screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for the first data-collection step of regulated onboarding flows (banking, lending, investing, insurance) where jurisdiction determines legal terms, product availability, or compliance requirements. It's ideal when you need to:

  • Capture a single critical piece of data before proceeding.

  • Bundle mandatory legal consent with a natural forward-progress action to minimize friction.

  • Set a trustworthy, premium tone early in a financial or high-stakes onboarding journey.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Regulations in your jurisdiction require explicit, separate opt-in checkboxes for each legal document (implicit "by continuing" consent may not be legally sufficient everywhere, e.g., GDPR-strict contexts).

  • The screen needs to collect multiple related fields, bundling too many fields here would break the single-focus benefit.

  • Users are already deep in a trusted relationship with the brand (e.g., returning users), where re-surfacing full legal text on every flow entry may feel redundant and annoying.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users signing up for a regulated financial product (banking, neobank, or payments app) who are early in a KYC (Know Your Customer) onboarding funnel. Because financial services are jurisdiction-dependent, capturing country of residence upfront is both a legal necessity and a personalization trigger (subsequent screens/terms will adapt based on this answer).

Psychologically, the screen leverages reduced decision fatigue (only one choice to make) and trust signaling (premium dark gradient, banking partner names like "Lead Bank" mentioned transparently) to reassure users that their money and data are handled by legitimate, regulated entities. The passive, bundled consent mechanism reduces perceived friction, which is critical at this vulnerable point in the funnel (right before requesting sensitive personal/financial information) where drop-off risk is highest.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Only one interactive input (country dropdown) is presented, eliminating any ambiguity about what action is required.

  • Implicit consent via CTA: Legal agreement is bundled into the primary button press rather than requiring a separate checkbox, reducing friction while still satisfying compliance via explicit copy.

  • Atmospheric gradient for hierarchy: The deep blue-to-black gradient creates a premium, trustworthy fintech aesthetic while naturally guiding the eye without extra chrome or dividers.

  • Inline hyperlinked legal text: Multiple legal documents (Revolut Privacy Policy, Lead Bank Privacy Policy, E-sign Consent) are surfaced compactly within a single sentence rather than as separate rows, saving vertical space.

  • Thin progress indicator: A minimal pill-shaped progress bar at the bottom subtly communicates onboarding flow position without overwhelming the screen.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Identity verification (KYC/AML) flows for fintech, banking, or crypto apps.

  • Any onboarding step requiring legally precise data entry where user error is common (e.g., legal name, tax ID, passport details).

  • Government, healthcare, or insurance apps needing exact official information distinct from casual profile data.

  • Multi-step forms where isolating one or two related fields per screen improves completion rates over long single-page forms.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Casual social or consumer apps where a nickname or display name is perfectly acceptable (the formal tone would feel unnecessarily bureaucratic).

  • Flows where users are highly familiar with the process and repeated single-field screens would feel slow; consider consolidating into one screen with multiple fields if the audience prioritizes speed over guidance.

  • Low-stakes forms where the extra explanatory micro-copy is unnecessary and adds visual clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users undergoing identity verification for a regulated product (likely a crypto exchange, neobank, trading platform, or other financial service subject to AML/KYC regulations). The audience spans first-time signups who may be unfamiliar with why legal precision matters, making the explanatory micro-copy essential for reducing verification friction and abandonment.

Psychologically, the screen leverages authority and legitimacy cues (formal language, document-based framing) to signal seriousness and build trust that the platform is compliant and secure (important for users about to share sensitive PII). The minimal, single-task design also reduces decision fatigue, keeping users in a low-friction flow state during what is typically a tedious onboarding requirement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual micro-copy example: "e.g. Daniel, not 'Dan'" proactively prevents a top KYC rejection reason (use of nicknames) at the point of entry rather than after submission.

  • Progressive visual emphasis: Field opacity/contrast decreases from First name → Last name → Alias, visually encoding required vs. optional priority without extra labels or icons.

  • Persistent, thumb-reachable CTA: The Continue button remains fully visible above the keyboard, eliminating the need to dismiss the keyboard to proceed.

  • Single-focus screen: Isolating name capture from other KYC fields (DOB, address, etc.) reduces perceived form length and keeps cognitive load low per screen.

  • Auto-focused first field: The cursor is already active in "First name," removing an unnecessary tap and speeding up task completion.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 17
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when an app must offer multiple verification or data-entry methods with different effort/speed tradeoffs, such as identity verification, bank account linking (instant vs. manual), or address confirmation. It's especially effective when one method is machine-verified/instant and another requires manual document submission, and you want to nudge users toward the faster, more reliable option without eliminating choice.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there is only one viable verification method, as presenting a false choice adds unnecessary decision friction. It's also inappropriate for regions/products without a trusted third-party verification service (like Singpass), since the "faster" option's credibility depends entirely on that institutional trust (without it, this hierarchy could look arbitrary or manipulative). Additionally, avoid heavy dark/gradient theming if the broader app uses a light, minimal design system, as inconsistency can undermine trust at this sensitive step.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users onboarding into a regulated financial, fintech, or government-adjacent service (likely in Singapore, given Singpass/NRIC references) who must complete mandatory identity verification before accessing core product features. This includes banking apps, insurance platforms, digital wallets, or gig economy apps requiring KYC compliance.

The psychological driver at play is friction reduction via choice architecture: by defaulting attention to the faster option through visual weight and badging, the design nudges users toward the path that also reduces business-side manual review costs and fraud risk. Users motivated by convenience (the majority) will gravitate to Singpass; users without accounts or with mismatched records retain a fallback via the manual path, preventing drop-off.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Effort-based visual hierarchy: The faster, automated option is placed first and styled with higher contrast/brightness, guiding users toward the path that benefits both user (speed) and business (data accuracy, lower fraud).

  • Social/institutional proof via Singpass branding: Leveraging a trusted government database name and logo builds instant credibility and reduces anxiety about data misuse.

  • "Faster" badge as a micro-nudge: A tiny, high-contrast chip communicates a key decision-making benefit at a glance, appealing to System 1 (fast, intuitive) thinking.

  • Consistent card pattern for binary choice: Using identical card structures (icon + title + description + chevron) for both options makes comparison effortless and scannable.

  • Atmospheric gradient background: The deep blue-to-black gradient signals security and importance, appropriate emotional framing for a sensitive identity task.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 18
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern during onboarding for multi-product platforms (super-apps, fintech, all-in-one tools) where understanding user intent early enables downstream personalization of content, feature discovery, and marketing. It's ideal when:

  • The product has many disparate features/verticals and needs to avoid overwhelming new users with all of them at once.

  • You want to collect soft-signal data for personalization without a hard compliance form feel.

  • You need to justify a data request that might otherwise feel like unnecessary friction.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The product has a single, narrow use case: the multi-select taxonomy would feel unnecessary and add friction for no personalization payoff.

  • Onboarding needs to be extremely fast (e.g., high-intent transactional apps) since browsing a long chip list can slow momentum.

  • You don't actually act on the data: asking without visible personalization payoff erodes trust and feels like data harvesting.

  • Users are likely to feel decision fatigue; if the list grows too large without strong grouping and search, it can become a negative, overwhelming experience.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users during first-time account setup, most likely immediately after identity/basic KYC info has been collected. Revolut leverages this data ostensibly for regulatory/compliance segmentation (financial products require different licensing based on declared use), but strategically, it also serves as an implicit segmentation and personalization tool for the product team, enabling Revolut to tailor upsell messaging, feature spotlights, and push notifications (e.g., promoting crypto to a user who selects "Crypto," or promoting the metal card to someone who selects "Metal card").

Psychologically, this taps into the IKEA effect / commitment consistency principle: by having the user actively select their intentions early, subsequent in-app upsells and feature recommendations feel more relevant and less intrusive, since the user themselves indicated interest.
screens.keyHighlights:
Notable UX decisions on this screen:

  • Transparent data-request justification: Explicitly stating the "regulatory" reason for asking preempts user suspicion about why a fintech app wants this data.

  • Emoji-led chip design: Each option pairs an emoji with text, aiding rapid visual scanning and adding personality to what could be a dry compliance form.

  • Thematic grouping over flat list: Segmenting into "Everyday needs" and "Global spending" (with more categories below) reduces the perceived length of the list and aids mental categorization.

  • Non-blocking optional selection: The Continue button remains active/available regardless of selection count, respecting user autonomy and preventing forced engagement.

  • Progressive disclosure via scroll: Partially cut-off content at the bottom (Stocks/Crypto row) hints at more categories, nudging exploration without cluttering the initial viewport.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 19
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during onboarding for products with a wide, diverse feature set where personalization can meaningfully change the user's experience (fintech super-apps, SaaS tools with multiple modules, content platforms with varied verticals). It's ideal when you need to collect self-reported intent data to drive segmentation, feature discovery, or marketing personalization, and when you can be transparent about why the data is being collected to maintain trust.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, single-purpose apps where use-case branching adds unnecessary friction before the user reaches core value. It also breaks down if the list of options grows too long without strong grouping/scannability, or if the copy fails to explain why the data is being collected, turning an inviting quiz into an invasive interrogation. Additionally, avoid this on returning-user flows or when speed-to-value is more critical than personalization (e.g., time-sensitive utility apps).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new sign-ups during account creation, spanning everyday banking users, freelancers, frequent travelers, and investors. Revolut's famously broad, all-in-one target market. By asking about intent up front, Revolut can immediately tailor the subsequent onboarding path, marketing messages, and feature highlights to each user's stated goals (e.g., prioritizing FX features for a "Foreign exchange" selector, or crypto education for "Crypto" selectors).

Psychologically, the pattern leverages the IKEA effect and commitment & consistency principle: by actively selecting several relevant use cases, users mentally invest in the product and become more likely to explore and adopt the features they endorsed. The multi-select format also reduces the friction/anxiety of committing to just one label, since real users often have multiple financial needs.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent regulatory framing: Explaining the "why" behind a mandatory data point turns a potentially annoying compliance question into a moment of trust-building honesty.

  • Emoji-led chip taxonomy: Using emoji + label pills grouped by theme (Everyday, Global spending, Investing) makes a long list of options feel light, fast, and browsable instead of overwhelming.

  • Immediate visual feedback: Selected chips flip to a high-contrast white background, giving instant, unambiguous confirmation of state without extra UI chrome.

  • Multi-select instead of single-choice: Allows Revolut to capture a much richer, multi-dimensional user profile in a single screen, fueling more precise downstream personalization (e.g., surfacing crypto features to users who selected "Crypto").

  • Progressive disclosure via scroll: Categorizing and partially cropping the last row cues the user there's more below, encouraging exploration without cluttering the initial viewport.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Regulated onboarding flows (banking, fintech, crypto exchanges) that require identity verification and support multiple verification data sources (government ID APIs vs. manual document upload).

  • Any screen where you need to guide users toward a faster/preferred path while still legally/functionally supporting an alternative route.

  • Markets with government digital identity infrastructure (e.g., Singpass in Singapore, Aadhaar in India, GOV.UK Verify) where an API-based instant verification can meaningfully reduce friction versus manual document scanning.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if only one verification method is legally required or available, presenting a false choice adds unnecessary decision friction.

  • Don't use subtle visual-weight nudging if regulatory compliance requires neutral, unbiased presentation of options (some jurisdictions mandate equal prominence for consumer protection).

  • Not suitable if the "faster" option has significantly worse success/completion rates in practice, as this would create a bait-and-switch experience once users discover the API-based route often errors out or falls back to manual anyway.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users in a specific regulatory market (Singapore, evidenced by Singpass/NRIC references) who are onboarding into Revolut as a licensed financial product. The audience spans students, freelancers, professionals, and digital nomads: many of whom may be foreigners on employment/dependent passes and thus need the document-based fallback rather than Singpass.

Psychologically, KYC screens are a classic drop-off point because they introduce friction and feel bureaucratic. By offering an "instant" government-linked path first, Revolut leverages the path-of-least-resistance principle to keep completion rates high, while the secondary manual option prevents total funnel abandonment for users without Singpass eligibility (e.g., newly arrived expats).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-path choice architecture: Offers both an instant government-database verification and a manual fallback, respecting different user contexts (e.g., non-Singpass holders, foreigners, permit holders).

  • Visual hierarchy as persuasion: The brighter, glowing card for the faster Singpass option versus the muted, flat card for manual upload subtly steers behavior without restricting choice.

  • "Faster" badge as social/functional proof: A tiny, high-contrast pill communicates a comparative benefit in two words, reducing decision paralysis.

  • Consistent card anatomy: Icon, title, description, chevron (repeated structure lowers cognitive load when comparing options).

  • Inclusive fallback option: Explicitly naming NRIC/Passport/Permit signals the flow accounts for both citizens, residents, and foreigners, which matters for Revolut's global/traveler audience.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Sign-up or KYC flows requiring legally mandated age verification (dating, alcohol, gambling, finance apps).

  • Any onboarding sequence where isolating a single input increases completion rates.

  • Personalization flows where birth date drives downstream content curation (e.g., horoscopes, age-appropriate content).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when collecting multiple related fields where grouping would reduce total taps and screens (e.g., combining DOB with gender in one lightweight step for less critical apps).

  • Not ideal for users on older devices or accessibility contexts where three separate small tap targets could cause input errors (consider a full calendar/date-wheel picker instead).

  • Should not be used without a clear reason presented elsewhere in the flow; regulatory or personalization context should be communicated before or after this screen to avoid feeling like unnecessary data harvesting.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users during account creation, particularly in apps with legal age requirements (dating apps, alcohol/gambling-adjacent products, social platforms with age gating, or fintech apps needing KYC compliance). The design leverages the psychological principle of the Zeigarnik effect: by showing an incomplete form with an inactive CTA, users feel compelled to finish the task to relieve the tension of an unfinished action.

The one-field-per-screen approach is also rooted in commitment and consistency bias: after answering one simple, low-friction question, users are more likely to continue through subsequent onboarding steps rather than abandon the flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented Input Fields: Breaking the date into Day/Month/Year individually reduces input errors and cognitive effort compared to a single free-text field.

  • Progressive Disabled State on CTA: The greyed-out "Continue" button acts as a built-in validation mechanism, visually signaling incompleteness without needing an error message.

  • Full-Screen Focus: Removing all other navigation chrome (no back arrows, no tab bars) forces total attention on this one task, a hallmark of high-conversion onboarding flows.

  • Native Keypad Utilization: Leveraging the OS numeric keypad rather than a custom date-picker wheel speeds up entry for users comfortable with typing numbers directly.

  • High-Contrast Gradient Background: The deep blue-to-black gradient creates a premium, focused atmosphere that visually separates this step from more content-heavy screens elsewhere in the app.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during onboarding or account-setup flows when you need to collect a birthdate quickly and unambiguously, especially in age-gated apps (dating, alcohol, gambling, fintech) or apps needing DOB for personalization/legal compliance. It's ideal when speed of entry is prioritized over data verification nuance, and when your user base is comfortable typing versus scrolling.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if your audience skews older or less tech-savvy, where a guided date-wheel picker with explicit calendar context may reduce input errors. It's also risky without inline validation (invalid dates (e).g., day 32, month 13) need real-time error handling, which isn't visible here. Additionally, if legal/compliance requires explicit justification for collecting DOB (e.g., GDPR), omitting an explanation of "why we need this" could hurt trust and conversion; a brief supporting line should be added in such contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets any general consumer audience going through app registration, particularly for products with legal age-gating requirements (dating apps, alcohol/vaping brands, gambling or fintech apps) or products that use age for personalization (fitness, dating, content curation). The design leverages the psychological principle of reduced cognitive load through chunking: breaking one field into three small, scannable units mirrors how humans already mentally parse dates. The custom keypad also taps into habit and familiarity, resembling PIN-entry screens, which subconsciously signals security and quick completion, keeping drop-off low at this potentially sensitive data-collection step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented Date Fields: Splitting DOB into Day/Month/Year removes ambiguity around date formats and allows for isolated, easy correction of a single component.

  • Custom Numeric Keypad: Bypassing the native scroll-wheel date picker in favor of direct numeric entry drastically speeds up input for users who know their birthdate by heart.

  • Inline Clear Icon: The (x) button on the active field enables instant field-level reset, reducing friction from manual backspacing.

  • Thumb-Zone CTA Placement: The "Continue" button sits directly above the keypad, keeping the primary action always visible and reachable without scrolling.

  • Pre-filled Example Values: Showing plausible-looking values (18/02/1995) can function as a subtle format hint even before the user starts typing (though in a live product these would be empty states).

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any regulated onboarding flow requiring precise, document-matched personal data (KYC, account verification, insurance applications, government services). It's ideal when data accuracy is critical and errors have downstream consequences (e.g., verification rejection).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes or exploratory data entry where a single-field-per-screen approach would feel unnecessarily slow. If the flow contains many address-adjacent fields (unit number, delivery instructions, etc.), breaking each into separate full screens rather than a single grouped form could frustrate users with excessive step counts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users going through mandatory identity verification (KYC/AML) for a regulated digital product (likely a neobank, crypto exchange, or investment app). The design leverages the psychological principle of reducing perceived friction by isolating one data point at a time, which is critical during compliance flows known for high abandonment rates.

The explanatory subtext taps into uncertainty reduction: users are anxious about identity verification being rejected, so clarifying the exact requirement (matching ID documents) increases user confidence and compliance accuracy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Isolating just the address search field eliminates cognitive load and reduces form abandonment during a sensitive KYC step.

  • Predictive search input: Using a "Search address" field instead of raw text boxes anticipates integration with an address autocomplete API (e.g., Google Places), minimizing typos and manual entry of multi-part addresses.

  • Disabled CTA state: The greyed-out "Continue" button gives immediate visual feedback that further input is required before proceeding, preventing invalid submissions.

  • Contextual justification copy: Explaining that the address must match the ID document manages user expectations and reduces downstream verification failures.

  • Atmospheric gradient background: Reinforces a premium, secure, trustworthy brand feel appropriate for sensitive personal data collection.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any app with a global or contextual search feature (e-commerce catalogs, content libraries, messaging/contact search, file management, or settings search). It's ideal when:

  • Users need fast, frequent access to a specific item within a large dataset.

  • You want to minimize preamble and get users typing immediately.

  • The product supports voice input as an accessibility or convenience feature.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this stark, full-screen takeover pattern when:

  • Search is a secondary, rarely-used feature: a lighter inline search bar without a full modal takeover may suffice.

  • You want to surface recent searches, trending terms, or suggestions immediately (this screen shows a true blank empty state instead, which could be a missed opportunity to seed engagement).

  • The app has a strong brand identity requiring more visual richness (this generic dark search state is functional but forgoes any brand expression).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets any general consumer mobile app user who needs to quickly locate content, products, or contacts. It leans on the psychological principle of reducing cognitive load by matching platform conventions (iOS native search UI) so users don't need to learn anything new (familiarity breeds instant usability).

The immediate keyboard pop-up leverages the path-of-least-resistance principle: by removing the need for an extra tap to summon the keyboard, the design shortens the time-to-value and keeps momentum in the task funnel, which is especially important for power users performing frequent searches.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-state guidance: Explicitly telling the user "Start typing to see your results" removes ambiguity about why the results area is blank, reducing perceived system failure.

  • Immediate keyboard focus: The search input is auto-focused with cursor visible and keyboard already raised, eliminating an extra tap and reducing friction to first keystroke.

  • Dimmed/dark overlay context: Visually isolates the search task, signaling a distinct interaction mode separate from the underlying app content.

  • Multi-modal input: Voice search (microphone) and keyboard language switching (globe) are surfaced directly in the accessory bar, catering to different user preferences and accessibility needs.

  • Clear escape hatch: The "Cancel" button is persistently visible, giving users a low-friction way to abandon search at any time.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 6
screens.whereToUse:
• Checkout and shipping address entry flows in e-commerce or delivery apps.

  • Any form requiring precise geolocation data (ride-hailing, food delivery, service booking).

  • Regions with reliable, granular postal/zip code systems that can shortcut full address typing.

  • Any search-first input experience where you want to combine autocomplete speed with a graceful fallback for unmatched queries.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• In countries/regions with unreliable or overly broad postal code systems (where one code maps to thousands of addresses), this pattern loses its precision advantage and should fall back to full address-line search.

  • Avoid if your backend address database is incomplete or stale, since users will hit the "not here" fallback too often, eroding trust in the feature.

  • Not suitable for freeform location searches (e.g., landmarks, points of interest) where map-based search/pin-drop would serve users better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users in transactional contexts (e-commerce checkout, food delivery, ride-hailing pickup/drop-off, or account setup) where accurate address capture is mission-critical for service fulfillment. It is particularly tuned for regions like Singapore where postal codes are highly granular (each code often maps to a single building), making postal-code-only search a fast, reliable shortcut.

Psychologically, this reduces cognitive load and typing effort (a key driver of form abandonment), while the visible escape hatch reduces anxiety for users whose address may be new, unlisted, or non-standard (e.g., new developments), building trust that the flow won't dead-end them.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Real-time postal-code-to-address resolution: Typing a 6-digit numeric postal code alone surfaces the complete, formatted address, drastically reducing typing effort and typo risk.

  • Escape hatch as a first-class citizen: "My address is not here" is placed above the actual result, not buried at the bottom, acknowledging that failure/edge-cases deserve equal visual priority to success paths.

  • Context-aware keyboard: Because postal codes are numeric, the numeric/symbol keyboard is presented by default, reducing friction and taps needed to enter digits.

  • Non-intrusive modal presentation: The search sheet overlays the previous screen (visible faded bar at top) rather than fully replacing it, preserving context and signaling this is a lightweight, transient step.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 7

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 9

It is ideal for consumer apps, subscription services, and any flow where user drop-off during registration is a key metric to optimize. Also effective when supporting platform-native privacy features (like Hide My Email or Sign in with Apple) to build trust.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this fully atomized single-field approach in enterprise/B2B contexts or forms where users expect to see the full scope of required information upfront (e.g., long compliance forms), as excessive step-by-step fragmentation can feel slow and patronizing.   • Keyboard-first layout: Content is pre-composed to sit correctly above the system keyboard, eliminating jarring layout shifts when the keyboard appears.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 10
screens.whereToUse:
• Sign-up or login flows where maximizing conversion/completion rate is the primary business goal.

  • Multi-step onboarding sequences where breaking data collection into digestible, single-purpose screens reduces perceived effort.

  • Products targeting mobile-first, on-the-go users who benefit from thumb-reachable CTAs and auto-focused inputs.

  • Brand experiences aiming for a premium, minimalist, distraction-free first impression.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this single-field-per-screen approach for internal/enterprise tools or data-heavy forms where users expect to see multiple related fields at once (e.g., billing address forms) - excessive fragmentation here creates fatigue rather than reducing it.

  • Not ideal when users need to reference multiple fields simultaneously (e.g., password confirmation fields benefit from being visible together).

  • Should be avoided if analytics show users abandon due to "step fatigue" from too many sequential screens rather than field complexity.

  • The stark, dark, minimal aesthetic may not suit brands requiring more warmth, imagery, or trust-building context (e.g., healthcare or financial services needing more reassurance copy).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users in the critical first-conversion moment of an app's lifecycle (the sign-up funnel). Because drop-off rates are highest during account creation, every element is engineered to minimize friction and cognitive burden.

Psychologically, breaking the form into single-field steps leverages the Zeigarnik effect (the tendency to feel compelled to complete a task once started) and reduces the intimidation of a long form by making progress feel incremental and effortless. The immediate keyboard presence exploits momentum (once a user is already typing, they are less likely to abandon the flow than if they had to first tap into a field).

This approach is best suited for consumer apps (social, entertainment, fintech onboarding) where maximizing sign-up completion is a primary KPI, and where the brand wants to project a slick, modern, low-friction identity.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Isolating email capture to its own screen (rather than bundling with password/name) dramatically reduces perceived effort and abandonment risk.

  • Auto-invoked keyboard: The keyboard is already active on screen load, saving the user a tap and creating a frictionless, momentum-driven entry experience.

  • Thumb-zone CTA placement: The "Continue" button sits directly above the keyboard, optimizing for one-handed reachability rather than being stranded at the top of the screen.

  • High contrast, distraction-free visual design: The deep gradient background with stark white typography creates a focused, premium "spotlight" effect on the single task at hand.

  • Inline clear (x) affordance: Allows instant field clearing, reducing friction for correcting typos in a field notorious for entry errors.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-screen camera capture pattern when the primary task requires scanning a physical object (payment cards, ID documents, QR/barcodes, receipts). Always pair it with:

  • A manual/alternate entry fallback for accessibility and failure recovery.

  • A clear, singular dismiss action.

  • Native-feeling capture controls (shutter, flash, gallery) to minimize cognitive load.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the data being captured can be reliably and faster entered via text input (e.g., short alphanumeric codes), as forcing a camera flow adds unnecessary friction. It's also unsuitable in low-connectivity or low-light contexts without robust fallback messaging, and should not be used without clearly communicating why camera access is needed (privacy/permission concerns) - a missing permission-priming step here could increase drop-off if this is the user's first camera-related ask.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets mainstream mobile users performing a transactional task (e.g., adding a payment card, scanning a QR/barcode coupon, or registering a loyalty card) who expect speed and minimal friction. It leverages the psychological principle of familiarity bias: by mimicking the stock iOS Camera app's control layout, the designer taps into years of existing muscle memory, meaning zero learning curve and higher completion rates. The manual fallback also addresses loss-aversion/frustration avoidance: users who fear wasting time on a failed scan are reassured there's always a guaranteed alternative path forward.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Manual entry fallback: Placing "Enter manually" prominently prevents a hard dead-end for users whose camera fails to recognize the object, respecting accessibility and real-world lighting/condition variance.

  • Familiar native camera affordances: Reusing the iOS system camera's shutter/flash/gallery layout dramatically lowers the learning curve (users don't need onboarding for how to operate the scanner).

  • Single, unambiguous exit: The circular X button is isolated top-right, matching platform conventions for modal dismissal, so users always know how to back out.

  • Distraction-free full-bleed canvas: No navigation chrome competes with the live camera feed, keeping 100% of visual attention on correctly framing the scan target.

  • Photo library shortcut: The "Select" option lets users scan from an already-captured photo instead of requiring a live camera pass, useful when the object isn't physically present.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for document/ID/card capture flows, KYC onboarding, receipt or check scanning, and any flow requiring an image of a physical object where camera access may fail or be inconvenient. Always pair the primary camera capture action with secondary import options (library, file) and a manual fallback to keep conversion high.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this multi-option action sheet for simple, low-stakes avatar or profile photo uploads where a single "choose photo" option is sufficient (too many choices can add friction). Also avoid if manual entry would violate compliance requirements (e.g., when optical capture is mandatory for fraud prevention), or if offering file upload introduces unnecessary security/format-validation complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users completing identity verification, document upload, or payment-card linking flows (e.g., KYC, check deposit, expense receipt capture) where camera access is the primary path but not all users have the physical document on hand or a working camera at that moment. Offering photo library, file choice, and manual entry reduces drop-off by accommodating edge cases (scanned PDFs already on device, accessibility limits, poor lighting) and leverages the psychological principle of perceived control: giving users choice reduces anxiety and abandonment in sensitive flows like identity verification.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multiple capture fallbacks: Camera, photo library, file picker, and manual entry are all offered from a single surface, respecting different user contexts (e.g., document already saved vs. needing to snap a new photo).

  • Non-blocking modal overlay: The action sheet appears without fully replacing the camera screen, preserving spatial context and reducing perceived navigation depth.

  • High-contrast, distraction-free capture UI: Pure black background and minimal chrome keep focus on the real-world subject being captured.

  • Escape hatch always visible: The persistent close (X) button ensures users never feel trapped in the camera flow.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 5
screens.whereToUse: Use the native OS photo/file picker (with its built-in limited-access messaging) whenever an app needs occasional, user-initiated access to personal media (such as attaching receipts, profile photos, documents, or support-ticket screenshots). It's ideal for expense management, customer support, document scanning, and social apps where trust and minimal permission footprint matter more than deep custom gallery curation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid relying solely on the native picker if your product requires rich, branded media-browsing experiences (e.g., a photo-editing app, a social network's camera roll integration with custom filters/previews) where a custom UI with deeper curation, tagging, or AI-based suggestions adds real value. Also, if the app needs frequent, repeated media access (e.g., continuous background photo sync), prompting for full library access with a clear value explanation may be more appropriate than repeatedly surfacing the limited-access picker, which can create friction if users must reselect photos each time.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
The target user here is a Brex business cardholder or employee submitting an expense report who needs to attach a photo of a physical receipt. This persona is typically on the go, often in a hurry (e.g., right after a client dinner or purchase), and may be privacy-conscious about granting full photo library access to a finance/corporate app.

Psychologically, this screen addresses the "privacy paradox" tension in B2B fintech apps: users want convenience (quickly finding a photo) but are wary of corporate software having blanket access to personal photos (family pictures, personal moments). The limited-access disclosure directly defuses this anxiety, increasing the likelihood a user completes the attach-receipt flow instead of abandoning it or granting access reluctantly.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Leverages OS trust instead of rebuilding it: By using the native picker, Brex inherits Apple's privacy guarantees and polished interaction patterns for free, rather than building a bespoke (and less trusted) media picker.

  • Transparent limited-access disclosure: The "Private Access to Photos" card is a best-in-class example of proactive, in-context privacy communication rather than a one-time blocking permission dialog.

  • Dismissible, non-blocking education: The explanation is informative but optional (closable via the X), respecting the user's time if they already understand the concept.

  • Low-friction task completion: Search, sort, and collections toggle allow power users to quickly locate the exact receipt photo needed, reducing time-to-task-completion for an inherently tedious expense-reporting workflow.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when designing camera-capture flows embedded within a larger workflow (not a standalone camera app), especially when the captured artifact needs to be associated with an existing record (e.g., receipts, documents, ID verification). It's especially valuable when there's a possible mismatch between user intent and system state (proactively surfacing that mismatch before the user invests effort (e).g., taking a photo) saves frustration. The dual-path bottom CTA ("scan" vs. "manual entry/alternative") pattern is ideal whenever the primary capture method may not always be the right fit for every user's situation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid overlaying warning banners on a camera viewfinder when the warning is purely informational and not actionable (this adds visual clutter and can obscure the subject being photographed). If the warning condition is rare or edge-case only, consider handling it via a toast or pre-emptive screen before entering the camera, rather than cluttering the capture UI itself. Additionally, this pattern should not be used when receipt/document capture is the primary, context-free action of the app (e.g., a dedicated scanner app), since the "no expenses to attach" framing assumes a specific linked-record workflow that may not apply universally.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets business travelers, employees, and finance/ops teams who need to digitize paper receipts for expense reporting and reimbursement, likely within a corporate expense management or spend platform (e.g., similar to Ramp, Brex, or Expensify). The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion and effort-justification prevention: by warning the user before they waste time scanning a receipt that has nowhere to go, the app respects the user's time and avoids a frustrating "scan completed, but now what?" dead-end experience. The inline "Add to existing" and "create reimbursement" options also reduce decision paralysis by making the next best action obvious and low-friction, appealing to time-pressed professional users who value speed and certainty over exploration.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual Just-in-Time Guidance: Rather than letting the user scan a receipt into a dead end, the app proactively surfaces a system-state warning banner the moment it detects there's nothing to attach the receipt to, with an inline fix via "Add to existing."

Branching Escape Hatch: The "Or create reimbursement" button acknowledges that not all expense-logging starts with a physical receipt, offering a graceful fallback path without forcing the user to exit the flow and start over elsewhere.

High-Contrast Overlay Controls: White solid-fill circular buttons (close, retake) against the dark camera viewfinder ensure maximum legibility and touch-target confidence regardless of the background scene being photographed.

Minimal Chrome, Maximum Viewfinder: By stripping away navigation bars and status elements, the design maximizes the available frame for accurately capturing the receipt image, which directly impacts OCR/data-extraction accuracy downstream.

screens.name: Cash App Login 1
screens.whereToUse: This Verification + Smart Defaults combination fits any account login or sensitive-action flow requiring two-factor or step-up authentication, where defaulting to the user's most likely-accessible method speeds up the common case while still supporting recovery scenarios.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a first-time account creation flow, where no default verification method or masked identifier yet exists and the user must actively supply contact information rather than confirm a pre-filled one.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• PayPal (2FA code request screen): uses the same masked-contact-plus-"Next" pattern for sending a one-time login code via email or SMS.

  • Venmo (login verification screen): offers a comparable default verification method with an alternate "try another way" fallback option.

  • Chase Mobile (identity verification for login): presents a similar pre-selected contact method with a masked identifier and a secondary path for alternate verification.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart defaults reduce friction: pre-selecting email as the verification method with the radio dot already filled lets most users complete this step with a single "Next" tap.

  • Privacy by design: masking the actual email address protects the user's personal information from shoulder-surfing while still confirming which account/method is in use.

  • Graceful degradation: "Verify another way" ensures users without access to this email (e.g., changed providers, lost access) aren't blocked, supporting account recovery scenarios.

  • Minimalism at a high-friction step: keeping the screen to a single option, two buttons, and no extraneous content reduces cognitive load at a step users want to move through quickly.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for signup flows in regulated or trust-sensitive verticals (fintech, marketplaces, gig platforms, healthcare, travel) where legal identity data must be collected but could otherwise raise user suspicion. Ideal when you want to compress several account-setup micro-steps into a single scrollable screen to reduce step-count anxiety, and when proactive field-level guidance (e.g., password rules) can meaningfully reduce validation errors and support ticket volume.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid combining this many fields on one screen for low-trust or high-abandonment audiences (e.g., casual consumer apps, low-commitment sign-ups) where a shorter, deferred-registration or progressive profiling approach would convert better. Also avoid requesting legal name/identity data without contextual justification in verticals where it's not expected (e.g., a simple content app), as it will trigger privacy concerns. If the target audience is highly mobile and speed-sensitive, a multi-step wizard with fewer fields per screen may reduce cognitive load better than this single dense form.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new users at the highest-risk drop-off point in an app's funnel: account creation requiring real identity information (likely a fintech, gig-economy, or regulated marketplace app given the legal name requirement, possibly identity-verification driven like ride-sharing, delivery, or payments platforms). The design leans on trust-building through transparency: by explaining the "why" behind sensitive data collection, it reduces the psychological reactance users feel when asked for legal names early in a relationship with a brand. The optional avatar step taps into self-expression and identity investment, a small personalization commitment that increases the odds of full onboarding completion (sunk-cost/foot-in-the-door effect). Proactive password guidance and visibility toggles serve less tech-confident or anxious users who are prone to abandoning forms after repeated errors.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Justification microcopy before friction: Explaining why legal name is required preempts user hesitation and builds trust at a moment where users are most likely to abandon (identity verification steps).

  • Optional, low-pressure photo upload: The "Add photo" circle with pencil icon signals customization without blocking progress, using a familiar avatar-editing convention users already know from other apps.

  • Persistent password rules instead of reactive errors: Requirements are shown proactively, not just after a failed validation attempt, which reduces retry frustration and shortens task completion time.

  • Password visibility toggle: Reduces typos in a field users cannot otherwise visually verify, especially important on mobile keyboards.

  • Consolidated single-scroll form: Reduces perceived step-count of a lengthy signup by grouping related fields, avoiding excessive multi-step pagination fatigue.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this consolidated single-screen form pattern when:

  • The number of required fields is moderate (4-6) and splitting them into multiple steps would feel artificially padded.

  • You need to collect legally sensitive information (full legal name, DOB, SSN, etc.) and must justify why it's being requested to maintain user trust.

  • Regulatory or compliance requirements mandate explicit e-sign/consent acknowledgment before proceeding.

  • Users are already primed to expect a longer sign-up (e.g., financial services, ride-sharing driver onboarding, healthcare apps).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The target audience is highly impatient or the product category expects ultra-low-friction sign-up (e.g., casual games, social apps) - in these cases, defer non-essential fields via progressive/deferred onboarding.

  • Fields exceed 6-7 inputs; at that volume, a multi-step wizard with visible progress will reduce perceived effort and abandonment better than one long scroll.

  • You have no strong justification for collecting sensitive data, asking for legal name without explanation elsewhere would increase distrust and drop-off.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users onboarding into an identity-verified platform: likely a fintech, gig-economy, or regulated marketplace app (the request for "legal name" and E-Sign consent strongly suggests financial or contractual obligations, similar to Uber, Lyft, or a banking app). The audience is mainstream consumers who may be unfamiliar or uneasy with providing legal identity information to an app, so the design leans heavily on trust-building copy and transparency to reduce abandonment.

Psychologically, the screen uses friction-reduction and pre-emptive reassurance: by answering the "why" before the user asks it, anxiety about surveillance or data misuse is minimized. The consent checkbox leverages the foot-in-the-door principle: getting explicit, active agreement (unchecked by default) builds a small commitment that increases follow-through to complete registration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Just-in-time password rules: Requirements are shown directly under the password field instead of only appearing after a failed validation error, preventing frustration before it starts.

  • Contextual explanation for sensitive data: Explaining why a legal name (not a nickname) is required builds trust and reduces drop-off from users wary of over-collection of PII.

  • Deep-link tip for personalization: Proactively telling users where to set a "preferred name" later removes a support-ticket-worthy point of friction.

  • Password visibility toggle: Reduces failed submissions caused by typos in a field users can't normally see.

  • Explicit, linked legal consent: The checkbox pairs an age/eligibility gate with a clear hyperlink to full legal text, satisfying compliance needs without resorting to dark-pattern pre-checked boxes.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Identity-verification-heavy onboarding flows (fintech, ride-share, marketplaces) where legal name collection needs justification.

  • Forms requiring redundant, accessible error signaling (icon + color + text) for compliance with accessibility standards.

  • Any multi-field form where explaining the purpose of sensitive fields upfront can reduce perceived friction.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid triggering full-form validation errors before the user has interacted with any field (this pattern should only fire per-field on blur or globally on submit attempt, never on initial page load). Doing so punishes the user visually for an action they haven't taken yet, increasing perceived difficulty and potential drop-off. For low-stakes forms, this level of aggressive, multi-field simultaneous error styling is overkill and should be reserved for cases with real compliance/security stakes.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This flow targets new users signing up for a platform that likely has identity-verification or regulatory requirements (e.g., fintech, gig-economy, or social platforms requiring real-name policies). The psychological trigger at play is trust-building through transparency: by explaining the "why" behind sensitive data requests, the product reduces abandonment at a high-friction step. However, the all-fields-errored state may inadvertently trigger a negative psychological response (a sense of failure or incompetence) for users who haven't even begun typing, which could increase early drop-off if this is truly the default/initial state rather than a post-submit state.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual justification copy: Explaining why legal name is required builds trust and reduces the "why do you need this?" friction common in KYC-heavy signup flows.

  • Optional-first ordering: Placing the low-commitment photo upload before the mandatory, higher-friction identity fields eases the user into the form.

  • Multi-signal error indication: Combining border color, label color, icon, and helper text creates redundant, accessible error cueing (helpful for color-blind users relying on the icon/text).

  • Password visibility toggle: The eye icon on the password field is a well-established affordance that reduces input errors on a field users can't visually verify.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Onboarding flows for apps requiring verified real identity (marketplaces, fintech, ride-share, delivery).

  • Any registration form collecting both public-facing (username, photo) and private/legal (legal name, email) data, where the distinction needs to be communicated clearly.

  • Situations where password complexity rules are non-trivial and should be shown before the user attempts submission to reduce error rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, multi-field pattern for low-stakes apps (e.g., a note-taking or utility app) where minimal signup (email + magic link) would suffice and this level of detail would feel excessive.

  • Not ideal when the platform doesn't legally require real names, asking for "legal" name unnecessarily increases perceived risk and abandonment.

  • Avoid combining photo upload with mandatory fields in markets/cultures where profile photos raise privacy concerns unless clearly marked optional (as done well here).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users mid-signup for a consumer app that likely has identity/compliance requirements (e.g., fintech, gig-economy, or social platform requiring real-name verification (the "legal name" language strongly suggests KYC-adjacent or trust & safety needs, similar to Airbnb or Uber)).

Psychologically, the screen leverages reciprocity and transparency (explaining why legal name is needed) to lower resistance to a normally sensitive data request. The optional, friendly avatar step at the top primes the user with a low-commitment, low-risk action before asking for higher-commitment personal data, using a foot-in-the-door technique to build momentum through the form.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive password guidance: Requirements are shown upfront, not just after a failed validation attempt, preventing frustration.

  • Trust-building microcopy: Explains exactly why legal name is required and immediately offers a workaround (preferred name), reducing perceived surveillance/friction.

  • Optional avatar placed first but visually de-emphasized with a neutral outline and "Add photo" placeholder text, signaling it's a nice-to-have, not a blocker.

  • Password visibility toggle (eye icon) reduces failed submissions from typos in a masked, high-stakes field.

  • Persistent thin progress bar at the bottom subtly communicates flow length without a heavy stepper UI cluttering the screen.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for account creation flows that require legally verifiable identity data (banking, lending, gig platforms, age-restricted marketplaces) where trust and regulatory compliance must be balanced with conversion. Ideal when the product needs to pre-empt user hesitation about sensitive data collection and reduce password-related support tickets.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, multi-field single-screen approach for low-stakes consumer apps (social, casual games) where legal name and heavy password rules would feel excessive and increase drop-off. Also avoid pre-checking legal consent checkboxes in jurisdictions (e.g., EU/GDPR) where affirmative, unambiguous opt-in is legally mandated (pre-ticked boxes can invalidate consent and create compliance risk).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets mainstream consumer app users (likely fintech, gig-economy, or regulated marketplace apps) who are wary of providing legal/government-matching information during signup. The explicit rationale for the legal name field leverages the psychological principle of "reason-giving" - people are far more compliant with a request when given even a minimal justification. Front-loading password rules exploits the "path of least resistance" bias, guiding users to success on the first attempt rather than through trial-and-error, which increases completion rates and reduces frustration-driven abandonment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Upfront justification copy explaining why legal name is required, reducing perceived invasiveness.

  • Persistent (not just on-error) password requirement text, preventing failed submission attempts.

  • Bottom-anchored page/progress indicator that signals flow length without cluttering the header.

  • Bundled single checkbox for age verification + terms acceptance to minimize decision steps.

  • Inline password visibility toggle to reduce entry errors on a high-friction field.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 6
screens.whereToUse:
• Any sign-up or account-creation flow that must satisfy legal consent (cookies/GDPR) and bot/fraud prevention requirements simultaneously.

  • Fintech, healthcare, or other regulated apps where identity verification credibility matters more than onboarding speed.

  • Use lightweight, single-checkbox CAPTCHA widgets (like hCaptcha) instead of distorted-image challenges to minimize friction on mobile.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid stacking two separate interruption modals (CAPTCHA + cookie banner) back-to-back during a single critical conversion flow like sign-up; combine or sequence them more gracefully, or trigger the cookie notice earlier (e.g., on app launch/splash) rather than mid-form.

  • Do not present cookie consent with an asymmetric visual hierarchy (prominent Accept, buried Manage/Decline) in jurisdictions requiring equal-weight consent options.

  • Avoid CAPTCHA challenges positioned directly over active form fields where users may lose their place or accidentally trigger validation errors upon return.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Venmo's "Busy Urban" audience wants to get from download to sending/requesting money as fast as possible. At registration, however, Venmo (as a money-transmitter) is legally obligated to verify humanness (fraud/bot prevention) and disclose cookie usage (GDPR/CCPA compliance) before the user proceeds. The design trades a small amount of onboarding speed for regulatory and security necessity (an acceptable tension for a fintech app where trust and compliance directly affect the user's willingness to link a bank account or card later in the flow).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Modal dimming for focus: The greyed-out background clearly communicates that the form is temporarily unavailable, reducing accidental taps on underlying fields.

  • Minimal-friction bot check: hCaptcha's checkbox-only interaction (versus distorted-text CAPTCHAs) keeps fraud prevention nearly invisible for legitimate users on a small screen.

  • Transparent ad-personalization disclosure: The cookie banner explicitly names the secondary use (cross-site personalized ads), which is more honest than many bundled consent banners.

  • Dismissible without full-screen takeover: Both overlays are compact and non-blocking of the entire viewport, letting users see the form context they're returning to.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a product legally requires explicit user consent to terms of service, privacy policies, or fee schedules during onboarding, especially in regulated industries like fintech, healthcare, or insurance. It's ideal when you want to soften the friction of mandatory legal steps without diminishing their legal weight (combine a fixed, low-friction CTA with scrollable, well-organized supporting content and injected personality/tone to keep users engaged rather than disengaging from a wall of text).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if your legal/compliance team requires explicit itemized consent (e.g., individual checkboxes per document) for audit or regulatory reasons (a single blanket "Agree" button may not satisfy stricter jurisdictions (e).g., GDPR granular consent requirements). Also avoid injecting humor into legal copy for products in serious/high-stakes contexts (e.g., medical consent, legal contracts with liability implications) where levity could undermine perceived seriousness or trust. If the fee structure is complex, oversimplifying it here could create trust issues later when hidden costs are discovered.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users signing up for a peer-to-peer payments app (Venmo) who are eager to start sending/receiving money and are likely to skim or skip legal text. The design leverages the path of least resistance psychological principle: by making the required reading feel light and by placing the CTA persistently at the bottom, the app respects the user's impatience while still fulfilling legal/regulatory obligations (financial services require explicit agreement to terms).

The reassuring fee language also targets fee-anxious users (a known drop-off point in fintech onboarding) pre-emptively addressing the objection "will this app quietly charge me?" before it becomes a blocker to activation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Humor to defuse boredom: The witty headline reframes a mandatory legal step as something almost welcome, lowering psychological resistance to reading (or skipping) dense content.

  • Sticky bottom CTA: The "Agree" button and consent text remain fixed at the bottom, decoupled from the scrolling legal content, so the user is never more than one tap away from completing the step.

  • Implicit consent via hyperlinks: Instead of separate checkboxes for each document, a single "Agree" action paired with inline linked document names streamlines consent capture without sacrificing legal coverage.

  • Progressive disclosure of fees: Rather than hiding fee information in a separate menu, key fee philosophy is surfaced directly in the onboarding flow, proactively building trust before the user commits.

  • Lettered mini table of contents: "A. User Agreement / B. Privacy Statement" gives structure and scannability to what is otherwise unglamorous legal content.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 8
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech, banking, or wallet app onboarding flows where regulatory fee disclosure is mandatory before account activation.

  • Any product where cost transparency is a key differentiator or objection-handler (e.g., subscription apps clarifying trial-to-paid pricing).

  • Situations where you need to bundle legal consent with informational content to avoid an extra confirmation step.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for products with complex, tiered, or usage-dependent pricing (a simple fact-box grid oversimplifies and could mislead users, creating compliance risk).

  • Not ideal if the fee structure is genuinely unfavorable; the friendly tone paired with hard cost data could feel dissonant or manipulative if fees are actually high.

  • Should not be used as a substitute for full, detailed terms (this format is a supplement/summary, not a replacement for the legally binding agreement it references).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users signing up for a peer-to-peer payments/digital wallet product (e.g., Venmo) who may have prior negative experiences with hidden bank fees. The design leverages the psychological principle of anticipated regret reduction: by proactively disclosing fees before the user commits, the product reduces the perceived risk of "gotcha" charges later, which is a major churn/distrust driver in fintech.

It also exploits the authority/trust heuristic: presenting fees in a formal, tabular disclosure format (like a bank's Schedule of Fees) borrows credibility from traditional financial institutions, making the product feel regulated and safe even though the tone remains casual.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fact-box fee table: Using a bordered, structured 2x2+ grid of "$0"-forward numbers mirrors regulated banking disclosures, instantly signaling legitimacy and transparency.

  • Emotional framing before data: Leading with empathetic, benefit-driven copy ("we minimize or eliminate fees") primes the user to interpret the subsequent numbers positively rather than skeptically.

  • Bundled consent + education: Combining fee disclosure and legal agreement into a single screen with one CTA reduces the number of steps needed to complete onboarding without skipping required compliance messaging.

  • Zero-cost emphasis via typography: "$0" values are set in oversized bold type, drawing the eye immediately to the free actions, while smaller fees (ATM out-of-network) are visually de-emphasized.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 9
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial services onboarding flows requiring regulatory fee/risk disclosures (banking, prepaid cards, crypto, lending).

  • Any screen combining mandatory legal text with optional educational/FAQ content, where you want to keep the CTA persistently accessible.

  • Use accordions when you have multiple related but distinct topics (e.g., "Opening an account" vs "Spending money") that not every user needs to read in full.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the legal content is short enough to display without scrolling, forcing an accordion/scroll pattern on brief text adds unnecessary friction. Also avoid softening critical risk disclosures (e.g., FDIC insurance exclusions) with too much visual "friendliness" if it risks burying material information users are legally required to notice; regulators may require such text remain prominent and unobscured by decorative elements. Do not use a single blanket "Agree" CTA if regulations require granular, itemized consent to distinct terms.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The FAQ-style reframing reduces anxiety by making the fee structure feel accessible and answerable rather than an opaque legal trap. screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Verifying 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this modal pattern any time an application needs to gate access to an irreversible, high-value secret or destructive credential (such as private keys, seed phrases, API secrets, admin recovery codes, or master passwords). It's ideal whenever the request could plausibly originate from an untrusted third party (e.g., a connected dApp, browser extension, or integration) and the user needs a moment of forced reflection before granting access.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this exact low-friction pattern (single tap "Allow") for irreversible financial actions if the risk profile is very high (consider adding a secondary layer such as biometric confirmation, a typed phrase, or a short delay/cooldown to prevent rushed or coerced taps (e).g., during a social-engineering call). Also avoid overusing system-style dialogs for low-stakes permissions, as it dilutes the perceived severity and trains users to dismiss these prompts reflexively, which is dangerous precisely in scenarios like this one.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets cryptocurrency wallet users (ranging from newcomers to experienced holders) at the exact moment a dApp, browser extension, or malicious script attempts to access the most sensitive credential in crypto: the seed phrase or private key. This is the single point of failure that, if leaked, results in irreversible and unrecoverable loss of funds.

The psychological trigger at play is protective friction: by pausing the user with an explicit, unavoidable checkpoint, the design counteracts "automation blindness" (users reflexively tapping "Allow" on permission prompts) and encourages a deliberate, conscious decision. It also builds product trust, showing that the wallet actively "detects" and flags sensitive requests reassures users that the app is looking out for them, which is a key retention and brand-trust driver in the security-anxious crypto space.
screens.keyHighlights:
• System-style trust borrowing: Mimics native OS permission dialogs to leverage users' existing trust and familiarity with that pattern, making the warning feel authoritative and non-skippable.

  • Embedded risk education: The body copy explicitly tells users the only valid reason to allow the request, turning a simple permission gate into a phishing-prevention micro-lesson.

  • Modal interruption: Full-focus dialog with dimmed backdrop ensures the user cannot proceed with a background action or ignore the prompt inadvertently.

  • Symmetrical, non-coercive button layout: Cancel and Allow are given equal visual weight and size, avoiding manipulative dark patterns that push users toward disclosure.

Apply this pattern whenever an application must present irreversible, security-critical secrets (API keys, recovery codes, encryption keys, backup codes) that the user must safeguard. It is ideal for:

  • Any one-time-display secret credential flow
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, warning-laden pattern for low-stakes or reversible data (e.g., a username change or a non-critical setting), where excessive caution language would create unnecessary anxiety and friction. Also avoid recommending cloud-based backup as the primary path if the product's threat model explicitly discourages internet-connected storage of secrets (e.g., cold-storage-focused hardware wallet apps), since this could contradict the product's core security promise.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new self-custody wallet users (ranging from crypto novices to experienced users) at the most vulnerable point of onboarding: seed phrase generation. The psychological drivers at play include loss aversion (emphasizing that anyone with the words "can steal all of your crypto"), authority/trust signaling (Coinbase distancing itself from phishing behavior), and reduction of choice paralysis via a clearly recommended default path (iCloud). The design must balance urgency and caution without inducing so much fear that users abandon the flow, making tone calibration especially critical here.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-path CTA with visual bias: The gradient-filled iCloud button visually outranks the flat-gray manual button, steering novice users toward the lower-friction, less error-prone recovery method while still respecting power-user choice.

  • Explicit phishing inoculation copy: Stating "Coinbase will never ask you for them" arms users against future scam attempts, a proactive trust and security-education tactic rare in most onboarding flows.

  • Obfuscated/blurred sensitive data: The seed phrase is shielded from casual view, protecting privacy in public settings or during screen recording/sharing.

  • Single-focus, distraction-free layout: Removal of all secondary navigation elements reinforces the gravity and singular importance of this step.

It's ideal for fintech, crypto, password managers, and enterprise security tools where a single social-engineering mistake causes catastrophic, unrecoverable loss. Pairing it with reversible or supportive recovery mechanisms (like "contact support to reset") would undermine the self-custody warning's credibility.

This pattern targets users who are prone to skimming onboarding flows and are the most vulnerable to seed-phrase phishing scams (a leading cause of crypto theft). By interrupting the flow with a mandatory, emotionally resonant checkpoint, Coinbase leverages loss-aversion psychology ("Anyone who learns them can steal all of your crypto") and the authority/trust heuristic (explicitly stating what the legitimate company will never do) to inoculate users against social engineering before they've even finished setup.

The dark, low-stimulation UI and unambiguous labeling cater to users making high-stakes decisions (protecting real monetary value), where any confusion or dark-pattern-like ambiguity could cause severe loss of trust or actual financial harm.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, ranging from crypto-native power users managing multiple addresses to newcomers who may not fully grasp the irreversible nature of losing a seed phrase. The psychological driver here is loss aversion: the screen is designed to trigger a proactive security action by reminding users of the catastrophic, irreversible consequence of losing access to funds if keys aren't backed up.

By presenting this as a checklist-style review rather than a one-time forced action during onboarding, the product respects user autonomy while still nudging them toward best security practices, likely triggered periodically or after wallet creation/import events.

• Dual-Method Support: The screen elegantly handles both passkey-based and seed-phrase-based wallets in the same list structure, future-proofing the UI for Web3's shift toward passwordless security.

  • Strategic Placement of Sign Out: Placing the destructive/exit action at the bottom, visually distinct and separated by a divider, prevents it from competing with the primary security task.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any transactional flow where a single numeric value is the primary input and must be verified before an irreversible action. P2P payments, tipping, invoicing, in-app currency top-ups, or bill-splitting features. It's especially effective when:

  • The action has two symmetrical directions (pay vs. request, buy vs. sell, add vs. withdraw).

  • Speed and low cognitive load are more valuable than rich formatting options.

  • A custom keypad can meaningfully reduce input errors compared to the system keyboard.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex financial inputs requiring multiple fields, currency conversion, or itemized breakdowns (e.g., invoicing with tax/line items) - the single giant number affordance breaks down when more than one value needs simultaneous visibility. It's also unsuitable for accessibility-sensitive contexts unless the custom keypad and buttons are rigorously tested with screen readers, since non-native keyboards can sometimes degrade assistive technology support. Finally, avoid dual equally-weighted CTAs (Request/Pay) in flows where one action is destructive or significantly higher-risk than the other, as visual parity can encourage mis-taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets mainstream consumer P2P payment users (e.g., Venmo, Cash App audiences) - largely younger, mobile-first users splitting bills, paying rent, or gifting money to friends and family. The design leans on social proof and casualness (memo field, gift icon, friendly tone) rather than the sterile formality of banking apps, because trust in this context comes from familiarity and simplicity rather than institutional gravitas.

Psychologically, the oversized amount display exploits the Von Restorff effect (isolation effect) - the number visually dominates so users double-check the figure before committing, reducing regret and support tickets from mistaken amounts. The proximity of "Request" and "Pay" buttons reduces the perceived friction of switching intent, appealing to users who make split-second decisions in social settings (e.g., splitting a check at a restaurant).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom numeric keypad: Overrides the system keyboard to optimize digit entry speed and prevent accidental non-numeric input in a financial context.

  • Giant, high-contrast amount display: The $1 figure is the single largest element on screen, immediately confirming the entered value at a glance (critical for reducing transaction errors).

  • Inline clear (X) affordance: Placed directly next to the amount for instant correction, avoiding tedious character-by-character backspacing.

  • Dual-intent CTA pattern: Presenting "Request" and "Pay" as equally weighted, adjacent pill buttons lets users flip the direction of money flow without navigating to a different screen.

  • Contextual memo field: Placed just above the CTAs so the "why" of the transaction is captured before the irreversible action, reinforcing social/contextual money transfers.

  • Minimal chrome: Only back and close icons are present, keeping the modal feel tightly scoped to a single task and reducing decision fatigue.

Adapt this pattern for rewards, loyalty, cashback, or coupon wallets where the goal is to maximize redemption rates and repeat visits. It works well for:

  • Fintech/neobank cashback and offer centers

  • Loyalty programs with rotating, time-limited perks

  • Gamified engagement surfaces (referral rewards, streak bonuses, spin-to-win outcomes)

  • Any context where you want to make a routine list feel like an exciting "prize reveal" moment
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this casino-esque, "you won" framing in contexts requiring trust, sobriety, or regulatory caution (such as investment products, insurance, loan offers, or any financial decision with real risk, where gamified urgency language could be seen as manipulative or even run afoul of financial advertising regulations).

It is also inappropriate for older, more conservative user bases or B2B/enterprise financial tools where a playful, gambling-adjacent tone could undermine perceived credibility. Additionally, artificial urgency (identical "expires in 05 days" on every card) should be used carefully and truthfully, reusing a static countdown across unrelated offers can erode trust once users notice the pattern is fake or non-dynamic.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of fintech, super-app, or cashback/rewards platforms (likely an Indian neobank or bill-payment/rewards aggregator given the Axis Bank/IOCL/RuPay branding) who respond well to gamified, dopamine-driven engagement loops rather than plain transactional lists.
