The design leans on the testing effect (retrieval practice strengthens memory more than re-reading) and reduced choice paralysis (only two options to compare) to keep the exercise approachable for users who may have math anxiety.

The minimalist, academic visual language (serif-italic table headers, clean sans-serif body text, generous whitespace) signals credibility and calm focus, appealing to users who want a "gym for the brain" experience rather than a flashy, dopamine-chasing app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Move-before-explain sequencing: the lesson text sets up a definition, but the actual learning happens via the tactile act of comparing and selecting a table, not by reading more.
  • Low-stakes binary choice: reducing the answer set to exactly two tiles keeps cognitive load minimal while still requiring genuine evaluation of x/y pairs against the equation.
  • Non-judgmental selection state: the blue selection border is neutral in valence (neither green=correct nor red=wrong), preserving suspense until "Check" is pressed and avoiding premature feedback leakage.
  • Persistent progress + streak iconography: the segmented progress bar and lightning bolt in the header keep the user oriented in the lesson arc and subtly reinforce the gamified streak system without needing a dedicated screen.
  • Low-friction recovery: "Start over" gives users permission to reconsider without a confirmation dialog, respecting the exploratory, game-like nature of the exercise.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (math) - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this fused instruction-and-interaction pattern when teaching discrete, verifiable concepts (math, logic, data literacy, coding syntax) where correctness can be binary and visually compared. It's ideal for:

  • Microlearning / edtech apps building a linear skill-tree curriculum.
  • Any onboarding or tutorial flow where you want users to "prove" comprehension immediately after a short explanation.
  • Gamified habit-building apps that reward small wins with visible, instant feedback (XP, streaks, badges).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The subject matter requires open-ended reasoning or multi-step derivation that can't be reduced to a binary choice, oversimplifying complex concepts into a two-option tap can create false confidence.
  • Users need to revisit and deeply review prior mistakes; the strong forward-only spine and weak backward review here would frustrate learners who need remediation or spaced repetition.
  • The app's primary value is content consumption or exploration (e.g. reference material) rather than guided skill-building, where forcing an interaction before information disrupts flow.
  • Accessibility is a major concern and color-only differentiation (green border/grey distractor) isn't paired with sufficiently strong non-color cues for colorblind users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed learners: students or lifelong-learning professionals (who want bite-sized, screen-by-screen mastery of STEM concepts without the passive overhead of video lectures). The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Active recall & generation effect:
  • Immediate reward (operant conditioning): The instant "+15 XP" and celebratory copy create a dopamine loop that encourages continued engagement lesson after lesson.
  • Low-stakes comparison framing: Choosing between two tables rather than freeform input reduces math anxiety for users intimidated by equations.
  • Momentum bias: The forward-only progress bar and lack of a back button nudge users to keep moving rather than second-guessing, reinforcing habit formation over perfectionism.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fused instruction + interaction: The lesson text and the question live on the same screen as the answer mechanism, embodying the "move something before it explains" ethos (here, "move" is a tap/selection rather than passive reading).
  • Side-by-side comparative choice: Presenting two visually identical table structures (one correct, one with transposed/wrong values) forces precise attention to the data rather than guessing from format.
  • Immediate layered feedback: Border color, checkmark badge, greyed-out distractor, and a bottom sheet all reinforce correctness through multiple redundant visual channels simultaneously.
  • Non-blocking "Why?" affordance: Offers an escape hatch to deeper explanation for curious users without forcing everyone through it, respecting the "low density, one idea per screen" design principle.
  • Persistent XP + streak lightning icon: Keeps gamification visible but unobtrusive, in the top bar rather than dominating the primary content area.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (math) - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any educational or skill-building product where active recall improves retention: coding exercises, language learning conjugation drills, finance/numeracy trainers, or certification prep apps. It's ideal whenever a concept can be scaffolded with a concrete example (table/visual) alongside its abstract/symbolic representation, and when the product's goal is mastery through repetition rather than content consumption.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for open-ended or creative tasks where there isn't a single correct answer, as the binary Check/validate model will feel punitive or reductive. It also doesn't suit time-pressured or casual browsing contexts (e.g., news, social feeds) where forcing an input before progression would feel like friction rather than engagement. Finally, avoid disabling the primary button without clear guidance on what's missing (pair it with inline validation or hints to prevent user frustration).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets self-directed learners: students, professionals upskilling, or lifelong learners (who want active, bite-sized STEM practice rather than lecture-style video content). The design leverages the generation effect (psychological finding that people retain information better when they produce an answer rather than passively receive it) and testing effect (retrieval practice strengthens memory more than re-reading). The disabled button and required input exploit the completion/consistency bias: once a user starts filling in a field, they feel compelled to finish the micro-task. The clean, judgment-free "Start over" option reduces performance anxiety, appealing to users who may have had negative past experiences with math.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled-until-valid CTA: The grayed "Check" button enforces input completion before advancing, reducing accidental skips and reinforcing active engagement.
  • Dual-representation scaffolding: Presenting both a symbolic equation and a concrete value table lets learners solve via pattern recognition or algebra, accommodating different cognitive styles.
  • Minimal chrome, maximal focus: No tab bar, no sidebar, just a close icon and progress bar (the entire screen real estate is devoted to one task).
  • Inline "Start over" affordance: Offers a low-stakes retry without leaving the screen, reducing fear of making mistakes.
  • Streak/lightning icon: Subtly gamifies the linear lesson spine without needing a full gamification dashboard on-screen.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (math) - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse:
• Educational or skill-building apps teaching quantitative, symbolic, or notation-heavy content (math, physics, chemistry, music theory, coding syntax).
  • Any product where the "doing" is the explanation (i.e., interaction precedes exposition) to boost retention via active recall.
  • Linear, step-based courses where a persistent micro-progress indicator helps reduce drop-off anxiety.
  • Scenarios requiring specialized input (equations, chemical formulas, musical notes) where the native keyboard is insufficient.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Content-heavy or narrative apps where context and explanation must precede action (e.g., legal, medical, or financial disclosures) - stripping away explanatory text here would confuse or mislead users.
  • Apps targeting casual or low-commitment users who may be frustrated by a custom keyboard replacing familiar system input.
  • Non-linear or exploratory experiences where forcing one-task-per-screen would feel overly restrictive or slow down power users.
  • Contexts needing quick review of past work: this pattern's "weak backward review" trade-off penalizes users who want to jump back and check earlier steps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-directed adult and student learners pursuing STEM fluency who are motivated by mastery rather than passive content consumption. The design leans heavily on the generation effect (people remember information better when they produce an answer rather than read it) and pattern-completion psychology: the table invites the brain to spot an arithmetic relationship before formal algebra is even introduced, lowering the intimidation barrier for math-anxious users.

The minimalist, single-idea-per-screen layout caters to users with limited attention spans who want short, gym-like "reps" of cognitive effort. The custom keyboard and tactile input cater to users who want precision and a sense of craftsmanship in their answer, appealing to their intrinsic motivation and self-efficacy rather than extrinsic rewards.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom math input keyboard: A bespoke keyboard with operators, fractions, exponents, and radicals elevates the interaction from generic text entry to authentic mathematical reasoning, which is central to the brand's "doing not watching" ethos.
  • Inline answer slot: The input box is typographically fused into the equation ("x = 10 y = [ ]"), making the blank feel like a natural extension of the math rather than a separate UI widget.
  • Table-driven inductive reasoning: Instead of explaining the rule, the screen presents a data table and lets the user extrapolate the pattern themselves (active construction of knowledge over passive consumption).
  • Persistent macro-progress bar: The segmented green bar at the top keeps global lesson progress visible at all times without needing a separate progress screen.
  • Non-punitive "Start over" affordance: Normalizes experimentation and failure as part of the learning loop.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (math) - Screen 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any educational or skill-building product where retention and comprehension matter more than passive consumption speed (math/coding/language-learning apps, certification prep tools, or interactive tutorials). It's ideal when a concept can be distilled into a single, gradable micro-task that reinforces one specific idea per screen. It is also effective for onboarding flows that want to prove product value experientially ("try it yourself") rather than through marketing copy.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for content that is primarily informational/reference-based rather than skill-practice oriented, where forcing interaction before revealing information would frustrate users seeking quick answers. It's also inappropriate for time-constrained or low-commitment contexts (e.g., a quick lookup tool) since the deliberate friction of "input before proceeding" slows down the flow. Additionally, this rigid one-question-per-screen, linear structure can frustrate advanced learners who want to skip ahead or review multiple concepts at once (the weak backward-review noted in the app's UX profile).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-motivated adult learners and lifelong students (often professionals or students supplementing formal education) who specifically want active, effortful practice rather than passive video consumption (the exact demographic Brilliant markets to versus competitors like Khan Academy or YouTube edu-content).

Psychologically, it leverages the generation effect (information is retained better when self-produced rather than read) and the testing effect (retrieval practice strengthens memory more than re-reading). The immediate, low-stakes check-your-work loop also taps into intrinsic mastery motivation rather than external rewards, appealing to users who enjoy the "click" of understanding a concept through their own derivation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline answer embedded in notation: The input box ("y = [5]") is placed directly within the mathematical expression rather than below it in a generic form, keeping the user's mental model anchored to the math itself.
  • Scaffolded data table: A pre-filled x/y lookup table is given as a crutch/pattern-recognition aid, letting users infer the relationship before solving algebraically (a subtle hint system baked into the layout rather than a separate "hint" button).
  • Segmented progress bar: Converts lesson completion into a visible, granular countdown, leveraging the Goal-Gradient Effect to motivate finishing.
  • Single, unmissable CTA: "Check" is the only actionable button, eliminating decision paralysis and enforcing the "do, then verify" loop central to active-recall learning.
  • Low-stakes "Start over": A safety net that reduces fear of irreversible mistakes, encouraging experimentation.

screens.name: Dave Setting Up 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this icon-grid + promo-card pattern for account/settings hub screens where users need fast access to a handful of frequently used, disconvnected actions (e.g., banking apps, wallet apps, utility/service apps). It's ideal directly beneath an account's top-level landing view, and works well to cross-sell secondary features (savings tools, upgrades, add-ons) without resorting to hard interruption or modals.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are more than 6-8 actions, as the grid loses scannability and needs pagination or scroll fatigue sets in. Also avoid stacking too many promotional cards below the grid (more than 2-3 will make the screen feel like an ad feed rather than a utility hub, undermining the "low-drama" trust the brand is trying to build). Not suitable for first-time users who haven't yet learned the icon meanings; in that case, add labels-only or a guided tour first.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Dave's target user is a busy, often financially-stretched urban consumer who needs quick, judgment-free access to banking basics. This screen's grid layout assumes the user already knows roughly what they want to do (deposit, withdraw, pay a bill) and simply needs the fastest path (this matches the "advance-first, one-tap balance check" ease-of-use philosophy stated in the app's design principles).

The direct deposit and budgeting nudges specifically target the psychological pain point this audience faces: cash flow timing gaps. By promoting "paid 2 days early" here, Dave subtly reinforces its core retention loop (get users on direct deposit so Dave can predict paychecks and safely offer advances) while framing it as a user benefit rather than a business requirement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-first grid navigation: Six equally-weighted rounded tiles let users recognize actions via icon + label combo, speeding up scanning versus a text-only list.

  • Progressive disclosure of value: Core utilities (transfers, cash handling, bill pay) are given top billing; growth/engagement features (direct deposit, budgeting) are pushed below as secondary, low-pressure suggestions.

  • Benefit-forward nudge cards: Each promo card leads with the user outcome ("get paid early", "stay on top of spending") rather than the feature name, increasing perceived relevance and reducing feature-explanation friction.

  • Consistent mint-green iconography against neutral grey tiles reinforces brand color while maintaining low visual noise, aligning with the "low-drama" positioning of the brand.

screens.name: H&M - Home - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for fashion, beauty, lifestyle, or luxury apps where brand perception and emotional engagement are as critical as conversion. It's ideal for:

  • Seasonal campaign launches or "New Arrivals" merchandising moments
  • Brands with strong visual identity/content assets (video, photography)
  • Home screens where storytelling should precede product grids
  • Apps targeting younger, trend-driven demographics who expect social-media-like immersive content
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for utility-first, task-driven, or data-heavy apps (banking, productivity, B2B tools) where users need immediate access to information or functionality rather than brand immersion. It's also risky for:

  • Users on slow or metered connections, since autoplay video increases load time and data usage
  • Accessibility-sensitive contexts, since text-over-video can suffer contrast/legibility issues and motion can affect users with vestibular sensitivities
  • Repeat-visit home screens where users expect fast access to search, cart, or order status rather than a campaign splash every time
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious shoppers who respond to aspirational, lifestyle-driven imagery rather than feature lists or price-first messaging. The cinematic, editorial presentation taps into psychological triggers around desirability, identity, and aspiration: the model's styling and the moody black-and-white treatment invite the user to project themselves into the "look," a technique long used in print fashion advertising now translated to mobile.

The autoplay video format also leverages novelty and motion to capture attention within the first seconds of app open, increasing dwell time and emotional engagement before any product browsing occurs. The uncluttered interface additionally reduces cognitive load for casual browsers while still serving power users via the persistent bottom navigation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-screen video as hero content: Uses autoplaying video instead of static imagery to create a premium, dynamic first impression that differentiates H&M from static catalog-style competitors.
  • Minimal floating UI controls: Pause and mute icons are unobtrusively placed top-right, giving users control without cluttering the visual composition.
  • Invisible navigation integration: The translucent, floating tab bar blends with content while remaining persistently accessible, preserving full-bleed immersion without sacrificing wayfinding.
  • Typography as branding: Oversized, editorial-style type treatment for "NEW ARRIVALS" functions almost as a logo/campaign lockup rather than plain UI text.
  • Single, unambiguous CTA: Only one actionable button on screen eliminates decision fatigue and funnels all attention toward one next step.

screens.name: Brex Assistant options 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any AI/automation feature's activity log or history view when there is no real data yet (especially in B2B, fintech, or productivity tools where trust and transparency around automated actions are critical). It's ideal for onboarding users to a new AI agent capability, or for any feed-based history screen that benefits from a "preview card" teaching the expected format before real entries appear.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the sample data could be mistaken for real, actionable data (ambiguity between "demo" and "live" content can cause costly user errors in financial contexts, so visual differentiation (blur, dimming, "Example" label) must be unmistakable). Also avoid for simple, low-stakes features where a lightweight empty state with just text/illustration would suffice; the extra visual complexity here is only justified when building trust in opaque automated behavior.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets finance/ops professionals and employees at companies using Brex who are being introduced to an AI-driven expense assistant feature. Because AI automation can feel opaque or risky in a financial context (auto-approving expenses, adding memos, inviting attendees), the design leans heavily on trust-building psychology: showing exactly what the AI did, citing its data source (calendar), and visually anchoring it in a believable, realistic example rather than an abstract icon.

The empty state copy also serves a expectation-setting function for first-time users or those with zero AI-assisted transactions yet, reducing the "is this broken?" anxiety that blank screens often trigger.
screens.keyHighlights:
Demonstrative empty state: Instead of a generic illustration, the screen reuses the actual card component the user will see once data exists, pre-filled with a realistic example (merchant, amount, approval, attendees, memo). This teaches the feature's value and format simultaneously, turning a "dead end" screen into an educational moment.

Transparency of AI reasoning: The "Based on your calendar" footer line is a small but powerful trust-building detail (it tells the user *why* the assistant made a particular inference, demystifying the AI's decision-making and building confidence in automation).

Layered card stack cue: The partially visible second card behind the primary one visually implies "there will be more of these," setting an expectation of an ongoing activity log/feed pattern.

screens.name: Venmo Inviting Teammates & Friends 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for growth-loop features in consumer apps with viral potential (especially fintech, marketplaces, delivery, and social apps) where both the referrer and referee benefit financially. It's ideal when the app already has contact/address book access and a well-defined, trackable reward structure.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy monetary-incentive approach for B2B or enterprise software where financial referral bonuses may be inappropriate or against compliance policies. Also avoid if the app cannot reliably track and pay out referrals quickly, as broken promises of "$10 per friend" can severely damage trust. Overusing contact-list access for invites can also trigger privacy concerns if not clearly opt-in and transparently explained.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets existing, engaged users of a peer-to-peer payments app (evidenced by the Cash App-style branding and iconography) who are likely to have friends within the same target demographic (young, mobile-first, social spenders). The design exploits several psychological triggers:

  • Loss Aversion / Endowed Progress: Pre-filling a sliver of the progress bar makes users feel they've already started and don't want to "lose" that momentum.

  • Reciprocity & Social Currency: Users are incentivized to share a "gift" of money with friends, which also flatters the referrer as generous.

  • Scarcity of Effort: By capping earnings at $100 (10 friends x $10), the product creates a bounded, achievable goal rather than infinite/vague earning potential, which increases perceived attainability.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual Progress Metrics: Tracking both "Referred" count and "$ Earned" in parallel gives users two satisfying ways to watch their progress grow.

  • Reward-First CTA Copy: Labeling each contact row button "Earn $10" instead of "Invite" keeps the financial incentive front-and-center at the moment of decision.

  • Frictionless Contact Integration: Surfacing the user's own address book with searchable, one-tap invite actions removes the multi-step hassle of manually finding and sharing a link.

  • Celebratory Illustration: The confetti-and-hand-holding-phone illustration visually reinforces the joyful, rewarding nature of referring friends.

  • Modal Presentation: Using a swipe-up sheet with a close "X" keeps the referral flow contextual and easily dismissible without derailing the user's main task.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-screen selection modal pattern when:

  • A user must make a required, single selection from a known, named list of entities before proceeding deeper into a multi-step flow (e.g., selecting a project, workspace, repository, or team).
  • The list of options could grow large, benefiting from a built-in search affordance.
  • The task benefits from being framed as a deliberate step (full screen) rather than a lightweight contextual choice (which would suit a popover or bottom sheet instead).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The list of choices is very short (2-3 items): a popover, action sheet, or inline segmented control would be less disruptive and keep the user in context.
  • The selection is optional or secondary; forcing a full-screen interruption for a minor preference adds unnecessary friction.
  • Users need to compare multiple attributes of each item before choosing, as this flat list lacks space for rich metadata (e.g., last updated, issue count) that could aid decision-making.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen directly serves engineers and technical PMs who manage work across multiple codebases/repositories. Because Linear integrates tightly with GitHub/GitLab workflows, the need to associate an issue with a specific repo is a core, frequent action. The design leans on recognition over recall: showing a scannable list of existing known repos rather than requiring the user to type anything by default, while still offering search for teams with large repo counts.

The minimal, no-frills tone also caters to this audience's preference for tools that stay out of the way and move fast, avoiding the decision fatigue that heavier enterprise tools often introduce at this stage of issue creation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Clear two-tier header pattern: Bold primary title with a muted descriptive subtitle efficiently communicates both the macro-task (create issue) and the micro-step (choose repository) without extra UI chrome.
  • Persistent bottom search bar: Anchoring the search field to the bottom of the screen (within thumb's reach) rather than at the top is an ergonomic mobile-first decision, making filtering fast even with one-handed use on large lists.
  • Consistent list iconography: Using the same repository icon/avatar for every row maintains visual consistency while the list labels do the differentiation work, reducing visual noise.
  • Explicit drill-down affordance: The chevron icon sets clear expectations that this is a selection step within a larger flow, reducing user anxiety about losing context.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any "quick create" flow where speed of capture is more valuable than completeness of data (note-taking apps, task managers, bug trackers, or CRM lead capture). It's ideal when the core object has one mandatory field (title/name) and several optional metadata fields that can be added later. Auto-focusing the primary input and disabling submission until it's valid is a strong default for any lightweight creation modal.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the created object genuinely requires several mandatory fields upfront (e.g., a detailed support ticket needing severity and category for proper routing) - hiding required fields below the fold or behind extra taps could lead to incomplete, unusable records. Also avoid auto-focusing the keyboard if the form contains a prominent single-choice control (e.g., a type selector) that should be set before text entry, as immediate keyboard pop-up can obscure context or feel jarring on first load.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engineers, PMs, and designers who need to log a bug, idea, or task the instant it occurs to them (often while away from their desktop). The design leverages the psychological principle of minimizing "friction to capture": the fewer steps between having a thought and recording it, the more likely the thought gets captured before being lost. screens.name: Home Screen 25
screens.whereToUse: This fits the end of a content funnel where artist- or item-specific material is exhausted and cross-catalogue suggestions are the only remaining path to continued browsing.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (You Might Also Like shelves): Identical component, heading convention, and badge treatment; inherited directly from the parent product.

  2. Spotify (Fans Also Like on artist pages): Cross-artist recommendations appended after an artist's own catalogue, comparable in position and purpose within the page.

  3. YouTube Music (related tracks after a search result): Same terminal placement of taste-based suggestions below artist-specific content.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Honest hedging in a heading: "You May Also Like" claims possibility rather than confidence, which is the appropriate register for recommendations built on one data point.

  2. Consistent shelf grammar at depth: Paging, badging, and play overlays repeat unchanged, so the deepest sections require no new learning.

  3. Widening the funnel at its end: Once the artist's catalogue is exhausted, cross-artist suggestions are the only remaining way to extend the session.

  4. Inline content marking: The explicit badge sits with the metadata rather than on the artwork, keeping thumbnails uncluttered though slightly harder to scan.

  5. Alignment cost of variable titles: A two-line title beside single-line neighbours breaks the row's baseline, which a fixed-height title block would prevent.

screens.name: Home Screen 26
screens.whereToUse: This fits the foot of a detail screen where reference metadata belongs, and where an optional permission can be requested beside data that already demonstrates what it would add.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Photos and Camera (location metadata): Location attached to a captured item as context rather than as a feature, with the same framing that place completes a record which already has a time.

  2. Google Maps Timeline / Google Photos: Comparable in treating where-and-when as the pair that makes a log entry memorable, and in asking for the permission where the resulting value is displayed.

  3. Last.fm scrobble history: A listening log where per-item metadata and timestamps are the product; a fair comparison for why Shazam surfaces recognition time at all.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Permission priming by adjacency: Placing the location ask next to a filled timestamp row lets the surrounding data explain the benefit, so no explanatory copy is needed.

  2. Contextual timing over launch-time asking: Requesting location deep in a result the user chose to explore, rather than at first run, means the ask arrives when its purpose is visible.

  3. Metadata as memory: The "Recognized" timestamp converts a catalogue record into a personal log entry, which is the foundation of the app's library value.

  4. Optional framing through visual weight: The location prompt is a text link rather than a button, so it reads as an available action rather than a required one.

  5. Restraint at the terminus: Ending on a teal share action rather than another Apple Music CTA respects a user who has already scrolled past several asks.

  2. Theme matched to task: Dark-on-light for extended reading is a legitimate reason to break the app's dark theme, unlike the earlier commerce sheet where the switch signalled a context change.

  3. Editorial voice as differentiation: Prose that reads like a profile rather than a database entry is what makes this worth surfacing at all; a Wikipedia-style summary would add nothing.

  4. Dismiss affordance mismatched to content: A confirm-shaped control on a read-only sheet implies a decision that does not exist, and it abandons the close position used consistently everywhere else.

  5. Unbounded scroll after a bounded summary: Expanding from four lines to full text with no intermediate step means the user cannot gauge length before committing to scroll.

screens.name: H&M - Adding to Cart & Bag - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-bleed hero + minimal CTA pattern for:

  • Time-boxed promotional campaigns (flash sales, seasonal sales, early access drops) where urgency is the primary driver.
  • Brand-first retail/fashion apps that want to maintain an editorial, premium look even when communicating discounts.
  • App-exclusive perks designed to boost app installs/retention versus web.
  • Landing/home moments where a single dominant message should take priority over navigation or browsing.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Users need immediate access to multiple categories or products (the lack of visible product imagery/content here could frustrate users wanting to browse quickly).
  • The brand/product requires more explanation (e.g., SaaS, financial products) where terse, bold typography alone can't convey necessary nuance or terms.
  • Accessibility is a strong concern: relying on color (red) alone to convey urgency can fail for colorblind users without additional text/icon reinforcement.
  • Running on small or low-contrast displays where oversized type may not render well or may overwhelm smaller screen real estate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets deal-seeking, fashion-conscious shoppers and existing loyal H&M app users who respond to urgency and exclusivity cues. The "today only" + "early app access" framing specifically rewards and retains the app-installed segment, differentiating app value from the website, which drives higher app engagement and retention metrics for H&M's business.

Psychologically, the screen leverages scarcity (today only), exclusivity (early access), and visual dominance (oversized red sale typography) to trigger impulse engagement. The minimal chrome also appeals to fashion-forward users who expect a visually polished, non-salesy-looking retail experience despite the message being a discount promotion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Editorial whitespace as a design tool: Using ~70% empty canvas space around a single bold message creates a premium, fashion-magazine feel rather than a cramped discount-bin aesthetic.
  • Dual-tier CTA structure: Separating the emotional hook (SALE 60% OFF) from the functional action (SHOP NOW) into two distinct zones reduces cognitive load and lets each message breathe.
  • Floating minimal tab bar: The pill-shaped, outline-icon tab bar visually recedes so it doesn't compete with campaign art, yet remains persistently accessible.
  • Exclusivity framing: "Early App Access" rewards app engagement, directly incentivizing app installs/usage over mobile web or desktop.

screens.name: H&M - Adding to Cart & Bag - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a core transactional container (cart, wishlist, order history) can be empty, especially in e-commerce or marketplace apps. It's ideal when:

  • You want to convert an empty state into a re-engagement or merchandising opportunity instead of a dead end.
  • Authentication is optional but beneficial: frame sign-in around tangible user value (saving progress, syncing across devices).
  • You want to build pre-purchase trust early by surfacing payment options and policies before checkout, reducing anxiety during the actual conversion moment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, information-dense empty state in contexts where:

  • The app has a simpler, single-category catalog where "Selected For You" recommendations would feel generic or forced.
  • Mandatory authentication is required for checkout, mixing optional sign-in framing with payment/trust badges on an empty cart could create false expectations about guest checkout.
  • Screen real estate is limited (e.g., smartwatch or compact widget), where policy text and payment logos would overwhelm a simple "add items" prompt.
  • The brand tone is more minimal/quiet: the bold, shouty typography here may clash with softer, premium brand positioning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets casual browsers and first-time or logged-out users who may have navigated to the bag out of habit or curiosity rather than intent to purchase. For this segment, an empty bag is a moment of potential drop-off, so the design leverages several psychological levers:

  • Reciprocity/convenience framing: Explaining the benefit of signing in (saving items) rather than demanding login outright respects user autonomy and reduces reactance.
  • Trust transference: Displaying familiar payment logos (Visa, PayPal, Klarna, Apple Pay) and clear return policies taps into recognition heuristics, reassuring price-sensitive and risk-averse shoppers before they've even added a product.
  • Loss aversion mitigation via recommendations: "Selected For You" immediately re-engages users with alternative products, countering the slight disappointment of an empty bag with new discovery opportunities, exploiting the fashion shopper's love of browsing.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empty state as recovery funnel: Instead of a dead-end, the empty bag immediately pivots into a personalized product carousel ("Selected For You"), keeping the user engaged in the shopping loop.
  • Soft authentication framing: Sign-in is presented as a value-add ("save or access saved items") rather than a gate, lowering resistance to account creation/login.
  • Pre-emptive trust signals: Payment method logos and return/shipping policy text are shown even with an empty bag, building confidence ahead of the purchase decision.
  • Persistent discount entry: The "Discounts / Add" row is shown regardless of cart state, priming users to think about promo codes early.
  • Consistent tab bar access: The bottom navigation remains fully accessible, letting users quickly jump back to Home, Search, Wishlist, or Profile without feeling stuck.

screens.name: H&M - Adding to Cart & Bag - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any e-commerce cart/bag review screen, especially in sale-driven retail contexts. It's ideal when:

  • Users frequently return with items already decided upon and want quick checkout access.
  • The product catalog has frequent discounts/promotions that benefit from price-anchoring visuals.
  • Offering installment/BNPL options to reduce price sensitivity at the point of commitment.
  • You want to reduce outright deletions by offering a "save for later" alternative alongside removal.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid duplicating the top-of-page checkout CTA in contexts where users typically need to review multiple complex line items first (e.g., B2B bulk orders, grocery carts with substitution rules) - premature CTAs there can cause checkout errors or oversight of important details like substitution options or stock issues.

Also avoid persistent promotional banners inside the cart for premium/luxury brands, where this can feel undercutting of the full-price perception the brand is trying to project, or where it may distract from completing an already-decided purchase.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious, value-driven shoppers, many of whom are arriving via a sale/discount hook (the 60% off banner persists even here). The design assumes a mixed audience: both deal-seekers who need price reassurance (strikethrough pricing, discount line-item) and convenience-driven repeat H&M customers who want the fastest possible path to checkout.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss aversion (wishlist as an alternative to deletion), anchoring (crossed-out original prices), and friction reduction (top-loaded CTA, pre-answered cost/tax/installment questions) to minimize cart abandonment (one of the highest-risk drop-off points in any retail funnel).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Top-anchored primary CTA: "Continue to Checkout" is placed immediately below the title, reducing scroll-to-convert distance for intent-driven users.
  • Dual-path item disposition: Wishlist (heart) and delete (trash) icons sit side-by-side, letting users defer a purchase decision instead of forcing a binary buy/delete choice.
  • Price anchoring: Strikethrough original price next to a red discounted price reinforces the perceived savings and justifies the purchase decision at the exact moment of commitment.
  • Buy-now-pay-later nudge: Installment messaging embedded directly in the cost summary lowers the perceived financial barrier.
  • Persistent merchandising banner: The sale bar remains visible even in the cart, continuously cross-selling.

screens.name: H&M - View products in H&M - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Seasonal or collection launch moments (new arrivals, capsule collections, collaborations) where emotional branding should precede product browsing.
  • Apps wanting to differentiate from competitors by leading with lifestyle/editorial content instead of immediate product grids.
  • Flagship or campaign-driven entry points where a single, strong CTA is more effective than multiple competing options.
  • Brands with strong visual/video assets that can sustain engagement without text-heavy explanation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Utility-first or price-sensitive shopping contexts where users need quick access to categories, filters, or deals immediately upon opening the app.
  • Low-bandwidth or data-constrained markets, where autoplaying video as the primary landing experience can hurt load times and increase churn.
  • Return-visit, task-oriented flows (e.g., users re-opening the app to check an order or search a specific item) where a cinematic hero adds friction instead of value.
  • Accessibility-critical contexts, since heavy reliance on background video and low-contrast text overlays can reduce legibility and increase motion-sensitivity issues for some users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for fashion-conscious browsers and existing H&M customers who open the app seeking inspiration, not just a transaction. The cinematic, editorial treatment taps into aspirational psychology: by evoking a natural, sunlit, almost dreamlike setting, H&M associates its "New Arrivals" collection with freshness, season change, and lifestyle rather than mere merchandise.

The minimal-choice interface (one CTA, one headline) leverages the psychological principle of reduced cognitive load (shoppers arriving on this screen are given a single, clear path forward, which increases the likelihood of engagement compared to a cluttered homepage). The story-like format also appeals to younger, social-media-native users who are accustomed to swipe-driven, video-first content consumption (e.g., Instagram/TikTok), making the shopping experience feel contemporary and less like a static catalog.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-bleed cinematic video background: Using motion instead of a static image dramatically increases perceived production value and emotional engagement, setting H&M apart from typical e-commerce screens.
  • Floating, translucent tab bar: Keeps core navigation persistently accessible without breaking the immersive visual, a clever balance between utility and aesthetics.
  • Single, high-contrast CTA: "SHOP NOW" is isolated with no competing actions, reducing decision fatigue and funneling all attention toward one next step.
  • Unobtrusive media controls: Pause/mute icons are present for user control but visually de-emphasized so they don't compete with the brand message.
  • Story-style progress indicator: Suggests a swipeable sequence of branded moments, borrowing a familiar interaction pattern from social media (Stories) to make a shopping app feel more dynamic and content-driven.

screens.name: H&M - View products in H&M - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for fashion, lifestyle, or editorial-driven e-commerce catalogs where brand perception and aspirational imagery are as important as conversion efficiency. It's ideal when:

  • The product itself benefits from contextual/lifestyle presentation (apparel, home decor, beauty).
  • The brand wants to differentiate from generic grid-based marketplaces (Amazon-style) by leaning into visual storytelling.
  • Users are expected to browse leisurely in addition to performing targeted searches.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this full-bleed single-image card pattern for high-density comparison shopping contexts such as electronics, groceries, or B2B catalogs, where users need to scan many SKUs, prices, and specs quickly. In such cases, a dense grid with smaller thumbnails and visible pricing/ratings is more efficient. This pattern can also slow down power users who know exactly what they want and prefer rapid, information-rich scanning over aspirational single-item presentation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious shoppers who browse for inspiration as much as for specific purchases. The large editorial photography triggers aspirational desire and lifestyle association (a well-documented psychological driver in fashion retail where customers buy an identity, not just a garment).

The segmented control and filter/sort bar cater to the pragmatic, time-pressed segment of the audience (parents, repeat H&M customers) who need to narrow down selection quickly amid vast inventory. By combining emotional (imagery) and functional (filtering) triggers on one screen, H&M serves both the browsing-for-fun shopper and the mission-driven shopper simultaneously.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Editorial-first product cards: Replacing a traditional square product thumbnail with a full-bleed lifestyle photo elevates perceived brand value and encourages emotional, aspirational engagement over purely transactional browsing.
  • Inline category segmented control: Allows instant filtering between All/Clothes/Shoes & Accessories without a page reload or navigation stack push, keeping users in flow state.
  • Unobtrusive wishlist affordance: The heart icon is placed directly on the image with high contrast, enabling one-tap saving without disrupting the visual composition.
  • Floating pill tab bar: A modern navigation treatment that maximizes content real estate while remaining universally accessible.
  • Persistent Sort & Filter bar: Positioned immediately below category tabs, this reduces the number of taps needed to refine a large catalog, critical for a global retailer with extensive inventory.

The wishlist heart icon exploits the Zeigarnik effect and loss-aversion psychology (by making saving effortless, users are encouraged to "collect" items they like even if not ready to purchase, increasing the likelihood of return visits and eventual conversion). The minimal sort/filter controls respect the user's primary goal (visual discovery) while still offering control for power users who want to refine by price or popularity.
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: H&M - View collection - Screen 1

It's ideal for fashion, beauty, travel, and lifestyle apps aiming to differentiate from purely transactional competitors, and works well when the brand has access to high-quality video assets and wants to reinforce premium/editorial positioning.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for utility-first or price-sensitive shopping contexts where users expect to see products, prices, and promotions immediately (e.g., grocery, electronics, or discount retail apps) - the lack of visible merchandise can feel like friction. It's also risky for low-bandwidth markets or users on data caps, as autoplay video increases load time and data usage. Additionally, it should not be the permanent home state for returning high-intent users who want quick repeat purchases; a lighter, product-forward view or quick toggle should be available for them.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious, visually-driven shoppers: particularly younger audiences accustomed to social media's short-form video and Stories formats. By opening with video instead of a product catalog, H&M leverages the mere exposure and mood-congruence effects: pleasant, sunlit, natural imagery primes positive affect, which transfers to brand perception and purchase willingness.

The single, bold CTA exploits the paradox-of-choice principle: reducing cognitive load by giving the user exactly one path forward. The muted/pause controls cater to users who want control over autoplay media (a nod to accessibility and bandwidth-conscious users), while the floating tab bar respects power users who want to jump straight to search, wishlist, or bag without waiting for the video narrative to play out.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Story-style progress bar: The thin indicator at the bottom signals multiple hero "slides," borrowing a familiar Stories/Reels mental model to encourage continued engagement.

screens.name: H&M - View collection - Screen 2

The large, cinematic lifestyle photography taps into aspirational psychology, showing the garment worn, styled, and contextualized in a real-world setting (travel, sunlight, movement) rather than a sterile studio cutout, which increases desirability and purchase intent.

The persistent wishlist heart leverages the low-commitment "save for later" psychological trigger, letting undecided browsers bookmark desire items without the friction of full purchase decision-making.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

By presenting one large, stylized image per product instead of a dense grid, the design slows the user down and encourages emotional engagement with each item, which is a well-documented tactic in fashion e-commerce to increase dwell time and perceived desirability.

screens.keyHighlights:

  • Narrative-First Hierarchy: Delaying the price and product name until after the emotional hero image lets the fashion styling sell the product before the commercial details are even introduced.
  • Multi-Image Storytelling via Dots: The page control signals additional styled shots are swipeable, extending engagement time and giving multiple angles/context without cluttering the UI with thumbnails.
  • Persistent Floating Nav: The transparent top bar and floating bottom tab bar maximize the visible image real estate while keeping core navigation always within thumb's reach.
  • Outfit-Based Cross-Sell: By tagging an entire outfit (bag, pants, top) in one photo, H&M naturally encourages basket-size growth without needing separate "complete the look" modules.

screens.name: H&M - Size guide - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any e-commerce product configuration screen where a product has multiple visually distinguishable variants (color/pattern) plus a discrete, bounded set of secondary options (size, quantity). It is especially effective for:

  • Fashion, footwear, and accessories apps where variant appearance materially differs.
  • Retailers with omnichannel fulfillment (BOPIS - buy online, pick up in-store).
  • Products with a limited, well-known option set (standard sizing) that can be fully displayed without pagination or scrolling.
screens.whereNotToUse:
This pattern becomes less effective when:

  • Products have a very large number of variants (e.g., 20+ colors or custom sizes), where a full grid of photographic swatches would overwhelm the screen and require scrolling, negating the "scan at a glance" benefit.
  • Products require more complex configuration (e.g., bundles, engraving, multiple simultaneous attributes), where a single-screen form becomes cluttered and a multi-step or wizard flow is more appropriate.
  • Brands without physical retail presence, where the "Free pickup" option would be irrelevant and should be removed to avoid clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious shoppers, including existing H&M app users who already browsed a product and are now in high-intent, decision-making mode. The psychological design levers at play include:

  • Reduction of decision fatigue:
  • Loss-aversion/fit-anxiety mitigation: The adjacent Size Guide link addresses the #1 driver of apparel returns (incorrect sizing) directly at the point of hesitation.
  • Convenience-driven omnichannel behavior: The free in-store pickup option appeals to shoppers who want to avoid shipping costs/delays or wish to try before fully committing, which is common among budget-conscious young adults and families.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Photographic color swatches: Using cropped product photos instead of flat color chips lets shoppers preview texture, pattern, and fit nuances specific to fashion (e.g., pleat visibility) before switching variants.
  • Full-size-grid visibility: All 7 sizes (XXS. XXL) are shown simultaneously in a tappable grid, eliminating scrolling or dropdown friction at the highest-anxiety decision point in apparel shopping.
  • Contextual Size Guide placement: Positioning "SIZE GUIDE" directly above the CTA, right after size selection, intercepts doubt exactly when it occurs, reducing returns and cart abandonment.
  • Omnichannel pickup toggle: The "Free pickup at store" checkbox merges e-commerce and physical retail inventory, a strength unique to H&M's large store footprint.
  • High-contrast monochrome CTA: The pure black "ADD" button against white space follows strong visual hierarchy principles, impossible to miss amid otherwise neutral UI.

screens.name: H&M - Size guide - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a product has variable, user-dependent fit (apparel, footwear, accessories, even furniture dimensions) and the catalog spans a wide size range that would otherwise require excessive scrolling. It's ideal for:

  • E-commerce PDP (Product Detail Page) size charts
  • Any global app needing to reconcile multiple measurement systems
  • Catalogs with sub-categories of fit (maternity, petite, plus, youth) that benefit from segmented tabs
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense tabular approach for products with simple, single-dimension sizing (e.g., one-size-fits-all accessories) where a full chart would add unnecessary complexity. It's also not appropriate for mobile contexts with very limited horizontal space if the table requires excessive horizontal scrolling (consider a simplified "find your size" quiz or recommendation algorithm instead for very small screens or less engaged users who may abandon a dense data table).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets online shoppers uncertain about fit: a universal pain point in fashion e-commerce where the inability to try on clothing physically drives purchase hesitation and high return rates. By front-loading detailed, categorized measurement data, H&M reduces the psychological risk associated with "will this fit me?" and builds purchase confidence before checkout.

The inclusion of Maternity and Petite tabs alongside Regular, plus "curvy" hip measurements, demonstrates an awareness of body diversity, appealing to a broader segment of the target audience (young adults, families) and reinforcing trust that H&M has sized thoughtfully for different body types, not just a generic standard.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Two-tier filtering (fit type + size range chips): Breaks an overwhelming size matrix into small, scannable chunks instead of one giant table.
  • Bottom sheet modal presentation: Keeps the user anchored to the product page context; dismissing the sheet returns them exactly where they left off.
  • Expandable "How to Measure" accordion: Keeps instructional content collapsed by default to prioritize the data table, but available on-demand for first-time or unsure users.
  • Dual-unit measurements (inch & cm): Serves a global audience without requiring a separate unit toggle.
  • Inclusive sizing (Maternity, Petite, Curvy hip measurements): Signals brand inclusivity and reduces return rates by helping diverse body types self-select correctly.

screens.name: H&M - Size guide - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern in any e-commerce or marketplace app selling physical apparel, footwear, or accessories where fit is subjective and return rates due to sizing errors are a business concern. It's ideal for:

  • Product detail pages with a "Size Guide" link near the size selector.
  • Categories with non-obvious measurement points (pants, bras, rings, hats).
  • Global apps needing to standardize understanding across different regional sizing norms.
  • Any flow where you need to educate users on a physical/manual process using diagrams rather than pure text.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, illustrated approach for:

  • Digital-only or simple products where sizing is binary or self-evident (e.g., one-size accessories, digital goods).
  • Contexts where screen real estate or user patience is extremely limited (this detailed modal adds a step before purchase and could feel excessive in a quick-buy/impulse checkout flow).
  • Products with universal/standardized sizing where users already have strong size intuition (e.g., basic unisex t-shirts across a single market), as the added friction of opening a modal may not be worth the marginal comprehension gain.
  • If illustrations aren't anatomically precise or lack sufficient contrast (e.g., poor color choices for colorblind users), this pattern can create false confidence and actually increase sizing errors.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern directly serves fashion-conscious online shoppers who cannot physically try on garments before purchase (a core friction point in apparel e-commerce). It is especially critical for first-time H&M shoppers unfamiliar with the brand's specific fit/sizing conventions, as well as international customers (H&M being a worldwide market) who may be used to different regional sizing standards.

Psychologically, this screen combats the fear of returns/wrong fit, which is one of the single largest drop-off points in fashion checkout flows. By proactively educating the user with clear, authoritative visuals, H&M builds purchase confidence and reduces anxiety, which in turn lowers cart abandonment and return rates.

The inclusion of "Maternity" and "Petite" size ranges signals an inclusive design consideration for specific body types/life-stages within the target demographic, widening the pattern's appeal to a broader segment of women shoppers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-Mode Instruction: Combining a labeled anatomical illustration with numbered text creates redundancy that dramatically reduces measurement errors.
  • Numbered Visual Legend: Using matching circled numerals on both the diagram and the instructions creates an intuitive, language-agnostic mapping system (valuable for H&M's global/worldwide audience where visual cues transcend translation issues).
  • Front & Back Silhouettes: Showing both views clarifies measurements (like low hip) that wrap around the body and aren't fully visible from one angle alone.
  • Segmented Size Range Control: Surfacing Regular/Maternity/Petite options directly within the sizing modal ensures the educational content and the subsequent data table stay contextually relevant to the user's body type.
  • Collapsible Section: The minus/accordion icon lets returning or confident users skip the tutorial and go straight to the numeric chart, respecting varying levels of user expertise.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any account/profile settings hub where users need to view and edit a small number of personal data fields alongside higher-stakes account lifecycle actions (export, deactivate, delete). It's ideal for:

  • Apps with GDPR/CCPA data export or deletion requirements.
  • Products prioritizing trust and transparency over retention tactics.
  • Any screen where visual calm and low cognitive load are priorities (education, wellness, productivity apps).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat, undifferentiated styling when:

  • Destructive actions carry severe, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., financial account closure) - these typically warrant stronger visual warning cues (red text, icons) and additional confirmation friction.
  • The settings list grows large (15+ items): at that scale, labeled section headers and search/filter become necessary instead of relying on dividers alone.
  • Regulatory or legal contexts require more prominent disclosure before data export/deletion, where a neutral chevron row may be seen as insufficiently informative.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Brilliant's audience is self-directed, intrinsically motivated learners (students, professionals, hobbyist problem-solvers) who value efficiency and clarity over flashy gamification. This settings screen caters to that same mindset: it respects the user's time and intelligence by not over-explaining or decorating basic account management.

Psychologically, grouping sensitive actions (export, delete) separately from everyday identity fields reduces the "fear of accidental taps" - users scanning for "Password" won't fear brushing against "Delete account" because of the clear visual separation. The neutral tone around deletion also reduces reactance; by not guilt-tripping or hiding the exit, Brilliant signals confidence in its product's value, which paradoxically builds trust and retention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Three-tier grouping via dividers: Separates identity, credentials, and account-lifecycle actions into clear risk tiers without needing labeled section headers, keeping the screen visually calm.
  • Non-alarming destructive action: "Deactivate or delete account" uses the same typography and black text as benign rows instead of red warning styling, avoiding unnecessary anxiety while still being fully accessible/transparent.
  • Consistent drill-down affordance: Every row uses the same chevron-and-value pattern, making the entire screen instantly scannable and predictable on first glance.
  • Privacy-aware masking: Password is hidden entirely (no value shown) while email is partially visible, reflecting sensible information-sensitivity tiering.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any subscription or account-based product's offboarding/deactivation flow, particularly when:

  • You want structured churn analytics without resorting to intrusive exit surveys or forced phone calls.
  • The brand value proposition relies on trust and non-manipulative design (e.g., education, wellness, productivity apps).
  • You want to close the loop gracefully, preserving goodwill for potential win-back campaigns later.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this exact pattern when:

  • The business genuinely needs a retention intervention (e.g., presenting a discount, pause option, or feature education) - in those cases, a reason selector should precede a tailored save-attempt screen rather than go straight to confirmation.
  • The checkbox list is so long or granular that it creates decision fatigue right as the user wants to leave quickly (simplicity and speed should be prioritized in exit flows).
  • Legal/compliance requirements mandate additional verification steps (e.g., re-authentication) before deactivation, which this screen does not surface.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already decided to leave (at this point, persuasion is futile and potentially damaging to brand perception). Instead, the design targets the company's internal product and growth teams as the secondary "audience," optimizing for structured churn-reason data collection. Psychologically, offering a reason selector gives departing users a sense of closure and voice, which can reduce negative word-of-mouth even among churned users ("they asked why, and listened").

The inclusion of options like "I am spending too much time on Brilliant" also signals self-awareness toward digital wellbeing-conscious users, appealing to the global, reflective STEM-learner demographic who may value a company that doesn't shame them for setting boundaries.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reframing churn as contribution: The headline positions the act of leaving as helpful to "future generations," softening the emotional friction of deactivation.
  • Multi-select checkboxes over radio buttons: Allows richer, more honest qualitative signal since churn is rarely caused by a single factor.
  • No dark patterns or last-minute discount offers: The screen respects user intent rather than inserting manipulative retention interstitials, which builds long-term brand trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Consistent minimalist chrome: Reusing the same top bar, typography, and spacing system as the rest of the app keeps even a "negative" flow feeling coherent and non-jarring.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any account-deletion or subscription-cancellation flow where:

  • You want structured, qualitative churn data without adding friction that feels manipulative.
  • Users need to choose between reversible (deactivate) and irreversible (delete) actions, and the distinction must be crystal clear.
  • Brand trust and long-term reputation (word-of-mouth, win-back potential) matter more than squeezing out one more retention save.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this low-friction approach if the business model depends heavily on short-term retention saves (e.g., subscription services with aggressive LTV targets) - some products legitimately need a single, well-crafted retention offer before this screen. Also avoid mixing checkbox and radio semantics on the same screen without a visual divider, as it can confuse users about whether multiple selections are allowed. Finally, never allow a "permanent delete" radio option without the explicit irreversibility disclaimer used here, as that invites support disputes and reduces trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves users who have already decided to leave (the target "demographic" here is a departing user, often someone who found Brilliant too difficult, redundant (duplicate accounts), privacy-conscious, or time-constrained). Pre-checked example states (shown with checkmarks) in the mock suggest common real-world churn reasons: difficulty, accidental duplicate accounts, and privacy concerns, implying Brilliant's actual churn data skews toward perceived difficulty and account-hygiene issues rather than lack of perceived value.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the sunk-cost-free exit principle (by not fighting the departure, Brilliant preserves brand goodwill and increases the odds of a future "boomerang" return (reinforced by the "temporarily deactivate" option)). The privacy-concern checkbox also signals awareness that STEM/edtech audiences (often data-conscious, intellectually engaged users) care about data ownership, hence offering a hard-delete path with explicit irreversibility language builds long-term trust even in the exit moment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Exit research, not exit prevention: No retention offer, discount, or guilt-trip modal precedes the actual deactivation choice (the product respects the user's decision and instead optimizes for learning).
  • Checkbox vs. radio button semantic clarity: Switching input type from checkboxes (top, multi-select reasons) to radio buttons (bottom, single-select severity) communicates selection rules without needing any instructional copy.
  • Transparent irreversibility disclosure: Explicitly stating deletion "can't be recovered, even by staff" removes ambiguity and builds trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Two-tier choice architecture: Separating "why" from "how severe" into two distinct question blocks, divided by a hairline rule, prevents cognitive overload and keeps the one-idea-per-section rhythm consistent with the app's lesson design philosophy.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any account deletion or cancellation flow where you want to (1) capture structured churn-reason data for product improvement, (2) differentiate between reversible and irreversible actions, and (3) add a final security/intent-confirmation gate. It's especially valuable for subscription, education, or SaaS products where re-engagement after a "cool-off" period is possible and worth protecting via a temporary deactivation default.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, multi-step flow for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., unsubscribing from a newsletter), where the added friction would feel punitive and out of proportion to risk. Also avoid for apps with no account recovery infrastructure, where offering a "temporary" option would be misleading. If legal/compliance requires immediate, frictionless deletion (e.g., GDPR right-to-erasure requests), this length of flow may need to be shortened or supplemented with a direct deletion path.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already decided to leave (learners who found the STEM content too difficult, privacy-conscious users, or those who created accidental duplicate accounts). Rather than fighting churn with dark patterns, Brilliant leans into transparency and data collection, which suits its brand as a trustworthy, pedagogically serious edtech platform aimed at a global, education-first audience.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss aversion (bold warning about permanent, unrecoverable deletion) and commitment/consistency (requiring users to articulate their reason and re-enter a password) to slow impulsive cancellations while still respecting user autonomy (an ethical approach appropriate for an app whose value proposition is built on sustained, deliberate practice).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multi-select churn survey captures granular, actionable reasons for leaving before the deletion flow proceeds, turning an offboarding moment into a product-research opportunity.
  • Asymmetric default framing between "temporarily deactivate" and "permanently delete" nudges users toward reversible action without removing agency.
  • Password re-authentication gate as a final friction point, preventing impulsive, accidental, or malicious deletions.
  • Explicit irreversibility warning ("can't be recovered, even by staff") sets honest expectations and builds institutional trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Consistent one-idea-per-screen minimalism is preserved even in a utilitarian settings flow, keeping cognitive load low despite the emotionally charged context.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this multi-stage confirmation pattern (reason → reversibility choice → re-authentication → consequence disclosure → final action) for any high-stakes, irreversible user action: account deletion, financial withdrawal, data purge, or subscription cancellation with sunk-cost implications (e.g., losing saved progress or paid content).

It is especially valuable in subscription-based products where deletion has a secondary financial consequence (active billing) that users may not immediately realize.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, multi-step friction pattern for low-risk or reversible actions (e.g., removing a single saved item, logging out, or unsubscribing from a single notification type) - excessive friction on low-stakes tasks frustrates users and feels punitive rather than protective.

Also avoid requiring password re-entry if the user already recently re-authenticated in the same session, as redundant verification steps increase abandonment without adding security value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves users who have already decided to leave (likely frustrated, overwhelmed, or re-prioritizing their time) and targets two underlying psychological needs: agency (the explicit choice between temporary vs. permanent action respects that not everyone wants to fully sever ties) and trust (radical transparency about irreversibility and billing consequences signals the company isn't trying to trap or trick them).

For Brilliant specifically, whose brand promise is calm, focused, friction-light learning, maintaining that same respectful, low-pressure tone even during offboarding reinforces brand integrity (a company that is honest when you're leaving is more likely to be trusted if you return).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Password re-authentication gate: Converts a single destructive tap into a two-factor-like confirmation, preventing accidental or unauthorized deletion.
  • Inline password-reset recovery link: Solves the "I forgot my password and now I'm stuck" dead-end proactively within the flow itself.
  • Transparent subscription-cancellation disclosure: Surfaces a consequential business fact at the precise decision moment instead of hiding it in fine print, respecting informed consent.
  • Color-coded severity: The lone coral-red button amid an otherwise monochrome screen visually isolates risk without needing extra copy.
  • Reason capture before action: Collecting churn reasons (visible above the fold scroll) turns an exit into usable product feedback data.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
• First-touch splash/welcome screens for subscription or edtech apps where the product's core mechanic (interactivity, motion, hands-on learning) can be visually encoded into the hero graphic itself.
  • Apps that want to differentiate from generic stock-photo onboarding by using brand-specific illustration or kinetic typography.
  • Funnels where you want to softly bias users toward sign-up while still offering a low-friction path back to sign-in.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Apps where the core value proposition is emotional or social (e.g., dating, social networking) - an abstract typographic illustration would fail to build the human connection those categories require.
  • B2B or enterprise tools where users expect immediate utility/functional clarity rather than brand storytelling on the first screen (this pattern spends a full screen on persuasion before any functional UI is shown, which could frustrate task-driven users).
  • Contexts where regulatory or compliance screens (e.g., consent, age-gating) must appear before any marketing content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets a broad, worldwide audience of self-directed learners (likely skewing toward curious professionals, students, and lifelong learners who are often comparing Brilliant against competitors like Duolingo, Khan Academy, or Coursera in an app store search). Because this is the very first impression, the design leans heavily on the von Restorff effect (the oversized, unusual typographic illustration stands out from typical SaaS/EdTech splash screens that use photos of smiling people) to create immediate brand memorability.

The "15 minutes a day" claim taps into the psychological principle of minimal viable commitment: by framing the ask as small and time-boxed, it lowers the perceived barrier to trying the product, which is critical for conversion at the top of a mobile acquisition funnel where attention spans are short and competing apps are one tap away.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Typography-as-illustration: Instead of screenshots or stock imagery, the brand's core differentiator (interactivity) is literally woven into the headline using fake drag-tags, axes, and dotted plot lines (a highly original and on-brand way to visualize "doing" rather than "watching)."
  • Single, unmissable CTA: One full-bleed green button with no competing buttons of equal visual weight (removes decision paralysis at the most critical conversion point of the funnel).
  • Specific, benefit-driven subcopy: "Get smarter in 15 minutes a day" quantifies the value proposition, making an abstract benefit (intelligence growth) feel concrete and attainable.
  • Deferred sign-in: "Sign in" is present but visually subordinate, correctly prioritizing new-user acquisition while not alienating returning users.

screens.name: Loom - Logging out - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Reuse this pattern for any settings or account management screen that combines routine account actions with one or more irreversible/destructive actions, such as:

  • Account/profile settings in SaaS, productivity, or collaboration apps
  • Subscription cancellation or data deletion flows
  • Any screen mixing "safe" exits (logout, sign out, archive) with "dangerous" ones (delete, deactivate, permanently remove)

It's particularly effective when you need users to quickly distinguish risk levels at a glance and want to funnel destructive actions through an additional confirmation step.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The destructive action needs much stronger friction (e.g., typing "DELETE" to confirm) - this screen alone is too lightweight if the stakes are extremely high (e.g., deleting an entire organization's data).
  • There are many account-related settings to manage (a flat single-section list won't scale and would need categorized sections, search, or an accordion).
  • The brand doesn't use a color system where red/orange reliably signals danger (e.g., color-blind accessibility concerns should always be paired with iconography or explicit copy, not color alone).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Loom's broad professional user base (individuals and team members who may need to manage credentials, switch accounts between work/personal emails, or exit the platform entirely (e).g., offboarding from a company, or consolidating tools). Since Loom targets professionals and teams, account email visibility is important for confirming "which identity am I logged in as," a common point of confusion in B2B SaaS tools used across multiple organizations.

The deletion flow specifically caters to users exercising data ownership/control (often driven by privacy regulation awareness like GDPR), or those leaving the platform. Isolating and color-flagging this option leverages loss-aversion psychology and caution-conditioning: red signals danger, prompting users to pause and consider before proceeding, which protects both the user and Loom's support team from accidental, hard-to-reverse requests.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded action hierarchy: blue for benign actions (sign out), red/orange for destructive ones (delete account) - enabling instant risk recognition without reading text.
  • Deliberate spatial isolation: the delete action lives in its own grouped section, separated from account details, reducing accidental selection via Fitts's Law and visual grouping principles.
  • Progressive disclosure for destruction: the chevron on "Delete my account" indicates this leads to a confirmation step rather than instant deletion, respecting the principle that destructive actions should never be a single tap.
  • Minimalist grouped-list layout: uses native platform conventions (iOS settings style) so the screen feels instantly familiar and trustworthy, lowering cognitive load for a sensitive task.

screens.name: Loom - Logging out - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for moderate-consequence, easily reversible actions such as signing out, discarding unsaved changes, leaving a shared document, or removing a non-critical integration. It's ideal when you want to catch accidental taps without fully blocking or heavily penalizing the user with multi-step confirmation flows.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this lightweight dialog pattern for truly irreversible or high-stakes actions (e.g., permanent account deletion, billing cancellation, data purges) - these warrant stronger friction such as typed confirmation text, re-authentication, or a secondary review screen. Overusing simple confirm dialogs for low-risk, frequent actions (e.g., closing a panel) also causes "dialog fatigue," training users to blindly tap through without reading.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Loom's audience is busy professionals and teams who move quickly between devices and accounts. A sign-out confirmation prevents accidental taps (especially on mobile, where fat-finger errors are common) from disrupting an in-progress recording or losing access unexpectedly mid-workflow.
