The pattern leverages loss-aversion psychology: users pause for a split-second to confirm intent, reducing support tickets and frustration from accidental logouts, while still respecting the user's time with a single-tap resolution either way.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded button hierarchy: Blue "Cancel" (safe/default) vs. red "Sign Out" (destructive) gives instant visual affordance without needing to read text.
  • Dimmed background scrim: Forces single-task focus and visually subordinates the settings list beneath the decision point.
  • Proportional friction: A lightweight, one-tap-to-cancel dialog is used for a reversible action (sign out), reserving heavier friction for truly destructive actions like account deletion.
  • Grouped settings architecture: Separating benign account info from destructive actions ("Delete my account" in its own isolated row) pre-signals risk before the modal even appears.

screens.name: Loom - Logging out - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern as the opening screen of a value-proposition carousel for any app with a core feature that is visually demonstrable (collaboration tools, creative/media apps, productivity SaaS). It is ideal when you need to communicate a product's primary differentiator before requiring any sign-up commitment, and when you want to support both new-user acquisition and returning-user sign-in from a single, low-friction entry screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy illustrative, multi-screen onboarding approach for utility apps, tools used under time pressure, or returning-user-dominant apps where users expect to land directly on login or their last-used screen (the extra carousel steps would feel like unnecessary friction). Also avoid if the core value proposition cannot be meaningfully illustrated visually, as the mock-UI technique would lose its impact and risk looking generic or decorative.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets busy professionals, remote/distributed teams, and knowledge workers worldwide who are evaluating Loom for the first time, often during a quick app-store driven trial decision. The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Show-don't-tell / concrete imagery bias: people trust and understand a realistic mock screenshot faster than abstract marketing copy, lowering the barrier to understanding what the product actually does within seconds.
  • Social/collaborative cues: the avatar and reaction emojis (👍, 💬) imply other humans are already engaging, subtly invoking social proof and reducing the feeling of a solitary tool.
  • Autonomy and flexibility framing ("wherever, whenever," "on the go") appeals to professionals who value asynchronous work and want to avoid being tied to scheduled meetings (directly aligned with Loom's core pitch of replacing live meetings).
screens.keyHighlights:
Illustrative product preview instead of abstract graphics: showing a mocked real UI (document + video thumbnail + reactions) builds instant product comprehension over generic illustrations.

Two-tone headline typography cleverly splits emphasis between the core value ("Watch & engage," dark/bold) and the flexibility modifier ("wherever, whenever," light gray), guiding the eye and reading rhythm.

Dual-path CTA footer (Sign in / Sign up) removes friction for returning users while still prioritizing acquisition via visual weight on Sign up.

Page-control dots set correct expectations that this is step 1 of a short, skippable multi-screen story, reducing bounce from perceived long commitment.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for:

  • Any in-app help/feedback entry point where user-reported issues need to be pre-categorized for internal routing (support vs. product teams).
  • Productivity, B2B, or SaaS tools with power users who generate frequent, specific feedback.
  • Situations where you want to reduce free-text ambiguity before a user reaches a longer form.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Your feedback categories overlap heavily or users frequently can't tell bugs from feature requests (in that case, a single unified form with a dropdown may reduce decision paralysis).
  • You need to capture urgent, time-sensitive issues (e.g., payment failures) - those deserve a dedicated, higher-visibility escalation path rather than being buried in a generic help sheet.
  • The target audience is non-technical and may not understand the bug/improvement distinction, risking mis-categorization.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers and developers actively working in Figma who hit a snag or have a fleeting idea mid-workflow. Because Figma's audience is technically literate and detail-oriented, they appreciate precision (hence the explicit distinction between a defect report and a feature suggestion rather than a generic "Contact Us" funnel).

Psychologically, this taps into the Zeigarnik effect: capturing a user's frustration or idea at the exact moment it occurs (in-context) dramatically increases the likelihood of them actually submitting feedback, compared to asking them to remember and report it later via email.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Intent-based bifurcation: Splitting feedback into "bug" vs "improvement" at the entry point does the routing work upfront, saving triage time downstream.
  • Descriptive subtitles: Each choice is reinforced with a clarifying sentence, preventing mis-selection and reducing support team back-and-forth.
  • Native OS pattern: Leveraging the iOS action sheet convention makes the interaction feel instantaneous and familiar, requiring no onboarding.
  • Low-friction exit: A clearly separated "Cancel" button respects the user's right to back out without penalty or guilt.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any professional/productivity tool with complex workflows where users encounter technical issues mid-task (design tools, IDEs, project management apps).
  • Support or feedback flows where automatically capturing diagnostic context (screenshots, logs, device info) would significantly improve the quality of reports without burdening the user.
  • Apps targeting technical or semi-technical users who value transparency and control over what data is being shared (hence the editable attachment list).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer apps with casual, non-technical users may find "steps to reproduce" and screen-recording language intimidating or confusing; simpler one-tap feedback (e.g., emoji rating) may be more appropriate.
  • Avoid auto-attaching screenshots or session data without explicit disclosure/consent in contexts involving sensitive or regulated information (e.g., healthcare, finance) to avoid privacy or compliance violations.
  • Not ideal for extremely time-sensitive critical bug escalation flows where a direct chat/ticket with a human support agent would be faster than a self-service form.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Figma's core audience of designers and developers, many of whom are highly technical and expect efficient, low-friction feedback channels embedded directly in their workflow tool. Because these users are often mid-task when they encounter a bug, the design minimizes typing (pre-filled email, auto-captured screenshot and repro steps) so they can report the issue and return to work quickly.

Psychologically, the screen reduces the perceived effort and uncertainty of bug reporting (a task users often abandon because they don't know what information is "useful" to include). By auto-capturing technical context (screenshot, steps to reproduce) and only asking for a free-text description, the app leverages the principle of reducing cognitive load, increasing the likelihood that users will actually complete and submit the report rather than give up.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-filled email field: Removes a trivial but annoying data-entry step by using the logged-in account's email automatically.
  • Guided placeholder copy: The description placeholder acts as an inline template/prompt (expected vs. actual behavior), improving the quality of bug reports submitted without extra UI.
  • Automatic context capture with user control: A screenshot and reproduction-steps log are auto-attached, with a visible close "X" and "Edit list" link giving the user editorial control and transparency over what's being sent.
  • Layered evidence options via bottom sheet: Screen recording, screenshot, and gallery selection are tucked into a secondary action sheet, keeping the main form minimal while still offering rich diagnostic capture.
  • Minimal chrome, clear exit/submit actions: A simple close (X) and send (paper plane) icon pair in the top bar keeps the interaction model obvious and low-friction.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for app "About" or "System Info" screens where you need to surface static metadata (version numbers, build IDs, legal documents) alongside rarely-used but necessary account-level destructive actions. It's ideal when:

  • You need to comply with app store or legal requirements to expose account deletion.
  • You want to separate informational, non-actionable content from interactive/destructive content on the same screen.
  • Your audience is technical and doesn't need extensive explanation of version/build terminology.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The target audience is non-technical and would benefit from plain-language explanations of what "Version" or "Build" mean, or why they'd need this information.
  • Account deletion is a frequently needed or urgent action (e.g., privacy-focused apps) - burying it two levels deep could frustrate users or violate "easy opt-out" expectations (e.g., GDPR "right to erasure" guidance favors more direct access).
  • The screen has multiple destructive or high-stakes actions (a single flat list with only color-coding may not provide enough differentiation or warning at scale; a dedicated confirmation flow or grouped "Danger Zone" section would be more appropriate for multiple risky actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves existing, logged-in Figma users: designers and developers (who need to reference their app version/build (often for bug reports or support tickets) or who are seeking to manage/delete their account). The audience is technically sophisticated, so no extra explanation of "Version" or "Build" is required.

Psychologically, the design leverages friction as a safety mechanism: by nesting the destructive "Delete account" action inside a secondary "About" screen rather than directly in the main Account menu, Figma reduces the chance of accidental or impulsive deletions, while still satisfying platform/legal requirements that users must have an accessible self-service deletion path. The red color coding taps into universal danger signaling, triggering caution before the user even reads the label.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-interactive vs. interactive differentiation: Version and Build rows have no chevron and gray static values, clearly signaling they are read-only, while "Legal" has a chevron indicating further navigation (a subtle but effective affordance cue).
  • Isolation of destructive action: "Delete account" is visually separated by a divider and distinct red color, preventing accidental taps and signaling irreversibility at a glance.
  • Burying high-risk actions: Placing account deletion two navigation levels deep (Account > About) is an intentional friction pattern that discourages impulsive or accidental account deletion while still technically providing the required self-service option.
  • Consistent dark header pattern: The dark navigation bar with back-chevron and centered title maintains visual consistency with the rest of the Account section, reinforcing a sense of place within the settings hierarchy.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any in-app feedback, support, or bug-reporting flow where reducing friction and capturing technical context quickly is critical (especially in professional/B2B tools, developer tools, or QA-heavy products). It's ideal when:

  • You want to boost bug report submission rates by minimizing manual steps.
  • Users are mid-task and need a fast way to flag issues without losing their place.
  • You can auto-capture useful diagnostic context (screenshots, logs, steps) to enrich reports for your support/engineering team.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, auto-capturing approach in consumer-facing apps with strong privacy sensitivities (e.g., health, finance, messaging) unless capture is clearly opt-in and consented to, as silently generating "reproduction steps" or screen recordings could feel invasive. It's also unnecessary for simple, low-complexity apps where a plain text feedback box is sufficient and a multi-option attachment sheet would just add complexity for minimal benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets designers and developers using Figma who encounter a bug mid-workflow and want to report it with minimal interruption to their creative process. Precision-focused users (Figma's core demographic) expect accurate, detailed bug reports to be easy to generate without needing to manually describe technical context.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduction of perceived effort (pre-filled fields, auto-attached screenshots) to overcome the natural reluctance to stop and fill out a support form. The transparency microcopy also taps into a need for control and trust, especially for a technically sophisticated audience who may be wary of what diagnostic data is being silently transmitted.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-filled & Smart Defaults: The email field is already populated, removing a step and reducing drop-off on a task users typically want to finish quickly.
  • Automatic Evidence Capture: A screenshot appears to be pre-attached with an in-line annotation/edit icon, turning a manual "take and upload a photo" task into a near-zero-effort action.
  • Transparency on Metadata Collection: Explicitly informing the user that reproduction steps are included builds trust and sets expectations for support/engineering teams reviewing the ticket.
  • Layered Bottom Sheet for Attachments: Rather than navigating away, a native action sheet surfaces additional capture methods (record, screenshot, gallery) contextually, preserving the user's place in the form.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
• Terminal confirmation step after any user-submitted form where the outcome is important enough to warrant a blocking acknowledgment (bug reports, support tickets, applications).
  • Scenarios where you want to end a potentially frustrating task (e.g., reporting an error) on a positive, appreciative note.
  • Any flow where preserving visual context of the submitted content reassures the user that nothing was lost.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid blocking modals for low-stakes, frequent actions (e.g., saving a file, liking a post) - use a lightweight toast/snackbar instead to prevent interrupting flow.
  • Do not use for flows requiring immediate next steps (e.g., "verify your email") since the lack of actionable CTA could leave users unsure how to proceed if auto-dismiss isn't implemented.
  • Avoid generic "thank you" messaging in contexts needing specific follow-up information (e.g., ticket number, expected response time) as it may feel dismissive of a more serious issue.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers and developers who have just taken time out of their workflow to report a bug (often a mildly disruptive, unpaid act of goodwill toward the product). Closing the loop with immediate, warm acknowledgment is a psychological reward (reciprocity and validation) that reduces the perceived "cost" of reporting issues and encourages users to continue submitting quality feedback in the future.

By avoiding a sterile "Submitted" message and instead directly thanking the user, Figma reinforces its brand ethos of valuing community and collaboration, which matters deeply to its professional, detail-oriented audience who expect transparency and respect for their time.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose modal: No competing CTAs or secondary actions. Just closure, respecting the user's mental model that the task is finished.
  • Soft, reassuring iconography: A blue checkmark in a pale circular badge visually encodes success without alarming colors (e.g., green success banners), fitting Figma's calm, precision-focused visual language.
  • Preserved context via dimmed background: Keeping the original form faintly visible behind the overlay reassures the user their input wasn't lost and maintains spatial continuity.
  • Gratitude-driven microcopy: Explicitly thanking the user converts a routine confirmation into a small moment of positive reinforcement, encouraging future engagement with feedback tools.

screens.name: Figma - About - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-list settings pattern when:

  • Designing account/profile management screens for productivity or B2B SaaS tools where clarity and speed outrank visual flourish.

  • You need to support multi-tenant or multi-organization switching (the Teams and organizations block with checkmark is ideal for this).

  • The settings screen is a secondary, modal-style destination accessed frequently but briefly.

  • You want to expose both routine settings (Notifications) and power-user utilities (Shake to report) in the same screen without overwhelming the primary nav.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat, text-only grouped list when:

  • The target audience is less technical and would benefit from icons, illustrations, or more visual scaffolding to aid recognition.

  • The settings surface needs to highlight monetization or upsell opportunities (this minimal style under-communicates urgency or value and would bury a paywall/upgrade CTA).

  • Account switching involves many organizations (10+), where a flat list without search/filter would become unwieldy and require a dedicated picker screen instead.

  • Destructive actions like "Log out" need extra friction (e.g., shared/kiosk devices) - this pattern provides no confirmation step, which could cause accidental logouts in those contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, developers, and team administrators who need to quickly verify their identity, switch between organizational contexts, or manage account-level preferences without leaving their current design flow. The target audience values efficiency and predictability over delight (hence the stripped-down, native-feeling UI).

Psychologically, the modal "Done" pattern (vs. a stacked push navigation) reinforces that this is a transient, task-focused detour from the main canvas-first experience, not a core destination, respecting the user's primary goal of returning to their design work as fast as possible.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grouped list architecture: Logical sectioning (Identity → Teams → General → Help) mirrors native iOS settings conventions, minimizing the learning curve.

  • Checkmark for active context: The checkmark next to "JudySmith" under Teams communicates current workspace context at a glance, critical for multi-org users who switch between client/team accounts frequently.

  • Chevron affordance discipline: Only navigable rows get a chevron, creating a reliable visual grammar for tap behavior across the entire list.

  • Isolated destructive action: "Log out" is styled identically to neutral items (no red text, no icon) and positioned mid-list rather than buried or over-emphasized, balancing discoverability with accident prevention.

  • Power-user utility surfaced early: "Shake to report" toggle exposes an advanced debugging/feedback mechanism directly in top-level settings, reflecting Figma's developer-friendly culture.

screens.name: Figma - About - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for terminal settings screens that combine static diagnostic metadata with legal/compliance links and a single destructive action. It's ideal for app "About" pages, developer tools, or any B2B/productivity software where support teams will ask users for version/build numbers. The physical separation technique for destructive actions is reusable anywhere a low-frequency, high-consequence action (delete, logout, deactivate) needs to be present but de-prioritized.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal approach if the destructive action (account deletion) carries significant consequences that warrant more friction (here it's only one tap away from a confirmation dialog, which may be too lightweight for highly sensitive consumer apps (e).g., banking). Also avoid this bare-bones layout for consumer-facing apps where users may not understand technical jargon like "Build" numbers; those audiences benefit more from help links or a support chat shortcut rather than raw version strings.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves Figma's core audience of designers and developers who may need build/version numbers for bug reporting or support tickets, as well as compliance-conscious users seeking legal documentation or account deletion rights (a requirement under GDPR/CCPA). The psychological design intent is to build trust through transparency (clear version/build data) while discouraging impulsive account deletion through visual de-emphasis and separation, without blocking the user's right to do so.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Spatial isolation of destructive action: "Delete account" is separated from the Legal/Version group by a large gap, acting as a non-verbal confirmation pattern that reduces accidental mis-taps.

  • Dark header, light body contrast: The near-black header anchors global navigation context visually, distinguishing chrome from content in a way consistent with Figma's branded dark-UI identity.

  • Non-interactive rows clearly marked: Version and Build rows have no chevron, correctly signaling they are copy-only/display-only data, avoiding user frustration from tapping dead rows.

  • Minimalist information architecture: Only four rows exist on the entire screen (an intentional reduction of an "About" screen to its legal and diagnostic essentials).

results.query: First-time user onboarding welcome walk-through tour

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Immediately after account creation or login, as a bridge screen before a guided tour, checklist, or setup wizard.

  • Any product where a brief orientation period benefits from framing as a personal, time-boxed favor rather than an administrative requirement.

  • B2C or B2B SaaS apps aiming to increase feature adoption by priming users mentally before showing them functionality.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the onboarding tour itself is lengthy or optional, overpromising "quickly" and then delivering a 10-step wizard erodes trust.

  • Not ideal for returning/power users who already know the product; showing this screen repeatedly would feel patronizing and add unnecessary friction.

  • Should be skipped or made dismissible for users who signed up anonymously or where personalization data (like a name) isn't yet available, to avoid an awkward generic greeting.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users immediately post-registration, a critical moment where activation and retention are most fragile. The psychological trigger at play is the Cognitive Fluency effect: simple, uncluttered screens with a single action feel easier to process and therefore are perceived as trustworthy and low-effort, increasing the likelihood the user will proceed rather than abandon the app.

The personalized greeting also leverages the Cocktail Party Effect / Personal Relevance bias: humans are neurologically wired to pay closer attention to anything bearing their own name, which increases retention of the message and emotional buy-in to the onboarding journey.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Name Personalization: Injecting the user's actual name ("Alex") transforms a static template into a one-to-one conversation, significantly boosting perceived care and engagement from the very first interaction after sign-up.

  • Single Focal CTA: With only one button on the entire screen, decision fatigue is eliminated and the conversion path to begin onboarding is maximized.

  • Expectation Setting Copy: Telling the user the walkthrough will be "quick" pre-emptively defuses the most common objection to onboarding flows (the fear of a long, tedious setup).

  • Generous Whitespace: The sparse layout communicates confidence and calm, reducing the anxiety that can accompany a new, unfamiliar app environment.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Onboarding sequences for apps with non-standard or complex gestures (e.g., reordering, swiping, pinch-to-zoom).

  • Productivity, design, or project management tools (Trello-like boards, Kanban, document editors) where manual manipulation of content is core to the UX.

  • Situations where you want to increase feature discovery for a "power" feature that is otherwise hidden behind a long-press or hidden gesture.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this for simple, universally understood gestures (e.g., tapping a button or scrolling a list), as it adds unnecessary friction for an obvious interaction.

  • Not suitable for very short onboarding flows where minimizing time-to-value is critical and the interactive gesture isn't essential for day-one usage.

  • Risky on older devices or with accessibility constraints where drag-and-drop might not be supported by assistive technology, potentially blocking users from proceeding.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users of Craft, a productivity/note-taking app where spatial organization (moving blocks, images, and text) is central to the user experience. Because drag-and-drop is a non-obvious gesture on mobile (as opposed to a simple tap), the designers used this screen to proactively prevent the "feature blindness" that occurs when users don't realize an app supports a specific interaction.

Psychologically, this leverages the Testing Effect: people retain information significantly better when they actively practice a skill rather than passively observing it. It also uses the Zeigarnik Effect (the disabled button creates a small, unresolved task that nudges the user to complete the drag action to achieve closure).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Learn-by-Doing Interaction: Replaces passive swiping through screens with a hands-on task, drastically increasing retention of the gesture.

  • Disabled State as a Guide: The grayed-out "Next" button acts as a subtle gatekeeper, implicitly telling the user "you aren't done yet" without needing an error message.

  • Self-Documenting UI: The draggable tile contains the instruction text directly on it, eliminating ambiguity about what to interact with.

  • Low-Friction Escape: A persistent "Skip" option in the top right respects the time of power users or those who already know the gesture.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when onboarding users to a novel, non-obvious, or app-defining gesture (e.g., drag-and-drop, swipe actions, pinch-to-zoom) that is central to the core value proposition of the product. It's especially effective for productivity, design, or organizational tools where a specific manual interaction model differentiates the app from competitors.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, universally-understood gestures (e.g., basic tapping or scrolling) where forcing an interactive tutorial would feel condescending or add unnecessary friction. Also avoid it in onboarding flows where user drop-off risk is high; forcing a physical action (even with a skip option) adds a layer of required effort that can increase abandonment compared to a simple 'Next' tap. Ensure a Skip option always remains to prevent hard-blocking repeat users or power users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets new users of a complex, gesture-rich productivity/note-taking app (Craft) who may be unfamiliar with drag-and-drop content manipulation as a core interaction model. It specifically serves users transitioning from simpler, tap-based apps who need a muscle-memory bridge before they can be productive. Psychologically, it leverages the "learning by doing" (constructivist) principle and the Zeigarnik effect (an incomplete task (the undragged tile) creates mental tension that motivates the user to complete the action, resulting in much higher retention of the gesture than passive reading would).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Learn-by-doing mechanic: Forces active engagement with the real gesture (long-press + drag) instead of passive video/illustration consumption, dramatically improving feature retention.

  • Disabled CTA as implicit gate: The grayed 'Next' button visually signals incompletion without an intrusive error message, using affordance rather than friction-heavy pop-ups.

  • In-context microcopy: Instructions live directly inside the interactive element, reducing cognitive load versus separate instructional text.

  • Escape hatches preserved: Skip and Back controls remain available, respecting advanced users who don't need hand-holding.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when onboarding users to a non-standard gesture that is critical to the core function of the app (e.g., swipe-to-delete, pinch-to-zoom, long-press-to-reorder). It is highly effective for complex software (like design tools, project management apps, or block-based editors) where textual explanation alone is insufficient to convey the physics or usability of an interaction.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, intuitive apps where gestures are already standard OS conventions (e.g., standard scrolling), as it adds unnecessary friction. Additionally, forcing interaction (rather than allowing a skip) can frustrate users who are already familiar with the app paradigm (e.g., return users or power users migrating from a similar tool), so ensure a robust "Skip" mechanism is always visible, as seen in this example.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users of a productivity/note-taking tool (Craft) who are likely accustomed to standard tap-based interfaces (like Notes or Word) but may be unfamiliar with block-based, drag-and-drop editing paradigms (like Notion or Craft).

The psychological trigger here is the Von Restorff effect combined with kinesthetic learning principles; by making the user physically perform the action, the app leverages muscle memory and active recall, which are proven to be more effective for skill retention than passive reading. This specifically targets users who might otherwise ignore long-press gestures because they are not standard "tap" interactions, ensuring a core app differentiator isn't missed.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Interactive Coach Mark: Rather than a static screenshot or video showing the gesture, the app embeds a live, functional element that users must manipulate themselves, significantly increasing muscle memory and feature retention.

  • Self-Contained Instructions: The instruction text ("Long press, and move me to the top") is placed directly on the object of interaction, eliminating the cognitive load of referencing a separate instruction block above.

  • Escape Hatches: The combination of "Skip" (to bypass the lesson) and "Reset" (to retry the specific interaction) gives power users an exit while still allowing engaged users to sand box the feature without fear of failure.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Introducing a non-obvious gesture-based interaction (swipe, long-press, pinch) that is core to the app's value proposition.

  • Feature tours for creative tools (editors, styling engines, customization panels) where "showing" beats "telling."

  • Onboarding flows where you want to guarantee behavioral engagement rather than passive click-through, especially for features with historically low discovery/adoption rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid gating the "Next" button behind a gesture if the feature being taught is trivial or already well-known (it adds unnecessary friction for experienced users).

  • Not appropriate for accessibility-constrained contexts where swipe gestures may be difficult; always pair with an alternative tap-based path or ensure screen-reader/switch-control compatibility.

  • Risky for time-sensitive flows (e.g., checkout, account recovery) where forcing interaction before progression could increase abandonment.

  • Should not be used repeatedly across many onboarding screens, as the novelty of the anthropomorphic/gated-CTA technique wears off and can start to feel gimmicky or patronizing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users of a content creation, note-taking, or design/formatting tool (e.g., a rich-text editor, social posting app, or presentation builder) who need to discover formatting/styling capabilities that are not immediately obvious from the main UI. It specifically serves users who learn better through kinesthetic interaction than through reading static feature lists.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Zeigarnik effect and commitment/consistency bias: by requiring the user to perform the actual gesture (swipe) before being allowed to proceed, the app ensures the behavior is encoded into muscle memory, increasing the likelihood of future spontaneous use of the feature post-onboarding. The playful first-person voice also taps into parasocial/anthropomorphic engagement, a technique known to increase emotional investment in otherwise mundane UI tutorials.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anthropomorphic, first-person instructional copy: "Swipe on me" personifies the UI element, making the tutorial feel conversational and reducing the sterility typical of onboarding screens.

  • Gated progression via disabled CTA: The greyed-out "Next" button enforces interaction completion before advancement, converting a passive tutorial into an active, muscle-memory-building exercise.

  • Inline directional iconography in copy: Embedding arrow symbols directly within the sentence structure communicates the gesture instantly without needing a separate diagram.

  • Distinct visual callout box: The light-blue tinted instruction panel visually separates "action" copy from "explanation" copy, letting users scan for what to do next.

  • Low-commitment escape hatch: The persistent "Skip" control respects user autonomy and prevents the required interaction from feeling like a hard wall.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 6
screens.whereToUse:
• Rich text / outline editors where multiple block types (headings, lists, checklists, toggles) need contextual, non-modal formatting controls.

  • Any editing surface where you want to teach a gesture (swipe, long-press, drag) through embedded sample content rather than a separate modal tutorial.

  • Apps that benefit from scoping toolbar actions to a clearly highlighted/selected element to avoid accidental edits to the wrong block.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Simple note or memo apps with a single content type (e.g., plain text journaling) where this level of formatting complexity would be unnecessary overhead.

  • Screens with limited vertical space (e.g., small-screen devices or landscape split-view) where a multi-row persistent toolbar would crowd out content.

  • First-time user flows where the user hasn't yet created real content, embedding tutorial copy into production notes/documents could feel unprofessional if left unedited.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets power users of note-taking and outlining apps (writers, PKM (personal knowledge management) enthusiasts, students, and professionals who value both structured hierarchy (outlines, checklists) and visual polish (styling, color)). The psychological driver is mastery and control: by exposing granular formatting (list types, indentation, color) through a discoverable but non-intrusive tray, the app rewards curious users who explore the toolbar while not punishing casual users who ignore it.

The gamified, friendly microcopy ("Swipe ← or → on me") also appeals to users who respond well to delight and whimsy, a differentiator for consumer-grade productivity apps competing against more austere, enterprise tools.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Self-documenting sample content: The demo text doesn't just fill space (it actively teaches the gesture (swipe to restyle) in the voice of the content itself, embedding onboarding directly into the canvas rather than a separate tutorial screen).

  • Tiered toolbar architecture: Separating "what kind of block" (Heading/Body/Page) from "what list/structure" (checkbox, bullet, numbered, indent) from "meta actions" (Focus, Block, Color, More) keeps a feature-dense tool from feeling cluttered.

  • Explicit selection state: The combination of a highlighted block background and a filled (vs. outlined) circular toggle removes any ambiguity about which content the toolbar will act upon (critical in a multi-block outline editor).

  • Full-spectrum color wheel icon: Signals deep customization (text/highlight color) is available without consuming toolbar real estate for a full palette.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern in content-creation or document-editing apps (notes, blogging, outlining, page builders) where users need access to multiple layers of formatting (text style, block type, page-level settings) without overwhelming a single toolbar. It's ideal when introducing a non-obvious interaction (like swipe-to-restyle) that benefits from being demonstrated via live, interactive sample content rather than static instructions. Also effective in onboarding flows for editor tools where you want users to "learn by doing" on dummy content before they commit to their own document.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense multi-tab toolbar approach in simple, consumer-facing text inputs (e.g., chat apps, basic to-do apps) where only 1-2 formatting options are needed (the segmented control adds unnecessary navigation overhead). Also avoid embedding instructional copy directly as fake content blocks in production/real documents, since it can confuse users about what is real content versus system guidance if not visually/contextually distinct enough, or if left behind after the user has already learned the gesture (should be dismissible or shown only once).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets productivity-app power users (writers, note-takers, PKM/outline tool enthusiasts) who value fine-grained control over typography and content structure but want it exposed without clutter. The psychological trigger at play is progressive disclosure: hiding advanced formatting behind clearly labeled, segmented tabs respects the user's limited attention while still offering depth. The playful, instructional copy taps into curiosity and self-efficacy: by framing a gesture as a fun discovery ("swipe on me"), the product encourages exploration and makes users feel clever for finding a shortcut, which increases feature adoption and perceived app sophistication.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual gesture coaching embedded in content: Instead of a generic overlay tutorial, the app teaches a swipe gesture using an actual interactive content block styled as a call-out, making the lesson feel native and discoverable at the moment of relevance.

  • Segmented formatting scope (Heading/Body/Page/More): Dividing style controls by content hierarchy level rather than showing all options at once simplifies a traditionally complex rich-text toolbar into digestible, context-aware tabs.

  • Dual-row toolbar with mode toggles: Separating atomic formatting actions (lists, checkboxes, indent) from broader editing modes (Focus, Block, Color) in two visually distinct rows clarifies the mental model of "what am I formatting" vs "how am I viewing/editing."

  • Non-destructive Reset/Done pairing: Placing "Reset" opposite "Done" at the top gives users a clear escape hatch before committing to style changes, reducing fear of permanent mistakes.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this interactive-demo-in-onboarding pattern when introducing a feature that relies on a specific gesture or manipulation (swipe, pinch, drag) that is not obvious from a static UI. It's ideal for creative tools, editors, customization features, or any flow where "trying it" is faster to understand than "reading about it." It pairs well with progressive, step-based onboarding flows with skip/reset escape hatches for returning or power users.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, self-explanatory features where an interactive tutorial would feel condescending or add unnecessary friction before value delivery. It's also risky if the live demo component is buggy or slow, since a broken interactive element during onboarding damages first-impression trust far more than a static screenshot would. Finally, avoid stacking multiple interactive demos back-to-back without pacing, as this can cause onboarding fatigue.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users of a content/design/writing app (likely a blogging, note-taking, or page-builder tool) who need to learn a non-obvious styling feature before they start creating content. It's aimed at users who may abandon a product if its core differentiator (easy styling) isn't immediately understood.

Psychologically, this leverages the testing effect/active recall: users who physically perform an action (swiping) during onboarding retain the behavior far better than those who only read about it. The personified, conversational copy ("Swipe on me") also reduces the perceived distance between user and interface, building early rapport and reducing onboarding drop-off anxiety.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Show, don't tell: Instead of a static screenshot, the onboarding embeds a live, swipeable card so users learn the gesture by doing it, which drives higher retention than text-only tutorials.

  • Inline iconography in copy: Using directional arrow symbols (←/→) directly in the instructional sentence makes the required gesture unambiguous at a glance.

  • Visual hierarchy via accent bar: A single vertical blue bar on the left edge of the card guides the eye straight to the actionable element amid a sparse layout.

  • Low-friction escape hatches: "Reset" and "Skip" are present but visually de-emphasized (smaller, muted gray for Skip) so they don't compete with the primary learning task.

  • Single-focus minimalism: No other UI clutter competes for attention, ensuring the one feature being taught is fully absorbed before moving on.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern as the final screen in a multi-step guided tour or coach-mark sequence, especially for creative or productivity tools where users might feel overwhelmed by features. It is effective for:

  • Summarizing that the tutorial has ended without a lengthy recap.

  • Transitioning the user’s mental state from "learning" to "doing."

  • Providing a clear, single exit path back to the live application.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimalist "That's it!" closing screen if:

  • The user has not actually retained critical information; in high-complexity apps, a visual summary or checklist of what was learned might be more effective than vague affirmation.

  • The app requires the user to take an immediate mandatory next step (e.g., payment or permissions), as the lighthearted tone might undersell the importance of that action.

  • Localizing for markets where overly casual, exclamation-point-heavy copy may feel unprofessional.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users immediately following account creation or first launch, specifically those who have just completed a guided tour of core features (likely a note-taking or productivity app given the "Craft" branding).

The psychological trigger here is the Peak-End Rule: users tend to judge an entire experience based on its peak moments and its ending. By ending the onboarding tutorial on a high, encouraging, and friendly note, the app ensures the user's overall memory of the "learning phase" is positive, increasing the likelihood of continued usage and reducing early churn.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Graceful Exit Signal: The drastic increase in whitespace compared to a typical tooltip step visually cues the user that the guided tour has concluded.

  • Human, Congratulatory Microcopy: Using "Well done" and "Have fun" builds a positive emotional association with the app immediately before the user is set free to use it.

  • Action-Oriented CTA: "Explore Craft" encourages continued engagement and curiosity rather than simply closing a modal.

screens.name: Craft Get started with Craft 10
screens.whereToUse:
• Productivity, note-taking, or document management apps needing to soften the "blank workspace" problem for new users.

  • Any app where self-serve education (handbooks, how-tos) should be persistent and revisitable rather than a one-time dismissible overlay.

  • Personal workspace apps that benefit from naming/personalizing containers (e.g., "Alex's Space") to increase perceived ownership.

  • Apps wanting to visually differentiate primary creation actions from routine navigation via an isolated FAB.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise or compliance-heavy tools where whimsical emoji and informal copy may undermine perceived professionalism.

  • Data-dense dashboards (analytics, admin panels) where a large hero carousel of help content would waste premium above-the-fold real estate needed for critical data.

  • Apps with very high document volume per user, where a horizontal carousel of only 3 featured docs would get buried and should instead prioritize recent/frequently-used file surfacing immediately.

  • Multi-tenant/team-first products where emphasizing a single named personal space (vs. shared/team space) could conflict with collaborative workflows.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new and returning knowledge workers, note-takers, and small teams evaluating or using Craft as a daily-driver document tool, likely switching from Apple Notes, Notion, or Google Docs. The friendly tone and visual polish target users who value aesthetics and personal ownership of their workspace (prosumers, creatives, solo founders) rather than enterprise IT buyers.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the IKEA effect and ownership bias by naming the space after the user and visually treating default content as "their" documents from minute one. The carousel of help docs reduces onboarding anxiety via reduction of cognitive load: new users aren't dumped into an empty void; they're given curated, low-effort first content to explore, satisfying the need for early competence and reducing abandonment risk.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Document-as-card onboarding: Instead of generic tutorial screens or modals, onboarding content is delivered as real, dismissible/navigable documents that live permanently in the workspace (users can revisit them anytime like any other file).

  • Stacked paper visual metaphor: The carousel cards use layered shadow/offset styling to mimic a physical stack of papers fanned out, reinforcing the "documents" mental model skeuomorphically while staying modern/flat elsewhere.

  • Floating pill tab bar with isolated FAB: Separating the 4-item navigation pill from a distinct circular create button prevents accidental taps and visually prioritizes content creation as a distinct, elevated action.

  • Educational empty states: The "Star Docs to keep them close" placeholder turns a lack of content into a feature-discovery moment instead of a dead end.

  • Personalized search scoping: Naming the search bar after the user's space ("Alex's Space") adds a layer of personalization and clarifies search scope (personal vs. shared/team spaces).

screens.name: Venmo Post-Onboarding 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for the first-session home/dashboard of transactional or utility apps (fintech, marketplaces, productivity tools) where the app has a persistent, multi-tab home that would otherwise render empty or overwhelming for a new user. It's ideal when you have 2-4 clear "first actions" you want to nudge users toward, and want to teach core navigation (search, tabs) in the same moment.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the app requires mandatory setup steps (KYC, permissions, payment method linking) - a full-screen guided setup wizard would be more appropriate to ensure completion. It also becomes clutter if left visible after the user has completed their first action; it must be dismissed, replaced, or hidden once real content/data exists. Overloading the carousel with more than 3-4 cards dilutes focus and reintroduces the decision paralysis it's meant to solve.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets brand-new Venmo users immediately post-signup, a critical activation moment where drop-off risk is highest. The design leverages the peak-end rule and choice architecture: by presenting a short, curated list of "what to do first" options instead of an overwhelming feature set, it reduces decision paralysis. The friendly illustration and exclamatory welcome copy trigger a positive emotional association early, which is proven to increase retention and completion of first-use tasks (a well-documented driver of long-term app stickiness). The promo code card taps into user curiosity/incentive-seeking behavior for growth-marketing acquisition (referral codes, sign-up bonuses) without being intrusive.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Repurposed Home Screen as Onboarding Surface: Instead of a separate onboarding flow, the app's actual Home tab becomes the first task screen, teaching navigation and driving activation simultaneously.

  • Illustrated, Emotionally Warm Cards: Playful hand-drawn illustrations (cash flying from a phone) make a financial app feel approachable and fun rather than intimidating or transactional.

  • Peek-a-boo Carousel: Sliver of the next card visible at the edge invites horizontal exploration without needing explicit instructions or page dots.

  • Prioritized Action Hierarchy: The primary CTA (first payment) is large and prominent; the secondary, less-common action (promo code) is visually subdued below it.

  • Persistent Global Search & QR Scan: Keeping search and QR-pay accessible at the very top, even during onboarding, reinforces these as core, always-on utilities.

screens.name: Venmo Post-Onboarding 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when onboarding requires the user to complete a small number of optional or semi-optional setup tasks (payment methods, profile completion, preferences) but you don't want to force a rigid, blocking wizard. It's ideal for apps where the "home" screen would otherwise be empty for new users, turning dead space into a conversion opportunity. Works well for fintech, e-commerce, and subscription apps needing to drive a specific activation action (add card, invite friends, verify identity) while still allowing full app exploration.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the setup task is strictly mandatory for the app to function (e.g., identity verification for regulatory compliance) - in that case a blocking modal or dedicated wizard is more appropriate to guarantee completion. Also avoid stacking too many low-priority cards in the carousel, as it can dilute focus and reduce completion rates of the primary task; and be cautious of leaving this state active too long after the user has already completed setup, as it can then read as clutter or a broken/stuck state.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets newly registered users in the critical first-session window, where activation (linking a payment method) is the key metric determining long-term retention. The design leverages the Zeigarnik effect and progress cue psychology: by visually presenting onboarding as a set of discrete cards, users feel compelled to complete the sequence. The friendly illustration and casual copy reduce the anxiety often associated with entering banking/financial information, a critical trust-building moment for a fintech app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Repurposed empty state: Instead of showing a blank/empty transaction feed for new users, the home screen is transformed into an actionable onboarding surface.

  • Card carousel for sequential tasks: Peeking cards at the edges hint at additional setup steps, encouraging horizontal exploration without a hard multi-step wizard.

  • Visual hierarchy between primary and secondary tasks: The payment-method card is large and illustrated; the promo code card is compact and utilitarian, correctly signaling priority.

  • Non-blocking onboarding: Full navigation (tab bar, search, QR) remains accessible, so power users aren't forced through onboarding before using the app.

screens.name: Venmo Post-Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this benefit-reframed gating pattern whenever a mandatory but unappealing step (KYC, permissions, data collection) blocks access to a desirable feature. Pair a friendly illustration and outcome-focused headline with a low-pressure, dismissible carousel card format so users don't feel forced, while still being nudged strongly toward completion. Ideal for fintech, marketplace, or gig-economy apps where identity verification unlocks money movement, payouts, or increased limits.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this soft, carousel-based approach when verification is an absolute hard blocker for core functionality (e.g., regulated trading platforms) - in that case a hard paywall/dedicated full-screen flow is more appropriate to avoid users missing or dismissing the swipeable card. Also avoid vague "unlock" language for steps that carry real legal/compliance stakes without disclosing why the data is needed, as vague framing can create distrust or later feel manipulative once the user discovers the "reward" was actually a legal requirement all along.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets brand-new Venmo users, likely younger, mobile-first consumers who signed up primarily to split a bill, receive money from a friend, or pay someone quickly. These users have low patience for friction and may abandon if asked to complete a lengthy KYC flow with unclear benefit. By naming the outcome ("Unlock your balance") instead of the mechanism ("Verify identity"), Venmo taps into loss-aversion and curiosity psychology (the user is made to feel they already have a balance/benefit waiting, and verification is simply the key, not a burdensome hurdle). This dramatically increases completion rates for a step that is legally mandatory but emotionally unappealing.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Benefit-framed compliance gate: Instead of a scary "Verify Identity" CTA, the card is framed as "Unlock your balance," turning a regulatory KYC requirement into a desirable unlock mechanic.

  • Carousel with peeking cards: Sliver previews of adjacent colored cards on both edges signal swipeability without needing instructional copy or arrows.

  • Task-oriented empty state: Rather than showing a blank dashboard for a new user with $0 balance and no transactions, the screen replaces the void with a prioritized action list (verification, promo code).

  • Consistent core-action anchor: The elevated circular Venmo logo button in the tab bar stays visually dominant even during onboarding, reinforcing "pay/request" as the app's gravitational center.

  • Low-commitment secondary card: The promo code entry sits below the primary card as a lightweight, optional secondary task, correctly prioritized beneath identity verification.

screens.name: Venmo Post-Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when launching a product that has a "cold-start" dependency on user-generated content, contacts, or connections (social apps, payment apps, marketplaces). It's ideal when you have 3-5 distinct onboarding actions of varying importance that don't need to be completed in a strict sequence, and when you want to preserve the user's sense of control by keeping core navigation accessible rather than locking them into a forced flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when a task is truly mandatory for compliance or safety (e.g., identity verification, legal consent) - the optional, skippable framing here would undermine urgency and could be exploited or ignored. Also avoid it if there are more than 4-5 cards, as swipeable carousels suffer from poor discoverability past the first couple of items and low completion rates for anything not immediately visible; in that case a persistent checklist widget or progress tracker would perform better for surfacing remaining tasks.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets brand-new Venmo signups in their very first session (a moment of maximum uncertainty ("what do I actually do with this app)?") but also maximum openness to guidance. The design leans on the Zero Moment of Truth psychology: give the user a fast, easy win (syncing contacts) to generate the network effect that makes Venmo useful (i.e., having people to actually pay).

Framing contact sync as step one exploits the cold-start problem inherent to social/payment apps. Venmo is worthless without a network of payees, so this card is engineered to solve the app's core activation metric disguised as a user benefit ("find people to pay") rather than a data-permission request. The promo code card beneath targets acquisition-channel users (referred by a friend, or arriving via a marketing campaign) who need a frictionless way to redeem an incentive immediately upon arrival, capturing attribution while intent is highest.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Modular carousel over rigid wizard: Onboarding tasks are broken into independently swipeable cards, letting users self-select priority and skip anything irrelevant to them, drastically reducing perceived friction versus a linear multi-screen wizard.

  • Non-blocking overlay pattern: Full navigation chrome (search, QR, tab bar) stays interactive underneath the onboarding cards, so power users can bypass onboarding entirely and dive into the product, respecting user autonomy.

  • Friendly, human illustration: The custom illustration of two people high-fiving with chat bubbles visually reinforces the social, peer-to-peer nature of Venmo before the user has any real network built, using imagery to substitute for social proof that doesn't exist yet.

  • Peeking edge cards: Partial visibility of adjacent cards (yellow/blue slivers) is a strong discoverability affordance signaling "there's more here, swipe me" without needing explicit instructional copy.

  • Outline (secondary) CTA styling: Using a lower-visual-weight button choice subtly communicates "this is optional" and avoids the aggressive feel of a hard-gated permission request.

screens.name: Venmo Post-Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when you need to present multiple optional onboarding actions immediately after signup without blocking access to core app functionality. It's ideal for:

  • Introducing supplementary revenue products (debit/credit cards, subscriptions, premium tiers) right after account creation.

  • Surfacing promo codes, referral incentives, or account setup tasks as dismissible, swipeable suggestions.

  • Apps where the home/dashboard screen is the primary landing surface and you want engagement prompts to coexist with normal usage rather than gate it.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The onboarding action is mission-critical (e.g., identity verification, required legal consent) - a dismissible carousel risks users skipping essential setup steps entirely.

  • Too many cards are stacked in the carousel, causing important actions to be buried past the first swipe and rarely seen.

  • The visual weight of the promotional card (debit card) overwhelms genuinely useful native features, creating a "salesy" first impression that erodes trust in a financial app.

  • Users are returning, experienced users: repeatedly showing "Welcome!" messaging to non-new users feels tone-deaf and cluttered.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets newly registered or recently reactivated Venmo users at their first meaningful session on the home screen (a moment of high attention and low habitual routine, making it the ideal time to introduce revenue-generating features like the debit card).

Psychologically, it leverages the choice-supportive framing ("What would you like to do first?") to make the user feel in control, reducing reactance to what is effectively a monetization prompt. The cashback benefit and card visual trigger loss-aversion and reward-anticipation: showing a tangible, physical card object builds trust and desirability. The carousel's partial reveal of additional cards leverages the curiosity gap / Von Restorff effect, encouraging exploration through the swipeable stack.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking onboarding: The welcome prompts are overlaid on the fully functional home screen rather than a separate modal/wizard, letting users skip straight to core functionality if desired.

  • Peeking carousel affordance: A visible sliver of the next (purple) card on the left edge is a subtle, icon-free way of communicating "swipe for more options" - reducing need for explicit instructional text or arrows.

  • Business-goal-first ordering: The debit card upsell is placed as the first and most visually dominant card (large illustration, filled CTA button), prioritizing monetization while still framing it as a user benefit ("Earn cashback").

  • Visual differentiation of card types: Using a colored icon badge (red tag icon) and different card style for the promo code entry visually separates "primary revenue" actions from "secondary utility" actions.

  • Persistent global navigation: Search bar and QR/tab bar remain accessible above and below the onboarding content, so exploration is never blocked by the welcome messaging.

screens.name: Venmo Post-Onboarding 6
screens.whereToUse:
• Use a similar promotional card pattern on home/dashboard screens to spotlight underused features without a full paywall or forced onboarding flow.

  • Combine search + QR/scan icon pairing when an app supports both text-based lookup and physical/in-person quick actions (payments, tickets, check-in).

  • Use a branded, elevated center tab icon when the brand identity (logo) is strong enough to double as a primary navigation anchor.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid leaving large unstructured empty space on a home screen for returning/active users (it can appear broken or make the app feel under-populated; ensure this only appears as a true empty state with a clear reason (e).g., no transactions yet).

  • Don't rely on a single feature promo card as the primary home content if users expect an activity feed (this can reduce perceived app utility and engagement).

  • Avoid vague low-commitment CTAs like "Try it out" for critical conversion flows requiring urgency or clear action framing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both new and existing Venmo users who may not be aware of, or habitually use, certain payment features (e.g., paying merchants/charities directly vs. just splitting bills with friends). The search bar copy ("People, Businesses, & Charities") signals an intent to expand usage beyond peer-to-peer transfers into broader commerce and donation use cases.

Psychologically, the screen leverages feature discovery via low-commitment framing: by using playful illustration and casual language, it reduces the intimidation factor often associated with financial apps. The empty space below may also be intentional breathing room that avoids overwhelming users, in line with mobile fintech's minimalist trust-building design language.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Branded FAB in Tab Bar: The circular Venmo "V" logo elevated above the tab bar doubles as a home indicator and a strong brand touchpoint, breaking the monotony of a standard 5-icon tab bar.

  • Dual-purpose header: Combining a broad search bar with a QR code scanner icon caters to two distinct payment discovery behaviors (searching by name and in-person/instant scanning) without cluttering the UI.

  • Illustration-driven promo card: The hand-drawn dollar sign and coin illustration adds warmth and approachability to an otherwise transactional/financial action, softening the "money" topic.

  • Low-friction CTA copy: "Try it out" invites exploration rather than commitment, reducing perceived risk for a financial feature.

screens.name: Figma - View prototype - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when onboarding users into a complex, blank, or canvas-based workspace (design tools, whiteboards, no-code builders) where a static modal would feel disconnected from the real experience. It's ideal for:

  • Introducing shared resources/libraries/templates within a collaborative tool.
  • Demonstrating "what good looks like" using the actual components/styles the user will consume.
  • Soft-launching a feature to existing users without forcing a blocking walkthrough.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach when:

  • The target audience is non-technical and needs more explicit, step-by-step hand-holding (a wizard or coach marks would serve better).
  • The canvas/workspace is small or mobile-first, where embedding instructional content directly into the workspace can clutter the real estate needed for actual work.
  • The content needs to be dismissed permanently or tracked for completion (on-canvas tutorials are harder to mark "done" or gate behind onboarding checklists).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new team members or design-system newcomers being introduced to a shared component/style library for the first time, likely added via an invite or onboarding flow in a design org. The psychological trigger here is reduction of cognitive load via self-explaining artifacts: instead of asking the user to read documentation and then go find the library, Figma shows the output and the explanation simultaneously, reinforcing learning through direct example (a well-known adult-learning principle ("show, don't tell")).

It also leverages the social/organizational framing ("JudySmith's team library") to build trust and context (the user understands this asset was intentionally curated by a teammate, increasing perceived value and adoption likelihood).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Tutorial-as-artifact: The onboarding content is built using real Figma frames and components rather than a native modal overlay, making the lesson self-referential and instantly demonstrating the product's capability.
  • Directional anchor: The bold "Start here ↓" arrow solves the "blank canvas" orientation problem elegantly without needing a coach-mark or tooltip system.
  • Horizontal Carousel on Canvas: Peeking the edge of the next card creates a natural scroll affordance, encouraging exploration without explicit "Next" buttons.
  • Non-blocking chrome: Keeping the standard file toolbar visible (Play, Comment, Share) lets advanced users skip the tutorial and interact with the file immediately.

screens.name: Figma - View prototype - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• When introducing a gesture, shortcut, or interaction method that has no visual affordance on screen (e.g., swipe, pinch, multi-finger tap).
  • For power-tool or professional apps (design, CAD, video editing) being adapted to touch where desktop interaction metaphors must be re-taught.
  • As a just-in-time tip shown the first time a user enters a context where the gesture becomes relevant, rather than in a generic onboarding carousel.
  • When the feature being taught is important enough to justify blocking interaction momentarily, but simple enough to communicate in a single screen.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for gestures that are already standard OS conventions (e.g., pull-to-refresh, swipe-back) where users already have muscle memory, showing a tip here feels patronizing.
  • Don't use for low-priority or rarely-used features; a blocking modal is too heavy-handed and will create onboarding fatigue if overused across many small tips.
  • Avoid stacking multiple such modals in sequence without spacing them across sessions/contexts, as this creates "tooltip fatigue" and gets dismissed without reading.
  • Not ideal if the gesture can be demonstrated via a lighter-weight, non-blocking coach mark or animated tooltip anchored to the relevant UI area instead of a full modal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers and developers on mobile/tablet devices who are accustomed to Figma's desktop interaction model (right-click for context menu) but now need an equivalent gesture-based trigger on a touchscreen. Because two-finger long-press is not an intuitive or standard mobile gesture outside of Figma's own ecosystem, the app cannot rely on "mobile conventions" as a crutch (it must explicitly teach it).

Psychologically, the pattern leverages the Von Restorff effect (isolating the tip visually from the rest of the UI via a modal and scrim) and the recognition-over-recall principle (diagram + text together) to maximize the chance the gesture is remembered before it's actually needed, reducing future frustration and failed attempts to access the context menu.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual gesture diagram over text-only instructions: Using two animated-looking touch-point circles with halo rings communicates a spatial, multi-touch gesture far more effectively than words alone could.
  • Single, unambiguous CTA ("Got it"): Removes decision paralysis (there is only one way forward, reinforcing that this is a mandatory one-time acknowledgment, not an optional tutorial step).
  • Scrim + centered card isolation: Dimming the background canvas focuses full attention on the tip without permanently navigating the user away from their current context (when dismissed, they land right back where they were).
  • Teaches a non-discoverable gesture at the moment it becomes relevant rather than bundling it into a generic onboarding tour, increasing the odds of retention since it ties learning to functional need.

screens.name: Figma - View prototype - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Professional/productivity tools where the target user is a returning, trained user rather than a first-time prospect.
  • Apps with meaningful load times (asset-heavy, file-heavy, or sync-dependent apps) where a determinate progress indicator can genuinely reflect load percentage.
  • Brands with strong, instantly recognizable marks that can stand alone without supporting copy.
  • Situations where you want to set an expectation of speed, precision, and no-fluff experience from the very first frame.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer apps targeting first-time users who need value-proposition reinforcement; a bare splash screen wastes a high-attention moment that could pitch the product.
  • Apps with lesser-known branding, where an unlabeled logo may confuse rather than reassure new users.
  • When load times are unpredictable or near-instant (a determinate bar can look jittery, jump erratically, or flash too briefly to be perceived, which can feel buggy rather than reassuring).
  • Growth-focused products that rely on splash/launch real estate for seasonal promotions, feature announcements, or re-engagement messaging.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Figma's audience is designers, developers, and cross-functional product teams who are typically returning, habitual users rather than first-time visitors being "sold" on the product. This screen correctly assumes familiarity (there's no need to re-explain value propositions or run an onboarding carousel at launch, unlike apps targeting new/casual users). The psychological trigger here is efficiency and trust: fast, no-nonsense professionals want friction-free re-entry into their workspace, and the stripped-back visual communicates that the app respects their time and won't waste it with marketing noise on every open.

The determinate progress bar also taps into a well-documented UX principle: users tolerate waits better when given visible proof of progress (versus ambiguous spinners), which matters heavily for a performance-sensitive canvas tool like Figma where users expect large files/projects to load.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Determinate progress bar: Using a filled-percentage bar instead of an indeterminate spinner gives users a tangible sense of how much longer the wait will be, reducing perceived latency and abandonment risk.
  • Logo-as-anchor layout: Centering the mark vertically and horizontally with no competing elements maximizes brand recall in the few seconds users spend here.
  • Extreme minimalism: Zero copy, zero color, zero decoration (a bold editorial choice that reinforces brand identity (precision, neutrality) rather than relying on marketing messaging typical of consumer app splash screens).
  • Proximity grouping: Placing the progress indicator directly beneath the logo (rather than screen-bottom) visually binds "brand" and "progress" into one cohesive loading unit.

screens.name: Figma Pages 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this "Start here" canvas-orientation pattern whenever you ship a template, boilerplate file, or shared workspace inside an infinite-canvas product (whiteboarding tools, design systems, roadmapping boards). It's especially valuable for:

  • Design system or component library cover pages distributed to a whole org.

  • Onboarding templates in whiteboard apps (FigJam, Miro, Mural).

  • Any freeform canvas meant to be consumed once by many different people with no verbal walkthrough available.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in linear, single-purpose product UIs (e.g., a checkout flow or settings screen) where the reading order is already obvious from standard top-to-bottom layout, adding a "Start here" label there would feel patronizing. It's also ill-suited for small mobile viewports in general: infinite canvases are optimized for large displays, and forcing users to pinch/zoom/pan on a phone to read a style guide creates real usability friction and should be flagged as a context mismatch rather than emulated wholesale.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves design teams and cross-functional collaborators (PMs, engineers, new hires) who need to be onboarded into a shared design system file on mobile. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of cognitive load via explicit sequencing: canvas tools are powerful but disorienting without guidance, so the "Start here" arrow exploits our instinct to follow directional cues and read left-to-right, converting an open-ended workspace into a guided tour.

Secondary trigger: authority/credibility building: showing an actual, polished style guide (not a mockup) reassures the viewer that the system is mature, well-organized, and worth adopting, reducing resistance to switching workflows.
screens.keyHighlights:
The standout decision here is the explicit "Start here" + arrow affordance placed directly on the infinite canvas. Because whiteboard/canvas tools (Figma, FigJam, Miro) have no built-in reading order, this simple typographic cue solves a major wayfinding problem for new collaborators opening a shared file for the first time.

  • Using a real, populated style-guide artboard (colors, type scale, text field states) as the "proof" artifact immediately next to the explanatory text (show, don't just tell).

  • Pairing an abstract benefit statement ("Don't reinvent the wheel") with a concrete visual example builds instant credibility and comprehension.

  • Leveraging native file-level chrome (close, share, comment, present) keeps the experience consistent with the rest of the tool, so viewing documentation doesn't feel like a separate mode.

screens.name: Figma Pages 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Multi-page or multi-document apps (design tools, note apps, slide decks) where users need a lightweight way to jump between pages/sections.

  • Any canvas-based or immersive full-screen viewer where you want to minimize UI chrome but still offer quick navigational overlays.

  • Scenarios where preserving background context (via partial bottom sheets) helps users maintain spatial orientation during a navigation task.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this minimal list pattern when there are many pages requiring search, filtering, grouping, or thumbnails (a flat checklist won't scale and should be replaced with a searchable/thumbnail grid view).

  • Not suitable for consumer-facing apps where users need richer visual cues (thumbnails, previews) rather than plain text rows to identify content.

  • Avoid embedding instructional text like "Start here" directly in production content for end-users; it's acceptable in internal/shared design files but would look unpolished in a finished product UI.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets designers and product teams collaborating via a shared mobile design system/library (e.g., Figma mobile viewer). The audience is professional, technically literate, and familiar with design tooling conventions like pages, components, and style guides. The psychological driver is wayfinding and control: users need to quickly confirm their location (which page) within a potentially large multi-page file without losing their place, hence the minimal, no-frills page list with a clear active-state indicator.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving modal: The Pages sheet is a partial-height overlay rather than a full-screen takeover, allowing the user to retain visual context of the canvas they were just viewing.

  • Clear selection state: A simple checkmark next to "Page 1" immediately communicates current location within the file's page hierarchy, reducing cognitive load during navigation.

  • Dimmed backdrop with dark top bar: Creates visual hierarchy and focus on the canvas/content while signaling an immersive, distraction-free viewing mode consistent with professional creative tools.

  • In-canvas onboarding ("Start here" + arrow): A clever low-tech pattern where the design file's author embeds literal navigational guidance as design elements, compensating for the lack of structured onboarding UI in a shared library context.

screens.name: Airtable -  Fields tutorial - Screen 22
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern as the final screen of a value-proposition or onboarding carousel, especially for products that carry a steep perceived learning curve (data tools, project management, complex B2B software). It's most effective when the product itself is powerful but intimidating, and you want to counterbalance that complexity with a moment of warmth and encouragement right before first use. It also works well for apps targeting broad audiences (including non-technical users) who benefit from confidence-building before being faced with a blank canvas or empty state.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for highly technical, expert-focused tools (e.g., developer IDEs, enterprise admin consoles) where users expect efficiency over charm and may perceive playful illustration as unprofessional or time-wasting.
