screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid bottom sheets for complex multi-field configuration flows (these are better suited to a full Multi-Step Form or dedicated screen).

  • Don't use vague benefit copy for financial automation features where users need precise numeric details (e.g., threshold amounts) before proceeding (this sheet is only an entry point, not a substitute for detailed configuration).

  • Not appropriate when the action has irreversible or high-stakes consequences; a lightweight sheet with a simple "Set up" link may under-communicate risk versus a full confirmation flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets busy urban users and students who need predictable cash flow without manually monitoring balances. Low balance reloads reduce the anxiety of a declined payment mid-purchase, while scheduled reloads support recurring bill-like payments (rent splits, subscriptions). By presenting these as optional, off-by-default toggles, PayPal respects the audience's need for control and avoids the friction/psychological discomfort of auto-charging students or lower-income users without explicit consent (a deliberate trust-building design choice aligned with the "cautious, ledger-minded" brand positioning).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Progressive Disclosure: Tapping "Set up" doesn't navigate away from the balance screen; it surfaces a bottom sheet, preserving context and reducing perceived navigation cost.

  • Dimmed Background for Modality: The underlying screen is greyed out but still legible, giving users a spatial anchor and reinforcing that this is a temporary, dismissible layer.

  • Binary OFF State Badges: Clear "OFF" chips immediately communicate current configuration status before the user even reads the copy, reducing scanning effort.

  • Benefit-Led Microcopy: Each auto-reload option pairs a functional label with a one-line real-world benefit, helping non-technical users self-select the right option instantly.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 9
screens.whereToUse:
• Recurring/subscription-style financial setups (auto-invest, autopay, recurring transfers) where the user must review and explicitly authorize a scheduled money movement.

  • Any settings flow with multiple interdependent parameters (source, frequency, amount) that benefit from being grouped into digestible cards rather than one long form.

  • Situations requiring regulatory or trust-building disclosures, placing the fine print directly above the commit button ensures it's seen without adding an extra confirmation screen.

  • Onboarding a savings/spending habit feature where a benefit-driven headline can motivate adoption of an otherwise mundane automation setting.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, text-heavy disclosure pattern for low-stakes preference toggles (e.g., notification settings) where such heavy legal framing would feel disproportionate and reduce completion rates.

  • Not suitable when the recurring amount/frequency should be instantly editable inline, forcing a drill-down chevron adds unnecessary taps for power users who frequently adjust values.

  • Risky for audiences who need same-day funding certainty, since the vague "3-5 days" disclosure could erode trust if users expect instant reloads (e.g., emergency low-balance situations).

  • Don't reuse the plain black rounded CTA styling if the action carries irreversible high-risk consequences (e.g., large one-time transfers) - a stronger, more explicit confirmation dialog step may be warranted instead of a single button.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Busy Urban users and Students who want to avoid the friction of manually topping up their PayPal balance before every purchase. Automating small recurring reloads ($25/week) matches the low, frequent spending patterns typical of students and gig-economy or hourly workers who don't keep large balances sitting idle.

The psychological trigger at play is reduced decision fatigue via automation combined with loss-of-control anxiety mitigation: because this audience is budget-conscious, PayPal counters the fear of an uncontrolled recurring debit by making every parameter editable, showing the exact linked source (Chime Savings, masked digits), and explicitly stating the transfer can be canceled up to 24 hours prior, building trust through radical transparency rather than urgency or excitement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Natural-language recap: The plain-English summary sentence above the cards translates structured settings into a single readable sentence, acting as a low-effort confirmation step that reduces user error before authorization.

  • Chunked settings cards: Grouping "funding source" separately from "schedule mechanics" makes a potentially complex recurring-payment setup feel like two simple decisions instead of one dense form.

  • Consistent tap affordance: Blue text + chevron on every editable value creates an unambiguous, learnable pattern for drilling into pickers (frequency, amount, source) without cluttering the screen with open text fields.

  • Pre-CTA disclosure placement: Positioning the timing/legal info banner immediately above the primary button ensures visibility right at the moment of commitment, satisfying compliance needs without a separate modal interruption.

  • Benefit-driven headline: Leading with an emotional/practical outcome ("ready to shop") rather than a technical label softens what is otherwise a financial automation feature.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 10
screens.whereToUse:
Use this single-decision, full-screen pattern with inline contextual sub-controls when:

  • A choice has secondary configuration that only applies conditionally (e.g., picking a day only matters if "Weekly" is chosen).

  • The decision has real financial or scheduling consequences and benefits from being isolated rather than bundled into a longer form.

  • You want to reduce ambiguity by translating technical/abstract options into concrete, human-readable outcomes.

  • The audience needs a low cognitive-load, unhurried, one-decision-per-screen flow (e.g., during multi-step setup wizards for subscriptions, bill pay, or automations).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The set of configuration options is very large (e.g., custom recurrence with multiple days, exceptions, end dates) - a single screen with a nested picker would become cluttered and require a more robust custom recurrence builder.

  • Users are power users who would prefer a fast, single-line dropdown/combobox to avoid extra navigation and tapping through a full screen for a minor setting.

  • Screen real estate or user attention is limited (e.g., embedded widgets, smartwatch companion apps) where a full dedicated screen for one field is excessive.

  • The frequency selection is rarely changed after initial setup (in which case, exposing it inline in settings (an accordion or inline editing) may be more efficient than a dedicated wizard step).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Busy Urban professionals and Students who are setting up recurring transfers (rent splits, subscription payments, allowance transfers, or bill-pay automation). These users need to configure a financial commitment quickly but without ambiguity, since an incorrect frequency could mean money leaving their account at the wrong time.

The psychological trigger at play is certainty and control: by showing the literal resulting schedule in text ("Every Wednesday") rather than just an abstract label ("Weekly"), the design reduces the anxiety of setting up an automated money flow. This is especially important for students or budget-conscious urban users who may be tracking cash flow tightly and fear "losing control" of when money moves.

The stark, minimal navy-on-white / black-on-white visual treatment (no color, no imagery) reflects PayPal's positioning as a serious, ledger-like utility rather than a flashy fintech product, reinforcing trust for a task (recurring payments) that inherently requires trust.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual sub-picker: The day-of-week selector only appears nested under the "Weekly" option when selected, keeping unrelated controls hidden and reducing visual clutter for other frequency choices.

  • Human-readable previews: Every option pre-computes what the schedule will actually look like ("Every Wednesday," "Every month on the 4th"), removing ambiguity before commitment.

  • Redundant selection signaling: Combining a checkmark icon with a filled dark circle for the chosen day ensures the selection state is legible to colorblind users and glanceable at a distance.

  • Single dedicated screen for one decision: Isolating frequency selection avoids overwhelming the user within a larger multi-field form, consistent with a Multi-Step Form pattern that reduces per-screen cognitive load.

  • Persistent, unambiguous CTA: The full-width black "Confirm" button anchors the flow and signals irreversible commitment intent, appropriate for money-related actions.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 11
screens.whereToUse:
• Any fintech, subscription, or billing flow where a user must define a recurring cadence (subscriptions, recurring transfers, bill pay, savings auto-deposits).

  • Scenarios where combining two decisions (frequency + date) into one screen reduces friction without overloading the user, especially when options are few and mutually clarifying.

  • Contexts requiring high trust and predictability, where showing the resolved outcome in plain language (rather than relying on the user to infer it) prevents costly misunderstandings.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when frequency options are numerous or highly configurable (e.g., custom multi-day-of-week rules); a single flat list won't scale and a dedicated rule-builder UI would serve better.

  • Not ideal for touch targets on very small screens if descriptive subtitles cause rows to become too tall (consider condensing for lower information density needs).

  • Should not be used without clearly disabling/graying invalid dates, as this is the mechanism that prevents user error in date-dependent financial commitments.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Busy Urban professionals and Students who need to automate recurring transfers (rent, subscriptions, allowances, bill splits) without manually re-initiating payments each cycle. For students on tight, irregular budgets, the "Every 2 weeks" and "Monthly" options map naturally to paycheck or stipend cycles, while busy urban users benefit from "set it and forget it" automation that removes a recurring task from their mental load.

Psychologically, the screen leans on certainty and control: the two things a "ledger-minded" money app must deliver to overcome anxiety around automated money movement. By resolving frequency into a concrete date preview and disabling invalid days, the design proactively removes the fear of "what did I actually just schedule?" which is the primary trust barrier for recurring payment features.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Plain-language cadence previews: Each frequency option shows its real-world resolved outcome (e.g., "Every month on the 4th"), eliminating mental math and reducing the risk of a mis-scheduled payment.

  • Disabled past-date treatment: Strikethrough styling on dates 1 and 2 communicates unavailability instantly, avoiding a dead-tap or error toast.

  • Editable date summary with inline pencil icon: Gives users a quick way to jump back into manual date entry without losing the context of the selected frequency.

  • Single, unmissable CTA: The full-width black "Confirm" button leaves no ambiguity about the next step, appropriate for a financial commit action.

  • Persistent checkmark on selected frequency: A lightweight checkmark (rather than a heavier radio button) keeps the row aesthetic clean while still confirming selection state.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Recurring payment or subscription setup screens (auto-pay, auto-invest, auto-save).

  • Any flow where multiple related settings need grouping before a single commit action (e.g., budget rules, transfer schedules).

  • Fintech or utility apps introducing automation where trust and reversibility must be communicated to reduce commitment anxiety.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for one-time, immediate transactions where scheduling language and recurring disclosures would only add confusing friction.

  • Not ideal when defaults cannot be reliably pre-filled (an empty version of this pattern loses its key "quick review" advantage and becomes just another long form).

  • Skip heavy legal disclosure blocks if the action is low-risk or non-financial, where such text would feel like unnecessary friction or over-explanation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets busy urban users and students who want to avoid the mental overhead of manually topping up their balance before every purchase. Automating "keep balance ready to shop" removes a recurring micro-decision from their day, aligning with PayPal's ledger-minded, paper-trail-focused brand promise (every dollar moved is scheduled, disclosed, and reversible).

Psychologically, the screen leverages the endowment of control paired with automation: users get the convenience of "set and forget" money management while being explicitly reassured they retain the power to edit or cancel, which reduces the loss-of-control anxiety common in recurring financial commitments (especially important for students or lower-balance users who need tight cash-flow visibility).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Natural-language rule summary: Converts abstract config fields into a single readable sentence so users can sanity-check the whole automation before saving.

  • Pre-filled smart defaults: Linked funding source, cadence, and amount are already populated, turning setup into a quick review-and-edit task rather than a blank-form chore.

  • Card-based field grouping with drill-down chevrons: Clean separation between "source" and "schedule" settings, each independently tappable, keeping the primary screen uncluttered.

  • Trust-building disclosure placed right before commitment: Transfer timing, editability, and cancellation policy are surfaced at the exact moment a user is about to authorize recurring money movement.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: One full-width black button with action+consequence copy avoids any confusion about what happens next.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 13
screens.whereToUse:
Use this error-recovery modal pattern whenever a multi-step or sensitive transactional flow (payments, transfers, scheduled automations, KYC/verification steps) encounters a backend or network failure mid-flow. It is especially effective when:

  • The user has already invested time/data into a form and abandoning entirely would be costly.

  • The failure is likely transient (network blips, temporary server issues) and a retry has a reasonable chance of succeeding.

  • You want to preserve user trust in a finance, health, or other high-stakes vertical where technical jargon or alarming visuals could spike anxiety.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this soft, reassuring pattern when:

  • The error is caused by user input (e.g., invalid amount, insufficient funds) - those cases need specific, actionable Inline Validation rather than a generic "something went wrong" message, since generic messaging won't help the user fix the actual problem.

  • The failure is a hard block (e.g., account restricted, compliance hold) where offering "Try Again" would be misleading since retrying won't resolve the underlying issue (a more specific explanation and alternate path is needed).

  • Repeated failures occur; showing this same generic modal on every retry without escalating detail or support routing will frustrate and erode trust rather than protect it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern directly serves Busy Urban users and Students who are setting up automated recurring transfers (e.g., monthly $25 reloads from a Chime savings account) to keep their PayPal balance topped up for daily purchases. These users are often managing tight budgets and juggling multiple financial apps/accounts, so a broken automation setup could cause real anxiety about missed payments or inconsistent cash flow.

The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion and trust preservation: a failed setup for something as sensitive as recurring money movement could easily cause a user to abandon the feature entirely or lose trust in the app's reliability. By softening the error tone and offering a "Finish later" escape valve, PayPal reduces the likelihood of total task abandonment and keeps the user re-engaged with the automation setup at a more convenient time.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-alarming iconography: Using a neutral blue "info" icon instead of a red warning/error icon reduces perceived severity and anxiety around a failed money-related action.

  • Dual recovery paths: Offering both an immediate retry (primary CTA) and a deferred option ("Finish later") respects that users may not have time or patience to troubleshoot right away, especially when setting up recurring financial automations.

  • Preserved context: The dimmed but still-visible underlying form ensures the user doesn't lose their place or configured settings (funding source, frequency), reducing the cost of the error.

  • Reassuring, blame-free language: Framing the issue as temporary ("at the moment") rather than definitive maintains user trust in the platform's reliability.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 14
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a product needs users to configure and explicitly authorize a recurring financial or subscription-like action: e.g., auto-invest contributions, subscription renewals, recurring bill pay, or automatic savings transfers. It's ideal when:

  • The action involves moving money or committing to a recurring charge that requires informed consent.

  • Users benefit from seeing a plain-language summary of a rule before final confirmation.

  • Legal/regulatory disclosures (timing, cancellation rights) must be surfaced at the point of decision, not buried in ToS.

  • The target audience values transparency and control over speed (e.g., budget-conscious or first-time recurring-payment users).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, disclosure-first pattern for:

  • Low-stakes or instantaneous actions (e.g., a one-tap peer-to-peer payment) where extra confirmation text and rows would feel like unnecessary friction.

  • Power users or repeat flows who already understand the mechanics and would benefit from a condensed, faster re-authorization (e.g., "same as last month" quick toggle) instead of a full form each time.

  • Contexts where lifestyle-benefit headlines would feel misleading or salesy for a purely mechanical setting, such as internal admin tools or B2B dashboards where users expect direct, functional labels rather than aspirational copy.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets busy urban users and students who want to avoid the friction of manually topping up their PayPal balance before purchases, but who are also budget-conscious and wary of surprise debits. Automating small, fixed reloads ($25/month) fits a student's limited, predictable cash flow and a busy professional's desire to "set and forget" routine finances.

Psychologically, the screen leverages certainty and control as trust triggers: by explicitly restating the rule, showing the funding source, and disclosing timing/cancellation policies upfront, it counters the natural anxiety around authorizing a recurring automatic transfer. This is critical for a "ledger-minded" app whose entire value proposition is reassurance over excitement (the design intentionally avoids any hype or urgency language, replacing it with auditable facts).

The chevron-driven secondary editing pattern also serves less financially sophisticated users (e.g., students newer to recurring transfers) by presenting one decision at a time rather than a dense multi-field form, lowering the chance of misconfiguration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Plain-English rule summary: The dynamic sentence recapping amount, frequency, and start date acts as a human-readable confirmation layer before the user commits, reducing errors on a recurring financial action.

  • Progressive disclosure via chevron rows: Frequency and amount are edited in secondary screens/sheets rather than cluttering the main form with steppers and pickers, keeping the primary screen scannable.

  • Compliance copy positioned right above the CTA: Placing transfer-timing and cancellation policy text immediately before the "Authorize" button ensures informed consent at the exact decision moment.

  • Source account transparency: Showing the linked institution (CHIME), account type (SAVINGS), and masked account digits builds confidence that the correct funding source is selected.

  • Benefit-oriented headline paired with precise data: Combining an emotional/lifestyle headline with exact numeric details balances warmth with the precision financially cautious users expect.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Use for single, low-complexity numeric or short-text inputs within a larger setup/onboarding wizard (e.g., reload thresholds, savings goals, spending limits).

  • Ideal when you want to offer a smart default to speed up completion while still allowing full user control via inline editing.

  • Appropriate when the action is easily reversible or adjustable later in settings, making a 'Skip' escape hatch safe to offer.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this level of minimalism when the input carries high-stakes consequences (e.g., large one-time transfers) that require more context, confirmation, or explanation before the user commits.

  • Not suitable when users need comparative information (e.g., fee structures, interest rates) to make an informed choice (bare numbers without context can feel opaque).

  • Skip should not be offered if skipping the step leaves the account in a broken or unusable state downstream.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets budget-conscious students and busy urban professionals who want automatic funds without babysitting their balance, but who are also wary of losing control over their money (hence the transparent, editable, skippable design). The psychological trigger at play is 'default with control': offering a sensible pre-set amount reduces the effort of decision-making (leveraging the default effect), while the visible pencil and Skip option reassure more cautious users that they are not being locked into an amount by a faceless algorithm. This mirrors PayPal's overall positioning as a ledger-minded app that favors reassurance and transparency over flashy automation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-decision screen: Reducing the entire interaction to one editable value eliminates decision paralysis and speeds completion, ideal for a busy, on-the-go audience.

  • Inline pencil-edit affordance: The pencil icon next to the prefilled amount clearly signals editability without requiring an open text field or keyboard by default, keeping the screen visually calm.

  • Smart default prefill: Presenting $25 as a pre-populated suggestion lets cautious or busy users simply tap Save rather than compute a custom figure, reducing friction and abandonment.

  • Non-punitive Skip option: Placing a low-emphasis 'Skip' link under the primary button respects user autonomy and prevents the setup flow from feeling coercive.

  • Bottom-anchored CTA: The pill-shaped Save button sits within comfortable thumb reach, consistent with the app's one-tap interaction philosophy.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 16
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for single-value financial or numeric configuration steps such as reload amounts, budget caps, savings goals, or subscription tier customization (especially within onboarding or settings flows where you want to isolate one decision per screen). It's ideal when there's a clear minimum/maximum business constraint that benefits from real-time inline messaging, and when you want to give users a low-pressure way to defer/skip a non-mandatory setup step.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when multiple related inputs need to be configured together (e.g., amount + frequency + payment method), as isolating just the amount may require an awkward multi-screen flow. Also avoid showing the validation error before any user interaction, as it can read as alarmist or broken (better UX would defer the warning until the user starts editing or attempts to save). Not suitable for critical, non-skippable financial commitments where offering a "Skip" could create compliance or downstream account issues (e.g., mandatory KYC or minimum balance requirements).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers setting up auto-reload/auto-top-up for a prepaid balance, transit pass, or digital wallet (a moment where users are often price-sensitive and hesitant to commit to recurring charges). The design leverages several psychological levers:

  • Reduced friction bias: Simplifying the input to one giant editable number lowers the perceived effort of the task.

  • Loss-aversion softening via Skip: Offering an easy escape hatch reduces anxiety about being locked into an unwanted financial commitment, which can actually increase overall funnel completion because users don't feel trapped.

  • Rule transparency: Displaying the $25 minimum upfront builds trust and prevents the frustration/distrust that comes from hidden business rules discovered only after a failed attempt.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Direct-manipulation input: The dollar amount itself is the interactive element (with an edit pencil affordance) rather than a conventional boxed text field, keeping the UI clean and focused.

  • Proactive inline validation: The minimum-amount rule is surfaced immediately and persistently, not just after a failed submit, reducing trial-and-error friction.

  • Clear action hierarchy: A single bold, full-width "Save" CTA paired with a low-emphasis "Skip" link avoids decision paralysis while still respecting user autonomy to defer.

  • Generous whitespace: The screen commits almost the entire vertical space to breathing room, keeping the user's attention locked onto the one decision that matters.

screens.name: PayPal Setting Up 17
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any single-value confirmation step embedded in a multi-step setup or onboarding flow (e).g., configuring auto-reload thresholds, savings round-up amounts, subscription budgets, or notification thresholds. It's ideal when you have a good smart-default to offer and want to minimize typing while preserving edit access.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal pattern when the value being set carries significant risk or requires more context (e.g., large one-time transfers, investment allocations) - in those cases, additional explanatory copy, validation, or confirmation dialogs are needed so users aren't confirming a consequential number they don't fully understand. Also avoid an unexplained 'Skip' if skipping silently disables a feature the user expected to be active, as that can create confusion later.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets busy urban users and students who want financial automation (auto-reload/top-up) without spending mental energy configuring it. By pre-filling a sensible default, PayPal leverages the default effect: a well-documented behavioral economics principle where users overwhelmingly accept whatever option requires the least effort, especially in low-stakes financial micro-decisions.

The edit-pencil icon caters to detail-oriented or budget-conscious users (e.g., students managing tight funds) who want precise control, while the prominent Skip option caters to cautious users who are wary of committing to automatic recurring money movement (directly reflecting the app's "cautious, ledger-minded" identity described in its brand positioning).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Default Pre-fill: The $26 amount is likely algorithmically suggested (e.g., based on average spend), removing the burden of a blank-field decision and letting most users simply tap Save.

  • Single-Focus Screen: Isolating one editable value per screen (instead of bundling it into a longer form) dramatically increases completion rates for setup flows.

  • Explicit Skip Path: Offering a low-commitment escape hatch respects user autonomy and prevents drop-off/rage-quits during optional setup steps.

  • Visual Hierarchy via Typography Scale: The contrast between the small header, huge dollar figure, and pill button creates an unmistakable reading order with zero ambiguity.

results.query: Video screen recording annotation and review comments

screens.name: Loom - Commenting on the video - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any platform centered on long-form or recorded media where contextual, time-anchored feedback adds value (e).g., design review tools, e-learning platforms, podcast/video critique apps, or customer support screen-recording tools. It's ideal whenever asynchronous collaboration needs to replace or supplement live meetings, and when you want to surface social engagement data directly on the scrub bar to drive curiosity.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for short-form, ephemeral content (e.g., Stories, Reels) where timeline-anchored comments add unnecessary complexity and clutter. It's also unsuitable for highly formal or regulated communication contexts where casual emoji reactions could undermine professionalism, or for very short videos where timestamp granularity provides little added value. Additionally, overloading the scrubber with too many reaction markers on heavily-viewed videos can create visual noise and reduce readability.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets professionals and distributed teams who rely on async video for status updates, feedback, and demos instead of live meetings. The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Social proof via visible reactions: seeing emoji on the timeline nudges new viewers to react similarly (herd behavior) and signals the video is worth engaging with.
  • Reduced friction for feedback: one-tap emoji and short-form text replies lower the activation energy needed to respond, which is critical in workplace tools where time is scarce.
  • Precision context: timestamp-linked comments satisfy the professional need for clarity and traceability ("what exactly are you referring to?"), avoiding the ambiguity of untimed comment threads.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emoji markers on the scrubber: Reactions are anchored directly to the timeline, creating an at-a-glance sentiment map that drives curiosity and re-watch behavior.
  • Timestamped threaded replies: Every comment is tagged with the exact video moment it refers to, eliminating ambiguity common in generic comment sections.
  • Activity/Transcript segmented toggle: Gives power users a text-based alternative to scrubbing audio, supporting accessibility and skimmability.
  • One-tap emoji reaction tray: Persistent at the bottom, it reduces the response to a single tap, maximizing engagement rate on async content.
  • Minimalist player chrome: Skip ±5s, speed control, and PiP/fullscreen icons are the only controls shown, keeping focus on content over chrome.

screens.name: Loom - Commenting on the video - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any time-based media review workflow: video feedback tools, podcast annotation, design-review recordings, async standups, or e-learning platforms where feedback needs to be tied to a specific moment rather than the whole asset. It's ideal when the core value proposition is replacing synchronous meetings with contextual, asynchronous commentary.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for static content (documents, images) where there's no "timestamp" to anchor to (a simpler inline or margin comment pattern would be more appropriate). It's also overkill for very short clips (under a few seconds) where timestamp precision adds little value, or for casual social video apps where frictionless, non-contextual reactions (likes, simple emoji taps) are more fitting than a full comment composer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets remote and distributed teams: designers, engineers, marketers, and managers (who need to give precise, contextual feedback on recorded walkthroughs, demos, or bug reports without scheduling a live call). Tying comments to exact timestamps saves the reviewer from writing "at around the 15 second mark, when you.." and eliminates ambiguity for the creator.

Psychologically, this leverages reduced cognitive load (the system remembers the timestamp so the user doesn't have to describe it) and social proof via emoji markers (seeing where others reacted encourages new viewers to engage at those same hotspots, driving more comments and interaction, which increases video stickiness and time-on-platform).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Timestamp-locked commenting: The header dynamically reflects the exact second ("Comment at 0:14"), giving users confidence their note will be contextually anchored.
  • Emoji reaction markers on the scrubber: Prior viewer reactions are plotted directly on the timeline, turning the scrubber into a mini engagement heatmap.
  • Non-destructive modal overlay: The video frame stays dimly visible behind the comment sheet, preserving context so the commenter can still see what they're reacting to while typing.
  • Frame-precise scrubbing controls: 5/10-second jump buttons let users pinpoint the exact moment to comment on with minimal effort.
  • Single-tap exit and send: Clear X and send affordances keep the interaction reversible and fast.

screens.name: Loom - Commenting on the video - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever feedback or discussion needs to be tied to a specific point in time-based media: video reviews, podcast annotations, design walkthroughs, e-learning platforms, or video-based bug reports. It's ideal for products built around asynchronous collaboration where precision and context preservation are more valuable than real-time dialogue.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for short-form or ephemeral content (e.g., Stories, Reels) where timestamp precision adds unnecessary complexity and friction. It's also unsuitable for live/real-time communication tools where immediate, non-anchored chat is more natural, or for content without a meaningful timeline (static images, documents without time dimension). Overusing emoji/timestamp markers on short videos can also clutter the scrubber and overwhelm rather than clarify.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets distributed teams, remote workers, and async-first professionals (engineers reviewing demos, designers giving feedback, managers responding to updates) who need to communicate precise feedback without scheduling a live call. The psychological driver is reducing ambiguity and social friction: commenting at a specific timestamp mimics the physical act of pointing at a screen during a meeting, satisfying the need for precise, contextual communication even when parties aren't co-present.

The emoji reaction trail also taps into social proof and lightweight engagement: seeing that colleagues reacted with 😍 or 😂 at certain points lowers the barrier for a viewer to add their own reaction, leveraging herd behavior to increase engagement with minimal cognitive effort.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Timestamp-anchored commenting: Ties every comment to an exact video frame, eliminating the "what are you referring to?" ambiguity common in async feedback.
  • Reaction markers on the scrubber: Emoji icons plotted along the timeline act as a visual heatmap of audience sentiment, letting viewers jump straight to emotionally charged moments.
  • Non-blocking modal design: The video remains partially visible and paused behind the comment sheet, keeping the user oriented in context rather than navigating away.
  • Low-friction composer: Keyboard auto-opens, cursor is pre-focused, and a single tap on the send arrow submits, minimizing steps between watching and reacting.
  • Skip ±5s and speed controls present: Allows quick re-watching of the exact moment before commenting, supporting accuracy of feedback.

screens.name: Loom - Commenting on the video - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any async video, audio, or long-form content review product: design feedback tools, podcast/video platforms, e-learning courseware, or code review tools with recorded walkthroughs. It's ideal whenever feedback needs to be anchored to a specific moment in time-based media, and when you want to encourage lightweight, low-effort engagement (emoji reactions) alongside deeper threaded discussion.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for short-form content (under ~15 seconds) where timestamp granularity adds more clutter than value, or for purely text/document-based products where there's no natural "timeline" to anchor comments to. It can also overwhelm the screen on very short or simple videos with few comments (the heavy chrome (reaction bar, scrubber, transcript tabs) assumes a reasonably rich, multi-viewer feedback scenario; for solo or low-engagement content, a simpler linear comment list is more appropriate).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

screens.name: H&M - Product filter - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adapt this pattern for any e-commerce, marketplace, or content-browsing app with a large catalog and multiple independent facets (price, category, attributes). It's particularly effective when:

  • The product set is large enough that unfiltered browsing is inefficient.
  • Filters are largely independent/non-hierarchical (so a flat list makes sense).
  • You can compute result counts cheaply/quickly enough to show live feedback without lag.
  • Omnichannel inventory (e.g., in-store stock) is a meaningful differentiator for the buying decision.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat drill-down filter pattern when:

  • There are very few filterable attributes: a single-screen filter with all options visible (no drill-down) would be faster.
  • Filters are highly interdependent (e.g., selecting one changes the validity of others) and need more sophisticated faceted-search UI with inline counts per option.
  • Result-count computation is slow or expensive, which would make the live "Showing X products" counter feel laggy or misleading.
  • The catalog is small enough that search or simple category browsing suffices, making a dedicated filter screen unnecessary overhead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

  • Scarcity/Urgency: the countdown timer plays on loss aversion, pushing users to complete payment before losing their reserved seat.

  • Trust & Transparency: itemized fees and tax-inclusive totals reduce anxiety around hidden costs, a common purchase blocker in ticketing apps.

  • Reduced Friction: prefilled contact details and a single persistent CTA minimize the effort required at the most fragile point of the funnel (payment), where every extra tap increases abandonment risk.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent sticky "Pay" button with live total ($16.00) eliminates the need to scroll back up to confirm cost, reducing drop-off.

  • Countdown timer overlay on the movie poster creates urgency and communicates that the selected seat is being temporarily held, preventing users from feeling rushed without explanation.

  • Transparent fee breakdown (ticket price, convenience fee, total, tax-inclusive note) builds trust and avoids surprise costs at the final step (directly combating cart abandonment caused by hidden fees).

  • Pre-filled contact info (name, email) reduces friction by leveraging smart defaults from the user's account/profile.

  • Content rating badge (M18) gives fast regulatory context without interrupting flow.

screens.name: Google Pay Booking & Reserving 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any high-intent, time-boxed purchase flow such as ticketing, ride-hailing, or flash-sale checkouts where speed and trust are paramount. It's ideal when integrating third-party payment providers (Apple Pay/Google Pay) to reduce PCI compliance overhead and checkout abandonment. The layered modal-over-context approach works well whenever you want to preserve purchase context while collecting a final confirmation or credential.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex purchases requiring multiple decisions (e.g., selecting insurance add-ons, splitting payment methods, applying multiple promo codes) since the native payment sheet offers little room for customization or additional messaging. Also avoid relying solely on countdown timers for low-stakes or non-inventory-constrained purchases, as artificial urgency can erode trust if the scarcity isn't genuine.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday consumers booking movie tickets who expect a fast, low-friction checkout comparable to e-commerce standards. The design leans on several psychological triggers: loss aversion and urgency via the visible countdown timer (fear of losing the reserved seat), trust transference by using Google Pay's recognized branding and stored card data instead of a custom checkout form, and cognitive ease through a single-tap 'Continue' action that requires no manual data entry. This caters well to mobile-first, on-the-go users who are often booking tickets last-minute before a showtime.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native payment sheet overlay: Leveraging the OS-level Google Pay UI instantly borrows platform trust and familiarity, lowering abandonment risk at the final payment step.

  • Dimmed/blurred background retains context: Users can still see the movie, seat, and price details behind the modal, reinforcing what they are paying for without needing to backtrack.

  • Visible countdown timer: The 09:43 hold timer creates urgency and prevents cart abandonment by signaling that the seat reservation is temporary.

  • Pre-filled saved card: Zero re-entry of payment details drastically reduces friction and completion time.

  • Transparent fee breakdown: Listing 'Convenience Fees' separately from the ticket price builds trust and avoids surprise costs at the final step.

screens.name: Google Pay Booking & Reserving 10
screens.whereToUse:
• Embedded/SDK-based payment flows where a third-party merchant integrates a trusted payment provider's sheet.

  • Any checkout flow with time-sensitive inventory (event tickets, flights, limited stock) where minimizing steps and typing directly impacts conversion.

  • Scenarios where preserving background context (cart contents, item image, price) during a modal payment step increases user confidence and reduces abandonment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this ultra-minimal single-CTA pattern when the transaction requires the user to review/confirm multiple variable details (e.g., shipping address, promo codes) - those need explicit inline summary within the sheet itself.

  • Don't dim/obscure background content so heavily that users can't quickly re-verify order details if the payment sheet lacks a full order recap.

  • Not suitable for flows requiring strong re-authentication (large payments) without an added verification step, as the single "Continue" button may feel too lightweight for high-value or fraud-sensitive transactions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets any mobile-app or mobile-web user in the middle of a purchase (here, cinema tickets) who has already chosen Google Pay as a checkout option. The design leverages the trust-transfer effect: because Google Pay is a recognized, secure utility, its appearance at checkout in a third-party app reduces the perceived risk of entering payment details on an unfamiliar merchant site.

Psychologically, the countdown timer (09:43) on the underlying screen creates mild urgency (seat reservation expiring), which makes the frictionless one-tap "Continue" flow of Google Pay especially valuable (it removes any extra typing or card entry that could cause the user to lose their seat hold).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving overlay: The merchant's order details (movie, seat, price breakdown, countdown timer) remain dimly visible behind the sheet, so users retain full situational awareness instead of feeling transported to a separate "payment app."

  • Radical minimalism: Only one payment method, one CTA, and one line of copy are shown, eliminating decision fatigue at the final, highest-stakes step of the funnel.

  • Brand restraint: Google Pay doesn't try to visually dominate; it uses light gray/white tones and a small logo so it feels like an embedded utility layer rather than a competing brand experience within Shaw Theatres' red-branded flow.

  • Chevron affordance on payment row: Signals the card is tappable/changeable without needing extra explanatory text.

screens.name: Google Pay Booking & Reserving 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this modal blocking pattern whenever an app makes a call to an external payment processor, bank API, or any operation where duplicate submission (double-charging, double-booking) would cause real harm. It's also appropriate for irreversible or slow, high-stakes async actions like submitting a legal form, finalizing a purchase, or completing a booking with limited inventory (e.g., a countdown-reserved seat).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid fully blocking modals for lightweight, fast, or reversible actions (e.g., saving a draft, toggling a setting) where an inline spinner or optimistic UI update would feel less intrusive. Also avoid this pattern if the operation can take an unusually long time (>10-15s) without providing any escape option (like a "cancel" or background-and-notify option), as users may feel trapped or assume the app has frozen (consider adding a timeout message or fallback after a threshold).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern serves any consumer completing a monetary transaction (here, moviegoers booking cinema tickets through Shaw Theatres, likely integrated via Google's in-app/web payment flow). The target user is transaction-anxious by nature (anyone paying money wants confirmation nothing went wrong), so the psychological goal is to reduce uncertainty and prevent erroneous repeat actions. By blocking interaction and showing a clear, singular message, the design leverages the trust heuristic: a locked screen signals "we are handling something sensitive carefully," similar to how ATMs lock the interface while dispensing cash.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Blocking modal with dimmed/blurred backdrop clearly communicates a system-busy state and prevents accidental double-taps on "Pay" that could cause duplicate charges.

  • Context preservation: keeping the checkout summary faintly visible behind the overlay reassures users their order details (movie, seat, total) are still intact.

  • Indeterminate loading indicator is honest about the unknown wait time of a real payment authorization call, avoiding a misleading fake progress bar.

  • No escape hatches (no back button, no close 'X') during payment processing, correctly preventing user actions that could corrupt the transaction state.

  • Visible countdown timer in the background subtly communicates urgency/scarcity of the reserved seat, justifying why speed matters.

screens.name: Google Pay Booking & Reserving 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any transactional flow ending in a physical redemption step (event tickets, boarding passes, restaurant reservations, retail pickup orders). It is ideal when you want to consolidate multiple redemption needs (e.g., seat + concessions) into one single scan point to speed up on-site logistics.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid overlaying transient, auto-dismissing toasts on top of static reference screens like a ticket/QR code, as demonstrated by the "Order summary will be dismissed" banner here. Users may need to reference this screen for several minutes while walking to the venue; interrupting overlays can obscure critical info like the address or showtime. Additionally, avoid this heavy "hero image" header style if the movie poster art competes visually with the QR code needed for scanning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets moviegoers who have just completed a purchase and need quick, stress-free physical access to the venue. The psychological trigger here is reduction of friction and anxiety at the point of entry (users want confidence that they have "the thing" they need to get past the ticket taker without fumbling through emails or apps). The large QR code size ensures easy scanning even in the dim lighting typical of cinema lobbies.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unified QR Code: Merging cinema entry and F&B collection into a single scannable code drastically reduces physical friction at the venue (no need to juggle two tickets/receipts).

  • Visual Hierarchy Shift: The transition from a dark, cinematic branded header to a clean white utility card signals a clear mental shift from "browsing" to "using/redeeming."

  • Content Rating Badge: The prominent "M18" chip ensures compliance and passenger awareness before entry, preventing confusion at the door.

screens.name: Google Pay Booking & Reserving 13
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for post-purchase confirmation screens involving time-sensitive physical/digital goods (event tickets, transport boarding passes, food delivery receipts) where the payment and the deliverable asset need to be viewed together. Ideal for wallet apps, super-apps, or messaging platforms that facilitate business-to-consumer (B2C) chat commerce.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex B2B invoicing or multi-item cart purchases where itemized breakdowns, tax details, and multi-page line items are required (the compact card format lacks the space for dense financial data). It is also unsuitable for purchases without a physical/digital "ticket" outcome, as the bottom "View ticket" CTA and seat map metaphor would be irrelevant.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday consumers using digital wallets (Google Pay) for daily purchases like movie tickets, who need immediate, low-friction proof of purchase. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of post-purchase anxiety: by immediately displaying "Paid" and "Confirmed" statuses with green checkmarks, the user's brain registers transaction success instantly. The bundling of support access directly caters to users who may be rushing to a cinema and need instant help without digging through menus, respecting their time-sensitive context (e.g., checking a ticket right before a movie starts).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unified Payment + Fulfillment Card: Merging the financial receipt (amount paid) with the actual deliverable (the movie ticket) in one continuous scroll removes the cognitive gap between "I paid" and "I have my goods."

  • Embedded Support Chip: Placing a one-tap "Shaw Theatres help" pill directly on the ticket card anticipates user anxiety about ticket issues (wrong seat, wrong time) and resolves it without app-switching.

  • Chat-as-Receipt Metaphor: Using a messaging timestamp header to frame a payment card leverages the familiarity and trust users have with chat interfaces, making transactional data feel less intimidating.

  • Merchant Enrollment Nudge: The bottom banner "Shaw Theatres in Google Pay" acts as a lightweight upsell to link/save the merchant loyalty card without interrupting the primary confirmation task.

screens.name: Wealthfront Logging & Tracking 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech/investing apps introducing new users to single-stock or themed-portfolio investing.

  • Any product needing to show a zero-state balance alongside historical/reference data without alarming or confusing the user.

  • Screens where you want to visually differentiate "potential/historical" data from "your actual" data using line style variation.

  • Detail pages that need persistent, thumb-reachable primary/secondary transactional CTAs (buy/sell, add/remove, accept/decline).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the zero balance/empty state could be mistaken for an error or broken data feed (always pair a $0).00 state with clear microcopy or visual cues (like the dotted line) explaining why. Also avoid combining a volatile historical chart with a static $0.00 balance without disambiguation, as it can raise trust concerns for financially anxious users. This layout is unsuitable for professional/pro-trader tools where information density and advanced charting (candlesticks, volume, indicators) are expected over simplified area charts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets novice or first-time retail investors using a guided/beginner-friendly investing app (similar to Plum, Moneybox, or Robinhood's curated collections). The "Your first stock portfolio" framing and the encouraging "Add more investments" CTA suggest this is aimed at users who may feel overwhelmed by traditional brokerage interfaces and need hand-holding, gamified milestones, and simplified single-asset entry points.

Psychologically, the design leverages the endowment effect and ownership framing: by pre-labeling this as "your" portfolio before any money has been invested, the app creates a sense of psychological ownership that nudges the user toward completing the actual investment (funding it via the Invest button).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dotted vs. solid line charting: A clever, non-verbal way to indicate "this is illustrative/no current position" data versus real market history, preventing user confusion about owning zero shares despite volatile-looking history.

  • Contextual dual deltas: Showing both "today" and "all time" performance side-by-side gives immediate short-term and long-term framing in one glance.

  • Disabled Sell / Active Invest button pairing: Visually communicates account state (no holdings yet) and guides the user toward the only actionable path forward.

  • Themed portfolio metaphor: Bundling a single security under a friendly "portfolio" label with a custom icon (Alphabet logo/avatar) makes single-stock investing feel like curated, guided investing rather than raw stock picking.

  • Segmented time-range control: Provides fast, low-friction historical reframing, a well-established best practice for financial charting.

results.query: Relational database table column schema field configuration

screens.name: Craft - Adding an option - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Any app that lets users define custom structured properties/fields inside otherwise freeform content (notes, docs, or hybrid databases).
  • Settings or configuration sheets where committing changes should be explicit rather than autosaved, due to downstream structural impact (e.g., changing a column type).
  • Power-user features that need to stay optional/invisible to casual users (surfaced only via contextual entry points like "Add Field," keeping the main document experience clean).
  • Mobile schema/field builders where screen space is limited and progressive disclosure (type → type-specific options) is essential.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for simple, single-purpose apps where users never need custom structured data (it adds unnecessary conceptual overhead).
  • Don't use explicit Cancel/Apply confirmation for trivial, non-destructive edits where autosave and inline editing would feel faster and less ceremonious.
  • Avoid dense database terminology ("schema," "enum," "field type") for consumer-facing, non-technical audiences (plain language is critical if the feature is meant to be approachable).
  • Not suitable when field types have many interdependent, complex configuration options that won't fit comfortably in a single scrollable bottom sheet on small screens.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets power users and "second-brain" builders (writers, PMs, researchers, and makers who use Craft not just for prose but for lightweight structured tracking (content pipelines, trackers, inventories) embedded directly in their notes). The pattern mirrors familiar mental models from Notion databases and Airtable fields, lowering the learning curve for anyone transitioning from those tools.

Psychologically, the modal's isolation and the "Cancel/Apply" pairing reduce anxiety around destructive schema changes (users feel safe experimenting with field types because nothing commits until they explicitly apply it). The icon-labeled type picker also leverages recognition over recall, a key usability heuristic for infrequently used configuration screens.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Database-in-a-document: Embedding a structured "Items" field inside an otherwise freeform document blurs the line between note and database, giving Craft Notion/Airtable-like power without sacrificing its document-first identity.
  • Layered modal isolation: The bottom sheet uses a distinct white surface and rounded top corners over a dimmed/softened background, clearly communicating "this is a temporary, focused task" versus the persistent document underneath.
  • Iconography-led type selector: The field type dropdown pairs a small icon with the label ("Single Select"), aiding fast visual scanning for users who will eventually manage many field types.
  • Safe, reversible editing: Explicit Cancel/Apply buttons (rather than auto-save) make this configuration feel deliberate and low-risk, appropriate for structural changes that affect an entire column of data.
  • Progressive disclosure: "Possible Values" and "Add Value" only make sense once "Single Select" is chosen (the UI reveals exactly what's relevant to the current type without a cluttered all-type form).

screens.name: Craft - Adding an option - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any flow where users create tags, labels, statuses, or categorical options within structured or semi-structured content (databases, Kanban boards, CRM tools, note apps with properties).
  • Mobile contexts where minimizing taps and keeping the keyboard pre-engaged meaningfully speeds up high-frequency micro-tasks.
  • Situations requiring lightweight customization (like color-coding) without overwhelming the user with a full settings screen.
  • When you want to preserve the user's spatial context by using a dimmed-background modal instead of a full-screen takeover.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for complex, multi-field creation tasks (e.g., creating a full contact or detailed record) - a single-field modal becomes cramped and should instead be a multi-step form or full screen.
  • Not ideal for first-time or novice users encountering database/property concepts for the first time without any inline explanation of what "Category" or "Option" means contextually.
  • Disabled buttons without any messaging can confuse users who don't realize typing is required to enable the action; pair with subtle affordance cues (e.g., placeholder emphasis) in simpler apps.
  • Avoid fixed color palettes when brand/categorization needs exceed 8 options or require precise hex matching (add a custom color picker option instead).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves power users and knowledge workers (writers, PMs, researchers, designers) who use Craft not just for prose but for structured planning (content calendars, component inventories, project trackers) within the same document canvas. The presence of "Items" as an empty structured field and the ability to add categorized options suggests this document is being used as a lightweight database (e.g., tracking "Hero section v1" variants or component states).

Psychologically, the disabled button and color-coded options reduce cognitive load and decision fatigue: the user doesn't need to worry about making an error (the system prevents invalid submission) and can quickly assign visual meaning (color) to categories for fast scanning later. The pastel, muted color palette also reinforces Craft's calm, editorial aesthetic rather than a loud, saturated "productivity app" feel, appealing to design-conscious users who care about visual craft even in utilitarian moments.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled-until-valid primary button: The "Add" button is greyed out until text is entered, providing implicit inline validation without error messages or wasted taps.
  • Pre-selected color default with full palette control: A pastel color (pink, indicated by the blue selection ring) is pre-chosen, giving smart defaults while still exposing an 8-color palette for quick customization, balancing speed with personalization.
  • Context-preserving modal: The background document (title, Items field, Add Field row) remains dimly visible behind the scrim, so the user never loses their place in the broader document hierarchy.
  • Auto-focused input with keyboard pre-summoned: Zero extra taps needed to start typing, optimizing for the high-frequency, low-friction task of tagging content.
  • Native, OS-aligned bottom sheet styling: Rounded corners, soft shadows, and iOS-standard button shapes make the custom feature feel like a first-party system component.

screens.name: Craft - Adding an option - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when adding structured metadata (tags, categories, statuses, labels) to items within a flexible document or database-like system. It's ideal for:

  • Tag/category creation flows in note-taking, project management, or CRM-like tools
  • Any lightweight "create new option" flow where color-coding aids visual scanning (Kanban boards, select fields, status pickers)
  • Apps wanting to preserve context (showing background content) rather than forcing a full-screen takeover for a simple creation task
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The number of color options would overwhelm users on very small screens or when color isn't a meaningful differentiator for the data type
  • Users need to configure multiple properties at once (e.g., name + color + icon + description) - a fuller form or dedicated screen would serve better than a compact modal
  • Accessibility is a strong concern and color is the only differentiator - without text labels or patterns, colorblind users may struggle to distinguish options
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves power users and knowledge workers (PMs, designers, engineers, writers) who use Craft not just for linear notes but for lightly structured data (databases, kanban-like fields, categorized lists) inside documents. The target user values speed (hence auto-focused input and keyboard), personalization (color-coding for visual scanning), and aesthetic consistency (soft palette matching the app's editorial branding).

Psychologically, the pre-selected color and pre-focused cursor reduce cognitive load and friction, encouraging users to actually tag/categorize content rather than skip the step (a common abandonment point in tagging UIs).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-focused input with active keyboard: Removes an extra tap, letting users start typing the option label immediately.
  • Smart default color selection: A color is pre-selected (shown by the focus ring) so users aren't forced to make a choice, but can still personalize it in one tap, balancing speed with customization.
  • Soft, pastel color palette: Matches Craft's editorial, designed-document aesthetic rather than generic saturated system colors, keeping tag/category visuals tasteful.
  • Context preservation: The modal doesn't fully obscure the underlying document, maintaining spatial orientation and reducing the feeling of a hard context switch.
  • Clear action hierarchy: High-contrast "Add" button vs. neutral "Cancel" reduces decision friction and errors.

screens.name: Craft - Adding an entry - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern when building hybrid document/database tools, note-taking apps with structured metadata, or any content object that benefits from both freeform writing and lightweight structured tracking (e.g., content calendars, task docs, CRM notes, design specs). It's ideal when you want users to layer organization onto content without forcing them into a rigid spreadsheet or table view first.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, single-purpose note apps where metadata would add unnecessary cognitive overhead, or for purely narrative/long-form writing contexts (journals, novels) where structured fields feel intrusive and break creative flow. It's also unsuitable for data-heavy use cases requiring bulk editing, filtering, or sorting across many records (at that scale, a true table/database view with multi-select and batch actions would serve users better than this single-document property list).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets power users and knowledge workers (designers, PMs, writers managing structured content like design specs, content calendars, or project trackers) who need lightweight database-like organization without leaving their writing tool. The "Hero section v1" example suggests use cases like design documentation or product spec tracking.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages familiarity bias: status/priority/owner fields mimic Jira, Linear, and Notion conventions, so experienced users feel immediate competence and control. The soft, pastel color coding taps into fast pre-attentive processing, letting users triage priority and status without reading. The extensible "+ Add Field" option satisfies users' need for autonomy and personalization, a key driver of retention in productivity tools where one-size-fits-all forms often cause abandonment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metadata-as-document-citizen: Properties are rendered inline above the content, not hidden in a separate settings screen, keeping context and structure unified.

  • Soft pastel status chips: Color-coded values communicate state instantly while staying visually consistent with Craft's editorial, non-corporate aesthetic.

  • Floating pill toolbars: Top and bottom controls float over a white canvas rather than anchoring to opaque bars, reducing visual noise and maximizing content focus.

  • User-extensible schema ("+ Add Field"): Empowers power users to customize structure per-document without forcing rigid templates on casual users.

  • Icon-led labels: Each property row pairs a minimal line icon with its label, aiding quick visual scanning for returning users who learn to recognize icons over time.

screens.name: Craft - Adding an entry - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Productivity, note-taking, or knowledge-management apps that want to offer lightweight database functionality without launching a separate app surface.

  • Project documentation tools where narrative context (briefs, goals) and structured tracking (tasks, assets, categories) need to coexist.

  • Any app aiming to support power users who value flexible, Notion-like block composition inside a single canvas.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Apps targeting casual or first-time users who need guided table creation (the lack of labels/tooltips here assumes prior familiarity with database concepts).

  • Mobile-first contexts where wide tables with many columns would require heavy horizontal scrolling and hurt usability on small screens.

  • Use cases requiring complex relational logic (formulas, filters, rollups) - this lightweight table may not scale to true database needs without added complexity that could clutter the minimalist aesthetic.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets power users, designers, PMs, and knowledge workers who use notes apps as lightweight project databases (people migrating from Notion, Airtable, or Coda who want the flexibility of structured data but with Craft's more polished, editorial visual language).

Psychologically, embedding a table directly in a document reduces the cognitive overhead of context-switching between "writing mode" and "database mode," appealing to users who value a single source of truth. The understated, icon-driven UI (no onboarding copy, no tooltips) builds a sense of craftsmanship and trust that the tool is powerful but not cluttered, reinforcing the brand promise of treating "every note like a designed document."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Database block embedded in a document: blurs the line between note-taking and database apps, letting a single doc hold narrative text and structured tables side by side.

  • View switcher ("Table ⌄"): hints at multiple view types (kanban, gallery, list) for the same underlying data, a powerful customization pattern borrowed from best-in-class workspace tools.

  • Inline "Add" CTA: primary action is contextually placed next to the table it affects, reducing travel distance and supporting fast capture.

  • Typed columns with icons (Aa for text, tag icon for Category/select) give instant visual affordance of data type without needing labels explained.

  • Persistent minimal bottom toolbar: keeps editing tools one tap away while maximizing vertical space for content (classic offline-first, writing-focused ergonomics).

screens.name: Craft - Adding an entry - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse:
• Productivity or knowledge-management apps where users need both narrative and tabular content in a single living document.

  • Tools targeting creative/technical professionals who value document aesthetics (type, spacing, dividers) as much as raw functionality.

  • Any "blocks" editor (notes, wikis, PRDs, project briefs) where embedding a mini-database view alongside prose adds value without forcing a full spreadsheet app.

  • Collaborative documentation tools wanting to reduce app-switching between writing and light data tracking.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Apps centered on heavy, relational data management (a lightweight inline table cannot replace a full spreadsheet/database app's filtering, formulas, and scale).

  • Simple note-taking apps aimed at quick capture, where adding table/block complexity would slow down the core "jot it down fast" use case.

  • Mobile-first contexts with very small viewports, where wide tables force horizontal scrolling and degrade the elegant editorial reading experience.

  • Contexts requiring strict data validation or large-scale collaboration on structured data, where a dedicated database tool with real-time multi-user editing is more appropriate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen speaks to knowledge workers, designers, and PMs who use Craft to combine narrative context (briefs, goals) with lightweight structured tracking (asset lists, status tables) inside one document, rather than juggling a separate notes app and spreadsheet. The target user values aesthetics and editorial polish as much as functionality (someone who wants their internal "Project Overview" doc to look presentable enough to screen-share or export).

Psychologically, the design taps into the sense of ownership and craftsmanship: by letting users mix typography-rich text with flexible tables, Craft reduces the friction of context-switching between apps, which lowers the perceived "cost" of documentation and encourages more frequent, higher-quality note-taking.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Blended content model: Prose and a structured table live in the same scrollable document, collapsing the usual divide between "notes app" and "database app."

  • Inline schema editing: The "+" affordances on both rows and columns let users extend the table's shape without leaving the canvas or opening a separate modal.

  • View-switchable collection block: The "Table ▾" control signals the same data could be rendered as other views, future-proofing the block for different workflows.

  • Minimal contextual toolbar: Only four icons persist at the bottom (attach, draw, style, undo), keeping the canvas uncluttered and letting slash-commands/menus handle the long tail of formatting options.

  • Editorial typography: Clear heading/body hierarchy and a subtle divider rule give the document a printed, designed feel consistent with the brand's "treat every note like a designed document" ethos.

screens.name: Airtable -  Adding a field - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-list settings pattern when:

  • Exposing structural/administrative configuration options for an object (table, document, project, list) that are distinct from everyday content editing.
  • You need to combine a renaming field, navigational actions, and destructive actions on one screen without overwhelming the user.
  • Your audience is already familiar with native OS settings conventions (iOS/Android), making this low-learning-curve and fast to scan.
  • You want to enforce an intentional modal/drill-down flow for sensitive operations (e.g., delete, duplicate) to prevent accidental changes from the main interface.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The configuration options are so numerous that a flat grouped list becomes a long scroll (in that case, consider tabs or a search-enabled settings hub instead).
  • You're targeting a highly visual, consumer-facing audience where a plain list may feel sterile or "unbranded"; richer card-based settings may better fit the product's tone.
  • The destructive action (delete) has catastrophic, non-undoable consequences at scale (in such cases, a simple list row is insufficient and should be paired with an additional confirmation dialog or typed-confirmation step beyond just tapping into the row).
  • Users frequently need to compare or bulk-edit multiple tables' settings simultaneously (a single-table drill-down becomes inefficient at scale).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations leads, project managers, and "builder" personas who are configuring Airtable bases as lightweight databases/business systems rather than simple spreadsheets. These users need confidence that structural changes (renaming a table, editing fields, duplicating, or deleting) are safe, reversible where possible, and clearly separated from everyday row/record editing.

The psychological trigger at play is reduction of anxiety around irreversible actions: by isolating "Delete table" visually (red, at the bottom, separated by whitespace) from benign actions, Airtable reduces the chance of catastrophic misclicks (vital trust-building for a tool whose core value proposition is being a reliable system of record for teams).

Secondarily, the pattern serves efficiency-seeking power users who want quick, low-friction access to schema management without navigating complex menus, reflecting Airtable's "flexible navigation" ethos noted in its UX philosophy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded action hierarchy: Blue for constructive/navigational actions, red for destructive ones, allowing rapid visual triage in a tool used by non-designers managing structural data.
  • Grouped-list / native OS settings pattern: Leveraging a UI convention (iOS Settings app) that millions of users already know intuitively, minimizing learning curve for a power-user feature.
  • Single-purpose sections: Isolating the "NAME" field alone prevents accidental edits to structural elements while renaming, reducing error rate.
  • Clear exit paths: Both a contextual back ("Edit Base") and an explicit commit action ("Done") give users confidence their changes are scoped and saved correctly (crucial in a tool where schema changes can be high-stakes).
  • Disclosure chevron on "Customize fields": Signals deeper hierarchy exists, setting correct expectations about navigation depth before the tap occurs.

screens.name: Airtable -  Adding a field - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when designing schema/configuration editors for no-code or low-code tools, form builders, CMS content-type editors, or any admin panel where non-technical users must define structured data fields. It's ideal when:

  • You need to expose complex backend concepts (data types, constraints) to non-developers.
  • Users benefit from seeing a live preview of how a field will render/behave.
  • Reordering and prioritizing attributes is a frequent task (drag handles).
  • Some fields need protection from accidental edits (lock icons on primary keys).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, row-based field editor for simple consumer apps with only a handful of static fields, where this level of configurability would feel like unnecessary overhead. It's also not appropriate for highly technical audiences (e.g., developers in a database console) who would prefer compact, keyboard-driven schema editors (like SQL DDL or JSON schema) over large touch-friendly cards, since this pattern trades information density for approachability, sacrificing efficiency for power users managing hundreds of fields.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations managers, builders, and non-technical team members who are configuring an Airtable base without any coding or database background. These users often arrive from Excel/Google Sheets mental models, so Airtable deliberately avoids technical database terminology and instead reuses familiar metaphors (blueprint, record, field) to lower the learning curve.

The psychological trigger at play is reduction of perceived complexity: by chunking schema editing into discrete, color-coded, previewable rows, users feel in control of a process (data modeling) that would otherwise feel intimidating or developer-only. The lock icon also leverages loss-aversion safety: reassuring users that core identifying data can't be accidentally broken while they experiment with the rest of the structure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live Field Previews: Each row doesn't just label the data type (it renders a miniature interactive preview of that field (toggle, text bar, numeric placeholder, attachment icons), letting users understand the behavior of a field type instantly without having to open a record).
  • Color-Coded Type Icons: A unique glyph and background color per field type (blue "A" for text, green eye for checkbox, orange hash for number, pink paperclip for attachment) creates fast visual scanning and type recognition across large tables.
  • Dual Row Affordance (Lock vs. Drag Handle): Clearly differentiates protected primary fields from freely reorderable fields, preventing destructive actions while still enabling flexible customization.
  • Embedded Video Onboarding: The contextual banner with an inline playable video reduces reliance on external documentation and meets users exactly at the point of confusion.
  • Persistent Add Action: The "Add a new field" row is anchored at the bottom of the list, mimicking the "add row" pattern of spreadsheets users are already fluent in.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when designing schema, settings, or configuration screens for flexible, structured-data products (form builders, CRMs, database tools, spreadsheet apps). It excels anywhere users must:

  • Define or reorder a list of structured attributes/fields/columns on mobile.
  • Understand abstract data types via immediate visual feedback instead of pure text labels.
  • Be gently onboarded into complex technical mental models (e.g., "schema," "primary key," "data validation") through metaphor-driven contextual tooltips.

It's especially effective for productivity, no-code, and database-adjacent apps serving non-technical users who need progressive education layered onto powerful functionality.
screens.whereNotToUse:
