Avoid this dense, icon-and-preview-heavy list approach for simple apps with few or fixed fields, where the overhead of type icons, lock indicators, and drag handles would be unnecessary complexity. It's also not ideal for extremely field-heavy tables (50+ fields) on small screens, where scrolling through a long vertical list becomes tedious (a searchable/filterable field list or grouped categories would serve better at scale).

Additionally, embedding a video coach mark directly in a frequently-visited settings screen can become annoying for repeat visitors if not properly dismissed/persisted; this pattern should only show once per user or be easily permanently dismissible to avoid frustration for power users who already understand the concept.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations managers, project coordinators, and "no-code builders" who are migrating processes from spreadsheets into Airtable but lack formal database training. The psychological driver here is reducing intimidation: concepts like field types, locked primary keys, and data validation can feel like "real coding" to a non-technical audience.

By using visual previews and plain-language metaphors ("blueprint"), Airtable lowers the perceived skill barrier, building user confidence and encouraging deeper customization (which increases product stickiness and reduces churn, since a highly customized base is harder to abandon). The reorder handles and coach marks also speak to power users and team admins who need precise control over how data entry is structured for an entire team, reassuring them that changes are safe, reversible (non-destructive drag), and clearly understood by every collaborator.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline Type Previews: Each field row shows a live, miniature rendering of its input type (toggle, text bar, number placeholder, attachment thumbnails), turning an abstract concept (data type) into something visually self-evident.
  • Color-Coded Type Icons: Consistent iconography and color per field type creates a quick visual language that scales as the field list grows long.
  • Contextual Coach Mark with Video: A dismissible, metaphor-driven explanation embedded directly in the workflow (with an inline video) teaches the "fields as blueprint" concept exactly when the user needs it, rather than in a generic onboarding flow.
  • Locked Primary Field: Visually distinguishing the primary field with a lock icon protects data integrity and prevents destructive mistakes in a highly interconnected system.
  • Persistent Add Field CTA: A fixed, always-visible button for the primary action of the screen reduces friction for the most common task (extending the schema).

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for schema editing or settings configuration where a single object (like a column, field, or variable) has multiple distinct properties (Name, Type, Constraints) that need to be edited in one view.
  • Ideal for No-code/Low-code platforms where you need to translate complex technical configurations (data types) into simple, mobile-friendly toggles and list selectors.
  • Effective when you need to provide contextual safety nets, such as combining an editing action with a destructive delete action in a logically separated way.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the "Field Type" selection requires extensive sub-configuration (e.g., complex Formula fields or Linked Records with multiple options) that cannot be summarized in a single helper line; this would require a dedicated sub-screen rather than an inline toggle.
  • Do not use this dense, stacked form layout for simple, single-input tasks (like just renaming a file), as the heavy sectioning would feel bureaucratic and slow down a simple interaction.
  • Not suitable for public-facing consumer apps where users are unfamiliar with technical "Field Type" terminology; this density works for professional tools but could alienate casual users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Operations Managers, Project Managers, and Database Builders who need the flexibility to modify their business logic (the "schema") while on the go, perhaps during a meeting where a new business requirement arises.

The psychological trigger here is Mastery and Control. By exposing granular field-type controls directly in a mobile modal, Airtable reinforces the user's identity as a "builder" or "admin" of their own system, rather than just a passive data-entry clerk. The simplicity of the toggle and dropdown reduces the intimidation factor often associated with "editing a database," making the user feel capable of making structural changes without engineering help.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Type-Specific Contextual Help: The dynamic helper text ("Useful for checklists.") that changes based on the selected Field Type acts as an inline tooltip, educating users on database schema design without leaving the current screen.
  • Grouped Table Hierarchy: Using distinct card groupings for Name, Description, and Type creates clear visual rhythm and reduces the perceived complexity of editing a database schema on a small screen.
  • Isolated Destructive Action: Placing "Delete Field" in its own distinct section at the bottom, separated by whitespace/dividers from the editing fields, prevents accidental data deletion via fat-fingering.
  • Icon-based Type Identification: Using a colored icon (green circle) next to the field type name allows users to quickly visually scan and identify field types across the app, creating a consistent visual language for data types.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Apply this pattern whenever a user-initiated action is irreversible and affects data beyond the immediate view (e.g., deleting a column/field, removing a user from a shared workspace, deleting a database table, or archiving a project with dependent records). It's especially valuable in collaborative, multi-user tools where one person's action can silently affect others' data.

Use the inline expansion technique (Checkbox toggle appearing within the Field Type row) for simple configuration options to avoid unnecessary drill-down navigation, reserving full-screen or secondary modals only for field types requiring multiple settings.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy-handed confirmation flow for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., toggling a UI preference, hiding a column temporarily) - doing so would create unnecessary friction and training users to blindly dismiss dialogs ("confirmation fatigue"), which weakens the pattern's effectiveness when it truly matters.

Also avoid echoing overly long or technical field names verbatim in a confirmation button if space is constrained; truncate gracefully or use a secondary text input requiring the user to type the field name for extremely high-risk deletions (e.g., deleting an entire base).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations managers, database administrators, and power users who are actively structuring or maintaining a shared Airtable base (often under time pressure or while collaborating with a team that depends on data integrity). Because Airtable fields can hold months of accumulated team data, the psychological stakes of an accidental deletion are high (irreversible data loss affecting colleagues).

The design leans on loss aversion and friction-as-safety principles: by making the deletion path require multiple deliberate taps and explicit acknowledgment of data loss, Airtable reduces anxiety for cautious users while still allowing expert users to move through quickly once they've internalized the pattern.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit consequence messaging: The dialog doesn't just ask "are you sure?" - it educates the user on exactly what will be lost (data across every record), reducing the chance of regret-driven support tickets.
  • Named re-confirmation: The button reads 'Delete "Visited?"' rather than a generic "Delete," reinforcing which specific field is about to be destroyed and guarding against misclicks when editing multiple fields in a session.
  • Inline type configuration: The Checkbox toggle and description appear directly within the Field Type row, minimizing navigation depth for simple field types.
  • Spatial separation of destructive action: Placing "Delete field" far below the primary editable fields, with a divider and trash icon, uses visual hierarchy to signal danger and reduce accidental taps.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Schema/configuration screens in no-code or low-code platforms where users define data structure (e.g., database builders, form builders, CRM customization panels).
  • Any settings list where each item represents a configurable "type" that benefits from a live visual preview rather than a text-only description.
  • Admin panels that need to onboard non-technical users to technical concepts through embedded contextual video and analogy-driven microcopy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Simple, flat forms with a small, fixed number of fields, adding live previews and type pickers would be over-engineering for a one-time contact form, for instance.
  • Screens targeting highly technical users (e.g., developers using a SQL schema editor) who may find the playful icon/analogy treatment patronizing and prefer dense, code-like table editors instead.
  • Contexts where field reordering has no real functional impact (e.g., static reports), since drag handles would add unnecessary complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations leads, project managers, and "citizen developers" who build business systems without formal engineering backgrounds. These users need to configure data structures but are often unfamiliar with database terminology like "schema" or "field types." The design leans on recognition over recall (visual previews, icons, color coding) and analogy-based education (the blueprint metaphor) to build confidence and reduce the intimidation factor typically associated with database configuration tools.

The locked primary field and drag-to-reorder handles also speak to power users who need structural control and customization once they're comfortable, supporting Airtable's dual audience of beginners and advanced builders.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live mini-previews per field type: Each row visually simulates its data type (progress bar, numeric input, file icons) instead of relying on text labels alone, dramatically improving scannability and comprehension.
  • Color-coded type icons: Each field type has a distinct icon/color combo (blue "A" for text, orange "#" for number, pink paperclip for attachment) creating a quick visual taxonomy that scales well as tables grow to dozens of fields.
  • Locked primary field affordance: The padlock icon on "Location" clearly communicates an immutable schema rule without needing a modal or error message.
  • Embedded contextual video/coach mark: Using a tappable video thumbnail inside the explanatory banner caters to varied learning styles (read vs. watch) and is dismissible via the "X" for repeat users.
  • Persistent "Add a new field" CTA: Anchored at the bottom of the list, it keeps the primary creation action always accessible regardless of scroll depth.

screens.name: Airtable - Editing table - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any settings or metadata-editing surface tied to a structural object (a table, a project, a collection) where users need to rename, duplicate, reconfigure, or delete that object. It's ideal for:

  • Admin/config panels in B2B SaaS tools
  • Mobile apps requiring a condensed equivalent of a desktop properties panel
  • Multi-level hierarchies (workspace → base → table → field) where breadcrumb-style headers reduce disorientation
  • Any screen combining low-risk edits with high-risk destructive actions that must be visually distinguished
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat grouped-list pattern when:

  • The object has many configurable attributes that would overwhelm a single scrollable list (consider tabs or an accordion instead).
  • Destructive actions need stronger friction (e.g., irreversible data loss affecting multiple collaborators) - a simple red label without an immediate confirmation step may be too lightweight; ensure a confirmation dialog follows.
  • The target audience is non-technical consumers who may not recognize iOS-settings conventions; in that case more explicit labeling or icons may be needed.
  • Field customization is simple enough to be shown inline, forcing an extra drill-down tap would then add unnecessary friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves power users and database administrators: team leads, ops managers, and builders who are structuring Airtable bases rather than just entering data. These users need fast, low-friction access to schema-level controls (rename, duplicate, delete, field customization) while on mobile, often making quick adjustments between meetings or in the field.

Psychologically, the design leans on familiarity and reduced cognitive load: by mimicking native iOS Settings patterns, Airtable removes the learning curve for an already complex product. The red/blue dichotomy exploits pre-attentive color processing to let users triage risk instantly, which matters heavily for a destructive action like "Delete table" that could affect an entire team's shared workspace.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grouped settings layout: Clear section headers (NAME, FIELDS) create scannable zones without needing dividiing illustrations or heavy visual weight.
  • Color-coded affordances: Blue for safe/navigational actions, red for destructive ones (an instantly recognizable visual grammar borrowed from iOS HIG that requires zero reading to parse risk level).
  • Progressive disclosure via chevron: "Customize fields" doesn't open complexity inline; it drills into a dedicated screen, keeping this root settings screen lightweight.
  • Breadcrumb-like header: "Edit Base" back-label plus "Edit Table" title communicates exact position in a nested hierarchy without a separate breadcrumb component.
  • Inline name editing: The table name field is directly editable in place, avoiding an extra tap into a dedicated rename dialog.

screens.name: Airtable - Editing table - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when building any schema/structure editor for non-technical users (form builders, database GUIs, CMS content-type editors, or survey builders). It's ideal whenever you must expose a list of configurable "slots" (fields, questions, columns) that each have a type, and you want users to understand the type's behavior without reading documentation.

The live-preview-per-row technique is particularly valuable when there are many possible field/data types, as it replaces a mental lookup table with instant visual recognition.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this density of per-row preview and configuration controls on screens targeting power users who manage large tables (50+ fields) - the vertical list becomes unwieldy to scan and reorder compared to a compact table/grid editor. In such cases, a dense settings table with inline type selectors is more scalable.

Also avoid heavy onboarding banners with embedded video if the audience is highly technical or revisiting the screen frequently, as repeated interruptions reduce efficiency; the banner should be dismissible (as it is here) and shown only on first visit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations managers, marketers, and "accidental builders" - people who are comfortable with spreadsheets but have no formal training in databases. The design's core psychological strategy is metaphor transfer: by labeling this the "blueprint" for records and using spreadsheet-like type names, Airtable lowers the intimidation factor of what is functionally a schema editor.

The persistent coach mark and video tutorial cater to users who may feel apprehensive about "breaking" their table by changing field types, directly addressing fear of irreversible technical mistakes. The live preview inputs exploit the recognition-over-recall principle (users don't need to remember what a "Checkbox" field does; they see the toggle and immediately understand its behavior).
screens.keyHighlights:
Live, Type-Specific Field Previews: Instead of abstract labels, each row renders an actual functioning preview of its input type (a real toggle switch for Checkbox, an editable text bar for Single Line Text, thumbnail stubs for Attachment). This "what you see is what you get" preview dramatically reduces the cognitive gap between configuring a field and seeing it in use.

Color-Coded Type Icons: Each field type gets a distinct colored circular icon (blue "A" for text, green eye for checkbox, orange hash for number, pink paperclip for attachment), enabling rapid visual scanning of a table's structure without reading every label (a pattern borrowed from Airtable's own grid-view column headers for consistency).

Embedded Video Coach Mark: The onboarding banner includes a play button over an illustration, offering an optional short video walkthrough directly in context instead of forcing users into a separate help center, respecting user autonomy while still proactively educating.

Lock Icon on Primary Field: The "Location" field shows a lock instead of a drag handle, subtly communicating that the primary field is structurally special (can't be deleted/reordered) without needing an explanit warning dialog.

results.query: AI conversational assistant chat financial advice checkup

screens.name: Cleo Adding & Creating 1
screens.whereToUse: Use a chat-first, single-input pattern when the product's core value is condensing complex, multi-variable calculations (budgeting, health metrics, recommendations) into a simple human-readable verdict. It's ideal for anxiety-prone tasks where a conversational, empathetic tone can reduce avoidance, and for apps that want to build habitual daily/weekly check-ins through a personality-driven mascot.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for power users or professional contexts (e.g., accountants, financial analysts) who need to see granular, exportable data, multi-account comparisons, or bulk transaction management (chat threads scale poorly for dense data review). It also fails when speed is paramount and the user already knows exactly what screen/action they need; forcing a conversational back-and-forth adds unnecessary steps compared to a direct form or dashboard tile.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets younger, mobile-native users (e.g., Gen Z/Millennial gig workers or students) who find traditional budgeting apps intimidating, tedious, or shame-inducing. By framing financial literacy as a text-message exchange with a witty "friend," Cleo lowers the psychological barrier to checking one's own finances (a task many avoid due to anxiety). The technique leverages the foot-in-the-door principle: starting with a fun, low-stakes prompt ("visualize that thing") before asking for real financial commitment (the price), and uses instant gratification (immediate, definitive answer) to keep users engaged rather than abandoning the task out of overwhelm.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Conversational Decisioning: Complex affordability math (balance, burn rate, cost) is resolved into one clear, plain-English verdict instead of raw dashboard numbers.

  • Minimal-Friction Input: The user only has to type a number ("20") rather than filling out a form, drastically lowering the effort to get an answer.

  • Actionable Follow-up Link: The "Set income" chip is contextually surfaced right where a data gap is implied, driving profile completion without an interruptive modal.

  • Personality-First Mascot Branding: The floating "CLEO" pill logo constantly reinforces brand identity mid-scroll, distinct from generic chat UIs.

screens.name: Cleo Adding & Creating 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Use for web-view handoffs, third-party SDK loads (Plaid/bank linking), or payment processing steps where load time is unpredictable but progress can be estimated.

  • Appropriate anytime a native app needs to bridge to external, non-native content and wants to mask the jarring transition.

  • Ideal for finance/fintech apps where user trust and perceived transparency during sensitive data exchanges are critical.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for near-instant operations (<1s) where a loading screen would only introduce unnecessary flicker.

  • Don't use a static "Loading.." label for very long processes (>10-15s) without additional context, humor, or progress messaging (users may abandon or assume the app has frozen).

  • Not suitable when brand personality/engagement is the goal (this pattern intentionally suppresses character voice, so overusing it can make the product feel cold if deployed for non time-sensitive interactions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves any Cleo user who has tapped into a flow requiring third-party or heavier data processing (most commonly linking a bank account, verifying identity, or loading a payment/subscription web-view (e).g., Stripe checkout). These are moments of elevated user anxiety since money and personal data are involved, so the design leans on trust-building mechanics: transparency (progress bar), control (close button), and consistency (brand color) rather than distraction or humor.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Determinate progress bar: Gives the user a sense of forward motion and expected completion, rather than an ambiguous spinner alone.

  • Escape hatch (X button): Always-visible dismiss control prevents the user from feeling stuck if the load takes too long or the underlying service (e.g., bank link) fails.

  • Brand-colored loader: Even in a neutral, functional screen, the pulsing circle is rendered in Cleo's core electric-blue/purple brand hue, keeping visual identity consistent even during "boring" system moments.

  • Restrained tone: Knowing when *not* to be funny (system loading states) preserves the comedic brand voice for moments that matter, avoiding "personality fatigue."

screens.name: Cleo Adding & Creating 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for onboarding flows in fintech, budgeting, or health apps where the required input (income, weight, habits) is sensitive or emotionally charged. It's ideal as a preparatory/explainer step immediately before a data entry step, priming the user's motivation ("why") before asking "how." Effective when paired with a warm, branded mascot/AI persona and when the overall flow is short enough that a single per-step screen doesn't feel padded.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for expert/power-user tools or B2B contexts where users want to move quickly and see filler explainer screens as friction rather than reassurance. Also avoid if the app lacks a consistent brand mascot/persona, as the anthropomorphized copy ("She'll guide you") would feel out of place or gimmicky. Overusing single-topic interstitials across many steps can also elongate onboarding and increase abandonment if not tightly scoped.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets primarily younger, financially anxious users (Cleo's core demographic is Gen Z/Millennials, often with irregular income or debt concerns) who may feel stress or shame around tracking money. The design leans heavily on approachable, meme-adjacent tone (emojis, personified AI) and playful illustration to disarm this anxiety and keep engagement high during a typically high-abandonment onboarding step (financial data entry).

Psychologically, it leverages the foot-in-the-door technique: asking for a low-friction categorical acknowledgment ("add income") before the harder task of entering specific numbers, and uses anthropomorphism to trigger parasocial trust, making users more willing to disclose sensitive financial details to "Cleo" as if confiding in a friend rather than filling out a form for a corporation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anthropomorphized AI Guide: Referring to the assistant by name ("Cleo") and gendered pronoun creates a companion-like trust dynamic, reducing the intimidation of financial disclosure.

  • Single Focused Ask: The screen asks for exactly one thing (income) with zero distracting inputs or competing CTAs, adhering to progressive disclosure principles in a Setup Wizard.

  • Playful Data Visualization Metaphor: The stacked coin illustration converts a dry financial category into an inviting, tangible visual, easing the emotional weight of talking about money.

  • Escape Hatch Preserved: The visible close (X) icon respects user autonomy and reduces feeling of being funneled, which can lower onboarding drop-off induced by claustrophobic flows.

  • Minimal Progress Bar: A subtle, non-numeric progress indicator communicates forward motion without emphasizing how many steps remain, avoiding perceived friction.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building AI-driven or bot-first applications targeting audiences fatigued by clinical, corporate app tones (especially in FinTech, health, or productivity apps trying to build daily habit loops). It works well for opt-in "entertainment" features where the user actively chooses a heightened emotional tone (e.g., "Roast me" vs. "Hype me").
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this aggressive comedic tone for critical transactional flows, such as reporting fraud, disputing charges, or during KYC/verification processes, where users require clarity and trust rather than comedy. It is also inappropriate for older demographics or enterprise/B2B contexts where a professional, dashboard-centric UI is expected.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets a younger, Gen-Z/Millennial audience that finds traditional finance apps boring, shameful, or intimidating. By using humor and "roasting" (mock insults about spending habits), Cleo lowers the psychological barrier associated with checking one's bank balance.

The psychological trigger here is reframing shame as humor. Instead of a stark red "You are overspending" alert, users voluntarily ask to be "roasted," turning a potentially anxiety-inducing money conversation into a game or joke, which increases the frequency of engagement with financial data.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Meme Integration: Injecting a recognizable meme (Grumpy Cat) directly into the chat log blurs the line between a financial tool and a social messaging app, increasing relatability.

  • Persona Consistency: The "unhinged roast" persona is maintained through the CTA chip ("yes let's 🔥") matching the fiery visual theme of the background.

  • Utility Escape Hatch: The floating Home button next to the chat input ensures that despite the deep conversational engagement, users are never trapped and can instantly return to core banking functions.

  • Asymmetrical Bubbles: Different colors (Orange vs. Red) for user vs. AI, rather than the standard Grey vs. Blue, keeps the aesthetic consistent with the "fire/roast" theme rather than generic chat UI defaults.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Apps targeting habit-change or behavior-monitoring (finance, fitness, diet) where blunt data can trigger shame or avoidance, wrapping it in humor/conversation increases engagement and retention.

  • Products aiming to differentiate through personality/mascot branding rather than pure utility.

  • Onboarding or retention flows where you want to re-engage users with negative/critical information (overspending, missed goals) without causing churn.

  • Youth-oriented or meme-literate audiences who respond to internet culture references and informal tone.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise, B2B, or professional financial tools where users expect precision, auditability, and neutral tone (e.g., accounting software, tax platforms).

  • Contexts requiring quick scanning of multiple data points (e.g., comparing spending across categories) - chat format buries data in a linear scroll, making retrieval/comparison inefficient.

  • Older or less meme-literate demographics who may find the humor confusing, unprofessional, or even offensive given the "roast" framing of their financial mistakes.

  • High-anxiety financial situations (debt collections, overdraft crises) where jokes about "sinking" money could feel tone-deaf or trivializing rather than supportive.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets younger, digitally-native users (likely Gen Z/younger Millennials) who are chronically online, meme-fluent, and fatigued by traditional finance apps' guilt-inducing, spreadsheet-heavy tone. These users respond better to humor and personality than to clinical dashboards; shame delivered as comedy is more palatable and shareable than shame delivered as a red bar chart.

Psychologically, the pattern exploits the Foot-in-the-door and gamified compliance techniques: by opting into a "roast," the user pre-commits to accepting critical feedback in a lighthearted frame, making it easier for Cleo to deliver harsh financial truths without triggering defensive avoidance. The chat format also leverages the social proof/parasocial relationship effect. Cleo behaves like a sassy friend group chat, satisfying a need for companionship/accountability that traditional apps don't provide.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Data-as-dialogue: Financial facts are embedded inside conversational bubbles rather than charts/tables, making spending review feel like banter rather than an audit.

  • Meme/GIF reinforcement: Reaction GIFs contextually amplify tone (judgment, sass) without requiring extra reading, leveraging pre-existing internet culture literacy for instant emotional resonance.

  • Single suggested-reply chip: "Keep em coming" reduces friction to zero (the user doesn't need to think of what to say to continue engaging with their financial data).

  • Color-coded roles: Consistent red-for-Cleo vs orange-for-user bubble coloring lets users track the "conversation" at a glance, just like iMessage's blue/grey convention.

  • Named/personal address: Using the user's first name inside the roast increases perceived personalization and emotional stakes.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 3
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for consumer apps targeting anxiety-inducing categories (finance, health, fitness) where standard data reporting causes user disengagement. It works well when the brand has a strong, distinct mascot/persona that can carry the weight of "difficult" news. It is highly effective for retention, as the conversational format encourages daily "check-ins" akin to texting a friend rather than "auditing" a spreadsheet.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for enterprise, B2B, or high-stakes financial dashboards (e.g., stock trading, wealth management) where users require precise, scannable data at a glance rather than narrative context. Additionally, this level of "roasting" humor can alienate users during moments of genuine financial distress or crisis, where a blunt, comedic tone might feel tone-deaf rather than empowering. It also does not scale well for complex data comparisons (e.g., comparing 12 months of spending), as chat bubbles are inefficient for dense data analysis.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This design targets a younger, digitally-native demographic (likely Gen Z and Millennials) who are fluent in meme culture and group chat vernacular but are often disengaged or anxious about traditional finance apps. By adopting the visual language of a messaging app (like iMessage or WhatsApp) rather than a bank, Cleo lowers the psychological barrier to entry.

The psychological trigger here is the reframing of "shame" into "humor." Instead of a red warning banner that says "You are over budget" (which triggers avoidance), Cleo uses playful roasting that triggers engagement and even amusement, encouraging users to check their finances more often because the "punishment" (in the form of a joke) is actually entertaining.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Data as Dialogue: Financial metrics (spend, income) are delivered as bite-sized, emotionally charged text bubbles rather than complex data visualizations, making financial literacy accessible to users who are intimidated by traditional budgeting apps.

  • Multimedia Roasting: The use of a pop-culture GIF within the chat thread breaks the monotony of text and reinforces the app's "comedian friend" persona, making the app feel alive and current rather than static.

  • Frictionless Quick Replies: By offering pre-written, personality-driven responses ("Keep em coming"), Cleo keeps the user engaged in the loop without requiring typing effort, sustaining conversation momentum.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Apps targeting younger demographics who prefer conversational, low-friction interfaces over dashboards.

  • Moments where you need to deliver potentially negative or sensitive data (spending totals, health metrics, performance stats) and want to reduce user defensiveness through humor and pacing.

  • Growth-loop moments (review asks, referrals) that benefit from being embedded in a high-goodwill emotional beat rather than presented as a cold interstitial.

  • Products with a strong mascot/personality-driven brand voice that can carry sarcasm without feeling corporate or robotic.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise, B2B, or high-stakes financial products (e.g., tax software, wealth management) where users expect precision, data tables, and a professional, neutral tone rather than jokes about their spending.

  • Users who need to scan/compare historical data: a linear chat feed makes it very hard to revisit, sort, or audit specific transactions later.

  • Accessibility-sensitive contexts, since GIFs, emoji-heavy copy, and color-coded bubbles without labels can be harder to parse for users relying on screen readers.

  • Any moment where the user is already stressed/anxious about money (excessive sarcasm can feel dismissive of real financial hardship if not carefully tuned).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, digitally-native users (likely Gen Z/younger Millennials) who are fatigued by traditional banking UI and who consume most of their information via messaging apps and social media. The psychological trigger at play is social framing and humor-as-anesthetic: delivering financially shameful or surprising data ($9,004 spent) is softened via comedic timing and meme reference, reducing defensive/anxious reactions and increasing the likelihood the user stays engaged rather than closing the app.

The follow-up review ask exploits the reciprocity/relief effect: having just been "let off the hook" emotionally by Cleo's humor, users are primed to say yes to a low-cost favor (leaving a review).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-as-OS: Replacing an entire "yearly spending report" feature with a scrollable chat bubble is a radical simplification that removes the need for charts, filters, or date pickers.

  • Embedded GIF as emotional pacing tool: Using a reaction meme mid-conversation lets the product "pause" after delivering a hard number, giving the user room to laugh instead of panic.

  • Zero-effort replies via Quick-Reply Chips: Both user turns in this thread are one-tap, pre-written responses, keeping engagement high while eliminating typing friction.

  • Contextual referral ask woven into narrative: The review request isn't a modal interruption (it's stitched into the conversational flow right after a positive emotional beat (relief that the "yearly wrap" is over)).

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 5
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (mixed-content curated card grid + tone modulation by sensitivity + feedback channel) fits any app where the "home" or primary landing screen needs to surface diverse, personalized content types (alerts, prompts, educational material) without overwhelming the user, and where the underlying recommendation system benefits from direct user feedback.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for utility-focused entry points where users expect immediate access to a specific function (e.g., a dedicated "send money" screen) - burying a direct action behind a curated content feed would add unnecessary friction for users with a clear, specific task in mind.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: evolves its home screen over time from a fixed lesson path into a broader feed mixing practice prompts, streak reminders, and supplementary content, mirroring Cleo's Chat-to-insights-feed evolution.

  • Headspace: mixes actionable content (meditation reminders) with educational/wellbeing articles in a similar card-grid home feed format.

  • Rocket Money: surfaces upcoming-bill alerts as prominent dashboard cards, matching Cleo's "Upcoming Bills" card treatment here.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Content feed replaces static Chat entry over time: evolving the Chat landing screen from onboarding quick-replies into a personalized insights feed reflects a maturing relationship between the user and the product, surfacing relevant prompts rather than generic conversation starters.

  • Mixed content types under one framework: combining financial alerts (bills), interactive prompts (affordability check), motivational content, and educational articles under "insights" broadens Cleo's perceived value beyond pure budgeting utility.

  • Tone modulation by topic sensitivity: maintaining playful copy for low-stakes prompts while shifting to plain, serious language for sensitive topics (gambling addiction) shows appropriate content-aware tonal judgment.

  • Direct feedback channel on the feed itself: "Got feedback about your feed?" invites correction/tuning of the recommendation algorithm, similar in spirit to the "Something not right?" link seen on the budget dashboard.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 6
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (chat-routed coach-mark dismissal) fits products where the entire interface is built around a conversational paradigm, keeping tutorial/guidance interactions consistent with the rest of the interaction model rather than introducing a jarring standard-UI interruption.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for products without an underlying chat/conversational interface, forcing a coach-mark acknowledgment through a chat-style interaction in a traditional app would feel unnecessarily indirect compared to a simple "Got it" button.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Intercom-style product tours: similarly route in-app guidance acknowledgments through conversational UI patterns rather than standalone modal dismissals, matching Cleo's approach here.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Coach-mark acknowledgment via chat interaction: routing tooltip dismissal through an actual chat bubble (rather than a standard toast or modal dismiss button) maintains full immersion in the conversational interface paradigm even for UI guidance moments.

  • Consistent all-caps card headers persist regardless of state: maintaining the same visual hierarchy and typography across both icon states (arrow vs. checkmark) ensures the underlying content remains identifiable and scannable.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 7
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (self-aware humor + three-way engagement choice + accessible opt-out) fits any product introducing an optional gamified or supplementary feature within a broader content feed, where respecting user choice not to engage matters as much as encouraging those who will.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for mandatory or core product features, offering an easy "Opt out" is only appropriate for genuinely optional add-ons; a core budgeting or bill-tracking feature shouldn't be presented with the same take-it-or-leave-it framing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: uses similarly playful, achievement-framed language to promote practice activities and games within its app, matching Cleo's ironic "win self respect" tone.

  • Robinhood Learn: offers gamified financial-literacy content with comparable low-pressure, opt-in framing.

  • Headspace: provides similar equal-weight "try it / see your stats / not now" choice structures when introducing optional engagement features.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Self-aware humor lowers the stakes of engagement: framing a financial quiz/game with ironic reward language ("win self respect") makes participation feel playful rather than like an obligation to prove financial competence.

  • Three-way choice respects varying user intent: offering Play, Game stats, and Opt out as equal options accommodates new players, returning players checking progress, and disinterested users, rather than forcing a binary yes/no.

  • Accessible, non-punitive opt-out: placing "Opt out" as a full, clearly-labeled row (not hidden in settings) respects user preference without requiring extra navigation effort to decline.

  • Modal doesn't fully obscure context: the underlying insight cards remain partially visible around the modal's edges, helping the user retain spatial awareness of where they are in the app.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 8
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (reassurance-first status summary + cross-navigation shortcuts) fits any app with a persistent home/insights feed where surfacing condensed versions of deeper data, plus direct links to that detail, reduces navigation friction for common check-in tasks.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if the underlying status is actually concerning (e.g., over budget) - leading with "You're good" framing would be actively misleading in a genuinely negative status; this pattern only works when paired with accurate, context-appropriate emotional framing that changes based on actual budget health.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Mint (Intuit), historically: surfaced condensed budget-status summaries with reassuring framing and drill-down shortcuts within its own notification/insights feed.

  • Copilot Money: provides similar cross-navigation shortcut cards summarizing budget status with links to detailed category views.

  • Duolingo: uses comparable reassurance-first framing ("You're on track!") before presenting supporting progress data in its own feed cards.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reassurance-first framing reduces anxiety: leading with "You're good" before the number softens what could otherwise read as a cold, potentially stressful budget statistic.

  • Cross-navigation shortcuts reduce friction: surfacing direct links to Income/Bills/Budget detail screens from within the Chat feed avoids forcing a tab-switch-then-drill-down sequence for users who want a quick check.

  • Consistent data across surfaces: restating the identical budget remaining figure seen on the main Budget dashboard builds trust that the numbers are consistent regardless of where in the app they're viewed.

  • Compact summary as a discovery mechanism: this card likely helps surface the existence of the Budget tab's detail views to users who might not otherwise navigate there directly.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 9
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (conversational framing + engagement-normalizing copy + equal-weight feedback shortcut) fits any personal finance app's recurring insights feed where daily/frequent engagement is desired and where ongoing user correction meaningfully improves the underlying categorization or recommendation system.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for financial products where frequent checking should be actively discouraged (e.g., long-term investment apps, where research suggests less frequent portfolio checking correlates with better outcomes) - normalizing daily engagement would work against the product's own best-practice guidance in that context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: normalizes daily engagement through similar encouraging framing ("Good to check every day" mirrors streak-encouragement language) embedded in feed content.

  • Copilot Money: offers comparable "top spending" and full-month view shortcuts within its own insights/notification feed.

  • Mint (Intuit), historically: included user-feedback mechanisms for improving auto-categorization accuracy, framed collaboratively rather than as bug reporting.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Normalizing frequent check-ins: "Good to check every day" reframes repeated app engagement as a positive habit rather than obsessive monitoring, supporting healthy daily use without inducing anxiety.

  • Feedback mechanism given equal visual weight: placing "Make Cleo smarter" alongside pure data-viewing shortcuts treats AI-improvement feedback as a routine, everyday action rather than a rarely-used settings toggle.

  • Consistent card structure across a varied carousel: reusing the same title + subtitle + stacked-options layout across distinct card topics (game, budget status, spending breakdown) maintains a coherent, learnable pattern even as content varies.

  • Scope-expanding shortcut: "Whole month" as a distinct option from an implied shorter default view lets users quickly widen their perspective without extra navigation steps.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 10
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (tiered self-service + human-escalation support card, integrated into a broader content carousel) fits any product where support needs vary in urgency/complexity and where normalizing help-seeking as a routine, easily accessible action reduces user frustration.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for products where human support isn't actually available or where offering "Humans pls" as an option would set an expectation the product can't fulfill (the option's self-aware, casual framing only works if the escalation path genuinely connects to real support).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Intercom-powered support widgets: commonly offer tiered self-service/human-escalation options structured similarly to this card, across many SaaS and consumer apps.

  • Duolingo: provides comparable in-app help/tutorial-revisit options accessible from a persistent feed or menu rather than a buried settings page.

  • Robinhood: offers a similar help-center-plus-human-support escalation structure within its own support access points.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Tiered support options respect varying need levels: offering tutorial review, self-service help center, and human escalation as distinct paths avoids forcing all support-seekers through an identical funnel.

  • Self-aware human-escalation option: "Humans pls" acknowledges (rather than resists) the common desire to skip AI/chatbot support, building trust by not obstructing access to a real person.

  • Consistent carousel format extends to support access: treating "Need help?" as a peer card within the same visual system as feature promotion and budget summaries normalizes seeking help as a routine action.

  • Register shift for functional clarity: dialing back personality-forward language for the descriptive copy (while keeping one characterful label) shows appropriate tonal calibration for a support-access context.

screens.name: Brex - Chatting with support - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Customer support flows within B2B SaaS or fintech apps where a high volume of repetitive, categorizable questions exist (billing, card issues, account status).
  • Any conversational interface where you want to blend automated triage with human escalation to balance cost-efficiency and user satisfaction.
  • Scenarios where quick, confident resolution builds trust in a financial product, reducing anxiety around money-related issues.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid pure chatbot-only flows (no escalation option) for high-stakes financial issues like fraud disputes or account lockouts (users need a guaranteed path to a human).
  • Not ideal when the majority of user queries are highly unique or complex, since quick-reply chips lose relevance and clutter the UI without added value.
  • Don't omit the expectation-setting message in regulated industries (finance, healthcare) - users must understand they're interacting with an automated, non-advisory agent for compliance and trust reasons.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees, finance admins, and founders who encounter operational friction (a lost card, a pending reimbursement, a delivery delay) and need fast resolution without opening a support ticket or waiting on hold. Given Brex's audience skews toward busy operators and finance teams managing time-sensitive spend, the chatbot's quick-chip shortcuts directly target the 80% of inquiries that are repetitive and transactional (card status, replacements), freeing human agents for complex escalations.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduced cognitive load (tap vs. type) and trust-building transparency (bot admits its limits and offers a human fallback) to keep users engaged in self-service rather than abandoning the app to call support (which is costlier for Brex and slower for the user).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Quick-reply chips for top intents: Surfacing "Replace card," "Card delivery status," and "Submit reimbursement" as tappable shortcuts dramatically reduces resolution time for the most frequent support requests, bypassing typing and NLP ambiguity entirely.
  • Expectation-setting copy: The bot proactively tells users it may hand off to a human, which reduces frustration and builds trust in an AI-first support flow.
  • Dual input modes: Supporting both structured taps and freeform text caters to different user preferences and query complexity, maximizing self-service containment.
  • Visible escape hatches: A persistent back arrow and "End Chat" button give users full control to exit at any time, avoiding the "trapped in chatbot" anxiety common to poor support UX.
  • Humanized bot identity: A named avatar ("Help Bot") with emoji personality makes the automated interaction feel less transactional and more approachable.

screens.name: Brex - Chatting with support - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any B2B or B2C product with a self-service support layer, especially in finance, SaaS, or operations tools where:

  • Users have common, repeatable questions that can be anticipated and pre-populated as quick replies.
  • There's a need to triage support volume between bot-resolvable and human-required tickets.
  • Trust and tone matter: injecting light personality can offset the stress of needing support in a serious domain (finance, healthcare, legal).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The support issue is urgent/critical (e.g., fraud, card lockout) - in these cases, a direct hotline or priority escalation should be surfaced immediately rather than funneling through a bot flow.
  • The bot's knowledge base is too shallow to handle nuanced financial queries, which could cause user frustration and erode trust if quick-reply suggestions consistently miss the mark.
  • Users are in a high-friction task already (e.g., mid-transaction) where introducing a conversational detour could cause task abandonment; a contextual inline help tooltip may serve better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets time-pressed business employees and finance admins who need quick, self-serve answers to operational questions (e.g., "how to send or receive funds") without waiting on hold or filing a ticket. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of friction and anxiety: financial tasks carry higher stakes than typical consumer app support, so users need reassurance that help is immediate, judgment-free, and escalatable to a real human if needed.

The quick-reply chips leverage the path-of-least-resistance principle: rather than forcing users to compose a question from scratch, Brex anticipates common pain points and surfaces them, increasing the likelihood of first-contact resolution and improving perceived efficiency of the support experience.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual input modality: Combines quick-reply suggestion chips with an open text field, accommodating both novice and specific-need users.
  • Honest expectation-setting: The bot explicitly states its limitations and the fallback to human support upfront, building trust rather than creating false expectations of AI omniscience.
  • Low-friction exit controls: Both a back button and an explicit "End Chat" CTA give users full control to disengage at any point, reducing the "trapped in a chatbot" anxiety common to poor support UX.
  • Human-like typing indicator: The three-dot animation after a user query maintains conversational rhythm and signals active processing, reducing perceived wait-time anxiety.
  • Branded personality: The waving emoji and robot avatar inject warmth into a finance app that otherwise relies on minimal, serious dashboards.

screens.name: Brex - Chatting with support - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for customer support ecosystems where bots need to handle Tier-1 queries (FAQs, account status) before escalating to human agents.
  • Ideal for B2B SaaS or Fintech apps where linking to detailed documentation (rather than trying to explain complex policies in a chat bubble) is more effective.
  • Effective when you need to capture feedback on bot accuracy in real-time to improve NLU models.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for urgent, time-sensitive issues (e.g., reporting a stolen card) where a bot interaction might delay access to a human agent or emergency hotline.
  • Do not use heavy "Knowledge Article" cards if the support platform cannot guarantee articles are up-to-date; broken or irrelevant links erode trust in the automated system.
  • Not suitable for high-emotion complaint scenarios where users need empathetic human interaction rather than templated bot responses.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective or non-verified users interacting with the app pre-login or without a full business account, as evidenced by the bot's specific detection of "not logged in" status. It also serves existing employees/admins seeking quick self-service answers regarding fund transfers.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Path of Least Resistance principle (by offering immediate self-service links alongside human agent options, it reduces the "effort" cognitive load associated with support tickets). The inclusion of the "Apply for Brex business account" button specifically targets curious non-users, using the support context as a soft-sell trigger to convert window-shoppers into lead applicants.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Rich Media Embeds: Instead of just linking out, the bot presents a structured "Knowledge Article" card with a title and summary, allowing users to gauge relevance before clicking.
  • Dual Escape Hatches: The footer offers both a support escalation ("Speak with a Brex Specialist") and a sales conversion path ("Apply for Brex business account"), cleverly turning a support interaction into a potential lead-gen opportunity for non-customers.
  • Binary Feedback Loop: The simple thumbs up/down ("Was this helpful?") allows for low-friction AI training data collection without interrupting the chat flow.
  • Clear Session Control: The "End Chat" button is persistently visible in the header, giving users explicit control to exit the automated flow at any time.

screens.name: Airtable -  Editing a record (note field) - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when designing mobile experiences for data-dense desktop-first products (spreadsheets, CRMs, inventory systems) that need a lightweight way to preview structured records. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to browse multiple fields per record without opening full detail view.
  • The underlying data model supports multiple views (filtered, grouped, sorted) that should be independently switchable.
  • Aggregate values (sums, counts) add immediate value to the user's at-a-glance understanding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense card/toolbar combination for casual consumer apps with simple, single-purpose data (e.g., a to-do list or social feed) where exposing Filter/Group/Sort controls would feel like unnecessary complexity. It also breaks down on very small screens if too many fields are configured to show per card, causing excessive vertical scrolling and card-height inconsistency. For first-time users unfamiliar with database concepts, this level of control should be progressively disclosed rather than shown upfront.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations-minded and detail-oriented users: project managers, trip planners, small business owners (who need the flexibility of a spreadsheet but the usability of a consumer app). The psychological trigger here is mastery and control: by exposing filter/sort/group tools alongside a friendly visual card design, Airtable reassures users they aren't sacrificing powerful data manipulation for simplicity.

The playful illustrated icons and informal notes tone build emotional familiarity, lowering the intimidation factor that traditionally accompanies database tools, making it approachable for non-technical users while still satisfying power users' need for structured, queryable data.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Card-based grid translation: Converts a traditionally dense spreadsheet row into a readable, touch-friendly card without losing column context (via small field labels and icons).
  • Dual-layer navigation: Separates "Table" (bottom tab bar: Places, Packing List, Friends) from "View" (top dropdown: Main View), letting users maintain multiple saved perspectives on the same dataset.
  • Automatic column aggregation: The "26 sum" footer under Days shows live computed totals, reinforcing Airtable's spreadsheet power even in a simplified mobile layout.
  • Persistent manipulation toolbar: Hide fields, Filter, Group, and Sort are always one tap away, keeping power-user data control accessible without a separate settings screen.
  • Attachment overflow badge ("+1"): Elegant compression of multiple images into a single thumbnail with a counter badge, preserving card height consistency.

screens.name: Cash App Dashboard 23
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when introducing a new loyalty/status tier, feature update, or premium capability to existing users, especially in fintech, subscription, or rewards-based products. It's ideal when you want to: (1) announce a change without forcing immediate action, (2) show rather than tell what the feature looks like via embedded previews, and (3) clearly communicate qualifying criteria to avoid confusion or perceived unfairness. Great for post-login interstitials, app-update announcements, or re-engagement campaigns.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for time-sensitive, critical account actions (security alerts, required verification) since the soft CTA and dismissible nature deprioritize urgency. Don't use it for entirely new/unproven features without clear qualifying criteria (vague benefit lists without concrete numbers can feel like marketing fluff and erode trust). Also avoid stacking multiple full-screen interstitials in a row, as this increases dismissal fatigue and can be perceived as intrusive, especially in a finance app where users expect quick access to their money.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing, active Cash App users (a personalized greeting "Hi Emma" is shown in the preview) who use Cash App Card and direct deposit features but haven't yet unlocked the new "Green" status tier. It's designed to re-engage users who are close to or capable of meeting the qualifying spend/deposit thresholds, nudging behavior change (increasing card usage or switching direct deposit) through a loyalty/status framing.

Psychologically, it leverages status/aspiration triggers (naming a tier "Green" implies exclusivity and achievement), loss-aversion-adjacent framing (highlighting benefits you could be missing), and reciprocity/gamification (rewarding an existing habit (spending/depositing) with tangible perks like interest and overdraft protection). The concrete numeric thresholds also tap into achievable-goal psychology, making the reward feel attainable rather than aspirational-only.
screens.keyHighlights:
• In-context product preview: Embedding a mock of the actual in-app card experience inside the promotional screen gives users a tangible, believable glimpse of the feature rather than an abstract illustration.

  • Quantified, concrete incentives: Specific numbers (3.5% interest, $500 spend, $300 deposit) build credibility and let users self-assess eligibility instantly.

  • Low-commitment CTA language: "Explore updates" invites discovery instead of pressuring an immediate financial decision, reducing drop-off from anxious users.

  • Brand-consistent color signaling: Using green gradients to represent the "Green" tier reinforces status/tier identity visually, not just verbally.

  • Easy escape hatch: The prominent top-left X ensures the interstitial doesn't feel forced, respecting user autonomy (important for financial apps where trust is paramount).

screens.name: Cash App Dashboard 24
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when announcing a significant new feature (especially AI/automation features) to an existing user base, particularly when the feature benefits from being seen "in action" rather than described abstractly. Ideal for fintech, productivity, and SaaS apps introducing copilots, assistants, or major redesigns. Effective as a post-login interstitial, especially timed right after an app update.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy full-screen takeover for minor feature tweaks or when users are in the middle of a critical task (e.g., mid-transaction), as it interrupts flow and can feel intrusive. Also avoid if the feature cannot be meaningfully previewed visually (a fake screenshot with no real substance can feel misleading if the actual feature underdelivers). Should not be shown repeatedly to users who have already dismissed or engaged with it once, as it will read as nagging.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets existing, engaged users of a personal finance/banking app (evidenced by the personalized "Emma" greeting) who are being introduced to a new AI feature post-login or after an app update. The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Personification/Anthropomorphism:

  • Concrete Specificity Bias: Real numbers ($120, 12%, $60) are more persuasive and believable than vague promises, demonstrating tangible value immediately.

  • Curiosity Gap: The truncated paragraph and "Explore updates" CTA exploit the human drive to complete unfinished information.

  • Loss Aversion Avoidance: Framing insights as proactive help (savings streaks, overspending alerts) taps into users' anxiety around finances, positioning the AI as a stress-reducing ally.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Nested UI Preview: Showing an actual screenshot of the chat feature inside a gradient frame builds credibility and sets accurate expectations versus abstract illustrations.

  • Personalized Mock Content: Using the user's name ("Hi Emma!") and realistic, specific financial callouts (12% less on groceries, $120 Uber split, $60 savings) makes the abstract AI concept tangible and immediately valuable.

  • Low-Commitment CTA: "Explore updates" invites curiosity rather than demanding a decision, reducing friction to proceed.

  • Truncated Body Copy: Cutting off the description text creates a subtle curiosity gap/Bento-style teaser encouraging further exploration.

  • Dual Exit Points: Both the outer X and an implied inner X on the mock UI reinforce that dismissal is always safe and non-intrusive.

screens.name: Cash App Dashboard 25
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a regulated product (fintech, healthcare, insurance, lending) must legally disclose partner institutions, risk factors, or eligibility terms tied to a feature announcement, paywall, or account action, but you don't want that legal content to gate the primary user flow. It's appropriate for footnotes/appendices attached to marketing or update screens, terms-of-service addenda, or expanded disclosure modals launched from an info icon.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for time-sensitive or consent-critical disclosures where the user must demonstrably read and acknowledge terms (e.g., loan agreements, binding arbitration clauses) - a skippable wall of text with an unrelated CTA is legally weaker than an explicit checkbox/acknowledgment flow. Also avoid for casual consumer content where dense monospace legal text will feel jarring, off-brand, and erode trust rather than build it; in those cases, summarized plain-language disclosures with a "Learn more" expandable would serve users better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves two very different audiences simultaneously: (1) regulators and legal/compliance reviewers, who require exhaustive, state-by-state, product-by-product disclosure of banking partners, risk factors, and eligibility rules; and (2) everyday Cash App users, who are functionally uninterested in this text and simply want to reach the feature update or dismiss the screen.

Psychologically, the design leans on the "wall of text" pattern to discourage close reading while technically satisfying disclosure obligations (most users will skim or skip straight to the CTA, a predictable behavior the design silently accommodates by keeping the button always accessible).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent, high-contrast CTA: The black "Explore updates" button remains anchored at the bottom, ensuring the legal wall of text never blocks the user's path forward.

  • Footnote/asterisk system: Using *, **, ***, etc. lets the product surface concise marketing claims elsewhere while deferring full legal nuance to this dedicated screen, keeping upstream screens clean.

  • Inline hyperlinks: Key terms ("terms," "Bitcoin disclosures," "View state licenses") are underlined and tappable, allowing users who need detail to drill deeper without cluttering this screen further.

  • Simple exit affordance: The "X" close icon offers an obvious, low-friction escape hatch for users who have no interest in reading disclosures.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Setting Up 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any flow where a user must select a recurring date, deadline, or billing cycle (such as subscription billing, loan/installment repayment scheduling, recurring transfers, or reminder scheduling). It works well when there's a sensible default (e.g., end-of-month) but real user needs vary (e.g., aligning with payday).

Also appropriate whenever an interface benefits from progressive disclosure, presenting a simple binary choice first, then expanding to detailed controls only when the non-default path is selected.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this exact numeric-grid calendar when the day-of-week is contextually important (e.g., scheduling a one-time event, meeting, or delivery), since omitting weekday labels would cause confusion. Also avoid an isolated single-step confirmation for highly complex scheduling logic (e.g., multiple recurring rules, exceptions, or timezone-sensitive events) - those require a multi-step wizard with more explicit validation and preview rather than a single static grid.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users managing recurring bills, loan repayments, or subscription services within a personal finance or banking app (likely BNPL (Buy Now Pay Later), lending, or utility payment products where aligning payment dates with payday or cash-flow cycles is a common user need).

Psychologically, the screen leverages certainty and control: financial anxiety is reduced when users can explicitly choose and confirm a date rather than have one imposed on them. The confirmation sentence at the bottom exploits the reduction of ambiguity principle: by restating the outcome in natural language, it prevents a "did I set this right?" doubt loop, which is especially important for automated/recurring financial commitments where mistakes have real monetary consequences.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive disclosure: the calendar grid only becomes meaningful/interactive after "Other Date" is chosen, keeping the default path simple.

  • Plain-language summary footer: restates the selected date's real-world impact in a full sentence, reducing ambiguity and anxiety around automated payments.

  • Simplified calendar UI: a numbers-only grid (no weekday labels) that matches the actual mental model needed (day-of-month, not day-of-week).

  • High-contrast single CTA: the blue circular checkmark button is the only saturated color element on the screen, making the primary action impossible to miss.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

screens.name: Apple Wallet Setting Up 9

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The design leverages the certainty/closure principle: explicit confirmation reduces the nagging worry of "did that actually work?"

The explanation of the skipped payment date leverages transparency as a trust-building mechanic, common in fintech products, where unexplained automated behavior (e.g., a payment appearing to not happen) can trigger fear of a system error or fraud. By preemptively answering the "why," the product reduces perceived risk and cognitive dissonance.

The notification opt-in nudge uses the psychological principle of contextual relevance: asking for permission at the exact moment its value is obvious (right after setting up recurring payments) dramatically increases conversion compared to a generic onboarding-time request.
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday Apple Card users trying to locate a specific charge, understand a spending spike, or audit recurring subscriptions.
