  • Screens combining a goal-progress visualization with a transactional audit trail (e.g., gift registries, trip funds, event pools).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy hero-visualization approach for high-frequency financial screens (e.g., primary transaction history) where users need dense, at-a-glance data rather than large decorative elements.

  • Not appropriate for enterprise or B2B finance dashboards where users expect immediate access to numeric detail without scrolling past a large graphic.

  • Avoid retaining "in-progress" visual metaphors (like a progress ring) for closed/completed states if it risks confusing users into thinking the goal is still active (supplement with unmistakable status text as done here).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using peer-to-peer payment apps (like Cash App) for informal group fundraising, splitting costs for parties, gifts, trips, or shared purchases with friends. The target demographic is socially-driven, mobile-first users who value transparency and quick visual confirmation over detailed financial statements.

Psychologically, the screen leverages "closure and resolution" cues: humans crave definitive endings to open loops (the pool being "open" until it's paid out), and this screen closes that loop with unambiguous status language and a visual receipt. The circular progress ring also taps into goal-gradient psychology, visually rewarding participants for having contributed toward a shared, tangible target, even retroactively.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent progress ring on a closed goal: Retaining the circular goal-tracking visualization even after closure creates continuity between the "active" and "resolved" states, so users immediately recognize the object type without re-orienting.

  • Explicit closure receipt: The bordered "Closed Oct 3 / Money transferred to Cash balance" card acts like a mini-receipt, giving users a clear, confident answer to "what happened to this pool" in one glance.

  • Scroll affordance cue: The "↓ Scroll for activity" microcopy solves the discoverability problem created by a very tall hero section, ensuring users don't miss the transaction history below.

  • Unified activity ledger: Mixing the pool-closure event and the resulting cash-balance transfer into one chronological feed lets users audit the full lifecycle of their money in a single view, reinforcing transparency and trust.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 24
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you need to request a sensitive permission (contacts, location, notifications) but don't want to block or delay the user's primary task. It's ideal for social or network-effect products where the value of the app increases with more connected users, and where the ask can be naturally embedded within an existing, relevant screen (e.g., asking for contacts sync during a payment/sharing flow rather than immediately at onboarding).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the permission request is unrelated to the current task context (it will feel like a non-sequitur and erode trust). Also avoid stacking multiple soft-asks on the same screen as the primary CTA, as it can dilute focus from the core transaction (here, completing the payment). For highly regulated or privacy-sensitive apps (health, finance-only utilities), a more explicit, dedicated consent screen with legal disclosure may be required instead of this lightweight card treatment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday consumers making small, casual peer-to-peer payments (splitting bills, paying back friends) - a highly habitual, low-cognitive-load action. The psychological trigger of social proof is used via the visible contacts list (showing checked/synced contacts) to imply that friends are already active on the platform. The reciprocity and utility framing ("find friends," "prevent fraud") lowers the perceived risk of granting contact access, appealing to users' underlying anxiety about security while dangling a social utility (finding more friends) as the primary hook (classic growth-loop mechanics for network-effect apps like Cash App).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Amount-as-title pattern: Placing the dollar amount ($1) as the top navigation title reinforces focus on the core transaction value at every step of the flow.

  • Non-blocking permission priming: Instead of a native OS contact-permission modal or interruptive dialog, the sync request is embedded as a soft card within the natural scroll flow, respecting user autonomy while still surfacing the ask contextually (right where contacts are relevant).

  • AI/sparkle icon on memo field: The sparkle icon beside the "For" field hints at AI-assisted note suggestions, adding a delightful, modern touch to a mundane input.

  • Reused mental model: The To/For/Use structure echoes a checkbook/paper form, leveraging a familiar real-world metaphor to make digital payments feel tangible and trustworthy.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 25
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for terminal confirmation states in transactional flows (especially in fintech, payments, bookings, or any action with real-world consequences (money, contracts, irreversible submissions)). It's ideal when a follow-on conditional event (like recipient acceptance) needs to be clearly communicated to prevent confusion. Best used as a full-screen or bottom-sheet takeover to enforce a moment of clear acknowledgment before returning to the main app flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen treatment for low-stakes or highly frequent actions (e.g., liking a post, saving a draft), where a lightweight toast or inline success state would be less intrusive and better suited to maintaining flow. Also avoid vague success language when the underlying action is actually pending/conditional (always be explicit like this example, rather than implying full completion when it hasn't occurred, as that erodes trust).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using P2P payment or banking apps (e.g., Cash App, Venmo-style transfers) who need immediate, unambiguous confirmation that their financial action was successful. Financial transactions carry high emotional stakes and anxiety, so the psychological trigger here is relief and closure: the green checkmark and affirmative headline resolve the tension created by the "will this payment go through?" uncertainty.

Additionally, by explaining the conditional deposit, the design leverages the trust-through-transparency principle, which is essential for fintech products where user confidence directly impacts retention and repeat usage.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose screen: No distractions, navigation, or secondary CTAs. Just confirmation and exit.

  • Iconography as instant feedback: The large green checkmark communicates success at a glance, before the user even reads the text, leveraging pre-attentive visual processing.

  • Expectation-setting copy: Proactively communicates the conditional nature of the transaction (pending recipient acceptance) to reduce anxiety and support inquiries.

  • Bold, oversized typography: Ensures the message is legible and reassuring even for a quick glance, appropriate for a financial transaction confirmation.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 26
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any in-person or proximity-based payment, ticketing, check-in, or identity verification flow where a QR/barcode needs to be scanned or displayed. It's ideal when you need to support both "I am scanning someone else's code" and "someone is scanning my code" within one unified interaction, such as transit fare apps, event ticketing, or contactless payment wallets.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this full-screen camera takeover pattern for scenarios where scanning is a rare, secondary action rather than a core flow, forcing users into a dedicated dark screen for infrequent use cases adds unnecessary navigation weight. Also avoid it if the target audience frequently lacks camera permissions or operates in environments where QR codes are impractical (e.g., no smartphone camera access, accessibility-impaired users who cannot align a viewfinder), in which case a manual code entry fallback should be prioritized instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users of digital wallets, P2P payment apps, or point-of-sale systems (e.g., Venmo, Cash App, Alipay-style checkout) who need to complete a transaction quickly, often in a live retail or social setting with time pressure. The psychological trigger here is reduction of friction and anxiety around payment: by making the interface unmistakably functional and instruction-driven, users feel confident they are performing the action correctly, which is critical when money is involved. The flashlight toggle also anticipates low-light environments (restaurants, market stalls), showing empathy for real-world usage contexts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented Control for Bidirectional Flow: The "Scan" vs "My Code" toggle elegantly handles both the payer and payee use cases within a single screen, avoiding navigation sprawl.

  • Dark, Camera-Native Aesthetic: The near-black background reduces light pollution/glare on the camera sensor and visually reinforces "this is a camera tool," setting correct user expectations instantly.

  • Visual Scan Frame Affordance: The rounded rectangle guide removes guesswork about where to aim the device, a critical usability aid for QR scanning tasks.

  • Minimal Controls, Maximum Focus: Only a close button and flashlight toggle exist as chrome, keeping the interface distraction-free and task-focused.

results.query: When to avoid conversational chatbot UI for high-stakes banking transactions

screens.name: Brex - Chatting with support - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-list settings pattern when an app has heterogeneous account-level functions (banking integrations, AI assistant access, referrals, support) that don't fit a single mental model. It's ideal for:

  • B2B SaaS/fintech apps where users need fast, non-decorative access to settings.
  • Surfacing real-time support SLAs directly in a menu to help users self-select the fastest resolution path.
  • Embedding referral/growth CTAs contextually within account pages rather than via disruptive modals.
  • Any app needing to expose a version/build identifier for support triage.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, text-heavy list style for consumer apps targeting less technical or younger audiences, where more visual/card-based settings screens improve approachability. It's also unsuitable when settings need heavier emphasis on personalization or visual customization (e.g., theming), since the plain list underserves image-based or toggle-heavy preferences. Additionally, embedding live metadata (like "1 min" response times) requires reliable, real-time backend data (stale or inaccurate SLAs here would damage user trust more than omitting the information entirely).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves business employees, founders, and finance admins who need quick, low-friction access to account-level controls and support while managing company spend. Because these users are often multitasking amid high-stakes financial tasks (e.g., resolving a declined card or requesting reimbursement), the design prioritizes speed and predictability: clear grouping, consistent iconography, and visible response-time expectations for support reduce anxiety and decision fatigue.

The referral incentive specifically targets founders/admins who have influence over purchasing decisions for other businesses, leveraging monetary incentive ($250) as a powerful driver of B2B word-of-mouth growth (a highly effective lever in SMB fintech markets where trust and peer recommendation drive adoption).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live response-time badges: Color-coded pills (green for fast channels, gray for slow) on Chat, Call, and Email let users make an instant cost/benefit decision on which support channel to use without opening each option.
  • Embedded growth loop: The referral incentive ($250) is placed contextually within account settings where users are already thinking about their relationship with Brex, maximizing conversion likelihood versus a separate promotional screen.
  • Visual isolation of destructive action: "Sign out" is separated by a whitespace gap and styled in red, reducing accidental taps while still keeping it easily accessible.
  • External link iconography: The Help Center row uses a distinct "external link" icon instead of a chevron, correctly signaling that this action leaves the app context (opens browser), which is a subtle but important wayfinding detail many apps get wrong.
  • Debug-friendly version string: Exposing the full build hash at the bottom aids support/troubleshooting conversations without cluttering the primary UI.

screens.name: Brex - Chatting with support - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Customer support flows within B2B SaaS or fintech apps where a high volume of repetitive, categorizable questions exist (billing, card issues, account status).
  • Any conversational interface where you want to blend automated triage with human escalation to balance cost-efficiency and user satisfaction.
  • Scenarios where quick, confident resolution builds trust in a financial product, reducing anxiety around money-related issues.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid pure chatbot-only flows (no escalation option) for high-stakes financial issues like fraud disputes or account lockouts (users need a guaranteed path to a human).
  • Not ideal when the majority of user queries are highly unique or complex, since quick-reply chips lose relevance and clutter the UI without added value.
  • Don't omit the expectation-setting message in regulated industries (finance, healthcare) - users must understand they're interacting with an automated, non-advisory agent for compliance and trust reasons.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees, finance admins, and founders who encounter operational friction (a lost card, a pending reimbursement, a delivery delay) and need fast resolution without opening a support ticket or waiting on hold. Given Brex's audience skews toward busy operators and finance teams managing time-sensitive spend, the chatbot's quick-chip shortcuts directly target the 80% of inquiries that are repetitive and transactional (card status, replacements), freeing human agents for complex escalations.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduced cognitive load (tap vs. type) and trust-building transparency (bot admits its limits and offers a human fallback) to keep users engaged in self-service rather than abandoning the app to call support (which is costlier for Brex and slower for the user).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Quick-reply chips for top intents: Surfacing "Replace card," "Card delivery status," and "Submit reimbursement" as tappable shortcuts dramatically reduces resolution time for the most frequent support requests, bypassing typing and NLP ambiguity entirely.
  • Expectation-setting copy: The bot proactively tells users it may hand off to a human, which reduces frustration and builds trust in an AI-first support flow.
  • Dual input modes: Supporting both structured taps and freeform text caters to different user preferences and query complexity, maximizing self-service containment.
  • Visible escape hatches: A persistent back arrow and "End Chat" button give users full control to exit at any time, avoiding the "trapped in chatbot" anxiety common to poor support UX.
  • Humanized bot identity: A named avatar ("Help Bot") with emoji personality makes the automated interaction feel less transactional and more approachable.

screens.name: Brex - Chatting with support - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any B2B or B2C product with a self-service support layer, especially in finance, SaaS, or operations tools where:

  • Users have common, repeatable questions that can be anticipated and pre-populated as quick replies.
  • There's a need to triage support volume between bot-resolvable and human-required tickets.
  • Trust and tone matter: injecting light personality can offset the stress of needing support in a serious domain (finance, healthcare, legal).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The support issue is urgent/critical (e.g., fraud, card lockout) - in these cases, a direct hotline or priority escalation should be surfaced immediately rather than funneling through a bot flow.
  • The bot's knowledge base is too shallow to handle nuanced financial queries, which could cause user frustration and erode trust if quick-reply suggestions consistently miss the mark.
  • Users are in a high-friction task already (e.g., mid-transaction) where introducing a conversational detour could cause task abandonment; a contextual inline help tooltip may serve better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets time-pressed business employees and finance admins who need quick, self-serve answers to operational questions (e.g., "how to send or receive funds") without waiting on hold or filing a ticket. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of friction and anxiety: financial tasks carry higher stakes than typical consumer app support, so users need reassurance that help is immediate, judgment-free, and escalatable to a real human if needed.

The quick-reply chips leverage the path-of-least-resistance principle: rather than forcing users to compose a question from scratch, Brex anticipates common pain points and surfaces them, increasing the likelihood of first-contact resolution and improving perceived efficiency of the support experience.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual input modality: Combines quick-reply suggestion chips with an open text field, accommodating both novice and specific-need users.
  • Honest expectation-setting: The bot explicitly states its limitations and the fallback to human support upfront, building trust rather than creating false expectations of AI omniscience.
  • Low-friction exit controls: Both a back button and an explicit "End Chat" CTA give users full control to disengage at any point, reducing the "trapped in a chatbot" anxiety common to poor support UX.
  • Human-like typing indicator: The three-dot animation after a user query maintains conversational rhythm and signals active processing, reducing perceived wait-time anxiety.
  • Branded personality: The waving emoji and robot avatar inject warmth into a finance app that otherwise relies on minimal, serious dashboards.

screens.name: Brex - Chatting with support - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for customer support ecosystems where bots need to handle Tier-1 queries (FAQs, account status) before escalating to human agents.
  • Ideal for B2B SaaS or Fintech apps where linking to detailed documentation (rather than trying to explain complex policies in a chat bubble) is more effective.
  • Effective when you need to capture feedback on bot accuracy in real-time to improve NLU models.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for urgent, time-sensitive issues (e.g., reporting a stolen card) where a bot interaction might delay access to a human agent or emergency hotline.
  • Do not use heavy "Knowledge Article" cards if the support platform cannot guarantee articles are up-to-date; broken or irrelevant links erode trust in the automated system.
  • Not suitable for high-emotion complaint scenarios where users need empathetic human interaction rather than templated bot responses.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective or non-verified users interacting with the app pre-login or without a full business account, as evidenced by the bot's specific detection of "not logged in" status. It also serves existing employees/admins seeking quick self-service answers regarding fund transfers.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Path of Least Resistance principle (by offering immediate self-service links alongside human agent options, it reduces the "effort" cognitive load associated with support tickets). The inclusion of the "Apply for Brex business account" button specifically targets curious non-users, using the support context as a soft-sell trigger to convert window-shoppers into lead applicants.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Rich Media Embeds: Instead of just linking out, the bot presents a structured "Knowledge Article" card with a title and summary, allowing users to gauge relevance before clicking.
  • Dual Escape Hatches: The footer offers both a support escalation ("Speak with a Brex Specialist") and a sales conversion path ("Apply for Brex business account"), cleverly turning a support interaction into a potential lead-gen opportunity for non-customers.
  • Binary Feedback Loop: The simple thumbs up/down ("Was this helpful?") allows for low-friction AI training data collection without interrupting the chat flow.
  • Clear Session Control: The "End Chat" button is persistently visible in the header, giving users explicit control to exit the automated flow at any time.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech or wellness apps targeting younger demographics who respond better to conversational, personality-driven interfaces than clinical dashboards.

  • Products aiming to build daily habitual engagement by blending content discovery (tips, articles) with an interactive AI companion.

  • Apps that need to deliver sensitive behavior-change nudges (spending, addiction, health) where humor and informality can lower defensiveness.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth financial products where users expect a formal, authoritative tone and precise data (memey copy would undermine trust).

  • Regulated contexts requiring unambiguous, compliance-safe language; playful phrasing risks being misread as unprofessional financial advice.

  • Older or less digitally-native user bases who may find internet-slang tone confusing or off-putting rather than endearing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets Gen Z and young millennial users, particularly those who find traditional banking apps intimidating, boring, or shame-inducing. The persona is someone who scrolls Instagram/TikTok daily and responds better to a witty, informal "financial hype friend" than a spreadsheet or bank statement. Psychologically, the design leverages anthropomorphism (talking to a character named Cleo) to reduce the emotional friction of confronting overspending, and uses Socratic questioning (asking users to self-report the cost of a purchase) to trigger self-awareness through active recall rather than passive lecturing (a well-documented behavior-change technique). The subscription-cost callouts exploit loss aversion
screens.keyHighlights:
• Personality-Driven AI Chat: The bot doesn't just answer queries (it proactively interrogates the user's spending intent ("visualize that thing you wanna buy," "How much does that cost, roughly)?"), turning budgeting into a guided cognitive-behavioral exercise.

  • Hybrid Feed + Chat Architecture: Merging a swipeable insight/content feed with a persistent chat thread lets Cleo deliver both passive content marketing (subscription reminders, articles) and active conversational coaching in one continuous scroll.

  • Responsible-Use Content Injection: Surfacing a gambling-addiction educational card inside a financial app demonstrates ethical design, using the same punchy visual system for serious wellbeing content as for playful "Hype Mode" content.

  • Brand Voice as Retention Mechanic: The irreverent, meme-forward tone converts a mundane task (subscription tracking) into an entertaining, shareable moment, increasing daily engagement likelihood.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 13
screens.whereToUse: Utilize this conversational pattern for financial wellness apps, health tracking, or any utility where the underlying data (spending, calories, screen time) is emotionally sensitive. It works exceptionally well for micro-decisions (quick queries that benefit from an immediate, natural-language answer rather than requiring the user to navigate multiple menus to find raw data and interpret it themselves).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex data visualization needs, such as detailed multi-month trend analysis or portfolio management, where a chat bubble format cannot adequately display graphs, charts, or granular transaction lists. Additionally, this high-frequency, casual tone may alienate high-net-worth users or enterprise clients who require a more formal, data-dense interface for serious financial planning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious or budget-novice users (likely Gen Z/Millennials, as evidenced by the casual tone and meme-adjacent language) who find traditional banking apps intimidating or boring. The primary psychological trigger is the reduction of decision fatigue: by outsourcing the "can I afford this?" calculation to an AI, the user avoids the mental math and shame spiral often associated with checking their bank balance.

The use of a "friend" persona (Cleo) rather than a "bank" persona leverages the parasocial relationship trigger, making users more likely to engage honestly and frequently with their finances because it feels like texting a buddy, not confessing to a bank teller.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anthropomorphized Financial Guardrails: Instead of a static "Available Balance" widget, the app frames budgeting as a dialogue, making the restrictive nature of budgeting feel like helpful advice from a friend rather than a punitive system.

  • Zero UI Input Friction: The user doesn't need to navigate to a "calculator" tool; they simply type a number ("20") directly into the chat, and the system contextually understands it refers to the previous question about cost.

  • Actionable Insight Injection: The chat bubble intelligently appends a "Set income" link when it detects incomplete data, turning a simple answer into an opportunity for data enrichment/onboarding completion.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 14
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern when building financial, wellness, or habit-forming apps aimed at a younger demographic that needs its subject matter de-stigmatized or made more approachable. It's ideal for products layering an AI assistant/chatbot as the core interaction model, where a feed of proactive insights can prime users before they even type a query. Also effective for apps needing to blend transactional utility with content marketing/education in a single screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this tone and layout for enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth financial products where users expect precision, gravity, and density of real data over personality-driven content cards. This pattern is also risky for regulatory-heavy contexts where irreverent humor about money ("Bezos" comparisons) could be seen as undermining trust or seriousness. Additionally, a chat-input-first home screen can frustrate power users who want instant access to structured dashboards/data rather than needing to phrase a query.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This design clearly targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z/Millennials) who are often intimidated, bored, or alienated by traditional banking/budgeting apps. The meme aesthetics, playful quizzes, and chatbot-first framing lower the psychological barrier to engaging with personal finances, a topic often associated with shame or anxiety for this demographic.

Psychologically, the design leverages anthropomorphism (the "Cleo" persona acting as a sassy financial friend) to build parasocial trust and habitual engagement, similar to how users interact with Duolingo's owl or a horoscope app. The gamified quiz card exploits curiosity gaps ("What's Your Spend Style?") to drive click-through, while the "Balance vs. Bezos" card uses social comparison humor to make abstract net-worth numbers feel relatable and less clinical.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-first architecture: Placing a persistent natural-language input bar at the bottom transforms complex financial queries into a single, low-friction text box, bypassing traditional menu-diving.

  • Personality-driven content cards: Using bold meme-style typography and irreverent copy ("Your Balance vs. Bezos") to reframe potentially stressful financial data as entertaining, shareable content.

  • Dual-intent content grid: The "Explore" (quiz/gamified) vs "Get Smarter" (educational) split elegantly serves both users seeking entertainment and users seeking utility within the same visual real estate.

  • Feedback loop invitation: The subtle "Got feedback about your feed?" link demonstrates a lightweight, low-commitment mechanism for improving algorithmic content relevance without a disruptive survey modal.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 15
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this conversational-dashboard pattern when a product deals with inherently intimidating or emotionally charged data (personal finance, health, mental wellness) and wants to reduce anxiety through personality and plain language. It's especially effective for apps targeting audiences fatigued by traditional enterprise-style dashboards, or for AI-assistant-driven products where natural language querying is a core value proposition. Quick-reply chips work well anywhere you want to reduce typing effort and guide exploration paths.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for power users, analysts, or B2B contexts where dense, comparative, at-a-glance data visualization (charts, tables, trends over time) is essential (chat-based delivery is slower to parse than a well-designed graph when users need to compare many data points). Also avoid an overly casual/meme tone in contexts requiring institutional trust and gravitas (e.g., large wealth management, enterprise banking, regulatory disclosures), where humor can undermine perceived competence or trustworthiness.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z/millennial) who are often financially anxious, under-served by legacy banking UX, and more receptive to informal, meme-based communication than corporate financial jargon. The design leans on parasocial trust: talking to "Cleo" like a witty friend rather than a bank (which lowers the psychological barrier to engaging with sensitive money topics).

The quick-reply suggestions leverage the path-of-least-resistance principle: users are far more likely to tap a button than compose a follow-up question, increasing engagement depth and data the app can use to personalize further insights or upsell premium features (a common freemium chatbot monetization funnel).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-as-Dashboard: Replacing static charts with a conversational Q&A format makes financial data feel personal and less intimidating, especially for anxious or first-time budgeters.

  • Suggested Quick Replies: Pre-written follow-up prompts remove typing friction and actively guide users toward deeper engagement (categories, merchants, insights feed) - a classic chatbot UX best practice.

  • Editorial Content Carousel: The top "Explore" cards inject discovery and light-hearted engagement (personality quiz, tax season tips) into what would otherwise be a purely utilitarian finance app, increasing session time and emotional connection to the brand.

  • Emoji-Enhanced Data: Using emoji as visual affordances (💰💸📈) within plain text speeds up scanning and softens the seriousness of money talk.

  • Persistent Multi-Product Tab Bar: Chat sits equally alongside Spend/Budget/Save/Borrow/Habits, signaling it's a first-class navigation destination, not a hidden support feature.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial wellness apps targeting younger or first-time banking users who benefit from simplified, guided data exploration.

  • Any AI-assistant interface where you want to constrain user queries to a supported subset via suggested replies.

  • Products aiming to humanize dry, numeric data (finance, health metrics, analytics) through personality-driven microcopy.

  • Apps building trust with anxious users around sensitive topics (money, health) where a friendly tone can reduce avoidance behavior.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise or B2B financial/accounting tools where users need precise, exportable, tabular data rather than conversational summaries.

  • Contexts requiring rapid multi-metric comparison (e.g., comparing 12 months of spend) - chat bubbles do not scale well for dense tabular analysis.

  • Older or less tech-savvy demographics who may find playful/casual tone at odds with the seriousness of their financial situation (e.g., debt collection, hardship notices).

  • Regulated disclosures or compliance-sensitive information where emoji and informal tone could undermine clarity or legal precision.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, mobile-native users (Gen Z/Millennial) who are more comfortable texting than navigating spreadsheets or complex dashboards. Cleo's brand is explicitly built around demystifying and destigmatizing personal finance through humor, making it approachable for users who may feel anxiety or avoidance around traditional banking apps.

Psychologically, the conversational format leverages the same engagement loops as social messaging apps (familiarity, low friction, and instant gratification) to keep users returning to check their finances rather than avoiding a stressful task. The playful emoji use also reduces the shame/anxiety often associated with reviewing spending (e.g., overdraft fees), reframing financial literacy as entertainment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Quick-reply chips instead of free text: Constrains user input to a finite, answerable set of queries, dramatically improving AI reliability and reducing dead-end conversations.

  • Emoji-coded financial categories: Using emoji (💀 for bills, 💩 for bank charges, 💰 for income) creates instant visual/emotional association and injects brand personality into raw numeric data.

  • Chat bubble math transparency: Explicitly showing "+/-/=" arithmetic builds trust and comprehension without needing a chart.

  • "See more" progressive disclosure: Truncates the category list to the top 3 spend categories, avoiding overwhelming the chat window while still allowing drill-down.

  • Persistent conversational memory: The chat retains context of the date range (Feb 1 (23) across follow-up queries, so the user doesn't need to re-specify the timeframe).

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 17
screens.whereToUse:
• Finance, health, or habit-tracking apps where raw data is emotionally sensitive and benefits from a softened, personality-driven delivery.

  • Products aiming to differentiate from data-dense competitors by offering a low-friction, query-based alternative to dashboards.

  • Scenarios where users have varied, unpredictable questions (ad hoc reporting) better served by NL queries than by pre-built dashboard views.

  • Apps targeting younger or first-time users unfamiliar with financial jargon/charts, where a guiding conversational voice reduces intimidation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Power users or professionals (e.g., accountants, active traders) who need to scan large datasets quickly (chat bubbles are slower and harder to compare at a glance than tables/charts).

  • Contexts requiring precise multi-dimensional analysis (e.g., comparing 12 months side-by-side) where a conversational thread becomes unwieldy to scroll through.

  • Situations where trust and seriousness are paramount (e.g., displaying a loan default warning) - excessive humor/emoji could undermine credibility or feel tonally inappropriate.

  • Accessibility-critical contexts where emoji-heavy, informally-formatted text may not read well with screen readers or for users who prefer structured, literal data.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets financially anxious or dashboard-averse users (often younger, less financially literate audiences (Gen Z/millennials) who find bank apps' bar charts and category tables intimidating or boring). By reframing financial review as a casual text conversation with a witty "friend," Cleo lowers the emotional barrier to checking one's spending.

Psychologically, this leverages the conversational interface heuristic: humans are wired to trust and engage with dialogue more readily than static reports (parasocial rapport with the Cleo mascot). The humor (skull/poop emojis) also uses tension release: talking about being broke or overspending is stressful, and comedy defuses shame, encouraging users to keep checking in rather than avoid their finances (a common behavior called financial avoidance).

The chip-driven follow-ups exploit the path of least resistance: users are more likely to continue engaging when the next action is pre-written for them, increasing session depth and data engagement metrics for the app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-UI data exploration: Complex financial querying (date-ranged aggregation, category breakdown) is accessed via plain-language chat rather than filters/dropdowns, removing the learning curve typically associated with finance dashboards.

  • Progressive disclosure via quick-reply chips: Each bot response ends with a suggested next action, guiding the user deeper into their data one bite-sized step at a time instead of overwhelming them with a full report.

  • Personality-infused data: Emoji annotations (💀 for Bills, 💩 for Bank Charges) turn dry financial categories into emotionally resonant, meme-able content, making the mundane act of expense tracking feel entertaining.

  • Typing indicator for perceived liveness: The animated dots reinforce a real-time, human-like conversational rhythm that increases trust and engagement compared to instant static loads.

  • Persistent bottom input + tab bar: The chat input stays anchored at the bottom, always ready for a new query, while Chat remains a top-level tab alongside Spend/Budget/Save, cementing it as the app's primary interaction surface, not an add-on.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 18
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for consumer fintech, wellness, or habit-building apps targeting younger demographics where reducing anxiety and building daily habitual engagement is the primary goal. It works well when the brand has permission to be irreverent and when the core function (chat/AI assistant) benefits from a distinct, memorable personality to differentiate from competitors' clinical UIs.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this tone and visual density for enterprise, B2B, wealth management, or older/high-net-worth demographics where credibility and seriousness are paramount trust signals. Overly meme-heavy language on sensitive topics (like debt or addiction) can also backfire if not carefully balanced, potentially seeming dismissive of genuine user distress; the graphic tone must be tested carefully against user financial stress levels.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen is clearly engineered for a younger, digitally-native audience (Gen Z / younger Millennials) who are typically disengaged or intimidated by traditional banking apps. The design leverages the psychological principle of "approachability through humor" - by using meme formats and casual slang, it lowers the guard of users who associate finance with shame or stress. The juxtaposition of a serious topic (gambling addiction awareness) within the same visual carousel as lighthearted content ("Hype Mode") signals emotional versatility, positioning Cleo as a "friend who gets it" rather than an institution, which is critical to building trust and daily engagement (retention) with users who might otherwise avoid opening a banking app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Personality-driven content merchandising: Using vibrant, poster-like cards instead of generic list items to market financial education content makes literacy topics feel like entertainment.

  • Emoji-augmented navigation: Placing expressive emojis directly in tab/section titles reduces the emotional distance typically felt with money apps.

  • Humor as an anxiety-reduction tool: Visualizing "Bills" with an exaggerated, comedic graphic acknowledges the dread of bill season while diffusing it with humor before the user engages with the underlying feature.

  • Persistent floating identity badge: The circular "CLEO" wordmark bridges scroll states and view transitions, keeping brand presence anchored even mid-animation.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 19

It works well for younger demographics or brands aiming to disrupt a stodgy incumbent industry.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth financial products where users expect clinical precision, trust signals, and formal data visualization (e.g., wealth management dashboards). Humor and memes can undermine perceived credibility for serious transactions like large loans, tax filing, or legal documents, and may not translate well across different cultural/international meme literacy levels.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets Gen Z and Millennial users who are digital natives fluent in meme culture and internet shorthand, and who are often disengaged or anxious about traditional, jargon-heavy banking apps. By adopting the visual and tonal language of texting a witty friend rather than a bank, Cleo lowers the psychological barrier to entry for financial engagement.

The psychological trigger here is parasocial relationship building: users are more likely to open a finance app daily if it feels like checking a message from a friend rather than confronting a spreadsheet of debts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Personality-Driven Interface: Using a chat bubble UI transforms a mundane task (bill review) into a relatable conversation, lowering the emotional barrier to engaging with finances.

  • Meme Integration: Embedding a recognizable pop-culture GIF/image directly in the chat feed creates an immediate emotional connection and shareability factor.

  • Quick Reply Chips: The pill-shaped suggested replies ("live", "laugh", "bills") allow for frictionless continuation of the conversation without requiring typing.

  • Hub & Spoke Navigation: The bottom tab bar cleanly separates the "fun" AI chat from the functional modules (Spend, Budget, Save, Borrow, Habits).

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 20
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building financial wellness, budgeting, or fintech products targeting younger or financially-anxious demographics who benefit from friendly framing rather than clinical data display. Effective for delivering potentially stressful information (low balance, bills due, overspending alerts) in a way that maintains user retention and reduces app abandonment/avoidance. Also useful in coaching, habit-tracking, or health apps where an AI persona can soften hard truths and drive daily re-engagement through conversational check-ins.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for enterprise, B2B, or professional financial tools (e.g., accounting software, investment platforms) where users expect precise, dense data and a serious, authoritative tone (playful chat bubbles would undermine credibility). Also inappropriate for older or less tech-savvy demographics who may find the chatbot metaphor confusing or prefer direct numerical dashboards. Overuse of full-screen typographic interruptions can also feel gimmicky or slow down power users who want quick, scannable data across multiple accounts at once.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern is targeted at younger users (Gen Z / young millennials), particularly those living paycheck-to-paycheck who experience financial anxiety around bill due dates. The conversational, meme-inspired tone and Cleo's "sassy but supportive friend" persona is specifically engineered to reduce the shame and avoidance behavior that often accompanies checking bank balances or bills.

Psychological triggers at play include: loss aversion/urgency (bills due before payday creates a ticking clock), social/emotional validation (removing blame lowers defensive avoidance), and anthropomorphism (chatting with "Cleo" as a friend increases trust and daily habitual engagement compared to a sterile balance screen).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Conversational UI as financial dashboard: Replacing charts/tables with a chatbot persona humanizes cold financial data and increases engagement/return visits.

  • Emotional pre-framing before data delivery: The bot validates the user's feelings ("no one's fault") before hitting them with a bill amount, reducing defensive/anxious reactions.

  • Oversized typographic "shock card": Using massive, bold, high-contrast type as a mid-conversation visual break dramatically increases recall and scannability of the single most important fact (amount + deadline).

  • Color-coded hierarchy: Light blue for narrative words vs. vivid orange for the critical number creates instant visual parsing without needing to read every word.

  • Chat input bar mimics native messaging apps (iMessage/WhatsApp), exploiting existing user muscle memory to make a finance app feel effortless and familiar.

screens.name: H&M - Product filter - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adapt this pattern for any e-commerce, marketplace, or content-browsing app with a large catalog and multiple independent facets (price, category, attributes). It's particularly effective when:

  • The product set is large enough that unfiltered browsing is inefficient.
  • Filters are largely independent/non-hierarchical (so a flat list makes sense).
  • You can compute result counts cheaply/quickly enough to show live feedback without lag.
  • Omnichannel inventory (e.g., in-store stock) is a meaningful differentiator for the buying decision.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat drill-down filter pattern when:

  • There are very few filterable attributes: a single-screen filter with all options visible (no drill-down) would be faster.
  • Filters are highly interdependent (e.g., selecting one changes the validity of others) and need more sophisticated faceted-search UI with inline counts per option.
  • Result-count computation is slow or expensive, which would make the live "Showing X products" counter feel laggy or misleading.
  • The catalog is small enough that search or simple category browsing suffices, making a dedicated filter screen unnecessary overhead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves fashion-conscious shoppers browsing large, fast-rotating H&M catalogs (hundreds to thousands of SKUs per category) who need to quickly narrow results by concrete, decision-relevant attributes like size, fit, price, and store availability. The inclusion of "Store Availability" as a top-level facet specifically reflects H&M's omnichannel model, appealing to users who want to buy online but pick up or try on in-store.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduction of choice overload (Hick's Law) by collapsing all but the most critical filter into single-line entries, and uses loss-aversion mitigation via the live product count, which prevents the frustrating experience of applying filters only to discover zero results. The uppercase, gender-neutral, utilitarian typography avoids alienating any customer segment (young adults, families, existing loyalists) since filtering is a universal, non-aspirational task.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live result count above the CTA: Showing "765 products" dynamically updates as filters are adjusted, giving users real-time confidence that their narrowing criteria haven't eliminated all inventory (a subtle but powerful anti-frustration mechanism).
  • Dual CTA footer (Clear All / Apply): Separates the "reset" and "commit" actions with equal visual weight, letting power users quickly start over without navigating back out of the sheet.
  • Price Range expanded by default: Elevates the statistically most-used filter to the top and renders it inline with a slider and numeric labels, saving a tap compared to the drill-down pattern used for every other facet.
  • Flat, accordion-style list architecture: Every other filter category collapses into a single row with a disclosure chevron, keeping the initial view digestible and letting users self-select which facets matter to them rather than forcing a long scroll of expanded options.
  • Minimalist, high-contrast typography: Uppercase labels and thin rules keep the screen feeling editorial and on-brand even in a purely functional context, reinforcing H&M's fashion-retail identity.

screens.name: H&M - Product filter - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a single filter facet (color, size, brand, material) has many enumerable options in an e-commerce or content-discovery context. It's ideal when:

  • The attribute has a strong visual component (color, pattern) that benefits from swatches rather than text alone.
  • You want to prevent zero-result dead ends by showing live counts per option.
  • Filters are hierarchical/nested and a drill-down approach with a dedicated back button is appropriate.
  • Multi-select behavior is expected and a persistent Apply/Clear footer can batch the user's choices before committing.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this full-screen, list-based approach when:

  • There are only 2: 4 filter options (a simple chip row or segmented control inline on the results page would be faster and avoid unnecessary navigation).
  • Real-time count computation is expensive or slow, as stale/delayed counts would undermine the core trust benefit of this pattern.
  • The product catalog is small enough that filtering adds more friction than value (in these cases, direct browsing is preferable).
  • Screen space is extremely limited (e.g., smartwatch) where swatch+text+count density would be unreadable.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves fashion-conscious shoppers who often shop with a specific aesthetic or wardrobe-matching goal in mind (color is frequently the single most decisive attribute for apparel purchases, more so than brand or even price for casual browsing). By giving color its own dedicated full-screen filter (rather than burying it in a dropdown), H&M acknowledges how central this decision point is to its worldwide, trend-driven audience.

The psychological driver here is reduction of choice paralysis combined with confidence-building feedback. Showing live counts taps into the user's desire for efficient decision-making (nobody wants to select "Purple" only to discover there's a single ugly option). It also leverages the scarcity signal subtly (low counts like "[ 1 ]" or "[ 2 ]" implicitly communicate rarity, which can increase perceived desirability for niche shoppers).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual visual encoding: Pairing text labels with actual color swatch dots lets users filter by color recognition rather than relying purely on language, which is especially helpful for ambiguous terms like "Multi" or distinguishing shades.
  • Live inventory counts per option: Displaying product counts next to every color (e.g., "[ 1 ]" for Purple vs. "[ 440 ]" for Blue) lets users gauge selection impact before applying, preventing dead-end empty states.
  • Persistent result preview footer: "Showing 765 products" updates contextually, giving continuous feedback and confidence before the user commits to the APPLY action.
  • Clear escape hatches: Both a back arrow (return to filter list) and an X (dismiss entirely) are offered, respecting different user mental models of "cancel."
  • Disabled Clear All state: Graying out "CLEAR ALL" when no filters are selected communicates current state and prevents unnecessary taps.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 31
screens.whereToUse:
• Support/help flows in fintech, e-commerce, or subscription apps where a user has drilled down into a specific order/transaction/item and self-service content failed to resolve their issue.

  • Any screen where you want to escalate from automated/self-serve help to human-assisted support without offering too many competing channels.

  • Use the "contextual anchor card" pattern whenever the support conversation needs to reference a specific object (order, transaction, booking) to avoid re-explaining context.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this minimal single-channel approach for complex B2B or enterprise support scenarios where users may need phone support, ticket tracking, or SLA-backed responses (chat-only may feel insufficient).

  • Not appropriate for urgent/critical issues (e.g., fraud, account lockout) where a phone number or emergency contact option should be prominently offered alongside or instead of chat.

  • Should not be used if the underlying chat support is slow or bot-only with poor resolution rates, as funneling all traffic into a single weak channel will amplify user frustration rather than reduce it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already attempted self-service resolution (likely via an FAQ or help article list prior to this screen) and were unsuccessful, making them moderately frustrated and time-sensitive. This is common in fintech/payments apps (e.g., Cash App, Venmo) where transaction disputes or failed transfers cause real anxiety about money.

The psychological trigger at play is reduction of cognitive load during stress: when users are anxious about money, presenting a single clear path forward (Chat) rather than a menu of choices reduces decision fatigue and perceived effort, increasing the likelihood they complete the escalation rather than abandoning the app or venting on social media/app store reviews.

Referencing the specific transaction also leverages the Zeigarnik effect: showing the "incomplete" or in-question task keeps it top-of-mind and reassures the user that the support system has retained context from their prior navigation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual anchoring: Surfacing the specific transaction ($1 add money) at the top of the support screen removes the need for the user to explain "which" transaction they have an issue with, reducing agent back-and-forth and user effort.

  • Single, decisive CTA: Rather than overwhelming the user with multiple support channels, the screen funnels to one clear action (Chat), eliminating decision paralysis at a moment when the user may already be frustrated.

  • Escape hatches preserved: Both a back arrow and a close (X) icon are present, respecting user autonomy and preventing a "trapped in a flow" feeling common in poorly designed support funnels.

  • Human, first-person heading: "I need more help" is written from the user's perspective, which is a subtle but effective microcopy trick that increases perceived relevance and click-through on support escalation paths.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 32
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any customer support surface in transactional, fintech, or utility apps where a small set of issues account for the majority of support volume. It's especially effective when:

  • Users are likely to be stressed, frustrated, or unsure how to articulate their problem.

  • You want to deflect tickets to automation without feeling dismissive.

  • The support experience benefits from asynchronous, notification-based follow-up rather than forcing live engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when support issues are highly varied or complex and can't be reduced to a handful of canned intents, forcing users through irrelevant quick-replies when their issue doesn't match any option creates frustration. Also avoid purely bot-driven flows for emergency, time-critical situations (e.g., suspected active fraud) without an immediate, prominent escalation path to a live human agent, as delayed async responses could increase user distress rather than alleviate it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets the full spectrum of Cash App's mass-market user base, particularly users experiencing financial stress or anxiety (e.g., fraud concerns, declined transactions, missing cards) who need fast reassurance. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of cognitive load during a high-anxiety moment: when money is involved, users want immediate, low-effort paths to resolution rather than navigating complex support taxonomies or typing lengthy explanations.

The pre-filled prompts also serve Cash App's business need to deflect support volume: by anticipating and pre-answering the most frequent tickets via bot, they reduce human agent load while still making the user feel heard and quickly served.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Predictive Quick-Reply Chips: Surfacing the top 5 most common support intents as tappable bubbles dramatically reduces user effort and support ticket ambiguity.

  • Asynchronous Expectation-Setting: Explicitly telling users they can leave and be notified later removes the pressure of a live-chat "wait" state, a major source of support frustration.

  • Familiar Messaging UI Paradigm: Reusing the iMessage-style bubble layout creates zero learning curve for users already fluent in mobile texting.

  • Humanized Bot Persona: "Cashbot" with a friendly avatar reduces the coldness typically associated with automated support, priming users for a more tolerant, patient interaction with an AI.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 33
screens.whereToUse: Use a bottom-sheet account switcher when: (1) your product supports multiple account types (personal/business, multiple profiles) under one login, (2) you want switching to feel lightweight and reversible rather than a full-page navigation event, and (3) you need to keep the primary screen's context visible/dimmed behind the action to reduce disorientation. Combine with profile completion nudges and incentive-based cross-promotion (referrals, rewards) on the parent screen to keep engagement high while account management remains just a tap away.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for apps with only a single account type or no valid use case for multiple identities (it adds unnecessary complexity). Also avoid stacking too many incentive nudges (photo, invite, verification) on one profile screen, as it can overwhelm users and dilute the purpose of the page from "profile management" into "notification center." For account switching with heavy legal/compliance implications (e.g., switching between entirely separate banking entities), a full-screen confirmation flow with more explicit disclosures may be safer than a lightweight bottom sheet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday consumers of a peer-to-payment or fintech app who may also run a side hustle or small business, needing to toggle between a personal and business identity without separate logins. The design leverages loss-aversion and reciprocity (the $5 referral incentive), social proof/pressure (profile photos help "people find you," implying social visibility matters), and Zeigarnik effect (the red dot signaling incomplete personal information nags at the user's need for closure).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Layered modal architecture: The account switcher is presented as a bottom sheet over a dimmed background, preserving context and signaling this is a lightweight, dismissible action rather than a full navigation change.

  • Incentivized profile completion: Pairing "Add a profile photo" with a soft benefit and "Invite friends" with a hard monetary reward ($5) uses two different motivational levers (social trust vs. financial gain) to drive engagement.

  • Attention-directing red dot: A minimal status dot on "Personal information" nudges users toward an incomplete or important task without an intrusive banner.

  • Clear active-state indicator: The checkmark badge on the currently selected account avatar in the sheet gives instant, unambiguous confirmation of context.

  • Dashed/outline "+" for account creation: Visually differentiates the "add new" action from existing account rows using an established plus-in-circle convention.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 34
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any account/profile settings screen where a small set of identity attributes (name, handle, avatar) need to be edited and where users benefit from previewing the public representation of their profile before saving. It's ideal for social, fintech, or marketplace apps where a username or public alias carries reputational or transactional significance (e.g., payment apps, social networks, marketplace seller profiles).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are many editable fields that would make drill-down navigation tedious (e.g., a fully-featured e-commerce seller profile with dozens of fields) - in that case, a single scrollable form or accordion layout would reduce navigation overhead. It's also unnecessary for private/internal-only data with no public preview value, since the Edit/Preview toggle would add complexity without benefit. Skip the drill-down pattern if fields are trivial (e.g., a simple bio checkbox) where inline editing would be faster.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday Cash App users: often younger, mobile-first consumers (who want quick, low-friction control over their public payment identity (name, $cashtag, avatar) without navigating complex account settings). The psychological trigger here is identity ownership and control: allowing a user to preview their public-facing profile taps into self-presentation concerns, similar to social media profile editing, which increases engagement and reduces anxiety about how they appear to peers when sending/requesting money.

The simplicity and lack of clutter also serve trust-building: in a financial app, an overly complex or cluttered settings screen can create doubt about security or reliability, so Cash App keeps this screen deliberately spare.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Edit/Preview toggle: Lets users instantly verify how their public profile will look before leaving the screen, closing the feedback loop that most profile editors leave open.

  • Contextual photo affordance: The floating camera icon on the avatar is a universally understood micro-interaction that avoids extra buttons or text instructions.

  • Progressive disclosure via drill-down rows: Sensitive/validated fields like $cashtag are pushed to their own screens, keeping this overview screen simple and reducing error surface area.

  • Explanatory microcopy: A single reassuring sentence at the top of the Basic Info section preempts confusion about visibility/consequences of the edit.

screens.name: H&M - Filtering products (price range) - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• E-commerce search/category results pages where reinforcing brand tone alongside functional browsing is a priority.
  • Retail apps running frequent promotions, where a persistent discount banner and corner badges can consistently drive conversion.
  • Multi-audience retailers (women/men/kids) needing to let users pivot segments without re-searching.
  • Any product grid where high-quality imagery is the primary selling tool and text should be minimized.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid oversized editorial headlines on results pages for utilitarian or B2B software, where users expect density and efficiency over brand flourish.
  • Persistent sale banners can feel manipulative or cause banner-blindness fatigue if used outside of genuine promotional periods or across every single screen indefinitely.
  • Truncated product titles are risky for categories where specification details (size, material, model) are critical to the purchase decision, such as electronics or furniture.
  • Heavy discount badges can cheapen a premium/luxury brand's perceived positioning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets value-conscious, fashion-forward shoppers who browse by category or keyword rather than committing early to a single item. The heavy use of discount badges, red pricing, and a sitewide sale banner leverages scarcity and urgency psychology to accelerate purchase decisions among price-sensitive young adults and families (a core H&M demographic).

The oversized, editorial typography for the search term speaks to the "fashion-conscious shopper" persona who expects a stylish, magazine-like browsing experience even in utilitarian moments like search results, reinforcing brand affinity alongside functional task completion.

The segmented category counts (WOMEN, MEN, BABY) also reflect H&M's family-oriented customer base, allowing a single search to serve multiple shopping missions (e.g., a parent shopping for themselves and their child) within one session.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized editorial query echo: Rendering the search term "DENIM JEANS" in huge bold type turns a mundane results page into a fashion-magazine-style moment, reinforcing brand identity even in a transactional flow.
  • Inline result counts on category chips: Showing [765], [429], [122] builds confidence in inventory depth and lets users self-filter by audience segment instantly.
  • Persistent sale banner: The "SALE: UP TO 60% OFF" bar stays fixed above all navigation, continuously nudging toward discounted inventory regardless of where the user browses.
  • Dual badge-and-strikethrough pricing: Combining a percentage-off corner badge with a strikethrough original price and red sale price creates multiple reinforcing cues of value, appealing to bargain-driven psychology.
  • Floating wishlist heart on tiles: Enables one-tap saving directly from the grid without entering product detail, reducing friction for comparison shopping.

screens.name: H&M - Filtering products (price range) - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any e-commerce or content-browsing app with a large catalog and multiple independent filter dimensions (price, category, attributes). It's ideal when:

  • The number of filter types exceeds 5-6, making a single flat screen with all options expanded impractical.
  • Real-time or near-real-time result counts can be computed cheaply, so users get instant feedback as they adjust filters.
  • Users need both coarse (price slider) and granular (drill-in list) filtering in the same session.
screens.whereNotToUse:
This pattern is less suitable when:

  • The catalog is small or has few meaningful attributes (a lightweight inline filter bar or chip-based filter row would be faster and less heavy-handed).
  • Result counts are expensive or slow to compute, which would force a stale or delayed counter that undermines the trust this pattern relies on.
  • Users are on very short, task-focused flows (e.g., a single-category micro-store) where a full-screen modal with 9+ options would feel like over-engineering and add unnecessary friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves fashion-conscious shoppers browsing large, varied inventories who need to narrow results efficiently (whether a parent filtering kids' sizes, a shopper with a strict budget, or someone seeking a specific color or material). The sheer number of filter facets (store availability, fit, style, customer group) speaks to H&M's broad, cross-demographic catalog spanning menswear, womenswear, kidswear, and home goods.

Psychologically, the design leverages the certainty principle: showing the live product count reduces the perceived risk of "filtering into nothing," a common abandonment trigger in e-commerce filter UIs. The collapsed-list structure also taps into chunking: breaking a complex decision (which of 9 filter types to adjust) into small, independently explorable units rather than overwhelming the user with all options expanded simultaneously.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live result counter: Surfacing "Showing 765 products" directly above the Apply button gives users immediate confidence about the impact of their filter choices before committing, preventing the frustration of a zero-result dead end.
  • Progressive disclosure via drill-down facets: Only Price Range is expanded by default; all other filters collapse into single-line entries with chevrons, keeping the screen digestible despite housing nine+ distinct filter categories.
  • Dual-handle range slider: A tactile, visual way to set min/max price bounds that's far more intuitive than two numeric text fields, with live numeric labels ($6.99 ($109).00) updating above the track.
  • Separated destructive vs. committing actions: "Clear All" and "Apply" are placed side-by-side but are visually and functionally distinct, reducing accidental resets.

screens.name: H&M - Filtering products (price range) - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this two-level filter pattern for any large e-commerce catalog, marketplace, or content library where the number of filterable attributes exceeds 5-6 (fashion, electronics, real estate, or travel listings are ideal candidates). It's especially effective when:

  • The product set is large enough that a single-screen filter panel would require heavy scrolling or accordion nesting.
  • You want to maintain a lightweight, fast-loading filter tray while still offering deep faceted search.
  • Real-time result counts can be computed cheaply enough to update live as users navigate between filter categories.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the catalog is small or when there are only 2-3 filter dimensions (in that case, a single flat list of chips or a simple segmented control would be faster and avoid the extra navigation hop). It's also a poor fit for touch contexts where network latency makes the live product counter sluggish or inaccurate, as a stale/slow counter undermines the trust this pattern is designed to build. Finally, for category sets so large that browsing is more exploratory than attribute-driven (e.g., open-ended content discovery feeds), a more visual/faceted browse or algorithmic recommendation surface may serve users better than a plain textual filter list.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves high-intent fashion shoppersbrowsing H&M's large, frequently-refreshed worldwide catalog who need to narrow thousands of SKUs down by concrete attributes like brand, material, or fit. For young adults and families shopping across multiple categories (kids, licensed collabs, basics), granular filters like "Customer Group" and "Licensed Item" directly address real purchase blockers (e.g., finding the right size group or character-branded merchandise).

Psychologically, the screen leverages progressive disclosure to reduce choice overload, showing only category names first lowers the cognitive barrier to engaging with filters at all. The live counter taps into a sense of control and certainty, which is particularly important for mobile shoppers who are impatient and want assurance their taps are productive before committing to viewing results.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live result count above the CTA: Continuously updating the "Showing X products" label right next to the Apply button closes the feedback loop instantly, preventing the frustrating experience of applying filters and landing on an empty state.
  • Two-tier filter architecture: Separating "categories" (this screen) from "values" (sub-screens) keeps each screen cognitively light (no single screen overwhelms the user with hundreds of checkboxes at once).
  • Disabled-state button styling: Both Clear All and Apply appear greyed out/disabled in this default state, visually communicating that no changes have been made yet and nothing is actionable until the user engages with at least one filter.
  • Expandable "More Filters" entry point: Using a "+" icon instead of a chevron subtly differentiates this row as an expansion/reveal action rather than a drill-down navigation, respecting iconographic consistency.

results.query: How to handle high cognitive load in multi-account balance overviews

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building detail views for financial or resource containers (budgets, project codes, wallets, team accounts) where a user needs to see a roll-up of related entities (transactions, instruments, permissions) in one scrollable surface. It is ideal for B2B SaaS admin panels where hierarchy (Budget > Cards > Members) needs to be flattened into a single, digestible view.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, multi-section list approach for consumer-facing apps or simple personal finance tools where users manage only a single account; the "Managed by/Members" governance sections would be unnecessary clutter. Additionally, if the number of cards or members is very high (e.g., hundreds), this flat list will require pagination or search filtering to remain usable, as the current design assumes a relatively small, finite list of associated items.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves Finance Admins and Team Managers who are responsible for overseeing a specific budget, project, or department's spending. It answers three key managerial questions instantly: "What was just spent?", "What cards draw from this budget?", and "Who is allowed to spend here?"

The psychological trigger here is control and accountability. By surfacing "Managed by" and "Members" so prominently, Brex reinforces the mental model that spending is not anonymous (it is attributed to specific people and overseen by specific managers, which subtly encourages responsible spending behavior among employees who know their activity is transparently logged against this view).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Modular Section Headers: The grey background bars for "Cards," "Alerts," "Managed by," and "Members" create strong visual chunking, acting as an organic table of contents that aids rapid orientation in a long scrolling list.
  • Inline Status Iconography: The top transaction row displays sync/receipt/approval icons directly in the list, eliminating the need to tap into the transaction just to check its compliance status.
  • Dual-Card Visualization: Displaying both a physical/virtual card art alongside the masked card number provides quick visual recognition for multi-card holders.
  • Non-Modal Close Affordance: The 'X' icon paired with a drag handle gives users two intuitive ways to dismiss the sheet (a swipe-down gesture or a direct tap) catering to different interaction habits.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a feature has multiple distinct notification triggers tied to a single object (e.g., a budget, subscription, project, or threshold) and users need fine-grained, independent control over each. It's ideal for finance, project management, or monitoring tools where different alert types have different urgency or relevance per user. Also effective as a contextual "mini settings" modal launched from an overflow menu, keeping deep configuration close to the object it affects rather than forcing navigation to a separate settings area.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are very few notification options (a single toggle would suffice and this adds unnecessary modal overhead), or when notifications are critical for compliance/safety (in those cases, defaulting to off could cause users to miss essential alerts, so an opt-out default or mandatory notification might be more appropriate). Also avoid duplicating the exact same toggles in both a contextual modal and the global settings screen without synchronization, as this can create confusing or conflicting states for the user.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves finance team members, budget owners, and employees managing a company card or spend limit who want proactive visibility into their spending status without manually checking balances. The psychological driver is loss aversion and control: employees and admins fear hitting a limit unexpectedly (which can block a purchase or cause embarrassment) or missing an expiration that disrupts ongoing work. Giving users granular control over exactly which alerts they receive (approaching limit, expiring soon, expired) satisfies the need for autonomy while reducing the anxiety of being caught off guard financially.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual entry point: Notification settings are scoped to the specific spend limit being viewed, reducing the need to hunt through global settings.
  • Grouped, labeled toggle rows: Each alert type has its own header and one-line explanation, making the consequence of enabling/disabling instantly clear.
  • Opt-in defaults: All toggles start off, respecting user attention and avoiding notification fatigue by default.
  • Escape hatch to global settings: The "View all notification settings" button bridges local and global configuration without adding complexity to this focused screen.
  • Modal dismissal pattern: A clear circular "X" signals this is a lightweight overlay, not a core navigation screen, letting users quickly return to their prior context.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building threshold-based or event-based notification settings for any metered resource (budgets, data usage, storage quotas, subscription limits, or inventory counts). It's ideal when a user needs to customize both whether they get notified and at what threshold, especially when that threshold has both a relative (%) and absolute (currency/unit) meaning. The toast-confirmation + grouped toggle layout is well suited to any settings screen with multiple related-but-distinct alert types.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of granularity for casual consumer apps where users are unlikely to want to fine-tune thresholds (a simple on/off toggle with a sensible default is less overwhelming for low-stakes notifications). Also avoid combining percentage and currency sliders if the resource has no natural dollar equivalent, as that would add confusing, non-applicable units. For mobile screens with limited vertical space, excessive sections (3+) with descriptions and toggles can feel long; consider collapsing into an accordion if more alert types are added in the future.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets finance admins, budget owners, and employees who have been assigned a spend limit or card budget and want proactive visibility into their spending without manually checking the app. The psychological driver here is control and anxiety reduction: by letting users set a custom threshold (e.g., 80%) rather than a fixed system default, Brex gives users a sense of ownership over how and when they are interrupted, which increases trust and reduces alert fatigue.

The toggle-based structure also appeals to the target audience's need for customization at scale: finance teams managing multiple budgets need fine-grained, predictable alerting so they aren't caught off guard by overspending or an expired limit, which could cause embarrassment or business disruption (e.g., a failed company purchase).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-unit slider readout: Simultaneously displaying percentage and dollar equivalent ($480.00 / 80%) removes the need for users to mentally convert between relative and absolute spend thresholds.
  • Immediate toast confirmation: The green-check "Budget limit alert: On" toast provides instant, low-friction feedback that a toggle change was successfully persisted.
