  • Progressive disclosure of slider: The percentage slider is only relevant and presumably only interactive when its parent toggle is active, keeping the UI decluttered for disabled states.
  • Grouped settings sections with dividers: Clear visual separation between the three alert types prevents accidental misconfiguration and aids scannability.
  • Escape hatch CTA: "View all notification settings" acknowledges this is a scoped/contextual settings view and offers a path to the broader preference center.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial apps needing to display a primary account balance alongside secondary linked accounts without overwhelming the user.

  • Products that want to soften potentially stressful data (low balances, debt) with tasteful illustration and typography instead of sterile numbers.

  • Multi-account fintech tools where horizontal carousels can efficiently surface a "connect more accounts" upsell in situ.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in enterprise, B2B, or professional financial dashboards where users need to compare multiple accounts simultaneously (horizontal carousels hide information and require extra swiping, which is inefficient for power users or accountants). Also avoid playful illustration/emoji treatments in contexts requiring high formality or trust signals (e.g., mortgage or investment platforms) where seriousness reinforces credibility. Truncated transaction labels should be avoided if users frequently need to distinguish between similarly-named transactions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday users: likely younger, financially-anxious millennials/Gen Z (who want quick reassurance about their balance without diving into a spreadsheet-like banking app). The low balance shown ($58.96) suggests the target demographic lives close to paycheck-to-paycheck and needs an approachable, non-judgmental way to check in on money.

Psychologically, the whimsical illustrations (space theme, cartoon thumb) reduce the shame or stress often tied to checking a low balance, aligning with Cleo's brand promise of a "blunt but caring" money coach. The quick-glance balance and simplified transaction feed cater to users who want financial awareness with minimal cognitive load, deferring deeper analysis to the Chat or Budget tabs.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Illustrated Balance Card: Turning a boring numeric balance into a mini illustrated scene (glowing planets, bold typography) reduces the anxiety typically associated with checking bank balances, especially low ones like $58.96.

  • Card Carousel with Edge Peek: The partially visible red "Connect" card teases additional functionality (linking more accounts) without needing an explicit label or arrow, driving curiosity-based interaction.

  • Emoji Iconography for Transactions: Using expressive icons (money bag, skull with sparkle) instead of flat bank logos for each transaction row adds character and makes scanning transaction types faster and more memorable.

  • Balanced Typography Hierarchy: The dollar amount uses a large integer with a smaller decimal suffix ($58.96), a common fintech trick to make numbers feel more impactful and readable at a glance.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when an app needs to expose granular, auditable data (transactions, logs, order history) as a secondary layer beneath a primary conversational or dashboard experience. It's ideal for fintech, expense tracking, or any AI-assistant product where users need an escape hatch to verify the source data behind automated insights. The modal/sheet presentation is especially useful for maintaining focus on a core flow (like chat) while still offering full detail on demand.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the transaction/data list is the primary user journey (in that case it deserves a dedicated tab or full-screen view rather than a dismissible modal, which can feel like a dead-end). Also avoid injecting playful icons/emoji into financial ledgers for enterprise, B2B, or highly formal financial products where users expect strict, unembellished bank-standard presentation for compliance or trust reasons.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves users who've connected an external bank account (RBC) to Cleo and want to audit recent activity behind the AI's chat-based summaries. It appeals to users who want reassurance and transparency (verifying that Cleo's snarky commentary about their spending is backed by real data) while still being anchored in Cleo's brand identity through icon choices. The psychological trigger is trust-building through transparency: by making raw transaction data easily accessible, Cleo reduces skepticism that could arise from an AI-only interface with no visible ledger.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Modal-based drill-down: Presenting the transaction ledger as a dismissible sheet/modal (X icon) rather than a full navigational push keeps users anchored to the chat-first flow, reinforcing that this is supplementary detail, not the primary interface.

  • Personified iconography: Swapping generic bank/merchant icons for whimsical emoji (skull, flame, money bag) injects brand personality into an otherwise mundane financial ledger.

  • 'Left to spend' reframing: Converts a neutral balance figure into coaching language, subtly nudging budget-consciousness even in a data view.

  • Two-tier amount typography: Large dollar digits paired with smaller cents improves scanability of financial figures at a glance.

  • Color-coded transaction direction: Green credits vs. black/dark debits allow instant visual parsing without reading each line.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Use illustrated, personality-driven empty states when the primary blocking action is emotionally sensitive (e.g., linking financial/health data) to reduce perceived risk.

  • Show "shell" content modules (e.g., empty transaction lists) pre-activation to preview future functionality and create anticipation.

  • Pair a bold carousel CTA with secondary, less prominent utility actions (add/manage) to accommodate users at different readiness levels.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid overly playful illustration and humor in contexts requiring high trust/formality, such as legal consent screens or actual credential-entry forms.

  • Don't rely on an empty-state carousel if the user has already dismissed or declined the action multiple times (repeated nagging can feel patronizing rather than charming).

  • Not suitable for data-dense finance apps targeting professional/enterprise users who expect immediate charts and figures rather than mascot illustrations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially disengaged or anxious users (Cleo's core demographic of younger, spending-conscious consumers) who may find traditional bank-linking flows intimidating or boring. By using humor, bold color, and mascot-driven illustration, Cleo lowers the psychological barrier to a high-stakes action (sharing bank credentials via Plaid/Open Banking) and frames it as fun and low-risk rather than clinical.

The empty "Recent Transactions" state leverages the Zeigarnik effect and curiosity gap (an incomplete visual promise (the card exists but is empty) nudges the user toward closing that loop by connecting an account).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empty state used as a feature preview: Showing the "Recent Transactions" card even when empty telegraphs future value and motivates the connect-a-bank action rather than hiding the module entirely.

  • Illustration-led CTA card: Using an oversized, comedic thumbs-up illustration to soften the friction of a sensitive action (bank linking) is a clever emotional design choice unique to Cleo's brand voice.

  • Carousel with page dots: Signals there is more content/mascot personality to swipe through, keeping the header area feeling alive rather than static.

  • Dual low-commitment entry points: "Add account" and "Manage accounts" icon buttons give users choice/control without forcing a single funnel.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern during any OAuth handoff, bank-linking, or third-party data integration step (e.g., Plaid, Yodlee, SSO providers).

  • Ideal for moments where the user must wait for an external API/service to authenticate, and you want to visually reassure them of a secure partnership rather than leave a blank spinner.

  • Effective when transitioning tone from playful brand voice to a more neutral, trust-building register for compliance-sensitive tasks.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for long-running processes without any progress feedback (if the actual connection takes more than a couple of seconds, a determinate progress indicator or looping animation state is needed to avoid perceived freezing).

  • Don't use this fully brand-muted, copy-free approach in flows unrelated to security/trust building, as it would waste an opportunity to reinforce Cleo's distinctive comedic voice.

  • Not suitable if the user needs specific instructions (e.g., "keep this window open") - pure iconography without any supporting microcopy can confuse users unfamiliar with the linking process.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new users (or existing users adding a new account) at the most vulnerable point of the financial app funnel: granting access to their actual bank credentials/transaction data. The psychological trigger being managed here is risk aversion and security anxiety. Financial app users abandon linking flows at extremely high rates if the process feels opaque or sketchy. By stripping the UI down to a clean, neutral "connecting" state and briefly suppressing Cleo's usual irreverent personality, the app signals "this part is serious and secure," borrowing credibility from the trusted banking aggregator logo shown alongside its own.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Brand-to-Partner Handshake Visual: Using two distinct circular logos joined by an animated dotted connector instantly communicates "these two systems are talking to each other" without needing any explanatory copy.

  • Anxiety Reduction via Whitespace: Removing all other UI chrome (tab bars, menus) during a sensitive OAuth/bank-linking handoff prevents the user from feeling like they can "break" something by tapping elsewhere.

  • Retained Exit Control: The persistent 'X' button ensures the user never feels trapped in a third-party redirect, which is essential for maintaining trust during financial data sharing.

  • Modal-over-Modal Structure: The visible sliver of the previous blue screen at the top signals a layered navigation stack, reassuring the user they can back out to their previous context.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an app must request sensitive, high-stakes permissions (bank linking, health data, identity verification) mid-onboarding. It's ideal immediately before a native SDK handoff (e.g., Plaid Link) to prime the user with reassurance, reducing drop-off and support complaints. Also effective for apps integrating trusted third-party infrastructure providers, where co-branding can borrow credibility.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy reassurance pattern for low-stakes or already-trusted actions (e.g., enabling notifications), where it would feel like overkill and add unnecessary friction. Also avoid injecting brand humor or mascot personality here, as levity during a security/consent moment can undermine perceived seriousness and trust. Don't use if your legal/compliance team requires more prominent, unmissable disclosure (the small privacy policy link may be insufficient for stricter regulatory contexts).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are already engaged and motivated (having progressed through onboarding) but are hitting the highest-friction step of any finance app: authorizing bank access. This population skews toward users with some hesitancy or prior data-privacy anxiety, especially younger, mobile-first users who may not fully trust dashboards run by a lesser-known fintech "AI coach" app.

Psychologically, it leverages authority/third-party credibility bias (Plaid is a recognizable infrastructure brand many banking apps use) and loss-aversion framing ("Your data belongs to you," "Protect your accounts") to reduce perceived risk immediately before the ask.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-brand trust transfer: Overlapping Cleo and Plaid logos visually signal a secure "handoff" partnership rather than Cleo alone vouching for security.

  • Objection-based content architecture: Each of the three benefit blocks directly answers a specific psychological objection (ease, privacy, safety) rather than generic marketing copy.

  • Tone-shift as UX signal: Cleo intentionally suppresses its comedic brand voice here, using sober, plain language to signal seriousness at a high-stakes consent moment.

  • Low-friction dismissal: The X button offers an escape hatch without forcing a decision, respecting user control over sensitive financial permissions.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any settings/management surface involving sensitive, linked third-party accounts (banking, calendars, health data, connected apps). It's ideal when:

  • Users need to review, hide, or disconnect linked data sources.

  • The action is infrequent and doesn't warrant a full dedicated screen (a modal/bottom sheet keeps it lightweight).

  • Trust and clarity are more important than brand personality or delight.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stripped-down, low-personality approach for flows where brand engagement or delight is the primary goal (e.g., core dashboards, celebratory moments) as it would feel flat. Also avoid relying solely on a hidden "swipe to remove" gesture for destructive actions if your target audience skews toward users unfamiliar with swipe gestures (e.g., less tech-savvy or older demographics) - always pair with a visible fallback like an edit/kebab menu for accessibility. Additionally, removing a bank account is a fairly destructive action; consider adding a confirmation step before finalizing a swipe-to-remove to prevent accidental disconnects.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already onboarded and linked at least one bank account with Cleo, and are now in a maintenance/trust-verification mindset rather than a discovery mindset. Psychologically, users visiting a "Manage bank accounts" screen are often driven by a need for control and reassurance: checking that their sensitive financial data is handled correctly, or preparing to add another account/paycheck source for more complete AI coaching.

The single bold "Connect another bank" CTA also serves Cleo's core business need: the more accounts linked, the richer and more accurate the AI money coach's insights and roasts become, directly improving retention and perceived value of the product.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Tonal restraint as a design decision: Cleo deliberately drops its comedic mascot voice here, using neutral, precise language because this screen touches real financial credentials and balances (a rare and smart example of a brand knowing when *not* to be funny).

  • Account visibility toggle: Letting a user hide an account (rather than only fully disconnect it) is a subtle but powerful feature for shared-finance or multi-account users who want Cleo's coaching/roasts to ignore certain accounts without losing the underlying bank connection.

  • Inline hint over icon clutter: Instead of showing a visible delete icon on every row, the "Swipe left to remove" caption teaches the gesture once, keeping the row minimal while still ensuring discoverability.

  • Freshness timestamp: "updated 20 minutes ago" builds trust in the accuracy of Open Banking data sync, addressing a common user doubt ("is this balance still correct?").

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet stepper pattern when a single, low-complexity numeric preference needs to be set (e.g., "items per page," "reminder frequency," "list length"). It's ideal for settings that don't require multi-field forms and benefit from an oversized, playful primary control.

The illustrated card carousel approach works well for surfacing multiple linked accounts/entities in fintech apps, especially when trying to soften the emotional weight of raw financial data.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stepper pattern for settings involving many options, ranges, or multi-variable configuration (a slider or full picker would be more space-efficient). Also avoid oversized illustrated financial cards in contexts requiring high information density (e.g., professional trading or business banking apps) where users expect precise, no-frills data.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves financially anxious or disengaged users (Cleo's core demographic) who need lightweight control over data density without being overwhelmed by complex settings menus. Users with low balances (like the $58.96 shown) benefit from Cleo's non-judgmental, illustrated presentation that reduces shame around checking finances.

The stepper's simplicity caters to users who want quick customization without navigating deep settings hierarchies, aligning with Cleo's "chat-first, no dashboards" philosophy (even traditional list-based settings are minimized to a single adjustable number).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Whimsical Bank Cards: Turning a linked checking account into a stylized "card" with illustrated planets softens the anxiety typically associated with checking a low balance ($58.96).

  • Oversized Stepper UI: The giant numeral and large circular +/- buttons make a normally minor settings adjustment feel tactile and satisfying rather than fiddly.

  • Layered Modal Pattern: Placing the settings sheet over a dimmed/scaled background screen preserves context, letting the user see they haven't left the accounts view.

  • Clear Exit Path: A single, unambiguous "Done" button removes any doubt on how to confirm the setting.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you need to present a comparative or ratio-based financial/health/usage metric (budget vs. actual, goal vs. progress) to a mainstream consumer audience who may be intimidated by traditional charts. It's especially effective in apps trying to differentiate on personality/tone (fintech, wellness, habit trackers) where injecting warmth and illustration can drive daily engagement and reduce avoidance behavior around sensitive data (money, weight, calories).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for power users, accountants, or B2B/enterprise dashboards where precision, density, and comparability across many data points are required (illustrated metaphors don't scale well past 2-3 categories and can obscure exact values). Also avoid if the brand tone is meant to convey trust through seriousness (e.g., wealth management, insurance), where playful mascots and cartoon coins may undermine credibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are budgeting-averse or intimidated by traditional finance dashboards (typically younger, mobile-first users (Gen Z/millennials) who find spreadsheets and bank apps boring or shame-inducing). By using playful illustration (coin stacks, a thumbs-up mascot) and informal copy, Cleo lowers the emotional barrier to checking one's own spending, a task many people avoid due to anxiety or guilt.

The psychological triggers at play include loss aversion (visualizing how close "Out" is getting to the "Limit" stack height), social/conversational rapport (the mascot's casual check-in mimics a friend rather than an institution), and progress framing (the "11 days left" bar taps into planning and pacing behavior, similar to a fitness ring).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metaphorical Data Visualization: Replacing bar/line charts with tactile, illustrated coin stacks makes abstract numbers feel physical and instantly comparable, reducing cognitive load for financially anxious or non-numerate users.

  • Dual-Tone Layout Hierarchy: The dark hero zone for macro visualization paired with a white card for granular numeric detail cleanly separates "feeling" from "fact" on a single screen.

  • Time-Elapsed Progress Bar: The "11 days left" segmented bar contextualizes spending against the calendar, nudging users to pace themselves rather than just showing a static total.

  • Conversational Check-in Banner: Embedding a mascot-voiced prompt directly in the dashboard blurs the line between "data screen" and "chat," reinforcing Cleo's chat-first identity even on a numbers-heavy page.

  • Inline Editable Goal: The small pencil icon next to "$1,463" lets users adjust their spending ceiling in-place without navigating to a settings screen, reducing friction for budget customization.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this layered bottom-sheet-over-dashboard pattern when you want users to adjust settings related to data they can still visually reference (e.g., editing a budget while seeing the budget chart). Use illustrated/metaphorical data visualizations (coin stacks, jars, plants) for younger or finance-anxious audiences where literal charts may feel cold or overly technical. The countdown progress bar is ideal for any cyclical/period-based tracking (billing cycles, challenges, subscriptions).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid whimsical illustrated charts for professional/enterprise financial tools, accountants, or power users who need precise, comparable data at scale (e.g., multi-category breakdowns, trend lines) - coin stacks don't scale well past 2-3 categories and lack precision for detailed analysis. Also avoid stacking a bottom sheet over a dashboard when the underlying context isn't needed for the task at hand, as it can feel like unnecessary visual clutter versus a clean full-screen settings page.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets everyday consumers: likely younger, budget-conscious users (Gen Z/Millennial) who find traditional banking apps and spreadsheets intimidating or boring. The illustrated, game-like coin visualization taps into a familiarity with mobile games and gamified finance apps, lowering the psychological barrier to engaging with what is normally an anxiety-inducing topic (spending limits, overspending).

The "11 days left" countdown leverages a mild urgency/scarcity trigger to nudge users toward checking in on their spending pace before month-end, while the settings sheet's simplicity (single paycheck row, clear $ amount) caters to users who want quick, low-effort control rather than deep customization.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Coin-stack data visualization: Replaces boring bars/donuts with a playful, on-brand metaphor (stacked coins) that still conveys quantitative comparison (In vs Out vs Limit) at a glance.

  • Layered Bottom Sheet pattern: Keeps the user's spatial context (the breakdown screen is still peeking out at the top) while surfacing deeper settings, reducing the feeling of a full context switch.

  • Time-remaining progress bar: Pairs a simple two-color bar with "11 days left" text to make budget pacing instantly scannable without requiring math.

  • Swipeable month navigation: Chevron arrows imply horizontal carousel navigation across months without needing a calendar picker or extra screen.

  • Freshness indicator: The "last refreshed" timestamp with a manual refresh icon builds transparency and trust in the linked financial data.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, health, or habit-tracking apps targeting users who feel intimidated or bored by traditional data dashboards. It's ideal for surfacing a single "north star" metric (balance, calories, streak count) at the top of a home screen, paired with modular scrollable cards below for secondary info (bills, categories, charges). The inline-editable target and carousel-embedded CTA are great for reducing friction on recurring setup tasks like adding bills or budgets.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this style for enterprise, B2B, or professional finance tools (e.g., accounting, investment platforms) where users expect density, precision, and multi-metric comparison (oversized single-stat displays would feel unserious or hide critical detail). Also avoid heavy illustration/mascot elements in contexts where users need to process large volumes of transactional data quickly, as decorative graphics can compete for attention and slow scanning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious or budgeting-averse users (often younger, gig-economy or paycheck-to-paycheck demographics) who are turned off by traditional finance apps' spreadsheet aesthetics. The playful illustrations and blunt, large-type numbers reduce the shame/anxiety typically associated with checking a bank balance, leveraging a psychological principle of "friendly authority" - Cleo delivers hard truths (like 52% of income going to essentials) but wraps them in humor and color to keep the user engaged rather than avoidant.

The daily spend allowance ("$115.90 per day") taps into the psychology of chunking a large abstract number into a manageable, actionable daily budget, which is proven to improve adherence to spending goals compared to a single monthly figure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero metric hierarchy: The remaining balance and daily spend allowance are rendered in massive, bold numerals, instantly answering the user's core anxiety ("Am I okay?") without requiring interpretation of charts or graphs.

  • Illustrated mascot hands as emotional punctuation: Rather than a full mascot character, isolated hand illustrations (thumbs-up, rock-on gesture) act as reaction emojis to financial data, injecting personality without cluttering the numeric content.

  • Bills-as-carousel with inline Add CTA: Embedding the "Add a bill" action as a card within the horizontal scroll (rather than a separate button) makes the empty/incomplete state feel like an invitation, not a nag.

  • Editable target inline: The "until $1,463" with a pencil icon allows quick inline editing of a payday/budget target directly within the hero stat, avoiding a separate settings screen.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 21
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a user is issued a piece of information that is irrecoverable if lost and non-transmittable by the app itself (e.g., recovery codes, encryption keys, master passwords, backup codes for 2FA). It's ideal anywhere the cost of user error is catastrophic and silent (no error message will ever fire later (the user just loses access one day)).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavier verification friction for low-stakes or easily recoverable data (e.g., a username or a preference setting) - it will feel like unnecessary busywork and increase drop-off. Also avoid it if the underlying system can recover the credential another way (e.g., email-based password reset), since the security theater isn't justified by real risk.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new crypto wallet users, many of whom are unfamiliar with self-custody and the irreversible nature of losing a seed phrase. The design leans on the psychological principle of the testing effect (retrieval practice improves retention far better than re-reading), ensuring the user has genuinely internalized or physically recorded their recovery phrase before they can proceed.

It also mitigates a well-documented support burden for wallet providers: users who skip past the seed-phrase screen without saving it, then lose access permanently. By gating progression behind a verification quiz, the product protects both the user and its own support/reputation costs.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Active recall over passive confirmation: Instead of a checkbox ("I saved my phrase"), the app requires the user to prove retention by identifying specific words, dramatically reducing the number of users who lose funds due to unsaved seed phrases.

  • Conversational microcopy: "You saved it, right?" injects personality and urgency without being alarming, softening an otherwise high-anxiety security step.

  • Segmented progress bar: Gives users a clear sense of finite, short remaining effort, which is especially important during friction-heavy security setup.

  • Escape hatch via back navigation: Lets users who didn't actually save the phrase return and fix their mistake rather than being trapped or forced to guess.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 22
screens.whereToUse: Use a bottom sheet wallet/account switcher pattern whenever an app supports multiple identities, profiles, or accounts that a user must frequently toggle between (multi-wallet crypto apps, multi-account banking apps, team/workspace switchers in SaaS tools). It's ideal when the switch action is frequent but shouldn't warrant a full-screen navigation, and when preserving background context aids orientation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if there are more than 8-10 accounts, since an unpaginated flat list in a sheet becomes hard to scan and would benefit from search/filter instead. It's also unsuitable for irreversible, high-stakes account switches (e.g., switching a live trading session) without an additional confirmation step, since a simple tap in a sheet may be too frictionless for consequential state changes. Additionally, avoid stacking too much financial complexity (fees, gas, chain indicators) inside this compact layout, as it can quickly overload the minimal design.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets busy urban professionals who likely manage multiple crypto identities (a personal wallet, a work/DAO wallet, an NFT-flexing ENS identity) and need to switch between them rapidly and confidently while on the go. The design leans on the psychological principle of reducing choice friction: by surfacing avatars and human names instead of addresses, it triggers faster System-1 recognition rather than slow, effortful System-2 verification of long strings.

The checkmark and balance-per-wallet also tap into loss-aversion and safety reassurance: self-custody users are highly anxious about sending assets from/to the wrong address, so this screen's clarity directly mitigates a top source of crypto-native anxiety.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Human-readable identity resolution: Displaying "alexsmithmobbin.cb.id" instead of a 42-character hex address dramatically improves trust and reduces the risk of sending funds to the wrong place.

  • Non-blocking modal context: The bottom sheet only covers ~60% of the screen, keeping the home dashboard peeking through above, so users retain spatial orientation.

  • Explicit active-state indicator: The blue checkmark next to "Address 1" removes any ambiguity about which wallet is currently in use before performing a transaction.

  • Persistent management CTA: "Add & manage wallets" is pinned at the bottom, always reachable regardless of list length, following the thumb-zone ergonomics best practice for one-handed mobile use.

  • Aggregate total balance: Showing "Total: $0.00" at the sheet header gives an at-a-glance portfolio snapshot across all wallets before drilling into any single one.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 23
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for settings/preferences screens where legal, help, or secondary informational links need to be grouped without dedicating a full screen. Ideal for:

  • Financial, healthcare, or regulated apps needing quick access to Privacy Policy/ToS.

  • Any settings hub with a mix of high-frequency (Security, Notifications) and low-frequency (Legal) actions, where the bottom sheet keeps low-frequency items decluttered.

  • Apps with deep settings trees that benefit from an in-page search bar for quick filtering.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when legal documents are lengthy and require full reading/scrolling (a bottom sheet with only links is fine, but rendering full ToS text inside a sheet is poor UX (use a full screen or in-app browser instead)). Also avoid using a bottom sheet for items requiring complex multi-step interaction; sheets work best for short, binary-choice or link lists like this one.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday users of a crypto/finance wallet app (likely Coinbase Wallet or similar) who need to configure security and privacy settings (a population that is often anxious about fund safety and data privacy). Grouping "Security" first and giving it a lock icon builds immediate trust and signals that the app prioritizes asset protection.

The Legal bottom sheet caters to compliance-conscious or skeptical users who want quick access to Privacy Policy/Terms without friction, and to the platform's own regulatory obligation to surface these documents discoverably without cluttering the main settings list.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Descriptive subtitles on every row: Each settings item previews its contents (e.g., "Dark mode, currency, balances, language") so users don't need to tap-and-check, saving time and reducing navigation anxiety.

  • Differentiated affordances: Chevron arrows indicate in-app drill-down, while the diagonal arrow icon on "Help" clearly signals it opens an external browser/support center (a subtle but important expectation-setting detail).

  • Lightweight bottom sheet for low-complexity choices: Rather than navigating to a full new screen for two links, the app surfaces them in a compact sheet, minimizing navigation depth and preserving context.

  • Search bar at the top of Settings: Acknowledges that as feature-rich apps grow, users prefer typing over hunting through nested menus.

screens.name: Wealthfront Dashboard 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when you want to cross-sell a related product within a financial aggregation or dashboard context, especially when the user has no current usage of that product. It works well:

  • In personal finance apps with multiple product lines (banking, investing, insurance) to surface unused features contextually.

  • When the target action requires low cognitive effort framing ("set it and forget it") to overcome activation-energy hesitation.

  • Directly beneath real account data, so the pitch feels relevant rather than intrusive.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The user has already opted out of or dismissed this upsell multiple times (repeated exposure can feel like nagging and erode trust in the aggregation feature's neutrality).

  • The screen's primary job is transactional or urgent (e.g., checking balance before a payment) - inserting merchandising here adds friction and distraction.

  • Regulatory constraints require prominent risk disclosures near investment offers; burying compliance text only in a small "Disclosures" link at the bottom may not meet fintech compliance standards.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday banking/finance app users who have already linked external accounts (savings, credit cards) and are engaged enough to check balances regularly (a warm audience for an owned investment product). The psychological trigger is effortless aspiration: by pairing "never lift a finger" messaging with a friendly leaf/growth icon, the design taps into the desire for passive wealth growth without expertise or ongoing labor, appealing especially to novice or busy investors who feel intimidated by traditional brokerage complexity.

Placing this pitch right after showing the user their real liabilities (credit card debt) subtly primes an emotional response (a nudge toward productive financial behavior (investing) as a counterbalance to visible debt).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual upsell placement: The investing pitch appears directly beneath real account balances, capitalizing on the moment a user is already thinking about their money.

  • Masked balances with skeleton-style blur: Protects sensitive data in screenshots/demos while preserving realistic layout proportions.

  • Freshness indicators ("8 minutes ago"): Builds trust by showing the aggregation is near real-time, not stale.

  • Dual CTA hierarchy: A strong filled primary button ("Start Investing") paired with a low-friction text link ("How it works") caters to both ready-to-convert and still-researching users.

  • Consistent institution branding: Reusing the same bank icon for both accounts reinforces recognizability and reduces cognitive load when scanning multiple linked accounts.

screens.name: Wealthfront Dashboard 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this aggregated stacked-list + category-subtotal pattern when:

  • Building personal finance / net-worth tracking dashboards that pull from multiple linked institutions (Plaid-like integrations).

  • Users need to monitor sync health of multiple external data sources and self-serve reconnect broken links.

  • The product benefits from encouraging users to add more data sources to increase engagement and personalization (more accounts = stickier product).

  • Sensitive numeric data needs an optional privacy/obfuscation mode for public use cases.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The user only has a single account/data source: grouped categorization and rollups would add unnecessary complexity.

  • Real-time precision is critical (e.g., active trading) since relative "time ago" sync indicators may mask actual staleness risk.

  • The blurred-balance privacy technique could confuse users into thinking there's a loading/error state rather than an intentional privacy mask (always pair with a clear toggle or icon explaining the behavior).

  • Highly regulated contexts where hiding numeric data by default could conflict with required at-a-glance compliance/disclosure visibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially engaged consumers who use multiple banks, credit unions, or brokerages (Bank of America for daily banking, SoFi for savings/checking, plus a stock portfolio) and want a single pane of glass to view their net worth. This is common among younger, digitally-native users consolidating accounts across various fintech apps rather than sticking with one traditional bank.

Psychologically, the design leverages:

  • Completeness/Zeigarnik effect: Seeing "$0.00" on an empty portfolio or a stale "Update" account creates a mild itch to complete/fix data, encouraging engagement.

  • Loss aversion via liabilities framing: Explicitly surfacing "Liabilities" alongside assets reinforces net-worth awareness and encourages debt paydown behavior.

  • Trust through transparency: Timestamps and disclosures build credibility necessary for handling sensitive financial data.

  • Privacy control: Blurred balances cater to users who check finances in public (transit, work) but don't want onlookers to see exact figures.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Balance obfuscation: Blurred/gradient placeholders over dollar figures protect user privacy in shared or public viewing contexts without breaking the visual layout.

  • Categorized rollups: Cash, Investments, and Liabilities are grouped with subtotal headers, giving a mental model similar to a personal balance sheet.

  • Inline reconnection prompts: "Update" links appear directly next to stale SoFi accounts instead of a generic error banner, reducing friction to fix broken syncs exactly where the problem is noticed.

  • Institution-branded iconography: Color-coded bank logos (e.g., red Bank of America flag icon) aid rapid visual recognition across a long list of accounts.

  • Freshness timestamps: "1 day ago" / "4 hours ago" build trust by showing data recency transparently.

  • Low-friction account expansion CTA: The soft, rounded "+ Add account" button encourages further aggregation to increase the product's stickiness and data completeness.

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when designing budget/limit tracking features where users need an at-a-glance sense of remaining allowance alongside itemized historical detail (e).g., subscription usage meters, data/storage caps, corporate expense categories, or gift card balances. It's also effective for embedding a primary CTA naturally inside a transactional list rather than as a disconnected floating button, especially in finance or task-management contexts where the action is directly tied to the list's content (e.g., "Add expense," "Log activity").

The card-over-card modal approach is ideal for secondary/drill-down detail views accessed from a dashboard, letting users peek back at the parent context via the visible handle/peek bar.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid the circular progress ring when the metric being tracked isn't naturally bounded (e.g., unlimited spend, open-ended savings) (a gauge implies a finite cap and could mislead users into thinking there's a hard ceiling that doesn't exist. Also avoid stacking multiple small status icons (sync/receipt/approval) in contexts where users are not already familiar with their meaning; without a legend or onboarding, these icons risk being ignored or misunderstood by first-time or casual users. Finally, embedding a primary CTA inside a list (like "Request reimbursement") can get visually lost or feel inconsistent if the list grows long or if users don't scroll far enough to notice it) a persistent sticky button might better serve high-urgency actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for employees managing a discretionary spending category (e.g., a daily meal/transportation allowance tied to a specific budget or trip) within a corporate card program. The target user is likely a traveling employee or in-office staffer who needs quick confidence that they are within policy limits before making another purchase.

Psychologically, the progress ring taps into the same "fuel gauge" heuristic used in fitness rings and data-usage meters (humans process circular depletion/fullness far faster than reading raw numbers, reducing cognitive load for a user who may be standing in line at a register). The itemized receipt-status icons serve the compliance-driven psychology of finance teams and auditors by making transaction completeness self-evident, reducing follow-up friction and anxiety about missing documentation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Circular progress ring as instant budget comprehension tool: converts an abstract dollar figure into a glanceable visual state (full ring = full budget remaining).
  • Inline primary action within the list ("Request reimbursement" styled like a list item with an accent-colored icon), reducing extra taps and keeping the CTA contextually relevant to the expense feed it populates.
  • Triple status iconography per transaction: communicates sync status, receipt attachment, and approval state simultaneously, giving finance oversight without needing to tap into each record.
  • Modal/card-over-card navigation pattern (visible peeking sheet above) preserves the user's place in the parent screen, encouraging quick in-and-out interactions typical of expense checking on the go.
  • Multi-currency transparency: explicit currency codes on every line item prevent costly misreading for a globally distributed workforce.

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: This pattern is ideal for B2B SaaS admin panels where a single object (like a budget, project, or team) has multiple associated resources (people, assets, rules). Use a bottom-sheet/modal detail view when you want users to drill down for specifics without losing their place in a master list. It is particularly effective for financial or project management tools where "who is responsible" and "what assets are attached" are critical pieces of metadata.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, stacked-section layout for consumer-facing apps where users expect a more visual, card-based, or narrative experience. Additionally, if the number of "Members" or "Cards" associated with an entity is very high (hundreds), this flat list approach will fail; it would require pagination or a search/filter mechanism integrated into the section itself rather than an infinite vertical scroll.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Finance Admins and Team Managers who require a "single pane of glass" view over a specific spending entity. The psychological driver here is control and oversight: by consolidating the cards, the people who can spend (Members), and the person accountable (Managed by) into one view, Brex reduces the anxiety associated with decentralized spending.

The inclusion of an "Alerts" section specifically targets the need for proactive risk management, allowing finance leads to set up guardrails rather than only reviewing spend retroactively.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Status Iconography: The small icons next to the transaction amount (receipt matching, policy compliance checks) provide immediate visual confirmation of expense status without requiring the user to tap into the transaction.
  • Modal Drag Handle: The use of a swipe-down gesture to dismiss the detail view keeps the interaction lightweight and native to iOS conventions, differentiating "detail" views from "primary" navigation screens.
  • Chevron Consistency: The right-aligned chevrons (>) on "All expenses" and "Add alert" create a clear visual language that these rows lead to deeper views or forms, distinct from the static list items below them (Cards, Members).

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any resource/quota detail screen where a user needs to understand a finite allowance and take immediate corrective action - examples include:

  • Subscription usage dashboards (API quotas, storage limits, seat counts)
  • Corporate card / budget management tools
  • Gift card or prepaid balance screens
  • Project budget tracking in PM tools

It's especially effective when the user's primary need is a single number (balance/quota) followed by secondary diagnostic detail and related records.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense, list-heavy layout for casual consumer-facing apps where emotional engagement or visual storytelling matters more than raw data density (the utilitarian, spreadsheet-like tone would feel cold or intimidating in a consumer lifestyle or social app).

Also avoid surfacing a blocking warning banner this prominently if the constraint is minor or temporary; overusing amber "unavailable" banners can create alert fatigue and erode trust if limits are frequently and arbitrarily restricted. Additionally, if the target user is not already familiar with financial terminology ("limit," "assignment," "expires"), this screen would need more onboarding or tooltips to avoid confusion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves employees and budget owners inside a company who have been allocated a specific spending limit (e.g., a department budget, project card, or vendor limit) and need to quickly check how much remains, understand restrictions, and take corrective action (requesting more budget or logging an expense).

Psychologically, the design leverages immediacy and clarity under financial accountability: employees managing company money are often anxious about overspending or being blocked, so leading with the exact remaining balance and expiry date reduces uncertainty. The warning banner leverages loss-aversion framing: by explaining why the limit can't be reassigned, it prevents the frustration of a failed action, which is critical for B2B tools where trust and reliability directly impact daily productivity.

The "Request limit increase" CTA appeals to autonomy and self-service, a key need for finance-adjacent but non-finance employees (e.g., marketers, ops managers) who want to resolve budget constraints without manually emailing finance teams.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero metric placement: The available balance is the largest, boldest element on screen, immediately satisfying the user's top intent.
  • Integrated progress visualization: A simple horizontal bar communicates budget consumption at a glance without requiring a chart or additional screen.
  • Proactive constraint messaging: Surfacing the "unavailable for assignment" warning directly below the relevant actions pre-empts user error and reduces support tickets.
  • Inline quick action: The orange "+" Request reimbursement row acts as a contextual shortcut embedded within a list rather than requiring a separate FAB or navigation flow.
  • Collapsible sections: "Documentation & reviews" uses an accordion chevron to keep the primary screen lightweight while still offering access to deeper detail/audit data.
  • Modal/sheet presentation: Using an "X" dismiss rather than back navigation signals this is a focused, task-oriented overlay, not a page the user needs to navigate out of hierarchically.

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when displaying rules-based or policy documentation where specific variables (thresholds, roles, dates, limits) are embedded in explanatory text (such as compliance pages, terms summaries, permission matrices, or tiered pricing rules). It's effective whenever users need to quickly extract 2-3 key facts from otherwise verbose text.

The paired error-banner + stale-cached-content approach is valuable for any data-sensitive app (finance, health, legal) that must stay usable offline or during partial outages, since it preserves trust by being transparent about data freshness rather than hiding the failure or blocking the whole screen.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid dense bold-in-paragraph formatting for policies with many more than 3-4 variables per rule (at that point a structured table or key-value list would scan far faster than embedded bold text in sentences). Avoid showing potentially stale financial/compliance data without the connectivity warning; silently displaying such data in an offline state risks real financial/compliance errors if thresholds have since changed.

Also avoid stacking a generic top-of-screen error message with functioning content below it without clarifying what specifically failed (users may be confused about whether the whole screen, or just one section, is unreliable).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees submitting expenses/reimbursements and finance admins setting policy who need to quickly verify compliance rules (e.g., "do I need a receipt for this $15 purchase?"). The psychological driver is reducing policy-violation anxiety: employees want certainty before submitting an expense, so surfacing exact dollar thresholds and required approvers builds confidence and reduces back-and-forth with finance teams.

The bolded key terms leverage selective attention, helping busy, non-finance-expert employees extract actionable facts without parsing legalistic paragraphs. The offline/error banners serve risk transparency: in a finance app, silently showing possibly-stale compliance data could lead to real monetary consequences, so Brex proactively flags uncertainty rather than letting users unknowingly act on outdated rules.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Bold-for-variables typographic pattern: Dynamic policy thresholds and approver names are bolded within gray descriptive sentences, letting finance/employee users scan for "what matters" (the number, the approver) without re-reading full sentences.
  • Graceful partial failure: Rather than showing a blocking full-screen error, the screen renders an inline error notice at top while still displaying cached/available documentation content below, prioritizing continued usefulness over strict correctness.
  • Persistent connectivity banner: The sticky red "No connectivity" toast at the bottom keeps the user continuously aware that displayed data (critical compliance rules) may be stale, which is especially important for financial policy accuracy.
  • Collapsible section with chevron affordance: The up-chevron next to "Documentation & reviews" signals this is an expandable/collapsible accordion, letting users collapse dense policy text once reviewed.

results.query: Irreversible backend transaction confirmation blocking modal pattern

screens.name: Venmo Banning & Blocking 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any screen where a user directly interacts with another individual's identity or content (profile pages, chat headers, comment threads, marketplace listings). It's ideal whenever you need to offer moderation/safety controls without cluttering the primary UI, deferring them to a contextual overflow menu and action sheet.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal, unconfirmed pattern for truly irreversible or high-stakes actions (e.g., permanently deleting an account or an unrecoverable financial transaction) - those warrant an additional confirmation dialog rather than a single tap. Also avoid on Android-first products, where the native pattern should shift to a Bottom Sheet or Material dialog styling instead of the iOS Action Sheet aesthetic to maintain platform consistency.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets any user of a social-payment platform (Venmo-like) who encounters an uncomfortable, spammy, or suspicious contact (particularly relevant given Venmo's public-by-default transaction feed, which can expose users to unwanted attention or harassment tied to their spending activity).

Psychologically, the pattern leverages loss-of-control anxiety mitigation: users who feel exposed (their payment history is visible) need a fast, low-friction escape valve. Placing Block/Report on the very screen where the discomfort originates (the offending user's profile) minimizes the effort required to act, which is critical because safety features with high friction are statistically underused.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native platform conventions: Using the iOS Action Sheet component instead of a custom modal builds instant familiarity and trust, reducing cognitive load for safety-critical actions.

  • Color-coded severity: Red for "Block" immediately communicates irreversibility/consequence versus the neutral blue "Report" and "Cancel", letting users triage risk at a glance without reading.

  • Isolated Cancel action: Separating "Cancel" into its own visually distinct card (with a gap) from "Block/Report" prevents accidental destructive taps and gives users a clear, low-effort exit.

  • Contextual placement of moderation tools: Surfacing Block/Report from the profile overflow menu (rather than burying it in settings) makes safety controls discoverable exactly at the point of potential harm/friction.

screens.name: Venmo Banning & Blocking 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a destructive, socially-sensitive account action (blocking, removing a connection, disabling a shared feature) has non-obvious side effects. It's ideal for social or marketplace apps where two-way relationships (payments, friending, messaging) need explicit teardown, and where user anxiety about "what happens next" or "will they know" must be proactively addressed in the copy itself.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of dense, bulleted legal-style copy for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., muting a notification, unfollowing a public account) - it will feel like overkill and add unnecessary friction. Also avoid this pattern if the underlying action doesn't actually preserve reversibility; promising an "unblock" path in the dialog only works if that setting is easy to find and honors user expectations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Venmo's core UX conceit: publicizing payments as a social feed (creates a unique liability: strangers, exes, scammers, or trolls can see and comment on financial activity, and payment requests can be weaponized for harassment (e).g., demanding money via mentions/comments). The busy urban target demographic often interacts with acquaintances, roommates, gig-economy counterparties, or dating contacts they may want to cut off entirely.

This screen serves anyone needing to end an unwanted financial/social connection (a critical trust-and-safety touchpoint that lets Venmo maintain its open social model without exposing users to indefinite unwanted contact). It targets users experiencing harassment, awkward social fallout, or scam attempts, and the clear informational design is meant to make an emotionally charged action (cutting someone off) feel procedural and safe rather than confrontational.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit consequence itemization: Rather than a vague "Are you sure?", the dialog lists the exact four capabilities lost, preventing surprise and building user trust in the action.

  • "Will not be notified" reassurance: Directly defuses the biggest psychological barrier to blocking someone (fear of confrontation) which is essential in a payments app where financial disputes can turn hostile.

  • Discoverable reversibility: Mentioning the unblock path inside the dialog itself lowers the perceived stakes/risk of the decision, making users more willing to act decisively rather than hesitating.

  • Native platform pattern conformity: Using the standard iOS destructive-confirmation dialog shape/typography makes the safety feature instantly recognizable and trustworthy, rather than a custom in-app design that might feel less authoritative.

screens.name: Venmo Banning & Blocking 3
screens.whereToUse:
Utilize this pattern of combining a status modifier (e.g., "(Blocked)", "(Archived)", "(Restricted)") in the header with a standard Empty State pattern when:

  • Displaying history or content lists for entities that are in a restricted or inactive state.

  • You need to maintain a consistent list-view template across different states (active vs. blocked) to reduce engineering complexity, while still communicating the specific state change contextually in the header.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid reusing generic "empty" CTAs (like "tap Pay to start") in a blocked-state context if the action is actually disabled or heavily gated. If the "Pay" action is not immediately available due to the block, the microcopy should be updated to reflect this specific restriction (e.g., "Unblock this contact to start a new payment") to avoid user frustration when the suggested action fails.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves users of a financial or social payment app (like Venmo, Cash App, or Zelle) who are managing their safety and privacy by blocking specific contacts. The primary psychological driver here is Trust & Safety: users need confirmation that blocking a contact was successful and that the interface reflects this restricted state.

The design caters to the "Digital Boundary Setter" persona: someone who wants to cut off financial interaction with a specific person (e.g., an ex-partner, a scammer, or an unwanted acquaintance) but wants to verify via the UI that the block is currently active and enforced.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent Status Contextualization: The "(Blocked)" tag is intelligently placed directly in the Top Navigation Bar next to the username, ensuring the block status is visible regardless of which sub-tab (Profile, Chat, Transactions) the user is currently viewing.

  • Calm Visual Hierarchy: By using generous whitespace and vertical centering for the empty state message, the UI avoids alarming the user, treating the "blocked" financial history as a standard empty list rather than a system error.

  • Consistent Overflow Menu: The three-dot "..." menu (Toolbar) remains accessible in the top right, allowing the user to manage the block (e.g., unblock) directly from this restricted view without needing to navigate away.

screens.name: Dave Deleting & Removing 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any irreversible or hard-to-reverse account/data deletion flow (closing accounts, deleting recurring goals, canceling subscriptions with data loss).

  • Financial products where an action affects automated processes (auto-transfers, recurring payments, round-ups) that the user may forget are tied to the object being deleted.

  • Situations where the destructive action has multiple downstream effects that aren't obvious from the action's label alone.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for low-stakes, easily reversible actions (e.g., removing an item from a wishlist) - this level of friction would feel excessive and annoying.

  • Do not use plain, low-emphasis styling for the destructive button when the action carries severe, non-financial risks (e.g., permanently deleting a user account with personal data) - in higher-risk contexts, add extra friction like typed confirmation or a stronger visual (red) warning treatment.

  • Avoid vague bullet points; if the consequences listed are generic or non-specific, the transparency benefit is lost and it becomes just visual noise.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users managing an active financial savings goal (e.g., a round-up savings or micro-investing product) who are reconsidering their commitment. The design assumes the user may be acting on impulse (frustration, changed circumstances) and uses friction as a protective mechanism: slowing the user down with information rather than blocking them outright. This serves both the user (avoiding regret from irreversible action) and the business (reducing accidental churn/account closures that could have been avoided with more information, such as pausing instead of ending).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consequence-first disclosure: Instead of a generic "Are you sure?" prompt, the dialog itemizes the exact functional impacts (deactivation, round-up pausing, recurring transfer cancellation), giving users full transparency before they commit.

  • Irreversibility called out explicitly: A dedicated sentence isolates the permanence of the action, reducing the chance of accidental, regretful deletions (critical in a financial app where trust is paramount).

  • Human, conversational button labels: "Keep it" / "End goal" replace generic "Cancel/OK" labels, making the decision feel more personal and reducing the sterile, legalistic feel of typical confirmation dialogs.

  • Non-alarmist visual tone: Despite being a destructive action, the dialog avoids red warning colors or aggressive iconography, keeping the brand's calm, trustworthy tone intact even during a "bad news" moment.

screens.name: Dave Deleting & Removing 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a user-initiated action is destructive, irreversible, and has hidden downstream side effects (e.g., canceling a subscription that also cancels linked add-ons, deleting an account that removes connected integrations, closing a financial product tied to automations). It is especially valuable in fintech, SaaS account settings, and any workflow involving recurring/automated processes that the user might forget about.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, list-based confirmation pattern for low-risk, easily reversible actions (e.g., removing a favorite, archiving a note) - it would feel like overkill and create unnecessary friction/anxiety. Also avoid it when the consequences are simple enough to state in one short sentence; forcing a bulleted list for a trivial action dilutes the pattern's power for truly critical moments. Additionally, never show both action buttons in a simultaneous loading state without clear disabling/visual distinction, as it can momentarily confuse the user about which action is being processed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday banking/fintech app users (e.g., Chime, Varo, or similar neobank "round-up savings" products) who are managing an automated micro-savings goal. The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion combined with informed consent: by clearly listing what will be lost (automatic round-ups, recurring transfers, reactivation ability), the design leverages the user's natural aversion to losing an established system/habit, prompting a final moment of reconsideration before an irreversible action.

It also serves risk-averse or forgetful users who may not remember they have automated transfers tied to this goal, protecting them from unintentionally disrupting their broader savings strategy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consequence-first messaging: Instead of a generic "Are you sure?" the dialog explicitly enumerates the three concrete downstream effects, setting accurate expectations and reducing post-action confusion or support tickets.

  • Isolated irreversibility statement: Placing "you can't reactivate it" as a standalone sentence (rather than burying it in the bullet list) ensures it isn't skimmed over.

  • Dual loading states on both buttons: Showing spinners on both the cancel and confirm buttons simultaneously (likely disabling both while the request processes) prevents race conditions and accidental double submissions during an irreversible API call.

  • Dimmed background retains context: Users can still see they were editing "Savings" with a "$75" goal amount, anchoring the decision to the specific object being deleted rather than an abstract concept.

screens.name: Dave Deleting & Removing 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an automated or recurring user action naturally terminates due to a triggering condition being met (e.g., goal completion, subscription cycle ending, challenge finishing). It's ideal for:

  • Habit-based features (savings automation, streak-based challenges, recurring reminders) that need a graceful "what's next" moment.

  • Situations where you want to immediately re-capture engagement momentum right after a milestone/completion event.

  • Any flow where reassuring users that "nothing was lost" is critical to prevent anxiety-driven drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The termination event is neutral or expected and doesn't require re-engagement (adding unnecessary friction/interruption).

  • The user has explicitly indicated they do not want to continue the feature (repeatedly prompting to "resume" could feel naggy and erode trust).

  • The screen would be better served by inline/contextual messaging rather than a full-screen interstitial, especially for low-stakes or minor completions where a toast alone would suffice.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday banking/fintech app users who have engaged with an automated micro-savings feature (Round Up) tied to a specific savings goal. These are habit-driven savers who may not realize their automation silently paused when their goal completed (a critical retention risk moment).

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete/paused tasks create tension that drives completion) by immediately offering to "resume" the interrupted habit. It also uses loss-aversion mitigation: explicitly stating past data is preserved (to prevent the user from feeling punished for the goal having ended). The soft dismissal option respects user agency, which builds long-term trust in the app rather than pressuring users, which is critical for financial products where trust is the core currency.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive reassurance banner: Confirms data isn't lost ("Past Goals section") before the user worries about it, reducing churn-inducing anxiety at a moment of feature interruption.

  • Friendly mascot illustration: Diffuses the potentially negative connotation of a "stopped" automation with a warm, relatable visual instead of a sterile system alert.

  • Benefit-oriented CTA framing: "Resume" language implies continuity and low effort, increasing likelihood of immediate re-engagement.

  • Non-committal exit path: "Not now" avoids permanent-feeling rejection language, keeping future conversion opportunities open.

  • Single, focused decision: No competing navigation elements or distractions. Just one clear action to take.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any safety, moderation, or privacy-control flow where users need to quickly locate a specific entity (account, contact, item) by name and take an immediate, single-tap action on it. It's ideal for block lists, mute lists, contact removal, or permission revocation screens where the target is known by name and the action is binary (add/remove, block/unblock).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the destructive action has significant, hard-to-reverse consequences that warrant an explicit confirmation step (e.g., permanently deleting an account) - in such cases, a confirmation dialog should be inserted before the action executes. Also avoid inline one-tap destructive buttons in exploratory browse contexts where accidental taps are likely, such as dense grids or fast-scrolling feeds, since the reduced friction that helps in a deliberate search flow can become a liability in casual browsing contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users who need to proactively manage their safety and privacy on a social platform (often in response to harassment, spam, or unwanted contact). The design assumes the user already knows (at least partially) the username or handle they want to block, hence the search-first approach rather than browsing a follower/following list.

Psychologically, the screen is built to minimize the emotional and cognitive burden of a defensive action: fewer steps, fewer decisions, and immediate visual feedback all reduce the time between intent and resolution, which matters when a user is anxious or upset about another account's behavior. The neutral, non-judgmental tone avoids adding friction or shame to what can be a difficult social decision.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-friction entry: Keyboard is pre-summoned and search field auto-focused so the user can type the instant the screen appears.

  • Inline destructive action: "Block" button is exposed directly on each search result row, eliminating the need to navigate to a full profile page to complete the task.

  • Dual exit affordances: Both a global "X" close and a local "Cancel" for the search field give users flexible, low-anxiety ways to back out.

  • Color-coded severity: Red "Block" chips instantly communicate the destructive/serious nature of the action via color alone.

  • Real-time typeahead: Results filter live as characters are typed, reducing perceived latency and effort.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Any irreversible or high-consequence action (blocking, deleting an account, canceling a subscription, removing a payment method).

  • Financial or social platforms where the action affects another party's ability to interact with the user.

  • Situations where users need to understand a specific, non-obvious side-effect (e.g., "pending payments will be canceled") before committing.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for low-stakes, easily reversible actions, adding friction here annoys users and trains them to blindly tap through dialogs (alert fatigue).

  • Don't use vague, generic confirmation copy ("Are you sure?") when specific consequences exist (users need concrete information to make an informed choice, especially with money involved).

  • Not ideal when the destructive action needs to be done in bulk/rapidly (e.g., mass moderation) - a full modal per action would be too slow; a bulk confirmation would be better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday consumers of P2P payment apps who need protection from harassment, scams, or unwanted repeated payment requests (e.g., splitting bills gone wrong, ex-partners, spam accounts). The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion combined with irreversible-action anxiety: financial apps must overcome users' fear of "breaking" something, so the confirmation dialog acts as a safety net that increases confidence to act. It also serves risk-averse users who might hesitate to block someone for fear of unintended consequences (e.g., losing money they were expecting), so transparency about pending payment cancellation directly addresses that anxiety.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Two-step destructive action: Tapping "Block" in the list doesn't block immediately (it requires a second, explicit confirmation, protecting users from accidental taps).

  • Consequence-specific messaging: Instead of generic "Are you sure?" copy, the dialog states the precise financial impact (pending payments canceled), which is essential in a money-transfer context.

  • Personalized title: Injecting the specific contact's name into "Block [Name]" (rather than a generic "Block user") increases clarity and reduces the chance of blocking the wrong person.

  • Visual restraint on destructive CTA: The red "Block" button is not a filled/heavy button, avoiding accidental muscle-memory taps and keeping visual weight balanced with "Cancel".

  • Dimmed background retains context: The underlying search screen is visible but desaturated, letting the user maintain spatial orientation without being distracted from the decision.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 13
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for confirming any destructive or protective account action (block, unfollow, unmatch, mute) in social or transactional apps.

  • Ideal when the consequences of the action are non-obvious (e.g., "pending payments canceled") and users would otherwise need to guess or contact support.

  • Pair a low-emphasis secondary action (like Report) with the primary dismissal action when there's a natural next step tied to the same context (safety, moderation).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, full-screen treatment for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (a simple toast/snackbar would suffice and reduce interruption).

  • Don't use this pattern if the block/action itself still requires confirmation, mixing "are you sure" logic with "this is done" messaging on the same screen creates confusion.

  • Not appropriate for actions with no meaningful consequences to explain, as the extra copy would feel padded and unnecessary.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday users of a P2P payment platform who need to protect themselves from unwanted contacts, scams, or harassment (a common occurrence in apps where usernames/phone numbers are semi-public and money requests can be sent unsolicited). The design leverages the psychological principle of closure: after taking a defensive action, users need explicit confirmation that the threat (unwanted transactions) has been neutralized, which this screen delivers through direct, unambiguous language.

It also serves trust & safety objectives for the platform itself, using the moment of heightened user vigilance (having just blocked someone) as a low-friction opportunity to funnel them toward reporting, which helps the company detect bad actors and fraud patterns.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Outcome-first messaging: Instead of a generic "Success" toast, the app confirms the specific action taken and its exact financial implications, reducing post-action anxiety.

  • Bundled Report CTA: Surfacing "Report" immediately after a block, rather than burying it in settings, capitalizes on the user's already-heightened emotional state to capture safety-relevant reports while it's top of mind.

  • Redundant exit paths: Both the top-left X and bottom "Done" button dismiss the screen, accommodating different user habits (modal-dismissal vs. explicit CTA-tapping).

  • Financial consequence transparency: Explicitly stating that pending payments were canceled prevents confusion or support tickets from users who might otherwise wonder where a pending transaction went.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 14
screens.whereToUse:
• End-of-flow confirmation screens for security, verification, or compliance actions (2FA setup, KYC, fraud reports, password resets).

  • Any moment where you want to reduce user anxiety after a sensitive or effortful task by clearly confirming success.

  • Flows where reinforcing platform trust and community stewardship (rather than pure self-interest) can deepen emotional engagement.

  • Situations requiring a hard stop/checkpoint before returning to the main app experience.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this ultra-minimal pattern when the user needs additional context or next steps (e.g., if further account action is required, omitting that information could cause confusion or repeat support requests). It's also unsuitable for flows where the outcome could have partial success or conditional states, since binary "success only" messaging may mislead users if edge cases exist. For high-stakes financial confirmations (e.g., large transfers), consider including a summary of what was done for the user's records, rather than only a generic acknowledgment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday Cash App users who have just completed a security-sensitive action (likely identity verification, suspicious transaction reporting, device confirmation, or fraud dispute resolution). Given Cash App's demographic skews toward younger, mobile-first, often first-time financial-app users, clarity and reassurance are paramount; these users may have limited patience for jargon-heavy compliance language and high sensitivity to anything that feels like a scam or error.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the completion/closure effect (a clear checkmark and affirmative statement satisfy the user's need to know "did this work?") and social contribution framing (positioning the user's action as helping the broader Cash App community, not just themselves) to leave users with positive brand sentiment even during what could otherwise be a mundane or friction-filled security task.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single, unmistakable success signal: The oversized green checkmark communicates completion instantly via color and shape, before any text is even parsed.

  • Empowering, community-framed messaging: "Thanks for helping keep Cash App safe" reframes a routine security/compliance step as a meaningful contribution, increasing perceived value of the interaction.

  • Zero-decision exit: Only one primary action ("Done") is presented, removing any friction or ambiguity about what to do next.

  • Restrained, breathable layout: Extensive white space and minimal copy reduce anxiety and reinforce a sense of resolution and trust.

  • Dismissible via X: Offering a top-left close affordance in addition to "Done" respects varying user mental models for exiting a flow.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern during onboarding for social or utility apps where the app's value increases significantly once populated with the user's personal data (contacts, favorites, shortcuts).

  • Ideal for introducing "quality of life" features that are technically optional but drive long-term retention (e.g., pinning items, adding contacts, setting default preferences).

  • Effective when you want to break a complex setup process into small, digestible, single-purpose screens to maintain high completion rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the "Favorites" or list-building feature is not immediately useful without a critical mass of other data (e.g., if the user has no contacts on the app yet, showing this screen might lead to an empty/frustrating experience).

  • Do not use this for mandatory security or compliance steps (like ID verification), as the light, spacious layout undersells the seriousness/urgency required for those tasks.
