  • Avoid if user testing shows high drop-off/skip rates for this specific step, as dedicating a full screen to an optional feature may unnecessarily lengthen the onboarding funnel.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users during the critical first-session "Aha moment" window, specifically those who are likely to have recurring transactions with the same group of people (roommates paying rent, friends splitting bills, family sending allowances). The psychological trigger here is efficiency framing: by promising future speed ("pay faster"), the app leverages the user's desire to reduce friction in future interactions, which is a stronger motivator during onboarding than a vague feature description.

It also relies on the Investment Loop psychological principle: by getting the user to invest a small amount of effort now (adding favorites), the app increases the likelihood of retention and habitual return, as the user has now personalized the app to their specific social graph.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Benefit-oriented microcopy: The body text ties a mundane setup task (creating a list) directly to a tangible user benefit (paying people faster), increasing motivation to complete the step.

  • Single Task Focus: By isolating one setup action per screen with massive negative space, the app minimizes decision fatigue and makes the onboarding feel like a quick series of "wins" rather than a long form.

  • Iconography as Semantic Anchor: The bright green star icon immediately communicates the concept of "Favorites" visually before the user even reads the text, speeding up comprehension.

  • Non-modal, Skippable Flow: The presence of a back button (rather than an "X" or being trapped) suggests this step is skippable/optional, respecting user autonomy while still nudging toward feature adoption.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 16
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any feature requiring users to curate a subset from a larger existing dataset (e.g., adding members to a group, favoriting products from a catalog, or selecting recipients for a share). It excels when:

  • The source list is long enough to require searching rather than just scrolling.

  • The action taken (adding) is non-destructive and reversible.

  • Users benefit from repeated, identical action buttons for scanability and speed.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the "add" action requires additional configuration (e.g., setting a nickname or permission level), as a single-tap button oversimplifies a decision that needs more context. It's also unsuitable for very short lists (fewer than 5-10 items) where a full search overlay with keyboard invocation adds unnecessary friction compared to a simple checklist. Additionally, if multiple attributes need comparison before selection, a richer detail/list view would serve users better than this compact row format.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users of a social, messaging, or dialer app who already have an established list of contacts and want to curate a smaller, prioritized "Favorites" subset for quick access. The design leverages the psychological principle of "recognition over recall" by displaying avatars and names rather than requiring the user to remember contact details, and it reduces decision fatigue by using a single repeated action button. This flow is typically used by power users of communication apps who value speed (e.g., quickly re-adding favorites after a data migration, or curating a new favorites list) and expect an efficient, list-based search-to-add mechanism similar to patterns seen in iOS Contacts, WhatsApp, or Phone Favorites.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Immediate Search Focus: The keyboard is invoked automatically on screen load, removing an extra tap and signaling this is a search-first, not browse-first, experience.

  • Consistent, Low-Friction CTA: Every row uses an identical black pill-shaped "Add" button rather than a checkbox or toggle, making the action state ("not yet added") and the required tap target instantly obvious and easy to hit.

  • Non-Destructive Modal Pattern: Using an 'X' to dismiss (instead of a back arrow) correctly signals to the user that this is an overlay task they can cancel at any point, reducing anxiety about making a wrong selection.

  • Clear Content Grouping: The "Results" header separates the input mechanism from the output list, giving the eye a clear anchor point after typing.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 17
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when users need to manage a curated subset (favorites, pinned items, shortlists) from a larger searchable dataset such as contacts, products, or channels. It's ideal when:

  • The action (add/remove) is low-risk and instantly reversible.

  • Users benefit from quick visual state feedback across many list items.

  • Search-first filtering is more efficient than browsing a long unfiltered list.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the "add" action has significant consequences (e.g., financial commitments, irreversible deletions) since it lacks a confirmation step. It's also unsuitable for very small lists (under 5-10 items) where search overhead outweighs benefit, or in flows where users need more contextual information (e.g., mutual connections, last-active status) before deciding (in such cases richer list items or detail previews would be more appropriate than a flat Add/Remove button pattern).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of communication-heavy apps (messaging, social, CRM, or contact-management tools) who need to curate a shortlist of frequently contacted people from a potentially large directory. The design assumes moderate-to-high familiarity with the app and prioritizes speed and efficiency over explanation.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect and completion-oriented behavior: presenting an open-ended list with clear "Add" affordances nudges users to complete their favorites list. The color-coded button states also exploit pattern recognition and peripheral vision scanning, letting users quickly audit "who's already favorited" without reading every label, which reduces friction and decision fatigue in a repetitive curation task.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Stateful button styling: Unselected contacts get a bold black "Add" pill; already-favorited contacts get a light gray "Remove" pill. This instantly communicates state through color/contrast alone, reducing cognitive load during fast scanning.

  • Persistent live search: The search field retains the typed query and shows an inline clear (X) button, letting users quickly iterate on searches without extra taps to a separate clear control.

  • Modal dismiss via X, not back: Signals this is a self-contained task (adding favorites) that can be abandoned at any point without disrupting a multi-step flow.

  • Single-tap reversible actions: Adding or removing a favorite requires no confirmation dialog, treating the action as low-risk and easily reversible (appropriate given it's a preference rather than destructive data change).

  • Flat, scannable list rhythm: Consistent avatar-text-button alignment across all rows creates a predictable reading pattern, letting users process many results quickly.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 18
screens.whereToUse:
Use this explicit-list-with-remove-button pattern when:

  • The list of saved/favorited items is typically short (under 10-15 items) so an uncluttered, non-gesture-based approach remains scannable.

  • Your user base includes less tech-savvy users who may not intuitively know swipe-to-delete gestures.

  • Accessibility is a priority (screen reader/voice control users benefit greatly from a tappable, labeled button over a hidden gesture).

  • The favorited items carry real-world utility (locations, contacts, shortcuts) that benefit from quick management and a strong "add more" CTA.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The favorites/saved list is expected to grow very large (50+ items), where an always-visible remove button per row adds unnecessary visual noise (swipe actions or bulk-select/batch delete would scale better).

  • Screen real estate is constrained (e.g., smaller list-item heights in dense dashboards) where a persistent button competes with other inline metadata.

  • The product's visual language favors gesture-driven interactions consistently across the app; mixing swipe-only actions elsewhere with an explicit button here could create inconsistency.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves frequent, repeat users of a location/transportation/delivery service who want to save recurring destinations (home, work, favorite venues) for quick future selection, reducing address re-entry friction. The target demographic is habitual daily commuters or busy professionals who value speed and one-tap access over rich customization.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the sunk-cost/investment loop: once a user favorites a location, they are more likely to return to and rely on the app because their personalized data lives there, increasing retention and switching costs. The explicit "Remove" control also reduces anxiety around irreversible mistakes, since destructive actions are clearly labeled and intentional rather than accidental swipe-triggers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit "Remove" button instead of swipe gesture: Increases discoverability and accessibility for users unfamiliar with swipe-to-delete patterns, at the cost of slightly more visual clutter per row.

  • Star badge overlay on avatar: A compact visual affordance that communicates "this is a favorite" status without adding extra text or icons elsewhere in the row.

  • Persistent high-contrast CTA: The black "Add favorites" button is anchored low on the screen, always accessible and visually dominant, driving the primary growth action of the screen (adding more favorites).

  • Radical minimalism: Sparse layout with large empty space below the list gracefully accommodates dynamic list length without a broken or awkward look when only one item exists.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 19
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a product facilitates financial or high-stakes transactions between users who may not know each other: P2P payment apps, marketplace escrow flows, rental deposit platforms, or freelance payment tools. It's especially valuable right before a "point of no return" action (sending money, releasing funds, confirming a booking) where surfacing trust signals can meaningfully reduce fraud and buyer's remorse.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy trust-signal treatment for interactions between already-verified or frequently-contacted users (it would add unnecessary friction and feel patronizing to repeat, trusted contacts). It's also inappropriate for low-stakes social interactions (e.g., liking a post, following a user) where transactional risk isn't present, and could unnecessarily flag new users as suspicious purely due to account age, potentially harming legitimate new user retention if overused without nuance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets mainstream P2P payment app users (Venmo, Cash App, Zelle-like audiences) who are about to transact with a stranger, often in scenarios like marketplace sales, splitting bills with a new acquaintance, or responding to a payment request from an unknown handle. It exploits/serves several psychological triggers:

  • Loss aversion:

  • Social proof (absence of): Highlighting the lack of social graph overlap and zero shared payment history removes the false comfort of "everyone else trusts them."

  • Cognitive ease via familiar iconography: Circle-slash and warning triangle icons are universally recognized, reducing the cognitive load needed to interpret risk.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Prohibition icon (circle-slash) reuse: The same "not allowed" icon is used for both informational risk flags and the destructive "Block" action, subconsciously linking unfamiliarity with actionable defense mechanisms.

  • Zero-state as a safety signal: Instead of hiding an empty transaction history, the screen prominently displays "0" total transactions in large type, turning an empty state into a deliberate warning rather than a gap in data.

  • Dual-CTA persistence: Pay and Request remain sticky at the bottom through all the risk-context scrolling, ensuring friction is informative but never blocking (the user retains full agency).

  • Progressive disclosure of danger controls: Block/Report are placed at the bottom, below the trust signals, so they're discovered contextually rather than being alarmingly front-and-center.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any transactional flow where a numeric value is the primary input and the directional intent (send vs. receive, buy vs. sell, debit vs. credit) can reasonably be decided last. Ideal for P2P payments, invoicing tools, bill-splitting features, in-app wallets, or POS-style checkout flows where speed and familiarity are paramount.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the transaction involves multiple line items, complex tax/fee calculations, or requires strong upfront confirmation of recipient identity (e.g., high-value wire transfers) - in those cases, a multi-step review/confirmation screen is safer. Also avoid combining two high-stakes primary actions (Pay/Request) with equal visual weight if one action is significantly riskier or more common than the other, as this can lead to accidental taps in a financial context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using P2P payment or digital wallet apps (e.g., splitting rent, paying back a friend, requesting money for a group gift). The design leverages several psychological principles:

  • Cognitive load reduction: By separating "how much" from "which action," the interface avoids forcing a premature commitment.

  • Familiarity/mental model reuse: The layout mirrors dominant apps like Venmo, so users transfer existing muscle memory instantly, reducing learning curve.

  • Micro-delight & friendliness: Casual copy ("What's this for?") and the Gift icon soften the inherently transactional/financial nature of the task, easing anxiety around money movement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Deferred decision pattern: Amount and note are entered before choosing "Request" or "Pay," letting users focus on one decision at a time.

  • Custom calculator keypad: Built-in math operators (+, -, ×, ÷) allow on-the-fly calculations (e.g., splitting a bill) directly in the amount field.

  • Large, unmissable amount display: Oversized typography with a live cursor makes the primary input the clear visual anchor of the screen.

  • Quick-clear affordance: The circular "x" next to the amount enables instant reset without multiple backspace taps.

  • Contextual "Gift" toggle: Surfaces a monetization/feature differentiator (gift payments) inline without a separate settings screen.

  • Add-recipient "+" control: Enables multi-person requests/payments directly from the entry screen.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a user's in-progress action holds non-trivial value (financial transactions, drafted content, multi-field forms) and an accidental exit would cause real loss of effort or data. It's ideal for guarding "close" or "back" gestures on flows the user has already invested time or attention into, especially transactional flows involving money, irreversible submissions, or long forms.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., closing a search filter, dismissing an informational card) - over-confirming trivial dismissals creates friction fatigue and trains users to blindly tap through dialogs, undermining the pattern's effectiveness when it truly matters. Also reconsider using the same brand-accent color for a destructive confirmation button; a distinct color or icon could better differentiate "cancel/destroy" actions from "affirm/proceed" actions to prevent misclicks.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Venmo's "Busy Urban" audience frequently multitasks while sending or requesting money (interruptions like phone calls, notifications, or second-guessing an amount are common). This confirmation dialog serves as a safety net against accidental exits (like a stray tap on the "X" during the payment flow) that would otherwise silently discard a half-completed transaction.

Psychologically, this leverages the commitment and consequence principle: by forcing an explicit confirmation step before discarding work, Venmo reduces regret-driven support tickets and repeated re-entry of payment details, which is especially valuable to users who are transacting quickly between other tasks and may not want to redo an entry.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving dim/blur overlay: The payment screen remains visible but de-emphasized behind the sheet, so users retain a mental model of what they're about to lose.

  • Redundant, low-friction dismissal: Swipe handle, "X" icon, and "Back" text link all lead to the same safe outcome, accommodating different user habits and reducing rage-taps.

  • Plain-language button labels: "Yes, cancel it" removes any ambiguity about what the affirmative action does, unlike generic "OK/Cancel" dialogs.

  • Minimal sheet real estate: Only the essential decision is presented (no upsells, no extra copy) respecting the urgency of a decision point.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any transactional flow where a single numeric value is the primary input and must be verified before an irreversible action. P2P payments, tipping, invoicing, in-app currency top-ups, or bill-splitting features. It's especially effective when:

  • The action has two symmetrical directions (pay vs. request, buy vs. sell, add vs. withdraw).

  • Speed and low cognitive load are more valuable than rich formatting options.

  • A custom keypad can meaningfully reduce input errors compared to the system keyboard.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex financial inputs requiring multiple fields, currency conversion, or itemized breakdowns (e.g., invoicing with tax/line items) - the single giant number affordance breaks down when more than one value needs simultaneous visibility. It's also unsuitable for accessibility-sensitive contexts unless the custom keypad and buttons are rigorously tested with screen readers, since non-native keyboards can sometimes degrade assistive technology support. Finally, avoid dual equally-weighted CTAs (Request/Pay) in flows where one action is destructive or significantly higher-risk than the other, as visual parity can encourage mis-taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets mainstream consumer P2P payment users (e.g., Venmo, Cash App audiences) - largely younger, mobile-first users splitting bills, paying rent, or gifting money to friends and family. The design leans on social proof and casualness (memo field, gift icon, friendly tone) rather than the sterile formality of banking apps, because trust in this context comes from familiarity and simplicity rather than institutional gravitas.

Psychologically, the oversized amount display exploits the Von Restorff effect (isolation effect) - the number visually dominates so users double-check the figure before committing, reducing regret and support tickets from mistaken amounts. The proximity of "Request" and "Pay" buttons reduces the perceived friction of switching intent, appealing to users who make split-second decisions in social settings (e.g., splitting a check at a restaurant).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom numeric keypad: Overrides the system keyboard to optimize digit entry speed and prevent accidental non-numeric input in a financial context.

  • Giant, high-contrast amount display: The $1 figure is the single largest element on screen, immediately confirming the entered value at a glance (critical for reducing transaction errors).

  • Inline clear (X) affordance: Placed directly next to the amount for instant correction, avoiding tedious character-by-character backspacing.

  • Dual-intent CTA pattern: Presenting "Request" and "Pay" as equally weighted, adjacent pill buttons lets users flip the direction of money flow without navigating to a different screen.

  • Contextual memo field: Placed just above the CTAs so the "why" of the transaction is captured before the irreversible action, reinforcing social/contextual money transfers.

  • Minimal chrome: Only back and close icons are present, keeping the modal feel tightly scoped to a single task and reducing decision fatigue.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for peer-to-peer payment confirmation, checkout confirmation, or any "review and confirm" step where a monetary or high-stakes action needs a final, deliberate user gesture. It's ideal when you want to combine transaction summary, configurable options (payment source, privacy, protections), and legal disclosures on a single scrollable screen without forcing a multi-step wizard.

Particularly effective for social-payment apps, marketplace checkouts, or bill-splitting tools where humanizing the transaction (via memo, avatar, social visibility) increases engagement and repeat usage.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for complex B2B or high-value transactions where additional verification, itemization, or multi-party approval is required (the single-screen simplicity here would be insufficient and risky). Also avoid defaulting sensitive financial activity to "Public" visibility in contexts where privacy regulations or user expectations demand private-by-default behavior (e.g., healthcare payments, salary transfers, enterprise expense platforms).

Not suitable when the payment method or optional add-ons (like protection plans) require detailed comparison, cramming that into a confirmation screen would increase cognitive load and reduce conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers: largely younger, social-media-native users, splitting small, informal costs with friends (e.g., splitting a $1 bottle of water). The design leans on social proof and normalization psychology: by defaulting to "Public" visibility, Venmo nudges users toward sharing payment activity as a social signal, similar to a social media post, which reinforces habitual usage and network growth.

The optional Purchase Protection toggle appeals to trust and loss-aversion psychology, protecting non-power users from being scammed in peer transactions that resemble commercial purchases, thereby reducing friction and anxiety for first-time or infrequent users making similar payments to strangers or sellers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single, high-contrast CTA: The pill-shaped teal "Pay" button is the only strong color on the screen, ensuring zero ambiguity about the next action.

  • Progressive disclosure of risk/fees: Purchase protection terms and fee implications are shown inline with a toggle rather than hidden behind a separate settings page, letting users make an informed decision at the point of payment.

  • Funding source transparency: Displaying the live balance ($150.11) directly on the payment method row lets users mentally verify affordability without navigating away.

  • Social-first framing: Treating the payment like a mini social post (avatar, name, memo, public/private setting) leverages Venmo's differentiator versus purely transactional apps like bank transfers.

screens.name: Wealthfront Deleting & Removing 2
screens.whereToUse: Utilize this pattern (swipeable list with dual-account iconography) for any interface managing scheduled or recurring financial events, such as subscription management, recurring bill pay, or investment auto-invest schedules. It is ideal for lists where each item represents a relationship between two distinct entities (accounts, users, locations) and where users need the ability to cancel/delete pending items before they execute.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for transactions that have already been fully processed/settled, as offering a "Delete" swipe action might mislead users into thinking they can reverse a completed transfer (which is usually not possible in real banking systems and could cause confusion or support tickets). Additionally, for touch-only interfaces where discoverability of swipe gestures is a concern, ensure an explicit "Edit" button or visible delete icons are always present, rather than relying solely on hidden swipe gestures.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves active investors and banking users (likely on a platform like Robinhood or a similar brokerage app) who have set up recurring or one-time transfers between their brokerage cash account and external bank accounts. The target user is someone who needs granular control over their pending money movements (perhaps realizing they scheduled a duplicate transfer or need to cancel a withdrawal before it processes).

The psychological trigger at play is "control and reversibility." In financial apps, users often feel anxiety about money movements; by providing a clear, editable list of pending (not yet finalized) transactions, the app reduces this anxiety and reinforces the perception that the user is always in command of their funds.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-Iconography for Flow Direction: Using two overlapping circular icons (e.g., a bank icon and a stock/cash icon) to visually represent the "Source" and "Destination" of funds is a brilliant way to convey complex relational data at a glance.

  • Destructive Action Redundancy: Showing both the swipe-revealed "Delete" state and the standard "minus" icon edit state provides a clear illustration of the interaction model, ensuring the user understands how to remove an item they no longer want.

  • Data Redaction: Masking the last 4 digits of the bank account number with a gray box (rather than displaying it in plain text) is a subtle but important security/privacy UX decision that builds trust.

  • Modal Containment: Using a "X to close, Done to save" header pattern signals to the user that this is a temporary, task-focused overlay rather than a permanent part of the navigation stack, appropriate for a settings-adjacent management task.

screens.name: Wealthfront Deleting & Removing 3
screens.whereToUse:
Utilize this confirmation dialog pattern specifically for actions that are irreversible or have significant real-world consequences, such as:

  • Deleting scheduled financial transactions, recurring payments, or subscriptions.

  • Canceling pending orders or trades.

  • Removing linked bank accounts or payment methods.

  • Any "Edit Mode" list deletion where data loss is permanent and consequential (e.g., financial data, legal documents).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, blocking modal pattern for low-stakes or easily reversible actions, such as deleting a draft note, removing an item from a wishlist, or dismissing a notification. In these low-risk scenarios, a lighter-weight "Undo" toast/snackbar is superior, as it doesn't interrupt the user's flow with an unnecessary tap-to-confirm step for actions that carry no real financial or permanent risk.

Additionally, avoid using this pattern if the list allows for bulk deletion of many items simultaneously without differentiation, stacking multiple generic "Delete transfer?" dialogs in a row can lead to "dialog fatigue," causing users to blindly tap "Delete" without reading the specific consequences.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users of a financial/investment app (likely Robinhood or a similar brokerage, based on the iconography) who are actively managing their automated finances, such as recurring deposits, withdrawals, or internal transfers between a cash account and a linked bank account.

The psychological trigger at play is the mitigation of "action anxiety." Financial apps deal with real money, so users are highly risk-averse. By interrupting the flow with a modal confirmation, the app leverages the user's need for certainty and control, effectively saying "we know this is serious, so we are double-checking with you." This builds trust in the platform's reliability while simultaneously protecting the user (and the company) from support tickets/losses resulting from erroneous, irreversible deletions of pending money movements.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Layered Destructive Confirmation: The design requires two distinct steps to delete a transfer (tapping the minus icon, then confirming in the dialog), creating a robust safety net against accidental deletion of financial transactions.

  • Contextual Account Masking: The bank account number is partially obscured ("ending in ****"), reinforcing security best practices even within a management/deletion flow.

  • Dual-Avatar Iconography: Using two stacked icons (institution logos) for each list item allows users to scan the "Pending Transactions" list quickly to identify the specific transfer they wish to remove without reading full sentences.

  • iOS Native Modal Standards: Adherence to native UIAlertController styling (rounded card, distinct button dividers, red for destructive) ensures the interaction feels trustworthy and familiar to iOS users, reducing cognitive load during a high-stakes decision.

screens.name: Wealthfront Deleting & Removing 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any screen that lists scheduled, recurring, or in-flight financial transactions (transfers, payments, subscriptions) where users need at-a-glance status plus an immediate cancellation option. It's ideal when the list is typically short (a handful of items) and the primary user goal is auditing/canceling rather than browsing or analyzing. Also effective for showing directional relationships (money, data, or content moving from A to B) via dual-icon compositions.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid always-visible destructive icons when the list can grow large or when accidental taps carry high risk (in high-volume lists, a swipe-to-reveal or long-press pattern paired with a confirmation dialog is safer. This flat list-only approach also breaks down if transfers need richer detail (e.g., transfer method, fees, recurring schedule)) in that case a drill-down/detail view would be more appropriate. Finally, since there's no confirmation dialog shown before deletion, this pattern should only be used if a confirmation step follows the tap (to prevent costly accidental cancellations of real money movements).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday retail investors or banking app users who have set up recurring or one-time transfers between a brokerage cash account and an external bank account. The psychological driver here is control and reassurance: users transferring money, especially withdrawals, want confidence that a mistaken or unwanted transfer can be easily stopped before it executes. By foregrounding the cancel affordance and clearly labeling direction/amount/date, the design directly addresses transactional anxiety common in fintech products, where users fear "losing" money to an error or fraud. The redacted account numbers also serve a trust-building purpose, subtly reminding the user their financial data is being handled securely.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Directional Dual-Icon Avatars: Stacking a source-account icon and destination-account icon creates an instant visual mental model of money flow direction, reducing cognitive load versus reading text alone.

  • Always-Visible Destructive Action: Rather than hiding cancel/delete behind a swipe gesture, the red minus button is persistently visible, which is optimal for a screen whose entire purpose is transaction management/cancellation.

  • Clear Information Hierarchy: Amount and transaction type lead the row in bold, larger type, with supporting metadata (date, account routing detail) visually subordinate, matching how users scan for the most decision-relevant info first.

  • Masked Account Numbers: Redacting the last digits of linked bank accounts reinforces security best practices even in a post-authentication context.

results.query: Where to avoid using swipe-to-confirm in non-destructive flows

screens.name: Craft - Deleting a comment - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when building collaborative document, content, or design review tools where feedback needs to be anchored to specific content segments. It's ideal for:

  • Writing/note apps adding team or client review workflows
  • Design tools with annotation/commenting on specific layers or text
  • CMS or content-approval platforms needing inline editorial feedback
  • Any product where preserving the relationship between source content and discussion is critical to comprehension
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in single-player, private-only apps where no multi-user collaboration exists (the added UI weight (avatars, threads, menus) would be unnecessary clutter). It's also a poor fit for very short-form content or chat-like apps where comments-on-comments could cause excessive nesting and confusion. On small screens, stacking a highlighted block plus a bottom sheet can feel cramped if the source text is lengthy; in that case, consider a dedicated full-screen comments view or side panel (on larger viewports) instead of an overlay.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets professional and team-oriented users of Craft (product managers, founders, designers, or writers who use the app not just for private notes but for collaborative drafting and review (e).g., drafting a "Web3 Platform Landing" brief with stakeholder input). The psychological driver here is collaborative accountability and social validation: seeing named avatars and real critique ("may attract the wrong audience") builds trust that the document is being rigorously vetted, while the quick "agree. will revise it" reply shows responsiveness and closes the feedback loop quickly, satisfying the commenter's need to be heard.

The persistent "type your comment" field and low-friction contextual menu reduce the activation energy needed to participate, catering to users who want fast, async collaboration without the formality of a suggestion-mode redline.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Highlighted-text-to-comment linkage: The light blue highlight on the source paragraph visually ties the comment thread back to the exact passage being discussed, a technique borrowed from professional editing tools (Google Docs, Medium) that is rare and valuable in a "note-taking" app.
  • Non-disruptive bottom sheet: Comments slide up as an overlay rather than a full-screen takeover, preserving spatial context and making it easy to dismiss and return to writing.
  • On-demand contextual menu: Edit/Delete actions only appear via long-press, keeping the comment thread visually quiet and uncluttered during normal reading.
  • Comment affordance on the source block: The "2 comments · Just Now" meta-row under the highlighted paragraph acts as a lightweight entry point/summary, so users can gauge discussion activity without opening the thread.

screens.name: Craft - Deleting a comment - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this confirmation dialog pattern whenever an action is:

  • Irreversible or costly to reverse (deleting comments, documents, folders, accounts).
  • Infrequent enough that added friction won't meaningfully slow down core workflows.
  • High-stakes relative to the user's effort invested (e.g., long-form comments, collaborative threads, financial transactions).

It's especially valuable in collaborative or document-based apps where content often represents significant user or team effort, and in any interface where a single mis-tap (like a swipe or long-press) could otherwise trigger permanent loss.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes, easily reversible, or high-frequency actions (e.g., deleting a character, dismissing a notification, or unchecking a checklist item) where a confirmation dialog would feel like unnecessary friction and train users to blindly tap "Delete" out of habit (alert fatigue). In such cases, prefer undo-instead-of-confirm patterns (e.g., a toast with an "Undo" action) that preserve speed while still offering a safety net. Overusing hard confirmation dialogs across an app also dilutes their perceived importance, making users numb to genuinely critical warnings.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Craft's audience is writers, knowledge workers, and teams collaborating on richly formatted documents (people who invest real effort into structuring comments, feedback, and critique threads (as seen with Alex Smith and Sam Lee's exchange on the Web3 platform copy)). For this audience, accidental loss of a thoughtful comment is a real pain point, especially given the editorial, document-centric nature of the app where comments often contain substantive feedback, not throwaway chat messages.

The psychological trigger here is loss aversion: by forcing a confirmation step and explicitly stating permanence, Craft reduces the anxiety of interacting with destructive controls, which in turn encourages users to use comment/delete features more confidently, knowing a safety net (the confirmation) exists before anything is truly lost.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native platform conformance: The dialog mimics iOS's native alert styling almost exactly (rounded card, blurred backdrop, stacked pill buttons), reducing cognitive load since users already have a learned mental model for this interaction.
  • Contextual backdrop preservation: Rather than a full-screen takeover, the dimmed/blurred background keeps the underlying comment thread and highlighted text visible, so users retain situational awareness of exactly what they're about to delete.
  • Asymmetric visual weight on buttons: Both buttons share equal size and shape, but color alone (red vs. neutral gray) communicates risk (a subtle but effective use of color psychology without needing icons or extra copy).
  • Irreversibility disclosure: Explicitly stating "This action cannot be undone" rather than silently deleting or offering a generic alert builds trust and reduces regret-driven support requests.

screens.name: Craft - Deleting a comment - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any collaborative document, note-taking, or content-authoring tool where feedback needs to stay tied to specific passages (specs, contracts, briefs, scripts).
  • Design or writing tools aiming for a "quiet," non-intrusive collaboration layer that doesn't disrupt the primary reading/writing experience.
  • Products where asynchronous, threaded feedback is more valuable than real-time chat, such as review cycles, editorial workflows, or async product documentation.
  • Apps wanting to combine resolution/triage controls (checkmark) directly into the comment thread to streamline review completion.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Real-time collaborative editors with many simultaneous commenters may need a persistent margin/sidebar view instead of a modal sheet, since bottom sheets can obscure concurrent discussions happening elsewhere in the doc.
  • Short-form or highly visual content (images, diagrams) where inline text highlighting doesn't translate (a pin/marker-based commenting system would serve better).
  • Data-dense enterprise tools where comment threads need rich formatting, mentions, or attachments; this minimal sheet may feel too lightweight for complex review cycles.
  • Public-facing or social contexts where comment visibility and moderation controls (beyond a simple overflow menu) are essential.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets knowledge workers, product teams, and writers who use Craft collaboratively for specs, briefs, and planning documents (as evidenced by the Web3 product-strategy content). The target user is someone reviewing or co-authoring a document asynchronously, needing to leave feedback without disrupting the document's polished, editorial presentation.

Psychologically, the design leverages contextual anchoring: humans retain feedback far better when it's tied to its exact source rather than abstracted into a list. The soft blue highlight also triggers a spotlight effect, drawing the eye precisely where discussion is needed. The low-friction bottom sheet and persistent input field cater to users' desire for quick, frictionless exchanges typical of async remote collaboration, reducing the activation energy needed to participate in a conversation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline highlight-to-thread binding: The commented text is visually tinted directly in the document body, so context is never lost (a major differentiator from tools that rely on disconnected sidebar comment lists).
  • Non-intrusive comment affordance: The avatar + "1 comment · Just Now" summary sits unobtrusively below the highlighted passage, acting as a quiet invitation rather than a blocking UI element.
  • Bottom sheet thread view: Keeps the user anchored to the document (visible, dimmed, behind the sheet) while reading/replying, preserving spatial context and avoiding a jarring full-screen navigation.
  • Inline resolve action: A checkmark icon in the sheet header allows marking the thread as resolved without extra menus, respecting the reviewer's momentum.
  • Persistent reply field: Always-visible "Type your comment" input reduces the steps needed to respond, encouraging quick, in-flow collaboration.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for schema editing or settings configuration where a single object (like a column, field, or variable) has multiple distinct properties (Name, Type, Constraints) that need to be edited in one view.
  • Ideal for No-code/Low-code platforms where you need to translate complex technical configurations (data types) into simple, mobile-friendly toggles and list selectors.
  • Effective when you need to provide contextual safety nets, such as combining an editing action with a destructive delete action in a logically separated way.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the "Field Type" selection requires extensive sub-configuration (e.g., complex Formula fields or Linked Records with multiple options) that cannot be summarized in a single helper line; this would require a dedicated sub-screen rather than an inline toggle.
  • Do not use this dense, stacked form layout for simple, single-input tasks (like just renaming a file), as the heavy sectioning would feel bureaucratic and slow down a simple interaction.
  • Not suitable for public-facing consumer apps where users are unfamiliar with technical "Field Type" terminology; this density works for professional tools but could alienate casual users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Operations Managers, Project Managers, and Database Builders who need the flexibility to modify their business logic (the "schema") while on the go, perhaps during a meeting where a new business requirement arises.

The psychological trigger here is Mastery and Control. By exposing granular field-type controls directly in a mobile modal, Airtable reinforces the user's identity as a "builder" or "admin" of their own system, rather than just a passive data-entry clerk. The simplicity of the toggle and dropdown reduces the intimidation factor often associated with "editing a database," making the user feel capable of making structural changes without engineering help.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Type-Specific Contextual Help: The dynamic helper text ("Useful for checklists.") that changes based on the selected Field Type acts as an inline tooltip, educating users on database schema design without leaving the current screen.
  • Grouped Table Hierarchy: Using distinct card groupings for Name, Description, and Type creates clear visual rhythm and reduces the perceived complexity of editing a database schema on a small screen.
  • Isolated Destructive Action: Placing "Delete Field" in its own distinct section at the bottom, separated by whitespace/dividers from the editing fields, prevents accidental data deletion via fat-fingering.
  • Icon-based Type Identification: Using a colored icon (green circle) next to the field type name allows users to quickly visually scan and identify field types across the app, creating a consistent visual language for data types.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Apply this pattern whenever a user-initiated action is irreversible and affects data beyond the immediate view (e.g., deleting a column/field, removing a user from a shared workspace, deleting a database table, or archiving a project with dependent records). It's especially valuable in collaborative, multi-user tools where one person's action can silently affect others' data.

Use the inline expansion technique (Checkbox toggle appearing within the Field Type row) for simple configuration options to avoid unnecessary drill-down navigation, reserving full-screen or secondary modals only for field types requiring multiple settings.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy-handed confirmation flow for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., toggling a UI preference, hiding a column temporarily) - doing so would create unnecessary friction and training users to blindly dismiss dialogs ("confirmation fatigue"), which weakens the pattern's effectiveness when it truly matters.

Also avoid echoing overly long or technical field names verbatim in a confirmation button if space is constrained; truncate gracefully or use a secondary text input requiring the user to type the field name for extremely high-risk deletions (e.g., deleting an entire base).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations managers, database administrators, and power users who are actively structuring or maintaining a shared Airtable base (often under time pressure or while collaborating with a team that depends on data integrity). Because Airtable fields can hold months of accumulated team data, the psychological stakes of an accidental deletion are high (irreversible data loss affecting colleagues).

The design leans on loss aversion and friction-as-safety principles: by making the deletion path require multiple deliberate taps and explicit acknowledgment of data loss, Airtable reduces anxiety for cautious users while still allowing expert users to move through quickly once they've internalized the pattern.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit consequence messaging: The dialog doesn't just ask "are you sure?" - it educates the user on exactly what will be lost (data across every record), reducing the chance of regret-driven support tickets.
  • Named re-confirmation: The button reads 'Delete "Visited?"' rather than a generic "Delete," reinforcing which specific field is about to be destroyed and guarding against misclicks when editing multiple fields in a session.
  • Inline type configuration: The Checkbox toggle and description appear directly within the Field Type row, minimizing navigation depth for simple field types.
  • Spatial separation of destructive action: Placing "Delete field" far below the primary editable fields, with a divider and trash icon, uses visual hierarchy to signal danger and reduce accidental taps.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Schema/configuration screens in no-code or low-code platforms where users define data structure (e.g., database builders, form builders, CRM customization panels).
  • Any settings list where each item represents a configurable "type" that benefits from a live visual preview rather than a text-only description.
  • Admin panels that need to onboard non-technical users to technical concepts through embedded contextual video and analogy-driven microcopy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Simple, flat forms with a small, fixed number of fields, adding live previews and type pickers would be over-engineering for a one-time contact form, for instance.
  • Screens targeting highly technical users (e.g., developers using a SQL schema editor) who may find the playful icon/analogy treatment patronizing and prefer dense, code-like table editors instead.
  • Contexts where field reordering has no real functional impact (e.g., static reports), since drag handles would add unnecessary complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations leads, project managers, and "citizen developers" who build business systems without formal engineering backgrounds. These users need to configure data structures but are often unfamiliar with database terminology like "schema" or "field types." The design leans on recognition over recall (visual previews, icons, color coding) and analogy-based education (the blueprint metaphor) to build confidence and reduce the intimidation factor typically associated with database configuration tools.

The locked primary field and drag-to-reorder handles also speak to power users who need structural control and customization once they're comfortable, supporting Airtable's dual audience of beginners and advanced builders.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live mini-previews per field type: Each row visually simulates its data type (progress bar, numeric input, file icons) instead of relying on text labels alone, dramatically improving scannability and comprehension.
  • Color-coded type icons: Each field type has a distinct icon/color combo (blue "A" for text, orange "#" for number, pink paperclip for attachment) creating a quick visual taxonomy that scales well as tables grow to dozens of fields.
  • Locked primary field affordance: The padlock icon on "Location" clearly communicates an immutable schema rule without needing a modal or error message.
  • Embedded contextual video/coach mark: Using a tappable video thumbnail inside the explanatory banner caters to varied learning styles (read vs. watch) and is dismissible via the "X" for repeat users.
  • Persistent "Add a new field" CTA: Anchored at the bottom of the list, it keeps the primary creation action always accessible regardless of scroll depth.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 35
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any "manage an existing commitment" moment (savings goals, budgets, subscriptions, recurring transfers, habit trackers, or fitness targets) where the two realistic next actions are "adjust" or "cancel/delete." It's ideal when:

  • The action set is naturally binary and mutually exclusive.

  • You want to reduce anxiety around creating the original commitment by proving it's reversible.

  • The context is emotionally sensitive (money, health, personal goals) and benefits from calm, minimal-jargon copy.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are more than two realistic actions available (e.g., pause, edit amount, edit deadline, delete) - cramming more choices into this minimal layout will break the clean binary decision framing and require a list/menu pattern instead. Also avoid pairing a destructive action with a full-black high-contrast button, as done here only for the safe action; if removal carries real, permanent financial consequences (not just UI removal), add a secondary confirmation step (e.g., a destructive confirmation dialog) rather than a single tap on "Remove goal."
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday banking/fintech app users managing personal savings pots or sub-accounts (e.g., "Emergency Fund," "Vacation," "New Laptop"). These users are often in a reflective, low-urgency mindset (checking in on progress rather than in a transactional rush) so the screen is designed to feel calm and consequence-free.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Zeigarnik effect and loss-aversion mitigation: by explicitly stating removal is a safe, available option (rather than forcing users to hunt for a hidden "delete" deep in settings), the app reduces the anxiety of commitment. Users are more likely to create new goals in the future if they trust they can painlessly undo or adjust them later (a classic strategy to increase feature adoption by lowering the perceived cost of trying something).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Binary decision architecture: Reducing the interaction to exactly two mutually exclusive choices eliminates decision paralysis on a topic (personal savings) that can otherwise feel emotionally loaded.

  • Visual weight signals intent: The primary "Update goal" button uses high-contrast black to subtly encourage retention/editing over deletion, while "Remove goal" is styled in a lower-contrast gray without being hidden or buried in a menu.

  • Friendly, literal icon: The target-with-pencil icon reduces reliance on text alone to convey "you're editing a goal," aiding fast scanning and reducing translation/localization burden.

  • Non-punitive microcopy: Framing removal as an equally valid option ("You can either... or") avoids shaming the user for changing their mind about a savings goal.

  • Escape hatch (X): A persistent, unambiguous close control reduces the perceived risk of opening the sheet at all.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 36
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a user is about to delete, cancel, or unsubscribe from something that has downstream financial, data, or relationship consequences (especially in fintech, subscription management, or account settings contexts). It's ideal when:

  • The action is irreversible or has non-obvious side effects (e.g., money movement, data loss, subscription cancellation).

  • You need to reduce support burden by preemptively answering "what happens next?"

  • Trust and transparency are core brand values (banking, healthcare, legal apps).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen confirmation pattern for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., removing a single line item from a cart, dismissing a notification) - it would feel like overkill and add unnecessary friction. Also avoid it when speed is critical to the user's workflow, such as bulk-management screens where repeated deletions should use lighter-weight inline confirmations or undo-snackbar patterns instead of a modal interruption. If the consequences list becomes too long, it risks overwhelming users and causing them to skim past important details.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday banking/fintech app users who are managing personal savings goals (e.g., an "Extra cash" goal in what appears to be a neobank or savings automation app like Chime, Current, or Varo). The design assumes a non-technical, mainstream consumer who needs financial actions explained in plain language, not jargon.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss aversion mitigation: by proactively explaining that funds are safely rerouted to Savings rather than lost, it neutralizes the fear that typically accompanies deleting a financial goal. It also uses the default safe-choice bias (gray Cancel button styled as the "path of least resistance") paired with a color-coded warning system (red for irreversible/impactful actions) to guide decision-making without being manipulative.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consequence transparency: Three distinct bullet points explain exactly what happens to funds, round-ups, and paycheck distributions, eliminating ambiguity that could cause support tickets or user anxiety.

  • De-escalated iconography: A friendly green trash icon (rather than a red warning triangle) keeps the emotional register calm despite the destructive nature of the action.

  • Button hierarchy & spatial safety: Cancel is neutral gray and positioned above the red "Remove goal" CTA, following the convention that the safer action is easier/first to reach, while the destructive action is visually loud but requires deliberate final commitment.

  • Dual exit paths: Both the top-left "X" and the "Cancel" button allow escape, reducing the chance of unintended deletions.

  • Reassurance copy: "You can always change this" reduces loss-aversion friction and builds confidence to proceed.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 37
screens.whereToUse:
• Confirming completion of destructive or edit actions (deletions, unsubscribes, cancellations) where the user needs certainty the action succeeded.

  • Any flow where you want to give the user a clean "exit ramp" after completing a task, before returning them to a list or dashboard.

  • Situations where brevity and lack of ambiguity are more valuable than rich visual storytelling.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this stripped-down pattern for actions the product wants to incentivize reversing (e.g., cancellations you want to prevent) - here an "Undo" option or reason-for-removal capture would be more strategic.

  • Don't use for celebratory milestones (e.g., completing a goal) - the neutral tone here would undersell an achievement; use a more festive/animated confirmation instead.

  • Not ideal when the user might benefit from next-step guidance (e.g., "Create a new goal?") since this screen offers no forward momentum, only exit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of goal-tracking, habit, fitness, or finance apps who are actively managing/pruning their list of active goals. It serves users who want quick, low-friction confirmation that their action succeeded without needing to parse extra text or make further decisions.

Psychologically, it leverages the Von Restorff effect (the isolated green checkmark stands out against a blank canvas) and satisfies the user's need for closure, confirming that the system state now matches their intent, which reduces anxiety about whether the deletion "really happened."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single, unambiguous CTA: Only one button ("Done") is present, removing any decision fatigue after the transaction is complete.

  • Iconography reinforces text: The green checkmark visually front-loads the meaning before the user even reads the headline, aiding fast comprehension and scannability.

  • Multiple dismissal paths: Close icon, primary button, and swipe-down drag handle all lead to the same outcome, respecting different user habits/mental models.

  • Restraint in visual noise: No extraneous stats, upsells, or secondary CTAs dilute the confirmation (the screen respects the user's time).

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 38
screens.whereToUse: Use this dashboard pattern for any balance-based financial product (savings, wallets, rewards points, gift cards) where you want to combine a headline balance, a primary CTA, sub-account breakdown, and automation settings in one scrollable view. It's ideal for consumer finance apps aiming to increase deposit frequency and habitual engagement through visible progress and effortless automation toggles.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex or professional financial dashboards (e.g., investment/brokerage platforms) where users need dense analytical data, multiple accounts comparison, or charts (the oversized single balance and simplified list would feel underinformative). Also avoid disabling critical actions (like Withdraw) without an explanatory tooltip/microcopy, as silent disabled states can confuse users unfamiliar with why the action is unavailable.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday consumers, particularly younger or financially novice users (Gen Z/Millennials) who use neobanking apps for budgeting and micro-saving. The psychological drivers include the endowment/goal-gradient effect (progress bars motivate completion), loss aversion reduction via effortless automated saving (Round Ups) that doesn't feel like an active sacrifice, and friction reduction for the primary "Add money" action to encourage habitual, frequent deposits.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-state monetization hook: Turning the empty "$0.00" balance state into an interest-earning upsell rather than a dead end.

  • Contextual button disabling: The Withdraw button is greyed out when balance is zero, preventing user error and communicating state at a glance.

  • Automation as first-class citizens: Round Ups and Paycheck splitting are surfaced prominently on the main dashboard, encouraging passive, "set it and forget it" saving behavior.

  • Goal progress visualization: The "0% complete" label under Extra Cash primes users to view savings as a game with a finish line, encouraging continued contributions.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 23
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech or budgeting apps targeting younger demographics who respond better to informal, meme-literate communication.

  • Any product delivering potentially negative or sensitive information (bill increases, overspending) where humor can soften the blow and keep users engaged rather than churning out of anxiety.

  • AI assistant products where building a distinct, memorable personality is a core differentiator and retention driver.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth financial products where users expect formal, data-dense, precise reporting rather than jokes.

  • Situations involving serious financial hardship, fraud alerts, or compliance/legal disclosures, where levity could feel dismissive or inappropriate.

  • Markets/cultures where humor styles (memes, GIFs, internet slang) don't translate well or could be perceived as unprofessional/untrustworthy for money matters.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z / millennials) who are often intimidated or bored by traditional banking apps and spreadsheets. By using humor, memes, and casual texting conventions, Cleo lowers the emotional guardedness people have around discussing debt, subscriptions, and spending habits.

Psychologically, framing the bot as a sarcastic "friend" rather than an institutional "bank" reduces shame and defensiveness, a key trigger for the target demo who may otherwise avoid checking their finances due to anxiety. The chat format also leverages the same neural pathways as texting with friends, making financial engagement feel habitual and low-stakes rather than a dreaded chore.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-as-Dashboard Pattern: Replacing static financial reports with a conversational thread makes bill review feel like getting advice from a witty friend instead of reading a bank statement.

  • Comedic Loading State: The Tom Hanks GIF plus repeated 🤔 emoji acts as a playful "typing/thinking" indicator, masking backend processing time while building anticipation and reducing perceived wait friction.

  • Message Reactions: Thumbs-down and emoji reaction affordances turn a one-way notification into a two-way social interaction, implicitly collecting sentiment/feedback data on AI responses.

  • Personality-Driven Copy: Deliberate lowercase/casual typos ("mayBE") and playful analogies humanize the AI, making financial guilt-inducing topics (overspending) feel less punitive.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 24
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription management or expense-review flows where users need to make many quick binary decisions (keep/cancel, approve/reject).

  • Onboarding flows for fintech apps that want to feel more like a friendly assistant than a bank.

  • Any AI chatbot experience that needs to elicit structured input (yes/no, like/dislike) without breaking the conversational flow.

  • Content curation or recommendation review tools (e.g., reviewing photos, matches, or product suggestions).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for high-stakes financial actions (e.g., actually cancelling a subscription) without a confirmation step, since swipe gestures can be accidental or misread.

  • Not suitable for users who may have motor/accessibility impairments unless an alternative button-based method is also provided.

  • Avoid in enterprise/B2B contexts where a more formal, data-dense table view is expected and swipe gestures may feel gimmicky or untrustworthy.

  • Don't use if the underlying decision requires more context/data than a single card can display (e.g., complex contract terms).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, mobile-native users (Gen Z/Millennials) who are highly familiar with swipe gestures from dating apps (Tinder) and short-form content (TikTok/Instagram Stories). These users are often anxious or avoidant about tracking their subscriptions and recurring bills, so Cleo leverages a familiar, low-friction, almost addictive gesture pattern to overcome that avoidance.

Psychologically, this taps into the Tinder effect: binary decisions framed as a game reduce decision fatigue and make users more willing to process an entire backlog of items quickly. The playful tone and swipe mechanic also reduce the shame/guilt often associated with confronting unused subscriptions, turning a negative task into a satisfying, almost cathartic decluttering experience.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Gamified Subscription Audit: Converts a boring financial chore (reviewing recurring bills) into a swipeable, game-like micro-interaction, drastically increasing engagement and completion rates.

  • Directional Color Semantics: Blue (keep/positive) vs Red (ditch/negative) chat bubbles visually pre-train the user on the swipe mechanic before interaction, reducing errors.

  • Redundant Affordance Cues: Emoji hand icons are repeated both in the chat text and directly on the card itself, ensuring the gesture is understood regardless of where the user's attention lands.

  • Card Stack Depth Cue: A visible second card peeking from behind the top card communicates that this is a queue/sequence, setting expectations for multiple swipes.

  • Hybrid Navigation: Combines a persistent bottom Tab Bar with an in-context chat interface, letting the AI-guided task live inside the broader app ecosystem without feeling siloed.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 25
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription/expense audit or "bill triage" flows where users must make many quick binary decisions.

  • Onboarding flows that need to sort large data sets (e.g., categorizing transactions, selecting interests) in an engaging way.

  • Any AI assistant or chatbot experience that needs to hand off from conversational guidance to a hands-on interactive task seamlessly.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for irreversible or high-stakes financial actions (e.g., actual subscription cancellation or fund transfers) without a secondary confirmation step, since swipe gestures can be triggered accidentally.

  • Not ideal for accessibility-first contexts or older/less tech-savvy demographics unfamiliar with swipe gestures, unless paired with equally prominent tap-based alternatives (as done here).

  • Avoid if the underlying data set requires nuanced, multi-factor evaluation rather than a simple binary keep/ditch decision, swiping encourages snap judgments.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, mobile-native users (Cleo's core demographic is Gen Z/millennial subprime and budget-conscious consumers) who are accustomed to swipe-based interactions from apps like Tinder and Bumble. By repurposing a familiar dating-app gesture for financial decision-making, Cleo lowers the cognitive and emotional barrier to confronting "wasteful" spending.

The psychological trigger at play is the Sunk Cost / Zeigarnik Effect combined with gamification: once a user starts swiping through cards, the incomplete stack creates a compulsion to finish, and the swipe motion itself feels effortless and rewarding compared to manually toggling settings in a boring list.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-to-Action Bridge: Uses conversational bubbles to teach a non-standard gesture (swipe left/right) before the interactive card appears, reducing discoverability friction.

  • Redundant Signifiers: The card includes explicit "Keep" text, a thumb emoji, and a green circular button (three separate visual cues for the same action, ensuring accessibility for users who don't intuit swipe gestures).

  • Progress Peek: A glimpse of the "You're done swiping" completion card underneath the current card gives users a subtle sense of how close they are to finishing, reducing perceived effort.

  • Gamified Decluttering: Converts a traditionally tedious finance task (subscription review) into a quick, dopamine-driven swiping game reminiscent of dating apps.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 26
screens.whereToUse: Use this chat-first, personality-driven pattern when building products in emotionally sensitive categories (finance, health, mental wellness) where a friendly, humanized interface can lower user resistance and shame. Effective for youth-oriented or Gen Z-targeted products where informal tone builds trust faster than corporate polish. Also useful when the AI/bot needs to feel proactive and stateful (sending unprompted encouragement, insights or content (like the story cards)) turning a reactive utility into a habitual daily check-in destination.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for enterprise, B2B, or high-stakes regulatory contexts (e.g., tax filing, wealth management for HNW clients, insurance claims) where users expect precision, authority, and a professional tone rather than jokes and slang. Also inappropriate for users who need quick, scannable data (e.g., checking exact balances) since a chat-log format buries structured data beneath conversational filler, increasing time-to-information. Overuse of humor can also alienate users during genuinely distressing financial moments (e.g., overdraft, debt collection) if tone isn't dynamically adjusted.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, digitally-native users (largely Gen Z/Millennial) who are fatigued by traditional banking UI and spreadsheet-style budgeting tools, and who respond better to conversational, meme-literate communication. The design leverages the psychological principle of parasocial relationship building: by giving the AI a distinct voice, personality, and even slang, Cleo becomes something closer to a texting buddy than software, which increases daily engagement and reduces the shame/anxiety typically associated with confronting personal finances.

The "hype me" / encouragement request also taps into self-affirmation psychology: users experiencing financial stress or low motivation can request a dopamine boost, which increases app stickiness and creates positive associative conditioning with opening the app.
screens.keyHighlights:
Multi-bubble message chunking: Instead of a single dense paragraph, Cleo's reply is broken into 4 sequential bubbles, replicating naturalistic human texting rhythm and increasing engagement/read-through.

Story carousel above chat: Borrowing a proven social-media UX pattern (Stories) to surface promotional/educational content without interrupting the primary chat flow.

Emotionally-tuned quick-reply chip: "My spirit is ready" is a humor-first CTA that reduces the cognitive/emotional barrier of initiating a finance conversation.

Chat as a primary tab, not a support overlay: Placing "Chat" centrally in the tab bar (flanked by Spend, Budget, Save, Borrow, Habits) signals it is the app's primary interaction surface, not an afterthought.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 27
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for consumer fintech, wellness, or coaching apps targeting younger, less finance-savvy audiences where the goal is to reduce shame/anxiety around a sensitive topic (money, health, habits) and increase daily engagement frequency. It works well when the brand wants a distinct, ownable personality and when data can be meaningfully summarized in short, digestible bursts rather than dense tables.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth financial products where users need precise, scannable data (multi-account balances, detailed transaction histories, tax documents) - chat bubbles bury and dilute critical numbers. It also fails users who prefer efficiency over personality, or in regulated contexts where casual tone could undermine trust or clarity around compliance-sensitive information.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets younger users (Gen Z/millennials) who are financially anxious, distrustful of traditional banks, and highly fluent in meme/chat culture. By wrapping potentially stressful information (overspending) inside a humorous, informal conversation, the design leverages the familiarity heuristic: users already spend hours daily in messaging apps, so this interface requires zero learning curve. The comedic tone and self-deprecating quick replies ("I'm v good at spending") also employ social validation and humor as an anxiety-reduction mechanism, making users more willing to return and engage with their finances rather than avoid them.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-as-Dashboard: Financial statements are delivered as conversational bubbles rather than dry stat cards, making mundane data ("$181 spent") feel like a message from a friend.

  • Quick-Reply Chips: Pre-written response pills reduce friction and typing effort while keeping the user engaged in a two-way "dialogue" with the AI.

  • GIF/Meme Integration: Embedding pop-culture reaction GIFs directly into financial commentary humanizes the brand and makes budgeting content inherently more shareable and re-engaging.

  • Personified Brand Voice: The "Cleo" persona with a bold logo and personality-driven copy converts a utility app into a relationship, driving daily emotional engagement.

results.query: When to display full-page interstitial versus inline permission priming

screens.name: Figma - Browse FigJam resources - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Content libraries or marketplaces (templates, plugins, stickers, assets) where the catalog is large and heterogeneous enough to need both search and browse paths.
  • Tools aimed at mixed audiences (experts + non-experts) where grouping by use-case/outcome rather than technical category improves discoverability.
  • Any modal/sheet that sits atop a persistent workspace, where keeping core tools visible reduces the feeling of a disruptive context switch.
  • Collaborative products where showing active participant avatars on content cards can drive social engagement and perceived popularity.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, multi-section browse pattern for simple apps with a small, flat set of options (it adds unnecessary scrolling and visual overhead).
  • Not ideal when users need a fast, single-purpose action (e.g., quick insert of one recent asset); in that case a simpler recents-first list would reduce friction.
  • Outcome-based grouping can backfire for expert power-users who already know exact template/object names and prefer direct, alphabetized or type-based browsing.
  • Showing collaborator avatars/social proof may feel unnecessary or cluttered in single-player or privacy-sensitive contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both professional designers and the broader "team" audience Figma has expanded toward (PMs, facilitators, marketers) via FigJam. The outcome-oriented section labels ("Run a meeting," "Brainstorm together") indicate Figma is designing for non-designer personas who think in terms of workshops and meetings, not design primitives.

Psychologically, the screen leverages reduced choice paralysis by pre-curating templates into digestible, goal-based clusters, and uses social proof (avatar stacks, "+7" counts) to build confidence that these templates are battle-tested and popular among peers. The friendly, assistant-like search copy reduces the intimidation factor of an empty canvas or blank search field, a common onboarding friction point for creative tools.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual discovery model: Combines a prominent search bar with scrollable category tabs, serving both intent-driven and exploratory users simultaneously.
  • Outcome-based grouping: Templates are organized by team activity/goal ("Brainstorm together," "Run a meeting") rather than by object taxonomy, dramatically lowering the learning curve for non-designers.
  • Persistent creation toolbar: The canvas toolbar remains docked beneath the discovery sheet, reinforcing that browsing is a lightweight, interruptible overlay rather than a context switch.
  • Social proof via avatars: The stacked collaborator avatars with a "+7" overflow badge on the "Simple Vote" card visually communicates active team participation and encourages FOMO-driven engagement.
  • Collaboration-aware header: Live collaborator avatars and share icon in the top bar keep multiplayer context visible even while browsing a modal.

screens.name: Figma - Browse FigJam resources - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Content marketplaces or plugin/extension directories embedded inside a core product (e.g., app stores, template galleries, asset libraries).
  • Tools that need to surface both "utility" and "delight" content within the same workspace without forcing a context switch away from the user's active work.
  • Collaborative or creative software where injecting personality and curated editorial content increases engagement and session enjoyment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern in dense, enterprise-grade admin tools where users need fast, predictable, alphabetized access to a large catalog rather than editorial browsing.
  • Not suitable for safety-critical or highly regulated contexts where playful copywriting ("slightly-more-talkative total strangers") would undermine trust or professionalism.
  • Avoid if the asset catalog is small: curated carousels and category tabs add unnecessary overhead when a simple flat list would suffice.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for designers, developers, and workshop facilitators running live collaborative sessions (brainstorms, retros, icebreakers) inside FigJam/Figma boards. The emphasis on stickers, photo booths, and icebreaker templates signals a target use-case of remote team workshops and creative facilitation, not just solo UI design work.

Psychologically, the screen leverages novelty and playfulness to drive engagement (curated collections with whimsical illustrations (a cartoon face, a Polaroid camera) tap into users' desire for fun, low-effort ways to energize a meeting). The low-friction "tap to insert" mental model (implied by the grid of ready-made assets) reduces the effort barrier for non-expert users who may not want to build an icebreaker activity from scratch.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent Canvas Context: The bottom sheet deliberately leaves the toolbar and canvas edge visible, preserving spatial awareness and reducing the "where was I?" disorientation common in full-screen takeovers.
  • Editorial Merchandising: Content is grouped into curated, named collections ("Break the ice") with rich imagery rather than a plain alphabetized plugin list, dramatically increasing discoverability and delight.
  • Dual-Mode Browsing: Combining a prominent search bar with category tabs serves both the user who knows exactly what they want and the user who is just browsing for inspiration.
  • Lightweight Exit & Actions: The close (X), share, and overflow (•••) icons in the header keep the modal's controls minimal and predictable, following standard iOS modal conventions.

screens.name: Figma - Browse FigJam resources - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when building insertable-content pickers within a canvas or editor tool (e).g., emoji/GIF pickers, icon libraries, template galleries, or sticker packs. It is ideal when:
