  • Users repeatedly insert from a large, categorized asset pool and would benefit from frequency-based shortcuts (Recents).
  • The product supports both personal and team/shared content libraries that need separate visual grouping.
  • The insertion flow must happen without leaving the current canvas/document context (modal-over-canvas).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, multi-tab browsing pattern for simple, single-category selections (e.g., picking one of five brand colors) where a lightweight popover or inline picker would suffice (the overhead of tabs, search, and sectioning would feel bloated). It's also unsuitable for first-time or new users with no usage history, since the "Recents" section (the pattern's core value) would be empty and the Libraries section alone may feel sparse or confusing without onboarding guidance. Finally, on very small screens or low-dexterity contexts, the dense icon grid may need larger touch targets.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This panel primarily serves teams running collaborative workshops, brainstorms, or FigJam-style sessions: designers, PMs, and facilitators who need to quickly inject visual flair (stars, eyes, "Start Here" banners) to guide attention or add levity during real-time collaboration. The playful sticker set (feedback-wanted poster, googly eyes, hand-drawn stars) suggests this is tuned for workshop facilitation and asynchronous commenting rather than UI design itself.

Psychologically, the Recents row exploits the mere-exposure and habit-loop effect: showing what was just used reduces cognitive load and reinforces repeated behaviors (e.g., always starting a workshop with the same "Start Here" banner). The Libraries section taps into social/organizational belonging by surfacing team-branded asset packs (e.g., "Construction Zone"), encouraging on-brand consistency across a team's files.
screens.keyHighlights:
Recents-first content ordering is the standout decision (it treats the sticker library like a muscle-memory tool (similar to emoji pickers) rather than a static catalog, dramatically speeding up repeat workflows for frequent collaborators).

  • The tabbed segmentation (All/Stickers/Templates/Widgets/Plugins) allows the same search surface to serve multiple asset types without fragmenting navigation into separate screens.
  • Persistent canvas toolbar beneath the modal keeps tool context (cursor, pen, fill color, AI tool) accessible, reinforcing that this is an in-flow overlay, not a context switch.
  • The "Add your own" library tile uses a plus-icon card pattern consistent with empty-state call-to-actions elsewhere in Figma, lowering the barrier to building custom libraries.

screens.name: Figma - Browse FigJam resources - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern (modal template/asset picker with visual grid + categorized sections) when:

  • Your app has a library of pre-built content/assets (templates, stickers, components) that benefit from visual preview over text description.
  • You want to allow users to insert content without leaving their current working context (overlay vs. full navigation).
  • You have enough content variety to warrant segmenting via tabs/categories to prevent an overwhelming single list.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The asset library is small (fewer than ~10 items) - in this case, a simple dropdown or inline menu would be more efficient and reduce the extra navigation step of opening a full modal.
  • Users need precise technical specs/metadata (e.g., file size, version, permissions) to make a decision, as the visual-grid format prioritizes aesthetics over detailed data and would require a secondary detail view.
  • Screen real estate is extremely limited (very small screens), where a 2-column visual grid may render thumbnails too small to be useful, undermining the pattern's core benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for active collaborators (designers, PMs, facilitators) mid-session, likely preparing for or actively running a workshop, brainstorm, or planning meeting. The "Brainstorms" category and templates like "Empathy Map" and "Pros & cons" specifically target facilitators who need to quickly scaffold a structure for group thinking without building it from scratch.

The psychological trigger at play is the reduction of the "blank canvas" anxiety. By providing a visual catalog of pre-built structures, Figma lowers the barrier to entry for non-expert FigJam users (e.g., a product manager or stakeholder) who may not know how to structure a workshop but recognizes the visual pattern of an Empathy Map or Brainstorm grid when they see it.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual-First Browsing: Unlike typical file pickers that rely on text lists, this screen uses high-fidelity, actual-content thumbnails for every template. This allows users to assess relevance at a glance, drastically speeding up the selection process.
  • Non-Modal Dismissal Pattern: The top-left 'X' (rather than a back arrow) correctly signals that this is an overlay sitting on top of the canvas, setting the correct mental model for "cancel/return to board" rather than "navigate back a level."
  • Contextual Grouping: Organizing templates by category ("Brainstorms") instead of a flat alphabetical or chronological list significantly improves scannability and acts as a lightweight recommendation engine.
  • Attribution as Trust Signal: Displaying the author (Figma vs. community creators) under each template helps users gauge quality and official support level before committing to a choice.

screens.name: Dave Setting Up 25
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern of presenting a native permission dialog immediately after establishing feature value when the permission is required for the feature to function usefully (e.g., location for job-matching by proximity). Effective for:

  • Feature-gated permission requests tied to a specific sub-flow (not the whole app).

  • Situations where users have opted into exploring a feature and need only one more click to unlock its core benefit.

  • Apps that want to preserve trust by offering graduated consent options rather than a single binary allow/deny.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid firing the native OS dialog directly without a custom "pre-permission" explainer screen when the system's default rationale text doesn't match the current user context (as seen here, where the reasoning mentions ATMs/fraud instead of job-matching). This mismatch can create confusion, erode trust, or cause users to decline out of suspicion. Also avoid interrupting a value-prop screen before the user has fully absorbed the pitch or reached the natural CTA, surfacing the OS prompt mid-read can feel jarring and disrupt the persuasive flow. Instead, trigger permission requests only when the user takes an explicit action requiring that permission (e.g., tapping "Find gigs near me").
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets existing Dave banking app users being cross-sold into a secondary "Side Hustle" job-marketplace feature (likely users showing financial stress signals (low balance, overdraft usage) who are being nudged toward supplemental income opportunities). The psychological trigger is need-based motivation: framing extra income as easily accessible ("flexible work that fits your schedule") taps into financial anxiety and the desire for quick relief.

The location permission request piggybacks on this emotionally primed moment, hoping that users focused on the promise of "more money in your pocket" will grant location access with less scrutiny, since compliance now feels like a small next step toward a desirable goal rather than an isolated data-privacy decision.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual placement: The permission prompt is deliberately surfaced during a feature-specific onboarding flow rather than at generic app launch, aiming to link the ask to a moment of user intent.

  • Value stacking before friction: Users see concrete benefits (flexible work, extra money) before being asked to grant a permission, softening the perceived cost of compliance.

  • Three-tier consent granularity: "Allow Once," "Allow While Using App," and "Don't Allow" give users graduated control, respecting privacy norms and reducing the feeling of an all-or-nothing demand.

  • Dismissible feature modal: The "X" close button on the Side Hustle screen ensures users aren't trapped in the promotional flow, maintaining a low-pressure, non-blocking exit.

screens.name: Dave Setting Up 26
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing an optional, secondary feature or partner integration inside a primary app, especially when the feature requires the user to leave their core mental model (e.g., banking app promoting job search). It's ideal for:

  • Cross-sell or upsell moments discovered via a card/banner elsewhere in the app.

  • Announcing new modules that need a quick value-prop explanation before the user commits to exploring them.

  • Situations where a single clear CTA increases funnel conversion into a new feature area.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed full-screen interstitial for minor, self-explanatory features where a tooltip or inline banner would suffice, forcing a full takeover screen for something trivial creates unnecessary friction and can feel intrusive. Additionally, avoid this pattern if the underlying feature is core to the primary use case (e.g., mandatory KYC or account setup), since the "X" dismiss option implies it's skippable, which could lead to critical feature drop-off if misapplied to essential flows.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users of a cash-advance/budgeting app (Dave) who are likely living paycheck-to-paycheck and are actively seeking ways to increase their income, not just manage existing funds better. The psychological trigger here is the promise of quick, tangible financial relief ("quick cash," "more money in your pocket") combined with low commitment framing ("flexible work that fits your schedule").

By cross-promoting a job/gig marketplace inside a financial wellness app, Dave capitalizes on a moment of high financial anxiety or need, positioning itself as a one-stop solution for both spending and earning. This is a monetization/engagement play: driving users to a partner job board likely generates referral revenue while also increasing user stickiness and perceived value of the core app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single CTA discipline: Only one primary action (Get started) is presented, removing choice overload and driving high conversion into the feature funnel.

  • Mascot-driven illustration: The laptop bears the Dave bear logo, subtly reinforcing brand ownership of a feature that is likely powered by a third-party job aggregator, building trust through familiar branding.

  • Benefit-first bullets over feature lists: Each bullet emphasizes an emotional or lifestyle outcome (flexibility, extra cash, control over schedule) rather than a dry functional description.

  • Non-blocking dismissal: The visible close "X" and bottom drag handle signal that this is an optional, skippable promotional moment, respecting user autonomy while still merchandising the feature.

screens.name: Dave Setting Up 27
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern when you have a moderate number (5-12) of discrete categories that users need to choose between before drilling into filtered results.

  • Ideal for marketplace, job board, or content-discovery apps where categories map to user intent/context rather than a rigid hierarchy.

  • Effective when the destination categories are mutually exclusive enough to be visually represented by a single illustrative icon.

  • Great for financial wellness or earnings-focused apps trying to build trust with first-time or anxious users via a friendly, low-pressure visual style.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid when there are more than ~12 categories: the grid will require excessive scrolling and a search/filter mechanism becomes more efficient.

  • Not suitable when categories overlap heavily or aren't mutually exclusive, as users may struggle to choose the "right" one (e.g., "Gig Jobs" vs "Flexible Hours" could cause decision paralysis if not clearly differentiated).

  • Skip illustration-heavy tiles if the brand requires a more professional, enterprise tone (e.g., B2B recruiting tools) where photography or data-driven cards may build more credibility.

  • Not ideal if users typically know exactly what job title/keyword they want (a search-first approach would be faster for that use case).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets cash-constrained users seeking supplemental income: likely students, parents, freelancers, or workers in the gig economy who need money quickly and value flexibility over prestige. The psychological hook is autonomy and control: by letting users filter by their own constraints (time availability, location, commitment) rather than forcing them through a generic job search, the design reduces the perceived effort and anxiety of job hunting.

The friendly illustrations and casual copy also target users who may not have a traditional "job search" mindset and could be intimidated by formal recruiting platforms (like LinkedIn). This screen instead borrows visual cues from consumer apps (e-commerce-style category tiles) to feel more like browsing a marketplace than filling out a job application.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Constraint-based taxonomy, not role-based: Categories are organized by user lifestyle constraints (flexible hours, part-time, work-from-home) rather than job titles or industries (a much more relevant filter for the side-hustle audience who care more about "when/where" than "what)."

  • Illustration-led visual language: Consistent flat illustration style across all six cards creates a cohesive, friendly, low-intimidation brand feel, ideal for users who may be job-searching for the first time or feel anxious about gig work.

  • Value-driven subheading: The one-line benefit statement under "Categories" reframes a plain navigational list into a motivational moment.

  • Symmetrical grid with equal visual weight: No category is visually prioritized over another, signaling neutrality and letting the user self-select based on personal need rather than platform bias (e.g., no "featured" badge pushing one job type).

screens.name: Incognito Mode
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any feature requiring an unambiguous mode switch with real user consequences (privacy, safety, data handling), where a strong, consistent visual signal (theme change) paired with explicit text confirmation reduces the risk of the user being unaware of their current state.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for low-stakes preference toggles where a full theme change would be an outsized, disruptive visual response to a minor setting adjustment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Chrome (Incognito mode): uses the same dark theme plus explicit "You've gone Incognito" messaging and a spy/mask icon as its mode indicator.

  2. Safari (Private Browsing): similarly shifts to a dark UI theme with explicit labeling when private mode is active.

  3. DuckDuckGo (default private browser): reinforces its always-private nature with consistent dark/muted theming and privacy-focused messaging.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Distinctive Mode Signaling: full dark theming plus explicit labeling creates an unambiguous, hard-to-miss visual distinction from standard browsing mode.

  2. Consistency (Jakob's Law): reusing dark theme plus footprint iconography follows an established cross-browser convention for private browsing, reducing learning cost.

  3. Visibility of System Status: the explicit "You're browsing Incognito" text removes any doubt about whether the mode switch succeeded.

  4. Trust Through Explicit Confirmation: pairing a visual cue (dark theme) with a written statement (not just color alone) reduces the risk of a user misunderstanding their privacy state.

screens.name: Site Settings
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits browsers offering granular, per-site control over privacy and interaction features, where users benefit from adjusting settings for a specific troublesome site without changing global app-wide defaults.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings that are inherently global and don't make sense scoped per-site (e.g., account-wide preferences), where offering a per-site override would create confusing, hard-to-track inconsistencies across different sites.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Brave Browser's per-site Shields panel: offers an almost identical grouped set of per-site privacy toggles (ad blocking, tracker blocking, cookie handling) scoped to the current site.

  2. Safari's per-website settings (Reader, content blockers): provides comparable site-specific toggles accessible from a similar settings sheet.

  3. 1Blocker / AdGuard's per-site rules: group ad, tracker, and cookie-banner blocking as distinct toggles scoped to individual domains, matching this panel's structure.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive Sheet Expansion: allowing the modal to grow from a partial to full-screen presentation (standard iOS sheet-detent behavior) gives users control over how much context they want to see at once.

  2. Clear Escape from Scoped to Global Settings: the "App Settings" row, now fully visible, offers an obvious, separate path to broader configuration beyond the current site's scope.

  3. Consistency (Jakob's Law): the expand/collapse drag-handle behavior matches standard iOS sheet conventions, requiring no new learning.

screens.name: App Settings 01
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any app needing a comprehensive, well-organized settings hub covering diverse concerns (branding, content preferences, behavior toggles), where grouping by functional category helps users navigate a long list efficiently.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for apps with only a handful of settings, where this level of categorization and grouping would be unnecessary structural overhead for a short, simple list that could be presented flatly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS Settings app (grouped preference sections): uses a comparable card-grouped structure separating different categories of app behavior, closely matching this screen's organization.

  2. Chrome's Settings (Default browser, search engine, privacy): groups similar categories of settings (browser identity, search preferences, browsing behavior) in a comparable structure.

  3. Safari's Settings (Auto-Fill, Search Engine, Privacy): offers a similar range of app-wide preference categories accessible from one central settings screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Feature Continuity Post-Onboarding: surfacing "Set as Default Browser" and "Change App Icon" here confirms features introduced during onboarding remain accessible for later reconsideration, not one-time-only prompts.

  2. Logical Grouping by Concern: separating identity/branding, content preferences, and behavioral toggles into distinct card sections aids scanability across a long settings list.

  3. Value-Revealing Rows: showing current values inline (Google, After 1 day, Native App) lets users understand current state at a glance without opening each sub-page.

  4. Novel Gesture Discovery: "Raise to Call Arc" introduces a previously unseen activation method for the voice assistant feature, expanding on the tap-based invocation shown in earlier screens.

screens.name: App Settings 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits comprehensive settings screens where account/sync features, referral promotions, and support/legal information all need a home, grouping and visually differentiating each category (toggle behaviors, sync, promotional banner, support links) keeps a long list navigable.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit to place a referral banner prominently within core settings if referral/growth isn't a meaningful part of the product's strategy (for purely utility-focused apps, a promotional banner here could feel like unnecessary clutter distracting from configuration tasks).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo's Settings ("Restart tutorial"): similarly allows users to voluntarily re-trigger onboarding content from within settings.

  2. Any referral-driven app's Settings ("Invite a friend" banner): uses a comparable visually-distinct promotional row within an otherwise neutral settings list.

  3. Standard iOS app Settings screens (Contact Us, Privacy Policy, version footer): follow the same closing structure seen at the bottom of this screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Revisitable Onboarding: "Show Onboarding" treats the first-run tour as an on-demand resource rather than a one-time gate, respecting that users may want to rediscover features later.

  2. Visual Differentiation for Promotional Content: the gradient "Gift Arc to a friend" banner stands apart from neutral settings rows, appropriately signaling it as an optional, non-utility action.

  3. Standard Settings Screen Conventions: grouping support/legal rows (Contact, Privacy Policy, Licenses) with a version footer at the bottom follows familiar app-settings patterns, aiding predictability.

  4. Account-Gated Sync Confirmation: showing "Sign in" under "Sync with Arc Desktop" clarifies this is a genuine account feature requiring authentication, not a passive or automatic sync.

screens.name: App Icon Change 01
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any personalization choice (like app icon) that's worth offering both during onboarding (for first impressions) and later via settings (for users who want to reconsider), with the settings version benefiting from contextual preview (like a dock mockup) since the choice here is more deliberate.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit to duplicate the exact same static-grid presentation from onboarding in settings without adapting to context (a carousel-with-dock-preview format (as shown here) provides more real-world context appropriate for a considered, deliberate revisit rather than a fast first-run decision).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Instagram/Telegram's in-app icon picker (Settings): similarly offers icon customization from within app settings, often with a dock or home-screen preview context.

  2. iOS's own "Home Screen Customization" (alternate app icons): uses comparable preview treatments showing how an icon would appear once selected.

  3. Spotify's icon/theme customization within Settings: offers a similar post-onboarding, deliberate revisit path for a personalization choice first introduced during setup.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Contextual Preview: showing icon options resting on a simulated dock lets users evaluate a choice in its real-world visual context, rather than as an isolated icon tile.

  2. Format Adaptation by Context: using a carousel here (versus onboarding's static grid) suggests the interface adapts its presentation to the browsing context (a scrollable format works well for a focused, single-purpose revisit, while a full grid suited the more exploratory first-run moment).

  3. Post-Onboarding Feature Access: confirming this customization option remains available and easily reachable after onboarding reinforces that first-run features aren't disposable, one-time-only choices.

  4. Low-Friction Exit: the prominent "X" dismiss button ensures users can back out without committing to a change if none of the visible options appeal.

screens.name: App Icon Change 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (accepting an unavoidable system dialog) applies whenever an app uses a platform API that mandates its own confirmation UI (designers should plan custom flows (like Arc's App Icon sheet) knowing this system interruption will occur and can't be visually customized or suppressed).
screens.whereNotToUse: Not applicable in the traditional sense, since this is OS-enforced rather than a design choice an app team makes (the only "avoidance" would be not offering alternate icons at all).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Any iOS app supporting alternate icons (Instagram, Telegram, etc.): all trigger this identical system dialog upon icon change, since it's OS-level behavior rather than an app-specific design choice.

  2. Apple's Human Interface Guidelines on alternate icons: explicitly documents this required system confirmation as part of the platform's icon-change API.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Platform-Mandated Transparency: iOS requires this confirmation specifically so apps can't silently alter their icon without the user's clear awareness, an intentional trust-preserving system design.

  2. Unavoidable Interruption: this dialog necessarily breaks the visual continuity of Arc's own custom App Icon picker, illustrating that some interruptions are outside an app's design control.

  3. Visual Contrast as a Signal: the plain system-dialog styling (versus Arc's colorful custom UI) subtly signals to attentive users that this specific moment is OS-level, not app-level, behavior.

  4. Simple Acknowledgment Model: a single "OK" button with no alternative action reflects that this is a notification of a completed fact, not a decision point requiring a choice.

screens.name: App Icon Change 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any horizontally-arranged option picker where a minimal, unobtrusive selection indicator (rather than a full checkmark overlay or border highlight) is sufficient to communicate current state.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when selection state needs to be highly prominent or immediately obvious at a glance (e.g., safety-critical settings), where a subtler dot indicator might be too easy to overlook compared to a bolder visual treatment like a checkmark or colored border.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS home-screen page-indicator dots: use an identical small-dot convention to indicate current position/selection among several options, a pattern this icon picker borrows directly.

  2. Spotify/Telegram's icon selection carousels: similarly move a selection indicator to reflect the currently active choice after a change.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Persistent Selection Indicator: the dot correctly relocating to the newly selected icon confirms the underlying state accurately reflects the just-completed change.

  2. Non-Verbal Confirmation: using a simple positional dot (rather than requiring text or a checkmark overlay) keeps the confirmation visually minimal and consistent with the carousel's clean layout.

  3. Consistency with Prior Selection Patterns: this dot-based indicator echoes the checkmark used in the earlier "Swipe to Navigate" popover, showing the app reuses a recognizable "current selection" visual language across different setting types.

screens.name: Global Site Setting 01
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any settings system where most users want consistent baseline behavior across all contexts, but some sites or contexts warrant individual exceptions, providing both a global default screen and per-instance override screens (with a clear explanation of their relationship) supports both needs without forcing users to configure every site individually.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings that should never vary by context (e.g., core account security settings), where offering a per-site override option would introduce unnecessary complexity or potential inconsistency for something that should behave identically everywhere.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's global vs. per-website settings: uses an identical default-plus-override model, where global settings (Content Blockers, Reader) apply everywhere unless a specific site's settings override them.

  2. Chrome's site settings hierarchy (global defaults vs. per-site permissions): follows the same cascading structure for privacy and behavior settings.

  3. Brave Browser's global Shields defaults vs. per-site Shields settings: closely mirrors this exact two-tier structure for ad/tracker blocking specifically.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Explicit Override Hierarchy: stating plainly that these are defaults "unless overridden" prevents confusion about whether this screen or a per-site panel takes precedence.

  2. Consistent Structure Across Scopes: reusing the identical toggle set and grouping between the global default screen and the per-site screen minimizes relearning when navigating between them.

  3. Detectable Customization Evidence: the differing "Swipe to Navigate" value between this global screen and the earlier per-site screen provides concrete confirmation that per-site overrides genuinely function as described.

  4. Sensible Defaults: shipping privacy toggles (Block Ads, Cookie Banners, Trackers) enabled by default at the global level extends the protection promised throughout onboarding to every site by default, not just ones a user manually configures.

screens.name: Global Site Settings 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits binary or small-option-set settings where a compact, in-place popover with a clear checkmark indicator is more efficient than navigating to a dedicated sub-screen, especially for settings whose two options represent a clear, nameable trade-off.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings with many possible values or those requiring additional explanatory context, where a compact popover wouldn't have room to adequately describe each option's implications, and a dedicated screen with more detail would serve users better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS system-level "Swipe from edge" gesture settings: offer a very similar edge-only vs. anywhere-based interaction choice for back-navigation gestures.

  2. Android's system-wide gesture navigation settings: provide a comparable binary choice between edge-triggered and more permissive gesture zones.

  3. Reddit's mobile app "swipe to navigate" preference: offers a similar two-option selector for customizing swipe-back gesture sensitivity.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Clear Selection Indication: a checkmark unambiguously shows which of the two options is currently active, avoiding any doubt about the setting's present state.

  2. Lightweight In-Place Selection: using a compact popover rather than a full navigation to a new screen keeps the interaction efficient for a setting with only two possible values.

  3. Trade-off Transparency Through Naming: the option names themselves ("From Anywhere" vs. "From Screen Edges") communicate the underlying trade-off (convenience vs. gesture-conflict avoidance) without needing additional explanatory text.

  4. Resolving Prior Ambiguity: this screen provides the missing context for a setting whose display-only value ("From Screen Edges" / "From Anywhere") appeared in two earlier screens without showing how it was actually changed.

screens.name: Global Site Settings 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any settings system where most users want consistent baseline behavior across all contexts, but some sites or contexts warrant individual exceptions, providing both a global default screen and per-instance override screens (with a clear explanation of their relationship) supports both needs without forcing users to configure every site individually.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings that should never vary by context (e.g., core account security settings), where offering a per-site override option would introduce unnecessary complexity or potential inconsistency for something that should behave identically everywhere.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's global vs. per-website settings: uses an identical default-plus-override model, where global settings (Content Blockers, Reader) apply everywhere unless a specific site's settings override them.

  2. Chrome's site settings hierarchy (global defaults vs. per-site permissions): follows the same cascading structure for privacy and behavior settings.

  3. Brave Browser's global Shields defaults vs. per-site Shields settings: closely mirrors this exact two-tier structure for ad/tracker blocking specifically.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Immediate Commit on Selection: choosing an option in the popover applies the change instantly upon dismissal, without a separate confirm step, reducing friction for a low-risk preference change.

  2. Consistent Value Display: the updated "From Anywhere" label matches the exact wording used in the selection popover, ensuring no disconnect between the choice made and its displayed result.

  3. Full Interaction Loop Demonstrated: across this and the two preceding screens, the complete cycle (view value → open selector → choose option → see updated value) is fully shown, confirming the setting behaves as expected end-to-end.

screens.name: Craft - Editing a separator pattern (washi gallery) - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Document or note-taking apps aiming to differentiate from plain, spreadsheet-like data entry by offering decorative, personalizable block types (dividers, backgrounds, stickers).

  • Any editor where users benefit from seeing a live, in-context preview of a style change rather than a disconnected settings panel.

  • Creative tools targeting users who value personalization and are willing to spend a few extra seconds choosing aesthetic details (journaling apps, mood boards, portfolio builders).

  • Situations where a feature has multiple sub-dimensions (type, color, pattern) that benefit from layered/progressive disclosure in a single bottom sheet rather than multiple nested screens.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise or data-heavy applications (CRMs, spreadsheets, admin dashboards) where users expect speed and neutrality over decorative flourishes (this would feel frivolous or slow down task completion).

  • Accessibility-critical contexts where decorative pattern-heavy dividers could reduce legibility or add visual noise for users with cognitive or visual processing difficulties; a toggle to disable decorative elements should exist.

  • Collaborative/shared documents where one user's personal taste in washi tape patterns could clash with team branding or professional document standards (better suited to personal/private note contexts).

  • Low-end devices or contexts with limited rendering performance, since pattern-rich assets (tape textures, illustrations) add visual complexity and asset loading overhead versus a simple CSS line.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets detail-oriented creative professionals, writers, and designers who use Craft for project briefs, documentation, or idea boards and who derive satisfaction from making their documents visually distinctive (per Craft's "editorial type, custom accents, cover images" identity). It appeals to the psychological drivers of aesthetic ownership and craftsmanship pride: a plain divider line is utilitarian, but a hand-picked washi-tape pattern makes the document feel personally curated, similar to scrapbooking or bullet journaling communities. The low-friction, reversible customization (reset icon, swatch tray) taps into a safe-exploration mechanism, lowering the barrier to experiment with visual flourishes during otherwise "boring" structural tasks like inserting a separator.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background document: The note stays partially visible behind the sheet, giving a live preview-in-context effect so style changes feel connected to real content rather than an abstract settings screen.

  • Decorative dividers as a first-class block type: Treating a simple horizontal rule as a customizable "washi tape" object with patterns elevates a mundane editor primitive into an expressive, scrapbook-like design touch (core to Craft's editorial, cover-image-driven aesthetic).

  • Layered disclosure in the sheet: Type selector (list/tape/pen icons) → color/pattern swatch row → deeper "Pattern" section creates a clear information hierarchy, letting users drill down only as far as they want.

  • Inline reset icon next to the sheet title: A small circular-arrow icon beside "Separators Style" offers an immediate undo path for experimentation, encouraging playful trial without fear of permanently messing up formatting.

  • Persistent block selection dots: Every content block carries a selection toggle, implying a consistent, learnable interaction model for selecting/restyling any element in the document, not just dividers.

screens.name: Craft - Editing a separator pattern (washi gallery) - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Rich-text or document editors offering stylistic customization (dividers, headers, themes, covers).

  • Any settings panel where live, in-context preview materially improves decision confidence (fonts, colors, layouts).

  • Tools targeting creative/prosumer audiences who value aesthetic differentiation over purely functional UI.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for high-frequency, low-stakes micro-decisions where a bottom sheet adds unnecessary friction (e.g., simple bold/italic toggles should stay inline).

  • Not appropriate for enterprise/B2B tools where playful decorative assets (washi tape) could undermine a serious, formal brand tone.

  • Risky on small screens if the sheet's height plus background blur obscures too much editing context, hurting the very preview benefit it aims to provide.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets writers, note-takers, and knowledge workers who care about the visual craftsmanship of their documents—bloggers, designers, PMs drafting polished specs, or anyone treating Craft docs as presentation-ready artifacts rather than disposable scratch notes. The washi-tape motif specifically appeals to users with a journaling/scrapbooking sensibility, tapping into nostalgia and tactile aesthetics (similar to physical bullet journals) to differentiate from sterile competitors like plain Markdown editors. The live-preview mechanic exploits the psychological principle of immediate feedback, reducing the cognitive load of imagining "what will this look like" and increasing confidence to customize further.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed/blurred background with live preview: The underlying document stays partially visible and updates in real time as styles are chosen, letting users judge the result in context instead of guessing from a thumbnail.

  • Decorative, playful asset (washi tape) in a productivity tool: Offering a physical-world, scrapbook-style divider option elevates the "designed document" feel over generic horizontal-rule separators found in most note apps.

  • Icon-first segmented control: Three divider "families" (rule, tape, hand-drawn) are switched via compact icon buttons, keeping the sheet dense yet scannable without text clutter.

  • Undo/reset affordance next to the panel title: Placing a quick-revert icon directly in the header reduces the risk of commitment, encouraging experimentation with styles.

screens.name: Craft - Editing a separator pattern (washi gallery) - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when an app wants to offer lightweight, optional visual customization layered on top of a core content object (notes, documents, profile covers, playlist art). It's ideal for apps with an editorial or craft-like brand voice where personalization reinforces emotional ownership. Works well whenever you need to balance a small set of curated defaults with deeper library/upload access without overwhelming first-time users.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, swatch-preview modal in utilitarian, data-dense, or enterprise productivity tools where visual decoration would distract from task efficiency. It's also unsuitable for contexts where users need to apply customization in bulk or make rapid consecutive selections (the full-screen modal interrupts flow each time it's invoked). Additionally, whimsical preset names like "Childhood" may feel inappropriate or confusing in B2B, technical, or highly localized/international markets without careful naming adaptation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets creative, detail-oriented knowledge workers and personal-note takers who treat their documents as designed artifacts (journalers, PKM enthusiasts, designers, and writers who value aesthetic ownership over their workspace). The psychological trigger at play is aesthetic investment and identity expression: by letting users "decorate" a note cover the same way one might choose a washi tape or notebook cover, Craft deepens emotional attachment to the document, increasing retention and perceived product value beyond pure text editing.

The curated "Suggested" list also leverages choice reduction to avoid decision fatigue, while the escape hatches (Upload, Washi Gallery) satisfy users seeking more control, supporting both novice and power-user segments simultaneously.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed/blurred background context: The underlying note stays legibly visible, so users never lose the thread of what they're decorating.

  • Washi-tape inspired selection indicator: The jagged/dashed blue border on the selected swatch is a tactile, material-inspired affordance rather than a generic checkmark overlay.

  • Named, personality-driven presets: Playful naming ("Childhood," "Groovy Water") turns a utilitarian picker into a moment of delight and self-expression.

  • Dual path for depth: "Upload" and "Washi Gallery" buttons balance fast defaults for casual users with deep customization for power users, without cluttering the main suggested list.

  • Segmented Control for mode switching: Cleanly separates "Pattern" vs. photo-based choices, reducing cognitive load versus one long mixed grid.

screens.name: Craft - Editing a separator pattern (washi gallery) - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any product offering cosmetic/decorative personalization (note covers, document headers, profile banners, widget skins).

  • Collectible or thematic content pickers where users browse visually rather than by name (stickers, themes, icon packs, wallpaper selection).

  • Features meant to deepen emotional attachment/brand affinity rather than drive core task completion.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, illustration-rich visual browsing pattern for high-frequency, functional choices (e.g., selecting a file type or permission level) where speed and clarity trump aesthetic browsing.

  • Not suitable when option count is very large: a 2-column static grid without search/filter would become tedious beyond ~20-30 items.

  • Don't use playful/whimsical naming conventions in contexts requiring precision or accessibility (e.g., screen reader users benefit more from descriptive alt labels than purely whimsical names).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users who treat their notes/documents as creative, personal artifacts (journalers, designers, students, and knowledge workers who value aesthetic ownership over their workspace, aligning with Craft's positioning as an "editorial," design-forward note-taking tool rather than a plain database-like note app).

Psychologically, this leans on self-expression and identity signaling: letting users decorate their documents the way they'd decorate a physical notebook taps into the same satisfaction loop as sticker collecting or washi tape journaling communities (popular on platforms like Pinterest/Instagram). The curated, named options (vs. raw color swatches) also reduce decision fatigue while still feeling personal and whimsical, increasing emotional attachment to the app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Physical metaphor done tastefully: die-cut tape edges and shadow give tactile realism without skeuomorphic excess.

  • Evocative naming over generic labels: turns a cosmetic setting into a delightful, brand-reinforcing micro-interaction.

  • Background blur/dim: maintains context (user still sees they're decorating this specific doc) while focusing attention on the picker.

  • Low-friction selection state: a simple outline ring communicates selection instantly without extra chrome or checkmarks.

  • Scannable visual grid: 2-column card layout suits a "pick by feel" decision, far better than a text list would.

screens.name: Craft - Editing a separator pattern (washi gallery) - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when offering lightweight visual customization of a container object (document covers, profile banners, playlist art, project boards) where users benefit from instant, reversible previews. It's ideal when you have a finite but expandable asset library, want to avoid a full-screen takeover for a minor styling decision, and need to preserve context of the underlying content being styled. Works well for creative/productivity tools aiming for a personal, editorial feel.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for decisions with significant downstream consequences (e.g., irreversible data actions) since the lightweight bottom-sheet treatment signals low stakes. It's also unsuitable when the asset library is very large (an unpaginated vertical list of full-width banners would become unwieldy and should instead move to a grid or dedicated full-screen gallery). Finally, skip it in utilitarian/enterprise contexts where cover imagery adds little functional value and may be perceived as frivolous.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern serves design-conscious knowledge workers and creatives who treat their notes as artifacts worth visually curating (journal-keepers, indie makers, and writers who want their documents to feel bespoke rather than templated). The psychological driver is ownership and identity expression: letting users pick a quirky, named pattern like "Groovy Water" transforms a plain doc into something personally branded, increasing emotional attachment and long-term retention of the app. The curated "SUGGESTED" list also reduces decision fatigue via smart defaults, while the Upload/Washi Gallery options satisfy power users who want full control, covering both ends of the customization-appetite spectrum.
screens.keyHighlights:
• True WYSIWYG swatches: each pattern preview is rendered in the exact banner aspect ratio it will appear as on the document cover, eliminating guesswork.

  • Clear single-select state: the active swatch gets a colored border and matching label color, giving instant confirmation without a separate "Apply" button.

  • Context preservation via blur: the dimmed, blurred document behind the sheet keeps the user anchored to the task (styling *this* document) while focusing attention on the sheet.

  • Dual-mode toggle: a compact segmented control cleanly separates abstract patterns from photographic images without needing separate screens.

  • Expandable library: Upload and Washi Gallery tiles future-proof the pattern set, letting users personalize beyond curated defaults.

screens.name: Craft - Editing a separator pattern (washi gallery) - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this contextual bottom-sheet customization pattern when:

  • Offering optional, non-critical styling choices (dividers, covers, accent colors, fonts) that shouldn't interrupt the primary editing flow.

  • The app's value proposition includes personalization or aesthetic differentiation (journaling, note-taking, document design, presentation tools).

  • You want to preserve spatial/document context while opening a secondary configuration panel (ideal for tablet/mobile editors with limited screen real estate).

  • Providing multiple tiers of choice (category → specific variant) that benefit from a two-row picker rather than a long single list.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The target use case is purely utilitarian/enterprise documentation where styling decorative dividers would be seen as feature bloat or distraction (e.g., legal, technical, or data-heavy documents).

  • Users are on a first-time or basic workflow: surfacing deep stylistic customization too early can overwhelm new users before they understand core block/document functions.

  • Screen real estate is extremely limited (very small devices) where stacking a persistent document header, selection rail, and a tall bottom sheet could cause visual crowding or obscure too much content.

  • Speed is paramount: for users who just want to insert a plain divider quickly, forcing a style-picker sheet adds unnecessary friction; a sensible smart default should always be available with styling as opt-in only.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets creative professionals, writers, and designers who view their notes and documents as an extension of personal brand or craft (bullet journalers, indie makers, and knowledge workers who want Notion/Craft-style structure but with aesthetic warmth analog tools (like washi tape and scrapbooking) provide).

Psychologically, this leans on the IKEA effect and aesthetic-usability effect: letting users customize decorative details increases perceived ownership and satisfaction with the document, and a beautifully styled note is judged as higher quality and more trustworthy even if the underlying content is unchanged. The tactile, physical-world metaphor of "washi tape" also triggers nostalgia and playfulness, differentiating Craft from sterile productivity tools.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Decorative, non-utilitarian dividers: Treating a simple divider as a styleable, artistic element (washi tape, hand-drawn squiggle) directly reflects the "treats every note like a designed document" brand promise.

  • Non-blocking contextual bottom sheet: The editor remains partially visible and the selected block stays highlighted in blue, maintaining spatial context and reducing cognitive reload when the user returns to the canvas.

  • Layered picker UI: A segmented icon switcher for divider type combined with a swatch row for specific pattern variants gives fast access to deep customization without nested menus.

  • Reset affordance: The undo/reset icon next to the panel title lowers the risk of experimentation, encouraging users to explore styles freely.

  • Selection rail with radio buttons: Likely part of an outline/multi-select mode, showing Craft's commitment to structured, block-based editing even for stylistic micro-decisions.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Introducing a signature, high-leverage feature (like a command palette, keyboard shortcut, or gesture) that differentiates the product from competitors.

  • Onboarding flows for productivity, developer, or power-user tools where speed and efficiency are core selling points.

  • Any scenario where the interaction method varies by device/input type and both paths need clear instruction.

  • Multi-step onboarding sequences where you want to balance education with user autonomy (skip option) and progress visibility.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, full-screen interruption pattern for minor or rarely-used features (reserve it for truly high-value, differentiating functionality).

  • Not ideal for first-time, non-technical consumer audiences who may find keyboard shortcut callouts (⌘K) confusing or irrelevant.

  • Should not be used if the feature can't actually be demonstrated/tried in context, forcing a "try it" prompt without real interactivity creates false expectations and frustration.

  • Avoid stacking too many of these full-screen coach mark steps in a row (fatigue risk) without allowing users to skip or revisit later via a help menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets productivity-focused, often technical users (engineers, designers, PMs) evaluating Linear as a project management tool. These users are typically efficiency-driven and skeptical of long onboarding flows, so the screen must quickly prove tangible value (speed) rather than rely on generic feature tours.

Psychologically, this leverages the testing/generation effect: users retain information far better when they perform an action themselves rather than just reading about it. It also uses reciprocity and competence framing: by immediately demonstrating a "power user" shortcut, Linear signals the product respects the user's time and skill level, which builds early trust and perceived product sophistication.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Device-adaptive instructions: The screen smartly provides both a touchscreen gesture ("tapping with two fingers") and a keyboard shortcut (⌘K), ensuring relevance regardless of input method.

  • Learn-by-doing microinteraction: Instead of just describing the feature, the card frames it as a task to "try," encouraging active engagement and muscle-memory formation over passive reading.

  • Keycap UI chips: Rendering the shortcut as skeuomorphic key chips (⌘ and K) rather than plain text instantly communicates "this is a keyboard shortcut" using a familiar visual convention.

  • Progress transparency: The page control dots at the bottom set expectations about onboarding length, reducing abandonment anxiety.

  • Low-friction exit: A persistent close (X) button respects user autonomy, letting advanced users skip onboarding entirely.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 13
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any OAuth/third-party authentication handoff, especially when:

  • The integration requires sensitive or broad-sounding permissions (e.g., code, financial data, contacts, calendar).

  • You want to pre-explain *why* the permission is needed in your own branded voice before the native OS/platform permission dialog appears (which you cannot customize).

  • You need to differentiate your request from what users might assume (e.g., "we only need X, not Y") to reduce abandonment.

  • The feature is optional/supplementary rather than core, so offering a clear "skip for now" path is appropriate.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavier priming pattern when:

  • The permission requested is trivial or expected (e.g., basic notification permission) - adding an extra screen here only adds friction without added trust value.

  • The integration is mandatory for the app to function; in that case, framing it as skippable ("I'll do this later") would be misleading.

  • Users are already deep in a time-sensitive task, inserting a full-screen interstitial here could feel like an interruption rather than a helpful primer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets software engineering teams and technical project managers who use Linear to track issues and want to connect their existing GitHub repositories. This audience is highly security-conscious and often skeptical of third-party tools requesting broad repo access, making trust and transparency the primary psychological lever at play.

The design leverages loss-aversion and risk-mitigation triggers: by explicitly ruling out code-read access, it removes the single biggest psychological barrier (fear of IP/code exposure) that would otherwise cause a drop-off at this step of the funnel. It also leverages the authority/competence heuristic: a clean, well-organized explanation signals that Linear is a professionally built, trustworthy product worthy of elevated permissions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive Objection Handling: Explicitly stating what the integration will not do (read code) directly inside the value-prop list, rather than letting users discover/fear this on the native GitHub OAuth screen.

  • Permission Priming Pattern: A branded, friendly pre-screen before handing off to GitHub's native, less-customizable OAuth consent page, allowing Linear to control the narrative and context.

  • Low-Friction Opt-Out: The "I'll do this later" link ensures the integration prompt never feels like a hard gate blocking core app usage.

  • Checkmark Visual Language: Using checkmarks (vs. plain bullets) subconsciously signals "these boxes are already ticked/safe for you," increasing perceived trustworthiness.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse:
• B2B SaaS products where value scales with number of collaborators (project management, communication, whiteboarding tools).

  • Early onboarding flows where you want to seed network effects before the user's enthusiasm decays.

  • Any flow where you want to encourage an action but must not block progress for users unwilling to comply immediately.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Single-player or personal-use apps where there is no collaborative value proposition (invites would feel irrelevant or pushy).

  • Highly privacy-sensitive contexts where asking for colleague emails this early could raise trust/compliance concerns.

  • Flows where the user hasn't yet experienced core value, asking for a team invite before the product has proven itself can increase drop-off instead of reducing it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new signups: typically a team lead, founder, or early adopter evaluating Linear for their organization. Since Linear's value is inherently networked (a project/issue tracker is far more useful with teammates present), this step exploits the "viral loop" growth pattern: converting a single-user trial into a multi-seat team account as early as possible. Psychologically, it capitalizes on the user's current high-motivation state (freshly signed up, curious, exploratory) to ask for an investment (inviting colleagues) before intent fades. It also uses social facilitation (once co-workers are invited, the user has public accountability to actually adopt and use the tool).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-exit strategy: Both "Continue" and "I'll do this later" give users multiple non-blocking ways to skip, drastically reducing onboarding abandonment risk.

  • Batch email input: A single text area accepting comma-separated emails lets power users invite an entire team in one action instead of repeating a form multiple times.

  • Visual progress transparency: The dot-based page control at the bottom sets expectations for how many steps remain, reducing onboarding fatigue/anxiety.

  • Strategic CTA hierarchy: The filled purple "Send invites" button draws the eye first, while skip options are intentionally muted in gray, nudging the desired behavior without forcing it.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Post-onboarding or settings flows where you want to capture marketing/notification consent without blocking the primary task.

  • SaaS products with a technical or privacy-conscious audience where transparency drives higher-quality opt-ins.

  • Any flow requiring compliance with opt-in consent regulations (GDPR, CAN-SPAM, CCPA).

  • Situations where you want to separate distinct communication types (product updates vs. marketing) to improve long-term engagement and reduce unsubscribe rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this soft, skippable pattern if email capture is a core business-critical conversion metric that must be maximized (a more assertive single-choice prompt may perform better for growth-stage products).

  • Don't use pre-toggled OFF switches if your business model depends on default opt-ins and your jurisdiction does not legally require explicit consent (though this is generally not recommended).

  • Not ideal mid-task, where interrupting with a preference screen would break flow and frustrate users (e.g., during checkout or active editing).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded or existing Linear users at a natural checkpoint (likely post-signup or post-settings-visit) where communication preferences are most relevant. The audience is primarily technical/product teams who are highly sensitive to unsolicited marketing noise, so Linear's restrained, honest approach to opt-in (rather than pre-checked boxes) is tailored to a sophisticated, trust-sensitive user base that would otherwise bounce or immediately unsubscribe if manipulated into a list.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages the principle of autonomy (user controls every choice), reciprocity (transparent value exchange: "subscribe to learn about changes" implies tangible benefit), and reduced cognitive load (binary toggles, no required fields) to maximize genuine, lower-churn opt-ins rather than inflated but low-quality subscriber counts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Opt-in by default (toggles OFF): Respects user consent norms and regulatory best practice, building long-term trust over short-term list-growth metrics.

  • Frictionless exit via "X": Clearly communicates this is a non-mandatory step, reducing perceived pressure and modal fatigue.

  • Granular, specific choices: Separating "changelog" from "marketing/onboarding" emails lets users tailor exactly what they want, avoiding the all-or-nothing subscription trap.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Stating frequency ("bi-weekly," "occasional") directly addresses the top objection to subscribing (fear of spam).

  • Correct component semantics: Using a toggle for binary preferences but a button/pill for the external "Follow on X" action avoids UI pattern misuse.

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this bottom-sheet invite pattern when a feature requires rapidly pulling other people into a collaborative, real-time or near-real-time session (co-listening, watch parties, multiplayer games, collaborative documents). It's ideal when you have multiple invite channels of differing effort/reach tradeoffs and want to let users self-select the fastest path for their situation. The dimmed-background-plus-sheet approach is best for lightweight, task-focused interruptions that shouldn't break the user's sense of place in the app.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-stakes or infrequent invite flows (e.g., inviting a business collaborator to a formal workspace) where a full-screen flow with more configuration (roles, permissions) is warranted. Also avoid stacking too many invite mechanisms if your audience skews non-technical (the QR code and Bluetooth auto-invite options add complexity that could overwhelm users who just want a simple share link). If proximity-based auto-invite requires significant permissions (Bluetooth, location), be cautious about implying it's low-effort, as permission prompts can introduce unexpected friction or privacy concerns.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets social, group-listening users: people at parties, road trips, or hangouts who want to collaboratively control a shared queue. The psychological drivers at play are:

  • Social facilitation:
  • Reduced friction for viral/network growth: Every Jam invite is an implicit growth loop (non-Spotify users who click a share link or scan a QR code are exposed to the product, functioning as a soft acquisition channel).
  • Context-matching convenience: By offering Bluetooth/Wi-Fi auto-invite for in-person scenarios, the app removes the awkwardness of manually sending links to people standing in the same room, reducing the social cost of using the feature in a live setting.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background context preservation: The Home screen is visible-but-darkened behind the sheet, keeping spatial continuity so the invite flow doesn't feel like a full context switch.
  • Reach-ordered option hierarchy: Share link (universal) → Auto-invite nearby (proximity-based) → QR code (in-person), guiding users to the fastest path for their specific social context.
  • Self-explanatory microcopy: Every advanced feature (auto-invite, QR) includes a one-line plain-language explanation, eliminating the need for a separate help screen or tooltip.
  • Multi-modal invite redundancy: Offering three distinct sharing mechanisms (link, proximity, visual code) maximizes the odds that at least one method matches the recipient's context (remote friend vs. person standing next to you).

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any native OS permission request (camera, microphone, location, Bluetooth, notifications, contacts) especially when the permission isn't immediately self-evident in value. It's ideal for:

  • Features gated behind sensitive hardware/data permissions where context is not obvious.
  • Flows where permission denial would be costly to recover from (since the system prompt usually can't be re-triggered easily).
  • Onboarding or feature-discovery moments where building long-term trust outweighs the cost of one extra screen/tap.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The permission's purpose is already self-evident from context (e.g., asking for camera access directly after tapping a camera icon) — adding an extra screen here is redundant friction.
  • The app needs the permission immediately and urgently; an extra educational step may slow down a time-critical task.
  • Used too frequently across many permissions in a row, which can create "priming fatigue" and make users suspicious of over-justification.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are about to engage in a social/offline listening feature (e.g., Spotify's "Group Session" or device-sharing flows) that technically requires Bluetooth. The target demographic is broad — essentially any Spotify user on a flow that needs Bluetooth — but the design specifically counters the general public's heightened wariness of granting background hardware permissions (Bluetooth, in particular, is often associated with tracking concerns).

Psychologically, it leverages the foot-in-the-door technique: agreeing to a low-stakes, well-explained "Continue" makes users far more likely to also tap "Allow" on the subsequent native iOS prompt. It also uses reciprocity/transparency framing — by proactively disclosing data usage and reversibility, Spotify builds trust, which increases the probability of permission grant and reduces later distrust or app uninstalls tied to perceived overreach.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-permission priming: Explains value before invoking the native OS prompt, which research shows significantly increases opt-in rates versus a cold system dialog.
  • Benefit-first headline: Leads with the social use case ("listen with friends nearby") instead of the technical permission name.
  • Dual reassurance blocks: "How we'll use this" and "You're in control" preemptively answer privacy objections using calm iconography instead of warning symbols.
  • Warm, human illustration: Diverse hands and floating music notes humanize an otherwise cold technical request and reinforce the social/sharing use case.
  • Single low-friction CTA: "Continue" (not "Allow") lowers perceived commitment and funnels the user smoothly toward the actual OS permission dialog.

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a feature involves real-time collaborative sessions (shared playlists, watch parties, multiplayer games, collaborative docs) and you need to lower the barrier to inviting others. Ideal for scenarios with mixed invite contexts (remote, proximity-based, and in-person) where offering multiple invite channels in a single, dismissible surface increases conversion to multi-user engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-stakes or privacy-sensitive invites (e.g., financial account sharing) where "auto-invite nearby" could unintentionally expose data to unintended parties (proximity-based auto-invite requires very clear consent framing or it risks feeling invasive). Also unsuitable for single-user or non-collaborative features where surfacing invite options would be irrelevant clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Targets Spotify's highly social, group-listening user segment (friends at parties, in cars, or in shared physical spaces who want synchronized music control (Spotify Jam/Group Session feature)). The psychological driver is social facilitation and shared experience: music is inherently communal, and making group participation nearly effortless (auto-invite nearby) taps into spontaneity and reduces the setup tax that typically kills group activities. The QR code option additionally serves offline/low-connectivity social gatherings where typing or app-switching is impractical.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multi-modal invite strategy: Combines link sharing, proximity auto-invite, and QR code in one sheet, covering remote, ambient, and in-person social contexts.
  • Context-preserving dim overlay: Background Home screen remains visible (blurred/dimmed), anchoring the user in their existing session rather than navigating away.
  • Iconography reinforces concept: The pulsing-wave Bluetooth/nearby icon visually communicates the "auto-invite nearby" radius concept at a glance.
  • Low-commitment UI: Swipeable grabber handle and non-blocking design make it easy to dismiss without friction.

screens.name: Linear - Adding a link to texts - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Rich-text editors where users need to insert supplementary inline data (links, mentions, dates) without leaving the compose context.
  • Mobile apps where screen real estate is limited and a full-screen takeover would feel disproportionate to a simple, single-input task.
  • Productivity tools targeting power users who value speed and minimal friction over guided/explanatory UI.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this terse, no-context dialog for consumer-facing apps or less technical audiences (a placeholder example URL or helper text would reduce input errors for novice users).
  • Not suitable when additional metadata is needed at link-creation time (e.g., custom link text, open-in-new-tab toggle) - a bottom sheet with multiple fields would serve better in that case.
  • Avoid native alert-style dialogs when brand consistency/theming is critical, since these often inherit OS-level styling that can clash with custom design systems.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern directly serves engineers and PMs writing detailed issue descriptions on mobile: a secondary but important use case for Linear, which is primarily a desktop-first tool. The psychological trigger here is momentum preservation: by using a quick, native-feeling dialog instead of a heavier modal flow, Linear avoids breaking the user's writing flow when they need to cite a design file, PR, or external doc while filing a ticket on the go.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native system dialog pattern: Using a familiar iOS alert-style component for link insertion reduces design and engineering overhead while meeting user expectations instantly (zero learning curve).
  • Context preservation via dimming, not navigation: The background issue content stays visible (dimmed), signaling this is a transient sub-task, not a new screen, which reduces disorientation and preserves flow state.
  • Toolbar docked above keyboard: Formatting controls are positioned exactly where the thumb naturally rests during typing, minimizing hand travel and supporting Linear's "fast capture" ethos.
  • Single-field, single-purpose dialog: No extra fields (like link text) clutter the dialog (it assumes the user has already selected text to hyperlink, keeping the task atomic and fast).

screens.name: Linear - Adding a link to texts - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any rich-text editor where users need to quickly embed hyperlinks without navigating away from their current context.
  • Mobile-first productivity tools where minimizing taps and keyboard dismiss/reopen cycles directly impacts perceived speed.
  • Scenarios where the target audience is technically fluent and does not require explanatory copy or guided validation.
  • Any flow where preserving visual context of the underlying document (dimmed background) is more valuable than a full-screen takeover.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer-facing apps with less technical audiences, where a bare "mobbin.com" input with no placeholder or format hint (e.g., "https://") could cause confusion or malformed entries.
  • Flows requiring link previews, metadata fetching, or validation (e.g., checking if a URL resolves) - this bare-bones dialog offers no feedback on link validity.
  • Situations where multiple link attributes are needed (display text + URL), since this dialog only captures a raw URL and likely applies it to pre-selected text or as a bare link.
  • Any context where accessibility requires more explicit labeling, since a generic "Add link" + input offers minimal screen-reader context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves engineers, PMs, and designers who are rapidly documenting issues on mobile and need to attach supporting references (designs, docs, PRs, Figma links) without breaking their flow. These users are keyboard- and shortcut-literate, so a dense, no-frills dialog that behaves exactly like the OS they already know is far more efficient than a custom-branded, heavier modal.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages familiarity bias (reusing a well-known iOS interaction) to make an otherwise secondary action feel effortless, and progress preservation cues (visible dimmed content behind the modal) to reduce anxiety about losing in-progress writing.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native-pattern dialog: Mimics the iOS system "Add Link" prompt almost exactly, instantly reducing the learning curve for mobile users.
  • Keyboard persistence: The software keyboard stays open and the text field is auto-focused, letting users paste or type the URL with zero extra taps.
  • Context preservation: The dimmed background still reveals the issue title and property chips underneath, reassuring users their draft is intact and unaffected.
  • Rich-text toolbar integration: The link action lives in a compact, icon-only formatting bar (B / I / S / link / code), keeping the editor interface dense but uncluttered.
  • Minimal decision surface: Only two possible exits (Cancel, OK) prevent decision paralysis during a quick inline task.

screens.name: Linear - Adding a link to texts - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any quick-capture or create flows in productivity, task-management, or note-taking apps where speed and minimal cognitive load are priorities (e).g., creating tickets, notes, reminders, or journal entries. It's especially effective when:

  • Users need to jot down an idea quickly before context-switching away
  • Metadata (tags, assignees, priorities) is secondary to the core content
  • The target audience is technically fluent and values efficiency over hand-holding
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense, chip-heavy single-screen approach when:

  • Onboarding new or non-technical users who need guided, step-by-step input (a Multi-Step Form would reduce overwhelm)
  • The required metadata set is large or mandatory, since horizontally scrollable chips can hide important fields off-screen
  • Users are on very small screens where the floating toolbar and chip row may compete for limited vertical space with the keyboard
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers who need to capture a task or bug the moment it's top of mind, often on mobile while away from their desk. The psychological driver here is reducing capture friction: the longer it takes to log an issue, the more likely it is abandoned or forgotten.

By front-loading the title and description and deferring metadata to lightweight chips, Linear leverages the "progressive disclosure" principle: users aren't forced to make decisions (priority, assignee) before they've even articulated the problem, respecting natural human thought order (idea first, categorization second).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-surface composition: Title, description, and metadata chips all live on one screen, eliminating the typical multi-step "create issue" wizard found in competitors like Jira.
  • Inline rich-text linking directly within the description field, letting users reference other issues or docs without breaking flow.
  • Contextual floating toolbar that appears only when the keyboard is active, maximizing vertical space for content when not needed.
  • Horizontally scrollable property chips (Backlog/Priority/Assignee/Label) act as lightweight, tappable popovers rather than full-screen forms, preserving the "fast capture" ethos.
  • Non-intrusive modal dismissal via the "X" button and clear primary submit action via the up-arrow, following standard compose-sheet conventions users already know from Messages/Notes apps.

screens.name: Airtable - Managing collaborators - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adapt this pattern for any multi-tenant or nested-permission system (e.g., workspace → project → document hierarchies) where:

  • Users need to understand layered/inherited access rather than a flat permission list.
  • Admin tasks are infrequent but high-stakes, justifying a lower-density, highly legible layout.
  • Multiple invitation methods (direct add vs. shareable link) need to coexist without overwhelming the primary view.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this sparse, single-column pattern when:

  • Managing large teams with dozens or hundreds of collaborators (this layout would require excessive scrolling and lacks search/filter/sort controls needed at scale).
  • Granular per-user role assignment is needed on this same screen; a flat list without visible role badges or permission levels would be insufficient for complex RBAC systems.
  • Real-time collaboration context (e.g., who's currently viewing) is needed (this is a static audit view, not a live presence indicator).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves base owners, workspace admins, and project leads responsible for controlling who can view or edit a specific Airtable base. These users are typically operations managers or team leads who are not deeply technical but need confidence that sensitive data (e.g., financial trackers, client CRMs) is shared only with the right people.

The psychological driver here is control and accountability. Admins need to audit access quickly before sharing a base externally or during security reviews. The explicit labeling of "1 workspace collaborator" combined with the inheritance explanation reduces anxiety around accidental over-sharing (a critical trust signal for teams handling proprietary or regulated data).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline permission transparency: The explanatory caption demystifies why a user appears in the list without manual intervention, turning a potential confusion/trust issue into a moment of clarity.
  • Clear separation of inherited vs. explicit access: Grouping workspace-level and base-level collaborators into distinct visually separated sections prevents admins from misunderstanding the scope of their permission changes.
  • Low-density, high-legibility layout: Despite Airtable's grid-heavy brand identity, this settings screen deliberately uses generous whitespace and large touch targets, appropriate for an infrequent, high-consequence administrative task.
  • Dual invitation pathways: Offering both direct collaborator addition and a shareable invite link accommodates different team workflows (controlled vs. self-service onboarding).

screens.name: Airtable - Managing collaborators - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use just-in-time permission priming whenever an app needs access to sensitive OS-level resources (contacts, camera, location, notifications) that are not essential to the core app experience. Trigger the request at the exact moment the user initiates a related action (e.g., requesting camera access only when the user taps "Add Photo"), and ensure the underlying screen offers a functional fallback for users who decline.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid front-loading this permission request during onboarding or first launch, before the user understands why it's needed (this significantly lowers acceptance rates and can trigger the "Don't Allow" default reflex).
