Also avoid this pattern for permissions that are mission-critical and non-optional (e.g., location for a navigation app); in those cases, a custom pre-permission educational screen should precede the native OS dialog to maximize opt-in rates rather than relying on the system prompt's generic framing alone.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Airtable's audience: teams, operations staff, project managers (frequently need to onboard multiple collaborators quickly, often from an existing professional network stored in their phone's contacts or Gmail). By requesting contact access precisely at the "Add Collaborators" step, Airtable leverages the Reciprocity and Relevance Heuristic: users are far more willing to grant sensitive permissions when the request is explicitly tied to the action they just initiated.

This pattern also mitigates drop-off anxiety common among B2B/enterprise users who are cautious about data privacy; delaying the ask until it's contextually justified reduces perceived risk and signals that Airtable respects user data boundaries, which is critical for building trust with operations and IT-conscious teams evaluating the platform.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual (Just-in-Time) Permission Priming is the standout decision here. Instead of requesting contacts access during onboarding (when the user has no context for why it matters) Airtable waits until the user actively navigates to "Add Collaborators," a moment when the value exchange is self-evident.

  • Graceful Degradation: The screen offers multiple fallback paths (manual search, Gmail import) so declining the native prompt doesn't dead-end the user's workflow.
  • Visual Hierarchy Preservation: Dimming rather than hiding the background screen keeps spatial context intact, reducing the disorientation that full-screen modals can cause.
  • Low-Friction Opt-Out: "Don't Allow" is given equal visual weight to "OK," respecting user autonomy and complying with Apple's Human Interface Guidelines, which builds platform-level trust.

screens.name: Airtable - Managing collaborators - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any B2B SaaS product that depends on multi-user adoption (project management, docs, CRM) where inviting teammates is a core growth lever.
  • Collaboration or sharing flows where users may invite people via multiple identifiers (email, username, phone).
  • Screens where leveraging a native contact list or third-party address book can meaningfully speed up a tedious manual-entry task.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for single-player or personal-use apps where there is no concept of collaborators or shared access.
  • Not ideal for highly regulated environments (healthcare, finance) where surfacing a user's personal contacts/Gmail data could raise privacy or compliance concerns without explicit, separate consent screens.
  • Should not be used as the only invite path if the target audience may not have the invitee's contact synced anywhere (e.g., external clients) - a manual email entry path must always remain primary via the search field.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations leads, project managers, and team builders who are setting up or scaling a shared Airtable base. The core psychological driver is reducing invite friction: collaboration tools live or die by how easy it is to get a second person into the workspace. Every extra tap or required field at this stage risks abandonment of the entire sharing action.

By defaulting to "Recent Collaborators" and contact-list integration, Airtable taps into familiarity bias (users are more likely to add known/recent colleagues) and reduces the activation energy needed to grow a multiplayer workspace, which is directly tied to Airtable's business model of expanding paid seats per account.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Tiered discovery hierarchy: Recent Collaborators → Contacts → Import creates a frictionless funnel that surfaces the most likely matches before asking the user to do more work.
  • Unified search-first entry point: A single search bar for name OR email avoids forcing users to choose an invite method upfront, reducing decision fatigue.
  • Native integration leverage: Pulling from device Contacts and Gmail dramatically lowers the barrier to populating a workspace with real collaborators, which is critical for Airtable's network-effect-driven value proposition.
  • Consistent affordances: Chevron indicators on every row set a predictable expectation that tapping leads to a next step (role/permission selection), maintaining system consistency.

screens.name: Airtable - Managing collaborators - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Reuse this pattern for any people-picker or invite flow in collaborative SaaS products (project management tools, document editors, chat apps, or shared calendars). It's especially effective when:

  • Users frequently re-invite the same small set of people across different projects/workspaces.
  • You want to reduce typing by surfacing device contacts or recent history before search.
  • The invited entity requires a secondary confirmation step (e.g., setting permission level) rather than one-tap addition.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen, multi-sourced picker for simple, single-use invites (e.g., a one-off share link) where a lightweight share sheet would be faster. Also avoid surfacing "Contacts" and "Import" sections if the app has strict data-privacy constraints or a young/consumer audience wary of permission requests (in those cases, a pure search-by-email field is safer and less intrusive).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets team leads, project managers, and operations staff who are setting up shared bases and need to quickly onboard collaborators without leaving their workflow. Because Airtable is fundamentally a multiplayer tool, frictionless invitation is core to activation and network-effect growth.

The psychological drivers at play include reduced search effort (recency bias leveraged via "Recent Collaborators" since people tend to re-invite the same colleagues across projects) and trust-building through transparency (showing exactly what import sources are available rather than silently scanning contacts).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-focused search input: The keyboard is already active on screen load, eliminating an extra tap and getting users typing immediately (ideal for a high-frequency, low-friction task like inviting a teammate).
  • Tiered contact sourcing: Recent Collaborators → Contacts → Import creates a prioritized, zero-query browsing experience before the user even types a character.
  • Low-commitment entry points: Chevrons on every row signal "tap to continue a flow" rather than "instantly perform an irreversible action," which builds trust around a sensitive permission-granting task.
  • Branded import source icon: Using the recognizable Gmail logo instantly communicates what data will be accessed and builds confidence in the integration.

screens.name: Airtable - Managing collaborators - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any invite, share, or add-collaborator flow where the target audience may not yet exist in the system's contact graph. It's especially effective for:

  • B2B SaaS tools with team-based collaboration (project management, docs, CRMs).
  • Flows where email is the primary identifier for invitations.
  • Scenarios where you want to simultaneously support "invite existing user" and "invite new user via email" in one unified search experience.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The product doesn't support external invitations (e.g., closed, approval-only team rosters) - showing an invite CTA would be misleading.
  • Privacy regulations prevent email-based invites without pre-consent, which could create legal/compliance risk (e.g., GDPR-sensitive contexts).
  • The user base skews toward in-app username/handle identity rather than email, where email-pattern matching logic would be less relevant.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets team admins, project managers, and operations leads who are the primary drivers of workspace expansion in Airtable (the people responsible for bringing collaborators onto a base). These users are often mid-task (e.g., setting up a project) and want to add teammates quickly without leaving their workflow.

Psychologically, the design exploits the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete tasks demand closure) by making the invite action feel like the natural, frictionless next step after typing an email, and reduces decision fatigue by only showing two clear, relevant options instead of a long list of unrelated contacts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dynamic Echo Confirmation: The input text is mirrored back inside the result row ("Email an invitation to 'X'"), giving the user real-time confirmation that their entry will be processed correctly.
  • Graceful Fallback for No Match: Instead of showing a generic "no results found" empty state, the UI pivots to an actionable invite CTA, turning a potential dead-end into a conversion point.
  • Secondary Growth Loop: The Google Contacts import option is surfaced contextually within the search flow, increasing the odds of acquiring multiple new collaborators from a single interaction.
  • Keyboard-First Interaction: Auto-focusing the search field and keeping the keyboard open removes extra taps, respecting the efficiency-driven workflows of power users.

screens.name: Airtable - Managing collaborators - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app needs to grant role-based or tiered access to a shared resource (documents, boards, projects, folders). It's ideal when:

  • There are a small, fixed number of permission tiers (3 (5) that benefit from full-list visibility rather than a collapsed dropdown).
  • The action is high-stakes enough to warrant an explicit confirmation sentence restating the object and recipient.
  • Users may be unfamiliar with the exact meaning of each tier, justifying an inline help link.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this full-screen modal approach when:

  • There are many more than 4-5 permission levels: a long scrollable checkmark list becomes unwieldy compared to a dropdown or combobox.
  • The sharing action is low-stakes or highly frequent (e.g., sharing a casual note), where a lightweight popover or inline share sheet would reduce friction better than a full navigational context switch.
  • Collaborators are added in bulk: this single-recipient form would need to be replaced with a multi-select or CSV/bulk-invite flow to avoid repetitive, tedious entry.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets team leads, operations managers, and project owners who need to invite collaborators into a specific Airtable base while controlling the blast radius of access (view-only vs. full edit/admin rights). Because Airtable powers business-critical workflows (CRMs, inventories, project trackers), granular permissioning is a trust-and-safety necessity, not a nice-to-have.

Psychologically, the design leans on loss-aversion and error-prevention: by explicitly restating who is being invited and to what base, it reduces the anxiety of "did I just give the wrong person edit access?" The checkmark-based selection list also taps into recognition over recall: users don't need to remember what each permission tier means in the abstract; they can tap through tiers and reference the help link if uncertain.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dynamic confirmation sentence: Injecting the live base name and invitee email directly into the body copy prevents misdirected shares (a subtle but powerful error-prevention mechanic).
  • Inline permission explainer link: "About permission levels" is positioned exactly where doubt would arise, rather than requiring users to leave the flow.
  • Single, obvious selection mechanism: Using a checkmark list instead of a dropdown/segmented control makes the four permission tiers immediately scannable and reduces mis-taps on a touch screen.
  • Clear modal chrome: Cancel/Add placement mirrors system-standard iOS modal conventions, so users instantly know how to commit or abandon the action.

screens.name: Airtable - Managing collaborators - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse:
• Permission/access management screens in any multi-tenant or hierarchical collaboration product (workspace → project → document).
  • Admin panels where inherited vs. explicit permissions need to be clearly differentiated to avoid user confusion.
  • B2B SaaS tools with team-based billing or role-based access control, where explaining the "why" behind a permission state reduces support burden.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer-facing social apps where a simpler, flat "friends/followers" list suffices (the extra explanatory text would feel overly bureaucratic).
  • Flows with only a single level of access control (no inheritance), where distinguishing "workspace vs base" collaborators would add unnecessary complexity.
  • High-frequency, low-stakes sharing actions (e.g., sharing a photo) where imperative admin-style language would feel too formal/heavy.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves workspace admins, team leads, and ops managers who are responsible for governing data access across a base (a high-stakes task since Airtable bases often house sensitive business data (CRM records, financials, project pipelines)). The psychological driver here is control and trust: admins need absolute clarity on who can view/edit data, and ambiguity in permission systems creates anxiety about data leaks or unauthorized edits.

By explicitly distinguishing workspace-inherited access from base-specific grants, Airtable reduces the "who can see this?" anxiety that is common in collaborative SaaS tools, building trust that the system is transparent and auditable.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Permission Education: Inline caption text demystifies why certain users appear on the list without requiring a separate help doc or tooltip.
  • Clear Separation of Inherited vs. Explicit Access: Workspace collaborators and base-specific collaborators are visually and structurally segmented, preventing admins from accidentally assuming they can remove someone who actually has workspace-level rights.
  • Dual Invitation Pathways: Offering both "Add base collaborators" (direct, controlled) and "Create an invite link" (viral, self-serve) caters to different team-scaling behaviors (from tightly controlled enterprise onboarding to rapid ad-hoc sharing).
  • Low-friction Row Actions: The blue "Manage" affordance next to each collaborator keeps the list scannable while still surfacing a clear per-user action entry point.

screens.name: Airtable - Managing collaborators - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-settings-with-visual-picker pattern when users need to configure metadata for a container object (projects, workspaces, folders, boards) that will later be recognized by color/icon in a list or switcher view. It's ideal for:

  • Multi-workspace or multi-project tools where visual differentiation aids navigation.
  • Any settings screen combining textual metadata (name, description) with branding controls (color, icon) in one place.
  • Scenarios where collaborative context (who else has access) is relevant to the configuration decision.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for single-user, non-shared contexts where collaborator information would be noise. It's also unsuitable for simple objects that don't benefit from heavy visual customization (e.g., a single to-do item), where exposing a full color/icon picker would add unnecessary complexity. Additionally, a full-screen modal is overkill for trivial edits like renaming only (consider an inline rename or lightweight popover instead to reduce perceived friction).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets team leads, operations managers, and power users who are setting up or maintaining a shared workspace used by multiple collaborators. Letting users assign a distinctive color and icon taps into a basic psychological need for spatial/visual memory and ownership: in a tool where users may juggle dozens of Bases, color-coding and iconography reduce cognitive load when scanning a crowded workspace list later.

The "Guide" description field serves a different psychological function: it encourages intentionality and documentation, prompting the creator to articulate the Base's purpose for teammates, which increases adoption and reduces onboarding friction for collaborators joining later.

Showing collaborator avatars reinforces social accountability: users are reminded that this isn't a private file but a shared asset, which subtly encourages more thoughtful naming and organization.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grouped settings architecture: Cleanly separates identity, collaboration, description, and branding into digestible, independently scrollable sections.
  • Inline collaborator preview: Stacked avatar icons plus names ("Jiho Lim, John doe") give an at-a-glance social snapshot without requiring a tap into the full collaborator list.
  • Visual self-reference loop: The chosen red color and cloud icon are mirrored in the nav bar's red theme and checkmark state, giving users immediate confirmation of how their choices manifest in the product chrome.
  • Horizontal swatch/icon carousel with pagination dots: Efficiently houses dozens of options in limited vertical space while signaling there's more to explore.
  • Guide field as a soft-onboarding nudge: Using a whimsical example text teaches new users the purpose of the field through demonstration rather than instruction.

screens.name: Airtable - Creating a new record - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an app must support file or media uploads from multiple competing storage ecosystems (documents, images, attachments) and when the audience is likely to have assets scattered across both local devices and professional cloud drives, such as B2B SaaS tools, productivity suites, CRM systems, and project management apps.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this exhaustive multi-source pattern for casual consumer apps where users almost always upload from a single source (e.g., a camera-only social app), as the extra choices add unnecessary decision fatigue. It is also not ideal when an app wants to funnel users toward its own proprietary storage/ecosystem (in that case, a single primary CTA with an "other options" fallback would be better).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Airtable's target users: operations teams, marketers, and project managers (frequently work across disparate tools and storage ecosystems (a marketer might store assets in Google Drive, an ops person in Dropbox or Box, enterprise users in OneDrive)). This screen respects that diversity instead of forcing a single workflow, which builds trust and reduces abandonment at the point of attaching critical files to records.

The psychological trigger here is reduced cognitive load through familiarity: by mirroring the native iOS share-sheet/file-picker pattern, users don't need to learn a new interaction model (it feels like an extension of the OS rather than a bespoke in-app control, lowering the perceived risk of connecting external accounts).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unified multi-source picker: Consolidates five cloud providers and three local sources into one coherent list, reducing fragmentation across integrations.
  • Iconographic recognition: Each row uses the source's actual brand icon/color, leveraging users' existing mental models (e.g., Dropbox's blue box, Google Drive's triangle) for near-instant scanning instead of reading.
  • Clear sectioning: Dividing "Local" from "Cloud" with bold section headers helps users quickly navigate to the storage type most relevant to their workflow (e.g., mobile camera roll vs. enterprise cloud drive).
  • Low-friction exit: A persistent, clearly labeled "Cancel" affordance in the header respects user control and prevents dead-end modals.

screens.name: Airtable - Creating a new record - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use contextual permission priming whenever a native OS capability (camera, microphone, location, notifications) is needed to fulfill a specific user-initiated action, attaching a photo, scanning a document, tagging a location, etc. Pair it with a record/detail view pattern for any app that lets users edit structured, multi-field data objects on mobile (CRMs, inventory apps, field-service tools, no-code database apps).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid requesting system permissions at app launch or before the user has expressed clear intent (this leads to higher denial rates and users being unable to understand the "why)." Also avoid the flattened field-row layout for extremely wide or highly relational data (e.g., linked records with many columns) where a tab-based or grouped-section layout would reduce scroll fatigue. Destructive actions like "Delete record" should never be placed this close to neutral actions without sufficient visual separation or confirmation step on less experienced user bases.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This flow targets operations staff, project managers, and mobile field workers who use Airtable to capture real-world data (e.g., travel logs, site visits, inventory checks) directly from their phone. The psychological trigger at play is reciprocity and trust-building through transparency: by explaining exactly why camera access is needed and tying it to a concrete, just-performed action, Airtable reduces the anxiety typically associated with permission requests, increasing opt-in rates and preserving user trust in the brand as a serious productivity tool rather than an intrusive consumer app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Just-in-time permission request: The camera prompt fires only after the user actively taps the Pics field, not preemptively on app load (dramatically increasing the likelihood of "OK" being tapped).
  • Field-as-row mobile reinterpretation: Complex relational table columns are elegantly flattened into a single scrollable record form, preserving Airtable's structured-data power while staying mobile-friendly.
  • Iconography per field type: Each field label has a distinct small icon (text "A", "#", paperclip, calendar) that mirrors the field-type icons used in Airtable's desktop grid, creating cross-platform consistency.
  • Clear destructive vs. constructive footer actions: Color and iconography (red trash vs. blue icon) make the irreversible "Delete record" action visually distinct from safe "Customize fields," reducing accidental data loss.

screens.name: Airtable - Creating a new record - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this native capture-confirm pattern whenever an app needs users to quickly document something visually as part of a larger workflow (e.g., attaching receipts, proof-of-delivery photos, damage reports, or asset photos to a record/field). It's ideal for data-entry-heavy, utility-first apps where speed and reliability trump custom branding at the capture moment. It's especially effective in CRMs, inventory/asset management tools, inspection apps, and expense trackers.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid relying solely on the native camera UI when the brand experience or guided framing is critical to data quality (for example, ID verification or KYC flows that require specific overlays/guides (e).g., aligning a card within a frame), or consumer social apps where a branded, filter-rich capture experience is part of the core product value. In those cases, a custom capture screen with guide overlays, filters, or branded chrome would better serve the user's needs and the business's conversion goals.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This flow directly serves operations teams, field inspectors, and project managers who use Airtable to document physical assets, conditions, or progress (e.g., furniture condition audits, construction site logs, inventory checks) - evidenced by the image subject (a worn wooden surface, likely documenting damage or wear for a report/record). The psychological driver is trust-building through verification: by forcing a review step (rather than auto-saving the first capture), Airtable gives users confidence that the correct, well-framed evidence enters their database, which matters greatly in professional and compliance-driven use cases where attachment quality has downstream consequences.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native OS Camera Delegation: Reusing the system camera/photo-confirmation UI instead of a custom in-app capture screen ensures familiarity, reliability, and lower development cost.
  • Binary Decision Point: Only two possible actions (Retake vs. Use Photo) eliminate decision paralysis and keep the flow moving quickly toward record attachment.
  • Full-Bleed Image Preview: Maximizing the captured image on-screen allows users to verify quality (sharpness, lighting, crop) before confirming, reducing the need for later re-uploads.
  • Non-Destructive Review Step: Giving an explicit "Retake" option before the photo is actually saved to the Airtable record prevents accidental low-quality attachments from polluting the data table.

screens.name: Airtable - Creating a new record - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when designing record/detail views for flexible, user-defined data models: CRMs, inventory trackers, content calendars, or no-code database apps. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to view/edit many heterogeneous field types within a single entity.
  • Field types vary (text, number, date, attachment) and benefit from visual differentiation.
  • Mobile users need parity with desktop table functionality without horizontal scrolling.
  • You want to support both quick-glance scanning and deep editing in the same screen.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense, form-style detail pattern when:

  • The underlying data model is simple or fixed (e.g., a single-purpose app with only 2-3 fields) - the overhead of icons/labels per field becomes unnecessary visual noise.
  • Users need to compare multiple records simultaneously, where a table/grid view is more efficient than drilling into one record at a time.
  • The app targets non-technical consumers who may be intimidated by schema-like labels (field-type icons, all-caps labels) rather than simple, friendly form fields.
  • Speed of bulk editing is critical: this single-record view is inherently slower than inline table editing for mass updates.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations and project managers, marketers, and "systems builders" who use Airtable to replace rigid spreadsheets with flexible, structured databases (in this case a lightweight travel-planning base). The target user is comfortable thinking in rows/fields but wants mobile convenience to quickly check or update a record (e.g., adding a photo on-site, jotting a note) without opening a laptop.

Psychologically, the design leverages structure-as-comfort: by labeling every field with its type and keeping a strict list format, the user never feels lost even with a completely custom, user-defined schema. The inline progress indicator exploits the Zeigarnik effect: showing incomplete tasks (uploading) keeps users engaged and confident the system is working rather than silently failing.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Field-type iconography: Each label is prefixed with an icon representing its underlying data type, turning an abstract schema into a visually scannable, almost "wayfinding" system.
  • Inline attachment uploader with progress bar: Users see real-time upload status directly within the field, with camera/gallery/more-options shortcuts right next to it, collapsing a multi-step attach flow into one row.
  • Record switcher in header: The "Singapore ▾" dropdown lets users jump to the next/previous record without leaving the detail view or returning to the table (a huge efficiency win for data entry workflows).
  • Separated footer actions: "Customize fields" vs. destructive "Delete record" are visually and spatially isolated from data fields, preventing accidental taps while keeping power-user configuration one tap away.
  • External link icon on Date field: Signals that date values can expand into a richer picker/modal, hinting at depth without cluttering the base view.

results.query: Recovering user trust after failed identity document camera scan

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern during identity verification, account setup, or compliance flows where the user must choose between a small, well-defined set of document types or credential options before proceeding to capture/upload steps. It's ideal when:

  • The choice set is small (2-4 options) and mutually exclusive.

  • A sensible default can be inferred from context (geolocation, prior input) to speed up the majority path.

  • You need to set expectations/rules before the next step (e.g., "no scans or copies") to reduce failed submissions.

  • The flow benefits from a calm, low-distraction UI due to its sensitive or compliance-driven nature.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this exact heavy, full-bleed gradient treatment for casual or high-frequency screens where users need speed and lightness over gravitas (it may feel overly dramatic for trivial settings choices). Also avoid pre-selecting a default when there is no reliable signal for which option is most likely correct, as an incorrect default may cause user confusion or accidental submission of the wrong document type. If more than 3-4 document options exist, a radio list may become unwieldy and should be replaced with a searchable list or dropdown instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users undergoing mandatory identity verification (KYC/AML compliance) for regulated services such as digital banks, crypto exchanges, or fintech apps operating in Singapore. The demographic spans from young digital-first consumers to non-native residents needing passport-based verification.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduction of choice overload (only two options), default bias (pre-selecting the most common document type), and anxiety reduction (clear instructions and progress indication) to keep users moving through what is typically perceived as a tedious, high-friction compliance step. The premium visual styling also triggers a sense of institutional trust, which is essential when asking users to submit sensitive personal documents.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Default Pre-Selection: "National ID" is pre-checked based on the detected country (Singapore flag), removing an unnecessary tap for the majority path.

  • Pre-emptive Error Prevention Copy: Explicitly stating "We don't accept scans or copies" upfront prevents wasted user effort and downstream verification failures.

  • Visual Hierarchy & Focus: Only one primary action (Continue) is emphasized with a high-contrast white pill button against the dark background; the secondary "Change citizenship" link is intentionally subdued to avoid distracting from the main path.

  • Trust-Building Atmosphere: The deep blue-to-black gradient and clean iconography evoke security and seriousness appropriate for identity verification.

  • Progress Transparency: The bottom page-control indicator reassures users of their place in a finite multi-step journey.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Any document/photo capture flow (ID verification, check deposit scanning, passport/visa scanning) where image quality is critical to downstream processing.

  • Compliance-heavy onboarding flows (banking, crypto, healthcare, age-gated services) where retries must be fast and low-friction to prevent funnel drop-off.

  • Any camera-based scanning UI (barcode, receipt, business card scanners) that requires specific framing and lighting conditions.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for catastrophic or unrecoverable errors (e.g., account suspended, document rejected for fraud) - those require a full-screen blocking state with distinct next steps, not an inline retry banner.

  • Not suitable for flows where multiple simultaneous errors could occur, stacking multiple inline banners would clutter the viewfinder and overwhelm the user.

  • Avoid if the camera hardware/permissions themselves are the issue (e.g., camera access denied); that requires a distinct permission-request state rather than an image-quality error banner.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users undergoing mandatory identity verification, common in fintech, banking, crypto exchanges, and gig-economy onboarding flows (e.g., account opening, age verification, KYC/AML compliance). This demographic is often anxious about handing over sensitive personal documents and may be verifying identity on a mobile device for the first time in a low-light or improvised environment.

The psychological trigger at play is friction reduction under stress: identity verification is a non-negotiable gate the user must pass to access a service (e.g., open a bank account, receive a paycheck, access a crypto wallet), so any perceived failure elevates anxiety. The immediate, actionable feedback loop (error → guidance → retry) reduces abandonment risk at a critical conversion funnel step. The persistent camera view also leverages the sunk-cost/momentum principle, keeping the user "in the moment" rather than forcing a restart.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking error banner: Uses an inline banner instead of a disruptive modal, allowing users to immediately retry the action without an extra dismiss step.

  • High-contrast iconography: The red circular alert icon against a black banner immediately draws the eye and signals severity using color psychology, even before reading the text.

  • Live camera persistence: Keeping the camera feed active during the error state (rather than showing a static failed image) reduces the number of steps needed to retry, respecting the user's time.

  • Clear visual guide-frame: The rounded rectangle overlay with corner accents removes guesswork about framing, directly addressing the root cause of the blur/positioning error.

  • Trust branding: The "Onfido | Real Identity" watermark reassures users that a reputable, specialized third-party service (rather than the host app itself) is handling sensitive biometric/document data.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 17
screens.whereToUse:
• Biometric or liveness-check flows (face scan, video selfie, passport/ID verification) in fintech, banking, crypto, insurance, or gig-platform onboarding.

  • Any camera-driven capture task requiring the user to remain still or follow a precise physical action (e.g., document scanning, AR try-on calibration).

  • Security-sensitive flows where minimal, non-distracting UI increases user focus and task completion accuracy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Casual, brand-personality-driven consumer apps where a cold, clinical tone would feel jarring or untrustworthy.

  • Flows where users need more contextual guidance (e.g., first-time users may need an explainer/coach mark before this stark screen, otherwise they may be confused about why the camera is black or what's expected).

  • Situations lacking a real-time active camera feed (this pattern depends on a live preview; using it for static forms or non-camera tasks would be misapplied).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets any user undergoing mandatory identity verification (typical in fintech, banking, crypto exchanges, gig-economy platforms, or age-restricted services requiring KYC/AML compliance). Users here are often anxious about privacy, camera access, and correctly completing an unfamiliar biometric task under time pressure.

Psychologically, the design leverages authority and trust cues (third-party verification badge) to offset anxiety about handing over facial biometric data. The stark, clinical dark UI reduces distraction-driven errors, while the direct imperative copy exploits minimal cognitive load
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dark, distraction-free theme: Nearly all UI chrome is suppressed so the live camera feed and instructions are the sole focal point, reducing user anxiety and errors during biometric capture.

  • Combined status + instruction pill: Merging the loading spinner with the directive "Hold still" into one compact overlay is an elegant micro-interaction that tells the user both what the system is doing and what they must do, without needing separate UI elements.

  • Framed capture viewport: The rounded, outlined frame around the video clearly demarcates the active recording area, guiding face/head positioning intuitively.

  • Persistent third-party trust badge: The Onfido "Real Identity" logo at the bottom footer reassures users the process is handled by a specialized, secure verification provider, increasing confidence in submitting sensitive biometric data.

  • Page indicator dot: The subtle horizontal bar at the very bottom hints at a multi-step flow (likely a swipe/progress indicator for verification stages), giving a sense of finite progress.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 18
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a system performs automated quality/validation checks on user-submitted media (documents, selfies, receipts, signatures) and needs to reject the submission before it moves further down a pipeline. It's ideal for:

  • KYC/AML identity verification flows

  • Document/receipt scanning in expense or banking apps

  • Selfie-based liveness or profile photo checks

  • Any file/photo upload requiring OCR or ML processing accuracy
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed, full-screen interruption pattern for low-stakes or cosmetic image issues (e.g., a social media post photo that's slightly blurry) (a lighter inline warning or toast would suffice and preserve flow. Don't use this pattern if failure detection is unreliable, as false-positive blur rejections will frustrate users with correctly captured images; ensure detection thresholds are well-tuned before shipping. Also avoid stacking multiple error states or vague messaging ("Something went wrong")) specificity is essential to this pattern's effectiveness.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets any end-user going through a mandatory identity verification process (e.g., opening a bank account, fintech onboarding, age-gated services, or gig-economy driver/rider verification). These users are often verifying under time pressure or on unfamiliar devices/lighting conditions, making capture failures common.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (the discomfort of an incomplete task) to motivate immediate correction, while the non-judgmental "system detected" framing reduces the shame or annoyance that could otherwise cause users to abandon the flow. Showing the actual failed image taps into transparency and procedural fairness (users are more likely to trust and comply with automated rejections when they can see the evidence themselves).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Automated Quality Gate: Client-side blur detection catches unusable images before they're submitted for verification, saving backend processing costs and reducing verification turnaround time.

  • Visual Evidence + Enlarge Control: Showing the actual blurry capture (with a zoom option) builds user trust by proving the system's judgment rather than issuing an opaque rejection.

  • Single, Unambiguous CTA: Only one action is offered ("Retake photo"), eliminating decision paralysis and funneling the user directly back into the capture loop.

  • High-Contrast Alert Styling: The red-bordered banner with icon uses conventional error semantics (color, icon, border) so the severity is instantly recognizable even at a glance.

  • Contextual Coaching Repeated: Guidance text appears twice (in the error banner and above the CTA), reinforcing the fix without needing the user to scroll or re-read.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 19
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any server-side or on-device processing step that follows a photo/document capture, especially in identity verification, KYC, document scanning, or biometric enrollment flows. It's ideal when:

  • Processing takes 1: 5 seconds and full-screen focus is needed.

  • You want to reduce user anxiety by explaining exactly what the system is validating.

  • Brand/vendor trust (e.g., a security partner) needs reinforcing during sensitive data handling.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, blocking full-screen loading pattern when:

  • Processing time is highly variable or could exceed 10-15 seconds without a determinate progress indicator (users will assume the app has crashed).

  • The task is low-stakes; an inline spinner or skeleton loader would be less disruptive.

  • Users may need to cancel or go back: this screen offers no escape route, which could frustrate users if the check hangs indefinitely.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users going through onboarding for a regulated product (fintech, banking, crypto exchange, gig-economy, or sharing-economy platform) that requires KYC/AML identity verification. These users are often slightly anxious about handing over biometric/ID data, so the design leans on authority and trust signals (the Onfido brand) and transparency of system state (explicit status text) to reduce drop-off during this friction-heavy but necessary step.

The psychological driver here is reducing perceived wait-time anxiety: by explaining exactly what's being checked, the app frames any delay as diligence/security rather than a technical glitch, increasing tolerance for the pause.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-black immersive background: eliminates distraction and visually signals "camera/scanning mode," consistent with the preceding capture screen.

  • Specific, action-oriented status text: "Checking image quality..." manages expectations and subtly primes the user for possible retake feedback if the image fails.

  • Persistent third-party trust branding: Onfido's logo and "Real Identity" tagline at the footer reassure users that a specialized, secure vendor is processing their sensitive biometric data.

  • No dismiss or cancel action: reinforces that this is a quick, mandatory checkpoint rather than an interruptible state, reducing decision fatigue during a short wait.

  • Progress bar at the very bottom hints this is one step within a larger multi-step verification sequence, giving implicit macro-progress context.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 20
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app needs to request a sensitive permission or biometric capture (camera, microphone, location for identity purposes) and abandonment or failed-attempt rates are a concern. It is ideal for:

  • KYC/AML identity verification flows in banking, fintech, and crypto apps

  • Age or identity verification for regulated content/services

  • Any biometric enrollment step (Face ID setup, liveness checks)

  • Pre-permission "priming" screens before triggering native OS permission dialogs
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, instructional pre-screen for low-stakes or frequently repeated camera interactions (e.g., casual photo uploads, chat attachments) where it would add unnecessary friction. It's also unsuitable for flows where speed is paramount and the data being captured is not sensitive (over-explaining trivial actions can feel patronizing and slow down conversion). Additionally, if the disclosure language is too legally dense or buried, it defeats the transparency purpose and can increase distrust instead of reducing it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets any end-user undergoing mandatory identity verification: typical in fintech onboarding, banking apps, crypto exchanges, gig-economy driver/worker verification, or age-restricted services. These users are often mid-funnel in a high-intent action (e.g., opening a bank account, accessing funds) but are simultaneously wary of privacy and biometric data misuse.

The psychological triggers at play include reducing perceived risk through transparency (the disclosure banner), lowering anxiety through preparation (clear physical instructions prevent failed/retry attempts, which is a major drop-off point in KYC flows), and authority/trust transfer via the recognizable Onfido brand, which signals institutional-grade security rather than an unknown or ad-hoc capture mechanism.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive objection handling: Explicitly stating "Eyeglasses are okay" removes a common point of hesitation before the user even thinks to ask.

  • Transparent biometric disclosure: A dedicated, visually distinct banner informs users their face/background will be captured, satisfying both legal compliance and user trust needs at the exact moment of highest sensitivity.

  • Zero-decision layout: Only one button exists on screen ("Take selfie"), removing any friction or ambiguity about the next step.

  • Icon-led scannability: Pairing simple line icons with each instruction lets users absorb requirements in seconds rather than reading dense paragraphs.

  • Trusted third-party branding (Onfido): Displaying the identity verification vendor's logo reassures users that a specialized, reputable service (not the host app itself) is handling sensitive biometric data.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 21
screens.whereToUse:
• Identity verification / KYC flows requiring a live selfie or facial liveness check.

  • Any biometric capture step (passport scan, face match, liveness detection) where precise framing is critical for backend processing accuracy.

  • Security-sensitive onboarding flows (banking, crypto, healthcare, age verification) where user trust and regulatory compliance must be visually reinforced.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this stark, feature-stripped pattern for casual or low-stakes photo capture (e.g., profile picture upload) where a friendlier, branded camera UI with filters/retake options would feel more appropriate.

  • Not suitable when users need supplementary guidance beyond simple framing (e.g., complex multi-angle scans) without additional coach marks or animated cues.

  • Avoid if the brand's tone is playful/casual, as the clinical dark UI may feel overly cold or intimidating for lower-risk use cases.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets any user undergoing mandatory identity verification (common in fintech, banking, crypto exchanges, gig-economy platforms, and rental/sharing apps where regulatory KYC (Know Your Customer) or AML compliance is required). Users at this stage are often anxious or hesitant about sharing biometric data, so the design leans on psychological triggers of control and clarity (a single, well-defined instruction), authority and trust (third-party vendor branding), and procedural transparency (progress indicator) to reduce abandonment and anxiety during a highly sensitive, friction-prone step of onboarding.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Distraction-free full-screen camera view: Removing all UI elements except the essential oval guide and shutter button ensures maximum focus and reduces failed capture attempts.

  • Native camera affordance: The bottom-centered circular shutter button borrows heavily from iOS/Android native camera conventions, requiring zero learning curve.

  • Dark, low-glare background: Improves face detection algorithm performance and reduces visual noise/distraction, subtly reinforcing a secure, controlled environment.

  • Progress bar footer: Provides subtle reassurance of flow progression without cluttering the primary capture area.

  • Third-party trust branding: Displaying the Onfido logo builds confidence that a specialized, compliant vendor is handling identity checks.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 22
screens.whereToUse: Use this confirm-before-submit pattern whenever a user captures sensitive or hard-to-redo content (ID photos, signatures, document scans, biometric selfies) where server-side rejection is costly or slow. It's ideal for KYC/AML flows, age verification, insurance claims photo evidence, and any camera-based capture step where quality directly impacts downstream processing success.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed confirm screen for low-stakes photo uploads (e.g., casual profile picture changes in a social app) where an extra confirmation step only adds friction without meaningful benefit. Also avoid it if your capture pipeline already includes automatic real-time quality detection (e.g., liveness/face-bounding checks during capture) that renders a manual "is my face visible?" check redundant.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users onboarding into a regulated product (fintech, crypto exchange, gig marketplace, sharing-economy platform, or age-restricted service) that legally requires Know Your Customer (KYC) or identity verification. These users are often moderately anxious about handing over biometric data, so the design leans on psychological triggers such as perceived control (ability to retake), procedural transparency (explicit instructions on what "good" looks like), and third-party authority/trust transfer (Onfido branding) to reduce drop-off at this sensitive step of the funnel.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Binary decision architecture: Only two possible actions are presented, eliminating decision paralysis at a high-stakes checkpoint.

  • Clear visual hierarchy between CTAs: The solid purple "Upload photo" button signals the recommended/default path, while the outlined "Retake photo" button offers a low-friction alternative without competing visually.

  • Full-screen photo review: Letting the user visually confirm their own captured image before submission builds confidence and reduces failed verification attempts caused by poor image quality.

  • Third-party trust branding: The Onfido "Real Identity" watermark reassures users that a specialized, security-focused vendor (not just the host app) is processing sensitive biometric data.

  • Dark, distraction-free canvas: The black background isolates the face photo as the sole focal point, mimicking a camera viewfinder aesthetic that feels native to identity-capture contexts.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 23
screens.whereToUse:
• Onboarding flows for multi-product platforms (super-apps, fintech, SaaS suites) where personalization can drive relevant feature discovery.

  • When you want to collect regulatory/compliance data but need to soften the ask with transparency and personality.

  • Early in the funnel, before heavier friction steps like identity verification, to build rapport and momentum.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for single-purpose apps with only one core use case (the categorized chip wall adds unnecessary complexity).

  • Don't use if the collected data won't actually be used for personalization; asking without follow-through erodes trust.

  • Avoid overloading with too many options (20+) without strong grouping, as decision fatigue can cause drop-off despite the playful tone.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets new users at the account-creation stage, most of whom are evaluating whether Revolut fits their financial lifestyle (freelancers, travelers, investors, or everyday spenders). By surfacing the full breadth of offerings as selectable "needs," Revolut leverages the IKEA effect and commitment/consistency bias: once a user actively picks "Crypto" or "Stocks abroad," they're psychologically primed to expect and engage with those features later, increasing feature adoption and reducing early churn. The playful, honest copy also targets users wary of over-invasive fintech onboarding, building early trust before deeper KYC steps (ID verification, etc.) that typically follow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent regulatory framing: Explicitly telling users why the data is needed ("regulatory reasons") pre-empts skepticism about invasive-feeling questions.

  • Emoji-as-icon system: Using native emojis instead of custom icons speeds up development, adds warmth, and aids fast visual scanning across a long list of options.

  • Categorized chip wall: Grouping into "Everyday needs," "Global spending," and (implied) "Investing" turns a flat checklist into a structured mental model that also doubles as a product feature showcase.

  • Implicit feature marketing: The selection list doubles as a soft tour of Revolut's full product suite (metal card, crypto, stocks, lounge access), priming users for upsells later.

  • Non-blocking multi-select: No hard limit is visually implied, encouraging generous selection which yields richer personalization data.

screens.name: Craft - Scanning a document - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Rich text/document editors needing to insert varied content types (notes apps, CMS editors, wikis).
  • Any "+" or slash-command menu where the option set exceeds ~6-8 items and benefits from categorization.
  • Tools serving both novice (visual browsers) and expert (keyboard/search-driven) users simultaneously.
  • Mobile contexts where a full-screen modal would be too disruptive to ongoing work.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense grid approach when there are only 2-3 insertion options (a simple inline toolbar or small popover would be lighter-weight).
  • Not ideal for first-time users without any onboarding/tooltips, since the sheer number of icon tiles can be intimidating without prior exposure to what each represents.
  • Should not be used if block types require significant configuration before insertion (better served by a wizard/dialog rather than instant-insert tile).
  • Avoid on very small screens where a 4-column grid forces icons/labels to be cramped or truncated.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets power users, writers, and knowledge workers (PMs, researchers, designers (evidenced by the Web3 UX research content visible in the background) who need to embed diverse content types (tables, code, formulas, whiteboards, scanned documents) directly into a single flowing document). The psychological driver is reduced friction for creative flow: by surfacing all block types in one tap-accessible, well-organized sheet, Craft minimizes the "what tool do I need" decision paralysis and keeps the user inside their writing momentum rather than forcing an app-switch (e.g., to Excel for a table, or a separate scanner app).

The inclusion of advanced blocks like Formula, Code Block, and Whiteboard signals this app is optimized for technical/creative professionals rather than casual note-takers, aligning with Craft's "every note is a designed document" positioning.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed but visible background document: preserves spatial context and writing flow instead of fully obscuring the canvas.
  • Icon-first, label-second tile design: visually previews each block type's output, leveraging recognition over recall.
  • Categorized grouping (Rich Blocks / Files): chunks a long list of insertion options into digestible, scannable sections.
  • Embedded search bar: gives power users an instant typeahead shortcut without scrolling through the grid.
  • Native bottom-sheet affordance (drag handle, rounded top corners) - matches iOS system conventions for muscle-memory dismissal.

screens.name: Craft - Scanning a document - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any in-app document, receipt, whiteboard, or business-card scanning flow embedded within a productivity or note-taking app.
  • Moments where you want to borrow the user's existing mental model from native camera apps to minimize onboarding.
  • Utility capture flows that should feel like a brief detour, not a branded destination (keep chrome minimal and get the user back to their primary task (the document/note) fast).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this stripped-down approach if the scanning feature requires teaching new, non-standard controls (e.g., custom multi-page batch scanning) - additional coach marks or labels would be needed.
  • Not suitable if edge-detection/auto-crop feedback is critical to the task; this screen as shown lacks any visible document-boundary overlay, which could cause failed captures without on-screen guidance.
  • Don't reuse this minimal pattern for flows requiring multiple simultaneous settings (exposure, white balance, grid lines) where more sophisticated camera controls are necessary.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Craft users who need to digitize physical source material (handwritten notes, whiteboard sketches, printed documents, book pages) directly into a note without switching to a separate scanning app. This is a power-user/knowledge-worker behavior: students, researchers, and professionals who treat Craft as a thinking tool and want frictionless capture of real-world artifacts.

Psychologically, the design leverages familiarity bias (reusing native camera UI patterns so users feel zero hesitation) and reduction of extraneous cognitive load (one instruction, one giant button) so the user's attention stays entirely on physically aligning the document rather than learning new UI.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single, unmistakable primary action: The oversized circular shutter button dominates the lower third of the screen, impossible to miss or mis-tap.
  • Minimal cognitive load: Only one line of instruction and three secondary icons keep the user focused purely on framing the document.
  • Familiar camera-app grammar: Placement of close (X), flash, filters, and shutter mirrors iOS/Android native camera and scanner apps, reducing onboarding friction to zero.
  • High-contrast black canvas: Full black background maximizes contrast against any document (usually white paper), implicitly aiding auto-edge-detection and keeping visual noise away from the live feed.
  • Escape hatch always visible: The X button is persistently available top-left, respecting user control and easy exit from the modal flow.

screens.name: Craft - Scanning a document - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Reuse this pattern whenever an app needs a lightweight, embedded capture experience that feeds directly into content creation (notes, chat attachments, document covers, inline images). It's ideal when:

  • Users need to capture and immediately use an image without context-switching to a separate camera app.
  • The brand wants full-bleed immersive focus with minimal chrome.
  • Only a small set of camera options (flash, filter, mode) are needed (not pro-level manual controls).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal pattern when users require advanced photography controls (manual exposure, ISO, grid lines, multiple lens switching) - power users will find the lack of options frustrating. It's also unsuitable for apps where camera capture is a core, frequently-used primary feature (e.g., a dedicated camera or social app), where a richer, more discoverable control set and live filter previews would better serve engagement. Additionally, for accessibility-first contexts, the icon-only bottom cluster should be paired with sufficient contrast and larger touch targets if testing reveals mis-taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves writers and note-takers who want to quickly capture a photo (a receipt, a whiteboard sketch, a scenic cover image, a reference photo) and insert it directly into a Craft document. Because Craft positions itself as a thoughtfully designed, offline-first writing tool where "every note is a designed document," embedding a dedicated capture flow (rather than routing through the OS photo picker) keeps the creative act of writing and the act of visually enriching a document inside one seamless, branded loop.

Psychologically, the stark black interface and oversized shutter button exploit familiarity with native camera apps (iOS/Android), reducing the learning curve to zero. The minimal control set also respects the user's current task-focus state (they came here to grab a quick image, not to explore a feature-rich camera app, so anything beyond flash/filter/shutter would be noise).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-bleed, chrome-less viewfinder: Removing all unnecessary UI maximizes the preview area and keeps visual focus on composing the shot.
  • Single large capture button: The oversized white shutter circle is unmistakable, highly tappable, and uses strong figure-ground contrast against the black background.
  • Grouped secondary controls: Flash, Filters, and Shutter mode are visually grouped as equal-weight circular icons with labels, reducing cognitive load versus a cluttered icon-only toolbar.
  • Inline status confirmation: "Auto Shutter Off" gives immediate textual feedback on toggle state without a modal or settings detour.
  • Dismiss affordance in a predictable corner: The top-left "X" matches platform conventions for exiting modal/full-screen flows, minimizing relearning cost.

screens.name: Craft - Scanning a document - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Reuse this pattern whenever an app needs the user to confirm or correct the geometry of a captured image before committing it (document scanners, receipt/invoice capture, ID/passport photo capture, whiteboard photography, or any OCR-adjacent feature). It's ideal when:

  • Automatic edge/corner detection may be imperfect and benefits from manual override.
  • The source image needs perspective correction before further processing (OCR, PDF export, embedding).
  • You want a lightweight, two-choice decision point (retry vs. accept) rather than a complex multi-step editor.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple photo attachments where cropping precision isn't functionally important (e.g., casual inline images, social posts) (it adds friction without benefit. It's also unsuitable when the source image aspect ratio must remain fixed (e.g., profile avatars), or when users are likely to be scanning multiple pages rapidly in batch mode, where a manual corner-adjustment step per page would be too slow; in that case, auto-crop with an optional "edit later" affordance is preferable. Additionally, avoid stark black loading/processing backgrounds without any progress or contextual labeling if the correction step can take a non-trivial amount of time) users may wonder if the app has frozen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves knowledge workers, students, and creatives who use Craft to digitize physical materials (meeting notes, book pages, whiteboard sketches, receipts, or handwritten ideas) directly into a structured, designed document. The target user values precision and polish (consistent with Craft's "editorial" positioning), so an auto-detected but user-adjustable crop appeals to their desire for control rather than blind trust in automatic processing.

Psychologically, the design leverages direct manipulation (dragging corners feels tactile and satisfying, similar to tangram puzzle-solving) and low-commitment framing (easy Retake escape hatch removes anxiety about "messing up" the shot). The uncluttered black canvas and soft rounded UI also reflect Craft's broader brand promise of calm, considered design even in a utilitarian task like scanning a document.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-bleed image canvas: The photo fills essentially the entire screen with no distracting labels or metadata, keeping focus entirely on the content being captured.
  • Isolated control bar: Retake/Keep buttons are placed in a neutral band physically separated from the image, preventing accidental interaction with the crop handles and avoiding visual clutter over the photo.
  • Draggable corner-handle crop overlay: Circular handles at all four detected corners with connecting guide-lines give precise, direct-manipulation control over perspective correction (a tactile, confidence-inspiring interaction model).
  • Pill-shaped buttons with soft contrast: Rounded, light buttons against a muted gray background create a calm, low-pressure decision point rather than an urgent modal interruption.
  • Binary, reversible decision: Only two choices are offered (Retake or Keep), removing decision paralysis and making the capture flow feel fast and frictionless.

screens.name: Craft - Scanning a document - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an app needs to let users capture visual content for immediate insertion into a larger artifact (notes, chat messages, listings, forms) and speed/familiarity matters more than brand differentiation. It's ideal for secondary, task-interrupting flows (image attachment, cover photo selection, document scanning) where the goal is to minimize time spent on the camera screen itself.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid heavily customizing or re-skinning core camera controls if the result confuses users accustomed to native conventions (novelty here adds risk, not delight). This pattern is also unsuitable for apps where photography is the core value proposition (e.g., a dedicated photo-editing or social camera app), since those products benefit from richer, differentiated camera UI (manual controls, live filters, AR effects) rather than a stripped-down utilitarian overlay.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves writers, researchers, and note-takers who need to quickly capture a whiteboard, book page, receipt, or inspiration photo to embed into a Craft document without breaking their writing flow. The psychological driver is frictionless capture: any delay or unfamiliar control at the moment of inspiration risks losing the thought entirely. By borrowing the exact mental model of the native camera app, Craft minimizes cognitive load and taps into users' existing procedural memory, making this feel like a trusted, zero-learning-curve extension of the OS rather than a third-party feature.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native camera metaphor reuse: Mirrors OS-level camera conventions (shutter, flash, thumbnail) so users need zero onboarding to use it.
  • Single accent-color anchor: The lone blue checkmark against all-black/white chrome draws the eye directly to the confirm action, embodying Craft's "custom accents" visual identity even inside a utility screen.
  • Thumb-zone optimized bottom bar: Primary actions (capture, confirm, dismiss) are all placed within easy one-handed reach, critical for a mobile capture-on-the-go moment.
  • Persistent last-shot thumbnail: Lets users quickly review/re-access the most recent capture without leaving the camera, supporting rapid multi-shot workflows (e.g., attaching several reference photos to a note).

screens.name: Craft - Scanning a document - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this floating-chrome, editorial-document pattern for:

  • Content-first apps (notes, docs, journaling, long-form reading) where the writing/reading experience should dominate over UI chrome.
  • Apps where users create artifacts meant to be re-read, shared, or presented (reports, briefs, specs) rather than quick disposable captures.
  • Any screen embedding mixed media (files, images, PDFs) where rich preview cards can replace generic file-link rows to improve scannability.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for:

  • High-frequency, utilitarian capture tools (e.g., quick checklists, voice memos) where speed of input matters more than visual polish and floating chrome could feel like unnecessary friction.
  • Data-dense or tabular content (spreadsheets, dashboards) where generous whitespace and large typography would waste screen real estate and hurt information density.
  • Contexts requiring persistent, always-visible navigation (e.g., multi-step forms, critical safety actions) since floating/translucent controls can be less discoverable or accidentally obscured over busy backgrounds.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves knowledge workers, designers, and creative professionals who use Craft to draft project briefs, concept documents, and research notes they intend to revisit, share, or present (not just capture fleeting thoughts). The editorial typography and document-like treatment of attachments cater to users who value aesthetics and want their internal docs to feel as polished as a finished deliverable.

Psychologically, the minimal floating chrome exploits the principle of focused attention: by receding navigational elements into translucent pills, the brain registers the content as the primary object, increasing perceived quality and reducing the "utility app" feeling common in bare-bones note apps. The rich PDF preview card also leverages recognition over recall, letting users instantly identify attached files visually rather than parsing filenames alone.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Floating pill-shaped navigation chrome instead of a solid top app bar, keeping focus on the writing canvas and reinforcing a borderless, editorial reading experience.
  • Editorial-grade typography: large bold headline, generous paragraph spacing, and hairline divider under the title (makes a simple note feel like a designed document or article).
  • Rich inline file-attachment card with live thumbnail, name, and metadata, elevating a PDF attachment into a visually integrated part of the document rather than a generic file icon link.
  • Dual-cluster floating bottom toolbar that separates content-insertion tools from formatting/history tools, reducing visual noise and clarifying intent-based grouping.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this layered bottom-sheet + action-sheet pattern when:

  • You need to let users drill into contextual details (like a specific card or account) without a full page transition, preserving spatial context.

  • The underlying task has multiple related but distinct sub-actions (e.g., reimbursement vs. mileage vs. drafts) that don't warrant separate screens.

  • You want to display compliance/status metadata compactly via iconography for power users scanning many rows quickly (expense reports, approvals, order history).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid stacking multiple modal sheets when:

  • The user needs to compare data across the obscured background screen and the sheet simultaneously, stacking reduces visible context the deeper it goes.

  • Actions require significant input (e.g., long forms); deeply nested sheets make it harder to back out gracefully and can disorient users on smaller screens.

  • Status icons are undocumented or inconsistent: icon-only communication risks confusing new users who haven't learned the meaning of each glyph; a tooltip or legend would be needed for first-time use.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets employees of a company using Brex for corporate card and expense management: likely non-finance staff who need a fast, low-friction way to check their remaining budget and submit reimbursement claims for out-of-pocket purchases (e.g., transit, coffee, travel). The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Loss aversion / budget anxiety:

  • Trust through transparency: Visible approval/reimbursement status icons reduce anxiety about whether a submitted expense is "stuck" or complete.

  • Reduced friction for compliance tasks: Separating "Request reimbursement" from "Request mileage" acknowledges that expense submission isn't one-size-fits-all, letting users self-select the correct flow quickly.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive disclosure via stacked sheets: Dashboard → Card detail sheet → Action sheet, each layer revealing only what's relevant to the current task without full-page navigation.

  • Status iconography row: Small compliance icons (upload, approval, reimbursement checkmarks) on each expense line let finance/ops users audit a list at a glance.

  • Persistent context card: Keeping the Brex card partially visible behind the sheet reinforces "which account am I looking at" without extra chrome.

  • Draft count transparency: Showing "(0)" next to View drafts manages expectations and subtly nudges completion behavior.

  • Grabber handles on both sheets: Reinforces the gesture-driven, dismissible nature of the modals, keeping the primary dashboard just one swipe away.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-screen camera capture pattern when the primary task requires scanning a physical object (payment cards, ID documents, QR/barcodes, receipts). Always pair it with:

  • A manual/alternate entry fallback for accessibility and failure recovery.

  • A clear, singular dismiss action.

  • Native-feeling capture controls (shutter, flash, gallery) to minimize cognitive load.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the data being captured can be reliably and faster entered via text input (e.g., short alphanumeric codes), as forcing a camera flow adds unnecessary friction. It's also unsuitable in low-connectivity or low-light contexts without robust fallback messaging, and should not be used without clearly communicating why camera access is needed (privacy/permission concerns) - a missing permission-priming step here could increase drop-off if this is the user's first camera-related ask.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets mainstream mobile users performing a transactional task (e.g., adding a payment card, scanning a QR/barcode coupon, or registering a loyalty card) who expect speed and minimal friction. It leverages the psychological principle of familiarity bias: by mimicking the stock iOS Camera app's control layout, the designer taps into years of existing muscle memory, meaning zero learning curve and higher completion rates. The manual fallback also addresses loss-aversion/frustration avoidance: users who fear wasting time on a failed scan are reassured there's always a guaranteed alternative path forward.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Manual entry fallback: Placing "Enter manually" prominently prevents a hard dead-end for users whose camera fails to recognize the object, respecting accessibility and real-world lighting/condition variance.

  • Familiar native camera affordances: Reusing the iOS system camera's shutter/flash/gallery layout dramatically lowers the learning curve (users don't need onboarding for how to operate the scanner).

  • Single, unambiguous exit: The circular X button is isolated top-right, matching platform conventions for modal dismissal, so users always know how to back out.

  • Distraction-free full-bleed canvas: No navigation chrome competes with the live camera feed, keeping 100% of visual attention on correctly framing the scan target.

  • Photo library shortcut: The "Select" option lets users scan from an already-captured photo instead of requiring a live camera pass, useful when the object isn't physically present.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for document/ID/card capture flows, KYC onboarding, receipt or check scanning, and any flow requiring an image of a physical object where camera access may fail or be inconvenient. Always pair the primary camera capture action with secondary import options (library, file) and a manual fallback to keep conversion high.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this multi-option action sheet for simple, low-stakes avatar or profile photo uploads where a single "choose photo" option is sufficient (too many choices can add friction). Also avoid if manual entry would violate compliance requirements (e.g., when optical capture is mandatory for fraud prevention), or if offering file upload introduces unnecessary security/format-validation complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users completing identity verification, document upload, or payment-card linking flows (e.g., KYC, check deposit, expense receipt capture) where camera access is the primary path but not all users have the physical document on hand or a working camera at that moment. Offering photo library, file choice, and manual entry reduces drop-off by accommodating edge cases (scanned PDFs already on device, accessibility limits, poor lighting) and leverages the psychological principle of perceived control: giving users choice reduces anxiety and abandonment in sensitive flows like identity verification.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multiple capture fallbacks: Camera, photo library, file picker, and manual entry are all offered from a single surface, respecting different user contexts (e.g., document already saved vs. needing to snap a new photo).

  • Non-blocking modal overlay: The action sheet appears without fully replacing the camera screen, preserving spatial context and reducing perceived navigation depth.

  • High-contrast, distraction-free capture UI: Pure black background and minimal chrome keep focus on the real-world subject being captured.

  • Escape hatch always visible: The persistent close (X) button ensures users never feel trapped in the camera flow.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 5
screens.whereToUse: Use the native OS photo/file picker (with its built-in limited-access messaging) whenever an app needs occasional, user-initiated access to personal media (such as attaching receipts, profile photos, documents, or support-ticket screenshots). It's ideal for expense management, customer support, document scanning, and social apps where trust and minimal permission footprint matter more than deep custom gallery curation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid relying solely on the native picker if your product requires rich, branded media-browsing experiences (e.g., a photo-editing app, a social network's camera roll integration with custom filters/previews) where a custom UI with deeper curation, tagging, or AI-based suggestions adds real value. Also, if the app needs frequent, repeated media access (e.g., continuous background photo sync), prompting for full library access with a clear value explanation may be more appropriate than repeatedly surfacing the limited-access picker, which can create friction if users must reselect photos each time.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
The target user here is a Brex business cardholder or employee submitting an expense report who needs to attach a photo of a physical receipt. This persona is typically on the go, often in a hurry (e.g., right after a client dinner or purchase), and may be privacy-conscious about granting full photo library access to a finance/corporate app.

Psychologically, this screen addresses the "privacy paradox" tension in B2B fintech apps: users want convenience (quickly finding a photo) but are wary of corporate software having blanket access to personal photos (family pictures, personal moments). The limited-access disclosure directly defuses this anxiety, increasing the likelihood a user completes the attach-receipt flow instead of abandoning it or granting access reluctantly.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Leverages OS trust instead of rebuilding it: By using the native picker, Brex inherits Apple's privacy guarantees and polished interaction patterns for free, rather than building a bespoke (and less trusted) media picker.

  • Transparent limited-access disclosure: The "Private Access to Photos" card is a best-in-class example of proactive, in-context privacy communication rather than a one-time blocking permission dialog.

  • Dismissible, non-blocking education: The explanation is informative but optional (closable via the X), respecting the user's time if they already understand the concept.

  • Low-friction task completion: Search, sort, and collections toggle allow power users to quickly locate the exact receipt photo needed, reducing time-to-task-completion for an inherently tedious expense-reporting workflow.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 6
