screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when designing camera-capture flows embedded within a larger workflow (not a standalone camera app), especially when the captured artifact needs to be associated with an existing record (e.g., receipts, documents, ID verification). It's especially valuable when there's a possible mismatch between user intent and system state (proactively surfacing that mismatch before the user invests effort (e).g., taking a photo) saves frustration. The dual-path bottom CTA ("scan" vs. "manual entry/alternative") pattern is ideal whenever the primary capture method may not always be the right fit for every user's situation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid overlaying warning banners on a camera viewfinder when the warning is purely informational and not actionable (this adds visual clutter and can obscure the subject being photographed). If the warning condition is rare or edge-case only, consider handling it via a toast or pre-emptive screen before entering the camera, rather than cluttering the capture UI itself. Additionally, this pattern should not be used when receipt/document capture is the primary, context-free action of the app (e.g., a dedicated scanner app), since the "no expenses to attach" framing assumes a specific linked-record workflow that may not apply universally.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets business travelers, employees, and finance/ops teams who need to digitize paper receipts for expense reporting and reimbursement, likely within a corporate expense management or spend platform (e.g., similar to Ramp, Brex, or Expensify). The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion and effort-justification prevention: by warning the user before they waste time scanning a receipt that has nowhere to go, the app respects the user's time and avoids a frustrating "scan completed, but now what?" dead-end experience. The inline "Add to existing" and "create reimbursement" options also reduce decision paralysis by making the next best action obvious and low-friction, appealing to time-pressed professional users who value speed and certainty over exploration.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual Just-in-Time Guidance: Rather than letting the user scan a receipt into a dead end, the app proactively surfaces a system-state warning banner the moment it detects there's nothing to attach the receipt to, with an inline fix via "Add to existing."

Branching Escape Hatch: The "Or create reimbursement" button acknowledges that not all expense-logging starts with a physical receipt, offering a graceful fallback path without forcing the user to exit the flow and start over elsewhere.

High-Contrast Overlay Controls: White solid-fill circular buttons (close, retake) against the dark camera viewfinder ensure maximum legibility and touch-target confidence regardless of the background scene being photographed.

Minimal Chrome, Maximum Viewfinder: By stripping away navigation bars and status elements, the design maximizes the available frame for accurately capturing the receipt image, which directly impacts OCR/data-extraction accuracy downstream.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Expense management, corporate card, and reimbursement workflows where receipt capture is the core input.

  • Any financial form where cross-currency clarity is needed for distributed or international teams.

  • Tasks that are frequently interrupted mid-completion, warranting a visible draft-save option.

  • Scenarios where showing a real-time balance/limit constraint upfront can prevent invalid submissions downstream.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, single-focus modal pattern for simple, single-field forms (it adds unnecessary ceremony).

  • Don't surface a 'Save draft' button if the backend doesn't reliably support autosave/draft retrieval, as it creates false expectations.

  • Avoid displaying currency conversions using potentially stale/cached rates without a timestamp or disclaimer, as this could erode trust if the actual rate differs at processing time.

  • Not ideal for high-volume bulk expense submission flows, where a tabular/multi-row entry pattern would be more efficient than one modal per expense.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees at a company using a corporate card/spend management platform who need to request reimbursement for out-of-pocket business expenses. The psychological drivers at play include loss aversion (draft-saving prevents the frustration of re-entering data) and reduction of financial ambiguity (currency conversion and visible spend limits prevent surprises or distrust). The design also reduces the friction/dread typically associated with expense reporting (a notoriously tedious task) by minimizing the number of visible fields and emphasizing a single primary action (photo capture) before submission.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-currency display: Automatically converting the available balance into the user's local currency removes a mental math step and builds trust in global teams.

  • Draft-saving affordance: Positioning 'Save draft' as equal-sized but visually secondary to 'Submit' respects that reimbursement requests are often filled out in multiple sittings (e.g., waiting on a receipt).

  • Large receipt/photo upload area: Dedicating the majority of above-the-fold space to the attachment reinforces that proof-of-purchase is the most critical and often most friction-inducing step.

  • Contextual spend limit surfaced inline: Showing the 'Assigned spend limit' directly in the form (rather than requiring the user to navigate elsewhere) prevents the user from submitting requests that are likely to be rejected.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, expense, or transactional forms where some data can be reliably pre-filled from an external source (receipts, calendar, transaction history, OCR). It's ideal for reducing friction in repetitive administrative tasks like expense reports, invoices, or tax forms. The draft-save + submit pattern is well suited to any multi-field form that users might need to pause and resume, especially on mobile where interruptions are common.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid heavy automation indicators (lightning bolts) if the underlying prefill confidence is low, mislabeling guesses as 'smart' erodes trust if users frequently need to correct them. This pattern is also unsuitable for simple, single-field transactional screens where a lightweight single-field flow would be faster, or for consumer apps where financial jargon like 'Merchant category' might feel overly corporate and reduce approachability.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees of a company using a corporate expense management platform (e.g., finance teams, remote/traveling staff) who need to file reimbursement claims for out-of-pocket business expenses, such as travel bookings. The psychological drivers at play include reduction of perceived effortcontrol and trust (users verify rather than blindly accept automation, which is essential when real money and accounting accuracy are involved).
screens.keyHighlights:
• AI/Automation Indicators: Green lightning bolt icons clearly flag which fields were auto-populated by the system, building trust through transparency while still allowing manual override via clear ('x') icons.

  • Inline Currency Conversion: Automatically displays the converted balance in a secondary currency, removing cognitive load for cross-border expense reporting.

  • Progressive Disclosure Toggle: The 'different currency' switch keeps the form uncluttered by default and only expands complexity when relevant.

  • Dual CTA Footer: Separates low-commitment ('Save draft') from high-commitment ('Submit') actions, reducing abandonment risk for incomplete expense reports.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Document, receipt, or ID scanning flows within finance, expense, tax, or productivity apps.

  • Any feature requiring quick, repeatable image capture where speed and minimal friction outweigh the need for contextual instructions.

  • Flows where users may already have a relevant photo saved, justifying a "Select from library" fallback alongside live capture.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this stripped-down approach for first-time users or complex scanning tasks (e.g., multi-page documents, precise alignment needs) without adding guidance overlays, bounding boxes, or edge-detection cues.

  • Not suitable when accuracy requires auto-cropping or real-time edge detection feedback (without visual guides, users may submit poorly framed or angled receipts leading to OCR errors).

  • Avoid if the app targets a less tech-savvy audience unfamiliar with standard camera iconography; in that case, add brief contextual tooltips or sample framing illustrations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of finance, expense-management, budgeting, or accounting apps (e.g., employees submitting reimbursements, freelancers tracking deductible purchases, or personal finance app users logging spending). These users are typically task-driven and want to complete receipt capture as fast as possible, often while standing at a checkout counter or shortly after a purchase.

Psychologically, the design leverages familiarity and reduced cognitive load: by mimicking the native camera UI almost exactly, it reduces hesitation and decision fatigue. The prominent, oversized shutter button exploits Fitts's Law for fast, error-free tapping, while the flash toggle addresses a common pain point (dim receipts/lighting in stores) proactively, building user trust that the app anticipates real-world scanning conditions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-screen immersive camera view that maximizes the scanning area and visually reinforces focus on the task at hand.

  • Dual capture pathways (live shutter + "Select" from gallery) accommodate both in-the-moment captures and previously taken photos, reducing friction for users who already snapped a receipt.

  • Familiar native camera control placement (flash toggle top-center-bottom, shutter bottom-center, gallery bottom-left) leverages existing muscle memory from iOS Camera and social apps, eliminating the need for onboarding.

  • Unobtrusive exit affordance (circular X) lets users back out instantly without hunting for a back gesture, important in a modal full-screen context.

  • Minimal, high-contrast labeling ("Scan receipt", "OFF", "Select") keeps the interface legible against variable real-world backgrounds seen through the camera feed.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this real-time inline validation pattern whenever a user performs a capture/input action that might be unnecessary or mismatched with system state (e.g., no matching record, duplicate submission risk). It is ideal for mobile camera-based capture flows where an immediate contextual banner can guide correction without forcing a full-screen interruption.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this lightweight banner approach for critical, irreversible errors (e.g., duplicate payment risk) where a modal confirmation with explicit acknowledgment is safer. Also avoid when the resolution path is ambiguous (a single "Add to existing" link assumes the user understands the expense-matching concept; novice users may need more explanation or an inline help affordance).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets traveling employees and expense submitters who scan receipts in real time (e.g., right after a meal or taxi ride) rather than batching paperwork later. The psychological trigger here is reducing friction and anxiety around expense compliance (by immediately flagging that the scanned receipt may not be needed, Brex prevents the user from feeling their scanning effort was wasted and offers an immediate alternative action, reinforcing trust that the app is "watching out" for them in real time).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline contextual error recovery: Instead of a blocking dialog, the warning is embedded as a dismissible banner that still allows the user to retake or exit, keeping control with the user.

  • Actionable recovery link: "Add to existing" directly resolves the problem by offering to attach the receipt to a prior transaction, turning a dead-end state into a productive path.

  • Minimal camera chrome: Stripped-back UI (just title, close, retake) keeps focus on the capture task and reduces cognitive load during a quick, on-the-go expense task.

  • Non-destructive framing: The warning triangle icon signals caution without being a hard error/red stop sign, matching the low-severity nature of the issue.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this modal bottom-sheet selection pattern when a user must link, attach, or match one record (like a receipt) to an existing item (like an expense) in a finance, accounting, or document-management workflow.

  • Appropriate for short-to-medium lists where date grouping aids recall more than alphabetical or categorical sorting.

  • Ideal when the action is secondary/supporting (e.g., attaching evidence) rather than primary navigation, since the full-screen sheet with dual-cancel affordances clearly signals "temporary task" rather than "new section of the app."
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for very large datasets without a search bar, relying solely on date-grouped scrolling will frustrate users hunting for an older or infrequent transaction.

  • Not suitable if multiple items need to be selected simultaneously (this layout implies single-select; bulk actions would need checkboxes and a different action footer).

  • Don't use when the list is frequently empty: without a dedicated empty-state illustration/message, a near-empty single-result list (as shown here) can feel broken or raise doubts about whether the app is loading correctly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets business professionals, freelancers, and finance teams using expense-management or corporate card platforms (e.g., Ramp, Brex, Expensify-style apps) who need to quickly reconcile a scanned receipt or uploaded document against an existing expense entry. The psychological driver is reduction of cognitive load during a repetitive administrative task: by presenting a filtered, chronologically sorted list instead of a search field, the design assumes the user remembers roughly when the expense occurred, leveraging recency and temporal memory rather than forcing exact-match recall.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Redundant dismissal controls: Both a top-right "X" and a bottom "Cancel" button let users exit from wherever their thumb naturally rests, reducing friction and frustration.

  • Date-grouped list: Chronological sectioning with sticky-style date headers helps users orient themselves when scrolling through transaction history.

  • Attachment status iconography: The small receipt/upload glyph next to the amount communicates receipt-linking status at a glance without extra text.

  • Filter chip pre-applied: "All expenses" as a chip (rather than a dropdown) implies this is one of potentially several quick filters (e.g., "Unmatched," "This month"), supporting fast narrowing without leaving the sheet.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any expense-tracking, receipt-scanning, or point-of-sale verification flow where speed is critical. It is ideal for financial apps, expense reports, or social payment apps where bridging a physical receipt to a digital ledger entry needs to feel instantaneous and effortless.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if your OCR/scanning technology has a high failure rate, as users will become annoyed if they have to rely on the "manual" fallback every time, making the scanning UI feel like unnecessary friction. Do not use this layout if the memo/notes field is optional or rarely used, as forcing the keyboard open immediately would be an intrusive UX decision that obscures the camera viewfinder unnecessarily.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users engaging in expense tracking, bill splitting, or budget logging (e.g., friends splitting a dinner bill or a user logging a reimbursable expense). The psychological trigger here is "reduction of friction in categorization." Users are notoriously lazy about manually typing receipt details; by using the camera to auto-detect the amount and merchant, the app leverages technology to save cognitive load, increasing the likelihood that the user will actually log the expense rather than abandoning the task.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Graceful Degradation: The "Select manually" link provides an immediate fallback for failed object/text recognition, preventing user frustration with the camera scanner.

  • Floating Context Card: Overlaying the detected data on top of the live camera view keeps the user oriented in the physical world (pointing the camera) while interacting with digital data simultaneously.

  • Proactive Keyboard Invocation: By triggering the keyboard immediately upon entering this view, the app reduces the friction of a subsequent tap, speeding up the "scan-then-annotate" workflow.

  • Minimalist Exit: The clear "X" button in a high-contrast white circle ensures users can always easily abort the camera/scanning flow.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this hybrid scan+manual-correct pattern whenever an app relies on computer vision or OCR to extract structured data (receipts, business cards, ID documents, barcodes) and accuracy cannot be 100% guaranteed. It's especially valuable in financial, logistics, or data-entry-heavy apps where errors have real consequences and user trust must be earned through visible fallback options.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, single-field scans (e.g., scanning a QR code) where a manual fallback adds unnecessary complexity. It's also inappropriate in flows where speed is paramount and interrupting the scan with editable text fields would break an otherwise seamless automated experience. If OCR accuracy is consistently very high, exposing a manual correction UI by default (rather than only on low-confidence detections) may undermine user confidence in the automation itself.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of expense-tracking, cashback/rewards, or receipt-scanning apps (e.g., fintech, loyalty, or budgeting apps) who need to digitize paper receipts quickly on the go. The primary psychological driver is reduction of friction and cognitive load: rather than forcing users to manually type out a merchant name, date, and amount, the camera does the heavy lifting, and the UI only asks for human intervention when the system isn't confident.

The immediate availability of a keyboard alongside a visual scan reduces anxiety for users who don't trust OCR accuracy (a common hesitation with scan-based features), reinforcing trust through transparency and control.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live camera + floating result card: Keeps the viewfinder fully unobstructed while surfacing parsed data in a compact, non-intrusive card, letting users visually verify the scan is aligned with the real receipt beneath it.

  • Graceful degradation to manual entry: The "Select manually" link and immediate keyboard access ensure that OCR failure or ambiguity never results in a dead end (a critical resilience pattern for computer-vision-powered features).

  • Skeleton-style placeholder bars: Gray redaction bars communicate "we detected something here, still processing/confirming" without committing to potentially wrong data, reducing perceived error rate.

  • Single, obvious exit: The circular X button offers unambiguous, thumb-friendly dismissal from this full-screen camera takeover.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any OCR- or AI-driven capture flow (receipts, business cards, checks, ID documents) where you need users to validate automatically extracted data before submission. It's ideal when speed and accuracy both matter, and when there's a reasonable chance the automated extraction could be imperfect, requiring a fallback.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if OCR/extraction accuracy is very low, as surfacing unreliable data overlaid on a live camera feed can erode user trust quickly. It's also unsuitable for complex multi-field data entry where a single card overlay would be too cramped (in those cases, a dedicated review screen with full-width fields and clear field-by-field editing is more appropriate). Additionally, avoid combining capture and annotation (memo field) on one screen if the data entry task is lengthy, as it could overwhelm the camera-first context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users of a fintech/payments app (likely a bill-splitting or expense app given the receipt-scanning and memo context) who want to quickly digitize a paper receipt rather than manually typing amounts and merchant names. The psychological trigger here is effort reduction and automation trust: by instantly surfacing extracted data, the app reduces the perceived effort and anxiety of trusting an automated process, while the manual fallback reduces the fear of being "stuck" if OCR misreads the receipt. The Retake/Keep binary choice also reduces decision fatigue by offering just two clear paths forward.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live OCR overlay: Parsed merchant and amount data appears instantly on the card, giving the user real-time confidence that the scan worked correctly before they commit.

  • Familiar Retake/Keep pattern: Mirrors iOS's native photo confirmation UI, minimizing cognitive load since users already know this interaction from their camera roll.

  • Manual override escape hatch: "Select manually" link gracefully handles OCR failure cases, preventing dead-ends and preserving user trust.

  • Inline memo field: Lets users annotate the transaction in the same flow, avoiding a disruptive multi-screen process.

  • Minimal chrome: Only a close (X) button and title appear up top, keeping full focus on the capture task.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this full-screen camera capture pattern whenever the core user goal is document, barcode, QR, or receipt digitization: expense trackers, banking/reimbursement apps, inventory scanners, or tax-filing tools. It's ideal when users may need to capture multiple items in one session (multi-page documents, batches of receipts) and when minimizing steps-to-completion is a priority metric.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stripped-down pattern when users need real-time guidance, such as auto-crop framing guides, edge-detection overlays, or lighting-quality warnings (without these aids, poorly lit or skewed receipts may fail OCR processing, frustrating users after the fact). Also avoid it for first-time users without any onboarding tooltip explaining the badge/counter behavior, as the "Done" vs. continuing-to-scan logic may not be self-evident to everyone. Not suitable for flows requiring metadata entry (e.g., category, amount) before capture, since this screen offers no fields for context capture.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of finance, expense-management, budgeting, or accounting apps (e.g., freelancers, employees submitting reimbursements, or budget-conscious consumers) who need to digitize paper receipts quickly and repeatedly. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Reduced friction/effort justification: A fast, familiar capture flow lowers the perceived "cost" of the tedious task of logging expenses, increasing the likelihood users will log every receipt rather than abandoning the habit.

  • Batching/commitment consistency: The badge counter leverages the Zeigarnik effect, showing an incomplete batch (1 item) nudges users to keep scanning until they feel the task is truly "done."

  • Familiarity bias: Reusing native camera UI patterns reduces cognitive load and builds instant trust, since the interface looks and behaves exactly like the trusted system camera.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Badge counter on Done button: The small orange "1" badge on the checkmark icon cleverly communicates that at least one receipt has already been captured and is queued, enabling multi-page/multi-receipt batch scanning without forcing the user back to a review screen after every shot.

  • Native camera parity: By replicating the iOS Camera app's bottom-bar layout (gallery/select, shutter, confirm), the designer eliminates the learning curve entirely (users transfer existing muscle memory instantly).

  • Single, unambiguous exit point: The circular "X" in the top-right is the only way out, reducing decision paralysis and accidental navigation.

  • Minimal top bar reinforces focus: No extra icons, settings, or tabs compete for attention (the entire screen funnels toward one action: capture).

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 19
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when onboarding a "primary" user (parent, admin, team owner) into a flow that will eventually grant delegated access to a secondary/dependent user (teen, employee, family member). It's ideal for:

  • Multi-step setup wizards where trust and control need to be established before permissions are granted.

  • Regulated financial or health products requiring both persuasive marketing copy and mandatory legal disclosures on the same screen.

  • Any flow introducing a feature that could be perceived as relinquishing control, where reassurance language ("optional," "if you want") can reduce drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy educational/legal pattern for simple, low-stakes toggles or non-regulated features (the dense disclosure text and full-screen real estate would feel disproportionate and slow down the flow unnecessarily). It's also not appropriate for expert/power-user flows where the audience already understands the feature and just needs a quick confirmation, or for screens where the user is the actual end-consumer (the teen) rather than the intermediary decision-maker, since the tone here is specifically calibrated for a supervisory parent.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
The primary audience is parents or legal guardians (not the teen) who are setting up a supervised financial account for a 13-17 year old. This demographic is motivated by a desire to teach financial responsibility while retaining oversight, but is also wary of privacy, security, and unwanted financial exposure for their child.

Psychologically, the screen leverages autonomy-supportive framing (the "if you want" qualifier) to reduce reactance (parents are more likely to proceed when they feel in control of the pace and scope of access granted). It also uses social/relatable imagery (handwritten ledger, casual home setting) to invoke trust and everyday practicality rather than a cold banking-app aesthetic.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Parenthetical reassurance in the headline ("if you want") directly addresses parental control anxiety and reduces perceived commitment before the user even reads the body text.

  • Authentic lifestyle photography instead of a sterile illustration (showing a real hand, a real phone, and a handwritten notebook) builds trust and relatability, subtly implying "budgeting/financial responsibility" without saying it outright.

  • Dual-tier information architecture: consumer-friendly value prop up top, legally required fine print below, clearly separated by a divider so neither dilutes the other.

  • Low-commitment secondary action ("Learn more") placed beneath the primary CTA gives cautious parents an offramp to gather more information without abandoning the flow entirely.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 20
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app must collect sensitive identity documents for regulatory compliance (banking, lending, crypto, insurance, gig-economy driver/worker verification). It's ideal when:

  • Multiple document types can satisfy a single requirement, and you want to communicate flexibility upfront.

  • Users need reassurance about photo quality before they attempt an upload, to reduce failed OCR/verification attempts.

  • The step is part of a longer onboarding flow and progress indication will reduce perceived effort.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, form-like presentation for low-stakes or optional profile completion tasks (it may feel disproportionately serious). Also avoid bundling too many document requirements onto a single screen; if more than 2-3 uploads are required, consider breaking them into separate steps within a wizard to prevent overwhelming the user. Additionally, don't use vague photo placeholders without accompanying example images/guidelines for users in regions where document formats vary widely, as this can increase upload errors.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users onboarding into a regulated financial product (neobank, payments app, crypto exchange, or lending platform) where identity verification is legally required under KYC/AML regulations. The audience spans a broad demographic, so the design leans on plain language rather than legal terminology to remain accessible to less financially sophisticated users.

Psychologically, the screen leverages trust-building through transparency: by explicitly stating why the data is needed and what will satisfy the requirement, it reduces the anxiety and suspicion often associated with being asked for government ID and SSN, which are frequent targets of fraud. The structured, itemized checklist format also taps into the completion/closure motivation, showing users a clear, finite set of tasks standing between them and account access.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empathetic reframing: Turns a mandatory regulatory checkpoint into a friendly, collaborative request, lowering perceived friction.

  • Document flexibility: Offering multiple acceptable document types (passport, license, ID / SSN card, W2, paystub) per requirement reduces abandonment from users lacking one specific document.

  • Visual affordance clarity: Camera icon placeholders inside bordered tiles unmistakably communicate "tap to capture/upload photo" without requiring additional labels.

  • Progressive disclosure: The "Requirement details" link keeps the primary screen lightweight while still offering deeper explanation for cautious or confused users.

  • Progress transparency: The bottom progress bar sets expectations that this is a finite, multi-step process, not an open-ended demand.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 21
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial or wallet-style apps where balance visibility, quick fund transfer, and payment method management are core jobs. Ideal for fintech apps that need to softly convert unverified users by pairing a benefit-driven CTA with an inline explanation rather than a blocking modal. The card-shaped empty state for adding a payment method is broadly reusable in any app requiring bank/card linkage.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy visual chrome (curved header, large avatar) in data-dense enterprise or B2B financial dashboards where information density and scanability matter more than brand personality. Also avoid soft-gating verification indefinitely if verification is legally required for core functionality (at some point a harder gate or more assertive prompt may be necessary to ensure compliance completion rates).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday Venmo users managing peer-to-peer balances, particularly those who have received money but haven't yet linked a bank or verified identity. The design leverages the endowed progress effect and loss aversion: showing "$0 in Venmo" alongside a verification prompt subtly implies money-in-waiting, motivating users to complete verification to "unlock" funds. The empty bank/card slot exploits the Zeigarnik effect (an incomplete visual pattern (a card that isn't there yet) creates a subconscious pull to complete the setup).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Curved header silhouette: The scalloped blue-to-white transition creates a soft, distinct anchor for the avatar, elevating profile identity above transactional content.

  • Segmented Control for context switching: Wallet/Transactions toggle keeps related financial views one tap apart without a full navigation change.

  • Verification framed as a feature unlock: Rather than a blocking wall, the KYC/verification nudge is presented as an inline benefit card, reducing perceived friction.

  • Empty-state CTA as a visual affordance: The 'Add a bank or card' tile mimics the shape of an actual card, making the empty state intuitively actionable.

  • Notification badge + settings gear: Clear iconography for alerts (5 unread) and account settings sits consistently in the header for quick access.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 22
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when presenting users with multiple payment/funding source options that carry different cost structures (fintech, marketplaces, subscription apps). It's ideal for any screen where fee transparency at the point of selection can reduce downstream confusion, support tickets, or cart abandonment.

Also effective when a platform wants to gently steer users toward a lower-cost-to-platform option without removing user choice, pairing subtle visual emphasis (background tint) with honest information rather than dark patterns.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern if fee structures are complex or conditional (e.g., tiered by amount, region, or promo), as a simple flat-list format may oversimplify and mislead. It's also unsuitable for very short flows where inserting a modal decision point could feel like unnecessary friction, or for premium/luxury products where highlighting fees front-and-center may clash with a frictionless, high-end brand narrative.

If the app wants to actively promote credit card usage (e.g., to earn interchange fees or drive rewards partnerships), this transparent fee-comparison layout would work against that business goal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets everyday consumers managing peer-to-peer payments and personal finance who are fee-sensitive and value transparency. Many Venmo users are younger (Gen Z/Millennial) and have been trained by fintech apps to expect no hidden fees; explicitly stating the 3% credit card surcharge preempts complaints and support tickets while subtly steering behavior toward bank linking, which reduces payment processing costs for Venmo/PayPal.

The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion framing: presenting the card fee prominently makes users consciously avoid it, while the "No fee" framing on Bank and Amex options creates a rewarding, cost-free feeling that reinforces continued app usage.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radical fee transparency: Every payment method explicitly states its cost (or lack thereof) directly in the selection list, eliminating surprise fees at the point of decision rather than at checkout.

  • Implicit default via visual weight: The "Bank" option is pre-highlighted with a subtle background tint, nudging users toward the free, lowest-friction (for Venmo) option without restricting choice.

  • Contextual layering: Using a bottom sheet over a dimmed but still-visible dashboard maintains orientation and reduces the feeling of a jarring context switch.

  • Branded partner integration: The Amex Send™ Account option demonstrates how a platform can surface co-branded/partner financial products as a first-class option alongside generic bank/card entries.

results.query: Avoiding banner blindness in transactional receipt screens

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any single-record detail view that mixes static facts with required follow-up actions, such as expense reports, invoice line items, order details, or claims processing. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to audit or verify a transaction/record after the fact.
  • Some fields are immutable (amount, merchant) while others need completion (tax, receipts, categorization).
  • Status at-a-glance matters more than exhaustive detail on first glance.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, sectioned detail pattern for high-frequency, low-complexity records where users just need a quick glance (e.g., a simple notification or balance check) - the multiple stacked sections and inline inputs would be overkill and slow. It's also unsuitable for consumer-facing, casual finance apps where terms like "assigned limit" and "tax rate" would be confusing jargon rather than clear context; in those cases, simplify to plain-language summaries instead of compliance-grade fields.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves employees and cardholders who need to reconcile a specific purchase, and secondarily finance admins auditing spend compliance. The psychological driver is reducing anxiety around accountability: employees spending company money want fast confirmation ("Approved") that they didn't do anything wrong, while incomplete items (tax info, unverified receipt) are flagged clearly so nothing slips through and creates friction later with finance/audit teams.

The inline "Switch limit" CTA targets users who may have accidentally charged the wrong budget/limit, giving them agency to self-correct rather than waiting on an admin, which reduces back-and-forth and support tickets.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded status pills (green Approved / orange Not verified) give instant visual triage of transaction health without reading text.
  • Inline actionable control ("Switch limit") embedded directly in a read-only detail view lets users correct a misapplied budget without navigating away.
  • Contextual compliance prompts ("This expense requires additional information") appear only when relevant, keeping the form lean for transactions that don't need tax handling.
  • Sectioned grey divider headers break a data-dense screen into clear, labeled zones (Amount/Merchant, Assigned limit, Tax rate, Receipts), reducing cognitive load.
  • Persistent back navigation and bottom Tab Bar keep the user oriented within the larger Wallet/Tasks ecosystem even while deep in a detail view.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any compliance-driven detail screen where a record (expense, application, claim, order) must pass through verification states before being finalized. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to supply supporting documents (receipts, IDs, proof of purchase).
  • There's a multi-stage review/approval workflow that benefits from a visible timeline.
  • Policy-specific messaging can reduce confusion (e.g., insurance claims, expense management, loan applications, KYC flows).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, warning-heavy layout for low-stakes or purely informational detail screens where no action is required (excessive banners and status indicators can create false urgency and alarm fatigue). It's also unsuitable for consumer-facing apps with casual, high-volume transactions (e.g., a coffee loyalty app), where this level of compliance friction would feel disproportionate and degrade the experience. Additionally, if policies vary widely or are too complex to summarize in one line, a static banner may oversimplify and mislead users about next steps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves employees who have made a small purchase on a corporate card and must now provide documentation to satisfy finance/compliance policies, as well as finance admins auditing the same record. The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion/compliance anxiety: by clearly flagging "Not verified" and explaining the consequence (manual review), the design nudges the employee to resolve the issue quickly to avoid being personally flagged or having the expense rejected.

The transparent status timeline also leverages the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to complete unfinished tasks) by visually showing an incomplete process, motivating the user to finish uploading valid receipts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive policy explanation: Instead of just flagging an error, the banner tells the user exactly *why* the receipt is problematic and references their specific company policy, reducing confusion and support escalations.
  • Inline character counter on Memo: The 50/800 counter gives real-time feedback, preventing surprise truncation and encouraging sufficiently detailed justifications for auditors.
  • Visual status timeline: Using a vertical checklist/stepper for "Status" turns an opaque back-office process (compliance review) into a transparent, trustworthy narrative the end-user can follow.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 4

This screen primarily serves employees whose expenses have been flagged and finance admins/auditors who need to verify compliance status. For the employee, seeing a transparent timeline of "flagged → reviewed" reduces the stress and ambiguity of having a purchase questioned, invoking the psychological principle of procedural justice: people are far more accepting of a process outcome when they can see the steps taken to reach it, even before knowing the final verdict.

For finance teams, the structured transaction details satisfy the need for completeness and defensibility: every field needed for bookkeeping, tax categorization, or dispute resolution is present in one place, reducing back-and-forth queries. The comment/@-mention system taps into workplace familiarity with tools like Slack, lowering the learning curve and encouraging asynchronous resolution instead of requiring a meeting or email thread.

  • Balanced action hierarchy: "Add comment" (collaborative, low-stakes) and "File a dispute" (escalation, higher-stakes) are styled identically to avoid alarming the user, yet are clearly separated as distinct next steps.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this layered bottom-sheet + chip-based error pattern when:

  • An automated verification/validation process (OCR, fraud check, data matching) fails and the user needs specific, itemized reasons rather than a blanket error.
  • The failure is recoverable or has a fallback path (manual review, memo, re-upload) and shouldn't fully block the user's workflow.
  • You want to preserve form context and avoid navigating the user away from their in-progress task.
  • Financial, compliance, or document-verification flows where transparency about *why* something failed builds user trust.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The error is critical and must hard-block the user (e.g., legal/compliance violation) - a bottom sheet may under-communicate severity; a full-screen interstitial or disabled submit button may be more appropriate.
  • There are more than 3-4 failure reasons, as the chip row could wrap awkwardly or overwhelm the limited bottom-sheet real estate (consider a scrollable list or accordion instead).
  • The underlying cause is highly technical; surfacing raw field names like "Merchant" without guidance on remediation could confuse less technical users if no next-step CTA is provided within the sheet itself.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets employees submitting expenses on the go, often from imperfect conditions (bad lighting, crumpled receipts, foreign currency receipts, or no receipt at all as implied by the memo). It also serves finance/admin teams indirectly by ensuring exceptions are flagged and routed to manual review rather than silently approved, protecting compliance integrity.

Psychologically, the design reduces anxiety around making a financial mistake by externalizing the error to a system limitation rather than user fault, while the granular breakdown (Date/Amount/Merchant) gives the user actionable next steps (e.g., re-upload or add memo justification) instead of leaving them stuck. The manual-review fallback also builds trust that legitimate business expenses won't be rejected outright due to OCR failure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Bottom Sheet over Dimmed Background: Preserves the user's place in the underlying form while delivering a focused, modal-style alert, avoiding a jarring full-screen takeover for a non-blocking issue.
  • Field-Level Error Chips: Breaking the verification failure into discrete, labeled chips (Date, Amount, Merchant) gives granular diagnostic feedback instead of a vague generic error message.
  • Non-Blocking Error Pattern: The flow explicitly allows the user to proceed via manual review and memo justification rather than hard-locking submission, respecting real-world edge cases (e.g., lost receipts).
  • Dual-Surface Status Communication: The "Not verified" status label on the Receipts section header and the warning banner work together with the modal to reinforce the same message across multiple visual layers.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
