The inline "Add to existing" and "create reimbursement" options also reduce decision paralysis by making the next best action obvious and low-friction, appealing to time-pressed professional users who value speed and certainty over exploration.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual Just-in-Time Guidance: Rather than letting the user scan a receipt into a dead end, the app proactively surfaces a system-state warning banner the moment it detects there's nothing to attach the receipt to, with an inline fix via "Add to existing."

Branching Escape Hatch: The "Or create reimbursement" button acknowledges that not all expense-logging starts with a physical receipt, offering a graceful fallback path without forcing the user to exit the flow and start over elsewhere.

High-Contrast Overlay Controls: White solid-fill circular buttons (close, retake) against the dark camera viewfinder ensure maximum legibility and touch-target confidence regardless of the background scene being photographed.

Minimal Chrome, Maximum Viewfinder: By stripping away navigation bars and status elements, the design maximizes the available frame for accurately capturing the receipt image, which directly impacts OCR/data-extraction accuracy downstream.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Expense management, corporate card, and reimbursement workflows where receipt capture is the core input.

  • Any financial form where cross-currency clarity is needed for distributed or international teams.

  • Tasks that are frequently interrupted mid-completion, warranting a visible draft-save option.

  • Scenarios where showing a real-time balance/limit constraint upfront can prevent invalid submissions downstream.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, single-focus modal pattern for simple, single-field forms (it adds unnecessary ceremony).

  • Don't surface a 'Save draft' button if the backend doesn't reliably support autosave/draft retrieval, as it creates false expectations.

  • Avoid displaying currency conversions using potentially stale/cached rates without a timestamp or disclaimer, as this could erode trust if the actual rate differs at processing time.

  • Not ideal for high-volume bulk expense submission flows, where a tabular/multi-row entry pattern would be more efficient than one modal per expense.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees at a company using a corporate card/spend management platform who need to request reimbursement for out-of-pocket business expenses. The psychological drivers at play include loss aversion (draft-saving prevents the frustration of re-entering data) and reduction of financial ambiguity (currency conversion and visible spend limits prevent surprises or distrust). The design also reduces the friction/dread typically associated with expense reporting (a notoriously tedious task) by minimizing the number of visible fields and emphasizing a single primary action (photo capture) before submission.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-currency display: Automatically converting the available balance into the user's local currency removes a mental math step and builds trust in global teams.

  • Draft-saving affordance: Positioning 'Save draft' as equal-sized but visually secondary to 'Submit' respects that reimbursement requests are often filled out in multiple sittings (e.g., waiting on a receipt).

  • Large receipt/photo upload area: Dedicating the majority of above-the-fold space to the attachment reinforces that proof-of-purchase is the most critical and often most friction-inducing step.

  • Contextual spend limit surfaced inline: Showing the 'Assigned spend limit' directly in the form (rather than requiring the user to navigate elsewhere) prevents the user from submitting requests that are likely to be rejected.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, expense, or transactional forms where some data can be reliably pre-filled from an external source (receipts, calendar, transaction history, OCR). It's ideal for reducing friction in repetitive administrative tasks like expense reports, invoices, or tax forms. The draft-save + submit pattern is well suited to any multi-field form that users might need to pause and resume, especially on mobile where interruptions are common.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid heavy automation indicators (lightning bolts) if the underlying prefill confidence is low, mislabeling guesses as 'smart' erodes trust if users frequently need to correct them. This pattern is also unsuitable for simple, single-field transactional screens where a lightweight single-field flow would be faster, or for consumer apps where financial jargon like 'Merchant category' might feel overly corporate and reduce approachability.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees of a company using a corporate expense management platform (e.g., finance teams, remote/traveling staff) who need to file reimbursement claims for out-of-pocket business expenses, such as travel bookings. The psychological drivers at play include reduction of perceived effortcontrol and trust (users verify rather than blindly accept automation, which is essential when real money and accounting accuracy are involved).
screens.keyHighlights:
• AI/Automation Indicators: Green lightning bolt icons clearly flag which fields were auto-populated by the system, building trust through transparency while still allowing manual override via clear ('x') icons.

  • Inline Currency Conversion: Automatically displays the converted balance in a secondary currency, removing cognitive load for cross-border expense reporting.

  • Progressive Disclosure Toggle: The 'different currency' switch keeps the form uncluttered by default and only expands complexity when relevant.

  • Dual CTA Footer: Separates low-commitment ('Save draft') from high-commitment ('Submit') actions, reducing abandonment risk for incomplete expense reports.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an external attendee - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any financial transaction, order, or request detail screen where users need both a clear status/outcome and the ability to supply supporting information. It's especially effective for:

  • Reimbursement, refund, or payout tracking screens where ETA transparency reduces support tickets.
  • Expense or invoice detail views requiring receipt attachment and categorization.
  • Any record that mixes read-only system data (amount, status) with user-editable metadata (attendees, memo, limit assignment).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, form-like detail pattern for simple, instantaneous transactions (e.g., a completed card swipe with no reimbursement component) where showing empty "Attendees" or "Memo" sections would add noise without value. It's also unsuitable for high-frequency micro-interactions where users need a quick glance rather than a full scrollable record (in those cases, a compact summary card or bottom sheet would be more efficient than a full-page drill-down with multiple collapsible sections).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees awaiting reimbursement for an out-of-pocket business expense (e.g., a quick lunch purchase at Pret a Manger while traveling). The psychological trigger being addressed is loss aversion and payment anxiety: employees who front money want certainty about when and how they'll be repaid. By surfacing the ETA and destination bank account proactively, Brex reduces perceived risk and builds trust in the platform's reliability.

Secondarily, this screen serves finance/admin reviewers indirectly, since the same record structure (attendees, receipts, assigned limit) supports audit and compliance needs, ensuring expenses are properly categorized and backed by documentation, satisfying corporate controllership requirements.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive ETA banner: Surfaces the reimbursement arrival date and masked destination account inline, eliminating the need to contact support (a major reduction in service load and user anxiety).
  • Masked sensitive data: Bank account and limit identifiers are partially obscured by default, balancing transparency with security best practices on a potentially unlocked/shared device.
  • Inline contextual actions: "Switch limit" button and "+" add-receipt icon are embedded directly within the relevant data row instead of requiring a separate edit screen, minimizing navigation depth.
  • Repeated merchant/amount anchor: Header subtitle and body fields both reinforce the core transaction identity, reducing the chance of acting on the wrong expense.
  • Modular card sections: Assigned Limit, Receipts, Attendees, and Memo are chunked into independent, scannable blocks that could be reordered or expanded without disrupting the whole page.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an external attendee - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any expense, invoice, or reimbursement flow requiring proof of meeting participants for audit or tax purposes.
  • Calendar/meeting scheduling apps where attendees must be selected from an org directory plus external guests.
  • B2B SaaS tools needing to attach people (internal + external) to a record quickly via search.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for high-volume bulk selection tasks (e.g., selecting 50+ people) - a full-screen multi-select list with checkboxes would scale better than a modal search sheet.
  • Not ideal if external attendees require extensive metadata (company name, email, relationship) since the single-line entry here is too lightweight for such data capture.
  • Should not be used as a persistent navigation screen; it's designed strictly as a transient, task-completion overlay.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees and finance teams submitting or auditing meal/entertainment expenses, where attendee documentation is often mandated by company policy or tax law (e.g., IRS requires business purpose and attendees for meal deductions over certain thresholds). The psychological trigger here is friction reduction for compliance tasks: by pre-filling the submitter and offering fast search/typeahead, Brex lowers the barrier to properly documenting expenses, increasing the likelihood employees comply rather than skip the field or submit incomplete reports.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-focused search with keyboard pre-triggered: Eliminates an extra tap, optimizing for speed since this is likely a mid-task flow during expense submission.
  • Self-inclusion as default attendee: The "(You)" chip is pre-populated and greyed out, applying a smart default since the user submitting the expense is almost always a dining participant.
  • External attendee support: Explicitly separates internal employees (searchable) from external guests, addressing a critical compliance need in expense management without cluttering the primary search flow.
  • Lightweight modal pattern: Using a bottom-sheet-style overlay (rather than full navigation) keeps the user anchored in the expense context, reducing perceived task switching cost.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an external attendee - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for short, supplementary data-capture modals nested within a larger task flow (especially in contexts like expense substantiation, guest/attendee logging, contact capture, or quick metadata entry where only one or two fields are truly mandatory). It's ideal when:

  • The form has 2: 5 fields max and needs to stay fast/lightweight.
  • Only a subset of fields are compliance-critical or required for submission.
  • Users need example-driven guidance instead of lengthy instructional copy.
  • The task is often repeated multiple times in a row (e.g., adding several attendees) and should minimize friction per repetition.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the form requires complex, interdependent validation across many fields, as single-field inline errors won't adequately guide users through more intricate forms (a multi-step wizard or summary-level validation would serve better. It's also inappropriate for data capture where strict identity verification is needed (e.g., legal contracts, KYC), since placeholder examples and loose validation could encourage low-quality or placeholder-like data entry. Finally, avoid a dismissible X-only exit if the data entered is costly to lose without any autosave/draft protection) users could unintentionally discard information for a long attendee list.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves employees, travel coordinators, and sales/finance staff who need to document client meetings, entertainment expenses, or event attendees for expense reports and compliance (e.g., IRS substantiation rules requiring business purpose and attendee details for T&E deductions). The psychological trigger at play is reduction of friction and anxiety around compliance tasks: by only requiring the bare minimum (a name) and clearly flagging what's missing, Brex lowers the activation energy needed to complete what is often perceived as tedious "paperwork," increasing the likelihood that users will accurately and promptly log attendee information rather than skipping it or providing incomplete data later.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline validation with specific messaging: The red border, icon, and precise error text appear directly under the offending field, keeping the user's eyes anchored rather than forcing them to scan the whole form or wait for a generic alert.
  • Placeholder-as-example pattern: Using realistic sample values (John Doe, VP of Sales, Acme Inc.) instead of generic instructions ("Enter name") reduces cognitive load and clarifies exactly what format is expected.
  • Minimal required fields: Only the name is mandatory, while job title and company are optional enrichment data (this respects user time while still capturing compliance-relevant detail when available).
  • Persistent bottom CTA: The "Add external attendee" button stays fixed at the bottom, ensuring the primary action is always accessible even as the user interacts with fields above.
  • Lightweight modal dismissal: The X icon in the header offers an unambiguous, low-friction way to abandon the task without data loss anxiety, which is standard for short supplementary forms nested inside a larger flow (e.g., expense/travel report).

screens.name: Brex - ETA information - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any financial transaction detail view where a user needs reassurance about status/timing combined with the ability to edit supporting metadata (category, attachments, participants). It's ideal for:

  • Reimbursement and expense report detail screens
  • Payment/transfer status pages (e.g., "money is on its way")
  • Invoice or bill detail views with editable allocation fields
  • Any record-based screen needing proactive ETA/status messaging to preempt support inquiries
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, section-stacked detail layout for simple, instantaneous transactions (e.g., a completed card swipe with no pending reimbursement) where showing an ETA banner, limit-switching, and attendee fields would be irrelevant clutter. It's also unsuitable for read-only audit contexts where allowing inline edits (like switching the assigned limit) could compromise financial compliance or create reconciliation conflicts if multiple people can alter categorization after submission. In highly condensed mobile list contexts, this amount of sectioned detail should be collapsed or paginated rather than shown in full on first load.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees awaiting reimbursement for out-of-pocket business expenses (e.g., a coffee purchase at Pret a Manger during travel) as well as finance-savvy users who need to verify budget attribution before an expense gets reconciled. The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion and uncertainty reduction: employees who front their own money are naturally anxious about repayment timing, so Brex proactively surfaces ETA and destination bank account to close that anxiety loop immediately upon opening the transaction.

The "Switch limit" CTA serves power users/admins who need control and correctness over how spend is categorized against company budgets, appealing to the finance team's need for accurate ledgering and the individual's desire to avoid being flagged for miscategorized spend.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive status transparency: The ETA chip and inline banner answer "when will I get paid back?" without the user needing to ask, reducing support tickets and anxiety.
  • Inline limit reassignment: The "Switch limit" button lets a user correct budget attribution directly from the detail view, avoiding a context switch to a separate screen.
  • Smart default for Attendees: Pre-populating "(You)" for single-party expenses while supporting expansion for group spend covers the common case with zero extra taps.
  • Persistent header summary: Repeating merchant + amount in the nav bar keeps context anchored while scrolling through a long detail record.
  • Lightweight receipt management: Thumbnail + "add" tile pattern makes multi-receipt attachment feel as easy as adding a photo in a messaging app.

screens.name: Brex - ETA information - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this contextual tooltip/popover pattern when:

  • A UI element displays a value or status (ETA, score, badge, calculated metric) whose underlying logic isn't self-evident from the label alone.
  • You want to preempt support requests for a recurring point of confusion without forcing users to leave the current screen.
  • The explanation is short enough to read in a few seconds and doesn't require a full help article or multi-step walkthrough.
  • You need to build trust around automated or backend-calculated values (timing, limits, scores) in finance, logistics, or SaaS products.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The information is critical enough that users need persistent access to it (a one-time dismissible tooltip may not resurface when needed later (pair with an inline help icon instead)).
  • The explanation requires lengthy content, multiple steps, or visuals (use a dedicated help/FAQ panel or bottom sheet instead).
  • It would appear too frequently or on every visit, which causes tooltip fatigue and gets reflexively dismissed without being read.
  • The screen is already dense with modals or interruptions, as stacking overlays harms usability and increases perceived complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets employees and finance admins who are reviewing expense or reimbursement transactions and may not be familiar with internal payment processing timelines. Non-finance employees in particular (e.g., someone expensing a coffee) may not understand why a payment has a variable arrival date, since consumer apps like Venmo or Apple Pay condition users to expect instant transfers.

Psychologically, this leverages the reduction of uncertainty/anxiety principle: unexplained delays in receiving money trigger distrust, especially in a workplace context where employees are waiting to be reimbursed for personal spend. By proactively addressing the "why" before the user has to ask, Brex builds credibility and reduces the volume of support tickets or Slack messages to finance teams, which is a major hidden cost for B2B fintech products supporting non-technical, non-finance end users across global time zones and banking systems.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Just-in-time contextual education: The tooltip appears exactly when and where confusion is likely to occur (next to an ambiguous "ETA" label), rather than burying the explanation in a help article.
  • Anchored pointer/tail design: The visual tail connecting the popover to the ETA chip reinforces exactly what is being explained, reducing cognitive load.
  • Dimmed background overlay: Focuses user attention entirely on the explanation while preserving context of the underlying screen, so users don't lose their place.
  • Single, frictionless dismissal action: "Got it" requires no decision-making, respecting the user's time and avoiding decision fatigue for a purely informational interstitial.
  • Demystifying financial jargon: Proactively explains how payment timing works, building trust and reducing support burden in a domain (corporate finance) where opacity breeds anxiety.

results.query: When to require two-step confirmation for destructive workspace entity deletion

screens.name: Brex Deleting a draft 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, administrative, or compliance-related task management within consumer or gig-worker apps (particularly where users must complete secondary, non-core actions (expense submission, document uploads, profile verification) that are easy to forget). It's ideal when you want to combine motivational content (ratings, streaks, performance stats) with a functional to-do list to keep engagement high. The floating CTA pattern works well when there's a single dominant action users should take regardless of list state.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for screens with high-volume, complex task management (e.g., enterprise project management) where a simple list and single FAB would be insufficient (those need robust filtering, bulk actions, and prioritization tools). Also avoid combining unrelated motivational banners (like performance ratings) with task lists if they create confusion about the screen's primary purpose, or if the praise content feels disconnected/irrelevant to the user's current need, which can come across as tone-deaf filler.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for gig economy workers (e.g., rideshare/delivery drivers) who need a lightweight, mobile-first way to manage financial admin tasks like expense reimbursements alongside their actual work metrics (ratings, earnings). The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Positive reinforcement / variable praise: The "High" rating celebration taps into achievement motivation, a technique borrowed from gamification to increase daily app opens.

  • Reduced friction via optionality framing: Labeling the task "Optional" lowers perceived obligation, making users more likely to engage voluntarily rather than avoid the screen due to dread.

  • Completion drive (Zeigarnik Effect): The badge count and half-finished draft state create a subtle itch to close the loop, especially for users motivated by clearing notifications.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Motivational micro-copy at the top of a task list: Surfacing a performance/rating compliment ("Way to go!") above the actual to-do items reframes a transactional screen into an emotionally rewarding one, increasing daily engagement likelihood.

  • Status/priority visualization via colored bar chart icon: The small tri-segment bar next to "High" gives an instant, scannable visual cue of standing without requiring the user to parse numbers.

  • Non-blocking floating action button: "Add receipts" is positioned to stay accessible during scroll without overlapping list content or the tab bar, following FAB best practices for primary actions.

  • Optional vs. required task labeling: The "Optional" chip is a simple but effective pattern for managing user cognitive load and preventing false urgency.

  • Badge on Tab Bar: The orange "1" badge on the Tasks tab creates a Zeigarnik-effect pull to return and resolve the outstanding item.

screens.name: Brex Deleting a draft 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this dual-layer destructive-confirmation pattern whenever a user action results in permanent or hard-to-recover data loss, especially in forms with multiple user-entered fields (memos, attachments, calculated values). It's ideal for financial, legal, or administrative tools where mistakes carry real costs or trust implications.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavier two-step confirmation for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., removing a single tag or dismissing a notification), where an undo toast would be faster and less intrusive. Overusing confirmation dialogs for trivial actions trains users to blindly tap through them, diminishing their effectiveness for genuinely critical actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for business travelers, field employees, sales reps, or contractors who log mileage for expense reimbursement (likely within a corporate expense management or HR tool (e).g., similar to Spendesk, Expensify, or SAP Concur). These users need speed and confidence that their financial data won't be lost by accident.

Psychologically, the design leverages loss aversion by explicitly confirming before deletion (users are more sensitive to losing already-entered data (distance, memo, attachments) than to the minor friction of an extra tap). The deferred confirmation also exploits the Zeigarnik effect, keeping the original form visible in the background as a reminder of what's at stake if they proceed with deletion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Automatic calculation transparency: Showing the per-mile rate (£0.45) alongside the total amount builds trust by letting users audit the math themselves rather than trusting a black-box total.

  • Two-step destructive action pattern: Separating the "Delete Draft" trigger from the actual confirmation dialog prevents accidental data loss from a single mis-tap.

  • Visual destructive hierarchy: Red text for the initial "Delete Draft" button and a bold orange fill for the final "Delete" button create consistent, escalating visual warning cues.

  • Context-preserving modal stacking: Rather than navigating away, the confirmation dialog stacks on top of the existing form, keeping the user's place and reducing cognitive reload.

screens.name: Brex Deleting a draft 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a task/notification/inbox-style screen can legitimately be empty for extended periods. It's ideal for:

  • Admin, compliance, or approval queues in B2B/gig-worker tools where "zero tasks" is a common and desirable state.

  • Any screen where you want to reduce compulsive re-checking behavior by clearly setting expectations about future notifications.

  • Apps that benefit from injecting secondary engagement content (ratings, tips, achievements) into otherwise empty real estate without cluttering primary navigation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, illustration-driven empty state in contexts where:

  • Users expect dense, high-frequency task lists (e.g., enterprise ticketing systems) - an overly playful empty state can feel inappropriate or juvenile for professional/serious use cases.

  • The "zero state" is actually a sign of a broken integration or sync failure (in such cases, a generic reassuring message could mask real errors and should be replaced with diagnostic messaging instead).

  • Screen space is premium and secondary content (like the rating card) could distract from a critical primary action the user needs to take elsewhere.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for gig-economy workers (e.g., drivers for Via Transportation) who use this app to manage reimbursements, wallet balances, and compliance/administrative tasks. These users are typically checking the app frequently throughout their workday or between shifts, often in brief, interrupted sessions.

The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Anxiety reduction: Gig workers often worry about missed paperwork affecting pay; explicitly confirming "no tasks" and promising future notification alleviates recurring low-level stress.

  • Variable positive reinforcement: The "High" rating card taps into the same motivational mechanics as performance dashboards in ride-share driver apps, rewarding users with status/esteem signals to encourage continued platform loyalty.

  • Reduced friction to monetize sunk cost: The "Add receipts" CTA capitalizes on an idle moment to encourage behavior (uploading receipts) that benefits both the user (reimbursement) and the platform (data completeness).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Repurposed empty space for engagement: Instead of leaving the empty state purely blank, the "High" rating insight card is surfaced above it, turning dead screen real estate into a retention/motivation touchpoint.

  • Friendly 3D illustration: A custom, on-brand character/object illustration softens the "nothing to do" moment and gives the empty state personality instead of feeling broken or unfinished.

  • Proactive reassurance copy: Explicitly stating "we'll notify you here" removes the need for users to habitually re-check the tab, reducing anxiety-driven app opens.

  • Persistent contextual CTA: The floating "Add receipts" pill ensures the screen is never a complete dead-end (there's always a low-friction next action available).

  • Layered transient feedback: The toast confirming a deletion demonstrates good system-status visibility without blocking the rest of the UI.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any subscription or account-based product's offboarding/deactivation flow, particularly when:

  • You want structured churn analytics without resorting to intrusive exit surveys or forced phone calls.
  • The brand value proposition relies on trust and non-manipulative design (e.g., education, wellness, productivity apps).
  • You want to close the loop gracefully, preserving goodwill for potential win-back campaigns later.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this exact pattern when:

  • The business genuinely needs a retention intervention (e.g., presenting a discount, pause option, or feature education) - in those cases, a reason selector should precede a tailored save-attempt screen rather than go straight to confirmation.
  • The checkbox list is so long or granular that it creates decision fatigue right as the user wants to leave quickly (simplicity and speed should be prioritized in exit flows).
  • Legal/compliance requirements mandate additional verification steps (e.g., re-authentication) before deactivation, which this screen does not surface.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already decided to leave (at this point, persuasion is futile and potentially damaging to brand perception). Instead, the design targets the company's internal product and growth teams as the secondary "audience," optimizing for structured churn-reason data collection. Psychologically, offering a reason selector gives departing users a sense of closure and voice, which can reduce negative word-of-mouth even among churned users ("they asked why, and listened").

The inclusion of options like "I am spending too much time on Brilliant" also signals self-awareness toward digital wellbeing-conscious users, appealing to the global, reflective STEM-learner demographic who may value a company that doesn't shame them for setting boundaries.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reframing churn as contribution: The headline positions the act of leaving as helpful to "future generations," softening the emotional friction of deactivation.
  • Multi-select checkboxes over radio buttons: Allows richer, more honest qualitative signal since churn is rarely caused by a single factor.
  • No dark patterns or last-minute discount offers: The screen respects user intent rather than inserting manipulative retention interstitials, which builds long-term brand trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Consistent minimalist chrome: Reusing the same top bar, typography, and spacing system as the rest of the app keeps even a "negative" flow feeling coherent and non-jarring.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any account-deletion or subscription-cancellation flow where:

  • You want structured, qualitative churn data without adding friction that feels manipulative.
  • Users need to choose between reversible (deactivate) and irreversible (delete) actions, and the distinction must be crystal clear.
  • Brand trust and long-term reputation (word-of-mouth, win-back potential) matter more than squeezing out one more retention save.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this low-friction approach if the business model depends heavily on short-term retention saves (e.g., subscription services with aggressive LTV targets) - some products legitimately need a single, well-crafted retention offer before this screen. Also avoid mixing checkbox and radio semantics on the same screen without a visual divider, as it can confuse users about whether multiple selections are allowed. Finally, never allow a "permanent delete" radio option without the explicit irreversibility disclaimer used here, as that invites support disputes and reduces trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves users who have already decided to leave (the target "demographic" here is a departing user, often someone who found Brilliant too difficult, redundant (duplicate accounts), privacy-conscious, or time-constrained). Pre-checked example states (shown with checkmarks) in the mock suggest common real-world churn reasons: difficulty, accidental duplicate accounts, and privacy concerns, implying Brilliant's actual churn data skews toward perceived difficulty and account-hygiene issues rather than lack of perceived value.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the sunk-cost-free exit principle (by not fighting the departure, Brilliant preserves brand goodwill and increases the odds of a future "boomerang" return (reinforced by the "temporarily deactivate" option)). The privacy-concern checkbox also signals awareness that STEM/edtech audiences (often data-conscious, intellectually engaged users) care about data ownership, hence offering a hard-delete path with explicit irreversibility language builds long-term trust even in the exit moment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Exit research, not exit prevention: No retention offer, discount, or guilt-trip modal precedes the actual deactivation choice (the product respects the user's decision and instead optimizes for learning).
  • Checkbox vs. radio button semantic clarity: Switching input type from checkboxes (top, multi-select reasons) to radio buttons (bottom, single-select severity) communicates selection rules without needing any instructional copy.
  • Transparent irreversibility disclosure: Explicitly stating deletion "can't be recovered, even by staff" removes ambiguity and builds trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Two-tier choice architecture: Separating "why" from "how severe" into two distinct question blocks, divided by a hairline rule, prevents cognitive overload and keeps the one-idea-per-section rhythm consistent with the app's lesson design philosophy.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any account deletion or cancellation flow where you want to (1) capture structured churn-reason data for product improvement, (2) differentiate between reversible and irreversible actions, and (3) add a final security/intent-confirmation gate. It's especially valuable for subscription, education, or SaaS products where re-engagement after a "cool-off" period is possible and worth protecting via a temporary deactivation default.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, multi-step flow for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., unsubscribing from a newsletter), where the added friction would feel punitive and out of proportion to risk. Also avoid for apps with no account recovery infrastructure, where offering a "temporary" option would be misleading. If legal/compliance requires immediate, frictionless deletion (e.g., GDPR right-to-erasure requests), this length of flow may need to be shortened or supplemented with a direct deletion path.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already decided to leave (learners who found the STEM content too difficult, privacy-conscious users, or those who created accidental duplicate accounts). Rather than fighting churn with dark patterns, Brilliant leans into transparency and data collection, which suits its brand as a trustworthy, pedagogically serious edtech platform aimed at a global, education-first audience.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss aversion (bold warning about permanent, unrecoverable deletion) and commitment/consistency (requiring users to articulate their reason and re-enter a password) to slow impulsive cancellations while still respecting user autonomy (an ethical approach appropriate for an app whose value proposition is built on sustained, deliberate practice).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multi-select churn survey captures granular, actionable reasons for leaving before the deletion flow proceeds, turning an offboarding moment into a product-research opportunity.
  • Asymmetric default framing between "temporarily deactivate" and "permanently delete" nudges users toward reversible action without removing agency.
  • Password re-authentication gate as a final friction point, preventing impulsive, accidental, or malicious deletions.
  • Explicit irreversibility warning ("can't be recovered, even by staff") sets honest expectations and builds institutional trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Consistent one-idea-per-screen minimalism is preserved even in a utilitarian settings flow, keeping cognitive load low despite the emotionally charged context.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this multi-stage confirmation pattern (reason → reversibility choice → re-authentication → consequence disclosure → final action) for any high-stakes, irreversible user action: account deletion, financial withdrawal, data purge, or subscription cancellation with sunk-cost implications (e.g., losing saved progress or paid content).

It is especially valuable in subscription-based products where deletion has a secondary financial consequence (active billing) that users may not immediately realize.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, multi-step friction pattern for low-risk or reversible actions (e.g., removing a single saved item, logging out, or unsubscribing from a single notification type) - excessive friction on low-stakes tasks frustrates users and feels punitive rather than protective.

Also avoid requiring password re-entry if the user already recently re-authenticated in the same session, as redundant verification steps increase abandonment without adding security value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves users who have already decided to leave (likely frustrated, overwhelmed, or re-prioritizing their time) and targets two underlying psychological needs: agency (the explicit choice between temporary vs. permanent action respects that not everyone wants to fully sever ties) and trust (radical transparency about irreversibility and billing consequences signals the company isn't trying to trap or trick them).

For Brilliant specifically, whose brand promise is calm, focused, friction-light learning, maintaining that same respectful, low-pressure tone even during offboarding reinforces brand integrity (a company that is honest when you're leaving is more likely to be trusted if you return).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Password re-authentication gate: Converts a single destructive tap into a two-factor-like confirmation, preventing accidental or unauthorized deletion.
  • Inline password-reset recovery link: Solves the "I forgot my password and now I'm stuck" dead-end proactively within the flow itself.
  • Transparent subscription-cancellation disclosure: Surfaces a consequential business fact at the precise decision moment instead of hiding it in fine print, respecting informed consent.
  • Color-coded severity: The lone coral-red button amid an otherwise monochrome screen visually isolates risk without needing extra copy.
  • Reason capture before action: Collecting churn reasons (visible above the fold scroll) turns an exit into usable product feedback data.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
• First-touch splash/welcome screens for subscription or edtech apps where the product's core mechanic (interactivity, motion, hands-on learning) can be visually encoded into the hero graphic itself.
  • Apps that want to differentiate from generic stock-photo onboarding by using brand-specific illustration or kinetic typography.
  • Funnels where you want to softly bias users toward sign-up while still offering a low-friction path back to sign-in.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Apps where the core value proposition is emotional or social (e.g., dating, social networking) - an abstract typographic illustration would fail to build the human connection those categories require.
  • B2B or enterprise tools where users expect immediate utility/functional clarity rather than brand storytelling on the first screen (this pattern spends a full screen on persuasion before any functional UI is shown, which could frustrate task-driven users).
  • Contexts where regulatory or compliance screens (e.g., consent, age-gating) must appear before any marketing content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets a broad, worldwide audience of self-directed learners (likely skewing toward curious professionals, students, and lifelong learners who are often comparing Brilliant against competitors like Duolingo, Khan Academy, or Coursera in an app store search). Because this is the very first impression, the design leans heavily on the von Restorff effect (the oversized, unusual typographic illustration stands out from typical SaaS/EdTech splash screens that use photos of smiling people) to create immediate brand memorability.

The "15 minutes a day" claim taps into the psychological principle of minimal viable commitment: by framing the ask as small and time-boxed, it lowers the perceived barrier to trying the product, which is critical for conversion at the top of a mobile acquisition funnel where attention spans are short and competing apps are one tap away.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Typography-as-illustration: Instead of screenshots or stock imagery, the brand's core differentiator (interactivity) is literally woven into the headline using fake drag-tags, axes, and dotted plot lines (a highly original and on-brand way to visualize "doing" rather than "watching)."
  • Single, unmissable CTA: One full-bleed green button with no competing buttons of equal visual weight (removes decision paralysis at the most critical conversion point of the funnel).
  • Specific, benefit-driven subcopy: "Get smarter in 15 minutes a day" quantifies the value proposition, making an abstract benefit (intelligence growth) feel concrete and attainable.
  • Deferred sign-in: "Sign in" is present but visually subordinate, correctly prioritizing new-user acquisition while not alienating returning users.

screens.name: Craft - Deleting a comment - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when building collaborative document, content, or design review tools where feedback needs to be anchored to specific content segments. It's ideal for:

  • Writing/note apps adding team or client review workflows
  • Design tools with annotation/commenting on specific layers or text
  • CMS or content-approval platforms needing inline editorial feedback
  • Any product where preserving the relationship between source content and discussion is critical to comprehension
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in single-player, private-only apps where no multi-user collaboration exists (the added UI weight (avatars, threads, menus) would be unnecessary clutter). It's also a poor fit for very short-form content or chat-like apps where comments-on-comments could cause excessive nesting and confusion. On small screens, stacking a highlighted block plus a bottom sheet can feel cramped if the source text is lengthy; in that case, consider a dedicated full-screen comments view or side panel (on larger viewports) instead of an overlay.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets professional and team-oriented users of Craft (product managers, founders, designers, or writers who use the app not just for private notes but for collaborative drafting and review (e).g., drafting a "Web3 Platform Landing" brief with stakeholder input). The psychological driver here is collaborative accountability and social validation: seeing named avatars and real critique ("may attract the wrong audience") builds trust that the document is being rigorously vetted, while the quick "agree. will revise it" reply shows responsiveness and closes the feedback loop quickly, satisfying the commenter's need to be heard.

The persistent "type your comment" field and low-friction contextual menu reduce the activation energy needed to participate, catering to users who want fast, async collaboration without the formality of a suggestion-mode redline.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Highlighted-text-to-comment linkage: The light blue highlight on the source paragraph visually ties the comment thread back to the exact passage being discussed, a technique borrowed from professional editing tools (Google Docs, Medium) that is rare and valuable in a "note-taking" app.
  • Non-disruptive bottom sheet: Comments slide up as an overlay rather than a full-screen takeover, preserving spatial context and making it easy to dismiss and return to writing.
  • On-demand contextual menu: Edit/Delete actions only appear via long-press, keeping the comment thread visually quiet and uncluttered during normal reading.
  • Comment affordance on the source block: The "2 comments · Just Now" meta-row under the highlighted paragraph acts as a lightweight entry point/summary, so users can gauge discussion activity without opening the thread.

screens.name: Craft - Deleting a comment - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this confirmation dialog pattern whenever an action is:

  • Irreversible or costly to reverse (deleting comments, documents, folders, accounts).
  • Infrequent enough that added friction won't meaningfully slow down core workflows.
  • High-stakes relative to the user's effort invested (e.g., long-form comments, collaborative threads, financial transactions).

It's especially valuable in collaborative or document-based apps where content often represents significant user or team effort, and in any interface where a single mis-tap (like a swipe or long-press) could otherwise trigger permanent loss.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes, easily reversible, or high-frequency actions (e.g., deleting a character, dismissing a notification, or unchecking a checklist item) where a confirmation dialog would feel like unnecessary friction and train users to blindly tap "Delete" out of habit (alert fatigue). In such cases, prefer undo-instead-of-confirm patterns (e.g., a toast with an "Undo" action) that preserve speed while still offering a safety net. Overusing hard confirmation dialogs across an app also dilutes their perceived importance, making users numb to genuinely critical warnings.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Craft's audience is writers, knowledge workers, and teams collaborating on richly formatted documents (people who invest real effort into structuring comments, feedback, and critique threads (as seen with Alex Smith and Sam Lee's exchange on the Web3 platform copy)). For this audience, accidental loss of a thoughtful comment is a real pain point, especially given the editorial, document-centric nature of the app where comments often contain substantive feedback, not throwaway chat messages.

The psychological trigger here is loss aversion: by forcing a confirmation step and explicitly stating permanence, Craft reduces the anxiety of interacting with destructive controls, which in turn encourages users to use comment/delete features more confidently, knowing a safety net (the confirmation) exists before anything is truly lost.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native platform conformance: The dialog mimics iOS's native alert styling almost exactly (rounded card, blurred backdrop, stacked pill buttons), reducing cognitive load since users already have a learned mental model for this interaction.
  • Contextual backdrop preservation: Rather than a full-screen takeover, the dimmed/blurred background keeps the underlying comment thread and highlighted text visible, so users retain situational awareness of exactly what they're about to delete.
  • Asymmetric visual weight on buttons: Both buttons share equal size and shape, but color alone (red vs. neutral gray) communicates risk (a subtle but effective use of color psychology without needing icons or extra copy).
  • Irreversibility disclosure: Explicitly stating "This action cannot be undone" rather than silently deleting or offering a generic alert builds trust and reduces regret-driven support requests.

screens.name: Craft - Deleting a comment - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any collaborative document, note-taking, or content-authoring tool where feedback needs to stay tied to specific passages (specs, contracts, briefs, scripts).
  • Design or writing tools aiming for a "quiet," non-intrusive collaboration layer that doesn't disrupt the primary reading/writing experience.
  • Products where asynchronous, threaded feedback is more valuable than real-time chat, such as review cycles, editorial workflows, or async product documentation.
  • Apps wanting to combine resolution/triage controls (checkmark) directly into the comment thread to streamline review completion.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Real-time collaborative editors with many simultaneous commenters may need a persistent margin/sidebar view instead of a modal sheet, since bottom sheets can obscure concurrent discussions happening elsewhere in the doc.
  • Short-form or highly visual content (images, diagrams) where inline text highlighting doesn't translate (a pin/marker-based commenting system would serve better).
  • Data-dense enterprise tools where comment threads need rich formatting, mentions, or attachments; this minimal sheet may feel too lightweight for complex review cycles.
  • Public-facing or social contexts where comment visibility and moderation controls (beyond a simple overflow menu) are essential.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets knowledge workers, product teams, and writers who use Craft collaboratively for specs, briefs, and planning documents (as evidenced by the Web3 product-strategy content). The target user is someone reviewing or co-authoring a document asynchronously, needing to leave feedback without disrupting the document's polished, editorial presentation.

Psychologically, the design leverages contextual anchoring: humans retain feedback far better when it's tied to its exact source rather than abstracted into a list. The soft blue highlight also triggers a spotlight effect, drawing the eye precisely where discussion is needed. The low-friction bottom sheet and persistent input field cater to users' desire for quick, frictionless exchanges typical of async remote collaboration, reducing the activation energy needed to participate in a conversation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline highlight-to-thread binding: The commented text is visually tinted directly in the document body, so context is never lost (a major differentiator from tools that rely on disconnected sidebar comment lists).
  • Non-intrusive comment affordance: The avatar + "1 comment · Just Now" summary sits unobtrusively below the highlighted passage, acting as a quiet invitation rather than a blocking UI element.
  • Bottom sheet thread view: Keeps the user anchored to the document (visible, dimmed, behind the sheet) while reading/replying, preserving spatial context and avoiding a jarring full-screen navigation.
  • Inline resolve action: A checkmark icon in the sheet header allows marking the thread as resolved without extra menus, respecting the reviewer's momentum.
  • Persistent reply field: Always-visible "Type your comment" input reduces the steps needed to respond, encouraging quick, in-flow collaboration.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for schema editing or settings configuration where a single object (like a column, field, or variable) has multiple distinct properties (Name, Type, Constraints) that need to be edited in one view.
  • Ideal for No-code/Low-code platforms where you need to translate complex technical configurations (data types) into simple, mobile-friendly toggles and list selectors.
  • Effective when you need to provide contextual safety nets, such as combining an editing action with a destructive delete action in a logically separated way.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the "Field Type" selection requires extensive sub-configuration (e.g., complex Formula fields or Linked Records with multiple options) that cannot be summarized in a single helper line; this would require a dedicated sub-screen rather than an inline toggle.
  • Do not use this dense, stacked form layout for simple, single-input tasks (like just renaming a file), as the heavy sectioning would feel bureaucratic and slow down a simple interaction.
  • Not suitable for public-facing consumer apps where users are unfamiliar with technical "Field Type" terminology; this density works for professional tools but could alienate casual users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Operations Managers, Project Managers, and Database Builders who need the flexibility to modify their business logic (the "schema") while on the go, perhaps during a meeting where a new business requirement arises.

The psychological trigger here is Mastery and Control. By exposing granular field-type controls directly in a mobile modal, Airtable reinforces the user's identity as a "builder" or "admin" of their own system, rather than just a passive data-entry clerk. The simplicity of the toggle and dropdown reduces the intimidation factor often associated with "editing a database," making the user feel capable of making structural changes without engineering help.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Type-Specific Contextual Help: The dynamic helper text ("Useful for checklists.") that changes based on the selected Field Type acts as an inline tooltip, educating users on database schema design without leaving the current screen.
  • Grouped Table Hierarchy: Using distinct card groupings for Name, Description, and Type creates clear visual rhythm and reduces the perceived complexity of editing a database schema on a small screen.
  • Isolated Destructive Action: Placing "Delete Field" in its own distinct section at the bottom, separated by whitespace/dividers from the editing fields, prevents accidental data deletion via fat-fingering.
  • Icon-based Type Identification: Using a colored icon (green circle) next to the field type name allows users to quickly visually scan and identify field types across the app, creating a consistent visual language for data types.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Apply this pattern whenever a user-initiated action is irreversible and affects data beyond the immediate view (e.g., deleting a column/field, removing a user from a shared workspace, deleting a database table, or archiving a project with dependent records). It's especially valuable in collaborative, multi-user tools where one person's action can silently affect others' data.

Use the inline expansion technique (Checkbox toggle appearing within the Field Type row) for simple configuration options to avoid unnecessary drill-down navigation, reserving full-screen or secondary modals only for field types requiring multiple settings.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy-handed confirmation flow for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., toggling a UI preference, hiding a column temporarily) - doing so would create unnecessary friction and training users to blindly dismiss dialogs ("confirmation fatigue"), which weakens the pattern's effectiveness when it truly matters.

Also avoid echoing overly long or technical field names verbatim in a confirmation button if space is constrained; truncate gracefully or use a secondary text input requiring the user to type the field name for extremely high-risk deletions (e.g., deleting an entire base).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations managers, database administrators, and power users who are actively structuring or maintaining a shared Airtable base (often under time pressure or while collaborating with a team that depends on data integrity). Because Airtable fields can hold months of accumulated team data, the psychological stakes of an accidental deletion are high (irreversible data loss affecting colleagues).

The design leans on loss aversion and friction-as-safety principles: by making the deletion path require multiple deliberate taps and explicit acknowledgment of data loss, Airtable reduces anxiety for cautious users while still allowing expert users to move through quickly once they've internalized the pattern.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit consequence messaging: The dialog doesn't just ask "are you sure?" - it educates the user on exactly what will be lost (data across every record), reducing the chance of regret-driven support tickets.
  • Named re-confirmation: The button reads 'Delete "Visited?"' rather than a generic "Delete," reinforcing which specific field is about to be destroyed and guarding against misclicks when editing multiple fields in a session.
  • Inline type configuration: The Checkbox toggle and description appear directly within the Field Type row, minimizing navigation depth for simple field types.
  • Spatial separation of destructive action: Placing "Delete field" far below the primary editable fields, with a divider and trash icon, uses visual hierarchy to signal danger and reduce accidental taps.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Schema/configuration screens in no-code or low-code platforms where users define data structure (e.g., database builders, form builders, CRM customization panels).
  • Any settings list where each item represents a configurable "type" that benefits from a live visual preview rather than a text-only description.
  • Admin panels that need to onboard non-technical users to technical concepts through embedded contextual video and analogy-driven microcopy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Simple, flat forms with a small, fixed number of fields, adding live previews and type pickers would be over-engineering for a one-time contact form, for instance.
  • Screens targeting highly technical users (e.g., developers using a SQL schema editor) who may find the playful icon/analogy treatment patronizing and prefer dense, code-like table editors instead.
  • Contexts where field reordering has no real functional impact (e.g., static reports), since drag handles would add unnecessary complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations leads, project managers, and "citizen developers" who build business systems without formal engineering backgrounds. These users need to configure data structures but are often unfamiliar with database terminology like "schema" or "field types." The design leans on recognition over recall (visual previews, icons, color coding) and analogy-based education (the blueprint metaphor) to build confidence and reduce the intimidation factor typically associated with database configuration tools.

The locked primary field and drag-to-reorder handles also speak to power users who need structural control and customization once they're comfortable, supporting Airtable's dual audience of beginners and advanced builders.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live mini-previews per field type: Each row visually simulates its data type (progress bar, numeric input, file icons) instead of relying on text labels alone, dramatically improving scannability and comprehension.
  • Color-coded type icons: Each field type has a distinct icon/color combo (blue "A" for text, orange "#" for number, pink paperclip for attachment) creating a quick visual taxonomy that scales well as tables grow to dozens of fields.
  • Locked primary field affordance: The padlock icon on "Location" clearly communicates an immutable schema rule without needing a modal or error message.
  • Embedded contextual video/coach mark: Using a tappable video thumbnail inside the explanatory banner caters to varied learning styles (read vs. watch) and is dismissible via the "X" for repeat users.
  • Persistent "Add a new field" CTA: Anchored at the bottom of the list, it keeps the primary creation action always accessible regardless of scroll depth.

screens.name: CRED Chatting & sending Messages 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for destructive or feature-disengaging actions (unsubscribing, deleting saved items, disconnecting integrations) where the business wants to reduce accidental drop-off without fully blocking the user.

  • Ideal for brands with a strong, distinct voice where a conversational confirmation reinforces brand personality instead of feeling like generic system UI.

  • Effective when the consequence of the action isn't just data loss but ongoing service/utility loss (subscriptions, reminders, tracking) - the "you'll miss out" framing works best here.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for high-frequency, low-risk actions (e.g., removing an item from a cart) - an elaborate chat-style confirmation adds unnecessary friction and slows down the user.

  • Not suitable for enterprise/B2B tools where users expect fast, efficient, no-nonsense confirmations; a chatty tone can feel patronizing or slow down power users.

  • Should not be used for truly irreversible, high-stakes actions (e.g., permanent account deletion, financial transfers) where a more formal, explicit double-confirmation (e.g., typing "DELETE") is safer than a casual chat bubble.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets CRED's affluent, engagement-conscious user base who use the Garage feature to track service reminders, insurance renewals, and challan/fine updates for their vehicles. The design assumes users may attempt to remove a vehicle impulsively (e.g., after selling a car) without realizing they'll lose ongoing utility notifications.

Psychologically, the screen exploits loss aversion (people weigh potential losses more heavily than equivalent gains) and the conversational trust heuristic: talking to a "bot" with personality feels less transactional and more like being counseled by a friend, which increases the likelihood a user reconsiders before churning off a feature that drives repeat app opens.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chatbot-styled confirmation: Uses an avatar + speech bubble instead of a generic system dialog, making a mundane deletion prompt feel like a personalized conversation.

  • Full-sentence action buttons: Eliminates ambiguity ("Yes, I confirm..." / "No, I want to keep...") so users always know exactly what they're agreeing to, even if they skim.

  • Loss-aversion copy: Frames the consequence as missing "important updates" rather than simply stating data will be deleted, tapping into FOMO to reduce accidental churn.

  • Neutral button styling: Both options use identical white pill buttons, forcing deliberate reading rather than allowing users to blindly tap a colored 'safe' button.

screens.name: CRED Chatting & sending Messages 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Consumer apps with a strong brand personality where standard system dialogs would feel too clinical or corporate.

  • Flows where you want to combine a destructive action confirmation with a feedback/exit-survey moment in a single continuous interaction.

  • Products already using a chatbot/assistant metaphor elsewhere in the app, so this pattern feels consistent rather than novel/jarring.

  • Situations where reframing "cannot be undone" language into loss-based benefits (what you'll miss) is more persuasive than generic warnings.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• High-frequency, low-stakes deletions (e.g., removing an item from a cart) where a lightweight modal or toast-with-undo is faster and less intrusive than a multi-turn chat exchange.

  • Enterprise/B2B tools where users expect efficiency over personality (a chat-style confirmation could feel slow and gimmicky for power users performing bulk operations).

  • Time-critical or high-severity actions (e.g., deleting a financial account, irreversible payment actions) where extra conversational steps could be misread as reducing the seriousness of the action.

  • Apps without an existing conversational/assistant paradigm, where introducing this pattern in isolation would feel inconsistent with the rest of the UI.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets CRED's core demographic of financially engaged, detail-oriented users who are used to more premium, personality-driven digital experiences (as opposed to generic banking UIs). The conversational format leverages the familiarity of messaging apps (WhatsApp/iMessage-like bubbles) to make an administrative task (vehicle data management) feel lightweight and low-stakes, reducing the psychological weight of "deleting" something.

The explicit confirmation sentence and the follow-up "why" question are aimed at users who might be removing the vehicle due to sale, ownership change, or app dissatisfaction. CRED uses this moment to extract churn/product feedback while the user is still engaged in the flow, rather than losing that signal entirely once the vehicle disappears from the garage.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-as-UI for destructive actions: Replacing a modal dialog with a conversational thread makes a mundane CRUD operation feel personal and branded.

  • Explicit confirmation phrasing: The button text is a full affirmative sentence, increasing intentionality and reducing rage-taps/misclicks.

  • Loss-framed warning copy: Focuses on what the user will miss out on rather than generic irreversible-action language, tapping into loss aversion psychology.

  • Post-action feedback capture: Asking "why" after the deletion is committed (not blocking it) turns a churn signal into a data collection opportunity without adding friction to the task itself.

  • Persistent Undo affordance: A floating Undo control near the input bar gives users a safety net, reducing anxiety around irreversible actions.

screens.name: CRED Chatting & sending Messages 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this conversational confirmation + feedback pattern when:

  • The action being confirmed is destructive or has downstream consequences (e.g., unsubscribing, deleting an asset, canceling a service) and you want to both confirm intent and capture the reason.

  • Your product has a strong, distinctive brand voice and benefits from consistent, personality-driven micro-interactions even in edge-case flows.

  • You want to combine confirmation and exit-feedback collection into a single, low-friction flow instead of separate dialogs/surveys.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The destructive action needs to be resolved extremely fast (e.g., emergency stop, critical security action) - a chat-style flow adds unnecessary steps and reading time.

  • Users are unfamiliar with or skeptical of chatbot-style interfaces, which could create confusion about whether a human or bot is responding.

  • Accessibility is a priority; a chat thread can be harder to scan quickly compared to a clear modal with distinct primary/secondary buttons.

  • The context demands strict compliance/legal confirmation language, where casual lowercase chat tone may undermine the seriousness of the action.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets CRED's affluent, tech-savvy user base that expects premium, polished, and non-generic interactions even for mundane account management tasks like removing a vehicle. By using a conversational tone and branded chat UI, CRED reinforces its distinctive product identity and keeps engagement high even during a 'negative' action (removal). Psychologically, the flow leverages loss aversion (highlighting missed updates), commitment consistency (explicit first-person confirmation), and the norm of reciprocity/curiosity (users feel compelled to answer why after being asked directly in a human-like tone). The embedded feedback collection also serves CRED's product team by gathering structured churn reasons in an unobtrusive, natural way.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-based confirmation instead of modal dialog: Converts a routine destructive-action confirmation into a branded, conversational experience consistent with CRED's design language.

  • Loss-aversion messaging: Explicitly states what the user will lose ('miss out on all important updates') to reduce accidental or impulsive removals.

  • First-person confirmation copy: 'Yes, I confirm...' makes the commitment explicit and intentional, reducing regret and mis-taps.

  • Post-action exit survey embedded in flow: Immediately asks 'why' after confirmation, capturing valuable churn data without adding a separate screen or form.

  • Quick-reply chips with Undo option: 'Sold it' and 'Undo' in the input bar reduce typing effort and offer an immediate escape hatch, respecting user autonomy even after confirmation.

screens.name: CRED Chatting & sending Messages 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a core feature of an app depends on user-supplied data that hasn't been entered yet (such as first-time dashboards, empty lists, or feature areas requiring setup (e).g., "no cards added," "no properties listed," "no pets added"). It's ideal for onboarding flows, post-signup states, or any screen where zero-content would otherwise look broken or unfinished.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen empty-state treatment for minor or secondary lists where a lightweight inline prompt would suffice, using a full illustration and centered CTA for trivial data (e.g., an empty search filter) can feel disproportionate and slow down power users. Also avoid it in flows where the user has already dismissed or skipped vehicle setup intentionally, as repeatedly showing a blocking empty state can feel naggy rather than helpful.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new or returning users of a vehicle-centric app (e.g., EV charging, parking, insurance, or fleet management) who have not yet completed the required setup step of registering a vehicle. The psychological trigger at play is the Zeigarnik effect: presenting an unfinished task (empty garage) creates a subtle discomfort that motivates the user to complete the action and "finish" the setup.

Additionally, the friendly, low-stakes tone reduces the anxiety often associated with empty states (which can otherwise feel like errors), reframing the moment as an invitation rather than a failure, which is especially important for onboarding-stage users who are still forming their first impressions of the product.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Domain-specific illustration: The retro-styled charging/monitor illustration with a warning icon visually communicates "missing setup" in a playful, on-brand way rather than using a generic stock empty-state graphic.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: Only one actionable button exists on the screen, eliminating decision paralysis and funneling the user toward the exact next step needed to unlock the app's core value.

  • High-contrast button styling: The stark white button against the pure black canvas guarantees the CTA is the most visually dominant element on the page.

  • Brand-aligned metaphor in copy: Reusing "garage" and "parked" terminology ties the empty state directly into the product's core mental model instead of a sterile system message.

results.query: Managing user anxiety during multi-minute asynchronous banking verification

screens.name: Cleo Creating Account 5
screens.whereToUse: This exact pattern (institution-specific consent statement + credential fields + inline password recovery) fits specifically within a genuine bank-aggregator credential flow (Plaid, Yodlee, MX, etc.), where real, sensitive login information is being collected and legal/trust clarity at the point of entry is essential.
screens.whereNotToUse: Not applicable to imitate outside a genuine credential-aggregation context (a host app should never build a custom-branded screen that mimics a bank's own login UI, as doing so would raise legitimate phishing/security concerns; this pattern only belongs to the trusted aggregator layer itself).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Venmo, Robinhood, Chime: all route through this identical Plaid-native credential screen when a user selects a specific bank via Plaid, since it's shared, standardized infrastructure across all Plaid integrations.

  • Coinbase, Acorns: likewise present the same per-institution consent statement and credential form at the equivalent point in their own Plaid-powered flows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Just-in-time, specific consent: restating exactly what's happening ("your RBC Royal Bank credentials," "retrieve your financial data") at the literal point of credential entry reinforces informed consent when it matters most, rather than relying solely on an earlier general disclosure.

  • Disabled-state error prevention: greying out "Submit" until both fields are filled avoids wasted submission attempts and premature error states.

  • Inline recovery path: surfacing "Reset password" directly on the login screen reduces abandonment for users who've forgotten credentials, avoiding a dead-end failure mode.

  • Neutral, non-alarming security framing: the consent statement's plain, declarative tone avoids either downplaying the sensitivity of the action or triggering unnecessary anxiety through overly formal/legal phrasing.

screens.name: Cleo Creating Account 6
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any multi-second backend processing step involving sensitive data transmission (credential submission, payment processing, identity verification) where breaking an opaque wait into visible sub-steps meaningfully reduces user anxiety and perceived duration.
screens.whereNotToUse: Overkill for near-instantaneous operations (sub-second responses) where inserting a staged, checkmarked progress screen would be unnecessary theater rather than genuinely informative feedback.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Venmo, Robinhood, Chime: all show this identical Plaid-native "Sending credentials" loading screen with checkmarked sub-steps, since it's shared standardized Plaid infrastructure.

  • Coinbase, Acorns: likewise display the same determinate-progress loading pattern during the equivalent bank-authentication wait in their own Plaid integrations.
