screens.name: Wealthfront Transferring Money 22
screens.whereToUse:
• Multi-step financial flows (transfers, payments, currency exchange) where source and destination must be unambiguous.

  • Any scenario with a small, finite set of selectable options where a rich list (name + balance/metadata) aids decision-making.

  • Flows benefiting from a visual "path" metaphor to communicate sequential steps (e.g., shipping origin/destination, itinerary building).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this single-purpose-per-screen pattern when users have many (10+) accounts, as it may require excessive scrolling or search functionality instead of a flat list.

  • Not ideal for expert/power-user tools where speed is prioritized over guided step-by-step flows (a single combined form may be faster for frequent transfers).

  • Avoid vague labels like "From?"/"To?" in contexts where regulatory or clarity requirements demand explicit terminology (e.g., legal/tax documents).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets existing Wealthfront users actively managing their cash and investment accounts (likely intermediate-to-advanced retail investors comfortable with self-directed transfers). The psychological trigger at play is reduction of financial anxiety through clarity: by showing exact balances and using friendly, human account nicknames, the design lowers the perceived risk of "getting it wrong" when moving money between financial instruments. The minimalist, one-decision-per-screen approach also caters to on-the-go mobile banking behavior, where users expect speed and simplicity over dense, all-in-one forms.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual Journey Metaphor: The connected "From/To" circles with a linking line make an abstract, two-part decision tree instantly scannable, reducing the mental effort of understanding transfer directionality.

  • Rich List Items with Contextual Balance: Displaying the live balance next to each account lets users make informed decisions in-line, without needing to navigate away to check funds first.

  • Single-Purpose Screen: By isolating "From" selection into its own dedicated step (rather than combining source/destination in one crowded screen), the design avoids decision fatigue and transfer errors.

  • Persistent Progress Bar: A subtle segmented indicator at the bottom sets expectations for flow length without cluttering the primary content area.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 23
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately before any third-party data-sharing integration (bank linking, calendar sync, contact import, health data access) in finance, health, or productivity apps. It's ideal when the next step involves leaving your app's UI (e.g., handing off to Plaid's or another SDK's authentication flow) and you need informed consent plus a fallback path for users who decline the primary integration.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed consent screen for low-risk, non-sensitive actions where it would only add friction (e.g., toggling a UI theme or basic app permission that doesn't involve financial/personal data sharing). Also avoid presenting this without a genuine manual/alternative path (if declining the third-party service simply dead-ends the user, the added disclosure will increase frustration and drop-off rather than build trust).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday consumers linking a bank account to a peer-to-peer payments app (Venmo), a moment of heightened financial-privacy sensitivity. The psychological triggers include: trust transference (leveraging the recognized Plaid brand and legal disclosures to borrow credibility), loss-aversion mitigation (offering a manual alternative so security-conscious users don't abandon the flow entirely), and reduction of ambiguity/anxiety (explicitly stating what data is used for and how to revoke access). This pattern is essential for fintech products where data-sharing consent directly impacts conversion and regulatory compliance.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Permission priming before third-party handoff: Explains what Plaid will access and why before triggering the actual bank-linking flow, reducing surprise and drop-off.

  • Dual-path CTA: Primary "Next" (Plaid/instant) and secondary "Verify bank manually instead" give users control and prevent hard stops for privacy-conscious users.

  • Proactive privacy reassurance: Preemptively explains how to revoke the Plaid connection, reducing anxiety without the user needing to search settings or FAQs.

  • Regulatory transparency: NMLS ID and PayPal entity disclosure at the footer builds institutional trust for a money-handling feature.

  • Non-disruptive modal presentation: Bottom sheet over a dimmed background preserves context and signals reversibility/low commitment.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 24
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for manual bank account linking flows in fintech, banking, payroll, or investment apps where instant bank verification (e.g., Plaid/Yodlee) isn't available or the user opts out. It's ideal any time you're asking users to input sensitive financial identifiers and there will be a multi-day delay before the action is complete (always pair delayed/invisible processes with clear upfront expectation-setting copy).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavier, delayed-verification pattern when a real-time bank-linking API is available, as forcing users through manual entry and a 3-day wait when instant verification exists adds unnecessary friction and drop-off risk. Also avoid over-explaining if the audience is already familiar with the flow (e.g., repeat users), as lengthy explanatory text can feel redundant and slow down power users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users who either don't use a supported instant-bank-login provider (e.g., smaller regional/credit union banks) or who are wary of sharing their bank credentials with a third-party aggregator. These users tend to be more privacy- and security-conscious, so the design compensates by leaning heavily on trust signals (lock icon, transparent explanation of the verification mechanism) rather than speed.

The psychological trigger at play is uncertainty reduction: financial actions involving real money movement trigger loss-aversion anxiety, so the copy and iconography work together to make an unusual process (small deposits/withdrawals over days) feel expected, safe, and legitimate rather than suspicious.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Security-signaling iconography: The prominent lock icon is placed before any sensitive data entry, priming users psychologically for a "safe" data exchange before they see the input fields.

  • Pre-emptive expectation-setting: Explaining the micro-deposit verification process in advance prevents user panic or fraud alerts when small unfamiliar transactions appear on their statement.

  • Confirm Account Number field: A double-entry validation pattern that guards against a high-cost, hard-to-reverse error (misdirected ACH transfer) - an appropriate use of friction given the stakes.

  • Escape hatch via "Done": Presented as a dismissible modal rather than a forced, un-exitable step, respecting user autonomy in a sensitive financial flow.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 25
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial onboarding flows requiring bank account linkage without third-party instant-verification APIs.

  • Any high-stakes data entry moment (banking, legal, medical) where a single typo has significant consequences (use double-entry confirmation fields).

  • Whenever a delayed, multi-day verification process will produce artifacts (charges, emails, codes) that could otherwise confuse or alarm the user (preemptively explain them).

  • Modal-based single-task flows where removing tab bars/navigation increases focus and reduces drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid manual micro-deposit flows when a real-time bank verification service (Plaid, Yodlee) can authenticate instantly, forcing users to wait 1-3 days for verification significantly hurts conversion and should only be a fallback.

  • Don't use double-entry confirmation fields for low-stakes or frequently-changed data, as it adds unnecessary friction.

  • Avoid vague security iconography without accompanying explanatory copy (a lock icon alone doesn't build trust; it must be paired with clear procedural transparency as seen here).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users of fintech, banking, investing, or payment apps (e.g., neobanks, crowdfunding platforms, payroll or peer-to-peer payment apps) who need to link an external bank account for transfers, deposits, or withdrawals. This flow is typically used when instant bank authentication (e.g., Plaid) is unavailable, declined, or the user opted for manual verification.

The psychological drivers at play are trust and risk-aversion: users are hesitant to share routing/account numbers, so the design leans on security visuals (lock icon) and radical transparency about what happens next to reduce anxiety. The confirm-field pattern leverages the user's own desire for accuracy to reduce error-driven support burden and delayed transactions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Security iconography: A large, centered lock icon visually reassures users before they input sensitive banking credentials, priming trust prior to disclosure.

  • Expectation-setting copy: Explaining the micro-deposit/withdrawal process in advance prevents user confusion and support inquiries when small unfamiliar transactions appear on their statement.

  • Double-entry confirmation field: "Confirm Account Number" reduces the risk of costly, hard-to-reverse errors in financial data entry.

  • Modal isolation: Presenting this as a full-screen modal with only a "Done" escape hatch keeps focus singularly on task completion.

  • Full-width loading CTA: Immediate visual feedback via a spinner within the button itself confirms the system is processing without requiring a separate loading screen.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 26
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech/wallet apps needing to nudge users toward identity verification or KYC completion without blocking core navigation.

  • Any dashboard where a primary numeric value (balance, score, count) should dominate visual hierarchy.

  • Multi-account or multi-payment-method management screens where a "wallet card" visual metaphor increases comprehension.

  • Apps with two closely related views (e.g., current balance vs. history) that benefit from a segmented control instead of full page navigation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid soft banner nudges for verification when the action is legally mandatory before ANY use of the product (in high-risk compliance contexts, a hard gate/paywall may be required instead).

  • The "wallet card" tile pattern doesn't scale well if users have many payment methods (5+), as horizontal scanning becomes tedious; a list/table pattern would be better for high-volume account management.

  • Large empty-state balances (like $0) prominently displayed can feel discouraging in apps oriented around savings/investment growth; better suited for transactional/utility apps like Venmo where zero balance is normal and expected.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday Venmo users managing peer-to-peer payments, checking balances after receiving money from friends, or setting up their account for the first time. The $0 balance and blurred/redacted bank info suggest this may be a fresh or lightly-used account, making the verification nudge highly relevant. Venmo is capturing the exact moment of intent (checking wallet balance) to drive KYC completion, which is critical for regulatory compliance and unlocking peer-to-peer transfer revenue (interchange, instant transfer fees).

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete verification creates a nagging sense of an unfinished task) and loss framing (money is "there" but inaccessible), motivating the user to complete verification to "unlock" their own funds.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual verification prompt: Rather than blocking the user with a hard paywall/gate, the verification requirement is surfaced as a soft, informative banner directly below the $0 balance (exactly where the friction point (inability to use funds) is felt, maximizing relevance and conversion likelihood).

  • Wallet metaphor card UI: Bank/card entries are rendered as literal wallet-card tiles with a "+" card of matching dimensions to add new ones, creating a strong, intuitive visual metaphor.

  • Segmented control for Wallet/Transactions: Avoids fragmenting into separate screens, keeping the balance and history one swipe/tap away from each other.

  • Prominent central Pay FAB: The raised circular Venmo icon in the tab bar visually breaks the grid to draw the eye to the primary monetization/engagement action (pay/request).

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 27
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for detail/management screens for a single linked financial account, card, or sensitive credential where the user needs to (a) confirm the identity of what they're managing, (b) understand its current trust/status, and (c) take one constructive and one destructive action. It's ideal for banking, payments, subscription billing, or identity-verification flows where a account/method can exist in multiple states (verified/unverified/expired).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal single-action layout when there are more than two possible actions to take (e.g., set as default, edit nickname, view transaction history) - cramming more options into this vertical list would require a more scalable settings/list pattern instead. Also avoid using generic iconography if brand recognition of the specific institution builds trust (e.g., showing the real bank logo increases confidence and reduces confusion for users with multiple linked banks). Do not omit a confirmation dialog before "Remove" is finalized on the next screen/step, as irreversible destructive actions should never fire immediately from a single tap.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of a fintech, banking, payments, or wallet app (e.g., neobank, P2P transfer app, investment platform) who have connected an external bank account via ACH/manual entry and must complete identity/ownership verification (often via micro-deposits or Plaid-style instant verification) before the account becomes usable for transfers.

Psychologically, the screen leverages status ambiguity resolution: users are uncomfortable with an "unverified" limbo state and are nudged, via a clearly visible blue CTA, to resolve it. The isolation of "Remove" preys on loss-aversion caution: since removing a bank account is consequential (may disrupt pending transfers), it's styled and positioned to require deliberate intent, not accidental discovery.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Redaction/blur of sensitive account data shown in the mock, illustrating a privacy-conscious pattern (masking PII by default until explicitly needed).

  • Clear visual hierarchy separating safe vs. destructive actions: "Verify" and "Remove" are spaced far apart and color-coded distinctly (blue vs. red) to prevent misclicks.

  • Status transparency: the "(Unverified)" label is surfaced prominently next to the account nickname, ensuring the user always understands the trust/functional state of this payment method before attempting to use it.

  • Iconography instead of a real photo for the bank header (a generic institution glyph works across any linked bank, avoiding reliance on possibly unavailable bank logos/branding assets).

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 28
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any asynchronous identity or ownership verification step where a user must retrieve external, real-world information (small deposit amounts, codes mailed to an address, etc.) and re-enter it into the app. It's ideal for banking/fintech onboarding, payroll setup, and any ACH-based payment linking. Keep the screen to a single task, use plain language, and pre-fill trust-signaling iconography to soften the wait/anxiety involved.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when instant verification (e.g., OAuth bank login, Plaid) is available and reliable, forcing users through a multi-day micro-deposit wait when a faster path exists adds unnecessary friction and drop-off risk. Also avoid using success-toned iconography (like a checkmark) before an action is actually verified, as it can mislead users or erode trust if verification later fails; consider a neutral or informational icon instead if there's a real risk of mismatch/error.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users completing account linking for fintech, banking, payroll, or payment apps (e.g., Venmo, Cash App, payroll direct-deposit setup, investment platforms) who selected the manual/ACH bank-linking route instead of an instant Plaid-style OAuth connection. These are typically users who either don't trust instant bank-login aggregators, whose bank isn't supported by instant verification, or who are completing a compliance-required identity/ownership check.

Psychologically, this screen relies on trust-building through transparency (explaining exactly what happened and why) and reduction of ambiguity anxiety: small unexplained deposits can feel alarming, so the calm, guided copy and success-coded visuals reassure the user they are in a safe, expected process.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose modal: Only one task is possible on this screen, minimizing cognitive load and drop-off risk during a critical financial trust step.

  • Premature success iconography: The green checkmark builds emotional confidence and momentum before the actual verification succeeds, subtly nudging task completion.

  • Plain-language explanation: Demystifies a technical banking process (micro-deposits) in one short, friendly sentence, preventing user confusion or support tickets.

  • Symmetrical paired inputs: Visually reinforces the mental model that two related, sequential values are expected together.

  • Persistent, full-width CTA: The "Verify" button anchored at the bottom follows platform conventions and is always reachable, reducing the effort to submit.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 29
screens.whereToUse:
• Any fintech or banking app offering ACH micro-deposit verification as a fallback to instant bank linking.

  • Identity or account verification flows requiring users to input externally-received codes or values.

  • Situations where trust and reassurance are critical, such as onboarding to payment or investment platforms.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for time-sensitive flows where users expect instant results (the multi-day wait for deposits can cause drop-off if not paired with reminder notifications).

  • Not suitable for low-stakes or non-financial verification, where a simpler OTP code would be less cumbersome.

  • Don't use vague or technical labels; if fields aren't clearly tied to real-world statement wording, users may enter values incorrectly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users linking a bank account to a fintech, payments, or investment app (e.g., Venmo, Robinhood, Wealthfront) who could not verify instantly via a service like Plaid, and must instead wait 1-3 business days for micro-deposits. This audience is often price-sensitive or wary of sharing bank credentials directly, so the fallback manual-verification path builds trust with users who are skeptical of instant-login bank connections.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the sunk-cost/commitment principle: since the user already waited days for the deposits, they are highly motivated to complete this final step. The simple, reassuring visual design also counteracts anxiety naturally associated with entering banking-adjacent information.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Trust-building success iconography: The green checkmark preemptively communicates "step completed successfully" before the user even reads the instructions, reducing anxiety around linking financial accounts.

  • Minimal, singular-focus modal: Removing tab bars and secondary navigation keeps the user locked into completing this one critical task without distraction.

  • Real-world mental model matching: Asking for "First amount" and "Second amount" in the order they'd typically appear on a bank statement reduces lookup friction.

  • Sticky, unmissable CTA: The full-width "Verify" button anchored at the bottom ensures the next step is always visible regardless of keyboard state.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 30
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any settings/detail screen tied to a single sensitive resource (payment methods, linked accounts, connected devices, API keys) where the primary user goal is to review identifying details and optionally disconnect/delete the resource. It's ideal when:

  • The resource has few editable properties, so a full form isn't needed.

  • Security or trust framing benefits from masked data and a dedicated visual icon.

  • You want to funnel users toward a single, clear, low-risk-of-error destructive action.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal single-action layout when:

  • The resource has multiple editable attributes (e.g., nickname, default payment toggle, notification prefs) - in that case a richer settings/edit form is more appropriate.

  • Users need more actions than remove (e.g., re-verify, set as default, view transaction history) - cramming those in later would break this clean layout.

  • The destructive action's consequences are severe/irreversible and require more context or friction than a plain red text link (a confirmation dialog or explicit re-authentication should be layered on top).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday consumers managing linked financial accounts inside a fintech, banking, or peer-to-peer payment app (e.g., Venmo, Cash App, PayPal-style products). The psychological driver is trust and control: users linking bank accounts are inherently security-conscious, so the design reduces cognitive load and reassures them that sensitive data is protected (masking) while giving them an obvious, easily-found "escape hatch" (Remove) to disconnect the account if they no longer trust or need the connection. The visual simplicity also reduces anxiety often associated with financial account management.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Singular focus / decision fatigue reduction: The screen offers exactly one actionable choice (Remove), eliminating any ambiguity about what a user can do here.

  • Iconography as trust anchor: Using a universally recognized bank/institution glyph in a large hero area builds immediate visual confirmation that this is a bank-linked account, not a card.

  • Masked sensitive data: Account numbers are truncated/masked by default, aligning with PCI-DSS-style best practices for displaying financial identifiers.

  • Destructive action isolation: Placing "Remove" in red, separated by significant vertical whitespace from informational content, reduces the chance of an accidental tap while still keeping it easily reachable.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Creating Account 8
screens.whereToUse:
• Any regulated onboarding flow (fintech, brokerage, healthcare, insurance) that legally requires explicit self-certification or attestation from the user.

  • Situations where a binary Yes/No compliance question has a statistically dominant "normal" answer that can be safely pre-selected to speed up flow completion.

  • Multi-step KYC/AML verification sequences where the final step needs to feel authoritative yet not overly bureaucratic to the end user.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid pre-selecting defaults on high-stakes questions where regulatory bodies require an explicit, un-biased choice with no default (this can create legal liability if regulations mandate neutral presentation).

  • Do not use dense legal blocks like this for casual, non-regulatory consent flows (e.g., marketing opt-ins), where such formality would feel excessive and increase abandonment.

  • Not suitable for screens with time pressure or A/B tested "friction increases conversion" flows (here, legal accuracy must always outweigh speed).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users undergoing KYC (Know Your Customer) verification for a financial/investment account (e.g., a brokerage, neobank, or robo-advisor). The audience is broad (ranging from first-time investors to seasoned users) but the design specifically caters to non-experts who find tax terminology ("backup withholding," "perjury") intimidating.

The psychological trigger at play is friction reduction via authority and reassurance: by pre-filling the safe default and labeling the alternative as "Uncommon," the design leverages the user's desire to complete the flow correctly and quickly without needing to research tax law, thereby preventing task abandonment at a critical regulatory hurdle.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Default Pre-Selection: The "No" radio button is pre-checked, aligning with the statistical majority and drastically speeding up completion for 99% of users.

  • Dynamic Legal Personalization: Auto-inserting the user's legal name and the current date into the certification text increases perceived seriousness and reduces the feeling of reading generic boilerplate.

  • Normalizing Language: The "(Uncommon)" tag next to the rare "Yes" choice acts as a micro-nudge, guiding users through an intimidating legal decision without needing a lawyer.

  • Progressive Disclosure of Legal Text: Separating the "Question" from the "Full Legal Copy" into two cards lets users who trust the system skim quickly, while offering full transparency for cautious readers.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Creating Account 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any multi-step, backend-dependent process where the user has no control and must wait for a third-party or server response (particularly in fintech, insurance, or KYC (Know Your Customer) verification flows). It's ideal for account creation, loan applications, or identity verification submissions where naming the processing entity adds legitimacy.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach if the backend process is extremely fast (under 1-2 seconds), as an explicit "Opening Account" screen would feel like unnecessary friction; a simple inline button spinner would suffice. Additionally, do not name a third-party processor if the wait time is unpredictable or very long (over 10-15 seconds) without adding a progress indicator or reassuring sub-copy, as static text with no progress signal can heighten anxiety if the user perceives it as frozen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users in the final, most vulnerable step of a financial onboarding funnel, having just submitted sensitive personal and financial data (SSN, income, banking details). At this moment, users are highly susceptible to anxiety about data security and application approval odds.

By invoking the Goldman Sachs brand name, the design leverages the Authority/Halo Effect psychological trigger: associating the interstitial wait time with a globally recognized, trusted financial institution reduces the likelihood of the user backgrounding the app or panicking mid-submission, which could otherwise cause a failed transaction or a support ticket.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent Backend Naming: Explicitly naming the underlying bank partner (Goldman Sachs) during processing builds significant institutional trust, especially crucial for neobanks/fintechs that rely on partner banks for FDIC insurance.

  • Non-Intrusive Spinner Placement: Placing the loading indicator inline next to the header text (rather than a large centered overlay) reduces perceived wait time anxiety and keeps the UI feeling lightweight.

  • Minimalist, Uncluttered Canvas: The vast empty space below prevents overwhelming the user during a moment where they have no control, allowing them to mentally pause without visual noise.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Creating Account 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this modal-based status pattern when communicating high-stakes, legally-sensitive outcomes (loan/account rejections, KYC failures, compliance holds) where: (1) the user must not miss the message, (2) the reason cannot be disclosed in-app due to regulatory constraints, and (3) a clear human-support escalation path is required. It's ideal for banking, lending, insurance, and other regulated verticals.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for less severe or reversible issues where showing a full-screen interruption would feel excessive (use inline banners or toasts instead). Also avoid leaving large unused white space as done here; if there is room for actionable next steps (reapply, explore alternative products, chat with support), they should be surfaced rather than leaving a dead-end screen with only a phone number and a close button.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets everyday retail banking customers (in this case, likely Apple Card / Goldman Sachs savings account applicants) who have just been declined for a financial product. These users are often anxious or frustrated, so the psychological design goal is to minimize perceived blame ("was not approved" vs "rejected"), provide a clear next step (call center), and avoid trapping the user in the flow (hence the simple Close button that returns them to a neutral state in the app).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Actionable phone number: The support number is styled and tappable (blue, likely tel: link), reducing the friction of escalation for a user who may be confused or upset.

  • Neutral tone under stress: Avoiding alarming red colors or aggressive language for a rejection helps de-escalate user emotion in a sensitive financial moment.

  • Single clear exit: One unambiguous 'Close' button prevents decision paralysis and lets the user quickly dismiss the modal once informed.

results.query: Where not to use gamified scratch cards in financial apps

screens.name: Brilliant - Setting a streak goal - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately after any effortful, multi-step task is completed (lesson finishes, workout completions, onboarding steps, course modules, or any point where you want to convert user effort into a felt sense of accomplishment). It's especially effective in habit-forming, streak-based, or educational products where intrinsic motivation needs an extrinsic nudge.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy celebratory treatment for low-effort or frequent micro-actions (e.g., saving a form field, toggling a setting) - overuse dilutes its emotional impact and feels patronizing. It's also inappropriate in professional/enterprise tools where a playful, game-like tone would undermine credibility, or in flows where users need quick access to detailed performance review rather than a simple forward push.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-directed learners (students, professionals, lifelong learners) who need external motivation to sustain a daily STEM learning habit. By leveraging variable, game-like reward feedback (XP, sparkles, glowing badge), Brilliant taps into the same dopamine-driven reinforcement loops used by games and fitness apps (e.g., Duolingo, Headspace) to combat the inherent friction of effortful cognitive practice.

Psychologically, this screen exploits the Goal-Gradient Effect and positive reinforcement: by immediately celebrating completion with a tangible number and visual spectacle, it increases dopamine release and the likelihood the user returns for another lesson, counteracting the "doing is harder than watching" friction central to Brilliant's active-learning philosophy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose screen: No tab bar, header, or competing UI (the entire screen is devoted to one emotional beat (completion + reward)).
  • Illustration as reward object: The glowing badge/gem floating above a pedestal gives an intangible XP gain physical, collectible presence, increasing perceived value.
  • Particle/sparkle accents: Scattered star glyphs around the XP number create a celebratory, game-like micro-interaction feel even in a static state.
  • High-contrast single CTA: The full-width dark pill button leaves no ambiguity and keeps momentum moving forward through the linear lesson spine.
  • Numeric feedback loop: Displaying a running "Total XP" ties immediate lesson completion to long-term progress/levels, reinforcing habit formation.

screens.name: Brilliant - Setting a streak goal - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Immediately after a user's very first completed lesson, workout, or core action in any habit-building app (education, fitness, meditation, language learning).
  • At the start of any streak/consistency mechanic, to clearly onboard the user to how the tracker visually works.
  • Anywhere you want to stack a primary reward (streak) with a teaser of a secondary reward system (badges/gems) without overwhelming the user.
  • In linear, single-path flows where you want zero decision fatigue and a single forward CTA.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for power users or repeat streak days: showing a full-screen celebration every single day quickly becomes friction and annoyance (reserve full-screen treatment for day 1, first milestone, or significant streak lengths).
  • Not suitable for apps with non-daily cadences (e.g., monthly billing tools, B2B dashboards) where a "streak" framing feels gimmicky or irrelevant to the user's goals.
  • Avoid in contexts where users are already annoyed/fatigued by gamification (over-reliance on streak mechanics can feel manipulative if not paired with genuine content value).
  • Don't use if the app lacks a true multi-day engagement loop to back up the promise, introducing a streak mechanic without server-side logic/reminders to support it will lead to broken promises and abandoned streaks.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users at the most fragile point in the lifecycle (immediately after their very first completed action) when habit-formation hooks are most effective. By introducing the streak mechanic here rather than burying it in a profile or stats page, Brilliant leverages the fresh-start effect and operant conditioning: rewarding the first rep instantly to create a positive association with the act of returning.

The weekly tracker visualization exploits the Zeigarnik effect and loss-aversion psychology (once a user sees empty circles for Tuesday and Wednesday, an open loop is created that nags at them to "fill in" the week, increasing D2 and D3 retention likelihood).

The worldwide, STEM-curious audience (students, lifelong learners, professionals brushing up on math/CS) responds well to restrained, non-childish gamification (the muted color palette and clean iconography avoid feeling like a kids' app, respecting the intelligence of the user while still using proven retention mechanics).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-focus celebration: No navigation, no distractions (the entire screen is designed around one emotional beat and one forward action).
  • Layered reward stacking: The small badge/gem icon peeking from behind the lightning bolt subtly teases a secondary collectible system without stealing focus from the primary streak reward.
  • Numeral-as-hero typography: Making "1" the largest element on the page gives the streak count totemic, trophy-like significance from the very first day.
  • Immediate mental model of the mechanic: The M/T/W row teaches the weekly streak-tracking UI in-context, right at the moment of first use, rather than via a separate tutorial.
  • Illustration as content: Consistent with the app's design philosophy, the glowing 3D bolt isn't decorative - it is the message, communicating energy/momentum before any text is read.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for loyalty/rewards ecosystems where you want to convert passive point balances into daily active engagement (e).g., fintech super-apps, banking rewards, subscription loyalty tiers, or gamified e-commerce loyalty hubs. It's especially effective when the parent app already has a strong daily-use case (like bill payments) that this feature can piggyback on to drive incremental session time.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavily gamified, casino-styled approach in contexts requiring trust and seriousness (e.g., core banking transactions, insurance, medical apps) where a game-show tone could undermine credibility. It also risks regulatory scrutiny or user backlash if it too closely resembles real gambling mechanics, especially for financial products. Avoid stacking multiple competing game loops (jackpot + deal carousel) on one screen for less engaged or first-time users, as it can overwhelm and confuse rather than delight.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets highly engaged, reward-motivated CRED users (typically financially savvy, credit-card-holding millennials/Gen Z in India) who already treat CRED as a habitual, gamified financial app. It leverages variable-reward psychology (similar to slot machines) and loss-aversion (accumulated coin balance) to drive daily re-engagement even outside of bill-payment cycles. The casino/game-show aesthetic specifically appeals to users motivated by status, novelty, and the thrill of "winning," converting a passive loyalty-point balance into an active daily habit loop.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-Layer Gamification: Combining a sticky jackpot teaser banner with an independent horizontal deal carousel creates layered engagement hooks, maximizing time-on-app.

  • Virtual Currency Visibility: Persistently displaying the CRED Coins balance (2,87,222) keeps users aware of their "wallet," nudging them to spend/engage to avoid coin stagnation (sunk cost psychology).

  • Reveal-Based CTA ("Show"): Using "Show" instead of "Claim" or "Redeem" adds mystery and a slot-machine-like anticipation before the user sees what's behind the deal.

  • Theatrical Visual Framing: The curtain-line illustration motif around each deal card visually reinforces the "prize reveal" metaphor, elevating a discount mechanic into an entertainment experience.

  • Peek of Next Card: The partially visible next carousel card creates a Zeigarnik-effect nudge to keep swiping and discover more deals.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Loyalty/rewards modules in super-apps where the goal is to increase session frequency and dwell time beyond core utility.

  • Brand-sponsored discovery placements where a "gamified reveal" increases engagement with advertised products vs static banners.

  • Apps with an existing virtual currency economy (coins, points) needing a compelling sink to drive earn-and-spend loops.

  • Contexts targeting younger or deal-motivated users comfortable with playful, casino-adjacent aesthetics.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Regulated financial contexts (banking, insurance, investing) where gambling-like visuals could raise compliance/trust concerns or regulatory scrutiny.

  • Enterprise, B2B, or utility-first apps where users expect efficiency and transparency, not mystery mechanics.

  • Markets/demographics where gamified spending patterns are viewed as predatory or where users have low tolerance for perceived manipulation (e.g., older or vulnerable user segments).

  • Any flow requiring clear, unambiguous next steps (the intentional ambiguity here would frustrate users seeking speed and clarity).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets high-frequency, deal-seeking users of a financial/payments app who are motivated by micro-rewards, gamified savings, and the thrill of "winning" discounts rather than straightforward coupon redemption. It is most effective on younger, mobile-first, price-sensitive demographics (common in Indian fintech apps like CRED, PhonePe, or Google Pay) who already engage with cashback and rewards programs. Psychologically, it exploits variable-ratio reinforcement (unpredictable reward reveals), sunk-cost coin accumulation, and curiosity gaps to convert a mundane app-open into a repeat, dwell-time-generating ritual (directly increasing daily active usage and ad/brand-partner impressions (note the sponsored Nutri Bears product placement)).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Casino-Core Visual Language: Deep black background, gold sparkles, and glow effects borrowed from real-world gambling environments to elevate perceived reward value and dopamine anticipation.

  • Tiered Coin Gating: Different unlock costs (100 vs 1000 coins) per card create a soft paywall/scarcity dynamic that pushes users to earn and accumulate more virtual currency.

  • Ambiguous Central Portal: The ringed circular button with only an arrow icon (no label) leverages the curiosity gap (users must tap to discover, driving exploration-based engagement).

  • Reward-Category Teasers: Semi-transparent 3D icons (bag, gift, cash) hint at upcoming reward types without fully disclosing them, sustaining anticipation.

  • Bespoke Tab Bar Icon: The oversized, glowing coin-like icon replacing a standard tab icon signals this feature's strategic importance to the business (likely driving retention/DAU metrics).

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for loyalty, rewards, or benefits hubs within finance, banking, or subscription apps where the goal is to drive engagement and card/product usage through curated third-party partner offers. It's ideal when you have a large catalog of offers that needs both a "quick recognition" path (logos) and a "guided browse" path (categories) to serve different user intents simultaneously.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy editorial/lifestyle treatment for core account functions like balance checks, statements, or bill payments, where users need speed and clarity over inspiration. Also avoid if the offer catalog is small (under ~20 items), as the multi-layered browse structure (logos + tabs + grid + CTA) would feel like overkill and create unnecessary navigation depth for a sparse dataset.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets credit card holders, likely of a premium or mid-to-premium tier card, who are motivated by maximizing rewards, cashback, and lifestyle perks. The demographic skews toward digitally savvy, urban shoppers who actively compare offers across shopping, travel, and dining categories (evident from brands like Myntra, Amazon, MakeMyTrip, Goibibo).

Psychologically, the design leverages reward salience (leading with numbers like "5x" and "2%"), recognition over recall (using familiar brand logos instead of text lists), and abundance framing (246 offers) to make the user feel their card unlocks disproportionate value, encouraging continued card usage and spend.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Editorial art direction: Serif typography and dark theme elevate a routine "rewards" screen into a premium lifestyle experience, differentiating it from generic banking UI.

  • Dual-path discovery: Users can either jump directly via recognizable merchant logos (goal-directed) or browse via category tabs (exploratory), covering both user intent types on one screen.

  • Quantified CTA: "Explore all 246 offers" uses a precise number to signal abundance and build anticipation, a subtle scarcity/social-proof-adjacent trick that increases click-through over a vague "See more".

  • Photography-led cards: Using real human lifestyle photos instead of generic icons for offer cards makes the reward emotionally resonant and aspirational.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any rewards, loyalty, or benefits marketplace where a single account/card unlocks a large catalog of third-party offers (e).g., banking apps, telecom loyalty programs, insurance wellness perks, or subscription bundle hubs (like Amazon Prime perks). It's especially effective when:

  • The offer catalog is large enough to warrant both search and categorical browsing.

  • Users may hold multiple accounts/cards/tiers and need clear context of which is active.

  • Brand recognition of partner merchants is high, making logo-based scanning faster than text descriptions.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, multi-section browsing pattern when the offer catalog is small (under ~15 items) - the overhead of categories, spotlight carousels, and trending sections would feel bloated and better replaced by a single flat list. It's also unsuitable for elderly or low-tech-literacy user bases where a dark theme and dense horizontal scrolling carousels can reduce discoverability and accessibility (low contrast, hidden off-screen content). Additionally, if the app's user rarely holds multiple cards, the card-switcher affordance becomes unnecessary complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets credit card holders who are value-conscious and reward-motivated: likely millennial and Gen-Z Indian consumers who actively seek to maximize cashback, discounts, and reward points across shopping, travel, and dining categories. The presence of an Axis Bank. Flipkart co-branded card suggests a user base that is digitally savvy and habituated to e-commerce platforms like Amazon, Myntra, and Ajio.

The spotlight logo carousel taps into brand recognition heuristics, letting users make snap decisions based on trusted merchant names rather than reading detailed copy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Quantified search placeholder: "search from 131 offers" turns a passive input field into a value statement, subtly reinforcing card membership benefits before the user even types.

  • Dual discovery pathways: Combining a search bar, brand-logo spotlight carousel, and image-based category tiles gives both intent-driven and exploratory users an efficient path to relevant offers.

  • Visual category tiles: Using evocative lifestyle photography (a model in glasses for shopping, hot air balloons for travel) instead of generic icons makes the category rail feel aspirational and editorial rather than utilitarian.

  • Persistent card context switcher: The card name and dropdown chevron at the top ensures multi-card holders always know which card's offer ecosystem they're browsing, reducing costly misredemption errors.

  • Dark, premium visual theme: The near-black background elevates the perceived exclusivity of the rewards program, differentiating it from standard banking UI chrome.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a product has a loyalty/points economy and you want to drive daily active usage through a habitual, time-gated reward mechanic. It's ideal for lifestyle, fintech, or rewards-based apps aiming to gamify commerce, convert dormant loyalty points into engagement, and create a "check back daily" habit loop. The animated unlock CTA works well when you want to soften the perception of a "purchase" and instead frame it as unlocking an earned reward.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in utilitarian or transactional-heavy contexts (e.g., B2B procurement, grocery essentials, or emergency services) where users need fast, predictable purchasing flows without theatrical delay. Overusing scarcity/urgency messaging without genuine limited inventory can erode trust once users realize deals reset identically every day. Also avoid the animated unlock delay for high-frequency purchases, as artificial waiting states can frustrate power users making repeat transactions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets CRED's core demographic: financially engaged, credit-card-paying millennials/young professionals in India who already use the app for bill payments and enjoy status/reward gamification. These users are motivated by exclusivity, aesthetics, and the feeling of "insider access" that CRED cultivates across its entire product (member-only credit score perks, curated brand deals, coin-based games).

The psychological triggers at play include: scarcity (limited units, one deal per day), variable/time-gated reward (return at 1 PM to see what's new, similar to loot-box mechanics), sunk-cost reinforcement (spending earned coins feels "free" and encourages redemption to avoid coin decay), and curiosity gap (edge-peeking carousel items hinting at more without full reveal).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Animated lock/capsule CTA: Replacing a boring "Buy Now" button with a suspended padlock visual that says "Unlocking..." adds theatricality and delight to a routine purchase action.

  • Edge-peeking carousel items: Partially visible products (coffee jar, ceiling fan) at the screen edges create curiosity and invite horizontal exploration without extra UI chrome.

  • Recurring time anchor ("1 PM Daily"): Encourages daily app visits by turning the deal into a scheduled ritual, similar to daily-reward mechanics in gaming apps.

  • Coin-based unlock, not cash-first: Leading with coin cost rather than currency price reframes the offer as a reward redemption, leveraging the sunk-cost/earned-currency psychology of CRED's point system.

  • Seamless transition to "Steal Deals": Immediately below the hero deal, a secondary scarcity-driven grid keeps momentum going and increases average session engagement.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 6

screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavily gamified "unlocked" framing on price-sensitive, utilitarian marketplaces (e.g., grocery or B2B procurement apps) where users expect transparent, straightforward pricing and may find gamification manipulative or confusing. screens.keyHighlights:

  • Gamified microcopy: "UNLOCKED" and "PRICE UNLOCKED" badges transform a routine discount into an earned reward, tapping into achievement psychology.

  • Coin reward tease: "you won 90 coins" nudges users toward the purchase by implying additional value/currency is attached to this specific deal.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when an app needs to perform an asynchronous data-fetching task (e.g., querying an external database, scanning a document, or processing an ID) that takes more than 2-3 seconds. screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen takeover for near-instantaneous actions, as the animation delay might actually slow down the perceived speed of the app. Additionally, if the backend process is prone to frequent errors or timeouts, relying on a single static loading screen without a fallback/cancel option could trap users in a dead-end state.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets vehicle owners, likely urban drivers or fleet managers who are anxious about undisclosed tickets, camera violations, or DMV holds. The psychological trigger here is the "Reveal" mechanic (by showing a loading/scanning state, the app builds suspense and perceived value, making the user feel that a rigorous, comprehensive check is being performed on their behalf before the "big reveal" of results (which likely follows on the next screen)).
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you want to increase engagement with an inherently infrequent or utilitarian check-in task (bill payments, compliance checks, health screenings, security audits). It's effective when the "good" outcome (zero violations, zero debt, clean record) can be framed as a countable streak worth protecting.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach when the underlying subject matter is severe or anxiety-driving for a meaningful subset of users (e.g., users who already have violations may feel shamed by streak-breaking framing). screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets everyday vehicle owners in markets with digital traffic-fine (challan) lookup services, likely India given the terminology. The design leans heavily on loss aversion (don't break the streak) and status/social comparison (being among the "select few") to drive repeat check-ins on what would otherwise be a low-frequency, utilitarian task.

By gamifying a compliance record, the product increases session frequency and retention, turning a purely functional government-data lookup into an emotionally engaging ritual similar to fitness or habit-tracking apps.
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use this celebratory empty-state pattern when:

  • A "zero" or "no results" outcome is objectively good news for the user (e.g., no fines, no errors, no security issues, inbox zero, no bugs found).

  • You want to increase engagement or retention for infrequently-used utility features by making the outcome feel rewarding.

  • The brand voice supports a more playful, human tone even within a serious or bureaucratic domain (finance, legal, compliance, health checks, security scans).

  • You want to differentiate a checking/scanning feature from a purely transactional tool, encouraging repeat usage or social sharing of good results.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • A "zero" result could actually be ambiguous or concerning (e.g., zero results due to a system/search error rather than genuinely no violations) - celebrating incorrectly could erode trust if data is wrong or incomplete.

  • The user base or context demands a strictly formal, neutral tone (e.g., official government portals, legal documentation, enterprise compliance dashboards) where celebratory language may seem unprofessional or trivializing.

  • There is no clear next action and the celebratory screen becomes a dead-end; if used, ensure there's still a path back to core app value (e.g., check another vehicle, view details, share).

  • Users check this frequently: over-celebrating a routine, expected outcome can feel patronizing or gimmicky over repeated exposures.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday vehicle owners in markets (likely India, given "challan" terminology) who use an app to check pending traffic fines associated with their vehicle registration number. The primary psychological trigger is positive reinforcement: users checking for fines often approach the screen with mild anxiety (fear of an unexpected penalty), and the app immediately converts that anxiety into relief and pride.

By labeling a "zero" result as an achievement ("mark of a great driver") rather than a neutral non-event, the app taps into identity-based motivation: users are subtly encouraged to see themselves as responsible, rule-abiding drivers, which can increase their emotional attachment to the app and likelihood of returning to check again (creating a habit loop around a otherwise infrequent utility action).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reframing a null state as a celebration: Rather than a sterile "No records found," the absence of data (0 challans) is turned into a badge of honor, creating a small dopamine hit for the user.

  • Bold typographic hierarchy: Oversized, high-contrast, colorful headline against a near-black background maximizes emotional impact and readability in a single glance.

  • Radial burst background motif: Subtle sunburst rays behind the text mimic celebratory/spotlight effects (similar to confetti or achievement unlocks) without needing heavy animation or illustration assets.

  • Color-coded data point: The "0 challans" figure is rendered in green, instantly communicating a positive status via color psychology before the user even parses the words.

  • Minimal, single-action dismissal: Only one interactive element (the X), keeping the moment focused purely on the emotional payoff rather than pushing the user toward another task immediately.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 10

Additionally, artificial urgency (identical "expires in 05 days" on every card) should be used carefully and truthfully, reusing a static countdown across unrelated offers can erode trust once users notice the pattern is fake or non-dynamic.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of fintech, super-app, or cashback/rewards platforms (likely an Indian neobank or bill-payment/rewards aggregator given the Axis Bank/IOCL/RuPay branding) who respond well to gamified, dopamine-driven engagement loops rather than plain transactional lists.

The psychological triggers at play include the variable reward mechanism (borrowed from gambling/slot machines) to keep users checking back for new "wins," loss aversion and urgency via the persistent countdown badges, and status/progress signaling via the lifetime voucher count that encourages users to keep accumulating for bragging rights or a sense of achievement. This approach is best suited to younger, mobile-first, engagement-sensitive demographics (e.g., Gen Z/millennial users in emerging markets) who are more receptive to playful, high-energy financial UX than to sober, traditional banking interfaces.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Casino/Jackpot Framing: Using "you won" language and playing-card/poker chip artwork to describe a fintech cashback offer taps into variable-reward psychology, making mundane credit card perks feel like slot machine payouts.

  • Lifetime Counter as Trophy Case: Displaying "lifetime: 127" alongside "active: 3" instantly signals social/self status and progress, encouraging users to view voucher collection as an ongoing game with a running score.

  • Consistent Urgency Badge: The "EXPIRES IN 05 DAYS" clock chip is applied uniformly across disparate card types, systematizing urgency as a core structural element rather than an occasional promotional flourish.

screens.name: Cleo Reviewing & Rating 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when introducing a new gamified feature, challenge, or habit-tracking module inside an existing app (especially for financial wellness, fitness, or productivity products where users need convincing before opting into a commitment (e).g., a savings challenge, workout streak, or reading goal). It works well as a feature-spotlight interstitial reached via a tab or nudge, not necessarily as first-run onboarding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, bold-typography sales-page style for features that are frequently revisited or purely utilitarian (e.g., settings, account info) since the emotional build-up would feel exhausting on repeat views. Also avoid mock "success state" previews if the feature is unlikely to produce quick wins in reality, overpromising a completed streak/savings result can create disappointment and erode trust if actual usage rarely matches the idealized preview.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets financially stressed, habit-driven spenders (Cleo's core Gen Z/young millennial demographic) who respond better to playful, meme-literate coaching than to spreadsheet-style budgeting tools. The screen leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Loss/shame framing ("vices," "finally"): subtly signals the user's current spending is a problem, creating motivation to act.

  • Vicarious success priming: showing a completed 21-day streak taps into modeling/observational learning ("if the example did it, I can too)."

  • Micro-reward anticipation: the "$85" savings figure and celebratory emoji give a concrete, near-term payoff that feels achievable rather than abstract.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Functional preview instead of static illustration: Showing an actual mock habit-tracker card with a progress bar and streak status lets users instantly understand the mechanic before opting in, lowering cognitive friction and hesitation.

  • Pre-completed social proof state: The example shown is "Day 21 of 21: on track" (a fully successful, completed cycle) priming the user with a vivid picture of success rather than an ambiguous empty state.

  • Simulated encouragement bubbles: Overlaying chat-style affirmations onto the preview card lets the product "demo" its own positive-reinforcement/gamification loop within a static onboarding screen.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: One large "Start 🚀" button removes decision paralysis and funnels 100% of intent toward challenge activation.

screens.name: Cleo Reviewing & Rating 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing a new, potentially unfamiliar feature inside an already-installed app, especially one that requires behavior change (habit formation, financial discipline, fitness, learning). It's ideal for:

  • Feature-specific onboarding accessed via a tab or menu item, not the app's initial first-run experience.

  • Features that benefit from framing as a "challenge" or game to increase motivation and follow-through.

  • Situations where you want to set expectations across 2 (4 distinct sub-capabilities before the user dives in).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for:

  • Frequently revisited screens: once a user has seen this explainer, it should not reappear on every visit to the Habits tab (it should convert into the actual challenge-creation flow going forward).

  • Features that are self-explanatory or icon-driven, where an explainer screen would feel like unnecessary friction before task completion.

  • Serious/regulated financial contexts (e.g., loan applications, tax tools) where playful, game-like language ("vice," "challenge") could undermine trust or feel tonally inappropriate.

  • Users who are already power users of the app: repeated exposure to marketing-style value props can feel patronizing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers: likely younger millennials/Gen Z users of a neobank or budgeting app (who struggle with impulse spending and are more motivated by gamified, competitive framing than by traditional budgeting spreadsheets or dry financial advice).

Psychologically, it leverages several triggers: loss aversion and self-competition (challenging your "vice" implies a battle with a personal flaw you want to overcome), goal-gradient effect (tracking savings growth visually motivates continued engagement), and curiosity/self-insight (the "Spot trends" card promises revealing, possibly uncomfortable truths about spending habits, which is intrinsically compelling). Framing money management as a game or "challenge" lowers the psychological barrier to engaging with a topic (personal finance) that often produces shame or avoidance.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotionally-charged reframing of a mundane task: Saving money is rebranded as a "challenge" against one's own "vice," tapping into gamification and self-improvement psychology rather than dry budgeting language.

  • Three-card benefit breakdown maps to a full behavioral loop (choose challenge → track progress → gain insight), giving users a mental model of the entire feature before they commit to using it.

  • Non-blocking onboarding: Persistent tab bar and back arrow ensure this educational screen never feels like a forced gate, preserving user autonomy and reducing bounce/frustration.

  • Consistent thematic iconography: The checkered flag emoji on the CTA button echoes the "challenge/race" metaphor set up in the headline, creating narrative and visual cohesion end-to-end.

  • High-contrast, bold typography immediately communicates energy and confidence, differentiating the feature from typically dry financial UI.

screens.name: Cleo Reviewing & Rating 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when trying to convert an infrequent, low-motivation task (financial reviews, health check-ins, journaling) into a recurring habit. It's ideal for apps with a defined cadence (e.g., twice weekly) where you want to visually preview upcoming touchpoints and reward consistency. Works well anywhere a "streak" or "path" metaphor can be layered onto a functional task to boost return visits.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for one-time or purely transactional tasks where a recurring cadence doesn't apply (the locked future nodes and streak framing would feel forced or confusing). Also avoid overly playful/gamified framing ("expose your vices") in contexts serving highly sensitive financial situations (e.g., debt collection, financial hardship tools) where a lighthearted tone could feel tone-deaf or trivializing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers using a neobank/budgeting app (likely similar to Cleo, Copilot, or Chime-style habit trackers) who need lightweight behavioral nudges to engage with financial self-reflection. The design leans heavily on gamification psychology: streak counters and locked/unlocked path nodes exploit the same reward loops found in fitness and language-learning apps, converting a chore (reviewing spend) into a game with visible progress and stakes.

The "0" streak paired with a flame icon leverages loss-aversion and a fresh-start effect, showing the user they're at zero creates a subtle itch to build the streak back up. The provocative "expose your vices" copy signals this is aimed at users who want blunt, judgment-free insight into impulsive spending habits, appealing to a self-improvement/accountability-seeking mindset rather than traditional spreadsheet budgeters.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Streak-as-navigation metaphor: The 3-step horizontal path (unlocked star → locked padlock → locked padlock) borrows directly from game/habit-app UX (Duolingo-style) to visualize progress and future commitment simultaneously.

  • Dual stat framing: Pairing "Review streak: 0" with "For review: 20 spends" creates both a motivational deficit (streak reset) and a tangible workload indicator, nudging the user to act now before the backlog grows.

  • Locked future nodes: Greyed-out padlocks for future review dates set expectation of a recurring cadence and imply that skipping today jeopardizes the whole sequence (a subtle loss-aversion cue).

  • Contextual explainer banner: The "why + when" info banner sits directly below the CTA, pre-empting the user's hesitation without requiring a separate onboarding flow.

screens.name: Cleo Reviewing & Rating 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when trying to convert a low-engagement, obligatory task (financial review, health logging, learning recaps) into a recurring habit loop. Ideal for apps that benefit from periodic (not daily) check-ins, where a calendar-based streak with witty personalized insights can re-engage users without feeling naggy. Effective in consumer fintech, wellness, and habit-tracking apps targeting younger demographics.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in serious, high-trust financial contexts (e.g., wealth management, tax, enterprise banking) where a jokey or sassy tone could undermine credibility and trust. Also avoid streak-based guilt mechanics for users managing financial stress or debt, as loss-aversion messaging around money habits can increase anxiety rather than motivation.
