screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for rewards, promotions, or incentives hubs within fintech, e-commerce, or loyalty-driven apps where the goal is to drive repeat engagement and behavior change (referrals, increased transaction volume, feature adoption). It's especially effective when you have a heterogeneous mix of offer types (partner deals, referral bonuses, cashback) that benefit from a unified scannable list format. The playful illustrated header works well for consumer apps trying to soften a transactional or financial context.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach in enterprise, B2B, or highly regulated financial contexts (e.g., investment platforms, tax tools) where a playful, game-like tone could undermine trust or perceived seriousness. Also avoid heavy truncation when the offer terms carry legal/compliance weight (e.g., interest rates, T&Cs) - users need enough information up front to avoid misunderstanding, and hidden critical details behind a tap can create compliance or trust risk. If the offer volume is very low (1-2 items), this full-page list format is overkill and a simpler banner or card would suffice.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets the broad base of everyday Google Pay users (particularly deal-seeking and cashback-motivated segments who are incentivized to increase their transaction frequency and volume through the app). It also targets users who are candidates for network-effect growth loops (referral offers).

Psychologically, the design leverages several triggers: variable reward (surprise vouchers, capped at 2/week, mimic slot-machine style unpredictability), reciprocity and social incentive (refer-a-friend cashback), and curiosity gaps (truncated copy). The gamified header art also taps into nostalgia and playfulness, lowering the psychological barrier associated with financial apps and making frequent return visits to the "Offers" tab feel more like checking a game inventory than reviewing a bank statement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Gamified Hero Illustration: The platform-game-style header with coins, stars, and a boat character reframes "earning offers" as a playful adventure rather than a financial chore, boosting emotional engagement before any content is read.

  • Consistent Card Anatomy: Every offer tile uses the same icon-title-description-chevron structure, drastically reducing the learning curve as users scroll through the list.

  • Curiosity-Driven Truncation: Ellipsis truncation on both title and body text creates an information gap that nudges taps without cluttering the compact card layout.

  • Mixed Partner & Native Offers: Blending third-party merchant offers (FavePay) with native Google Pay offers (referrals, vouchers, P2P incentives) increases perceived value density of the offers hub.

screens.name: Google Pay Redeeming 18
screens.whereToUse:
Use this stacked-card offer feed pattern when:

  • Aggregating heterogeneous reward types (cashback, vouchers, discounts) from multiple sources (first-party + partner brands) into one unified, scannable list.

  • You want to encourage habitual "checking" behavior (e.g., daily/weekly) without relying on aggressive gamification UI like points bars or countdown timers.

  • The underlying offers vary greatly in complexity/terms, so a summary-then-drill-down flow is preferable to cramming details into the list view.

  • Brand trust and calm visual tone are priorities over conversion-maximizing urgency tactics.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Offers are highly time-sensitive and truly urgent (e.g., expiring in hours) - the neutral, non-urgent visual treatment here would undersell real scarcity and needs badges/timers instead.

  • Users need to compare multiple offers side-by-side quickly; the vertical single-column list with truncated text makes comparison shopping slow.

  • The offer catalog is very large (100+), in which case flat lists without filtering/categorization (visible here only via an ambiguous overflow menu) will hurt discoverability (faceted browse or search would perform better).

  • The brand identity calls for high-energy, sales-driven merchandising (e.g., flash-sale apps) - this restrained Google-style treatment would feel underwhelming and reduce perceived urgency/value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday Google Pay users in a market with an active local merchant loyalty ecosystem (evidenced by DBS/POSB and HSBC card-linked promos, and Golden Village cinema chain (likely Singapore/SEA)). The design assumes a price-sensitive, deal-seeking user segment that checks the offers tab periodically to find cashback or voucher opportunities before making a purchase, particularly around entertainment (movies) and P2P transfers.

Psychologically, the screen leverages variable reward anticipation (surprise vouchers, capped at "max 2 a week") to create a lottery-like intermittent reinforcement loop that encourages repeat visits to the Offers tab, a classic gamification lever borrowed from casino/loyalty psychology but delivered with Google's understated visual restraint so it doesn't feel manipulative.

The "Send money to friends" reward simultaneously serves a growth/network-effects function (monetarily incentivizing P2P transfers to another Google Pay user helps expand the platform's active-user graph, disguised here as a simple offer rather than an explicit referral campaign).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Uniform card template: Avatar + brand + headline + subtext + chevron repeated identically across every row, enabling fast visual scanning without reading effort.

  • Curiosity-gap truncation: Ellipsis-truncated headlines and descriptions create a soft incentive loop, nudging taps without resorting to aggressive CTAs or banners.

  • Dual-source offer feed: Mixing first-party (Google Pay) and third-party (Golden Village) offers in a single unified feed maximizes perceived value density and offer inventory without needing separate tabs.

  • Restrained visual design: No badges, no red dots, no countdown timers (reward discovery feels calm and non-manipulative, matching the trust-first brand ethos).

  • Referral-style incentive embedded as an offer: "Send money to friends" reframes a peer-to-peer referral/growth loop as a passive reward card rather than a separate onboarding nudge.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 13
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech/neobank apps where the payment card is a core brand touchpoint and users need quick access to card-specific actions (freeze, share details, request replacement, settings).

  • Product detail screens for physical/digital hybrid objects (loyalty cards, ID cards, transit passes) where visual realism aids recognition.

  • Screens targeting returning, habitual users who prioritize speed over guidance and have already learned the iconography.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid icon-only controls for first-time users or complex/destructive actions (e.g., card cancellation) without labels or confirmation, as ambiguity can cause costly mistakes.

  • Not suitable for accessibility-critical contexts without added text labels or screen-reader support, since meaning relies entirely on icon shape recognition.

  • Avoid oversized decorative hero objects on data-dense utility screens where users need to scan multiple pieces of information (balance, transactions) simultaneously (this layout sacrifices information density for visual impact).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets digitally-native banking or neobank customers (e.g., users of apps like Revolut, N26, Cash App, or Dave) who expect their card to be a visual, ownable, personalized asset rather than a buried line item in a list. The neon color choice and stylized flat design appeal to a younger, design-conscious demographic that values aesthetic customization and brand identity in financial products.

Psychologically, presenting the card at near-life-size scale and allowing direct manipulation (flip, freeze, actions) creates a sense of tangible ownership and control over one's finances, reducing the anxiety often associated with abstract digital money by tethering it to a familiar physical object metaphor.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero card treatment: The card occupies ~70% of the vertical viewport, using scale and a saturated neon color to command attention and reinforce brand personality/ownership.

  • Symmetrical action clusters: Placing four actions above and four below the card creates balanced visual weight and implies these are peer-level, frequently used utilities (e.g., lock, share, refresh/replace, settings).

  • Single active-state button: The one filled black circle stands out instantly against six gray ghost buttons, guiding the eye to the most contextually relevant or currently selected action.

  • Realistic chip rendering: The photorealistic EMV chip graphic anchors the abstract color block as an unmistakable "credit/debit card" object, aiding instant recognition.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 14
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when:

  • Offering physical/virtual product personalization (cards, phone cases, merchandise) where the preview must match the final real-world object precisely.

  • Targeting a self-expressive, design-savvy audience for whom customization is a retention/virality lever.

  • Building creative tools where drawing, doodling, or freeform marking is the primary interaction (notes, whiteboards, signature capture).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The product is purely utilitarian/regulated and customization introduces compliance risk (e.g., legally required card number/logo placement rules could be violated by user drawings overlapping them).

  • Users are less tech-savvy and require labeled/tooltip-guided tools rather than icon-only affordances (icon-only UI can create ambiguity for first-time users without prior onboarding).

  • Performance-constrained devices where real-time freehand rendering could introduce lag, harming perceived quality.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets fintech/neobank usersownership and identity psychology: when users invest creative effort into a product (IKEA effect), they form stronger emotional attachment and brand loyalty. The doodle/signature format also evokes nostalgia (yearbook signing, sneaker customization) which drives shareability on social media, turning the card into organic marketing material.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-bleed live card preview: Editing happens directly on a 1:1 representation of the final product, including the true chip position and a reserved area for embossed text, giving true WYSIWYG confidence.

  • Clear active-state affordance: The pen tool is filled solid black against light-grey siblings, immediately communicating which mode is engaged without a label.

  • Symmetrical top/bottom toolbar split: Navigation/meta actions vs. creative tools are spatially separated, reducing cognitive load and mirroring familiar pro-creative-app conventions.

  • Minimal, icon-only chrome: Maximizes canvas real estate and keeps the emotional focus on the personalized artwork rather than UI decoration.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Sticker, emoji, GIF, or decal picker modals in photo/video editing and messaging apps.

  • Asset libraries for creative tools (tattoo design apps, scrapbooking, mood-board builders) where visual scanning trumps textual search.

  • Any "add embellishment" flow where the content itself is inherently graphical and self-explanatory.

  • Contexts where a lightweight modal overlay with a clear commit/cancel binary choice is preferable to a full navigational screen.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this chrome-less, label-free grid for functional or transactional content (e.g., settings, financial items) where users need textual context to make informed decisions.

  • Not suitable for large catalogs without search/filter/category navigation (pure infinite grid browsing breaks down past a few dozen items and users need Faceted/Filtered Browse or Search-First Navigation instead).

  • Rotated/sideways content orientation is risky for accessibility and general usability outside of a specific stylistic/creative-tool context; avoid for mainstream, task-oriented apps.

  • Disabled CTA without a hint/tooltip explaining why can confuse first-time users (pair with a coach mark if audience is not already familiar with the pattern).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets younger, visually-driven users (Gen Z/millennial) engaging with social/creative apps such as photo editors, BeReal-style camera apps, journaling apps, or sticker/tattoo design tools. The psychological driver is the "paradox of choice made fun" - a large gallery of playful, aesthetic options encourages exploratory browsing and self-expression rather than task-efficiency. The disabled Add button leverages a Zeigarnik-effect-like tension: users feel compelled to complete the task (pick something) to unlock progress, nudging engagement and selection completion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Content-first, chrome-less layout: Removing all labels, section titles, and search bars maximizes visual real estate for browsing purely by recognition rather than reading.

  • Disabled-until-valid CTA pattern: The greyed-out "Add" button enforces a clear selection requirement, preventing accidental empty submissions and giving unambiguous state feedback.

  • Symmetrical Cancel/Add placement: Mirrors standard iOS modal conventions (dismiss on one side, commit on the other), making the interaction instantly familiar despite the unconventional rotated grid.

  • Mixed content grid: Combining hand-drawn line icons with script typography stickers in one unified grid keeps visual density high while offering variety (graphic vs. text-based expression).

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 16
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a product wants to differentiate a otherwise commoditized physical or digital object (cards, avatars, profile covers, merch) through user-generated customization. It's ideal for consumer fintech, social, or lifestyle apps targeting younger demographics who value self-expression and are likely to share their creations. It works well as a delight/retention moment post-signup or during onboarding to build emotional investment early.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of playful freehand customization in enterprise, B2B, or highly regulated financial contexts where trust, security, and professionalism are paramount, doodling on a "serious" financial instrument could undermine credibility for older or risk-averse users. Also avoid if the underlying card art/branding has legal or compliance constraints that limit how much can be altered, or if users lack fine motor precision on small screens without a stylus.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets younger, design-conscious users (Gen Z / young Millennials) drawn to fintech products like Cash App, Revolut, or Cleo that differentiate through personality and personalization rather than pure utility. The psychological driver is ownership and identity expression: by letting users literally draw on their card, the product taps into the IKEA effect (people value things more when they helped create them) and turns a mundane financial object into a piece of self-expression worth sharing on social media, driving organic virality and brand affinity.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Card-as-canvas metaphor: Turning the literal card artwork into an editable drawing surface makes personalization tangible and emotionally resonant (users aren't picking a color from a swatch, they're literally drawing on "their" card).

  • Symmetrical dual toolbar: Splitting tools above and below the canvas keeps the drawing surface unobstructed by fingers/thumbs while still keeping all controls within easy thumb reach.

  • Color-coded primary action: The green back/confirm button stands out immediately from the uniform gray tool icons, preventing accidental exits and signaling "this is different from the other buttons."

  • Realistic chip rendering: Keeping the EMV chip photorealistic amid hand-drawn doodles grounds the fantasy in reality, reassuring the user this is still a functional, legitimate payment card.

  • Undo/Redo affordance: Prominent undo/redo icons reduce fear of "ruining" the design, encouraging experimentation.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 17
screens.whereToUse:
• Physical product customization flows (cards, merch, hardware) where showing a rendered final preview builds purchase confidence.

  • Final review/confirmation steps in a multi-step configurator, right before a commit action.

  • Any flow where you want to visually reduce the psychological distance between a digital choice and a physical real-world object.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for purely digital or intangible products where a physical mockup adds no value or could feel gimmicky.

  • Not appropriate when the customization involves financial risk or legal terms that need more prominent disclosure (a lightweight two-button footer would under-serve compliance requirements).

  • Avoid if the preview rendering cannot be generated quickly/accurately, as a slow or generic-looking preview undermines the "what you see is what you get" trust signal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets younger, design-conscious banking customers (Gen Z/Millennial) for whom a debit card is also a form of self-expression, similar to phone cases or sneaker customization. The psychological trigger at play is ownership bias / IKEA effect: by allowing the user to draw or stamp their own design, the resulting product feels more valuable and desirable, increasing the likelihood of completing the order. The "glow in the dark" feature also leverages novelty appeal and social shareability (a card that looks cool on social media), which is a growth/acquisition lever for challenger banks.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live, rendered product preview: Rather than a generic stock photo, the card mock-up dynamically reflects the user's actual customization (handwriting/doodle), closing the gap between digital configuration and physical expectation.

  • Redacted card number: The card number area is intelligently blurred/obscured in the preview even in a mock context, reinforcing security-conscious design patterns users expect from financial apps.

  • Clear CTA hierarchy: Two-tier button styling (neutral secondary vs. solid black primary) guides the user toward the intended "Order card" action while still surfacing the edit option without shame or friction.

  • Benefit-led headline over feature-led: "Glow in the dark" sells an emotional/sensory outcome rather than a spec sheet, increasing desirability of a mundane utility object (a debit card).

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 18
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when a single app offers multiple loosely-related financial or subscription products and you need a scalable, low-friction way to surface all of them without building separate dashboards or resorting to disruptive pop-ups. It's ideal for super-apps, neobanks, or platforms cross-selling investing, lending, insurance, or premium tiers to an existing user base that already trusts the core product for one primary use case (e.g., payments).

It also works well for personalized "recommended next steps" sections in fintech, healthtech, or any multi-service platform where each recommendation needs a consistent, scannable template (icon, benefit-led subtitle, single CTA) to reduce decision fatigue across many options.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern on a primary balance/home screen where users need immediate clarity on their current cash position, burying the actual account balance below a promotional module can feel manipulative and erode trust, especially in finance apps where users check balances frequently and urgently.

Also avoid when products being cross-sold require heavy regulatory disclosures or risk warnings (e.g., crypto, BNPL, investing) - a single-line subtitle and "Start" button can understate risk and lead to compliance or dark-pattern concerns if users don't fully grasp the commitment before drilling in. In such cases, add clearer risk framing or a short intermediate disclosure step before the deep-link into onboarding.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing peer-to-peer payment users (likely Cash App) who already trust the platform for sending/receiving money and are being nudged toward becoming full-service banking/investing customers. The design leverages the foot-in-the-door principle: by starting with trivial, low-stakes financial actions (invest $1, check tax refund estimate), the product incrementally escalates commitment and deepens wallet share.

The inclusion of "Family: Invite your teen" targets a specific demographic expansion strategy (parents of teens), using social/family motivation rather than personal finance motivation to drive a completely different acquisition channel. Similarly, "Afterpay ($200 available" targets budget-conscious or credit-averse users with an already-approved-feeling credit line, exploiting the endowment effect (money that's "available" feels like it's already theirs)).

The flat, non-intrusive presentation (list items, not full-screen modals or aggressive banners) suggests this targets users in a passive browsing mindset (checking their money screen for balance/status) who are then opportunistically shown relevant next-step products without disrupting their primary task.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unified cross-sell list pattern: Five distinct financial products (investing, crypto, tax, family, BNPL) are normalized into one repeatable icon/title/subtitle/CTA template, making a sprawling product suite feel like a single tidy feature list instead of five separate app pitches.

  • Friction-reducing microcopy: Subtitles like "Invest with $1" preemptively answer the biggest objection (cost/complexity) for each product in-line, right where the decision is made (no need to tap in to learn the barrier to entry).

  • Soft-commitment CTA labeling: "Start" instead of "Buy," "Invest," or "Apply" lowers perceived risk and encourages exploratory taps, increasing top-of-funnel conversion into onboarding flows.

  • Two-tier card hierarchy: The "Pools" balance card and "Direct deposit" card use elevated white surfaces against the grey background to visually separate "your data" modules from the flat-list "recommendation" modules below.

results.query: Designing for low-bandwidth offline connectivity during audio identification

screens.name: Home Screen
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits single-purpose, sensor-driven capture apps where one action dominates all others and the moment of use is fleeting (audio recognition, scanning, quick capture) and where secondary features exist mainly to store or extend the results.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for multi-purpose apps where two or more actions have comparable frequency, since elevating one to hero status makes the others feel buried; it also wastes a screen's worth of real estate in content-led products where the user arrives to browse rather than to act.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Snapchat: Opens directly on the capture surface with one dominant circular action and peer destinations relegated to a bottom rail. Same premise: the moment is perishable, so the app opens in the tool rather than in a menu.

  2. Yuka (and barcode-scanner apps generally): Hero scan button on the home screen, with scan history as a secondary tab. Structurally identical: a single sensor-driven capture that produces a saved record you can revisit.

  3. Google (Search a song / hum to search): The same audio-recognition task exposed as one prominent tap, and a fair comparison because it shows the pattern holds even when embedded inside a much larger app rather than given its own.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Fitts's law: Target acquisition time falls with size and rises with distance. A very large, centrally placed target is close to the theoretical best case for a task performed under time pressure and often without full visual attention.

  2. Signal-to-noise ratio: With one action in the content area, there is no visual search step. The user's eye does not have to scan, parse, or decide before acting.

  3. Recognition over recall: The hint text removes any need to remember what the circle does, which matters because Shazam is a low-frequency app for many users; sessions can be weeks apart.

  4. Progressive disclosure: Library, Concerts, search, and settings are all one tap away but contribute nothing to the primary task, so none of them occupy the primary zone.

  5. Thumb-zone ergonomics: Secondary navigation sits in the natural thumb arc at the bottom; the hero action sits higher, where a deliberate two-handed or reaching tap is fine because it is the action you are already committed to.

screens.name: Home Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits short, sensor-dependent operations of genuinely unpredictable length where success depends partly on the user's physical positioning (audio matching, live scanning, voice capture) and where abandoning mid-operation is free.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for operations whose duration is knowable, where a determinate bar sets better expectations, and for long-running or irreversible processes such as uploads or payments, where a bare indeterminate animation with a one-tap exit gives the user neither a sense of progress nor protection against cancelling something costly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Assistant / "Search a song": The same audio-capture wait rendered as an animated, level-responsive visual with a live status line. A fair comparison because it faces the identical constraint: unknown match time on a perishable input.

  2. Apple's Voice Memos and Siri: Waveform-as-loading-state, where the animation doubles as proof the microphone is receiving. Shazam is drawing on the same platform vocabulary, including the system-level recording indicator.

  3. Face ID enrollment / camera-based scanners: Concentric progress framing around a live sensor with a corner dismiss, comparable because the user must physically position a device correctly for the capture to succeed and needs real-time confirmation that they have.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status: Nielsen's first heuristic, executed twice over: one signal for process activity, one for input signal quality. The user is never left guessing whether the delay means working or stuck.

  2. Perceived duration and active waiting: Continuous motion plus a task to perform ("check it can hear") compresses felt wait time relative to a static spinner of identical real duration.

  3. User control and freedom: An always-available, unconfirmed exit from a running operation. Since abandoning costs nothing, adding a "Are you sure?" step would be pure friction.

  4. Feedforward, not just feedback: The audibility hint arrives at the only moment the user can still act on it, rather than after a failed match when it becomes a post-mortem.

  5. Continuity of the interaction model: The hero mark stays in place and grows into the pulse rather than being replaced by a new screen, so the button visibly becomes the process it started.

screens.name: Home Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: This fits short sensor-driven operations of unpredictable length where the user's physical positioning affects success and abandoning costs nothing (audio matching, device discovery, live scanning).
screens.whereNotToUse: Poorly suited to operations with knowable duration, where a determinate indicator sets better expectations, and to long or irreversible processes such as uploads or payments, where escalating full-screen motion with a bare one-tap exit gives neither progress information nor protection against accidental cancellation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Assistant / "Search a song": Same audio-capture wait rendered as expanding, audio-reactive motion around a fixed center; identical constraint of unknown match time on perishable input.

  2. Siri and Apple's Voice Memos: Waveform-as-status where the animation doubles as proof of microphone input, drawing on the same platform vocabulary including the OS recording indicator.

  3. Airdrop and Bluetooth pairing screens: Expanding concentric rings as the standard visual grammar for "sensing outward for something not yet found," a fair comparison because the wait is genuinely indeterminate and cancelling is free.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status, sustained: Activity remains legible not just at onset but throughout the wait, which is where most loading states quietly stop reassuring.

  2. Perceived duration: Rising amplitude resists the sense of stall that a constant-intensity loop invites after two or three seconds.

  3. Stable anchor amid motion: The opaque center gives the eye a fixed point, preventing a full-screen animation from becoming visually fatiguing or hard to focus on.

  4. Consistency of controls across states: Close and copy hold position between frames, so nothing the user might reach for moves while they are reaching for it.

  5. Motion restraint where it counts: The animation is slow, wide, and low-contrast; it fills the screen without flashing, strobing, or high-frequency movement.

screens.name: Home Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: This fits short two-phase operations where a local capture is followed by a remote lookup, and where naming the phases helps the user attribute any eventual failure correctly (audio or image recognition, scanning against a remote catalogue, lookup after sensor input).
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the phases are invisible to the user or complete in well under a second, since narrating them just adds flicker, and where latency is long or highly variable, in which case a bare indeterminate state with filler copy leaves the user with no basis to decide whether to keep waiting.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Assistant / "Search a song": Runs the same two-beat structure, shifting from an audio-reactive capture visual to a neutral processing indicator once the sample is sent. Same architecture, same constraint.

  2. Google Lens and barcode scanners generally: Capture phase with live camera feedback, then a distinct lookup phase against a remote index; a fair comparison because the user's physical contribution ends partway through and the interface must show that.

  3. Apple Pay / contactless payment sheets: Discrete named phases with tight, non-apologetic status strings and a persistent cancel affordance, comparable in how a short multi-stage wait is narrated without inflating it.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Match between system and the real world: Splitting "Listening" from "Searching" surfaces the app's actual two-stage architecture in plain language, which is what lets a failure be correctly attributed later.

  2. Honest signalling: The live meter is retired the moment it stops measuring anything real. Keeping an audio-reactive element running during a network call would be theatre.

  3. Consistency and standards: Close control, mark, and text block hold identical positions across states, so nothing the user might reach for shifts underneath them.

  4. Visibility of system status, weakened: This phase carries the thinnest feedback of the three states while being the one most exposed to network latency; a determinate or elapsed-time cue would be more useful here than in the capture phase.

  5. Aesthetic-usability tradeoff: The rings now animate without encoding anything, which keeps continuity and visual calm but converts a former information channel into decoration.

screens.name: Home Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits recognition and lookup products where the answer is delivered free but the natural next action is monetizable, and where the moment of resolution is also the moment of highest user affinity (music, product, and media identification).
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the query is functional rather than affective (a translation, a unit conversion, a support answer) since layering a trial offer over a utilitarian result reads as opportunism, and it fails where the user is in a hurry or a public setting and auto-playing video is unwelcome.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (free tier track pages): Delivers the content, then gates full playback behind an upgrade at the exact point of intent. A fair comparison because both convert a moment of demonstrated interest into a subscription ask rather than interrupting earlier.

  2. SoundHound: The direct competitor's result screen pairs identification with lyrics, sharing, and streaming handoffs, showing the pattern is category-standard rather than Apple-specific.

  3. Google Lens results: Answer delivered as a full-bleed visual with actions layered over it and related results below the fold; comparable in treating a resolved query as the entry point to a browsing session.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Peak-end rule and moment-of-affinity conversion: The subscription ask lands at the emotional high point of the session, when the user has just gotten what they wanted, rather than at launch or on exit.

  2. Visibility of system status via content, not chrome: Success needs no announcement because the answer is the announcement; adding a confirmation banner would delay the payoff it describes.

  3. Colour as a hierarchy instrument: A single accent hue used only for playback and conversion means the revenue paths are the only saturated pixels; everything else recedes into video and dark neutral.

  4. Social proof as accuracy signal: The recognition count simultaneously validates the match ("a million people found this too") and reduces the user's doubt about whether to trust the result.

  5. Session extension over task completion: Related content positioned immediately below the fold converts a thirty-second utility interaction into a browsable session, which is how a single-purpose app earns retention.

screens.name: Home Screen 6
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits media detail views where several related items of the same type exist and the user is browsing rather than searching (video shelves, trailer collections, artist media) particularly where a contained player with an opt-in fullscreen respects the user's surroundings.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit when only one item exists, where a carousel promises variety that is not there, and for long-form video, where a small contained player with a persistent CTA below is worse than a proper immersive player. It also fails where the horizontal swipe would compete with a vertical scroll of equal importance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (music video sections): Same card-based horizontal video shelf, same expand affordance, same visual language. Shazam is reusing the parent product's pattern, which is why the handoff to Apple Music feels continuous rather than like leaving the app.

  2. Spotify (canvas and video previews on free tier): Video content shown in a contained frame with full playback gated behind an upgrade; comparable in using media as the hook for a subscription ask.

  3. YouTube Shorts shelves inside search results: Horizontally swipeable video cards nested inside a larger result page, a fair comparison for how a carousel signals "more of this type" without leaving the current context.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Affordance through partial visibility: The clipped neighbouring card is a textbook use of the boundary as a signifier; showing that content continues is more reliable than any indicator explaining that it does.

  2. Consistency across states: Close remains top-left and the teal accent remains reserved for the single monetized action, holding the conventions established through listening, searching, and result.

  3. User control over immersion: Offering fullscreen as an explicit choice rather than defaulting to it respects the user's context, which matters for a video that may be playing audio in public.

  4. Recognition over recall: The persistent header keeps track and artist visible while the user browses videos, so context is never lost to scrolling or swiping.

  5. Focused leaf view: Stripping secondary actions reduces this screen to one content type and one forward path, which is appropriate for a destination the user chose deliberately.

screens.name: Home Screen 7
screens.whereToUse: This fits post-result contexts where a mixed set of related content can deepen a user's interest (artist, album, and video cards after an identification or search) particularly where editorial framing raises the value of a subsequent subscription ask.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the user's query was purely functional and time-boxed, since editorial prose after a utility answer is friction, and where the related content set is thin (a mixed carousel with two entries promises breadth the product cannot deliver).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (artist pages and editorial notes): The biography voice, the truncated-with-read-more treatment, and the card language are lifted directly from the parent product, which is why the eventual handoff feels continuous.

  2. Spotify (artist "About" cards): Portrait, short bio, expand affordance, positioned as context beside playback; a fair comparison for using editorial to convert casual listening into follows and subscriptions.

  3. Genius / SongMeanings-style pages: Contextual editorial attached to a specific track lookup, comparable because both extend a one-question query into a browsing session by answering questions the user did not ask.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Consistent template across heterogeneous content: A shared card structure with an explicit type label lets videos, artists, and albums coexist in one carousel without the user having to relearn each card.

  2. Progressive disclosure: Truncating the biography keeps card heights uniform and lets the user opt into depth, protecting the carousel's rhythm from variable-length prose.

  3. Orientation through clipping: Partial cards on both sides communicate position in a sequence more precisely than a single peek, and do it without a pager or index.

  4. Affinity before ask: Editorial content raises investment immediately before the conversion prompt, which is why the trial line is worth more here than on a screen the user is merely passing through.

  5. Colour discipline, partially broken: Teal has meant "this leads to Apple Music" through the entire flow; applying it to a free text expansion dilutes a signal the design had otherwise kept clean.

screens.name: Home Screen 8
screens.whereToUse: This fits the deepest level of a media drill-down where the user has explicitly asked to view an image at size (album art, photography, poster and cover art) and where any additional control would compete with the thing being looked at.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit as an intermediate screen in a browsing flow, since a dead-end view with a single exit forces a return trip for any next action, and it wastes a viewport where the image is incidental rather than the reason for the visit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (tap-to-expand album art): Identical treatment: artwork enlarged on a dark field with minimal chrome, which is where Shazam's behaviour is inherited from.

  2. Photos and Instagram lightbox views: Full-width image on black with a single dismiss and a share action; a fair comparison because both treat "look closer" as a mode that suppresses surrounding UI.

  3. Discogs / Bandcamp release pages: Album artwork given deliberate prominence for an audience that treats sleeve art as content in its own right, comparable in recognising that some users came for the image.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Content-first minimalism: Stripping chrome at the deepest level of a drill-down matches the user's intent: they asked to see the image, so the interface removes itself.

  2. Restraint at the point of attention: Declining to place a CTA on a view the user actively chose preserves the sense that the app is showing them something rather than selling to them, which protects the credibility of the asks made elsewhere.

  3. Contrast through surround: A pure black field around a dark, warm-toned image maximizes perceived contrast without touching the artwork, the same reason galleries and photo viewers default to neutral dark.

  4. Persistent escape route: Close holds the same top-left position it has occupied on every screen from listening onward, so exiting a three-level drill-down requires no learning.

  5. Orientation through inherited context: Keeping the originating track in the header prevents a deep leaf view from becoming a screen with no visible provenance.

screens.name: Home Screen 9
screens.whereToUse: This fits a single-offer trial reached from a specific blocked action, where the user's intent is already established and the only remaining decision is whether to start (particularly where carrying the triggering content into the sheet keeps the offer concrete).
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where multiple plans or tiers must be compared, since one headline and one button cannot express a pricing structure, and as an unprompted interstitial at launch or mid-session, where the same sheet with no triggering intent reads as an ad rather than an answer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple TV+ and Apple Arcade in-app offers: Identical system sheet: co-branded hero, one-sentence offer, all-caps blue CTA, terms below. Shazam is presenting Apple's standard commerce component, not a bespoke paywall.

  2. Spotify Premium upgrade sheets: Triggered from a gated playback attempt, framed around what the user just tried to do; a fair comparison for converting at the moment of blocked intent rather than at launch.

  3. YouTube Premium prompts on ad or background-play blocks: Same structure of hitting a limit, being offered a trial that removes it, with terms disclosed inline; comparable in that the block itself is the pitch.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Contextual continuity into a purchase: Carrying the album artwork across the boundary keeps the offer tied to the specific desire that produced the tap, which is what separates a well-timed trial from a generic paywall.

  2. Single decision, single action: No plan grid, no tier comparison, no secondary CTA. When the offer is one trial, presenting one button is the lowest-friction honest option.

  3. Disclosure at the point of commitment: Auto-renewal terms on the same screen as the button, above the fold, is materially more transparent than a "Terms apply" link.

  4. Honest context switching: Dropping Shazam's theme for Apple's system commerce styling signals that the user has entered a different kind of transaction, rather than disguising a purchase as continued browsing.

  5. Unbalanced vertical rhythm: The dead band between headline and CTA is the clearest usability flaw in the flow so far: the argument and the action should not be separated by an empty half-screen.

screens.name: Home Screen 14
screens.whereToUse: This fits result screens for probabilistic systems (recognition, search, recommendation) where several follow-on actions apply to one item and where an accessible correction path both helps the user and improves the underlying data.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the result is deterministic and cannot be wrong, since a correction row invites doubt where none exists, and where the action count grows past roughly seven, at which point a menu stops being scannable and needs a proper sheet with sections.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. SoundHound: Offers an equivalent "wrong result" correction path after identification; a fair comparison because both products' credibility depends on match accuracy and both surface the correction where the doubt occurs.

  2. Google Maps (report an error on a place): Correction embedded in the item's own overflow rather than in settings, comparable in treating user feedback as a data-quality mechanism placed at the point of noticing.

  3. Apple Music (track overflow with state-dependent add/remove): The library toggle, destructive red styling, and row composition are inherited from the parent product's menu component.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Error recovery as a trust instrument: Offering a correction path at the point of doubt turns the product's most damaging failure mode into a moment where it looks reliable rather than broken.

  2. State-reflective menus: Showing "Remove" rather than "Add" communicates library membership without a separate indicator, so the menu answers a status question while offering an action.

  3. Destructive styling convention: Red plus a trash glyph marks the one consequential row, so a compact uniform list still ranks its items by risk.

  4. Contextual action sets: "Find Concerts" appearing on the result screen but not the player shows the menu is composed per surface, not shipped as a fixed list.

  5. Grouping by divider: Four clusters give the seven rows a scannable structure, though the section header still describes only the first cluster.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 14
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any content-heavy, habit-forming app (music, video, news, shopping) where:

  • You have rich behavioral/listening/viewing data to power personalization.
  • Users return frequently and benefit from near-zero-decision re-entry points.
  • Content can be visually represented (cover art, thumbnails) to support fast recognition-based browsing over text-based decision making.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The app has sparse or no historical user data (new users will see empty or generic, low-relevance shelves, eroding trust in personalization).
  • Content needs to be consumed in strict chronological or sequential order (e.g., task managers, financial transaction logs) - algorithmic shelves obscure recency and completeness.
  • Accessibility or low-vision contexts are a priority, since dense horizontal carousels with small truncated text are harder to navigate via screen readers or keyboard-only input.
  • The brand needs a curated, editorial-first storefront feel rather than an infinite, algorithmically-reordered browse experience.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets returning, habitual users rather than new sign-ups (it assumes a rich listening history and uses it immediately (the entire feed is personalized off known favorites)). The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Choice reduction / decision fatigue relief: by pre-curating stations and mixes, Spotify removes the paradox-of-choice friction from a catalog of 100M+ tracks.
  • Mere-exposure & familiarity bias: repeatedly surfacing the same favorite artists (Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo) across different shelf types builds trust in the algorithm and increases click-through likelihood.
  • Momentum/resumption bias: the "Start listening" row exploits the Zeigarnik effect (an incomplete/previously started listening session is more compelling to resume than to start fresh).
screens.keyHighlights:
Key UX decisions worth stealing:

  • Top segmented pills as a lightweight feed filter: switching between Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks without a full page navigation or loss of scroll context.
  • Color-coded cards per shelf row: distinct saturated backgrounds (coral/mint/cyan) make each horizontal carousel instantly distinguishable from its neighbors even on a quick scroll.
  • Artist-list microcopy as implicit social/taste proof: reusing recognizable names (Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo) across multiple shelves reinforces personalization credibility.
  • "Start listening" resume row: placed last but functionally first-priority, it's a near-zero-effort way to re-engage with recently played content, using an overflow menu (•••) for secondary actions instead of cluttering the row.
  • Dense, scroll-first density: no onboarding chrome or empty states; the screen is 100% content, which is ideal for a daily-habit app where returning users want immediate value.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 15
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any content-rich, habitual-use app (media, streaming, news aggregators) where the primary goal is fast re-engagement rather than deep navigation. It's ideal when you have multiple content types that benefit from cross-promotion, and when personalization/recency can meaningfully reduce the user's search burden. The segmented filter-plus-carousel-shelves approach also works well for apps transitioning from single-content-type to multi-content-type offerings.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, shelf-based home pattern for simple, single-purpose apps where a flat list or singular focused screen would reduce cognitive load. It's also unsuitable for first-time or low-content users (brand-new accounts without listening history will see sparse or awkward empty shelves, requiring a separate cold-start/onboarding strategy). Additionally, this pattern can overwhelm users seeking a specific item rather than passive browsing, who would be better served by a search-first entry point.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Spotify's full worldwide user base, especially habitual daily listeners who want frictionless re-entry into music/podcasts rather than active discovery. The psychological driver is the reduction of decision fatigue: by surfacing recently played and recommended content immediately, Spotify exploits the "path of least resistance" - pressing play is easier than choosing what to play, directly matching the app's core design philosophy.

The avatar notification dot and "Good Hang with Amy Po.." badge leverage curiosity-gap and social/novelty cues to pull users deeper into unexplored shelves, while the segmented filter caters to users with singular intent (e.g., podcast-only listeners) without forcing them into a separate app section.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-decision resumption grid: The top row of recent/continue items requires no scrolling or searching (users can resume exactly where they left off within one tap of opening the app).
  • Inline filter chips: The All/Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks segmented control reshapes the entire home feed instantly without navigation, giving a sense of control without complexity.
  • Graceful offline empty state: Rather than blocking the UI with an error, the offline notice is presented as just another shelf in the feed, maintaining flow and app usability perception.
  • Mixed content shelving: Podcasts, radio stations, and personalized DJ features are shelved together using identical card patterns, letting Spotify cross-merchandise disparate content types seamlessly.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 16
screens.whereToUse: Use this shelf-based, dual-axis home pattern for any content-rich app where the primary job is "reduce time-to-first-engagement" rather than "support deep deliberate search" - e.g., streaming (video/audio/podcasts), news aggregators, e-commerce homepages, or any app with a strong recommendation engine. It's ideal when you have multiple distinct personalization signals (recent activity, trending, genre-based) that don't fit into a single ranked list and benefit from being segmented into legible, labelled groups.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for task-oriented or utility apps (banking, productivity, settings) where users arrive with a specific goal (shelf browsing adds unnecessary scanning cost when users need direct, predictable paths. It also underperforms for small catalogs: if there isn't enough distinct content to fill multiple meaningfully different rails, the shelves will feel repetitive or sparse, exposing the recommendation engine's weaknesses rather than hiding them. Finally, be cautious embedding temporary campaigns (like Wrapped) as persistent navigation chips if the campaign isn't genuinely timely) stale promotional chips erode trust in the personalization system.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is engineered for Spotify's broadest possible segment: casual-to-habitual listeners who want frictionless audio, not crate-diggers who want to browse a catalog. The design leans heavily on the psychological principle of choice reduction: presenting 3 confident picks instead of a blank search bar reduces decision fatigue and shortens the time-to-first-play, which correlates directly with session length and retention.

The "Recents" and "Based on your recent listening" shelves exploit the mere-exposure and consistency principles, showing content the user has already engaged with increases the likelihood of re-engagement because it requires zero cognitive evaluation of whether the content is "good." The Wrapped chip taps into social/temporal relevance (a culturally-charged seasonal event) to re-activate dormant interest and drive sharing behavior later in the funnel.
screens.keyHighlights:
Several micro-decisions on this screen are worth stealing:

  • Decision-removal design: By pre-populating "Start listening" with three concrete, named tracks instead of a generic "Resume" button, Spotify removes the single biggest point of friction in media apps (choosing what to play) using algorithmic confidence instead of user effort.
  • Dual-axis scroll economy: Stacking independently-scrolling horizontal rails inside one vertical feed allows an almost unlimited number of personalization contexts to be surfaced on one screen without overwhelming the user, since each rail is optional to explore.
  • Overflow menu on recommendation rows: The persistent ••• next to each "Start listening" track gives users an escape hatch (e.g., "not interested," add to playlist) right at the point of recommendation, which both improves control and quietly feeds the recommender system more signal.
  • Campaign-as-filter-chip: Embedding "Wrapped" as a selectable chip in the primary navigational filter row (rather than as a separate banner) lets a seasonal marketing push feel like a native, integrated part of the experience rather than an interruption.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 17
screens.whereToUse:
Use this shelf-based home pattern when:

  • Your product aggregates large, heterogeneous content libraries (media, shopping, learning) that benefit from multiple parallel recommendation algorithms.
  • You need a single landing screen that serves both returning/habitual users (resume content) and discovery-seeking users (recommended content) simultaneously.
  • Visual thumbnails are strong, recognizable brand/content assets that can carry meaning without heavy text labels.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Your content catalog is small or narrow: shelves will feel redundant or sparse, exposing an empty-feeling product.
  • Users need a single, linear primary action (e.g., task-based utility apps, checkout flows) - horizontal carousels add unnecessary navigational complexity.
  • Accessibility/screen-reader users are a primary audience (nested horizontal scrolling grids are notoriously harder to navigate via assistive tech than linear lists).
  • You lack sufficient behavioral data to personalize shelves meaningfully, which would default users to the same generic/static ordering, losing the pattern's core value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Spotify's broadest possible audience (from casual music listeners to dedicated podcast binge-listeners) by using behavioral personalization rather than demographic targeting. The psychological trigger at play is the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to finish unfinished tasks): surfacing "Recents" first exploits the itch to continue an interrupted playlist or episode.

The "Your shows" and "Episodes you might like" shelves leverage habit formation and variable reward: mixing guaranteed, subscribed content (predictable reward) with fresh recommendations (variable reward) in the same scroll session, a core mechanic for maximizing daily active usage and session length.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Content-type segmented control pinned at the top lets users instantly re-scope the entire home feed (Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks) without navigating away (a lightweight filter that prevents content-type fatigue).
  • Recency-first shelf ordering: "Recents" appears before any algorithmic discovery content, optimizing for the single most common use case: resuming what you were just listening to.
  • Dense, image-forward grid with minimal text maximizes scanability; users recognize album/show art faster than they can read titles, leveraging visual memory over literal reading.
  • Avatar-as-nav-item in the top-left doubles as profile entry and establishes personalization/identity framing right where the eye lands first.
  • Four-item tab bar keeps the global navigation surface minimal, reducing decision fatigue and keeping "Home" as the obvious default re-entry point.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 10
screens.whereToUse:
Use this compound stacked-list settings pattern when:

  • Your app has many distinct configuration categories that benefit from grouping (finance, security, or multi-account apps).

  • Users need to understand what's inside a section without tapping in (critical for high-stakes/finance UX).

  • You want to spotlight a primary object (account/wallet/profile) distinctly from secondary settings via card treatment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The settings list is short (under ~6 items): the extra visual weight of subtitles and cards becomes unnecessary overhead.

  • Users are unfamiliar with the vocabulary used in subtitles (e.g., "recovery phrase") without any onboarding context, which can increase confusion instead of reducing it.

  • The product is casual/low-stakes, where such heavy security emphasis (Face ID, backup, passcode) at the top may feel excessive or intimidating.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, ranging from onboarding newcomers to experienced multi-chain traders. The psychological anchor is trust and control: because losing a recovery phrase means permanent loss of funds, the design elevates Security and the wallet identity card to the top of the hierarchy to reduce anxiety and reinforce that the user is in command of their asset custody.

The ENS-style human-readable name (vs. a hex address) leverages the recognition-over-recall principle, making the wallet feel personal and less error-prone when sharing/verifying identity. The "Connect to Coinbase" row taps into familiarity bias for users migrating from custodial exchanges, bridging Web2 comfort with Web3 self-custody.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Identity-first architecture: The wallet name/ENS card is visually promoted above generic settings, anchoring the whole screen around "who you are" before "what you configure."

  • Compound subtitles: Grouping related sub-settings into one descriptive line (e.g., "Passcode, backup, Face ID") lets users predict content before navigating, reducing exploratory taps.

  • Persistent bottom tab bar: Settings remains part of the primary navigation shell rather than a full-screen takeover, letting users jump to swap/browse without back-tracking.

  • Search-first affordance: A prominent search bar at the top acknowledges the long-tail complexity of wallet settings and gives power users a fast escape from scrolling.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 11
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any settings surface governing access control, authentication, or protection of sensitive data/assets: banking apps, password managers, health record apps, and enterprise admin consoles. It's especially effective when:

  • Multiple independent security mechanisms need to coexist (lock method + trigger conditions + biometrics).

  • Users manage multiple protected entities (e.g., multiple wallets/accounts) requiring per-item configuration via drill-down.

  • You need to prevent invalid states (e.g., zero security enabled) and want to communicate that constraint before it's hit.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, text-heavy grouped-list approach for casual consumer apps where security is a background concern rather than a primary use case (it would feel overly clinical). Also avoid burying critical scope disclaimers (like "only affects standard wallet") in small gray subtext if the consequence of misunderstanding is severe; in extremely high-risk flows, consider an explicit confirmation dialog or tooltip instead of relying on passive helper text that can be skimmed past.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users: an audience that is inherently anxious about asset loss/theft and typically more security-literate than average mobile users. The psychological driver here is control and reassurance: by exposing granular toggles (unlock on app open vs. unlock only on transaction) and biometric options, the app signals that the user (not a custodian) is fully in charge of their security posture, reinforcing the self-custody value proposition.

The dark, low-stimulation UI and unambiguous labeling cater to users making high-stakes decisions (protecting real monetary value), where any confusion or dark-pattern-like ambiguity could cause severe loss of trust or actual financial harm.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Scoped toggle disclaimers: Inline sublabels (e.g., "Only affects standard wallet") sitting directly under a switch eliminate misunderstanding about what exactly a security control governs, which is essential when multiple wallets have different protection needs.

  • Proactive validation messaging: Stating "At least one option must be selected" before the user attempts an invalid state avoids a jarring error later and builds trust that the app has sane security defaults.

  • Segmented settings grouping: Dividing Backups, Lock, Unlock Triggers, and Biometrics into visually separated blocks with bold headers turns a long settings list into an easily scannable set of mental categories.

  • Drill-down chevrons for complex sub-flows: Wallet-specific backup and lock-method configuration are pushed to secondary screens, keeping this main security hub lightweight and focused on high-level toggles.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any app handling sensitive financial, health, or identity data where users need transparent, granular control over authentication behavior. Ideal for multi-account or multi-wallet products where different sub-entities may need independent backup/security states. Also effective whenever you need to prevent a user from disabling all protection accidentally (enforce a "cannot go below one" rule).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of granularity in low-stakes consumer apps where excessive security toggles create decision fatigue without real benefit. If an app only has a single account/wallet, per-item drill-down backup rows are unnecessary overhead (a single backup section suffices). Also avoid burying critical security actions (like backup) below the fold or without visual differentiation, as this reduces the likelihood users complete essential setup steps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets crypto-savvy users managing multiple wallets who hold real financial value on-device and are highly sensitive to both security and usability. The design leans on the psychological principle of loss aversion: by making backup and lock settings prominent and impossible to fully disable, the app reduces the anxiety of "what if I lose access to my funds." It also respects user autonomy by allowing biometric convenience for routine actions (opening app) while optionally hardening the more consequential action (transactions), aligning security friction with actual risk level.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Forced minimum security floor: The system explicitly requires at least one unlock trigger to remain active, preventing users from accidentally leaving their wallet completely unprotected.

  • Scoped disclosure text: "Only affects standard wallet" removes ambiguity about which assets a toggle governs, critical in multi-wallet architectures.

  • Per-wallet drill-down for backups: Treating each wallet's backup as its own navigable row scales cleanly to N wallets without cluttering the top level.

  • Granular unlock triggers: Separating "Opening the app" from "Making a transaction" gives users fine control over the security/convenience trade-off at different risk levels.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Editing & Updating 13
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-toggle-with-inline-preview pattern for any settings screen governing sensitive, irreversible, or security-critical actions: financial apps, password managers, health data apps, or enterprise admin consoles. It's ideal when:

  • Multiple related boolean settings need logical grouping under clear section headers.

  • Users need to see current configuration state without extra navigation (inline value labels).

  • Certain combinations of settings are invalid and must be prevented via inline constraint messaging rather than after-the-fact error dialogs.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense settings-list approach for onboarding or first-run experiences, where users are unfamiliar with terminology like "Lock method" or "Change protection" - a wizard or guided setup would be more appropriate there. It's also unsuitable for low-stakes preference settings where verbose helper text would feel like unnecessary friction. Additionally, if the toggles have complex interdependencies beyond a simple "at least one required" rule, a plain list of switches may not sufficiently communicate the logic, requiring a more visual or wizard-based configuration flow instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets crypto wallet users managing real financial assets, a demographic highly sensitive to security and prone to anxiety about irreversible mistakes (lost funds, compromised keys). The psychological drivers at play include loss aversion (users fear losing access or funds, so the screen reassures via explicit constraints and explanations) and need for control/transparency (crypto-native users expect granular, explicit toggles rather than opaque automatic security, reflecting Web3 values of self-custody and user sovereignty).

The inclusion of biometric and recovery-phrase safeguards also speaks to more advanced/security-conscious users who understand device compromise risks (e.g., someone else's fingerprint being added to a phone), while helper copy accommodates less technical users by explaining consequences in plain language.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline value preview on drill-down rows: "Lock method" shows "Face ID" directly in the list row, letting users confirm current configuration without an extra tap.

  • Enforced minimum security constraint: The explicit note "At least one option must be selected" prevents users from disabling all unlock requirements, protecting them from an insecure default.

  • Contextual safeguard messaging: Explaining that changing biometrics without "Change protection" enabled could bypass recovery-phrase verification builds user trust and educates on security trade-offs at the point of decision.

  • Scoped setting clarification: "Only affects standard wallet" clarifies toggle scope for multi-wallet setups, preventing false assumptions about hardware/other wallet types.

screens.name: Brex - Locking a card - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any screen managing a sensitive financial or identity instrument (physical/virtual cards, API keys, passwords) where users need both at-a-glance status and quick access to high-risk actions. It's ideal for:

  • Corporate card / fintech apps needing to balance security with usability.
  • Contexts where a single critical account issue (e.g., missing configuration, expiring document) should interrupt the flow via a dismissible bottom sheet rather than a hard block.
  • Any screen offering native wallet/Apple Pay integration as a primary conversion action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this masked-by-default pattern for low-sensitivity data where friction isn't justified (e.g., a simple username). Also avoid stacking a bottom sheet alert on first load if the underlying issue is not truly actionable or time-sensitive (overuse of interruptive sheets for non-critical items will train users to dismiss them blindly, reducing their effectiveness for genuinely urgent cases). Additionally, for less financially-literate audiences, the term "spend limit requests" may need more explanatory microcopy or a help link.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves employees and cardholders at companies using Brex for corporate spend (individuals who need quick, secure access to their card credentials and basic self-service controls (locking a lost card, replacing a damaged one) without needing to contact finance/IT). The psychological trigger at play is control and security reassurance: masking sensitive data by default signals that the app takes custody of financial information seriously, building trust. The spend-limit bottom sheet leverages a mild loss-aversion/urgency trigger: alerting the user to a problem before it causes embarrassment (a declined card at checkout), prompting immediate corrective action.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive disclosure of sensitive data: card number, expiry, and CVV are masked by default with an explicit reveal toggle and long-press-to-copy gesture, balancing security with convenience.
  • Thumb-zone optimized action row: Lock, Replace, and More are placed immediately below the card for one-handed, high-frequency use.
  • Native OS integration: the prominent "Add to Apple Wallet" button reduces time-to-value by letting users tap-to-pay immediately.
  • Contextual system alert via bottom sheet: surfaces a potential blocking issue (no spend limit) proactively rather than waiting for a failed transaction, paired with a single clear CTA to resolve it.
  • Visual hierarchy through contrast and color: dark neutral UI keeps focus on the card, while the single orange CTA pops for the one action that truly matters on this screen.

screens.name: Brex - Locking a card - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any screen governing high-stakes, reversible-but-impactful account actions: such as locking/unlocking payment instruments, pausing subscriptions, disabling access, or deactivating integrations. It's ideal when the action has a clear, explainable downstream consequence that the user may not intuitively anticipate.

The masked-by-default sensitive data pattern should be used whenever displaying PII, card numbers, passwords, or other confidential credentials on a shared or mobile surface.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid heavy confirmation modals for low-risk, easily reversible actions (e.g., toggling a notification setting) - this adds unnecessary friction and interrupts flow. Similarly, do not mask data that users need to reference frequently and that carries little security risk, as this reduces usability without added benefit.

For actions with severe permanence (like account deletion), this single-step confirmation may be insufficient; consider adding a secondary verification step (e.g., password re-entry or typed confirmation) instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves employees and business admins who need rapid, confident control over a lost, stolen, or temporarily misused corporate card. The design leverages the psychological principle of loss aversion and control restoration: giving users an immediate, low-friction way to "freeze" financial exposure the moment they suspect fraud or misplacement, which builds trust in Brex as a safety-conscious platform.

The confirmation modal exploits the pause-before-commit heuristic: by requiring an explicit secondary tap and surfacing the operational consequence, Brex protects non-technical users (e.g., founders or employees unfamiliar with card systems) from accidentally disrupting legitimate business spending.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Default-masked sensitive data: Card number, expiry, and CVV are hidden until explicitly revealed, reducing shoulder-surfing risk in public settings.
  • Three-tile quick action row: Lock, Replace, and More provide immediate access to the most common card-management tasks without additional navigation.
  • Consequence-driven confirmation copy: Instead of generic "Are you sure?" messaging, the dialog explains the real-world business impact (declined expenses), improving user comprehension and reducing accidental misuse.
  • Native wallet integration CTA: The "Add to Apple Wallet" button is prominently placed, encouraging frictionless real-world card usage.
  • Color-coded urgency: The orange "Lock card" button visually signals an impactful, state-changing action distinct from neutral navigation buttons.

screens.name: Brex - Locking a card - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Reuse this pattern for any account/instrument detail screen tied to a security-sensitive, reversible state: e.g., payment cards, SIM/eSIM management, API key management, or device management screens. It's ideal when:

  • An entity (card, key, device) has a binary lock/active state that materially affects user capability.
  • Sensitive identifiers (PANs, tokens, secrets) need masking with optional reveal.
  • You want to guarantee the user notices a blocking state via both ambient (inline banner) and interruptive (modal) messaging.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy dual-messaging approach for low-stakes or non-blocking states, where a modal would feel excessive and annoying (e.g., informational tooltips, minor settings toggles). Also avoid redundant inline + modal messaging if the user has already dismissed or acted on the modal once per session, repeating it on every visit could become an unwelcome, naggy interruption rather than a helpful safeguard. For less security-critical apps, masking data by default may add unnecessary friction rather than value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves employees and admins who need quick, confident control over a corporate card (often in moments of urgency, such as realizing a card was lost, suspecting fraud, or intentionally freezing spend). The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion and control restoration: by clearly stating "all transactions will be declined," Brex removes ambiguity about why a payment might fail, preventing panic or repeated failed purchase attempts at checkout.

For finance teams and founders who value auditability and control, the masked-by-default card data and locked-by-default state reflect Brex's "security-first" brand promise, building trust that the platform actively protects company funds rather than just tracking them.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-layer status communication: the locked state is shown both inline (persistent, scrollable context) and in a modal (urgent, action-forcing), covering both passive awareness and active decision-making.
  • Progressive disclosure of sensitive data: card number, expiry, and CVV are masked by default with an explicit "Press to load" / eye-icon reveal gesture, balancing security with on-demand utility.
  • Action-first card layout: three equally-weighted secondary actions (Unlock, Replace, More) sit directly beneath the card visualization, making card lifecycle management (lock/unlock/replace) immediately accessible without hunting through menus.
  • Native ecosystem integration: "Add to Apple Wallet" is surfaced prominently as its own full-width row, reducing friction to get the card into daily use at physical points of sale.
  • Single accent color discipline: orange is reserved exclusively for the highest-priority CTA, making the "unlock" action visually unmistakable in an otherwise monochrome UI.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any fintech, banking, or healthcare app settings area where multiple independent security layers (biometric, PIN, 2FA, trusted contacts) need to be surfaced together.

  • Products with multiple sub-products or data domains (e.g., core wallet vs. tax filing vs. investing) that warrant separate authentication requirements.

  • Settings screens where reducing user anxiety through plain-language explanations is more important than dense technical configuration.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this verbose, description-per-row pattern in settings with 15+ items, as it will create excessive scrolling (better to use a denser table or accordion grouping at that scale).

  • Not ideal for expert/developer-facing security consoles where users want fast, dense toggles without hand-holding copy.

  • Should not be used if the underlying settings change frequently, since maintaining accurate, friendly microcopy for many toggles increases content-ops overhead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers using Cash App for peer-to-peer payments, banking, investing, and tax filing (a broad demographic ranging from first-time banking app users to more security-conscious power users). Because Cash App handles real money movement and sensitive PII (SSN via Taxes), the design leans on the psychological principle of perceived control: giving users granular, clearly labeled toggles increases trust in the platform's handling of their financial data.

The "Off" status labels leverage a mild loss-aversion/completeness nudge: seeing an unprotected state listed plainly (without shaming) encourages users to close the gap, similar to a profile-completion prompt. The separation of Taxes security also signals institutional credibility to more cautious or first-time tax filers who may be wary of digitizing sensitive tax documents.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Self-explanatory rows: Every setting includes a one-line description so users never need to guess what a toggle does before interacting with it.

  • Segmented taxonomy: Splitting general "Security" from "Taxes access" acknowledges that tax data carries a different risk/sensitivity profile and deserves independent authentication (password + 2FA authenticator).

  • Consistent trailing affordances: Status text + chevron for navigational settings vs. a filled pill button for direct actions creates a predictable interaction language across the whole list.

  • Icon-led scanning: Distinct line icons (Face ID frame, asterisk/PIN, trusted contact, shield) let users visually locate a setting faster than reading text alone.

  • Progressive security layering: Offering both a password AND an authenticator app for taxes demonstrates defense-in-depth without forcing both simultaneously (the authenticator is offered as an optional upgrade).

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Any app handling sensitive data (banking, healthcare, password managers) where authentication frequency needs to be user-configurable.

  • Settings screens where you want to build trust around biometric or sensitive data usage via inline, contextual privacy statements.

  • Use this granular toggle pattern when different in-app actions carry meaningfully different risk levels (e.g., viewing balance vs. transferring funds).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this level of granularity in low-stakes apps where extra toggles would just add confusing, unnecessary decisions for users (e.g., a simple to-do list app).
