  • Don't use ambiguous action groupings: if "Move money" and "Unlock the app" toggles aren't clearly distinguished with helper text for less common flows, users may misconfigure their security and create a false sense of protection.

  • Not suitable if the underlying OS/device doesn't reliably support the biometric hardware, as offering the toggle without hardware compatibility checks could lead to a broken or misleading experience.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumer users of a peer-to-peer payment app (Cash App) who are security-conscious but not technically sophisticated. The psychological driver here is trust calibration: financial apps must balance perceived security (making users feel protected) with usability friction (not annoying users with constant Face ID prompts).

By exposing individual toggles rather than a single master switch, the design leverages the illusion of control heuristic: users feel more secure and in charge of their own data/money when they can fine-tune exactly when authentication is required, rather than accepting an opaque, one-size-fits-all policy set by the app.

The explicit privacy disclaimer addresses a well-documented psychological barrier to biometric adoption: fear of biometric data being stored/leaked. Removing this friction point increases the likelihood users will enable Face ID, which in turn increases account security and reduces support/fraud costs for Cash App.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Granular, action-based security triggers: Instead of a single blanket "enable security" toggle, the app lets users decide independently whether Face ID/PIN is required for moving money vs. simply unlocking the app, respecting that these have very different risk profiles.

  • Inline trust-building copy: The reassurance that Face ID data is never stored is placed directly under the toggle it concerns, at the exact moment of decision, rather than buried in a legal document.

  • Visual grouping via whitespace: Separating the "trigger conditions" from the "authentication method" toggle with vertical spacing creates an implicit two-tier mental model without needing section headers or dividers.

  • Minimalist, low-chrome UI: No icons, colors, or extra decoration (appropriate for a security screen where clarity and trust outweigh visual flourish).

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app needs OS-level sensitive permissions (biometrics, camera, location, contacts) tied to security or core functionality. Best practices to replicate:

  • Delay the system permission dialog until the user opts into the specific feature that requires it.

  • Provide a plain-language explanation of data usage immediately before the system prompt appears.

  • Offer granular toggles for related-but-distinct actions (e.g., unlocking app vs. authorizing transactions) instead of one master switch.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the permission is required for the app's core function to work at all (e.g., a camera scanning app) - in that case, blocking flows with clear value-prop framing before the first use is more appropriate. Also avoid stacking multiple permission primers in a single settings screen, as decision fatigue can cause users to decline reflexively. Do not use vague copy like "We use your data" without specifics, as this erodes trust rather than building it, especially in regulated fintech contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of a peer-to-peer payments app (Cash App) who are security-conscious but also wary of biometric data misuse. Financial apps face heightened scrutiny, so the design leans on trust-building through transparency: explicitly stating what data is collected and why, which reduces the psychological friction/fear response tied to biometric permissions.

The deferred/contextual permission request leverages the psychological principle that people are more willing to grant access when they understand the immediate, tangible benefit (securing their money) versus an abstract request at onboarding.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual, just-in-time permission request: The native Face ID prompt is triggered by direct user action (toggling a switch) instead of on first app launch, dramatically increasing the likelihood of "Allow" being tapped.

  • Granular control switches: Splitting "Move money" and "Unlock the app" into separate toggles gives power users flexibility while defaulting to safer, opt-in behavior.

  • Pre-permission education: Explanatory copy about data usage appears directly above the toggle, functioning as a priming layer before the OS-level dialog appears.

  • Non-blocking decline path: "Don't Allow" is offered with equal visual weight to "Allow," respecting user autonomy and avoiding dark-pattern coercion.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when designing settings for any app handling sensitive data (fintech, health, identity) where users need to configure when and how biometric/PIN authentication is triggered. It's especially effective when:

  • You have more than one authentication use-case (app entry vs. specific sensitive actions) that deserve independent granularity.

  • You're introducing biometric data collection and need to proactively address privacy concerns inline rather than relying on a separate policy page.

  • The default states matter for adoption: pairing a low-friction default with optional higher-friction protections.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The app has only one universal authentication behavior (in that case, a single toggle is simpler and multiple options would create unnecessary decision fatigue).

  • Users are in a highly regulated context (e.g., enterprise/healthcare) where security settings should be mandatory and not user-configurable, as offering opt-outs could create compliance risk.

  • The product needs to enforce mandatory biometric locks for legal/compliance reasons, presenting these as optional toggles would undermine required security posture.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumer fintech users (Cash App's broad P2P payment and banking user base) who are security-conscious but not technically sophisticated. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Loss aversion: Financial apps must overcome deep-seated fear of unauthorized fund transfers, hence the option to gate "Move money" specifically.

  • Privacy anxiety around biometrics: Many users are wary of Face ID/FaceID-adjacent tech being "stored" or shared; the explicit denial statement directly neutralizes this objection.

  • Autonomy/control: Giving users several independent toggles (rather than a single lock/unlock master switch) satisfies the need for perceived control over one's own financial security posture.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual trust copy: Privacy reassurance text appears directly beneath the toggle it concerns, reducing abandonment/anxiety at the exact decision point rather than burying it in a separate privacy policy link.

  • Granular permission control: Splitting "Move money" and "Unlock the app" into separate toggles gives users fine-tuned control over friction vs. convenience trade-offs, rather than an all-or-nothing security switch.

  • Smart default hierarchy: Only the least intrusive protection (Face ID enablement) is on by default; the two friction-heavy gates are opt-in, respecting the user's autonomy while still nudging general security awareness.

  • Whitespace-driven grouping: Uses vertical spacing instead of dividers or section headers to imply a dependency between toggles, keeping the visual design extremely clean.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 8
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any settings/preferences hub in apps handling sensitive personal, financial, or social data (particularly where some settings are simple binary toggles and others require multi-option configuration). Ideal for fintech, social, and marketplace apps needing to balance discoverability (letting others find/interact with you) against user safety.

Also effective whenever you want to reduce support burden by pre-empting "how do I stop X" questions with clear, benefit-framed descriptions rather than terse OS-style labels.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this verbose, two-line-description-per-row style in high-frequency utility settings screens where users already understand the options (e.g., simple developer/debug toggles) - it adds unnecessary vertical scroll and slows down power users. Also avoid mixing switches and chevrons without a clear, learnable visual rule, as inconsistent affordance mapping across an app can create confusion about what tapping a row will do.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets every active Cash App user, but is especially critical for privacy-conscious individuals, scam-wary older users, and anyone who has experienced unwanted payment requests or spam. Financial apps carry heightened scrutiny around personal data handling, so this screen exists to proactively reduce support tickets and churn caused by privacy anxiety.

Psychologically, it leverages the need for control: a foundational trust driver in fintech UX. By exposing granular switches (who can find you, who can request money, whether your profile is public) the app converts an abstract fear ("is my money/data safe?") into concrete, actionable levers, which measurably increases perceived security and reduces uninstalls or negative reviews tied to spam/scam experiences.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline current-value preview: "Payment requests" shows "Anyone" directly in the list, eliminating an unnecessary tap just to check the current state.

  • Dual affordance system: Switches for instant binary actions vs. chevrons for multi-option deep dives, letting icon/control shape communicate interaction complexity at a glance.

  • Benefit-first microcopy: Reframes potentially invasive permissions (contact sync) around user protection and spam prevention rather than data collection.

  • Consistent leading iconography for each row aids rapid scanning and builds a visual vocabulary users can memorize over time.

  • Transparent web profile URL displayed in-line (cash.app/$madedaley) so users see exactly what's public before deciding to toggle it off.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any settings screen governing lists that are commonly empty for most users (blocked users, muted accounts, saved items, notifications). It's ideal when you want to educate users about a feature's purpose while it's unused, and when the primary action (e.g., adding/blocking) should remain accessible regardless of list state.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal empty-state treatment when the absence of data might indicate an error (e.g., failed sync) rather than a true "zero state" - in those cases use a distinct error state with retry actions. Also avoid a neutral/de-emphasized CTA when the action is meant to be highly encouraged (e.g., adding contacts, subscribing), as low-contrast buttons can suppress conversion for growth-critical actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern serves any user managing their safety and privacy on a social platform, dating app, or messaging service. The target demographic is broad but particularly relevant to users who have experienced or want to prevent harassment, unwanted contact, or spam. Psychologically, the screen leverages a sense of control and safety: by proactively showing "no blocked accounts" rather than hiding the feature, the app reassures users that moderation tools exist and are easy to access, building trust in the platform's safety infrastructure even before they need to use it.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reassuring Empty State Copy: Clearly explains what the screen is for and what will happen when it's populated, reducing user confusion.

  • De-emphasized CTA Styling: The "Block an account" button uses a neutral gray pill instead of a vibrant brand color, subtly signaling this is a utility/safety action rather than a growth-oriented one.

  • Persistent Bottom Action: Keeping the primary action accessible even in an empty state avoids a true UX dead-end.

  • Minimal Visual Noise: No unnecessary icons or illustrations, keeping focus on clarity for a sensitive safety/privacy feature.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any short, non-cancelable background process critical to security or account setup (wallet/key generation, encryption setup, biometric enrollment, account provisioning, or backend account creation during sign-up). It's ideal whenever the operation takes a few seconds and cannot be meaningfully progressed by a progress bar (i.e., duration is unpredictable).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this indeterminate, full-screen blocking pattern for longer processes (over ~10-15 seconds) where users need a sense of progress (use a determinate progress bar with a percentage or step count instead). Also avoid it for interruptible or resumable tasks, where a cancel option should be provided to respect user control. Overusing full-screen blocking loaders across an app can also feel heavy-handed for trivial operations that could instead use inline skeleton loaders.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Coinbase Wallet's "Busy Urbans" target audience typically has low patience for friction and jargon. This screen is engineered to hold their attention for the few seconds required to securely generate a wallet without triggering doubt ("Did it freeze?") or drop-off. The dark, secure-vault aesthetic also plays to the psychological need for trust and safety when a user is about to be handed sole custody of their financial assets (a moment where perceived reliability of the underlying technology is critical to conversion).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radical minimalism: Removing all extraneous UI (no back button, no cancel, no branding clutter) signals to the user that this is a protected, atomic operation that shouldn't be interrupted.

  • Single-point focus: Pairing an indeterminate spinner with one short status line concentrates attention and reduces the perceived complexity of an inherently technical cryptographic task.

  • Reassurance through plain language: Translating a complex security operation into a simple, human sentence builds trust and reduces onboarding drop-off anxiety.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use native system permission dialogs with a custom rationale string whenever requesting sensitive OS-level permissions (biometrics, camera, location, notifications) in finance, health, or identity apps. Always trigger the prompt contextually (right after the user reaches a step where the permission's value is obvious) rather than immediately on app launch. Pair with a pre-permission "priming" screen beforehand when the ask is non-obvious, to increase acceptance rates since the system dialog itself cannot be visually persuaded.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid firing this system dialog blindly at first launch before the user understands why biometric access matters (this depresses opt-in rates and can trigger app-store-review-style rejection reflexes). Do not attempt to visually bias the "Allow" button (not possible on iOS, but relevant on Android custom equivalents) as it violates platform guidelines and erodes user trust. Also avoid re-prompting repeatedly after a "Don't Allow" response, since iOS suppresses re-prompting and repeated soft-asks feel naggy.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Targets "Busy Urbans" who need fast, frictionless access to their funds throughout the day (tapping to pay, checking balances on the go) without repeatedly entering PINs or passwords. Face ID satisfies both their need for speed (one-glance unlock) and their heightened need for security assurance, since this audience is managing real monetary value in a self-custody product with no bank-style fraud reversal safety net.

Psychologically, this leans on loss aversion (protecting money/data) and trust transfer from Apple's native biometric system, which users already trust for banking and payment apps, making them more willing to extend that trust to Coinbase Wallet.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom rationale string: Coinbase overrides the default system copy with a benefit-driven, security-framed sentence tailored to a financial wallet context.

  • Contextual timing: Presumably triggered after a relevant in-app moment (e.g., end of wallet setup) rather than an abrupt cold-start request, increasing acceptance likelihood.

  • Low-friction security upgrade: A single tap enables biometric lock, reducing future password/PIN entry friction while reinforcing the sense of a secure, self-custody product.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any dashboard, wallet, or account-balance screen that can legitimately be at zero (new accounts, financial apps, portfolio trackers). Ideal when there is one clear, dominant recovery action (e.g., "Add funds," "Connect account," "Import data") and you want to avoid a jarring blank screen. Especially effective when the product has an adjacent, trusted parent brand/account that can be leveraged as an easy funding source.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy illustration-driven empty state for screens where zero-state is rare or unexpected (e.g., a returning user who should have data (here an error state or reload prompt is more appropriate)). Also avoid duplicating the CTA at both top and bottom on very short-viewport screens, as it can feel repetitive or noisy if the whole screen already fits without scrolling. Not suitable when there are multiple equally important next steps, since the pattern is optimized for single-path conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Targets new or newly-onboarded crypto wallet users (including those migrating from a Coinbase exchange account) who have just created or imported a wallet and have zero on-chain assets. The design leverages the Zeigarnik effect and progress-oriented framing (presenting "$0.00" not as a dead end but as step one of an implied journey) plus reduction of decision paralysis by offering exactly one clear CTA. The Coinbase-brand link icon exploits trust transfer: users familiar with the centralized exchange are reassured that moving funds to the self-custody wallet is safe and easy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-illustration branding: The empty state graphic visually links the Coinbase (C) logo and Wallet logo via a chain icon, subtly reinforcing that funds can flow seamlessly from the Coinbase exchange account into the self-custody wallet (a key value proposition and cross-sell mechanic).

  • Persistent, redundant CTA: "Add crypto" appears both inline (attached to the empty state) and pinned near the tab bar, ensuring the primary action is always reachable regardless of scroll position.

  • Pre-populated navigation: Buy/Swap/Cash out and Crypto/NFTs/DeFi tabs remain visible and tappable even with $0 balance, letting curious users explore the app's structure before committing funds.

  • Contextual guidance over generic error: Instead of a blank void, the empty state proactively explains *why* it's empty and *how* to fix it in one sentence.

screens.name: Brex Add to Apple Wallet 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any fintech, banking, or corporate card management screen where sensitive payment credentials must be displayed, concealed, or copied. It's ideal for admin/self-service financial dashboards, virtual card issuance platforms, and any scenario where users need granular control (lock, replace, limits) over a tokenized payment instrument. The bottom sheet nudge pattern is reusable whenever a non-blocking but important account configuration gap needs surfacing in context.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid fully masking sensitive data by default in low-security contexts where users need constant visibility (e.g., a personal card display for a trusted single-user app) as the extra reveal/long-press step adds friction. Also avoid stacking a bottom sheet warning on top of an already dense screen if the issue isn't actionable immediately (this can feel like an interruption rather than a helpful nudge if the user lacks permission to resolve it themselves (e).g., non-admin employees seeing spend limit warnings they cannot act on).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets business professionals, finance administrators, and employees of a company using Brex for corporate spend management. These users are typically multitasking, cost-conscious, and security-aware, often accessing this screen in moments of urgency (e.g., lost card, need to make a purchase, verifying details for an expense report).

Psychologically, the design leverages the sense of control (lock/replace card instantly), trust through security transparencyloss-aversion framing in the bottom sheet (a pending/missing spend limit implies the card may not work, prompting quick resolution to avoid a blocked transaction later).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Security-first default masking of PAN/CVV/Expiry with a deliberate reveal toggle, balancing security compliance with user convenience.

  • Gesture-based copy interaction ("long press to copy details") that eliminates extra buttons while remaining discoverable via inline hint text.

  • Three-tile quick action row (Lock, Replace, More) gives users instant control over card security states (critical for fraud/loss scenarios) without navigating deeper menus.

  • Contextual bottom sheet nudge for spend limits that surfaces at the moment of card management, rather than as a generic notification, increasing the likelihood of action.

  • Apple Wallet integration CTA bridges the native OS payment ecosystem directly from the card management screen, reducing friction to real-world card usage.

screens.name: Brex Add to Apple Wallet 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an action depends on a third-party or OS-level service (payment provisioning, calendar sync, native share, push permission) that can fail unpredictably. It's ideal for:

  • Apple Wallet / Google Pay card provisioning flows

  • Payment processing failures

  • Any integration with external APIs where retry is a valid recovery path

  • Mobile contexts where a full-screen error would feel overly disruptive for a recoverable, non-destructive failure
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for silent, low-stakes background failures where interrupting the user adds more friction than value (use a toast instead). Also avoid it for critical/destructive errors (e.g., account security breaches, data loss) where a bottom sheet may under-communicate severity (a full-screen or modal dialog with stronger visual weight would be more appropriate. Don't use vague "try again later" messaging if the error is actionable by the user (e.g., permission not granted)) give specific remediation steps instead of a generic retry.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets business/corporate cardholders (Brex is a corporate card/spend management platform) who expect bank-grade security affordances (masked card numbers, lock card) alongside modern conveniences (Apple Wallet provisioning). The error-handling pattern specifically serves users attempting a device-level integration that depends on external APIs (Apple's PassKit/Wallet service), which can fail for reasons outside the app's control (network, device state, Apple servers).

Psychologically, the design reduces frustration by (1) not hiding the failure behind silent retries, (2) giving a human-readable apology-free but polite explanation, and (3) offering immediate recourse via "Try again" to restore a sense of control after a disrupted task flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Masked sensitive data by default: PAN, CVV, and expiry are hidden behind dots with an explicit reveal toggle, reducing shoulder-surfing risk for a corporate card.

  • Non-blocking, recoverable error pattern: The failure is surfaced in a bottom sheet rather than a full-screen takeover, preserving context of the underlying card screen.

  • Dual-path resolution: Offering both "Close" (dismiss) and "Try again" (retry) respects user agency (some users may want to retry immediately, others may want to abandon the Wallet flow and continue elsewhere).

  • Plain-language error messaging: Avoids technical jargon or error codes, reducing user anxiety around a failed native OS integration (Apple Wallet provisioning).

  • Visual hierarchy via color: The red alert icon and orange primary CTA create unambiguous visual cues about severity and recommended next action.

results.query: Avoiding choice paralysis in multi-tiered subscription pricing tables

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any free-trial paywall confirmation, especially for subscription products with auto-renewal. It is ideal when:

  • App Store/Play Store compliance requires clear trial-to-paid disclosure.
  • The target audience skews trust-sensitive (education, finance, health apps).
  • You want to reduce trial abandonment caused by fear of hidden charges.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The product has a true no-payment-required trial (the timeline/reminder framing would feel unnecessary and add friction).
  • Speed-to-conversion is critical and extra screens meaningfully hurt funnel completion rates in A/B tests.
  • Your brand strategy intentionally obscures renewal terms (not recommended, but some low-trust dark-pattern funnels skip this for short-term conversion gains at the cost of refund/chargeback rates).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective subscribers who are curious but price-sensitive or wary of being "tricked" into a recurring charge (a common friction point for STEM/edtech apps competing against free YouTube content). By front-loading transparency, Brilliant reduces the perceived risk of starting a trial, which is especially important for its worldwide audience that may include users unfamiliar with Western auto-renewal subscription norms.

Psychologically, this leverages the reciprocity and trust-building principles: by proactively disclosing the "gotcha" (the charge date and reminder), the brand positions itself as honest, which lowers the psychological barrier to commitment. The timeline format also taps into the Zeigarnik effect: once a user sees a multi-step journey mapped out, there's a subconscious pull to complete it, i.e., to tap 'Start'.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent Trial Timeline: Converts confusing subscription terms into a simple, scannable three-step narrative, building trust rather than relying on surprise billing.
  • Dual-purpose Connector Line: The gradient vertical line functions simultaneously as a timeline guide and an implicit progress bar, reinforcing forward momentum toward conversion.
  • Pre-emptive Reminder Disclosure: Explicitly stating the day-5 email reminder reduces anxiety about forgetting to cancel, which paradoxically increases trial sign-up rates.
  • Exact Charge Date: Stating "October 13" instead of a vague "7 days" removes ambiguity and satisfies platform compliance for subscription transparency.
  • CTA Reframing: "Start my free week" emphasizes value-received language over cost/commitment language.

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for subscription-based products with a strong brand identity and content-led value proposition (especially in education, fitness, and habit-building apps where the user has already sampled value before hitting the wall). It's ideal when you want to convert trial users softly, without alienating them via a hard paywall, and when annual plans are the primary revenue driver (since the small monthly price point reduces hesitation).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this soft, single-plan approach if your product benefits from tiered differentiation (e.g., Basic/Plus/Pro) where users need to compare feature sets (a single plan would feel restrictive or opaque). Also avoid closable 'X' exits if your business model relies on hard paywalls to force conversion at a critical gate. Finally, this slow, illustration-heavy, trust-building layout is unsuitable for fast transactional contexts (e.g., re-subscribing an already familiar lapsed user) where users want to skip straight to checkout.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets engaged trial users: people who have already clicked through a few lessons and are emotionally invested in the "gym for your brain" metaphor, but haven't yet committed financially. Brilliant's worldwide, largely self-motivated learner audience (students, professionals, lifelong-learning hobbyists) responds well to low-pressure, intellectually respectful sales tactics rather than aggressive urgency.

Psychological triggers at play include: Loss Aversion (don't lose access to the gym you've started building a habit in), Anchoring (monthly price framing), Risk Reversal (free trial + clear cancellation terms reducing commitment anxiety), and Consistency (maintaining the same illustrative visual language builds subconscious trust that this is 'part of the learning experience,' not a separate ad).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-plan focus: Avoids multi-tier comparison fatigue by presenting one annual plan as the default/only path, simplifying the decision to a binary yes/no.
  • Price reframing: Highlighting the small monthly-equivalent price ($13.33/mo) in large bold text while the actual annual charge ($159.99) is shown smaller, leveraging anchoring bias to reduce sticker shock.
  • Illustration continuity: Using the same hand-crafted 3D illustration style found throughout the learning content, making the paywall feel like a natural extension of the product rather than an ad interruption.
  • Transparent risk reversal: Explicit, un-hidden renewal terms build trust and reduce the "gotcha" feeling, which is crucial for a brand built on intellectual credibility.
  • First-person CTA: "Start my free week" personalizes the commitment and softens the perceived cost of the action.

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any subscription or payment confirmation flow where backend processing (App Store/Play Store/Stripe) takes more than ~500ms.
  • Flows where accidental double-taps could cause duplicate charges or errors.
  • Moments of high user anxiety (checkout, trial activation, irreversible actions) where reassurance copy reduces drop-off or support tickets.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for near-instantaneous actions where a modal would feel like unnecessary friction (a simple inline spinner or optimistic UI is better).
  • Don't use an opaque full-block modal if the backend call is unpredictable or could take very long (>10s) without a fallback/error timeout message, as users may think the app is frozen.
  • Not ideal for flows where you want to keep the user editing or exploring (this pattern deliberately halts all interaction, which is only appropriate for committed, final actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This moment targets any user who has just made the decision to start a free trial (typically someone already convinced by the value proposition and price anchoring on the screen beneath). The psychological goal here is purely to reduce transactional anxiety and prevent error states (double taps, perceived freezing, or uncertainty about whether the purchase went through). By showing a clear, branded, calm processing state rather than a blank screen or generic OS spinner, Brilliant maintains trust continuity through the riskiest step of the funnel: the moment money/commitment is on the line.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking context preservation: The pricing screen remains visible (dimmed) behind the loading modal instead of navigating away, reducing anxiety that the selection was lost.
  • Indeterminate spinner + status label: Combines a classic spinner with explicit copy ("Completing purchase..") so users understand exactly what stage of the transaction they're in.
  • Disabled CTA during processing: The "Start my free week" button is greyed out, preventing duplicate submissions/double billing (a critical e-commerce safeguard).
  • Persistent legal transparency: Trial and billing terms stay visible beneath the modal, reinforcing trust at the highest-anxiety moment of the funnel.

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any subscription or trial-based paywall flow where regulatory/App Store compliance requires explicit trial-to-paid disclosure (iOS/Android subscription apps). It's especially valuable for premium education, wellness, or productivity apps targeting trust-sensitive, detail-oriented users who are prone to subscription anxiety. Pair native purchase confirmations with reassuring, non-hype microcopy immediately after checkout to reduce chargebacks and improve trial retention.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid relying solely on a native system dialog as the "celebration" moment for products where onboarding momentum and emotional delight are critical to activation (e.g., gamified consumer apps) - a plain OS alert can feel flat and may need to be followed by a richer branded welcome/success screen. Also avoid repeating legal disclaimers so many times in playful, low-friction impulse-purchase contexts (e.g., in-app cosmetic purchases) where excessive fine print can introduce unnecessary doubt and hurt conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users who have just converted from a free to a trial-premium tier (the highest-intent moment in the funnel. The psychological goal here is to immediately reduce post-purchase dissonance ("did I just get tricked into a subscription?") through plain-language confirmation and explicit billing transparency. For a worldwide STEM-learning audience that skews toward analytically-minded, skeptical users (students, professionals, lifelong learners), over-explaining the billing terms builds credibility and trust rather than being perceived as noise) this audience actively reads fine print and rewards honesty with retention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native OS Confirmation Dialog: Leveraging the system-level purchase confirmation instead of a custom in-app modal borrows platform credibility and satisfies App Store trust conventions instantly.
  • Dual-Metaphor Illustration: The dumbbell-shaped key icon elegantly fuses the "mental gym" brand concept with the universal "unlock" symbol for premium content, reinforcing brand identity at the exact point of conversion.
  • Redundant Trial Transparency: Repeating the no-charge/cancel-anytime message in two separate places (fine print + micro-copy above CTA) pre-empts regret and subscription-fatigue anxiety, a key driver of trial abandonment.
  • Minimal Chrome: A single close (X) icon is the only escape hatch, keeping full visual focus on the value proposition and confirmation rather than navigation options.

screens.name: Brilliant - Premium - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this stacked-list settings pattern when:

  • You need to expose a mix of navigational (multi-field) and binary (single-value) preferences in one place.
  • Your brand voice is minimal/utilitarian and you want to avoid visual noise or heavy card chrome.
  • You want to passively surface a monetization entry point (e.g., Premium/Upgrade) without resorting to a modal or banner interruption.
  • The product has a clear primary flow that settings must not interfere with (hence modal presentation).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat single-list approach when:

  • The number of settings is very large (50+), where grouping into categorized sub-pages (e.g., a settings "hub" with cards per category) prevents excessive scrolling.
  • Settings require contextual explanation or risk (e).g., privacy/security options that need inline descriptions, warnings, or previews; a bare label + chevron may leave users uncertain of consequences.
  • The brand relies on strong visual merchandising (e.g., consumer social apps) where flat gray text for "Log out" might under-communicate an important, frequently used action.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves existing, already-onboarded learners who need occasional control over their account, subscription, and sensory/notification preferences (not new users being persuaded to join). The psychological design goal here is reducing friction and anxiety around configuration: by using familiar iOS-native list patterns (chevrons, toggles, hairline dividers), the screen leverages users' existing mental models from countless other apps, requiring zero learning curve.

Surfacing "Premium" as a dedicated, icon-matched row (not a plain text link) subtly primes free users every time they open Settings, applying a gentle, passive upsell trigger via mere repeated exposure rather than aggressive interruption, fitting for a calm, trust-building edtech brand targeting self-directed learners worldwide.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-led scanability: Every row pairs a simple line icon with its label, letting users visually scan and locate a setting without reading every word.
  • Immediate feedback toggles: Sounds and Haptics use inline switches (green = on) rather than drilling into a sub-page, respecting the user's time for simple binary preferences.
  • Visual hierarchy via grouping and whitespace: Four distinct sections separated by hairline dividers and blank space, rather than boxed cards, keep the screen feeling light and uncluttered.
  • De-prioritized destructive/meta actions: "Log out" and the version string are rendered in muted gray with no chevron on Log out, visually signaling lower importance/finality without burying them in a submenu.
  • Modal "X" dismissal: Reinforces that Settings is a utility layer, not part of the core learning flow, preserving the integrity of the linear lesson spine.

screens.name: Brilliant - Premium - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Account/billing sections of any subscription-based app (edtech, fitness, SaaS).
  • Screens where the user has already converted and needs reassurance/control rather than conversion pressure.
  • Any product wanting to reduce support ticket volume by pairing account data with an immediate, low-friction help entry point.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this passive, non-promotional tone on screens where you still want to upsell (e.g., trial-to-paid conversion) - the lack of urgency here would hurt conversion goals.
  • Not suitable if the business model requires in-app cancellation flow data capture (e.g., win-back offers) - deep-linking straight to the App Store forfeits that retention opportunity.
  • Avoid for complex multi-tier plans where users need comparison or plan-switching (this layout only supports a single, static plan view).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves existing paying subscribers who need transparency and control, not persuasion. The target psychology here is reducing "subscription anxiety" - a well-documented churn driver where users forget what they're paying for or panic about hidden renewal terms. By surfacing the renewal date and plan name plainly up front, Brilliant preempts support tickets and chargebacks, while the dedicated Help card reduces the perceived friction of canceling or asking questions, paradoxically building more trust (and retention) than hiding the exit would.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Restraint over upsell: No cross-sell, no "upgrade further" nudges on a page about an existing subscription (respects the user's prior decision).
  • Native delegation: "Manage Subscription" hands off to the OS-level subscription manager instead of building a custom (and riskier) cancellation flow in-app.
  • Consistent illustration language: The help card reuses the same soft, hand-drawn illustration style found in lessons/onboarding, keeping even a settings page feel on-brand.
  • Clear visual grouping: Dividers and bold section headers ("Current plan," "Help") create scannable zones without needing cards or heavy borders everywhere.

screens.name: Spotify - Manage subscription - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription management screens for any SaaS or media app needing to communicate trial status without inducing cancellation anxiety.
  • Apps with multi-faceted "bundle" subscriptions (e.g., Amazon Prime style) where users often forget which specific perks they are paying for.
  • Post-trial "nurture" flows designed to increase feature discovery before a renewal decision is made.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this passive "soft-sell" layout if the business goal is aggressive, immediate conversion (e.g., a trial ending in 24 hours), where a more urgent, high-contrast banner would be required.
  • Do not use this pattern for single-feature subscriptions where there is no "snapshot of benefits" to showcase, as the module would feel empty or redundant.
  • Not suitable for B2B admin dashboards where billing/seat management requires more granular, data-table driven interfaces rather than lifestyle-oriented illustrations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets trial users and existing subscribers who may be uncertain about the tangible value of their payment. By surfacing a "Snapshot of your benefits" (specifically Audiobook listening time), Spotify leverages the Endowment Effect: making users feel they already possess valuable assets (listening hours, discounts) that would be lost upon cancellation.

The "Get to know your benefits" carousel specifically targets users who signed up for the headline feature (ad-free music) but are unaware of bundled perks (Audiobooks, Family Mix, Discounts), aiming to increase feature adoption to drive down trial-churn rates.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-Tone Branding: Using a pink/magenta accent for "Individual" Premium status visually separates account-tier information from standard navigational green accents, preventing user confusion between "content" and "account" states.
  • Soft Retention Strategy: Instead of a hard paywall or urgent banner, the trial expiration is presented as a simple utility line item, reducing subscription anxiety while keeping the user informed.
  • Benefit Re-engagement Module: The "Get to know your benefits" card acts as a mini-onboarding flow embedded within the settings, ensuring users justify their subscription cost by discovering underutilized features (like Audiobooks).

screens.name: Spotify - Manage subscription - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription/account management screens in apps constrained by platform billing policies (iOS/Android IAP restrictions).
  • Any settings surface where transparency about limitations can preempt user frustration or support escalations.
  • Billing summary screens needing to clearly state renewal date, price, and plan tier in a scannable, low-anxiety format.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this passive "informational-only" pattern when the business goal is active plan conversion or upselling (a stronger CTA-driven layout would be needed instead).
  • Do not use self-deprecating/apologetic copy in contexts where it could undermine brand confidence (e.g., high-stakes financial or legal flows where users need assurance of control, not an admission of limitation).
  • Not suitable for platforms without billing restrictions, where native in-app editing of plans is expected and this redirect-style pattern would just add unnecessary friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing paying subscribers who are auditing or confirming their billing status (a moment of heightened scrutiny and potential anxiety (common triggers: unexpected charge, forgotten trial, or curiosity about price changes)). The design's psychological strategy is to reduce anxiety through radical clarity: dates, amounts, and plan names are stated plainly with no ambiguous jargon.

The apologetic disclaimer about not being able to edit plans in-app serves a dual audience: it manages expectations for new premium users unfamiliar with App Store billing restrictions, and it reassures frustrated users that Spotify is aware of the limitation, reducing perceived indifference from the brand.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radical transparency copy: Explicitly telling users they can't edit their plan in-app, with an empathetic, human tone, preempts frustration and support tickets.
  • Billing clarity: Exact renewal date, exact price, and offer-expiry are surfaced together, reducing surprise billing complaints (a major churn/trust driver for subscription apps).
  • Non-blocking navigation: Keeping the bottom tab bar visible on an account/settings screen signals this is a low-stakes, easily-exited destination, reducing anxiety around visiting billing settings.
  • Soft upsell placement: "Explore plans" is tucked low in hierarchy as a card row rather than a banner or modal, respecting user intent (they came here to check status, not necessarily to buy).

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse:
• B2B SaaS products where value scales with number of collaborators (project management, communication, whiteboarding tools).

  • Early onboarding flows where you want to seed network effects before the user's enthusiasm decays.

  • Any flow where you want to encourage an action but must not block progress for users unwilling to comply immediately.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Single-player or personal-use apps where there is no collaborative value proposition (invites would feel irrelevant or pushy).

  • Highly privacy-sensitive contexts where asking for colleague emails this early could raise trust/compliance concerns.

  • Flows where the user hasn't yet experienced core value, asking for a team invite before the product has proven itself can increase drop-off instead of reducing it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new signups: typically a team lead, founder, or early adopter evaluating Linear for their organization. Since Linear's value is inherently networked (a project/issue tracker is far more useful with teammates present), this step exploits the "viral loop" growth pattern: converting a single-user trial into a multi-seat team account as early as possible. Psychologically, it capitalizes on the user's current high-motivation state (freshly signed up, curious, exploratory) to ask for an investment (inviting colleagues) before intent fades. It also uses social facilitation (once co-workers are invited, the user has public accountability to actually adopt and use the tool).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-exit strategy: Both "Continue" and "I'll do this later" give users multiple non-blocking ways to skip, drastically reducing onboarding abandonment risk.

  • Batch email input: A single text area accepting comma-separated emails lets power users invite an entire team in one action instead of repeating a form multiple times.

  • Visual progress transparency: The dot-based page control at the bottom sets expectations for how many steps remain, reducing onboarding fatigue/anxiety.

  • Strategic CTA hierarchy: The filled purple "Send invites" button draws the eye first, while skip options are intentionally muted in gray, nudging the desired behavior without forcing it.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Post-onboarding or settings flows where you want to capture marketing/notification consent without blocking the primary task.

  • SaaS products with a technical or privacy-conscious audience where transparency drives higher-quality opt-ins.

  • Any flow requiring compliance with opt-in consent regulations (GDPR, CAN-SPAM, CCPA).

  • Situations where you want to separate distinct communication types (product updates vs. marketing) to improve long-term engagement and reduce unsubscribe rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this soft, skippable pattern if email capture is a core business-critical conversion metric that must be maximized (a more assertive single-choice prompt may perform better for growth-stage products).

  • Don't use pre-toggled OFF switches if your business model depends on default opt-ins and your jurisdiction does not legally require explicit consent (though this is generally not recommended).

  • Not ideal mid-task, where interrupting with a preference screen would break flow and frustrate users (e.g., during checkout or active editing).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded or existing Linear users at a natural checkpoint (likely post-signup or post-settings-visit) where communication preferences are most relevant. The audience is primarily technical/product teams who are highly sensitive to unsolicited marketing noise, so Linear's restrained, honest approach to opt-in (rather than pre-checked boxes) is tailored to a sophisticated, trust-sensitive user base that would otherwise bounce or immediately unsubscribe if manipulated into a list.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages the principle of autonomy (user controls every choice), reciprocity (transparent value exchange: "subscribe to learn about changes" implies tangible benefit), and reduced cognitive load (binary toggles, no required fields) to maximize genuine, lower-churn opt-ins rather than inflated but low-quality subscriber counts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Opt-in by default (toggles OFF): Respects user consent norms and regulatory best practice, building long-term trust over short-term list-growth metrics.

  • Frictionless exit via "X": Clearly communicates this is a non-mandatory step, reducing perceived pressure and modal fatigue.

  • Granular, specific choices: Separating "changelog" from "marketing/onboarding" emails lets users tailor exactly what they want, avoiding the all-or-nothing subscription trap.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Stating frequency ("bi-weekly," "occasional") directly addresses the top objection to subscribing (fear of spam).

  • Correct component semantics: Using a toggle for binary preferences but a button/pill for the external "Follow on X" action avoids UI pattern misuse.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Post-signup or onboarding flows where you need explicit communication consent (GDPR/CAN-SPAM compliance).

  • SaaS products that send multiple types of emails (product updates vs. marketing) and want to avoid conflating them.

  • Any screen attempting to grow social following organically as a secondary, non-intrusive ask.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the onboarding flow is already long, adding a dedicated full screen for email preferences can feel like unnecessary friction if users are eager to reach core product value. In such cases, consider deferring this to account settings instead of a blocking/interstitial step. Also avoid defaulting marketing-heavy toggles to "on," as it undermines the trust this screen is designed to build.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly signed-up users of Linear, a developer/PM-focused project management tool. The audience is technically sophisticated and typically averse to spammy marketing, so the design psychologically leverages autonomy and transparency: giving explicit, separated controls rather than a single bundled "opt-in to emails" checkbox.

By pre-enabling only the lower-frequency, highly relevant changelog email, the product nudges users toward retention-building communication (feature updates) without triggering the reactance that comes from being auto-subscribed to sales/marketing content. This builds long-term goodwill and likely improves opt-in rates and reduces churn-driven unsubscribes.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Ethical default selection: The low-commitment "changelog" toggle is pre-enabled while the higher-frequency "marketing and onboarding emails" toggle is off by default (a thoughtful, user-respecting use of smart defaults rather than opting users into everything).

  • Granular consent control: Splitting communications into two distinct toggles (product changelog vs. marketing) lets users curate exactly what they want, increasing trust and reducing future unsubscribe/spam complaints.

  • Non-blocking escape hatch: The ✕ close icon gives users an immediate way to skip the step entirely, signaling this isn't a mandatory gate.

  • Soft social CTA: Embedding the "Follow us on X" prompt as a tertiary, non-toggle element cleverly extends brand reach without cluttering the primary consent decision.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 17
screens.whereToUse:
• End of an onboarding flow where you want to transition users from setup to active usage without losing them to incomplete secondary tasks.

  • SaaS/B2B tools where team invites and integrations are critical for activation/retention.

  • Any scenario needing to communicate "setup complete" while surfacing optional, value-reinforcing next steps.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the secondary actions are critical/mandatory for the product to function (use a required setup wizard instead).

  • Not ideal for consumer apps with less patience for reading; shorter, icon-only checklists or progressive disclosure may work better for less technical audiences.

  • Avoid in flows already suffering from onboarding fatigue, stacking yet another screen with action items can increase drop-off if users are eager to reach the core app.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets newly onboarded professional users (likely engineering/product teams) who have just finished initial account/workspace setup in Linear. The psychological strategy here is to capitalize on the momentum and dopamine of a completed task ("You're good to go") by immediately presenting value-adding follow-up actions while the user is still engaged, using the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete team/integration setup nags at the user's attention) balanced against respect for autonomy by making it skippable. Highlighting team invites and integrations also serves Linear's business goal of network-effect driven growth and stickiness (the more a team integrates Slack/GitHub, the higher switching costs and daily usage).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking secondary checklist: Growth actions (invite team, integrations, mobile app) are presented as optional suggestions rather than mandatory gates, preserving momentum toward the core product.

  • Single, unmissable primary CTA: "Open Linear" is the only full-width, high-contrast button, eliminating decision paralysis about what to do next.

  • Dual exit paths: Users can close (X) or navigate the carousel back, respecting user control and avoiding a forced funnel.

  • Contextual deep links embedded in copy: The "installation guide" hyperlink is embedded inline within descriptive text rather than as a separate button, keeping the layout clean.

  • Progress closure signal: The page control dots confirm to the user they've reached the end of onboarding, reducing anxiety about "how much is left."

screens.name: Brilliant - Disabling notifications - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-list settings pattern whenever an app needs a single, exhaustive hub for account, preference, and support actions. It is ideal for:

  • Apps with a primary linear or task-focused flow (courses, fitness, meditation) where settings must stay out of the way until explicitly summoned.
  • Products targeting a global, OS-fluent audience that benefits from native-feeling, convention-following UI.
  • Screens combining toggles, drill-downs, and destructive actions that need clear visual hierarchy without heavy chrome.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat, single-list approach when:

  • The settings surface is large enough (e.g., 20+ items) that a searchable or categorized multi-tab settings experience would serve users better.
  • Monetization or account-health items (e.g., expiring subscription, security alerts) need urgent visual emphasis (this pattern's uniform styling would bury important alerts).
  • The brand voice is highly expressive or playful (the stark, utilitarian styling here would feel inconsistent with a more maximalist or illustration-heavy brand identity elsewhere in the product).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Brilliant's audience is self-directed, intrinsically-motivated STEM learners who value efficiency and clarity over flashy engagement loops. This screen is designed for that same user in a "maintenance" mindset (someone who wants to quickly toggle haptics off in a quiet room, check their subscription status, or log a bug, then return immediately to learning). The low-friction, text-dense-but-visually-sparse layout respects the user's time and avoids dark patterns like disguising Log out or burying cancellation flows in nested menus.

Psychologically, the grouped list format exploits the "recognition over recall" heuristic: by mimicking the native OS settings pattern worldwide users already know, cognitive load is minimized and trust is subtly reinforced (it feels like a "real," well-engineered app rather than a custom reinvented wheel).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Modal exit (X) instead of back arrow: correctly communicates that Settings is a detached utility layer, not a step in the linear lesson spine.
  • Inline toggles for binary prefs: Sounds and Haptics are resolved with a single tap via Switch controls, avoiding unnecessary navigation depth for simple on/off decisions.
  • Visual grouping via whitespace + dividers: four tiers of functionality (identity, sensory feedback, support, destructive/meta) are instantly scannable without needing section headers.
  • Color-coded affordance hierarchy: active/navigable rows are black with chevrons; de-prioritized items (Log out, Legal, version string) are rendered in light gray, communicating hierarchy without extra UI chrome.
  • Version number transparency: displaying build version (v9.8.3) at the bottom aids support/debugging conversations and signals engineering maturity.

screens.name: Brilliant - Disabling notifications - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this granular matrix pattern when an app has multiple distinct notification triggers tied to different value propositions (engagement streaks, social/competitive features, content updates, marketing) and multiple delivery channels (push, email, SMS). It's especially valuable in gamified or habit-forming products where users need confidence that turning off noisy categories (e.g., News) won't accidentally silence critical ones (e.g., streak-saving alerts).

It's also a strong pattern for any app aiming to reduce uninstalls/opt-outs caused by notification fatigue, since offering precise control is proven to increase overall long-term opt-in rates compared to a blunt master toggle.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this level of granularity for simple apps with only one or two notification types (a full matrix would be overkill and add unnecessary friction to settings). It's also unsuitable for first-time onboarding flows, where presenting a dozen individual toggles would overwhelm new users before they understand the value of each feature (a simplified permission prompt or smart defaults would work better there).

On very small screens or for users with low digital literacy, a long checkbox matrix without grouping/collapsing (e.g., accordions) can feel overwhelming; consider progressive disclosure or collapsed sections if the list grows much longer than what's shown here.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engaged, habit-driven learners who have already bought into Brilliant's streak and league gamification mechanics and now want to fine-tune how aggressively the app contacts them. Power users and privacy-conscious users alike benefit from this level of control, as it prevents notification fatigue from becoming a reason to churn or disable notifications entirely.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss aversion (streak/league expiry alerts) and autonomy (granular opt-in/opt-out per category and channel) simultaneously (the app wants to keep users engaged via timely nudges, but it earns trust by not forcing an all-or-nothing notification relationship, which increases the likelihood users leave high-value alerts (like streak expiry) enabled even if they mute lower-value ones (like News and Announcements)).
screens.keyHighlights:
Dual-channel granularity: Splitting every notification type into independent Mobile and Email checkboxes lets users tailor channel-specific noise levels (e.g., email digests but no push interruptions) rather than forcing an all-or-nothing choice.

Behavior-based categorization: Grouping by product feature (Streaks, Leagues, Learning Reminders) rather than by technical notification type mirrors the user's mental model of the app, making the settings feel organized around "what I care about" instead of "system plumbing."

Reminder vs. Alert distinction: Separating proactive reminders from risk-based alerts (e.g., streak about to expire, league demotion risk) acknowledges that users have different tolerance thresholds for routine nudges versus loss-prevention warnings (a subtle nod to loss-aversion psychology embedded directly into settings architecture).

Consistent minimalist checkbox styling: The bold black-filled checkboxes with white checkmarks are highly legible and scannable at a glance across a long list, reducing cognitive load despite the information density.

screens.name: Brilliant - Disabling notifications - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this dense matrix-style preference pattern when an app has multiple distinct notification triggers tied to multiple delivery channels, and when granular control materially improves retention (e.g., gamified habit apps, fitness trackers, social/competitive platforms). It is especially effective for apps with "streak" or "league/competition" mechanics where losing a streak or rank is emotionally charged and users want reassurance they'll be warned before penalty.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of granularity for casual or low-frequency apps where users have few meaningful notification categories (the matrix format adds cognitive overhead and decision fatigue unnecessary for simple on/off needs). Also avoid checkbox-styled toggles (rather than native switches) on platforms where users expect strict adherence to OS conventions, as it can create subtle affordance confusion about whether the control is a toggle or a selection checkbox.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets engaged, habit-forming learners who have already bought into Brilliant's streak and league mechanics but want fine-grained control over interruption frequency (a classic "power user" settings need). Giving granular control (rather than a single on/off master toggle) respects the autonomy of self-directed learners who are this app's core demographic: people motivated by intrinsic mastery rather than brute-force push notification pressure.

Psychologically, offering separate Mobile/Email toggles per category exploits the endowed control effect: users who feel they can finely tune exactly what interrupts them are statistically less likely to disable notifications entirely, preserving the app's ability to leverage streaks and league alerts (its strongest retention mechanics) for re-engagement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Channel x Category Matrix: Clean two-column (Mobile/Email) grid layout lets users make independent decisions per delivery channel without needing separate screens, respecting user autonomy and reducing notification fatigue.
  • Optimistic UI with Inline Loading State: The spinner replacing a checkbox mid-toggle demonstrates real-time async feedback, preventing the user from wondering if their tap registered.
  • Clarifying Parentheticals: Every ambiguous label is annotated with concrete trigger conditions, a small but high-leverage copywriting decision that builds trust and reduces accidental over-disabling.
  • Priority-Ordered Categories: Placing Streaks and Leagues (the app's core gamification/retention levers) above generic learning reminders subtly signals to the user (and to the product itself) what matters most for retention.

screens.name: Brilliant - Disabling notifications - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this granular channel-by-category checkbox matrix pattern when an app has multiple distinct retention mechanics (streaks, social competition, content recommendations, editorial content) that each warrant different urgency and channel treatment. It's ideal for subscription/habit apps, fitness trackers, language learning, and any gamified product where over-notifying is a top churn driver.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for apps with only one or two notification types, where a simple global toggle or a short list suffices (excessive granularity here would be over-engineering). Also avoid dense checkbox grids for less tech-literate or older user bases who may find a matrix of checkboxes across two channels confusing; a simpler single-channel toggle list or smart defaults with minimal exposed controls would be more appropriate in those contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves habit-driven learners who are motivated primarily by streaks, league competition, and daily practice cues (the core gamification loop of Brilliant). By exposing these systems as separately tunable notification categories, the design acknowledges that different users have different tolerance thresholds: a competitive league player may want every alert, while a solo learner may only care about streak preservation.

Psychologically, pre-checking most boxes leverages the default effect to maximize opt-in engagement (more notifications sent = more re-engagement triggers = higher retention), while the one unchecked box shows restraint to avoid notification fatigue on the single most interruptive channel (mobile push) for a secondary feature (leagues).
screens.keyHighlights:
Checkbox grid over single toggle: Splitting every notification type into Mobile and Email channels (rather than one blanket switch) respects user autonomy and reduces unsubscribe/uninstall risk by letting users tune intensity instead of going all-or-nothing.

Inline explanatory copy: Each reminder type includes a short, parenthetical description of its trigger condition, eliminating ambiguity at the point of decision.

Deliberate default asymmetry: League Alerts default to Email-only (Mobile off), likely because league-closing alerts are time-sensitive but less universally valued than streak alerts, suggesting the team calibrated defaults per-category based on expected annoyance tolerance rather than uniformly defaulting everything to "on."

Consistent visual rhythm: Bold black checkboxes with high contrast checkmarks make current state instantly scannable at a glance across a long, dense list.

results.query: When to use grouped stacked-lists instead of grid tiles for mobile settings

screens.name: Craft - Grouping entries - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern when an app needs to support structured, tabular data within otherwise free-form content: e.g., note-taking apps adding lightweight database features, project docs with embedded trackers, or any hybrid document/spreadsheet tool. The bottom-sheet "Group By" approach is ideal whenever you need to expose an advanced data-organization feature (grouping, sorting, filtering) without building a dedicated full-screen settings page (it keeps the user anchored to their content while making a quick configuration choice).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid embedding full database functionality directly in a document if your product's core differentiation is distraction-free, pure writing (added complexity can undermine the minimalist promise). This pattern also fails on very small screens or for simple tables with few columns/rows, where a bottom sheet for grouping is overkill. For power users needing advanced multi-level grouping, sorting, and filtering simultaneously, a cramped bottom sheet with a single field selector will feel insufficient and should be replaced by a dedicated full-screen or side-panel configuration view.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets knowledge workers, designers, and product managers who use Craft not just for personal notes but for structured project documentation (such as design critiques, feature trackers, or research repositories). The "Web3 Platform Landing" document with a tracked "Collection" of design artifacts (Multi-Chain Selector, Wallet card UI, Hero section) suggests a design team using Craft as a lightweight Notion/Airtable alternative embedded within a narrative doc.

Psychologically, offering database functionality inside a beautifully typeset document taps into the desire for "one tool to rule them all": users avoid context-switching between a writing app and a project-management tool. The low-friction Group By interaction respects the user's time and cognitive bandwidth, avoiding the intimidation that complex database configuration screens (like Airtable's) can induce.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Database-in-document hybrid: Embedding a fully functional table (with typed columns, tag chips, and add rows) inside a free-form document blurs the line between "note" and "database," giving Craft Notion-like power without forcing users into a separate app mode.
  • Minimal Group By sheet: Rather than a complex settings panel, grouping is reduced to a single combobox in a small bottom sheet, respecting progressive disclosure and keeping advanced features low-friction.
  • Soft pastel tag chips: Color-coded category chips provide at-a-glance scannability while staying muted enough not to clash with the editorial, document-first visual language.
  • Visible empty rows: Leaving rows 4-6 visible but empty invites continued data entry and avoids the abrupt "wall" feeling of a table that ends exactly at the last filled row.
  • Context preservation via bottom sheet: The modal dims but doesn't fully obscure the background table, letting users see the field names they're about to group, reducing cognitive load during the decision.

screens.name: Craft - Grouping entries - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any app combining free-form documents with embedded structured data (databases, tables, kanban) where users need lightweight, in-context configuration without leaving the page.
  • Productivity or knowledge-management tools where power users expect Notion/Airtable-like grouping, sorting, and filtering controls.
  • Scenarios where you want to preserve document context visually (dimmed background) while presenting a transient settings/action menu.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, label-only menu style for first-time or non-technical users who need descriptive guidance (add icons or short descriptions if the audience is less database-literate).
  • Not suitable for simple consumer apps where a single grouping dimension is sufficient; the added UI complexity would be unnecessary overhead.
  • Avoid stacking multiple overlapping sheets/menus (as partially suggested here) in production (ensure only one modal layer is active at a time to prevent z-index confusion and accidental taps).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves designers, product managers, and knowledge workers who use Craft to maintain living project documents that blend narrative context (briefs, goals) with structured tracking (collections of design assets, tasks, or references). The psychological trigger at play is cognitive offloading through structure: by letting users group rows by Owner, Status, or Priority on demand, the app reduces the mental burden of manually scanning unsorted data, giving a sense of control and order over a potentially sprawling design system or project backlog.

The dimmed-background overlay also leverages a focus/isolation effect: graying out peripheral content signals "this decision is temporary and reversible," lowering the stakes of experimenting with grouping options.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Grouping Action Sheet: Instead of a full settings screen, grouping options appear in a compact, bottom-anchored sheet that floats above the dimmed table, preserving spatial context and enabling instant preview-adjacent decisions.
  • Color-coded Category Chips: Using distinct chip colors per category (Interaction/green, Component/purple, Layout/blue) turns a plain data table into a scannable, visually organized system (classic Craft "designed document" polish applied to structured data).
  • Hybrid Document + Database Block: The same canvas holds free-form rich text (overview, goal) and a structured table, demonstrating Craft's core promise of flexible, composable blocks within one document.
  • Persistent Document Identity: The header retains the doc title and parent folder ("in Design") even while deep in a sub-interaction, so users never lose their place in the hierarchy.

screens.name: Craft - Grouping entries - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this dimmed-backdrop bottom sheet configuration pattern whenever:

  • A user needs to adjust a narrow, well-scoped setting (grouping, sorting, filtering) without losing visual context of the underlying content.
  • You want to make database/table configuration feel lightweight and native rather than opening a heavy modal or new screen.
  • The action is low-risk and benefits from an easily accessible inline delete/reset control.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the configuration requires multiple dependent steps or extensive input (better suited to a full-screen or multi-step form). It's also inappropriate for destructive or high-stakes actions that need an explicit confirmation step, since the inline trash icon here offers no "are you sure" safeguard. For first-time users unfamiliar with database concepts, the terse iconography (Aa, ⊟) and compact chips could be confusing without onboarding or tooltips.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prosumer knowledge workers, designers, and project leads who use Craft not just for notes but for lightweight project databases (e.g., tracking design collections, content inventories, or research). The psychological driver is mastery and control: by offering database-like grouping/sorting inside a writing app, Craft taps into users' desire to organize information without context-switching to a separate tool like Airtable or Notion.

The low-friction bottom sheet and reversible delete action reduce the cognitive load and risk anxiety typically associated with structured data manipulation, appealing to users who want spreadsheet power without spreadsheet intimidation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Dimmed Backdrop: Rather than navigating away, the underlying document and table remain dimly visible, preserving spatial and mental context while the user configures a sub-setting.
  • Compact Pill Controls: Grouping field and sort direction are represented as rounded chip/dropdown combos, keeping a dense configuration task visually light and tappable.
  • Inline Destructive Action: The trash icon sits directly beside the configuration controls, allowing immediate removal of the Group By rule without a separate menu or confirmation step for a low-risk, easily-undoable action.
  • Document-to-Database Continuity: The seamless scroll from prose to an embedded, spreadsheet-like Collection table exemplifies Craft's "block" philosophy, everything, including structured data, is just another block in the document.

screens.name: Craft - Grouping entries - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when designing hybrid document/database editors (notes apps, wikis, CRM-lite tools, project briefs) where users need to move fluidly between freeform writing and structured data entry. It's especially effective for:

  • Note-taking or documentation apps targeting professionals who maintain both narrative and tabular content.
  • Tools where lightweight categorization (grouped rows) adds organizational value without forcing users into a rigid database schema upfront.
  • Any screen requiring a persistent formatting toolbar for long-form content editing on mobile.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid embedding full spreadsheet-like tables directly in mobile documents when:

  • The target data requires complex relational operations (multi-table joins, formulas, large-scale filtering) - a dedicated database app would serve users better.
  • Screen real estate is highly constrained (small phones) and the table has many columns, leading to excessive horizontal scrolling and degraded readability.
  • Users are non-technical and may be intimidated by spreadsheet affordances (#, Aa icons) without clearer onboarding or tooltips.
  • The app's core use case is quick capture rather than structured organization (added table complexity could slow down fast note-taking).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers, product managers, and knowledge workers who need to combine narrative documentation (briefs, specs, notes) with structured tracking (asset lists, categorized tasks, inventories) in a single artifact. The psychological driver here is reduced context-switching cost: instead of jumping between a notes app and a spreadsheet/database tool, users get both affordances fused, which lowers cognitive load and keeps creative flow uninterrupted.

The understated, editorial visual language (soft blur, generous whitespace, neutral grays) appeals to users who value calm, distraction-free tools over flashy, gamified productivity apps, signaling trust, craftsmanship, and respect for the user's attention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Blurred Scroll-Under Header: The top bar uses a frosted-glass blur effect that lets content scroll beneath it, preserving context while keeping navigation persistently accessible (reduces jarring hard cuts between header and body).
  • Embedded Database Block: A full spreadsheet/table component lives inside a free-form document, letting users mix prose and structured data without switching apps or modes (a core differentiator of Craft's block system).
  • Grouped, Collapsible Rows: Table rows are organized into named sections (e.g., "None", "Layout") with disclosure chevrons, enabling lightweight categorization directly at the data layer.
  • Inline Row/Column Affordances: The "+" row and "#" column auto-numbering reduce friction for adding content, mimicking spreadsheet muscle memory for power users.
  • Persistent Bottom Toolbar: Attach, draw, format, and undo actions remain fixed at the bottom, ensuring editing tools are always within thumb's reach during long documents.
  • Breadcrumb-style Subtitle: "in Design" under the title acts as a lightweight breadcrumb, orienting the user within the folder hierarchy without consuming extra vertical space.

screens.name: Linear - Adding an assignee - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when designing mobile companion views for data-dense desktop tools (project management, CRM, analytics dashboards) where full feature parity isn't feasible. It's ideal for:

  • Issue/ticket tracking apps needing a condensed mobile browsing experience
  • Any list requiring grouped status sections with collapsible counts
  • Interfaces that integrate with third-party systems (GitHub, Jira) and need to mirror familiar taxonomies like labels and milestones
  • Situations where you must gracefully degrade a complex view (e.g., kanban board) into a simpler one on constrained viewports, with clear user communication
screens.whereNotToUse:
