Avoid this dense metadata-row-per-card pattern for consumer-facing or non-technical audiences, where unfamiliar iconography (branch icons, status circles) and jargon-heavy labels would create confusion rather than efficiency. It's also unsuitable for very small screens or contexts requiring one-handed quick glances, since each card still demands moderate vertical space and reading effort.

Silently disabling a feature (board view) without an explanatory banner would be a trust-breaking mistake in any context (this pattern of transparent fallback messaging should always accompany graceful degradation, not be treated as optional polish).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen directly serves engineers, product managers, and technical founders who are reviewing GitHub-synced backlog items while away from their desktop. The design assumes users already understand issue-tracking conventions (labels, milestones, assignees), so no explanatory onboarding is present (it's built for fluency, not first-time discovery).

The psychological trigger at play is cognitive consistency: because every card follows an identical metadata template, users build a mental model after the first card and can then skim subsequent cards at high speed, drastically reducing the time-to-decision when triaging a backlog on a small screen.

The honest limitation banner also taps into trust-building through transparency: for a technical audience that values precision and dislikes "magic" or silent failures, stating a limitation outright is more credible than hiding or fudging a feature gap.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Status-grouped accordion lists: Backlog/Done sections with counts and collapse affordance let users manage attention and avoid endless scrolling through large repositories.
  • Consistent metadata row pattern: Every issue card repeats the same iconography + label structure (Assignees, Status, Labels, Milestone, Repository), creating a scannable, learnable grid-like rhythm despite being a vertical list.
  • Transparent fallback messaging: Explicitly notifying users that board view isn't supported on mobile avoids confusion and sets accurate expectations instead of silently degrading.
  • Color-coded label chips: Fast visual categorization system ported directly from GitHub conventions, reducing the learning curve for its developer audience.
  • Dual iconography for issue type: The circular status icon (open/closed) and git-branch icon for PR-linked issues let power users distinguish issue types at a glance without reading text.

screens.name: Linear - Adding an assignee - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this consolidated "edit all properties" sheet pattern whenever an object (ticket, order, contact record, product listing) has many independent metadata fields that users frequently need to adjust in quick succession. It's ideal for admin/power-user tools, CRM records, project management tickets, and e-commerce product editors where jumping between many individual edit screens would be disruptive. The value-preview-as-button technique is broadly reusable anywhere a settings or detail list mixes populated and empty fields.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for consumer-facing apps where users are unfamiliar with domain terminology, as the field names assume prior knowledge (e.g., "Milestone," "Estimate") without any inline explanation or tooltip. It's also unsuitable when fields require complex, multi-step input (e.g., rich date ranges, nested relationships) that can't be meaningfully represented by a single "Edit" tap (in those cases, a full-screen dedicated editor is clearer). Finally, this dense list approach should be avoided for first-time users or onboarding flows, since it offers no contextual guidance and could feel overwhelming to someone unfamiliar with the data model.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers on fast-moving product teams who need to triage, estimate, and assign issues mid-sprint, often while away from their desktop. The design leverages the psychological principle of recognition over recall: by pairing icons with labels and showing live values, users don't need to remember which field controls what; they can scan visually.

The flat, no-frills tone and dense informational layout cater to technically sophisticated users who value speed and efficiency over hand-holding, consistent with Linear's broader brand promise of being the "fast" tool for serious engineering teams. The single modal consolidating nine fields also reduces the cognitive and physical friction of mobile multi-screen navigation, acknowledging that mobile issue-editing is typically a quick, in-between-meetings task rather than a deep work session.
screens.keyHighlights:
Unified metadata editing surface: Rather than forcing users to tap into nine separate screens, all editable issue properties are exposed in one scrollable list, drastically reducing the number of taps and screen transitions needed to fully triage or groom an issue.

Smart value-vs-edit distinction: Showing the actual current value (e.g., "Backlog," "v1.0") instead of a generic "Edit" label wherever data exists turns the field list into a quick-glance summary view in addition to an editing tool (a dual-purpose design decision that respects user time).

Consistent iconography system: Each row's leading icon is semantically tied to its field type (people icon for assignees, tag icon for labels, flag for milestone), which builds muscle memory and speeds up recognition for power users who manage dozens of issues a day.

Lightweight modal pattern: Using a card-style sheet with rounded corners and a dedicated close button (rather than a full-screen push) signals this is a transient, secondary task layered on top of the main issue view, preserving context and encouraging quick in-and-out interactions.

screens.name: Linear - Adding an assignee - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any multi-select assignment, tagging, or ownership picker where a clear distinction between "currently selected" and "available options" improves scanability.
  • Interfaces introducing AI agents or bots as assignable entities alongside human users, where visual/categorical separation builds trust and clarity.
  • Mobile modals that may later scale to long lists, where anchoring search to the bottom supports reachability.
  • Workflows requiring fast, low-friction toggling of membership (project collaborators, reviewers, watchers, labels).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when assignment requires additional metadata per person (e.g., role, permission level) - a simple list lacks the structure to convey that without added complexity.
  • Not ideal for single-select scenarios where a radio-button or simple list with a single checkmark would be less visually heavy than full add/remove iconography.
  • If the list of assignable entities is very short (2-3 people) permanently, a full-screen modal may be overkill versus an inline popover.
  • Risky if "Agents" or automated assignees aren't clearly explained elsewhere in the product (new users unfamiliar with AI agents could be confused by their presence in a people-picker).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, product managers, and designers who need to quickly delegate ownership of an issue (often mid-conversation or mid-triage, where speed matters more than exhaustive configuration). The minimal, keyboard/touch-shortcut-friendly design respects Linear's power-user audience who value frictionless task routing over decorative UI.

The explicit "Agents" section caters to teams adopting AI copilots into their sprint workflows, acknowledging a growing audience segment that delegates tickets to automated agents alongside humans (a forward-looking choice that signals Linear's product positioning at the frontier of AI-augmented engineering teams).

Psychologically, the design reduces "assignment anxiety" by making the current state crystal clear (who's already assigned) and making changes trivially reversible (tap X, tap +), which lowers the perceived cost of experimentation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Selected-state surfacing: Placing already-assigned people at the very top of the list eliminates the need to scroll/search to verify or edit current state.
  • Dedicated "Agents" category: Separating AI assignees (Copilot) from human teammates reduces ambiguity and reflects a thoughtful information architecture decision as AI becomes a workflow participant.
  • Symmetrical add/remove iconography: Using a circular "+" for adding and an "X" for removing creates instantly recognizable, low-friction toggle actions.
  • Bottom-anchored search: Positioning search near the thumb-reachable zone (rather than the top) optimizes for one-handed mobile use and fast filtering of large member/agent lists.
  • Single confirm action: A solitary blue checkmark avoids multiple competing CTAs, keeping the exit path unambiguous.

screens.name: Linear - Adding an assignee - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Any entity with many optional/structured metadata fields (tasks, tickets, CRM records, inventory items) where users need fast bulk access to edit multiple properties.
  • Mobile contexts where screen real estate is limited and drilling into separate screens per field would be too slow for power users.
  • Admin/back-office tools where information density and speed outweigh the need for guided, explanatory UI.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer-facing apps with novice users who need labels explained (this pattern offers zero affordance hints or tooltips and would confuse first-time users).
  • Flows requiring sequential logic or validation dependencies between fields (e.g., start date must precede target date) - a flat list doesn't enforce or visually indicate such relationships.
  • When fields have highly variable input complexity (e.g., rich text, file uploads) that don't fit cleanly into a label-value row (long-form content would break the layout's visual consistency).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers doing rapid issue triage or backlog grooming, often on mobile between meetings or when away from their desk. The density and lack of hand-holding assume power users who already know Linear's data model (Status, Size, Estimate, etc.) from the desktop app.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect and task-batching: by surfacing every editable property on one screen, it invites the user to complete the entire "fill out this issue" task in one continuous session rather than fragmenting it across multiple navigations, reducing the cognitive cost of context-switching and increasing the likelihood of fully-populated, well-groomed issues.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unified metadata editor: Instead of forcing users to tap into nine separate screens, Linear flattens all issue properties into one scrollable list, drastically reducing navigation depth for a core, high-frequency task (triaging/grooming issues).
  • Consistent iconography system: Every field has a bespoke, instantly recognizable glyph (people icon for Assignees, tag for Labels, calendar for dates), creating a visual index that speeds up scanning even before reading the text label.
  • Dual-state value display: Smartly differentiates between fields with a settable "chip" value shown inline (e.g., "Backlog", "v1.0") versus fields needing a dedicated flow ("Edit"), subtly communicating interaction complexity without extra UI chrome.
  • Lightweight modal dismissal: The circular "X" affordance combined with the sheet's visible rounded top corners and the peeking background screen reassures users they haven't left their primary context (ideal for a quick, non-destructive editing session).

screens.name: Linear - Adding an assignee - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any mobile companion app to a complex desktop tool (project management, CRM, dev tools, analytics dashboards) where full feature parity isn't feasible. Use grouped, collapsible status sections with counts whenever users need to triage queues of work items (tickets, orders, tasks, leads). The dense metadata card pattern is ideal for technical/B2B audiences who value information scent over visual polish, and the "unsupported feature" banner pattern is a best practice for any responsive feature degradation across platforms.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, text-heavy card pattern for consumer-facing or low-technical-literacy audiences, where icon-label-value stacks and jargon-heavy labels (enhancement, milestone, repository) would overwhelm rather than inform. Also avoid surfacing a "feature not supported" message without an actionable alternative or link to the desktop app (repeated across many screens, this could feel like a degraded, second-class mobile experience rather than an intentional design choice). For highly visual workflows (e.g., kanban-dependent teams), a collapsed list substitute may cause friction if it's the only way to view priority/status at a glance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, engineering managers, and technical PMs who need to triage GitHub-linked issues on the go, checking in on sprint/backlog status between meetings or outside their desk setup. The density and GitHub-native labeling (enhancement, documentation, help wanted) indicate this is tuned for developers who already think in repository/issue terms, not generalist project stakeholders.

Psychologically, the screen leverages status-grouping as a motivator (seeing items move from "In progress" to "Done" provides a visible sense of progress and closure) and transparency as trust-building (admitting a feature limitation rather than offering a broken experience). The compact metadata exposure also reduces the anxiety of "what am I missing" by front-loading context before a user commits to opening an issue.
screens.keyHighlights:
Key UX decisions worth emulating:

  • Graceful degradation messaging: Explicitly telling users a desktop-only feature (board view) isn't supported on mobile, rather than hiding it or crashing, preserves trust and sets accurate expectations.
  • Dense but digestible issue cards: Each card surfaces 5-6 metadata fields (assignee, status, labels, PRs, milestone, repo) in a compact, icon-led list, enabling triage without opening the issue.
  • Collapsible status groups with live counts: The chevron-and-count pattern (In progress · 1, Done · 2) gives an instant pulse-check on workload distribution and allows users to collapse completed work to reduce scroll fatigue.
  • AI-agent as first-class assignee: Showing "copilot-swe-agent" alongside human avatars normalizes AI pair-programming within existing team workflows without a separate UI paradigm.
  • Relative timestamps ("4 days ago"): Reduces cognitive load of parsing absolute dates, reinforcing a sense of recency/activity.

screens.name: Airtable - Grouping records - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a single object (a view, document, list, or record) has a large number of possible actions that would overwhelm a toolbar if all were shown at once. It's ideal for:

  • Table/database/spreadsheet apps with per-view configuration options (sort, filter, group, field visibility).
  • Any CRUD-heavy admin tool where destructive and non-destructive actions need visual separation.
  • Mobile contexts where screen real estate for a persistent toolbar is limited.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when actions need to be discoverable at a glance without an extra tap (burying a single critical action (e.g., "Save" or "Submit") inside an overflow sheet adds unnecessary friction. It's also inappropriate for a very short action list (2-3 items), where a simple inline toolbar or popover would be faster and require less motion/gesture. Finally, avoid greying out destructive actions without any tooltip or explanation if the reason for disabling isn't intuitively obvious to the user) this can cause confusion rather than reassurance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets operations managers, project coordinators, and data-savvy team members who treat Airtable views as living, reconfigurable reports rather than static spreadsheets. These users frequently reshape the same dataset for different stakeholders (e.g., filtering by status for one team, grouping by owner for another), so quick access to Filter/Sort/Group without leaving the current screen is essential to their workflow velocity.

Psychologically, this leverages the Hick's Law principle (by segmenting high-frequency actions into large touch targets at the top and relegating lower-frequency ones to a scannable list, decision time is minimized). The disabled "Delete view" also taps into error-prevention psychology, reducing anxiety around irreversible actions by making the system visibly block the action rather than letting the user attempt and fail.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Tiered action hierarchy: Frequent actions (Filter/Sort/Group) get prominent icon-button treatment at the top, while rarer actions are demoted to a simple list below (directly reflecting a frequency-of-use mental model).
  • Disabled state as implicit guidance: "Delete view" is greyed out rather than hidden, teaching the user that the action exists but is currently blocked, which reduces confusion versus simply removing the option.
  • Context preservation: The underlying table/record screen remains dimly visible behind the sheet, keeping users spatially oriented and reinforcing that this menu is a transient overlay, not a new destination.
  • Icon + label pairing: Every menu row combines a universally recognizable icon with explicit text, balancing speed for experts and clarity for novices.

screens.name: Airtable - Grouping records - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when building data-management tools, CRMs, or no-code platforms where users need to reorganize dense tabular data without leaving their current context. It's ideal for:

  • Mobile table/grid views where screen space demands a modal rather than a persistent sidebar for configuration.
  • Progressive disclosure of advanced features (grouping, sorting, filtering) that should feel optional and low-commitment.
  • Any tool mixing narrative/document content with structured records, where visual separation (divider, typography hierarchy) must clarify context switches.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The grouping/configuration action involves multiple dependent fields (a single-step bottom sheet will feel cramped and require awkward re-opening for each field, better suited to a full-screen multi-step form).
  • Users are highly technical and would benefit from more powerful, visible controls (e.g., desktop power users) - collapsing options into a shallow sheet can slow down expert workflows.
  • The underlying table/grid is not a core mental model for the audience; non-spreadsheet-literate users may struggle with icon-based type indicators (Aa, select-icon) without more explicit labeling.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets operations, product, and design teams who use Airtable as a flexible project tracker (in this case design ops cataloguing UI components for a Web3 project). The audience is comfortable with spreadsheet logic but wants more structure (typed fields, grouping, views) without writing code or SQL.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduction of perceived complexity: database concepts like "Group By" are notoriously intimidating to non-technical users, so Airtable disguises it as a simple, single-dropdown action in a friendly bottom sheet rather than a complex settings panel. This builds confidence and encourages experimentation, which is core to Airtable's self-serve, no-code value proposition.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hybrid doc+database layout: Freeform rich-text project notes live directly above a structured table, letting a single screen serve both narrative context and structured data without switching apps.
  • Typed column iconography: Small glyphs (Aa for text, select-icon for Category) teach users the data type of each field at a glance, reducing errors when adding data.
  • Lightweight Group By sheet: A single-field combobox in a compact bottom sheet keeps an advanced database operation (grouping) feel as easy as a filter toggle, avoiding intimidation for non-technical users.
  • Persistent context behind the modal: The dimmed-but-visible table beneath the sheet preserves spatial context, helping users remember what they're about to transform.

screens.name: Airtable - Grouping records - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when:

  • Your app exposes structured/tabular data that users need to organize dynamically (CRMs, project trackers, inventory apps).
  • You want to offer powerful desktop-class features (grouping, sorting, filtering) in a mobile-friendly way without overwhelming the primary view.
  • The set of available options is directly derived from user-defined schema/fields, ensuring the action list is always relevant and self-explanatory.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach when:

  • The underlying data model is simple or fixed: adding a "group by" sheet with few meaningful fields adds unnecessary complexity.
  • Users are casual/consumer-facing and unfamiliar with database concepts like grouping/fields (this pattern assumes some spreadsheet literacy).
  • Screen real estate is extremely limited (smaller devices) where stacking a bottom sheet over an already dense table could cause excessive scrolling or occlusion of critical context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations managers, designers, and project coordinators who use Airtable as a flexible project tracker (in this case, tracking a Web3 design sprint's deliverables (Hero section, Wallet UI, Multi-Chain Selector)). These users need spreadsheet-grade organization (grouping, filtering, categorizing) but expect app-grade touch ergonomics on mobile.

The psychological driver here is control and customization: by exposing every field as a potential grouping axis, Airtable signals to power users that the tool adapts to their mental model of the data, rather than forcing them into a rigid, pre-defined structure. This autonomy is central to Airtable's "build your own system" value proposition.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Schema-to-Action Mirroring: The grouping options are pulled directly from existing table fields, so users never have to learn a separate taxonomy (the data model IS the interface).
  • Layered Context Preservation: The bottom sheet dims but doesn't hide the underlying table and record details, letting users maintain spatial awareness of where they are in the hierarchy.
  • Color-Coded Chips as Scannable Metadata: Category values (Interaction, Component, Layout) use distinct pastel chip colors, enabling at-a-glance pattern recognition across rows without reading text.
  • Progressive Disclosure of Power Features: Complex database operations like grouping are tucked behind a single icon tap, keeping the primary table view clean while still surfacing advanced functionality on demand.

screens.name: Airtable - Grouping records - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Data table or spreadsheet apps that need to expose advanced view configuration (grouping, sorting, filtering) on constrained mobile screens.
  • Any scenario where you want users to configure a view transformation while still seeing the artifact being transformed (live feedback).
  • Power-user tools where density and directness are more valuable than hand-holding copy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer-facing apps targeting non-technical audiences (terms like "Group By" and "First → Last" would confuse users unfamiliar with database semantics).
  • Screens where the underlying content is already complex; dimming it behind a modal could overwhelm rather than orient the user.
  • Flows requiring frequent, rapid reconfiguration (a bottom sheet requiring re-open/re-close cycles would be slower than a persistent inline toolbar for expert users doing this repeatedly).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets operations leads, project managers, and power users who are already comfortable with spreadsheet mental models (fields, sorting, grouping) but need that power while working on mobile (e).g., triaging a project board during a commute or standup. The design assumes technical fluency: no onboarding tooltips or explanations accompany "Group By," because the target user already understands the concept from desktop spreadsheet or database tools.

Psychologically, the sheet leverages reduced cognitive load through familiarity: reusing the same mental model and iconography (chevrons, dropdown pills) found throughout Airtable's desktop app builds confidence and reduces the learning curve when switching contexts between platforms.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving bottom sheet: The underlying table and record description stay dimly visible, so users retain situational awareness of what they're grouping rather than being yanked to a blank config screen.
  • Live-preview feedback loop: The table above the sheet already shows a collapsed "None" group row, instantly validating that the chosen field is actively restructuring the view.
  • Compound chip controls: Combining the field selector and direction selector into two adjacent pill-shaped dropdowns within one rule row keeps the configuration dense but scannable (a hallmark of data-dense UI done well on a small screen).
  • Low-commitment affordance: The trash icon next to the rule signals that grouping is reversible and disposable, lowering the psychological barrier to experimentation.

screens.name: Airtable - Grouping records - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this embedded-table-in-document pattern when designing tools for knowledge workers who need both qualitative context and quantitative tracking on the same page (e).g., project briefs with linked task lists, CRM notes with linked deal records, or research docs with embedded datasets. It's ideal for flexible, user-configurable workspace products where rigid separation between "notes" and "database" would feel artificial.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in simple consumer apps or single-purpose tools where data density would overwhelm casual users (e).g., a to-do list app or a social feed. It is also risky on small mobile viewports if the table requires heavy horizontal scrolling, as cramming many columns into a narrow screen can hurt readability and touch-target accuracy. Products needing strict content/data separation for compliance or simplicity reasons should also avoid merging these surfaces.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets operations leads, project managers, and cross-functional builders who need to combine narrative context (goals, briefs) with structured tracking (deliverables, categories) in one place. The psychological trigger is reduced cognitive switching cost: by nesting a database table inside a descriptive document, Airtable removes the friction of jumping between a wiki/doc tool and a spreadsheet tool, which is the exact pain point its target "flexible workspace" audience experiences daily. The grouped, numbered rows also appeal to detail-oriented users who want visible structure and order (row counters, group labels) as a sense of control over complex projects.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Embedded table inside a document view: merges free-form writing with structured relational data in a single scrollable record, eliminating app-switching friction.
  • Grouped rows (None / Layout): automatically clusters records by category field with collapsible chevrons, giving spreadsheet power without manual filtering.
  • Persistent bottom edit toolbar: quick access to attach, format text, apply style/paint tool, and undo actions keeps authoring tools one tap away at all times.
  • Blurred sticky header on scroll: preserves navigation and record title while content scrolls beneath it, maximizing data density on a small screen.
  • Inline "Add" and overflow menu on the table: lets users add records or manage the collection without leaving the record detail context.

screens.name: Airtable - Grouping records - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-table pattern when:

  • Users need to manage a backlog of items that naturally fall into categories (e.g., Tasks by Status, Assets by Type, Leads by Source).
  • You want to allow quick-add functionality without forcing a full-screen form or modal for simple records.
  • The product needs to display both qualitative context (notes/briefs) and quantitative/structured data on the same screen to avoid context-switching.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The dataset is simple and flat with no logical grouping variable, forcing artificial categories adds unnecessary visual clutter.
  • Screen real estate is extremely limited (very small devices), as horizontal scrolling for additional columns (like "Category") can become cumbersome and hide critical data off-screen.
  • Users are non-technical and may be intimidated by spreadsheet-like density; in such cases, a card-based list might be friendlier.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen specifically targets Product Managers, Designers, and Operations leads who need to track discrete assets (like UI components or design iterations) within the context of a broader narrative or brief. The "Web3 Platform Landing" example suggests a design/engineering team tracking deliverables.

The psychological driver here is reducing cognitive load via structure. By grouping chaotic line items (various UI components) under clear headers, the tool exploits the "Chunking" principle of cognitive psychology, making a long list of disparate design assets feel organized and manageable. The inline "+" also leverages the "Path of Least Resistance" to encourage higher data completion rates.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline Grouped Rows: Data is automatically clustered by the "Category" field (Layout, Component, Interaction), turning a flat spreadsheet into a scannable, hierarchical outline.
  • Contextual "Add" Row: Each group contains its own dedicated "+" affordance, allowing users to add a new record directly into the correct category without manual re-sorting or tagging after creation.
  • Document-to-Database Hybrid: The screen seamlessly merges rich-text/document elements (the "Goal" paragraph) with a live database table, blurring the line between a wiki and a spreadsheet.
  • View Switcher: The "Table ∨" dropdown at the top of the collection block implies the same data can be toggled instantly into a Kanban, Gallery, or Calendar view.

screens.name: Craft - Uploading images - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any content-creation or block-based editor (note-taking, CMS, page builders, document editors) where users need to insert varied structural elements quickly. It's ideal when:

  • The app has many insertable block types that benefit from visual differentiation.
  • Users are expected to develop command fluency over time (keyboard-first workflows).
  • Maintaining editing context/flow is important (vs. navigating to a separate screen).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense visual grid for apps with only a handful of insert options (the categorization and thumbnail overhead would be unnecessary complexity for 3-4 choices (a simple inline toolbar suffices)). It's also unsuitable for primarily mouse/trackpad-driven desktop contexts where a slash command isn't a natural input pattern, or for novice-first onboarding experiences where unlabeled thumbnail icons could create ambiguity without a brief tour or tooltip support first.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets power users and design-conscious writers: people who care about the visual rhythm of a document (students, PMs, designers, writers) and who already have muscle memory from tools like Notion or Craft's own prior versions for "/" commands. The visual card grid appeals to users who think in layouts and typography rather than raw text, reflecting Craft's "designed document" value proposition.

Psychologically, the pattern reduces cognitive load via recognition over recall: rather than forcing the user to remember exact command names, the thumbnail previews let them recognize the desired format at a glance, speeding up decision-making and reducing errors (picking the wrong list type).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual command palette: Each block type renders as a miniature preview card instead of a plain icon+label row, making abstract formatting concepts (toggle, numbered list, separator weight) instantly recognizable.
  • Contextual dimming: The document stays visible but muted behind the sheet, maintaining spatial orientation and reducing the jarring "where did my content go" feeling common in full-screen modals.
  • Search-first entry point: Placing a search bar at the very top (above categorized grids) accommodates both power users (typing to filter instantly) and exploratory users (browsing by category).
  • Granular separator options: Offering four distinct separator weights (Extralight to Strong) as first-class visual options demonstrates Craft's document-design DNA (most note apps offer a single horizontal rule).

screens.name: Craft - Uploading images - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this rich, categorized grid-tile command palette when:

  • An app offers many distinct content/block types and users need fast visual recognition over textual scanning.
  • The product's brand identity is built on craftsmanship, creativity, or premium polish, where generic icon lists would undersell the experience.
  • Users are already familiar with the available options and benefit more from quick recall (icon recognition) than from explanatory text.
  • You want to preserve the user's editing context by using a bottom sheet overlay instead of full navigation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The list of insertable items is very short (2-4 options) - a simple inline toolbar or small popover would be faster and less heavy-handed.
  • Users are first-time/novice and need descriptive text to understand what each block does; icon-only tiles can be ambiguous without labels or onboarding.
  • Screen real estate is extremely limited (e.g., small widgets or smartwatch contexts) where a dense illustrated grid can't render legibly.
  • Performance-sensitive contexts where loading many custom icons/thumbnails could introduce lag on slower devices.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets prosumer writers, note-takers, and knowledge workers who treat documents as design artifacts (people who value aesthetics as much as function (a key differentiator from utilitarian tools like Google Docs or plain Markdown editors)). The psychological trigger here is mastery and delight: by presenting block insertion as a visually rich, almost app-store-like gallery, Craft signals that formatting and media embedding is a first-class creative act, not an afterthought. The inclusion of niche block types (Smart Link, Whiteboard, Live Text, code block with syntax highlighting) speaks to power users and creative professionals who need flexible, structured content beyond plain text, appealing to their desire for a tool that scales with sophistication without feeling cluttered.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual-first iconography: Each block type gets a bespoke, full-color illustrated icon instead of a generic line icon, making the palette feel like a curated toolbox rather than a settings menu, reinforcing Craft's "designed document" brand promise.
  • Search-first design: The search bar is placed at the very top of the sheet, acknowledging that as the block library grows, typeahead will be faster than scrolling for experienced users.
  • Dimmed context preservation: Keeping the underlying document faintly visible behind the sheet maintains spatial continuity and reduces the jarring feeling of a full context switch.
  • Unlabeled quick-access slot: Placing "Page Break" above the category groups suggests a smart/recent-use ordering layer sitting on top of the static taxonomy.
  • Dense but breathable grid: A 4-column tile grid balances information density with generous tap targets and whitespace, ideal for thumb reach on mobile.

screens.name: Craft - Uploading images - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a native, privacy-sensitive OS permission (camera, photos, contacts, microphone, location, notifications) is about to be requested and the value exchange isn't immediately obvious to the user. It's especially valuable for:

  • First-time feature triggers (e.g., first attempt to add a cover image).
  • Apps where trust and data privacy are brand differentiators.
  • Any permission request that is easily declined and hard to re-prompt (iOS only shows the system dialog once).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for permissions that are obviously necessary and expected (e.g., asking for microphone access inside a voice-memo recorder mid-recording), where an extra step only adds friction. It's also unnecessary for low-stakes permissions users grant without hesitation, or if used too frequently/early in onboarding before the user has experienced any value, as it can feel like a premature sales pitch for access rather than a justified, in-context need.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users who are about to insert a cover image or inline photo into a document (a core Craft feature given its "cover images, editorial type" positioning). The audience is likely privacy-conscious knowledge workers, writers, and note-takers who may be wary of granting broad photo-library access to a third-party app.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the foot-in-the-door technique: by first asking a soft, contextual, dismissible question ("Allow" vs. "X"), users are primed to say yes to the subsequent hard system dialog, since they've already mentally committed. The explicit "we don't scan" statement also leverages reactance reduction: directly naming and neutralizing the user's likely objection before they can form it.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-permission priming: Explains the "why" before triggering the native OS prompt, which is proven to increase opt-in rates significantly.
  • Native-pattern mimicry: Uses iOS-style list row (icon, label, description, trailing action) so the custom UI doesn't feel foreign or manipulative.
  • Explicit privacy reassurance copy: Directly addresses data-scanning fears, building trust at the exact moment of highest user hesitation.
  • Non-blocking dismissal: The visible close (X) affirms user control and avoids a dark-pattern feel.
  • Partial-height card: Keeps underlying UI dimly visible, reducing the perceived weight/intrusiveness of the interruption.

screens.name: Archive
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any browser or tab-management feature where content is automatically moved out of active view after a period of inactivity, requiring a dedicated, searchable, chronologically-organized location for users to retrieve or manage that archived content later.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if archived content should be permanently and irretrievably removed rather than stored for later retrieval (in cases requiring true deletion rather than archiving, a distinct "delete" flow (rather than an archive-and-search model) would be more appropriate).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Tab History / Recently Closed Tabs: organizes closed or archived tabs chronologically with title, URL, and favicon, closely matching this screen's structure.

  2. Chrome's History page: groups browsing history by date with search functionality, mirroring this Archive's date-grouped, searchable list.

  3. Arc Browser desktop's own Archive feature: the mobile app's Archive directly parallels the desktop Arc browser's auto-archiving tab-management system, maintaining feature consistency across platforms.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Feature Follow-Through: this screen delivers on the "auto-archive" promise made during onboarding and confirmed in Settings, showing archived tabs land somewhere retrievable rather than being silently lost.

  2. Chronological Grouping: organizing entries under date headers like "TODAY" follows familiar browser-history conventions, aiding quick temporal orientation.

  3. Scalable Management Tools: providing both Edit (bulk actions) and Search upfront anticipates the Archive growing significantly over time as tabs continue to auto-archive daily.

  4. Consistent Favicon Usage: using site favicons (the Google "G") alongside titles and URLs gives quick visual source recognition, consistent with standard browser history/bookmark list conventions.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 01
screens.whereToUse: This grouped Stacked List + Preference Center pattern fits any settings surface with a moderate-to-large number of independent preferences that benefit from being scanned at a glance, especially where some options are binary (toggle) and others need a dedicated picker screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when there are only a handful of settings (a flat list would suffice) or when settings are highly interdependent and better presented as a guided wizard rather than an unordered menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari (iOS Settings): same grouped Stacked List + chevron drill-down pattern for browser preferences, a near-identical information architecture.

  2. Chrome (iOS Settings): uses the same colored-icon-plus-label row convention and trailing value text for settings like default search engine.

  3. Notion (iOS Settings): groups toggles and drill-down rows into dividered sections in a comparable Preference Center layout.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking (Miller's Law): Dividers break ~14 settings into 5 digestible clusters instead of one long list.

  2. Recognition over recall: Trailing value text (e.g., "Google", "After 1 day", "Native App") shows current state inline, so users don't need to open each row to check it.

  3. Progressive disclosure: Chevron rows (Global Site Settings, Languages, Search Engine) push secondary complexity to nested screens, keeping this page scannable.

  4. Fitts's Law: Full-row tap targets (not just the switch/chevron) make toggles and navigation rows easier to hit on mobile.

  5. Consistency: Icon-label-value-chevron row pattern repeats identically throughout, lowering the learning curve as users scan down.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any automated content-management feature (archiving, auto-deletion, auto-logout) where users benefit from choosing a personally appropriate threshold, especially when a single fixed default wouldn't suit meaningfully different usage patterns across the user base.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings where offering multiple duration options would create confusing inconsistency (e.g., security-critical timeouts where a single, carefully chosen default is safer than user-configurable flexibility).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Close Tabs Automatically" duration picker: offers a nearly identical range of duration options (1 day, 1 week, 1 month) for automatically closing inactive tabs.

  2. Chrome's "Auto Tab Groups" or memory-saver duration settings: provides comparable configurable timeframes for tab-management automation.

  3. Firefox's tab-unloading/archiving thresholds: similarly lets users choose how long inactive tabs remain before being archived or unloaded.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Resolving Prior Ambiguity: this screen retroactively confirms the "After 1 day" value seen in earlier Settings screenshots was genuinely configurable, not a fixed label.

  2. Range Accommodates Diverse Habits: offering both very short (12 hours) and long (30 days) options serves meaningfully different tab-management styles without forcing a one-size-fits-all default.

  3. Consistent Selector Pattern: reusing the same compact popover-with-checkmark format as the earlier "Swipe to Navigate" setting maintains a predictable interaction model for similar types of choices throughout Settings.

  4. Feature Follow-Through: this control makes the onboarding-promised "auto-archive" feature concretely adjustable, giving users direct control over how aggressively that promise is enforced.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (immediate persistence without explicit save) fits virtually all mobile settings interfaces, where requiring a separate save action for individual preference changes would add unnecessary friction and risk of lost changes if a user navigates away.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit only for settings with significant, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., account deletion, irreversible data actions), where an explicit confirm/save step is appropriate specifically to prevent accidental changes (a distinction correctly reflected in this app's separate use of confirmation dialogs (like the earlier "Clear All" archive action) for higher-stakes actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS Settings app (immediate value persistence): uses an identical pattern where sub-screen selections instantly update and display in the parent settings list without requiring a save step.

  2. Any well-designed settings architecture (Safari, Chrome, etc.): follows this same immediate-persistence convention as a baseline usability expectation for modern mobile settings.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Reliable State Propagation: both changed settings correctly display their new values upon returning to the parent Settings screen, without requiring a manual refresh or save confirmation.

  2. Consistent Interaction Model Across Settings: the same select-then-confirm pattern (whether via popover or dedicated sub-screen) applies uniformly across different setting types (search engine, archive timing, language), giving the whole Settings experience a cohesive, predictable feel.

  3. Immediate Effect Without Explicit Save: no "Save" or "Apply" button was needed at any point in this sequence; each selection takes effect and displays immediately upon choice.

results.query: Preventing user drop-off in multi-step loan underwriting questionnaire

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Third-party integration or partner feature introductions within a host app (e.g., survey panels, cashback offers, affiliate features).

  • Monetization funnels where you want to quickly explain a value proposition and move users into an external SDK/webview flow.

  • Situations requiring lightweight legal consent capture without introducing a full multi-step legal review process.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid pre-toggling consent switches for sensitive data sharing (health, financial, biometric) in regulated markets (this can violate GDPR/CCPA "affirmative consent" requirements).

  • Not appropriate when the terms include material financial obligations or data risks the user genuinely needs to review before proceeding.

  • Avoid this sparse, single-message layout when the feature has meaningful onboarding requirements (e.g., eligibility criteria, survey length expectations) that affect user satisfaction and abandonment rates later in the flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing Dave app users (a cash-advance/banking app) who are already financially motivated and receptive to earning extra income opportunities. The psychological trigger is the reward/incentive loop: "Earn Rewards" taps into extrinsic motivation for users already primed to seek quick monetary gains via the host app.

The pre-checked consent switch leverages default bias / status quo bias, a well-documented psychological principle where users are far less likely to change a pre-set option, thereby increasing opt-in rates for the survey partner's data collection and terms.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-enabled consent toggle: Reduces the number of taps needed to proceed, streamlining opt-in at the cost of true informed consent.

  • Single CTA, zero distractions: No secondary buttons, links, or navigation compete with "Get Started," maximizing conversion probability.

  • Friendly illustration + speech bubble motif: Visually reinforces the concept of "surveys" (conversation/feedback) before the user reads any text, aiding rapid comprehension.

  • Contained legal card: Isolates compliance content into a bordered card so it reads as a discrete, skimmable unit rather than an interruption to the main flow.

  • Clear escape hatch: The top-left "Close" button respects user autonomy, reducing feelings of entrapment in a partner/ad-like flow.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 8
screens.whereToUse:
Use this single-question, large-tile, disabled-CTA pattern when:

  • Collecting sequential demographic or preference data in onboarding or survey flows.

  • You need to maximize completion rates on optional data-collection tasks by minimizing per-step effort.

  • The data collected feeds a reward, personalization, or matching engine and users need clear incentive/progress cues to stay engaged.

  • Designing for one-handed mobile use where large touch targets are critical (e.g., commute-time usage).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The question requires more than 2-3 mutually exclusive options, forcing binary choices (e.g., gender) can alienate users and produce inaccurate/incomplete data; an inclusive, expandable option set or free-text field is more appropriate.

  • The data collection process is very long, as splitting every single field into its own screen can feel tediously slow and increase abandonment despite low per-screen friction.

  • Users expect to edit/review multiple answers together (e.g., account settings), where a consolidated form is more efficient than one-question-per-screen pagination.

  • The survey purpose isn't transparently communicated, asking sensitive demographic questions without context on data usage can trigger privacy concerns and drop-off.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday users of a personal finance/banking app (Dave) who are being incentivized or prompted to complete profile/demographic surveys, likely in exchange for rewards, cash advances eligibility, or personalized offers. The demographic skews toward mobile-first, time-poor consumers who need extremely low-friction interactions to complete optional tasks.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to complete a task once started, especially when shown visible progress) and foot-in-the-door technique (starting with an easy, non-threatening question like gender builds momentum for a longer survey chain, likely including income, spending habits, etc.).

The binary gender options suggest the data is being used for basic demographic segmentation/panel matching (common in survey-reward monetization models), rather than for personalized user experience, where more inclusive options would typically be prioritized.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled-until-valid CTA: The greyed-out "Continue" button provides a passive validation cue, preventing errors before they happen rather than showing them after submission.

  • Large tap-target tiles: Converting standard radio buttons into full-width selectable rows dramatically improves thumb-reachability and tap accuracy on mobile.

  • Micro progress bar: A slim, low-emphasis progress indicator sets duration expectations without dominating the screen, reducing perceived effort.

  • Isolated single-question flow: Asking one question per screen (rather than a bundled form) keeps completion rates high by minimizing decision fatigue at any single step.

  • Clear exit path: The "Close" button in the top-left respects user autonomy, letting them abandon the survey without feeling trapped, which paradoxically increases willingness to start.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for:

  • Multi-step surveys, quizzes, or onboarding flows where you want to maximize per-step completion rates.

  • Data collection moments where each field carries cognitive weight (location, income, preferences) and benefits from undivided attention.

  • Optional/incentivized flows where users need a clear, guilt-free way to exit (e.g., "Close").

  • Situations where you want to convey progress without revealing the full scope of remaining steps (to avoid intimidating users with long forms upfront).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Collecting many related fields that logically belong together (e.g., full address) - splitting them across screens can feel excessively slow and annoying.

  • Users are power users or professionals who prioritize speed over guided simplicity (e.g., B2B admin tools) - a single dense form would be more efficient.

  • The survey is very long; too many single-question screens can cause fatigue from excessive tapping/navigation, even if each screen feels light.

  • Bandwidth/latency is a concern, since each screen transition may require a network round-trip, unlike a single scrollable form.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of a personal finance/cash-advance app (Dave) who are asked to complete short surveys, often in exchange for micro-incentives (points, cash, or eligibility for offers). The audience is typically on mobile, multitasking, and has low tolerance for long, tedious forms.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (the progress bar creates a subconscious desire to complete an already-started task) and foot-in-the-door commitment: once a user answers one easy question, they're more likely to continue answering subsequent ones. The low-friction single-field format also reduces perceived effort, which is critical for surveys where drop-off is the primary risk at every step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-question focus: Isolating one field per screen minimizes friction and decision fatigue, increasing completion rates.

  • Thin progress indicator: Gives a subtle sense of forward momentum without the pressure of an exact step count.

  • Disabled CTA state: The greyed "Continue" button acts as an implicit validation cue, preventing premature or empty submissions.

  • Contextual placeholder: "E.g. 12345" clarifies expected input format instantly, reducing errors and need for extra labels.

  • Clear exit path: The "Close" button respects user autonomy, which is critical for voluntary engagement flows like paid surveys.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this single-question survey pattern when collecting demographic, psychographic, or preference data incrementally in consumer apps, especially in trust-sensitive verticals like finance, health, or insurance. It's ideal for optional research surveys, onboarding personalization, or profile enrichment flows where you want to maximize completion rate without overwhelming the user with a long form. The disabled-CTA-until-selection technique is broadly applicable to any single-select required field.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for mandatory account-critical information (e.g., legal or compliance data) where skipping isn't actually permissible (the "Close" affordance would create false expectations). Also avoid single-question-per-screen pagination for long surveys with 15+ questions, as the number of screen transitions can fatigue users more than a scrollable grouped-question form would. Additionally, sensitive questions like marital status should always include a "Prefer not to answer" option, as omitting it here would create user friction and potential distrust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets existing app users of a personal finance product (Dave) who are being asked to voluntarily share demographic data, likely for personalization, financial product eligibility, or ad-targeting/research purposes. The psychological trigger at play is reciprocity and incremental commitment: by answering easy, low-stakes questions first (in a likely multi-question flow), users become more invested and are more likely to complete subsequent questions (the "foot-in-the-door" technique). The non-intrusive, skippable design also leverages autonomy preservation to reduce reactance in privacy-sensitive contexts like personal finance.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled CTA until valid input: The grayed-out "Continue" button enforces a required response while providing a clear, low-effort visual cue of what's needed to proceed.

  • Optional "Other" with inline expansion: Avoids a jarring navigation to a new screen for edge cases, keeping the flow contained and fast.

  • Explicit opt-out option: "Prefer not to answer" respects user privacy and autonomy, which is especially important for sensitive demographic data in a finance app.

  • Skippable via "Close": Reinforces that this is a voluntary, value-add survey rather than a blocking gate, reducing perceived coercion.

  • Minimalist progress indicator: A thin bar rather than a numbered "Step X of Y" avoids anchoring users to a potentially long remaining survey length, reducing dropout from length anxiety.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 11
screens.whereToUse:
Use this single-question, full-bleed-answer pattern for:

  • Demographic or profiling surveys where you need high completion rates on sensitive questions.

  • Any linear questionnaire/quiz flow (onboarding personalization, research panels, health intake forms) where showing one decision at a time reduces overwhelm.

  • Contexts where you want to preserve user trust by offering an opt-out ("Prefer not to answer") and an easy exit.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The survey has many questions and hiding total progress could feel manipulative once users realize the true length (consider showing a numeric step count for transparency in longer, non-incentivized flows).

  • Users need to compare or reference multiple questions simultaneously (e.g., dependent or branching logic) - a single-question-per-screen approach adds unnecessary friction here.

  • The audience is highly privacy-sensitive or regulated (e.g., healthcare) without proper consent/disclosure language accompanying the data collection.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing users of a personal finance app (Dave) who are being incentivized (typically via cash rewards, points, or app credit) to complete third-party or first-party market research surveys. The demographic skews toward budget-conscious, financially-stretched consumers who are motivated by small monetary incentives to spend a few minutes answering questions.

Psychologically, the design leverages the sunk-cost / momentum effect: once a user starts and sees a progress bar move, they are more likely to continue to avoid losing invested effort. The single-question-per-screen format also reduces perceived effort at any one moment (a form of "chunking"), making a demographically invasive question (marital status) feel like a quick, low-stakes tap rather than an interrogation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• High-contrast selected state: The solid teal fill with a bold checkmark icon makes the current selection instantly scannable, reducing cognitive load compared to subtle radio-dot changes.

  • Ambiguous progress bar: A thin, unlabeled progress indicator communicates movement through the survey without disclosing total length, mitigating the "how long is this going to take" abandonment trigger.

  • "Prefer not to answer" option: A respectful, trust-building inclusion that signals the product values user privacy over data completeness.

  • Expandable "Other" row: Uses a chevron to hint at inline expansion, keeping the user in flow rather than triggering a new screen or modal.

  • Explicit exit path: The "Close" button removes any sense of being trapped, which is especially important for optional, incentivized surveys.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for demographic data collection, onboarding personalization quizzes, market research surveys, or KYC-style questionnaires where you need one clear answer per screen. It's ideal when data accuracy and completion rate both matter, especially on mobile where fat-finger errors on small radio buttons are common.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this full-screen, one-question-per-page approach for very long surveys with 20+ questions unless progress feedback and time estimates are provided (users may abandon due to fatigue). Also avoid for questions that require multiple selections without clearly switching the UI to a multi-select pattern, and avoid for time-sensitive transactional flows where a single-question-per-screen pace would feel unnecessarily slow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday users of the Dave personal finance app (likely a broad, mainstream demographic including underbanked or budget-conscious consumers). Collecting education level allows Dave to segment users for personalized financial content, targeted product recommendations (e.g., cash advances, banking tiers), or to sell aggregated demographic insights to partners/advertisers.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (progress bar creates a subtle desire to complete the unfinished task) and choice simplification (large, clearly labeled options reduce decision fatigue). The non-judgmental phrasing and full inclusion of all education levels also reduce social-desirability bias, encouraging honest responses.

  • Lightweight progress indicator: A subtle top progress bar communicates flow position without adding numeric pressure or clutter.

  • Single-question focus: Isolating one question per screen (single-screen form pattern applied iteratively) minimizes cognitive load and keeps completion rates high.

  • Persistent exit option: The "Close" button respects user autonomy, letting them abandon the optional survey without feeling trapped.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 13
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for optional, low-stakes data-collection surveys embedded within onboarding or in-app engagement flows (especially in fintech, health, or subscription apps where segmenting users (e).g., by employment, income bracket, or life stage) improves personalization or underwriting. Ideal when questions are mutually exclusive and benefit from large touch targets (e.g., mobile-first, thumb-friendly forms). Not suitable for mandatory, business-critical data (e.g., KYC/compliance forms) where skipping via "Close" would leave incomplete records (in those cases, use a blocking wizard instead). screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of Dave, a mobile banking/cash-advance app whose core users are often financially stretched individuals (gig workers, hourly employees, students) who need quick access to credit or banking insights. Collecting employment status helps Dave's underwriting/personalization engine tailor credit limits, financial advice, or eligibility for cash advances.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (visible progress bar creates a desire to complete an unfinished task) and choice simplification (four broad categories instead of an open text field) to reduce friction and abandonment. The disabled button leverages a subtle affordance cue that guides users toward the "correct" next action without explicit error messaging, which is less punishing and more encouraging (important for a financial-wellness brand trying to build trust with users who may already feel financial stress or shame).

  • Chevron-per-option progressive disclosure: Each answer choice can expand to reveal follow-up detail, letting the form stay simple by default while still capturing granular data when needed.

  • Disabled CTA until valid input: The greyed-out "Continue" button acts as a built-in validation cue, preventing null submissions without needing an error toast.

  • Persistent progress bar: A slim top progress indicator sets expectations about survey length, reducing abandonment by showing the user is making measurable progress.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 14

Do not use a playful or humorous tone here, as it risks trivializing sensitive personal identity data. screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets Dave's broad "Busy Urban" user base during account setup or periodic profile enrichment, likely used for internal analytics, compliance (e.g., fair lending/EEOC-style reporting), or personalized financial content. screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 15
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for critical, high-stakes data inputs (like Date of Birth, SSN, or Legal Name) where accuracy is paramount and errors are costly (e.g., financial or medical apps). It is ideal for:

  • Isolating fields that require specific format validation (dates, currency).

  • Situations where you want to force sequential completion of a multi-step form without allowing users to skip ahead.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of granularity (breaking one field into three separate screens/steps or three separate pickers taking up a whole screen) for low-stakes or optional data. If you have many fields to collect, this "one field per screen" approach can feel bureaucratic and slow, leading to drop-off due to the sheer number of taps required to reach the end goal. In such cases, grouping related fields (e.g., Name + Birthdate) on a single screen is more efficient.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users undergoing an identity verification, KYC (Know Your Customer), or eligibility-check process, likely for a financial services app like Dave. The primary psychological driver here is reducing friction and anxiety associated with providing personal identifiable information (PII).

By presenting the request as a "Survey" rather than a rigid "Verification Form," the app leverages a softer framing to lower the perceived stakes of the interaction, making users more willing to comply and complete the required regulatory or eligibility data collection.
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 16

Additionally, in flows where user trust is already high and screen real estate is limited, splitting one field across an entire screen may feel like it artificially inflates the number of steps and could frustrate power users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users onboarding into or engaging with Dave, a neobank/fintech app known for cash-advance and budgeting features. Collecting birth date is almost certainly tied to regulatory age verification (18+) and identity verification (KYC/AML compliance) required for financial services in the US.

Psychologically, framing this as part of "Dave Surveys" rather than "Account Verification" softens the perceived intrusiveness of requesting a legally sensitive data point, making users more willing to comply. The instant age-reflection feedback taps into a small dopamine-triggering moment of self-recognition/personalization ("Oh yes, that's me"), building trust that the app is listening and responding accurately, which increases confidence in proceeding through the rest of the sensitive onboarding/KYC flow.
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: Figma Onboarding 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for high-intent sign-up flows where you want to combine account creation with lightweight personalization data collection (role, use-case) in a single step, rather than a separate onboarding quiz. It's ideal for B2B SaaS and productivity tools where segment-based defaults (e.g., "Design," "Engineering," "Marketing") can meaningfully customize the subsequent experience. The single-CTA, minimal-field approach is best for products where the brand is already trusted or the user arrived with clear intent (e.g., via invite link), so no additional persuasive copy is needed.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the product is unfamiliar and needs to build trust or communicate value before asking for commitment (in that case, a value-prop carousel or short explainer should precede this form. Avoid pre-checking consent/marketing checkboxes in jurisdictions with strict opt-in consent laws (e.g., GDPR in the EU), as this can create legal risk and erode user trust once discovered. Also avoid combining personalization questions with account creation if the use-case/role data isn't actually used downstream to tailor the experience) collecting unused data only adds friction without benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This flow targets new Figma users: likely designers, product managers, or team members being onboarded via an invite or organic sign-up (who are already somewhat familiar with the product's value (hence no persuasive marketing copy at this stage, unlike a landing page)). The psychological strategy leans on momentum and low friction: by minimizing required fields and pre-filling the most probable answer, Figma reduces the perceived time-to-value and keeps drop-off low at this critical conversion point. The pre-checked mailing list box exploits default bias (status quo heuristic) to maximize marketing list growth with minimal active user effort, a common but ethically gray growth tactic.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive personalization embedded in sign-up: Instead of a generic sign-up, the form captures role ("Design") and use-case intent during account creation, enabling immediate downstream personalization (templates, onboarding flow, UI defaults) without a separate quiz step.

  • Smart default pre-fill: The role dropdown is pre-populated with "Design," likely inferred from an invite link, referral source, or prior context, reducing friction and decision fatigue for the most common user segment.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: Only one full-width, high-contrast button is present, eliminating decision paralysis and visually anchoring the user's next action.

  • Minimal field count: Only one true text input (name) is required, with the rest being low-effort dropdown selections, keeping the perceived effort of account creation very low.

screens.name: Figma Onboarding 12
screens.whereToUse:
Utilize this pattern when you need to segment users for the purpose of tailoring subsequent onboarding content, feature recommendations, or marketing attribution, but you only have space for one single question.

screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid adding this to the sign-up form if the choice does not significantly alter the user's subsequent experience; asking for data you don't immediately act upon feels like unnecessary friction.

Do not use a simple text-based dropdown if the options require significant explanation or if you want to track more analytical/visual distinction between choices (in those cases, visual card selectors (tiles) perform better for engagement and clarity).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The psychological trigger at play here is the Consistency Principle: by asking the user to self-identify their category immediately, Figma can tailor the subsequent onboarding experience (templates, tutorials, and pricing recommendations) to match the expectations set by this specific answer, making the rest of the onboarding feel custom-built for them.
screens.keyHighlights:
The most brilliant decision here is the strategic placement of a personalization/segmentation question directly within the mandatory sign-up form, rather than saving it for a separate "Welcome" screen after email verification. This maximizes the data capture rate because it rides on the momentum of a user who is already committed to filling out a form (reducing drop-off compared to a standalone survey).

  • Visual Feedback: The distinct blue focus state on the input border immediately communicates which field is currently active, reducing cognitive load for the user navigating a potentially zoomed-in mobile browser view.

screens.name: Figma Onboarding 13

Also avoid pre-filled dropdowns if the defaults could skew data collection or mislead less attentive users into submitting incorrect information; in high-stakes forms (e.g., legal, financial), defaults should be used cautiously or avoided in favor of explicit empty states that force deliberate selection.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users: likely designers, product managers, or cross-functional collaborators, signing up for a professional design tool, captured mid-funnel after they've already supplied core credentials (email/password presumably on a prior screen). The role and use-case dropdowns are a lightweight personalization/segmentation mechanism, letting Figma tailor onboarding content, templates, or marketing messaging without resorting to an intrusive multi-screen quiz.

Psychologically, the form leverages the sunk-cost momentum of a user who has already started sign-up: by this point they are motivated to finish, so the form keeps friction minimal (few fields, defaults pre-filled, single CTA) to capitalize on that momentum before motivation decays.

screens.name: Figma Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for post-signup profiling screens where you need just enough data to personalize the subsequent experience (content, templates, pricing nudges) without overwhelming a brand-new user. screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if you need to collect more than 3-4 data points (long single-screen forms without progress indication cause fatigue and abandonment). screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new Figma sign-ups: designers, product managers, and students (immediately after account creation).
