screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern as the very first screen of a multi-step onboarding carousel for any product that needs to establish category positioning and emotional safety before asking for an account. It's ideal for:

  • Apps entering a category associated with difficulty or technical intimidation (math, coding, finance, data tools like Airtable).
  • Products wanting to differentiate instantly via a strong, literal visual metaphor tied to their core value prop.
  • Flows where you want to delay authentication friction and let users experience value messaging first.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy illustration-first splash pattern when:

  • The product's value proposition is highly functional/utilitarian and better demonstrated through live product screenshots or interactive demos rather than metaphorical art (e.g., enterprise dashboards where users want proof, not promise).
  • Users are already familiar with the brand and arrive with high intent (e.g., a deep link to a specific record) - inserting a full-screen marketing slide here would add unnecessary friction.
  • Time-to-value is critical and every extra screen before sign-up hurts activation metrics; in that case a direct sign-up or guest-mode entry may convert better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Although this specific screenshot stylistically resembles a math/CS learning app (e.g., Brilliant) rather than Airtable's own onboarding, the underlying pattern is highly relevant to Airtable's workspace-builder audience: teams, operations staff, marketers, and project managers who are often non-technical and may feel intimidated by a "database/spreadsheet" tool. The psychological trigger here (using a relatable, benefit-driven illustration and copy to de-risk a technically perceived product) is exactly the strategy Airtable itself could employ to reassure first-time users that "no-code power" is approachable, not engineering-only.

The screen leverages the authority/competence trigger (best-in-class claim), the reduction of perceived effort (bite-sized, guided), and low commitment entry (Continue vs. Sign up) - all critical for converting skeptical, time-poor professional users in a worldwide, cross-vertical market.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Domain-specific hero illustration: Using a rocket with an actual physics formula (J = u·δm) instantly communicates the app's subject matter and builds credibility with a technically-minded audience, far more effective than generic abstract shapes.
  • Deferred sign-up framing: The primary CTA says "Continue," not "Sign Up," lowering the psychological barrier to tapping forward into the funnel.
  • Dual-path hierarchy: A bold filled button for new users paired with a subtle text link for returning users ("Log in") cleanly segments two very different intents on one screen without adding visual clutter.
  • Single progress dash: Minimal onboarding-step indicator sets expectation of a short, respectful intro flow.

screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this single-select goal/persona capture pattern during onboarding when:

  • The product serves multiple distinct user segments that benefit from different content, pacing, or feature emphasis.
  • You want to increase perceived personalization and investment early in the funnel before asking for payment or deeper commitment.
  • You need lightweight, low-friction data collection that doesn't feel like a traditional form (e.g., consumer apps, edtech, habit trackers, wellness apps).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The product is strictly single-purpose or B2B utility software where goal branching doesn't meaningfully change the experience, as it adds friction without downstream payoff.
  • Users are already deep in a task-oriented workflow, inserting a conversational quiz mid-task breaks flow and feels patronizing.
  • The options list is long or ambiguous; too many categories (beyond ~6-7) increases decision fatigue and should instead use a searchable or grouped selector.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for new users at the very start of their lifecycle, immediately after signup or app install, when motivation and willingness to share information are at their peak (the "fresh start" effect). By asking about goals before showing any product functionality, the app leverages the IKEA effect and commitment-consistency bias: once a user explicitly states their goal, they are psychologically more likely to persist with an experience tailored to that stated goal.

The varied options (career, students, parents, teachers) indicate the app targets a horizontal, multi-persona audience rather than a single niche, and this question functions as an implicit segmentation/branching mechanism that will likely drive personalized content recommendations later in the onboarding or home feed.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Speech-bubble mascot framing: Turns a standard form question into a friendly, guided conversation, lowering the perceived effort of onboarding.
  • Emoji/icon-paired options: Each choice has a unique, instantly recognizable icon, enabling fast visual scanning and reducing cognitive load versus text-only lists.
  • Disabled CTA until selection: The greyed-out 'Continue' button enforces a mandatory choice while visually teaching the user the interaction model without extra copy.
  • Segment-spanning options: Covering professionals, students, parents, and teachers in one question efficiently captures persona data in a single tap, enabling downstream personalization.
  • Linear progress bar: Sets expectations about onboarding length, a key factor in reducing early drop-off.

screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Early onboarding flows where personalization of templates, dashboards, or content depends on user intent or goals.
  • Apps serving multiple distinct personas (e.g., students vs. professionals) that benefit from branching experiences.
  • Any product wanting to inject personality/warmth into an otherwise technical or data-heavy tool to reduce first-session drop-off.

• Avoid for returning/power users: repeating a quiz-style gate after initial setup feels patronizing and adds friction.
  • Not ideal for strictly enterprise B2B tools where users expect a professional, no-frills tone; overly playful mascots/emoji may undermine credibility with IT admins or procurement stakeholders.
  • Risky if the collected answer doesn't meaningfully alter the downstream experience, asking for input without visible personalization payoff breeds distrust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users during first-run onboarding, spanning professionals, students, parents, and educators. By asking "why are you here?" early, the product can segment users psychologically, triggering motivation-based personalization (a technique rooted in self-determination theory) so that subsequent screens, templates, or content recommendations feel tailor-made rather than generic.

The emotional, mascot-led tone specifically targets users who may be intimidated by a powerful but complex tool, using approachable visuals to reduce perceived learning curve and increase completion rates of the onboarding sequence.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emoji-as-icon system: Using expressive emoji instead of generic line icons makes each option feel distinct, human, and quick to parse at a glance.
  • Speech-bubble framing: Anchoring the question in a chat-bubble emanating from a mascot creates a conversational, guided feel rather than a sterile form.
  • Clear selected-state styling: The blue border/fill on the chosen card provides unambiguous confirmation of selection with no extra taps needed.
  • Persistent progress bar: Signals the user's position in a larger sequence, reducing abandonment anxiety common in multi-step onboarding.
  • Single persistent CTA: The fixed "Continue" button removes friction and decision fatigue about what to do next.

screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 5

• Early onboarding sequences for B2B SaaS, EdTech, or data tools where the user base is broad and new users may question fit or competency.
  • Post-signup, pre-personalization-quiz or pre-paywall moments where you need to build emotional buy-in before asking for more commitment (e.g., payment, deep setup).
