screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users immediately after sign-up, specifically those who may be uncertain if a tool is "for them" (e.g., non-technical operations staff evaluating a data-heavy platform like Airtable, or beginners unsure if they have the skill level for the product). By invoking scale ("Millions of professionals") and belonging, the screen reduces early-funnel anxiety and activation friction, which is critical for tools with a learning curve.

For Airtable specifically, this mirrors the real challenge of onboarding non-technical "builders" who may feel spreadsheets-to-database transitions are intimidating; normalizing the community broadens perceived accessibility.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-focus layout: Only one actionable element (Continue button) eliminates decision paralysis during onboarding.
  • Segmented progress bar: Builds a sense of momentum and sets a finite expectation for onboarding length, reducing drop-off.
  • Illustrative diversity cards: Visually represent multiple professional domains (engineering, analytics, coding) to help a wide range of users self-identify with the product instantly, without needing a personalization quiz result yet.
  • Persistent back navigation: The chevron back arrow preserves user control/agency even inside a guided funnel, lowering perceived pressure.
  • High-contrast, full-width CTA: Large tap target with strong color contrast mimics native iOS patterns, ensuring the action is instantly discoverable.

screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern during onboarding flows that require skill, interest, or preference calibration (e).g., language learning apps, fitness apps asking fitness level, finance apps asking investment experience, or any personalization quiz that feeds into adaptive content difficulty. It's especially effective when:

  • The product can meaningfully branch content/difficulty based on the answer.
  • Options can be visually differentiated (images, icons, or examples) rather than relying purely on text.
  • You want to increase completion rates in a multi-step onboarding sequence by making data collection feel conversational rather than transactional.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The underlying content/experience does not actually adapt based on the response, asking the question without delivering personalized value feels manipulative once discovered.
  • There are more than 4-5 options, as the 2x2 card grid will require scrolling or cramped cards, hurting scannability.
  • Speed is critical and users are already familiar with the product (returning users) - the illustrative, slow-paced conversational tone is best reserved for first-time onboarding, not routine settings changes.
  • The audience skews highly expert/professional (e.g., enterprise B2B tools) where a playful mascot and casual tone may undercut perceived credibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users entering an educational product (students, parents, or adult learners) during initial onboarding, before any content is served. The psychological drivers include:

  • Self-determination & autonomy:
  • Reduced evaluation anxiety: Because there's no "right or wrong" quiz being graded, users are more likely to answer honestly, leading to better personalization downstream.
  • Identity affirmation: First-person statements leverage the "self-referencing effect," where people remember and engage more with information framed around themselves.
  • Progress visualization: The green progress bar taps into the Zeigarnik effect (once users see partial completion, they're motivated to finish the sequence (a well-known onboarding pattern to reduce abandonment)).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual-first option cards: Each skill level is represented with an actual worked math snippet rather than a text-only label, letting users gauge their comfort instantly and accurately.
  • First-person micro-copy: "I can..." / "I understand..." phrasing invites honest self-identification rather than triggering a "test-taking" anxiety response.
  • Disabled CTA until selection: Prevents accidental skip and guarantees the personalization engine receives data for every quiz step.
  • Friendly mascot + speech bubble: Converts a data-capture form into a guided dialogue, increasing perceived warmth and lowering onboarding drop-off.
  • Persistent progress bar with back navigation: Sets clear expectations of flow length and gives users control/escape hatch, reducing commitment anxiety.

screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this single-screen card-selection pattern during onboarding personalization flows where skill level, interest, or content tier must be captured quickly (e).g., language learning apps, fitness apps (fitness level), educational platforms, or any adaptive-content product. Ideal when you have a small number (3-6) of mutually exclusive tiers that benefit from visual representation instead of plain text, and when you want to make a potentially judgmental self-assessment feel safe and affirming.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are many options (beyond ~6), as the grid will require scrolling and lose scannability (use a list or dropdown instead). Not suitable when precise, objective skill measurement is required (e.g., certification or compliance testing), since self-reported levels can be inaccurate; in those cases use an actual diagnostic quiz with scored questions. Also less effective if the options cannot be meaningfully visualized (e.g., abstract preferences), where the illustrative graphic advantage is lost.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Designed for new users of a math learning/tutoring app (likely students or lifelong learners) who need personalized content difficulty from the very first session. The psychological trigger is self-determination and autonomy: letting the user choose their own level fosters ownership and reduces the fear of being 'tested' and found lacking. The encouraging headline and graph/equation visuals also serve users with math anxiety by normalizing all starting points as valid ('every math genius starts here'), which increases onboarding completion and reduces early drop-off for a learning app targeting worldwide audiences across varying educational backgrounds.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual math previews on cards: Each tile shows an actual equation or graph relevant to that skill level, letting users instantly recognize their comfort zone without reading dense text.
  • First-person self-identification copy: Framing options as 'I can...' statements turns a test into a confidence-affirming self-selection, reducing performance anxiety.
  • Mascot + speech bubble: Builds an approachable, friendly brand voice right at a potentially vulnerable onboarding moment (admitting skill level).
  • Clear selected-state styling: Blue border/fill vs. neutral gray immediately communicates the current choice with high contrast.
  • Persistent progress bar: Signals near-completion of onboarding, sustaining motivation to finish.

screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when onboarding needs to gather behavioral/contextual data (not just demographics) to power personalization features like reminder scheduling, content curation, or notification timing. It's ideal for consumer apps, habit-building tools, learning platforms, wellness apps, and any product that sends time-sensitive nudges. The single-question-per-screen format is best when you have 3-6 steps total and want to maximize completion rates through incremental commitment.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, illustrative conversational style for B2B, enterprise, or productivity tools (like Airtable itself) where users expect efficiency over personality (dense data-driven audiences typically prefer compact multi-field forms or skip-able setup wizards instead of one-question-per-screen flows). Also avoid if the question doesn't lead to a visible, valued personalization payoff, as users will perceive it as a stalling tactic rather than meaningful setup.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users during first-run setup who are being profiled for personalization (e.g., scheduling reminders, content pacing, or notification timing). The psychological triggers include:

  • Commitment & Consistency: small, low-effort choices early in onboarding increase the likelihood of continued engagement later.
  • Personal relevance bias: by referencing daily life moments (breakfast, lunch, bed), the app signals it will adapt to the user's unique life rather than imposing a generic schedule.
  • Goal-gradient effect: the near-full progress bar subtly accelerates completion motivation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Conversational chat-bubble UI transforms a data-collection form into a dialogue, lowering perceived friction.
  • Scenario-based options instead of abstract labels (e.g., "during breakfast or my commute") help users self-identify faster than generic time-slot pickers.
  • Disabled CTA until selection clearly communicates the required action without using intrusive error messaging.
  • Progress bar near completion motivates users to push through via the near-finish effect (goal-gradient hypothesis).
  • Consistent visual rhythm of icon + bold keyword + description across all four cards aids fast scanning and reduces decision fatigue.

screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse: Reusable whenever a product needs to capture lifestyle/usage-context preferences early in onboarding to drive later personalization (e.g., notification scheduling, content recommendations, habit-based nudges). Works well for habit-tracking, learning, fitness, wellness, and productivity apps. Also effective anywhere a single-select multiple-choice question benefits from large touch targets and visual iconography to speed decision-making.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, personality-driven approach in enterprise, B2B, or professional data tools (ironically including Airtable itself) where users expect efficiency over whimsy (excessive mascot commentary can feel juvenile or slow down power users trying to get to the product quickly). Also avoid if the onboarding already has many steps, as redundant lifestyle questions can increase drop-off; keep such personalization quizzes short and clearly value-justified.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users during first-run onboarding who are being profiled so the app can tailor content, reminders, or notification timing to their lifestyle. By asking "when do you usually use this app," the product can later personalize push notification timing, content difficulty, or session length (a classic data-driven personalization strategy).

Psychologically, the screen leverages micro-commitment (each small, easy choice builds investment in the onboarding flow, a foot-in-the-door technique), the Von Restorff/Isolation Effect (icons help differentiate options instantly), and reciprocity via personality (the humorous mascot comment makes the user feel acknowledged, encouraging continued engagement).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Conversational mascot + speech bubble that reacts contextually to a previous answer, creating a sense of continuity and delight across onboarding steps.
  • Bold keyword + light descriptor text hierarchy inside each option for fast scanning.
  • Large card-based single-select options with icon, label, and clear selected-state styling (blue border/fill) for effortless, thumb-friendly interaction.
  • Persistent progress bar at the top communicating onboarding length and reducing drop-off anxiety.
  • Sticky bottom CTA that remains accessible regardless of list length or scroll position.

screens.name: Airtable - Onboarding - Screen 10
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before requesting any one-shot, non-reversible OS permission (notifications, camera, location, contacts) during onboarding or first-run flows. It is especially valuable when:

  • The permission is not immediately obvious in value to a first-time user.
  • You only get one native prompt attempt and want to maximize acceptance rate.
  • The app's core value proposition is tied to timely alerts (reminders, collaboration mentions, automation results, deadline nudges).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The permission's value is already self-evident from context (e.g., asking for camera access right as the user taps a 'scan' button) - an extra priming screen there only adds friction.
  • Onboarding is already lengthy; stacking another full-screen step can increase abandonment.
  • The app targets highly technical/power users (e.g., advanced Airtable admins) who may find an overly consumer-style, coach-like tone ("reach your daily goal") inconsistent with a professional B2B data tool (tone should be adapted to match enterprise credibility rather than gamified consumer apps).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users mid-onboarding who have not yet formed a usage habit. For a tool like Airtable (used by teams, operations staff, and project managers) notifications could cover record updates, automation triggers, mentions, or deadline reminders. Priming screens like this are critical because operations and productivity users are highly sensitive to notification overload, so framing the ask around tangible value (staying on track, not missing updates) increases opt-in likelihood versus a blind native prompt.

Psychologically, this leverages the foot-in-the-door technique (agreeing to a small, framed request primes agreement to the subsequent system dialog) and loss-aversion framing implied by "stay on track," suggesting that declining risks falling behind on goals or workflows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Simulated system dialog as a visual rehearsal tool: Showing a mock OS permission prompt with a pointing-hand illustration teaches the user exactly what to tap next, reducing confusion and accidental dismissal.
  • Soft-ask before hard-ask pattern: Decouples the explanation from the actual OS-level, one-time-only permission request, maximizing the chance of acceptance.
  • Benefit-first messaging: Ties the permission to a concrete user outcome (daily goals/reminders) instead of app-centric language.
  • Asymmetric CTA hierarchy: Bold filled button vs. plain text link clearly signals the preferred path while keeping the decline option accessible and non-punitive.
  • Progress indicator continuity: Keeps users oriented within the onboarding flow, reducing anxiety about how many steps remain.

screens.name: Oportun Cancelling Subscription 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern at the exact moment a user commits to canceling a paid subscription, deleting an account, or downgrading a plan. It's effective in SaaS, subscription commerce, fintech, and membership apps where churn reasons directly inform retention offers (discounts, pause options, educational content) or product roadmap prioritization. Best paired with a disabled CTA to nudge selection while still respecting user autonomy via a clear skip option.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for free-tier account deletions or low-stakes actions where forcing any interaction (even skippable) adds unnecessary friction and frustration. Do not omit or bury the skip option, making the survey feel mandatory, or following it with aggressive retention pressure/dark patterns, will damage trust and can violate consumer-protection regulations (e.g., FTC "click-to-cancel" rules) that require cancellation to be as easy as sign-up. Also avoid overly long or multi-select surveys here, as elongating the cancellation path itself is a compliance and reputational risk.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets paying subscribers who have already initiated a cancellation (a high-value, high-churn-risk segment). The psychological strategy leans on the norm of reciprocity (the app has given a service, so answering a quick question feels like a fair, low-cost favor) and sunk-cost/foot-in-the-door tactics (once a user engages with the form, they're more likely to continue through to a retention offer rather than abandon the flow). It also serves the business need for churn analytics, letting product/growth teams quantify why users leave (price sensitivity vs. confusion vs. competitor loss) and route each segment to a tailored save offer.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled-until-selected primary CTA: Forces at least one micro-decision before the user can proceed, maximizing feedback capture rate without technically blocking cancellation.

  • Non-punitive "Skip" escape hatch: Preserves user trust and avoids feeling coercive by giving an equally prominent, friction-free opt-out.

  • Diagnostic answer set: Reasons are pre-selected to map directly onto solvable business levers (pricing objection, confusion, awareness gap) enabling a targeted win-back offer on the next screen.

  • Empathetic microcopy: Frames a revenue-defense mechanism as a customer-care gesture, reducing perceived friction and negative sentiment during a moment of user frustration.

screens.name: Oportun Cancelling Subscription 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern in any subscription cancellation, account deletion, or unsubscribe flow where diagnostic churn data is valuable. It's ideal for SaaS, fintech, and subscription-box products that want to route specific cancellation reasons into different downstream retention offers (e.g., pricing objection → discount; confusion → tutorial). Always pair with a visible skip/escape option to keep it ethical and non-coercive.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when it's used purely as a delay tactic with no visible skip button, hidden cancellation flows, or multiple sequential surveys before allowing exit (these tip into dark-pattern territory and generate regulatory/reputational risk (e).g., FTC "click to cancel" scrutiny). Also avoid for free-tier downgrades or low-stakes actions where the friction cost outweighs the data value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets users who have already decided to churn (the goal is not to force retention on this screen, but to (a) capture actionable churn data for the product/growth team, and (b) create one last low-friction touchpoint where a save-offer (e.g., discount, pause) could be triggered based on the selected reason (e.g., "cost too high" could trigger a discount offer next). Psychologically, it leverages the sunk-cost/reciprocity principle) users who already trust the brand are often willing to spend 3 seconds helping "improve the service" even as they leave, especially when assured it won't block their exit.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking friction: A skip button is always visible, ensuring the survey never becomes a dark-pattern hard stop that traps the user.

  • Self-diagnostic reason list: Includes options like "I didn't know this was a paid app," which doubles as a covert audit of onboarding/paywall clarity issues.

  • Visual hierarchy nudge: Primary black "Continue" button is emphasized over the outlined "Skip," subtly encouraging data submission without blocking exit.

  • Single-select radio pattern: Keeps the ask lightweight (one tap) versus a multi-select or open text field, lowering abandonment of the survey itself.

screens.name: Oportun Cancelling Subscription 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern at the final step of a cancellation, uninstall, or offboarding flow when you want to capture unstructured qualitative data without adding friction to the exit. It is ideal for SaaS products, subscription services, or apps where retaining a golden opportunity for feedback is valuable, but forcing completion would increase support tickets or app store complaints about "dark patterns."
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the business goal is aggressive retention, as the low-friction "Skip" option will result in high skip-rates and low data capture, providing minimal actionable insight. Additionally, do not use this for critical account actions (e.g., legal consent, payment updates) where skipping could lead to downstream errors (reserve the "easy skip" treatment strictly for optional sentiment/feedback collection).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users who have already committed to canceling a subscription (post-decision), Product/Growth teams, and Customer Success stakeholders who rely on churn qualitative data. Psychologically, it leverages the "foot-in-the-door" technique in reverse, having already agreed to progress through several cancellation confirmation steps, the user is now primed to comply with one small, easy request (leaving a comment) before their exit is finalized. It also uses reciprocity: by making the exit process painless and non-manipulative up to this point, users may feel more inclined to reciprocate with honest, constructive feedback rather than blank apathy or hostility.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inverted CTA Hierarchy: The "Skip" button is styled with a bold, high-contrast outline while the "Continue" button is disabled/greyed out, visually nudging users toward finishing the flow without friction if they have nothing to add.

  • Optional Friction: By making the text area entirely optional (no character minimums or red asterisks), the design respects the user's time during an already negative-sentiment interaction (cancellation).

  • Whitespace Management: The vast empty space below the text field prevents the screen from feeling like a demanding "essay" form, keeping the cognitive load extremely low.

  • Persistent Exit: Keeping the "Exit" link visible in the header throughout the cancellation flow builds trust that the user is not being coerced into staying.

screens.name: Oportun Cancelling Subscription 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern in offboarding, cancellation, or account-deletion flows where qualitative exit feedback is valuable but must not create additional friction or resentment. Ideal for churn-analysis programs, free-text NPS-style follow-ups, or any optional feedback capture appended to a completed primary task.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the feedback request meaningfully delays a user's ability to complete a time-sensitive or urgent action (e.g., emergency account recovery, payment failure resolution). Also avoid making "Skip" visually indistinguishable or hard to find, as forcing feedback in a cancellation flow damages trust and increases negative sentiment/support complaints. Do not use playful/positive placeholder ghost-text if the brand tone or context calls for serious, formal acknowledgment (e.g., B2B enterprise cancellations).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already committed to canceling a paid subscription (a high-value, high-risk-of-churn moment for the product team). The design leans on psychological principles of reciprocity (the app has "given" the user value, subtly implying they might "give back" a comment) and foot-in-the-door technique (having already answered earlier cancellation-reason questions, the user is primed to continue engaging rather than break the pattern).

The soft, encouraging tone is calibrated for users who may feel some guilt or ambivalence about leaving, using empathetic design to keep the interaction pleasant and preserve brand goodwill even as the business loses a subscriber, increasing the odds of win-back later.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Optional-but-encouraged feedback: Skip is always available, respecting user autonomy while the visual weight of Continue nudges completion.

  • Empathetic placeholder copy: "You're doing great" as example text reframes an open text field from a chore into an easy, low-stakes affirmation opportunity.

  • Retention-team data capture: Positioned at the terminal step of cancellation, this maximizes the chance of capturing qualitative churn reasons before the user disengages entirely.

  • Dual exit paths: Both a back arrow (revisit previous step) and an "Exit" link (abandon flow entirely) are offered, reducing feelings of being trapped in the flow.

screens.name: Wealthfront Setting Up 16
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when collecting sensitive or high-friction personal/financial data (income, SSN, health info) as part of an onboarding or setup wizard. It's ideal when:

  • The data point directly drives a personalized outcome (recommendation, pricing, eligibility).

  • You need to justify a legally or ethically ambiguous ask.

  • You want to keep completion rates high by breaking a long form into single-question steps.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this single-question-per-screen approach for low-stakes, low-sensitivity fields (e.g., first name), where it would feel needlessly slow and patronizing. Also avoid omitting the "why" explanation for any field perceived as invasive, doing so without justification significantly increases abandonment and erodes trust. Not suitable for power users doing bulk data entry or account migrations, where a single consolidated form is more efficient.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective users of a robo-advisor or automated investing platform (e.g., Wealthfront, Betterment-style products) who are in the account-funding/setup phase. These are typically new-to-investing or busy professionals who want a guided, low-effort path to a personalized portfolio rather than manually picking assets.

Psychologically, the design leverages the reciprocity and transparency principle: by explaining the reasoning behind an intrusive question, users feel respected rather than interrogated, increasing willingness to disclose. The foot-in-the-door technique is also at play, having already committed to prior onboarding steps (implied by the progress bar), users are more likely to continue rather than abandon due to sunk-cost/consistency bias.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive Disclosure of Sensitive Data: Isolating one intrusive question per screen lowers the perceived effort and psychological resistance compared to a dense form.

  • Just-in-Time Justification: Explaining the "why" immediately adjacent to the input field pre-empts user distrust and reduces drop-off on a highly sensitive field.

  • Redundant Trust Layer: The secondary "Why do you need my income?" link offers deeper reassurance without cluttering the primary copy, catering to more skeptical or privacy-conscious users.

  • Native, Frictionless Input: Auto-focused numeric keypad with live currency formatting removes ambiguity and speeds up entry with minimal taps.

  • Transparent Progress: The thin segmented progress bar under the step title manages expectations about the length of the onboarding journey, reducing perceived burden.

screens.name: Wealthfront Setting Up 17
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for onboarding flows that must collect subjective, preference-based data (e.g., risk tolerance, goals, personality/preference quizzes) in financial, health, or personalization apps where the outcome directly shapes a downstream recommendation (portfolio, meal plan, content feed, etc.). It's ideal when:

  • The decision has real consequences and benefits from a moment of reflection.

  • Users may lack domain-specific vocabulary and need plain-language options.

  • The flow is long enough to warrant progress indication to sustain motivation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, one-question-per-screen wizard approach for low-stakes or frequently repeated interactions, as it will feel slow and paternalistic. It's also unsuitable when:

  • Users are highly experienced/expert and want dense, information-rich forms rather than guided hand-holding.

  • The number of questions is very large, where screen-per-question pacing would create excessive friction and drop-off.

  • Real-time responsiveness or bulk data entry is needed, where a single consolidated form would be more efficient.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new or prospective robo-advisor/investment app users during account setup (typically first-time or novice investors who are unfamiliar with formal financial terminology but have intuitive feelings about growth versus safety). By avoiding terms like "risk tolerance" and instead asking about desired outcomes ("grow savings," "avoid losing money"), the design leverages the psychological principle of reducing perceived complexity to increase completion rates and self-report accuracy.

The wizard format and visible progress bar tap into the Goal-Gradient Effect, motivating users to complete the flow since they can see they are partway through a defined process. Presenting distinct, binary-feeling extremes plus a middle "something in between" option also uses the psychological anchoring effect, making the choice feel simpler by bounding it between two poles.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Plain-language risk framing: Replacing technical risk-tolerance jargon with relatable, emotionally resonant statements lowers the barrier to accurate self-assessment.

  • Single-question-per-screen pacing: Isolating one decision at a time inside a multi-step wizard reduces overwhelm and increases completion accuracy for a high-stakes financial questionnaire.

  • Progressive disclosure via chevrons: Each option leads to a deeper follow-up rather than immediately committing the user, allowing for more nuanced calibration of risk profile.

  • Contextual just-in-time help: The "Why are my investing goals important?" link provides optional rationale exactly when the user might need reassurance, without cluttering the primary UI.

  • Visible progress + easy exit: The progress bar and close button together balance motivation to continue with the psychological safety of being able to leave anytime.

screens.name: Wealthfront Setting Up 18
screens.whereToUse:
• Any regulated onboarding flow where a binary eligibility/compliance question gates access to further features (e.g., accredited investor checks, age verification, jurisdiction restrictions, tax residency declarations).

  • Multi-step KYC/AML flows where isolating one legally significant question per screen improves auditability and reduces user error.

  • Situations where the two answer paths lead to meaningfully different subsequent flows, justifying the "chevron drill-in" affordance over simple toggles.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for low-stakes preference questions (the heavy, isolated single-question format will feel overly bureaucratic and slow down flows that don't require legal precision).

  • Don't use bare Yes/No chevron rows when the answer doesn't branch into different flows; a simple toggle or radio button pair is more efficient and less misleading.

  • Not ideal if the underlying concept is complex and users are highly likely to need clarification (in such cases, inline definitions or a preceding educational screen may reduce error rates better than a hidden help link).

  • Should be avoided if you need to collect multiple compliance answers at once for efficiency reasons; splitting every yes/no question onto its own screen can excessively lengthen the onboarding funnel and increase abandonment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets prospective users of investment platforms, private equity/venture crowdfunding apps, or alternative asset marketplaces (e.g., real estate syndications, startup equity platforms, hedge fund access apps) that are legally obligated under SEC Regulation D to distinguish accredited from non-accredited investors before showing certain offerings.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the authority and formality bias: the clinical, form-like presentation signals seriousness and legitimacy, priming the user to answer honestly rather than casually. The binary Yes/No framing also employs the choice-reduction principle, preventing analysis paralysis on a question many retail users may not fully understand, while the help link caters to the self-efficacy need of anxious or first-time investors who don't want to answer incorrectly.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-Question Focus: Isolating one high-stakes, compliance-driven question per screen eliminates ambiguity and ensures the user's attention and intent are unambiguous (critical for legal/audit purposes).

  • Chevron-as-Branch Pattern: Using ">" instead of checkmarks or radio buttons signals that each answer leads to a distinct downstream path (e.g., "Yes" may trigger document upload, "No" may trigger a different investment tier), setting correct expectations before the tap.

  • Dual Exit Points: Providing both "Back" and "Close" respects user autonomy on a screen that could otherwise feel like a forced gate, reducing anxiety and drop-off-driven frustration.

  • Deferred Definition Link: Placing "What's an Accredited Investor?" as a secondary link rather than inline text keeps the primary decision uncluttered while still meeting informed-consent/education needs.

  • Minimalist Progress Indicator: The slim bottom progress bar communicates forward motion in the onboarding funnel without resorting to a numbered "Step 3 of 7" label that could highlight how long the flow is.

screens.name: Wealthfront Setting Up 19
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a product must obtain informed, legally binding consent for financial, medical, or otherwise high-stakes actions (brokerage account opening, loan agreements, insurance policies, margin/credit agreements, or terms with arbitration clauses). It's ideal when regulatory bodies require explicit acknowledgment of multiple documents but the business wants to preserve a clean, non-intimidating UX. The slide-to-confirm mechanic is well suited to any "point of no return" action (fund transfers, account closure, contract signing).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-consent pattern for low-stakes or reversible actions (e.g., toggling a notification preference), where the added friction of a slide gesture and legal bullet list would feel bureaucratic and cause unnecessary drop-off. Also avoid burying critical clauses (like arbitration or fee structures) only inside linked PDFs without any on-screen summary, as it can create legal risk and erode trust (the bullet summary technique used here should be preserved, not omitted, in similar high-stakes consent screens).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets retail investors opening a self-directed or margin-enabled stock investing account, likely already engaged users who have progressed through several prior onboarding steps (evidenced by the near-complete progress bar). The design assumes a financially engaged but not necessarily legally trained audience, hence the translation of formal agreements into scannable bullets.

Psychologically, the screen leverages trust-building through transparency (explicit callouts of arbitration, margin, and electronic communication clauses) combined with effort-justification via the slide gesture: the physical act of sliding reinforces the seriousness and irreversibility of the commitment, which can increase perceived legitimacy and reduce buyer's remorse or regulatory disputes later.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Serif/sans-serif type pairing creates an emotional-to-functional reading hierarchy, softening an otherwise dense legal screen.

  • Plain-language bullet summary of dense legal agreements dramatically reduces cognitive load while preserving full legal transparency via linked source documents.

  • Slide-to-confirm CTA instead of a simple tap button adds appropriate friction for a high-stakes, binding financial commitment, preventing accidental agreement.

  • Persistent exit and back controls paired with a progress bar give the user a sense of control and context within the larger onboarding funnel, reducing signing anxiety.

  • Inline hyperlinked legal documents keep the primary content lightweight while ensuring full compliance disclosure is always accessible.

results.query: How to design soft paywalls that preserve content exploration before login

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when:

  • You have a freemium model with a clear, easily-tabulated feature delta between tiers (5 or fewer comparison rows works best for scannability).
  • The user has already had a taste of core value and is hitting a natural usage ceiling (not interrupting onboarding cold).
  • You want to visually bias a decision without resorting to pushy copy, letting color/elevation do the persuasion.
  • Offering a free trial, where a risk-reversed CTA can replace a harder "Buy Now" ask.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The feature list is long or nuanced: comparison tables degrade quickly past 6-7 rows and start requiring actual reading, which defeats the scan-based persuasion.
  • Pricing transparency is a regulatory or trust requirement in your market (e.g., some fintech or EU contexts) - deferring price could feel evasive rather than frictionless.
  • Your brand tone is utilitarian/enterprise: the playful gradient and floating-card treatment would feel incongruous in a B2B SaaS context.
  • Users haven't yet experienced core value: showing this paywall too early (before the "aha" moment) will read as aggressive and spike uninstall/decline rates.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets engaged free users who have already completed at least one daily lesson loop (people who've felt the tactile, drag-and-slide satisfaction Brilliant is known for and are now hitting a natural ceiling (limited daily lessons, locked course jumps)). The design assumes intrinsic motivation already exists; it doesn't need to sell the product, only the unlock.

Psychologically, it leans on loss aversion (seeing 4 of 5 rows X'd out under "Free" makes the user acutely aware of what they're missing) and anchoring (the visually dominant Premium card sets the "normal" expectation, making Free look like the compromised, crippled option rather than the default). The free trial CTA exploits the endowment effect: once a user commits to "my free week," they begin to feel ownership over the Premium features before ever paying.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Floating card overflow: The Premium column visually breaks out of the table grid, creating a 3D "lifted" card effect that signals superiority without extra copy.
  • Color-coded binary scanning: Orange checkmarks vs. grey X's let users compare tiers in under two seconds, no reading required.
  • Gradient brand tie-in: The rainbow border and gradient wordmark on "Premium" link the paywall aesthetically to the app's playful illustration-driven brand language rather than feeling like a generic commerce screen.
  • Deferred pricing: No price is shown on this screen, reducing sticker-shock and front-loading value before cost (classic foot-in-the-door sequencing).
  • Risk-reversal CTA: "Start my free week" instead of "Subscribe" or "Upgrade" removes perceived risk and commitment anxiety at the moment of decision.

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any free-trial paywall confirmation, especially for subscription products with auto-renewal. It is ideal when:

  • App Store/Play Store compliance requires clear trial-to-paid disclosure.
  • The target audience skews trust-sensitive (education, finance, health apps).
  • You want to reduce trial abandonment caused by fear of hidden charges.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The product has a true no-payment-required trial (the timeline/reminder framing would feel unnecessary and add friction).
  • Speed-to-conversion is critical and extra screens meaningfully hurt funnel completion rates in A/B tests.
  • Your brand strategy intentionally obscures renewal terms (not recommended, but some low-trust dark-pattern funnels skip this for short-term conversion gains at the cost of refund/chargeback rates).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective subscribers who are curious but price-sensitive or wary of being "tricked" into a recurring charge (a common friction point for STEM/edtech apps competing against free YouTube content). By front-loading transparency, Brilliant reduces the perceived risk of starting a trial, which is especially important for its worldwide audience that may include users unfamiliar with Western auto-renewal subscription norms.

Psychologically, this leverages the reciprocity and trust-building principles: by proactively disclosing the "gotcha" (the charge date and reminder), the brand positions itself as honest, which lowers the psychological barrier to commitment. The timeline format also taps into the Zeigarnik effect: once a user sees a multi-step journey mapped out, there's a subconscious pull to complete it, i.e., to tap 'Start'.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent Trial Timeline: Converts confusing subscription terms into a simple, scannable three-step narrative, building trust rather than relying on surprise billing.
  • Dual-purpose Connector Line: The gradient vertical line functions simultaneously as a timeline guide and an implicit progress bar, reinforcing forward momentum toward conversion.
  • Pre-emptive Reminder Disclosure: Explicitly stating the day-5 email reminder reduces anxiety about forgetting to cancel, which paradoxically increases trial sign-up rates.
  • Exact Charge Date: Stating "October 13" instead of a vague "7 days" removes ambiguity and satisfies platform compliance for subscription transparency.
  • CTA Reframing: "Start my free week" emphasizes value-received language over cost/commitment language.

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for subscription-based products with a strong brand identity and content-led value proposition (especially in education, fitness, and habit-building apps where the user has already sampled value before hitting the wall). It's ideal when you want to convert trial users softly, without alienating them via a hard paywall, and when annual plans are the primary revenue driver (since the small monthly price point reduces hesitation).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this soft, single-plan approach if your product benefits from tiered differentiation (e.g., Basic/Plus/Pro) where users need to compare feature sets (a single plan would feel restrictive or opaque). Also avoid closable 'X' exits if your business model relies on hard paywalls to force conversion at a critical gate. Finally, this slow, illustration-heavy, trust-building layout is unsuitable for fast transactional contexts (e.g., re-subscribing an already familiar lapsed user) where users want to skip straight to checkout.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets engaged trial users: people who have already clicked through a few lessons and are emotionally invested in the "gym for your brain" metaphor, but haven't yet committed financially. Brilliant's worldwide, largely self-motivated learner audience (students, professionals, lifelong-learning hobbyists) responds well to low-pressure, intellectually respectful sales tactics rather than aggressive urgency.

Psychological triggers at play include: Loss Aversion (don't lose access to the gym you've started building a habit in), Anchoring (monthly price framing), Risk Reversal (free trial + clear cancellation terms reducing commitment anxiety), and Consistency (maintaining the same illustrative visual language builds subconscious trust that this is 'part of the learning experience,' not a separate ad).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-plan focus: Avoids multi-tier comparison fatigue by presenting one annual plan as the default/only path, simplifying the decision to a binary yes/no.
  • Price reframing: Highlighting the small monthly-equivalent price ($13.33/mo) in large bold text while the actual annual charge ($159.99) is shown smaller, leveraging anchoring bias to reduce sticker shock.
  • Illustration continuity: Using the same hand-crafted 3D illustration style found throughout the learning content, making the paywall feel like a natural extension of the product rather than an ad interruption.
  • Transparent risk reversal: Explicit, un-hidden renewal terms build trust and reduce the "gotcha" feeling, which is crucial for a brand built on intellectual credibility.
  • First-person CTA: "Start my free week" personalizes the commitment and softens the perceived cost of the action.

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any subscription or payment confirmation flow where backend processing (App Store/Play Store/Stripe) takes more than ~500ms.
  • Flows where accidental double-taps could cause duplicate charges or errors.
  • Moments of high user anxiety (checkout, trial activation, irreversible actions) where reassurance copy reduces drop-off or support tickets.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for near-instantaneous actions where a modal would feel like unnecessary friction (a simple inline spinner or optimistic UI is better).
  • Don't use an opaque full-block modal if the backend call is unpredictable or could take very long (>10s) without a fallback/error timeout message, as users may think the app is frozen.
  • Not ideal for flows where you want to keep the user editing or exploring (this pattern deliberately halts all interaction, which is only appropriate for committed, final actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This moment targets any user who has just made the decision to start a free trial (typically someone already convinced by the value proposition and price anchoring on the screen beneath). The psychological goal here is purely to reduce transactional anxiety and prevent error states (double taps, perceived freezing, or uncertainty about whether the purchase went through). By showing a clear, branded, calm processing state rather than a blank screen or generic OS spinner, Brilliant maintains trust continuity through the riskiest step of the funnel: the moment money/commitment is on the line.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking context preservation: The pricing screen remains visible (dimmed) behind the loading modal instead of navigating away, reducing anxiety that the selection was lost.
  • Indeterminate spinner + status label: Combines a classic spinner with explicit copy ("Completing purchase..") so users understand exactly what stage of the transaction they're in.
  • Disabled CTA during processing: The "Start my free week" button is greyed out, preventing duplicate submissions/double billing (a critical e-commerce safeguard).
  • Persistent legal transparency: Trial and billing terms stay visible beneath the modal, reinforcing trust at the highest-anxiety moment of the funnel.

screens.name: Brilliant - Subscribing to Brilliant - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any subscription or trial-based paywall flow where regulatory/App Store compliance requires explicit trial-to-paid disclosure (iOS/Android subscription apps). It's especially valuable for premium education, wellness, or productivity apps targeting trust-sensitive, detail-oriented users who are prone to subscription anxiety. Pair native purchase confirmations with reassuring, non-hype microcopy immediately after checkout to reduce chargebacks and improve trial retention.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid relying solely on a native system dialog as the "celebration" moment for products where onboarding momentum and emotional delight are critical to activation (e.g., gamified consumer apps) - a plain OS alert can feel flat and may need to be followed by a richer branded welcome/success screen. Also avoid repeating legal disclaimers so many times in playful, low-friction impulse-purchase contexts (e.g., in-app cosmetic purchases) where excessive fine print can introduce unnecessary doubt and hurt conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users who have just converted from a free to a trial-premium tier (the highest-intent moment in the funnel. The psychological goal here is to immediately reduce post-purchase dissonance ("did I just get tricked into a subscription?") through plain-language confirmation and explicit billing transparency. For a worldwide STEM-learning audience that skews toward analytically-minded, skeptical users (students, professionals, lifelong learners), over-explaining the billing terms builds credibility and trust rather than being perceived as noise) this audience actively reads fine print and rewards honesty with retention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native OS Confirmation Dialog: Leveraging the system-level purchase confirmation instead of a custom in-app modal borrows platform credibility and satisfies App Store trust conventions instantly.
  • Dual-Metaphor Illustration: The dumbbell-shaped key icon elegantly fuses the "mental gym" brand concept with the universal "unlock" symbol for premium content, reinforcing brand identity at the exact point of conversion.
  • Redundant Trial Transparency: Repeating the no-charge/cancel-anytime message in two separate places (fine print + micro-copy above CTA) pre-empts regret and subscription-fatigue anxiety, a key driver of trial abandonment.
  • Minimal Chrome: A single close (X) icon is the only escape hatch, keeping full visual focus on the value proposition and confirmation rather than navigation options.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a user lands on a dashboard with an empty or near-zero primary metric (balance, inventory, tasks) and you want to convert that dead-end moment into a guided next action. Particularly effective for fintech, crypto, or SaaS products where the "next best action" is well-defined (deposit, invite, upgrade). Pairing a first-party feature promo with a dismissible sponsored unit is effective for monetizing engagement without heavy-handedness, provided sponsorship is clearly labeled.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid stacking multiple promotional modules when the user's zero-state is due to a routine action (e.g., just logging out and back in) rather than genuine inactivity (repeated upsells can feel tone-deaf or spammy). Also avoid this pattern in contexts where trust is fragile (e.g., first-time onboarding before KYC/verification) since pushing deposits too early can raise suspicion or regulatory concerns. Never omit the "Sponsored" label, and never remove the dismiss option, as forcing exposure to ads in a financial context erodes trust quickly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets crypto-native or crypto-curious users who already hold a self-custody wallet but haven't yet deposited funds (likely a new or dormant user segment). The design leans on psychological principles including loss aversion (idle crypto = wasted opportunity), social proof and legitimacy (via the Morpho brand and reward eligibility badge), and reward incentives ($MORPHO token rewards) to trigger a deposit action. The "Trending onchain" section beneath further taps into FOMO/curiosity to keep even non-depositing users engaged and scrolling.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-state monetization: Instead of a passive empty state for the $0.00 balance, the screen immediately pivots to high-intent upsell content, turning a potential drop-off moment into a conversion opportunity.

  • Labeled sponsorship transparency: The "Sponsored" label above the native ad maintains user trust and regulatory/ethical clarity while still blending stylistically with organic content.

  • Dismiss affordance: Giving equal visual footing to "Deposit Now" and "Dismiss" respects user agency and prevents ad fatigue/annoyance, a subtle but important trust-building UX choice in a financial app.

  • Dot-grid decorative background: The card's subtle dot pattern adds visual sophistication and a "premium fintech" feel without competing with the text or CTA.

  • Redundant persuasion loop: Two consecutive modules (first-party promo + sponsored ad) both push the same "deposit/earn yield" action, maximizing the chance of conversion via repeated exposure.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 7
screens.whereToUse: Adapt this pattern for any app combining a personal dashboard with a content discovery feed (e).g., crypto wallets, creator economy platforms, or fintech apps introducing new "drops" or features. It's especially effective when you want to surface community-driven or time-sensitive content (mints, drops, limited offers) directly on the home screen with low-friction CTAs.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for first-time users unfamiliar with domain jargon, as the icon-only tab bar and dense terminology (onchain, mint) can create confusion without onboarding support. It's also risky when balance is zero and the primary content pushes spending/minting actions immediately (this can feel tone-deaf or overly sales-driven for users who haven't yet funded their account). Not ideal for apps prioritizing simplicity or first-run clarity over content density.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for crypto-native and Web3-curious users who already hold a self-custody wallet and are comfortable navigating onchain jargon (mint, onchain, address). The target user is likely an early adopter or NFT collector seeking new mini-apps and drops rather than a total beginner requiring hand-holding.

Psychologically, the design leverages social proof (showing dozens of other minters) and curiosity/FOMO (curated "Trending" carousel, truncated descriptions) to drive engagement and minting actions. The $0.00 balance juxtaposed against enticing mint opportunities and trending content also subtly nudges users to fund their wallet in order to participate.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero Carousel for App/Mini-App Discovery: Using a full-width, immersive carousel (Paperview) to surface trending onchain mini-apps treats discovery like a curated editorial feed rather than a boring app list, increasing engagement.

  • Social Proof-Driven Mint Cards: Each NFT mint opportunity shows "@user and X others minted," leveraging bandwagon psychology to reduce decision friction and imply FOMO-driven scarcity.

  • One-Tap Mint CTA: The persistent, high-contrast "Mint" pill button on each list item removes navigation friction (users can act immediately from the home feed without drilling into a detail page first).

  • Icon-Only Tab Bar: A minimalist bottom navigation using pure iconography (no text labels) keeps the UI clean and signals a power-user, crypto-native audience.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 8
screens.whereToUse:
Use this feed-based discovery pattern for crypto wallets, Web3 super-apps, or any platform bridging a technical/financial product with a content-discovery layer. It's especially effective for:

  • Onboarding new-to-category users by making unfamiliar actions (minting, connecting to dApps) feel like familiar social browsing.

  • Driving engagement in wallets/portfolios that would otherwise be static and only visited during transactions.

  • Merchandising time-sensitive or curated content (drops, trending apps) above static financial data.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for professional trading platforms, institutional finance dashboards, or any context where users expect immediate, dense access to portfolio performance, charts, and transaction history, burying that data below a media carousel would frustrate power users. Also avoid unlabeled icon-only tab bars for first-time users without a brief onboarding/coach mark, and avoid mixing high-risk financial actions (minting/spending) with casual social-feed framing for products serving risk-averse or compliance-heavy audiences.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets crypto-native and crypto-curious users on iOS who need a low-friction way to discover legitimate onchain apps and NFT drops without navigating opaque marketplaces or Etherscan-style interfaces. The design specifically caters to users who are more comfortable with consumer app UX (Instagram, TikTok, App Store) than with traditional finance dashboards, easing them into Web3 behaviors (minting, connecting to dApps) through familiar visual metaphors.

Psychologically, the screen leans on social proof (mutual mint counts), curiosity gaps (truncated descriptions), and low commitment framing (a single tappable "Mint" pill button) to convert passive scrolling into onchain action. The immediate visibility of $0.00 without gating or a heavy empty-state message keeps a new/empty wallet from feeling like a dead end.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Feed-ification of Web3: Reframes NFT minting and dApp discovery using familiar social/app-store UI (carousels, thumbnails, social handles) to lower the intimidation barrier of blockchain jargon.

  • Embedded Social Proof on CTA rows: Showing "@handle and 46 others" next to each mint opportunity leverages bandwagon effect to drive conversion without needing star ratings or download counts.

  • Zero-state balance without an empty-state screen: Rather than blocking the user with an empty wallet message, the $0.00 balance sits quietly at the top while the feed below gives the user something to do immediately (mint, explore) - turning a potentially discouraging moment into an engagement opportunity.

  • Info icon on "NFT mints for you": A small transparency affordance clarifying that this is an algorithmic/personalized recommendation, building trust around a feed the user didn't explicitly curate.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this dashboard-as-discovery-feed pattern for platforms where the core home screen risks feeling empty for new or low-activity users (e.g., wallets, investment apps, marketplaces). It's ideal for surfacing sponsored/partner content and personalized recommendations directly on the primary landing screen to drive activation and habitual return visits.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in contexts where users expect immediate, uncluttered access to their core financial data (e.g., banking apps) since mixing promotional carousels and merchandising with balance information can feel like it dilutes trust or introduces conflict-of-interest concerns. Also avoid icon-only, jargon-heavy tab bars and copy for less experienced or mainstream consumer audiences without added labels or onboarding cues.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets crypto-native power users: early adopters, NFT collectors, and DeFi/onchain app explorers (who are comfortable navigating wallets without heavy hand-holding text). The design assumes familiarity with concepts like "minting," "onchain," and wallet addresses (shown as truncated "Address 1").

Psychologically, the screen leverages social proof (mint counts, handles), curiosity/FOMO (trending carousel, scarcity implied by "for you" personalization), and low-friction discovery (one-tap Mint buttons) to keep users engaged even when their wallet holds no funds, effectively using content merchandising to drive re-engagement and transaction volume.
screens.keyHighlights:
Turning an empty balance into an opportunity: Rather than showing a stark "$0.00" with nothing else, the screen immediately pivots to curated discovery content, softening the potentially discouraging empty wallet state.

Native ad/content carousel: The trending onchain card behaves like a full-bleed sponsored placement with an embedded interactive prompt field, blurring the line between content and product, increasing engagement with third-party onchain apps.

Social-proof-driven mint list: Attaching "@handle and X others" to each NFT mint leverages bandwagon psychology, making minting decisions feel validated by community activity rather than solitary speculation.

Minimal icon-only tab bar: Reduces visual clutter and reinforces a power-user, symbol-literate audience who already understands wallet iconography conventions.

screens.name: Spotify - Manage subscription - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription management screens for any SaaS or media app needing to communicate trial status without inducing cancellation anxiety.
  • Apps with multi-faceted "bundle" subscriptions (e.g., Amazon Prime style) where users often forget which specific perks they are paying for.
  • Post-trial "nurture" flows designed to increase feature discovery before a renewal decision is made.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this passive "soft-sell" layout if the business goal is aggressive, immediate conversion (e.g., a trial ending in 24 hours), where a more urgent, high-contrast banner would be required.
  • Do not use this pattern for single-feature subscriptions where there is no "snapshot of benefits" to showcase, as the module would feel empty or redundant.
  • Not suitable for B2B admin dashboards where billing/seat management requires more granular, data-table driven interfaces rather than lifestyle-oriented illustrations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets trial users and existing subscribers who may be uncertain about the tangible value of their payment. By surfacing a "Snapshot of your benefits" (specifically Audiobook listening time), Spotify leverages the Endowment Effect: making users feel they already possess valuable assets (listening hours, discounts) that would be lost upon cancellation.

The "Get to know your benefits" carousel specifically targets users who signed up for the headline feature (ad-free music) but are unaware of bundled perks (Audiobooks, Family Mix, Discounts), aiming to increase feature adoption to drive down trial-churn rates.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-Tone Branding: Using a pink/magenta accent for "Individual" Premium status visually separates account-tier information from standard navigational green accents, preventing user confusion between "content" and "account" states.
  • Soft Retention Strategy: Instead of a hard paywall or urgent banner, the trial expiration is presented as a simple utility line item, reducing subscription anxiety while keeping the user informed.
  • Benefit Re-engagement Module: The "Get to know your benefits" card acts as a mini-onboarding flow embedded within the settings, ensuring users justify their subscription cost by discovering underutilized features (like Audiobooks).

screens.name: Spotify - Manage subscription - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription/account management screens in apps constrained by platform billing policies (iOS/Android IAP restrictions).
  • Any settings surface where transparency about limitations can preempt user frustration or support escalations.
  • Billing summary screens needing to clearly state renewal date, price, and plan tier in a scannable, low-anxiety format.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this passive "informational-only" pattern when the business goal is active plan conversion or upselling (a stronger CTA-driven layout would be needed instead).
  • Do not use self-deprecating/apologetic copy in contexts where it could undermine brand confidence (e.g., high-stakes financial or legal flows where users need assurance of control, not an admission of limitation).
  • Not suitable for platforms without billing restrictions, where native in-app editing of plans is expected and this redirect-style pattern would just add unnecessary friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing paying subscribers who are auditing or confirming their billing status (a moment of heightened scrutiny and potential anxiety (common triggers: unexpected charge, forgotten trial, or curiosity about price changes)). The design's psychological strategy is to reduce anxiety through radical clarity: dates, amounts, and plan names are stated plainly with no ambiguous jargon.

The apologetic disclaimer about not being able to edit plans in-app serves a dual audience: it manages expectations for new premium users unfamiliar with App Store billing restrictions, and it reassures frustrated users that Spotify is aware of the limitation, reducing perceived indifference from the brand.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radical transparency copy: Explicitly telling users they can't edit their plan in-app, with an empathetic, human tone, preempts frustration and support tickets.
  • Billing clarity: Exact renewal date, exact price, and offer-expiry are surfaced together, reducing surprise billing complaints (a major churn/trust driver for subscription apps).
  • Non-blocking navigation: Keeping the bottom tab bar visible on an account/settings screen signals this is a low-stakes, easily-exited destination, reducing anxiety around visiting billing settings.
  • Soft upsell placement: "Explore plans" is tucked low in hierarchy as a card row rather than a banner or modal, respecting user intent (they came here to check status, not necessarily to buy).

results.query: Where to avoid using modal bottom sheets for complex multi-input forms

screens.name: Brilliant - Giving Feedbacks - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for in-context feedback or bug-reporting forms embedded directly in a product experience, especially in educational, SaaS, or content-heavy apps where surfacing content errors quickly is valuable. It's ideal when:

  • You want users to report issues without navigating away from their current context (e.g., triggered by a shake gesture or a persistent feedback icon).
  • The form only needs 2-4 fields and benefits from a simple, single-screen structure instead of a multi-step wizard.
  • You need lightweight required-field cues (red dot) rather than heavy-handed error messaging before the user has even attempted submission.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the report needs significant context (e.g., screenshots, logs, device diagnostics) without a clear, labeled way to attach them (here the unlabeled "+" button is ambiguous and could confuse users about its function). Also avoid for flows requiring multiple categorized attachments or longer narrative input, where a single small text field is insufficient. If the feedback type requires branching logic (e.g., different follow-up fields depending on ticket type), this flat single-screen form would need to evolve into a multi-step form to avoid overwhelming or under-collecting information.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engaged, detail-oriented learners: the type of self-motivated STEM learner who notices when an explanation is "a bit vague" and cares enough to report it rather than simply bouncing. Brilliant's audience skews toward analytically-minded users who appreciate having a direct, low-ceremony channel to influence content quality.

Psychologically, the design leverages investment and ownership: by making it fast and easy to report a flaw, Brilliant turns a moment of frustration into a moment of contribution, which can increase loyalty and perceived product quality. The pre-populated email (already known from the user's account) reduces friction and signals that the system "already knows you," reinforcing trust and reducing abandonment at the final required field.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Low-friction exit points: both a back arrow and a circular close "X" are available at the top, respecting the user's time and preventing the feedback flow from feeling like a forced detour.
  • Required-field red dots: a lightweight, unobtrusive validation pattern that flags missing information without resorting to intrusive error banners until submission is attempted.
  • Dedicated vertical breathing room: the large empty space before the Email field visually separates "what happened" from "who you are," subtly structuring the mental model of the form into two logical groups.
  • Third-party trust badge: the "We run on Shake" mark builds credibility and signals that feedback is taken seriously and routed through dedicated tooling.

screens.name: Brilliant - Giving Feedbacks - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• In-app bug reporting or feedback forms where visual evidence dramatically improves the quality of support tickets.
  • Any attachment-picker use case needing to differentiate between multiple capture/source types (camera, gallery, files, screen).
  • Contexts where you want to preserve underlying screen context rather than fully navigating away, such as lightweight utility actions nested inside a longer form.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the attachment options exceed 5-6 items (a bottom sheet list becomes unwieldy and should shift to a grid or dedicated screen).
  • Not ideal for destructive or security-sensitive actions (e.g., sharing device location) without additional permission priming, since this list mixes casual item like "Pick from gallery" with more sensitive "Browse other locations" without differentiated weight.
  • Should be avoided on flows requiring strict user focus, where a dimmed-but-visible background could distract or create unintended context bleed between the ticket and the attachment flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets engaged, detail-oriented learners and power users of Brilliant who notice friction points (vague explanations, unclear visuals) and want to report them. Offering screenshot/screen-recording capture directly in-flow caters to users who think visually and want to show, not just tell, what's wrong, reducing the effort barrier that normally causes most users to abandon feedback forms before submission.

Psychologically, this leverages the effort-justification/investment principle: by making it trivially easy to attach rich evidence, Brilliant signals that it genuinely values granular feedback, which increases the likelihood of higher-quality, more actionable submissions from its most invested users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed-but-visible background: The ticket form remains legible behind the sheet, maintaining context and reducing the cognitive cost of modal interruptions.
  • Color-coded icon system: Each attachment option gets a unique accent color, turning a plain text list into a fast, scannable menu without adding visual clutter.
  • Low-friction bug reporting: Native screen-grab and screen-record options are surfaced directly inside the feedback flow, removing the need for users to leave the app to attach evidence.
  • Dual exit paths: Both a back arrow and an explicit "X" close button give users flexible, low-risk ways to abandon or retreat from the flow.

screens.name: Brilliant - Giving Feedbacks - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Educational or training apps teaching quantitative, logical, or procedural concepts where a visual model can replace a wall of text.
  • Any linear micro-learning flow (language learning, coding, finance literacy) that benefits from one-question-per-screen pacing and instant feedback.
  • Gamified habit-building products wanting to reward correct actions with lightweight, non-intrusive XP/streak mechanics.
  • Products targeting global/multilingual audiences, since diagram-driven content minimizes localization burden.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Complex, multi-variable or open-ended problems that can't be reduced to a simple visual metaphor, forcing a diagram here could oversimplify or mislead.
  • Expert or advanced-level content where users want efficiency over hand-holding; the single-question-per-screen pacing would feel slow and condescending.
  • Contexts requiring robust review/backtracking (e.g., certification exams), since this app's "weak backward review" navigation would frustrate users needing to revisit prior questions.
  • Time-pressured assessment scenarios where XP/confetti celebrations would feel misplaced or distracting from serious evaluation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed adult learners and STEM-curious users (worldwide, language-agnostic since much of the content is mathematical notation and visuals) who want bite-sized, low-pressure practice rather than lecture-style video courses. The tactile, game-like mechanics (XP, streak icon, instant green checkmark) borrow proven psychological triggers from gamified habit apps: immediate positive reinforcement, small variable rewards (+15 XP), and visible incremental progress, all of which drive session completion and return visits.

The bar-diagram approach specifically appeals to visual/kinesthetic learners and those with math anxiety, since it reframes an intimidating equation as a concrete, colorful comparison task, lowering the barrier to engagement for non-expert audiences.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual proof before verbal explanation: The bar-model diagram lets users perceptually verify the algebra, embodying "move something before it explains anything."
  • Color-coded segment matching: Reusing purple/blue/orange across both bars creates an implicit visual legend that reduces the need for explanatory text.
  • Non-blocking feedback drawer: Correctness, XP reward, reporting, and deeper explanation ("Why?") are all bundled into one bottom sheet instead of separate modals, keeping flow momentum.
  • Granular progress bar: The segmented dash indicator at the top shows exact position within a short lesson, lowering perceived effort and anxiety about length.
  • Deferred depth via "Why?": Optional, low-commitment secondary action caters to varying learner needs without forcing extra steps on everyone.

screens.name: Brilliant - Giving Feedbacks - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Adapt this pattern whenever you need frictionless, contextual bug/feedback reporting embedded directly inside a core product flow (especially in education, productivity, or gaming apps where interrupting the user's task to file a support ticket risks total drop-off). It's ideal for:

  • In-app bug reporting SDKs (support/QA tooling)
  • Any flow where automatic screen capture can replace manual description
  • Products with authenticated users where email/identity can be auto-filled
  • Low-density, card-based forms for lightweight data entry
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex, multi-faceted support requests that require conversational back-and-forth, nuanced triage, or attachments of multiple document types (a single static form with one screenshot slot will feel limiting). It's also unsuitable for anonymous/logged-out flows where there's no identity to auto-populate, as the email field would need to become a manual, friction-adding step. Finally, in apps with a more playful or highly branded voice, this utilitarian system-field tone may feel jarringly generic compared to the rest of the product's personality.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engaged learners who hit a confusing or broken moment mid-lesson and want to flag it immediately rather than lose their place or motivation. Because Brilliant's core audience is self-directed, detail-oriented STEM learners, the design assumes they value efficiency and precision (hence the form favors structured fields (dropdown, description, auto-screenshot) over an open-ended chat-style support experience).

Psychologically, the auto-attached screenshot leverages the reduction of perceived effort: users are far more likely to complete a feedback loop when the system does the "showing" and they only need to do the "telling." The pre-filled email also exploits sunk-cost continuity: the user doesn't have to break flow to recall or type credentials, keeping the reporting action impulsive and immediate rather than deferred (and likely abandoned).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Automatic context capture: The exact in-lesson screen is auto-attached as a screenshot, eliminating the need for users to manually describe or recreate the bug.
  • Pre-filled email field: Removes friction by leveraging the logged-in user's identity, so the report can be routed and followed up on without extra typing.
  • Card-based field segmentation: Each form field is isolated in its own card, making the form feel scannable and low-density, consistent with the app's "one idea per screen" design philosophy.
  • Dual exit affordances: Both a back arrow (return to previous context) and a close "X" (abandon the flow entirely) are offered, respecting different user intents at the moment of quitting.
  • Required-field indicators: Red dots on Description and Email clearly communicate validation requirements before submission is attempted, pre-empting error states.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a product needs to present a single record with both a status history and granular metadata, especially in regulated or scrutinized domains (expense management, compliance review, order/shipment tracking, support ticket detail, or insurance claims). It's ideal when trust and auditability matter more than persuasion, and when multiple stakeholders (submitter + reviewer) need a shared source of truth.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, document-style layout for high-frequency, low-stakes interactions where speed matters more than completeness (e.g., quick balance checks or casual browsing). It would also be inappropriate for consumer-facing, emotionally-driven experiences where a utilitarian tone could feel cold or bureaucratic. If a transaction has no review history, this layout should degrade gracefully with an empty state rather than showing an empty or confusing timeline.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

For the employee, seeing a transparent timeline of "flagged → reviewed" reduces the stress and ambiguity of having a purchase questioned, invoking the psychological principle of procedural justice: people are far more accepting of a process outcome when they can see the steps taken to reach it, even before knowing the final verdict.

For finance teams, the structured transaction details satisfy the need for completeness and defensibility: every field needed for bookkeeping, tax categorization, or dispute resolution is present in one place, reducing back-and-forth queries. The comment/@-mention system taps into workplace familiarity with tools like Slack, lowering the learning curve and encouraging asynchronous resolution instead of requiring a meeting or email thread.
screens.keyHighlights:
