screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this layered bottom-sheet + chip-based error pattern when:

  • An automated verification/validation process (OCR, fraud check, data matching) fails and the user needs specific, itemized reasons rather than a blanket error.
  • The failure is recoverable or has a fallback path (manual review, memo, re-upload) and shouldn't fully block the user's workflow.
  • You want to preserve form context and avoid navigating the user away from their in-progress task.
  • Financial, compliance, or document-verification flows where transparency about *why* something failed builds user trust.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The error is critical and must hard-block the user (e.g., legal/compliance violation) - a bottom sheet may under-communicate severity; a full-screen interstitial or disabled submit button may be more appropriate.
  • There are more than 3-4 failure reasons, as the chip row could wrap awkwardly or overwhelm the limited bottom-sheet real estate (consider a scrollable list or accordion instead).
  • The underlying cause is highly technical; surfacing raw field names like "Merchant" without guidance on remediation could confuse less technical users if no next-step CTA is provided within the sheet itself.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets employees submitting expenses on the go, often from imperfect conditions (bad lighting, crumpled receipts, foreign currency receipts, or no receipt at all as implied by the memo). It also serves finance/admin teams indirectly by ensuring exceptions are flagged and routed to manual review rather than silently approved, protecting compliance integrity.

Psychologically, the design reduces anxiety around making a financial mistake by externalizing the error to a system limitation rather than user fault, while the granular breakdown (Date/Amount/Merchant) gives the user actionable next steps (e.g., re-upload or add memo justification) instead of leaving them stuck. The manual-review fallback also builds trust that legitimate business expenses won't be rejected outright due to OCR failure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Bottom Sheet over Dimmed Background: Preserves the user's place in the underlying form while delivering a focused, modal-style alert, avoiding a jarring full-screen takeover for a non-blocking issue.
  • Field-Level Error Chips: Breaking the verification failure into discrete, labeled chips (Date, Amount, Merchant) gives granular diagnostic feedback instead of a vague generic error message.
  • Non-Blocking Error Pattern: The flow explicitly allows the user to proceed via manual review and memo justification rather than hard-locking submission, respecting real-world edge cases (e.g., lost receipts).
  • Dual-Surface Status Communication: The "Not verified" status label on the Receipts section header and the warning banner work together with the modal to reinforce the same message across multiple visual layers.

screens.name: Linear - Creating a label - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:

screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The option list is very large (50+ labels), where a flat scrolling list without search/filter becomes inefficient (a searchable combobox or typeahead would be more appropriate).
  • True single-select behavior is required and radio-style circles are used (ensure the visual affordance (circle vs). checkbox) accurately reflects whether multiple selections are permitted, to avoid user confusion.
  • Label creation requires additional metadata (e.g., color, description) that can't be reasonably captured inline (in that case, a dedicated creation flow/dialog is more suitable than a bare text row).
  • Destructive or high-stakes categorization changes are being made, where an explicit Cancel button (not just swipe-to-dismiss) is needed for clarity and error prevention.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern directly serves engineers, product managers, and designers who need to rapidly triage and organize large volumes of issues or tasks. The psychological driver here is reducing cognitive load during categorization: by presenting labels as a flat, scannable list with minimal UI decoration, users can make quick binary decisions (apply/don't apply) without being distracted by color, iconography, or complex grouping.

The inline 'add new label' taps into the autonomy and control needs of power users who don't want to be gated behind an admin panel to create new organizational structures (this is a key value for teams who iterate on workflow terminology frequently (e).g., sprint-specific or client-specific labels as shown here with order-processing terms).

screens.name: Linear - Creating a label - Screen 3

screens.name: Craft - Adding a row - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Reuse this layered bottom-sheet pattern whenever an app needs to expose a large number of context-sensitive actions on a single selected object (a table, cell, shape, or block) without navigating away from the canvas. It's especially effective for:

  • Rich document/table editors (Notion, Craft, Coda, spreadsheet apps) where selection-based actions vary by context.
  • Any mobile UI where screen real estate is limited and a full toolbar can't be permanently docked.
  • Situations where you want to blend "quick action" tiles with "deep settings" drill-down menus in one coherent surface.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when the action set is small (2-4 items) - a simple popover or inline toolbar would be faster and less heavy-handed than a full sheet. It's also inappropriate for extremely high-frequency, repetitive actions (e.g., toggling bold/italic while typing), where an always-visible persistent toolbar is far more efficient than repeatedly invoking a sheet.

Additionally, this pattern should be reconsidered on larger screens (tablet/desktop) where a contextual right-click menu or a persistent side panel would better leverage available space rather than a bottom sheet designed for thumb reach on phones. Finally, destructive actions like "Clear Cell Contents" should always pair with an explicit confirmation step or undo affordance elsewhere in the flow, placing it at the bottom of a scrollable list is not sufficient protection against accidental taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets power users and professionals (PMs, designers, engineers, consultants) who use Craft not just for prose notes but for structured specs, like the "Web3 Platform Landing Page" document shown, which contains a feature/layer table. These users expect spreadsheet-grade table manipulation (sorting, formulas, formatting) without leaving their writing flow, a hybrid need that general-purpose notes apps often fail to serve well.

The psychological trigger at play is reduced friction for complex operations: by surfacing table commands as a bottom sheet rather than a separate app or dense ribbon toolbar, Craft lowers the perceived complexity of what is otherwise an advanced, spreadsheet-like feature set. The graduated hierarchy also taps into recognition over recall: users scan icons and labels rather than memorizing keyboard shortcuts, which is critical on mobile where modifier-key shortcuts aren't available.

  • Destructive action isolation: dangerous commands are pushed to the bottom and the final one uses red text, following platform HIG conventions for harm-avoidance.
  • Formula support surfaced directly in a note-taking app: "Insert Formula" signals Craft's ambition to blend document elegance with spreadsheet-like power, differentiating it from purely prose-focused writing apps.

screens.name: Craft - Adding a row - Screen 3

screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Users need to see live previews of the effect of their action (e.g., drag-to-reorder) - a sheet-based command interrupts the direct-manipulation mental model and adds an extra step.
  • The content behind the sheet is itself needed for decision-making (e.g., comparing two rows before deciding to delete) - in that case, a side panel or inline affordance that doesn't occlude content would be better.
  • On desktop/large-screen contexts, where a right-click context menu or persistent toolbar is more efficient and expected than a mobile-style bottom sheet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

These users need spreadsheet-like manipulation (insert/move/delete rows and columns) without leaving the fluid, document-first writing experience.

Psychologically, this satisfies the need for perceived control and precision: rather than fumbling with tiny drag handles on a touchscreen, the user gets large, tappable, explicitly labeled commands. The bottom sheet format also respects thumb-zone ergonomics on mobile, acknowledging that table editing on a phone is inherently more fragile than on desktop, so Craft compensates with a more deliberate, menu-driven interaction model instead of relying purely on direct manipulation gestures.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Icon-led scannability: Each action pairs a minimalist line icon depicting the table transformation (e.g., a grid with an arrow) with text, allowing power users to recognize actions by shape alone over time.
  • Semantic grouping via whitespace and dividers: Insert, Move, and Delete actions are visually clustered, mirroring how users mentally categorize table operations.
  • Destructive isolation: Delete actions are pushed to the bottom and colored red, following the "safe defaults, dangerous actions last" pattern to prevent slip errors.
  • Non-blocking overlay: The partially visible document and table behind the scrim preserves context, so users don't lose their place in a long document.

screens.name: Craft - Adding a row - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this contextual action-sheet pattern when:

  • Actions can be logically grouped by increasing risk level (safe → reversible → destructive).

screens.whereNotToUse:

  • The destructive actions (deletions) have high real-world cost and no easy undo (in that case, add an explicit confirmation dialog rather than relying on color alone).

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

Psychologically, the design leverages recognition over recall (icons + labels) and progressive disclosure: advanced table operations are hidden until needed, keeping the base editing experience clean and uncluttered, true to Craft's "document, not database row" philosophy. The red-flagged destructive actions tap into trained color-association heuristics (red = caution) so users self-moderate without needing a secondary confirmation step, preserving speed for power users while still signaling risk.

screens.name: Craft - Editing cell formatting styles - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use a bottom-sheet, document-anchored color picker pattern when:

  • Users need to apply fine-grained visual styling (text color, highlight, accents) without leaving their editing flow.
  • Your app's differentiator is document/content craftsmanship and visual customization (editorial tools, design docs, presentation builders).
  • You want to preserve spatial/content context during a secondary action rather than forcing a full navigation away from the task.
  • Your user base is sophisticated enough to benefit from an expanded palette instead of a simplified default set.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense grid approach when:

  • Your audience is non-technical or casual, where a smaller curated palette (brand colors only) reduces decision fatigue.
  • Screen real estate is very constrained (small phones) - a 10-column grid risks tiny, hard-to-tap targets and accessibility/tap-target issues.
  • The product's design language favors strict brand consistency over user customization (e.g., a tool where off-brand colors would break visual cohesion).
  • Color selection is a rare, low-frequency action (in that case, a simpler swatch row or system picker suffices and avoids unnecessary complexity).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets power users and creative professionals: designers, PMs, writers (who treat their notes as polished deliverables rather than disposable scratch space). The presence of a structured table with a "Layer/Description" schema embedded inside a prose document suggests a technical or design-adjacent professional organizing project specs.

Psychologically, the granular color grid taps into a sense of creative control and craftsmanship: giving users 50 precise swatch options (rather than 6-8 basic colors) signals that the app respects their aesthetic judgment and won't constrain their customization the way a "database row" tool would. This appeals to users who already use design software and expect parity in a note-taking context.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual overlay over live document: The color picker appears as a bottom sheet rather than a full-screen takeover, letting the user see the document bleed through at the edges (a subtle but powerful cue that formatting is a transient, lightweight action, not a mode switch).

Hue-family grid organization: Colors are arranged in rows by hue with tint/shade progression (left-to-right), a mental model borrowed from professional design tools (Figma, Keynote) rather than generic mobile pickers, signaling that Craft treats documents as designed artifacts.

Persistent editing context: The table structure and surrounding prose remain fully visible and legible above the sheet, so the user retains full situational awareness of what they're styling and why.

Icon-only, chrome-light top bar: Back, share, and overflow menu are the only persistent controls, keeping focus on content and deferring all formatting power into contextual, on-demand surfaces like this sheet.

screens.name: Craft - Editing cell formatting styles - Screen 10
screens.whereToUse:
• Rich-text or block-based editors where inline formatting (color, highlight, font) needs quick access without navigating away from the canvas.
  • Any tool targeting prosumer/creative users who value a design-system-like, curated set of options over a full-spectrum picker.
  • Document or note apps aiming for a native, platform-consistent feel (breadcrumb subtitle, back/share/more icons).
  • Table or structured content editors where cell-level or inline styling is a differentiator (specs, wikis, databases-as-documents).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid a dense swatch grid for casual or mainstream consumer apps where users just want 1-2 accent colors (simplify to fewer, bigger swatches).
  • Not ideal for small screens/phones in landscape or very compact viewports, where a 10-column grid may feel cramped and tap-targets too small.
  • Don't use a partial bottom sheet if the picker requires significant additional controls (e.g., custom hex input, opacity slider) - a full dialog with more room may serve better in that case.
  • Avoid for accessibility-critical contexts without text labels/alt descriptions per color, since color-only differentiation can be a problem for colorblind users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves power users, designers, and knowledge workers who treat their notes as polished artifacts (specs, proposals, project briefs) rather than throwaway text. The granular text-color control demonstrates Craft's appeal to users who care about visual hierarchy and personal branding within documents, distinguishing it from plain-text or minimalist note apps.

Psychologically, the non-full-screen sheet reduces the "interruption" feeling of a modal, keeping users in a state of flow since they never fully lose sight of their work. The checkmark and curated palette reduce decision fatigue, a key usability lever for creative tools that could otherwise overwhelm users with infinite color options.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual, non-blocking bottom sheet: The color picker rises only over the lower half of the screen, letting users see the live preview of their document above while editing, reducing cognitive disconnect between action and result.
  • Curated color ramp instead of a color wheel: Organizing swatches into tonal rows (grayscale, purple/blue, cyan, green, red/orange/yellow) reflects an editorial design sensibility and speeds up selection versus a raw HSB picker.
  • Clear state indication: The checkmark on the active green swatch immediately confirms the current selection without requiring the user to recall it.
  • Native-feeling document chrome: Back button, truncated title, parent-folder subtitle, and share/more icons mimic iOS system patterns, lowering the learning curve for new users.
  • Rich document composition: Headings, dividers, and tables rendered inline in the editor reinforce the "document, not database row" brand promise.

results.query: Preserving user input context during unexpected session expiration

screens.name: Figma - Deleting a comment - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this long-press contextual menu pattern when:

  • Users need quick access to multiple secondary actions (3 (6 items) tied to a specific list item, message, or object without navigating to a new screen).

  • The app already has an established commenting, messaging, or collaborative-feedback system and needs mobile parity with desktop controls.

  • You want to visually separate a destructive action from neutral ones using color rather than extra confirmation steps, for low-to-medium risk deletions.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The destructive action (like permanent deletion of shared, multi-user content) carries high stakes (in those cases, pair the red menu item with an additional confirmation dialog rather than relying on color alone).

  • The action list exceeds 6-7 items, as long-press menus on mobile become hard to scan and can get clipped by screen edges or keyboards.

  • Primary actions need high discoverability: contextual/long-press menus are inherently low-affordance and should never house a user's core workflow actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers and stakeholders reviewing work asynchronously on mobile: e.g., a product manager commenting on a design system update while commuting, or a designer triaging feedback threads between meetings. The target user already understands Figma's commenting conventions from desktop and expects the mobile experience to replicate that power without dumbing it down.

Psychologically, the menu exploits recognition over recall (icons + labels), and the red "Delete thread" leverages loss-aversion cues to slow down accidental destructive taps. The persistent visibility of the underlying thread reduces cognitive load and context-switching anxiety, a key concern for mobile power users who often fear losing their place in long comment chains.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-anchored menu placement: The action sheet appears directly adjacent to the triggering comment rather than centered on screen, maintaining spatial continuity between cause and effect.

  • Color-coded destructive action: "Delete thread" is isolated in red at the bottom of the list, leveraging color psychology to create hesitation before an irreversible action (without requiring an extra confirmation tap at this stage).

  • Icon-text pairing for scan speed: Every menu item pairs a label with a recognizable glyph on the trailing edge, allowing fast recognition for power users who memorize icon positions over repeated use.

  • Persistent context behind overlay: The comment thread and reply field remain visible beneath the semi-transparent menu, so users never lose their place in the conversation.

  • Parity with desktop commenting: Features like "Mark as unread" and "Copy text" mirror desktop-grade commenting controls, reinforcing Figma's cross-platform consistency ethos.

screens.name: Figma - Deleting a comment - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this confirmation dialog pattern whenever:

  • An action is irreversible or has cascading effects on data other users contributed (comments, threads, shared assets).

  • The content being deleted could easily be confused with similar items (e.g., multiple comment threads on a canvas), warranting a specific object name in the CTA.

  • Collaborative or multi-user contexts where "undo" isn't readily available or visible to all parties.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy modal confirmation pattern for:

  • Low-stakes, easily reversible actions (e.g., archiving a comment, muting a thread) - use an inline undo/snackbar instead to reduce friction.

  • High-frequency repeated actions, where a modal interruption every time would create workflow fatigue; consider a "don't ask again" option or swipe-to-delete with undo.

  • Situations where the destructive action only affects the current user's own private data with no collaborative impact (a lighter-weight confirmation may suffice).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers and collaborators working in shared Figma files, where comment threads often contain valuable design feedback, decisions, and discussion history from multiple stakeholders (not just the deleter). Because threads can include replies and reactions from teammates, accidental deletion has a real collaborative cost, losing someone else's input, not just your own.

The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion combined with social accountability: users are reminded that deleting affects not only their own content but also other people's contributions (replies/reactions), which raises the perceived stakes of the action and encourages a second thought before confirming. The dialog also serves a trust-building function for teams (by making destructive actions require explicit confirmation with clear consequences, Figma signals that collaborative work is protected from careless deletion).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit consequence messaging: Clearly states that replies and reactions cascade-delete, preventing silent data loss and surprise.

  • Color-coded action hierarchy: Blue "Cancel" (safe/default) vs. red "Delete thread" (destructive) leverages established color psychology to guide safe defaults.

  • Named action instead of generic label: "Delete thread" instead of "Delete" or "OK" removes ambiguity about what exactly will be removed.

  • Dimmed/blurred background: Visually locks focus onto the decision, preventing accidental interaction with underlying canvas or thread.

  • Context preserved behind the modal: The original thread (author, message, timestamp) remains partially visible, letting users mentally confirm they're deleting the correct thread before committing.

screens.name: Figma - Deleting a comment - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Steal this pattern whenever your app supports deep links or shareable URLs to transient or mutable content (comments, chat messages, notifications, tasks, cart items) that can be deleted, resolved, or expired independently of the link's lifetime. It's especially valuable for:

  • Collaboration tools with resolvable/deletable comment threads
  • Notification-driven deep links where the target object may no longer exist
  • Shared links in team environments where permissions or content change frequently

Always pair the dialog with a dimmed-but-visible background state so users retain context rather than feeling abruptly redirected or lost.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this exact pattern for frequent or expected empty states: if a piece of content is routinely and predictably unavailable (e.g., a brand-new user with no comments yet), a modal interruption is overkill; use an inline empty state instead. Modals should be reserved for unexpected exceptions, not normal flows.

Also avoid vague or apologetic phrasing in high-stakes error contexts (e.g., payment failures, data loss) where users need actionable next steps rather than just reassurance (a simple "OK" dismissal is insufficient when recovery actions (retry, contact support, undo) are available and expected).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves designers and developers collaborating asynchronously on shared Figma files, often via links shared in Slack, email, or task trackers. Comment threads in Figma are frequently resolved and auto-hidden (or deleted) once feedback is addressed, meaning stale links to those comments are common in fast-moving teams.

The psychological trigger at play is reducing anxiety around "broken" experiences. When a user clicks a link expecting to see specific feedback and it's gone, there's a moment of uncertainty: "Did I click the wrong thing? Is the app broken? Did I lose access?" By explicitly stating the comment used to exist and was resolved/deleted, Figma removes ambiguity and reassures the user that the system is working as intended (it's simply a case of stale state, not a technical failure).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving scrim: The canvas remains visible (dimmed) behind the dialog, so users retain spatial orientation instead of losing their place entirely.

  • Humanized error copy: Conversational phrasing turns a potentially frustrating dead-end (broken link) into a clear, blame-free explanation.

  • Single, unambiguous action: Only one button ("OK") removes decision fatigue (there is no recovery action needed since the comment is genuinely gone).

  • Graceful handling of stale deep links: Rather than crashing or silently redirecting, the app explicitly validates the referenced comment ID and responds with a meaningful message.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 22
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a growth or referral feature sends unsolicited communications (SMS, email) to third parties, especially in regulated industries (fintech, healthcare, insurance). It's ideal for reward-based referral programs where the cash incentive might otherwise drive users to spam their entire contact list. Also applicable to any action with legal/compliance implications that a simple upfront disclaimer wouldn't adequately cover.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid adding this extra confirmation step for low-stakes, non-regulated sharing actions (e.g., sharing a public link, inviting to a low-risk social app) where it would only add friction without meaningful legal benefit. Also avoid stacking multiple redundant consent dialogs across the same flow, as excessive interruptions train users to blindly tap through confirmations, defeating the pattern's purpose (dialog fatigue / banner blindness).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets any fintech, banking, or consumer app (the green person icon and "$5" reward suggest a peer-to-peer payments or banking app like Chime/Cash App) running a referral growth program via SMS. The audience is everyday consumers being incentivized with cash rewards to invite friends (a group motivated primarily by the monetary incentive ("Get $5 Each"), which can lead to careless mass-inviting of contacts who never opted in).

The psychological trigger being managed here is the tension between incentive-driven virality (users want to spam invite as many contacts as possible to earn rewards) and legal/compliance risk (unsolicited texts violate TCPA and carrier spam policies). The confirmation dialog leverages the commitment/consistency principle (by forcing an explicit acknowledgment, it shifts moral and legal responsibility onto the user and reduces the likelihood of thoughtless bulk invites).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consent-at-the-point-of-action: The legal confirmation is triggered contextually per-recipient rather than as a single blanket checkbox at the top of the flow, closing the loop between intent and legal accountability.

  • Personalized legal copy: Dynamically inserting the recipient's identifier into the consent sentence makes an otherwise generic disclaimer feel specific and serious, increasing genuine attention and reducing careless spam invites.

  • Native action-sheet pattern: Using the familiar iOS-style stacked dialog with dividers keeps the interruption feeling lightweight and platform-consistent rather than like a jarring custom legal wall.

  • Dual-layer disclosure: The underlying screen already states the consent requirement in body copy, and the modal reinforces it a second time immediately before the irreversible action, creating redundancy that protects both the user and the platform from liability.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 23
screens.whereToUse: Use this grouped-list-with-progress-meter pattern whenever an app needs to communicate metered resources, quotas, or tiered permissions: e.g., API rate limits, storage quotas, subscription usage caps, KYC-tiered transaction limits, or data plan usage. It's ideal any time a single numeric limit isn't enough context and users benefit from seeing consumption relative to a cap.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this static, read-only format when limits change dynamically in real time and require live updates (a purely static screen could show stale data, causing failed transactions). Also avoid mixing metered progress bars with flat non-metered rows on the same screen without a legend, as it can create ambiguity about why some items have visual indicators and others don't. For very simple apps with only one limit type, this level of sectioning would be over-engineered.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves active users of a peer-to-peer payment or crypto exchange app (pattern strongly resembles Cash App's Bitcoin/limits page) who need to plan a transaction (e).g., before attempting to withdraw or buy Bitcoin, they check whether they have enough remaining allowance. It's especially relevant to users who transact frequently or in larger amounts and need to avoid failed transactions due to limit caps.

Psychologically, this leverages the need for control and predictability in financial apps: users trust platforms more when limits are transparent rather than discovered only via an error message at the point of failure. It also reduces support tickets by proactively answering "why can't I send more money?" before it becomes a frustration point.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-value transparency: Showing both "remaining" and "per week" cap side-by-side eliminates the need for mental subtraction.

  • Visual progress meter: The cyan progress bar under Bitcoin Purchase converts a raw number into an instantly scannable proportion of usage.

  • Clear grouped taxonomy: Separating Cash Limits from Bitcoin Transactions via section headers keeps mental models for fiat vs. crypto operations distinct, avoiding confusion between asset types.

  • Honest disclosure of asymmetric limits: Explicitly stating "Unlimited" for Receive versus capped Send/Withdraw builds trust by being upfront about risk-based restrictions (fraud/AML controls) rather than hiding them.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 24
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any application handling sensitive personal data (banking, healthcare, crypto, enterprise SaaS) where users need to audit and revoke access to their account. It is essential for apps utilizing passwordless authentication (Magic Links/OTP), as users lose the traditional "password reset" mental model and need a replacement mechanism for security control.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of technical device-tracking detail for low-stakes consumer apps (e.g., a simple recipe app or weather app) where the friction of explaining session policies outweighs the security benefit. Additionally, if the app supports many concurrent devices, this pattern would need to be adapted to include bulk "log out of all other devices" actions, as a single-item list style doesn't scale well for enterprise environments with dozens of active sessions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves security-conscious users, specifically those managing sensitive data (financial services, health apps, or professional tools) who need assurance that their account isn't compromised across multiple browsers or devices.

The psychological trigger here is Locus of Control. By showing users exactly what has access to their data and explicitly telling them they can revoke it "at any time," the app alleviates the anxiety of losing control over their digital identity. It caters to power users who actively audit their security settings, as well as anxious users who land here after receiving a suspicious login notification.
screens.keyHighlights:
The most brilliant aspect of this screen is the pairing of a functional list with proactive, plain-language security education. Instead of just listing devices, the app immediately addresses the "why should I care?" question by explaining the standing security policy.

  • Distinct "Current Session" Grouping: Isolating "This device" under its own header before other devices prevents the user from mistakenly identifying their own session as a threat.

  • Passive Threat Detection Copy: Displaying "Unknown Location" acts as a built-in security nudge, encouraging vigilance without requiring a separate alert system.

  • Policy Transparency: Explicitly stating the auto-logout timeframe manages user expectations regarding session persistence, reducing support tickets asking "why was I logged out?"

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 25
screens.whereToUse: Use this categorized preference-center pattern for any product with multiple notification types spanning different risk/importance levels (fintech, healthcare, SaaS admin tools). It's ideal when you have 6+ notification types that would be unwieldy as a single flat toggle list, or when some notifications (security, legal) should never be fully silenced and need separate framing from discretionary/marketing notifications.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this multi-level drill-down approach for apps with only 2-3 notification types (the added navigation depth would introduce unnecessary friction versus a single-screen toggle list). Also avoid nesting critical safety toggles (e.g., fraud alerts) behind multiple taps if regulatory or safety requirements mandate they remain highly visible and always-on; in such cases, consider disabling the ability to turn them off entirely rather than allowing an "Off" state at depth.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets the full spectrum of Cash App's user base, but is particularly designed for privacy- and security-conscious users, and those experiencing notification fatigue who want to curate exactly what interrupts them. Financial apps carry high stakes (missing a fraud alert can be costly, but being spammed with marketing pushes erodes trust) so the design leans on transparency and granular control as psychological reassurance mechanisms.

The separation of "Security"/"Account changes" from "News & exclusives" also reflects a psychological trust-building tactic: by visually and structurally isolating promotional content ("More from Cash App") from critical account/security content, the app signals that it does not conflate marketing spam with essential safety alerts, which increases user confidence when toggling things off.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Categorized Grouping over Flat List: Segmenting notifications into Contact, Account, Activity, and Marketing groups reduces overwhelm and helps users mentally map controls to their real-world concerns (security vs. marketing spam).

  • Iconography as Quick-Scan Aid: Each row uses a distinct, semantically relevant icon, allowing users to visually locate a category faster than reading text alone.

  • Descriptive Subtext: Pairing each category name with a concrete example list (e.g., "Bank holidays, policy updates, support") removes ambiguity about what "Notices" actually means before the user drills in.

  • Deferred Granularity (Master-Detail): Aggregate on/off states are shown at the top level, with full channel-by-channel control (push/email/SMS) presumably nested one level deeper, balancing simplicity with power-user control.

  • Contextual Upsell via "Add": Turning an incomplete field (missing phone) into an actionable pill button nudges profile completion without being a disruptive modal or nag.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 26
screens.whereToUse: Use this dual-CTA numeric entry pattern whenever an app supports two closely related but directionally opposite actions on the same input (e.g., send/receive money, buy/sell shares, debit/credit an amount). It's ideal for high-frequency, low-friction financial or transactional flows where speed and error prevention outweigh the need for detailed explanation. It also works well as a full-screen modal for any "quick action" that should feel lightweight and interruptible.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex transactions requiring more context (e.g., international transfers with fees, currency conversion, or scheduled/recurring payments) where a single giant numeric field and two buttons would under-inform the user and risk costly mistakes. Also avoid saturated, high-brightness full-bleed color fields for screens requiring prolonged reading or multiple data points, as it can cause visual fatigue and lacks room for secondary information like recipient details, notes, or transaction history.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers making peer-to-peer payments, splitting rent, paying back a friend, requesting money for a group gift. The design assumes low patience and high frequency of use: speed and unambiguous feedback are prioritized over explanation or hand-holding, since target users already understand the mental model of "enter a number, then pay or request it."

Psychologically, the massive number display and satisfying tactile-feeling keypad play into a "counting cash" metaphor, making a digital, abstract action (moving electronic money) feel as concrete and satisfying as handling physical bills. The locked card skins subtly trigger collector/completionist psychology, encouraging continued engagement and exploration of the app beyond the core utility.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Deferred action choice: Users input an amount first, then choose Pay or Request, collapsing two flows into one screen and one keypad.

  • Oversized, legible amount display: The giant "$0" typography instantly confirms input with zero ambiguity, crucial for financial trust.

  • High-contrast, brand-saturated background: The neon green full-bleed color reinforces brand recognition (Cash App green) even in a purely functional, decision-heavy screen.

  • Card/skin carousel with lock icons: Locked skins are visible but unavailable, acting as a soft upsell/gamification hook (unlock more designs) embedded inconspicuously below the primary task.

  • Modal dismissal pattern: Clear X/Done affordances make the transactional flow feel contained and easily escapable, reducing anxiety around accidental money actions.

screens.name: Brex Send an email to support 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this minimalist single-field contact pattern when:

  • The support topic is already broad/general (post-categorization fallback).

  • You want to maximize submission completion rates for lower-stakes inquiries.

  • Email is an acceptable and expected response channel (not live chat/real-time).

  • You need a fast, low-engineering-cost support channel for MVP or early-stage products.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Support requests require specific metadata (order ID, device info, screenshots) to be actionable (in these cases a Multi-Step Form with structured fields and file upload would reduce back-and-forth).

  • Users expect real-time resolution (e.g., live chat widget) rather than asynchronous email reply.

  • The product serves enterprise/B2B customers who need ticket tracking, priority levels, or SLA visibility (a plain text box lacks the structure needed for triage at scale).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users who have a non-urgent, non-categorized issue and need a simple escape hatch to contact support after self-service options (FAQs, help articles) have failed to resolve their problem. It serves a broad demographic (essentially any app user experiencing friction) but is particularly suited to less tech-savvy users who prefer writing a free-form message over navigating ticket categorization systems.

Psychologically, the design leverages the reduction of perceived effort principle: by stripping the form to a single text area, it lowers the barrier to complaint/feedback submission, which increases completion rates for support tickets that might otherwise be abandoned in a more complex multi-field form.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Removing all non-essential fields (subject, category, attachments) minimizes cognitive load and speeds up submission for simple inquiries.

  • Disabled CTA until input: The greyed-out "Send" button provides an implicit, low-friction form validation cue without intrusive error messaging.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Explicitly stating the reply will arrive "directly by email" builds trust and reduces the likelihood of the user waiting anxiously in-app for a response.

  • Clean navigational affordance: The circular back button paired with a centered bold title keeps the header uncluttered and consistent with standard iOS navigation conventions.

screens.name: Brex Send an email to support 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Customer support or contact-us flows where the goal is a quick, low-friction message submission.

  • Any feedback or bug-report form where you want to avoid overwhelming the user with multiple fields.

  • Situations where response happens out-of-band (e.g., email, ticketing system) and you need to set that expectation clearly up front.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this minimal single-field pattern when the support team requires structured data (e.g., order ID, device info, severity level) to resolve issues efficiently (this would necessitate additional fields or smart defaults/prefill).

  • Not suitable for live support or chat-based experiences where real-time back-and-forth is expected; the "we'll reply by email" framing would feel mismatched.

  • If categorization of inquiries is important for routing (billing vs. technical vs. account), a bare text field without a topic selector could create downstream triage overhead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users who are already somewhat frustrated or confused (seeking "General support"), meaning the design must minimize additional friction and decision fatigue. Users in a support-seeking mindset are often impatient or anxious, so a single clear text field with no distracting options caters to a "get me help fast" psychological state.

The explicit mention of an email reply channel sets a mental model for response time (not instant), which preemptively manages frustration about a lack of live typing indicators or immediate replies. The large touch targets and simple keyboard-adjacent CTA also suggest this is optimized for one-handed mobile use, likely by users who are multitasking or quickly firing off a request between other app activities.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Only one input is required, dramatically lowering the barrier to submitting a support request and reducing abandonment.

  • Inline clear button: The (x) icon inside the text area allows instant content clearing without manual text selection, a small but high-value micro-interaction.

  • Persistent, thumb-friendly CTA: The orange "Send" button sits in a fixed, easily reachable position that remains visible even when the keyboard is open.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Explicitly telling users they'll be contacted "directly by email" manages expectations and reduces repeat-check anxiety.

  • High contrast CTA color: The vivid orange button against a white background ensures the primary action is unmissable.

screens.name: Brex Send an email to support 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a user is about to navigate away from a screen with unsaved, non-trivial input (multi-line text entry, forms with several filled fields, checkout flows, or any screen where back-navigation is easy to trigger accidentally (e).g., swipe-back gestures, hardware back buttons). It's especially valuable in support/contact forms, long-form content creation (posts, reviews, emails), and multi-step wizards.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this interruption pattern for trivial or easily-recoverable inputs (e.g., a single short-answer field, filters, or toggles) where the cost of re-entry is negligible (the friction would feel excessive and annoying). Also avoid it if autosave/draft persistence is already implemented, since there's no real risk of data loss and the confirmation becomes redundant friction. Overuse of confirmation dialogs across an app can lead to "dialog fatigue," where users reflexively tap through warnings without reading them.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets any user who has invested time or effort filling out a form (in this case, someone drafting a support inquiry, likely already frustrated or in need of help, making data loss doubly costly to their patience and trust in the product). Interrupting an accidental exit protects against the negative emotional spike of having to re-type an explanation of their problem.

Psychologically, this leverages the sunk cost effect and loss aversion: by explicitly naming what will be "lost," the dialog nudges the user to reconsider rather than abandon their progress impulsively, while still respecting their autonomy to exit if they truly intend to.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context preservation: The underlying form stays visible (dimmed) behind the sheet, letting users see exactly what they typed before deciding whether to lose it.

  • Unambiguous button labels: "No, go back" / "Yes, discard" eliminates the cognitive friction of interpreting generic Yes/No or OK/Cancel against the question asked.

  • Bottom sheet over full dialog: Using a swipeable bottom sheet (with drag handle) instead of a centered modal keeps the interaction feeling lightweight and native, reducing perceived interruption severity.

  • Protects user-generated content: Prevents accidental data loss from a stray back-tap, which is especially valuable on a support form where composing a message may take real effort/thought.

screens.name: Archive
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any browser or tab-management feature where content is automatically moved out of active view after a period of inactivity, requiring a dedicated, searchable, chronologically-organized location for users to retrieve or manage that archived content later.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if archived content should be permanently and irretrievably removed rather than stored for later retrieval (in cases requiring true deletion rather than archiving, a distinct "delete" flow (rather than an archive-and-search model) would be more appropriate).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Tab History / Recently Closed Tabs: organizes closed or archived tabs chronologically with title, URL, and favicon, closely matching this screen's structure.

  2. Chrome's History page: groups browsing history by date with search functionality, mirroring this Archive's date-grouped, searchable list.

  3. Arc Browser desktop's own Archive feature: the mobile app's Archive directly parallels the desktop Arc browser's auto-archiving tab-management system, maintaining feature consistency across platforms.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Feature Follow-Through: this screen delivers on the "auto-archive" promise made during onboarding and confirmed in Settings, showing archived tabs land somewhere retrievable rather than being silently lost.

  2. Chronological Grouping: organizing entries under date headers like "TODAY" follows familiar browser-history conventions, aiding quick temporal orientation.

  3. Scalable Management Tools: providing both Edit (bulk actions) and Search upfront anticipates the Archive growing significantly over time as tabs continue to auto-archive daily.

  4. Consistent Favicon Usage: using site favicons (the Google "G") alongside titles and URLs gives quick visual source recognition, consistent with standard browser history/bookmark list conventions.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 01
screens.whereToUse: This grouped Stacked List + Preference Center pattern fits any settings surface with a moderate-to-large number of independent preferences that benefit from being scanned at a glance, especially where some options are binary (toggle) and others need a dedicated picker screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when there are only a handful of settings (a flat list would suffice) or when settings are highly interdependent and better presented as a guided wizard rather than an unordered menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari (iOS Settings): same grouped Stacked List + chevron drill-down pattern for browser preferences, a near-identical information architecture.

  2. Chrome (iOS Settings): uses the same colored-icon-plus-label row convention and trailing value text for settings like default search engine.

  3. Notion (iOS Settings): groups toggles and drill-down rows into dividered sections in a comparable Preference Center layout.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking (Miller's Law): Dividers break ~14 settings into 5 digestible clusters instead of one long list.

  2. Recognition over recall: Trailing value text (e.g., "Google", "After 1 day", "Native App") shows current state inline, so users don't need to open each row to check it.

  3. Progressive disclosure: Chevron rows (Global Site Settings, Languages, Search Engine) push secondary complexity to nested screens, keeping this page scannable.

  4. Fitts's Law: Full-row tap targets (not just the switch/chevron) make toggles and navigation rows easier to hit on mobile.

  5. Consistency: Icon-label-value-chevron row pattern repeats identically throughout, lowering the learning curve as users scan down.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any automated content-management feature (archiving, auto-deletion, auto-logout) where users benefit from choosing a personally appropriate threshold, especially when a single fixed default wouldn't suit meaningfully different usage patterns across the user base.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings where offering multiple duration options would create confusing inconsistency (e.g., security-critical timeouts where a single, carefully chosen default is safer than user-configurable flexibility).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Close Tabs Automatically" duration picker: offers a nearly identical range of duration options (1 day, 1 week, 1 month) for automatically closing inactive tabs.

  2. Chrome's "Auto Tab Groups" or memory-saver duration settings: provides comparable configurable timeframes for tab-management automation.

  3. Firefox's tab-unloading/archiving thresholds: similarly lets users choose how long inactive tabs remain before being archived or unloaded.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Resolving Prior Ambiguity: this screen retroactively confirms the "After 1 day" value seen in earlier Settings screenshots was genuinely configurable, not a fixed label.

  2. Range Accommodates Diverse Habits: offering both very short (12 hours) and long (30 days) options serves meaningfully different tab-management styles without forcing a one-size-fits-all default.

  3. Consistent Selector Pattern: reusing the same compact popover-with-checkmark format as the earlier "Swipe to Navigate" setting maintains a predictable interaction model for similar types of choices throughout Settings.

  4. Feature Follow-Through: this control makes the onboarding-promised "auto-archive" feature concretely adjustable, giving users direct control over how aggressively that promise is enforced.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (immediate persistence without explicit save) fits virtually all mobile settings interfaces, where requiring a separate save action for individual preference changes would add unnecessary friction and risk of lost changes if a user navigates away.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit only for settings with significant, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., account deletion, irreversible data actions), where an explicit confirm/save step is appropriate specifically to prevent accidental changes (a distinction correctly reflected in this app's separate use of confirmation dialogs (like the earlier "Clear All" archive action) for higher-stakes actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS Settings app (immediate value persistence): uses an identical pattern where sub-screen selections instantly update and display in the parent settings list without requiring a save step.

  2. Any well-designed settings architecture (Safari, Chrome, etc.): follows this same immediate-persistence convention as a baseline usability expectation for modern mobile settings.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Reliable State Propagation: both changed settings correctly display their new values upon returning to the parent Settings screen, without requiring a manual refresh or save confirmation.

  2. Consistent Interaction Model Across Settings: the same select-then-confirm pattern (whether via popover or dedicated sub-screen) applies uniformly across different setting types (search engine, archive timing, language), giving the whole Settings experience a cohesive, predictable feel.

  3. Immediate Effect Without Explicit Save: no "Save" or "Apply" button was needed at any point in this sequence; each selection takes effect and displays immediately upon choice.

results.query: Handling out-of-stock variations gracefully in retail product detail pages

screens.name: H&M - Product detail - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-bleed video hero pattern on the entry point of fashion, beauty, lifestyle, or luxury retail apps where brand perception and emotional engagement are as important as conversion. It's ideal for seasonal campaign launches, new collection drops, or flagship moments where you want to differentiate from generic grid-based commerce apps.

Also effective for apps targeting younger, trend-driven audiences accustomed to short-form video content, or when a brand wants to reposition itself as editorial/aspirational rather than purely transactional.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for utility-driven, price-sensitive, or B2B apps where users expect immediate access to catalog, pricing, or search functionality (the lack of visible navigation and product information can frustrate task-focused users and increase bounce rate).

It's also risky on slow network connections or low-end devices where autoplay video can hurt performance and load times, and for accessibility-first contexts where motion, lack of text contrast, or missing alt content could exclude users with visual or vestibular sensitivities. Always pair with a fast skip-to-shop path for returning, task-oriented users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious shoppers and younger demographics who respond to aspirational, editorial-style content rather than overt discounting. By opening with cinematic, model-led imagery reminiscent of Vogue or runway campaigns, H&M leverages the halo effect and aspirational identity-signaling (users are invited to imagine themselves embodying the look, which builds emotional investment before any product is even shown).

The muted autoplay video also taps into modern social-media content consumption habits (familiar from Instagram/TikTok Stories), making the shopping experience feel native and current to younger users. The minimal, uncluttered design reduces cognitive load for casual browsers while still converting intent-driven users instantly via the single "Shop Now" CTA.
screens.keyHighlights:
Video-as-hero: Using an autoplaying, muted-by-default cinemagraph/video instead of a static banner creates a premium, dynamic first impression and increases dwell time before any navigation decision is made.

  • Minimal chrome, maximum imagery: Removing a traditional top nav bar and letting the photo bleed to the very edges (under the status bar) maximizes emotional impact and screen real estate for brand storytelling.
  • Floating, translucent tab bar: Keeps core navigation (Home, Search, Wishlist, Account, Bag) always within thumb reach without needing a solid background that would break the full-screen visual.
  • User control over media: Explicit pause and mute/unmute icons give users agency over an autoplaying video, respecting attention and data/sound preferences (a subtle but important accessibility and courtesy touch).
  • Single, unambiguous CTA: One button, one action ("Shop Now"), eliminates decision paralysis and funnels all engagement toward the "New Arrivals" collection.

screens.name: H&M - Product detail - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-bleed editorial hero pattern for:

  • Fashion, beauty, lifestyle, or luxury retail apps where brand perception and desirability drive conversion as much as price.
  • Launching seasonal collections, campaigns, or new arrivals where visual impact needs to dominate the first impression.
  • Home screen entry points where you want to set an emotional/brand tone before funneling users into deeper product discovery.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The app's value proposition is price/deal-driven (e.g., discount or clearance retailers), where users expect immediate pricing, offers, or product info rather than brand storytelling.
  • Users are typically returning for utility/task-based goals (e.g., reordering, order tracking) - a large non-functional hero would be an unnecessary barrier to speed.
  • Bandwidth/performance is a concern, since autoplay video on a home screen increases load time and data usage, which can hurt experience for users on slow connections.
  • Accessibility is a priority without strong fallback (pure image/video with overlaid text and no alt content can be problematic for screen reader users if not implemented carefully).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious shoppers and existing H&M customers who respond to aspirational, editorial-style imagery rather than aggressive discounting. The design leans heavily on the psychological principle of aspirational association: showing a model in a desirable setting and styling triggers identity-based purchase motivation ("I want to look/feel like this") rather than purely functional shopping behavior.

The scarcity-adjacent framing of "New Arrivals" taps into novelty-seeking behavior common among younger, trend-driven shoppers who frequently check the app for fresh drops. The minimal interface also reduces cognitive load for casual browsers, making the first touchpoint feel more like flipping through a lookbook than being sold to, which builds trust and brand affinity with style-conscious users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Immersive full-bleed hero video/photo that uses the entire screen as a canvas, deprioritizing chrome and UI in favor of brand storytelling.
  • Minimal, high-contrast typography overlaid directly on the image with no background scrim needed, thanks to careful placement over a darker area of the image for legibility.
  • Autoplay muted video with manual sound/play controls, giving users agency while defaulting to a non-intrusive, silent experience.
  • Single, unambiguous CTA ("Shop Now") that eliminates choice paralysis and drives a clear next action.
  • Persistent bottom tab bar ensures core navigation is never lost even during an immersive full-screen content moment.

screens.name: H&M - Product detail - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use a full-bleed video/motion hero combined with a floating minimal nav bar when launching seasonal campaigns, new collections, or rebranding moments where emotional engagement and brand storytelling should precede transactional browsing. It's ideal for fashion, lifestyle, travel, or beauty apps where visual identity and mood are core differentiators and the target audience already has purchase intent or brand familiarity.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for utility-driven apps, first-time user onboarding where clarity of navigation is critical, or low-bandwidth/emerging markets where autoplay video can cause performance issues, data costs, or slow load times. It's also unsuitable for conversion-focused screens needing multiple pathways (e.g., category shortcuts, promotions, personalized recommendations) since the single hero message intentionally limits information density, which could frustrate returning users seeking quick access to specific products.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for fashion-conscious shoppers and existing H&M loyalists who respond to brand storytelling and seasonal campaign cues rather than purely utilitarian shopping flows. The nature/sunlight motif evokes a seasonal (likely spring/summer) collection launch, tapping into emotional and aspirational triggers rather than price-based urgency.

Psychologically, the full-screen video leverages the aesthetic-usability effect: users perceive more beautiful, immersive interfaces as more usable and trustworthy, building brand affinity before any product is even shown. The singular "Shop Now" CTA exploits the paradox of choice reduction, directing motivated users straight into discovery without distraction, which benefits impulse-driven and discovery-oriented shoppers alike.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Video-first hero: Using ambient, nature-themed motion footage instead of static product photography immediately differentiates the brand experience and signals a seasonal/editorial campaign (likely tied to a "new arrivals" collection drop).
  • Floating pill tab bar: An elevated, rounded navigation bar that visually "floats" over content rather than anchoring to the screen edge, giving the interface a lighter, more contemporary feel while maximizing visible media.
  • Minimal overlay controls: Pause and mute icons are unobtrusively tucked in the top corner, giving users control over the autoplay video without cluttering the primary message.
  • Single, unambiguous CTA: Rather than offering multiple competing actions, the screen funnels all attention toward one "Shop Now" button, reducing decision fatigue.

screens.name: H&M - View collection - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for top-of-funnel brand/campaign launches, seasonal collection drops, or flagship home screens where emotional engagement and brand storytelling matter as much as conversion. It's ideal for fashion, beauty, travel, and lifestyle apps aiming to differentiate from purely transactional competitors, and works well when the brand has access to high-quality video assets and wants to reinforce premium/editorial positioning.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for utility-first or price-sensitive shopping contexts where users expect to see products, prices, and promotions immediately (e.g., grocery, electronics, or discount retail apps) - the lack of visible merchandise can feel like friction. It's also risky for low-bandwidth markets or users on data caps, as autoplay video increases load time and data usage. Additionally, it should not be the permanent home state for returning high-intent users who want quick repeat purchases; a lighter, product-forward view or quick toggle should be available for them.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious, visually-driven shoppers: particularly younger audiences accustomed to social media's short-form video and Stories formats. By opening with video instead of a product catalog, H&M leverages the mere exposure and mood-congruence effects: pleasant, sunlit, natural imagery primes positive affect, which transfers to brand perception and purchase willingness.

The single, bold CTA exploits the paradox-of-choice principle: reducing cognitive load by giving the user exactly one path forward. The muted/pause controls cater to users who want control over autoplay media (a nod to accessibility and bandwidth-conscious users), while the floating tab bar respects power users who want to jump straight to search, wishlist, or bag without waiting for the video narrative to play out.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-screen autoplay video as hero: Uses motion and natural lighting/atmosphere instead of static product photography to create an emotional, editorial first impression before any product is shown.
  • Minimal UI chrome over media: Only pause and mute icons intrude on the visual, both subtly placed and semi-transparent so they don't compete with the content.
  • Single, unmissable CTA: One high-contrast "SHOP NOW" button avoids decision fatigue and funnels all user intent toward a single next step.
  • Floating pill tab bar: A rounded, elevated navigation bar overlays the content rather than sitting in a fixed opaque container, preserving the immersive, borderless feel of the screen while keeping core navigation always reachable.
  • Story-style progress bar: The thin indicator at the bottom signals multiple hero "slides," borrowing a familiar Stories/Reels mental model to encourage continued engagement.

screens.name: H&M - View collection - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Fashion, beauty, or lifestyle e-commerce apps where brand imagery and aspirational styling are core differentiators.
  • Product listing pages where the brand wants to blend editorial/content browsing with functional commerce tools (filter/sort).
  • Catalogs with multiple sub-categories that benefit from quick, inline segment switching rather than deep navigation drill-downs.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for commodity or utility products (electronics, groceries, hardware) where shoppers prioritize spec comparison and density over lifestyle imagery.
  • Not ideal when users need to scan many SKUs quickly (a single large image per scroll significantly reduces the number of products visible, increasing time-to-decision for price-sensitive or bulk shoppers).
  • Risky for low-bandwidth or emerging markets where large full-bleed imagery increases load times and data costs.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious shoppers and existing H&M customers who respond to visual storytelling and trend inspiration rather than purely functional spec-driven shopping. The large, cinematic lifestyle photography taps into aspirational psychology, showing the garment worn, styled, and contextualized in a real-world setting (travel, sunlight, movement) rather than a sterile studio cutout, which increases desirability and purchase intent.

The segmented control and filter/sort bar cater to the more decisive, time-pressed segment of the audience who want quick category narrowing, balancing the editorial/inspirational browsing mode with a fast, utilitarian path to conversion. The persistent wishlist heart leverages the low-commitment "save for later" psychological trigger, letting undecided browsers bookmark desire items without the friction of full purchase decision-making.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-bleed editorial imagery as the primary content unit instead of a dense product grid, elevating perceived brand value and making browsing feel like flipping through a fashion magazine.
  • Inline segmented category switcher (View All / Clothes / Shoes & Accessories) placed directly under the title for instant scope refinement without navigation overhead.
  • Low-friction wishlist heart overlaid on the image itself, enabling a one-tap save at the point of visual interest.
  • Lightweight Sort & Filter affordances that stay visually minimal (icon + label, no heavy buttons) so they don't compete with the product photography.
  • Persistent bottom tab bar ensures users can always jump to search, wishlist, account, or bag regardless of scroll depth.

screens.name: H&M - View collection - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Fashion, beauty, home décor, or lifestyle e-commerce apps where mood and visual storytelling significantly influence purchase decisions.
  • Curated collections, "shop the look," lookbooks, or editorial/visual-search result feeds where inspiration browsing matters more than rapid comparison.
  • Brands wanting to reinforce premium or trend-led positioning through photography rather than discount-driven messaging.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for utilitarian or high-SKU categories (electronics, groceries, hardware) where users want to compare many items quickly (a single large image per product slows scanning and increases scroll fatigue).
  • Not ideal when users are price-driven or doing quick repeat purchases, since the format prioritizes emotional browsing over fast decision-making and comparison.
  • Risky on slower networks or low-end devices, as large full-bleed imagery increases load times and can hurt perceived performance without proper skeleton loading or image optimization.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets fashion-conscious shoppers who browse apparel the way they'd flip through a lookbook or Instagram feed, scrolling for inspiration as much as for a specific purchase. By presenting one large, stylized image per product instead of a dense grid, the design slows the user down and encourages emotional engagement with each item, which is a well-documented tactic in fashion e-commerce to increase dwell time and perceived desirability.

The psychological trigger at play is aspirational lifestyle association: showing the dress on a model in a sun-drenched poolside setting activates imagined-use imagery, helping shoppers project themselves into the scene and increasing purchase motivation beyond the garment's literal attributes. The persistent, low-friction wishlist heart also caters to the common fashion-browsing behavior of "saving for later" across multiple sessions before committing to buy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-bleed editorial photography as the primary content: Using large, atmospheric lifestyle imagery (poolside setting, natural model pose) instead of flat product shots elevates the perceived brand value and lets users visualize the garment in a real-world context, which is a key driver of fashion purchase intent.
  • Overlaid wishlist icon on the image: Placing the heart icon directly on the photo keeps the save action persistently accessible without cluttering the text metadata block, reducing friction for impulse-saving items while browsing.
  • Color swatches at the top, decoupled from the image: Showing available colorways as small squares next to the price allows users to gauge variety without needing to tap into the product detail page, speeding up the browse-to-decision loop.
  • Minimal chrome / content-first design: Stripping the UI down to a back button and a single header label maximizes screen real estate for imagery, aligning with H&M's image-led, minimalist look and feel.

screens.name: H&M - View collection - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this dense, image-first grid pattern for fashion, beauty, or lifestyle e-commerce apps where visual appeal and browsing volume are more important than detailed specs. It is ideal when:

  • The catalog is large and benefits from quick visual scanning (sort/filter accessibility).
  • The brand relies on strong photography/art direction to differentiate from competitors.
  • You want to encourage "discovery shopping" rather than targeted search-and-buy behavior.
  • Variant availability (color/size) needs to be communicated at a glance to reduce clicks.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for utility-based or spec-heavy products (e.g., electronics, hardware, B2B tools) where users need to compare technical details rather than aesthetics (a dense grid with minimal text would frustrate users needing to make informed comparisons quickly).

It is also less effective for small inventories, as the two-column grid and editorial breaks work best with high content volume; a small catalog would look sparse or require excessive scrolling padding. Additionally, this high-image approach is unsuitable for low-bandwidth markets or users on slow connections, as the full-bleed video/images increase load times and data usage significantly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious shoppers and young adults who are motivated more by aesthetic discovery and trend-shopping than by pure utility. The dense grid and swipe-able bottom carousel image cater to users accustomed to "scrolling" behavior similar to social media (Instagram-like browsing), making the shopping experience feel less like a utilitarian task and more like content consumption.

The psychological trigger here is aspiration via imagery: using high-production lifestyle shots (e.g., the model in the wind-blown hair video) instead of sterile product-on-white shots taps into identity-based purchasing, where the user buys into a "lifestyle" rather than just an "item." The ability to quickly favorite items (heart icon) caters to the "window shopping" behavior pattern, capturing purchase intent for later even if the user isn't ready to buy immediately.
screens.keyHighlights:
Key UX Highlights:

  • In-line Wishlisting: The heart icon sits directly atop the product image, allowing users to save items with zero navigation cost, encouraging higher save rates and reducing bounce.
  • Visual Variant Preview: Small color swatches beneath the price allow users to instantly see how many colorways exist without tapping into the detail page, drastically improving scan efficiency.
  • Editorial Content Breaks: Inserting a full-width lifestyle video/image between product rows breaks grid monotony and reinforces brand image, blending commerce with inspiration (a technique borrowed from print magazines).
  • Minimalist Chrome: By removing borders, card backgrounds, and shadows, the UI gets out of the way, letting the photography (the actual product) do the selling.

screens.name: H&M - Product filter - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a single filter facet (color, size, brand, material) has many enumerable options in an e-commerce or content-discovery context. It's ideal when:

  • The attribute has a strong visual component (color, pattern) that benefits from swatches rather than text alone.
  • You want to prevent zero-result dead ends by showing live counts per option.
  • Filters are hierarchical/nested and a drill-down approach with a dedicated back button is appropriate.
  • Multi-select behavior is expected and a persistent Apply/Clear footer can batch the user's choices before committing.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this full-screen, list-based approach when:

  • There are only 2: 4 filter options (a simple chip row or segmented control inline on the results page would be faster and avoid unnecessary navigation).
  • Real-time count computation is expensive or slow, as stale/delayed counts would undermine the core trust benefit of this pattern.
  • The product catalog is small enough that filtering adds more friction than value (in these cases, direct browsing is preferable).
  • Screen space is extremely limited (e.g., smartwatch) where swatch+text+count density would be unreadable.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves fashion-conscious shoppers who often shop with a specific aesthetic or wardrobe-matching goal in mind (color is frequently the single most decisive attribute for apparel purchases, more so than brand or even price for casual browsing). By giving color its own dedicated full-screen filter (rather than burying it in a dropdown), H&M acknowledges how central this decision point is to its worldwide, trend-driven audience.

The psychological driver here is reduction of choice paralysis combined with confidence-building feedback. Showing live counts taps into the user's desire for efficient decision-making (nobody wants to select "Purple" only to discover there's a single ugly option). It also leverages the scarcity signal subtly (low counts like "[ 1 ]" or "[ 2 ]" implicitly communicate rarity, which can increase perceived desirability for niche shoppers).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual visual encoding: Pairing text labels with actual color swatch dots lets users filter by color recognition rather than relying purely on language, which is especially helpful for ambiguous terms like "Multi" or distinguishing shades.
  • Live inventory counts per option: Displaying product counts next to every color (e.g., "[ 1 ]" for Purple vs. "[ 440 ]" for Blue) lets users gauge selection impact before applying, preventing dead-end empty states.
  • Persistent result preview footer: "Showing 765 products" updates contextually, giving continuous feedback and confidence before the user commits to the APPLY action.
  • Clear escape hatches: Both a back arrow (return to filter list) and an X (dismiss entirely) are offered, respecting different user mental models of "cancel."
  • Disabled Clear All state: Graying out "CLEAR ALL" when no filters are selected communicates current state and prevents unnecessary taps.

screens.name: H&M - Product filter - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any e-commerce, marketplace, or content-discovery app with a large, attribute-rich catalog (apparel, furniture, electronics, real estate) where users benefit from narrowing results by a single facet like color, brand, size, or price range. It's ideal when:

  • The attribute has a visual dimension (color, pattern) that benefits from swatch-based dual coding.
  • Inventory depth varies significantly across options, making live counts valuable for setting expectations.
  • Users commonly combine multiple values of the same facet (e.g., "black OR blue").
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dedicated single-facet screen pattern when:

  • The catalog is small enough that all products could be browsed directly without filtering overhead (the extra navigation step would add friction rather than remove it).
  • There are very few filter values (2-3), where inline chips or a segmented control on the main filter screen would be faster than a full drill-down page.
  • Real-time count computation is technically expensive or laggy, since stale or slow-loading counts would undermine the core trust benefit of this pattern.
  • The facet is not naturally represented by discrete values (e.g., continuous price range is better served by a slider, not a checklist).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves fashion-conscious shoppers browsing large catalogs who have a specific color preference in mind (e.g., shopping for a "black dress" or "blue jeans") and need to quickly narrow hundreds of SKUs. It's especially valuable for mobile users who can't visually scan dozens of product images at once and instead rely on structured filtering.

The psychological drivers at play include reduced decision fatigue (clear binary checkbox state), loss aversion mitigation (seeing counts before filtering prevents the fear of over-filtering into an empty result set), and sense of control (multi-select plus easy clear-all builds trust that exploration is low-risk and reversible).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live inventory counts per filter value: Each checkbox displays the exact number of matching products, helping users avoid dead-end filter combinations before applying.
  • Dual-coded swatches: Pairing text labels with actual color dots improves scannability and reduces ambiguity for terms like "Multi" or "Turquoise."
  • Running summary footer: "Showing 603 products" updates live as selections change, functioning as a confidence check prior to commitment.
  • Multi-select checkboxes: Square checkboxes (not radio buttons) correctly signal that multiple colors can be combined in a single query.
