  • Dual exit patterns: Back arrow for step-back navigation within the filter flow vs. "X" for full dismissal, respecting different user intents.
  • Balanced CTA pairing: Equal-width "Clear All" and "Apply" buttons prevent dead-ends and make resetting filters as effortless as applying them.

screens.name: H&M - Product filter - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• E-commerce search/category result pages where catalog depth is large and visual browsing drives purchase decisions (fashion, home goods, beauty).
  • Apps running frequent promotions/sales where urgency messaging needs to be baked into the grid itself rather than relying solely on banners.
  • Multi-audience retailers (Women/Men/Kids) that benefit from in-result audience segmentation chips.
  • Products with clear variant data (color, size) that can be previewed via swatches to reduce PDP taps.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Catalogs with low SKU counts, where an oversized headline and heavy filter/sort UI would feel like overkill for a handful of results.
  • B2B, enterprise or utility apps where discount-driven urgency styling (red pricing, badges) would undermine a professional or trustworthy tone.
  • Content types without strong imagery (e.g., digital services, subscriptions) where a two-column photo grid adds no value and could be replaced by a list view.
  • Contexts where accessibility/color-blind users need discount info, relying solely on red/strikethrough without a text label ("Save X%") could be improved.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets value-driven, visually-oriented fashion shoppers: a core H&M demographic of young adults and budget-conscious trend followers who browse by category/search rather than committing to a single item early. The heavy emphasis on discount percentages and red pricing exploits loss-aversion and scarcity psychology: showing the "was" price crossed out next to a red "now" price creates a perceived-savings anchor that increases conversion likelihood.

The segment chips (Women/Men/Baby) acknowledge that H&M serves whole households, letting a parent shopping for themselves pivot instantly to kids' or men's denim within the same search context, reducing the need to restart the search journey, which serves busy, multi-tasking shoppers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized editorial category title: Turns a mundane search result page into a styled, on-brand landing moment for the query.
  • Inline bracketed result counts (e.g., "ALL [603]", "WOMEN [342]") give users instant inventory-depth feedback for each segment before they even tap, aiding navigation decisions.
  • Discount badges overlaid on imagery rather than only in the text block, catching the eye during fast scroll/scan behavior.
  • Dual-purpose heart icon on each card enables immediate wishlist-saving mid-browse, reducing friction to return later without committing to purchase now.
  • Color swatch previews ("+2") communicate variant availability without needing to enter the PDP, saving a navigation step for comparison shopping.
  • Sticky promotional banner at the very top keeps the sitewide sale top-of-mind throughout the browsing session.

screens.name: H&M -  Sale info - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Seasonal sale launches, flash sales, or Black Friday/Cyber Monday campaigns needing maximum visual impact.
  • Driving app-exclusive engagement by offering early or privileged access to promotions.
  • Any retail/e-commerce home or landing screen where a single, time-sensitive message must outcompete all other content for attention.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for evergreen or non-promotional browsing screens, where users expect to see immediate product content, not a full-screen marketing takeover.
  • Risky for frequent/daily use: if every session opens on a hard sale screen, users may develop "banner blindness" or feel fatigued by constant urgency messaging.
  • Not suitable for users in a specific product-search mindset, as it delays access to search/browse functionality behind a promotional layer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets deal-motivated, fashion-conscious shoppers who respond to urgency and scarcity cues. The "TODAY ONLY" and "EARLY APP ACCESS" framing specifically rewards loyal app users, reinforcing retention and app-first behavior among existing H&M customers rather than new/casual browsers.

Psychologically, the screen relies on scarcity (limited-time sale), exclusivity (app-only early access), and visual dominance (oversized red sale typography, a color strongly associated with discounts/urgency) to short-circuit deliberation and drive an immediate tap on "Shop Now."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Negative space as a design weapon: Over 70% of the screen is empty, which (counterintuitively for e-commerce) increases perceived premium value and ensures the discount message is unmissable.
  • App-exclusive early access: A powerful channel-growth lever that incentivizes customers to use the app over web/desktop by gating a deal behind the app experience.
  • Persistent dual-layer CTA: The "SHOP NOW" bar sits above a floating tab bar, meaning the user always has two paths to purchase visible at once, reducing friction to conversion.
  • Lightweight department switcher: The "WOMEN +" control hints at quick category-switching without needing a heavier top navigation bar, preserving the clean hero layout.

screens.name: H&M -  Sale info - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for seasonal sales, flash promotions, or limited-time campaigns where you want maximum emotional impact before the user commits to browsing. It's ideal for:

  • App launch screens or category landing pages during sale events.
  • Driving urgency for time-boxed offers (clearance, holiday sales, member-exclusive drops).
  • Situations where legal/compliance text is mandatory but should not dilute the primary CTA's visual weight.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach for evergreen or non-promotional browsing screens, where oversized, interruptive typography would feel out of place and slow down task-oriented shopping. It's also risky if:

  • The brand needs a calmer, premium aesthetic (luxury positioning), since aggressive red sale typography can cheapen perceived brand value.
  • Users are already deep in a purchase funnel: this kind of hero teaser is better suited to entry points, not mid-checkout screens.
  • Accessibility is a priority without fallback, since relying on a swipe gesture to reveal critical pricing info could confuse less tech-savvy users if no visual cue (like the handle) is clear enough.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets deal-seeking and fashion-conscious shoppers: a core H&M demographic motivated by discounts and fast-fashion turnover. The large red "SALE" typography taps into well-established retail psychology: red signals urgency, discount, and loss-aversion ("don't miss this").

By cropping the percentage and requiring an upward swipe to reveal more, the design uses a curiosity gap / Zeigarnik effect: incomplete information compels users to engage further, increasing time-on-screen and the likelihood of discovering sale items. This is particularly effective for younger, mobile-native users accustomed to swipe gestures and bottom-sheet interactions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized, cropped typography creates visual tension and curiosity, encouraging the user to interact (swipe/expand) to reveal the actual discount percentage.
  • Draggable bottom sheet affordance transforms a simple promo banner into a progressively disclosed, gesture-driven experience rather than a static image.
  • Minimal top chrome (category label + expand icon) keeps focus entirely on the promotional message while still anchoring the user within the navigation hierarchy (Women's department).
  • Compliance text tucked at the bottom in a neutral tone satisfies legal requirements without competing visually with the primary sale message.

screens.name: H&M -  Adding an item to favorites - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this shoppable-lifestyle-image pattern for fashion, home decor, or beauty apps where styling context and outfit/look completion drives purchase intent. It's ideal for campaigns, lookbooks, seasonal collections, or any scenario where cross-selling multiple complementary SKUs from one scene is a business goal. It also works well for brands with strong photography/art direction budgets, as the pattern lives or dies by image quality.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for utilitarian, spec-driven, or commodity products (electronics, groceries, hardware) where users need immediate access to technical details, specifications, or comparisons rather than mood/atmosphere. It is also risky for small screens or low-bandwidth markets where heavy image loading delays perceived performance, and for accessibility-first contexts where text-sparse, image-reliant screens can disadvantage users relying on screen readers.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets fashion-conscious young adults who shop with their eyes first (they are drawn in by a complete styled look (outfit, bag, shoes, setting) rather than an isolated garment). The psychological trigger here is aspirational identity transfer: by showing the product worn in a desirable, well-art-directed real-world setting (a charming European street), the user imagines themselves living that scene, which increases perceived value and desirability beyond the $24.99 price tag.

The "VIEW PRODUCTS" overlay also leverages low-friction curiosity: it invites users who may not have the pants on their radar to discover complementary items (the bag, the sandals), driving incremental cross-sell revenue, a core objective for a high-volume fast-fashion retailer like H&M.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Shoppable Lifestyle Image: Embedding a "VIEW PRODUCTS" CTA directly inside an editorial photo turns inspirational content into a direct shopping funnel, capturing the user's desire for the full look at the exact peak-emotion moment.
  • Image-Dominant Real Estate: Dedicating ~75% of the screen to photography before any text appears builds a fashion-magazine feel appropriate for a style-conscious audience.
  • Persistent Thumb-Zone Actions: Back, Share, and Wishlist icons float over the image in the toolbar, keeping key actions accessible without interrupting the visual immersion.
  • Carousel Page Control: Dot indicators communicate additional lifestyle angles are available via swipe, encouraging further exploration before scrolling to purchase details.

screens.name: H&M -  Adding an item to favorites - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for fashion, home decor, or lifestyle product catalogs where visual context and aspiration significantly influence purchase decisions. It's ideal for marketing campaign tie-ins, seasonal "look" collections, or editorial content that needs to double as a shopping entry point. Especially effective when a single scene features multiple purchasable items, as it naturally promotes cross-selling and increases average order value.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for utility, commodity, or specification-driven products (electronics, groceries, hardware) where customers need technical details and direct comparison immediately rather than mood-setting imagery. It's also not advisable for repeat-purchase or search-driven shopping flows, since the extra step of tapping "View Products" to see the actual items adds friction for users who already know exactly what they want to buy.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets fashion-conscious shoppers who browse H&M for inspiration as much as for explicit need (a Gen Z/Millennial audience raised on Instagram and Pinterest-style visual discovery). The lifestyle photography taps into aspirational psychology: showing the garment as part of a lived, attractive lifestyle (a sunny European doorway, tousled hair, a wicker bag) rather than on a sterile mannequin triggers desire by association, a core technique in fashion marketing.

The heart/wishlist icon prominently placed top-right caters to browsing behavior typical of this demographic, who frequently save items to revisit later rather than purchasing immediately, supporting a considered, multi-session purchase journey common in fast fashion apps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Shoppable Lifestyle Imagery: Embedding a "View Products" CTA directly within an aspirational editorial photo rather than a sterile product grid merges content and commerce seamlessly.
  • Narrative-First Hierarchy: Delaying the price and product name until after the emotional hero image lets the fashion styling sell the product before the commercial details are even introduced.
  • Multi-Image Storytelling via Dots: The page control signals additional styled shots are swipeable, extending engagement time and giving multiple angles/context without cluttering the UI with thumbnails.
  • Persistent Floating Nav: The transparent top bar and floating bottom tab bar maximize the visible image real estate while keeping core navigation always within thumb's reach.
  • Outfit-Based Cross-Sell: By tagging an entire outfit (bag, pants, top) in one photo, H&M naturally encourages basket-size growth without needing separate "complete the look" modules.

results.query: When to prompt users for app store rating without disrupting critical tasks

screens.name: Brex Compliance rating 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for utility apps where users manage recurring administrative or compliance tasks (reimbursements, document uploads, compliance checklists) alongside performance metrics. Ideal for gig-work platforms, field-service apps, or B2B employee tools where motivating consistent, low-friction task completion is critical. The combination of a motivational status banner + filterable task list + persistent creation FAB works well whenever you need to balance "nice-to-know" performance data with "need-to-do" action items.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-stakes or complex task management (e.g., project management tools with many interdependent tasks) where a flat list lacks sufficient hierarchy, grouping, or due-date prioritization. Also avoid combining unrelated performance/rating banners with task lists if the metric isn't contextually tied to the tasks, doing so can feel like noise or manipulative gamification rather than genuine insight. If most tasks are mandatory/urgent, the soft "Optional" framing could undermine urgency and lead to critical items being ignored.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for gig economy workers (e.g., rideshare/delivery drivers) who need a lightweight, fast way to manage administrative to-dos (expense reimbursements, documentation) alongside their core work. The target user is likely checking this app in short bursts between jobs, so the UI prioritizes glanceable information and one-tap actions.

Psychologically, the screen leverages positive reinforcement (the "High" rating banner) to build trust and goodwill before presenting the user with tasks, increasing the likelihood of task completion. The "Optional" labeling also reduces the psychological friction/anxiety associated with an unfinished to-do list, a known driver of task abandonment or app avoidance.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Performance-as-Motivation Card: Surfacing a positive "High" rating banner at the top of a task list reframes the Tasks screen from a chore list into a rewarding check-in, boosting emotional engagement before the user even looks at pending work.

  • Priority-tagged, color-coded status bar: The green stepped indicator with a "High" label gives instant visual feedback on standing without requiring the user to parse numbers.

  • Dual-purpose FAB: The "Add receipts" pill button is labeled (not just an icon), clarifying intent immediately and reducing misclicks.

  • Optional vs Required task framing: Tagging tasks as "Optional" manages user expectations and prevents guilt/anxiety over incomplete, non-critical items.

  • Segmented filter (All/Drafts): Keeps the task list lightweight and lets power users jump straight to in-progress work.

screens.name: Brex Compliance rating 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any B2B SaaS or fintech product that needs to drive compliance, data completeness, or administrative hygiene behaviors from end users (e.g., expense receipts, KYC documents, profile completeness).

  • Admin/finance tools where the end user is not a domain expert and needs just-in-time education alongside a status indicator.

  • Scenarios where you want to turn a potentially punitive metric (audit risk, score, grade) into a motivating, improvable gauge rather than a static judgment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for highly technical or expert audiences who find oversimplified gauges patronizing and prefer raw data/detailed breakdowns instead.

  • Not ideal when the score is based on dozens of weighted factors that can't be honestly represented by a single pin on a 3-color scale (oversimplification could mislead users about what specifically to fix).

  • Avoid if the underlying "fix" requires significant effort disproportionate to the simplicity of the ask; the lightweight, friendly tone here could feel dismissive for more complex compliance failures.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees at a company using Brex corporate cards who are nudged (likely via a Tasks tab notification) to improve their expense documentation. The primary psychological lever is social/organizational accountability: tying personal behavior ("your rating") to company-level outcomes ("tax compliance," "[Company] relies on you") taps into a user's sense of responsibility to their team/employer.

Secondary triggers include gamification (the colored gauge mimics a score/level system) and reduction of uncertainty: non-finance employees often don't know what "compliant" documentation looks like, so the explicit definitions and examples reduce anxiety and task-abandonment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Traffic-light gauge visualization: Converts a multi-factor compliance score into one intuitive red-yellow-green gradient with a labeled pin, instantly communicating status without requiring the user to parse numbers.

  • Proactive self-service education: Anticipates user questions (calculation method, importance, definitions) directly on the results screen instead of hiding them behind a separate help center, reducing cognitive friction and support load.

  • Concrete, example-driven definitions: Using a real-world example for "memo" removes ambiguity that often causes incomplete expense submissions.

  • Positive framing of an accountability mechanic: Frames compliance as something the user actively "improves" rather than a static grade they failed, encouraging ongoing engagement rather than defensiveness.

screens.name: Brex Tasks 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you need users to resolve discrete, finite action items tied to compliance, data completeness, or account health (e.g., missing receipts, unverified identity documents, incomplete profile fields). It excels in B2B/fintech contexts where tasks have clear, quantifiable stakes (amounts, deadlines) and benefit from being decoupled from the main dashboard to avoid clutter.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for consumer apps where surfacing a dedicated "Tasks" tab may feel overly corporate or guilt-inducing for low-stakes actions. It also fails if task volume is very high and unfiltered, as the simple segmented-control filtering shown here would become insufficient, requiring more robust sorting, grouping by due date, or batch-resolution tools instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees or finance team members using a corporate spend/expense management platform (similar to Pleo, Ramp, or Brex) who need to reconcile receipts against card transactions. The psychological trigger at play is the Zeigarnik effect: the persistent badge count and explicit "missing" framing create a nagging sense of incompleteness that drives the user to close the loop quickly, which is crucial for compliance-heavy workflows where unresolved receipts can create audit risk or accounting delays.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Badge-driven Tab Bar: The red/orange numeric badge on the "Tasks" tab preemptively signals outstanding items before the user even opens the screen, driving habitual re-engagement.

  • Dual-layer header: The vibrant animated gradient header paired with a sliding white content sheet gives the utilitarian task list a premium, modern feel rarely seen in typically dry expense-management tools.

  • Context-rich list item: Combining the task description with the specific transaction amount (£2.50) on the same row eliminates the need to tap in for details just to assess urgency/importance.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: The orange "Add" button is the only strong color accent on the entire screen, ensuring zero ambiguity about the next required action.

screens.name: Brex Tasks 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for task/notification centers in productivity, gig-work, or financial apps where users need a prioritized, scannable to-do list combined with personalized performance feedback. Ideal for apps serving time-constrained users (field workers, drivers, freelancers) who need glanceable status plus quick-action completion flows. The persistent floating action button pattern is effective when one action (e.g., adding a receipt/record) dominates user intent across the task list.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in enterprise or B2B admin tools where task volume is high and users need advanced sorting/filtering/bulk actions (a single-task flat list will not scale well beyond a handful of items). Also avoid the "congratulatory banner + task list" combination in contexts where performance metrics could cause stress or comparison anxiety (e.g., underperforming users may find the self-rating banner demotivating if not handled with equally graceful messaging at lower tiers).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets gig workers (e.g., rideshare/delivery drivers) who need lightweight financial administration tools (expense/reimbursement tracking) integrated into their daily workflow app. The psychological hooks include:

  • Validation/Esteem triggers: The "High" rating congratulatory message taps into achievement motivation, reinforcing continued engagement with the platform.

  • Reduced anxiety via optionality: Labeling tasks as "Optional" respects user autonomy, which is critical for a user base that may already feel overburdened by platform requirements.

  • Low cognitive load: Minimal single-task view with one clear CTA caters to users who open the app briefly between shifts/rides, needing fast, frictionless task completion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Gamified status banner: The "High" rating banner with a tiered progress bar visualization turns an abstract performance metric into a tangible, motivating visual, reinforcing positive behavior (social proof/self-comparison).

  • Low-pressure task framing: Tagging the task as "Optional" prevents false urgency fatigue, building long-term trust with users who might otherwise ignore or distrust nagging reminder systems.

  • Persistent floating CTA: The "Add receipts" pill ensures the primary content-creation action is never more than one tap away, regardless of list length or scroll state.

  • Segmented filtering: Simple All/Drafts toggle lets power users quickly triage incomplete work without a complex filter UI.

screens.name: Brex Giving Feedbacks 1
screens.whereToUse:
• AI agent or copilot interfaces where users need to audit or trust automated actions taken on their behalf.

  • Any overflow/kebab menu requiring quick access to secondary actions (Settings, Feedback, Help) without leaving the current context.

  • Activity/history feeds for automation tools, where showing the "reasoning" behind an action increases user confidence and reduces support tickets.

  • Empty states for logs or feeds that haven't accumulated content yet, pairing the empty message with a forward-looking explanation of future content.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this level of granular action-by-action transparency in high-frequency, low-risk automations where it would create information overload instead of reassurance.

  • Don't use ambiguous scrims/dimming in contexts where users need to reference background information precisely (the semi-obscured content here could frustrate users who want to re-read the card while the menu is open).

  • Avoid playful empty-state copy ("Nothing to report yet!") in highly regulated or compliance-sensitive contexts where users expect strictly formal, auditable language.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets business professionals and finance/ops teams using Brex's expense management platform who are delegating repetitive tasks (expense categorization, memo writing, attendee tracking) to an AI assistant. The psychological driver here is trust calibration: users handing over financial workflows to an autonomous agent need constant, low-friction proof that the AI is acting correctly and based on legitimate data sources (like their calendar), not hallucinating or guessing. The transparency affordances reduce the anxiety typically associated with "black box" AI automation in a finance context where errors carry real monetary consequences.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explainable AI pattern: Each automated action (added attendees, added memo) is paired with a rationale ("Based on your calendar"), building trust in agentic automation by making the "why" visible rather than hidden.

  • Layered depth via dimming: The context menu uses a scrim over the background content rather than fully obscuring it, letting users retain spatial orientation of what they were doing before opening the menu.

  • Didactic empty state: Rather than a generic "no data" message, the empty state educates the user on what will appear here in the future, setting expectations for the assistant's role.

  • Dual-card stacking: A subtle second card peeking from behind the primary one hints at additional history items, implying a scrollable feed without needing explicit UI chrome.

screens.name: Brex Giving Feedbacks 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for post-interaction feedback capture on specific features (e.g., AI assistants, new betas, support interactions) where you want qualitative + quantitative signal without disrupting the user's primary workflow. Ideal for in-app micro-surveys, NPS-style check-ins, or beta feature feedback loops. Works well as a bottom sheet triggered from a settings menu, a "..." overflow action, or after task completion.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when feedback needs to be mandatory or highly structured (e.g., compliance surveys), as the lightweight, dismissible nature invites low completion rates. Also avoid presenting this immediately upon app launch or mid-critical-task, as interrupting a user's active workflow for feedback (even a lightweight one) can feel intrusive and lower goodwill. If deeper diagnostic data is needed (e.g., multi-choice categorization of complaint type), a single free-text field plus stars will be insufficient and should be expanded into a short multi-step form.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets business/finance professionals using Brex's AI assistant within a B2B fintech product. The design leverages the IKEA effect/co-creation bias: by explicitly asking "How can we improve," it signals to power users and early AI-feature adopters that their input directly shapes the roadmap, which increases the likelihood of candid, detailed responses from an audience that is typically time-constrained and skeptical of unprompted surveys. The low-friction design (short form, no mandatory fields, easy dismissal) acknowledges that B2B users have limited patience for feedback loops and will abandon anything that feels like extra "work" outside their core job tasks.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-mode feedback capture: Combines qualitative (free text) and quantitative (star rating) feedback in one lightweight screen, maximizing data richness without adding form steps.

  • Bottom sheet presentation: Keeps the user anchored to their current task/context (the AI Assistant) rather than forcing a full-page navigation, reducing perceived friction.

  • Sticky CTA: The orange Submit button is fixed to the bottom of the viewport, guaranteeing visibility and reachability even if the on-screen keyboard appears.

  • Optional-feeling inputs: Neither field is marked as required with asterisks or blocking validation visible, which lowers the psychological barrier to engagement for a low-stakes, voluntary action.

screens.name: Brex Giving Feedbacks 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for lightweight, in-context feedback collection immediately following a feature interaction (e.g., after using an AI chatbot, completing a support ticket, or finishing a task). It's ideal when you want quantitative (star rating) and qualitative (open text) signals without resorting to a full external survey tool. Pre-filling the text input with a plausible, editable default is particularly effective for low-engagement contexts where users are unlikely to type unprompted.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when you need statistically rigorous or unbiased qualitative data (pre-filled text can anchor user responses and skew sentiment toward the suggested answer (a form of priming bias)). It's also unsuitable for multi-dimensional feedback (e.g., NPS plus detailed diagnostics) where a single text field and rating are insufficient to capture nuanced issues. For high-stakes or compliance-related feedback (e.g., safety reports), a more structured, unbiased multi-step form should be used instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets business users of Brex (finance/expense management professionals) who have just interacted with an AI-powered assistant feature. Because these users are typically busy professionals with limited patience for lengthy surveys, the design leverages the path-of-least-resistance psychological principle: by prefilling an answer and limiting the ask to one rating plus one text field, Brex maximizes the likelihood of capturing a data point before the user's attention wanes.

The star rating also taps into familiar mental models from app-store reviews and e-commerce, so users instantly understand how to interact with it without instruction, reducing cognitive friction for a secondary (non-core) task like feedback-giving.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-filled smart default text: Populating the feedback field with "Easy to use" dramatically increases completion rates by giving users a starting point they can simply accept or tweak, rather than facing a blank-page problem.

  • Single, focused ask: Combining only one open text question and one rating control avoids survey fatigue, which is especially important for a feedback loop on an AI/assistant feature that may be used frequently.

  • Clear exit affordance: The circular back button ensures users never feel forced to complete the form, preserving a sense of control and reducing rage-quits or negative sentiment toward the app.

  • Thumb-friendly CTA placement: The large, high-contrast orange "Submit" button is docked at the bottom, matching natural mobile ergonomics and brand color for maximum visibility.

screens.name: Brex Giving Feedbacks 4
screens.whereToUse:
• AI/agent-based products where users need auditability of autonomous actions (fintech, ops automation, AI copilots).

  • First-run or low-activity states for a history/log/activity feed feature.

  • Anywhere a toast confirmation needs to coexist with a background empty state without feeling intrusive.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid if the feature has no real "memory" or history to eventually populate (the faded preview cards create an expectation that must be fulfilled).

  • Not suitable for screens where users need an immediate strong call-to-action (CTA) to generate content; this design is passive and could be paired with a prompt like "Try asking the assistant" for better activation.

  • Risky in contexts where AI transparency details (merchant, amount, attendees) are sensitive and shouldn't be shown even in blurred/ghost form to unauthorized viewers.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets business professionals and finance/ops teams using Brex's corporate card and spend management platform who are being introduced to an AI assistant feature for the first time. The psychological trigger at play is trust calibration: because AI agents can take autonomous actions (approving expenses, editing calendar memos), users need constant visibility into what the assistant has done and why, satisfying the need for control and predictability in high-stakes financial contexts. The empty state also leverages a curiosity gap, previewing the format of future automated reports to encourage continued engagement with the assistant.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent AI Reasoning: Cards explicitly cite sources for AI actions (e.g., "Based on your calendar"), which is a best-practice pattern for building trust in agentic/AI automation features.

  • Faded Context Stack: Rather than a blank white empty state, the design uses dimmed/blurred historical cards to hint at the type and format of future content, reducing ambiguity about what this screen is for.

  • Immediate Feedback Loop: The toast confirms the user's rating action was received instantly, reinforcing that their input into the AI's behavior matters (reinforcement learning framing).

  • Non-punitive Empty State Copy: "Nothing to report yet!" avoids technical or negative language (e.g., "No data"), keeping the tone encouraging.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Introducing a signature, high-leverage feature (like a command palette, keyboard shortcut, or gesture) that differentiates the product from competitors.

  • Onboarding flows for productivity, developer, or power-user tools where speed and efficiency are core selling points.

  • Any scenario where the interaction method varies by device/input type and both paths need clear instruction.

  • Multi-step onboarding sequences where you want to balance education with user autonomy (skip option) and progress visibility.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, full-screen interruption pattern for minor or rarely-used features (reserve it for truly high-value, differentiating functionality).

  • Not ideal for first-time, non-technical consumer audiences who may find keyboard shortcut callouts (⌘K) confusing or irrelevant.

  • Should not be used if the feature can't actually be demonstrated/tried in context, forcing a "try it" prompt without real interactivity creates false expectations and frustration.

  • Avoid stacking too many of these full-screen coach mark steps in a row (fatigue risk) without allowing users to skip or revisit later via a help menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets productivity-focused, often technical users (engineers, designers, PMs) evaluating Linear as a project management tool. These users are typically efficiency-driven and skeptical of long onboarding flows, so the screen must quickly prove tangible value (speed) rather than rely on generic feature tours.

Psychologically, this leverages the testing/generation effect: users retain information far better when they perform an action themselves rather than just reading about it. It also uses reciprocity and competence framing: by immediately demonstrating a "power user" shortcut, Linear signals the product respects the user's time and skill level, which builds early trust and perceived product sophistication.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Device-adaptive instructions: The screen smartly provides both a touchscreen gesture ("tapping with two fingers") and a keyboard shortcut (⌘K), ensuring relevance regardless of input method.

  • Learn-by-doing microinteraction: Instead of just describing the feature, the card frames it as a task to "try," encouraging active engagement and muscle-memory formation over passive reading.

  • Keycap UI chips: Rendering the shortcut as skeuomorphic key chips (⌘ and K) rather than plain text instantly communicates "this is a keyboard shortcut" using a familiar visual convention.

  • Progress transparency: The page control dots at the bottom set expectations about onboarding length, reducing abandonment anxiety.

  • Low-friction exit: A persistent close (X) button respects user autonomy, letting advanced users skip onboarding entirely.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 13
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any OAuth/third-party authentication handoff, especially when:

  • The integration requires sensitive or broad-sounding permissions (e.g., code, financial data, contacts, calendar).

  • You want to pre-explain *why* the permission is needed in your own branded voice before the native OS/platform permission dialog appears (which you cannot customize).

  • You need to differentiate your request from what users might assume (e.g., "we only need X, not Y") to reduce abandonment.

  • The feature is optional/supplementary rather than core, so offering a clear "skip for now" path is appropriate.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavier priming pattern when:

  • The permission requested is trivial or expected (e.g., basic notification permission) - adding an extra screen here only adds friction without added trust value.

  • The integration is mandatory for the app to function; in that case, framing it as skippable ("I'll do this later") would be misleading.

  • Users are already deep in a time-sensitive task, inserting a full-screen interstitial here could feel like an interruption rather than a helpful primer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets software engineering teams and technical project managers who use Linear to track issues and want to connect their existing GitHub repositories. This audience is highly security-conscious and often skeptical of third-party tools requesting broad repo access, making trust and transparency the primary psychological lever at play.

The design leverages loss-aversion and risk-mitigation triggers: by explicitly ruling out code-read access, it removes the single biggest psychological barrier (fear of IP/code exposure) that would otherwise cause a drop-off at this step of the funnel. It also leverages the authority/competence heuristic: a clean, well-organized explanation signals that Linear is a professionally built, trustworthy product worthy of elevated permissions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive Objection Handling: Explicitly stating what the integration will not do (read code) directly inside the value-prop list, rather than letting users discover/fear this on the native GitHub OAuth screen.

  • Permission Priming Pattern: A branded, friendly pre-screen before handing off to GitHub's native, less-customizable OAuth consent page, allowing Linear to control the narrative and context.

  • Low-Friction Opt-Out: The "I'll do this later" link ensures the integration prompt never feels like a hard gate blocking core app usage.

  • Checkmark Visual Language: Using checkmarks (vs. plain bullets) subconsciously signals "these boxes are already ticked/safe for you," increasing perceived trustworthiness.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse:
• B2B SaaS products where value scales with number of collaborators (project management, communication, whiteboarding tools).

  • Early onboarding flows where you want to seed network effects before the user's enthusiasm decays.

  • Any flow where you want to encourage an action but must not block progress for users unwilling to comply immediately.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Single-player or personal-use apps where there is no collaborative value proposition (invites would feel irrelevant or pushy).

  • Highly privacy-sensitive contexts where asking for colleague emails this early could raise trust/compliance concerns.

  • Flows where the user hasn't yet experienced core value, asking for a team invite before the product has proven itself can increase drop-off instead of reducing it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new signups: typically a team lead, founder, or early adopter evaluating Linear for their organization. Since Linear's value is inherently networked (a project/issue tracker is far more useful with teammates present), this step exploits the "viral loop" growth pattern: converting a single-user trial into a multi-seat team account as early as possible. Psychologically, it capitalizes on the user's current high-motivation state (freshly signed up, curious, exploratory) to ask for an investment (inviting colleagues) before intent fades. It also uses social facilitation (once co-workers are invited, the user has public accountability to actually adopt and use the tool).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-exit strategy: Both "Continue" and "I'll do this later" give users multiple non-blocking ways to skip, drastically reducing onboarding abandonment risk.

  • Batch email input: A single text area accepting comma-separated emails lets power users invite an entire team in one action instead of repeating a form multiple times.

  • Visual progress transparency: The dot-based page control at the bottom sets expectations for how many steps remain, reducing onboarding fatigue/anxiety.

  • Strategic CTA hierarchy: The filled purple "Send invites" button draws the eye first, while skip options are intentionally muted in gray, nudging the desired behavior without forcing it.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Post-onboarding or settings flows where you want to capture marketing/notification consent without blocking the primary task.

  • SaaS products with a technical or privacy-conscious audience where transparency drives higher-quality opt-ins.

  • Any flow requiring compliance with opt-in consent regulations (GDPR, CAN-SPAM, CCPA).

  • Situations where you want to separate distinct communication types (product updates vs. marketing) to improve long-term engagement and reduce unsubscribe rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this soft, skippable pattern if email capture is a core business-critical conversion metric that must be maximized (a more assertive single-choice prompt may perform better for growth-stage products).

  • Don't use pre-toggled OFF switches if your business model depends on default opt-ins and your jurisdiction does not legally require explicit consent (though this is generally not recommended).

  • Not ideal mid-task, where interrupting with a preference screen would break flow and frustrate users (e.g., during checkout or active editing).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded or existing Linear users at a natural checkpoint (likely post-signup or post-settings-visit) where communication preferences are most relevant. The audience is primarily technical/product teams who are highly sensitive to unsolicited marketing noise, so Linear's restrained, honest approach to opt-in (rather than pre-checked boxes) is tailored to a sophisticated, trust-sensitive user base that would otherwise bounce or immediately unsubscribe if manipulated into a list.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages the principle of autonomy (user controls every choice), reciprocity (transparent value exchange: "subscribe to learn about changes" implies tangible benefit), and reduced cognitive load (binary toggles, no required fields) to maximize genuine, lower-churn opt-ins rather than inflated but low-quality subscriber counts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Opt-in by default (toggles OFF): Respects user consent norms and regulatory best practice, building long-term trust over short-term list-growth metrics.

  • Frictionless exit via "X": Clearly communicates this is a non-mandatory step, reducing perceived pressure and modal fatigue.

  • Granular, specific choices: Separating "changelog" from "marketing/onboarding" emails lets users tailor exactly what they want, avoiding the all-or-nothing subscription trap.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Stating frequency ("bi-weekly," "occasional") directly addresses the top objection to subscribing (fear of spam).

  • Correct component semantics: Using a toggle for binary preferences but a button/pill for the external "Follow on X" action avoids UI pattern misuse.

screens.name: Brex Deleting a draft 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, administrative, or compliance-related task management within consumer or gig-worker apps (particularly where users must complete secondary, non-core actions (expense submission, document uploads, profile verification) that are easy to forget). It's ideal when you want to combine motivational content (ratings, streaks, performance stats) with a functional to-do list to keep engagement high. The floating CTA pattern works well when there's a single dominant action users should take regardless of list state.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for screens with high-volume, complex task management (e.g., enterprise project management) where a simple list and single FAB would be insufficient (those need robust filtering, bulk actions, and prioritization tools). Also avoid combining unrelated motivational banners (like performance ratings) with task lists if they create confusion about the screen's primary purpose, or if the praise content feels disconnected/irrelevant to the user's current need, which can come across as tone-deaf filler.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for gig economy workers (e.g., rideshare/delivery drivers) who need a lightweight, mobile-first way to manage financial admin tasks like expense reimbursements alongside their actual work metrics (ratings, earnings). The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Positive reinforcement / variable praise: The "High" rating celebration taps into achievement motivation, a technique borrowed from gamification to increase daily app opens.

  • Reduced friction via optionality framing: Labeling the task "Optional" lowers perceived obligation, making users more likely to engage voluntarily rather than avoid the screen due to dread.

  • Completion drive (Zeigarnik Effect): The badge count and half-finished draft state create a subtle itch to close the loop, especially for users motivated by clearing notifications.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Motivational micro-copy at the top of a task list: Surfacing a performance/rating compliment ("Way to go!") above the actual to-do items reframes a transactional screen into an emotionally rewarding one, increasing daily engagement likelihood.

  • Status/priority visualization via colored bar chart icon: The small tri-segment bar next to "High" gives an instant, scannable visual cue of standing without requiring the user to parse numbers.

  • Non-blocking floating action button: "Add receipts" is positioned to stay accessible during scroll without overlapping list content or the tab bar, following FAB best practices for primary actions.

  • Optional vs. required task labeling: The "Optional" chip is a simple but effective pattern for managing user cognitive load and preventing false urgency.

  • Badge on Tab Bar: The orange "1" badge on the Tasks tab creates a Zeigarnik-effect pull to return and resolve the outstanding item.

screens.name: Brex Deleting a draft 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this dual-layer destructive-confirmation pattern whenever a user action results in permanent or hard-to-recover data loss, especially in forms with multiple user-entered fields (memos, attachments, calculated values). It's ideal for financial, legal, or administrative tools where mistakes carry real costs or trust implications.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavier two-step confirmation for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., removing a single tag or dismissing a notification), where an undo toast would be faster and less intrusive. Overusing confirmation dialogs for trivial actions trains users to blindly tap through them, diminishing their effectiveness for genuinely critical actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for business travelers, field employees, sales reps, or contractors who log mileage for expense reimbursement (likely within a corporate expense management or HR tool (e).g., similar to Spendesk, Expensify, or SAP Concur). These users need speed and confidence that their financial data won't be lost by accident.

Psychologically, the design leverages loss aversion by explicitly confirming before deletion (users are more sensitive to losing already-entered data (distance, memo, attachments) than to the minor friction of an extra tap). The deferred confirmation also exploits the Zeigarnik effect, keeping the original form visible in the background as a reminder of what's at stake if they proceed with deletion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Automatic calculation transparency: Showing the per-mile rate (£0.45) alongside the total amount builds trust by letting users audit the math themselves rather than trusting a black-box total.

  • Two-step destructive action pattern: Separating the "Delete Draft" trigger from the actual confirmation dialog prevents accidental data loss from a single mis-tap.

  • Visual destructive hierarchy: Red text for the initial "Delete Draft" button and a bold orange fill for the final "Delete" button create consistent, escalating visual warning cues.

  • Context-preserving modal stacking: Rather than navigating away, the confirmation dialog stacks on top of the existing form, keeping the user's place and reducing cognitive reload.

screens.name: Brex Deleting a draft 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a task/notification/inbox-style screen can legitimately be empty for extended periods. It's ideal for:

  • Admin, compliance, or approval queues in B2B/gig-worker tools where "zero tasks" is a common and desirable state.

  • Any screen where you want to reduce compulsive re-checking behavior by clearly setting expectations about future notifications.

  • Apps that benefit from injecting secondary engagement content (ratings, tips, achievements) into otherwise empty real estate without cluttering primary navigation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, illustration-driven empty state in contexts where:

  • Users expect dense, high-frequency task lists (e.g., enterprise ticketing systems) - an overly playful empty state can feel inappropriate or juvenile for professional/serious use cases.

  • The "zero state" is actually a sign of a broken integration or sync failure (in such cases, a generic reassuring message could mask real errors and should be replaced with diagnostic messaging instead).

  • Screen space is premium and secondary content (like the rating card) could distract from a critical primary action the user needs to take elsewhere.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for gig-economy workers (e.g., drivers for Via Transportation) who use this app to manage reimbursements, wallet balances, and compliance/administrative tasks. These users are typically checking the app frequently throughout their workday or between shifts, often in brief, interrupted sessions.

The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Anxiety reduction: Gig workers often worry about missed paperwork affecting pay; explicitly confirming "no tasks" and promising future notification alleviates recurring low-level stress.

  • Variable positive reinforcement: The "High" rating card taps into the same motivational mechanics as performance dashboards in ride-share driver apps, rewarding users with status/esteem signals to encourage continued platform loyalty.

  • Reduced friction to monetize sunk cost: The "Add receipts" CTA capitalizes on an idle moment to encourage behavior (uploading receipts) that benefits both the user (reimbursement) and the platform (data completeness).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Repurposed empty space for engagement: Instead of leaving the empty state purely blank, the "High" rating insight card is surfaced above it, turning dead screen real estate into a retention/motivation touchpoint.

  • Friendly 3D illustration: A custom, on-brand character/object illustration softens the "nothing to do" moment and gives the empty state personality instead of feeling broken or unfinished.

  • Proactive reassurance copy: Explicitly stating "we'll notify you here" removes the need for users to habitually re-check the tab, reducing anxiety-driven app opens.

  • Persistent contextual CTA: The floating "Add receipts" pill ensures the screen is never a complete dead-end (there's always a low-friction next action available).

  • Layered transient feedback: The toast confirming a deletion demonstrates good system-status visibility without blocking the rest of the UI.

results.query: Where not to use push notification priming during cold app launch

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 18
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any regulated product needing to disclose jurisdiction-based feature limitations, where proactive, plainly-worded transparency (paired with a reassuring counterpoint) reduces user confusion and complaint volume better than silently disabling features.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for disclosures involving genuinely serious risk or compliance matters (e.g., fraud warnings, account suspension reasons) - the casual, softened tone used here would be inappropriate where the user needs to register real urgency or take corrective action.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Chime / Varo: similarly disclose state-based feature restrictions (e.g., cash advance eligibility) via a plain-language screen before full app access, a common fintech-compliance pattern.

  • Robinhood: uses comparable "heads up" style disclosure screens for state-restricted investment products, balancing legal necessity with approachable copy.

  • Klarna: pairs restriction/limitation messaging with reassurance about what's still available, matching this two-part bad-news/good-news structure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive disclosure reduces later frustration: surfacing the state-based restriction before app entry (rather than letting the user discover it mid-task) follows the trust principle that bad news is best delivered early and honestly.

  • Bad-news-then-good-news sequencing: splitting the message into two bubbles that pivot from limitation to reassurance is a copywriting technique that reduces perceived severity without hiding the fact.

  • Illustration as tone-softener: the playful mascot graphic counterbalances the seriousness of a regulatory disclosure, keeping the moment from feeling like a legal pop-up.

  • Forward-framed CTA: "Explore the app" reframes the moment as entering something positive rather than merely dismissing a warning.

screens.name: Cleo Pre-Onboarding 19
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any mobile app where push notifications carry real ongoing value (reminders, coaching, alerts) and where the one-time nature of the OS permission dialog makes a pre-ask conversion step worth the extra screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for apps where notifications are purely transactional/low-value (e.g., a single order-confirmation alert) - the extra priming screen would add friction disproportionate to the notification's actual utility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: uses nearly identical permission-priming screens with mock notification previews and benefit bullets before requesting push permissions.

  • Headspace: similarly frames notification permission asks around emotional/wellbeing benefit rather than pure feature description, matching Cleo's "you're only human" framing.

  • Robinhood: uses a comparable soft-ask screen with a realistic notification mockup before the system dialog, for the same conversion-optimization reasons.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Permission priming increases opt-in: showing value and a realistic preview before the irreversible OS dialog is a well-established mobile pattern for maximizing permission grants.

  • Outcome-framed value proposition: "Never miss a dollar" leads with user benefit, not the technical ask ("allow notifications"), which is more persuasive per standard conversion-copy principles.

  • Non-punitive decline option: "Not now" (rather than "No" or "Deny") keeps the door open for reconsideration later without making the user feel they're rejecting the product outright.

  • Emotional reassurance as differentiation: "Reminders that you're only human 💙" preemptively defuses the anxiety that budget notifications will feel shaming, a thoughtful trust-building touch specific to a finance app's notification content.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 13
screens.whereToUse:
Use this modal-escalation error pattern for:

  • OTP/2FA and account verification flows where errors must not go unnoticed.

  • High-stakes single-field validations (payment PINs, security codes) where inline errors risk being overlooked.

  • Any flow where a wrong attempt should pause the user and require explicit acknowledgment before retrying.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy modal interruption pattern for:

  • Low-stakes or frequent validation errors (e.g., form field typos) - a modal here would feel excessive and annoying, better served by inline validation.

  • Flows where users may fail multiple times in quick succession (e.g., typing a long password) since repeated modal interruptions create friction fatigue.

  • Contexts where speed is paramount and users benefit from an unobtrusive, real-time inline correction cue instead of a full stop-and-acknowledge interaction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets general consumer app users going through account security/authentication flows (login, sign-up, password reset, or sensitive transaction confirmation). It's especially relevant for fintech, crypto, banking, or social apps where phone verification is a security gate.

Psychologically, this leverages the interruption effect: a full-screen or near-full-screen modal captures attention far more reliably than a color change or small text label, which is important because the OTP entry moment is high-stakes and users are often anxious about being locked out. The red "X" icon triggers immediate recognition of failure via pre-attentive color processing, while the calm copy prevents escalation of user anxiety, balancing urgency with reassurance.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Escalated error visibility: Uses a modal bottom sheet instead of subtle inline validation, ensuring the error cannot be missed, which is critical in security-sensitive OTP flows.

  • Context preservation: The background OTP screen remains dimly visible behind the sheet, so users retain spatial awareness of where they are in the flow.

  • Segmented OTP input with visual grouping: The dash divider between the 3rd and 4th digit boxes improves scannability and mimics familiar SMS code formatting.

  • Throttled resend with countdown: Prevents abuse/spam of the resend action while setting clear time expectations for the user.

  • Single, low-friction recovery CTA: Only one action ("Got it") avoids decision paralysis and gets the user back into the input flow immediately.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app needs to request a system-level permission (push notifications, location, camera, contacts, Bluetooth, etc.) that is not immediately obvious in value to a new user. It is especially effective:

  • During onboarding, right before the feature that depends on the permission becomes relevant.

  • In finance, health, delivery, or on-demand apps where real-time alerts are a core value proposition.

  • When the platform only allows a single native permission prompt, making the "ask" a precious, non-repeatable moment worth maximizing through pre-framing.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The permission's benefit is already self-evident from context (e.g., asking for camera access directly after tapping a "Scan document" button) - an extra screen would add unnecessary friction.

  • It's used too early in onboarding before the user has any trust or context for the app, which can lower conversion versus asking in-context later.

  • Overused across many permissions in a row, causing "permission fatigue" and increased decline rates or user drop-off.

  • The copy oversells the benefit relative to actual notification frequency, which can lead to users feeling misled and disabling notifications entirely after a few days.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users of a fintech/challenger-bank or card-based payments app (indicated by the "R" logo and card imagery) immediately after account creation, during initial app setup. The audience is likely everyday consumers who value real-time visibility into their spending (a core need for budget-conscious or first-time digital banking users).

Psychologically, the screen leverages: reciprocity/value exchange (explaining the benefit before asking for permission increases perceived fairness of the request), loss aversion (missing instant fraud/spend alerts feels risky), and autonomy preservation (offering an easy opt-out reduces reactance and permission fatigue). Priming permissions this way is proven to substantially increase opt-in rates versus firing the bare OS dialog cold, which is critical for fintech apps since push notifications are often the primary channel for fraud alerts and balance updates.
screens.keyHighlights:
Custom pre-permission screen: Decouples the value explanation from the native OS dialog, allowing the app to make its best case before the one-shot system permission prompt is triggered (critical because iOS/Android permission dialogs can typically only be shown once without deep-linking to Settings).

  • Visual permission metaphor: The white notification-shaped card with the brand "R" icon visually simulates what an actual push notification will look like, priming user expectations and building familiarity before they even receive one.

  • Benefit-first messaging: Leads with user value (instant balance/spend awareness) instead of app-centric language, tapping into loss-aversion and security-consciousness common in banking/fintech contexts.

  • Non-punitive decline path: "Not now" is styled as a full-width, easily tappable secondary button (not a tiny dismiss link) respecting user choice and avoiding dark-pattern friction, which builds trust in a financial product.

  • Consistent progress signaling: The back arrow and bottom progress bar maintain orientation within a multi-step onboarding sequence.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for the first data-collection step of regulated onboarding flows (banking, lending, investing, insurance) where jurisdiction determines legal terms, product availability, or compliance requirements. It's ideal when you need to:

  • Capture a single critical piece of data before proceeding.

  • Bundle mandatory legal consent with a natural forward-progress action to minimize friction.

  • Set a trustworthy, premium tone early in a financial or high-stakes onboarding journey.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Regulations in your jurisdiction require explicit, separate opt-in checkboxes for each legal document (implicit "by continuing" consent may not be legally sufficient everywhere, e.g., GDPR-strict contexts).

  • The screen needs to collect multiple related fields, bundling too many fields here would break the single-focus benefit.

  • Users are already deep in a trusted relationship with the brand (e.g., returning users), where re-surfacing full legal text on every flow entry may feel redundant and annoying.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users signing up for a regulated financial product (banking, neobank, or payments app) who are early in a KYC (Know Your Customer) onboarding funnel. Because financial services are jurisdiction-dependent, capturing country of residence upfront is both a legal necessity and a personalization trigger (subsequent screens/terms will adapt based on this answer).

Psychologically, the screen leverages reduced decision fatigue (only one choice to make) and trust signaling (premium dark gradient, banking partner names like "Lead Bank" mentioned transparently) to reassure users that their money and data are handled by legitimate, regulated entities. The passive, bundled consent mechanism reduces perceived friction, which is critical at this vulnerable point in the funnel (right before requesting sensitive personal/financial information) where drop-off risk is highest.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Only one interactive input (country dropdown) is presented, eliminating any ambiguity about what action is required.

  • Implicit consent via CTA: Legal agreement is bundled into the primary button press rather than requiring a separate checkbox, reducing friction while still satisfying compliance via explicit copy.

  • Atmospheric gradient for hierarchy: The deep blue-to-black gradient creates a premium, trustworthy fintech aesthetic while naturally guiding the eye without extra chrome or dividers.

  • Inline hyperlinked legal text: Multiple legal documents (Revolut Privacy Policy, Lead Bank Privacy Policy, E-sign Consent) are surfaced compactly within a single sentence rather than as separate rows, saving vertical space.

  • Thin progress indicator: A minimal pill-shaped progress bar at the bottom subtly communicates onboarding flow position without overwhelming the screen.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Identity verification (KYC/AML) flows for fintech, banking, or crypto apps.

  • Any onboarding step requiring legally precise data entry where user error is common (e.g., legal name, tax ID, passport details).

  • Government, healthcare, or insurance apps needing exact official information distinct from casual profile data.

  • Multi-step forms where isolating one or two related fields per screen improves completion rates over long single-page forms.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Casual social or consumer apps where a nickname or display name is perfectly acceptable (the formal tone would feel unnecessarily bureaucratic).

  • Flows where users are highly familiar with the process and repeated single-field screens would feel slow; consider consolidating into one screen with multiple fields if the audience prioritizes speed over guidance.

  • Low-stakes forms where the extra explanatory micro-copy is unnecessary and adds visual clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users undergoing identity verification for a regulated product (likely a crypto exchange, neobank, trading platform, or other financial service subject to AML/KYC regulations). The audience spans first-time signups who may be unfamiliar with why legal precision matters, making the explanatory micro-copy essential for reducing verification friction and abandonment.

Psychologically, the screen leverages authority and legitimacy cues (formal language, document-based framing) to signal seriousness and build trust that the platform is compliant and secure (important for users about to share sensitive PII). The minimal, single-task design also reduces decision fatigue, keeping users in a low-friction flow state during what is typically a tedious onboarding requirement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual micro-copy example: "e.g. Daniel, not 'Dan'" proactively prevents a top KYC rejection reason (use of nicknames) at the point of entry rather than after submission.

  • Progressive visual emphasis: Field opacity/contrast decreases from First name → Last name → Alias, visually encoding required vs. optional priority without extra labels or icons.

  • Persistent, thumb-reachable CTA: The Continue button remains fully visible above the keyboard, eliminating the need to dismiss the keyboard to proceed.

  • Single-focus screen: Isolating name capture from other KYC fields (DOB, address, etc.) reduces perceived form length and keeps cognitive load low per screen.

  • Auto-focused first field: The cursor is already active in "First name," removing an unnecessary tap and speeding up task completion.

screens.name: Brex Onboarding 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for B2B, enterprise, or invite-only applications where the user base is pre-qualified (e.g., employees of client companies, SaaS tools distributed by IT/admin). It's ideal when the goal is rapid re-entry into an existing account rather than conversion of a brand-new, undecided visitor. Great for apps where trust and brand confidence matter more than feature education at this exact touchpoint.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal single-CTA pattern for consumer-facing apps that rely on self-serve growth, viral acquisition, or freemium sign-ups, since omitting a visible "Sign up" / "Create account" path will create friction and lost conversions for new users discovering the app organically (e.g., via app store search). Also avoid if the product requires upfront value-prop education (users unfamiliar with the brand may bounce without more context, carousels, or social proof before being asked to authenticate).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees and finance admins of companies that have already adopted Brex (most of whom are being prompted by HR/finance to download the app to manage a corporate card or submit an expense). Because the audience already has organizational buy-in, the screen doesn't need to "sell" the product; it only needs to confirm brand identity and get the user into the authenticated experience as fast as possible.

Psychologically, the design leverages the principle of least effort: by presenting a single, large, high-contrast button with no distractions, cognitive load is minimized and the likelihood of immediate action (tapping Sign in) is maximized. The confident, almost dismissive subhead copy also builds trust and authority: signaling that Brex doesn't need to over-explain itself to a professional, financially literate audience.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radical minimalism: Only one interactive element on screen eliminates decision paralysis and funnels 100% of attention toward authentication.

  • Single CTA, no sign-up option: Reinforces that this is a provisioned B2B tool, not a self-serve consumer app, setting correct user expectations immediately.

  • Thumb-zone button placement: The CTA sits in the bottom third of the screen, optimized for one-handed mobile use.

  • Brand-differentiating subhead copy: Uses competitive positioning language ("actually love") instead of generic feature bullet points, building emotional trust before the user even logs in.

  • Page control dots: suggests this welcome screen may be swipeable, hinting at an onboarding value-prop sequence hidden behind minimal first-frame design.

screens.name: Brex Onboarding 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this soft pre-permission pattern when:

  • Requesting push/SMS/communication permissions at the end of onboarding, right before a native OS or carrier permission prompt.

  • The permission is tied to a clear, specific user benefit that can be articulated in one sentence (e.g., reminders, deadlines, receipts).

  • You have multiple communication channels and want to let users self-select their preferred one(s) rather than force a single default.

  • Legal/regulatory consent (SMS/WhatsApp marketing) requires explicit, unchecked opt-in with visible terms.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The app has no urgent, time-sensitive reason for notifications, adding a whole screen for low-value notifications increases onboarding length without payoff.

  • You only support a single notification channel; a full screen with three toggle rows would be overkill for one switch (use a lighter inline prompt instead).

  • Users are already fatigued from a long onboarding flow (in that case, defer the ask to a contextual moment inside the app (e).g., right before the first receipt is due) rather than front-loading it here.

  • Legal copy becomes so dense it overwhelms the primary decision (if so, link out to a dedicated consent/legal screen instead of inlining paragraphs).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded business users and finance/ops teams (Brex is a corporate card/spend-management platform) who need timely nudges to complete expense-related tasks like uploading receipts. The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Reciprocity/context-setting: explaining the benefit before asking for permission increases perceived value and willingness to comply (foot-in-the-door technique).

  • Autonomy preservation: allowing granular, opt-in control over each channel reduces reactance and builds trust in the brand's handling of communications.

  • Loss aversion framing: "so you never forget" subtly implies the cost of missing a receipt upload (late reimbursements, compliance issues), motivating the user to enable at least one channel.

  • Global remote workforce consideration: WhatsApp support signals awareness of Brex's international user base, building affinity with non-US-based team members who rely on WhatsApp over SMS.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Soft permission priming: Explains the value of notifications before (or instead of) the hard native OS prompt, increasing opt-in rates and reducing permission fatigue.

  • Multi-channel choice architecture: Push, SMS, and WhatsApp are presented as independent, granular toggles rather than one bundled switch, respecting user preference and regional communication habits.

  • Default-off toggles: Protects user trust and regulatory compliance (especially for SMS/WhatsApp) by requiring explicit opt-in instead of pre-checked consent.

  • Non-blocking CTA: "Start using Brex" allows users to proceed regardless of toggle state, avoiding a frustrating permission gate.

  • Benefit-anchored copy: Ties the ask to a specific job-to-be-done (receipt/memo reminders) instead of generic "enable notifications" messaging.

  • Inline legal transparency: Embeds Terms/Privacy links directly in the SMS description at the point of consent, satisfying compliance without a separate screen.

screens.name: Brex Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any onboarding flow where push/SMS notifications materially improve user engagement or task completion (e.g., finance, productivity, habit-tracking apps).

  • Apps operating in multiple regions where alternative messaging channels (WhatsApp, SMS) may be more reliable or cost-effective than push notifications alone.

  • Scenarios requiring legal consent language (TCPA/GDPR) for SMS/marketing communications, embedding it contextually avoids extra friction-heavy legal modals.

  • Pre-permission "softening" screens before triggering native OS permission dialogs to increase acceptance rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid pre-enabling toggles by default in regions/jurisdictions where explicit opt-in consent is legally mandated (e.g., strict GDPR interpretation) - this could create compliance risk.

  • Not suitable for apps where notifications aren't core to the value proposition, as it may feel like an unnecessary forced step delaying time-to-value.

  • Avoid this heavy illustration-led layout if the app's brand tone is more utilitarian/enterprise-serious, as playful 3D art may undercut credibility in some B2B contexts.

  • Don't omit a skip/decline path entirely if regulatory environments require users be able to proceed without granting any communication consent.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users of Brex, a corporate card/expense management platform, during their first-run onboarding experience. The target persona is a busy finance team member or employee who needs timely reminders to perform expense hygiene tasks (uploading receipts, adding memos) - tasks that are easily forgotten without nudges.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the default effect (pre-checked toggles) and reciprocity/framing (notifications framed as helpful rather than invasive) to drive high opt-in rates. By addressing notification permissions proactively within the app's own branded UI before the OS-level prompt, Brex avoids the common pitfall of users reflexively denying system permission dialogs that offer no context.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-emptive Permission Priming: Explains value before the native OS permission dialog appears, significantly boosting opt-in conversion rates.

  • Smart Defaults: Push and SMS toggles are pre-enabled, using default bias to maximize subscription rates while still respecting user autonomy to opt-out.

  • Multi-Channel Choice Architecture: Offers three distinct communication channels (Push, SMS, WhatsApp) catering to different user geographies and preferences, particularly useful for Brex's global/international customer base.

  • Embedded Legal Compliance: Integrates required SMS consent language and policy links directly into the toggle description without needing a separate modal.

  • Single Forward Path: One primary CTA with no visible 'skip' reduces decision paralysis and funnels users directly into the product.

screens.name: Brex Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this layered modal NPS pattern when you want to capture sentiment at a high-engagement micro-moment (post-task completion, mid-onboarding) without derailing the user's current flow. It's ideal for B2B SaaS, fintech, and productivity apps where survey fatigue must be minimized and quick, large-target input is preferred for busy professional users on mobile devices.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid interrupting critical setup flows (like notification/permission grants) with a survey before the user has completed the primary task, as it can create conflicting cognitive load and lower both completion rates for the original task and the quality of survey responses. Also avoid this pattern for brand-new or first-session users who haven't yet formed an opinion of the product, and avoid stacking modals if the underlying screen itself requires an urgent decision (e.g., a permission system dialog), since competing modals can confuse or frustrate users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets active, engaged users of a B2B fintech/expense product (Brex) who are already mid-flow in configuring their account (enabling notifications). Triggering NPS here (rather than at random) leverages the recency and engagement effect: users who have just interacted positively with a useful feature (notification setup for receipt reminders) are statistically more likely to give favorable, thoughtful scores. The large numeric tiles also reduce friction for busy finance/operations professionals who want to answer quickly on mobile without precision-slider frustration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background pattern: The parent screen is grayed out but still visible, giving contextual continuity while clearly establishing modal hierarchy.

  • Large tile-based rating scale: Replacing a thin slider with big, bold number tiles dramatically improves tap accuracy and accessibility on touch devices.

  • Non-intrusive dismissal: The visible close button and drag handle ensure the survey never feels like a hard blocker, preserving goodwill during a feedback ask.

  • Strategic timing: Surfacing NPS during a permissions/onboarding-adjacent flow catches the user in a moment of active engagement with the app's value proposition.
