screens.name: Brex Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Use layered feedback sheets when you want to capture sentiment at a meaningful transition point (e.g., after permission requests, onboarding completion, or feature usage) without forcing a separate dedicated screen.

  • Ideal for B2B/fintech products where qualitative feedback loops inform roadmap prioritization and customer success outreach.

  • Pair permission priming screens with benefit-oriented copy and 3D/illustrated hero imagery when requesting sensitive permissions like notifications, to increase OS-level opt-in rates.

  • Mark feedback fields as explicitly "optional" whenever the primary goal is data collection without risking flow abandonment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid stacking a feedback modal on top of a permission screen if the user hasn't yet completed the primary action (it can create confusion about which task is actually being requested ("Am I being asked about notifications or giving feedback)?").

  • Do not use this pattern for time-sensitive or transactional flows (e.g., checkout, payment confirmation) where any interruption increases drop-off risk.

  • Avoid when user research shows survey fatigue; overusing feedback modals can degrade trust and perceived app quality.

  • Not appropriate if the feedback is actually mandatory for business logic, labeling it "optional" while silently requiring it elsewhere breaks trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets business cardholders and expense-management users within Brex, likely mid-onboarding or during a periodic in-app survey trigger. The psychological strategy leverages reciprocity and low-friction disclosure: by making feedback optional and quick, Brex increases the volume of qualitative insight it collects from engaged users who might otherwise ignore a dedicated survey.

The underlying notification screen targets users at a vulnerable decision point (granting OS-level permissions), using permission priming to pre-sell the value before the native iOS prompt appears (a well-documented technique to improve opt-in conversion rates by contextualizing the "why" before the "ask)."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Layered modal-over-screen architecture: capturing qualitative feedback without fully derailing the primary permissions flow underneath.

  • Optional-by-design text field: explicitly labeled "optional" to lower the barrier to engagement and avoid form abandonment anxiety.

  • Dual exit paths (X icon + Back button + swipe handle): gives users three equally accessible ways to dismiss, respecting user autonomy and reducing frustration.

  • Smart default toggles on the underlying screen pre-enable notification channels, leveraging the power of defaults to boost opt-in rates passively.

  • High-fidelity 3D illustration used as emotional "soft sell" before requesting a system-level permission, priming positive sentiment before the OS dialog appears.

screens.name: Brex Onboarding 6
screens.whereToUse: Use channel-specific notification opt-in screens when your app has multiple genuinely distinct communication channels (push, SMS, WhatsApp, email) and users benefit from controlling each independently. Pair the ask with a concrete, task-relevant benefit statement rather than generic "stay updated" copy. Use time-boxed, dismissible review-request toasts immediately after a demonstrably positive user action (e.g., task completion, positive feedback rating) to maximize conversion while preserving goodwill.
screens.whereNotToUse: Do not allow a review-request or marketing toast to visually overlap and block an in-progress settings/permission task (this creates cognitive overload, obscures UI controls (as seen with the hidden WhatsApp toggle), and can cause users to dismiss or rage-quit both flows). Avoid defaulting sensitive consent toggles (especially SMS, which carries legal/TCPA implications) to ON, as this can create compliance risk and erode trust if not clearly disclosed and genuinely optional. Avoid stacking unrelated asks (reviews, upsells) during a permission-granting flow; sequence them with sufficient temporal/contextual separation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets Brex's B2B finance/expense-management users (employees and finance admins at companies) who need timely reminders to stay compliant with expense policies. The notification ask leverages the psychological principle of reducing future friction/anxiety ("never forget") rather than generic engagement bait, which resonates with a professional, task-oriented audience.

The review-request toast exploits a positive-affect reciprocity moment
screens.keyHighlights:
• Channel-level granularity: Separate toggles for Push, SMS, and WhatsApp let users tailor exactly how they're reached, rather than a binary notifications on/off switch.

  • Contextual justification: Ties the permission ask directly to a concrete user benefit (not forgetting receipts/memos) instead of a generic "enable notifications" ask.

  • Inline legal compliance: SMS disclaimer and linked Terms/Privacy Policy are embedded contextually at the point of consent, satisfying compliance without a separate screen.

  • Dismissible, time-boxed review ask: The G2 review prompt is transparent about its auto-close behavior and offers an explicit manual close, respecting user agency.

screens.name: Figma - Activity - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use a pre-permission priming dialog like this whenever:

  • You need to request a system-level permission (notifications, location, camera, contacts) that has only one native prompt opportunity per install.
  • The permission's value isn't self-evident from the OS prompt alone and benefits from contextual explanation.
  • You can trigger the ask at a moment of high relevance (e.g., right after a user experiences the feature the permission supports).
  • You want to preserve the ability to re-ask later by avoiding triggering the native "hard no," which on iOS can only be reversed via Settings.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The permission ask is unrelated to the user's current context or task, which can feel jarring or manipulative.
  • It's shown too early (e.g., on first app launch before the user has experienced any value), increasing decline rates.
  • The app over-prompts repeatedly after "Not now," which erodes trust and feels like nagging.
  • The underlying feature doesn't meaningfully depend on the permission, making the interruption unjustified friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets collaborative teams: designers and developers working in shared Figma files (who rely on timely awareness of teammates' comments, replies, and mentions to stay synchronized asynchronously). For these users, missing a mention or comment can mean blocked work or delayed feedback loops, so the psychological trigger here is FOMO (fear of missing out) combined with a sense of team responsiveness.

By asking at the moment the user is actively engaging with the Activity feed, Figma leverages the context-of-use principle: users are primed to value notifications precisely because they're already looking at collaborative activity, making the ask feel helpful rather than intrusive.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-permission priming: A custom in-app dialog precedes the native OS prompt, allowing Figma to control messaging and timing rather than relying on the one-shot system dialog.
  • Contextual trigger: Surfaced specifically within the Activity tab, directly tying the ask to the feature it enhances.
  • Benefit-specific copy: Naming concrete triggers (comments, replies, @mentions) instead of generic notification language increases perceived relevance.
  • Soft decline path: "Not now" preserves the ability to re-prompt later without feeling like a hard rejection, protecting the native permission prompt's credibility for a better-timed future ask.
  • Branded illustration: On-brand abstract avatar/speech-bubble artwork reinforces the collaborative, social nature of the notification content.

screens.name: Figma - Activity - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern: triggering the native OS permission prompt from within a contextually relevant screen rather than during onboarding (whenever the permission's value is tied to a specific feature (e).g., asking for notification access inside an inbox, activity feed, or reminders screen). This is especially effective for collaboration, productivity, and social apps where push notifications drive re-engagement and real-time awareness.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid firing this system dialog immediately on first app open or before the user has experienced any feature that benefits from notifications (this leads to high "Don't Allow" rates since users have no basis to judge the value). Also avoid triggering it automatically without a clear contextual link (e.g., mid-onboarding flows or on random screen transitions), as this wastes the one native permission attempt iOS grants and often requires users to manually re-enable it in Settings afterward.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Figma's audience is professional designers, developers, and cross-functional teams who rely on real-time collaboration (comments, handoff requests, and file changes often require timely awareness even when the app isn't open). This permission prompt directly serves power users and team leads who need to stay in sync with collaborators' activity.

The psychological trigger at play is reciprocity and relevance-based consent: by waiting until the user proactively opens the Activity feed (a screen explicitly about updates and collaboration), Figma frames the notification permission as a natural extension of a need the user already expressed, rather than an interruption, increasing the likelihood of tapping "Allow."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual trigger placement: The prompt fires specifically when the user visits the Activity tab, not on app launch, aligning the permission ask with a concrete, self-evident use case.
  • Native system modal: Leveraging the OS-standard dialog increases perceived trustworthiness and familiarity, reducing user hesitation compared to a custom-styled popup.
  • Visible tab bar context: Keeping the bottom navigation and highlighted "Activity" tab visible behind the dialog subtly reinforces the connection between the permission and the feature that needs it.
  • Single-shot resource respected: Since iOS blocks repeat prompts if dismissed, Figma preserves this one chance for a high-intent moment rather than burning it during onboarding.

screens.name: Figma - Activity - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Companion mobile apps for primarily desktop-first collaboration tools, where the phone serves as a notification/review surface rather than the main editing environment.
  • Any B2B/collaboration product where @-mentions, comments, or approvals drive re-engagement (e.g., project management, design, or document tools).
  • Notification centers that benefit from separating "unread" from "all" to reduce cognitive load when scanning a mixed-urgency list.
  • Scenarios where quick contextual preview (showing the actual comment/mention text) can reduce unnecessary taps into the full source.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this stripped-down layout for consumer social apps where richer visual content (photos, reactions, previews) is expected (a text-only row may feel underwhelming).
  • Not ideal when notification volume is consistently high; a flat single-section list without grouping by type/date or filtering would quickly become unmanageable and should be paired with Filter & Sort or Faceted Browse at scale.
  • Don't rely on a mostly-empty canvas as a final design if the product expects frequent engagement (an empty state illustration or prompt (e).g., "You're all caught up") should be added once the unread item is cleared, otherwise the blank space can feel unfinished or broken.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers and developers working in teams who need lightweight, asynchronous awareness of collaboration happening in shared Figma files (e).g., being tagged in a comment while away from their desktop. The psychological trigger at play is social recognition and FOMO: being @-mentioned is inherently attention-grabbing, and the red dot/unread badge exploits the Zeigarnik effect (unresolved items create mental tension until "read" or acted upon).

The "Mark all as read" affordance caters to users who experience notification-count anxiety and want control over their badge count without reviewing every item individually (a common pattern for busy professionals juggling multiple tools).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unread count + bulk dismiss combo: Pairing "Unread (1)" with "Mark all as read" gives users both visibility into outstanding items and a one-tap way to clear them, respecting users who treat notifications as a queue to be emptied.
  • Dual-signal unread indicator: The red dot on the avatar plus the dedicated "Unread" section header creates redundant, low-effort cues so the unread status can't be missed even with partial attention.
  • Context-rich notification copy: Embedding the actual @mention and comment text directly in the feed lets users triage importance without opening the file, saving a navigation step for low-priority mentions.
  • Consistent root tab bar: Activity sits alongside Recents, Search, and Mirror, reflecting Figma's hub-and-spoke mobile strategy where the phone app is a lightweight review/mirror companion to the desktop canvas, not a full editing surface.

screens.name: Figma - Activity - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a collaborative/creative tool needs to extend desktop-centric work into a mobile companion experience focused on notifications, review, and lightweight replies rather than full editing. It's ideal for:

  • Design, documentation, or whiteboard tools with threaded commenting (Figma, Miro, Notion).
  • Any workflow where visual context (a screenshot, diagram, or canvas region) is essential to understanding a conversation.
  • Apps that want to keep users engaged on mobile without forcing complex editing tasks onto a small screen.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The underlying content isn't inherently visual: a text-only screenshot preview adds unnecessary weight and scrolling for non-visual apps.
  • Real-time co-editing on mobile is a core use case; in that scenario, bridging out to another app/view (rather than enabling inline editing) would frustrate power users who expect full parity.
  • Thread volume is extremely high (hundreds of replies) - a flat chronological list without collapsing/summarization would become unwieldy and require pagination or grouping instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers and cross-functional collaborators (PMs, developers, stakeholders) who need to stay looped into design feedback while away from their desktop. It specifically targets the moment when someone receives a push notification about a comment and wants to quickly triage it on their phone.

Psychologically, it leverages social validation and reciprocity: seeing teammates react with 👀 and 😍 emojis creates a sense of momentum and validates the work being discussed, encouraging further engagement. The casual tone and avatar-driven identity cues (colored initials) build a sense of team presence and belonging, reducing the feeling that feedback is a formal, high-stakes evaluation.

The "Open comment in file" CTA taps into task continuity psychology (users feel reassured that they can always pick up deeper work later, reducing anxiety about missing full context on a small screen).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual context first: Surfacing the actual canvas screenshot above the conversation ensures comments are never read out of context (essential for a visual design tool).
  • Emoji reactions with counts: Lightweight, low-friction engagement that lets team members acknowledge feedback without typing, reducing conversational overhead.
  • "Open comment in file" bridge button: A clear, well-placed escape hatch that respects the boundary between mobile (review/triage) and desktop (deep editing) workflows.
  • Persistent reply bar: Keeps the core action always within thumb's reach regardless of thread length.
  • Chronological threading: Simple, readable conversation flow with relative timestamps ("1 hour ago") reduces cognitive load versus absolute timestamps.

results.query: Segmented Control toggle for monthly versus annual billing

screens.name: CRED Logging & Tracking 33
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, subscription, or usage-tracking apps where users need a quick, glanceable summary before deciding whether to drill into details. Ideal for monthly billing summaries, expense trackers, fitness/usage dashboards, or any context where a trend-over-time chart plus categorical breakdown adds value. Works especially well for premium/lifestyle brands wanting to differentiate from utilitarian competitor dashboards through refined typography and color restraint.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when users need to perform frequent, detailed data manipulation (multi-metric comparisons, custom date ranges) - the simplified, editorial layout sacrifices density and flexibility. It's also not ideal for accessibility-critical products, as high-contrast dark themes with thin gray text and small-caps labels can strain readability for low-vision users. Additionally, if the brand needs to convey urgency (e.g., debt/collections apps), this calm, muted aesthetic would undercut the necessary tone.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially engaged users of a card/banking app (likely a premium credit/debit card or neobank) who want a quick, low-stress pulse-check on their spending rather than granular budgeting tools. The audience skews toward users who value aesthetics and simplicity over dense financial dashboards (e.g., Mint-style multi-widget screens).

Psychologically, the screen leverages:

  • Anchoring: leading with the big current-month number sets the frame for interpreting everything else on the page.

  • Social/self-comparison: comparing this month to last month triggers a simple win/loss evaluation, encouraging continued engagement with the app.

  • Reduced cognitive load: dark theme and generous whitespace reduce the "financial anxiety" often associated with looking at spend data.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Present-moment bar highlighting: The current month's bar in the 12-month chart is rendered in solid white while all past months are muted gray (an elegant, low-effort way to orient the user instantly).

  • Editorial serif typography: Breaks from typical fintech UI conventions to create a premium, non-alarmist tone around money management.

  • Progressive disclosure in category split: Only the top categories are shown with a clear "View all" escape hatch, avoiding cognitive overload.

  • Color-coded delta indicator: Immediate red/green comparison against the previous month gives instant emotional feedback without extra copy.

  • Single dominant CTA: The bold white "Show transactions" button stands out starkly against the dark UI, guiding the user toward the natural next action (drill into detail).

screens.name: CRED Logging & Tracking 34
screens.whereToUse: Use this dual-zone (dark summary header + light data list) pattern for any category-specific financial drill-down screen (such as spending by merchant, subscription tracking, or budget category breakdowns). It's ideal when users need both a quick aggregate answer and the ability to inspect individual transactions. The hybrid time-range selector (dropdown + quick chips) is excellent for analytics dashboards where users toggle between precise and common date ranges frequently.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for screens with very few transactions (fewer than 5-10), where the elaborate filtering/summary header would feel like overkill relative to content. Also avoid the plain minus-sign for negative amounts in contexts where quick red/green visual scanning of debits vs. credits is critical (e.g., trading or multi-currency apps), as it may cause user errors in fast scanning. Additionally, this heavy black-header/white-body split may feel visually jarring in a lengthy multi-screen flow that otherwise uses a single consistent theme.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen is designed for financially-aware banking/fintech app users (likely users of a debit/credit card or expense-tracking app in India, given the ₹ symbol and HP fuel station branding) who want to audit or budget recurring category spend, such as fuel costs. The psychological trigger at play is the "categorization for control" effect (by isolating one spending category and summing it over a year, the app leverages the human desire for financial clarity and control, helping users feel more in command of discretionary spending patterns). The prominent total also taps into loss-aversion/awareness psychology, prompting users to reflect on cumulative spend that might feel invisible in day-to-day small transactions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-zone color inversion: Black analytical header vs. white ledger body creates instant visual separation between "controls/summary" and "raw data," reducing cognitive load.

  • Hybrid time-range selector: Combining a flexible month dropdown with fixed quick-select chips (3M/6M/1Y) serves both casual and power users without cluttering the UI.

  • Explicit date-range confirmation: Stating "apr '23 - mar '24" removes ambiguity that a bare "1Y" toggle would otherwise create.

  • Prominent total spend metric: Placing the aggregate sum front-and-center answers the user's top-of-mind question before they even scan the list.

  • Sortable list header ("Most Recent"): Gives users control over ordering without needing a separate filter screen.

  • Consistent iconography: Repeated fuel-pump icon per row (with a branded HP logo appearing for a recognized merchant) helps users quickly identify recurring transaction types and specific vendors.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse:
• B2B SaaS products where value scales with number of collaborators (project management, communication, whiteboarding tools).

  • Early onboarding flows where you want to seed network effects before the user's enthusiasm decays.

  • Any flow where you want to encourage an action but must not block progress for users unwilling to comply immediately.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Single-player or personal-use apps where there is no collaborative value proposition (invites would feel irrelevant or pushy).

  • Highly privacy-sensitive contexts where asking for colleague emails this early could raise trust/compliance concerns.

  • Flows where the user hasn't yet experienced core value, asking for a team invite before the product has proven itself can increase drop-off instead of reducing it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new signups: typically a team lead, founder, or early adopter evaluating Linear for their organization. Since Linear's value is inherently networked (a project/issue tracker is far more useful with teammates present), this step exploits the "viral loop" growth pattern: converting a single-user trial into a multi-seat team account as early as possible. Psychologically, it capitalizes on the user's current high-motivation state (freshly signed up, curious, exploratory) to ask for an investment (inviting colleagues) before intent fades. It also uses social facilitation (once co-workers are invited, the user has public accountability to actually adopt and use the tool).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-exit strategy: Both "Continue" and "I'll do this later" give users multiple non-blocking ways to skip, drastically reducing onboarding abandonment risk.

  • Batch email input: A single text area accepting comma-separated emails lets power users invite an entire team in one action instead of repeating a form multiple times.

  • Visual progress transparency: The dot-based page control at the bottom sets expectations for how many steps remain, reducing onboarding fatigue/anxiety.

  • Strategic CTA hierarchy: The filled purple "Send invites" button draws the eye first, while skip options are intentionally muted in gray, nudging the desired behavior without forcing it.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Post-onboarding or settings flows where you want to capture marketing/notification consent without blocking the primary task.

  • SaaS products with a technical or privacy-conscious audience where transparency drives higher-quality opt-ins.

  • Any flow requiring compliance with opt-in consent regulations (GDPR, CAN-SPAM, CCPA).

  • Situations where you want to separate distinct communication types (product updates vs. marketing) to improve long-term engagement and reduce unsubscribe rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this soft, skippable pattern if email capture is a core business-critical conversion metric that must be maximized (a more assertive single-choice prompt may perform better for growth-stage products).

  • Don't use pre-toggled OFF switches if your business model depends on default opt-ins and your jurisdiction does not legally require explicit consent (though this is generally not recommended).

  • Not ideal mid-task, where interrupting with a preference screen would break flow and frustrate users (e.g., during checkout or active editing).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded or existing Linear users at a natural checkpoint (likely post-signup or post-settings-visit) where communication preferences are most relevant. The audience is primarily technical/product teams who are highly sensitive to unsolicited marketing noise, so Linear's restrained, honest approach to opt-in (rather than pre-checked boxes) is tailored to a sophisticated, trust-sensitive user base that would otherwise bounce or immediately unsubscribe if manipulated into a list.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages the principle of autonomy (user controls every choice), reciprocity (transparent value exchange: "subscribe to learn about changes" implies tangible benefit), and reduced cognitive load (binary toggles, no required fields) to maximize genuine, lower-churn opt-ins rather than inflated but low-quality subscriber counts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Opt-in by default (toggles OFF): Respects user consent norms and regulatory best practice, building long-term trust over short-term list-growth metrics.

  • Frictionless exit via "X": Clearly communicates this is a non-mandatory step, reducing perceived pressure and modal fatigue.

  • Granular, specific choices: Separating "changelog" from "marketing/onboarding" emails lets users tailor exactly what they want, avoiding the all-or-nothing subscription trap.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Stating frequency ("bi-weekly," "occasional") directly addresses the top objection to subscribing (fear of spam).

  • Correct component semantics: Using a toggle for binary preferences but a button/pill for the external "Follow on X" action avoids UI pattern misuse.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Post-signup or onboarding flows where you need explicit communication consent (GDPR/CAN-SPAM compliance).

  • SaaS products that send multiple types of emails (product updates vs. marketing) and want to avoid conflating them.

  • Any screen attempting to grow social following organically as a secondary, non-intrusive ask.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the onboarding flow is already long, adding a dedicated full screen for email preferences can feel like unnecessary friction if users are eager to reach core product value. In such cases, consider deferring this to account settings instead of a blocking/interstitial step. Also avoid defaulting marketing-heavy toggles to "on," as it undermines the trust this screen is designed to build.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly signed-up users of Linear, a developer/PM-focused project management tool. The audience is technically sophisticated and typically averse to spammy marketing, so the design psychologically leverages autonomy and transparency: giving explicit, separated controls rather than a single bundled "opt-in to emails" checkbox.

By pre-enabling only the lower-frequency, highly relevant changelog email, the product nudges users toward retention-building communication (feature updates) without triggering the reactance that comes from being auto-subscribed to sales/marketing content. This builds long-term goodwill and likely improves opt-in rates and reduces churn-driven unsubscribes.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Ethical default selection: The low-commitment "changelog" toggle is pre-enabled while the higher-frequency "marketing and onboarding emails" toggle is off by default (a thoughtful, user-respecting use of smart defaults rather than opting users into everything).

  • Granular consent control: Splitting communications into two distinct toggles (product changelog vs. marketing) lets users curate exactly what they want, increasing trust and reducing future unsubscribe/spam complaints.

  • Non-blocking escape hatch: The ✕ close icon gives users an immediate way to skip the step entirely, signaling this isn't a mandatory gate.

  • Soft social CTA: Embedding the "Follow us on X" prompt as a tertiary, non-toggle element cleverly extends brand reach without cluttering the primary consent decision.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 17
screens.whereToUse:
• End of an onboarding flow where you want to transition users from setup to active usage without losing them to incomplete secondary tasks.

  • SaaS/B2B tools where team invites and integrations are critical for activation/retention.

  • Any scenario needing to communicate "setup complete" while surfacing optional, value-reinforcing next steps.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the secondary actions are critical/mandatory for the product to function (use a required setup wizard instead).

  • Not ideal for consumer apps with less patience for reading; shorter, icon-only checklists or progressive disclosure may work better for less technical audiences.

  • Avoid in flows already suffering from onboarding fatigue, stacking yet another screen with action items can increase drop-off if users are eager to reach the core app.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets newly onboarded professional users (likely engineering/product teams) who have just finished initial account/workspace setup in Linear. The psychological strategy here is to capitalize on the momentum and dopamine of a completed task ("You're good to go") by immediately presenting value-adding follow-up actions while the user is still engaged, using the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete team/integration setup nags at the user's attention) balanced against respect for autonomy by making it skippable. Highlighting team invites and integrations also serves Linear's business goal of network-effect driven growth and stickiness (the more a team integrates Slack/GitHub, the higher switching costs and daily usage).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking secondary checklist: Growth actions (invite team, integrations, mobile app) are presented as optional suggestions rather than mandatory gates, preserving momentum toward the core product.

  • Single, unmissable primary CTA: "Open Linear" is the only full-width, high-contrast button, eliminating decision paralysis about what to do next.

  • Dual exit paths: Users can close (X) or navigate the carousel back, respecting user control and avoiding a forced funnel.

  • Contextual deep links embedded in copy: The "installation guide" hyperlink is embedded inline within descriptive text rather than as a separate button, keeping the layout clean.

  • Progress closure signal: The page control dots confirm to the user they've reached the end of onboarding, reducing anxiety about "how much is left."

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 18
screens.whereToUse:
• When introducing a feature or concept that has non-obvious terminology or state logic (filters, statuses, pipelines).

  • For B2B/productivity tools where users need quick clarity without leaving their workflow.

  • When you want to reinforce learning with a visual icon/pictogram alongside brief text.

  • As a replacement for a modal dialog when you want to keep the underlying screen content visible and in context.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for critical, blocking information the user must process before proceeding (a non-modal card can be ignored or scrolled past).

  • Don't use for highly simple or self-evident features; it adds unnecessary clutter and can feel condescending to experienced users.

  • Avoid repeating this explainer every session: it should be dismissible permanently to prevent annoyance (persistent fatigue).

  • Not ideal on very small screens where the card could push essential content out of the viewport.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets new or returning users of a project management tool (Linear) who are unfamiliar with the specific semantics of "Active" vs "Todo" vs "Backlog" - terminology that varies across PM tools. The psychological trigger is reducing cognitive dissonance: a user filtering by "Active" but seeing a group labeled "Todo" could be confused, so Linear proactively closes that gap. Offering a lightweight "Got it" exit respects the user's time and autonomy (self-determination), while the "Documentation" link serves power users or admins who want to understand status workflows deeply before configuring their team.
screens.keyHighlights:
• In-context education: The explainer card is docked to the bottom of the exact view it describes, rather than a generic tutorial carousel shown pre-use.

  • Visual pictogram before text: Four circular icons depicting issue-state progress let users grasp the concept visually before reading.

  • Dual dismissal paths: "Got it" for quick acceptance vs. "Documentation" for users wanting more depth, catering to different engagement levels.

  • Non-blocking placement: Card sits below live content instead of a modal overlay, preserving visibility of the actual UI being explained.

  • Status-group affordances: Collapsible "Todo" group header with count badge and inline "+" to add new issues directly into that state.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 01
screens.whereToUse: This grouped Stacked List + Preference Center pattern fits any settings surface with a moderate-to-large number of independent preferences that benefit from being scanned at a glance, especially where some options are binary (toggle) and others need a dedicated picker screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when there are only a handful of settings (a flat list would suffice) or when settings are highly interdependent and better presented as a guided wizard rather than an unordered menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari (iOS Settings): same grouped Stacked List + chevron drill-down pattern for browser preferences, a near-identical information architecture.

  2. Chrome (iOS Settings): uses the same colored-icon-plus-label row convention and trailing value text for settings like default search engine.

  3. Notion (iOS Settings): groups toggles and drill-down rows into dividered sections in a comparable Preference Center layout.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking (Miller's Law): Dividers break ~14 settings into 5 digestible clusters instead of one long list.

  2. Recognition over recall: Trailing value text (e.g., "Google", "After 1 day", "Native App") shows current state inline, so users don't need to open each row to check it.

  3. Progressive disclosure: Chevron rows (Global Site Settings, Languages, Search Engine) push secondary complexity to nested screens, keeping this page scannable.

  4. Fitts's Law: Full-row tap targets (not just the switch/chevron) make toggles and navigation rows easier to hit on mobile.

  5. Consistency: Icon-label-value-chevron row pattern repeats identically throughout, lowering the learning curve as users scan down.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any automated content-management feature (archiving, auto-deletion, auto-logout) where users benefit from choosing a personally appropriate threshold, especially when a single fixed default wouldn't suit meaningfully different usage patterns across the user base.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings where offering multiple duration options would create confusing inconsistency (e.g., security-critical timeouts where a single, carefully chosen default is safer than user-configurable flexibility).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Close Tabs Automatically" duration picker: offers a nearly identical range of duration options (1 day, 1 week, 1 month) for automatically closing inactive tabs.

  2. Chrome's "Auto Tab Groups" or memory-saver duration settings: provides comparable configurable timeframes for tab-management automation.

  3. Firefox's tab-unloading/archiving thresholds: similarly lets users choose how long inactive tabs remain before being archived or unloaded.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Resolving Prior Ambiguity: this screen retroactively confirms the "After 1 day" value seen in earlier Settings screenshots was genuinely configurable, not a fixed label.

  2. Range Accommodates Diverse Habits: offering both very short (12 hours) and long (30 days) options serves meaningfully different tab-management styles without forcing a one-size-fits-all default.

  3. Consistent Selector Pattern: reusing the same compact popover-with-checkmark format as the earlier "Swipe to Navigate" setting maintains a predictable interaction model for similar types of choices throughout Settings.

  4. Feature Follow-Through: this control makes the onboarding-promised "auto-archive" feature concretely adjustable, giving users direct control over how aggressively that promise is enforced.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (immediate persistence without explicit save) fits virtually all mobile settings interfaces, where requiring a separate save action for individual preference changes would add unnecessary friction and risk of lost changes if a user navigates away.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit only for settings with significant, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., account deletion, irreversible data actions), where an explicit confirm/save step is appropriate specifically to prevent accidental changes (a distinction correctly reflected in this app's separate use of confirmation dialogs (like the earlier "Clear All" archive action) for higher-stakes actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS Settings app (immediate value persistence): uses an identical pattern where sub-screen selections instantly update and display in the parent settings list without requiring a save step.

  2. Any well-designed settings architecture (Safari, Chrome, etc.): follows this same immediate-persistence convention as a baseline usability expectation for modern mobile settings.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Reliable State Propagation: both changed settings correctly display their new values upon returning to the parent Settings screen, without requiring a manual refresh or save confirmation.

  2. Consistent Interaction Model Across Settings: the same select-then-confirm pattern (whether via popover or dedicated sub-screen) applies uniformly across different setting types (search engine, archive timing, language), giving the whole Settings experience a cohesive, predictable feel.

  3. Immediate Effect Without Explicit Save: no "Save" or "Apply" button was needed at any point in this sequence; each selection takes effect and displays immediately upon choice.

screens.name: Brex All expenses 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this layered hero-card-plus-draggable-sheet pattern for any app where a single physical/visual asset (a card, a device, a ticket) is the primary mental anchor but needs to coexist with a long scrollable list of related records (transactions, logs, bookings). It's especially effective for fintech, loyalty cards, ticketing, or transit pass apps where users value seeing "the object" before diving into its history.

The tri-icon compliance row pattern is reusable anywhere a list item represents a multi-stage workflow item (e.g., document approval chains, order fulfillment stages, task checklists) and users need at-a-glance status across many items simultaneously.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the primary object (the card) isn't actually central to the user's task, forcing a large decorative hero at the top wastes vertical space on screens primarily used for fast, repetitive data scanning (e.g., a pure transaction ledger app). Also avoid dense tri-icon status systems for consumer-facing audiences unfamiliar with the icon meanings; without a legend or onboarding tooltip, new users may find unlabeled status icons confusing or ignore them entirely, defeating their purpose.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees at a company using Brex for corporate card and expense management (likely knowledge workers, sales reps, or traveling staff who need to quickly check their remaining spend limit and submit/verify expenses). The design assumes moderate financial literacy but low patience for bureaucratic friction, since expense reporting is a secondary task to their actual job.

Psychological triggers at play include: trust-building through visual realism (the card mockup feels authentic and "owned"), reduction of anxiety via transparency (clearly showing "$36.14 USD available" prevents overspending surprises), and compliance nudging through status iconography (visually incomplete rows with red/missing icons would implicitly pressure the user to complete documentation, leveraging the Zeigarnik effect of unfinished tasks).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Physical card metaphor header: Rendering the actual card design with brand mark (Brex) and an "eye" toggle to reveal/hide full card number builds trust and familiarity, borrowing the mental model of a physical wallet.

  • Compressed compliance iconography: Three small status icons per transaction row (receipt, approval, sync) let a user triage dozens of expenses for missing documentation without tapping into each one (a significant efficiency gain for expense workflows).

  • Draggable bottom sheet over persistent card: Keeps the card and glanceable balance always partially visible while letting the user scroll an effectively infinite transaction feed underneath, a strong use of layered z-axis navigation on a small screen.

  • Separation of balance view from action items: Pushing "Tasks" (likely approvals/missing receipts) into its own tab with a badge keeps the Wallet screen calm and read-only in feel, reducing anxiety-inducing clutter.

screens.name: Brex All expenses 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any financial transaction history, expense tracking, or reconciliation screen where users need to quickly scan multiple records grouped by date and verify compliance/status at a glance. It's especially effective for:

  • B2B SaaS tools (expense management, invoicing, procurement) needing both individual and team-wide views.

  • Any list requiring quick visual categorization via icons plus compact status indicators.

  • Modal/bottom-sheet contexts where users need to dip into a sub-task (reviewing expenses) without losing their place in a parent flow.
screens.whereNotToUse:
This dense, icon-heavy, text-light approach is not well suited for consumer-facing apps where users are unfamiliar with financial iconography: new users may not understand what each status glyph means without onboarding or tooltips, leading to confusion. Avoid this pattern when:

  • The audience is non-expert or uses the feature infrequently (icons require learned recognition).

  • Transaction volume is very low (grouping and segmented controls add unnecessary complexity for just a few items).

  • Accessibility is a primary concern: small icon clusters with subtle color coding (green checkmarks) can be hard to parse for users with visual impairments unless paired with text labels or accessible alt-text.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets business travelers, employees submitting expense reports, and finance/team administrators within a corporate travel management platform. The dual-toggle (My vs. All members') directly serves two distinct personas: the individual contributor reconciling their own spend, and the manager/finance admin auditing team-wide expenditure.

Psychologically, the design leans on reducing anxiety around financial accountability: by surfacing clear verification status icons per transaction, users (and auditors) gain immediate reassurance that receipts are attached and reimbursements are tracked, reducing the fear of "lost" or unreconciled expenses. The explicit currency tagging also builds trust for frequent international travelers who deal with multi-currency transactions and need certainty during expense report submission.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-mode segmented control: "My expenses" vs. "All members' expenses" toggles scope instantly without a page navigation, serving both IC and manager/admin personas in one screen.

  • Status iconography triad: Each expense row displays three compact status glyphs (reimbursement, document/receipt verification, card linkage) giving at-a-glance compliance state without extra taps.

  • Date-grouped chronological feed: Clear sticky-style date headers segment the list for fast temporal scanning.

  • Category iconography: Distinct icons per expense type (train, restaurant logo, rail ticket) aid rapid visual categorization over text alone.

  • Bottom sheet modal with drag handle: Signals a non-destructive, dismissible overlay that preserves the user's place in the underlying Wallet/Tasks navigation.

screens.name: Brex All expenses 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Expense management, corporate card, or accounting apps where both individual and aggregate views of transactional data are needed.

  • Any admin/oversight tool where a single toggle can reframe the same list structure from "mine" to "everyone's" to avoid duplicating UI.

  • Audit or compliance-heavy interfaces where per-item status indicators (receipt attached, approved, synced) need to be visible without drilling into detail views.

  • Long transactional lists benefiting from date-based grouping to aid scanning and mental chunking.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, icon-heavy layout for consumer-facing apps where users are unfamiliar with financial iconography (the three unlabeled status icons could confuse non-expert users without onboarding or tooltips).

  • Not ideal when transaction volume per user is very low; the overhead of a scope-switching control and grouped headers would be unnecessary complexity for a short list.

  • Avoid presenting this as a full-screen modal on larger viewports (tablet/desktop) where a persistent sidebar or split-view master-detail would better serve power-user workflows.

  • Do not omit labels/tooltips for the status icons in production, relying purely on color (green) risks accessibility issues for color-blind users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets finance administrators, team managers, or bookkeepers within SMBs or startups who are responsible for reconciling corporate card spend across multiple employees. The "All members' expenses" toggle specifically serves admins who need oversight authority beyond their own spending.

Psychologically, the dense grid of green checkmarks exploits the "all clear" visual pattern: humans are wired to scan for anomalies against a uniform baseline, so a sea of green checks makes any red flag or missing icon instantly conspicuous, reducing the audit burden from reading-every-line to pattern-scanning.

The explicit currency labeling and precise dating serve loss-aversion and accountability motivations: in financial contexts, ambiguity creates anxiety, so removing it (exact dates, explicit currency codes) builds user trust in the system's accuracy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Scope-switching segmented control: "My expenses" vs "All members' expenses" is an elegant way to give a single screen dual utility (personal tracking and team oversight) without separate navigation paths.

  • Triple status iconography: Embedding three micro-icons (likely receipt, review, and reimbursement status) directly under each amount lets admins audit compliance at a glance across dozens of transactions without opening each one.

  • Consistent merchant iconography: Real brand logos (Pret a Manger) mixed with generic category icons (train, generic card) help users pattern-match transactions visually faster than reading text alone.

  • Chronological grouping with sticky-feeling date headers: Reduces the need to re-read dates per row, a classic bank-statement pattern that scales well to long lists.

  • Modal presentation with drag handle: Signals this is a contextual, dismissible layer (via the X and bottom handle), preserving the user's place in the underlying Wallet tab.

screens.name: Brex All expenses 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for financial, expense, or transaction-ledger screens where users need to audit multiple data points per line item (amount, status, category) at speed. It's ideal for:

  • Expense management and corporate card reconciliation apps

  • Banking/transaction history screens requiring compliance or sync status

  • Any list where users must confirm multi-step processing (e.g., payment → invoice → receipt matching) without drilling into each item
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, icon-heavy list style for consumer-facing, emotionally-driven experiences (e.g., social feeds, lifestyle apps) where the utilitarian tone would feel cold or overly clinical. Also avoid stacking three small status icons per row for users unfamiliar with their meaning (without onboarding or tooltips, the iconography risks being ambiguous for first-time users; a legend or progressive disclosure (tap to see full status) should accompany this pattern). Not suitable when screen real estate is very limited (small smartwatch or narrow widget views), as the information density would compromise legibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets business travelers, corporate employees, or freelancers who need to track and reconcile expenses incurred during travel (trains, rideshare, food) against a corporate card or reimbursement wallet. The psychological driver here is reduction of anxiety around financial accountability: employees often worry about whether their expenses have been properly logged, categorized, and approved. The green checkmark badges exploit the "completion/closure" bias, giving users a dopamine-lite sense of relief and control knowing their line items are already validated, reducing the need for manual follow-up or end-of-month reconciliation stress.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Status-at-a-glance iconography: The triple-icon system (sync/refund, doc-check, receipt-check) with green badges lets users instantly verify the reconciliation/compliance state of each expense without opening a detail view (a huge time-saver for frequent travelers submitting many small transactions).

  • Merchant recognition via logos: Using real brand marks (Pret a Manger, Uber) alongside generic icons for unbranded services speeds up visual scanning and builds trust that data was captured automatically and accurately.

  • Chronological grouping with date dividers: Breaks a long, dense list into digestible temporal chunks, reducing the perceived complexity of the ledger.

  • Dual-purpose bottom tab (Wallet/Tasks): Allows contextual switching between viewing transactions and completing related action items without leaving the modal flow.

  • Modal presentation with drag handle: Signals temporary, dismissible context (reviewing expenses) layered over a primary app flow, preserving navigational state in the background.

screens.name: Spotify - Manage subscription - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription management screens for any SaaS or media app needing to communicate trial status without inducing cancellation anxiety.
  • Apps with multi-faceted "bundle" subscriptions (e.g., Amazon Prime style) where users often forget which specific perks they are paying for.
  • Post-trial "nurture" flows designed to increase feature discovery before a renewal decision is made.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this passive "soft-sell" layout if the business goal is aggressive, immediate conversion (e.g., a trial ending in 24 hours), where a more urgent, high-contrast banner would be required.
  • Do not use this pattern for single-feature subscriptions where there is no "snapshot of benefits" to showcase, as the module would feel empty or redundant.
  • Not suitable for B2B admin dashboards where billing/seat management requires more granular, data-table driven interfaces rather than lifestyle-oriented illustrations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets trial users and existing subscribers who may be uncertain about the tangible value of their payment. By surfacing a "Snapshot of your benefits" (specifically Audiobook listening time), Spotify leverages the Endowment Effect: making users feel they already possess valuable assets (listening hours, discounts) that would be lost upon cancellation.

The "Get to know your benefits" carousel specifically targets users who signed up for the headline feature (ad-free music) but are unaware of bundled perks (Audiobooks, Family Mix, Discounts), aiming to increase feature adoption to drive down trial-churn rates.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-Tone Branding: Using a pink/magenta accent for "Individual" Premium status visually separates account-tier information from standard navigational green accents, preventing user confusion between "content" and "account" states.
  • Soft Retention Strategy: Instead of a hard paywall or urgent banner, the trial expiration is presented as a simple utility line item, reducing subscription anxiety while keeping the user informed.
  • Benefit Re-engagement Module: The "Get to know your benefits" card acts as a mini-onboarding flow embedded within the settings, ensuring users justify their subscription cost by discovering underutilized features (like Audiobooks).

screens.name: Spotify - Manage subscription - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription/account management screens in apps constrained by platform billing policies (iOS/Android IAP restrictions).
  • Any settings surface where transparency about limitations can preempt user frustration or support escalations.
  • Billing summary screens needing to clearly state renewal date, price, and plan tier in a scannable, low-anxiety format.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this passive "informational-only" pattern when the business goal is active plan conversion or upselling (a stronger CTA-driven layout would be needed instead).
  • Do not use self-deprecating/apologetic copy in contexts where it could undermine brand confidence (e.g., high-stakes financial or legal flows where users need assurance of control, not an admission of limitation).
  • Not suitable for platforms without billing restrictions, where native in-app editing of plans is expected and this redirect-style pattern would just add unnecessary friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing paying subscribers who are auditing or confirming their billing status (a moment of heightened scrutiny and potential anxiety (common triggers: unexpected charge, forgotten trial, or curiosity about price changes)). The design's psychological strategy is to reduce anxiety through radical clarity: dates, amounts, and plan names are stated plainly with no ambiguous jargon.

The apologetic disclaimer about not being able to edit plans in-app serves a dual audience: it manages expectations for new premium users unfamiliar with App Store billing restrictions, and it reassures frustrated users that Spotify is aware of the limitation, reducing perceived indifference from the brand.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radical transparency copy: Explicitly telling users they can't edit their plan in-app, with an empathetic, human tone, preempts frustration and support tickets.
  • Billing clarity: Exact renewal date, exact price, and offer-expiry are surfaced together, reducing surprise billing complaints (a major churn/trust driver for subscription apps).
  • Non-blocking navigation: Keeping the bottom tab bar visible on an account/settings screen signals this is a low-stakes, easily-exited destination, reducing anxiety around visiting billing settings.
  • Soft upsell placement: "Explore plans" is tucked low in hierarchy as a card row rather than a banner or modal, respecting user intent (they came here to check status, not necessarily to buy).

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 13
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a system can algorithmically infer structured data (bills, subscriptions, categories, tags) from a larger raw dataset and needs lightweight human confirmation rather than full manual entry. It's ideal for financial apps, subscription trackers, or any onboarding flow where reducing data-entry friction significantly boosts completion rates. Pair it with a disabled primary CTA to prevent empty/null submissions, and group results by clear, scannable metadata (like date) to aid recognition-based decision-making over recall.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when transaction/data volume is very high, as an unfiltered or noisy candidate list will overwhelm users and undermine the "we did the work for you" value proposition (pagination or smarter filtering would be needed). It's also unsuitable when the underlying detection algorithm has low confidence or high false-positive rates, since repeatedly asking users to correct wrong suggestions erodes trust in the AI's competence. Finally, this bare-bones list works only for simple binary confirmation tasks; more nuanced editing (adjusting amounts, frequency, due dates) would need a richer detail/edit screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users setting up Cleo's bill-tracking/budgeting feature, likely during onboarding or a "connect your bank" flow, who want automated financial organization without manually inputting every recurring payment. The psychological trigger at play is reduced cognitive load via smart defaults: by pre-filtering the transaction history down to only plausible bill candidates, Cleo lowers the activation energy needed to complete setup, increasing the likelihood the user finishes the task instead of abandoning a longer manual entry form. The conversational tone also builds parasocial trust with the Cleo mascot/persona, positioning it as a helpful, witty assistant rather than a cold utility.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Editorial, oversized bold typography for the question injects brand personality and a chat-like informality into an otherwise dry financial categorization task.

  • Auto-surfaced candidate detection: Cleo does the pattern-matching work for the user by identifying recurring transactions of identical amounts, drastically reducing manual data entry.

  • Disabled "Done" CTA as a passive validation mechanism (prevents users from confirming zero bills and visually cues that an action is still required).

  • Date-grouped stacked list with colorful avatars aids fast visual recall and scanning of past transactions.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 14
screens.whereToUse:
• Any flow where the system can infer structured data from unstructured input (e.g., transaction history, email parsing, calendar events) and wants to convert it into a trackable recurring item.

  • Bill trackers, subscription managers, budgeting apps, or expense categorization confirmation flows.

  • Whenever you want to reduce a "create new record" task down to a "confirm this record" task to boost completion rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if your detection/inference accuracy is low (incorrect pre-filled data erodes trust faster than an empty form, since users may not carefully review pre-filled values before submitting).

  • Not suitable for highly sensitive financial commitments (e.g., loan agreements) where users should deliberately input data rather than passively confirm auto-detected values.

  • Avoid mascot/playful elements if the context is a serious compliance or legal disclosure screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets users who are trying to get a handle on recurring expenses but are too disorganized or busy to manually track bills in a spreadsheet. Cleo's core demographic of financially anxious, spreadsheet-averse young adults. By automatically detecting the pattern (an e-transfer sent monthly to the same recipient), Cleo reduces the activation energy required to build a complete financial picture, leveraging the psychological principle of reduced friction increases task completion. Pre-filled fields also build trust and a sense of "the AI actually gets me," reinforcing Cleo's coach positioning rather than a passive ledger tool.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Pre-fill (Zero-Effort Data Entry): Cleo has already parsed the transaction and populated amount, frequency, and next date, turning a tedious manual entry task into a one-tap confirmation.

  • Mascot Injection: The purple skull emoji humanizes a purely administrative screen, keeping brand personality present even in utilitarian flows.

  • Bottom Sheet Modality: Presenting this as a sheet (not a full navigation push) keeps the task lightweight and reversible, implying "quick edit" rather than "big commitment."

  • Single Primary CTA: Only one clear action ("Add to bills") is presented, eliminating decision paralysis.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 15
screens.whereToUse: Use this coin-stack/illustrated comparison pattern when translating category comparisons (income vs. expense, actual vs. target, before vs. after) for audiences who may disengage from standard bar/line charts. It's ideal for consumer fintech, gamified habit trackers, or wellness apps where emotional engagement and quick comprehension outweigh the need for granular data precision. Pair with a secondary "facts" panel (as done here) for power users who still want exact figures.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in professional, B2B, or high-stakes financial contexts (e.g., accounting, tax, investment platforms) where users need precise multi-variable comparisons, historical trend lines, or exportable data (illustrations like coin stacks lack the precision and scannability of true charts at scale). Also avoid if the target demographic skews toward users who perceive playful visuals as undermining trust or seriousness around their finances.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets financially anxious or budget-avoidant users (often younger adults who find traditional banking apps (tables, graphs, percentages) intimidating or boring). By gamifying the visualization (coin stacks, thumbs-up mascot reaction, progress bar countdown) Cleo taps into reward/loss framing psychology: a rising "Out" stack nearing the "Limit" ghost stack creates a visceral, almost game-over anxiety that's more motivating than a static number. The thumbs-up illustration provides immediate positive reinforcement/social-proof-like validation ("you're doing fine"), appealing to users who need encouragement rather than shame to stay engaged with money management.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Coin-stack metaphor: Converts abstract dashboard data into an intuitive, physical visual (height = money), removing the need to interpret charts or legends.

  • Ghost/ghosted "Limit" stack: Using a translucent overlay stack to show the untouched budget ceiling creates an implicit progress-bar effect layered directly into the illustration, rather than a separate UI element.

  • Dual-zone contrast layout: Bold color block for narrative/visual summary, clean white card for hard numeric truth, serving both emotional and analytical user needs on one screen.

  • Mascot-driven proactive check-in: The floating chat prompt turns a passive dashboard into a two-way conversation starter, staying true to Cleo's chat-first identity even on a data screen.

  • Editable target amount: The small pencil icon next to "$1,463" invites inline goal editing without leaving the dashboard, reducing friction for adjusting budget targets.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 16
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for budget creation, goal setting, or any multi-variable numeric configuration screen where precision is less important than user buy-in. It is especially effective for:

  • Financial goal-setting flows (savings targets, spending caps).

  • Fitness or habit-tracking apps where users set daily/weekly targets.

  • Any "commitment" screen where you want the user to feel psychologically invested in a number they are about to see repeatedly.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, playful, stepper-based UI for professional or enterprise financial tools where users need to input large, precise figures quickly (e.g., business accounting or expense reporting), as tapping +/- buttons repeatedly for large deltas becomes inefficient and frustrating. Additionally, the informal, coach-like CTA copy ("Alright, I can do this") would feel inappropriate or condescending in a B2B or high-net-worth wealth management context where users expect neutral, authoritative language.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious users: often younger adults or those new to budgeting (who have historically been intimidated or bored by traditional finance apps (like Mint or bank dashboards)). By using large, bold typography and a coaching tone, Cleo leverages the psychological principle of self-efficacy: telling the user "I can do this" reframes the budget limit as an achievable goal set by an ally, not a restrictive cage imposed by an institution.

The pre-filled "smart default" numbers exploit the anchoring effect and reduce decision fatigue; users are statistically more likely to accept a suggested default than to build a budget from a blank slate, satisfying the need for quick wins during onboarding or monthly resets.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotionally-coded CTA copy: "Alright, I can do this" replaces a generic confirm button, turning a financial commitment into a motivational, first-person affirmation.

  • Smart Defaults: The limit and category breakdowns are pre-filled based on historical average spending, drastically lowering the effort required to complete setup.

  • Granularity Toggle: A single switch lets users collapse complex category-level budgeting into one simple master number, catering to both power users and minimalists.

  • Tactile Steppers: Using +/- buttons instead of direct text input makes fine-tuning budget numbers feel like a game-like interaction rather than a spreadsheet task.

  • Playful Iconography: Custom illustrated icons (e.g., a flying dollar bill for 'Transfer Out') inject personality into standard financial categories.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 17
screens.whereToUse: Use this stepper-list pattern when users need to configure multiple numeric values across many categories in one sitting (budgets, nutrition macros, inventory counts, notification frequency per channel). It's ideal when values are typically small, incremented in fixed steps, and precision to the cent/unit isn't critical. The sticky CTA + dismiss (X) combo works well for any long-form configuration modal where you want to reduce list-scroll anxiety while preserving an easy exit.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid steppers when users need to enter large, arbitrary, or highly precise numbers (e.g., entering an exact salary or large one-off transaction) - tapping + or - dozens of times becomes tedious and frustrating. In those cases, pair the stepper with a tappable numeric field or slider for direct entry. Also avoid this dense, single-column list approach if the category count is very high (30+), as it may still overwhelm users even with a sticky CTA; consider grouping, search/filter, or progressive disclosure instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users who are actively engaging with Cleo's budgeting/coaching feature after being shown their spending breakdown (likely people who feel overwhelmed or anxious about tracking finances and need a low-friction way to set limits). The design leans on reducing perceived effort (steppers vs. forms) and self-determination psychology (framing the confirmation as a personal capability statement) to keep users engaged rather than abandoning the task out of frustration or shame, which is common in traditional budgeting apps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Stepper-over-keyboard input: Using large tappable +/- controls instead of a numeric text field removes friction and typing errors for a repetitive, tedious task.

  • Disabled state clarity: Greyed-out minus buttons on $0 categories visually communicate a floor limit without any explanatory copy needed.

  • Sticky bottom CTA: The persistent, high-contrast button ensures the primary action is always one thumb-tap away, regardless of scroll depth in a long list.

  • Playful iconography per category: Distinct, colorful emoji-in-circle icons make a long, otherwise monotonous list instantly scannable and add brand personality.

  • Emotionally-framed CTA copy: "Alright, I can do this" turns a mundane confirmation into an act of self-affirmation, reducing the psychological weight of budget-setting.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 18
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial or health apps targeting users prone to shame or avoidance around negative metrics (overspending, missed workouts, calorie overages).

  • Products aiming to differentiate from clinical/corporate competitors through mascot-driven personality and humor.

  • Summary/recap screens where a period-over-period comparison (month, week) needs to be understood instantly without requiring numeracy or chart literacy.

  • Apps that want to bridge passive reporting screens with an active conversational/support channel (e.g., embedding a chat CTA within a dashboard).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise, B2B, or professional finance tools where users expect precise, chart-based analytics (e.g., accounting software, investment platforms) - illustration-heavy metaphors can feel unserious or imprecise.

  • Contexts involving serious financial hardship or debt where humor could feel dismissive or insensitive rather than supportive.

  • Situations requiring exact data comparison across many categories, where illustrated coin stacks lack the precision of bar/line charts.

  • Older or more conservative user demographics who may perceive mascot humor as unprofessional or untrustworthy for money management.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious, budget-averse young adults (likely Gen Z/Millennial) who have historically avoided traditional finance apps because of their clinical, judgmental tone. By using humor, illustration, and casual language, Cleo lowers the psychological barrier to confronting bad financial news.

The psychological trigger at play is shame mitigation via humor: users are more likely to return to and re-engage with an app that makes them laugh about failure rather than one that flags it in red alarming text. The chat prompt also leverages the social/parasocial trigger: being "checked in on" by a mascot creates a sense of accountability similar to a friend or coach, increasing retention and engagement with the chat feature.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anthropomorphized data visualization: Coin stacks and a mascot skull replace charts, making the abstract concept of overspending immediately legible and emotionally engaging.

  • Humor as a shame-reduction mechanic: "RIP budget" and the winking skull defuse the anxiety typically associated with overspending, keeping users from abandoning the app out of guilt.

  • Proactive conversational nudge: The dismissible chat bubble embedded directly in the data screen invites reflection and funnels users toward Cleo's core chat interface, blurring the line between passive dashboard and active coaching.

  • Consistent hub navigation: The bottom tab bar keeps budgeting contextually tied to Spend, Save, Borrow, and Habits, reinforcing a holistic money-coach narrative rather than siloed features.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 19
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, health, or habit-tracking dashboards where the goal is to reduce anxiety around numbers by softening zero/empty states, injecting mascot personality, and blending data display with conversational engagement hooks. Ideal for apps that want to minimize navigational complexity while still surfacing periodic (weekly/monthly) summaries.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for power users, accountants, or B2B financial tools where dense, precise data (multi-account breakdowns, transaction-level granularity, exportable reports) is expected (the playful illustration and large whitespace would feel unserious and would waste valuable screen real estate). Also avoid dash-based placeholders in contexts where users need immediate confirmation that a value is genuinely zero versus not-yet-loaded, as ambiguity could cause confusion in high-stakes financial decisions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets financially anxious or budgeting-averse users (often younger, gig-economy or paycheck-to-paycheck demographics) who are put off by traditional finance-app spreadsheets and charts. By using mascot illustrations, playful copy, and a countdown to payday, Cleo taps into loss-aversion and anticipation triggers in a way that feels supportive rather than punitive. The dismissible chat prompt exploits the Zeigarnik effect and social reciprocity, having a 'friend' check in creates a mild obligation to respond, nudging users back into the retention-driving chat interface.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dash placeholders instead of $0: Using "-" for empty monetary data avoids the false signal of zero balance, a subtle but important trust-preserving detail.

  • Crystal ball mascot moment: A whimsical illustration used as a functional divider between top-level totals and the spend/day breakdown, turning a boring stat block into a branded moment.

  • Persistent chat nudge card: The dismissible Cleo speech-bubble card at the bottom keeps the AI coach 'present' even on a non-chat screen, driving re-engagement into the core conversational loop.

  • Payday countdown progress bar: A minimal, wordless progress bar paired with "11 days until payday" gives an instant temporal anchor for budgeting decisions.

  • Bold color-blocking: The stark purple-to-white split visually segments 'period context' from 'financial data' without needing dividers or cards.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 20
screens.whereToUse: Use this hero-stat + grouped list pattern for any screen summarizing recurring financial commitments, such as subscription trackers, upcoming invoices, loan repayment schedules, or utility bill dashboards. It's ideal when users need a fast "at-a-glance" total before drilling into line-item details, and when grouping by time horizon (current vs. future) adds clarity to planning.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the underlying data set is large or highly variable (e.g., dozens of daily micro-transactions), as the oversized hero number loses meaning and the flat list becomes unwieldy without search or filtering. It's also unsuitable for screens requiring bulk actions or edits, since there are no checkboxes, swipe actions, or batch controls present (a limitation for power users trying to manage many bills at once).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious users, particularly younger millennials/Gen Z who live paycheck-to-paycheck and often get blindsided by forgotten subscriptions or automated bill withdrawals. The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion reduction: by proactively surfacing the exact dollar amount due before it happens, Cleo removes the dread of surprise overdrafts, positioning itself as a protective "money coach" rather than just a tracker.

The visual softness (rounded cards, pastel lavender, playful cash illustrations) targets users who typically avoid traditional banking apps because they feel cold, judgmental, or overly clinical. The design reduces the shame often associated with looking at debts/bills by making the screen feel more like a friendly notification than a stern financial audit.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero Stat Pattern: Leading with a giant, oversized dollar figure immediately orients the user without requiring any cognitive parsing of a table or chart.

  • Illustrated Money Motifs: The floating 3D-style cash illustrations around the header reinforce the "money" theme emotionally, softening what could otherwise feel like a stressful debt reminder.

  • Temporal Grouping: Splitting bills into "this budget" vs "Future bills" helps users mentally separate immediate obligations from what's coming, reducing overwhelm.

  • Brand Recognition Icons: Using the actual Netflix logo instead of a generic icon speeds up scanning and builds trust that Cleo has accurately synced real transaction data.

  • Persistent Sticky CTA: "Add a bill" stays fixed at the bottom, ensuring the user can always take the next logical action regardless of scroll position.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 21
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when confirming auto-detected recurring data (subscriptions, bills, income) where you have partial certainty from transactional/behavioral data. It's ideal for onboarding flows, bill/subscription managers, or budgeting apps where reducing manual entry directly correlates with activation and retention. Also effective anywhere a bottom sheet is preferable to a full-screen push for a lightweight, interruptible task.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the underlying data confidence is low (auto-filling incorrect values (wrong amount or date) can erode user trust faster than manual entry would build it). Also avoid for complex forms with many fields, where a bottom sheet's limited vertical space and lack of persistent navigation context could frustrate users. Not suitable for irreversible financial commitments without an explicit secondary confirmation step.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users setting up bill tracking/budgeting features (typically financially anxious or disorganized users who signed up for Cleo specifically because they don't want to manage spreadsheets). By pre-filling the data, Cleo removes the friction and effort that would normally cause this exact demographic to abandon a manual bill-tracking setup. The psychological trigger is reduced effort/cognitive load combined with automation-driven trust: the user feels the app "already knows" their finances, reinforcing Cleo's value proposition as an AI money coach rather than a passive tracker.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Defaults / Prefill: Amount, frequency, and next due date are automatically populated from transaction history, drastically reducing manual data entry and the associated drop-off risk.

  • Brand Consistency in Utility Screens: Even a mundane form uses the Netflix brand icon and Cleo's distinct bold typography to keep the experience visually on-brand.
