  • Progressive Disclosure via Bottom Sheet: Presenting this as a modal sheet (with a swipe-to-dismiss handle) rather than a full navigation push keeps the task feeling lightweight and reversible.

  • Icon-Assisted Field Affordance: The chevron and calendar icons clearly communicate interaction type (dropdown vs. date picker) without extra copy.

screens.name: Cleo Logging & Tracking 22
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (real-logo bill cards + equal-weight add action + dual-framed category spending figures + visible category-editing) fits any personal finance app's budget-detail view, where users need both to review upcoming obligations and understand spending proportionally, not just in absolute terms.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for extremely high-volume or highly granular category systems (e.g., dozens of narrow spending categories) where a card-based layout with large illustrative elements would become inefficient compared to a denser table or list view.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Rocket Money, Truebill: use nearly identical "upcoming bill card + add bill" layouts within their own bill-tracking dashboards.

  • Mint (Intuit), historically: displayed spending-by-category cards with both dollar amount and percentage-of-budget/income framing, matching Cleo's dual-figure approach.

  • Copilot Money: offers a comparable "edit categories" action prominently placed near auto-categorized spending totals, respecting user correction of automatic classification.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Real brand logo for bill recognition: using Netflix's actual icon (rather than a custom illustrated icon) prioritizes instant recognizability for a real, specific merchant, showing Cleo's icon system flexes between playful abstraction and literal branding depending on what best serves the user's need to quickly identify the item.

  • Dual-framing of spending figures: pairing an absolute dollar amount with a percentage-of-income figure gives users two ways to judge whether a spending category is reasonable, supporting better self-assessment than either number alone.

  • Equal-weight add action: sizing "Add a bill" identically to an actual existing bill (rather than as a small icon or link) treats bill-tracking as an ongoing, always-available task rather than a one-time setup step.

  • User-correctable categorization: the visible "edit categories" action signals that automatic spending classification is a starting point, not a fixed judgment, respecting that auto-categorization is often imperfect and users need an easy correction path.

screens.name: Oportun Adding & Creating 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when users need to select from a finite set of common, recognizable categories as the first step of goal creation, onboarding, or configuration (especially in personal finance, budgeting, habit-tracking, or preference-setup flows where reducing typing and decision fatigue improves completion rates).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the category list is very long (>8-10 items), as a flat scrollable list without search or grouping becomes tedious; in such cases a search bar or grouped/faceted browse would perform better. Also avoid if users' needs are highly unique or non-standard, since a preset list may feel irrelevant and add an extra tap before reaching the "custom" option.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets budget-conscious consumers, likely younger or financially-stressed users using an app like Qapital, Digit, or a similar automated-savings product, who need help proactively setting aside money for recurring bills. The psychological trigger at play is reducing decision fatigue: by pre-populating the most common bill types, the app leverages the "path of least resistance" bias, nudging users to commit to a savings goal quickly rather than abandoning the task due to a blank-canvas input field. The reassuring subtext and flexible fallback option also address loss-aversion and autonomy needs (users don't feel forced into a rigid taxonomy, which increases completion likelihood for this onboarding-style micro-flow).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Recognition over recall: Presenting curated, common bill categories as tappable tiles removes the cognitive load of typing a goal name from scratch.

  • Built-in escape valve: The "Create a unique goal" option at the list's end ensures no user feels unsupported by the presets, preventing drop-off for edge cases.

  • Dual exit pattern: Separate back arrow and "Cancel" affordances give users granular control depending on whether they want to revisit a previous step or abandon the whole flow.

  • Friendly iconography: Circular emoji icons soften the financial subject matter, making bill management feel less stressful and more human.

screens.name: Oportun Adding & Creating 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this single-screen form pattern when collecting a small, well-defined set of related inputs (3-5 fields) for object/entity creation (such as setting up bills, budgets, recurring transactions, reminders, or subscription trackers). It's ideal when you want to front-load all required inputs before a review/confirmation step, and when the domain (finance, health, habits) benefits from a "goal-oriented" framing to increase completion motivation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are many fields (7+) as it will create a long scroll and increase abandonment (a multi-step wizard would serve better). Also avoid disabled/greyed CTAs without clear inline messaging on what's missing, as this can frustrate users who don't understand why they can't proceed; pairing disabled buttons with inline validation hints or error states is recommended to avoid a dead-end feeling.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of personal finance, budgeting, or bill-tracking apps who are setting up recurring payment goals (e.g., subscriptions, phone bills, rent). The psychological driver here is reducing financial anxiety through structure: by breaking down a bill into discrete, guided fields (frequency, due date, amount), the app makes an otherwise stressful task (money management) feel procedural and controllable.

The "goal" framing also taps into self-efficacy and motivation psychology: users are more likely to engage with financial planning when it's framed as achieving a goal rather than merely tracking a liability.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon + Name pairing: The circular category icon next to the editable name field instantly communicates "what this goal represents" visually, reducing reliance on text alone.

  • Asterisk-based required field marking: A minimal, non-intrusive way to communicate validation requirements upfront rather than after a failed submit attempt.

  • Disabled state CTA: The greyed-out "Review" button visually communicates incompleteness, nudging the user to fill all required fields before proceeding, preventing premature submission errors.

  • Consistent pill-shaped field design: Creates a friendly, approachable aesthetic uncommon in traditional dry financial forms.

screens.name: Oportun Adding & Creating 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet single-select pattern when:

  • You need to capture one discrete choice from a short, finite list (typically 3-7 options) without derailing the user from a multi-field parent form.

  • The decision is important enough to warrant focused attention but not complex enough to need a dedicated full page.

  • You want to enforce a deliberate, validated selection before allowing progression (via a disabled CTA state).

  • Financial, scheduling, or preference-setting flows where plain-language explanations can demystify technical fields (e.g., recurrence, billing cycles, notification cadence).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The option list is long (10+ items): a searchable list, dropdown with search, or full-screen picker would perform better than a scrollable radio list in a constrained sheet.

  • Users need to select multiple frequencies or complex custom recurrence rules (e.g., "every 2nd Tuesday") - this would require a more robust custom scheduler UI, not simple radio buttons.

  • The decision is trivial or low-stakes, where a bottom sheet interruption would feel like unnecessary friction compared to an inline segmented control or dropdown.

  • On larger screens (tablet/desktop) where a modal dialog or inline expansion may be more appropriate than a mobile-style bottom sheet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using a personal finance or budgeting app to set up recurring bill-based savings goals (e.g., saving incrementally for a phone bill, insurance, or subscription). The audience likely includes financially cautious or budget-conscious users who need structure and reassurance rather than open-ended flexibility.

Psychologically, offering a fixed, curated set of frequency options (rather than a free-text or complex custom recurrence builder) reduces decision fatigue and taps into the "paradox of choice" - five clear options feel manageable and confidence-inspiring, whereas a fully custom scheduler could induce hesitation or errors. The bill-payment framing also triggers relevance and urgency: users are reminded this goal is tied to a real, recurring financial obligation, which increases motivation to complete the setup accurately.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual bottom sheet over full navigation: Keeps the user anchored to the parent form, reducing perceived task complexity and avoiding a jarring full-screen transition for a single-field decision.

  • Disabled CTA until selection: The greyed-out "Save frequency" button acts as a built-in validation mechanism, preventing null-state submissions without needing an error message.

  • Human-centric explanatory subtext: Ties an abstract financial term to a real-world action (paying a bill), improving comprehension for less financially-savvy users.

  • Drag handle affordance: Signals the sheet is dismissible via swipe, aligning with native iOS interaction conventions and reducing reliance on an explicit close button.

screens.name: Oportun Adding & Creating 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this contextual bottom-sheet-with-radio-list pattern when:

  • A single field within a larger form requires selecting one option from a small, finite set (typically 3-7 items).

  • You want to preserve the user's sense of place within a longer flow (e.g., multi-field forms, settings, wizards).

  • There's a clear, data-backed default that applies to the majority of users, allowing for one-tap acceptance.

  • Mobile-first contexts where native sheet gestures (drag to dismiss) are expected and improve perceived responsiveness.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The option list is long (10+ items) or requires search/filtering (a full-screen picker or searchable list would perform better).

  • Multiple related fields need to be configured together, in which case a dedicated screen or multi-step form may reduce excessive sheet-to-sheet navigation.

  • The choice carries high stakes or complexity requiring more explanation than a two-line description can provide (e.g., legal or irreversible financial commitments) - these deserve a full screen with more educational content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users setting up personal finance or budgeting goals (likely a fintech/banking app) who need to configure recurring bill reminders or savings targets. This audience ranges from financially novice to intermediate users who benefit from simplified language and reduced decision fatigue.

Psychologically, the smart default ("Every month" pre-selected) leverages the path-of-least-resistance bias: most users will simply accept the default and tap save, speeding up onboarding completion rates. The bottom sheet's partial reveal of the underlying form also leverages the Zeigarnik effect, subtly reminding users that a task is incomplete and encouraging them to finish configuring the goal.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Bottom Sheet over full navigation: Keeps users tethered to the parent form visually (dimmed background) while focusing attention on a single decision, preventing loss of context or flow.

  • Smart Default Pre-Selection: "Every month" is pre-selected in green, reflecting the most statistically common billing cycle and reducing friction for the majority of users.

  • Full-Row Radio Targets: Entire list rows are likely tappable, not just the small radio circle, improving accuracy and speed on mobile touchscreens.

  • Persistent, Reachable CTA: The primary action button sits at a fixed, thumb-friendly position at the bottom, all options visible without scrolling.

  • Drag Handle Affordance: Signals native swipe-to-dismiss gesture support, reinforcing a lightweight, non-committal feel to the interaction.

screens.name: Oportun Adding & Creating 6
screens.whereToUse:
• Any mobile form requiring discrete date/time selection where precision matters more than open-ended flexibility (billing dates, appointment scheduling, subscription renewals).

  • Multi-field forms where you want to preserve the user's place and prevent the "lost context" feeling of full-screen navigation.

  • iOS-first or cross-platform apps aiming for native look-and-feel to reduce onboarding friction for date inputs.

  • Financial, health, or utility apps where recurring/periodic actions need clear due-date configuration.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid wheel pickers when users need to select dates far in the future or past (e.g., birthdates decades away) since scrolling becomes tedious (a searchable/typed date input or full calendar grid is better there).

  • Not ideal for selecting date ranges or multiple non-contiguous dates, where a calendar view with range-highlighting is more appropriate.

  • Avoid on Android or Material Design contexts without adaptation, since the spinner metaphor is distinctly iOS; Android users expect a calendar-dialog picker instead.

  • Don't use if users frequently need to cross-reference a calendar (e.g., checking day-of-week context) since the wheel format omits calendar grid visualization.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers managing personal finances (particularly users setting up recurring bill reminders or savings goals (e).g., phone bills, subscriptions, rent). The design assumes a moderately tech-comfortable iOS user who benefits from familiar system-level interaction patterns rather than a custom-built calendar grid.

Psychologically, the picker leverages the "recognition over recall" principle: instead of forcing users to type a date (error-prone) or navigate a full calendar (higher cognitive load for a date months away), the scrollable wheel format allows fast, tactile browsing especially efficient for near-future dates. The dimmed backdrop exploits the Gestalt principle of figure-ground to direct 100% of attention to the current micro-task (choosing a date) while subtly signaling "you'll return here" - reducing anxiety around losing context or progress in a multi-field form.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native platform picker pattern: Using the iOS wheel/spinner picker instead of a custom calendar component leverages users' existing muscle memory, drastically reducing the learning curve for date selection.

  • Dimmed background context preservation: Rather than navigating to a new screen, the form remains visible (dimmed) behind the picker, reassuring the user that their previously entered data (Name, Frequency) is safe and unaffected.

  • Redundant exit paths: Both an implicit "tap outside" affordance and an explicit "Cancel" button beneath "Confirm" give anxious users multiple ways to back out without fear of accidentally submitting wrong data.

  • Required field marking (*): Efficient use of asterisks front-loads expectation-setting, so users aren't surprised by validation errors later.

  • Icon-based goal categorization: The circular phone icon adds a visual, scannable identifier that helps users quickly recognize goal type in list/dashboard views later.

screens.name: Oportun Adding & Creating 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this native date-picker bottom sheet pattern when collecting a single, unambiguous date value in a mobile context (especially for recurring events, deadlines, reminders, or bill due dates). It's ideal for finance, calendar, booking, or task management apps where platform consistency and reduced input errors are priorities. Pairing it with clearly marked required fields is effective for any multi-field setup/creation flow where users must supply several distinct pieces of structured data before proceeding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid native wheel pickers when users need to select dates far in the future/past without efficient scrolling shortcuts (e.g., selecting a birth year decades ago) - a calendar grid or direct year input would be faster. Also avoid this pattern on Android without adapting to Material Design date picker conventions, as inconsistency with platform norms can feel jarring. For power users or data-dense B2B tools, a compact inline date field with keyboard input may be more efficient than a full-screen modal interruption.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users of personal finance or budgeting apps who need to set up recurring bill reminders or savings goals (likely a mainstream consumer audience seeking help with financial organization and discipline). The psychological driver here is reducing friction and anxiety around financial admin tasks: by breaking the goal creation into clearly labeled, bite-sized fields and using familiar native controls (like the iOS date wheel), the app minimizes perceived effort and the risk of input errors, which is critical for retention in finance apps where users can easily abandon tedious setup flows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native platform-consistent date picker: Using the iOS wheel spinner instead of a custom calendar UI leverages user familiarity and reduces interaction errors.

  • Required field markers (*): Immediately communicates form completion requirements upfront, preventing surprise validation errors later.

  • Iconography as visual anchor: The circular icon avatar (phone icon) gives immediate, scannable context to what "Cell phone" represents as a goal/category before the user even reads the label.

  • Dual dismissal options (Confirm/Cancel): The bottom sheet clearly separates commit vs. discard actions, reducing accidental confirmations.

  • Dimmed background scrim: Focuses full attention on the date selection task while preserving context of the underlying form.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 10
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (validating a real pain point + low-burden confirmation framing + consistent visual grammar) fits any feature-introduction screen for an automation-style feature (the app does detection/tracking, the user just confirms), especially where the underlying task (like bill management) is widely perceived as tedious.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for features requiring extensive manual setup rather than simple confirmation, framing something as low-effort ("so I can track 'em for you") when it actually requires significant user input would create a mismatch between promised and actual effort, undermining trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Rocket Money: uses similarly blunt, relatable copy ("we hunt down your forgotten subscriptions") when introducing bill/subscription-tracking features.

  • Mint (Intuit), historically: introduced bill-tracking and reminder features with comparable illustrated, headline-driven interstitials before requiring user confirmation of detected bills.

  • Truebill/Rocket Money: matches the "confirm what we found" interaction pattern, where the user's role is verification rather than manual entry.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Honest acknowledgment builds credibility: "Bills suck" validates a real negative feeling before offering help, which tends to land as more trustworthy than pure positive-spin marketing copy.

  • Low-burden framing of the ask: "so I can track 'em for you" reframes bill verification as delegating a chore rather than adding a task, reducing perceived friction.

  • Consistent visual grammar across distinct features: reusing the headline + chat-bubble + single-CTA structure from prior onboarding screens for what's likely a different feature module reinforces a coherent design system across Cleo's broader product surface, not just its first-run flow.

  • Distinct CTA color for a distinct action type: the mint-green "Verify bills" button (versus the blue CTAs elsewhere) may help users visually distinguish confirmation/verification actions from standard navigation actions, though this can't be fully confirmed without seeing more of the app's color system.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an app can algorithmically infer structured data (subscriptions, contacts, calendar events, expenses) on a user's behalf during onboarding or data import. It's ideal for finance, subscription-tracking, or CRM apps where confirming pre-filled data is far less taxing than manual entry, and where building early trust in automated intelligence is a core value proposition.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the underlying detection/categorization accuracy is poor, as showing wrong data erodes trust immediately at first use. It's also unsuitable when the dataset is very large (dozens of transactions), since a simple list without search/filtering or bulk actions would become unwieldy (a batch review or table view would be more appropriate). Additionally, if users have no context on why data was detected this way, the lack of an explanation/source citation could feel intrusive or "creepy."
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users onboarding onto Cleo who have just linked a bank account, likely younger, mobile-first consumers (Gen Z/Millennial) who are put off by traditional budgeting apps' manual entry requirements. The psychological trigger here is reduced effort + delegated authority: by having the AI pre-populate bills, Cleo signals competence and does the "boring" work, letting the user simply validate rather than labor through data entry, which increases completion rates for the onboarding funnel. The editable/removable list also builds trust and a sense of control, mitigating anxiety about an AI misreading personal financial data.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-detected pre-fill: Instead of asking users to manually input recurring bills, Cleo does the heavy lifting via transaction analysis and asks for a lightweight yes/no-style confirmation, converting a tedious form task into a quick review task.

  • Embedded interaction hint: The subheader copy ("Tap to edit or swipe to remove") teaches the gesture vocabulary inline, avoiding a separate coach-mark overlay and reducing onboarding friction.

  • Custom playful iconography: Whimsical icons (a winged dollar coin, a bank building) for each bill category reinforce Cleo's fun, mascot-driven brand identity even in a purely functional financial screen.

  • Typographic price hierarchy: Large integer + smaller decimal formatting for amounts improves scannability and mirrors familiar receipt/pricing conventions.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern after a user completes a moderately effortful, potentially tedious task (form completion, budget setup, goal creation) within onboarding or key flows. It's most effective when the underlying task is functional/dry and needs an injected moment of levity to prevent drop-off or negative sentiment before continuing to the next step.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen celebratory treatment for minor, frequent micro-actions (e.g., every single toggle change), as it will quickly become obtrusive and slow down power users. It's also inappropriate for enterprise, B2B, or highly formal financial products where overly casual tone or slang ("Like a Boss") could undermine perceived trust or professionalism.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z/Millennials) who are fatigued by traditional, dry banking UX and respond better to meme-adjacent, humor-forward interfaces. The psychological trigger here is the Peak-End Rule: by inserting a high point of delight at the end of a setup task, Cleo ensures users remember the budgeting process positively, increasing the likelihood they'll complete future onboarding steps or engage with the app again. The "Like a Boss" framing also taps into self-affirmation and identity reinforcement, making financial responsibility feel cool and validating rather than restrictive.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotional Reward Before Data: Leads with a dopamine-triggering celebration screen instead of dumping the user straight into a budget dashboard, making a boring finance task feel like an achievement.

  • On-Brand Mascot Illustration: Uses whimsical, oversized donut illustrations (a nod to indulgent spending/reward) bleeding off-canvas to create scale and joy, avoiding generic checkmark/confetti clichés.

  • Persistent Chat Metaphor: Even in a full-screen celebratory moment, the confirmation is delivered via chat bubbles, keeping the entire app experience conversational and consistent.

  • Single, Curiosity-Driven CTA: One button with playful emoji copy reduces decision fatigue and nudges forward momentum.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 13
screens.whereToUse: Use this illustrative, narrative-driven data pattern when the goal is to encourage habitual engagement with otherwise dry or emotionally sensitive data (budgets, health metrics, screen time). It's ideal for apps with a strong mascot/brand voice trying to differentiate from clinical competitor dashboards, and for periodic (weekly/monthly) summary screens meant to be swiped through like a story or carousel.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for power users, accountants, or B2B financial tools where precision, comparability, and data density matter more than charm (illustrative metaphors like coin stacks scale poorly for detailed multi-category comparisons). Also avoid if brand tone is meant to convey stability/trust (e.g., mortgage or investment platforms), since playful mascot commentary can undercut perceived seriousness for high-stakes financial decisions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious or budget-averse users (often younger, Gen Z/Millennial) who find traditional banking dashboards boring, shameful, or overwhelming. By using humor, mascot reactions, and playful iconography instead of stark red/green deficit charts, Cleo lowers the emotional barrier to checking one's own finances regularly.

Psychological triggers at play include: Loss aversion softened by humor (a thumbs-up mascot makes even a review of spending feel non-judgmental), the Zeigarnik effect (the "11 days left" progress bar creates a sense of an unfinished task driving return visits), and social-style feedback loops (mascot commentary mimics receiving a text from a friend rather than a bank).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metaphorical Data Visualization: Replacing bar/line charts with a "coin stack" illustration makes raw financial data feel tactile, gamified, and less intimidating.

  • Emotional Reaction Overlay: The purple mascot thumb floating in front of the chart delivers an instant qualitative judgment on financial behavior, adding personality where a normal fintech app would show a neutral chart.

  • Layered Information Density: The dark "story" zone (visual/emotional) and light "data" zone (precise numbers) are cleanly separated by a rounded card, letting users choose how deep they want to go.

  • Editable Goal Inline: The "until $1,463" edit pencil lets users adjust their spending ceiling directly inline without navigating to a settings screen.

  • Conversational Re-engagement Banner: A dismissible chat-bubble nudge at the bottom of a data screen pulls users back into Cleo's core AI-chat loop.
