screens.name: Brex Account information 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped settings-sheet pattern when:

  • Building account/settings hubs for B2B SaaS, fintech, or productivity apps where users need quick, low-friction access to disparate configuration categories.

  • You want to surface support channels with trust-building SLA indicators (e.g., estimated response times) to reduce pre-contact anxiety.

  • You need to embed a growth/referral mechanism non-intrusively within an existing high-traffic screen rather than as a separate marketing push.

  • Settings functionality is secondary to the app's core workflow and benefits from being presented as a dismissible overlay rather than permanent navigation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The settings area is extensive enough (20+ items) that a single scrolling sheet becomes unwieldy (consider a dedicated full-screen settings page with search instead).

  • Users frequently need to cross-reference settings while performing other tasks, since a modal sheet blocks the underlying content and discourages multitasking.

  • The product targets consumers unfamiliar with financial/support SLAs (overly specific wait-time badges could set expectations that are hard to maintain operationally).

  • Referral incentives are not yet finalized or could change frequently, as hardcoding monetary values inline increases the maintenance/legal review burden.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets business/finance professionals and company admins using Brex's corporate card and spend management platform. These users are typically busy, task-oriented, and expect enterprise-grade reliability and quick access to account controls, support, and banking configuration.

Psychologically, the design leverages:

  • Reduced anxiety through transparency (support wait times) - critical for financial products where users may be dealing with time-sensitive issues (fraud, failed payments).

  • Incentive-driven virality (referral cash reward) - tapping into extrinsic financial motivation, which resonates strongly with a finance-savvy audience.

  • Trust via information affordance: the info icon next to the account identity reassures users that verification/detail is readily accessible, important in a banking context where identity and account status matter.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grouped sectioning with shaded headers: Clearly partitions unrelated settings domains (General vs. Banking vs. Support) improving scannability.

  • Inline value previews: Showing "Automatic" next to Appearance lets users know the current state without an extra tap (a small but high-leverage efficiency pattern).

  • SLA transparency badges: The "1 min" green pill next to Chat and Call preemptively answers "how long will this take?", directly reducing support friction and anxiety.

  • Monetized referral incentive inline: Placing the $250 earning potential directly under "Refer a friend" (rather than requiring a tap-through) maximizes conversion by front-loading the value proposition.

  • Modal dismissal via explicit X: Signals this is a secondary/utility layer, not a primary tab, letting users exit without ambiguity (avoiding reliance on swipe-only gestures).

screens.name: Brex Account information 2
screens.whereToUse:
• When certain administrative or security-sensitive actions are intentionally desktop-only (e.g., legal documents, complex bank linking, compliance forms).

  • To explain feature parity gaps between platforms without leaving users confused by missing/disabled controls.

  • For fintech, B2B SaaS, or enterprise apps where desktop remains the primary management surface.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the redirected action could easily be supported natively on mobile (unnecessary redirection increases friction and task abandonment).

  • Don't use for frequently-needed actions; constant context-switching to a browser harms retention and perceived app completeness.

  • Avoid stacking multiple redirects/deflections in a single flow, as it signals an unfinished or secondary mobile experience.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets business professionals and finance teams using Brex's corporate card/expense platform, a demographic that frequently alternates between mobile (for quick checks) and desktop (for administrative tasks). The design leverages the psychological principle of reducing frustration through transparency: explicitly stating a limitation builds trust rather than letting users feel the app is broken or incomplete.

It also taps into task-appropriate channeling: sensitive account/security changes (email, identity) are nudged toward a more secure, verifiable desktop environment, which can also subtly serve as a soft security measure against mobile-based account takeover attempts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Graceful Feature Deflection: Instead of silently disabling the edit function or hiding it, the app explains *why* an action isn't available on mobile and offers an immediate alternative path (opening the dashboard in browser).

  • Context Preservation via Dimmed Background: The settings list remains visible but dimmed behind the sheet, reinforcing spatial context and signaling this is a temporary, dismissible overlay rather than full navigation.

  • Scannable Settings Hierarchy: Clear bold section labels (General, Personal bank account, Brex Assistant, Referrals) paired with right-aligned secondary text (e.g., "Automatic") let users scan state at a glance without extra taps.

  • Drag Handle & Close (X) Redundancy: Both a swipe-down drag handle on the sheet and an explicit X button on the parent screen give users multiple intuitive ways to dismiss, accommodating different interaction habits.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Managing Accounts 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Final confirmation steps for financial transactions, subscriptions, or recurring billing setup where user trust and error-prevention are critical.

  • Any flow where you want to reuse a platform's native authentication gesture to inherit trust and reduce cognitive load.

  • Multi-step setup wizards where a modal summary/confirmation screen should reference all previously chosen parameters (date, source, frequency) in one glanceable place before commit.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Low-stakes or reversible actions: imposing a hardware-confirmation step for something trivial adds unnecessary friction and frustrates users.

  • Non-native/web contexts where you cannot legitimately trigger or reference a physical side-button/biometric gesture; faking this pattern outside its OS context breaks trust and platform consistency guidelines.

  • Flows requiring fast, high-frequency repeat actions (e.g., approving multiple small items in a row), where added friction meaningfully slows throughput without safety benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers setting up automated bill payments on a high-trust financial product (Apple Card). The primary psychological trigger being managed here is loss-aversion anxiety around recurring, automatic money movement (users fear "set and forget" payments going wrong). Apple counters this by making every parameter (bank, amount, cadence, start date) explicitly visible and by requiring a deliberate physical confirmation gesture rather than an easily mis-tapped button.

It also targets users already embedded in the Apple ecosystem who are highly familiar with Face ID / Touch ID / Side Button confirmation from Apple Pay, reducing the learning curve to near zero and increasing conversion on setup completion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Layered context preservation: Dimming and blurring the background screen (rather than fully replacing it) keeps the user oriented within the multi-step setup flow.

  • Hardware-level confirmation: Using the physical side button as the "commit" gesture instead of an on-screen button adds a deliberate, deniable-friction security checkpoint appropriate for recurring financial commitments.

  • Chunked information architecture: Separating funding source, recurrence schedule, and amount into distinct grouped rows lets users verify each fact independently before authorizing.

  • Reused system patterns: Borrowing the exact visual language of Apple Pay's authentication sheet (icon, "Double-Click to Pay" ghost text, blue checkmark) leverages existing user muscle memory and increases perceived trust/security.

  • Escape hatch always visible: The "X" close button and "Change Bank Account" row give the user control to back out or adjust before finalizing, reducing commitment anxiety.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Managing Accounts 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Payment/checkout flows where a user must choose from a small set of previously saved payment sources (bank accounts, cards, wallets).

  • Settings screens for managing default payout or billing accounts.

  • Any scenario where selection needs to be paired with an easy "add new" escape hatch.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when there are many (10+) accounts/options, as a flat list without search/filter would become unwieldy (a searchable list or combobox would be more appropriate).

  • Not suitable when accounts have complex metadata (balances, statuses, fees) that need more space than a simple two-line list item can convey.

  • Should not be used for irreversible high-stakes selections without an additional confirmation step, since a single tap immediately changes state with no explicit "Save"/"Confirm" button visible.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers managing money movement in a banking, P2P payment, or fintech app (e.g., paying bills, funding a wallet, or completing a purchase) who already have multiple linked bank accounts. The design assumes returning, somewhat financially engaged users who need quick account switching rather than first-time setup.

Psychologically, the screen reduces cognitive load by presenting a short, finite list rather than a dropdown, leveraging recognition over recall (users see their bank's name and icon and instantly recognize which account is "checking" vs "savings" without memorizing account numbers). The clear checkmark exploits the human preference for visual confirmation of state, reducing hesitation before completing a payment flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single checkmark for selection state: Instead of using bulky radio buttons, a single blue checkmark next to the currently active account keeps visual noise low while remaining instantly recognizable as the "current choice."

  • Grouped card separation between selection and creation: Placing "Add Bank Account" in its own isolated card below the account list visually distinguishes a navigational/creation action from a selection action, reducing accidental taps.

  • Masked account numbers with real bank iconography: Balances security (hiding full account digits) with identifiability (bank icon + last digits + full legal name), letting users pattern-match to their real-world bank cards/apps.

  • Lightweight modal dismissal: A circular 'X' button in a soft, well-padded touch target in the top-left offers an unambiguous, low-friction way to back out without committing to a change.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Managing Accounts 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for final-step confirmations of high-stakes, recurring, or irreversible financial actions (e.g., autopay setup, subscription billing changes, fund transfers) within an ecosystem that has native biometric/hardware authentication. It's ideal when you want to reduce accidental confirmations by requiring a deliberate physical gesture instead of a simple tap.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern on platforms without native hardware authentication support (e.g., Android, Web) as it cannot be replicated and would need a fallback (like a standard PIN or tap button), breaking consistency. It is also overkill for low-stakes, easily reversible actions where a simple confirm button would suffice and add unnecessary friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets existing Apple ecosystem users setting up recurring bill payments for their Apple Card. It relies on the psychological trigger of familiarity and trust transfer: since users already trust the Side Button gesture for Apple Pay purchases, applying the same gesture to authorize an autopay schedule instantly signals "this is secure and Apple-verified," lowering the anxiety typically associated with linking bank accounts and automating money movement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hardware-based Confirmation: Repurposing the physical Side Button (usually reserved for Apple Pay/Face ID) to confirm a financial setup adds a tangible, high-trust layer of security to an otherwise "soft" software toggle.

  • Context Preservation via Blur: The background remains visible (though blurred/dimmed), reassuring the user of where they are in the flow and that this is a temporary overlay, not a full context switch.

  • Grouped Information Card: Bank name, masked account, and recurrence details are bundled into a single scannable card, reducing cognitive load before the final commit action.

  • Easy Escape Hatch: "Change Bank Account" is prominently available, reducing anxiety that this is a point-of-no-return without an obvious edit path.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Managing Accounts 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Account/settings screens for regulated financial products (credit cards, loans, BNPL) where clarity and trust outweigh visual flair.
  • Any screen mixing informational display (balances, rates) with actionable security controls (lock, replace, freeze).
  • Contexts where users need fast self-service to avoid support calls (ideal for busy, time-constrained audiences).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for high-risk irreversible actions (e.g., closing an account) - these deserve stronger visual differentiation (red text, confirmation dialogs) rather than the same blue-link treatment as benign links.
  • Not suitable for marketing or acquisition-focused screens where tone needs to be persuasive rather than purely informational.
  • Poor fit for data-dense power-user dashboards needing charts/trends rather than simple list rows.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves Apple Card holders who need to self-manage financial details without calling support (a key efficiency driver for the "Busy Urban" persona who values speed and autonomy). The psychological reliance here is on trust transference: by using identical visual grammar to iOS Settings, Apple leverages the user's existing mental model of "safe, reversible toggles" to make financial actions (locking a card, viewing APR) feel as low-risk as changing a ringtone, lowering the anxiety barrier typically associated with credit management.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grouped rounded sections cleanly segment unrelated financial data (payments vs. credit vs. physical card vs. travel) without needing headers for every subgroup, reducing cognitive load.
  • Inline disclaimers placed directly beneath the relevant data (credit availability lag) pre-empt confusion at the exact point of potential doubt.
  • Non-alarming security actions: "Lock Card" uses the same calm blue-link style as benign actions, reducing user hesitation to act quickly in an emergency.
  • Progressive disclosure via chevrons on Card Information and Bank Accounts keeps the primary screen lightweight while allowing deeper detail on demand.

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 37
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech, neobank, or crypto wallet onboarding flows where getting the user to complete one real transaction quickly drives long-term retention (activation metric).

  • Any flow requiring identity/recipient verification before a sensitive action, where trust signaling is critical to conversion.

  • Guided, checklist-style onboarding sequences where isolating a single task per screen improves completion rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for repeat/power users who need quick access to full transaction history, multiple recipients, or advanced payment options (the single-focus layout would feel restrictive).

  • Not ideal for B2B or high-volume payment tools where batch actions and detailed recipient management take priority over a guided, milestone-style narrative.

  • Should not be used if the brand tone is conservative/traditional banking, since the gamified "achievement" framing may feel inappropriately casual for high-stakes financial contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new users during activation/onboarding for a fintech, neobank, or crypto payments app (likely users who are digitally native but cautious about financial security). The design leans on social proof and authority (verified badge), reduction of loss-aversion anxiety (privacy blurring + verification), and goal-gradient/achievement psychology (framing the payment as a milestone to complete, similar to a checklist item) to nudge the user past the friction of their first real money movement in the app. The dark, high-contrast, minimal aesthetic also signals to a younger, design-conscious audience that this is a modern, premium financial tool rather than a legacy bank app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-focus task framing: Isolating the flow to one recipient and one action removes decision fatigue for a first-time user.

  • Privacy-by-default blurring: Masking the sensitive account/name text while still showing verification status is an elegant way to protect PII without withholding trust signals.

  • Gamified milestone copy: Framing the transaction as "MAKE YOUR FIRST TRANSACTION" turns a routine financial action into an onboarding achievement, increasing completion motivation.

  • Trust-reinforcing visual system: The verified checkmark badge, "VERIFIED NAME" label, and card-style container work together to reduce first-transaction anxiety.

  • Skeuomorphic CTA button: The layered/beveled green "Pay" button visually pops against the dark background, making the next action unmistakable.

  • Progress indicator: The bottom page-control dot subtly communicates that this is one step within a larger guided sequence, setting expectations without a heavy progress bar.

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 38
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet account/method-selector pattern when:

  • Users must choose among multiple saved payment instruments (bank accounts, cards, wallets) mid-transaction.

  • Different payment sources may be in different setup/verification states requiring different CTAs.

  • You want to preserve context of the parent flow without a full navigation transition.

  • Quick utility actions (like balance check) can reduce transaction failure.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • There is only a single payment method available (the extra selection step adds unnecessary friction).

  • The list of methods is very long (more than 5-6), as a bottom sheet becomes cramped and scrolling may hide the primary CTA; a full page might serve better.

  • Users need to compare more complex account details (e.g., fees, exchange rates) that require more screen real estate than a compact row allows.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday digital payment users in markets with UPI (Unified Payments Interface) infrastructure, such as India, who commonly link multiple bank accounts to a single payment app. The design assumes users are moderately tech-savvy but may not remember bank-specific setup states (like whether mPIN is configured), so the UI proactively surfaces that status.

Psychologically, the screen reduces the "paradox of choice" anxiety of selecting where money leaves from (a decision with real financial consequence) by using familiar bank branding (logos) and a simple radio-selection metaphor, borrowed from universal payment mental models.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual trailing action per row: Instead of a generic "select" affordance, each account shows a different actionable state (already-selected radio, needs mPIN setup, needs linking) - reducing user confusion about why an account might be unusable.

  • Dimmed background retains context: Keeping the parent payment screen visible (dimmed) behind the sheet preserves task continuity and spatial memory.

  • Inline "Check balance" utility: Letting users check balance right at the point of account selection reduces failed payment attempts due to insufficient funds.

  • Progressive disclosure via bottom sheet: Avoids a jarring full-screen navigation for what is a secondary, quick decision within a larger payment flow.

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 39
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern when you want to drive repeat usage of a core transactional action (payments, check-ins, submissions) by layering a lightweight, visible progress/reward mechanic directly into the primary task flow. It works well for fintech, loyalty, and subscription-adjacent products where the reward is small but the frequency of the underlying action is high. It's especially effective when the incentive is placed at the point of decision rather than buried in a separate rewards hub.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-value, low-frequency, or emotionally weighty transactions (e.g., large bank transfers, medical payments, legal document actions) where gamified visuals could feel dissonant or trivializing. It's also inappropriate for enterprise/B2B tools where users expect a purely functional interface, or in contexts where regulatory/compliance concerns make "gamifying" money movement risky or where users may perceive it as manipulative dark-pattern design if reward criteria are unclear.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday retail UPI users in India who make frequent, small peer-to-peer or merchant payments (a mass-market audience for whom small cashback amounts (₹10) ₹40) meaningfully influence habit formation. The psychological triggers at play include the Zeigarnik effect (an unfinished progress chain creates a mental itch to complete it), variable/near-term reward anticipation, and loss aversion once the first reward node is already checked off, making users reluctant to "waste" the ₹10 already earned by not continuing the streak. The suggested contacts and quick-action shortcuts serve a secondary audience motivation: minimizing the number of taps required for extremely frequent, low-friction repeat behavior.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Gamified progress chain: Turning a repeat-transaction incentive into a visual, node-based progress tracker (like a mini quest map) taps into completion bias and the sunk-cost effect, nudging users toward habitual UPI usage.

  • Contextual reward placement: Surfacing the cashback progress directly on the payment initiation screen (rather than in a separate rewards tab) ensures the incentive is seen at the exact moment of decision, maximizing behavioral impact.

  • Dual-zone visual hierarchy: The stark black/white split cleanly separates "inspiration & incentive" (dark, hero) from "utility & action" (light, dense) without needing dividers or labels.

  • QR affordance on avatar: Embedding a scan icon directly on the profile photo cleverly reuses the same visual real estate for two different sharing/identification mechanisms.

  • Suggested contacts with mixed identity cues: Combining photos, initials, and icons (heart, silhouette) in the same avatar grid keeps the recipient list scannable even when profile images are missing.

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 40
screens.whereToUse:
• Payment/wallet apps seeking to increase transaction frequency through visible, gamified incentive tracking.

  • Any app where a personal QR code or shareable identifier is central to the core loop (payments, business cards, event check-ins).

  • Home/dashboard screens that need to balance a "status/identity" moment with immediate task-oriented actions via a layered sheet.

  • Contexts with a small, repeat set of destinations (contacts, favorite merchants) where avatar-based quick-select can replace search for the majority of use cases.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid gamified progress trackers for high-stakes or infrequent transactions (e.g., large bank transfers, investments) where playful reward framing may feel inappropriate or reduce perceived trust.

  • Do not use ambiguous dual-purpose icons (avatar-as-QR-trigger) in flows where users may not intuitively understand the icon's second function (always pair with a clear affordance or first-use coach mark).

  • Layered bottom sheets over hero content can bury critical primary actions if the sheet's peek height is too small on smaller devices (ensure the initial action row remains visible without scrolling).

  • Not suitable for enterprise/B2B payment tools where users expect dense, table-based data over playful visual gamification.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This design targets mass-market mobile payment users in markets with high UPI/QR adoption (e.g., India), where payment apps must differentiate on speed and incentives rather than novelty. The target user pays frequently (multiple times daily for small transactions (chai, groceries, bill splits) and is highly price-sensitive to cashback/rewards).

The psychological triggers at play include: variable/near-term reward proximity (visible progress toward ₹40 cashback creates a near-complete goal gradient effect, motivating continued use), identity reinforcement (personal QR/avatar hero treatment builds a sense of ownership and pride akin to a debit card), and reduced cognitive load (suggested contacts and quick-action chips remove decision fatigue for the 80% of payments that go to the same handful of people/services).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Gamified cashback path: The 5-node hex progress tracker turns routine bill payments into a visible, near-complete quest, leveraging the Zeigarnik effect (unfinished tasks linger in mind) to drive repeat transactions.

  • Dual-purpose avatar: The profile photo acts simultaneously as identity display and QR/scan trigger, reducing UI clutter by overloading one element with two functions.

  • Frictionless VPA sharing: The one-tap copy icon next to the UPI handle removes typing/memory burden when sharing payment details over calls or chat.

  • Layered bottom sheet: Partial reveal of the white action sheet over the dark hero view maintains context (identity + rewards) while prioritizing the next action (who to pay).

  • Zero-search repeat payments: Suggested contacts as colorful initials avatars let frequent payees be tapped instantly, bypassing search entirely for the most common use case.

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 41
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for referral, invite, or growth-loop features where you want to convert a flat, one-time action (share/invite) into an ongoing, motivating campaign. It's ideal for consumer social, gaming, fintech cashback, or marketplace apps running limited-time referral incentives, especially when you can offer tiered/escalating rewards for multiple invites.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy gamified treatment for B2B, enterprise, or professional tools where playful quest metaphors can feel unserious or patronizing. It's also inappropriate when the underlying reward mechanics are weak or unclear (a flashy countdown and locked nodes without a compelling payoff can breed cynicism). Similarly, don't use urgency countdowns for evergreen/non-time-bound programs, as repeated false urgency erodes trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users already engaged enough with the app to be considering inviting friends (likely mid-funnel or loyal users being nudged into a growth loop). The psychological levers used are loss aversion/urgency (countdown timer), gamification/variable reward (locked gem nodes hinting at mystery/future rewards), and social proof/low-friction suggestion (pre-filled suggested contacts reduce the effort of manually searching, exploiting the default bias). Together these push the user toward completing more "nodes" by inviting more people, driving viral growth.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual mode-switching: The black gamified header vs. white utilitarian list instantly communicates two different jobs-to-be-done on one screen without needing extra copy.

  • Node-based progress path: A tactile, jewel-like 5-step tracker with one checked node makes the referral program feel like an unfolding quest rather than an abstract counter.

  • Countdown timer: Injects urgency ("ENDS IN 6D:13H") to accelerate action before the reward window closes.

  • Segmented control for context switching: Lets users toggle between "who to invite" and "what they get" without navigating away from the flow.

  • Search bar positioned immediately below the incentive banner: Places the primary conversion action right where attention is highest post-motivation.

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 42
screens.whereToUse:
• Apps seeking to inject viral/referral growth loops into naturally high-frequency touchpoints like search or home screens.

  • Reward or loyalty programs that benefit from visualized progress trails to drive multi-step task completion.

  • Premium or aspirational brands wanting to make transactional referral prompts feel elevated rather than spammy.

  • Products with time-bound campaigns needing urgency without resorting to aggressive red countdown banners.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Utility-first apps (banking core flows, healthcare, government tools) where gamification could undermine trust or perceived seriousness.

  • Contexts where search needs to remain hyper-fast and distraction-free, inserting reward content here could frustrate users trying to complete a quick task.

  • New users unfamiliar with the platform who may find a quest trail confusing without prior onboarding context explaining the reward mechanic.

  • Situations where referral incentives are not genuinely valuable, as an artificial "already completed" first node can feel manipulative if the reward payout process is unclear or delayed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets CRED's core demographic: affluent, credit-conscious urban Indian millennials/Gen-X who value status, exclusivity, and financial optimization. The gamified quest trail appeals to users' intrinsic motivation for completion and mastery (Zeigarnik effect), while the ₹250 cashback appeals to extrinsic, tangible reward motivation. By blending both into the search experience, CRED maximizes daily active engagement, nudging users who opened the app just to search for a bill or transaction into also completing quest actions and inviting friends, thereby driving viral growth loops alongside retention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Endowed Progress Node Trail: Pre-completing the first step of a 5-step quest visually to boost completion motivation via the sunk-cost/endowed-progress bias.

  • Dual-Purpose Search Screen: Repurposing the search modal's empty state to house a monetizable rewards quest instead of a blank or purely functional suggestion list.

  • Segmented Toggle Between Utility and Incentive: "Suggestions" vs "Win Rewards" lets users choose their own path (functional or gamified) without forcing either.

  • Countdown Timer for Urgency: A ticking clock above the quest trail creates time-based pressure to keep engaging with the app.

  • Premium Editorial Styling: Serif typography and monochrome illustration elevate what would normally be a low-trust "refer & earn" spam banner into a tasteful, on-brand moment.

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 43
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when trying to drive repeat, habitual usage of a specific transaction type (payments, check-ins, purchases) by tying a tangible, quantified reward to a small number of remaining actions. It's especially effective for:

  • Fintech/rewards apps encouraging repeat UPI/card transactions

  • Referral or streak programs with a clear "X more to unlock" framing

  • Any funnel where keeping the incentive visible during task completion (e.g., above a keypad or form) increases completion rates

  • Calm, factual microcopy for low-stakes failures (test transactions, verification pings) to avoid unnecessary user alarm
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavily gamified visual treatment in enterprise, B2B, healthcare, or high-stakes financial contexts (e.g., large fund transfers, tax payments) where users expect sober, functional UI rather than game-like ornamentation (it can undermine perceived seriousness and trust). Also avoid downplaying failure messaging when the failed transaction involves a meaningful amount of money or requires urgent user action; in those cases, clearer error states with recovery CTAs are necessary rather than a passive notification-style log entry.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday UPI users in India (likely on a rewards-driven fintech/credit app like Cred) who are motivated by micro-incentives and gamified streaks to increase their transaction frequency on the platform. The target demographic skews toward younger, smartphone-native, credit-card-holding urban Indians who respond well to premium, dark-mode "gamer aesthetic" design and cashback-driven engagement loops.

Psychologically, the design exploits the goal-gradient effect (motivation increases as one nears a finish line) and variable/near-complete reward visualization: showing 1 of 5 already lit up makes the remaining 4 feel more attainable than starting from zero. The failed ₹1 payment notification, likely part of a bank account verification flow, is designed to reassure rather than alarm, protecting user trust during a technical hiccup.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Gamified progress nodes instead of a boring progress bar: Using glossy 3D gem/hexagon icons with a glowing "completed" state taps into game-reward psychology (think Duolingo path or loot crates) far more effectively than a percentage bar.

  • Reward framing tied directly to the action in progress: Placing the cashback tracker directly above the active payment input keeps the incentive top-of-mind exactly when the user is about to commit the transaction that advances it.

  • Calm, non-punitive failure messaging: The ₹1 failed payment notification uses neutral, lowercase language and a soft pastel avatar rather than alarming red error iconography, reducing user stress around failures.

  • Contextual small-value transaction transparency: Surfacing even a ₹1 failed transaction as a discrete notification builds trust (the user knows the app tracks every rupee, however small).

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 44
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any high-frequency, low-friction transactional flow where speed and error prevention are paramount. P2P transfers, quick bill splits, in-store QR payments, or topping up wallets. It's ideal when the primary input is a single numeric value and the user is likely to perform the action repeatedly (daily/weekly), justifying investment in a specialized keypad UI over generic OS controls.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, keypad-dominant layout for complex transactions requiring multiple inputs (e.g., invoices with line items, international transfers requiring additional compliance fields) - the layout doesn't scale well beyond amount + note + payment method. Also avoid for first-time/unfamiliar recipients without stronger identity verification, since the minimal chrome here relies on the user already trusting the "verified" system; new-to-crypto or new-to-fintech audiences may need more explicit safety copy and confirmation steps before this stripped-down UI would feel safe.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday retail and P2P payment users in markets with UPI infrastructure (primarily India), spanning a very broad demographic from small merchants to individuals splitting bills with friends. The design assumes variable literacy and tech-savviness, hence the oversized, high-contrast numeric keypad and minimal reliance on text.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss-aversion mitigation (verified badge, dynamic pay label) to reduce the anxiety inherent in sending money digitally. The large, unambiguous amount display and repeated confirmation of value at the button level exploit the peak-end rule: ensuring the last thing a user sees before committing is a completely unambiguous confirmation of intent.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dynamic CTA Label: The primary button updates in real time to reflect the exact amount ("Pay ₹1"), which is a powerful anti-error, confidence-building microinteraction before an irreversible financial action.

  • Full-Bleed Numeric Keypad: Dedicating the entire lower half of the screen to a custom keypad (rather than the OS-default keyboard) speeds up entry and keeps focus locked on the single task of amount input.

  • Verified Recipient Badge: The green checkmark next to the masked recipient name reduces fraud-related anxiety, a critical trust signal in P2P payments.

  • Persistent Payment Method Selector: "PAY USING" with the bank/UPI chip and a chevron allows last-second account switching without leaving the flow, avoiding a costly context switch.

  • Inline History Access: The collapsible "VIEW HISTORY" affordance lets users verify past transactions with this same contact contextually, aiding decision confidence (e.g., "did I already pay this person today?").

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 45
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial transaction entry points where a single critical identifier (account number, ID, handle) must be captured with zero distraction.

  • Flows where cross-platform/interoperability confusion needs to be proactively addressed via inline educational copy.

  • Any screen benefiting from a search-like input pattern to imply real-time verification before submission.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this ultra-minimal single-field pattern when multiple related inputs (amount, note, recipient name) are required simultaneously (it would force excessive multi-step navigation and slow down frequent-use flows).

  • Not suitable for contexts where users need to compare multiple saved recipients or payment methods at a glance, since this layout has no list/history affordance visible.

  • The lowercase, casual typographic tone may undermine perceived seriousness/security in enterprise or B2B financial products where users expect formal, authoritative UI language.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday retail UPI users in India (or similar real-time payment markets) who are used to apps like Google Pay, PhonePe, or Paytm but may be trying a new app for the first time. The design leverages simplicity bias and reduced cognitive load to build immediate trust in a money-movement context, where any friction or confusion could cause transaction abandonment. The reassurance copy directly targets first-time or less tech-savvy users who may not understand that UPI IDs are interoperable across apps, addressing a real adoption barrier.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-focus input design: Only one interactive element (the UPI ID field) is present above the fold, eliminating decision paralysis for a high-stakes financial action.

  • Search-style affordance on a payment field: Using a search icon and placeholder pattern ("enter upi") subtly signals real-time validation/lookup behavior, setting the right mental model before the user even types.

  • Preemptive trust-building microcopy: The "pay anyone" explainer tile answers the unspoken user question about UPI interoperability, reducing hesitation and support inquiries.

  • Distinctive typographic branding: Serif headline mixed with rounded lowercase body text gives the screen personality without sacrificing clarity (rare in transactional banking flows).

screens.name: CRED Transferring Money 46
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any flow requiring entry of a unique identifier (UPI ID, wallet address, username, email) where real-time resolution/validation can build confidence before a high-stakes action like a payment or transfer. It's ideal when:

  • The action is irreversible or costly to undo (money transfers, wire payments, crypto sends).

  • The identifier format is non-trivial or error-prone (compound strings like username@handle).

  • You can offer autocomplete shortcuts for common suffixes/domains to speed up entry.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimalist single-field pattern when:

  • The identifier system has no reliable real-time verification/lookup service, showing an unconfirmed "match" could create false confidence and increase fraud risk.

  • First-time or unfamiliar users need contextual guidance; the complete absence of helper text or examples could confuse novices unfamiliar with the ID format.

  • Multiple matches or ambiguous results are possible (this layout assumes a single clean match and doesn't gracefully demonstrate handling for multiple/conflicting results or error states).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers in India's UPI payment ecosystem (a mass-market audience ranging from tech-savvy urban users to less experienced users in tier-2/3 cities who transact peer-to-peer or with merchants daily). Because sending money to the wrong UPI ID is largely irreversible, the psychological driver here is anxiety reduction through verification: showing the resolved payee name and a verified badge before the user commits taps into loss-aversion and the need for certainty in financial transactions.

The suffix chips cater to users who know their own bank but forget the exact "@handle" syntax, reducing frustration and abandonment for a demographic that may not be fully technically fluent but transacts frequently via mobile.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Real-time identity resolution: The moment a valid UPI ID is typed, the recipient's masked name and verified badge appear instantly, converting an anxiety-inducing blind data-entry task into a confirmed, low-risk action.

  • Bank-suffix chip shortcuts: Common PSP handles (@okaxis, @okicici, @okhdfcbank) are surfaced as tappable chips, dramatically reducing typing effort and typo risk for the trickiest part of a UPI ID.

  • Verified badge trust signal: The green checkmark next to the resolved name leverages a universally recognized "verified" visual language to instantly reassure the user they're sending money to the correct, legitimate person.

  • Distraction-free single-purpose layout: No tab bar, no extraneous navigation. Just back button, headline, input, and result, keeping cognitive load minimal during a sensitive financial action.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Setting Up 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any irreversible or financially significant action (payments, subscriptions, money transfers, or destructive account changes) where you want to combine OS-level biometric security with a summary confirmation screen. It's ideal for confirming recurring commitments (autopay, subscriptions) where the user needs a final, tamper-resistant checkpoint.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy hardware-gesture pattern for low-stakes or high-frequency actions (e.g., liking a post, saving a draft) as the added friction of biometric authentication would frustrate users and slow down the app for no security benefit. This is also not suitable for Android or web platforms lacking a dedicated Side Button/Face ID hardware integration (alternative confirmation (e).g., PIN code or simple button tap) should be used instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Who: This targets existing Apple Card users managing their credit line via iOS Wallet, specifically users setting up "Autopay" to avoid missing payments and interest fees.

Why: Financial actions carry high emotional and security stakes. By requiring a physical biometric gesture (Side Button + Face ID/Touch ID) rather than a simple tap, Apple leverages the psychological principle of "effort justifies commitment" - the physical action makes the digital commitment feel more real and secure, reducing user anxiety about unauthorized or accidental transactions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hardware Integration: Bypassing a standard software "Confirm" button in favor of the physical Side Button creates a higher-friction, higher-trust interaction for financial commitments, reducing the chance of accidental payment setup.

  • Consolidated Summary Card: Bank account, recurrence frequency, and start date are grouped into a single visual card, allowing users to verify all payment parameters in one glance before authenticating.

  • Context Preservation: The dimmed background retains the previous "Payment Date" screen, visually confirming to the user which specific action (setting the due date) triggered this confirmation sheet.

  • Zero Cognitive Overload: No numbers, dollar amounts, or complex terms are shown yet for "Monthly Balance" - the system intentionally simplifies to the type of payment rather than a distracting dynamic number at this stage.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Setting Up 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this consolidated confirmation-sheet pattern when finalizing any recurring or sensitive commitment (subscriptions, autopay, recurring donations, scheduled transfers) where the user needs a last-glance summary of multiple previously configured settings before committing. It's especially effective when the setup involved multiple prior screens and you want to reunify the choices into one trustworthy checkpoint.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, low-stakes toggles or single-field settings where a full summary sheet would feel like unnecessary friction. Also avoid stacking a bottom sheet like this on top of an already complex background screen (like a full calendar) for users on smaller devices, as it can feel visually cluttered or cause information to be obscured behind the modal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday Apple Card users setting up automated bill payments, a demographic that values simplicity, trust, and reduced financial anxiety over granular configurability. The design leans on the psychological principle of reducing perceived risk before a recurring financial commitment: by surfacing all the terms (source, cadence, date) in one final review card, it satisfies the user's need for reassurance and control ("Am I sure this is right before I commit money automatically?").

The use of a bottom sheet rather than a full-screen takeover also signals a low-friction, lightweight decision, subtly telling the user "this is easy to reverse and not a big deal," which lowers anxiety around automating finances.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual layering: The dimmed background calendar screen remains partially visible, preserving spatial memory and reducing disorientation during the confirmation step.

  • Single consolidated summary card: Bank, recurrence, and start date are grouped into one glanceable card instead of being scattered across multiple screens or rows.

  • Non-destructive escape hatch: "Change Bank Account" is offered inline without forcing the user to abandon the current confirmation flow.

  • Unambiguous single CTA: The circular checkmark "Done" button is visually isolated and impossible to confuse with a cancel or secondary action.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Setting Up 9
screens.whereToUse:
• Final confirmation screens for any recurring/scheduled financial transaction (autopay, subscriptions, standing orders).

  • Any flow where automated system logic might produce a non-obvious outcome (e.g., skipped charge, delayed shipment) that needs proactive explanation.

  • Permission requests for notifications, calendar access, or reminders (always pair the request with a clear, contextual benefit statement rather than a bare system prompt).

  • Multi-step setup wizards that need a clear, low-anxiety terminal "success" state.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when the confirmation message requires urgent action (e.g., an error needing user input) - a purely celebratory/informational layout would undersell urgency.

  • Not suitable if there are multiple next-best-actions of equal importance; the single-CTA layout works only when there is truly one primary exit path.

  • If the skipped/edge-case explanation is highly technical or lengthy, this compact card format may need to be replaced with an expandable FAQ or help link instead of dense inline paragraph text.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have just configured a recurring/automatic bill or credit card payment (a moment of moderate financial anxiety where users want certainty that their money is being handled correctly). The design leverages the certainty/closure principle: explicit confirmation reduces the nagging worry of "did that actually work?"

The explanation of the skipped payment date leverages transparency as a trust-building mechanic, common in fintech products, where unexplained automated behavior (e.g., a payment appearing to not happen) can trigger fear of a system error or fraud. By preemptively answering the "why," the product reduces perceived risk and cognitive dissonance.

The notification opt-in nudge uses the psychological principle of contextual relevance: asking for permission at the exact moment its value is obvious (right after setting up recurring payments) dramatically increases conversion compared to a generic onboarding-time request.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive edge-case disclosure: Rather than silently skipping a payment date, the copy explicitly explains why, preventing user confusion and support tickets.

  • Decoupled primary/secondary messaging: The core confirmation and the optional notification nudge are visually separated into distinct blocks, so the secondary ask never dilutes the primary success message.

  • Contextual, value-driven permission priming: The notification request is framed around user benefit (payment reminders/confirmations) rather than a blind system permission dialog, increasing opt-in likelihood.

  • Single, unambiguous exit action: One large "Done" button removes any decision paralysis at the terminal step of the flow.

screens.name: Apple Wallet Setting Up 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an automated or recurring system action deviates from the user's expectation (skipped charge, delayed shipment, paused subscription, rescheduled event). Also apply the grouped read-only settings list for any configuration summary (subscriptions, recurring transfers, scheduled reports) where users need quick confirmation rather than frequent editing. Isolate and color-code any irreversible or high-consequence action (cancel, delete, downgrade) away from informational content.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid silently changing scheduled financial or recurring actions without notice (this erodes trust). Don't use a dense settings-list format for actions requiring frequent editing; instead provide inline edit controls or explicit "Edit" affordances if changes are common. Avoid placing destructive actions like cancellation in the same visual card as neutral information, as it increases risk of accidental taps in dense financial UI.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers managing recurring bill payments or credit card/loan balances (users who set up autopay to avoid missed payments and late fees but who need periodic reassurance that the automation is behaving correctly). The design leverages the psychological need for certainty and control over money: automating payments creates anxiety about "what if it messes up," and this screen directly counters that anxiety with transparent status reporting.

It also relies on the trust-through-transparency principle common in fintech: by explaining *why* a payment is skipped instead of just changing the schedule silently, the app avoids triggering suspicion or the perception of an error/bug, which could otherwise drive users to disable autopay altogether or contact support.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive skip notification: Explicitly informing users when a scheduled autopay will NOT occur, and why, rather than leaving a payment gap to be discovered later.

  • Settings-style grouped list: Familiar stacked rows reduce learning curve and let users audit their autopay rules in seconds.

  • Isolated destructive action: "Cancel Autopay" is visually separated and color-coded red, preventing accidental cancellation while keeping it easily accessible.

  • Masked sensitive data: Partial redaction of the bank account number balances usability (recognition) with security/privacy best practice.

  • Compliance micro-copy: Linking to the Customer Agreement grounds the automated financial behavior in legal terms without cluttering the primary UI.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 21
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial or wallet-style apps where balance visibility, quick fund transfer, and payment method management are core jobs. Ideal for fintech apps that need to softly convert unverified users by pairing a benefit-driven CTA with an inline explanation rather than a blocking modal. The card-shaped empty state for adding a payment method is broadly reusable in any app requiring bank/card linkage.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy visual chrome (curved header, large avatar) in data-dense enterprise or B2B financial dashboards where information density and scanability matter more than brand personality. Also avoid soft-gating verification indefinitely if verification is legally required for core functionality (at some point a harder gate or more assertive prompt may be necessary to ensure compliance completion rates).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday Venmo users managing peer-to-peer balances, particularly those who have received money but haven't yet linked a bank or verified identity. The design leverages the endowed progress effect and loss aversion: showing "$0 in Venmo" alongside a verification prompt subtly implies money-in-waiting, motivating users to complete verification to "unlock" funds. The empty bank/card slot exploits the Zeigarnik effect (an incomplete visual pattern (a card that isn't there yet) creates a subconscious pull to complete the setup).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Curved header silhouette: The scalloped blue-to-white transition creates a soft, distinct anchor for the avatar, elevating profile identity above transactional content.

  • Segmented Control for context switching: Wallet/Transactions toggle keeps related financial views one tap apart without a full navigation change.

  • Verification framed as a feature unlock: Rather than a blocking wall, the KYC/verification nudge is presented as an inline benefit card, reducing perceived friction.

  • Empty-state CTA as a visual affordance: The 'Add a bank or card' tile mimics the shape of an actual card, making the empty state intuitively actionable.

  • Notification badge + settings gear: Clear iconography for alerts (5 unread) and account settings sits consistently in the header for quick access.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 22
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when presenting users with multiple payment/funding source options that carry different cost structures (fintech, marketplaces, subscription apps). It's ideal for any screen where fee transparency at the point of selection can reduce downstream confusion, support tickets, or cart abandonment.

Also effective when a platform wants to gently steer users toward a lower-cost-to-platform option without removing user choice, pairing subtle visual emphasis (background tint) with honest information rather than dark patterns.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern if fee structures are complex or conditional (e.g., tiered by amount, region, or promo), as a simple flat-list format may oversimplify and mislead. It's also unsuitable for very short flows where inserting a modal decision point could feel like unnecessary friction, or for premium/luxury products where highlighting fees front-and-center may clash with a frictionless, high-end brand narrative.

If the app wants to actively promote credit card usage (e.g., to earn interchange fees or drive rewards partnerships), this transparent fee-comparison layout would work against that business goal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets everyday consumers managing peer-to-peer payments and personal finance who are fee-sensitive and value transparency. Many Venmo users are younger (Gen Z/Millennial) and have been trained by fintech apps to expect no hidden fees; explicitly stating the 3% credit card surcharge preempts complaints and support tickets while subtly steering behavior toward bank linking, which reduces payment processing costs for Venmo/PayPal.

The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion framing: presenting the card fee prominently makes users consciously avoid it, while the "No fee" framing on Bank and Amex options creates a rewarding, cost-free feeling that reinforces continued app usage.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radical fee transparency: Every payment method explicitly states its cost (or lack thereof) directly in the selection list, eliminating surprise fees at the point of decision rather than at checkout.

  • Implicit default via visual weight: The "Bank" option is pre-highlighted with a subtle background tint, nudging users toward the free, lowest-friction (for Venmo) option without restricting choice.

  • Contextual layering: Using a bottom sheet over a dimmed but still-visible dashboard maintains orientation and reduces the feeling of a jarring context switch.

  • Branded partner integration: The Amex Send™ Account option demonstrates how a platform can surface co-branded/partner financial products as a first-class option alongside generic bank/card entries.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 23
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately before any third-party data-sharing integration (bank linking, calendar sync, contact import, health data access) in finance, health, or productivity apps. It's ideal when the next step involves leaving your app's UI (e.g., handing off to Plaid's or another SDK's authentication flow) and you need informed consent plus a fallback path for users who decline the primary integration.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed consent screen for low-risk, non-sensitive actions where it would only add friction (e.g., toggling a UI theme or basic app permission that doesn't involve financial/personal data sharing). Also avoid presenting this without a genuine manual/alternative path (if declining the third-party service simply dead-ends the user, the added disclosure will increase frustration and drop-off rather than build trust).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday consumers linking a bank account to a peer-to-peer payments app (Venmo), a moment of heightened financial-privacy sensitivity. The psychological triggers include: trust transference (leveraging the recognized Plaid brand and legal disclosures to borrow credibility), loss-aversion mitigation (offering a manual alternative so security-conscious users don't abandon the flow entirely), and reduction of ambiguity/anxiety (explicitly stating what data is used for and how to revoke access). This pattern is essential for fintech products where data-sharing consent directly impacts conversion and regulatory compliance.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Permission priming before third-party handoff: Explains what Plaid will access and why before triggering the actual bank-linking flow, reducing surprise and drop-off.

  • Dual-path CTA: Primary "Next" (Plaid/instant) and secondary "Verify bank manually instead" give users control and prevent hard stops for privacy-conscious users.

  • Proactive privacy reassurance: Preemptively explains how to revoke the Plaid connection, reducing anxiety without the user needing to search settings or FAQs.

  • Regulatory transparency: NMLS ID and PayPal entity disclosure at the footer builds institutional trust for a money-handling feature.

  • Non-disruptive modal presentation: Bottom sheet over a dimmed background preserves context and signals reversibility/low commitment.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 24
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for manual bank account linking flows in fintech, banking, payroll, or investment apps where instant bank verification (e.g., Plaid/Yodlee) isn't available or the user opts out. It's ideal any time you're asking users to input sensitive financial identifiers and there will be a multi-day delay before the action is complete (always pair delayed/invisible processes with clear upfront expectation-setting copy).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavier, delayed-verification pattern when a real-time bank-linking API is available, as forcing users through manual entry and a 3-day wait when instant verification exists adds unnecessary friction and drop-off risk. Also avoid over-explaining if the audience is already familiar with the flow (e.g., repeat users), as lengthy explanatory text can feel redundant and slow down power users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users who either don't use a supported instant-bank-login provider (e.g., smaller regional/credit union banks) or who are wary of sharing their bank credentials with a third-party aggregator. These users tend to be more privacy- and security-conscious, so the design compensates by leaning heavily on trust signals (lock icon, transparent explanation of the verification mechanism) rather than speed.

The psychological trigger at play is uncertainty reduction: financial actions involving real money movement trigger loss-aversion anxiety, so the copy and iconography work together to make an unusual process (small deposits/withdrawals over days) feel expected, safe, and legitimate rather than suspicious.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Security-signaling iconography: The prominent lock icon is placed before any sensitive data entry, priming users psychologically for a "safe" data exchange before they see the input fields.

  • Pre-emptive expectation-setting: Explaining the micro-deposit verification process in advance prevents user panic or fraud alerts when small unfamiliar transactions appear on their statement.

  • Confirm Account Number field: A double-entry validation pattern that guards against a high-cost, hard-to-reverse error (misdirected ACH transfer) - an appropriate use of friction given the stakes.

  • Escape hatch via "Done": Presented as a dismissible modal rather than a forced, un-exitable step, respecting user autonomy in a sensitive financial flow.

results.query: OTP 6-digit verification Text field with automatic SMS autofill

screens.name: Craft Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any email or SMS-based OTP verification step, including account creation, passwordless login, password reset, or sensitive action confirmation (e.g., changing payment details). It's ideal when security requires a secondary channel of trust but you still want to preserve a fast, low-friction experience.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, single-purpose full-screen treatment for low-stakes confirmations where a lighter inline or toast-based verification would suffice. Also avoid if your user base frequently has delayed email delivery without a resend/countdown timer (the screen as shown lacks a visible resend button or cooldown timer, which could frustrate users whose codes take longer than expected to arrive).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets any user who has just signed up or triggered a passwordless/2FA login flow (essentially all new or security-conscious users across consumer apps, fintech, SaaS, and marketplaces). It leans on the psychological principles of commitment and momentum (the user has already invested effort by entering their email, so a short, frictionless final step keeps them moving toward task completion) and trust-building through transparency (showing exactly where the code was sent reduces anxiety about phishing or misrouted communications). The auto-advancing numeric keypad also taps into the user's expectation of low-effort, "it just works" interactions common in modern mobile UX.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-surfaced numeric keypad: Matches input type to the keyboard shown, eliminating friction and keypad-switching taps.

  • Segmented 3+3 code input: Grouping digits visually (like a phone number) improves scannability and reduces entry errors.

  • Email address embedded in the headline: Builds confidence that the code was routed to the correct account without requiring the user to recall it themselves.

  • Proactive spam-folder nudge: Anticipates the most frequent drop-off reason and resolves it inline instead of waiting for a support request.

  • Minimal chrome: Single back arrow and no tab bar keeps the user locked into the verification task with no escape routes other than going back.

screens.name: Craft Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any two-factor authentication, email/phone verification, or sensitive action confirmation flow where a short numeric or alphanumeric code must be validated. It's ideal whenever the code is delivered via a channel (SMS/Email) that the OS can automatically parse for autofill, significantly reducing drop-off during security-critical moments like sign-up, login, or checkout verification.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the code delivery channel cannot be parsed by the OS (e.g., a third-party authenticator app code that isn't SMS/Email-based), as the autofill benefit disappears and users will face full manual entry friction. Also avoid lengthy delays in code delivery without a visible countdown/resend timer, as users may assume the system failed and abandon the flow before the email/SMS arrives.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is aimed at any user undergoing account security verification (typically during sign-up, login from a new device, or sensitive account changes (like password reset)). It targets general consumer audiences who are not tech-savvy and may be frustrated by friction; the autofill integration is a psychological relief mechanism that reduces perceived effort and task abandonment.

The pattern exploits the "reduce cognitive load" principle: by removing manual memorization and typing of a 6-digit number, the design taps into users' aversion to tedious, error-prone tasks, which is especially critical on mobile where app-switching to retrieve a code is cumbersome.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native OTP AutoFill Integration: Surfacing the code via the iOS QuickType bar ("From Gmail: 326945") removes nearly all manual effort, turning a tedious copy-paste task into a single tap.

  • Explicit Email Confirmation: Restating the destination email address reassures the user that the system is working correctly and reduces confusion if they manage multiple inboxes (especially relevant given the test '+3' alias suffix shown).

  • Proactive Spam Folder Nudge: Anticipating delivery failure and giving a self-serve fix lowers support burden and keeps users from feeling stuck.

  • Segmented Code Input Styling: Grouping digits (3 2 6 / 9 4 _) visually communicates progress and expected length without needing a counter or label.

screens.name: Craft Onboarding 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for short, unpredictable-duration waits such as API calls, authentication, or screen-to-screen transitions where the next screen's layout is already known. It's especially effective when you can blur the actual destination screen's skeleton, as it previews structure and smooths the transition. Pair with skeleton loaders for longer waits or when content shape needs to be more explicitly communicated.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid relying solely on an indeterminate spinner for processes that take longer than a few seconds (users lose confidence without a determinate progress indicator or time estimate). Also avoid this on first-run/cold-start splash screens where branding opportunity is lost; a logo-based splash is more appropriate there. If the blurred background doesn't match the actual incoming content, it can create a jarring mismatch when the real content snaps into place.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern serves any general consumer-facing app audience during moments of data fetching, authentication checks, or screen transitions (e.g., post-login, post-onboarding-step, or app cold start after splash). Psychologically, it leverages the "progress illusion" - showing movement (the spinner) and shape (the blur) to make the wait feel shorter and more intentional than an abrupt blank or frozen screen, which can trigger anxiety that the app has crashed.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Blurred content preview instead of blank screen: Using a gaussian-blurred ghost of the underlying layout gives users a subconscious cue that content is "almost there," reducing perceived latency compared to a stark white screen.

  • Indeterminate spinner for unknown duration tasks: Signals ongoing activity without over-promising a specific completion time, appropriate for network calls of variable length.

  • Minimal visual noise: Stripping away all text and chrome during the loading state prevents cognitive load and keeps focus on the single animating element.

screens.name: Craft Onboarding 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Early onboarding flows where personalization will be used throughout the app experience (greetings, personalized content, certificates).

  • Signup flows for apps that defer full account creation (email/password) until after rapport is built with lighter-weight questions.

  • Any multi-step wizard where breaking a form into atomic single-purpose screens would reduce perceived effort and abandonment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for transactional or utility apps where users expect speed and have no need for personalization (e.g., a quick calculator tool) - it adds unnecessary friction.

  • Not ideal in B2B/enterprise contexts where account provisioning is tied to company directories/SSO, making manual name entry redundant.

  • Risky if overused across many sequential single-field screens, as it can make onboarding feel artificially long and tedious if not paced with progress indicators.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets new users in the critical first-session window, where every point of friction risks drop-off. By personalizing the product early with the user's name, the app can later use their first name in greeting copy, push notifications, and emails (a well-documented psychological trigger (the "own name effect") that increases perceived relevance and emotional investment in the product). This is broadly applicable to consumer apps (fitness, finance, social, edtech) that want to build a relationship-driven, personalized experience from the very first interaction.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-Question Focus: Isolating just the name fields on their own screen dramatically increases completion rates versus a long multi-field registration form.

  • Auto-Focused Keyboard: The keyboard is already active on load, removing a tap and accelerating time-to-input.

  • Disabled State Button: The grayed-out "Continue" CTA provides a clear, low-pressure visual cue of form completion status without needing an error message.

  • Native Autofill Leverage: Surfacing the OS-level QuickType name suggestion dramatically reduces the effort required to complete the step.

screens.name: Oportun Login 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for returning-user authentication screens in any mobile app, especially those where speed and low cognitive load are priorities (fintech, e-commerce, utility apps). It's ideal when:

  • The app already has a separate onboarding/sign-up flow, so this screen can stay lean.

  • Biometric authentication (Face ID/Touch ID) is supported by the underlying OS/device.

  • You want to minimize drop-off by removing all non-essential content from the critical conversion path.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this ultra-minimal approach when:

  • The product needs to reinforce brand identity or trust signals at every touchpoint (e.g., a brand-new fintech app might want a logo or security badge visible for reassurance).

  • Users are likely to need more guidance (e.g., first-time users, less tech-savvy audiences) - in these cases, visible field labels and inline validation messaging are preferable to placeholder-only labels.

  • The disabled button pattern isn't paired with any inline hint about why it's disabled, which can confuse users if the empty-state reasoning isn't obvious.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for existing, returning users who already have an account and simply need to re-authenticate (likely arrived via a "Log in" CTA from a preceding welcome/splash screen). The inclusion of a Face ID toggle targets users on biometric-capable devices who value speed and low friction on subsequent logins, appealing to the psychological principle of reducing perceived effort for habitual actions.

The disabled-until-valid button leverages a subtle error-prevention psychology: rather than letting users fail and see an error, the interface withholds affordance until the input is plausible, reducing frustration and reinforcing a sense of guided competence.

The stark, no-frills visual design also builds trust for a security-sensitive task (over-designed login screens can feel less "serious," whereas this austere approach mirrors patterns seen in banking and fintech apps where credibility and focus are paramount).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Face ID toggle inline on the login form: rather than only offering biometrics after a first successful manual login, the toggle is exposed immediately, letting returning users opt in proactively.
