Overusing decorative illustration on a money app aimed at high-frequency power users may feel like unnecessary friction or "fluff" instead of efficiency.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets a broad, mainstream mobile payments audience (both first-time users being onboarded gently into the ecosystem, and repeat users who need fast access to peer-to-peer payments and merchant offers. The empty "People" state specifically targets new users, using social-proof-adjacent framing ("people who you've recently paid") to imply the feature is normal and habitual once adopted. The "Spend and earn" and "Explore" sections target monetization/retention personas) casual users who might otherwise only open the app rarely (by injecting rewards, offers, and lifestyle use cases (dining, movies) to increase session frequency beyond pure bill-splitting or transfers). The overall trust-first, whitespace-heavy design speaks to a risk-averse financial user who needs calm, uncluttered visual cues before performing money-based actions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent floating CTA: The pill-shaped "New payment" button stays anchored mid-screen, guaranteeing the core action is always reachable without hunting through menus.

  • Educational empty state: Instead of a blank "People" section, a dashed placeholder avatar plus explanatory copy turns a void into an onboarding cue.

  • Localized hero illustration: Region-specific art (Merlion, Singapore icons) personalizes a global utility app and builds emotional warmth atop a purely functional product.

  • Card-based modular content: Explore and Spend & Earn sections use uniform card tiles, allowing Google to merchandise new services (food, movies, offers) without redesigning the core navigation.

  • Top-corner utility icons: Scan/QR icon and avatar are tucked into corners, keeping the primary canvas free for content while preserving one-tap access to camera-based payments and account settings.

screens.name: Google Pay Pre-Onboarding 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for early-onboarding jurisdiction, language, or regional variant selection when a product's core functionality (currency, compliance, payment rails, legal terms) fundamentally differs by country. Ideal when the option set is small (2-5 items) and can be fully displayed without scrolling or search. Pre-fill with a smart default from device locale/IP whenever possible to minimize interaction cost.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this flat-list approach if supporting dozens or hundreds of countries (at that scale, a searchable list or combobox is required to prevent excessive scrolling). Also avoid gating this early if the region selection isn't truly critical to core functionality, as any mandatory pre-step before value delivery increases drop-off risk unless it's absolutely necessary (as it is here for payment compliance).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets brand-new installers across multiple geographies (India, Singapore, US being Google Pay's distinct regional product variants, each with different backend rails like UPI vs. cards). The psychological trigger at play is reduction of decision fatigue: by pre-selecting the most probable answer, Google leverages the default effect to accelerate the user past a mandatory but low-engagement step as quickly as possible, preserving momentum toward the "aha moment" of adding a card or making a payment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Default Pre-Selection: Auto-checking the likely country (based on locale) turns a decision screen into a single-tap confirmation screen for most users.

  • Radical Minimalism: Only three options and zero decorative elements keep focus entirely on the one required action.

  • Graceful Exclusion Messaging: The footer disclaimer preempts frustration for unsupported regions instead of leaving users to guess why their country is missing.

  • Overflow Menu for Edge Cases: The "..." icon in the top right likely houses help/support links without cluttering the primary flow.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any identity or security verification step (phone, email, 2FA) in fintech, banking, or any app handling sensitive personal/financial data. It's ideal when you need to confirm real-world contact ownership before granting access to money-movement features, and when you want to minimize distraction so users complete the step quickly without confusion.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this bare-bones approach in contexts where users need more reassurance or guidance, such as first-time onboarding for less tech-savvy audiences who may not understand OTP conventions (here, additional micro-copy or an illustration explaining 'why we verify' would help). Also avoid indefinite or overly long resend timers, which frustrate users who legitimately did not receive the code; and don't use this stripped-down layout if the product needs to reinforce brand personality or emotional connection at this touchpoint.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets every Google Pay user at account setup or re-authentication (a universal, non-segmented audience since phone verification is mandatory for all). The psychological trigger at play is trust-through-friction: users psychologically associate a short, slightly annoying verification step with heightened security, which increases confidence in a financial app. The countdown timer also taps into loss-aversion/patience conditioning, subtly discouraging premature exits by giving a concrete, finite wait time rather than an ambiguous 'please wait.'
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native keyboard reuse: Leverages the OS-level numeric keypad instead of a custom in-app one, reducing engineering overhead and matching user muscle memory instantly.

  • Masked phone number confirmation: Shows (a blurred/obscured) destination number so the user has confidence the OTP is going to the right place without fully exposing PII on screen.

  • Segmented underline OTP field: Six discrete slots visually communicate exactly how many digits are expected, reducing input anxiety and errors.

  • Timed resend gating: The 00:27 countdown next to 'Request a new OTP' prevents accidental spam-tapping while still communicating that recovery is possible.

  • Radical minimalism: Removing all non-essential UI (illustrations, tips, branding) keeps focus entirely on the single task of digit entry.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 9
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this segmented-OTP-with-native-keypad pattern whenever:

  • You need to verify phone number or email ownership as part of onboarding, login, or a sensitive account change.

  • The code has a fixed, known length (4-8 digits) that can be visually chunked.

  • Speed and low cognitive load are priorities: e.g., financial, delivery, or ride-hailing apps where users are often in a hurry.

  • You want to discourage abuse of resend functionality without blocking the user from recovering permanently.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this exact pattern when:

  • The verification code has variable length or is alphanumeric (segmented boxes lose their visual clarity advantage and can feel constraining).

  • You're on a form with many other fields on the same screen; dedicating a full screen to just OTP entry would feel disproportionately heavy for a secondary or optional verification step.

  • Users may need to paste a code copied from an email/SMS app (ensure paste support is included, as purely segmented inputs sometimes block clipboard paste, causing frustration).

  • Accessibility is a major concern for very low-vision users (six discrete tap targets can be harder to navigate with screen readers than a single labeled field).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves virtually every Google Pay user at a critical trust-and-safety gate, during initial account setup, adding a new payment method, or re-authenticating after a suspicious login. Because Google Pay moves real money, verifying phone ownership is a foundational anti-fraud control that protects both the user and Google from account takeover and unauthorized transactions.

Psychologically, the design leans on reduction of friction under urgency: users entering an OTP are almost always mid-task (trying to complete a payment or finish setup) and want zero cognitive overhead. The progressive visual feedback (underline fill) taps into the same completion-bias psychology as a progress bar (each digit typed feels like a small win, keeping momentum high and abandonment low).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented digit boxes with progressive underline fill: Turns an abstract 6-digit code into a visual progress bar, giving the user constant positive feedback as they type.

  • Auto-advancing cursor: The blinking caret automatically jumps to the next empty slot, so the user never has to manually tap between fields.

  • Countdown-gated resend CTA: Prevents abuse/spam while transparently telling the user exactly when they'll regain control, avoiding dead-end frustration.

  • Full-bleed native keypad: Uses the system numeric keyboard instead of a custom one, ensuring familiarity, correct key hit-targets, and haptic consistency with the OS.

  • Masked destination display: Shows a redacted/blurred phone number to confirm the OTP's destination without fully exposing PII on screen.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 10
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any identity or account-security verification step (phone, email, 2FA) in flows where speed and trust are paramount (financial apps, fintech onboarding, or any registration gate requiring SMS-based verification. It's especially valuable when the OTP can be programmatically read (via SMS Retriever API / Autofill APIs) to eliminate manual copy-paste friction. Use the segmented-box UI whenever the code has a fixed, short length (4) 8 digits) to aid scanning and error detection.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid auto-submission when the OTP length or format is unpredictable, or when users might need to review/edit the code before submitting (e.g., in regions with unreliable SMS parsing, where false-positive autofill could trigger premature, incorrect submissions). This pattern should be avoided if the platform doesn't reliably support SMS autofill (e.g., certain Android OEM restrictions or web contexts without the WebOTP API), since users would then face empty boxes but expect the app to "know" the code, increasing confusion. Also avoid over-blurring or hiding the phone number entirely without an option to reveal/edit it, since users need to confirm they're verifying the correct number.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets every new or returning Google Pay user attempting to link/verify a phone number (an near-universal audience given phone-number verification is often the very first mandatory step in a payments app, essential for both identity assurance and regulatory compliance (KYC)). The psychological driver here is reducing perceived effort and anxiety around security steps: financial onboarding is inherently trust-sensitive, and users are primed to abandon flows that feel slow or overly manual. By auto-filling and auto-submitting the OTP, Google Pay leverages the "path of least resistance" principle, keeping momentum in the funnel and minimizing drop-off at a step known for high abandonment rates industry-wide.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Autofill + Auto-Verify: The OTP is automatically read from SMS and submitted without requiring the user to tap "Continue," collapsing two steps into one and removing manual entry friction entirely.

  • Segmented digit boxes: Each digit occupies its own cell, making the code highly scannable and reducing perceived complexity versus a single long text field.

  • Inline loading state within the input row: Rather than a separate spinner or full-screen loader, the seventh box repurposes itself into a circular progress indicator, keeping the loading feedback spatially tied to the action.

  • Masked phone number blur: The destination number is obscured (blurred) in this instance, a subtle privacy-conscious detail useful for screenshots/demos while preserving realistic layout proportions.

screens.name: Google Pay Login 11
screens.whereToUse:
• Consumer fintech apps where repeat transactions to a known set of people/merchants dominate usage (P2P payments, food delivery wallets, super-apps).

  • Apps needing to soften a utilitarian task (money transfer) with brand personality via a hero illustration.

  • Home screens that must balance promotional real estate with core task shortcuts without letting marketing overwhelm utility.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise or B2B finance tools where balance/ledger data is more critical than a "who to pay" contact list, burying account balance below the fold would frustrate power users.

  • Apps serving a high volume of one-off/unknown-payee transactions, where a contact-first UI adds friction instead of removing it.

  • Compliance-heavy contexts where a playful, emoji-driven promo tone could undermine perceived trust or seriousness (e.g., wealth management, insurance).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves a mass-market, mobile-first consumer who already has an established social/payment graph (friends, group chats like "Foodies", local merchants) and wants near-instant repeat transactions. The design leans on familiarity and habit-formation psychology: by front-loading known contacts and businesses, it reduces the cognitive load of remembering names or numbers, exploiting the recognition heuristic.

The promotional banner exploits reward/lottery-style triggers (win vouchers) to nudge transaction frequency, targeting price-sensitive users in Southeast Asian markets where voucher/cashback culture drives app engagement. The gentle, illustrated splash panel signals Google's brand trust transplanted onto a financial use case, easing anxiety for users who may be new to digital payments.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dismissible, non-blocking promo banner: The travel deals card is contained and closable (X icon), respecting user attention without gating core functionality behind it.

  • Contact-first spoke navigation: Surfacing recent People and Businesses as tappable avatars turns "who do I pay" into a one-tap decision, mirroring the recall-over-recognition mental model used in messaging apps.

  • Persistent floating action button: "New payment" stays anchored regardless of scroll position, guaranteeing the core task is always one thumb-reach away.

  • Localized illustration as brand warmth layer: Region-specific art (Merlion, dragon boat) softens the utilitarian nature of a payments app and builds local relevance/trust.

  • Dual quick-entry icons in header: Scan (left) and Avatar/Profile (right) bookend the screen, covering the two most frequent non-list actions without extra taps.

results.query: Progress Indicator multi-step stepper header for identity verification

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 17
screens.whereToUse: Use this single-field, justified-request pattern when collecting sensitive personal identifiers (SSN, tax ID, bank details) during onboarding. It's ideal for KYC/compliance flows in fintech, lending, insurance, or credit products where trust-building copy and minimal-friction UI are critical to reducing drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes or non-sensitive data collection, where the added justification copy and heavy visual staging would feel like unnecessary overhead. Also avoid isolating fields one-per-screen for lengthy forms with many low-risk fields, as this would elongate the flow unnecessarily and increase abandonment due to excessive step count.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users onboarding into a financial services or credit-tracking product (likely in the Indian market, given "PAN" = Permanent Account Number, an Indian tax ID). These users are typically financially engaged individuals seeking loans, credit score monitoring, or investment services who expect a secure, trustworthy, yet frictionless data collection process.

Psychologically, the design leverages reciprocity and value framing (explaining that PAN unlocks "accurate credit reports") to justify the sensitive ask, and reward/gamification cues (the gift icon) to leverage intermittent reinforcement, keeping users motivated to push through what could otherwise feel like an invasive step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Isolating the PAN number field from other data (name, address, etc.) minimizes overwhelm for a high-sensitivity field.

  • Contextual justification copy: Directly explains the “why” behind the data request, reducing perceived intrusiveness and building trust.

  • Reward affordance: A floating gift icon persists on-screen, hinting at a completion incentive to motivate users through friction-heavy KYC steps.

  • Editorial visual tone: Serif typography and lowercase headers elevate what is normally a dry compliance form into a premium-feeling experience.

  • Bottom-anchored progress bar: Subtly communicates flow progress without cluttering the primary content area.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 18
screens.whereToUse:
• Use during backend-heavy verification steps (KYC, credit checks, identity verification) where the user must wait for a third-party API response.

  • Ideal for financial, insurance, or lending apps where trust signals and data-privacy reassurance are critical to prevent abandonment.

  • Effective when the wait time is unpredictable and you want to keep users engaged with meaningful status updates rather than a generic spinner.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, message-dense loading pattern for very short (sub-second) loading operations, where a simple spinner or skeleton screen would be less distracting. Also avoid over-explaining technical backend steps ("fetching questions from bureau") to users in non-financial contexts where such transparency adds no value and could feel like unnecessary jargon. If the actual data flow is not privacy-safe, avoid making explicit "we don't store your data" claims, as this creates legal and trust liabilities if untrue.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially engaged, credit-conscious users (CRED's core demographic of high-credit-score individuals) who are applying for a new credit product and are being asked to authorize a credit bureau soft/hard pull. This is a psychologically sensitive moment because users are wary of unnecessary credit inquiries affecting their score, and of sharing PII with third parties.

The design leverages the anxiety-reduction principle: by explaining what is happening ("fetching questions from bureau") and reassuring on data handling, it reduces drop-off during a step where users have no control and might otherwise abandon the flow due to uncertainty or distrust.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-layer progress communication: A high-level reassuring headline paired with a granular, technical status label ("FETCHING QUESTIONS FROM BUREAU") gives users both emotional comfort and functional transparency.

  • Privacy-first trust card: Explicitly stating "CRED does not store your data" with a lock icon during a moment of high data-sensitivity (credit bureau pull) directly targets and defuses the user's primary objection to continuing.

  • Premium serif typography: Using a serif font for the headline on a pure black background elevates the perceived trustworthiness and premium positioning of the brand, differentiating it from generic banking apps.

  • Persistent security badges: Displaying PCI-DSS, encryption, and card network logos even on a loading screen (not just checkout) reinforces security at every touchpoint of the sensitive data flow.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 19
screens.whereToUse:
• Identity verification flows for fintech, banking, or credit-reporting apps where OTP alone is insufficient.

  • Fraud-prevention checkpoints before granting access to sensitive account linking or credit data.

  • Any KYC/AML compliance step requiring proof of "something you know" beyond standard credentials.

  • Multi-step verification wizards where breaking questions into single-focus screens reduces abandonment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for low-stakes, casual onboarding flows where it would feel excessive or intrusive and increase drop-off.

  • Not suitable when the underlying data source is unreliable, as incorrect "correct answers" (e.g., outdated loan records) will wrongly block legitimate users and damage trust.

  • Should not be used as the sole authentication factor for highly sensitive actions (it works best combined with OTP/2FA, not as a replacement).

  • Avoid vague or ambiguous multiple-choice options; if the user genuinely doesn't recognize any option (e.g., data mismatch), there should always be a "None of these" or skip/escalation path to prevent hard lockouts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets users attempting to link financial accounts, unlock a credit report, or verify identity within a fintech "credit management" app like CRED. The primary psychological trigger is trust and security assurance: financial apps must overcome deep-seated user hesitancy to share personal financial history. By asking a question that only the real account holder could answer, the flow leverages a sense of "this app really knows my exact financial history," which paradoxically increases user trust in the platform's legitimacy and data partnerships (e.g., credit bureaus).

The demographic is likely urban, credit-card-owning, financially literate Indian users (SBI, RuPay presence) who are accustomed to formal bank verification steps and expect this level of rigor before being granted access to sensitive financial features.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Knowledge-Based Authentication (KBA): Uses obscure personal financial history (loan institution names) that only the genuine user would recognize, making it far more secure than OTP or password-based checks alone.

  • Explicit Privacy Reassurance: The "CRED does not store your responses" microcopy directly counters user anxiety about sharing sensitive financial data at the exact decision point.

  • Trust Badges Placement: Payment network and PCI-DSS compliance logos are anchored right below the CTA, reinforcing security credibility at the moment of commitment.

  • Single-Question Focus: Isolating one decision per screen (versus a long form) minimizes error rate and cognitive fatigue during a high-stakes verification flow.

  • Disabled CTA State: Submit button remains visually inactive until a choice is made, preventing premature/empty submissions.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 20
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech or lending apps requiring step-up identity verification beyond SMS/email OTP (e.g., for high-value transactions, credit report access, loan disbursal).

  • Any KYC/AML compliance flow where knowledge-based authentication is an available/legal method to confirm identity.

  • Screens where reducing user anxiety around data privacy is critical to completion rates (use explicit "we don't store this" style disclaimers).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for low-stakes or casual data collection (the heavy, serious tone would feel jarring and overly bureaucratic for non-critical actions).

  • Do not use if the underlying data source is unreliable or frequently outdated, as an incorrect "correct answer" (e.g., wrong bank name on file) will incorrectly lock out legitimate users, causing severe frustration and support tickets.

  • Not suitable for markets/users where credit bureau data coverage is thin, as many users may not recognize any of the presented options.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing or prospective CRED users undergoing credit-linked verification, typically triggered when checking a credit score, applying for a CRED loan/EMI product, or unlocking a new financial feature that requires proof of identity beyond OTP.

The psychological trigger at play is authority and legitimacy signaling: by asking a question that only official credit bureaus would have record of (past loan issuers), the app subconsciously convinces the user that CRED has deep, verified access to their credit history (which increases perceived security and trustworthiness of the platform). Simultaneously, the stark, serious visual design reduces the likelihood of the user treating this step frivolously, increasing focus and answer accuracy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-Question Focus: Isolating one KYC question per screen prevents overwhelm and reduces error rates on a high-stakes verification task.

  • Explicit Privacy Disclaimer: "CRED does not store your responses" preemptively neutralizes the user's biggest objection/fear at the exact moment of highest sensitivity.

  • Borrowed Trust Signals: Reusing payment security badges (PCI-DSS, card networks) on a non-payment KYC screen to transfer established e-commerce trust cues to an identity-verification context.

  • Distractor Design: The multiple-choice options are non-obvious (mix of real and plausible-but-wrong bank names), which is a hallmark of legitimate bureau-based identity verification (similar to Experian's "out-of-wallet" questions).

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 21
screens.whereToUse:
• Multi-step financial or identity verification flows where an external, latency-prone API call (bank, KYC, credit bureau) is in progress.

  • Any process where user action (navigating away, closing app) could break the verification, requiring explicit "stay here" messaging.

  • Onboarding sequences where you want to maintain brand tone and reduce perceived wait-time anxiety through custom illustration rather than a generic spinner.

  • Situations needing to reinforce trust via third-party/partner branding (bank, payment network) during a sensitive handoff.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for very short loading states (under 1-2 seconds) - the elaborate illustration and copy would feel like overkill and could actually make the wait feel longer.

  • Not suitable when the underlying process is instantly cancellable or reversible; the "don't leave" messaging implies real stakes and shouldn't be used for trivial actions.

  • Should not be used without an actual progress mechanism (skeleton, determinate bar) if the wait can be long (indefinite dark screens with no time estimate can increase abandonment for waits over 10-15 seconds).

  • Avoid mixing unrelated engagement elements (like the gift icon) if they risk distracting users from a critical security-sensitive task.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users in the middle of a high-stakes fintech onboarding flow (likely linking a bank account for UPI-based payments (common in Indian fintech apps like a neobank, wallet, or investment app)). At this exact moment, users are psychologically primed for anxiety: they've just handed over sensitive banking details and are waiting for an external verification. The design leverages calm, confident language and premium visual polish (serif type, dark theme, smooth animation) to reduce this anxiety and project institutional trustworthiness, borrowing credibility from the recognizable Axis Bank/UPI marks.

The persistent reward icon suggests this product uses gamification/incentive loops (e.g., referral rewards, cashback) as a core retention mechanic, targeting younger, digitally-native users who respond to game-like engagement even in utilitarian banking flows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom illustrated loader: Instead of a generic spinner, a bespoke dial-and-layers illustration communicates "secure connection being built," reinforcing brand identity even in a transient state.

  • Explicit behavioral instruction: "Stay on this screen while we verify your account" directly reduces drop-off/failure caused by users backgrounding the app mid-verification.

  • Persistent gamification affordance: The floating gift/reward icon remains accessible even during a technical wait state, subtly reinforcing an engagement loop without distracting from the primary task.

  • Trust-building partner branding: Axis Bank and UPI logos are prominently placed to reassure users that a licensed financial institution is handling the sensitive connection.

  • Editorial typography: Serif headline paired with tracked uppercase label gives a premium, calm tone to an otherwise stressful "waiting on bank" moment.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 22
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when requesting sensitive, high-friction permissions (e.g., linking bank accounts, enabling biometrics, or requesting location) during a setup flow. It is highly effective when the action requires an external verification step (like an SMS confirmation) because it preempts confusion. It is best suited for finance, banking, or utility apps where building immediate trust is paramount to the user's decision to proceed.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, benefit-justification approach for low-stakes or non-sensitive permissions where a simple system dialog would suffice, as it may cause unnecessary friction. Additionally, avoid dark, high-contrast text-heavy screens like this if the target demographic includes older, less tech-savvy users who may find low-contrast body text (as seen in the grey"we will send an sms" copy) difficult to read.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new users of a mobile payments app (likely a Neobank or UPI-based wallet in India) who have already downloaded the app and are moving through the initial account setup. The psychological trigger relies heavily on the Sunk Cost/Endowment effect ("Almost There") to push users through the final friction point of linking sensitive bank data. It also uses Trust Transference by prominently displaying the "Axis Bank" and official "UPI" logos, borrowing credibility from established, regulated financial institutions to reassure the user that their data is safe with this potentially newer or lesser-known app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparency Box: Explicitly explaining that "we will send an SMS to your bank" demystifies the technical background process, significantly reducing user hesitation before granting permissions.

  • Progress Signaling: The "ALMOST THERE" label combined with the bottom progress bar reduces perceived effort and combats onboarding drop-off by indicating the finish line is near.

  • Value-First Benefit Tag: The green checkmark benefit ("lightening fast payments") reframes a technical requirement (linking bank details) into a tangible user benefit.

  • High-Contrast CTA: The solid white button against the black background ensures the single required action is impossible to miss, driving a clear, singular path forward.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 23
screens.whereToUse: Use this permission-priming + progress-reassurance pattern whenever an app must request a sensitive OS-level permission (SMS, contacts, location, camera) mid-onboarding, especially in regulated or trust-sensitive verticals like fintech, healthcare, or identity verification. It's ideal right before a native permission dialog, at a point where the user has already invested some effort (so framing it as "almost there" feels earned rather than manipulative).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the permission being requested is not clearly necessary for the stated benefit, overpromising ("simpler payments") while requesting broad SMS read access can backfire and increase distrust if users later feel the permission scope exceeds the stated purpose. Also avoid heavy stylistic flourishes (serif fonts, dark themes) if your brand identity is already established with a different visual language, as inconsistency can undercut trust. Not suitable for low-stakes permissions where a simple one-line native prompt would suffice without added friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers in India setting up a UPI-linked payment app (e.g., for peer-to-peer transfers, bill pay, or merchant payments). The audience skews toward mobile-first, mass-market users who may be wary of granting SMS permissions due to privacy/security concerns around banking apps.

Psychologically, the screen leverages:

  • Reciprocity/Momentum: "Almost there" plus a completed checkmark exploits the sunk-cost/goal-gradient effect (users are more motivated to finish a task the closer they perceive themselves to be to completion).

  • Reduced Ambiguity Anxiety: Clearly stating why SMS access is needed removes the fear of "why does this app want to read my texts," a major trust barrier in financial apps.

  • Authority/Trust Transfer: Displaying a recognized bank (Axis Bank) and UPI logos borrows institutional credibility to reduce perceived risk.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Permission Priming before OS prompt: Explaining exactly what SMS access will be used for ("verify your phone number") before triggering the native permission dialog is a best-practice pattern that dramatically improves acceptance rates.

  • Progress reassurance microcopy: "ALMOST THERE" combined with a completed green checkmark reduces perceived remaining effort and fights onboarding fatigue/drop-off.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: Only one high-contrast button ("Continue to setup") is present, eliminating decision paralysis at a step where hesitation is costly.

  • Trust branding: "Powered by Axis Bank UPI" logos at the bottom leverage established financial institution credibility to offset anxiety about sharing SMS/phone data.

  • Ambient gamification teaser: The gift icon in the corner subtly seeds a rewards/referral hook without competing with the primary task.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 24
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for loyalty programs, gamified habit-trackers, subscription tier displays, or community/social apps where reinforcing a user's rank or membership status drives engagement and retention. It's especially effective in apps that want an aspirational, premium feel (space, cosmic, or fantasy themes work well for younger or hobbyist audiences).

Also well-suited to screens meant to be revisited often (e.g., a home/profile tab) since the ambient reward badge and progress visualization invite repeat check-ins.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, atmospheric visual treatment in utilitarian, task-focused apps (e.g., banking transaction screens, enterprise dashboards, healthcare tools) where users need fast, literal information rather than emotive theming.

It's also not ideal for accessibility-first contexts (low-contrast blurred text, dark backdrops, and small decorative iconography can hinder legibility for visually impaired users). Overuse of mystery/ambiguity (e.g., unlabeled progress rings) can also frustrate users who need clear, immediate understanding of their exact status or next steps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users in gamified or loyalty-driven products (such as fitness apps, fintech reward programs, gaming platforms, or subscription services) where retention depends on making users feel a sense of ongoing status and progression. The demographic is likely younger, digitally-native users familiar with game-like reward loops (levels, XP, unlockables) from mobile gaming or streaming platforms.

Psychologically, it leverages the endowed progress effect (showing a partially-filled ring makes users want to complete it), status signaling (naming and visually distinguishing a "Lunar" tier makes users want to advance to the next visible tier), and curiosity gap triggers (the unclaimed gift icon implies a reward is waiting, prompting exploration).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Avatar-as-progress-ring fusion: Merging the user's avatar with a circular progress track transforms a mundane progress bar into an identity-driven status symbol, increasing emotional investment in advancement.

  • Atmospheric dark theme with a single color accent: The near-monochrome cosmic palette makes the vivid pink gift icon and glowing planet pop instantly, guiding attention without any bright chrome or clutter.

  • Tier naming ("Lunar") as identity marker: Naming membership levels after celestial bodies creates a collectible, aspirational ladder (e.g., Lunar → Solar → Stellar) that taps into completionist psychology.

  • Floating reward beacon: The persistent gift icon acts as a lightweight, non-intrusive nudge that there's unclaimed value waiting, encouraging return visits and exploration.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 25
screens.whereToUse:
• Any onboarding or KYC/underwriting flow where a user may fail an automated eligibility check (loans, credit cards, BNPL, insurance).

  • Waitlist-based product launches where scarcity or gating is used intentionally (feature drops, beta access).

  • Situations where you want to retain a "rejected" or "not yet qualified" user in the funnel for future re-engagement rather than losing them entirely.

  • Any moment where you need to soften bad/negative news with empathetic copy and offer a constructive path forward.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this soft-landing/waitlist framing for regulated financial decisions where clear, compliant, unambiguous denial language is legally required (e.g., formal adverse action notices in the US under ECOA/FCRA) - softness can create compliance risk if it obscures the factual decision.

  • Don't use vague "financial irregularities" language without a way for users to see specifics or dispute errors; this can erode trust if users feel misled about a permanent rejection disguised as a "wait."

  • Not appropriate for time-sensitive transactional failures (e.g., payment processing errors) where users need immediate, clear resolution rather than a hopeful holding pattern.

  • Avoid if your brand voice is formal/enterprise: the casual lowercase, editorial tone would feel inconsistent for B2B or high-trust institutional financial products.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of a fintech/neobank credit product (likely younger or credit-building demographics (e).g., Gen Z, first-time credit card applicants, or those with thin/blemished credit files) who are more likely to be declined or deferred. These users are emotionally sensitive to rejection, especially around financial products, and are prone to abandoning the app entirely if told bluntly "no."

Psychologically, the screen leverages the loss aversion and sunk cost principles (by keeping the user "in line" (waitlisted) rather than rejected, it discourages them from switching to a competitor). The "what can you do next" section leverages the locus of control principle: giving people actionable steps reduces frustration with algorithmic decision-making and increases perceived fairness, even if those steps don't guarantee approval.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reframing rejection as anticipation: Instead of a blunt "you don't qualify" message, the copy positions the user as "on the waitlist," preserving hope and reducing emotional friction/churn.

  • Personalization: Using the user's first name in a large serif headline humanizes an automated decision engine's output.

  • Actionable next steps instead of a dead end: The "what can you do next?" module gives the user concrete levers (pay bills on time, verify info) to influence a seemingly opaque algorithmic decision, restoring a sense of control.

  • Opt-in re-engagement hook: The "Notify me" button captures continued interest/permission to re-contact the user later, turning a negative outcome into a retained lead.

  • Tonal softening via typography: Consistent lowercase and serif/sans-serif mixing reduces the perceived severity of a financial rejection.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 26
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately after account creation or KYC in fintech, banking, or subscription apps where users must complete multiple setup actions (verification, payment method linking, profile completion) before unlocking full value. It's ideal when you have 2-4 concrete, high-value next actions and want to increase activation rate without a rigid, forced wizard flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this loose, browsable card format when a task is legally or functionally mandatory (e.g., KYC compliance) - in those cases a forced, blocking Setup Wizard is more appropriate since users may skip optional-feeling cards. Also avoid the low-contrast, all-lowercase serif typography for elderly or accessibility-sensitive audiences, as it can reduce legibility and feel less authoritative for banking contexts requiring high trust and clarity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded users of CRED, a premium credit-card rewards app aimed at financially responsible, high-income/high-credit-score individuals in India. The tone assumes a sophisticated, design-conscious user who responds to minimalist luxury aesthetics rather than typical bright, busy banking UIs.

Psychologically, it leverages the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete tasks create mental tension) by explicitly listing "what can you do next," nudging users toward completing setup. It also uses social proof (7 million+ members) and authority/security signaling (PCI-DSS, card network logos) to overcome the natural skepticism users have about linking bank/credit details to a new app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Task Prioritization via Card UI: Converts an onboarding checklist into a visually engaging, swipeable card carousel rather than a plain bulleted to-do list, increasing perceived value of each action.

  • Strategic Trust Placement: The security/PCI-DSS/card network badges are placed directly after the "verify personal information" CTA, pre-emptively resolving the exact objection (data safety) a user would have at that moment.

  • Social Proof at Scale: "7 million+ members pay on CRED every month" uses the bandwagon effect to normalize the sensitive act of linking financial payment behavior to a third-party app.

  • Anxiety-Reducing Empathetic Copy: Framing FAQs around curiosity being "a valuable skill" is a subtle, humanizing brand touch rare in fintech onboarding flows.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for the first data-entry step of any account creation or onboarding funnel, especially in regulated industries (fintech, healthcare, insurance) where legal consent must be captured early. It's ideal when you want to:

  • Reduce drop-off by starting with the fewest possible fields.

  • Bundle legal/compliance consent invisibly into the primary CTA rather than an extra checkbox tap.

  • Signal multi-step progress without revealing the full length of the flow (avoiding "step 1 of 12" discouragement).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Regulatory requirements mandate an explicit, separately-checked consent checkbox rather than implied agreement via a button tap (some jurisdictions/GDPR contexts require this).

  • The flow needs to communicate exact progress length upfront (e.g., enterprise B2B forms where users expect to see "Step X of Y" for planning purposes).

  • Users are already authenticated elsewhere and re-entering credentials would feel redundant or annoying (in that case, a magic-link or SSO option may reduce friction better than a password field).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective users of Dave, a neobanking/fintech app aimed at budget-conscious consumers, often those who may have been underserved by traditional banks. The design leverages the commitment and consistency principle: by starting with an easy, low-effort action (email + password), users become psychologically invested and more likely to complete subsequent, harder steps (identity verification, linking a bank account, etc.).

The sparse layout and lack of distracting marketing content also reduces decision fatigue at a moment when the user has already decided to sign up (the job here is purely operational (credential creation), not persuasive, so the UI gets out of the way).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Minimal field count: Only two inputs are requested at this stage, deferring more sensitive/lengthy data (SSN, income, etc.) to later steps, which increases completion likelihood.

  • Implicit consent bundling: Legal agreement is tied to the primary action button rather than a separate checkbox, removing a friction point common in many sign-up flows.

  • Disabled CTA as guidance: The greyed "Agree and continue" button visually communicates incomplete input state without needing explicit error messaging.

  • Escape hatch preserved: The "X" close icon respects user autonomy and reduces the perceived risk of starting the flow.

  • Micro progress indicator: A subtle progress bar sets expectations of a multi-step journey without a discouraging step counter (e.g., "1 of 8").

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 5

Also avoid a bare progress bar without step labels/count if your flow is very long, as ambiguity about total steps can increase anxiety instead of reducing it; in such cases, use a numbered step indicator (e.g., "Step 1 of 5") instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

These users are often financially stressed and motivated by urgency, so the onboarding flow is deliberately kept short and low-friction to prevent abandonment before value is delivered.

Psychologically, the progress bar leverages the goal-gradient effect: users push harder to finish a task as they perceive proximity to completion (while the single-column, two-field form reduces the intimidation factor common in financial signups that typically require SSNs, bank links, and identity verification later in the funnel).
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 6

Pair with a visible progress bar to set expectations of a short, finite process.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes, high-familiarity forms (e.g., a simple login) where users expect to complete multiple fields on one screen and would find single-field pagination unnecessarily slow. Also avoid on flows where users are returning/repeat users who already expect a fast, one-screen experience (repeated screen transitions can feel tedious and increase abandonment for form types with many fields (e).g., 10+ step KYC without a clear payoff).

This screen's brevity and gentle tone directly counteract "form fatigue" and payday-loan shame by making sign-up feel more like a quick chat than a bank application. Requiring "legal name" upfront (rather than deferring it) is a regulatory necessity for a chartered banking product, but framing it as the very first, simplest step builds early trust and momentum before requesting more sensitive data (SSN, income, bank linking) in later steps.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 7

Also effective for any multi-step form where breaking fields into single-question screens will improve completion rates over a monolithic form.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users mid-way through account creation for a service that requires identity verification (likely fintech, given the green branding and security-forward tone reminiscent of apps like Cash App or Chime). The explicit security rationale also taps into trust-transfer: users are more willing to share sensitive data when the reason is framed around protecting their own account rather than the company's benefit.
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 8

Also avoid this pattern for high-frequency/low-friction re-authentication (e.g., app biometric unlock) where a full-page form would feel like unnecessary friction. screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users completing account creation or phone-based identity verification for a consumer app (likely retail, fintech, or subscription service given the SMS marketing consent language typical of US commerce apps). The design leverages the psychological principle of commitment and progress: the visible progress bar exploits the sunk-cost/completion bias, encouraging users to push through the friction of retrieving and typing a code rather than abandoning the flow.

The clean, uncluttered layout also targets users on mobile devices in potentially distracted contexts (checking a text message on another app/screen), so minimizing choices and text ensures the user can quickly refocus and complete the field.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progress indicator retention: Keeping the top progress bar visible reassures the user they are partway through a finite process, reducing onboarding drop-off anxiety.

  • Masked phone number: Balances confirmation (user trusts the right number was used) with privacy (full number not exposed on-screen).

  • Inline resend affordance: Placing "Resend code" immediately below the reference text preempts the most likely user friction point (delayed/lost SMS) without requiring navigation away from the screen.

  • Ethical opt-in default: The marketing consent checkbox defaults to unchecked, respecting user autonomy and reducing legal risk (a best-practice deviation from manipulative pre-checked patterns).

  • Single fixed CTA: One clear, large, thumb-friendly action button eliminates decision paralysis at a critical conversion point.

screens.name: Dave Creating Account 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when a product has regulatory or compliance-mandated fine print (banking, lending, insurance, subscriptions) that must legally accompany marketing claims. It's ideal for:

  • Account-opening or paywall screens in fintech apps where trust and legal transparency are paramount.

  • Any screen that must balance persuasive marketing copy with mandatory disclosures without overwhelming the primary conversion path.

  • Situations where a sticky, always-visible CTA is needed to keep conversion rate high despite lengthy supporting content.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy disclosure-dump approach in:

  • Low-stakes consumer apps (e.g., games, casual utilities) where legal fine print isn't required (it would feel unnecessarily bureaucratic and erode simplicity).

  • Screens where the fine print materially changes the offer's value (e.g., very high fees); burying critical caveats in gray footnotes can be seen as a dark pattern and damage long-term trust if the "free" claims are misleading.

  • Contexts requiring quick, one-tap decisions (e.g., in-line upsells) - a full-screen modal with this much text creates friction and drop-off if used too early or too often in a flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially underserved or paycheck-to-paycheck consumers considering a neobank/cash-advance product (Dave). These users are often highly price-sensitive and wary of hidden fees given past experiences with overdraft charges at traditional banks, so the design leans heavily on trust signals: FDIC insurance, fee-free ATM count, and 24/7 support.

Psychologically, the screen employs reciprocity and risk-reversal: by front-loading tangible perks (instant advances, free ATMs) before showing the fine print, users form a positive impression that primes them to accept the disclosures as a minor formality. The checkmark list also taps into the Zeigarnik/completion effect, visually suggesting these benefits are "unlocked" the moment the user signs up.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Card-contained benefit list: Grouping benefits in a shaded rounded container visually separates "sales pitch" from "legal text," letting users self-select their depth of engagement.

  • Checkmark iconography: Using checkmarks instead of bullets subtly implies these features are guaranteed/verified, increasing perceived trustworthiness.

  • Footnote superscripts: Numbers like "²" next to claims signal rigor and transparency without breaking the flow of the main benefit statement, letting power-users verify claims while casual users skim past.

  • "See Terms 1-5" link: Provides an explicit, low-visual-weight escape hatch for the legally cautious user, satisfying transparency requirements without cluttering the primary CTA path.

  • Persistent bottom CTA: The "Get Started" button remains anchored regardless of scroll position within the disclosures, reducing the number of scroll-to-convert steps.

screens.name: Dave Creating Account 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for:

  • Sensitive, regulated data collection (SSN, DOB, ID numbers) where trust and precision matter more than speed.

  • Multi-step onboarding or KYC/AML flows where breaking down a large form into single-question screens reduces abandonment.

  • Situations where you need to validate one discrete, unambiguous data point before proceeding (age gating, identity confirmation).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach when:

  • Collecting many simple, related fields (e.g., name + email + phone) where splitting into separate screens would create unnecessary friction and increase total time-to-complete.

  • The user base is highly task-driven and speed-sensitive (e.g., power users, B2B tools) where a consolidated single-page form is more efficient.

  • Network/data-fetch latency between micro-steps would introduce jarring loading delays for what should be an instant transition.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users onboarding into a regulated financial product (banking, neobank, crypto exchange, lending, or investment app) where KYC (Know Your Customer) and age/identity verification are legally mandated. The primary psychological trigger is trust-building through transparency: showing progress and framing questions simply reduces the anxiety typically associated with sharing sensitive personal data like birthdate.

The minimalist, distraction-free layout is designed for users who may already be experiencing onboarding fatigue after multiple prior steps (implied by the progress bar being ~40% filled), so the interface intentionally avoids adding any additional visual or cognitive burden.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field-per-screen design: Isolating one data point drastically reduces perceived effort and cognitive load compared to a long form.

  • Disabled CTA until valid input: Prevents errors proactively and gives a clear visual signal of form state without extra messaging.

  • Progress bar without step count: Shows tangible advancement through the flow, motivating completion (sunk cost / goal-gradient effect) without overwhelming the user with "Step 3 of 9" anxiety.

  • Dual exit affordances (back arrow + close X): Gives users control to either go back or abandon entirely, respecting user autonomy even in a mandatory compliance flow.

  • Conversational framing of a compliance requirement: Turns a rigid legal necessity into an approachable, low-friction micro-interaction.

screens.name: Dave Creating Account 6
screens.whereToUse:
• Any KYC/AML identity-verification step requiring SSN, national ID, or tax ID collection in fintech, neobank, or lending apps.

  • High-sensitivity data entry moments where user trust is fragile and drop-off risk is high.

  • Steps deep in a multi-step onboarding flow where a progress indicator can reduce perceived remaining effort.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy-friction, double-entry pattern for low-sensitivity or optional fields (it will feel like overkill and slow down casual data entry unnecessarily).

  • Do not use vague "bank-level security" reassurance without it being backed by real compliance/certifications, or in regions where such phrasing has no regulatory teeth (it can create a false sense of security).

  • Not suitable for contexts where the field can be validated/auto-verified instantly (e.g., via a trusted ID document scan), since manual double-entry becomes redundant extra effort.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Dave's target user is often underbanked, credit-invisible, or has been burned by predatory payday lenders and traditional banks in the past (this audience is inherently more skeptical about sharing an SSN with a mobile-only bank). The design directly addresses that skepticism with legal justification, security badging, and visual restraint (no ads, no upsells, no clutter) that signals seriousness and safety. Busy urban users completing account setup on the go need a fast, unambiguous form; the single-field-focus layout minimizes cognitive load and lets them complete this step in seconds, one-handed, without hunting for what's required.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Masked-by-default input with reveal toggle: Borrows the password-field convention to visually communicate that sensitive data is being safeguarded, even before any backend encryption occurs.

  • Double-entry confirmation field: Reduces silent typo errors on a field that cannot be easily auto-corrected or validated in real time, preventing costly identity-verification failures later in onboarding.

  • Regulatory framing as trust anchor: Citing "U.S. Federal Law" reduces the user's perception that Dave is being invasive, shifting the request from a company preference to a legal necessity.

  • Security microcopy placed adjacent to the CTA: Timed reassurance exactly at the decision point maximizes its persuasive/anxiety-reducing effect.

screens.name: Dave Creating Account 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Identity verification (KYC/AML) steps in banking, lending, or crypto onboarding flows.

screens.whereNotToUse:

  • Do not use for flows where data has already been verified upstream and re-confirmation adds redundant friction.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users onboarding into a regulated financial product (likely a cash-advance or banking app like Dave) who must pass identity verification to access credit or banking features. The design leverages the psychological principle of "commitment and consistency" - by having users actively review and confirm their own data, they become more personally invested in the accuracy of the submission, reducing fraud and typos. The explicit mention of SSA and Socure (a known identity-verification vendor) builds institutional trust by naming real regulatory/verification partners rather than hiding the process behind vague language, which reduces user anxiety around sharing an SSN. The single-column, low-decoration layout signals seriousness and reduces cognitive load so users focus solely on verifying accuracy rather than being distracted by branding or promotions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline Review-and-Edit Rows: Each data point (name, DOB, SSN, address) is independently tappable, letting users jump directly to fix a single field instead of restarting the entire form, reducing friction and abandonment risk at a highly sensitive step.

  • Dual Exit Points: Offering both a back arrow (edit/step back) and an X (abandon flow) gives users agency without trapping them, which is critical for trust in high-stakes financial data collection.

  • Bolded "IMPORTANT" Warning: A pre-emptive accuracy nudge reduces costly downstream verification failures caused by typos or mismatched legal names.

screens.name: Dave Creating Account 8

screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this full-screen blocking pattern for short operations (under 2-3 seconds), where a lightweight inline spinner or skeleton loader is less disruptive. Also avoid it if you can measure actual progress (e.g., file upload percentage) - in that case, a determinate progress bar builds more trust than an indeterminate spinner. Additionally, ensure a timeout/error fallback state exists; leaving users stuck on this screen indefinitely without an error path (e.g., "still confirming" after 5+ minutes) can severely damage trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users going through mandatory identity verification (KYC/AML) flows common in fintech, banking, crypto, or gig-economy driver/seller onboarding. These users are often slightly anxious about submitting sensitive personal documents (ID, selfie, SSN) and want reassurance that the system is actively working rather than frozen or lost. The psychological trigger at play is uncertainty reduction: by clearly communicating both the action ("confirming your identity") and the expected wait duration, the design curbs anxiety-driven behaviors like repeatedly force-closing the app or resubmitting forms.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose blocking screen: No tab bar, back button, or escape hatch is present, correctly signaling to the user that this step is mandatory and non-skippable.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Explicitly stating a time range ("a couple minutes") preempts user frustration and reduces premature app abandonment or support tickets during long verification calls.

  • Indeterminate loading pattern: Correctly chosen over a determinate progress bar since verification duration is variable and unpredictable, avoiding the false precision that could break trust if a progress bar stalls.

  • Minimalist visual design: Ample negative space and centered content reduce cognitive load and signal calm, controlled process rather than urgency or error.

screens.name: Dave Creating Account 9
