screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for demographic data collection, onboarding personalization quizzes, market research surveys, or KYC-style questionnaires where you need one clear answer per screen. It's ideal when data accuracy and completion rate both matter, especially on mobile where fat-finger errors on small radio buttons are common.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this full-screen, one-question-per-page approach for very long surveys with 20+ questions unless progress feedback and time estimates are provided (users may abandon due to fatigue). Also avoid for questions that require multiple selections without clearly switching the UI to a multi-select pattern, and avoid for time-sensitive transactional flows where a single-question-per-screen pace would feel unnecessarily slow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday users of the Dave personal finance app (likely a broad, mainstream demographic including underbanked or budget-conscious consumers). Collecting education level allows Dave to segment users for personalized financial content, targeted product recommendations (e.g., cash advances, banking tiers), or to sell aggregated demographic insights to partners/advertisers.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (progress bar creates a subtle desire to complete the unfinished task) and choice simplification (large, clearly labeled options reduce decision fatigue). The non-judgmental phrasing and full inclusion of all education levels also reduce social-desirability bias, encouraging honest responses.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Large, full-row tap targets: Instead of small radio buttons, the entire row is tappable, drastically improving mobile usability and reducing selection errors.

  • Immediate visual feedback: The selected answer flips to a bold teal fill with a white checkmark, giving instant, unmistakable confirmation of the user's choice.

  • Lightweight progress indicator: A subtle top progress bar communicates flow position without adding numeric pressure or clutter.

  • Single-question focus: Isolating one question per screen (single-screen form pattern applied iteratively) minimizes cognitive load and keeps completion rates high.

  • Persistent exit option: The "Close" button respects user autonomy, letting them abandon the optional survey without feeling trapped.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 13
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for optional, low-stakes data-collection surveys embedded within onboarding or in-app engagement flows (especially in fintech, health, or subscription apps where segmenting users (e).g., by employment, income bracket, or life stage) improves personalization or underwriting. Ideal when questions are mutually exclusive and benefit from large touch targets (e.g., mobile-first, thumb-friendly forms). Also effective when some answers require additional detail, since the chevron/expand affordance keeps the primary flow uncluttered while still enabling deeper data capture.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, one-question-per-screen approach for long surveys with many questions, as excessive screen transitions can fatigue users and increase drop-off; consider grouping related quick-answer questions instead. Not suitable for mandatory, business-critical data (e.g., KYC/compliance forms) where skipping via "Close" would leave incomplete records (in those cases, use a blocking wizard instead). Also avoid disabled-button-only validation for accessibility-critical flows; screen reader users benefit from explicit inline error messaging in addition to a disabled state.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of Dave, a mobile banking/cash-advance app whose core users are often financially stretched individuals (gig workers, hourly employees, students) who need quick access to credit or banking insights. Collecting employment status helps Dave's underwriting/personalization engine tailor credit limits, financial advice, or eligibility for cash advances.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (visible progress bar creates a desire to complete an unfinished task) and choice simplification (four broad categories instead of an open text field) to reduce friction and abandonment. The disabled button leverages a subtle affordance cue that guides users toward the "correct" next action without explicit error messaging, which is less punishing and more encouraging (important for a financial-wellness brand trying to build trust with users who may already feel financial stress or shame).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-question-per-screen pacing: Isolating one question at a time minimizes cognitive load and increases completion rates compared to long, scrollable forms.

  • Chevron-per-option progressive disclosure: Each answer choice can expand to reveal follow-up detail, letting the form stay simple by default while still capturing granular data when needed.

  • Disabled CTA until valid input: The greyed-out "Continue" button acts as a built-in validation cue, preventing null submissions without needing an error toast.

  • Persistent progress bar: A slim top progress indicator sets expectations about survey length, reducing abandonment by showing the user is making measurable progress.

  • Non-committal exit path: The visible "Close" button respects user autonomy, an important trust signal for optional data-collection flows.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 14
screens.whereToUse: Use this single-question, opt-outable, progressively-disclosed pattern for any legally or ethically sensitive demographic data collection (race, gender, income bracket) in onboarding or profile-completion surveys. It's ideal when the data isn't required to unlock core functionality but is valuable for personalization, compliance reporting, or fair-lending audits.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when demographic data is mandatory for account creation, forcing sensitive disclosures early increases drop-off. Do not use a playful or humorous tone here, as it risks trivializing sensitive personal identity data. Also avoid stacking many single-question screens back-to-back without a visible progress indicator, as this can make an already sensitive survey feel endless and invasive.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets Dave's broad "Busy Urban" user base during account setup or periodic profile enrichment, likely used for internal analytics, compliance (e.g., fair lending/EEOC-style reporting), or personalized financial content. Because Dave serves underbanked and diverse urban communities, capturing race/ethnicity data responsibly signals to users that the company is tracking equitable access to its cash-advance and banking products, which can build trust with historically underserved groups (provided the "why" is transparently communicated elsewhere in the flow).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit Opt-Out: Including "Prefer not to answer" reduces user anxiety and friction around answering a legally sensitive question, improving overall survey completion.

  • Progressive Disclosure via Chevron: Selecting a broad category (Asian) reveals a secondary, more specific sub-choice (Chinese) inline, avoiding an extra full-screen step.

  • Single-Question Focus: Isolating one question per screen with a thin progress bar keeps the task perceived as short and manageable, reducing survey fatigue.

  • Consistent Branding in a Neutral Flow: Even a compliance/data-collection screen retains Dave's mint-green CTA and rounded-card language, keeping brand trust intact.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 15
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for critical, high-stakes data inputs (like Date of Birth, SSN, or Legal Name) where accuracy is paramount and errors are costly (e.g., financial or medical apps). It is ideal for:

  • Regulatory compliance flows (KYC/AML).

  • Isolating fields that require specific format validation (dates, currency).

  • Situations where you want to force sequential completion of a multi-step form without allowing users to skip ahead.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of granularity (breaking one field into three separate screens/steps or three separate pickers taking up a whole screen) for low-stakes or optional data. If you have many fields to collect, this "one field per screen" approach can feel bureaucratic and slow, leading to drop-off due to the sheer number of taps required to reach the end goal. In such cases, grouping related fields (e.g., Name + Birthdate) on a single screen is more efficient.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users undergoing an identity verification, KYC (Know Your Customer), or eligibility-check process, likely for a financial services app like Dave. The primary psychological driver here is reducing friction and anxiety associated with providing personal identifiable information (PII).

By presenting the request as a "Survey" rather than a rigid "Verification Form," the app leverages a softer framing to lower the perceived stakes of the interaction, making users more willing to comply and complete the required regulatory or eligibility data collection.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled State Guidance: The "Continue" button is greyed out by default, clearly communicating that the form is incomplete and preventing null submissions.

  • Segmented Date Input: Breaking the date into three separate native pickers (Day/Month/Year) simplifies interaction compared to a calendar widget, and enforces valid syntax automatically.

  • Clear Exit Path: The "Close" button is prominently placed in the top left, respecting the user's autonomy to abandon the survey at any point without being trapped.

  • Minimalist Focus: By isolating a single question on a mostly empty canvas, the app ensures 100% user focus on the specific data point required.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Any onboarding or KYC flow requiring precise date-of-birth capture, especially where regulatory compliance (age eligibility) matters.

  • Financial, insurance, healthcare, or age-restricted apps (alcohol, gambling, dating) where date accuracy and format clarity are critical.

  • Multi-step onboarding wizards where isolating one data point per screen improves completion rates and reduces form abandonment.

  • Any scenario where instant feedback (like computed age) can reassure users their input was correctly understood.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this granular, multi-step-per-field approach for low-stakes or frequently-used forms where speed matters more than precision (e.g., a native date picker or calendar widget would be faster for filling in an event date or reminder). This pattern is also unnecessarily heavy for internal tools or contexts where users are entering dozens of dates rapidly (a single compact date input or native OS date picker would be more efficient). Additionally, in flows where user trust is already high and screen real estate is limited, splitting one field across an entire screen may feel like it artificially inflates the number of steps and could frustrate power users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users onboarding into or engaging with Dave, a neobank/fintech app known for cash-advance and budgeting features. Collecting birth date is almost certainly tied to regulatory age verification (18+) and identity verification (KYC/AML compliance) required for financial services in the US.

Psychologically, framing this as part of "Dave Surveys" rather than "Account Verification" softens the perceived intrusiveness of requesting a legally sensitive data point, making users more willing to comply. The instant age-reflection feedback taps into a small dopamine-triggering moment of self-recognition/personalization ("Oh yes, that's me"), building trust that the app is listening and responding accurately, which increases confidence in proceeding through the rest of the sensitive onboarding/KYC flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Real-time age calculation as implicit inline validation (confirms correct parsing of the date before submission, catching typos or nonsensical dates (e).g., Feb 30) early.

  • Segmented Day/Month/Year steppers instead of a single free-text field or ambiguous native date picker, eliminating locale-based date format confusion and reducing malformed input.

  • Single-question-per-screen design minimizes cognitive load and keeps focus entirely on one decision point.

  • Persistent exit ("Close") and progress indicator give the user a sense of control and location within the flow, reducing abandonment anxiety.

  • Large, single, high-contrast Continue CTA removes any ambiguity about the next action.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 17
screens.whereToUse:
• After a user completes onboarding, a setup wizard, or a qualification screening in reward/incentive-based apps.

  • Before transitioning users into a potentially tedious or effortful task (surveys, forms, assessments) to boost motivation.

  • At key milestone completions (first task done, profile 100% complete, first payout unlocked) to reinforce positive behavior and encourage retention.

  • Any consumer app relying on gamification loops where celebrating small wins drives continued engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid using full-screen celebratory interstitials for minor, frequent actions (overuse desensitizes users and turns delight into annoyance/friction).

  • Not appropriate in enterprise, B2B, or professional productivity tools where a playful tone may undermine perceived credibility.

  • Should not be used to mask or distract from an actual lack of tangible reward (e.g., celebrating before real value has been delivered) as it can breed user distrust if repeated without payoff.

  • Avoid in time-sensitive or task-critical flows where an extra screen adds unnecessary friction to power users who want to move quickly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of reward/incentive apps (like paid survey platforms) who need positive reinforcement to stay engaged through what is often a tedious process (surveys, screening questions, profile setup). The target demographic is likely value-conscious consumers seeking supplemental income, who respond well to gamification and instant gratification cues.

Psychologically, this screen leverages the peak-end rule: by inserting a strong positive emotional spike (celebration) at a transition point, the app increases the likelihood that users perceive their overall experience positively and remain motivated to continue through subsequent, potentially less exciting screens (i.e., actual survey completion). The trophy and confetti trigger dopamine release associated with achievement, even though no tangible reward (money, points) has been granted yet (it's an anticipatory reward that primes the user for the "real" survey-taking task ahead).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Illustration-led storytelling: Using a trophy and celebrating characters instead of text to communicate "success" taps into universal visual literacy, making the moment feel rewarding regardless of language or literacy level.

  • Single CTA, zero friction: Only one primary action is presented, eliminating decision fatigue at an emotionally charged moment.

  • Non-blocking exit: The "Close" option in the header respects user autonomy while the visual hierarchy still nudges toward continuing.

  • Full-bleed brand color header: Reinforces brand identity (green) at a moment of positive association, strengthening emotional brand linkage.

  • Confetti micro-animation: Implied motion/particle effects add a dopamine-triggering, game-like reward sensation typical of gamified reward apps.

screens.name: Dave Giving Feedbacks 18
screens.whereToUse: Use this dual-metric card pattern (payout + time) in any gig-economy, task-marketplace, or micro-earning product (such as survey platforms, cashback apps, or freelance gig aggregators) where users need to rapidly triage opportunities by effort-to-reward ratio. The color-tiered grouping strategy is also effective for prioritizing premium vs. quick-win content in reward-based apps, loyalty programs, or task lists.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for content where dollar amount and time aren't the primary decision drivers, such as educational or entertainment content, where richer context (titles, thumbnails, descriptions) is needed to drive engagement. Also avoid oversimplifying to just two data points in domains with legal or compliance implications (e.g., financial products, insurance) where users need more disclosure before committing, as this could feel deceptive or lead to poor decision-making.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially stretched users, likely gig workers, hourly employees, or those living paycheck-to-paycheck, who are already using Dave for cash advances or budgeting. These users are motivated by immediate, small-dollar income opportunities and are highly sensitive to time-value tradeoffs.

Psychologically, the design leverages instant gratification cues (visible dollar amounts), reduced cognitive load (no need to read survey descriptions before deciding), and reciprocity/trust-building (transparent FAQ addressing disqualification frustration). The tiered color system also taps into a subtle "reward hierarchy" bias, nudging users toward higher-value surveys first.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-metric card design: Every survey card foregrounds both payout and time cost, enabling instant value assessment without extra taps, reducing decision fatigue.

  • Color-coded tiering: Green vs. blue tile backgrounds visually segment "premium/high-value" surveys from "quick" ones, creating an intuitive priority system.

  • Proactive friction mitigation: The FAQ block preemptively answers disqualification concerns, a known pain point in survey monetization that erodes trust if unaddressed.

  • Contextual cross-sell: The "Try a Side Hustle" card at the bottom smartly funnels engaged, income-seeking users toward another monetization feature, maximizing session value.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 11
screens.whereToUse:
Adapt this pattern for any app curating a themed collection of locations, products, or content pieces that benefits from strong visual merchandising (e).g., travel guides, food delivery collections, retail "shop the look" lists, or event venue directories. It's especially effective when:

  • You want to merchandise a "why should I care" hero image before diving into a list of items.

  • The collection has a natural, trackable completion goal (visited places, watched episodes, read articles) that benefits from progress gamification.

  • You need lightweight save/follow and share mechanics to drive organic distribution of curated content.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy photo-hero + progress-bar treatment for purely transactional or time-sensitive tasks (e.g., checkout, account settings) where visual flourish adds friction rather than delight. It's also unsuitable for very large or frequently-changing datasets where "visited/completed" tracking becomes meaningless or stale, or for B2B/utility apps where users expect dense data tables over lifestyle imagery. If the list has fewer than a handful of items, the progress-bar gamification will feel gimmicky rather than motivating.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Google Pay users in Singapore (or similar markets) who dine out and want a frictionless, cashless ordering experience. The audience is likely tech-comfortable smartphone users who already trust Google's payment and Maps ecosystem and are open to discovering new restaurants through curated, algorithmically-scored lists rather than manual search.

Psychologically, the screen leverages several triggers: appetite appeal via large sensory food photography to create desire before any text is read; curiosity and collection-completion bias via the "Visited 0 of 44" progress bar, which taps into the same psychology as loyalty stamp cards or achievement trackers; social proof via star ratings and review counts on each restaurant card; and reduced decision friction by explicitly instructing users how to act (scan QR, order in-app) removing any ambiguity about the payment flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Photo-first hero with overlaid floating controls: Back and overflow buttons sit in translucent dark circles directly atop the image, preserving full visual impact of the food photo while keeping navigation always reachable.

  • Card-over-photo composition: The rounded white content panel overlapping the bottom of the hero image creates depth and a clear visual handoff from "inspiration" (photo) to "information" (list details).

  • Progress/completion bar ("Visited 0 of 44"): Turns a static content list into a trackable, gamified checklist, encouraging users to return and "complete" the collection.

  • Dual low-friction CTAs (Follow / Share): Both actions are reversible, free, and social (ideal for driving list distribution and repeat engagement without asking for money or heavy commitment).

  • Relevance scoring ("57% match"): Personalizes an otherwise generic list by hinting the algorithm has ranked each restaurant against the user's known preferences.

  • Cross-surface integration: Combines Google Maps-style place data (ratings, hours) with a Google Pay-specific instructional use case (QR-scan ordering), demonstrating tight ecosystem integration.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this segmented progress + minimal header pattern for any linear, multi-step transactional flow such as checkout, onboarding, form wizards, or reservation/booking processes where users benefit from knowing exactly how far along they are. It's especially effective when each step requires focused attention with no distracting side content.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this bare-bones progress-only header for flows where steps vary significantly in effort/time (the equal-width segments would misrepresent true completion). Also avoid leaving the body area blank for more than a few hundred milliseconds (if this is meant to be a loading state, it should include a skeleton loader or indeterminate spinner rather than a completely empty white canvas, which can appear broken or unresponsive to users).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday consumers using a food ordering/delivery app who are moving through a multi-step task (e.g., selecting a pickup time, confirming a location, or reviewing an order). The progress bar leverages the Goal Gradient Effect: showing users partial completion increases motivation to finish the remaining steps rather than abandon the flow. The stripped-back header also reduces decision fatigue by presenting only essential navigation controls (back, title, more options) at this stage of a transactional journey where speed and clarity are paramount.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented progress bar: Clearly communicates multi-step flow progress at a glance, reducing user anxiety about how many steps remain.

  • Minimal chrome navigation: Back button, centered title, and overflow menu keep the header lightweight and predictable, adhering to native iOS patterns for reduced cognitive load.

  • Contextual overflow menu: Placing secondary actions (cancel, edit, help) behind a "..." icon avoids cluttering the primary flow while still offering an escape hatch.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 13
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a primarily utility-based app (payments, banking, super-apps) wants to introduce an adjacent commerce vertical without building a separate app. It's ideal when there's a clear incentive (cashback, discounts) to tie the new vertical back to the core product's value proposition (payments). It also works well for location-based discovery flows where filtering by proximity, category, and availability status is essential to reduce a large catalog to actionable choices.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the parent app has no natural incentive mechanism (like cashback or rewards) to justify the cross-sell (without it, users may perceive the feature as bloat or scope creep unrelated to the app's core promise). It's also unsuitable for apps with sparse restaurant/merchant coverage in a region, since an empty or thin results list under "Restaurants near [location]" would undermine trust rather than build engagement. Additionally, if fulfillment options are inconsistent (e.g., many listings support delivery but the UI implies pickup-first), mismatched expectations can cause user frustration.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday Google Pay users: likely in Singapore given "islandwide," Queenstown, and SGD pricing (who already trust Google Pay for payments and are being cross-sold into a food discovery use case). The psychological hook is incentivized habit expansion: by attaching a cashback reward to food ordering, Google converts a single-purpose payment app into a multi-purpose daily utility, increasing app engagement frequency and stickiness.

The pre-checked "Order on Google Pay" filter subtly exploits the path-of-least-resistance bias (users are shown a curated list where paying with Google Pay is already the default expectation, reducing any friction or decision point about payment method later in the funnel). The star ratings and review counts leverage social proof to build trust in unfamiliar establishments quickly.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Illustration teaser strip: A row of stylized food icons builds appetite appeal and category anticipation before real restaurant data is even shown.

  • Pre-applied smart filters: "Open" and "Order on Google Pay" chips are selected by default, ensuring the first results shown are always actionable and relevant, not stale or unpayable.

  • In-app incentive banner: The cashback offer is contextually placed exactly where the user is about to browse restaurants, maximizing the chance it influences the payment method choice at the point of highest relevance.

  • Dense yet scannable restaurant cards: Each list item packs price tier, cuisine, fulfillment method, payment support, rating, review volume, and distance into a compact card without feeling cluttered, thanks to consistent typographic hierarchy.

  • Payment-method as a first-class filter: Treating "Order on Google Pay" as a filter chip (not just a badge) is a clever platform-lock-in tactic that quietly nudges the ecosystem toward using Google Pay for food transactions.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 14
screens.whereToUse: Use this image-forward card list pattern when the product needs to drive quick, low-friction purchase decisions based on visual and social-proof cues (local discovery, food/restaurant browsing, marketplace listings, or any vertical where photos materially affect conversion). It's especially effective when embedding a new transactional vertical inside an existing trusted app, since repeating a recognizable payment/trust badge on each item reduces perceived risk of a new feature.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy card-per-item layout when the catalog is large and comparison-driven (e.g., grocery SKUs, financial products, flight search) since large photo cards slow scanning and increase scroll fatigue. It's also unsuitable when photos are not user-differentiating (e.g., generic stock icons) as the visual investment yields low return, or when screen real estate must prioritize dense filtering/sorting controls over imagery.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday Google Pay users who already trust the app for bill splitting and transfers and are being nudged into using it as a broader commerce and payments hub. By surfacing local pick-up restaurants inside the wallet app, Google leverages existing session intent (users already open Google Pay frequently for money-related tasks) to cross-sell food ordering, increasing daily active engagement. The psychological trigger is convenience plus trust transfer: since users already trust Google Pay with their financial data, extending that trust to a new transactional category (food ordering) lowers the adoption barrier compared to installing a dedicated food app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Payment-as-badge: Embedding "Order on G Pay" directly into every merchant card reinforces platform trust and turns a payment method into a discovery filter simultaneously.

  • Photo-first card hierarchy: Large edge-to-edge food imagery leverages appetite appeal to drive taps, a proven pattern borrowed from food-delivery apps but rendered in Google Pay's cleaner card style.

  • Consistent scan pattern: Rating, review count, and distance are placed in the same position on every card, enabling fast visual comparison without reading full text.

  • Expectation-setting labels: "Pick-up only" preempts confusion about delivery availability before the user commits a tap.

results.query: Interactive Slider for loan repayment term duration calculation

screens.name: Oportun Setting Up 22
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a product needs to let users temporarily disable a recurring automated action (subscriptions, auto-payments, savings transfers, habit trackers, workout plans) without fully canceling their engagement. It's ideal for:

  • Fintech apps managing recurring transfers or auto-invest rules

  • Subscription or membership pause flows (e.g., gym memberships, meal kits)

  • Habit-formation or wellness apps allowing "snooze" on goals

  • Any scenario with both a bulk toggle and itemized list of dependent settings
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for irreversible or destructive actions (the reassuring, low-friction tone here is inappropriate when higher-stakes confirmation or friction is needed (e).g., account closure, fund withdrawal). It's also unsuitable for time-sensitive financial actions where an ambiguous "learn more" link isn't enough; regulatory or compliance-heavy actions may require more explicit, itemized disclosures rather than an optional inline link. Additionally, if a product only ever has one savings goal, the bulk "Pause/Resume all" control becomes redundant clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers of a personal finance or neobank app who use automated "round-up" or scheduled savings features (e.g., Chime, Qapital, Acorns-style products). The target user is likely someone experiencing temporary cash-flow constraints (a very common and recurring scenario for budget-conscious or lower-to-middle income users who rely on paycheck-to-paycheck cycles).

Psychologically, the design leverages loss-aversion mitigation: by making "pausing" feel safe and reversible instead of punitive, the app prevents users from disabling notifications entirely or churning from the savings feature altogether. The dated pause end-state also taps into commitment and consistency bias: giving a resume date makes users more likely to follow through, similar to calendar-based habit reminders.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empathetic reframing of a "failure" state: Instead of treating paused savings as a negative outcome, the copy normalizes it, reducing user guilt and preserving trust in the app.

  • Disabled state as implicit feedback: The greyed-out "Pause all" button communicates current system state without additional copy, adhering to the "recognition rather than recall" heuristic.

  • Granular + bulk control coexistence: Users can manage goals individually (snooze/resume per card) or in bulk (Pause/Resume all), catering to both power users and quick-action users.

  • Proactive transparency link: Pre-empting the "what happens next" anxiety with an inline "learn more" link reduces support tickets and builds confidence in an automated financial decision.

  • Concrete resume dates: Turning an indefinite pause into a dated commitment leverages the psychological principle of implementation intentions, increasing the likelihood users will actually resume saving.

screens.name: Oportun Setting Up 23
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a user is about to take a semi-reversible or ambiguous action (pausing, canceling a partial feature, downgrading) that carries lesser-known side effects. It's ideal for subscription services, financial automation tools, or any product where continued billing/behavior might not be intuitively obvious to the user. Also effective for reducing support burden by front-loading FAQ-style content contextually rather than requiring users to seek out a help center.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, fully-reversible actions with no hidden consequences (e.g., toggling a display setting) - the extra explanatory step would be unnecessary friction. Also avoid stacking multiple modals/sheets if the underlying screen content is itself critical for decision-making, as double-layering (dimmed screen + sheet) can feel visually heavy or claustrophobic if overused across a flow. If the disclosed information is likely to cause immediate cancellation anxiety (e.g., surprise fees), consider pairing this pattern with an easy escape hatch or fee-waiver option to prevent it from being a churn trigger instead of a trust builder.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets budget-conscious or cash-flow-variable users of an automated micro-savings app (e.g., gig workers, freelancers, or anyone with irregular income) who need the flexibility to pause recurring transfers without losing their subscription benefits or feeling penalized. The design leverages the psychological trigger of loss aversion mitigation: by clarifying that pending/manual transfers and subscription access continue, it removes the fear of "losing progress" or "being locked out," which is often the top objection preventing users from using pause features at all (they'd rather cancel entirely, which is worse for retention).

It also uses reciprocity/trust-building: being upfront about the continued fee (which could seem unfavorable to the user) paradoxically increases trust and reduces the perceived risk of dishonesty in the broader app relationship.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anticipatory FAQ Pattern: Proactively answers "What happens when I pause?" before the user has to search for it or contact support, reducing cognitive load and support tickets.

  • Transparent Fee Disclosure: Clearly states the subscription fee continues during a pause, an ethical design choice that preempts dispute/chargeback friction and builds long-term trust.

  • Layered Context via Bottom Sheet: Preserves the underlying screen state visibility (dimmed) so users retain spatial orientation while consuming supplementary detail.

  • Metaphorical Illustration: The pause-button-on-a-check-with-a-clock visual instantly communicates the temporal, reversible nature of the action without needing text.

  • Low-friction Acknowledgment CTA: The single "Got it" button, styled as a secondary/outline button, correctly signals this is informational, not decision-forcing.

screens.name: Oportun Setting Up 24
screens.whereToUse:
• Subscription or recurring-billing extension/pause flows where users need to adjust a time-bound setting (trials, holds, snoozes).

  • Any decision requiring a duration input where translating relative time to an absolute date reduces user error (e.g., "snooze until," "remind me in," "delay shipment by").

  • Financial or health apps where hidden costs/consequences of a choice must be disclosed upfront to maintain regulatory compliance and trust.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this bottom-sheet, radio-list pattern for decisions with many options (>4-5) or that require custom date input (a full date picker or dedicated screen would serve better).

  • Don't bury important cost/consequence disclosures in fine print if using this pattern for billing-related decisions; the value here depends on the transparency being prominent, not an afterthought.

  • Not ideal when the action is irreversible or high-stakes enough to warrant a full-screen confirmation flow with more visual weight and friction (e.g., account cancellation).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of a savings/fintech app who have already paused automated contributions to a goal (e.g., due to a cash-flow crunch) and are now near or past the end of that pause window. It's likely triggered by a reminder notification or an in-app banner prompting the user to decide whether to resume or extend.

The psychological driver here is loss-aversion mitigation and control: users pausing a savings goal are often in a moment of financial stress, and this screen respects their need for continued flexibility without forcing an immediate resumption of contributions they may not be ready for. By offering pre-set durations with clear end dates, the design reduces decision paralysis and anxiety, while the fee disclosure respects the user's right to informed consent (critical for retaining trust in a money-management context).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Relative + absolute date pairing: Each duration option shows both the increment ("Add 1 week") and the resulting calendar date ("until Jul 11"), eliminating mental math and increasing decision confidence.

  • Proactive fee transparency: The screen explicitly states the subscription fee continues during the pause, addressing a likely point of user confusion or frustration before it becomes a support ticket.

  • Contextual goal card: A visual snapshot of the specific paused goal (icon, name, balance, pause badge) anchors the decision to a concrete object, reducing the risk of the user extending the wrong goal.

  • Sensible default selection: "Add 1 week" is pre-selected, letting low-effort users complete the task with a single tap on the CTA.

  • Layered modal with dimmed backdrop: Preserves the sense of place within the flow while focusing full attention on the decision at hand.

screens.name: Oportun Setting Up 25
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a product needs to offer a reversible, non-punitive opt-out from a recurring commitment (subscription pauses, habit-tracking streak freezes, recurring donations, or automated transfers). It's especially effective in fintech, wellness, and habit-forming apps where forcing a hard cancellation would drive churn, but silently continuing to charge/transfer would erode trust.

Also apply the toast + explanatory banner combo whenever a user completes a state-changing action (extend, pause, resume) that has downstream financial or scheduling consequences and benefits from a "why this is safe" reassurance message.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this soft-pause pattern for actions with real compliance, safety, or contractual consequences (e.g., insurance coverage lapses, legal deadlines) where ambiguity about "paused vs. cancelled" could create liability or user harm (in those cases, a more explicit, harder confirmation flow is required).

Also avoid stacking a toast directly over body copy as seen here (the toast overlaps and obscures the first line of the explanatory paragraph), since it can cause important information to be clipped or misread, especially for accessibility/screen-reader users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers using an automated micro-savings or round-up savings app (e.g., similar to Digit, Qapital, or Chime-style savings goals) who are experiencing a temporary cash crunch. The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion mitigation: instead of forcing users to cancel a goal outright (a hard, guilt-inducing decision), the product offers a soft, reversible "pause" mechanic that preserves the user's long-term commitment to the goal while removing immediate financial pressure.

The reassuring copy and lack of blocking dialogs suggest the target user is price-sensitive, potentially living paycheck-to-paycheck, and prone to abandoning savings apps when they feel punished for pausing. By making pause/resume low-friction and stigma-free, the product increases long-term retention and re-engagement odds once the user's cash flow stabilizes.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empathetic reframing of a negative action: Pausing savings is framed as a supportive feature ("No worries") rather than a failure, reducing user shame and churn risk.

  • Toast confirmation with iconography: The checkmark-in-circle toast gives immediate, low-friction feedback that the extend action succeeded, without requiring a full-screen interruption.

  • Bulk + granular controls coexisting: "Pause all/Resume all" segmented control at the top complements individual per-goal alarm/play icons, giving users both macro and micro control in the same view.

  • Progressive disclosure via "learn more": Keeps the core screen scannable while still answering the anxious user's follow-up question about account-wide impact.

  • Explicit resume dates: Each paused goal shows a hard "Paused until [date]" instead of an ambiguous "paused" label, setting clear expectations and building trust.

screens.name: Oportun Setting Up 26

screens.whereNotToUse:

  • Do not use if the underlying system cannot reliably persist a "resume date," as showing an incorrect date would erode trust.

  • Avoid stacking too many contextual icons (snooze, divider, play) if the list can exceed 10+ items, as it may increase visual clutter and scanning time on smaller screens.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The target demographic likely includes budget-conscious individuals or those with variable income who need flexibility to pause automated transfers during tight cash-flow periods without abandoning their long-term goals entirely.

The specific "Paused until [date]" framing also uses defaults and pre-commitment psychology, nudging the user back into saving behavior automatically at a future point, capitalizing on the human tendency toward inertia (auto-resume) rather than requiring active re-engagement.

  • Reassuring Empty Judgment Copy: Explicitly reassuring language reduces financial shame, a strong retention/trust-building technique.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a feature has multiple distinct notification triggers tied to a single object (e.g., a budget, subscription, project, or threshold) and users need fine-grained, independent control over each. It's ideal for finance, project management, or monitoring tools where different alert types have different urgency or relevance per user. Also effective as a contextual "mini settings" modal launched from an overflow menu, keeping deep configuration close to the object it affects rather than forcing navigation to a separate settings area.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are very few notification options (a single toggle would suffice and this adds unnecessary modal overhead), or when notifications are critical for compliance/safety (in those cases, defaulting to off could cause users to miss essential alerts, so an opt-out default or mandatory notification might be more appropriate). Also avoid duplicating the exact same toggles in both a contextual modal and the global settings screen without synchronization, as this can create confusing or conflicting states for the user.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves finance team members, budget owners, and employees managing a company card or spend limit who want proactive visibility into their spending status without manually checking balances. The psychological driver is loss aversion and control: employees and admins fear hitting a limit unexpectedly (which can block a purchase or cause embarrassment) or missing an expiration that disrupts ongoing work. Giving users granular control over exactly which alerts they receive (approaching limit, expiring soon, expired) satisfies the need for autonomy while reducing the anxiety of being caught off guard financially.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual entry point: Notification settings are scoped to the specific spend limit being viewed, reducing the need to hunt through global settings.
  • Grouped, labeled toggle rows: Each alert type has its own header and one-line explanation, making the consequence of enabling/disabling instantly clear.
  • Opt-in defaults: All toggles start off, respecting user attention and avoiding notification fatigue by default.
  • Escape hatch to global settings: The "View all notification settings" button bridges local and global configuration without adding complexity to this focused screen.
  • Modal dismissal pattern: A clear circular "X" signals this is a lightweight overlay, not a core navigation screen, letting users quickly return to their prior context.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building threshold-based or event-based notification settings for any metered resource (budgets, data usage, storage quotas, subscription limits, or inventory counts). It's ideal when a user needs to customize both whether they get notified and at what threshold, especially when that threshold has both a relative (%) and absolute (currency/unit) meaning. The toast-confirmation + grouped toggle layout is well suited to any settings screen with multiple related-but-distinct alert types.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of granularity for casual consumer apps where users are unlikely to want to fine-tune thresholds (a simple on/off toggle with a sensible default is less overwhelming for low-stakes notifications). Also avoid combining percentage and currency sliders if the resource has no natural dollar equivalent, as that would add confusing, non-applicable units. For mobile screens with limited vertical space, excessive sections (3+) with descriptions and toggles can feel long; consider collapsing into an accordion if more alert types are added in the future.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets finance admins, budget owners, and employees who have been assigned a spend limit or card budget and want proactive visibility into their spending without manually checking the app. The psychological driver here is control and anxiety reduction: by letting users set a custom threshold (e.g., 80%) rather than a fixed system default, Brex gives users a sense of ownership over how and when they are interrupted, which increases trust and reduces alert fatigue.

The toggle-based structure also appeals to the target audience's need for customization at scale: finance teams managing multiple budgets need fine-grained, predictable alerting so they aren't caught off guard by overspending or an expired limit, which could cause embarrassment or business disruption (e.g., a failed company purchase).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-unit slider readout: Simultaneously displaying percentage and dollar equivalent ($480.00 / 80%) removes the need for users to mentally convert between relative and absolute spend thresholds.
  • Immediate toast confirmation: The green-check "Budget limit alert: On" toast provides instant, low-friction feedback that a toggle change was successfully persisted.
  • Progressive disclosure of slider: The percentage slider is only relevant and presumably only interactive when its parent toggle is active, keeping the UI decluttered for disabled states.
  • Grouped settings sections with dividers: Clear visual separation between the three alert types prevents accidental misconfiguration and aids scannability.
  • Escape hatch CTA: "View all notification settings" acknowledges this is a scoped/contextual settings view and offers a path to the broader preference center.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when configuring threshold-based alerts or limits in finance, budgeting, health, or usage-tracking apps (e.g., data caps, calorie budgets, savings goals). It's ideal when:

  • A single continuous value (percentage, quantity) needs user-defined customization.
  • Users benefit from seeing the value translated into a more meaningful real-world unit (currency, time, count).
  • Multiple related-but-distinct notification triggers exist and warrant separation rather than a single master toggle.
  • You want to reduce form friction by using autosave instead of requiring an explicit submit action.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this granular, multi-section toggle/slider layout when:

  • Users only have one simple preference to configure (excessive subdivision would feel bureaucratic and overwhelming).
  • The setting is high-risk or irreversible, where autosave without a confirmation step could lead to accidental misconfiguration.
  • Screen real estate is very limited (e.g., smartwatch), where showing dual units and slider endpoints would clutter the interface.
  • Your users are non-technical and would be confused by percentage-based abstractions rather than a simple toggle.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets finance-conscious employees, founders, and finance team admins who are monitoring a specific card or budget limit and want proactive visibility rather than having to manually check balances. The psychological driver is loss-aversion and control: by letting users set a custom early-warning threshold (vs. a fixed default), Brex reduces the anxiety of unexpectedly hitting a spend cap, which is especially important for business spenders who could face declined transactions mid-task (e.g., during travel or client meetings).

The autosave/toast pattern also builds trust with financially cautious users, confirming "your setting is live" instantly satisfies the need for certainty in a money-management context where ambiguity about whether a setting "stuck" is highly undesirable.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-unit slider: Simultaneously displays percentage and dollar equivalents at the handle and at both slider endpoints, eliminating cognitive math for the user.
  • Autosave with toast confirmation: No save button required; dragging the slider instantly persists the value and surfaces a non-blocking success toast.
  • Decomposed alert types: Splitting notification logic into three independent toggles (limit alert, expiring soon, expired) gives users precise control instead of one blunt on/off switch.
  • Progressive disclosure: The slider and percentage detail only appear once the parent toggle is switched on, keeping the UI clean when the feature is disabled.
  • Escape hatch CTA: "View all notification settings" link lets users navigate to the global settings hub without cluttering this contextual screen.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet radio-selection pattern when:

  • You want to preserve the user's place in a longer settings or configuration flow rather than navigating to a new screen.
  • The decision is low-stakes and benefits from quick, reversible selection (e.g., notification timing, sort order, unit preferences).

The paired toggle-plus-slider pattern for threshold alerts is ideal for any app involving budgets, usage caps, or quota management (telecom data plans, cloud billing alerts, fitness goal tracking).
screens.whereNotToUse:

Also avoid it for choices requiring additional context, explanation, or multi-field input, since the compact sheet format doesn't accommodate supporting copy well.

The slider-plus-numeric pattern should be avoided when precision matters more than approximation (sliders are imprecise for exact financial inputs, so a direct numeric text field (with optional slider as a secondary aid) would be safer in contexts requiring exact threshold compliance (e).g., regulatory spend caps).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves finance admins, budget owners, and employees with discretionary spend limits (e.g., card holders on a monthly budget) who need proactive visibility into their spending without manually checking balances. The psychological driver here is loss aversion and anxiety reduction: nobody wants to be surprised by a declined card or an expired budget mid-transaction, especially in a professional context where that could cause embarrassment or operational delay.

By allowing users to self-select their alert threshold (80% rather than a fixed default) and lead time (3 days rather than a forced 1-day notice), Brex caters to varying risk tolerances and planning styles (some users want early warnings to plan ahead, others only want alerts close to the deadline to avoid notification fatigue). screens.keyHighlights:

  • Synced slider + numeric input: The percentage slider dynamically displays both relative (%) and absolute ($) values, letting users intuitively drag to a round percentage while instantly seeing real-world dollar impact.
  • Non-disruptive bottom sheet selection: Using an action sheet with radio buttons for the "days before" selector keeps users anchored in their settings flow, avoiding a jarring full-page navigation for a single-field decision.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 6

screens.keyHighlights:

  • Specific confirmation toast: Rather than a generic "Saved" message, the toast states the exact value selected ("1 day before"), giving users immediate, unambiguous feedback.

screens.name: Brex - Adding an alert - Screen 7

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 18
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern at the end of any document-generation or form-completion flow where the next step requires external distribution (sharing, signing, submitting to a third party) - e.g., tax forms, contracts, applications, invoices. Ideal when you want to reduce cognitive load with a prefilled/automated next action while still allowing manual review.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal success-only pattern when the user needs to take multiple follow-up actions or when additional error-prone steps remain (in which case a checklist or status tracker is more appropriate). Not suitable for flows where the "success" message could be misleading (e).g., if the deposit setup isn't actually complete until the employer confirms it, the copy should clarify remaining dependencies to avoid false confidence.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets Cash App users setting up direct deposit, often gig workers, hourly employees, or unbanked/underbanked individuals who may not have handled payroll paperwork independently before. The design leans on the peak-end rule (ending a task on a positive, celebratory note) and reduction of perceived effort (prefilled email) to counter form-related anxiety. The reassuring green checkmark and simple language build trust for a financially sensitive action, authorizing where paychecks go.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-focus success screen: No distractions, no upsells (pure task-completion affirmation using color (green check) and typography scale to communicate success instantly).

  • Pre-filled action reduces friction: By stating the email is already drafted, the user's perceived effort for the next step drops to nearly zero, increasing likelihood of completion.

  • Dual-path CTA hierarchy: "View form" (secondary/verify) vs. "Email form" (primary/commit) lets cautious and confident users both proceed comfortably.

  • Just-in-time legal consent: Placing the e-signature disclosure immediately above the commit button ties consent directly to the action, rather than requiring a separate acknowledgment step.

  • Non-modal exit (X): Preserves user control and reduces perceived lock-in, important for financial/legal documents.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 19
screens.whereToUse:
Use this circular/radial allocation pattern when:

  • Users need to split a whole (100%, a budget, or a fixed resource) across a small number (3-6) of mutually exclusive categories.

  • You want the interaction to feel more like a "control panel" than a "spreadsheet," increasing engagement and reducing perceived complexity of financial or resource planning.

  • The categories benefit from strong visual color-coding, and there's a natural "remainder" bucket that can be automatically calculated instead of manually input.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • There are many categories (8+) to distribute, since the ring becomes visually cluttered and precise dragging becomes difficult (fat-finger problem).

  • Users need extremely precise, granular control (e.g., allocating to the exact decimal or cent) - a numeric text field with real-time validation would be faster and more accurate.

  • The user base is less visually/spatially inclined or using assistive technology, where a radial drag gesture may be harder to operate than standard form controls; ensure an accessible numeric fallback is always available.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets fintech/neobank users setting up automated "paycheck splitting" or round-up investing rules (e.g., Chime, Current, Step, or Acorns-style products). The audience is typically younger, mobile-first savers who want to automate good financial habits (saving, investing in crypto/stocks) without manually transferring money each payday.

Psychologically, the design leverages the endowment/ownership effect by visualizing "your money" as a tangible pie that the user physically carves up, making the abstract act of saving feel concrete and rewarding. The locked, ever-present "Cash Balance" also exploits the default effect: money stays as spendable cash unless the user takes deliberate action to reroute it, which is honest and non-manipulative, but the "Add" prompts nudge the user toward habitual investing behavior via friendly, actionable framing rather than guilt or pressure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radial drag-to-allocate control: Converts an abstract percentage-splitting task into a satisfying, spatial, tactile gesture that's more intuitive than typing numbers.

  • Color-synced legend: Each segment's color is mirrored in the list below via colored dots, creating instant visual mapping between the abstract ring and concrete categories.

  • Locked derived value: "Cash Balance" is shown as a locked, calculated remainder (100% minus allocations), removing the need for the user to manually balance percentages to 100%, preventing math errors.

  • "Add" as empty-state CTA: Replacing "0%" with "Add" for Bitcoin/Stocks turns an empty state into an actionable upsell moment for investment products.

  • Deferred help: A dedicated "?" icon keeps the primary UI clean while still providing contextual education for less confident users.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 20

Use a circular/radial drag input combined with quick-select presets when:

  • The action is low-stakes or frequent (e.g., adjusting a filter), where a simpler stepper or standard slider would be faster and less heavy-handed.

  • Accessibility is a top priority without a robust alternative input (drag gestures can be difficult for users with motor impairments unless paired with equally prominent tap targets (as done here with the presets)).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets retail investors and everyday consumers (likely users of a fintech/neobank or micro-investing app (similar to Acorns, Cash App, or SoFi)) who want to automate Bitcoin accumulation without manually executing trades each pay period. The design leverages the "set it and forget it" mental model popular in dollar-cost-averaging (DCA) investment strategies.

Psychologically, the circular slider exploits the endowment and effort-justification effect: physically dragging a dial to "set" a commitment feels more deliberate and personally owned than typing a number, which can increase follow-through and reduce regret/cancellation later. The preset chips also leverage anchoring: by displaying 5%, 10%, 15%, 20% as "normal" choices, the app subtly nudges users toward larger allocations than they might have chosen unprompted.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Real-time numeric feedback: The giant "0%" recalculates live as the ring is dragged, satisfying the user's need for instant confirmation of their action.

  • Dual input modality: Combining the slider with tappable preset chips (1% (20%) respects different user preferences) precision draggers vs. quick tappers (without cluttering the UI).

  • Disabled CTA as a soft guardrail: The greyed "Continue" button at 0% prevents users from unintentionally proceeding without setting an allocation, embedding a subtle commitment device into the flow.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 21

Psychologically, the design leverages the completion/closure effect: the checkmark and affirmative headline trigger a sense of accomplishment and closure, similar to a task being "checked off." Restating the specific percentage also invokes the commitment and consistency principle: by seeing their own choice reflected back in bold text, users feel ownership over the automated behavior, making them less likely to second-guess or immediately disable it.

Because this action has real, recurring financial consequences (a portion of every future paycheck being diverted into a volatile asset), the confirmation screen also functions as a trust-building and anxiety-reducing checkpoint, essential for retention in fintech products where users are highly sensitive to feeling in control of their money.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Numeric restatement as a verification layer: Repeating the exact 40% figure the user selected acts as an implicit final confirmation for a recurring, automated financial action, reducing the risk of costly configuration mistakes.

  • Single focal icon + headline hierarchy: The oversized checkmark badge and bold headline create an unmissable "success" signal, ideal for high-stakes financial flows where users need instant, unambiguous feedback.

  • Minimal cognitive load: No competing UI elements, charts, or upsells. Just confirmation and exit, respecting the user's mental bandwidth right after committing to an automated investment.

  • Dual exit paths: Both the top-left X and the bottom "Done" button close the flow, catering to different user mental models (dismiss vs. complete) without adding complexity.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 23
screens.whereToUse:
Use this radial allocation pattern when:

  • Users need to split a fixed total (100%, budget, time, storage) across a small number of mutually exclusive categories.

  • You want to visually reinforce that categories are interdependent (increasing one lowers others).

  • The task benefits from a single glanceable "hero" metric alongside a supporting breakdown list.

  • You want to gently upsell additional categories (e.g., new asset classes) within the same allocation context.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • There are more than 5-6 categories to allocate, as the ring segments become too thin to grab or read accurately.

  • Users need high-precision input (e.g., exact currency amounts down to the cent) - a numeric stepper or text field would be more reliable.

  • The audience skews toward power users/accountants who prefer fast keyboard-driven entry over drag gestures.

  • Accessibility is a major concern, since radial drag targets are harder to operate via screen readers or switch control than standard form fields.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of a fintech/crypto investing app (likely a "round-up" or automated investing product like Acorns or Cash App-style tools) who want to automate recurring savings and crypto purchases from their paycheck. The primary psychological driver is reducing decision fatigue and friction around recurring financial commitments: by setting a percentage split once, the user achieves a "set it and forget it" sense of control and automation, appealing to behavioral finance principles like the endowment effect and commitment devices (pre-committing savings before it can be spent).

The visual, game-like ring interaction also appeals to less financially sophisticated or younger users who may find spreadsheet-like percentage entry intimidating, making investing feel approachable and almost playful.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radial percentage manipulation: Converts an abstract math problem (splitting 100%) into a tangible, draggable visual, lowering cognitive load versus typing numbers into multiple fields.

  • Locked residual category: The "Cash Balance" segment auto-calculates and locks, making it mathematically impossible for the user to create an invalid allocation that doesn't sum to 100%.

  • Live numeric feedback in the center: Placing the most relevant real-time metric inside the ring itself keeps the user's eyes anchored to one spot while adjusting.

  • Inline upsell via greyed row: The disabled "Stocks. Add" row surfaces a growth opportunity (adding another asset class) contextually, without an intrusive modal or banner.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 24
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when introducing a new financial product, premium feature, or account type that requires user buy-in before a multi-step setup flow (e.g., savings accounts, investment products, credit lines, insurance add-ons). It's ideal when you have 3-5 clear, differentiated benefits that can be communicated in a single short phrase plus subtitle, and when a dismissible modal is appropriate because the feature is optional/opt-in rather than mandatory.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for mandatory flows (e.g., required KYC/compliance steps) where an exit (X) affordance could cause users to abandon a necessary process. Also avoid it when the feature has many nuanced conditions or fine print that cannot be honestly compressed into a single line, oversimplifying complex financial terms (like conditional interest rates) risks user confusion or complaints later if expectations aren't met. Not suitable for screens needing detailed comparison data (e.g., pricing tiers), where a table or more structured layout would serve better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday Cash App users: often younger, mobile-first, and previously underbanked or dissatisfied with traditional banks (who are being cross-sold into a savings product from within a peer-to-peer payments app). The design assumes limited patience for financial jargon and leverages simple, benefit-oriented language to build trust quickly.

Psychologically, it relies on anchoring (leading with a high interest rate number), loss aversion reduction (no fees, no minimum balance removes common objections to opening a savings account), and reciprocity/low-friction commitment (an easily dismissible modal lowers resistance to continuing). The plant/money illustration reinforces a "growth" metaphor, subtly triggering associations with nurturing and long-term reward, which supports savings behavior motivation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Benefit-led headline over feature-led headline: "A better way to save" evokes emotion and outcome before any mechanics are explained, priming the user positively.

  • Icon-anchored scannable list: Four value props are reduced to icon + bold title + one-line subtitle, making the entire value proposition digestible in seconds.

  • Strategic incentive disclosure: The high-interest rate is presented boldly to hook attention, with the unlock condition (direct deposit) placed subordinately so it doesn't reduce the initial appeal.

  • Low-commitment exit affordance: The visible "X" close icon reduces perceived risk of engaging further, which paradoxically increases the likelihood users will proceed rather than abandon out of anxiety.

  • Compliance text unobtrusively placed: Legal/interest disclaimer is present for regulatory transparency but styled to avoid competing with the primary CTA.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 25

It's ideal for sub-account dashboards (savings, goals, rewards balances) where you need to balance core transactional actions (add/withdraw) with secondary feature discovery (automations, goals) and monetizable upsells (higher interest tiers) in a single, scannable screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this layout for accounts that always carry non-trivial balances or complex multi-currency/multi-asset holdings, where a single large balance figure oversimplifies the data. Also avoid greying out an action like "Withdraw" if the disabled state isn't self-explanatory to first-time users (supplement with a tooltip or microcopy if the reason for disablement isn't obvious). Additionally, stacking too many promotional banners in this style can overwhelm the zero-balance user; limit to one clear incentive at a time.

This pattern targets everyday consumers and younger, mobile-first banking users (e.g., Chime, Cash App, Current-style neobank audiences) who are motivated more by simplicity and automation than by traditional banking features. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Automation appeal: Round Ups and Paycheck splitting appeal to users who struggle with manual saving discipline, leveraging "set it and forget it" behavioral design.

screens.name: Wealthfront Logging & Tracking 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a form needs to branch based on a key qualifying question (e.g., renter vs. owner, employed vs. self-employed) where the answer significantly changes subsequent input fields or logic. It's ideal for financial, insurance, tax, or health apps where personalization depends on early binary classification. It's also effective for reducing form abandonment by breaking a long profile-building task into bite-sized, contextual micro-decisions with clear value statements attached to each.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy modal-interruption pattern for low-stakes or purely cosmetic settings, as the friction of a full-card dialog is disproportionate to trivial choices. It also shouldn't be used if the branching logic doesn't meaningfully alter the following screens, forcing a decision that doesn't change anything downstream feels like unnecessary friction. Additionally, avoid stacking multiple such modals in sequence without a progress indicator, as users may feel unsure how many more interruptions remain before reaching their goal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users engaging with a personal finance or retirement-planning app who are building out a net-worth or budget profile. The design assumes users may be reluctant to manually enter granular data (like exact rent or mortgage details), so it uses micro-commitments (a simple yes/no tap) to lower the barrier to starting the task. The linking CTA leverages the psychological principle of least effort: users are nudged to connect a financial account (auto-import) rather than manually calculate and type figures, increasing data accuracy and completion rates. The reassurance copy about "cash flow and net worth" appeals to users motivated by long-term financial clarity and control, a core driver for retirement-planning app engagement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Modal Interruption for Critical Branching Logic: Using a focused card/dialog to ask a single yes/no question before continuing prevents the user from providing incomplete or inaccurate financial data further down the flow.

  • Justification-Before-Ask Microcopy: Explaining "we'll analyze how your housing situation impacts your cash flow" builds trust and reduces the perceived intrusiveness of a personal question.

  • Actionable, Specific CTAs: "No, I rent" and "Yes, link it" replace generic binary buttons, reducing ambiguity and making the next step obvious (linking a bank/mortgage account vs. manual entry).

  • Persistent Goal Anchor: The sticky bottom button "How will I live in retirement?" keeps the emotional payoff of the exercise visible even while the user completes granular data-entry tasks.

  • Contextual Nudge/Upsell: The "Do you own a home? Link it!" prompt beneath the rent field reinforces account-linking (likely driving higher-fidelity data via bank integrations) at the exact moment of relevance.

screens.name: Wealthfront Logging & Tracking 10
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when a product needs to present a complex, personalized calculation (financial, health, nutrition, fitness) and wants users to fine-tune assumptions quickly. It's ideal for:

  • Financial planning tools (retirement, budgeting, loan calculators) where inputs are numerous but can be abstracted into simple presets.

  • Any onboarding/quiz flow where showing a smart default first, then allowing lightweight adjustment, increases completion rates versus asking users to input raw numbers.

  • Screens that benefit from progressive disclosure, showing a headline number with optional expandable detail for power users.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Precision is critical and a 3-tier preset would oversimplify important individual variance (e.g., regulated financial disclosures requiring exact user-entered data).

  • Users need to compare multiple scenarios side-by-side rather than toggle a single estimate (a static segmented control can't show trade-offs simultaneously).

  • The underlying calculation logic is opaque; if users don't trust the "smart estimate," a single big number without transparent methodology can feel manipulative or reduce credibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets a broad consumer audience: likely users of a personal finance or retirement-planning app (e.g., similar to NewRetirement, Boldin, or Empower) - who are financially engaged enough to plan for retirement but not necessarily sophisticated in actuarial math or budgeting.

Psychologically, it leverages the anchoring effect (showing a pre-calculated $4,432/mo figure so users don't start from a blank slate), reduced cognitive load (a 3-option segmented control instead of open-ended sliders or forms), and curiosity/goal-gradient effect (the CTA promises to answer "how soon can I retire," a highly desirable and emotionally charged outcome that motivates continued engagement).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-tap lifestyle recalibration: The Thrifty/Moderate/Spendy segmented control lets users adjust an entire financial model instantly instead of manually editing dozens of budget line items.

  • Progressive disclosure of complexity: The total is shown big and bold first; tapping the chevron reveals the housing/other breakdown only for users who want more detail, keeping the primary screen clean.

  • Editable sub-components: The pencil/edit icon next to "Other future spending" gives power users a manual override path without cluttering the default experience for everyone else.

  • Motivating CTA reframing: Rather than a generic "Next," the button asks "How soon can I retire?" - tying a mundane data-review step to the emotional payoff the user actually wants.

  • Contextual help affordances: Small "?" icons next to each figure offer inline definitions without needing to leave the screen or break flow.

screens.name: Wealthfront Logging & Tracking 11
screens.whereToUse:
• Long-term financial planning tools (retirement, FIRE calculators, investment growth projections).

  • Any "simulator" style feature where users benefit from adjusting one variable (savings rate, contribution, age) and seeing a real-time recalculated outcome.

  • Health/fitness or goal-tracking apps projecting future milestones based on current behavior trends.

  • Scenarios requiring both a quick answer for casual users and deep methodology transparency for skeptical/power users.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for short-term or highly volatile predictions (e.g., day-trading tools) where a long smooth projection curve could mislead users into false confidence.

  • Not suitable when the underlying data is incomplete or unlinked, presenting a confident verdict ("you're covered") without robust data risks users making poor financial decisions based on false assurance.

  • Avoid excessive interactivity (scrubbers + sliders + collapsible sections) for one-time or low-engagement informational screens where simplicity is more valuable than exploration.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-directed retail investors or personal finance app users (e.g., Origin, Copilot, Monarch Money-style tools) who have linked bank/investment accounts and want ongoing visibility into long-term financial health without hiring a human advisor. The audience skews toward digitally-savvy millennials/Gen X users comfortable self-serving complex financial decisions via an app.

Psychologically, the design leverages uncertainty reduction: retirement is an abstract, distant, anxiety-inducing concept, and translating it into a concrete number ("$900K") and a simple verdict ("more than covered") satisfies the need for closure. The editable slider and scrubbable chart also tap into agency and control: showing users they can actively influence their outcome (rather than being a passive forecast recipient) increases engagement and trust in the product as a planning tool rather than just a report generator.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Verdict-first architecture: Leads with the plain-English outcome ("on track," "$900K," "you're more than covered") before any chart or number crunching, satisfying the 80% of users who just want a yes/no answer.

  • Interactive time-scrubbing chart: The prev/next arrow pill under the timeline lets users scrub through projected years, turning a static forecast into an explorable simulation rather than a flat report.

  • Comparative overlay lines: Two trend lines (current plan vs. an alternate scenario like 'Retire at 25') allow instant visual comparison of outcomes, leveraging pattern recognition over reading numbers.

  • Live 'what-if' slider with undo: Adjusting "My planned savings" likely recalculates the projection in real time, and the adjacent undo icon removes the risk of experimentation, encouraging engagement.

  • Contextual help icons: Placing "?" tooltips directly next to potentially confusing claims lets novice users get clarification without cluttering the primary copy for advanced users.

  • Progressive disclosure of assumptions: "My assumptions" is collapsed at the bottom, keeping methodology transparent (for trust/credibility) without overwhelming the primary experience.

screens.name: Wealthfront Logging & Tracking 12
screens.whereToUse:
Use this interactive slider-to-outcome pattern in any tool where a numeric input has a clear, immediate downstream financial or health impact (e.g., loan calculators, budgeting apps, fitness calorie trackers, retirement calculators). It is highly effective for "what-if" scenario planning where instant feedback drives better decision-making.

The "Assumptions" disclosure pattern should be used whenever an app performs a complex calculation that users might distrust; always give users the option to inspect the "ingredients" of an algorithmic output.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for simple, single-variable inputs where a text field or stepper would be faster and more precise than a slider (sliders are imprecise for exact figures like currency).

Do not use overly cheerful, congratulatory copy ("You're nailing it") if the underlying data is actually negative or concerning (e.g., user is significantly behind on savings), as this creates a jarring, untrustworthy dissonance between the UI tone and the harsh financial reality.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
