  • You want to maintain a lightweight, fast-loading filter tray while still offering deep faceted search.
  • Real-time result counts can be computed cheaply enough to update live as users navigate between filter categories.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the catalog is small or when there are only 2-3 filter dimensions (in that case, a single flat list of chips or a simple segmented control would be faster and avoid the extra navigation hop). It's also a poor fit for touch contexts where network latency makes the live product counter sluggish or inaccurate, as a stale/slow counter undermines the trust this pattern is designed to build. Finally, for category sets so large that browsing is more exploratory than attribute-driven (e.g., open-ended content discovery feeds), a more visual/faceted browse or algorithmic recommendation surface may serve users better than a plain textual filter list.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves high-intent fashion shoppersbrowsing H&M's large, frequently-refreshed worldwide catalog who need to narrow thousands of SKUs down by concrete attributes like brand, material, or fit. For young adults and families shopping across multiple categories (kids, licensed collabs, basics), granular filters like "Customer Group" and "Licensed Item" directly address real purchase blockers (e.g., finding the right size group or character-branded merchandise).

Psychologically, the screen leverages progressive disclosure to reduce choice overload, showing only category names first lowers the cognitive barrier to engaging with filters at all. The live counter taps into a sense of control and certainty, which is particularly important for mobile shoppers who are impatient and want assurance their taps are productive before committing to viewing results.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live result count above the CTA: Continuously updating the "Showing X products" label right next to the Apply button closes the feedback loop instantly, preventing the frustrating experience of applying filters and landing on an empty state.
  • Two-tier filter architecture: Separating "categories" (this screen) from "values" (sub-screens) keeps each screen cognitively light (no single screen overwhelms the user with hundreds of checkboxes at once).
  • Disabled-state button styling: Both Clear All and Apply appear greyed out/disabled in this default state, visually communicating that no changes have been made yet and nothing is actionable until the user engages with at least one filter.
  • Expandable "More Filters" entry point: Using a "+" icon instead of a chevron subtly differentiates this row as an expansion/reveal action rather than a drill-down navigation, respecting iconographic consistency.

screens.name: H&M -  Sorting products - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any high-SKU e-commerce or marketplace search/category results page where users need to quickly scan, filter, and compare many visually-driven items (fashion, home goods, electronics). It's especially effective when running active promotions, as the layout is built to foreground pricing and discounts without cluttering the primary grid.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, promotion-heavy layout for low-SKU catalogs, luxury/premium branding where aggressive red discount badges would undermine perceived exclusivity, or for content types that aren't primarily visual (e.g., services, B2B SaaS). Also reconsider the oversized query-as-headline treatment on screens with long or multi-word search phrases, as it can wrap awkwardly or dominate the viewport, pushing results below the fold.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious, deal-driven shoppers: particularly young adults and existing H&M customers browsing high-turnover denim inventory during a sitewide sale. The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Scarcity & Urgency: Red discount badges and strikethrough pricing exploit loss-aversion and anchoring biases, making the sale price feel like a time-sensitive win.
  • Choice architecture: Segmented category chips with counts reduce decision fatigue by letting users narrow 765 results into digestible, gender/age-based subsets instantly.
  • Low-commitment saving: The heart icon on every tile supports impulsive wishlisting, appealing to browsers who aren't ready to purchase but want to curate options for later (a key behavior for the fashion-shopping demographic who compare before buying).
screens.keyHighlights:
Treating the search query as a hero headline: Rendering "DENIM JEANS" in huge bold type turns a mundane search results page into an editorial moment, reinforcing brand identity even in a transactional flow.

  • Inline category counts (ALL [765], WOMEN [429]) give users instant inventory confidence and help them self-select the most relevant filter without guesswork.
  • Dual-badge discount system: a corner percentage badge plus red sale pricing (creates two redundant urgency cues that reinforce each other at a glance).
  • Persistent global sale banner + bottom tab bar keep promotional and navigational affordances always visible, reducing friction to re-engage with the sale funnel from any screen.
  • Swatch previews under each product let users gauge color variety without tapping into the PDP, saving time during high-volume browsing.

screens.name: H&M -  Sorting products - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for e-commerce search/category result pages where users need to quickly reorder large inventories by relevance, recency, or price. It's ideal when:

  • The catalog is large enough that sorting materially changes the browsing experience (hundreds of SKUs).
  • You want to keep users anchored in their current results context rather than navigating away to a new screen for simple preference changes.
  • Category segmentation (gender, age group, etc.) is a natural, high-value way to narrow large result sets.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid a lightweight inline popover when the number of sort/filter options is large or multi-dimensional (e.g., combined sort + filter + multi-select attributes) - in that case, a dedicated bottom sheet or full-screen filter page is more appropriate to avoid overcrowding. Also avoid stacking a persistent promotional banner above critical navigation/search context on smaller screens, as it reduces above-the-fold space for actual results and can feel like clutter for users not motivated by discounts (e.g., full-price/loyalty shoppers).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets fashion-conscious, price-sensitive shoppers browsing a large seasonal catalog (767+ denim results) who need fast, low-friction ways to narrow and prioritize options. The sort-by popover reduces cognitive load for decisive shoppers who know they want "cheapest first" or "newest arrivals," while the segmented category filter (Women/Men/Baby) serves family shoppers managing multiple needs in one session.

Psychologically, the discount badges (-63%, -60%) and the top sale banner exploit scarcity and deal-seeking behavior, nudging users toward purchase urgency. The heart/wishlist icon on every tile caters to users in a comparison or "save for later" mindset typical of fashion browsing, where decisions are deferred across multiple sessions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-intrusive popover sort menu: Opens inline below its trigger rather than consuming the full screen, letting users retain spatial context of the results grid.
  • Category counts in segmented pills: Showing "[767]," "[433]," "[121]" builds trust in catalog depth and helps users decide whether to narrow by gender/age instantly.
  • Persistent sale banner across navigation depth: The promotional strip remains visible even deep into a search journey, maximizing upsell exposure without a dedicated interstitial.
  • Consistent, scannable product card template: Wishlist heart, discount tag, crossed-out original price, and color swatch previews let users compare multiple items at a glance without tapping in.

screens.name: H&M -  Sorting products - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any visually-driven e-commerce catalog or search results screen, especially in fashion, home goods, or lifestyle retail apps where product imagery is a primary driver of purchase decisions. It's ideal when:

  • The catalog is large and benefits from audience/category segmentation (chips with counts).
  • Visual merchandising matters more than dense textual specs.
  • You need to combine promotional messaging (sales banners) with functional browsing without cluttering the UI.
  • A floating/pill tab bar suits a content-forward, minimal-chrome aesthetic.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for spec-heavy or comparison-driven verticals (electronics, B2B tools, groceries) where users need to compare detailed attributes (specs, nutritional info, reviews) before deciding (large hero imagery with minimal text would frustrate rather than assist decision-making).

Also avoid persistent promotional banners in flows where they could distract from critical tasks (e.g., checkout, account recovery) or in markets/regulatory contexts where sale banners must be more restrained. The floating tab bar may also overlap content on smaller screens or when more than 5 primary nav items are needed, requiring an overflow pattern instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves fashion-conscious shoppers and existing H&M customers actively searching for a specific product category (denim). The design assumes a user with intent-driven behavior rather than passive browsing, so it prioritizes fast refinement tools (sort, filter, audience chips) over inspirational content.

Psychological triggers at play include:

  • Scarcity/Urgency: "SALE: UP TO 60% OFF" in red exploits loss-aversion and FOMO to drive immediate action.
  • Social proof via volume: Large result counts (765, 429, 122) imply extensive choice and brand credibility/assortment depth.
  • Aesthetic-usability effect: High-fashion, editorial-style photography builds desirability and trust, aligning with H&M's brand image despite being a results/utility screen.
  • Low-friction wishlisting: The heart icon reduces the cost of "maybe later" decisions, capturing interest even when purchase intent isn't immediate.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Query confirmation as hero content: The oversized "DENIM JEANS" headline acts as a visual confirmation of search intent, reducing cognitive dissonance and reassuring the user they landed in the right place.
  • Chip-based audience segmentation with live counts: Horizontally scrollable filter chips (ALL/WOMEN/MEN/BABY) with bracketed counts let users self-filter instantly without opening a separate filter panel.
  • Floating pill tab bar: A modern, space-efficient navigation bar that stays unobtrusive while keeping core destinations one tap away.
  • Persistent sale banner: The sticky promotional strip at the very top maximizes conversion opportunity across every screen without disrupting the browsing flow.
  • Minimalist product cards: Large photography with condensed metadata (name, price) and an unobtrusive wishlist heart icon keeps the grid visually clean and editorial.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 24
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any app acting as an aggregator or directory of third-party destinations (marketplaces, loyalty/rewards hubs, deal aggregators, or super-apps linking out to partner services). It's ideal when the list can grow large and users need fast scanning combined with both structured (category) and unstructured (search) filtering.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this flat, logo-heavy list approach when partners lack strong visual brand recognition (e.g., small local businesses without polished logos), as the pattern relies heavily on instant visual identification. It's also unsuitable when each entry requires differentiated metadata (e.g., price, distance, ratings) that a generic "Shop" subtitle can't convey (in that case, a richer card-based layout would be more appropriate).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Afterpay's core demographic: budget-conscious, often younger shoppers (Gen Z/Millennial) who use installment payments to make retail, beauty, and travel purchases more affordable. The presence of fast-fashion (SHEIN, Temu, Fashion Nova) and lifestyle brands (Ulta, Gap, Expedia) suggests the audience skews toward frequent, smaller-ticket discretionary spending rather than big-ticket purchases.

Psychologically, the screen leverages brand familiarity as social proof: seeing trusted, well-known retailers listed as "partners" reduces perceived risk of using a financial product and signals that BNPL is mainstream and widely accepted, easing anxiety for first-time or hesitant users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Logo-led recognition: Using full-color, high-fidelity brand logos instead of generic icons dramatically speeds up visual scanning and builds instant trust via association with known retailers.

  • Frictionless search-to-browse hybrid: Combining a search bar, a category filter, and a "Suggested" curated list gives users multiple entry points depending on whether they know what they want or are browsing.

  • Consistent, predictable list architecture: Every row follows an identical Avatar + Title + "Shop" subtitle + tap-target structure, which lowers the learning curve as the list scales to hundreds of partners.

  • Persistent bottom navigation: Keeps payment and history utilities accessible, reinforcing that shopping discovery is one spoke of a larger financial hub rather than an isolated flow.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 25
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet category filter pattern when:

  • You need to let users narrow a large, unstructured list (brands, products, articles) by a single dominant attribute.

  • Screen real estate is limited (mobile), making a full dropdown or sidebar impractical.

  • You want to preserve navigational context while still giving filtering options full visual priority.

  • The category set is small-to-medium (under ~12 items) so it fits without requiring internal scrolling or search within the sheet.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Users need to select multiple categories simultaneously (radio buttons here would need to become checkboxes with a "Multi-Select" pattern instead).

  • The category list is very long (50+), where a searchable list or dedicated full-screen page would perform better than a bottom sheet.

  • The action requires heavy contextual explanation, since bottom sheets have limited vertical real estate and compete with the keyboard/gesture areas on smaller devices.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using Afterpay's Buy-Now-Pay-Later ecosystem who want to quickly discover which merchants support installment payments within a specific shopping category. The design assumes a broad, non-technical audience motivated by efficient browsing and decision-making rather than exploration for its own sake.

Psychologically, the single-select radio buttons (rather than checkboxes) suggest the product intentionally limits users to one category at a time, simplifying decision-making and reducing choice overload (a nod to Hick's Law). The clean, icon-driven list also reduces perceived effort, which increases the likelihood users will engage with filtering rather than skipping it and endlessly scrolling.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Layered bottom sheet over persistent context: The partial visibility of the underlying screen (search bar, "Suggested" header) keeps the user oriented to where they are in the app hierarchy, reducing the disorientation common with full-screen modals.

  • Icon + label pairing: Each category uses a bespoke line icon (hanger, flower, shoe, lamp, sofa, jacket, swimmer, headphones) alongside text, leveraging dual-coding (visual + verbal) to speed up recognition and add personality to an otherwise plain list.

  • Disabled Apply state as implicit guidance: Rather than an error message, the grayed-out "Apply" button non-verbally communicates that a selection is a prerequisite, which is a subtler and less intrusive form of validation.

  • Symmetrical dual-button footer: Placing "Clear" and "Apply" side-by-side with matching pill shapes but different visual weights creates clear affordance hierarchy while keeping both actions equally accessible.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 26
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet single-select filter pattern when:

  • You need to let users narrow a large catalog/directory by one mutually-exclusive dimension (category, sort order, region).

  • Mobile screen real estate is limited and a full-page filter screen would feel disruptive to the browsing flow.

  • You want to preserve context of the underlying list/search screen while performing the refinement task.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Users need to select multiple categories simultaneously (in that case checkboxes and a multi-select facet UI (with count badges) are more appropriate).

  • The category list is very long (30+): a searchable list or grouped/alphabetized list would work better than a flat scroll.

  • The filter needs to combine with several other facets at once (price, size, brand) - a full-page or multi-tab filter experience may be clearer than a single bottom sheet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers browsing Afterpay's partner merchant directory who want to quickly narrow down hundreds of retail brands to a specific vertical (e.g., only Furniture stores) before making a BNPL purchase decision. The design assumes users are on mobile, often mid-shopping-journey, and want minimal friction to filter results.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages choice architecture: by forcing a single-select radio pattern instead of open multi-select checkboxes, it reduces decision paralysis and keeps result sets meaningfully differentiated. The icon-driven list also taps into recognition-over-recall: users spot the shoe icon or hanger icon faster than reading text, which speeds up the filtering task on a small screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Layered context preservation: The background screen (search bar, "Category" chip, "Suggested" header) remains visible and dimmed behind the sheet, reminding users what page they'll return to and reducing the feeling of a full navigational jump.

  • Icon + label pairing: Each category row includes a unique, simple line icon that speeds up visual scanning and adds personality without heavy illustration.

  • Clear single-select signaling: Radio buttons (not checkboxes) make it immediately obvious that only one category can be active at a time, preventing user confusion about multi-select expectations.

  • Balanced footer actions: "Clear" as a muted pill vs. "Apply" as a bold black pill establishes clear visual priority without hiding the reset option.

  • Drag handle + partial peek layout: The sheet doesn't cover the full screen at rest, giving a spatial cue that it's dismissible via swipe and is a temporary overlay, not a new page.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 27
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any B2B2C marketplace, aggregator, or financial services app that needs to direct users to third-party partners or affiliate destinations. It is ideal for loyalty programs, cashback apps, or fintech products where the core value proposition is connecting a user to an external ecosystem of merchants. The combination of search bar + category filter + suggested list works well when the catalog is too large for a single screen but users often have specific known targets in mind.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this flat list pattern if the partner catalog spans thousands of entries without further sub-categorization, as an infinite un-sectioned scroll will become tedious; in that case, alphabetical indexing or more robust faceted filtering would be necessary. Additionally, if brand recognition is low (e.g., lesser-known local businesses), relying solely on a logo/name/generic "Shop" label pattern will fail to communicate value (richer contextual data (e).g., cashback rate, distance, ratings) would be needed instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing Afterpay users who are in an active shopping-discovery mindset (likely opening the app not to check a balance, but specifically to find where they can use their installment payment plan). The psychological driver here is choice facilitation: by surfacing a curated "Suggested" list rather than an exhaustive alphabetical directory, Afterpay reduces decision fatigue and implicitly endorses these retailers, which can also serve a merchandising/commercial function (featured brand placements).

The furniture category filter suggests behavioral or intent-based personalization (perhaps triggered by a prior search or seasonal promotion), targeting users currently in a bigger-ticket purchase consideration phase, where "buy now, pay later" financing is most psychologically appealing due to its ability to reduce sticker-shock/friction on larger purchases.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Category Filter Chip: The "Furniture" pill with a chevron acts as a lightweight entry point into a full category taxonomy without cluttering the UI with a full filter bar, keeping the search-first design clean.

  • Consistent Brand Iconography: Using recognizable, high-contrast circular logos (IKEA, Redbubble, Anthropologie) leverages brand recognition to build trust and speed up decision-making, since users often decide whether to explore further based on retailer familiarity alone.

  • Repeated 'Shop' CTA: Rather than a single header CTA, embedding "Shop" as secondary text under every single list item reinforces the action affordance at the item level, making every row feel individually clickable and purposeful.

  • Persistent Tab Bar Context: Keeping the global tab bar visible (with badge notification) ensures users don't feel "lost" in a deep directory screen and can easily jump back to their financial overview.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 28
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for help center articles, FAQ deep-dives, or policy explanations in any transactional app (fintech, e-commerce, marketplaces) where you need to explain fees, limits, or rules clearly without causing alarm. It's especially effective for:

  • Explaining monetization/fee structures transparently

  • Support flows that need a clear "escape hatch" to human help

  • Situations where you want to nudge users toward a specific behavior (e.g., enabling direct deposit) via incentive framing
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, text-heavy pattern for time-sensitive or emotionally charged support issues (e.g., fraud, account lockout) where users need immediate visual reassurance, escalation options, or status indicators rather than long paragraphs. Also avoid on tasks requiring urgent action (the passive, read-only format isn't suited for flows needing form inputs or immediate decisions). For less financially-savvy users, a purely text-based explanation of conditional fee waivers may still require an FAQ or visual chart supplement.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday Cash App users, likely lower-to-middle income individuals who receive paycheck direct deposits and rely on cash-based transactions (paper money), a demographic Cash App has specifically targeted (versus traditional banking apps). The explanation of fee waivers via direct deposit is also a subtle behavioral nudge/growth mechanic. Cash App wants to convert casual users into full direct-deposit customers, increasing stickiness and reducing churn to traditional banks.

Psychologically, this leverages loss-aversion and reciprocity: users feel they are being rewarded (fee waived) for loyalty (direct deposit), which builds trust in a category (fintech apps handling cash) where trust is a major adoption barrier.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fee-Waiver Framing: Instead of leading with "this costs $1," the copy quickly reframes to "but it's free if you do X," turning a potential objection into a loyalty/engagement driver (encouraging direct deposit usage).

  • Related Articles Stack: Anticipates follow-up questions (locations, limits, instructions) directly beneath the main content, reducing the need to search again.

  • Progressive Disclosure to Human Support: The "Contact us > Chat" option is placed last, following the standard support funnel of self-serve first, human-assisted second (this reduces support ticket volume and costs).

  • Modal Dismissal Pattern: Using an "X" instead of a back arrow correctly signals this is a supplementary help layer, not a step in a task flow, letting users return to a base state instantly.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 29
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when presenting location-based service details (ATMs, deposit partners, pickup points, service centers) where the user needs actionable next steps (navigate vs act now) plus critical fine print (fees, limits) before committing. Ideal for fintech cash deposit networks, retail pickup/return flows, or any "find a partner location" feature layered on a map.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the underlying data (fees, minimums) is variable/unreliable, since displaying stale numeric commitments can erode trust. Also avoid stacking too many bottom sheets on a map for complex multi-step flows (if the user needs to compare multiple locations side-by-side, a full list/table view with filtering would serve better than a modal-per-location approach).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets underbanked or cash-reliant users of a neobank/fintech app (e.g., Chime, Varo, Cash App-style products) who need to convert physical cash into their digital account balance via retail partner networks. These users are often deposit-fee sensitive, so surfacing exact costs and minimums before the trip is a critical trust and retention lever, nothing frustrates this segment more than driving to a store and discovering unexpected fees or a $20 minimum they can't meet with a small bill.

The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion and effort justification: by disclosing fees and minimums before the user commits time/gas money to visit the location, the app prevents a wasted trip and the resulting distrust/churn that would follow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Map + Sheet layering preserves spatial context so users don't lose their place on the map while reviewing details.

  • Upfront fee transparency with an inline info icon builds trust and reduces surprise/chargeback disputes at checkout.

  • Dual-path CTAs ("Show barcode" vs "Directions") elegantly serve both in-store and en-route user states from a single screen.

  • Icon-led fact list (dollar sign, barcode, card) enables rapid scanning of deposit method minimums without reading full sentences.

  • Branded avatar for the retailer builds immediate recognition and trust for a third-party deposit partner.

results.query: Floating Action Button FAB for quick issue logging

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for:

  • Account/settings surfaces in B2B SaaS or productivity tools, especially those with multi-tenant/team-switching needs.
  • Modal-style settings screens that should feel detached from primary navigation stacks (mobile apps that are companions to a desktop-first product).
  • Screens needing to clearly separate navigational rows (with chevrons) from terminal/destructive actions (flat rows) for scannability.
  • Any tool targeting professional/technical users where a lightweight, always-available bug-reporting mechanism (like shake-to-report) adds real value.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal, text-only pattern when:

  • The target audience is less tech-savvy and needs more visual cues, icons, or explanatory copy to understand settings (e.g., consumer apps aimed at broad demographics).
  • The app has only a single workspace/account: the "Teams and organizations" switcher becomes unnecessary clutter.
  • You need to surface account security actions (2FA, password changes) prominently; this flat list structure can bury critical security settings without strong visual emphasis.
  • The brand personality calls for warmth or delight (this layout is purely functional and offers no opportunity for brand expression or emotional connection).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves professional designers, developers, and team administrators who need quick access to account identity, team/organization switching, and support channels while deep in a design workflow. Because Figma is fundamentally collaborative, the "Teams and organizations" section addresses the very real need to confirm or switch context between a personal account and client/employer organizations (a frequent pain point for freelancers and consultants working across multiple workspaces).

The inclusion of "Report issue" and "Shake to report" reflects the target audience's technical sophistication; these are power-user affordances aimed at professionals who will proactively surface bugs to improve a tool they rely on daily for their livelihood, rather than casual consumers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Modal "Done" pattern: Using "Account" + "Done" in the nav bar (instead of a back arrow) correctly communicates that this is a self-contained settings sheet that can be dismissed at any point without losing navigational state in the main app.
  • Active organization checkmark: A minimal, elegant way to indicate the currently selected team context without needing radio buttons or extra labels (critical for a multi-tenant collaboration tool).
  • "Shake to report" toggle: A delightful, low-friction power-user feature that turns physical device gestures into a bug-reporting shortcut, reducing the friction of filing issues during active design work.
  • Clear visual hierarchy via section headers: Grouping settings into "Teams and organizations," "General," and "Help" lets users build a mental model of where destructive (Log out), navigational (Notifications/About), and support (Report issue) actions live.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for:

  • Any in-app help/feedback entry point where user-reported issues need to be pre-categorized for internal routing (support vs. product teams).
  • Productivity, B2B, or SaaS tools with power users who generate frequent, specific feedback.
  • Situations where you want to reduce free-text ambiguity before a user reaches a longer form.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Your feedback categories overlap heavily or users frequently can't tell bugs from feature requests (in that case, a single unified form with a dropdown may reduce decision paralysis).
  • You need to capture urgent, time-sensitive issues (e.g., payment failures) - those deserve a dedicated, higher-visibility escalation path rather than being buried in a generic help sheet.
  • The target audience is non-technical and may not understand the bug/improvement distinction, risking mis-categorization.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers and developers actively working in Figma who hit a snag or have a fleeting idea mid-workflow. Because Figma's audience is technically literate and detail-oriented, they appreciate precision (hence the explicit distinction between a defect report and a feature suggestion rather than a generic "Contact Us" funnel).

Psychologically, this taps into the Zeigarnik effect: capturing a user's frustration or idea at the exact moment it occurs (in-context) dramatically increases the likelihood of them actually submitting feedback, compared to asking them to remember and report it later via email.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Intent-based bifurcation: Splitting feedback into "bug" vs "improvement" at the entry point does the routing work upfront, saving triage time downstream.
  • Descriptive subtitles: Each choice is reinforced with a clarifying sentence, preventing mis-selection and reducing support team back-and-forth.
  • Native OS pattern: Leveraging the iOS action sheet convention makes the interaction feel instantaneous and familiar, requiring no onboarding.
  • Low-friction exit: A clearly separated "Cancel" button respects the user's right to back out without penalty or guilt.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any professional/productivity tool with complex workflows where users encounter technical issues mid-task (design tools, IDEs, project management apps).
  • Support or feedback flows where automatically capturing diagnostic context (screenshots, logs, device info) would significantly improve the quality of reports without burdening the user.
  • Apps targeting technical or semi-technical users who value transparency and control over what data is being shared (hence the editable attachment list).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer apps with casual, non-technical users may find "steps to reproduce" and screen-recording language intimidating or confusing; simpler one-tap feedback (e.g., emoji rating) may be more appropriate.
  • Avoid auto-attaching screenshots or session data without explicit disclosure/consent in contexts involving sensitive or regulated information (e.g., healthcare, finance) to avoid privacy or compliance violations.
  • Not ideal for extremely time-sensitive critical bug escalation flows where a direct chat/ticket with a human support agent would be faster than a self-service form.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Figma's core audience of designers and developers, many of whom are highly technical and expect efficient, low-friction feedback channels embedded directly in their workflow tool. Because these users are often mid-task when they encounter a bug, the design minimizes typing (pre-filled email, auto-captured screenshot and repro steps) so they can report the issue and return to work quickly.

Psychologically, the screen reduces the perceived effort and uncertainty of bug reporting (a task users often abandon because they don't know what information is "useful" to include). By auto-capturing technical context (screenshot, steps to reproduce) and only asking for a free-text description, the app leverages the principle of reducing cognitive load, increasing the likelihood that users will actually complete and submit the report rather than give up.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-filled email field: Removes a trivial but annoying data-entry step by using the logged-in account's email automatically.
  • Guided placeholder copy: The description placeholder acts as an inline template/prompt (expected vs. actual behavior), improving the quality of bug reports submitted without extra UI.
  • Automatic context capture with user control: A screenshot and reproduction-steps log are auto-attached, with a visible close "X" and "Edit list" link giving the user editorial control and transparency over what's being sent.
  • Layered evidence options via bottom sheet: Screen recording, screenshot, and gallery selection are tucked into a secondary action sheet, keeping the main form minimal while still offering rich diagnostic capture.
  • Minimal chrome, clear exit/submit actions: A simple close (X) and send (paper plane) icon pair in the top bar keeps the interaction model obvious and low-friction.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for app "About" or "System Info" screens where you need to surface static metadata (version numbers, build IDs, legal documents) alongside rarely-used but necessary account-level destructive actions. It's ideal when:

  • You need to comply with app store or legal requirements to expose account deletion.
  • You want to separate informational, non-actionable content from interactive/destructive content on the same screen.
  • Your audience is technical and doesn't need extensive explanation of version/build terminology.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The target audience is non-technical and would benefit from plain-language explanations of what "Version" or "Build" mean, or why they'd need this information.
  • Account deletion is a frequently needed or urgent action (e.g., privacy-focused apps) - burying it two levels deep could frustrate users or violate "easy opt-out" expectations (e.g., GDPR "right to erasure" guidance favors more direct access).
  • The screen has multiple destructive or high-stakes actions (a single flat list with only color-coding may not provide enough differentiation or warning at scale; a dedicated confirmation flow or grouped "Danger Zone" section would be more appropriate for multiple risky actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves existing, logged-in Figma users: designers and developers (who need to reference their app version/build (often for bug reports or support tickets) or who are seeking to manage/delete their account). The audience is technically sophisticated, so no extra explanation of "Version" or "Build" is required.

Psychologically, the design leverages friction as a safety mechanism: by nesting the destructive "Delete account" action inside a secondary "About" screen rather than directly in the main Account menu, Figma reduces the chance of accidental or impulsive deletions, while still satisfying platform/legal requirements that users must have an accessible self-service deletion path. The red color coding taps into universal danger signaling, triggering caution before the user even reads the label.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-interactive vs. interactive differentiation: Version and Build rows have no chevron and gray static values, clearly signaling they are read-only, while "Legal" has a chevron indicating further navigation (a subtle but effective affordance cue).
  • Isolation of destructive action: "Delete account" is visually separated by a divider and distinct red color, preventing accidental taps and signaling irreversibility at a glance.
  • Burying high-risk actions: Placing account deletion two navigation levels deep (Account > About) is an intentional friction pattern that discourages impulsive or accidental account deletion while still technically providing the required self-service option.
  • Consistent dark header pattern: The dark navigation bar with back-chevron and centered title maintains visual consistency with the rest of the Account section, reinforcing a sense of place within the settings hierarchy.

screens.name: Figma - Reporting an issue - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any in-app feedback, support, or bug-reporting flow where reducing friction and capturing technical context quickly is critical (especially in professional/B2B tools, developer tools, or QA-heavy products). It's ideal when:

  • You want to boost bug report submission rates by minimizing manual steps.
  • Users are mid-task and need a fast way to flag issues without losing their place.
  • You can auto-capture useful diagnostic context (screenshots, logs, steps) to enrich reports for your support/engineering team.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, auto-capturing approach in consumer-facing apps with strong privacy sensitivities (e.g., health, finance, messaging) unless capture is clearly opt-in and consented to, as silently generating "reproduction steps" or screen recordings could feel invasive. It's also unnecessary for simple, low-complexity apps where a plain text feedback box is sufficient and a multi-option attachment sheet would just add complexity for minimal benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets designers and developers using Figma who encounter a bug mid-workflow and want to report it with minimal interruption to their creative process. Precision-focused users (Figma's core demographic) expect accurate, detailed bug reports to be easy to generate without needing to manually describe technical context.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduction of perceived effort (pre-filled fields, auto-attached screenshots) to overcome the natural reluctance to stop and fill out a support form. The transparency microcopy also taps into a need for control and trust, especially for a technically sophisticated audience who may be wary of what diagnostic data is being silently transmitted.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-filled & Smart Defaults: The email field is already populated, removing a step and reducing drop-off on a task users typically want to finish quickly.
  • Automatic Evidence Capture: A screenshot appears to be pre-attached with an in-line annotation/edit icon, turning a manual "take and upload a photo" task into a near-zero-effort action.
  • Transparency on Metadata Collection: Explicitly informing the user that reproduction steps are included builds trust and sets expectations for support/engineering teams reviewing the ticket.
  • Layered Bottom Sheet for Attachments: Rather than navigating away, a native action sheet surfaces additional capture methods (record, screenshot, gallery) contextually, preserving the user's place in the form.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any productivity, dev-tools, or B2B SaaS product where speed-of-capture outweighs completeness-of-metadata at creation time (e).g., issue trackers, note-taking apps, CRM quick-add, or task managers. It's especially effective when:

  • The user base is technical/power-users comfortable with Markdown or plain-text shorthand.
  • Secondary metadata (assignee, priority, due date) can reasonably be added later without blocking workflow.
  • You want to reduce abandonment on creation flows by minimizing required fields to just one (title).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal-field, Markdown-first pattern when:

  • Your audience is non-technical and would be confused or intimidated by raw Markdown syntax without a WYSIWYG toolbar.
  • Compliance, reporting, or downstream automation requires mandatory structured metadata (e.g., priority, category) at the moment of creation, deferring these fields could create backlog hygiene problems.
  • The product relies on heavy upfront categorization for routing (e.g., support ticketing systems that must classify issues immediately for SLA purposes).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and founders who need to capture a technical task the instant it comes to mind (often mid-conversation or mid-code-review) without breaking flow. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of friction to intention-to-record latency: by not forcing the user through dropdowns for priority, labels, or assignee before they can even write the issue body, Linear captures the thought before it's lost, a core tenet of fast-moving engineering teams praised for valuing speed over process ceremony.

The structured Acceptance Criteria formatting also reflects target-user behavior: teams that already think in Definition-of-Done checklists, so the tool is meeting them where their existing documentation habits already are rather than imposing new templates.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Markdown-native authoring: Users can type raw Markdown syntax (bold, bullet lists) directly in the description field, aligning with how engineers already write specs/tickets elsewhere, removing the need to learn a new formatting UI.
  • Minimal mandatory fields: Only a title is strictly required; everything else (labels, assignee, priority, cycle) is optional and deferred, dramatically lowering the activation energy to log an issue.
  • Contextual breadcrumb in header: Showing the repo/project path ("SLMobbin/padel-score-c...") directly under the modal title keeps the user oriented about where this issue will land without needing a separate dropdown field cluttering the body.
  • Full-screen modal over navigation: Using a card-style sheet that overlays rather than navigating away preserves the user's prior context/scroll position on the underlying screen.
  • Disabled Submit with loader: Prevents premature or duplicate submissions while background validation/sync resolves, an unobtrusive way to enforce data integrity.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any collaborative, stateful record that evolves over time (issue trackers, support tickets, order statuses, approval workflows, or CRM deal pages). It's ideal when users need both the current state (header/status) and historical context (activity feed) in a single scroll, and when a lightweight persistent action (comment, reply, approve) should remain accessible during review.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, static content (e.g., a profile view or a read-only article) where an activity log would be noise. It also breaks down on screens where many competing primary actions exist (the single floating action bar works because Linear limits itself to one dominant interaction (commenting); adding more buttons would clutter the thumb zone). For consumer apps prioritizing emotional engagement over auditability, this dense, log-style timeline would feel cold and overly technical.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engineers, PMs, and founders who need to triage or update issues on the go (e).g., reviewing acceptance criteria during a commute or quickly commenting from a phone during a standup. The density and GitHub-like structure cater to technically literate users who value information density over whitespace-heavy consumer UI.

Psychologically, the activity log leverages the Zeigarnik effect and transparency bias, seeing a running history of actions (assignment, labeling, milestone) builds trust that nothing is lost and creates accountability among collaborators. The always-visible comment action reduces friction for in-the-moment feedback, exploiting the "strike while the iron is hot" principle to increase engagement velocity.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent floating action bar: The "Comment" + info-icon cluster floats above the tab bar, keeping the primary interaction always within thumb reach regardless of scroll position.
  • Status pill as instant state signal: The green "Open" badge with a circular icon lets users parse issue state in a glance, no reading required.
  • Unified timeline of content + metadata events: Comments, labels, milestones, and assignments are rendered in one continuous feed, giving a single source of truth for issue history without separate tabs.
  • Breadcrumb-style repo context: "SLMobbin / padel-score-counter #2" instantly orients the user within the larger project hierarchy.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 10
screens.whereToUse:
• Any detail view for a record that has lifecycle state (tickets, orders, tasks, bugs) where status needs to be understood in under a second.
  • Collaborative tools where mentions, ownership, and accountability need lightweight visual emphasis inline with free-text content.
  • Apps with nested/hierarchical content (parent issue → sub-issues) that benefit from inline expansion rather than forced navigation.
  • Mobile companion experiences for desktop-first power tools, where users need fast read/triage/comment actions rather than full editing capability.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, text-heavy layout for casual consumer apps where users expect visual-first browsing (e.g., media, social feeds) - the information density here would feel overwhelming.
  • Not ideal when the primary user task is rapid bulk triage of many items; a list/table view with batch actions would serve that need better than a single-item detail drill-down.
  • If the target audience is non-technical or unfamiliar with issue-tracker conventions (acceptance criteria, sub-issues), this structure may require additional onboarding or simplification.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers who need to triage or action issues on the go (often between meetings or away from their desk). The dense but well-organized layout caters to power users who already understand issue-tracking conventions (acceptance criteria, sub-issues, status states) and simply need fast confirmation or lightweight commenting rather than full authoring.

Psychologically, the clear status badge and structured acceptance criteria reduce anxiety around ambiguous task ownership (everyone can see exactly what "done" looks like). The Owner tag and mention highlighting leverage social accountability, subtly encouraging responsiveness from tagged collaborators. The persistent bottom navigation exploits the Von Restorff/habit-loop principle: no matter how deep a user drills into a single issue, the path back to inbox or home never disappears, lowering the fear of "getting lost" in a dense tool.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Status pill as a first-class citizen: The green "Open" badge with icon is placed directly under the title, making state scannable before reading any detail (critical for triage-heavy workflows).
  • Breadcrumb-lite identity line: "SLMobbin / padel-score-counter #3" compresses team, project, and issue ID into one glanceable line, preserving context when deep-linked or shared.
  • Inline collaborator mention highlighting: Yellow-highlighted @mentions inside body text improve scanability of ownership/action items embedded in prose.
  • Progressive disclosure of sub-issues: A dedicated "Sub-issues" section with a quick-add (+) button supports hierarchical issue breakdown without leaving the detail view.
  • Persistent global tab bar: Even on a deep, content-dense detail screen, Home/Inbox/Explore/Copilot remain one tap away, reinforcing a hub-and-spoke IA.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 11
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when building detail/record views for technical or operational tools (issue trackers, CI/CD dashboards, support ticketing systems) where users need to see rich structured content, an audit trail, and a cross-tool shortcut all on one screen. It's especially effective when:

  • The record has a strong external linkage (e.g., GitHub, Jira, Figma) that deserves a persistent CTA.
  • An activity/audit trail adds trust and traceability for collaborative, asynchronous teams.
  • Content is naturally list/checklist-based (acceptance criteria, requirements, specs).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, log-heavy layout for consumer-facing apps or for users unfamiliar with technical/engineering jargon (the activity feed and checklist format can feel cold or overwhelming to non-technical audiences). It's also not ideal when the detail record has minimal metadata, as the extra chrome (breadcrumb, activity log, sub-issues) would feel like empty scaffolding on a simple object. Additionally, if the primary external action changes contextually (not always "Open in GitHub"), a static persistent button could create confusion or false affordances.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for engineers, founders, and technical product managers who need to triage or review issues while away from their desktop (e).g., approving acceptance criteria from a phone during a commute, or quickly checking an issue's status before a standup.

Psychologically, it leverages reduced cognitive load through familiar developer mental models (git-style activity logs, checklist-style acceptance criteria) so users don't have to re-learn a new paradigm on mobile. The immediate "Open" button also taps into minimizing perceived effort: engineers who live in GitHub expect a frictionless bridge between tools, and surfacing this action prominently builds trust that Linear won't trap them in a walled garden.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent "Open" CTA: Anchored directly under the header outside the scroll area, ensuring the primary cross-tool action (opening the linked GitHub resource) is never lost as content grows.
  • Inline Activity Timeline: Combines system events (label, milestone, assignee) into a single connected vertical thread, eliminating the need for a separate audit log screen.
  • Structured Acceptance Criteria as native checklist copy: Presents QA/test requirements as scannable bullet points directly within the issue body, supporting async engineering handoff.
  • Dual-layer bottom actions: Comment and Info buttons sit above the OS tab bar, cleanly separating "issue-level" actions from "app-level" navigation.
  • Compact metadata breadcrumb: Repo path (SLMobbin/padel-score-counter) under the title keeps full project context visible without consuming a dedicated header row.

screens.name: Figma - Turning on commenting - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet action menu pattern when a full-screen immersive view (prototype playback, media player, map, game) needs to expose secondary controls without permanently consuming screen real estate. It's ideal for:

  • Presentation/viewer modes where the primary content must stay unobstructed by default.
  • Grouping toggle states and navigation actions that are used infrequently but must remain discoverable.
  • Scenarios requiring a dynamic, context-aware title to re-orient the user mid-flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when actions are used frequently or need to be accessed instantly, as the extra tap to open the sheet adds friction. It's also unsuitable when more than 7-8 options are needed, since a flat list without grouping or search becomes hard to scan. Additionally, mixing destructive actions (like "Exit prototype") with harmless toggles in a single undifferentiated list (without visual separation or color coding) can create risk of accidental taps for high-stakes actions in other contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This overlay primarily serves designers presenting prototypes and the stakeholders/clients viewing them on mobile devices (a scenario common when sharing a Figma prototype link for review outside the desktop app). The psychological driver is control and reassurance: viewers need confidence that they can restart, exit, or inspect the underlying file without breaking anything, which is why "Restart" and "Exit prototype" are given prominent, unambiguous placement near the top of the list.

"Turn on commenting" and "Turn on hotspot hints" cater to collaborative review workflows, letting non-designers annotate feedback or discover interactive hotspots, lowering the barrier for less technical participants to engage meaningfully in the design review loop.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual title binding: The sheet header dynamically displays the file and page name ("JudySmith's team library - Page 1"), keeping the viewer oriented about exactly what they're interacting with even after navigating away from the main canvas.
  • Disabled state teaching: Greying out "Flow" rather than hiding it communicates the feature's existence while signaling it's currently unavailable, preserving menu consistency across different files.
  • Single primary exit via "Done": Placing the confirmatory action top-right (rather than a stacked button) keeps the list below purely for navigation/toggles, avoiding competing calls-to-action.
  • Icon-label pairing: Every action is reinforced with a recognizable icon (arrow, reverse arrow, feather/pen, speech bubble, pointing hand), aiding rapid recognition for repeat use.

screens.name: Figma - Turning on commenting - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Multi-step onboarding carousels introducing complex platform-specific concepts (e.g., design systems, workspaces, templates) to new users.
  • Feature education screens for B2B/collaborative SaaS tools where demonstrating a "real" screenshot builds more trust than abstract illustration.
  • Any product with a reusable-asset/library concept (components, snippets, templates) that benefits from showing a concrete before-you-build example.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, information-rich screenshot approach for first-touch, top-of-funnel onboarding meant for total beginners (it may overwhelm users unfamiliar with basic design terminology).
  • Not suitable for consumer apps with simple, single-purpose use cases where the feature being described doesn't warrant a dedicated carousel slide.
  • Avoid if the screenshot used isn't pixel-accurate/up-to-date, as outdated UI previews can create confusion or mistrust once users reach the real interface.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is aimed at new signups who are likely professional or aspiring UI/UX designers and front-end developers evaluating Figma for team-based work. The messaging assumes familiarity with design system vocabulary (styles, components, text fields, color tokens), indicating this step targets users past the very first "what is Figma" stage (likely a mid-funnel onboarding screen introducing more advanced collaborative capabilities).

Psychologically, it leverages the efficiency/avoidance-of-redundant-work trigger (not reinventing the wheel) and social validation/belonging (team library, "everyone on your team") to position Figma as the tool that eliminates duplicated design effort and fosters consistency, which is a major pain point for design teams migrating from tools like Sketch or standalone static files.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Authentic Product Screenshot as Proof: Rather than a generic illustration, the screen shows a real, detailed example of a color/typography/component library, which builds immediate credibility and sets accurate expectations.
  • Icon-as-Avatar Branding: The rounded library icon with a letter avatar ("J") subtly reinforces the "team" and personalization aspect of libraries, hinting this content belongs to a specific team member/org.
  • Benefit-First Headline Structure: Leads with the outcome ("Build your own team library") before explaining the mechanism, aligning with best practice for scannable onboarding copy.
  • Split-Canvas Layout: Visually mirrors Figma's own product layout (canvas + panel), subtly onboarding users into the app's spatial mental model even during marketing-style education.

screens.name: Figma - Turning on commenting - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Use the side-by-side "artifact + explanation" layout when introducing any feature that produces a visible output (templates, themes, design systems) - it builds trust faster than text-only marketing.
  • Use comment/mention overlays with bolded deadlines in any collaborative tool (docs, whiteboards, project management) where asynchronous feedback needs light urgency without full task-management overhead.
  • Apply the resolve/checkmark affordance in any threaded commenting system to help teams track outstanding vs. addressed feedback at a glance.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid overlaying comment sheets on top of dense, information-critical screens where obscuring context could cause users to lose their place or misunderstand what's being referenced.
  • Don't use casual @mention-with-deadline patterns for high-stakes or compliance-related tasks (these require formal, trackable task-assignment systems rather than lightweight chat-style mentions).
  • Avoid the "artifact + headline" educational format for abstract or non-visual features where there's nothing meaningful to preview visually.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves design teams and cross-functional collaborators (PMs, developers) who rely on Figma not just as a design tool but as a shared source of truth. The team-library promotion targets designers early in adoption, using the psychological trigger of reduced cognitive/manual effort ("don't reinvent the wheel") to drive feature adoption. The comment thread targets active collaborators already inside a file, leveraging social accountability (named mention, deadline) and FOMO/urgency (a due date tied to a specific colleague) to drive timely engagement with feedback.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Show-don't-tell content pairing: The actual UI library artifact (colors, text field states) is placed adjacent to its explanatory headline, letting users visually validate the claim instantly instead of trusting copy alone.
  • In-context collaboration overlay: Comments live as a dismissible bottom sheet layered over the content itself, preserving spatial context so the commenter's feedback remains tied to what they're discussing.
  • @Mention with bolded deadline: Combining a tappable mention chip with bold text ("by Monday") creates a lightweight task-assignment mechanic inside a casual comment, blurring the line between chat and project management.
  • Resolve toggle affordance: The circular checkmark icon gives a one-tap way to mark feedback as addressed, reducing thread clutter and giving teams a lightweight accountability loop.

screens.name: Figma - FigJam file options - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when designing mobile companion experiences for complex desktop-first canvas or document tools (whiteboards, diagramming, design tools, map editors). It's ideal when:

  • The core interaction is spatial/freeform and benefits from an infinite canvas metaphor.
  • You need to preserve a large visual viewport while still exposing creation tools without modal interruptions.
  • Real-time collaboration/presence is a core value proposition that should be visible at all times.
  • Users will perform short, frequent "check-in" sessions rather than long focused work, justifying a reduced/simplified toolset versus the desktop version.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal floating-toolbar-on-canvas pattern when:

  • The tool requires dense, frequent access to many simultaneous options (e.g., full desktop-grade vector editing) - icon-only compressed toolbars will cause excessive nested menus and friction.
  • Users are predominantly first-time/non-technical and need labeled, explicit actions rather than icon-only affordances.
  • The app's primary content is linear/text-based rather than spatial, where an infinite dot-grid canvas would add confusion instead of clarity.
  • Precise, fine-grained manipulation is required that finger-based touch targets cannot adequately support without a stylus or zoom affordances.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers, product managers, and cross-functional team members who need to check in on, contribute to, or react to a brainstorming session while away from their desktop (e).g., during a stand-up, commute, or hallway conversation. The simplified mobile toolset assumes users are performing lightweight actions (adding a sticky note, reacting with an emoji, moving an object) rather than deep design work.

Psychologically, the design leans on social presence (avatars) and low-commitment engagement (big tap targets, undo-friendly canvas tools) to encourage spontaneous participation. The playful "FigJam basics" sticky and sticker pack also serves as implicit onboarding/demo content, lowering the intimidation factor for first-time FigJam mobile users by showing rather than telling them what's possible.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-mode floating toolbar: Separates navigation (select/pan) from creation (pen/shape) tools into distinct pill-shaped clusters, reducing accidental tool switches on a small touchscreen.
  • Infinite canvas affordance via dot grid: Instantly communicates spatial freedom and orientation without any onboarding copy.
  • Persistent collaborator avatars: Builds real-time social presence awareness at a glance, reinforcing FigJam's multiplayer value proposition even in a condensed mobile header.
  • Expandable tool trays (chevrons): Keeps the primary toolbar compact while still surfacing deeper customization (colors, shapes, sticky variants) on demand.
  • Minimal top bar with clear exit path: The "X" close button gives users unambiguous, low-friction control to leave the board, critical for a mobile companion/viewer experience.

screens.name: Figma - FigJam file options - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when a desktop-grade application needs to expose a long tail of secondary, power-user commands on a space-constrained mobile surface. It's ideal for:

  • Productivity, creative, or technical tools porting a rich menu-bar feature set to mobile/touch.
  • Contexts where command frequency varies widely (some used constantly, others rarely) and a flat always-visible toolbar would be impractical.
  • Apps that already have an established keyboard-shortcut/menu-bar culture on desktop, where consistency across platforms builds user confidence.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense list-menu approach for:

  • Consumer-facing, first-time-use apps where cognitive load must stay minimal (a 14-item menu would overwhelm casual users).
  • Primary, high-frequency actions that deserve dedicated, always-visible buttons rather than being buried in an overflow list (forcing two taps instead of one hurts efficiency for core workflows).
  • Situations lacking logical grouping: if items can't be clearly clustered, the undifferentiated list becomes a scroll-heavy, hard-to-scan wall of text.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This menu targets intermediate-to-power users: designers and developers already fluent in Figma's desktop conventions who need parity when working on a tablet/phone during a review, a quick edit, or while away from their workstation. The inclusion of niche commands like "Show timer" (a FigJam collaboration/workshop tool) and "Find in file" signals this is built for active collaborators, not first-time visitors.

Psychologically, the design leverages recognition over recall: by mirroring the structure of Figma's desktop right-click menu, returning users don't need to relearn where functions live, reducing friction and reinforcing platform consistency across devices, which builds trust and perceived reliability in a professional tool.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Grouping via Dividers: Related actions (clipboard, history, view) are clustered with subtle separators instead of labelled headers, saving vertical space while preserving scannability.
  • Disabled-but-Visible Pattern: Unavailable actions (Cut, Copy, Undo) are grayed out rather than hidden, maintaining a predictable, muscle-memory-friendly menu structure across sessions.
  • Icon + Label Redundancy: Every action pairs a trailing icon with its text label, speeding recognition and supporting accessibility/localization.
  • Porting Desktop Power to Mobile: The menu condenses Figma's desktop right-click/menu-bar functionality into a single scrollable sheet, proving that a touch-first surface can still support an expert, keyboard-shortcut-level workflow.
  • Persistent Trigger Visibility: The top bar (avatars, share, "...") stays visible above the menu, letting users understand the menu's origin and dismiss ambiguity about where it came from.

screens.name: Figma - Turning on hotspot hints - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet action menu pattern when:

  • Surfacing secondary, session-level controls (settings, navigation shortcuts, mode toggles) without permanently occupying screen real estate in a content-first view like a prototype player or media viewer.
  • You need to expose several independent toggles/actions that don't warrant their own dedicated screen.
  • Context (the underlying canvas/content) should remain visible/dimmed behind the sheet so users retain spatial orientation.
  • Your users are power users familiar with domain terminology, allowing terse, label-only rows without extra explanatory copy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Actions have significant, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., deleting a file) - these need explicit confirmation dialogs, not a simple one-tap row in a list.
  • The target audience is non-technical and would be confused by jargon like "hotspot hints" or "Flow" without additional explanation or tooltips.
  • Too many options exist (>7-8), which would require scrolling and undermine the quick-access value of an action sheet; a full settings screen would serve better.
  • You need to show rich previews or visual state (e.g., thumbnails of flows) - plain text rows lose important visual context in those cases.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This menu is built for designers and stakeholders reviewing or presenting interactive prototypes on mobile devices (a secondary but important use case for Figma beyond the desktop canvas). The audience includes both the prototype's creator (who may want to restart the flow or jump to the source file) and collaborators/clients viewing a shared link (who may want to leave feedback via commenting).

Psychologically, the design leverages reduced choice overload by limiting the menu to six clearly scoped actions, and state disclosure (explicit on/off wording) to build user confidence that toggling a setting won't produce a surprising or hidden effect (critical in a collaborative tool where turning on commenting changes what other viewers can do).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual disabling of irrelevant options: "Flow" is greyed out rather than hidden, teaching users the feature exists but isn't applicable right now, preserving a consistent menu structure across all prototypes.
  • Dismiss without data loss: "Done" and the background dim let users peek at the underlying prototype state, reducing fear of losing their place in a presentation.
  • State-transparent toggles: Labels like "Turn on hotspot hints" explicitly communicate the current state and the resulting action in one phrase, eliminating ambiguous iconography-only toggles.
  • Native platform conventions: Drag handle, right-aligned "Done," and list-row icons mirror iOS/Android system action sheets, so the control feels instantly familiar despite being Figma-specific tooling.

screens.name: Figma - Turning on hotspot hints - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when onboarding a sophisticated, visually literate audience to a complex feature that benefits more from demonstration than explanation. Ideal for:

  • Introducing design-system, component library, or theming features in professional tools.
  • Any value-prop carousel step where showing a real-looking artifact builds more trust than an abstract icon or illustration.
  • Positioning collaboration/team-based features early to seed future multiplayer engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, screenshot-heavy approach for first-time or non-technical users who may feel overwhelmed by seeing raw UI complexity (text field state names, hex-like tokens) before they understand basic app navigation. It is also unsuitable for mobile-first, lightweight consumer apps where screen real estate is better spent on simplified iconography rather than literal screenshots. If the feature being marketed isn't visually rich (e.g., a backend/API feature), this screenshot-led layout loses its persuasive power.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new or evaluating Figma users who are likely designers or design-adjacent team members (developers, PMs) being introduced to Figma's collaborative design system capabilities during initial app onboarding. The psychological trigger at play is competence signaling and aspiration: showing a polished, organized design system (named color tokens, systematic text field states) appeals to professional designers' desire for order, scalability, and best practices.

It also leverages social dependency framing ("across files, with everyone on your team") to subtly nudge solo users toward inviting teammates, which drives Figma's core growth loop of collaborative, multi-seat adoption.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Authentic artifact as proof: Using a real, detailed screenshot of color/typography/component libraries instead of an abstract illustration builds immediate credibility with a design-literate audience who can self-identify with the content.
  • Idiom-driven pain-point hook: "Don't reinvent the wheel" instantly communicates the core value proposition (reusability) without requiring technical explanation.
  • Visual-to-text ratio: Roughly 65% of the screen is dedicated to the product screenshot, respecting that for a visual tool, seeing the interface is more persuasive than reading about it.
  • Soft color-blocked text panel: The pale blue background box subtly distinguishes marketing copy from the product screenshot above without needing a hard divider line.

screens.name: Figma - Turning on hotspot hints - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Teaching users how to interact with shared/global assets (design tokens, team libraries, style guides) where mistakes have broad consequences.
  • Any onboarding flow for complex desktop software where a tiny icon or affordance is easy to miss without explicit visual pointing.
