screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving dim/blur overlay: The payment screen remains visible but de-emphasized behind the sheet, so users retain a mental model of what they're about to lose.

  • Redundant, low-friction dismissal: Swipe handle, "X" icon, and "Back" text link all lead to the same safe outcome, accommodating different user habits and reducing rage-taps.

  • Plain-language button labels: "Yes, cancel it" removes any ambiguity about what the affirmative action does, unlike generic "OK/Cancel" dialogs.

  • Minimal sheet real estate: Only the essential decision is presented (no upsells, no extra copy) respecting the urgency of a decision point.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any transactional flow where a single numeric value is the primary input and must be verified before an irreversible action. P2P payments, tipping, invoicing, in-app currency top-ups, or bill-splitting features. It's especially effective when:

  • The action has two symmetrical directions (pay vs. request, buy vs. sell, add vs. withdraw).

  • Speed and low cognitive load are more valuable than rich formatting options.

  • A custom keypad can meaningfully reduce input errors compared to the system keyboard.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex financial inputs requiring multiple fields, currency conversion, or itemized breakdowns (e.g., invoicing with tax/line items) - the single giant number affordance breaks down when more than one value needs simultaneous visibility. It's also unsuitable for accessibility-sensitive contexts unless the custom keypad and buttons are rigorously tested with screen readers, since non-native keyboards can sometimes degrade assistive technology support. Finally, avoid dual equally-weighted CTAs (Request/Pay) in flows where one action is destructive or significantly higher-risk than the other, as visual parity can encourage mis-taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets mainstream consumer P2P payment users (e.g., Venmo, Cash App audiences) - largely younger, mobile-first users splitting bills, paying rent, or gifting money to friends and family. The design leans on social proof and casualness (memo field, gift icon, friendly tone) rather than the sterile formality of banking apps, because trust in this context comes from familiarity and simplicity rather than institutional gravitas.

Psychologically, the oversized amount display exploits the Von Restorff effect (isolation effect) - the number visually dominates so users double-check the figure before committing, reducing regret and support tickets from mistaken amounts. The proximity of "Request" and "Pay" buttons reduces the perceived friction of switching intent, appealing to users who make split-second decisions in social settings (e.g., splitting a check at a restaurant).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom numeric keypad: Overrides the system keyboard to optimize digit entry speed and prevent accidental non-numeric input in a financial context.

  • Giant, high-contrast amount display: The $1 figure is the single largest element on screen, immediately confirming the entered value at a glance (critical for reducing transaction errors).

  • Inline clear (X) affordance: Placed directly next to the amount for instant correction, avoiding tedious character-by-character backspacing.

  • Dual-intent CTA pattern: Presenting "Request" and "Pay" as equally weighted, adjacent pill buttons lets users flip the direction of money flow without navigating to a different screen.

  • Contextual memo field: Placed just above the CTAs so the "why" of the transaction is captured before the irreversible action, reinforcing social/contextual money transfers.

  • Minimal chrome: Only back and close icons are present, keeping the modal feel tightly scoped to a single task and reducing decision fatigue.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for peer-to-peer payment confirmation, checkout confirmation, or any "review and confirm" step where a monetary or high-stakes action needs a final, deliberate user gesture. It's ideal when you want to combine transaction summary, configurable options (payment source, privacy, protections), and legal disclosures on a single scrollable screen without forcing a multi-step wizard.

Particularly effective for social-payment apps, marketplace checkouts, or bill-splitting tools where humanizing the transaction (via memo, avatar, social visibility) increases engagement and repeat usage.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for complex B2B or high-value transactions where additional verification, itemization, or multi-party approval is required (the single-screen simplicity here would be insufficient and risky). Also avoid defaulting sensitive financial activity to "Public" visibility in contexts where privacy regulations or user expectations demand private-by-default behavior (e.g., healthcare payments, salary transfers, enterprise expense platforms).

Not suitable when the payment method or optional add-ons (like protection plans) require detailed comparison, cramming that into a confirmation screen would increase cognitive load and reduce conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers: largely younger, social-media-native users, splitting small, informal costs with friends (e.g., splitting a $1 bottle of water). The design leans on social proof and normalization psychology: by defaulting to "Public" visibility, Venmo nudges users toward sharing payment activity as a social signal, similar to a social media post, which reinforces habitual usage and network growth.

The optional Purchase Protection toggle appeals to trust and loss-aversion psychology, protecting non-power users from being scammed in peer transactions that resemble commercial purchases, thereby reducing friction and anxiety for first-time or infrequent users making similar payments to strangers or sellers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single, high-contrast CTA: The pill-shaped teal "Pay" button is the only strong color on the screen, ensuring zero ambiguity about the next action.

  • Progressive disclosure of risk/fees: Purchase protection terms and fee implications are shown inline with a toggle rather than hidden behind a separate settings page, letting users make an informed decision at the point of payment.

  • Funding source transparency: Displaying the live balance ($150.11) directly on the payment method row lets users mentally verify affordability without navigating away.

  • Social-first framing: Treating the payment like a mini social post (avatar, name, memo, public/private setting) leverages Venmo's differentiator versus purely transactional apps like bank transfers.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing a toggle, setting, or classification choice that has downstream financial, legal, or policy implications the user might not intuitively understand (e.g., payment type selection, privacy visibility settings, subscription auto-renewal toggles). It's ideal for:

  • Fintech apps clarifying fee structures or protection eligibility tied to a binary choice.

  • Any moment right after a user toggles a setting, to reinforce understanding without requiring them to seek out help documentation.

  • Situations where you want to preempt support tickets or user confusion with a single, friendly, dismissible explainer.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for trivial or self-explanatory settings (over-explaining low-stakes toggles creates unnecessary friction and modal fatigue). It also should not be used as a substitute for proper legal consent flows; if the setting carries binding terms (e.g., fee agreements), a simple "Got it" acknowledgment may be legally insufficient and a more explicit consent mechanism (checkbox, "I agree" with T&Cs link) should be used instead. Additionally, avoid stacking multiple such explainer sheets in a single flow, as repeated interruptions frustrate users and encourage blind "Got it" tapping without actual comprehension.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using a peer-to-peer payment app who may be unfamiliar with the legal distinction between "paying a friend" (informal transfer) and "paying for goods/services" (a regulated commercial transaction with buyer/seller protections and often fees). The primary psychological trigger is reduction of uncertainty and perceived risk: by explaining the "why" behind a toggle before the user commits, Venmo lowers hesitation and builds trust in the platform's fairness and safety mechanisms.

It also leverages reciprocity and fairness framing ("safer marketplace," "both you and the seller will be covered") to make what could feel like an extra fee or friction point (goods/services fees) feel like a protective benefit rather than a cost. This is especially important for casual sellers (e.g., marketplace resellers, freelancers) who need confidence that Venmo will back them if a transaction goes wrong.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Illustration mirrors the live UI: The hand-holding-phone graphic replicates the exact toggle and Pay button the user just saw, creating instant visual continuity between context and explanation.

  • Dimmed background retains context: Rather than a full-screen takeover, the underlying payment screen remains dimly visible, reminding the user why this sheet appeared without letting them lose their place.

  • Anticipatory objection handling: The copy proactively answers "what if I'm not buying anything?" before the user has to ask, reducing support burden and toggle-related anxiety.

  • Single, low-friction CTA: "Got it" is the only actionable button (no complex choices, no risk of the user picking the "wrong" option in an informational moment).

  • Drag handle affordance: The visible pill/handle at the top signals the sheet is dismissible via swipe, reinforcing that this is a lightweight, non-blocking helper rather than a hard gate.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this balance-card-plus-action-stack pattern for consumer fintech home screens where you need to combine (1) a critical numeric status, (2) immediate transactional CTAs, and (3) an evolving feed of secondary promos/notifications. It's ideal for apps with a "primary metric" (balance, score, streak) that benefits from being visually anchored at the top with supporting actions bundled tightly beneath it.

The mascot/illustration softening technique is especially valuable in financial, health, or other anxiety-prone verticals where raw numbers alone could feel harsh or judgmental.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for B2B, enterprise, or data-dense dashboards where users expect density and multiple accounts/metrics visible simultaneously (the single hero-card approach doesn't scale well beyond one or two primary numbers). Also avoid whimsical mascots in contexts requiring high trust/seriousness (e.g., large business banking, legal, insurance claims) where playful illustration could undermine credibility. Additionally, be cautious mixing promotional upsell banners (like the advance CTA) too close to sensitive financial states, as regulators in some markets scrutinize cash-advance marketing tied to low-balance triggers.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially underbanked or paycheck-to-paycheck consumers, evidenced by the $0.02 balance shown as a normalized default/example state and the prominent surfacing of the ExtraCash advance feature. Dave's core user base often lives close to overdraft, so the design intentionally avoids alarming red color-coding for a low balance, instead using neutral black text and a friendly mascot to keep the emotional tone non-punitive.

The psychological trigger at play is relief and support-seeking behavior: by immediately offering "Get some ExtraCash" right where a user would feel stressed about a low balance, Dave capitalizes on a moment of financial anxiety to drive engagement with its most profitable product (advances/subscriptions), while simultaneously building trust through a non-shaming, human tone.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Balance-anchored action pairing: Add Money/Withdraw buttons sit immediately below the balance, minimizing distance between information and action.

  • Anxiety-softening mascot: A friendly 3D bear character is placed adjacent to a near-zero balance, using character design to reduce the emotional sting of a low-balance state.

  • Proactive logistics messaging: Surfacing the physical card's estimated arrival date with an immediate digital-card fallback reduces support tickets and anxiety about "where is my card."

  • Soft framing of credit products: The ExtraCash (cash advance) banner uses gentle, non-judgmental language and a full-width green banner to funnel users to a monetizable feature without shame-based messaging.

  • Stacked card feed pattern: Using a vertical stream of dashboard cards allows Dave to merchandise new features/promos without redesigning the primary balance view.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-screen numeric entry pattern whenever the primary and singular action on a screen is entering a specific numeric value (especially currency, quantities, or measurements) in contexts like:

  • Wallet top-ups, money transfers, or deposit/withdrawal flows in fintech and banking apps

  • Bill splitting, invoicing, or payment request amount entry

  • Any single-input flow where you want to eliminate distraction and enforce input validation before allowing progression
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for multi-field forms, flows requiring additional context (e.g., payment method selection alongside amount), or situations where users need to reference other on-screen data while typing. It's also unsuitable when supporting multiple currencies simultaneously without clear currency-switching affordances, or when the target audience needs guidance/hints (e.g., minimum/maximum amount) since this stripped-down layout offers no room for inline help text without cluttering the design.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of fintech, banking, wallet, or peer-to-peer payment apps (e.g., Cash App, Venmo, PayPal) who need to quickly deposit or transfer funds. The design assumes a goal-directed user who already knows their objective ("I want to add $50") and simply needs the fastest, least obstructed path to enter that value.

Psychologically, the massive amount display exploits the "picture superiority" and salience effect (larger, high-contrast text draws attention and reinforces the user's sense of control over their input). The disabled button leverages a subtle behavioral nudge (a soft constraint) to guide correct behavior without explicit scolding, reducing frustration and perceived friction in a money-handling context where trust and precision are paramount.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized, dynamic amount display: The giant "$0" typography functions as instant visual confirmation of input, a pattern borrowed from calculator and POS interfaces that users already trust.

  • Disabled CTA until valid input: The grayed-out "Next" button prevents users from submitting a zero-value transaction, an elegant inline validation technique that avoids the need for an error toast or dialog.

  • Full-screen custom numeric keypad: Bypassing the native OS keyboard keeps the user contained within the app's branded environment and allows for a decimal point and backspace key tailored specifically to currency entry.

  • Minimal chrome / single exit point: The lone "X" in the top-right is the only way out, reducing decision paralysis and keeping the user hyper-focused on completing the single task at hand.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any transactional flow requiring numeric-only input, such as payment amounts, top-ups, tips, or budget entries.

  • Situations where you want to eliminate ambiguity by making the current value the dominant visual element.

  • Mobile-first flows where one-handed usability and thumb reach are priorities.

  • Apps needing consistent, branded input controls instead of relying on inconsistent native OS keyboards.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for complex forms requiring multiple fields or contextual data (e.g., recipient details, notes) - a single giant number field doesn't scale to multi-input scenarios.

  • Not ideal when users need to reference other information (like account balance or transaction history) while entering the amount, since the minimalist layout offers no space for supporting context.

  • Risky in flows where input errors carry irreversible consequences without a strong confirmation step afterward (the simplicity here should always be paired with a review/confirmation screen before finalizing).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using peer-to-peer payment or digital wallet apps (e.g., Cash App, Venmo, PayPal, banking apps) who need to quickly top up their balance. The design assumes users are often multitasking or in a rush (e.g., transferring money before a purchase), so speed and clarity are prioritized over education or upsell messaging.

Psychologically, the large numeral leverages the "focal point" principle, drawing the eye and reinforcing a sense of control and confidence over the amount being entered, which is critical in financial contexts where errors cause anxiety. The stripped-back, almost blank canvas also reduces perceived complexity, making a potentially stressful action (moving money) feel simple and low-risk.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized amount display: Using an extra-large font size for the dollar figure creates an immediate focal point and lets users visually verify their input at a glance without eye strain.

  • Custom numeric-only keypad: Bypasses the OS-default number pad to enforce input constraints (digits + decimal only) and guarantees consistent cross-platform visual design.

  • Thumb-zone optimized layout: Critical interactive elements (CTA + keypad) are anchored at the bottom of the screen, matching natural one-handed grip and reach patterns.

  • Minimal chrome, maximum focus: Removing navigation clutter, tab bars, and secondary content creates a modal-like, distraction-free task flow appropriate for financial input.

  • Clear escape hatch: The "X" in the top-right gives users an unambiguous, low-risk way to abandon the flow at any point, reducing anxiety around a money-related action.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this stacked bottom-sheet pattern when a user needs to make a secondary selection (like choosing a payment method) without abandoning the primary transaction context. Ideal for money transfer, checkout, or booking flows where displaying cost/time trade-offs transparently for each option builds trust and reduces support inquiries. Also effective whenever there are 2+ categories of similar-but-distinct options (e.g., bank vs. wallet, shipping methods, delivery times).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid layering multiple modals when the underlying content isn't necessary for the current decision (it can feel visually cluttered or overwhelming, especially on smaller screens). Also avoid this pattern if there are more than 4-5 selectable options per category, as a bottom sheet may become cramped; a full-screen list or dedicated page would scale better. If fee structures are complex (tiered, variable, conditional), simple inline text may not be sufficient and could require a more detailed comparison table instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This flow targets everyday banking app users, likely lower-to-middle income consumers using Dave for early paycheck access, overdraft protection, or budgeting (a demographic highly sensitive to fees and speed of fund availability. Surfacing fee and timing information upfront respects their financial constraints and builds trust, a key retention lever for challenger banks competing against traditional banks perceived as fee-heavy and opaque. The choice architecture (free-but-slow vs fast-but-fee) leverages the classic time-value-of-money psychological trade-off, letting the user's own urgency dictate the fee they're willing to accept) a subtle monetization mechanism disguised as user choice.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Stacked modal context preservation: The underlying "Add money" summary stays visible (dimmed) behind the funding-source sheet, so users never lose track of the amount or destination while making their selection.

  • Transparent cost/speed trade-off labeling: Every payment method displays both delivery time and fee inline, enabling instant comparison without extra taps or hidden-fee surprises.

  • Categorized funding options: Grouping by "Bank account" and "Digital wallet" instead of a flat list improves scannability and mental modeling.

  • Inline-editable hero amount: The large $1 figure with an adjacent edit pencil keeps amount adjustment one tap away without navigating to a separate screen.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any single-purpose financial transaction flow (bank transfers, peer-to-peer payments, top-ups, or withdrawals) where the amount is the primary variable and the user must select between a small number of source/destination accounts. It's ideal when transparency (fees, timing) directly impacts user trust and conversion, and when you want to minimize steps by keeping everything on one screen instead of a multi-step wizard.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this single-screen approach for complex transfers involving multiple currencies, recipients, or additional compliance steps (e.g., large international wires) where more guided, multi-step verification is needed. It's also not ideal if there are many account options, as a simple dropdown/expandable card wouldn't scale (a searchable list or full selection screen would be more appropriate). Additionally, if legal/regulatory disclosures are extensive, burying them in small gray text may not meet compliance visibility standards.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday banking app users, likely including financially underserved or budget-conscious consumers (a core Dave demographic) who care deeply about transfer fees and processing times. The explicit "No fee" and "4-5 business days" labels directly address anxiety around hidden costs, which is a major pain point for this audience switching from traditional banks.

Psychologically, the screen leverages reduction of transactional friction (large tap targets, minimal fields, one clear CTA) and trust-building through transparency (fees, timing, balance all visible upfront). The mascot and rounded, friendly typography also invoke a sense of approachability and safety, important for users who may feel intimidated or anxious about managing money digitally.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized, editable amount display: The giant dollar figure with a subtle pencil icon makes the amount the clear focal point while keeping editing frictionless and discoverable.

  • Inline contextual metadata on accounts: Surfacing fee, timing, and current balance directly on the source/destination cards eliminates the need to tap through to find critical decision info.

  • Dynamic CTA label: "Transfer $1.00" mirrors the entered amount directly in the button, serving as a final glanceable confirmation before committing money.

  • Brand personality via mascot avatar: The friendly bear icon on the Dave Checking account softens the transactional, potentially stressful nature of moving money.

  • Compliance without friction: Legal disclosure text is present but visually de-emphasized and linked out, balancing regulatory requirements with clean UX.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any single-purpose financial transaction flow (bank transfers, P2P payments, top-ups, withdrawals) where the user needs to confirm an amount and a source/destination pairing. It's especially effective for:

  • Fintech/neobank deposit or withdrawal modals

  • P2P payment confirmation screens (e.g., Venmo/Cash App style "Add from/to" flows)

  • Recurring payment or subscription setup screens where amount and account selection are core inputs

  • Any flow that benefits from an inline, in-place loading state rather than a full navigation transition
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The transaction involves multiple line items or complex calculations (e.g., cart checkout with taxes/discounts) - the oversized single-amount hero treatment won't scale.

  • Users need to compare multiple funding sources side-by-side before choosing, as the vertical stacked-card layout limits comparison at a glance.

  • The transfer requires multi-factor confirmation or additional risk disclosures (e.g., large wire transfers) - a single scrollable modal may under-communicate the gravity of the action; a dedicated review/confirmation step would be safer.

  • The loading state might take a very long time (e.g., >10-15 seconds) - an in-button spinner without additional context (e.g., estimated wait time) could cause user frustration or repeated taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers of a neobank/cash-advance app (Dave) who are topping up their checking account balance, likely to enable overdraft protection, cash advances, or bill payments. The demographic skews toward users who are budget-conscious and possibly living paycheck-to-paycheck, making fee transparency ("No fee") and low minimum amounts (as low as $1) especially persuasive trust signals.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduction of friction and anxiety around moving money (a historically stressful action for financially strained users). The clear visual separation of "from" and "to," combined with real-time balance display ($0.02) creates urgency and relevance (motivating the top-up) while the inline progress state reduces the "did it work?" uncertainty that can cause repeated taps or app abandonment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized, directly-editable amount display: Treating the dollar figure as the visual hero (rather than burying it in a small input field) reinforces that this screen has one job: confirm how much money to move.

  • Dual-card source/destination selector: The "Add from" / "Add to" cards use consistent visual language (institution logo, account nickname, contextual metadata like fees and timing, balance) making it easy to scan and verify before committing.

  • Inline button-state loading: Rather than navigating to a new screen or showing a full-screen spinner, the primary CTA morphs in-place from an action label to a progress label with a spinner, preserving context and reducing perceived wait time.

  • Transparent fee/timing disclosure at the point of decision: Displaying "4-5 business days • No fee" directly inside the source account card, right where the user is choosing the funding source, prevents surprises and builds trust.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately after any successful transactional flow (payment, transfer, sign-up, purchase) where you want to introduce a complementary feature without derailing the user's primary goal. It's ideal for fintech apps introducing direct deposit, subscription upgrades, or referral programs, and for e-commerce apps suggesting related products post-purchase. It works best when the secondary offer is genuinely relevant and low-commitment to explore.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the primary confirmation message is critical/legal (e.g., large financial transactions, medical actions) where any visual competition could distract from important details or create distrust. Also avoid stacking multiple upsells on one confirmation screen, as this can feel manipulative and dilute the sense of task completion. If the secondary offer is unrelated to the user's current context, it will feel like noise and erode trust in the confirmation itself.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday banking/fintech app users (e.g., Dave, Chime, Cash App demographics) who are often underbanked or living paycheck-to-paycheck and are highly motivated by speed-of-access to their own money. The mention of "Dave Checking" suggests this is a neobank targeting cost-conscious consumers who value avoiding fees and getting paid faster.

Psychologically, this screen exploits the "peak-end rule" - users remember experiences based on their peak emotional moment and the ending, so placing an appealing offer right after a successful action (positive peak) increases receptivity and reduces the perceived friction of a sales pitch. It also uses loss-aversion/gain framing ("up to 2 days early") to nudge users toward adopting a stickier product feature (direct deposit) that increases their engagement and retention with the app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Success-Moment Cross-Sell: Injecting a relevant, high-value upsell (early direct deposit) at the peak of a positive emotional moment (task completion) rather than interrupting the transfer flow itself.

  • Visual Hierarchy Separation: Using distinct background colors and a card/shadow to clearly separate "required information" (confirmation) from "optional information" (upsell), so the user's core task is never obstructed.

  • Icon-First Communication: The custom illustration communicates the value proposition (faster money) instantly and emotionally, before the user reads a single word.

  • Non-Blocking CTA Priority: The primary "Done" button remains the dominant, always-available action, respecting user autonomy while the secondary CTA is offered as an opt-in, not a forced gate.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 8

It's ideal when a product offers multiple card form factors (virtual + physical) and needs to disambiguate them clearly. The masked-by-default approach should be used anywhere sensitive financial data is displayed in a shared or mobile context.

Do not mask data by default in contexts where users need frequent, low-friction access to card numbers (e.g., a dedicated "copy card details" utility) - in such cases, consider a persistent unmask toggle instead of hiding it within a settings-like list. Also avoid stacking too many toggle-based actions without grouping/hierarchy, as it can make the list feel like a flat settings dump rather than a curated action center.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday banking app users, particularly Dave's core demographic of budget-conscious, often underbanked consumers who value transparency and control over their finances. The psychological trigger here is security and control: masking sensitive card data by default builds trust, while giving users one-tap freeze and PIN controls empowers them to react quickly to lost cards or fraud without calling support, satisfying a need for autonomy and reducing anxiety around financial safety.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Security-by-default masking: Card number, CVV, and expiration are masked by default and only revealed via an explicit "Show card info" toggle, protecting against shoulder-surfing and screen-recording risks.

  • Carousel + Page Control combo: Enables users to browse between digital and physical card entities in a compact, swipeable format instead of a long scrolling list.

  • Contextual education card: Placing an explanatory blurb about the digital/physical card relationship directly in the flow (rather than in a help center) reduces confusion at the point of need.

  • Consolidated card controls: Freeze, PIN, and replace actions are grouped in one list, turning what could be 3+ separate screens into a single, efficient control panel.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 9

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 10

  • Low cognitive friction for users who may be hesitant to manually type a card number, achieved by isolating just two required inputs per screen.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual confirmation copy: Dynamically inserting the card name and target device into the subtitle reassures the user their action is correctly scoped before they invest effort filling out fields.

  • Minimal field surface area: Only two fields are shown at once, keeping the step lightweight and reducing form abandonment risk.

  • Embedded privacy transparency: Placing a plain-language data usage disclosure directly within the flow (rather than hiding it in Settings) builds trust at the exact moment sensitive financial data is being requested.

  • Consistent OS navigation chrome: Back/Next buttons in the same position as every other Apple system flow reduce learning curve and increase perceived reliability.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 14
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any single, critical numeric or currency input step within a multi-step financial or transactional flow (such as deposit amounts, loan amounts, budget goals, or transfer sums). It's ideal when you want to isolate a high-stakes value from distraction, ensure accuracy, and maintain flow momentum in an onboarding/setup wizard. Also effective in Multi-Step Forms where each step captures exactly one variable for clarity and lower error rates.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when multiple related fields naturally belong together (e.g., paycheck amount + frequency + pay date) - forcing them into separate single-field screens can feel tedious and increase completion time/friction. Also avoid excessive whitespace and single-field screens for low-stakes or frequently repeated inputs, where users will resent the extra taps. Not suitable for expert/power-user tools where speed and information density are prioritized over guided simplicity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users going through a financial onboarding or account-configuration flow (likely setting up automatic paycheck deposits or budget/paycheck tracking within a banking, budgeting, or early-wage-access app). The audience is likely everyday consumers, potentially including financially stressed or less tech-savvy users who benefit from reduced cognitive load and unambiguous instructions.

Psychologically, the single-field, single-task screen leverages the "one thing at a time" principle to reduce anxiety around financial data entry. The disabled button leverages a "Zeigarnik effect"-like nudge: users see an incomplete state and are motivated to complete the action to "unlock" progress. The dollar sign and plain-language copy build trust and reduce friction, both crucial for financial apps where hesitation or confusion can cause drop-off.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose screen: Only one input is presented, eliminating decision fatigue and errors from a cluttered form.

  • Disabled CTA as implicit validation: The greyed "Save" button communicates form state without needing an explicit error message, guiding the user naturally to complete the field first.

  • Currency affordance built into the field: The persistent "$" prefix removes ambiguity about input formatting instantly, without extra copy.

  • Large, bold typographic hierarchy: The oversized title mimics a conversational prompt, making a technical/financial task feel more human and approachable.

  • Minimal chrome: Simple back arrow only in the nav bar avoids distracting the user from the primary task.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 15

It's ideal for financial, fintech, or budgeting apps where precision and reduced cognitive load are critical, and for flows where you want to minimize drop-off by isolating one decision per screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when multiple related fields need to be captured together (e.g., amount + date + recipient), as splitting these into separate screens could increase the number of steps unnecessarily and frustrate users. It's also not ideal for use cases where a full alphanumeric keyboard is needed (e.g., notes or descriptions), or in dense dashboard-style apps where screen real estate for a single field would be inefficient. Additionally, if users frequently need to reference other account data (like current balance) while entering the amount, this stripped-down layout may omit necessary context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen likely targets users of a banking, budgeting, or paycheck-splitting app (e.g., early direct-deposit or savings automation apps) who need to quickly specify how much of their paycheck to allocate or deposit into a specific account/goal. The audience is likely mainstream consumers, potentially including financially cautious or first-time savers who benefit from a simplified, distraction-free flow.

Psychologically, the design leverages the focus effect (single input, single CTA) to reduce anxiety around entering financial data, and the reachability/ergonomics principle by locating the confirm action near the thumb's natural resting position during numeric entry. The large numerals and clear labeling also invoke a sense of control and transparency, which builds trust when handling money.
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 16
screens.whereToUse: Use this review-and-edit summary pattern whenever a multi-step form or wizard culminates in generating a document, submitting an application, or triggering an irreversible/hard-to-undo backend action (e.g., loan applications, tax forms, insurance claims, HR forms, contract generation). It's ideal any time you want to reduce error-driven support tickets or re-submissions by giving users one last, low-effort chance to verify their inputs field-by-field.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy confirmation pattern for low-stakes, easily reversible actions (e.g., changing a display name or toggling a preference), where an extra review screen only adds friction and feels redundant. It's also not ideal when the form has a very large number of fields, in which case a single flat review list becomes overwhelming (consider grouping fields into collapsible sections (Accordion) instead). Additionally, avoid separating the e-sign consent from the data being signed off on; here it's borderline problematic that the checkbox and CTA are only revealed after scrolling, which could be improved with a sticky footer to guarantee visibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users setting up automated payroll deductions or savings contributions (e.g., fintech apps like Chime, Dave, or employer-benefits platforms) who need to generate an official-looking payroll form to submit to HR/employer. The audience is likely everyday consumers, not enterprise users, given the casual tone and simplified field set (Name, Company, Amount).

Psychologically, the pattern leverages the need for control and error prevention: users handling money and legal documents are highly loss-averse and want a final checkpoint before committing. The inline Edit buttons satisfy the psychological need to feel in control, while the plain summary format reduces the perceived effort of verification (users can scan three short lines instead of re-reading a full form).

The e-sign checkbox taps into familiar patterns from tax software (TurboTax) and e-commerce checkout, so users don't need new mental models to understand that checking the box + tapping "Create form" finalizes the legally binding request.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Per-field inline editing: Each row has its own dedicated "Edit" button, letting users correct a single piece of information surgically instead of navigating back through multiple prior screens.

  • Review-before-commit pattern: Consolidating all inputs onto one confirmation screen builds user confidence and catches errors before an irreversible or hard-to-edit document (the form) is generated.

  • Legal consent bundled with final action: The e-signature checkbox is placed directly above the primary CTA, ensuring compliance/consent is captured in the same glance as the commit action, reducing legal risk without adding an extra screen.

  • High-contrast, low-distraction visual design: Bold black-on-white typography with no unnecessary color or imagery keeps full attention on data accuracy and the task at hand (appropriate for a financial/legal context).

  • Clear escape hatch: The top-left "X" gives users permission to abandon the flow at the point of highest commitment friction, reducing anxiety and rage-quits.

screens.name: Cash App Adding & Creating 17
screens.whereToUse: Use this granular summary-and-edit pattern in any multi-step form where the final output is a legally binding document, financial transaction, or irreversible action (e.g., loan applications, tax forms, subscription sign-ups, payroll deductions). It is ideal when the form contains 3-7 distinct data points that benefit from individual verification before a "point of no return" submission.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for very short forms (1-2 fields) where a full summary screen adds unnecessary friction/an extra step. It is also not suitable for high-frequency, low-stakes actions where a lightweight inline confirmation or toast would suffice instead of a dedicated review screen. Additionally, avoid pairing a pre-checked legal consent checkbox with a submit button in jurisdictions where explicit (unchecked-by-default) opt-in is legally required.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday consumers/employees setting up automated payroll deductions (likely for a savings, investment, or benefits app). The design assumes a non-technical audience by using plain language and avoiding financial jargon. The psychological trigger at play is reducing anxiety around financial commitments: by summarizing exactly what will happen (a fixed $10 deduction per paycheck) before the binding action, the user feels a sense of control and transparency. The granular edit capability specifically caters to users who are detail-oriented or anxious about errors in financial/legal documents, offering an escape hatch that prevents drop-off due to fear of mistakes.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Granular Inline Editing: Distinct "Edit" pill buttons per data row allow surgical correction of a single field without restarting or navigating a long back-stack, drastically reducing user frustration in a multi-step flow.

  • Legal Consent Coupling: The e-sign checkbox is placed immediately adjacent to the submit button, creating an unmissable visual link between "I agree" and "I am doing this now," which aids legal compliance and informed consent.

  • High-Contrast Single CTA: The absence of a competing secondary button (no visible "Back" button on the main summary) keeps the user focused on a singular path forward: confirm or edit specific fields.

  • Data Chunking: Breaking the review into three distinct titled sections instead of a dense paragraph or table improves scannability and lets users verify accuracy at a glance.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 35
screens.whereToUse:
• Configuring recurring or scheduled financial transactions (auto-deposits, subscriptions, bill pay) where a single date parameter needs isolated focus.

  • Any setup wizard step where you want to minimize distraction and force a deliberate, single-variable decision.

  • Mobile contexts where large touch targets and swipe gestures outperform dense grid-based date pickers.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• When users need to select a date far in the future or navigate across multiple months (this horizontal-only, day-of-month carousel doesn't scale well beyond a small range (like day 1) 31 for recurring billing).

  • Contexts requiring multi-parameter input (e.g., date + time + recurrence rule) where separating everything into full-screen single-question modals would create excessive step fatigue.

  • Desktop or data-dense enterprise tools where compact calendar widgets are more efficient and expected.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumer fintech users (e.g., Cash App, Venmo-style audiences) setting up automatic/recurring savings or cash deposits. The design assumes a mobile-first, often younger or less financially sophisticated audience that benefits from simplified, guided decision points rather than dense settings forms.

Psychologically, the screen leverages choice reduction and progressive disclosure: by only asking one question at a time in a modal, it prevents the user from feeling overwhelmed by a full recurring-transfer settings page (frequency, amount, account, date all together). The direct-manipulation carousel with immediate visual feedback (green highlight, scaled tile) taps into satisfaction from tactile, physical-feeling interactions, increasing engagement and confidence when configuring an automated money movement (a high-stakes, trust-sensitive action).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-question full-screen focus: Removes all UI chrome so the user's cognitive load is spent entirely on one decision.

  • Oversized carousel date tiles: Replaces a cramped calendar grid or wheel picker with large, glanceable, thumb-friendly cards, improving tap accuracy and readability.

  • Green "torn calendar page" motif: Instantly communicates "date" semantics using a familiar physical metaphor without any text label.

  • Dynamic CTA label ("Set 16th"): Closes the feedback loop, confirming exactly what action will be taken before the user commits.

  • Peeking neighbor cards: Non-verbal affordance signaling horizontal scrollability, reducing reliance on written instructions.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 36
screens.whereToUse: Use this full-screen numeric keypad pattern whenever the core task of a screen is entering a single monetary or numeric value (such as deposit amounts, savings goals, bill splitting, tipping, or recurring transfers). It's ideal when you want zero distraction and maximum focus on correctness of a single critical input, especially for financial or high-stakes numeric entries.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when multiple related fields need to be filled simultaneously (e.g., amount + date + recipient), as forcing users through a hyper-focused single-value screen for each field creates excessive multi-step friction. Also avoid it for non-numeric or complex data entry, and be cautious using a custom keypad instead of the native OS keyboard if accessibility (VoiceOver/TalkBack) support hasn't been rigorously tested, since custom controls can break screen-reader expectations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers setting up automated savings, investment contributions, or bill payments (likely within a neobank, savings app, or investing platform (e).g., Acorns, Chime, Copilot Money style flows). The audience values simplicity and reassurance when dealing with recurring money movement, since automating finances can trigger loss-of-control anxiety.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Commitment Consistency principle by starting the default amount low ($1), making the action feel low-risk and encouraging users to proceed rather than abandon the flow due to perceived high stakes. The live-updating CTA also exploits the Zeigarnik effect and reduces friction-induced drop-off by keeping the user's attention locked to a single, evolving number.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dynamic CTA Binding: The primary button text updates live with the numeric input ("Schedule $1"), giving the user constant confirmation of the value before submission.

  • Oversized Amount Display: The giant green currency figure acts as the emotional and visual anchor of the screen, making the number impossible to misread (critical for financial trust).

  • Distraction-Free Modal: Removing tab bars and secondary navigation via a full-screen modal with a simple 'X' dismiss keeps cognitive load low and task completion rates high.

  • Native-feeling Custom Keypad: A large-target, evenly spaced numeric pad optimized for one-handed thumb reach on mobile devices.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 37
screens.whereToUse:
• End of any multi-step setup flow (recurring payments, automated transfers, subscription creation, appointment booking) where the user needs unambiguous confirmation that their configured action was accepted by the system.

  • High-stakes actions (financial, medical, legal) where restating key parameters reduces user anxiety and prevents costly errors.

  • Flows where you want to create a strong, positive emotional "peak" at the end of an otherwise transactional or tedious process.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for low-stakes, frequent actions (e.g., liking a post) where a full-screen takeover would be excessive and disruptive (a toast/snackbar is more appropriate).

  • Not ideal if the user may need to immediately take a related follow-up action (e.g., view the transfer in a list) - in that case, offer a secondary link/button rather than only a single "Done" dead end.

  • Avoid if the confirmation details are complex or itemized (e.g., multi-line receipts), as this pattern works best for simple, single-fact confirmations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users of a fintech/banking or money-transfer app (e.g., remittance, savings, or peer-to-peer payment apps) who have just set up an automated, recurring financial commitment (likely a savings goal, subscription payment, or family remittance). This audience needs high reassurance and trust signals because recurring money movement carries real financial risk and anxiety if misconfigured.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Peak-End Rule: by ending the flow on a clean, positive, celebratory note (green checkmark, affirming copy), the app ensures the user's overall memory of the task is positive, even if earlier steps in the setup wizard were tedious. It also uses closure as a cognitive relief mechanism (clearly signaling "this task is complete, you can stop thinking about it now)."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-focus "dead end" screen: Deliberately strips away all navigation to prevent decision paralysis and confirm task completion.

  • Restated transaction parameters: Repeating the amount, currency, and date acts as a final, passive confirmation/audit step for the user.

  • Universal success iconography: The green circular checkmark is an instantly recognizable, language-agnostic symbol of success used across countless apps, reducing cognitive load to near zero.

  • Editorial-style typography: Using oversized, bold text for the confirmation message rather than a small system label elevates the perceived importance of the financial commitment.

  • Single full-width CTA: "Done" is the only actionable element, removing any ambiguity about the next step.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 38
screens.whereToUse: Use this dual-strategy toggle pattern whenever a product offers multiple valid automation rules for the same underlying action (e.g., subscription billing, savings auto-transfers, inventory reordering) and users benefit from choosing the trigger logic that matches their personal habits. It's especially effective for financial top-up, auto-pay, or recurring fulfillment features where showing collapsed inactive options and expanded active configuration keeps the page scannable.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when only one automation method is technically meaningful, as presenting a false choice adds unnecessary decision fatigue. It also breaks down if the two options are not truly mutually exclusive (if a user might reasonably want both active simultaneously with interacting logic, the collapsed/expanded asymmetry can hide important conflicts (e).g., both a scheduled and balance-based transfer firing on the same day) and the design should instead surface an explicit "these may combine" warning or a compare/summary view.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of a prepaid/transit/wallet-style card product (e.g., transit cards, prepaid debit apps) who want to avoid the friction and embarrassment of a declined balance at point-of-use. The psychological driver is loss-avoidance and cognitive offloading: users set up automation once so they never have to think about manual top-ups again, trading a small amount of upfront configuration effort for long-term peace of mind.

Offering two philosophically different automation triggers (event-based vs. time-based) caters to different user mental models: some users think in terms of "never let my balance run out" (balance-based, ideal for unpredictable spenders), while others think in terms of "payday routine" (scheduled, ideal for budget-disciplined users who reload after each paycheck).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Asymmetric disclosure: Only the active method (Scheduled) exposes its configuration fields, while the inactive method (Balance based) collapses to a single CTA, minimizing visual noise.

  • Live status microcopy: Naming the actual linked bank ("Coastal Community Bank") in the confirmation text builds trust and reassures the user the automation is truly active.

  • Segmented visual grouping: Grey full-width dividers cleanly separate the two auto-reload strategies, preventing users from conflating threshold-based and date-based rules.

  • Tappable summary chips: Amount and Frequency values are shown as pill buttons that double as both a status display and an entry point to edit, reducing extra taps for common re-configuration.

results.query: Toast notification snackbar for successful file upload confirmation

screens.name: Home Screen 15
screens.whereToUse: This fits low-consequence feedback submissions on probabilistic systems where the user needs a brief explanation of what their report does, and where asking for structured detail would cost more completions than the added data is worth.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for genuinely reversible actions where an immediate submit with undo is less friction, and for reports that require detail to be actionable - a bare confirm produces a signal too coarse to act on when the system needs to know what was wrong, not merely that something was.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. SoundHound: Offers an equivalent correction path with a confirm step after identification; the closest comparison since both products' credibility rests on match accuracy.

  2. Google Maps (report a problem with a place): Confirmation dialog framed around improving the map for everyone, comparable in converting user irritation into a data-quality contribution.

  3. Apple Maps and Siri feedback prompts: Same platform alert component and the same "help us improve results" register, which is where Shazam's phrasing and styling are inherited from.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Explanation before commitment: The dialog exists mainly to tell the user what reporting accomplishes, information the menu row had no room for; that is a legitimate use of a confirm step even where consequence is low.

  2. Framing feedback as contribution: Casting the report as improving results rather than filing a complaint is what makes an irritating moment into a two-tap gesture people will actually complete.

  3. Consistency between trigger and destination: Repeating the menu's exact wording in the dialog title eliminates any doubt about which action was invoked.

  4. Minimum viable signal: Asking for no detail keeps completion rates high at the cost of data richness, a reasonable trade when the user usually cannot supply the correct answer anyway.

  5. Overlay occlusion: The alert covers the track title it refers to, so the object of the report is not fully visible at the moment of confirming it.

screens.name: Home Screen 16
screens.whereToUse: This fits confirmation of low-consequence, non-blocking submissions where the user should be told their action registered but has nothing further to decide (feedback, reports, saves, and background syncs).
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the action has consequences the user may want to reverse, since a self-dismissing banner with no undo gives no recovery window, and where the user's underlying problem remains unsolved (an acknowledgment that ends the flow can read as dismissal when the user still needs an answer).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Maps (after reporting a place problem): Same pattern of a brief thanks-toast returning the user to the unchanged map; comparable in treating crowd-sourced correction as a background data process rather than a user-facing resolution.

  2. Apple Maps and Siri feedback: Platform-standard acknowledgment styling and register, which is where Shazam's toast component and phrasing come from.

  3. SoundHound: The direct competitor's correction flow ends similarly, confirming that "acknowledge, do not resolve" is the category norm rather than a Shazam-specific choice.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Acknowledgment without interruption: A self-dismissing banner confirms the action and costs the user nothing to clear, which is the correct weight for a low-consequence submission.

  2. Icon before text: The check mark communicates success pre-attentively; the words are confirmation for anyone who looks, not a requirement for understanding.

  3. Placement over chrome, not content: Occluding the header rather than the title, artwork, or CTA means the toast blocks nothing the user is currently reading.

  4. Closing the feedback arc: Menu row asks, dialog explains, toast thanks. Three touchpoints in one consistent voice, which is what makes the correction path feel like a conversation rather than a form.

  5. Acknowledged but unresolved: The user's data problem is solved; the user's actual problem is not. Nothing offers a re-scan, an alternative match, or a manual search after a reported error.

screens.name: Figma - Renaming file - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for quick, atomic metadata edits (renaming files, folders, layers, boards) where the action is reversible, low-risk, and doesn't require navigating to a dedicated settings screen. It's ideal for:

  • File/document management systems where renaming is a frequent micro-interaction.
  • Mobile contexts where screen real estate is limited and a full-page form would be overkill.
  • Situations where maintaining the user's current context (e.g., staying on the canvas) is more valuable than a dedicated settings flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the edit requires additional context, validation, or multiple related fields (e.g., renaming plus changing permissions or location) - a native alert input is too cramped for multi-field forms. It's also unsuitable for destructive or high-stakes actions requiring more deliberation, as the simple two-button layout doesn't provide space for warnings, previews, or undo explanations. Additionally, on platforms/devices where custom branded modals are the established pattern, suddenly using a native OS dialog could feel inconsistent with the rest of the product's visual language.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers and teams who are actively organizing and iterating on multiple FigJam boards or Figma files, often mid-collaboration session (note the two colored collaborator avatars in the top bar indicating a live multiplayer context). Renaming files is a frequent, low-stakes housekeeping task for professionals managing dozens of iterative files (e.g., "FigJam basics 1.0," suggesting versioning conventions).

Psychologically, the modal taps into the Zeigarnik effect and task-focus principles (by blocking interaction with the rest of the UI, it forces resolution of the naming task before the user can return to their creative flow, preventing abandoned or forgotten renames). The pre-selected/editable text also leverages the principle of least effort, respecting that power users want to make small edits quickly without retyping full strings.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native OS Dialog Pattern: Using the platform's native alert/input dialog style (rather than a custom branded modal) ensures familiarity, instant recognizability, and faster interaction for iOS users.
  • Pre-filled & Pre-focused Input: The current file name is already populated and the keyboard is instantly active, minimizing taps and cognitive load for a rename task that is inherently a quick edit.
  • Context Preservation: The dimmed canvas and visible thumbnail strip/top bar behind the dialog keep the user oriented within the larger file structure without fully navigating away.
  • Binary, Low-Risk Actions: Only two possible outcomes (Cancel/Rename) eliminate decision paralysis and make the destructive/non-destructive paths crystal clear.

screens.name: Figma - Renaming file - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any collaborative canvas, whiteboard, or document tool being adapted for mobile, especially where real-time multiplayer presence is a core value proposition.

  • Design/whiteboarding tools (Figma, Miro, FigJam) needing mobile parity.
  • Any app where background/system actions (renames, saves, syncs) need lightweight, non-intrusive confirmation via toast.
  • Tools migrating a complex desktop toolbar to mobile (use icon-only, horizontally scrollable toolbars with clear active-state highlighting).
  • Products wanting to reinforce trust and reduce "lost work" anxiety by surfacing live collaborator presence directly on content.
screens.whereNotToUse:
This minimal-chrome, icon-heavy approach can fail in contexts requiring more guidance or accessibility support.

  • Avoid for first-time or occasional users unfamiliar with canvas/design tool conventions (icon-only toolbars without labels create steep learning curves).
  • Not suitable for apps targeting non-technical or casual consumer audiences who need more explicit labels and onboarding cues.
  • Live cursor presence can become visually cluttered and distracting on very small screens if many collaborators are active simultaneously; consider collapsing to avatar-only indicators beyond 2-3 users.
  • Toast notifications for every minor background change (renames, moves) can become noisy if overused (reserve for meaningful state changes).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for professional designers, developers, and cross-functional teams who need to review, comment on, or lightly edit design files while away from their desktop (e).g., checking in during a commute, a stakeholder meeting, or a quick client review.

  • Trust through Transparency: Showing live collaborator cursors and names leverages social presence to reduce the anxiety of "working on the wrong version" or losing changes, a critical psychological need in collaborative, high-stakes design work.
  • Confirmation Reduces Uncertainty: The "File has been renamed" toast closes the feedback loop for an action likely taken by a teammate or on another device, preventing confusion about unexpected file state changes.
  • Expert-Mode Interface: The lack of explanatory labels on toolbar icons assumes familiarity, catering to Figma's core audience who already know the tool from desktop use (efficiency over discoverability).
screens.keyHighlights:
The most brilliant decision here is the successful compression of Figma's signature multiplayer, infinite-canvas experience into a mobile form factor without stripping away its core identity.

  • Real-time Cursor Presence on Mobile: Maintaining live collaborator cursors (not just avatars) on a touch device is a technically impressive and trust-building feature, reinforcing that the file is a living, shared document even when viewed on a phone.
  • Non-blocking Toast Placement: Positioning the confirmation toast low on the screen, above the toolbar, ensures system feedback is visible without covering canvas content or collaborator activity.
  • Toolbar Parity with Desktop: By keeping the same iconography and tool groupings as the desktop app (cursor, pen, shapes, comment), Figma reduces the learning curve for existing users switching between devices (a strong example of cross-platform consistency).
  • Overflow Menu for Secondary Actions: The ".." icon in the header offloads less-frequent actions, keeping the primary header lightweight and focused on identity (avatars) and sharing.

screens.name: Cleo Creating Account 9
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any two-step MFA flow (channel selection followed by code entry) where restating the delivery destination and restricting backward navigation post-dispatch meaningfully reduces user confusion and protects session integrity.
screens.whereNotToUse: Unnecessary for single-channel MFA flows where there's no ambiguity about where a code was sent (e.g., only one phone number on file) - the destination-reconfirmation copy becomes redundant when there was never a choice to begin with.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Venmo, Robinhood, Chime: all present this identical Plaid MFA code-entry screen as the second half of the channel-selection + code-submission sequence, since it's shared Plaid infrastructure.

  • Coinbase: matches the same destination-reconfirmation + single-field code entry pattern during equivalent bank-linking MFA challenges.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Destination reconfirmation reduces confusion: restating the masked email at the point of code entry (rather than assuming memory of the prior screen) reduces the chance of a user checking the wrong inbox.

  • Restricted backward navigation post-dispatch: removing the back button once a code has been sent is a deliberate security/state-integrity choice, preventing a user from re-triggering channel selection mid-verification.

  • Consistent gated-button feedback: the disabled "Submit" state follows the same visual language established throughout this entire flow (phone entry, credential entry, channel selection), reinforcing a coherent system.

  • Single-field simplicity: asking for only the code, with no additional fields, keeps this final verification step as low-friction as possible given it's the last gate before account access completes.

screens.name: Cleo Creating Account 10
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (reused celebration illustration + real-time status toast + distinctly-worded final CTA) fits best as the true final step of a multi-stage onboarding flow, where the goal is to mark genuine completion distinctly from intermediate progress steps.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for mid-flow milestones that aren't the actual final step, using this level of unique, escalated celebration and bespoke CTA copy too early would undercut its impact at the true completion point, leaving nothing left to differentiate the real ending.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: closes onboarding with a similarly celebratory, uniquely-worded final CTA (distinct from earlier "Continue" buttons) right before entering the main app experience.

  • Robinhood: displays a comparable connection-success toast layered over a positive full-screen state after Plaid linking completes.

  • Headspace: reuses consistent celebratory illustration motifs at multiple onboarding milestones, matching Cleo's bookending approach here.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Bookended celebration reinforces milestone parity: reusing the identical confetti illustration from the email-verification success screen visually signals "this achievement matters as much as that one did," building a consistent reward vocabulary across the flow.

  • Transient status doesn't block the milestone moment: layering the toast over (rather than replacing) the celebratory background lets the user register both pieces of information (technical status and emotional payoff) without one screen crowding out the other.

  • Reserved unique CTA copy for true completion: breaking from the "Next" pattern used at every prior step signals to the user, even subconsciously, that this step is different from the rest (a well-placed payoff after a long onboarding sequence).

  • Anticipation-building headline: "ARE YOU READY?" primes the user emotionally for entering the live app, rather than just neutrally confirming task completion.

screens.name: Cleo Creating Account 11
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (transient status toast over a persistent celebration screen, with the toast auto-clearing) fits any flow where a background process (data sync, account setup finalization) needs brief acknowledgment without permanently occupying space on the completion screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if the status information genuinely needs to remain visible or actionable (e.g., an error requiring user action) - auto-dismissing status messaging that the user still needs to reference or act on would hide important information prematurely.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood: similarly auto-dismisses connection-status toasts after Plaid linking completes, leaving a clean confirmation screen behind.

  • Duolingo: matches this pattern of transient status messaging fading out while a persistent celebration/CTA screen remains stable underneath.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transient feedback doesn't permanently alter the primary screen: the toast's auto-dismissal confirms Cleo treats system-status messaging as genuinely temporary, correctly distinct from the persistent celebration content underneath (appropriate use of toast/snackbar semantics).

  • Clean final state before app entry: presenting an uncluttered screen at the literal last moment before entering the live app avoids competing signals right before the user's most consequential tap.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA persists: "Unleash Cleo 👀" remains the only actionable element, maintaining decision clarity regardless of whether the toast was present.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately after any automated or AI-driven action completes successfully (auto-categorization, smart matching, auto-fill, OCR extraction, recommendation acceptance) where you want lightweight, high-signal feedback on whether the automation felt accurate/helpful. Ideal for fintech, expense management, productivity, and AI-assisted tools where trust-building in automation is critical. Best used sparingly and only after genuinely novel or "magic" moments to avoid survey fatigue.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid stacking a feedback request on every single automated action (if triggered too frequently, it creates interruption fatigue and trains users to dismiss sheets reflexively. Do not use this pattern for critical/blocking flows (e.g., payment confirmations, legal consent) where visual competition between confirmation data and a survey could cause users to miss important financial details. Also avoid binary-only feedback when you need diagnostic detail (e.g., why something failed)) in those cases a reason-capture follow-up or open text field is more appropriate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets business users and employees submitting expenses (likely via a corporate expense management tool such as Ramp, Brex, or Expensify) who have just uploaded or forwarded a receipt. The psychological trigger at play is the peak-end rule: by inserting the feedback ask directly after a moment of relief/delight (task automatically completed, no manual reconciliation needed), the product captures feedback when sentiment is highest and most favorable.

It also leverages the reciprocity principle: having just received a "free" benefit (time saved via auto-matching), users are more inclined to reciprocate with two seconds of feedback. The low-effort binary choice format specifically targets busy professionals who would abandon a multi-question survey but will tap a single icon.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual, in-moment feedback capture: The survey appears immediately after the exact feature it's evaluating (auto-matching), not in a generic "Rate our app" popup days later, which dramatically improves recall accuracy and response relevance.

  • Binary sentiment over Likert/NPS scales: Using only thumbs up/down instead of a 5-star or 1-10 scale reduces cognitive load and decision fatigue, likely boosting completion rates for passive, non-intrusive micro-surveys.

  • Non-blocking layered modal: By stacking the feedback sheet over (not instead of) the confirmation screen, users still get to see and verify their matched expense data while being prompted (no information is hidden or sacrificed for the ask).

  • Celebratory confirmation language: "Well done!" reframes an automated system action as user achievement, reinforcing positive reinforcement loops common in fintech/expense apps to build trust in automation.

  • Dual status iconography: The small icon pair (upload/card icon + verified receipt icon) on the expense line communicates two data states at a glance (payment recorded and receipt verified) without needing extra text.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 10
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for compliance-heavy, multi-field data entry flows such as expense reports, tax filings, insurance claims, or any workflow requiring document upload + categorization + manual policy checks. It's ideal when:

  • Users need async confirmation of background uploads (toast).

  • Certain submitted data triggers downstream manual review (status banners/chips).

  • Forms are long and benefit from sectioning with clear labels and dividers.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, multi-section form approach for simple, high-frequency transactions where speed is paramount (e.g., a one-tap purchase or quick note). Overloading a short-task flow with compliance banners and granular categorization fields will cause drop-off. Additionally, stacking a toast directly above a warning banner risks visual clutter or z-index collisions on smaller screens (ensure toasts auto-dismiss quickly so they don't visually compete with persistent in-page alerts like the "Not verified" banner).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets business travelers, employees submitting expense reports, or finance/operations teams who must document and categorize reimbursable spend (e.g., rideshare trips, as suggested by the receipt thumbnail referencing a "Pickup" vehicle confirmation). The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Reassurance via immediate feedback (toast) to reduce anxiety about whether the upload "worked."

  • Loss-aversion framing in the compliance banner, implying the expense may be delayed or rejected unless reviewed, nudging the user to ensure correctness.

  • Authority & procedural trust: referencing "your policy" reinforces that rules are externally governed (company policy), reducing the user's sense of being arbitrarily blocked by the app itself.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking success toast that confirms the receipt upload without halting form progress, preserving flow state.

  • Proactive compliance warning banner using color (amber/yellow) and iconography to flag "Not verified" receipts before the user submits, preventing downstream rejection surprises.

  • Inline status chip ("Not verified") next to the Receipts section header gives at-a-glance status without needing to open a detail view.

  • Character counter on Memo field sets clear expectations and prevents submission errors due to length limits.

  • Dedicated "+" add-receipt tile sitting next to existing thumbnails enables multi-receipt attachment using a familiar grid-plus pattern.

screens.name: Brex Adding a receipt 11
screens.whereToUse:
• When a user-initiated action (e.g., scan, search, sync) could lead to a logical dead-end due to zero matching data.

  • To explain complex business-logic-driven restrictions (e.g., policy-based rules on receipts, approvals, eligibility) in plain language.

  • When you want to redirect users toward alternative, still-valid workflows instead of just blocking them.

  • For modal interruptions that need a dimmed backdrop to ensure message comprehension before dismissal.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for frequent, low-stakes empty states where a lightweight inline message or toast would suffice (a full-screen dimmed modal is heavy-handed for minor non-issues).

  • Don't use if the user has a genuine error (e.g., no camera permission) - this should be a distinct permission/error state, not conflated with a feature-unavailable message.

  • Avoid stacking too much explanatory text; if the underlying business logic is too complex to explain in two sentences, consider a help link instead of overloading the sheet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets business/finance app users (likely employees submitting expenses in a corporate expense management tool) who triggered a "scan receipt" shortcut expecting to attach a receipt, but have no outstanding expense items flagged as requiring one. The psychological trigger here is reduction of frustration/confusion: by preemptively explaining the empty state rather than showing a blank scanner or silent failure, the product builds trust and reduces perceived complexity of the expense policy logic. It also subtly nudges education around the "reimbursement" feature, which serves the business goal of feature discovery and engagement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Empty-State Guidance: Rather than silently failing or showing a generic error, the app proactively explains *why* the scan-receipt flow has nothing to do, converting friction into education.

  • Dimmed Background Focus Lock: The camera/scan UI behind the sheet is nearly blacked out, forcing attention onto the explanation and preventing accidental interaction with the obscured scan controls.

  • Actionable Alternative Paths: The body copy proactively surfaces two alternative actions (add receipt to existing expense, create reimbursement), reducing the chance the user feels stuck.

  • Single, Unambiguous Exit: One full-width, high-contrast orange button removes any decision paralysis (the user can only acknowledge and move on).

results.query: Stacked List grouped settings navigation with chevrons

screens.name: Craft - Updating export settings - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any export/share flow where the user is sending a document, image, or file outside of the app (PDFs, image exports, print preview).
  • Situations where brand reinforcement via watermark is desirable in freemium or prosumer apps.
  • Flows benefiting from a "preview before commit" step to increase user confidence (invoices, contracts, reports, resumes).
  • When you want to offer both a fast default action (Share) and an escape hatch to deeper configuration (Export Options) without a multi-step wizard.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy preview pattern for trivial or instant exports (e.g., copying plain text) where a full-page PDF render would add unnecessary friction.
  • Not suitable for large multi-page documents without pagination/scroll affordances or a page counter (users could get lost without a quick way to jump between pages).
  • Avoid watermarking in paid/pro tiers or professional output contexts (e.g., enterprise contracts) where unsolicited branding may appear unprofessional or violate white-labeling expectations.
  • Skip this if export settings are simple enough to need no customization (in that case, a single confirmation step is more frictionless than opening a secondary "Export Options" path).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves knowledge workers, writers, and designers who use Craft to produce polished documents and need to export or send them outside the app (e.g., sharing a concept brief with a client or team).
