The target user cares about document aesthetics (hence the importance of seeing an exact visual preview before export, matching Craft's "every note is a designed document" ethos).

Psychologically, this leverages the principle of confirmation and control: users feel safer sharing a file when they've visually verified its final appearance. The dimmed backdrop and modal framing also tap into spatial persistence, reassuring users that canceling costs nothing since their original context remains intact.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live, accurate preview: Instead of an abstract "exporting..." state, the user sees the literal, pixel-accurate output document, building trust before committing to share.
  • Contextual dimming: Keeping the original screen faintly visible behind the sheet preserves the user's mental model of "where am I," reducing disorientation common in modal-heavy flows.
  • Progressive disclosure via "Export Options...": Advanced settings (format, quality, page size, etc.) are tucked behind a secondary action, keeping the primary screen focused on the binary decision to share or cancel.
  • Subtle watermark branding: The "created with Craft" tag turns every shared PDF into organic brand exposure, a low-friction viral/referral loop embedded in a core utility action.
  • Clear visual hierarchy of actions: The prominent blue circular share button versus the neutral pill-shaped "Cancel" button instantly communicates which action is primary.

screens.name: Craft - Updating export settings - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Reuse this grouped list + chevron/switch hybrid pattern whenever a settings screen mixes multi-value configuration (needing a picker) with binary toggles. It's ideal for export/print dialogs, document/PDF generation settings, sharing preferences, or any "preview-then-configure" workflow preceding a file output action. The grouped-section layout is also excellent for any native iOS-style Preferences screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when settings have interdependencies that benefit from live preview (users may want to see the document update in real time rather than toggle blind switches). Also avoid for complex, high-stakes export configurations requiring explanation (e.g., compression quality, legal formatting rules) since this screen provides no tooltips or help text. On Android or web, a flat Material list may be more appropriate than this iOS-specific grouped/floating-button aesthetic to maintain platform consistency.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves power users and professionals (writers, students, consultants) who need to share polished output (reports, essays, branded documents) outside the Craft ecosystem. The presence of "Watermark" and "Paper Size (A4)" suggests use cases spanning both personal and business/print contexts, and international paper standards (A4) signal a worldwide audience beyond US-centric Letter format defaults.

Psychologically, offering granular control (page numbers, watermark, tags) taps into a sense of authorial control and craftsmanship (the same reason users chose Craft over a plain note app in the first place). Giving them export-time control over presentation reinforces the brand promise that "every note is a designed document."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual control paradigm: Chevron rows for multi-option settings vs. Switches for binary ones, creating an intuitive, label-free interaction language.
  • Logical grouping: Structural export details separated from visual appearance settings, reducing decision fatigue.
  • Smart defaults: "Use Style" pre-enabled to preserve Craft's design identity even outside the app, while content-stripping toggles default to off to prevent accidental data loss on export.
  • Floating back button: A circular, elevated back chevron instead of a flat nav bar button, adding tactile, modern polish consistent with Craft's premium aesthetic.

screens.name: Craft - Updating export settings - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for short, single-select settings lists (3 (6 options) where selections are low-risk, instantly reversible, and benefit from immediate visual feedback) e.g., paper size, font family, theme, export format, or sort order. It's ideal when you want to let users experiment freely without an explicit save/cancel transaction cost.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for settings with many options (better suited to a searchable list or picker wheel), for choices that trigger destructive or costly side effects (which need explicit confirmation), or when options require additional explanation/preview (in those cases, add inline descriptions, icons, or a live preview rather than relying on label text alone).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves writers, students, and professionals worldwide who treat their notes as polished, print/export-ready documents rather than throwaway text. Offering both "US Letter" and "A4" alongside a "Dynamic" default demonstrates clear global market awareness, letting regional print conventions coexist without forcing a region-specific default on the user. The instant-apply checkmark pattern caters to power users who value speed and want to iterate quickly on document appearance (a key value prop for Craft's "designed document" positioning) without interrupting their writing flow with modal confirmations.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-tap, auto-committing selection: Tapping a row instantly applies the setting and shows a checkmark (no secondary confirmation step, reducing friction and cognitive load).
  • Native platform conventions: Grouped inset table list, pill "Close" button, and translucent dimmed backdrop mirror iOS system patterns, making the control feel instantly familiar and trustworthy.
  • Peeking background context: The underlying document remains partially visible, reassuring the user their work is preserved and this is a lightweight, non-destructive overlay.
  • Minimal option set: Limiting choices to three (Dynamic, US Letter, A4) avoids decision paralysis while covering the core global use cases (digital-native and the two dominant print standards).

screens.name: Craft - Updating export settings - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this grouped-settings-with-live-preview-value pattern whenever a user needs to configure multiple independent, non-sequential options before a single terminal action (like export, print, or share). It's ideal when settings are orthogonal (don't depend on each other) and when immediate visual feedback isn't required on this exact screen. Categorizing settings into 2-3 clearly labeled sections works well once you exceed ~5 total controls, preventing an undifferentiated wall of switches.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when settings are interdependent or sequential (e.g., a step-by-step wizard would serve better), or when users need a live preview of the exported output (in that case a split-screen or preview-pane layout would reduce trial-and-error). Also avoid unlabeled toggle lists for complex or ambiguous options; without tooltips or microcopy, unfamiliar users (e.g., "Hide Tags," "Use Style") may not understand consequences, so this pattern is best reserved for audiences already fluent in the product's terminology.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen is built for professional writers, consultants, and knowledge workers who treat their Craft documents as deliverables (people exporting polished PDFs for clients, print, or sharing outside the app. The granular controls (watermark, page numbers, tag visibility, custom style vs. system dark mode) speak to a user who cares about document presentation as much as content, aligning with Craft's "every note is a designed document" value proposition. The autosave/no-confirm interaction pattern caters to users who want frictionless iteration) toggling settings repeatedly to preview before the final export without a modal "Apply" step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-category grouping cleanly separates document semantics (Details) from visual theming (Appearance), making an otherwise long settings list scannable.
  • No explicit save action: every control is a live, auto-applied toggle/selector, reflecting Craft's autosave-everywhere philosophy and reducing friction/anxiety about "did my settings stick."
  • Disclosure rows with inline value preview (e.g., "US Letter," "Regular") let users confirm current state at a glance before deciding whether to drill in, avoiding unnecessary navigation.
  • Floating pill-shaped back button over a translucent/blurred backdrop is a distinctive, on-brand departure from the default iOS nav bar, reinforcing Craft's custom, designed-document aesthetic even in a purely functional settings screen.

screens.name: CRED Editing Profile 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this stacked-list profile hub pattern when an app has many loosely related account functions (rewards, credit, payments, support) that need a single entry point. It's ideal for fintech, banking, and loyalty-driven apps where users frequently check balances/scores and occasionally dive into settings. The KPI-row-with-arrow technique is excellent whenever you want to preview a headline metric while deferring detail to a secondary screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense list-based approach for apps with only 2-3 settings, as the multiple section headers would feel like unnecessary ceremony. It's also not ideal for first-time users still building context (new users may find "credit score" or "coins" without immediate explanation confusing; the pattern assumes prior familiarity with the app's reward economy). Additionally, in bright/light-brand-guideline products, this heavy dark theme may clash with overall brand tone and should be reconsidered.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday users of a digital lending/payments app (likely a BNPL or credit-card-style fintech product) in India, evidenced by Rupee (₹) currency formatting and localized copy conventions. The "member since" tenure marker and credit score exposure specifically appeal to users who are credit-conscious and value transparency into their financial standing.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the endowment effect (large coin/rewards balances make users feel they've "earned" something worth protecting), social/status signaling (credit score as a gamified personal metric), and loyalty reinforcement (membership since date). The referral banner exploits reciprocity and incentive-driven virality, nudging engaged users to invite peers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Editable Identity Block: The pencil/edit icon anchored beside the avatar makes profile ownership immediately actionable without navigating deeper.

  • KPI-as-Navigation Rows: Credit score and lifetime rewards are displayed as large, legible numbers paired with directional arrows, turning passive data display into an inviting tap target that promises more detail.

  • Section Chunking via Uppercase Labels: Grouping into "YOUR REWARDS & BENEFITS", "TRANSACTIONS & SUPPORT", and "PAYMENTS & BANK ACCOUNTS" creates strong information scent and reduces search time in a long list.

  • Embedded Referral Upsell: Placing "win upto Rs 1000 / refer and earn" directly inside the rewards section (rather than a separate menu) exploits contextual relevance to maximize referral conversion.

  • Dark Mode as Premium Signal: The near-black canvas paired with gold/amber avatar accent creates a premium, credit-card-like aesthetic that reinforces trust and status.

screens.name: CRED Editing Profile 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this stacked-list settings pattern for any app with a moderate-to-large number of account/preference controls that need clear grouping (fintech apps, subscription services, or B2B SaaS admin panels). It's ideal when users arrive with a specific task in mind (e.g., "change my password") and need fast scan-and-tap navigation rather than persuasion or discovery.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense list-only approach when settings require more context or preview (e.g., toggles with real-time state, or settings that benefit from inline switches/values). A pure "chevron-only" list hides current state, forcing an extra tap just to check a setting (problematic for toggles like notification preferences where users often want to see status at a glance). In such cases, mix in inline switches, badges, or summary text instead of forcing full drill-down navigation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets financially engaged, credit-card-holding millennials/Gen-X urban Indian users. CRED's core demographic of high-trust, high-credit-score individuals who value control and transparency over their financial data. The design leverages the psychology of trust through order: a clean, uncluttered, well-categorized settings menu signals that the underlying financial system is equally well-organized and safe.

The persistent support button exploits anxiety reduction: financial apps trigger higher scrutiny/fear (fraud, refunds, security), so constant visible access to help reduces hesitation to explore deeper settings like "manage CRED protect" or "security."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent Support Access: The floating "support" pill stays anchored in the header, guaranteeing users dealing with sensitive financial settings can always escalate to human help instantly.

  • Typographic Hierarchy via Case, not Weight: Uppercase tracked section labels vs. lowercase row labels create clear grouping using letter-casing rather than heavy borders or shadows (a clean, low-noise IA technique).

  • Consistent Drill-Down Affordance: Every row uses an identical chevron pattern, making the entire list instantly learnable (users know every tap leads one level deeper).

  • Dark Mode as Default Brand Identity: True black background reduces eye strain, saves OLED battery, and reinforces CRED's premium fintech positioning.

  • Logical Content Chunking: Sensitive/financial settings (payments, refunds, RuPay) are separated from account/legal settings, reducing cognitive load when scanning for a specific control.

screens.name: CRED Editing Profile 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any profile, avatar, or document image upload flow (KYC, ID verification, profile pictures).

  • Situations with exactly 2-4 mutually exclusive simple choices where a full-screen navigation would be excessive.

  • Contexts where preserving the underlying screen's context aids user orientation (e.g., editing while still seeing the profile being edited).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when more than 4-5 options are needed (a bottom sheet with too many rows becomes a scrollable list that loses the lightweight feel and may be better served by a dedicated screen).

  • Not ideal when the subsequent step requires significant additional input (e.g., cropping, filters, multi-image selection) - in that case a full-screen flow is more appropriate to avoid stacking sheets/modals.

  • Don't use in flows where the user needs to compare information from the background screen carefully, since dimming reduces legibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumer app users (likely of a fintech/rewards/lending app given the "credit score" and "coins" elements visible behind the sheet) who need a fast, frictionless way to personalize their profile. The design assumes low intent-friction: users opening this sheet have already decided to update their photo, so the interface should get out of the way as quickly as possible.

Psychologically, this leverages the Principle of Least Effort: by offering exactly the two expected pathways to obtaining an image (device storage vs. live capture) with zero additional configuration, the app respects the user's time and avoids overengineering a trivial task.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed contextual background: Rather than a full-screen takeover, the underlying profile screen remains partially visible, preserving context and reducing the jarring feeling of a hard navigation change.

  • Binary choice architecture: Only two clearly differentiated options are presented, avoiding decision paralysis for a simple, low-stakes task.

  • Icon-first scannability: Each option pairs a recognizable icon (gallery thumbnail icon, camera icon) with text, allowing near-instant recognition without reading.

  • Gesture-dismissible drawer: The drag handle signals native, swipe-to-dismiss behavior consistent with iOS/Android bottom sheet conventions, avoiding the need for an explicit close/cancel button.

screens.name: CRED Editing Profile 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this dual-gauge dashboard pattern when:

  • Presenting a single core metric (score, health index, rating) that benefits from a bounded-range visual (gauge/dial) rather than a raw number.

  • Multiple authoritative sources report slightly different values for the same underlying concept and transparency about the discrepancy builds trust (e.g., multiple credit bureaus, multiple health metrics from different wearables).

  • The subject matter (finance, health, credit) is emotionally loaded and benefits from softer, editorial tone and typography to reduce anxiety.

  • You want to create a hub screen that both informs and funnels users to deeper detail reports.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • There is only one authoritative score/value: showing multiple redundant sources would add confusion rather than trust.

  • The user needs to compare many data points at once; gauges are low-density and don't scale well beyond 2-3 comparisons on one screen.

  • Precision matters more than gist: dial-based visualizations are best for quick status reads, not for detailed numeric analysis (better suited to tables/line charts for trend-following).

  • The brand tone is highly formal/corporate, where playful editorial typography for a serious financial metric might undercut perceived seriousness or authority.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially-conscious consumers, particularly those who are credit-aware but not necessarily experts (likely users managing multiple loans/credit cards (6 cards, 8 loans) who want a consolidated view rather than checking multiple separate bureau sites or apps). It appeals to users in emerging or credit-education-focused fintech markets (the CRIF bureau branding suggests a market like India or similar) where credit literacy is being actively built by the product.

Psychologically, the design taps into loss-aversion and status-anxiety reduction (a poor or unclear credit score creates stress, and by softening the visual and verbal tone (friendly color gradients, reassuring copy, editorial typography) the app lowers the emotional barrier to actually checking one's score, a task users often avoid). The dual score comparison also builds trust through transparency, since discrepancies between bureaus are common and confusing; addressing this proactively increases user confidence in the app's credibility as a maker of financial truth.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-bureau transparency: Showing scores from two different credit bureaus (Experian, CRIF) side-by-side builds trust by acknowledging that "credit score" isn't a single universal number, educating users on a nuance most consumer apps hide.

  • Semantic color-coded gauges: The arc color (orange vs. yellow-green) reinforces the qualitative status label, allowing rapid visual scanning without reading text.

  • Contextual metadata per score: Including the account count and last-updated date builds trust and answers the implicit user question "is this data current and complete?"

  • Soft, editorial typography: The serif, lowercase headline reduces the emotional intimidation typically associated with credit/financial topics.

  • Progressive disclosure hub: The "Insights for You" teaser at the bottom hints at further personalized content, encouraging continued scroll/engagement.

screens.name: Archive
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any browser or tab-management feature where content is automatically moved out of active view after a period of inactivity, requiring a dedicated, searchable, chronologically-organized location for users to retrieve or manage that archived content later.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if archived content should be permanently and irretrievably removed rather than stored for later retrieval (in cases requiring true deletion rather than archiving, a distinct "delete" flow (rather than an archive-and-search model) would be more appropriate).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Tab History / Recently Closed Tabs: organizes closed or archived tabs chronologically with title, URL, and favicon, closely matching this screen's structure.

  2. Chrome's History page: groups browsing history by date with search functionality, mirroring this Archive's date-grouped, searchable list.

  3. Arc Browser desktop's own Archive feature: the mobile app's Archive directly parallels the desktop Arc browser's auto-archiving tab-management system, maintaining feature consistency across platforms.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Feature Follow-Through: this screen delivers on the "auto-archive" promise made during onboarding and confirmed in Settings, showing archived tabs land somewhere retrievable rather than being silently lost.

  2. Chronological Grouping: organizing entries under date headers like "TODAY" follows familiar browser-history conventions, aiding quick temporal orientation.

  3. Scalable Management Tools: providing both Edit (bulk actions) and Search upfront anticipates the Archive growing significantly over time as tabs continue to auto-archive daily.

  4. Consistent Favicon Usage: using site favicons (the Google "G") alongside titles and URLs gives quick visual source recognition, consistent with standard browser history/bookmark list conventions.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 01
screens.whereToUse: This grouped Stacked List + Preference Center pattern fits any settings surface with a moderate-to-large number of independent preferences that benefit from being scanned at a glance, especially where some options are binary (toggle) and others need a dedicated picker screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when there are only a handful of settings (a flat list would suffice) or when settings are highly interdependent and better presented as a guided wizard rather than an unordered menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari (iOS Settings): same grouped Stacked List + chevron drill-down pattern for browser preferences, a near-identical information architecture.

  2. Chrome (iOS Settings): uses the same colored-icon-plus-label row convention and trailing value text for settings like default search engine.

  3. Notion (iOS Settings): groups toggles and drill-down rows into dividered sections in a comparable Preference Center layout.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking (Miller's Law): Dividers break ~14 settings into 5 digestible clusters instead of one long list.

  2. Recognition over recall: Trailing value text (e.g., "Google", "After 1 day", "Native App") shows current state inline, so users don't need to open each row to check it.

  3. Progressive disclosure: Chevron rows (Global Site Settings, Languages, Search Engine) push secondary complexity to nested screens, keeping this page scannable.

  4. Fitts's Law: Full-row tap targets (not just the switch/chevron) make toggles and navigation rows easier to hit on mobile.

  5. Consistency: Icon-label-value-chevron row pattern repeats identically throughout, lowering the learning curve as users scan down.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any automated content-management feature (archiving, auto-deletion, auto-logout) where users benefit from choosing a personally appropriate threshold, especially when a single fixed default wouldn't suit meaningfully different usage patterns across the user base.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings where offering multiple duration options would create confusing inconsistency (e.g., security-critical timeouts where a single, carefully chosen default is safer than user-configurable flexibility).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Close Tabs Automatically" duration picker: offers a nearly identical range of duration options (1 day, 1 week, 1 month) for automatically closing inactive tabs.

  2. Chrome's "Auto Tab Groups" or memory-saver duration settings: provides comparable configurable timeframes for tab-management automation.

  3. Firefox's tab-unloading/archiving thresholds: similarly lets users choose how long inactive tabs remain before being archived or unloaded.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Resolving Prior Ambiguity: this screen retroactively confirms the "After 1 day" value seen in earlier Settings screenshots was genuinely configurable, not a fixed label.

  2. Range Accommodates Diverse Habits: offering both very short (12 hours) and long (30 days) options serves meaningfully different tab-management styles without forcing a one-size-fits-all default.

  3. Consistent Selector Pattern: reusing the same compact popover-with-checkmark format as the earlier "Swipe to Navigate" setting maintains a predictable interaction model for similar types of choices throughout Settings.

  4. Feature Follow-Through: this control makes the onboarding-promised "auto-archive" feature concretely adjustable, giving users direct control over how aggressively that promise is enforced.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (immediate persistence without explicit save) fits virtually all mobile settings interfaces, where requiring a separate save action for individual preference changes would add unnecessary friction and risk of lost changes if a user navigates away.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit only for settings with significant, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., account deletion, irreversible data actions), where an explicit confirm/save step is appropriate specifically to prevent accidental changes (a distinction correctly reflected in this app's separate use of confirmation dialogs (like the earlier "Clear All" archive action) for higher-stakes actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS Settings app (immediate value persistence): uses an identical pattern where sub-screen selections instantly update and display in the parent settings list without requiring a save step.

  2. Any well-designed settings architecture (Safari, Chrome, etc.): follows this same immediate-persistence convention as a baseline usability expectation for modern mobile settings.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Reliable State Propagation: both changed settings correctly display their new values upon returning to the parent Settings screen, without requiring a manual refresh or save confirmation.

  2. Consistent Interaction Model Across Settings: the same select-then-confirm pattern (whether via popover or dedicated sub-screen) applies uniformly across different setting types (search engine, archive timing, language), giving the whole Settings experience a cohesive, predictable feel.

  3. Immediate Effect Without Explicit Save: no "Save" or "Apply" button was needed at any point in this sequence; each selection takes effect and displays immediately upon choice.

screens.name: Brilliant - Premium - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this stacked-list settings pattern when:

  • You need to expose a mix of navigational (multi-field) and binary (single-value) preferences in one place.
  • Your brand voice is minimal/utilitarian and you want to avoid visual noise or heavy card chrome.
  • You want to passively surface a monetization entry point (e.g., Premium/Upgrade) without resorting to a modal or banner interruption.
  • The product has a clear primary flow that settings must not interfere with (hence modal presentation).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat single-list approach when:

  • The number of settings is very large (50+), where grouping into categorized sub-pages (e.g., a settings "hub" with cards per category) prevents excessive scrolling.
  • Settings require contextual explanation or risk (e).g., privacy/security options that need inline descriptions, warnings, or previews; a bare label + chevron may leave users uncertain of consequences.
  • The brand relies on strong visual merchandising (e.g., consumer social apps) where flat gray text for "Log out" might under-communicate an important, frequently used action.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves existing, already-onboarded learners who need occasional control over their account, subscription, and sensory/notification preferences (not new users being persuaded to join). The psychological design goal here is reducing friction and anxiety around configuration: by using familiar iOS-native list patterns (chevrons, toggles, hairline dividers), the screen leverages users' existing mental models from countless other apps, requiring zero learning curve.

Surfacing "Premium" as a dedicated, icon-matched row (not a plain text link) subtly primes free users every time they open Settings, applying a gentle, passive upsell trigger via mere repeated exposure rather than aggressive interruption, fitting for a calm, trust-building edtech brand targeting self-directed learners worldwide.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-led scanability: Every row pairs a simple line icon with its label, letting users visually scan and locate a setting without reading every word.
  • Immediate feedback toggles: Sounds and Haptics use inline switches (green = on) rather than drilling into a sub-page, respecting the user's time for simple binary preferences.
  • Visual hierarchy via grouping and whitespace: Four distinct sections separated by hairline dividers and blank space, rather than boxed cards, keep the screen feeling light and uncluttered.
  • De-prioritized destructive/meta actions: "Log out" and the version string are rendered in muted gray with no chevron on Log out, visually signaling lower importance/finality without burying them in a submenu.
  • Modal "X" dismissal: Reinforces that Settings is a utility layer, not part of the core learning flow, preserving the integrity of the linear lesson spine.

screens.name: Brilliant - Premium - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Account/billing sections of any subscription-based app (edtech, fitness, SaaS).
  • Screens where the user has already converted and needs reassurance/control rather than conversion pressure.
  • Any product wanting to reduce support ticket volume by pairing account data with an immediate, low-friction help entry point.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this passive, non-promotional tone on screens where you still want to upsell (e.g., trial-to-paid conversion) - the lack of urgency here would hurt conversion goals.
  • Not suitable if the business model requires in-app cancellation flow data capture (e.g., win-back offers) - deep-linking straight to the App Store forfeits that retention opportunity.
  • Avoid for complex multi-tier plans where users need comparison or plan-switching (this layout only supports a single, static plan view).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves existing paying subscribers who need transparency and control, not persuasion. The target psychology here is reducing "subscription anxiety" - a well-documented churn driver where users forget what they're paying for or panic about hidden renewal terms. By surfacing the renewal date and plan name plainly up front, Brilliant preempts support tickets and chargebacks, while the dedicated Help card reduces the perceived friction of canceling or asking questions, paradoxically building more trust (and retention) than hiding the exit would.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Restraint over upsell: No cross-sell, no "upgrade further" nudges on a page about an existing subscription (respects the user's prior decision).
  • Native delegation: "Manage Subscription" hands off to the OS-level subscription manager instead of building a custom (and riskier) cancellation flow in-app.
  • Consistent illustration language: The help card reuses the same soft, hand-drawn illustration style found in lessons/onboarding, keeping even a settings page feel on-brand.
  • Clear visual grouping: Dividers and bold section headers ("Current plan," "Help") create scannable zones without needing cards or heavy borders everywhere.

screens.name: Brilliant Account 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this stacked, sectioned settings pattern whenever an app has a moderate-to-large number of configuration options that need to be organized without overwhelming the user. It's ideal for:

  • Account/profile management hubs

  • Apps needing a dedicated monetization entry point (Premium/Upgrade) within a trusted, low-pressure context

  • Any screen mixing instant toggles (sound, haptics) with deeper navigational settings (notifications, account)

  • Products wanting to visually separate frequent settings from rare/destructive actions (logout, legal)
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat list pattern when:

  • The number of settings is very small (2-3 items) - a simpler single section suffices and extra grouping adds unnecessary visual noise.

  • Settings require rich contextual explanation per item (this layout has no room for descriptive subtext, which could confuse users on ambiguous toggles).

  • The product is complex/enterprise-grade and needs search or categorized tabs for dozens of settings (a flat scroll becomes unwieldy past ~15-20 items).

  • Destructive actions like "Delete Account" need more friction/visibility (this minimal de-emphasized styling is appropriate for "Log out" but should not be reused for truly irreversible, high-stakes actions without additional confirmation safeguards).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets mainstream consumer app users (likely a language-learning, wellness, or gamified habit app given the playful icon style) who need quick, low-friction access to account, monetization, and preference controls. The psychological driver is predictability and reduced cognitive load: by mimicking the native iOS Settings paradigm, the designer leverages users' pre-existing mental models so zero learning curve is required. Placing "Premium" high in the list exploits the mere exposure effect and proximity to account management to nudge free users toward conversion during a moment when they're already engaging with app configuration (a natural reflection point about their relationship with the product).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual affordance system: Chevrons for navigational drill-down vs. toggles for instant state changes lets users instantly distinguish "this opens another screen" from "this changes a setting right now" without reading extra copy.

  • Three-tier visual hierarchy via grouping and whitespace: Primary settings, support/info links, and destructive/meta actions are separated purely with spacing and dividers (no heavy borders or color needed).

  • De-emphasized destructive actions: "Log out" is given no icon, no container, and muted styling, reducing accidental logouts while still being easily reachable at the bottom.

  • Modal dismissal via "X": Correctly signals this Settings screen is a temporary overlay, reinforcing a mental model of "I can always close this and return to where I was."

  • Premium entry placed near the top, directly under Account, maximizing visibility for monetization without being obnoxious or forced.

screens.name: Brilliant Account 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this grouped stacked-list pattern for any account/profile management screen where users need to view and edit personal identity fields, credentials, and perform rare, high-stakes actions. Ideal for settings hubs, admin profile pages, or any CRUD-style preference screen where scannability and predictability matter more than visual flourish. Also appropriate whenever regulatory compliance (GDPR/CCPA) requires exposing data export and account deletion options clearly.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimalist list style when fields require rich context, previews, or validation feedback inline (e.g., password strength, profile photo cropping) - those need dedicated editing screens or inline components. Do not bury destructive actions at the bottom if your product has legal/UX requirements for more prominent warnings (e.g., financial or healthcare apps may need explicit red flagging even at the list level). Also avoid this flat layout for screens with more than 8-10 settings, where sectioned headers and search become necessary to prevent scroll fatigue.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets all authenticated users managing their personal account, especially those who are privacy-conscious or need to update credentials periodically. The design leverages the psychological principle of reduced cognitive load through familiarity: by mimicking native iOS Settings conventions, users immediately understand how to interact without onboarding. Placing destructive actions last exploits spatial memory and friction-by-distance: users must deliberately scroll/reach further down, reducing impulsive account deletion. The inclusion of "Export your data" signals trust and regulatory compliance, which can reduce user anxiety about lock-in (a known churn-reduction/trust-building tactic).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Logical grouping via whitespace/dividers: Separates identity, credentials, and account-lifecycle actions without needing heavy visual containers, keeping the page light.

  • Deferred alarm color: The destructive "Deactivate or delete account" action is not colored red on this list screen, avoiding premature anxiety; the warning is reserved for the confirmation step (progressive disclosure of risk).

  • Consistent chevron affordance: Every row uses the same right-chevron, teaching the user a single predictable interaction model across all items regardless of destination type (edit field vs. navigate to sub-flow).

  • Transparency-first data controls: "Export your data" is given equal visual weight to profile fields, normalizing data portability as a standard, non-scary account feature.

results.query: Avatar stack group presence indicator in collaborative canvas

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Apply this canvas-first pattern when designing freeform creative or collaborative tools (whiteboards, mind-mapping apps, mood boards, diagramming tools) on mobile, where:

  • The primary value is the content/canvas itself, not navigation chrome.
  • Real-time multi-user collaboration is core, warranting persistent presence indicators.
  • Users need frequent access to a small set of creation tools without context-switching away from their work.
  • Onboarding can be accomplished via example content rather than modal tutorials, preserving flow.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal-chrome, icon-only approach when:

  • The target audience is non-technical or first-time users who need explicit textual guidance (icon-only toolbars can be ambiguous without prior exposure to similar tools).
  • The app's primary tasks require frequent navigation between many distinct sections (a persistent bottom tab bar would serve better than a floating tool tray).
  • Precision input is critical and screen space is at such a premium that condensed toolbars would force excessive nested menus, increasing tap depth and errors.
  • Accessibility is a top priority and icon-only controls aren't paired with adequate labels/tooltips for screen reader users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, developers, and cross-functional team members collaborating remotely who need a lightweight, visual brainstorming space accessible from a phone (e).g., checking in on a team's FigJam board during a meeting, adding a quick sticky note, or reacting with a stamp while away from desk.

Psychologically, the design leverages several triggers: social presence (seeing collaborator avatars creates accountability and reduces the solitude of staring at a blank canvas), low cognitive load via familiarity (icon-only toolbar mirrors tools professionals already know from physical whiteboarding - pens, sticky notes, pointers), and playfulness as an anxiety reducer (the pun-filled sample content and emoji stickers make an otherwise intimidating infinite canvas feel approachable and non-precious, encouraging experimentation rather than perfectionism).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Minimal, canvas-first chrome: UI controls are reduced to two thin strips at the very top and bottom, maximizing screen real estate for the actual work surface (critical on small mobile viewports where every pixel of canvas matters).
  • Live presence indicators: Overlapping avatar bubbles in the header immediately communicate "you are not alone here," reinforcing FigJam's core real-time, multiplayer value proposition even before any content is touched.
  • Active-state tool highlighting: The purple-filled cursor icon in the toolbar gives unambiguous, glanceable feedback on which tool mode is currently engaged (important since mobile touch targets are small and mode errors are costly).
  • Inline color swatch next to the pen tool: Surfacing the current drawing color directly in the primary toolbar (rather than burying it in a submenu) reduces taps for the most common action, changing ink color mid-brainstorm.
  • Sample content as onboarding: Rather than a tutorial overlay, the board ships with real-looking sticky notes, stickers, and a flowchart, letting users learn affordances by exploring and manipulating existing objects (a "learn by doing" approach that respects user agency).
  • Dotted grid background: Subtly communicates "infinite canvas" and spatial freedom without needing explanatory text.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this edge-anchored minimal-chrome pattern for any canvas-based, direct-manipulation tool (whiteboards, design tools, mind-mapping, diagramming apps) where the content area must dominate the viewport, especially on mobile. Use live cursors with name labels whenever real-time multiplayer editing is a core value proposition, as it builds trust and transparency in collaborative work. The avatar-stack presence indicator is ideal for toolbars with limited horizontal space when more than one collaborator may be active.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid pure icon-only toolbars for first-time or non-technical audiences where tool literacy can't be assumed — add labels or onboarding coach marks instead. Live cursors and presence become visual noise in single-player contexts or in apps where collaboration is incidental rather than central, and should be gated behind a toggle. Overlapping avatar stacks break down with large numbers of simultaneous collaborators (10+) and need a "+N more" fallback to remain legible.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, developers, and cross-functional teammates collaborating synchronously on brainstorms, workshops, or planning sessions, often while mobile or away from their desktop. The mobile FigJam experience specifically targets users who need to quickly glance at, annotate, or react to a board started on desktop — e.g., joining a workshop from a phone during a meeting.

Psychologically, the live cursor and presence avatars tap into social presence and accountability: knowing a named collaborator is actively present and visibly moving around the board increases engagement and reduces the feeling of working in isolation. The minimal, icon-driven chrome also appeals to the target audience's assumed tool literacy — designers and technical users are comfortable inferring icon meaning without text labels, and the reduced UI signals a "professional, precision-focused" tool rather than a hand-holding consumer app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live multiplayer cursor with name tag directly on the canvas, making remote collaboration tangible and spatially contextual rather than abstracted into a sidebar list.
  • Edge-anchored, icon-only chrome (top and bottom bars) that maximizes canvas real estate on a small mobile screen while keeping essential actions reachable by thumb.
  • Overlapping avatar stack as a space-efficient presence indicator that scales gracefully as more collaborators join.
  • Expandable bottom toolbar with chevron affordances, hinting at deeper tool options (color/stroke, shape variants, note styles) without cluttering the default view.
  • Sample content as onboarding — the pre-built "FigJam basics" board acts as an implicit tutorial/demo rather than a modal walkthrough.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any real-time collaborative canvas, document, or whiteboard product where multiple users can be simultaneously active. It's ideal when:

  • You need a lightweight, non-blocking way to show who's present without permanent UI real estate cost.
  • Facilitation or teaching use-cases require pulling group attention to a single viewport (e.g., Spotlight/Follow).
  • You want to reinforce a sense of liveness and reduce the "am I alone here?" anxiety in multiplayer tools.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in single-player or asynchronous-only apps where presence/collaboration isn't a core value prop (the added UI would be noise). It's also unnecessary for tools with very large concurrent user counts (50+) where showing every avatar becomes unwieldy and a simplified count or grouped indicator would be more appropriate. Additionally, "Spotlight"-type forced-navigation actions should be used cautiously, as hijacking another user's viewport without clear consent/visual warning can feel intrusive or disorienting.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers, product managers, and distributed teams running collaborative brainstorming or workshop sessions on a tablet/mobile device (likely in a room together or hybrid remote setting). The psychological driver here is social presence and co-creation: seeing avatars and live cursors satisfies the human need to feel "together" even in a digital space, which increases engagement and trust in the collaborative output.

The Spotlight feature specifically serves facilitators/teachers who need control over group attention (a direct response to the common pain point of "losing" participants who wander off exploring a large FigJam board during a workshop).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Stacked Avatar Entry Point: Overlapping circular avatars in the nav bar double as both a presence indicator and a tappable trigger for the full collaborator list (an elegant, space-efficient affordance).
  • Spotlight Action: A single-tap mechanism to broadcast your viewport to all collaborators, purpose-built for workshop facilitators and teachers running remote sessions.
  • Live Cursor Labels: Named cursors on canvas ("Julian") create an ambient, game-like sense of co-presence without needing a persistent sidebar.
  • Non-Modal Popover: The roster list floats above the canvas without dimming or blocking it, letting users keep visual context of the board while checking who's online.
  • Thumb-Optimized Floating Toolbar: Tools are condensed into a pill at the screen's bottom edge, optimized for one-handed mobile/tablet use during a creative session.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this "follow mode" pattern for any real-time collaborative canvas, document, or whiteboard product where multiple users navigate a shared infinite space (e.g., diagramming tools, collaborative slide decks, virtual whiteboards, or live code review tools). It's especially valuable for remote presentations, guided walkthroughs, mentorship/pairing sessions, and onboarding where one expert leads others through complex content.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in single-player or non-real-time apps, or in contexts where simultaneous multi-user viewports aren't relevant (e.g., static document viewers, form-based apps). It can also backfire if overused without a clear exit path (always pair persistent "following" states with an obvious, instantly accessible way to break away (as the X button here does), since locked navigation can feel disorienting or claustrophobic if users feel trapped following someone else's pace).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern serves teams and designers conducting remote walkthroughs, brainstorms, or workshops in FigJam, especially useful on mobile when someone wants to passively observe a facilitator's presentation of a board (e.g., during a remote standup or design critique) without needing to manually navigate. The psychological trigger is reduced cognitive load through delegated navigation: users don't need to figure out where to look; the system does it for them, mirroring the comfort of being guided on a tour. It also leverages social presence theory: visible cursors and names make remote collaboration feel co-located and trustworthy.
screens.keyHighlights:
Why this screen is excellent:

  • Color-coded identity consistency: Julian's avatar, cursor label, and the "Following" pill all share the same yellow hue, letting users track identity across multiple UI surfaces without re-reading names.
  • Persistent, unobtrusive mode indicator: The floating pill clearly communicates a non-default navigation state (being driven by someone else) without blocking the canvas content.
  • Minimal chrome maximizes canvas space: Only essential controls are exposed, reinforcing the "canvas-first" philosophy where content always takes visual priority over UI.
  • Live cursor as social proof of activity: Seeing a real named cursor moving through content makes the collaboration feel alive and synchronous rather than static.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for canvas-based, creative, or collaborative tools (whiteboards, diagramming apps, design tools) being adapted to mobile or tablet form factors. It's ideal when:

  • The core value is a large, zoomable/pannable workspace that must not be obstructed by chrome.
  • Multiple simultaneous collaborators need lightweight, glanceable presence indicators.
  • Tool selection benefits from progressive disclosure (primary tool visible, sub-options behind a chevron) to conserve limited mobile screen space.
screens.whereNotToUse: This pattern is not suitable for form-heavy, linear, or transactional flows (e.g., checkout, settings, onboarding) where users need clear hierarchical navigation and persistent labels rather than icon-only, gesture-driven controls. It can also fail for new or first-time users without prior exposure to the desktop tool, since icon-only toolbars with minimal labeling rely heavily on learned mental models and may feel cryptic without onboarding/tooltips. Additionally, on very small screens, a floating toolbar can obscure canvas content near the bottom edge, so it should be paired with safe-area padding or auto-hide behavior.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for designers, product managers, and cross-functional teams who use FigJam for brainstorming, workshops, and collaborative ideation (now extended to mobile so participants can contribute or review boards away from their desktop). The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Social presence & FOMO: Seeing teammate avatars and live selections triggers a sense of shared activity and urgency to engage.
  • Low cognitive load: The pared-back UI reduces overwhelm for a touchscreen context where complex tool palettes would otherwise be unwieldy.
  • Familiarity transfer: Reusing iconography and layout patterns from the desktop app builds instant recognition and trust for existing Figma/FigJam users switching devices.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Minimal top chrome: Only essential global actions (close, share, overflow) and presence indicators are shown, maximizing canvas visibility.
  • Floating segmented toolbar: Condenses a desktop-class tool palette (select, pen, shape/color, sticky note, more) into a thumb-friendly floating bar with expandable chevrons for progressive disclosure of sub-tools.
  • Live presence avatars: Overlapping colored initials at the top instantly communicate who else is active on the board, reinforcing the real-time multiplayer value proposition.
  • Named live cursor label ("Julian"): Attributing an in-canvas selection to a specific collaborator builds trust and awareness during simultaneous editing.
  • Infinite dotted canvas: Reinforces spatial, exploratory mental model consistent with whiteboard/mind-mapping use cases.

screens.name: Figma - Reacting to a comment - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any collaborative tool (design, docs, project management) needing lightweight, contextual feedback loops tied to a specific object or location.
  • Mobile companion apps where users need to triage and respond to discussions quickly without the full desktop editing surface.
  • Threaded commenting systems where reactions can reduce reply volume and notification noise.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for high-stakes, formal approval workflows where reactions could be mistaken for official sign-off (a dedicated approve/reject action would be clearer).
  • Not ideal for extremely long, deeply nested discussion threads; a flat reaction+reply model doesn't scale well without threading/sub-replies.
  • Should not be used as the sole feedback mechanism in contexts requiring structured, trackable action items (e.g., bug tracking) - plain chat-style comments lack status/priority metadata.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets design teams and cross-functional collaborators (designers, PMs, developers) who review work asynchronously, often on mobile while away from their desktop. The psychological driver is social validation and low-friction acknowledgment: emoji reactions let teammates affirm or react to feedback without the cognitive and social cost of typing a reply, keeping collaboration momentum high. The familiar chat-thread visual language also lowers anxiety for non-technical stakeholders (e.g., clients, marketers) who may be intimidated by Figma's canvas tools but feel instantly at home in a comment thread.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline, per-message reactions instead of a global reaction bar (keeps emotional responses contextually tied to the exact comment that prompted them).
  • Persistent bottom composer ensures the reply action is always one tap away, reducing friction for quick back-and-forth design feedback.
  • Drag-handle bottom sheet preserves spatial context (the canvas remains "underneath," reinforcing that comments are annotations on the design, not a separate app).
  • @mention highlighting makes multi-person threads scannable at a glance.
  • Colored initial avatars (no need for profile photos) provide quick visual identity differentiation between collaborators using lightweight, consistent styling.

screens.name: Figma - Reacting to a comment - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when:

  • Feedback or discussion needs to stay tightly coupled to a specific visual or spatial element (design canvases, maps, images, documents with annotations).
  • You want to support collaborative review without forcing users to leave the primary content view.
  • Mobile companion experiences need parity with desktop commenting without overwhelming a small screen.
  • Lightweight social engagement (reactions) can increase participation rates on feedback threads.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Comments need to be reviewed in bulk or triaged (a dedicated inbox/list view would serve better than spatially-pinned threads).
  • The canvas or background content is dense/small, making overlay dimming counterproductive or distracting.
  • Formal approval workflows require structured status tracking (resolved/unresolved, assignees) rather than casual chat-style threads.
  • Screen real estate is too limited to show both the anchor point and readable sheet content simultaneously, risking a cramped or confusing experience.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, developers, and cross-functional stakeholders collaborating asynchronously or in near-real-time on a shared design file. It specifically targets the moment when a team member reviews work on mobile (e.g., during a commute or quick check-in) and wants to engage without opening a full desktop session.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages social validation (reaction counts), presence awareness (colored avatar initials), and low-commitment engagement (one-tap reactions) to encourage frequent, lightweight participation. The spatial pinning of comments taps into contextual relevance: feedback tied directly to the artifact it concerns is processed faster and with less misinterpretation than detached comment threads.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Spatially-anchored comments: The avatar pin on the canvas ties the conversation directly to the design element being discussed, eliminating ambiguity about context.
  • Non-destructive overlay: Using a bottom sheet instead of full-screen navigation keeps the underlying artboard visible and preserves mental context.
  • Inline emoji reactions with quick-add: Lightweight reactions (👀 1, 😍 2) let teammates acknowledge feedback without typing, lowering the barrier to engagement.
  • Persistent reply bar: Always-visible input field at the bottom removes friction for continuing the conversation.
  • Clear exit affordance: The "X" icon in the top bar gives users confidence they can dismiss the thread instantly.

screens.name: Figma - Reacting to a comment - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
• Onboarding flows for complex, abstract features (design systems, style guides, shared components) where a live example communicates faster than text.
  • Any collaborative tool introducing multiplayer concepts to solo users, showing avatars/presence on sample content builds anticipation for teamwork.
  • Mobile companion apps for desktop-first tools, where the goal is orientation and light review rather than full editing.
  • Template galleries or "starter kit" files meant to be duplicated by the user as a jumping-off point.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for simple, self-explanatory features where a sample canvas would add unnecessary friction compared to a one-line tooltip.
  • Not suitable for small-screen-only apps without a canvas/zoom paradigm, panning large content on tiny screens can frustrate users without pinch-to-zoom affordances.
  • Risky if the sample content isn't kept up to date with the current product UI (outdated mockups inside the sample file break trust).
  • Should not replace guided coach marks for critical, time-sensitive actions the user must complete immediately (e.g., permissions, account setup).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets design team leads and new team members who are being introduced to shared libraries for the first time, likely via an invite link opened on a mobile device. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of cognitive load through concrete example over abstraction: rather than explaining "what is a library" conceptually, Figma shows a finished, tangible artifact that the user can directly relate to their own future files.

The presence avatars also tap into social proof and belonging: seeing "J" avatars already engaged with the file signals that teammates are active and invested, nudging the new user to participate rather than abandon the workflow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Learn-by-example canvas: Instead of static instructional screens, Figma teaches the library concept using an actual editable/viewable file artifact, which doubles as a template users can reference or copy.
  • Directional microcopy + arrow: "Start here ↓" instantly orients new users on an otherwise open, directionless infinite canvas.
  • Simulated presence avatars: Colored initials bubbles on each card visually reinforce multiplayer collaboration, a core value proposition of Figma, even within a solo onboarding context.
  • Minimal chrome, maximal content: The top bar is reduced to a close action and title, keeping full visual focus on the canvas content itself.
  • Consistent bottom toolbar: Reusing the standard viewer toolbar (pages, present, comment, share) keeps the onboarding experience native rather than feeling like a separate tutorial mode.

screens.name: Figma Adding a comment 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this card-carousel pattern for in-product onboarding of complex internal tools, design systems, or shared workspace features where showing real artifacts (not just icons) builds credibility.

  • Appropriate when introducing a feature that benefits a team/organization (shared libraries, templates, brand kits) and you want to combine persuasive copy with functional preview content.

  • Good for documentation-style walkthroughs embedded directly inside the tool, letting users learn in-context rather than via an external help center.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for simple, single-concept features where a tooltip or single banner would suffice (multi-card carousels add unnecessary friction for trivial content).
