It's ideal when you want to present AI-generated or user-generated content with minimal chrome and maximum focus on the content itself.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal, accordion-first approach for data-heavy or multi-entity screens (e.g., dashboards, analytics, e-commerce listings) where users need to compare multiple data points simultaneously, collapsing key info by default would slow down task completion. Also avoid if your primary user base is non-technical and may not recognize icon-only toolbar actions (wand, history) without labels, which could create discoverability issues.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets creators, designers, and product builders who use AI-assisted tools to draft and organize concept documents (e.g., landing page briefs, product specs). The audience values speed and low-friction editing over heavy structure, which explains the sparse, document-like presentation rather than a traditional dashboard.

Psychologically, the collapsed accordion reduces overwhelm for a user re-opening a document (they see the gist first (title + one-liner) and can progressively disclose more detail, which respects the user's mental bandwidth and builds trust that the tool organizes information sensibly on their behalf).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Collapsed-by-default Accordion: Hides dense "Project Overview" content behind a single tap, reducing initial cognitive load and letting users choose their depth of engagement.

  • Floating Pill Toolbars: Grouping related icon actions (share/more, edit/attach, AI-wand/history) into soft rounded capsules keeps the canvas feeling open and uncluttered while still surfacing core actions persistently.

  • Magic Wand Icon: A strong visual cue signaling embedded AI/generative capabilities directly within the document action bar (lowers the barrier to discovering AI features).

  • Typography-led Hierarchy: Reliance on font weight/size differences instead of boxes or dividers to separate title, description, and section headers keeps the interface feeling light and editorial.

screens.name: Loom - Terms & conditions - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any settings area housing static, reference-only legal or compliance documents (Terms, Privacy Policy, Licenses, Acknowledgements). It's ideal when you need a low-maintenance, easily extensible list that can accommodate additional legal documents in the future without redesign. Appropriate for any B2B or consumer app that must satisfy App Store, GDPR, or enterprise procurement legal requirements.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this flat list pattern if legal content requires contextual flagging (e.g., "Updated" badges for recently changed policies) - users should be alerted to changes, which this plain design doesn't support. Also avoid for content requiring in-app reading with highlighted key points, as a chevron-only row doesn't signal document length or hint at import; a preview or summary might better serve users who need quick scanning rather than full navigation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves compliance-conscious professionals and enterprise teams who may need to verify Loom's data handling, terms of service, or open-source licensing (Acknowledgements) before adopting the tool organizationally (particularly relevant for IT/security reviewers vetting the app for workplace use). The psychological driver here is trust and transparency: by making legal documentation easily accessible and clearly labeled, Loom reduces friction for risk-averse B2B buyers and satisfies App Store/legal requirements without cluttering primary workflows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grouped list simplicity: Using a single stacked list section avoids overwhelming users with legal jargon up front (each document is one tap away, reducing cognitive load).
  • Consistent disclosure affordance: The chevrons on every row create a predictable interaction pattern, so users instantly know these rows navigate rather than toggle or expand inline.
  • Clear back navigation: The left-aligned chevron in the top bar maintains iOS-standard conventions, so users never feel lost in the settings hierarchy.
  • Intentional negative space: The large blank area below signals there's nothing else to find here, reducing scroll anxiety and confirming completeness of the list.

screens.name: Loom - Terms & conditions - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this consolidated legal-document pattern (dropdown switcher + dated policy header) whenever an app needs to host multiple related legal/compliance documents (Terms, Privacy Policy, DPA, Cookie Policy, Acceptable Use Policy) in one place. It's especially valuable for B2B/enterprise products where procurement and legal teams need quick access to version history and document switching without hunting through a footer or settings menu.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid over-designing legal pages with heavy visual flourishes, animations, or marketing language (legal/compliance content must prioritize clarity, searchability, and neutrality over persuasion). Additionally, this dropdown-switcher pattern becomes impractical if there are many more than 4-5 documents; in that case, a proper sidebar index or table of contents would scale better than a single dropdown.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This page primarily serves IT/security reviewers, legal/compliance teams, and procurement stakeholders at companies evaluating Loom for enterprise adoption, as well as individual users who want to verify data handling practices before recording sensitive screen content. Since Loom's audience includes professionals sharing internal/confidential work via screen recordings, trust and legal clarity are high-stakes conversion factors, especially for B2B sales cycles where legal sign-off gates purchase decisions.

The psychological trigger at play is trust-building through transparency: explicit effective dates, a consolidated terms hub, and consistent branding reduce perceived risk and signal organizational maturity, which is often an invisible but critical factor in B2B SaaS purchase decisions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consolidated legal hub: A single dropdown selector lets users switch between multiple legal documents (Terms, Privacy, etc.) without backtracking to a separate index page.
  • Branded even in boilerplate: Retaining the Loom logo and signature purple accent color on an otherwise generic legal page reinforces brand trust at a moment when users are specifically scrutinizing the company's credibility and commitments.
  • Visible effective date: Placing the "Effective: January 31, 2022" date immediately at the top of the body copy gives enterprise/legal reviewers an instant reference point without needing to scan the whole document.
  • Reader-mode compatibility: The clean semantic HTML structure (proper headings, paragraph spacing) is friendly to browser Reader Mode, improving accessibility and readability for users who strip away styling.

screens.name: H&M - Article detail - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for retail or e-commerce apps with multiple departments/categories that need a single consolidated menu combining navigation, search, and account utilities. It's ideal when:

  • The product catalog spans multiple shopper segments (e.g., gender/age-based departments) requiring quick top-level switching.
  • You want to blend merchandising (curated shopping moments) with standard taxonomy browsing in one screen.
  • Visual/camera-based search adds real value due to a highly visual product category like fashion, home decor, or beauty.
  • You need a scalable list for long-tail utility links (settings, support, store locator) without needing a separate drawer.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The catalog is small or single-category, making department tabs unnecessary overhead.
  • Visual/camera search isn't relevant to the product type (e.g., B2B software, digital services) - adding it would confuse rather than help.
  • Users need frequent, fast access to account settings; burying them at the bottom of a long undifferentiated list increases time-to-task for support-seeking users.
  • The brand identity calls for icon-assisted scannability (this flat, text-only list can feel sparse or hard to scan quickly for less design-literate audiences or accessibility-dependent users who benefit from icon redundancy).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves fashion-conscious shoppers who move fluidly between browsing by department and browsing by occasion or trend. The occasion-based shortcuts (Concert Shop, Workout Clothes) target younger, trend-driven users who think in terms of "what am I dressing for" rather than rigid categories, appealing to impulse and lifestyle-based purchasing psychology.

The camera/visual search icon specifically targets a psychological trigger of "I saw it, I want it now" - reducing friction for users inspired by social media or street style who don't know the product name. The scan icon serves existing in-store H&M customers, bridging physical and digital shopping behaviors, which reinforces loyalty and omnichannel convenience for repeat customers.

Utility links (Customer Service, Store Locator, Gift Card) cater to the practical needs of the broader "existing customer" segment, offering reassurance and reducing support friction without cluttering the primary shopping flows.
screens.keyHighlights:
Dual-mode search bar: Combining a text search field with both a camera icon (visual/image search) and a scan icon (barcode/product scanner) is a standout decision. It caters to different discovery mindsets (typing, snapping a photo of an outfit seen in real life, or scanning an in-store tag) collapsing three entry points into one compact, unobtrusive bar.

  • Segmented department tabs: Horizontal WOMEN/MEN/KIDS/HOME/BEAUTY tabs with a bold underline active state give instant context-switching without navigating away from the screen.
  • Content-first ordering: Editorial shopping destinations are placed above utility links, prioritizing revenue-driving discovery over account management.
  • Flat, chrome-free list design: No icons, borders, or cards (just typography and a single divider) keeps cognitive load low and lets the brand's minimalist aesthetic shine through even on a purely navigational screen.

screens.name: H&M - Article detail - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this single-field-first support pattern when:

  • You have one dominant, high-frequency user intent (e.g., order tracking, balance check, booking lookup) that can be resolved with minimal input.
  • You want to reduce support ticket volume by offering immediate self-service before funneling users to live chat or FAQs.
  • The brand wants to maintain commercial context (ads, promotions, navigation) even within utility/support flows.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Users have highly diverse support needs with no single dominant task (a search bar or categorized menu would serve them better than one prioritized form).
  • The required lookup data (e.g., order number) isn't readily available to the user, in which case alternative identifiers (email, phone) or account-based lookup should be offered alongside.
  • Retaining promotional banners above a support/help screen could feel tone-deaf, such as in cases of complaints, refunds for defective products, or sensitive service issues where marketing content may frustrate an already unhappy customer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves existing H&M customers who have already made a purchase and need post-purchase support (primarily order tracking and returns, the two highest-volume customer service inquiries in fashion e-commerce). The design assumes a time-pressed, task-oriented user (e.g., someone checking "where is my package?") rather than a browsing user, so it strips away marketing fluff in the main content area and gets straight to functional input.

Psychologically, the friendly greeting plus a single, obvious input field reduces the anxiety often associated with "where's my stuff" moments, reassuring the user that help is fast and requires minimal effort (just one field, not a multi-step form or login wall).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Task-first design: The most common support request (order tracking) is placed immediately below the headline, with zero scrolling required, rather than burying it under generic FAQ links.
  • Clear visual prioritization: A solid black primary button ("TRACK ORDER") versus an outlined secondary button ("REGISTER A RETURN") instantly communicates which action is more frequent/expected.
  • Input guidance via placeholder example: Showing a sample order number format proactively reduces input errors and support friction.
  • Persistent commerce context: Retaining the sale banner and tab bar even on a support screen keeps the user tethered to the shopping experience and avoids a jarring "exit" from the app's retail context.
  • Progressive disclosure: Additional help topics are tucked into an accordion list below, keeping the initial viewport uncluttered and focused.

screens.name: H&M - Article detail - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Customer support and FAQ sections in e-commerce or service apps where query volume needs to be organized without overwhelming the user.
  • Any screen where a short list of top questions should be shown first with an option to expand to the full knowledge base.
  • Contexts where live chat/support escalation should remain available as a fallback to self-service content.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid accordions for FAQs if answers are long and complex (nested scrolling inside expanded items can hurt readability; a dedicated detail page may be better).
  • Don't bury critical support options (like live chat) only as a small FAB (for urgent, failure-prone transactions (e).g., payment errors), a more prominent CTA may be warranted.
  • Persistent promotional banners should be removed or suppressed on support/help screens if user research shows this reads as tone-deaf during service recovery scenarios (e.g., a customer trying to report a defective product).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves existing H&M customers with active orders or in-store shopping intent (people searching for quick, specific answers (order cancellation, promotion disputes, in-store item location) rather than general brand information). The psychological driver is anxiety reduction and control: customers who reach a help screen are often already mildly frustrated (missed a sale, need to cancel), so the design prioritizes speed-to-answer over marketing flourish.

The persistent "SALE: UP TO 60% OFF" banner subtly exploits the moment (even a user seeking support is re-exposed to a purchase trigger, maximizing conversion opportunity without being intrusive).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Accordion-based progressive disclosure keeps the page short and scannable while housing dense support content.
  • "Show More" expansion prioritizes the top 3 most likely customer pain points before revealing the full list, reducing initial overwhelm.
  • Persistent promo banner + tab bar even within support screens keeps commerce top-of-mind and avoids dead-ending the user in a support silo.
  • Floating chat FAB provides an always-visible human/bot escalation path for issues the FAQ doesn't resolve.
  • Contextual placement of Klarna and Privacy Notice links exactly where payment-related anxiety is highest.

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when a user must link one resource (e.g., a card, device, or seat) to another governing resource (e.g., a budget, policy, or plan) before it becomes active. It's ideal for:

  • Financial or admin tools requiring assignment of budgets, limits, or permissions to an asset.
  • Any "activation" step gating further use of a feature until a required configuration is completed.
  • Scenarios with both a "create new" and "choose existing" path, where visual hierarchy can guide users to the most relevant option.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there is only a single possible path (e.g., only one limit always exists), as the dual-option layout would add unnecessary complexity. It's also unsuitable for consumer-facing apps where financial jargon like "spend limit" or "expires" could confuse non-business users. If the list of available limits could grow very large, this flat list would need to be upgraded with search, filtering, or grouping to remain scannable.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees and card administrators at a company using Brex, specifically those activating or reconfiguring a corporate card. The design assumes some familiarity with budget/limit concepts but keeps the interface simple enough for non-finance employees to self-serve without needing to contact their finance team.

The psychological driver here is reducing friction and decision paralysis at a critical activation step (without an assigned limit, the card is unusable, so the UI must make the "happy path" (selecting an existing limit) as fast as possible while still accommodating the edge case (requesting a new one)). The prominent orange CTA leverages color contrast to draw attention to the primary suggested action for users who don't yet have a limit, while existing-limit holders can bypass it and tap directly into the list.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-path action design: Clearly separates "create new" from "select existing" using contrasting visual treatment (bold orange tile vs. neutral list row), guiding users efficiently regardless of their starting context.
  • Transparent financial disclosure: Surfacing exact available balance and expiration date directly in the list item removes the need to tap in just to check basic eligibility, saving the user a step.
  • Masked sensitive data: Card number and limit names are obscured with placeholder bars/dots, reflecting a security-conscious design appropriate for financial data shown in screenshots or shared screens.
  • Lightweight modal pattern: Using an X-dismiss modal rather than a full page keeps this as a quick, non-disruptive sub-task within a larger card management flow.

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any screen involving a finite resource allocation (budgets, data caps, storage limits, subscription credits). It is highly effective for:

  • Enterprise expense management apps.
  • Telecom apps showing data/minutes usage.
  • SaaS platforms showing API usage or storage quotas.
  • Any "wallet" or "card" detail view where a user needs to see available balance vs. total limit instantly.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense, modal-stacked approach for:

  • Simple Consumer Apps: If the target audience is non-technical consumers who do not need granular "per diem" breakdowns, this level of detail (accordions, restrictions, documentation) may feel overwhelming or overly "corporate."
  • High-Frequency Glance Checks: If users need to check this balance dozens of times a day in under 2 seconds, a modal requiring a swipe-to-dismiss might be slower than a persistent dashboard widget.
  • Screens with volatile/real-time data: If the balance changes every few seconds (e.g., stock trading), a static progress bar might create distrust if it doesn't update with live animations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves mobile-first employees (e.g., sales reps, consultants, or traveling staff) who need to make a quick purchasing decision ("Do I have enough budget for this coffee/flight?") without opening a laptop or calling accounting.

The psychological trigger here is reduction of financial anxiety. By presenting the remaining limit as a massive, bold number alongside a visual bar, Brex alleviates the "fear of overspending" that corporate card holders often feel. Furthermore, the "Request limit increase" button taps into a sense of autonomy and trust, signaling to the employee that the company's tool empowers them to ask for more resources directly, rather than feeling micromanaged.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual Limit Gauge: The thick black progress bar beneath the balance is a brilliant micro-interaction that replaces mental math (calculating remaining budget) with an instant visual read.
  • Contextual Per Diem Tracking: The circular "Meals" icon with a green ring acts as a secondary, specific progress indicator nested within the general budget, allowing users to track specific spending categories (like food) without leaving the main limit screen.
  • Inline Compliance Status: The small icons (camera/receipt, checkmark) next to the "Recent expenses" list provide an immediate visual audit trail, showing which transactions are fully documented versus pending without requiring a tap-through.
  • Self-Service Deflection: The "Request limit increase" button is placed with equal visual weight to "View limit details," directly empowering users to solve their own budget constraints without needing to email a finance manager.

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any screen involving finite resource allocation (budgets, data caps, storage limits, vacation days) where a user needs to see "remaining capacity" alongside granular, rule-based exceptions. It is ideal for:

  • Expense management and corporate card dashboards.
  • SaaS usage limits (e.g., API calls, storage).
  • Project management budget tracking.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, text-heavy accordion approach for consumer-facing apps where the audience is less tolerant of reading policy text, or for very simple limits where a single line item would suffice. If the restrictions are too complex (e.g., more than 3-4 nested rules), this UI may need to be upgraded to a dedicated "Policy" full-screen page rather than a modal accordion, to avoid excessive scrolling within a sheet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves employees and business travelers who need to self-serve answers about their spending limits before making a purchase, reducing reliance on manual approval from a manager or finance admin. It also implicitly serves finance teams/admins by codifying and displaying the specific guardrails (thresholds, attendee requirements) they have configured.

The psychological trigger here is reduction of uncertainty and anxiety. Corporate spending often creates stress around "Will this be approved?" or "Am I over budget?". By surfacing the exact dollar limit, expiration date, and category-specific rules upfront, Brex removes the ambiguity, empowering users to spend confidently within the rules.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual Balance Hierarchy: The usage bar combined with the large dollar figure communicates "how much is left" far faster than a simple table of numbers would.
  • Progressive Disclosure via Accordions: Complex compliance rules for different spending categories (Meals, Airline) are hidden until needed, keeping the default view clean while supporting power-user auditing.
  • Contextual Self-Service: The "Request limit increase" CTA is placed directly next to the balance, turning a potential moment of friction (running low on funds) into an immediate, frictionless action.
  • Granular Policy Transparency: By breaking down review thresholds by category and even by booking duration (under/over 6 hours), the app manages expectations and reduces the surprise of a rejected expense report later.

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when designing budget/limit tracking features where users need an at-a-glance sense of remaining allowance alongside itemized historical detail (e).g., subscription usage meters, data/storage caps, corporate expense categories, or gift card balances. It's also effective for embedding a primary CTA naturally inside a transactional list rather than as a disconnected floating button, especially in finance or task-management contexts where the action is directly tied to the list's content (e.g., "Add expense," "Log activity").

The card-over-card modal approach is ideal for secondary/drill-down detail views accessed from a dashboard, letting users peek back at the parent context via the visible handle/peek bar.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid the circular progress ring when the metric being tracked isn't naturally bounded (e.g., unlimited spend, open-ended savings) (a gauge implies a finite cap and could mislead users into thinking there's a hard ceiling that doesn't exist. Also avoid stacking multiple small status icons (sync/receipt/approval) in contexts where users are not already familiar with their meaning; without a legend or onboarding, these icons risk being ignored or misunderstood by first-time or casual users. Finally, embedding a primary CTA inside a list (like "Request reimbursement") can get visually lost or feel inconsistent if the list grows long or if users don't scroll far enough to notice it) a persistent sticky button might better serve high-urgency actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for employees managing a discretionary spending category (e.g., a daily meal/transportation allowance tied to a specific budget or trip) within a corporate card program. The target user is likely a traveling employee or in-office staffer who needs quick confidence that they are within policy limits before making another purchase.

Psychologically, the progress ring taps into the same "fuel gauge" heuristic used in fitness rings and data-usage meters (humans process circular depletion/fullness far faster than reading raw numbers, reducing cognitive load for a user who may be standing in line at a register). The itemized receipt-status icons serve the compliance-driven psychology of finance teams and auditors by making transaction completeness self-evident, reducing follow-up friction and anxiety about missing documentation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Circular progress ring as instant budget comprehension tool: converts an abstract dollar figure into a glanceable visual state (full ring = full budget remaining).
  • Inline primary action within the list ("Request reimbursement" styled like a list item with an accent-colored icon), reducing extra taps and keeping the CTA contextually relevant to the expense feed it populates.
  • Triple status iconography per transaction: communicates sync status, receipt attachment, and approval state simultaneously, giving finance oversight without needing to tap into each record.
  • Modal/card-over-card navigation pattern (visible peeking sheet above) preserves the user's place in the parent screen, encouraging quick in-and-out interactions typical of expense checking on the go.
  • Multi-currency transparency: explicit currency codes on every line item prevent costly misreading for a globally distributed workforce.

screens.name: Brex - Available limit - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: This pattern is ideal for B2B SaaS admin panels where a single object (like a budget, project, or team) has multiple associated resources (people, assets, rules). Use a bottom-sheet/modal detail view when you want users to drill down for specifics without losing their place in a master list. It is particularly effective for financial or project management tools where "who is responsible" and "what assets are attached" are critical pieces of metadata.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, stacked-section layout for consumer-facing apps where users expect a more visual, card-based, or narrative experience. Additionally, if the number of "Members" or "Cards" associated with an entity is very high (hundreds), this flat list approach will fail; it would require pagination or a search/filter mechanism integrated into the section itself rather than an infinite vertical scroll.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Finance Admins and Team Managers who require a "single pane of glass" view over a specific spending entity. The psychological driver here is control and oversight: by consolidating the cards, the people who can spend (Members), and the person accountable (Managed by) into one view, Brex reduces the anxiety associated with decentralized spending.

The inclusion of an "Alerts" section specifically targets the need for proactive risk management, allowing finance leads to set up guardrails rather than only reviewing spend retroactively.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Status Iconography: The small icons next to the transaction amount (receipt matching, policy compliance checks) provide immediate visual confirmation of expense status without requiring the user to tap into the transaction.
  • Modal Drag Handle: The use of a swipe-down gesture to dismiss the detail view keeps the interaction lightweight and native to iOS conventions, differentiating "detail" views from "primary" navigation screens.
  • Chevron Consistency: The right-aligned chevrons (>) on "All expenses" and "Add alert" create a clear visual language that these rows lead to deeper views or forms, distinct from the static list items below them (Cards, Members).

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a product legally requires explicit user consent to terms of service, privacy policies, or fee schedules during onboarding, especially in regulated industries like fintech, healthcare, or insurance. It's ideal when you want to soften the friction of mandatory legal steps without diminishing their legal weight (combine a fixed, low-friction CTA with scrollable, well-organized supporting content and injected personality/tone to keep users engaged rather than disengaging from a wall of text).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if your legal/compliance team requires explicit itemized consent (e.g., individual checkboxes per document) for audit or regulatory reasons (a single blanket "Agree" button may not satisfy stricter jurisdictions (e).g., GDPR granular consent requirements). Also avoid injecting humor into legal copy for products in serious/high-stakes contexts (e.g., medical consent, legal contracts with liability implications) where levity could undermine perceived seriousness or trust. If the fee structure is complex, oversimplifying it here could create trust issues later when hidden costs are discovered.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users signing up for a peer-to-peer payments app (Venmo) who are eager to start sending/receiving money and are likely to skim or skip legal text. The design leverages the path of least resistance psychological principle: by making the required reading feel light and by placing the CTA persistently at the bottom, the app respects the user's impatience while still fulfilling legal/regulatory obligations (financial services require explicit agreement to terms).

The reassuring fee language also targets fee-anxious users (a known drop-off point in fintech onboarding) pre-emptively addressing the objection "will this app quietly charge me?" before it becomes a blocker to activation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Humor to defuse boredom: The witty headline reframes a mandatory legal step as something almost welcome, lowering psychological resistance to reading (or skipping) dense content.

  • Sticky bottom CTA: The "Agree" button and consent text remain fixed at the bottom, decoupled from the scrolling legal content, so the user is never more than one tap away from completing the step.

  • Implicit consent via hyperlinks: Instead of separate checkboxes for each document, a single "Agree" action paired with inline linked document names streamlines consent capture without sacrificing legal coverage.

  • Progressive disclosure of fees: Rather than hiding fee information in a separate menu, key fee philosophy is surfaced directly in the onboarding flow, proactively building trust before the user commits.

  • Lettered mini table of contents: "A. User Agreement / B. Privacy Statement" gives structure and scannability to what is otherwise unglamorous legal content.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 8
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech, banking, or wallet app onboarding flows where regulatory fee disclosure is mandatory before account activation.

  • Any product where cost transparency is a key differentiator or objection-handler (e.g., subscription apps clarifying trial-to-paid pricing).

  • Situations where you need to bundle legal consent with informational content to avoid an extra confirmation step.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for products with complex, tiered, or usage-dependent pricing (a simple fact-box grid oversimplifies and could mislead users, creating compliance risk).

  • Not ideal if the fee structure is genuinely unfavorable; the friendly tone paired with hard cost data could feel dissonant or manipulative if fees are actually high.

  • Should not be used as a substitute for full, detailed terms (this format is a supplement/summary, not a replacement for the legally binding agreement it references).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users signing up for a peer-to-peer payments/digital wallet product (e.g., Venmo) who may have prior negative experiences with hidden bank fees. The design leverages the psychological principle of anticipated regret reduction: by proactively disclosing fees before the user commits, the product reduces the perceived risk of "gotcha" charges later, which is a major churn/distrust driver in fintech.

It also exploits the authority/trust heuristic: presenting fees in a formal, tabular disclosure format (like a bank's Schedule of Fees) borrows credibility from traditional financial institutions, making the product feel regulated and safe even though the tone remains casual.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fact-box fee table: Using a bordered, structured 2x2+ grid of "$0"-forward numbers mirrors regulated banking disclosures, instantly signaling legitimacy and transparency.

  • Emotional framing before data: Leading with empathetic, benefit-driven copy ("we minimize or eliminate fees") primes the user to interpret the subsequent numbers positively rather than skeptically.

  • Bundled consent + education: Combining fee disclosure and legal agreement into a single screen with one CTA reduces the number of steps needed to complete onboarding without skipping required compliance messaging.

  • Zero-cost emphasis via typography: "$0" values are set in oversized bold type, drawing the eye immediately to the free actions, while smaller fees (ATM out-of-network) are visually de-emphasized.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 9
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial services onboarding flows requiring regulatory fee/risk disclosures (banking, prepaid cards, crypto, lending).

  • Any screen combining mandatory legal text with optional educational/FAQ content, where you want to keep the CTA persistently accessible.

  • Use accordions when you have multiple related but distinct topics (e.g., "Opening an account" vs "Spending money") that not every user needs to read in full.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the legal content is short enough to display without scrolling, forcing an accordion/scroll pattern on brief text adds unnecessary friction. Also avoid softening critical risk disclosures (e.g., FDIC insurance exclusions) with too much visual "friendliness" if it risks burying material information users are legally required to notice; regulators may require such text remain prominent and unobscured by decorative elements. Do not use a single blanket "Agree" CTA if regulations require granular, itemized consent to distinct terms.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new or existing Venmo users who are opening or upgrading a Venmo balance account (a prepaid/FBO account issued by PayPal, Inc.) and, by the crypto disclaimer, likely users engaging with Venmo's crypto buying feature. The audience spans everyday consumers who are not financial experts, so the design must balance legal obligation (full disclosure of fees, FDIC insurance limits, crypto risk) with usability.

Psychologically, the screen leverages authority and transparency cues (referencing CFPB.gov, explicit issuer naming "PayPal, Inc.") to build trust despite delivering somewhat alarming information (crypto not FDIC insured). The FAQ-style reframing reduces anxiety by making the fee structure feel accessible and answerable rather than an opaque legal trap. The single, unmissable "Agree" button reduces decision friction at the point of commitment, banking on the fact that most users skim rather than read fully (a known dark-pattern-adjacent but industry-standard practice for terms acceptance flows).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Sticky footer CTA + consent text: The "Agree" button and its supporting legal microcopy remain fixed at the bottom, decoupled from the long scrollable legal content above, ensuring the action is never lost regardless of scroll depth.

  • Progressive disclosure via accordions: Converting dense fee-related FAQs into collapsible sections prevents an overwhelming wall of text and lets users self-select which details matter to them.

  • Visual segmentation of legal vs. friendly content: A hard-bordered box isolates the strictly regulatory disclosure text from the softer, illustrated FAQ section, helping users mentally categorize "official terms" vs. "helpful explanation."

  • Brand personality injection: Colorful speech-bubble illustrations next to the "Answers about Venmo account fees" heading humanize an otherwise sterile compliance screen.

  • Explicit risk callouts: Bolding/capitalizing "NOT eligible for FDIC pass-through insurance" ensures critical risk disclosures aren't glossed over, satisfying regulatory transparency requirements.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 10
screens.whereToUse:

  • Ideal for consumer/social apps where brand personality and emotional tone matter (fintech-with-a-social-layer, lifestyle, gaming).

  • Effective when paired with a multi-step progress indicator so users understand it's transient and part of a larger flow.
screens.whereNotToUse:

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users mid-onboarding (likely post-signup, pre-account-activation) on Venmo, a peer-to-peer payments app whose core demographic is younger, socially-driven users who split bills, gift money, and casually transact with friends. The illustration of a toast/cheers moment specifically evokes social camaraderie - the psychological trigger being positive anticipation and social belonging rather than transactional utility.

Using diverse skin tones in the illustrated hands signals inclusivity, which builds trust and relatability with a broad user base during a vulnerable onboarding moment (when trust in a financial app is still being established).

  • Distraction-free single focus: No nav bar, buttons, or competing elements, nothing to tap, which eliminates decision fatigue during a forced wait.

  • Progress transparency: The bottom progress bar subtly communicates onboarding sequence position without being overtly gamified.

  • On-brand illustration style: Diverse hands, playful confetti/sparkle marks, and warm color palette reinforce Venmo's inclusive, social-first identity.

  • Anticipation copy: "We can't wait to celebrate" builds excitement for what's next rather than apologizing for the wait.

screens.name: Venmo Setting Up 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an app needs to request a sensitive OS-level permission (contacts, location, notifications, camera) and wants to maximize opt-in rates. It's ideal for social, marketplace, or communication apps where the permission directly unlocks a visible, desirable feature (finding friends, nearby deals, etc.). Always pair the ask with a tangible benefit statement and a visible, low-friction way to decline or defer.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for permissions with no clear user-facing benefit, as the priming copy will feel like padding or manipulation. Do not use if the permission is mandatory for core app function (in that case, blocking flows with a hard paywall/requirement is more honest than presenting a "skip" option that leads to a broken experience later). Also avoid over-explaining trivial permissions, as excessive justification can trigger suspicion ("why do they need to explain so much?").
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new Venmo users mid-onboarding, most of whom are social, peer-to-peer payment users motivated by ease of splitting bills and paying friends. The psychological trigger at play is social utility and loss-aversion: users are shown that without contact syncing, finding friends on the platform will be harder, subtly making non-compliance feel like a downgrade in experience. Simultaneously, the explicit "protect your account" language taps into security-conscious reasoning, appealing to more risk-averse users who might otherwise decline access. The optional "Skip for now" respects user autonomy, which is critical for privacy-sensitive demographics who would otherwise abandon onboarding entirely if forced.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-permission priming: Explains value and reversibility before triggering the native OS permission dialog, increasing opt-in acceptance rates.

  • Security framing: Frames contact sync as a way to "protect your Venmo account," turning a privacy trade-off into a security benefit.

  • Explicit reversibility disclosure: Tells users exactly where to undo the action (Friends & Social Settings), lowering the perceived risk of commitment.

  • Non-blocking secondary path: "Skip for now" lets users progress without friction or forced compliance, preserving onboarding completion rates.

screens.name: Wealthfront Searching & Finding 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you need to help users navigate a large, potentially overwhelming catalog (stocks, products, content) by grouping items under narrative-driven, benefit-oriented themes rather than raw taxonomies. Ideal for fintech/investing apps, content discovery platforms, or e-commerce apps aiming to curate collections around lifestyle or interest-based hooks. Also effective for surfacing "what's new" alongside evergreen curated content to balance freshness with reliability.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for professional/institutional trading tools where users need precise, unfiltered access to raw data, screeners, and full ticker lists (thematic packaging can feel patronizing or imprecise to expert users). Also avoid when regulatory/compliance concerns require full transparency of holdings upfront (truncated lists could be seen as obscuring material information in some jurisdictions). Not suitable if the underlying catalog is small, as artificial "theming" would feel forced or sparse.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed retail investors, particularly younger or novice users (Millennials/Gen-Z) who are drawn to investing through cultural or narrative hooks (gaming, crypto, ESG, etc.) rather than pure fundamental analysis. The psychological trigger at play is thematic relevance/identity investing: people are more likely to engage with an investment idea framed around something they already care about (esports, crypto culture) than a raw list of tickers.

The "Newly added" section leverages novelty and curiosity, while "Targeted strategies" leverages a sense of sophistication and control, appealing to users who want to feel like tactical investors without needing deep financial literacy. The truncated "+4 MORE" list creates a mild curiosity gap, nudging exploration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Theme-as-Product Packaging: Turning an investment thesis (e.g., indirect crypto exposure) into a named, ownable "collection" makes stock picking feel like curated shopping rather than dry research.

  • Progressive Disclosure via "+X More": Showing only 3 logos plus a counter keeps cards compact and scannable while still conveying depth and encouraging a tap-through for more.

  • Dual-Axis Organization: Combining vertical sections (by category type: "Newly added" vs "Targeted strategies") with horizontal carousels (by individual theme) allows dense content curation without long scrolling fatigue.

  • Logo-First Recognition: Using recognizable brand icons (AMD, NVIDIA, Roblox) instead of ticker symbols alone leverages brand familiarity to build instant trust and relevance.

screens.name: Wealthfront Searching & Finding 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern when offering multiple tiers or "flavors" of a single core product (subscription plans, investment strategies, workout programs) where visual differentiation aids quick comprehension.

  • Ideal for upsell/cross-sell moments where you want browsing to feel low-pressure and exploratory rather than a hard sales page.

  • Effective when each option benefits from strong visual/brand storytelling to differentiate otherwise similar underlying commodities (e.g., index funds).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid if there are more than 4-5 options: carousels hide content and can bury less-visited items, hurting discoverability at scale (use a grid or filterable list instead).

  • Not ideal for decisions requiring detailed side-by-side comparison (e.g., fees, minimums across many attributes) - a comparison table would serve users better than swiping between isolated cards.

  • Risky for accessibility/desktop contexts where horizontal swipe gestures are less discoverable than on touch-first mobile.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing app users (likely from a brokerage/investing app like Public, Robinhood, or Wealthfront) who already have a basic account and are being upsold into a higher-margin, fee-based automated investing product. The target user is someone who wants "set it and forget it" investing but is unsure which strategy fits their values or risk tolerance (hence multiple portfolio types like Classic vs. Socially Responsible).

Psychologically, the screen leverages choice architecture: presenting a curated, small set of portfolio "flavors" reduces decision paralysis compared to a raw list of fund options. The premium badge and elevated illustration style also tap into status signaling and aspiration, framing the automated portfolio as a lifestyle upgrade rather than a mere fee-generating product.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Card-based product carousel: Each investment strategy (Classic, Socially Responsible, etc.) is packaged as a swipeable, visually distinct card, making comparison shopping between portfolio types feel exploratory rather than overwhelming.

  • Intentional edge-peek affordance: The next card is deliberately cropped at the right edge, using the Gestalt principle of continuation to non-verbally communicate "swipe for more" without any instructional copy or UI chrome.

  • Premium badge for tiering clarity: A single, unobtrusive badge instantly communicates monetization status, letting free users self-select whether to explore further or immediately understand this is a paid upgrade.

  • Illustration as brand differentiation: Using rich, editorial-style artwork (vs. generic stock icons) for each portfolio type reinforces premium quality and helps each product feel memorable and distinct.

  • Embedded feedback capture: Placing a lightweight feedback CTA directly in the flow (rather than buried in settings) increases the likelihood of capturing in-the-moment sentiment about a new/complex feature.

screens.name: Wealthfront Searching & Finding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a platform has multiple upsell/premium features to surface without overwhelming the primary dashboard, particularly in fintech, subscription, or SaaS apps. It's ideal for a dedicated "Discover/Explore" tab where users are in a browsing mindset rather than a task-completion mindset. Also effective when a product wants to segment gating by account tier (e.g., balance thresholds) and needs to communicate premium value visually before pricing details are shown.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern on core transactional screens (e.g., checkout, account balance, transfer confirmation) where users need speed and clarity, not merchandising. It's also inappropriate for entry-level or low-trust user segments who may not yet have accounts large enough to qualify, as repeatedly showcasing inaccessible premium features can create frustration or a sense of exclusion. Additionally, avoid heavy illustrative/editorial visuals if the brand's positioning is utilitarian or trust-first (e.g., banks targeting risk-averse older demographics), since abstract art can obscure the concrete financial benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-directed retail investors who already use the app for core investing/banking and are being segmented for premium upsell (likely users with a moderate-to-high account balance (the copy explicitly gates "Direct Indexing" to accounts over $100k, targeting affluent or high-net-worth segments)). The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Aspiration & status signaling via the "PREMIUM" badge and sophisticated dark visual styling.

  • Authority & competence framing: automation, personalization, and tax optimization messaging implies the product is smarter than manual investing, building trust in the algorithm.

  • Low commitment exploration: framing this as "Discover" content rather than a hard sell reduces resistance, letting users self-select into the upsell funnel.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Nested carousel-within-scroll architecture: Peeking edges of adjacent cards clearly signal swipeability, encouraging users to browse multiple feature pitches in one session, increasing surface area for upsell conversion.

  • Scannable value checklist: Converting dense product terms (fee structure, personalization, tax optimization) into three short checkmarked bullets reduces cognitive load and mirrors high-converting SaaS landing page patterns.

  • Contextual feedback capture: Placing a feedback CTA directly after a discovery/upsell module captures qualitative sentiment about new features at the exact moment of exposure, which is a smart, low-friction research technique.

  • Clear premium gating badge: The "PREMIUM" pill immediately sets pricing expectations before the user reads further, preventing frustration/surprise later in the funnel.

screens.name: PayPal Pre-Onboarding 23

screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: PayPal Pre-Onboarding 24
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for financial or utility super-apps where a single "primary job" (e.g., sending money, hailing a ride) must coexist with a growing portfolio of secondary monetizable products. It's effective when:

  • You need to cross-sell multiple unrelated product lines (crypto, credit, retail partnerships) without overwhelming the primary task flow.

  • Trust is fragile (new user, first session): leading with crypto/debit-card ads before the user has even checked their balance may feel presumptuous rather than reassuring, undermining the "cautious, ledger-minded" brand promise.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Designed for Busy Urban users and Students who need fast, low-friction access to sending/requesting money as their primary use case, but who are also viable targets for supplemental revenue products (crypto, debit card, BNPL retail partnerships). The screen leans on:

  • Anchoring/Framing:

screens.name: PayPal Pre-Onboarding 25

It's ideal for fintech, wallet, or account-based apps where users check in frequently for quick glances but where the business also needs surface area for partner promotions or upsells.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid stacking multiple horizontal carousels below a primary balance/status card in apps where users need fast, single-purpose task completion (e.g., a pure P2P transfer app) - the offer clutter can distract from urgent account-checking behavior. The $0.00 empty state paired with a prominent 'Add money' CTA nudges cash-strapped or between-paycheck students toward funding their account, converting a potentially discouraging balance into an actionable next step. The Pay Later merchant carousel (Target, Home Depot) speaks directly to budget-conscious users seeking installment flexibility for everyday retail needs, while the cash-back offers (Grammarly, a productivity tool popular with students) tap into a demographic likely juggling schoolwork or side hustles, using cash-back savings as a psychological reward for continued app engagement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Elevated FAB-style Send/Request tab: Breaking the flat tab bar pattern with a raised circular icon instantly communicates the app's core value proposition (moving money) without needing a label to be understood.

  • Peeking carousel cards: The second account/crypto card is deliberately cut off at the screen edge, a classic affordance cue that signals horizontal scrollability without needing an explicit indicator or instruction.

  • Contextual CTA embedded in the balance card: Rather than a separate promotional banner, 'Add money' lives directly inside the balance card, tying the empty $0.00 state directly to its solution.

  • Layered monetization without disruption: Grammarly and retail offers are merchandised in the same visual language as core banking info, normalizing partner promotions as part of the everyday utility rather than an intrusive ad.

screens.name: Lemon8 - Commenting on a post - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for image/video-first social or content-discovery apps where individual posts benefit from a strong "hook" cover slide and sequential storytelling (e.g., lifestyle, beauty, DIY, recipe, or educational carousels). It's ideal when the goal is to maximize swipe-through completion rate and when a creator's authentic voice is central to brand trust. It also suits apps needing a lightweight, reusable engagement bar (save/like/comment/share) for scalable content feeds.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for data-dense, utility-first apps (banking, productivity, enterprise tools) where decorative typography and curiosity-driven copy would feel unprofessional or slow down task completion. It's also unsuitable for content requiring immediate, complete information delivery (e.g., safety alerts, legal disclosures), since the deliberate "cliffhanger" structure delays key information and could frustrate users seeking quick facts. Additionally, overlaying large stylized text on photos can hurt accessibility/readability for users with visual impairments if not paired with proper contrast and alt text.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets Gen Z and young millennial lifestyle consumers who browse Lemon8 for aesthetic inspiration and trustworthy peer recommendations (home décor, wellness, beauty). The creator's casual, warning-toned narrative exploits the curiosity gap and loss-aversion triggers (users fear they might be using something "toxic" and want the resolution). The Follow button in high-contrast yellow capitalizes on the moment of highest content-driven trust to convert a casual viewer into a subscriber, while the save/like/comment/share bar leverages social proof (counts) to validate the content's credibility before the user commits to reading further.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual slide-count affordance: Both a dot page-control and a numeric "1/4" badge tell users exactly how much content remains, encouraging full carousel consumption.

  • Editorial text-on-image overlay: Large, curved, shadowed typography transforms a simple product photo into a thumb-stopping "cover" slide, borrowing proven magazine/Pinterest visual hierarchy.

  • Curiosity-gap copywriting: The caption intentionally withholds the full explanation, driving continued swiping and engagement time.

  • Low-friction engagement bar: Save, like, comment, and share icons are paired with live counts, providing social proof at a glance while keeping the action targets large and thumb-friendly.

  • Minimal top chrome: Stripping navigation down to essentials (back, creator identity, Follow, more) keeps visual real estate dedicated to the content itself.

screens.name: Lemon8 - Commenting on a post - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for content or community platforms where discussion depth and creator-follower relationships drive retention: social apps, niche forums, creator economy platforms, or UGC-driven marketplaces. It's especially effective when:

  • You want to surface creator engagement transparently (badges, pinned replies) to incentivize creators to respond.

  • The product benefits from granular reactions (likes per comment) to extend session time and signal content quality.

  • You need a low-friction entry point to commenting for users who are intimidated by blank text fields (placeholder prompts + emoji shortcuts).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this density of social-engagement UI in utility-first, transactional, or professional contexts (e.g., banking apps, B2B SaaS dashboards, formal documentation tools) where playful comment prompts or emoji nudges would undermine credibility. Additionally:

  • In apps with low comment volume, a per-comment like system may look empty (zero-states) and signal lack of community activity, which can be discouraging rather than motivating.

  • If brand tone is more premium/editorial, overly casual placeholder copy like "Say 'Hi' to make friends" could feel juvenile or off-brand.

  • For sensitive or crisis-support content, lighthearted emoji prompts risk being tonally inappropriate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is engineered for Gen Z and young millennial lifestyle enthusiasts seeking niche community belonging (e.g., "clean living," "essential oils," wellness subcultures) rather than just content consumption. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Parasocial relationship building: The Creator badge and direct reply from Tay make followers feel personally acknowledged, deepening loyalty and increasing the likelihood of repeat visits to that creator's content.

  • In-group identity signaling: Hashtags and comment language ("found my people," "oily ladies") tap into tribal belonging (a powerful motivator for Gen Z who seek micro-communities around specific identities/interests).

  • Low-friction social validation: Heart icons on every comment allow users to receive validation not just on posts but on their individual thoughts, reinforcing the dopamine loop that drives return visits.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Creator badge in comments: Highlighting the original poster's reply with a yellow "Creator" pill instantly clarifies authorship in a flat comment list and rewards users whose comments get a creator reply, driving higher engagement rates.

  • Sticky Follow CTA in header: Placing the Follow button in the persistent top bar (not just on a profile page) captures conversion intent at the exact emotional peak (right after reading relatable content).

  • Per-comment like counters: Treating comments as first-class engageable content (not just text) deepens interaction depth and time-on-post.

  • Playful input placeholder with emoji shortcuts: Lowers the activation energy for commenting by suggesting a script ("Say Hi") and offering pre-loaded emoji reactions for zero-effort replies.

  • Unified bottom action bar: Consolidating save/like/comment/share counts into one bar at the thumb-reachable bottom zone optimizes for one-handed mobile use.

screens.name: Lemon8 - Commenting on a post - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern on any content/social screen where you want to maximize lightweight engagement without forcing users to leave the content context (social feeds, community forums, UGC platforms, and comment-heavy discussion apps). It's ideal when the goal is to lower the activation energy for first-time repliers via quick reactions, and when preserving visual context (dimmed background) helps users stay oriented to what they're responding to.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in enterprise, transactional, or data-dense applications where comments require more structured or formal input (e.g., code review tools, legal documents, B2B dashboards) - the playful emoji tray and casual copy would feel off-brand. It's also less suitable on small-screen devices where the combined overlay, emoji tray, and keyboard can consume excessive vertical space, obscuring too much original content and hurting usability for users needing to re-reference the post while typing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets Gen Z and young adult lifestyle users who are accustomed to fast, low-friction social interactions (akin to TikTok or Instagram commenting). The emoji quick-reply tray appeals to users who want to express approval or emotion without the cognitive effort of composing text, which is especially effective for casual browsers who may not otherwise engage.

The "make friends" framing specifically targets Lemon8's community-building growth loop, which relies on users feeling like the app is a space for genuine connection (e.g., niche hobbyist/wellness communities) rather than just passive content consumption. This nudges toward higher comment volume, which in turn boosts creator retention and feed algorithm signals.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Quick-reaction emoji strip: Placed directly above the keyboard for thumb-friendly, near-zero-effort engagement, lowering the barrier to replying.

  • Human, friendly placeholder copy: "Say 'Hi' to make friends" reframes commenting as a social/relationship action instead of a generic input task.

  • Persistent engagement metrics: The "5 comments" counter and visible existing comment thread leverage social proof to encourage further participation.

  • Clickable hashtag taxonomy: Converts free-text content into a structured discovery layer, reinforcing the algorithmic feed and niche community building.

screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when designing camera-capture flows embedded within a larger workflow (not a standalone camera app), especially when the captured artifact needs to be associated with an existing record (e.g., receipts, documents, ID verification). It's especially valuable when there's a possible mismatch between user intent and system state (proactively surfacing that mismatch before the user invests effort (e).g., taking a photo) saves frustration. The dual-path bottom CTA ("scan" vs. "manual entry/alternative") pattern is ideal whenever the primary capture method may not always be the right fit for every user's situation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid overlaying warning banners on a camera viewfinder when the warning is purely informational and not actionable (this adds visual clutter and can obscure the subject being photographed). If the warning condition is rare or edge-case only, consider handling it via a toast or pre-emptive screen before entering the camera, rather than cluttering the capture UI itself. Additionally, this pattern should not be used when receipt/document capture is the primary, context-free action of the app (e.g., a dedicated scanner app), since the "no expenses to attach" framing assumes a specific linked-record workflow that may not apply universally.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets business travelers, employees, and finance/ops teams who need to digitize paper receipts for expense reporting and reimbursement, likely within a corporate expense management or spend platform (e.g., similar to Ramp, Brex, or Expensify). The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion and effort-justification prevention: by warning the user before they waste time scanning a receipt that has nowhere to go, the app respects the user's time and avoids a frustrating "scan completed, but now what?" dead-end experience. The inline "Add to existing" and "create reimbursement" options also reduce decision paralysis by making the next best action obvious and low-friction, appealing to time-pressed professional users who value speed and certainty over exploration.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual Just-in-Time Guidance: Rather than letting the user scan a receipt into a dead end, the app proactively surfaces a system-state warning banner the moment it detects there's nothing to attach the receipt to, with an inline fix via "Add to existing."

Branching Escape Hatch: The "Or create reimbursement" button acknowledges that not all expense-logging starts with a physical receipt, offering a graceful fallback path without forcing the user to exit the flow and start over elsewhere.

High-Contrast Overlay Controls: White solid-fill circular buttons (close, retake) against the dark camera viewfinder ensure maximum legibility and touch-target confidence regardless of the background scene being photographed.

Minimal Chrome, Maximum Viewfinder: By stripping away navigation bars and status elements, the design maximizes the available frame for accurately capturing the receipt image, which directly impacts OCR/data-extraction accuracy downstream.
