• Continuous multi-month scroll instead of single-month pagination, reducing taps and allowing users to see date proximity across month boundaries at a glance.
  • Clear disabled-state styling (grayed-out past dates) communicates constraints instantly without extra copy or error messages.
  • High-contrast selected-date indicator (filled navy circle) makes the current selection unmistakable even in a dense grid of numbers.
  • Sticky primary CTA ("Select") pinned at the bottom ensures the action is always one tap away regardless of scroll depth.
  • Lightweight modal presentation with a drag handle and close icon, reinforcing it as a transient, dismissible overlay within a larger flow.

screens.name: Brex - Requesting new spend limit - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-screen scrolling calendar pattern when:

  • Users need to select a single future-dated deadline, expiration, or limit date (e.g., card expiry, budget caps, subscription renewals).
  • The valid date range spans multiple months and users benefit from seeing month transitions without pagination taps.
  • Precision and prevention of invalid selections (e.g., past dates) is business-critical, as in financial or compliance contexts.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Users need to select a date range (start + end) simultaneously (a dual-handle range picker would be more efficient).
  • The relevant date window is very large (e.g., selecting a birthdate decades in the past), where a scrolling month grid becomes tedious versus a dropdown/wheel-based year-month selector.
  • Screen real estate is limited and an inline, compact date field with native OS picker would suffice without needing a dedicated full-screen modal.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets finance admins and founders configuring corporate card spend limits within Brex, a task that requires precision and trust. Because financial controls carry real monetary consequences, the design leans heavily on clarity and error prevention (disabling invalid past dates) rather than delight or gamification. The straightforward, utilitarian tone builds trust with finance-savvy users who value speed and accuracy over flourish, and the large touch targets accommodate quick configuration during busy admin workflows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Continuous multi-month scroll instead of forcing users to paginate month-by-month, reducing friction for near-term date selection.
  • Disabled/greyed past dates proactively prevent invalid input, embodying an error-prevention-first design philosophy.
  • High-contrast selection indicator (solid navy circle) gives immediate, unambiguous visual confirmation of state.
  • Sticky bottom CTA keeps the primary action always accessible, ideal for one-handed thumb reach on long scrollable content.
  • Dual dismissal affordances (drag handle + X icon) respect differing user mental models for closing modals.

screens.name: Brex - Requesting new spend limit - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any multi-step financial or administrative request form where a single numeric input is central (budget, discount, limit, quota) but requires secondary configuration (duration, visibility, recurrence). It's ideal for:

  • Expense/budget approval request flows
  • Permission or role-elevation requests in B2B SaaS tools
  • Time-boxed resource allocation (e.g., temporary access, trial extensions)
  • Any form where defaults can meaningfully speed up completion for the majority of users
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this layout when the form involves many interdependent fields that don't logically fit a single linear step, as burying complex conditional logic in one screen can overwhelm users despite the clean visual design. It's also not ideal for low-stakes, one-off inputs (e.g., a simple preference toggle) where a full multi-step wizard with a progress bar would feel like overkill and add unnecessary friction. Additionally, if the target users are less finance-literate (e.g., casual consumer apps), the terse administrative tone and toggle-heavy structure may require more onboarding or inline education to avoid confusion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets finance team members, managers, and employees requesting incremental or temporary budget authority within Brex (for example, a department head requesting a one-time travel budget or an employee asking for a higher spend ceiling for a project). The psychological trigger at play is control and trust-building: because the request involves real company money, the interface reassures the requester with transparent defaults and explicit permission language, while reducing the admin's downstream review burden by collecting structured, well-formatted data (amount, dates, recurrence) upfront. The toggle for hiding the limit from members also speaks to the principal-agent dynamic in corporate finance (managers often want discretion over how much subordinates know about overall budgets, and Brex proactively surfaces that control point).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progress indicator: A segmented bar at the top gives immediate visual feedback on flow length and current position, reducing perceived effort.
  • Smart date defaults: Start and end dates are pre-populated with a sensible near-term range, letting power users tap "Next" immediately without manual input.
  • Inline permission explainer: The "Hide limit from members" toggle includes an immediate, specific consequence statement, preventing accidental misconfiguration of sensitive financial visibility settings.
  • Persistent clear-input affordance: The 'x' clear icon inside the amount field allows instant correction without multiple backspaces.
  • Single, unmissable CTA: One full-width orange gradient "Next" button eliminates decision paralysis and matches brand color for recognizability.

screens.name: Brex - Requesting new spend limit - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any multi-role setup flow (permissions configuration, team/project creation, budget allocation, or shared resource management) where a small number of distinct roles (e.g., owner, editor, viewer, member) need to be assigned to people. It's especially effective when:

  • The roles carry different levels of authority or risk, and users benefit from plain-language explanations.
  • The task is part of a short, linear wizard where progress visibility reduces abandonment.
  • A shortcut toggle can eliminate redundant data entry for a common use case (e.g., owner = member).
  • Form validity should be gated before allowing submission to protect downstream data quality.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • There are more than 2-3 roles to assign, as stacking multiple dropdowns with captions could overwhelm the single screen (a table or multi-select matrix would scale better).
  • The role distinctions are already well understood by the user base (e.g., power users configuring the 10th limit), where repeated caption text becomes noise and should be collapsed into a tooltip instead.
  • Speed is critical and the task is high-frequency (the verbose explanatory captions add friction for expert users doing this repeatedly).
  • Mobile real estate is extremely limited and the vertical whitespace here would be better used for inline validation or search-as-you-type picker previews instead of empty space.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for business admins, founders, and finance team members who are setting up budget governance for their company (a task that is infrequent but high-stakes, since it determines who can spend and who can oversee spending). These users are often not deeply technical and may be unfamiliar with formal "RBAC" (role-based access control) concepts, which is why the UI proactively defines "owner" vs "member" inline rather than assuming prior knowledge.

Psychologically, the progress bar and reduced-field layout combat the natural friction and tedium associated with administrative configuration tasks. Because setting spend limits is tied to real financial accountability, the disabled-until-valid submit button also reassures users that the system will catch missing information before an incomplete or erroneous request is routed to a reviewer, reducing the anxiety of "doing it wrong."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline role clarification: Helper text directly below each dropdown eliminates ambiguity between "owner" and "member" roles without needing a modal or tooltip.
  • Efficiency toggle: "Include limit owners as members" removes redundant manual entry for the common case where the approver is also a spender.
  • Segmented progress indicator: Clearly communicates this is the last of three steps, reducing perceived effort and drop-off risk.
  • Disabled CTA gating: Prevents premature or incomplete submission, reinforcing data integrity for downstream approval workflows.
  • Dual exit affordances: Back arrow for step navigation and X for flow termination accommodate different user intents simultaneously.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 33
screens.whereToUse: Use this large-question, single-column-choice pattern when configuring a single, isolated preference within a multi-step onboarding or setup wizard (especially for recurring/scheduled actions like subscriptions, reminders, or automated transfers). It's ideal when you want to maximize completion rate and minimize hesitation on a binary or ternary choice.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when more than 4-5 options are needed, as the large pill format would force excessive scrolling. It's also unsuitable for decisions requiring comparative context (e.g., pricing tiers) where users need supporting details, tooltips, or visual comparisons before choosing (the deliberate lack of information here would leave users under-informed for higher-stakes decisions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users setting up recurring/automated savings behavior (likely within Cash App's "Round Ups," direct deposit, or automatic investing features). The target user is someone who is comfortable with simple, guided decisions but may be intimidated by dense financial configuration screens found in traditional banking apps.

Psychologically, this leverages the Paradox of Choice mitigation: by capping options at three clear cadences, the user isn't overwhelmed and can quickly self-select a rhythm matching their pay cycle or spending habit, increasing completion rates for the automation setup.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-Question Focus: Isolating one decision per screen eliminates choice paralysis and keeps the multi-step flow feeling fast and effortless.

  • Massive Negative Space: Deliberate whitespace elevates the importance of the question and gives it an almost editorial, confident presentation uncommon in fintech forms.

  • Thumb-Zone Optimization: Placing all interactive options at the bottom of the screen accounts for natural one-handed phone usage and modern large-screen ergonomics.

  • Minimal Chrome: Only an exit 'X' and a subtle progress indicator frame the content, keeping the visual noise near zero.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 34
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when asking a user for a specific numeric or discrete value (like a day of the month, a quantity, or a specific size) within a checkout or setup flow. It works best for a single input requirement where visual/tactile scrolling is faster than typing. Ideal for mobile-first "sheet" based questions that block the main app flow until a required input is provided.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this modal-question pattern if the user needs to input multiple related pieces of data at once (e.g., date AND amount AND frequency), as it would require excessive modal stacking. Additionally, avoid the "picker" carousel style if the list of options is very long (e.g., selecting from 1-31 with only 3 visible at a time) without very obvious scroll affordances, as this hides information and might require excessive scrolling to find an out-of-view date.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users of fintech or neobanking apps (e.g., automated savings apps like Chime, Qapital, or Robinhood) who are setting up a recurring transfer or auto-invest feature. The primary psychological trigger here is the reduction of "friction" associated with financial planning. By framing the interaction as a simple question with a physical dial to spin, the app lowers the perceived effort of committing to a recurring financial habit, encouraging users to set up automated wealth-building behaviors (like Direct Deposit or Round-ups) without feeling overwhelmed by banking terminology.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-Task Focus: By using a modal overlay instead of a full page navigation, the app signals that this is a quick, temporary sub-task within a larger flow (likely setting up an automated savings/investing plan).

  • Generous Whitespace: The stark contrast between the minimal text/UI and the vast empty space simplifies the decision-making process, preventing decision paralysis.

  • Physical Carousel Metaphor: Using a horizontal scroller for dates mimics a physical dial, making the selection feel tactile and intuitive compared to a standard dropdown list.

  • Drag Handle Affordance: The handle at the bottom of the screen reinforces the "sheet" mental model, hinting to the user that they can swipe down to dismiss if needed, even though a specific 'X' is also provided.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 35
screens.whereToUse:
• Configuring recurring or scheduled financial transactions (auto-deposits, subscriptions, bill pay) where a single date parameter needs isolated focus.

  • Any setup wizard step where you want to minimize distraction and force a deliberate, single-variable decision.

  • Mobile contexts where large touch targets and swipe gestures outperform dense grid-based date pickers.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• When users need to select a date far in the future or navigate across multiple months (this horizontal-only, day-of-month carousel doesn't scale well beyond a small range (like day 1) 31 for recurring billing).

  • Contexts requiring multi-parameter input (e.g., date + time + recurrence rule) where separating everything into full-screen single-question modals would create excessive step fatigue.

  • Desktop or data-dense enterprise tools where compact calendar widgets are more efficient and expected.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumer fintech users (e.g., Cash App, Venmo-style audiences) setting up automatic/recurring savings or cash deposits. The design assumes a mobile-first, often younger or less financially sophisticated audience that benefits from simplified, guided decision points rather than dense settings forms.

Psychologically, the screen leverages choice reduction and progressive disclosure: by only asking one question at a time in a modal, it prevents the user from feeling overwhelmed by a full recurring-transfer settings page (frequency, amount, account, date all together). The direct-manipulation carousel with immediate visual feedback (green highlight, scaled tile) taps into satisfaction from tactile, physical-feeling interactions, increasing engagement and confidence when configuring an automated money movement (a high-stakes, trust-sensitive action).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-question full-screen focus: Removes all UI chrome so the user's cognitive load is spent entirely on one decision.

  • Oversized carousel date tiles: Replaces a cramped calendar grid or wheel picker with large, glanceable, thumb-friendly cards, improving tap accuracy and readability.

  • Green "torn calendar page" motif: Instantly communicates "date" semantics using a familiar physical metaphor without any text label.

  • Dynamic CTA label ("Set 16th"): Closes the feedback loop, confirming exactly what action will be taken before the user commits.

  • Peeking neighbor cards: Non-verbal affordance signaling horizontal scrollability, reducing reliance on written instructions.

screens.name: Cash App Setting Up 36
screens.whereToUse: Use this full-screen numeric keypad pattern whenever the core task of a screen is entering a single monetary or numeric value (such as deposit amounts, savings goals, bill splitting, tipping, or recurring transfers). It's ideal when you want zero distraction and maximum focus on correctness of a single critical input, especially for financial or high-stakes numeric entries.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when multiple related fields need to be filled simultaneously (e.g., amount + date + recipient), as forcing users through a hyper-focused single-value screen for each field creates excessive multi-step friction. Also avoid it for non-numeric or complex data entry, and be cautious using a custom keypad instead of the native OS keyboard if accessibility (VoiceOver/TalkBack) support hasn't been rigorously tested, since custom controls can break screen-reader expectations.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers setting up automated savings, investment contributions, or bill payments (likely within a neobank, savings app, or investing platform (e).g., Acorns, Chime, Copilot Money style flows). The audience values simplicity and reassurance when dealing with recurring money movement, since automating finances can trigger loss-of-control anxiety.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Commitment Consistency principle by starting the default amount low ($1), making the action feel low-risk and encouraging users to proceed rather than abandon the flow due to perceived high stakes. The live-updating CTA also exploits the Zeigarnik effect and reduces friction-induced drop-off by keeping the user's attention locked to a single, evolving number.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dynamic CTA Binding: The primary button text updates live with the numeric input ("Schedule $1"), giving the user constant confirmation of the value before submission.

  • Oversized Amount Display: The giant green currency figure acts as the emotional and visual anchor of the screen, making the number impossible to misread (critical for financial trust).

  • Distraction-Free Modal: Removing tab bars and secondary navigation via a full-screen modal with a simple 'X' dismiss keeps cognitive load low and task completion rates high.

  • Native-feeling Custom Keypad: A large-target, evenly spaced numeric pad optimized for one-handed thumb reach on mobile devices.

results.query: Switch toggle control for biometric Face ID authentication enablement

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 13
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when implementing app-level PIN/passcode security in fintech, healthcare, crypto, or any app handling sensitive personal data. It's ideal for:

  • Onboarding flows that require setting up a local security PIN.

  • Re-authentication or step-up security features.

  • Any two-step "create then confirm" credential flow where typos would lock the user out.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The app already relies on biometric authentication as the primary and sufficient security layer (adding a redundant PIN step increases friction unnecessarily).

  • The passcode length is variable or alphanumeric (the fixed 6-dot UI implies a strict numeric length, which won't scale to flexible password formats).

  • Users are in a highly casual, low-security context (e.g., a note-taking app) where this level of formality feels excessive and may increase drop-off during onboarding.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets any user setting up local app security (common in fintech, banking, crypto wallets, healthcare, or password manager apps where an additional PIN layer protects sensitive data beyond the OS-level lock screen). The psychological trigger here is trust through familiarity: by replicating the native OS passcode experience, the app signals that it takes security as seriously as the operating system itself, increasing user confidence in handling their sensitive data. The double-entry confirmation step also taps into error-prevention psychology, reassuring anxious users that they won't accidentally lock themselves out due to a typo.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Native pattern reuse: Mimicking the iOS system passcode entry UI reduces the learning curve to zero (users intuitively know how to proceed).

  • Dot-based progress indicator: Communicates input progress and passcode length without ever displaying the actual digits, balancing usability with security/privacy.

  • Auto-advance interaction model: No explicit "submit" button is needed; the keypad auto-validates once all 6 digits are entered, reducing steps and taps.

  • High-contrast, distraction-free visual hierarchy: The gradient-to-black background focuses cognitive attention entirely on the security task at hand.

  • Escape hatch via back arrow: Allows correction of a mistyped original passcode without forcing the user through a full restart or error dialog.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse:
• Immediately after signup/login in apps handling sensitive data (banking, health, crypto, password managers).

  • Any time you want to increase adoption of an optional-but-beneficial security or convenience feature.

  • When you want to reduce future login friction and increase daily active session speed.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid using this pattern too early, before the user has built any trust with the app (e.g., on the very first screen before signup) - it should follow a completed action.

  • Don't use it if the app has no real security differentiation to justify biometric login, as it may feel like unnecessary friction.

  • Not appropriate for apps where users frequently switch devices or share accounts, since Face ID binds the login to a single physical device/user.

  • Avoid stacking multiple permission primers back-to-back (e.g., notifications + Face ID + location) as it causes primer fatigue and increases decline rates.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new or returning users immediately post-authentication, most commonly in fintech, banking, crypto, or productivity apps where repeated password entry is a friction point. It's designed for mainstream mobile users who value speed and are already comfortable with biometric unlock at the OS level (Face ID/Touch ID), so the ask feels low-risk.

Psychologically, it leverages the consistency principle (once a user says "yes" to convenience, they're more likely to continue engaging) and authority/trust transfer from Apple's own Face ID iconography, borrowing the platform's credibility to reduce hesitation about a third-party app accessing biometric-gated login.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-permission priming: Asking in-app before the native OS Face ID dialog appears increases the odds of system-level acceptance, since the user is already primed with context and benefit.

  • Asymmetric button styling: High-contrast white primary CTA vs. muted grey secondary CTA visually nudges toward the desired action without removing user agency.

  • Benefit-first copy: Leads with an emotional/aspirational headline ("Log in with a look") before the rational justification, matching how users actually make quick trust decisions.

  • Non-blocking dismissal: "Not now" avoids guilt-tripping or dead-ending the user, preserving goodwill and trust in the brand.

  • Atmospheric gradient background: Deep blue-to-black gradient with a glowing icon creates a premium, secure, almost futuristic feel appropriate for an identity/security moment.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern during identity verification, account setup, or compliance flows where the user must choose between a small, well-defined set of document types or credential options before proceeding to capture/upload steps. It's ideal when:

  • The choice set is small (2-4 options) and mutually exclusive.

  • A sensible default can be inferred from context (geolocation, prior input) to speed up the majority path.

  • You need to set expectations/rules before the next step (e.g., "no scans or copies") to reduce failed submissions.

  • The flow benefits from a calm, low-distraction UI due to its sensitive or compliance-driven nature.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this exact heavy, full-bleed gradient treatment for casual or high-frequency screens where users need speed and lightness over gravitas (it may feel overly dramatic for trivial settings choices). Also avoid pre-selecting a default when there is no reliable signal for which option is most likely correct, as an incorrect default may cause user confusion or accidental submission of the wrong document type. If more than 3-4 document options exist, a radio list may become unwieldy and should be replaced with a searchable list or dropdown instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users undergoing mandatory identity verification (KYC/AML compliance) for regulated services such as digital banks, crypto exchanges, or fintech apps operating in Singapore. The demographic spans from young digital-first consumers to non-native residents needing passport-based verification.

Psychologically, the design leverages reduction of choice overload (only two options), default bias (pre-selecting the most common document type), and anxiety reduction (clear instructions and progress indication) to keep users moving through what is typically perceived as a tedious, high-friction compliance step. The premium visual styling also triggers a sense of institutional trust, which is essential when asking users to submit sensitive personal documents.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Default Pre-Selection: "National ID" is pre-checked based on the detected country (Singapore flag), removing an unnecessary tap for the majority path.

  • Pre-emptive Error Prevention Copy: Explicitly stating "We don't accept scans or copies" upfront prevents wasted user effort and downstream verification failures.

  • Visual Hierarchy & Focus: Only one primary action (Continue) is emphasized with a high-contrast white pill button against the dark background; the secondary "Change citizenship" link is intentionally subdued to avoid distracting from the main path.

  • Trust-Building Atmosphere: The deep blue-to-black gradient and clean iconography evoke security and seriousness appropriate for identity verification.

  • Progress Transparency: The bottom page-control indicator reassures users of their place in a finite multi-step journey.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Any document/photo capture flow (ID verification, check deposit scanning, passport/visa scanning) where image quality is critical to downstream processing.

  • Compliance-heavy onboarding flows (banking, crypto, healthcare, age-gated services) where retries must be fast and low-friction to prevent funnel drop-off.

  • Any camera-based scanning UI (barcode, receipt, business card scanners) that requires specific framing and lighting conditions.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for catastrophic or unrecoverable errors (e.g., account suspended, document rejected for fraud) - those require a full-screen blocking state with distinct next steps, not an inline retry banner.

  • Not suitable for flows where multiple simultaneous errors could occur, stacking multiple inline banners would clutter the viewfinder and overwhelm the user.

  • Avoid if the camera hardware/permissions themselves are the issue (e.g., camera access denied); that requires a distinct permission-request state rather than an image-quality error banner.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users undergoing mandatory identity verification, common in fintech, banking, crypto exchanges, and gig-economy onboarding flows (e.g., account opening, age verification, KYC/AML compliance). This demographic is often anxious about handing over sensitive personal documents and may be verifying identity on a mobile device for the first time in a low-light or improvised environment.

The psychological trigger at play is friction reduction under stress: identity verification is a non-negotiable gate the user must pass to access a service (e.g., open a bank account, receive a paycheck, access a crypto wallet), so any perceived failure elevates anxiety. The immediate, actionable feedback loop (error → guidance → retry) reduces abandonment risk at a critical conversion funnel step. The persistent camera view also leverages the sunk-cost/momentum principle, keeping the user "in the moment" rather than forcing a restart.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking error banner: Uses an inline banner instead of a disruptive modal, allowing users to immediately retry the action without an extra dismiss step.

  • High-contrast iconography: The red circular alert icon against a black banner immediately draws the eye and signals severity using color psychology, even before reading the text.

  • Live camera persistence: Keeping the camera feed active during the error state (rather than showing a static failed image) reduces the number of steps needed to retry, respecting the user's time.

  • Clear visual guide-frame: The rounded rectangle overlay with corner accents removes guesswork about framing, directly addressing the root cause of the blur/positioning error.

  • Trust branding: The "Onfido | Real Identity" watermark reassures users that a reputable, specialized third-party service (rather than the host app itself) is handling sensitive biometric/document data.

screens.name: Oportun Pre-Onboarding 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any high-security action requiring identity verification, such as login, password reset, high-value transactions, or account setting changes (e.g., adding a new payee). It is ideal when SMS/Phone verification is the standard security layer for the target demographic.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy OTP friction for low-stakes actions where security requirements are minimal, as it introduces unnecessary abandonment risk. Additionally, avoid relying solely on SMS if the target user base is international or highly mobile, as carrier delays can cause frustration; ensure "voice call" or "authenticator app" fallbacks are always visible, as demonstrated here.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets general users undergoing account login or sensitive transaction verification (likely financial services based on the green accent color and stark typography). The primary psychological trigger is security assurance: users expect friction during login for a banking app, and the presence of 2FA actually builds trust that their money/data is protected.

The secondary trigger is loss aversion, driven by the "avoid being logged out" copy, which motivates the user to complete the action swiftly rather than abandoning the flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented Digit Boxes: Breaking the numeric code into six distinct, high-contrast boxes rather than a single input field significantly improves scannability and reduces cognitive load during data entry.

  • Time-Bound Urgency Messaging: Explicitly stating the 5-minute expiration window sets clear expectations and prompts immediate action, reducing drop-off due to delayed code entry.

  • Multiple Recovery Paths: Offering both "Resend" (SMS) and "Request a voice call" ensures accessibility and resilience against carrier delivery issues, catering to users in poor signal areas or those who prefer audio.

  • Loading State on Auto-Submit: The button entering a loading state immediately upon code completion removes an unnecessary tap, streamlining the "time-to-value" of the verification process.

screens.name: Oportun Pre-Onboarding 12
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any native OS permission dialog (Face ID, push notifications, location, camera, contacts) where denial has UX consequences later. It's especially valuable for:

  • Post-signup or post-login flows introducing biometric shortcuts.

  • Any permission with a reversible "skip" path that shouldn't feel forced.

  • Apps where trust and security messaging matter (fintech, health, password managers).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The permission is mandatory for core app function, priming with an easy "Not now" escape hatch will just create a confusing dead-end later.

  • You're already deep into a task-oriented flow; injecting a full-screen interstitial here interrupts momentum. A contextual tooltip or inline prompt may be less disruptive.

  • The user has already denied the OS-level permission previously (re-priming without deep-linking to Settings will lead to a frustrating loop since the priming screen can't force the system dialog to reappear).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets all users during onboarding or post-login setup, particularly those who are security-conscious but also convenience-driven (the majority of modern mobile users). It leverages the psychological principle of reciprocity and framing: by presenting the ask as a gift ("easier login") rather than a demand ("we need access to your face"), users are primed to say yes.

It also reduces permission fatigue and distrust: a known driver of iOS/Android permission denial (by giving users agency and context before the irreversible system-level prompt appears (which, if denied, requires a trip to Settings to reverse)).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Priming before the OS prompt: Explains value before the native, context-less system dialog appears, significantly increasing opt-in acceptance rates.

  • Benefit-led copy: Leads with "won't need to enter your password" instead of technical/permission framing, lowering perceived risk.

  • Non-blocking dual CTA: "Not now" and "Enable" are both easily tappable and visually balanced (outline vs. solid), signaling that declining is a safe, judgment-free choice and preventing forced-action frustration.

  • Friendly iconography: A soft, pastel-toned Face ID glyph replaces cold system iconography, making biometric setup feel approachable.

screens.name: Oportun Pre-Onboarding 13
screens.whereToUse:
• Before any native OS permission prompt (notifications, location, camera, contacts) where a one-shot system dialog risk of denial is high.

  • In consumer apps where ongoing engagement (reminders, progress updates, streaks) is core to retention and habit formation.

  • Financial, health, or goal-tracking apps where milestone-based notifications provide clear emotional and practical value.

  • Onboarding flows, positioned after the user has seen enough core value to understand why notifications would help them.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid using this pattern too early in onboarding, before the user understands the app's core value proposition, priming without context can feel premature and increase decline rates.

  • Don't use for permissions that carry privacy sensitivity (e.g., location, contacts) with overly cheerful mock content, as it can appear manipulative if the actual data usage is more invasive.

  • Avoid repeating this soft-ask on every session if declined once, as it can become an annoying, nagging pattern (should be one-time or spaced very conservatively).

  • Not appropriate if the app's actual notification content doesn't match the emotional promise shown here (mismatched expectations damage trust after opt-in).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users of Oportun, a personal finance / lending and savings app aimed at underbanked and budget-conscious consumers. This demographic is highly motivated by tangible savings milestones and financial progress, making a "goal achieved" notification example especially resonant and relatable.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the peak-end rule and anticipated reward: showing users a preview of a positive emotional peak (celebrating a savings win) primes them to associate the app's notifications with good feelings, increasing the likelihood of granting permission. It also uses the principle of reciprocity/context: by first explaining "why" before asking "may I," the app frames the permission request as a mutual benefit rather than a system interruption, which meaningfully raises opt-in conversion versus a cold OS prompt.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Priming before the system prompt: Explains value first so the subsequent native OS permission dialog is met with an already-warmed, informed user, significantly boosting opt-in rates.

  • Simulated notification preview: Using a realistic device/lock-screen mockup with actual sample content lets users "pre-experience" the benefit instead of imagining it abstractly.

  • Positive, milestone-based sample copy: Choosing a goal-achievement notification (rather than a warning or reminder) frames notifications as good news, associating the feature with dopamine rather than anxiety.

  • Non-blocking dual CTA: Offers a graceful decline path ("Not now") alongside the primary action, preserving user agency and trust while still visually emphasizing the recommended choice.

  • Cadence preview mentioned upfront: Telling users they can pick Daily/Weekly frequency in advance reduces the fear of over-notification, a top reason users deny permissions.

screens.name: Oportun Pre-Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for subscription-based utility or fintech apps where the core value proposition requires slight technical explanation (e.g., how an algorithm works) before asking for payment. It is highly effective for:

  • Introducing complex automated features (round-ups, automatic transfers) in simple, benefit-driven language.

  • Softening the transition into a paywall by educating the user on value first.

  • Apps requiring bank linking, where trust and transparency (regarding fees) must be established immediately to reduce drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this lengthy, text-heavy explainer format for:

  • High-frequency, low-complexity apps (e.g., simple to-do lists) where the user already understands the value prop and this screen would just be an unnecessary barrier to entry.

  • Users who are already power-users: if this triggers for someone re-engaging with the app rather than a first-time user, the "start here" tone will feel condescending or repetitive.

  • Scenarios where regulatory copy is required to be more prominent than default styling allows (financial disclosures often need bolder, more legally structured presentation than this soft narrative approach).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets casual savers and financially anxious consumers (likely Gen Z/Millennials) who struggle with the discipline of manual saving. The psychological trigger here is "Set and Forget" relief (by automating the financial decision, the app removes the friction and guilt associated with spending decisions).

The "Try free for 30 days" trigger utilizes the standard freemium trial hook, but the immediate juxtaposition with hard pricing numbers suggests a "high-intent" user base that responds better to transparency than to surprise billing, likely reducing refund requests and App Store complaints regarding hidden costs.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transparent Pricing Disclosure: Unlike many apps that hide pricing until the final "wall," this screen states the exact monthly/annual cost and the cancellation policy upfront, building trust before the ask.

  • Benefit-Sequencing: The three icons follow a logical narrative arc: Capability (What it does) → Time-to-Value (How fast) → Cost (What it costs), mirroring a natural sales conversation.

  • Custom Iconography: The use of a bespoke "money plant" illustration alongside soft, rounded icon backgrounds (mint/sage tones) creates a calming, organic brand identity that contrasts with typical aggressive fintech "growth chart" imagery.

  • Persistent Escape Hatch: The top-left "X" ensures the user never feels trapped, which paradoxically increases conversion rates by lowering the perceived risk of engaging with the flow.

screens.name: Oportun Login 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for the core login/authentication screen of any app that has already funneled the user past onboarding/marketing screens and just needs a fast, no-nonsense credential entry point. Ideal for apps with a large returning-user base (banking, delivery, e-commerce, social) where speed and trust outweigh the need for visual flourish. The disabled-CTA + optional biometric toggle combo works well whenever security/convenience tradeoffs need explicit user consent.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stripped-down approach for first-time user acquisition flows where trust-building, branding, and value communication are still needed (a bare login form with no logo or context can feel cold or untrustworthy to a brand-new visitor). Also avoid disabling the CTA entirely if you want to allow users to tap-and-see-inline-errors as a validation strategy; for some audiences, an always-enabled button with post-tap validation feedback tests better. Finally, don't bury biometric setup here if the platform requires a dedicated permission-priming screen for Face ID/Touch ID for OS-level compliance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets returning, already-registered users who need frictionless re-entry rather than new users needing persuasion. The psychological drivers at play are:

  • Reduction of cognitive load via a stripped-back, single-task layout.

  • Autonomy/control bias: the Face ID switch is off by default, letting the user opt in rather than feeling forced into biometric data usage.

  • Error prevention over error correction: the disabled button state pre-empts failed submissions, reducing frustration and support/recovery flows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled-state CTA: The greyed-out "Log in" button provides a passive validation cue, visually communicating that required fields are incomplete without needing an error message.

  • Combined identifier field: Merging "Email or phone" into one field reduces perceived form length and supports multiple account recovery/login vectors.

  • Face ID opt-in toggle: Placing biometric login as an explicit, user-controlled switch (rather than auto-enabling it) builds trust and gives the user a sense of control over security tradeoffs.

  • Sticky bottom CTA: Anchoring "Log in" to the bottom edge follows thumb-reachability best practices for one-handed mobile use.

  • Minimal chrome: The lack of a logo or extraneous branding keeps focus entirely on completing the credential entry task.

screens.name: Oportun Login 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for returning-user authentication screens in any mobile app, especially those where speed and low cognitive load are priorities (fintech, e-commerce, utility apps). It's ideal when:

  • The app already has a separate onboarding/sign-up flow, so this screen can stay lean.

  • Biometric authentication (Face ID/Touch ID) is supported by the underlying OS/device.

  • You want to minimize drop-off by removing all non-essential content from the critical conversion path.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this ultra-minimal approach when:

  • The product needs to reinforce brand identity or trust signals at every touchpoint (e.g., a brand-new fintech app might want a logo or security badge visible for reassurance).

  • Users are likely to need more guidance (e.g., first-time users, less tech-savvy audiences) - in these cases, visible field labels and inline validation messaging are preferable to placeholder-only labels.

  • The disabled button pattern isn't paired with any inline hint about why it's disabled, which can confuse users if the empty-state reasoning isn't obvious.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for existing, returning users who already have an account and simply need to re-authenticate (likely arrived via a "Log in" CTA from a preceding welcome/splash screen). The inclusion of a Face ID toggle targets users on biometric-capable devices who value speed and low friction on subsequent logins, appealing to the psychological principle of reducing perceived effort for habitual actions.

The disabled-until-valid button leverages a subtle error-prevention psychology: rather than letting users fail and see an error, the interface withholds affordance until the input is plausible, reducing frustration and reinforcing a sense of guided competence.

The stark, no-frills visual design also builds trust for a security-sensitive task (over-designed login screens can feel less "serious," whereas this austere approach mirrors patterns seen in banking and fintech apps where credibility and focus are paramount).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Face ID toggle inline on the login form: rather than only offering biometrics after a first successful manual login, the toggle is exposed immediately, letting returning users opt in proactively.

  • Bottom-pinned CTA keeps the primary action within thumb reach and clear of the software keyboard, a strong mobile ergonomics decision.

  • Disabled button state as implicit validation feedback, avoiding intrusive error messaging while still guiding the user.

  • Radical minimalism: only the essential fields and actions are shown, reducing cognitive load and time-to-login.

  • Consistent back navigation affordance in the top-left corner for easy flow exit/reversal.

screens.name: Oportun Login 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any two-factor or one-time-password verification flow (login re-authentication, password reset, high-value transaction confirmation, or new device verification). It's ideal whenever you need a fast, low-error way for users to input a short numeric code delivered externally (SMS, voice, email).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for longer alphanumeric codes or passwords, where segmented boxes become cumbersome; a standard masked text field is better there. Also avoid strict time-bound messaging if your backend doesn't actually enforce a session timeout (false urgency erodes trust). For low-security use cases, a full OTP step may add unnecessary friction versus a magic link.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets any user attempting to log in or authenticate on a security-conscious platform (likely fintech, banking, or an app handling sensitive personal/financial data given the clean, trustworthy green-and-white design language). The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Progress visibility: The six-box layout leverages the human preference for visualizing task completion, similar to a progress bar.

  • Trust signaling: Masking the phone number while still showing partial digits builds confidence that the right channel was used without oversharing PII, which increases perceived security.

• Segmented OTP boxes: Six distinct input cells instead of one field, giving instant visual feedback on progress and expected length.

  • Auto-focused first cell: Reduces friction by eliminating an extra tap to start typing.

  • Time-bound urgency messaging: Sets clear expectations (5-minute window) to prevent user confusion if the session expires mid-task.

  • Fallback delivery options: "Resend" and "Request a voice call" provide accessible recovery paths for users who didn't receive the SMS, crucial for accessibility and delivery reliability across carriers.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any short, non-cancelable background process critical to security or account setup (wallet/key generation, encryption setup, biometric enrollment, account provisioning, or backend account creation during sign-up). It's ideal whenever the operation takes a few seconds and cannot be meaningfully progressed by a progress bar (i.e., duration is unpredictable).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this indeterminate, full-screen blocking pattern for longer processes (over ~10-15 seconds) where users need a sense of progress (use a determinate progress bar with a percentage or step count instead). Also avoid it for interruptible or resumable tasks, where a cancel option should be provided to respect user control. Overusing full-screen blocking loaders across an app can also feel heavy-handed for trivial operations that could instead use inline skeleton loaders.

This screen is engineered to hold their attention for the few seconds required to securely generate a wallet without triggering doubt ("Did it freeze?") or drop-off. The dark, secure-vault aesthetic also plays to the psychological need for trust and safety when a user is about to be handed sole custody of their financial assets (a moment where perceived reliability of the underlying technology is critical to conversion).
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Single-point focus: Pairing an indeterminate spinner with one short status line concentrates attention and reduces the perceived complexity of an inherently technical cryptographic task.

  • Reassurance through plain language: Translating a complex security operation into a simple, human sentence builds trust and reduces onboarding drop-off anxiety.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use native system permission dialogs with a custom rationale string whenever requesting sensitive OS-level permissions (biometrics, camera, location, notifications) in finance, health, or identity apps. Always trigger the prompt contextually (right after the user reaches a step where the permission's value is obvious) rather than immediately on app launch. Pair with a pre-permission "priming" screen beforehand when the ask is non-obvious, to increase acceptance rates since the system dialog itself cannot be visually persuaded.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid firing this system dialog blindly at first launch before the user understands why biometric access matters (this depresses opt-in rates and can trigger app-store-review-style rejection reflexes). Do not attempt to visually bias the "Allow" button (not possible on iOS, but relevant on Android custom equivalents) as it violates platform guidelines and erodes user trust. Also avoid re-prompting repeatedly after a "Don't Allow" response, since iOS suppresses re-prompting and repeated soft-asks feel naggy.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Targets "Busy Urbans" who need fast, frictionless access to their funds throughout the day (tapping to pay, checking balances on the go) without repeatedly entering PINs or passwords. Face ID satisfies both their need for speed (one-glance unlock) and their heightened need for security assurance, since this audience is managing real monetary value in a self-custody product with no bank-style fraud reversal safety net.

Psychologically, this leans on loss aversion (protecting money/data) and trust transfer from Apple's native biometric system, which users already trust for banking and payment apps, making them more willing to extend that trust to Coinbase Wallet.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom rationale string: Coinbase overrides the default system copy with a benefit-driven, security-framed sentence tailored to a financial wallet context.

  • Contextual timing: Presumably triggered after a relevant in-app moment (e.g., end of wallet setup) rather than an abrupt cold-start request, increasing acceptance likelihood.

  • Low-friction security upgrade: A single tap enables biometric lock, reducing future password/PIN entry friction while reinforcing the sense of a secure, self-custody product.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any dashboard, wallet, or account-balance screen that can legitimately be at zero (new accounts, financial apps, portfolio trackers). Ideal when there is one clear, dominant recovery action (e.g., "Add funds," "Connect account," "Import data") and you want to avoid a jarring blank screen. Especially effective when the product has an adjacent, trusted parent brand/account that can be leveraged as an easy funding source.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy illustration-driven empty state for screens where zero-state is rare or unexpected (e.g., a returning user who should have data (here an error state or reload prompt is more appropriate)). Also avoid duplicating the CTA at both top and bottom on very short-viewport screens, as it can feel repetitive or noisy if the whole screen already fits without scrolling. Not suitable when there are multiple equally important next steps, since the pattern is optimized for single-path conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Targets new or newly-onboarded crypto wallet users (including those migrating from a Coinbase exchange account) who have just created or imported a wallet and have zero on-chain assets. The design leverages the Zeigarnik effect and progress-oriented framing (presenting "$0.00" not as a dead end but as step one of an implied journey) plus reduction of decision paralysis by offering exactly one clear CTA. The Coinbase-brand link icon exploits trust transfer: users familiar with the centralized exchange are reassured that moving funds to the self-custody wallet is safe and easy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-illustration branding: The empty state graphic visually links the Coinbase (C) logo and Wallet logo via a chain icon, subtly reinforcing that funds can flow seamlessly from the Coinbase exchange account into the self-custody wallet (a key value proposition and cross-sell mechanic).

  • Persistent, redundant CTA: "Add crypto" appears both inline (attached to the empty state) and pinned near the tab bar, ensuring the primary action is always reachable regardless of scroll position.

  • Pre-populated navigation: Buy/Swap/Cash out and Crypto/NFTs/DeFi tabs remain visible and tappable even with $0 balance, letting curious users explore the app's structure before committing funds.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 4

The "Off" status labels leverage a mild loss-aversion/completeness nudge: seeing an unprotected state listed plainly (without shaming) encourages users to close the gap, similar to a profile-completion prompt. The separation of Taxes security also signals institutional credibility to more cautious or first-time tax filers who may be wary of digitizing sensitive tax documents.

  • Progressive security layering: Offering both a password AND an authenticator app for taxes demonstrates defense-in-depth without forcing both simultaneously (the authenticator is offered as an optional upgrade).

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 5

• Any app handling sensitive data (banking, healthcare, password managers) where authentication frequency needs to be user-configurable.

  • Settings screens where you want to build trust around biometric or sensitive data usage via inline, contextual privacy statements.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumer users of a peer-to-peer payment app (Cash App) who are security-conscious but not technically sophisticated. The psychological driver here is trust calibration: financial apps must balance perceived security (making users feel protected) with usability friction (not annoying users with constant Face ID prompts).

By exposing individual toggles rather than a single master switch, the design leverages the illusion of control heuristic: users feel more secure and in charge of their own data/money when they can fine-tune exactly when authentication is required, rather than accepting an opaque, one-size-fits-all policy set by the app.

The explicit privacy disclaimer addresses a well-documented psychological barrier to biometric adoption: fear of biometric data being stored/leaked.   • Visual grouping via whitespace: Separating the "trigger conditions" from the "authentication method" toggle with vertical spacing creates an implicit two-tier mental model without needing section headers or dividers.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app needs OS-level sensitive permissions (biometrics, camera, location, contacts) tied to security or core functionality. Best practices to replicate:

  • Delay the system permission dialog until the user opts into the specific feature that requires it.

  • Provide a plain-language explanation of data usage immediately before the system prompt appears.

  • Offer granular toggles for related-but-distinct actions (e.g., unlocking app vs. authorizing transactions) instead of one master switch.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the permission is required for the app's core function to work at all (e.g., a camera scanning app) - in that case, blocking flows with clear value-prop framing before the first use is more appropriate. Also avoid stacking multiple permission primers in a single settings screen, as decision fatigue can cause users to decline reflexively. Do not use vague copy like "We use your data" without specifics, as this erodes trust rather than building it, especially in regulated fintech contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of a peer-to-peer payments app (Cash App) who are security-conscious but also wary of biometric data misuse. Financial apps face heightened scrutiny, so the design leans on trust-building through transparency: explicitly stating what data is collected and why, which reduces the psychological friction/fear response tied to biometric permissions.

The deferred/contextual permission request leverages the psychological principle that people are more willing to grant access when they understand the immediate, tangible benefit (securing their money) versus an abstract request at onboarding.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual, just-in-time permission request: The native Face ID prompt is triggered by direct user action (toggling a switch) instead of on first app launch, dramatically increasing the likelihood of "Allow" being tapped.

  • Granular control switches: Splitting "Move money" and "Unlock the app" into separate toggles gives power users flexibility while defaulting to safer, opt-in behavior.

  • Pre-permission education: Explanatory copy about data usage appears directly above the toggle, functioning as a priming layer before the OS-level dialog appears.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 7

Use this pattern when designing settings for any app handling sensitive data (fintech, health, identity) where users need to configure when and how biometric/PIN authentication is triggered. It's especially effective when:

  • You're introducing biometric data collection and need to proactively address privacy concerns inline rather than relying on a separate policy page.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 8
