screens.whereToUse:
• Companion mobile apps for primarily desktop-first collaboration tools, where the phone serves as a notification/review surface rather than the main editing environment.
  • Any B2B/collaboration product where @-mentions, comments, or approvals drive re-engagement (e.g., project management, design, or document tools).
  • Notification centers that benefit from separating "unread" from "all" to reduce cognitive load when scanning a mixed-urgency list.
  • Scenarios where quick contextual preview (showing the actual comment/mention text) can reduce unnecessary taps into the full source.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this stripped-down layout for consumer social apps where richer visual content (photos, reactions, previews) is expected (a text-only row may feel underwhelming).
  • Not ideal when notification volume is consistently high; a flat single-section list without grouping by type/date or filtering would quickly become unmanageable and should be paired with Filter & Sort or Faceted Browse at scale.
  • Don't rely on a mostly-empty canvas as a final design if the product expects frequent engagement (an empty state illustration or prompt (e).g., "You're all caught up") should be added once the unread item is cleared, otherwise the blank space can feel unfinished or broken.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers and developers working in teams who need lightweight, asynchronous awareness of collaboration happening in shared Figma files (e).g., being tagged in a comment while away from their desktop. The psychological trigger at play is social recognition and FOMO: being @-mentioned is inherently attention-grabbing, and the red dot/unread badge exploits the Zeigarnik effect (unresolved items create mental tension until "read" or acted upon).

The "Mark all as read" affordance caters to users who experience notification-count anxiety and want control over their badge count without reviewing every item individually (a common pattern for busy professionals juggling multiple tools).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unread count + bulk dismiss combo: Pairing "Unread (1)" with "Mark all as read" gives users both visibility into outstanding items and a one-tap way to clear them, respecting users who treat notifications as a queue to be emptied.
  • Dual-signal unread indicator: The red dot on the avatar plus the dedicated "Unread" section header creates redundant, low-effort cues so the unread status can't be missed even with partial attention.
  • Context-rich notification copy: Embedding the actual @mention and comment text directly in the feed lets users triage importance without opening the file, saving a navigation step for low-priority mentions.
  • Consistent root tab bar: Activity sits alongside Recents, Search, and Mirror, reflecting Figma's hub-and-spoke mobile strategy where the phone app is a lightweight review/mirror companion to the desktop canvas, not a full editing surface.

screens.name: Figma - Activity - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a collaborative/creative tool needs to extend desktop-centric work into a mobile companion experience focused on notifications, review, and lightweight replies rather than full editing. It's ideal for:

  • Design, documentation, or whiteboard tools with threaded commenting (Figma, Miro, Notion).
  • Any workflow where visual context (a screenshot, diagram, or canvas region) is essential to understanding a conversation.
  • Apps that want to keep users engaged on mobile without forcing complex editing tasks onto a small screen.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The underlying content isn't inherently visual: a text-only screenshot preview adds unnecessary weight and scrolling for non-visual apps.
  • Real-time co-editing on mobile is a core use case; in that scenario, bridging out to another app/view (rather than enabling inline editing) would frustrate power users who expect full parity.
  • Thread volume is extremely high (hundreds of replies) - a flat chronological list without collapsing/summarization would become unwieldy and require pagination or grouping instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers and cross-functional collaborators (PMs, developers, stakeholders) who need to stay looped into design feedback while away from their desktop. It specifically targets the moment when someone receives a push notification about a comment and wants to quickly triage it on their phone.

Psychologically, it leverages social validation and reciprocity: seeing teammates react with 👀 and 😍 emojis creates a sense of momentum and validates the work being discussed, encouraging further engagement. The casual tone and avatar-driven identity cues (colored initials) build a sense of team presence and belonging, reducing the feeling that feedback is a formal, high-stakes evaluation.

The "Open comment in file" CTA taps into task continuity psychology (users feel reassured that they can always pick up deeper work later, reducing anxiety about missing full context on a small screen).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual context first: Surfacing the actual canvas screenshot above the conversation ensures comments are never read out of context (essential for a visual design tool).
  • Emoji reactions with counts: Lightweight, low-friction engagement that lets team members acknowledge feedback without typing, reducing conversational overhead.
  • "Open comment in file" bridge button: A clear, well-placed escape hatch that respects the boundary between mobile (review/triage) and desktop (deep editing) workflows.
  • Persistent reply bar: Keeps the core action always within thumb's reach regardless of thread length.
  • Chronological threading: Simple, readable conversation flow with relative timestamps ("1 hour ago") reduces cognitive load versus absolute timestamps.

screens.name: Figma - Activity - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Notification/activity feeds in collaborative or social products where zero-state confusion needs to be avoided.
  • Secondary/utility tabs where restraint (no heavy illustration or CTA) is appropriate to keep focus on primary workflows elsewhere in the app.
  • Any feed-based screen where teaching users "what will appear here" reduces future support questions and builds correct expectations.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this minimal approach on primary onboarding screens or core feature surfaces where a stronger illustration, CTA, or guided action would better drive first-time engagement.
  • Not ideal when the empty state should prompt an immediate action (e.g., "Invite teammates" or "Create your first file") - this pattern is purely informational and passive.
  • Risk of feeling too sparse/cold if used on a screen meant to feel warm or celebratory (e.g., a rewards or community feed).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers and developers who use the Figma mobile companion app primarily to check in on team collaboration while away from their desktop (e).g., checking comment replies or mentions during a commute or meeting. Because this is a secondary, glanceable surface (not the primary design workflow), the empty state is deliberately low-key and non-intrusive.

Psychologically, the design reduces anxiety around "Did I miss something?" by clearly confirming there is no unread activity, while the explanatory subtext builds anticipation and familiarity with the notification system for new or infrequent app users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive education via empty state: Rather than just saying "nothing to show," the subtext explicitly teaches the user what will trigger entries here (comments, replies, @mentions), setting mental models for collaborative behavior before it happens.
  • Tonal consistency with brand: The dark top bar against a light canvas mirrors the toolbar/canvas contrast of the Figma desktop app, reinforcing brand recognition across platforms.
  • Minimal cognitive load: No illustration, no CTA button. Just typography and whitespace, appropriate for a secondary/utility tab that doesn't need to drive conversion or action.
  • Persistent global navigation: Tab bar remains fully visible and functional even in a zero-data state, preventing the user from feeling "stuck."

screens.name: Linear - Inbox - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this dual-feed + faceted-tile pattern for any marketplace or content app where both algorithmic recommendations and manual exploration need to coexist (e-commerce, real estate, media libraries). The isolated favorite-icon approach is ideal whenever the primary content is itself a visual/creative asset that shouldn't be obscured by UI chrome.
screens.whereNotToUse: This pattern is less suitable for data-dense, task-oriented tools like Linear, where users need fast triage of structured issues rather than visual browsing. In such contexts, large image-first cards and curatorial copy would slow down scanning and reduce information density, conflicting with a keyboard-driven, list-based workflow optimized for speed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This design serves art collectors, enthusiasts, and casual browsers who value both personalized curation and the ability to self-direct discovery by style or size. The psychological triggers at play include social proof (curators' pick, increased interest), aspiration (named artists, gallery provenance), and the endowed progress of a personalized feed that implies the app "knows" the user's taste, increasing engagement and session depth.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual discovery model: combines algorithmic personalization ("New Works for You") with manual faceted browse tiles ("Our Picks," "Style," "Size") so both passive and intentional users are served.
  • Social proof micro-copy: tags like "Curators' Pick" and "Increased Interest" add credibility and urgency without needing numeric metrics, well-suited to a market where provenance and taste signal value.
  • Non-intrusive favoriting: the heart button sits below the artwork, not as an overlay, preserving uncluttered visual appreciation of the piece (critical in a visually-driven marketplace).
  • Flexible price display: gracefully handles both fixed pricing and "Price on request" states, reflecting real-world art sales nuance.

screens.name: Linear - Inbox - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for:

  • Any list/feed screen that can legitimately be empty for new users (e.g., bids, orders, saved items, notifications).
  • Re-engagement moments where you want to redirect an idle user toward a core revenue-driving action.
  • Marketplace or e-commerce apps where "browsing" is the natural next step after an empty transactional list.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The emptiness is due to an error (e.g., failed network request) - in that case, an error state with retry action is more appropriate, not a marketing-style CTA.
  • The user has already engaged extensively and would find a generic "explore" prompt irrelevant or redundant (returning power users expect data, not onboarding-style messaging).
  • The screen requires showing partial/loading data (this should use a skeleton loader instead of jumping straight to an empty state).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets new or inactive users who have not yet placed a bid in the auction section. Psychologically, it combats the "blank page anxiety" that occurs when a user navigates to a section expecting content and finds none. By immediately presenting a clear next step, it reduces drop-off and channels the user back into the core engagement loop (browsing and bidding) rather than letting them bounce due to perceived lack of value.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Actionable Empty State: Instead of a passive "nothing here" message, the screen actively redirects the user toward a value-generating action (exploring auctions).
  • Single, Unmissable CTA: The pill-shaped, full-contrast black button is the only interactive element on the screen, eliminating decision paralysis.
  • Persistent Context via Segmented Tabs: Users retain orientation (Bids vs. Inquiries) even when the content area is empty.
  • Minimalist Restraint: No illustrations or heavy graphics are used, keeping the tone premium and gallery-like, consistent with an art marketplace brand identity.

screens.name: Linear - Inbox - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when:

  • An event has a hard deadline or go-live time that gates user participation (auctions, live drops, scheduled launches, cycle/sprint starts).
  • There is exactly one blocking prerequisite action (registration, verification, approval) that must be visually inseparable from the countdown/status.
  • You need to reassure users that "zero results" is an intentional, verified state rather than a loading failure (e).g., empty dashboards, empty activity feeds, empty sprint boards.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Multiple competing actions exist: stacking several "complete X" banners dilutes urgency and creates decision fatigue.
  • The underlying data updates in real time without a hard deadline; a static countdown implies false urgency.
  • Users browse casually and don't need transactional status tracking (this format is overkill for passive content consumption screens).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets active bidders/collectors who need a trustworthy, time-critical status dashboard for auctions they're tracking. The psychological drivers are urgency (countdown to live bidding), loss-aversion (incomplete registration could mean missing the sale entirely), and transparency (explicit confirmation of zero bids avoids anxiety about whether an action succeeded).

For a Linear-style audience, the transferable lesson is about surfacing a single blocking action tied to a time-sensitive event (e.g., "cycle starts in 2 days (finish estimating issues") directly adjacent to the relevant status, rather than burying it in settings or a separate checklist).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Status-driven CTA placement: The registration prompt is injected directly below the live-bidding countdown, so the user sees cause (sale starting soon) and required action (register) in the same glance.
  • Explicit empty state: Rather than leaving blank space, the screen confirms "no bids placed" so users trust the absence of data is accurate, not a loading/error bug.
  • Segmented top tabs: Bids vs Inquiries cleanly separates two different transactional contexts without needing separate screens or deep navigation.
  • High-impact hero art: Using the actual lot artwork as a banner image builds immediate emotional/product recognition for collectors.

screens.name: Linear - Inbox - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any first-use or zero-data state within a messaging, notifications, or activity-based feature, particularly in marketplace, social, or CRM-like products. It's ideal when:

  • The feature's purpose isn't self-evident from its name alone (e.g., "Inquiries," "Bids," "Requests").
  • You want to convert an idle moment into a funnel back toward core content discovery.
  • The brand tone benefits from a calm, editorial, non-alarming empty state (premium, lifestyle, or curated marketplaces).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The inbox/feature is expected to have content almost immediately (e.g., transactional confirmations) - in that case, a loading or skeleton state is more appropriate than an explanatory empty state.
  • Users are already highly familiar with the feature (e.g., returning power users), where verbose explanatory copy can feel redundant or patronizing.
  • Multiple CTAs or secondary actions are needed: this single-CTA layout doesn't scale well if there are several relevant next steps (e.g., "Invite a gallery" vs "Browse works").
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets art collectors and buyers who are new to using the platform's messaging feature, or who simply haven't yet contacted any galleries. The psychological driver at play is reduction of ambiguity: new users often don't understand what an "Inquiries" tab is for in a marketplace context, so the screen proactively explains the mental model before the user has any data in it.

The CTA also leverages the path-of-least-resistance principle: rather than leaving the user stranded with no next step, it immediately redirects intent toward the discovery funnel, increasing the likelihood of future gallery contact and ultimately inquiries/sales.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Didactic empty state: Uses the empty inbox as a teaching moment rather than a dead end, explaining the feature's value proposition in plain language.
  • Single, unambiguous CTA: Only one pill-shaped black button is present, eliminating decision paralysis and funneling users back into content discovery.
  • Segmented Bids/Inquiries control: Cleanly separates two related but distinct relationship types (financial bids vs. conversational inquiries) within one inbox destination.
  • Restrained visual design: Generous white space and muted gray secondary text keep attention on the headline and CTA, consistent with a minimal, gallery-like aesthetic appropriate for an art marketplace.

screens.name: Linear - Inbox - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any marketplace, freelance, or service app where transactional conversations tied to specific listings or items need to be organized (e.g., real estate inquiries, e-commerce buyer questions, freelance gig proposals). It's ideal when users manage multiple concurrent conversations tied to visual/product context, and when splitting conversation types (e.g., formal offers vs. casual questions) aids prioritization.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this flat segmented-list approach for apps with high message volume or group/multi-party threads, where richer filtering, search, or folder systems are needed. It is also unsuitable for purely social messaging apps where read receipts, typing indicators, and real-time presence are expected, since this screen lacks those richer conversational affordances. For enterprise tools like Linear itself, this pattern is less relevant (issue/comment threads tied to tasks would require different metadata (status, assignee) rather than simple commerce-style inbox rows).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets sellers on an art/collectibles marketplace who need to quickly monitor and respond to buyer interest. The psychological trigger at play is responsiveness anxiety reduction: surfacing real-time inquiry activity with "a few seconds ago" timestamps nudges sellers toward fast replies, which increases buyer trust and conversion likelihood (reciprocity and urgency). The thumbnail-plus-preview format also leverages recognition over recall, a core usability heuristic, minimizing the mental effort needed to triage messages.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented Bids/Inquiries split: Separates negotiation-stage communications (Bids) from general questions (Inquiries), reducing clutter and helping sellers triage by urgency/intent.
  • Thumbnail-first list item: Including the artwork image directly in the inbox row lets sellers instantly recall which listing a message pertains to without opening the thread (a major efficiency win for multi-listing sellers).
  • Relative timestamps: "A few seconds ago" creates a sense of immediacy and liveness, encouraging quick responses.
  • Persistent bottom tab bar with active state: Keeps navigation context clear and messaging always one tap away, critical for time-sensitive commerce conversations.

screens.name: Brex Tasks 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a core feature or data view is legitimately empty due to a missing dependency (e.g., permissions not yet granted, setup incomplete, pending approval). It's especially effective in B2B/enterprise tools where end-users depend on an admin or workflow step outside their control. Pair an explanatory message with a friendly illustration and a single, clear recovery CTA, and surface alternative secondary actions below so the screen doesn't feel like a dead end.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for states that are the result of a true error (e.g., network failure, server error) - in those cases use an explicit error state with retry messaging rather than a soft, ambiguous "no limit selected" framing. Also avoid stacking decorative illustrations on screens where users need to act with urgency or scan data quickly, as the large graphic consumes valuable vertical space and delays access to information for power users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees of companies using Brex for corporate card/expense management who have been onboarded but not yet assigned a spending limit by their finance/admin team. The design acknowledges a common B2B onboarding gap (the employee has an account before the admin has finished configuration) and proactively addresses the resulting confusion.

Psychologically, the illustration and neutral tone reduce the frustration of hitting a "wall" in the app, while the single CTA leverages the Hick's Law principle (fewer choices, faster decisions) to drive immediate action rather than leaving the user stuck.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Illustration-led empty state: Uses a custom 3D illustration instead of a generic icon, softening what could otherwise feel like an error or broken experience.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: Only one primary button is shown, eliminating decision paralysis and guiding the user to the exact resolution path.

  • Contextual reassurance copy: Explicitly tells the user why the state is empty and hints at a likely cause (pending request), reducing support tickets and anxiety.

  • Partial card reveal behind sheet: The Brex card peeking above the modal sheet maintains context of "where you are" (inside the Wallet/card view) even while the detail panel is empty.

  • Secondary task surfaced below the fold: "Request reimbursement" gives users something productive to do even when the primary feature (spend limit) is unavailable.

screens.name: Brex Tasks 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any notification-style or task-inbox empty states in productivity, finance, or workflow apps where zero-items is the expected default state (e.g., approvals, alerts, moderation queues, to-do lists). It is especially effective when:

  • The absence of items is a positive outcome (nothing urgent to do).

  • You want to reduce perceived "systems is broken" anxiety.

  • There's a complementary action (like uploading receipts) users can proactively take even without pending tasks.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid overly whimsical illustrations in empty states where the absence of data is itself a problem signal (e.g., an empty "Orders" screen for a seller who expects sales, or an empty inbox for a support agent whose job depends on ticket volume) - in those cases, playful mascots can feel tone-deaf. Additionally, for enterprise/B2B dashboards where density and efficiency are valued over delight, this much vertical whitespace and illustration real estate may be seen as wasteful or unprofessional.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of a financial wallet/expense app (likely a corporate card or receipt-management tool like Ramp, Brex, or Expensify) who check the "Tasks" tab to resolve action items such as missing receipts, approvals, or disputes. Since the default state for most users on most days is "no outstanding tasks," this screen is seen frequently and must avoid feeling like an error or a punishment for having nothing to do.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Peak-End Rule and anti-anxiety design principles common in finance UX: by using warm color and a smiling character, it reduces the stress typically associated with financial "to-do" lists. It also uses the Zeigarnik effect in reverse, reassuring users that incomplete tasks will actively surface later, which permits them to mentally disengage from checking manually.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotionally intelligent empty state: Uses a friendly 3D character instead of a generic icon, transforming "nothing to do" into a moment of delight rather than a UX dead-end.

  • Proactive reassurance copy: Explicitly tells the user they will be notified of future action items, removing the need to manually re-check this screen.

  • Persistent secondary CTA: The floating "Add receipts" button ensures the screen is never fully passive (there's always a productive action available even when the primary list is empty).

  • Strong visual hierarchy via gradient header: The dark, textured top section clearly separates global navigation/utility icons from the content body, guiding focus downward.

  • Notification badge contrast: The orange dot on the bell icon creates a subtle tension/curiosity loop, prompting engagement despite the empty task list.

screens.name: Brex Tasks 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when:

  • Users have recurring, low-engagement administrative obligations (uploading documents, approving requests, confirming details) that are easy to forget.

  • You need a dedicated space separate from the primary content feed (e.g., separate from "Wallet"/transactions) so action items don't get lost.

  • The app ecosystem benefits from a badge-based nudge system to pull users back into the app for specific unresolved items.

  • You want to offer both a bulk-resolution shortcut (floating button) and item-level resolution (inline button) for flexibility.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The number of tasks is typically zero: an entire dedicated tab for a feature that's usually empty may feel like wasted navigation real estate; consider folding it into a notification center instead.

  • Tasks are extremely time-sensitive or high-stakes (in such cases, a passive tab-based list is too easy to ignore; a modal interrupt or push notification would be more effective).

  • Having two redundant CTAs ("Add" inline and floating "Add receipts") could feel cluttered on screens with multiple task rows; this works well with one item but may need consolidation with many.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees using a corporate card or business expense app who are required by their finance/ops team to submit documentation for every transaction. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Loss aversion / compliance anxiety:

  • Zeigarnik effect: An open, unresolved task (visually represented by a badge and a standalone tab) creates cognitive tension that nudges the user to complete it quickly.

  • Reduction of friction for a mundane chore: Since uploading receipts is a low-value, easily-forgotten chore, the design compensates with persistent visibility (badge + floating button) rather than relying on user memory.

This pattern is most useful for internal tools, fintech, or B2B SaaS products where users must be proactively reminded to complete low-engagement administrative tasks tied to policy compliance.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-entry CTA pattern: Both a persistent floating "Add receipts" button and a contextual inline "Add" button on the task row give users flexible paths to resolve the same task.

  • Badge-driven tab bar: The "1" badge on the Tasks tab icon creates a lightweight, non-intrusive nudge that pulls users into this screen from elsewhere in the app.

  • Category chips for scalability: The "All" / "Missing documentation" segmented chips imply a flexible task taxonomy, future-proofing the screen for more task types (approvals, disputes, etc.) without redesigning the layout.

  • Decorative header vs. functional body contrast: The expressive gradient header softens an otherwise purely functional, compliance-driven screen, preventing the app from feeling like a cold back-office tool.

  • Transaction context inline: Showing the merchant (redacted) and amount (£2.50) directly in the task row lets users identify which expense needs action without an extra tap.

screens.name: Brex Tasks 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you need users to resolve discrete, finite action items tied to compliance, data completeness, or account health (e.g., missing receipts, unverified identity documents, incomplete profile fields). It excels in B2B/fintech contexts where tasks have clear, quantifiable stakes (amounts, deadlines) and benefit from being decoupled from the main dashboard to avoid clutter.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for consumer apps where surfacing a dedicated "Tasks" tab may feel overly corporate or guilt-inducing for low-stakes actions. It also fails if task volume is very high and unfiltered, as the simple segmented-control filtering shown here would become insufficient, requiring more robust sorting, grouping by due date, or batch-resolution tools instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees or finance team members using a corporate spend/expense management platform (similar to Pleo, Ramp, or Brex) who need to reconcile receipts against card transactions. The psychological trigger at play is the Zeigarnik effect: the persistent badge count and explicit "missing" framing create a nagging sense of incompleteness that drives the user to close the loop quickly, which is crucial for compliance-heavy workflows where unresolved receipts can create audit risk or accounting delays.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Badge-driven Tab Bar: The red/orange numeric badge on the "Tasks" tab preemptively signals outstanding items before the user even opens the screen, driving habitual re-engagement.

  • Dual-layer header: The vibrant animated gradient header paired with a sliding white content sheet gives the utilitarian task list a premium, modern feel rarely seen in typically dry expense-management tools.

  • Context-rich list item: Combining the task description with the specific transaction amount (£2.50) on the same row eliminates the need to tap in for details just to assess urgency/importance.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: The orange "Add" button is the only strong color accent on the entire screen, ensuring zero ambiguity about the next required action.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Asset/instrument detail pages in fintech, trading, or crypto apps where users need both transactional controls and contextual education in one view.

  • Products serving a mixed audience of novices and experts, where progressive disclosure ("View more") lets each segment self-select their depth of engagement.

  • Any screen introducing a new or unfamiliar entity that benefits from paired "act now" and "learn more" affordances.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid an 8-icon flat action grid when only 2-3 actions are truly relevant to the current user state (e.g., a zero-balance user shown "Cash out" and "Send") - this creates decision paralysis and clutters the primary CTA. In such cases, prioritize the single most relevant action (e.g., "Buy") with greater visual weight and defer secondary actions to a "More" overflow. This pattern is also unsuitable for simple single-purpose apps where exhaustive action exposure would overwhelm a low-frequency or highly novice user base; a more guided, single-CTA flow would convert better.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both crypto-curious beginners and active traders simultaneously. The zero balance state ("0.00000 BTC") combined with an educational "About Bitcoin" module suggests this is likely a new user's first visit to an asset page before any deposit (the design anticipates onboarding-stage curiosity and provides just-in-time education to build confidence before a purchase decision).

Simultaneously, the exhaustive action grid (Bridge, Swap, Text send) caters to sophisticated DeFi users who expect granular control without extra taps. Psychologically, exposing all options at once leverages the availability heuristic: users feel the app is powerful and complete because every capability is visible, even if unused. The whitepaper/official site links serve as credibility signals, tapping into the trust deficit inherent to cryptocurrency products by pointing to primary-source, non-corporate documentation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full action transparency: Instead of a hamburger/overflow menu, all eight transactional capabilities are exposed as first-class icon buttons, reducing navigation depth to zero for power users.

  • Embedded education layer: The "About [Asset]" and "Resources" (Whitepaper, Official website) sections turn a transactional screen into a trust-building content surface, critical for reducing anxiety in volatile/unfamiliar asset classes.

  • External link affordance: Explicit diagonal arrow icons on Whitepaper/Official website links clearly signal that the user will leave the app context, setting correct expectations.

  • Consistent iconography system: Uniform circular dark-grey buttons with monochrome line icons create a calm, unified visual rhythm across a functionally busy grid.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any inbox, feed, or list screen that can legitimately be empty for new users (notification centers, activity feeds, order histories, chat lists, or saved/favorites screens). It's especially effective in fintech/crypto apps where user trust and guidance are paramount. Pair the empty state with a direct link or button to the action that generates content (e.g., "Browse Markets" or "Set a Price Alert") to shorten the path from empty state to first value.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this soft, welcoming approach for empty states caused by errors, failed loads, or connectivity issues (those require distinct error messaging and recovery actions (e).g., "Retry") rather than an onboarding-style welcome. Also avoid this pattern if the notification screen is a low-frequency, secondary feature; over-designing minor empty states can be unnecessary engineering/design effort. Additionally, ensure this state doesn't appear for returning users who previously had notifications, as it could confuse them into thinking their history was wiped.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets new users of a crypto trading/portfolio app who have just signed up or freshly installed the application and have not yet added assets, watchlists, or price alerts. Psychologically, empty states are critical "first impression" moments (a poorly handled one can make an app feel broken or abandoned). By using a positive, guiding tone ("Welcome!"), the design reduces the anxiety/confusion new users feel and instead frames the empty inbox as an opportunity, leveraging the curiosity gap and a subtle call-to-action to drive users toward core engagement actions (adding coins to watchlist, enabling price alerts) that will eventually populate this screen with content, increasing long-term retention and notification opt-in rates.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Actionable Empty State: Instead of a static "nothing here" message, the screen tells the user exactly what to do (explore crypto) to start receiving value from this section.

  • Settings Access Preserved: The gear/preferences icon remains accessible in the top bar even with zero notifications, letting proactive users pre-configure alert types.

  • Custom Illustration: A bespoke phone-with-notification-bubble illustration adds personality and visually communicates the concept of "notifications" better than generic empty-state art.

  • Persistent Navigation: The tab bar stays fully functional, preventing the empty state from feeling like a navigational dead-end.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logging & Tracking 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Any list, feed, or history screen (transactions, orders, messages, notifications) that a new user will encounter before generating data.

  • Situations where converting an empty state into an activation opportunity is valuable, e.g., prompting a first deposit, first post, or first connection.

  • Fintech, crypto, and banking apps where trust and clarity are paramount during onboarding.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Screens where the user has already completed the primary action but simply has no results due to filtering (here the CTA should be "Clear filters" rather than an unrelated onboarding action).

This demographic is often anxious about handing over sensitive personal documents and may be verifying identity on a mobile device for the first time in a low-light or improvised environment.

The psychological trigger at play is friction reduction under stress: identity verification is a non-negotiable gate the user must pass to access a service (e.g., open a bank account, receive a paycheck, access a crypto wallet), so any perceived failure elevates anxiety. The immediate, actionable feedback loop (error → guidance → retry) reduces abandonment risk at a critical conversion funnel step. The persistent camera view also leverages the sunk-cost/momentum principle, keeping the user "in the moment" rather than forcing a restart.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking error banner: Uses an inline banner instead of a disruptive modal, allowing users to immediately retry the action without an extra dismiss step.

  • High-contrast iconography: The red circular alert icon against a black banner immediately draws the eye and signals severity using color psychology, even before reading the text.

  • Live camera persistence: Keeping the camera feed active during the error state (rather than showing a static failed image) reduces the number of steps needed to retry, respecting the user's time.

  • Clear visual guide-frame: The rounded rectangle overlay with corner accents removes guesswork about framing, directly addressing the root cause of the blur/positioning error.

  • Trust branding: The "Onfido | Real Identity" watermark reassures users that a reputable, specialized third-party service (rather than the host app itself) is handling sensitive biometric/document data.

Don't use this pattern if failure detection is unreliable, as false-positive blur rejections will frustrate users with correctly captured images; ensure detection thresholds are well-tuned before shipping. Also avoid stacking multiple error states or vague messaging ("Something went wrong")) specificity is essential to this pattern's effectiveness.

screens.name: Venmo Scanning 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any payment, ticketing, loyalty, or identity app where a single interaction point needs to support both scanning someone else's code and presenting your own code interchangeably (e.g., transit apps, event check-in apps, P2P payment apps, boarding passes with peer transfer). It's ideal when the core actions are symmetrical (pay vs. receive) and users may need to switch roles rapidly and repeatedly in the same session.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the scanning use case is rare, one-directional, or highly complex, since collapsing a rarely-used camera scanner into a persistent tab may waste prime navigation real estate. The three-way segmented control also caters to context-switching speed (a user at a cash register (Show to pay), splitting a bill with a friend (Scan code), or requesting money from a friend (Venmo me) can pivot instantly without leaving the screen, which reduces abandonment during time-sensitive in-person transactions (e).g., a checkout line).

  • Photo library fallback: The gallery icon anticipates a real edge case (codes received as screenshots via text/email) that pure camera-only scanners often miss.
