screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
The target user here is a Brex business cardholder or employee submitting an expense report who needs to attach a photo of a physical receipt. This persona is typically on the go, often in a hurry (e.g., right after a client dinner or purchase), and may be privacy-conscious about granting full photo library access to a finance/corporate app.

Psychologically, this screen addresses the "privacy paradox" tension in B2B fintech apps: users want convenience (quickly finding a photo) but are wary of corporate software having blanket access to personal photos (family pictures, personal moments). The limited-access disclosure directly defuses this anxiety, increasing the likelihood a user completes the attach-receipt flow instead of abandoning it or granting access reluctantly.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Leverages OS trust instead of rebuilding it: By using the native picker, Brex inherits Apple's privacy guarantees and polished interaction patterns for free, rather than building a bespoke (and less trusted) media picker.

  • Transparent limited-access disclosure: The "Private Access to Photos" card is a best-in-class example of proactive, in-context privacy communication rather than a one-time blocking permission dialog.

  • Dismissible, non-blocking education: The explanation is informative but optional (closable via the X), respecting the user's time if they already understand the concept.

  • Low-friction task completion: Search, sort, and collections toggle allow power users to quickly locate the exact receipt photo needed, reducing time-to-task-completion for an inherently tedious expense-reporting workflow.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when designing camera-capture flows embedded within a larger workflow (not a standalone camera app), especially when the captured artifact needs to be associated with an existing record (e.g., receipts, documents, ID verification). It's especially valuable when there's a possible mismatch between user intent and system state (proactively surfacing that mismatch before the user invests effort (e).g., taking a photo) saves frustration. The dual-path bottom CTA ("scan" vs. "manual entry/alternative") pattern is ideal whenever the primary capture method may not always be the right fit for every user's situation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid overlaying warning banners on a camera viewfinder when the warning is purely informational and not actionable (this adds visual clutter and can obscure the subject being photographed). If the warning condition is rare or edge-case only, consider handling it via a toast or pre-emptive screen before entering the camera, rather than cluttering the capture UI itself. Additionally, this pattern should not be used when receipt/document capture is the primary, context-free action of the app (e.g., a dedicated scanner app), since the "no expenses to attach" framing assumes a specific linked-record workflow that may not apply universally.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets business travelers, employees, and finance/ops teams who need to digitize paper receipts for expense reporting and reimbursement, likely within a corporate expense management or spend platform (e.g., similar to Ramp, Brex, or Expensify). The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion and effort-justification prevention: by warning the user before they waste time scanning a receipt that has nowhere to go, the app respects the user's time and avoids a frustrating "scan completed, but now what?" dead-end experience. The inline "Add to existing" and "create reimbursement" options also reduce decision paralysis by making the next best action obvious and low-friction, appealing to time-pressed professional users who value speed and certainty over exploration.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual Just-in-Time Guidance: Rather than letting the user scan a receipt into a dead end, the app proactively surfaces a system-state warning banner the moment it detects there's nothing to attach the receipt to, with an inline fix via "Add to existing."

Branching Escape Hatch: The "Or create reimbursement" button acknowledges that not all expense-logging starts with a physical receipt, offering a graceful fallback path without forcing the user to exit the flow and start over elsewhere.

High-Contrast Overlay Controls: White solid-fill circular buttons (close, retake) against the dark camera viewfinder ensure maximum legibility and touch-target confidence regardless of the background scene being photographed.

Minimal Chrome, Maximum Viewfinder: By stripping away navigation bars and status elements, the design maximizes the available frame for accurately capturing the receipt image, which directly impacts OCR/data-extraction accuracy downstream.

results.query: Compare money transfer flow between Cash App and Venmo

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for multi-entity search experiences (marketplaces, social apps, payment apps, directories) where a single query can plausibly match different object types (users, orgs, products, locations). It's especially valuable when result availability varies wildly by category, since it avoids all-or-nothing empty states and preserves partial value from a single search action. Also ideal for financial apps where guiding users to unique identifiers (like @handles) reduces the risk of costly mis-sends.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this layout when the search domain only has one entity type (the segmented tabs and repeated section headers would add unnecessary visual clutter). It's also not ideal for extremely time-sensitive search-first flows (e.g., quick command palettes) where scanning three stacked sections and empty-state paragraphs would slow the user down. If categories rarely differ in result count, a single flat combined list is more efficient than segmented sections.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves everyday Venmo users searching for a specific person, merchant, or charity to send/request money or make a donation. The design assumes the user has a fuzzy or partial memory of a name/handle, so it prioritizes forgiving search UX with categorized fallback guidance rather than a strict exact-match system.

The psychological driver here is reducing search abandonment: by never showing a fully blank "nothing found" screen (since People still has a match), and by coaching the user toward @handle search syntax, Venmo increases the likelihood of successful task completion (finding the right recipient) and decreases the anxiety associated with financial transactions going to the wrong person.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented category filtering: "Top / People / Businesses / Charities" pills allow instant re-scoping of the same query without a new search action.

  • Graceful degraded empty states per section: Rather than treating "no results" as a single all-or-nothing outcome, each category independently renders success or a tailored empty state, maximizing perceived usefulness of the query.

  • Actionable empty-state copy: Each failure message offers a specific recovery tip (use @handle, check spelling), reducing dead-ends and educating the user on search syntax.

  • Persistent search bar with inline clear (X): Keeps the user anchored to their query, allowing instant edits or resets without navigating back.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any transactional flow where a numeric value is the primary input and the directional intent (send vs. receive, buy vs. sell, debit vs. credit) can reasonably be decided last. Ideal for P2P payments, invoicing tools, bill-splitting features, in-app wallets, or POS-style checkout flows where speed and familiarity are paramount.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the transaction involves multiple line items, complex tax/fee calculations, or requires strong upfront confirmation of recipient identity (e.g., high-value wire transfers) - in those cases, a multi-step review/confirmation screen is safer. Also avoid combining two high-stakes primary actions (Pay/Request) with equal visual weight if one action is significantly riskier or more common than the other, as this can lead to accidental taps in a financial context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using P2P payment or digital wallet apps (e.g., splitting rent, paying back a friend, requesting money for a group gift). The design leverages several psychological principles:

  • Cognitive load reduction: By separating "how much" from "which action," the interface avoids forcing a premature commitment.

  • Familiarity/mental model reuse: The layout mirrors dominant apps like Venmo, so users transfer existing muscle memory instantly, reducing learning curve.

  • Micro-delight & friendliness: Casual copy ("What's this for?") and the Gift icon soften the inherently transactional/financial nature of the task, easing anxiety around money movement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Deferred decision pattern: Amount and note are entered before choosing "Request" or "Pay," letting users focus on one decision at a time.

  • Custom calculator keypad: Built-in math operators (+, -, ×, ÷) allow on-the-fly calculations (e.g., splitting a bill) directly in the amount field.

  • Large, unmissable amount display: Oversized typography with a live cursor makes the primary input the clear visual anchor of the screen.

  • Quick-clear affordance: The circular "x" next to the amount enables instant reset without multiple backspace taps.

  • Contextual "Gift" toggle: Surfaces a monetization/feature differentiator (gift payments) inline without a separate settings screen.

  • Add-recipient "+" control: Enables multi-person requests/payments directly from the entry screen.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a user's in-progress action holds non-trivial value (financial transactions, drafted content, multi-field forms) and an accidental exit would cause real loss of effort or data. It's ideal for guarding "close" or "back" gestures on flows the user has already invested time or attention into, especially transactional flows involving money, irreversible submissions, or long forms.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., closing a search filter, dismissing an informational card) - over-confirming trivial dismissals creates friction fatigue and trains users to blindly tap through dialogs, undermining the pattern's effectiveness when it truly matters. Also reconsider using the same brand-accent color for a destructive confirmation button; a distinct color or icon could better differentiate "cancel/destroy" actions from "affirm/proceed" actions to prevent misclicks.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Venmo's "Busy Urban" audience frequently multitasks while sending or requesting money (interruptions like phone calls, notifications, or second-guessing an amount are common). This confirmation dialog serves as a safety net against accidental exits (like a stray tap on the "X" during the payment flow) that would otherwise silently discard a half-completed transaction.

Psychologically, this leverages the commitment and consequence principle: by forcing an explicit confirmation step before discarding work, Venmo reduces regret-driven support tickets and repeated re-entry of payment details, which is especially valuable to users who are transacting quickly between other tasks and may not want to redo an entry.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving dim/blur overlay: The payment screen remains visible but de-emphasized behind the sheet, so users retain a mental model of what they're about to lose.

  • Redundant, low-friction dismissal: Swipe handle, "X" icon, and "Back" text link all lead to the same safe outcome, accommodating different user habits and reducing rage-taps.

  • Plain-language button labels: "Yes, cancel it" removes any ambiguity about what the affirmative action does, unlike generic "OK/Cancel" dialogs.

  • Minimal sheet real estate: Only the essential decision is presented (no upsells, no extra copy) respecting the urgency of a decision point.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any transactional flow where a single numeric value is the primary input and must be verified before an irreversible action. P2P payments, tipping, invoicing, in-app currency top-ups, or bill-splitting features. It's especially effective when:

  • The action has two symmetrical directions (pay vs. request, buy vs. sell, add vs. withdraw).

  • Speed and low cognitive load are more valuable than rich formatting options.

  • A custom keypad can meaningfully reduce input errors compared to the system keyboard.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex financial inputs requiring multiple fields, currency conversion, or itemized breakdowns (e.g., invoicing with tax/line items) - the single giant number affordance breaks down when more than one value needs simultaneous visibility. It's also unsuitable for accessibility-sensitive contexts unless the custom keypad and buttons are rigorously tested with screen readers, since non-native keyboards can sometimes degrade assistive technology support. Finally, avoid dual equally-weighted CTAs (Request/Pay) in flows where one action is destructive or significantly higher-risk than the other, as visual parity can encourage mis-taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets mainstream consumer P2P payment users (e.g., Venmo, Cash App audiences) - largely younger, mobile-first users splitting bills, paying rent, or gifting money to friends and family. The design leans on social proof and casualness (memo field, gift icon, friendly tone) rather than the sterile formality of banking apps, because trust in this context comes from familiarity and simplicity rather than institutional gravitas.

Psychologically, the oversized amount display exploits the Von Restorff effect (isolation effect) - the number visually dominates so users double-check the figure before committing, reducing regret and support tickets from mistaken amounts. The proximity of "Request" and "Pay" buttons reduces the perceived friction of switching intent, appealing to users who make split-second decisions in social settings (e.g., splitting a check at a restaurant).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom numeric keypad: Overrides the system keyboard to optimize digit entry speed and prevent accidental non-numeric input in a financial context.

  • Giant, high-contrast amount display: The $1 figure is the single largest element on screen, immediately confirming the entered value at a glance (critical for reducing transaction errors).

  • Inline clear (X) affordance: Placed directly next to the amount for instant correction, avoiding tedious character-by-character backspacing.

  • Dual-intent CTA pattern: Presenting "Request" and "Pay" as equally weighted, adjacent pill buttons lets users flip the direction of money flow without navigating to a different screen.

  • Contextual memo field: Placed just above the CTAs so the "why" of the transaction is captured before the irreversible action, reinforcing social/contextual money transfers.

  • Minimal chrome: Only back and close icons are present, keeping the modal feel tightly scoped to a single task and reducing decision fatigue.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for peer-to-peer payment confirmation, checkout confirmation, or any "review and confirm" step where a monetary or high-stakes action needs a final, deliberate user gesture. It's ideal when you want to combine transaction summary, configurable options (payment source, privacy, protections), and legal disclosures on a single scrollable screen without forcing a multi-step wizard.

Particularly effective for social-payment apps, marketplace checkouts, or bill-splitting tools where humanizing the transaction (via memo, avatar, social visibility) increases engagement and repeat usage.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for complex B2B or high-value transactions where additional verification, itemization, or multi-party approval is required (the single-screen simplicity here would be insufficient and risky). Also avoid defaulting sensitive financial activity to "Public" visibility in contexts where privacy regulations or user expectations demand private-by-default behavior (e.g., healthcare payments, salary transfers, enterprise expense platforms).

Not suitable when the payment method or optional add-ons (like protection plans) require detailed comparison, cramming that into a confirmation screen would increase cognitive load and reduce conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers: largely younger, social-media-native users, splitting small, informal costs with friends (e.g., splitting a $1 bottle of water). The design leans on social proof and normalization psychology: by defaulting to "Public" visibility, Venmo nudges users toward sharing payment activity as a social signal, similar to a social media post, which reinforces habitual usage and network growth.

The optional Purchase Protection toggle appeals to trust and loss-aversion psychology, protecting non-power users from being scammed in peer transactions that resemble commercial purchases, thereby reducing friction and anxiety for first-time or infrequent users making similar payments to strangers or sellers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single, high-contrast CTA: The pill-shaped teal "Pay" button is the only strong color on the screen, ensuring zero ambiguity about the next action.

  • Progressive disclosure of risk/fees: Purchase protection terms and fee implications are shown inline with a toggle rather than hidden behind a separate settings page, letting users make an informed decision at the point of payment.

  • Funding source transparency: Displaying the live balance ($150.11) directly on the payment method row lets users mentally verify affordability without navigating away.

  • Social-first framing: Treating the payment like a mini social post (avatar, name, memo, public/private setting) leverages Venmo's differentiator versus purely transactional apps like bank transfers.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing a toggle, setting, or classification choice that has downstream financial, legal, or policy implications the user might not intuitively understand (e.g., payment type selection, privacy visibility settings, subscription auto-renewal toggles). It's ideal for:

  • Fintech apps clarifying fee structures or protection eligibility tied to a binary choice.

  • Any moment right after a user toggles a setting, to reinforce understanding without requiring them to seek out help documentation.

  • Situations where you want to preempt support tickets or user confusion with a single, friendly, dismissible explainer.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for trivial or self-explanatory settings (over-explaining low-stakes toggles creates unnecessary friction and modal fatigue). It also should not be used as a substitute for proper legal consent flows; if the setting carries binding terms (e.g., fee agreements), a simple "Got it" acknowledgment may be legally insufficient and a more explicit consent mechanism (checkbox, "I agree" with T&Cs link) should be used instead. Additionally, avoid stacking multiple such explainer sheets in a single flow, as repeated interruptions frustrate users and encourage blind "Got it" tapping without actual comprehension.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using a peer-to-peer payment app who may be unfamiliar with the legal distinction between "paying a friend" (informal transfer) and "paying for goods/services" (a regulated commercial transaction with buyer/seller protections and often fees). The primary psychological trigger is reduction of uncertainty and perceived risk: by explaining the "why" behind a toggle before the user commits, Venmo lowers hesitation and builds trust in the platform's fairness and safety mechanisms.

It also leverages reciprocity and fairness framing ("safer marketplace," "both you and the seller will be covered") to make what could feel like an extra fee or friction point (goods/services fees) feel like a protective benefit rather than a cost. This is especially important for casual sellers (e.g., marketplace resellers, freelancers) who need confidence that Venmo will back them if a transaction goes wrong.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Illustration mirrors the live UI: The hand-holding-phone graphic replicates the exact toggle and Pay button the user just saw, creating instant visual continuity between context and explanation.

  • Dimmed background retains context: Rather than a full-screen takeover, the underlying payment screen remains dimly visible, reminding the user why this sheet appeared without letting them lose their place.

  • Anticipatory objection handling: The copy proactively answers "what if I'm not buying anything?" before the user has to ask, reducing support burden and toggle-related anxiety.

  • Single, low-friction CTA: "Got it" is the only actionable button (no complex choices, no risk of the user picking the "wrong" option in an informational moment).

  • Drag handle affordance: The visible pill/handle at the top signals the sheet is dismissible via swipe, reinforcing that this is a lightweight, non-blocking helper rather than a hard gate.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a single action (posting, sharing, transacting) has variable audience implications and the user needs a lightweight way to adjust visibility without leaving the primary task flow. Ideal for social/financial apps, content sharing platforms, or any feature with a "who can see this" component. The dimmed backdrop technique is excellent for any modal decision that is a sub-step of a larger form.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the privacy implications are severe or legally sensitive (e.g., health or financial account details) - in those cases, a full-screen dedicated flow with more explanation and friction (e.g., re-confirmation) is safer than a lightweight bottom sheet. Also avoid if there are more than 4-5 options, as a simple list radio selector becomes harder to scan and may require search or grouping instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets Venmo's core demographic of younger, social-first users who use payments as a form of social expression (emoji captions, public feeds) but who are increasingly privacy-conscious due to past controversies over Venmo's public-by-default transaction feed. By offering granular, easy-to-understand control at the moment of send, Venmo mitigates regulatory/privacy criticism while preserving its social discovery feed for users who opt-in. The psychological trigger here is autonomy and trust: giving users a clear sense of control reduces anxiety about oversharing financial activity.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual disclosure: Privacy settings are exposed exactly where the decision matters (at the point of payment), not buried in a settings menu.

  • Icon-driven cognition: Globe, friends, and padlock icons let users grasp visibility scope instantly without reading full text.

  • Dimmed context preservation: The underlying payment details remain faintly visible, reassuring the user their transaction data (amount/memo) is preserved while they make this sub-decision.

  • Transparent default labeling: Explicitly calling out "(Your Default)" builds trust by making the platform's default behavior explicit rather than hidden.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for final-step payment or transaction confirmation screens where trust, clarity, and speed are equally critical (such as P2P payment apps, checkout flows, or money transfer confirmations). It's ideal when you need to consolidate recipient info, amount, funding source, and optional protections into one glanceable screen before an irreversible action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal single-CTA pattern for complex or high-value transactions (e.g., large wire transfers, investment purchases) where additional friction, multi-factor confirmation, or itemized breakdowns are legally or practically necessary. It's also unsuitable when multiple funding sources or split payments need simultaneous comparison, as the vertical single-focus layout doesn't support side-by-side decision-making.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers making small, informal peer-to-peer payments (splitting bills, reimbursing a friend for water, rent, etc.). The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Loss aversion mitigation: The purchase protection toggle and "full refund" language reduce the anxiety of sending money to someone for a good/service, especially relevant for marketplace-adjacent transactions.

  • Social trust cues: The privacy toggle reassures users that casual, sometimes embarrassing or private transactions (e.g., paying for "Water") won't be broadcast publicly, addressing Venmo's known social-feed privacy concerns.

  • Commitment consistency: By clearly showing the amount and recipient before the final CTA, users experience a small "review moment" that increases their sense of control and reduces buyer's remorse or accidental payments.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Receipt-style visual hierarchy: Large amount typography paired with recipient avatar mimics familiar payment mental models (checks, receipts), reducing cognitive friction at the moment of highest financial risk.

  • Contextual privacy transparency: Surfacing the "Private" visibility setting directly on the payment screen (rather than buried in settings) preemptively answers a common user concern about social feed exposure.

  • Opt-in purchase protection toggle: Presents an optional safety net with clear, benefit-driven copy and a visible fee trade-off, letting users self-select risk tolerance without a mandatory upsell interruption.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: The full-width "Pay" button with high-contrast color anchors the entire screen and eliminates decision paralysis at the point of conversion.

  • Non-disruptive modal presentation: The bottom sheet with drag handle keeps the flow feeling lightweight and easily dismissible, preserving user control over the transaction.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 9
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial or transactional apps where duplicate submissions carry real monetary or business risk (payments, orders, bookings).

  • Any form flow where accidental double-submission is a known failure mode due to network latency or user impatience.

  • Situations requiring a hard stop rather than a soft warning (use native modal alerts when the cost of the user missing the message is high).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid native generic "Error" alerts for low-stakes or frequent errors (the flat title and disruptive full-block modal will feel heavy-handed for minor issues (better suited to inline validation or a toast)).

  • Don't use this pattern if the user genuinely intends to send the same repeat payment quickly (e.g., legitimate repeated small tips) - provide an override/confirm option instead of an absolute block.

  • Avoid vague messaging; if you must block, always pair it with a clear, specific recovery instruction like this example does.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets everyday Venmo users conducting routine peer-to-peer payments (e.g., splitting a small purchase like "Water" for $1). The psychological trigger being defended against is habitual/impulsive re-tapping (users on mobile often double-tap buttons due to lag uncertainty or accidental screen touches, risking unintentional duplicate charges).

By intercepting this exact pattern, Venmo builds trust: it signals to the user (and protects the business from support burden) that the app is actively safeguarding their money against slips, which is essential for a financial app where trust and accuracy are paramount to retention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Actionable error messaging: Rather than a cryptic code, the alert explains exactly why the action failed and how to fix it (change note or amount).

  • Fraud/mistake prevention rule: The 10-minute duplicate-payment guard rail is a clever invisible safety net that protects users from costly double-taps or accidental resubmissions without requiring them to double check manually.

  • Hard interrupt via native modal: Using the OS-standard alert ensures the warning cannot be missed or accidentally swiped away, appropriate given real money is at stake.

  • Preserved context: The payment details (amount, note, recipient) remain visible behind the dimmed dialog, so once dismissed the user can immediately edit the specific field mentioned in the error without needing to re-enter information from scratch.

screens.name: Venmo Transferring Money 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for consumer P2P payment or money-request flows embedded in social/messaging contexts, especially where speed and low cognitive friction are paramount (splitting bills, casual reimbursements, gifting). It's ideal when the recipient context (identity, thread) is already established, allowing the UI to focus purely on amount and intent.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stripped-down pattern for high-value, formal, or business financial transactions where additional verification, itemization, tax details, or explicit confirmation steps are legally or contextually necessary. The dual Pay/Request buttons side-by-side could also be risky in contexts where accidental mis-taps might trigger irreversible large payments (a confirmation step or clearer visual differentiation should be added for high-stakes amounts).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers performing casual, social financial exchanges, splitting bills, paying back friends for concert tickets, or gifting small amounts within a chat conversation. The design assumes familiarity with mobile messaging and light financial literacy, targeting a mass-market, non-power-user audience.

Psychologically, the design exploits the reduction of friction principle: by keeping the amount entry and action buttons on a single uncluttered screen, it minimizes the "activation energy" required to complete a micro-transaction, which is critical for casual payments where users might abandon the flow if it feels like a "banking app" experience. The playful gift/sticker elements also leverage social reciprocity and warmth cues to make sending money feel like a friendly gesture rather than a formal transaction.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-focus numeric input: The oversized dollar amount dominates the visual hierarchy, ensuring zero ambiguity about the primary task.

  • Dual-intent action buttons: 'Request' and 'Pay' are presented together, letting the user decide direction of money flow at the last possible moment rather than pre-selecting a mode earlier in the flow.

  • Contextual memo field with smart default: Pre-filling "Ticket" reduces typing friction and anchors the transaction to a real-life context.

  • Inline clear (X) affordance next to the amount allows instant correction without needing a backspace-heavy re-entry.

  • Native keyboard + sticker tray integration: Blending social stickers with a financial input field shows deep integration into a messaging OS layer, keeping the user in-context rather than switching apps.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this hero-balance-plus-action-buttons pattern for any financial, wallet, or points/rewards app where the user's primary intent upon opening the screen is to check a balance and immediately act on it (deposit, withdraw, transfer). It's especially effective for neobanks, budgeting apps, or gig-economy earning apps where instant clarity on available funds reduces anxiety and builds trust. The card-grid segmentation for sub-accounts is ideal for products offering multiple money "buckets" (savings, joint pools, goals) that benefit from being visually distinct yet part of one unified dashboard.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this playful/illustrated approach for enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth wealth management products, where users expect a more serious, data-dense, and conservative visual language (whimsical illustrations could undermine trust in contexts involving large sums or institutional users). Additionally, if a user's core account has many concurrent sub-balances or complex multi-currency needs, this oversized single-number hero pattern may oversimplify and require users to drill down excessively for a fuller financial picture.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets a younger, digitally-native demographic (likely Gen Z/younger Millennials) who bank primarily through mobile and are drawn to brands with personality rather than traditional, sterile banking UI. The reliance on a whimsical illustration and playful iconography (the tab bar icons literally being "$1", "$", and a clock) signals a brand attempting to make personal finance feel less intimidating and more approachable, appealing to users who may be new to saving, direct deposit, or interest-bearing accounts.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Primacy Effect (leading with the balance) and reduces choice paralysis by limiting the primary actions to just two big buttons. The "Ready for first paycheck" and interest-rate callouts also exploit the endowment/goal-gradient effect, nudging users who haven't yet linked direct deposit or funded savings to complete these near-term financial goals.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero number treatment: The cash balance is rendered in an oversized, bold, extra-legible typeface that instantly answers the user's core question with zero scanning effort.

  • Action buttons anchored to context: "Add money" and "Withdraw" sit directly below the balance they affect, minimizing eye/thumb travel and reinforcing a clear mental model of cause and effect.

  • Inline account/routing display: Surfacing masked account and routing numbers directly on the dashboard (rather than buried in settings) removes friction for users setting up ACH transfers or payroll.

  • Personality injected via illustration: The quirky "Shipped" card banner breaks the monotony of a typical finance app, using humor and asymmetric color-blocking to build emotional brand affinity.

  • Modular bento cards for sub-accounts: Savings and Pools are visually separated into their own cards with unique iconography, letting users quickly parse different "buckets" of money at a glance.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any monetary top-up, recharge, or credit-purchase flow (wallets, ride-share credit, gift cards, prepaid SIM) where a small set of common amounts covers most user needs. It's ideal when you want to speed up a frequent, low-complexity transaction while still allowing custom input via an overflow option, and when you want to offer secondary/alternative fulfillment methods without competing for primary attention.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the amounts involved are highly variable or unpredictable (e.g., paying an exact invoice or bill amount), where forcing users through preset chips followed by a custom field adds an unnecessary extra step. Also avoid a disabled-until-valid CTA without a visible reason/tooltip for users who may not understand why the button isn't active (pair it with inline guidance if the disabled state isn't self-evident from context).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday consumer banking/P2P payment app users (e.g., Cash App, Venmo) who need to top up a balance quickly, often in-the-moment before a purchase or transfer. The psychological trigger is reduction of friction and decision fatigue: by anchoring users to common round-number amounts, the design leverages default bias, nudging users toward pre-selected values that are "good enough" rather than requiring deliberate numeric entry. The instant-transfer framing also taps into a desire for immediate gratification, critical for a financial app where delays increase abandonment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Preset Amount Chips: Replacing a numeric keypad with tappable denomination buttons ($10-$200) dramatically speeds up the most common task and reduces input errors.

  • Disabled State CTA: The greyed-out "Add" button is a strong affordance that communicates "select an amount first," preventing empty submissions without needing an error message.

  • Contextual Backdrop: Leaving the dimmed balance screen visible behind the sheet reinforces the motivation (low $1.00 balance) driving the user into this flow.

  • Progressive Disclosure of Methods: Instant bank transfer is prioritized above the fold, while less common methods (paper cash, check deposit) are tucked below, matching frequency of use to visual prominence.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-screen numeric-entry pattern whenever the core task is inputting a single critical numeric value (such as adding funds, setting a transfer amount, entering a tip, or setting a budget goal). It's ideal for fintech, banking, and payment apps where precision, trust, and speed matter more than exploration or browsing.

Also effective in any flow where you want to intentionally isolate the user from all other app chrome to prevent distraction during a sensitive or consequential action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for multi-field forms or when additional context (e.g., recipient, memo, currency conversion, fees) is essential to display simultaneously (the extreme minimalism here would force those elements into secondary screens, adding steps). Also avoid if the amount requires complex validation feedback (e.g., real-time balance checks, minimum/maximum warnings) that needs more visual space than this stripped-back layout affords. Not suitable for non-numeric or free-text-heavy inputs.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of fintech/digital wallet apps (e.g., Cash App, Venmo, PayPal, Apple Cash users) who need to quickly top up a balance, often in-the-moment before a purchase or transfer. The primary psychological trigger is reduction of friction and anxiety around money movement: by making the number huge and the interface simple, the user feels in full control and certain about exactly how much they are about to add, which is critical for trust in financial contexts.

The minimalist, native-feeling numeric pad also leverages pattern familiarity: mimicking calculator/ATM/phone dial conventions so no explanation is needed, satisfying System 1 (fast, automatic) thinking rather than requiring deliberate System 2 effort.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized Amount Display: The dollar amount dominates the screen, turning a mundane data-entry task into a clear, confidence-inspiring visual confirmation of intent.

  • Custom Numeric-Only Keypad: Replacing the system keyboard with a custom, large-target keypad increases speed and reduces input errors for a purely numeric context.

  • Dual CTA Placement: A "ghost" Add button up top (likely disabled until valid input) paired with a solid, always-visible Add button at the bottom reinforces the action without being redundant or confusing, and matches scroll/attention patterns.

  • Full-Screen Modal with Close (X): Presenting this as a modal with a clear escape hatch (X) signals it's a transient, focused task, not a permanent navigation destination.

  • Home Indicator/Drag Handle at bottom: Reinforces the sheet's modal/dismissible nature via gesture.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately following any transactional success state (payments, deposits, sign-ups) where you have a complementary feature that reduces future user effort. It's especially effective for:

  • Subscription/auto-pay upsells after a manual bill payment

  • Auto-reload/auto-invest features after a manual funding action

  • Feature discovery for power-user settings immediately after a relevant first-time action
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The user is in a high-stress or time-sensitive flow (e.g., completing a payment before a deadline) where any additional screen adds unwanted friction.

  • The transaction itself was a failure or partial success, pairing negative/neutral outcomes with upsells can feel tone-deaf or opportunistic.

  • The user has already dismissed or declined this same upsell multiple times, which can create banner blindness or annoyance (frequency capping should be applied).

  • Regulatory or compliance-sensitive financial contexts require the confirmation screen to remain uncluttered and strictly informational.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of a peer-to-peer payment or digital wallet app who have just manually reloaded a small balance (likely to cover an upcoming transaction, such as a debit card purchase). The $1 amount suggests either a test transaction or a minimal top-up to enable a purchase (a segment of users who are price-sensitive or new to using the balance feature).

The psychological trigger at play is the "warm glow" effect: capitalizing on the dopamine hit from completing a task successfully to introduce a related convenience feature (auto-reload) that reduces future friction. This is also an application of the Zeigarnik effect / momentum principle: users who just took a small action are more likely to take a related next action while still in a task-oriented mindset.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Success-moment upsell placement: Introducing the auto-reload feature directly after a successful top-up leverages peak positive emotion/dopamine to increase conversion likelihood for a secondary feature.

  • Clear visual hierarchy separation: Using a bordered card and whitespace to distinguish the core confirmation from the promotional content prevents message confusion and preserves the celebratory moment.

  • Non-blocking, dismissible upsell: The feature pitch is optional (via "Get started" link) and does not gate the primary "Done" action, respecting user autonomy and avoiding forced friction.

  • Iconography reinforces concept: The infinity-loop cash icon visually communicates the "continuous/automatic" nature of the feature before the user even reads the text.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app requests access to sensitive third-party data (banking, health records, contacts, location) especially through an intermediary API/SDK. It's ideal for:

  • Fintech account linking (banking, investment, lending apps)

  • Health apps requesting data from wearables or providers

  • Any OAuth-style consent screen where a named third party will handle credentials

  • Situations requiring both legal disclosure and conversion optimization
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, itemized consent pattern for low-risk permissions (e.g., notification access, camera roll for a single photo) where it would feel disproportionate and add unnecessary friction. Also avoid if the itemized list becomes long or overly technical (beyond 3-4 bullets, benefit framing loses effectiveness and should be replaced with a collapsible/expandable detail view or link to full documentation). Do not use this pattern without a clear escape/close action, as forcing consent screens without exit paths increases distrust and regulatory risk.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers linking a bank account to a peer-to-peer payments app (Cash App), a population that spans varying levels of financial and technical literacy. Many users are wary of sharing banking credentials with apps, so the design leans heavily on psychological safety mechanisms: authority (mentioning Plaid, a recognized aggregator), reciprocity framing (data use benefits you), and control (easy exit via X).

The design assumes users may hesitate or abandon at this step, which is a known drop-off point in fintech onboarding funnels. By preemptively answering "why do you need this?" before the user has to ask, the screen reduces support inquiries and cart/flow abandonment while satisfying regulatory disclosure requirements (e.g., GLBA, CFPB open banking guidance).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Benefit-Framed Permission List: Instead of listing raw data-access scopes, the screen translates them into user-centric benefits (fraud prevention, balance verification), lowering perceived risk.

  • Third-Party Transparency: Explicitly naming Plaid as the data intermediary builds credibility and pre-empts confusion or suspicion when a separate Plaid flow launches next.

  • Low-Friction Escape: The visible 'X' close button ensures users don't feel trapped, which paradoxically increases willingness to proceed since consent feels voluntary.

  • Single Primary Action: Only one clear CTA (Continue) avoids decision paralysis at a moment where trust and momentum are fragile.

  • Legal Compliance Without Clutter: Privacy policy consent language is present but visually subordinate, balancing regulatory needs with UX simplicity.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any terminal confirmation step in a financial or transactional flow (e.g., after a bank transfer, withdrawal request, subscription cancellation, or order placement) where the user needs unambiguous confirmation that an action succeeded and clear expectations about what happens next (timing, amount, destination). It's ideal for modal/sheet presentations that cap off a flow initiated elsewhere in the app.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stripped-down pattern when the user might need to take further action (e.g., verifying details, choosing a delivery speed, or troubleshooting an issue) - in those cases a more informative screen with additional options or context is needed. It's also unsuitable for celebratory milestones (e.g., first deposit, goal achieved) where more delightful, expressive visuals and copy would better reinforce positive emotion and engagement.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of a fintech, neobank, or peer-to-peer payment app (the visual style is evocative of apps like Cash App or Venmo) who are moving money between internal wallets and external bank accounts. The specific $1 amount and 'external bank account' language suggest this could be part of an instant/standard transfer flow or bank account linking verification.

Psychologically, this screen leverages the need for closure and certainty in financial transactions. Users experience latent anxiety when money "disappears" from a visible balance during a transfer; providing an explicit date (Friday) and reaffirming success reduces support-ticket-driving worry and builds long-term trust in the platform's reliability.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-message clarity: Only one sentence of body copy communicates amount, destination, and exact timing, eliminating ambiguity about fund status.

  • Dual dismissal paths: Both the top-left 'X' and the bottom 'Done' button let users exit in the way that feels most natural to them.

  • Iconography reinforces state: The large green checkmark badge is universally recognized as 'success,' allowing users to grasp the outcome before even reading text.

  • No distractions: Absence of tab bars, ads, or upsells keeps focus entirely on confirming the transaction outcome, which builds trust.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for peer-to-peer payment, money transfer, or point-of-sale style apps where speed and simplicity of a single numeric input are paramount. It's ideal when the primary user action is entering an amount before choosing a downstream action (pay, request, split), and works well when brand differentiation through bold visual identity is a goal.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex financial transactions requiring multiple fields (e.g., international transfers with currency conversion, memo fields, or recipient selection) since the minimalist single-focus layout has no room for additional context without redesign. Also avoid using such a visually loud, saturated full-screen color for use-cases requiring prolonged reading or where accessibility/contrast concerns exist for users with visual impairments (the black-on-green contrast, while high, should be tested for colorblind accessibility).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, mobile-first consumers (Gen Z/Millennials) who are used to sending money as casually as texting, splitting a dinner bill, paying rent, or requesting money from friends. The design leverages the psychology of immediacy and low friction: by removing all non-essential UI, it taps into the user's desire for instant gratification and speed, reducing the number of decisions between "opening the app" and "money sent."

The dual-purpose Pool/Request/Pay action set also serves social use-cases (group payments, splitting costs), acknowledging that money movement among peers is often collaborative, not just transactional (a psychological nod to social norms around shared expenses).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Giant, unmissable amount display that doubles as both input and validation, eliminating any ambiguity about what value will be transacted.

  • Tri-action footer hierarchy: Pool and Request as secondary, equal-weight pill buttons, with Pay elevated as a high-contrast full-width primary button, guiding user intent without extra copy.

  • Custom full-screen numeric keypad replacing the OS-native number pad, giving the brand full control over typography, spacing, and touch target size for a faster, more tactile input experience.

  • Bold, saturated brand color (neon green) used as a full-bleed background, creating instant brand recognition and emotional energy atypical of finance apps.

  • Notification badge on avatar subtly nudges the user toward social/inbox activity without interrupting the primary payment flow.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 10
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any high-frequency, single-value input task where speed and minimal cognitive load are paramount. P2P payment apps, tipping calculators, ATM-style withdrawal screens, or quick top-up/reload flows. It's ideal when the user already understands the mental model (numeric keypad) and doesn't need guidance text.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex or multi-field financial transactions (e.g., international wire transfers requiring routing numbers, recipient verification, or fee breakdowns) where hiding information behind a giant keypad would obscure important context the user needs before committing. Also avoid the borderless/flat key style in accessibility-sensitive contexts or for less tech-savvy audiences (e.g., older users) who may need explicit button affordances to feel confident tapping.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets mainstream, mobile-first consumers conducting peer-to-peer payments (splitting bills, paying rent, sending gifts) who want speed over ceremony. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of transactional friction and anxiety: by making the numeric entry feel like a simple calculator interaction rather than a "banking form," Cash App lowers the perceived stakes of moving money.

The aggressive, high-saturation green also serves a branding/recognition psychology goal (it's instantly identifiable in screenshots and social sharing (a growth loop Cash App leans on heavily), reinforcing brand recall every time a user pays a friend).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized amount display as the unambiguous focal point, reinforcing the emotional weight of a money transaction.

  • Full-bleed, borderless numeric keypad that trades conventional key affordances for bold brand-color immersion.

  • Segmented action row (Pool / Request) paired with a high-contrast black "Pay" button, creating clear visual priority between primary and secondary transaction types.

  • Subtle color-fade on unconfirmed trailing digit ("0") as a lightweight, non-intrusive input-state indicator.

  • Persistent bottom tab bar ensures the money-entry flow never feels like a dead-end modal, letting users bail out to other app areas instantly.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 11
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any transactional flow where a single numeric value is the entire point of the interaction. P2P payments, tipping, ATM-style withdrawals, splitting bills, or in-store checkout entry. It's ideal when you want to minimize decision fatigue and maximize speed/confidence for repeat, high-frequency actions.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stripped-down approach for complex transactions requiring context (e.g., invoice details, multi-item carts, or transfers needing memo/category fields) since the extreme minimalism leaves no room for supporting information. Also reconsider the bold full-screen color treatment for enterprise/B2B fintech products where a more conservative, "trustworthy" visual language is expected by users handling large sums or business accounts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers, particularly younger and mobile-first demographics (Gen Z / Millennials) who send money to friends, split bills, or pay small vendors informally. The design leans on simplicity bias and reduced cognitive load: by stripping away all non-essential UI, the user's full attention channels into typing an accurate amount, reducing costly entry errors in a financial context.

The bold, playful green also taps into brand distinctiveness as a psychological trigger: in a category where most competitors use safe blue/white palettes, Cash App's saturated color makes the app instantly recognizable in screenshots, social sharing, and muscle memory, reinforcing loyalty and lowering the perceived "seriousness/anxiety" often associated with moving money.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Giant, auto-scaling amount display: The typography for the dollar amount is the largest element on screen by a huge margin, making error-checking the entered value effortless at a glance.

  • Dual-purpose split CTA row: "Pool" and "Request" as secondary pill buttons let the user branch into alternate money flows without leaving the keypad context, while "Pay" remains the unmistakable primary action in high-contrast black.

  • Custom full-bleed keypad: Numbers floating directly on the brand-green background (no boxed keys) keeps the UI feeling light and modern rather than like a clunky calculator/ATM.

  • Notification badge on avatar: The small red "2" badge on the profile icon cleverly injects a re-engagement hook even within a transactional flow.

  • Backspace glyph integrated into grid: Placing the delete arrow in the last keypad slot (instead of a separate floating icon) keeps the numeric input path spatially efficient and thumb-reachable.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 12
screens.whereToUse:
• P2P payment or fintech apps introducing group/shared payment features (bill splitting, gift pooling, fundraising).

  • Any flow where a large "hero number" needs to remain visually anchored while a secondary, lightweight detail (name, note, category) is collected via an overlay.

  • Quick-action flows where you want to minimize steps between decision and confirmation (single field + adjacent CTA).

  • Casual social finance products where terminology like "pool," "start," and playful naming increases approachability over formal banking language.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for high-stakes or complex financial transactions (e.g., loans, investments, multi-party legal agreements) where more fields, disclosures, or confirmations are legally or contextually necessary.

  • Not suitable when multiple required fields are needed before submission, cramming more inputs into this compact sheet would break the minimalist promise and hurt usability.

  • Avoid oversized "hero number" treatment on screens where multiple pieces of information are equally important; it can visually crowd out other necessary context.

  • Don't use casual, playful copy ("Start a pool") in enterprise, B2B, or regulated financial contexts where formal, precise language is expected.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumer users of P2P payment apps (friends splitting a bill, roommates pooling for a gift, or groups collecting money for an event ("Mobbin Party" example)). The design leans on social financial behavior psychology: framing money collection as a "pool" rather than a "request" or "invoice" reduces the awkwardness typically associated with asking peers for money.

The oversized dollar figure taps into a well-known fintech UX convention where users mentally anchor on the number before anything else, similar to a calculator or till display, reinforcing trust and clarity around exactly how much is being committed before any social or naming details are added.

The minimal-friction, single-field approach is designed for young, mobile-native, fast-decision users who expect financial actions to feel as lightweight as sending a text message.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized hero amount: The $100 figure occupies the majority of visual real estate, making the transaction amount unmistakably the emotional and functional focal point of the screen.

  • Inline input + CTA pairing: Placing the "Start" button directly beside the "For" text field (rather than pinned to the bottom) keeps the action within thumb/eye reach without requiring keyboard dismissal.

  • Layered bottom sheet over persistent context: The sheet doesn't obscure the $100 hero number entirely, letting users visually confirm the amount while completing the secondary naming step.

  • Auto-focused input: The cursor is already active in the field with the keyboard raised, removing an extra tap and speeding up task completion.

  • Single-field minimalism: Only one piece of information (the pool name/purpose) is requested before launch, minimizing form fatigue for a low-stakes social action.

screens.name: Cash App Managing Accounts 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any fintech, banking, or healthcare app settings area where multiple independent security layers (biometric, PIN, 2FA, trusted contacts) need to be surfaced together.

  • Products with multiple sub-products or data domains (e.g., core wallet vs. tax filing vs. investing) that warrant separate authentication requirements.

  • Settings screens where reducing user anxiety through plain-language explanations is more important than dense technical configuration.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this verbose, description-per-row pattern in settings with 15+ items, as it will create excessive scrolling (better to use a denser table or accordion grouping at that scale).

  • Not ideal for expert/developer-facing security consoles where users want fast, dense toggles without hand-holding copy.

  • Should not be used if the underlying settings change frequently, since maintaining accurate, friendly microcopy for many toggles increases content-ops overhead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers using Cash App for peer-to-peer payments, banking, investing, and tax filing (a broad demographic ranging from first-time banking app users to more security-conscious power users). Because Cash App handles real money movement and sensitive PII (SSN via Taxes), the design leans on the psychological principle of perceived control: giving users granular, clearly labeled toggles increases trust in the platform's handling of their financial data.

The "Off" status labels leverage a mild loss-aversion/completeness nudge: seeing an unprotected state listed plainly (without shaming) encourages users to close the gap, similar to a profile-completion prompt. The separation of Taxes security also signals institutional credibility to more cautious or first-time tax filers who may be wary of digitizing sensitive tax documents.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Self-explanatory rows: Every setting includes a one-line description so users never need to guess what a toggle does before interacting with it.

  • Segmented taxonomy: Splitting general "Security" from "Taxes access" acknowledges that tax data carries a different risk/sensitivity profile and deserves independent authentication (password + 2FA authenticator).

  • Consistent trailing affordances: Status text + chevron for navigational settings vs. a filled pill button for direct actions creates a predictable interaction language across the whole list.

  • Icon-led scanning: Distinct line icons (Face ID frame, asterisk/PIN, trusted contact, shield) let users visually locate a setting faster than reading text alone.

  • Progressive security layering: Offering both a password AND an authenticator app for taxes demonstrates defense-in-depth without forcing both simultaneously (the authenticator is offered as an optional upgrade).

screens.name: Dave Setting Up 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this icon-grid + promo-card pattern for account/settings hub screens where users need fast access to a handful of frequently used, disconvnected actions (e.g., banking apps, wallet apps, utility/service apps). It's ideal directly beneath an account's top-level landing view, and works well to cross-sell secondary features (savings tools, upgrades, add-ons) without resorting to hard interruption or modals.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are more than 6-8 actions, as the grid loses scannability and needs pagination or scroll fatigue sets in. Also avoid stacking too many promotional cards below the grid (more than 2-3 will make the screen feel like an ad feed rather than a utility hub, undermining the "low-drama" trust the brand is trying to build). Not suitable for first-time users who haven't yet learned the icon meanings; in that case, add labels-only or a guided tour first.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Dave's target user is a busy, often financially-stretched urban consumer who needs quick, judgment-free access to banking basics. This screen's grid layout assumes the user already knows roughly what they want to do (deposit, withdraw, pay a bill) and simply needs the fastest path (this matches the "advance-first, one-tap balance check" ease-of-use philosophy stated in the app's design principles).

The direct deposit and budgeting nudges specifically target the psychological pain point this audience faces: cash flow timing gaps. By promoting "paid 2 days early" here, Dave subtly reinforces its core retention loop (get users on direct deposit so Dave can predict paychecks and safely offer advances) while framing it as a user benefit rather than a business requirement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-first grid navigation: Six equally-weighted rounded tiles let users recognize actions via icon + label combo, speeding up scanning versus a text-only list.

  • Progressive disclosure of value: Core utilities (transfers, cash handling, bill pay) are given top billing; growth/engagement features (direct deposit, budgeting) are pushed below as secondary, low-pressure suggestions.

  • Benefit-forward nudge cards: Each promo card leads with the user outcome ("get paid early", "stay on top of spending") rather than the feature name, increasing perceived relevance and reducing feature-explanation friction.

  • Consistent mint-green iconography against neutral grey tiles reinforces brand color while maintaining low visual noise, aligning with the "low-drama" positioning of the brand.

screens.name: Oportun Editing Profile 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for account/profile settings screens in fintech, banking, healthcare, or any regulated industry where certain PII fields (like legal name or SSN) require verified backend processes to change, while other fields (phone, email) can be self-serviced through in-app flows like OTP verification.

Also effective whenever you want to provide a clear support fallback for edge cases not covered by self-service UI, rather than blocking the user entirely.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this asymmetric editability pattern in low-risk consumer apps (e.g., social or productivity apps) where users expect to freely edit any profile field instantly, adding artificial friction there would feel bureaucratic and annoying.

Also avoid if you can't clearly communicate *why* a field isn't editable; users may perceive it as a bug if there's no explanatory copy (as provided here in the footer note).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of a regulated financial product (loans, cards, or banking) who need to manage their account contact details. The design assumes a security-conscious, compliance-first audience where identity fraud prevention outweighs pure self-service convenience.

Psychologically, masking the phone number and restricting name edits builds implicit trust: users subconsciously register that the company is protecting their identity data carefully, which is reassuring in a financial context. The clear support escape hatch also reduces anxiety for users who hit a wall, preventing them from feeling trapped or abandoning the app in frustration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Selective Editability: Deliberately omitting a "Change" action next to Full Name (while offering it for Phone/Email) subtly communicates a business/compliance rule without needing an explicit disclaimer next to the field itself.

  • Masked Phone Number: The phone number is shown as a blurred/redacted placeholder bar rather than plain digits, a subtle privacy/security affordance protecting PII from shoulder-surfing.

  • Human Fallback for Edge Cases: Rather than building complex in-app logic for name changes (which often require legal document uploads), the design punts to human support (a pragmatic MVP decision that avoids scope creep while still serving the user).

  • Consistent Action Color Coding: Using the same green for "Change" links and the support email creates a clear visual language for "things you can tap."

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for the first screen of an app's onboarding/acquisition flow when the goal is to create strong emotional resonance and brand differentiation before requesting any user effort or data. It's ideal for consumer fintech, lifestyle, or premium subscription apps competing in a crowded market where perceived quality and personality are conversion levers. It also works well when the product has a genuinely distinctive visual identity worth showcasing via motion/3D assets.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, animation-first approach for utility apps, enterprise/B2B tools, or contexts where users need fast, functional access (e.g., re-opening a banking app to check a balance) - repeated exposure to elaborate splash content becomes friction and annoyance for returning users. It's also risky on low-end devices or poor networks where a complex animated render may cause jank or slow load times, undermining the very premium feel it's meant to convey. Additionally, purely aspirational copy without any functional/security reassurance (FDIC, encryption, etc.) may reduce trust in more risk-averse or older banking demographics.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets a broad, digitally-savvy audience (travelers, freelancers, students, and young professionals) who are evaluating Revolut against both traditional banks and other neobanks (Monzo, N26, Wise). The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Novelty & spectacle bias: The dazzling motion visual creates a halo effect, making users unconsciously associate the app with innovation and technical sophistication.

  • Identity signaling: The irreverent copy ("money" as a verb) appeals to a self-image of being modern, tech-forward, and not tied to "old-school" banking norms.

  • Commitment priming: The progress bar exploits the human preference for completing started sequences (goal-gradient effect), increasing the odds a user continues through subsequent onboarding steps once they've begun.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Cinematic first impression: A high-production 3D coin/warp animation replaces a static logo screen, creating an emotional "wow" moment that differentiates Revolut from traditional bank apps within the first second of use.

  • Clear CTA hierarchy: A solid, high-contrast "Create account" button paired with a subtle ghost "Log in" button ensures new-user acquisition is prioritized while not alienating returning users.

  • Progress indicator on a splash screen: Placing a step/segment bar at the very top, even before any input is required, primes users to expect a short, finite onboarding journey rather than an open-ended one.

  • Provocative, on-brand copywriting: The verb-ified "money" headline is memorable, quotable, and instantly communicates brand personality over generic "Welcome" copy.

  • Full dark-mode immersion: The near-black background with luminous blue/white streaks reinforces the "premium/futuristic fintech" positioning called out in Revolut's brand look and feel.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Pre-authentication marketing/value-prop carousels for apps with a strong physical or visual product component (cards, devices, merchandise).

  • Onboarding flows where you need to communicate a core differentiator before asking for sign-up commitment.

  • Any app serving both new and returning users from the same entry screen, where CTA hierarchy needs to gracefully serve two audiences.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for utility or productivity apps where the core value isn't visually representable (an abstract illustration-heavy carousel may feel like empty marketing fluff).

  • Not ideal if legal/compliance disclaimers are extensive; a single small caption line works here, but heavier regulatory text would break the clean layout and require a different disclosure pattern (e.g., expandable footnote).

  • Should be skipped or shortened for returning users who've already seen onboarding (repeated exposure to the same static carousel can feel patronizing and slow down re-engagement).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen is engineered for Revolut's core acquisition funnel: travelers, digital nomads, and internationally-minded professionals who are anxious about currency friction and payment acceptance abroad. By foregrounding "home and away" usability with a vivid card visual, the design triggers aspirational travel/freedom associations and reduces the perceived complexity of switching banks. The rainbow card also signals brand inclusivity, appealing to socially-conscious younger demographics (students, freelancers) who value brands aligning with their identity. The low-friction dual CTA respects both new prospects and existing loyal users returning to check balances, minimizing abandonment at the very first touchpoint of the app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Product-as-hero visual: Instead of abstract illustrations, real stacked card designs (including a Pride-themed card) are shown, instantly communicating brand personality, customization options, and physical tangibility of the offering.

  • Dual-path CTA hierarchy: A visually lighter 'Create account' pill above a stronger, solid black 'Log in' button cleverly reverses the expected emphasis, putting acquisition (new users) visually secondary but positionally first, while returning users get the higher-contrast action, reducing friction for both cohorts.

  • Line-segment progress indicator: Communicates a short, scannable onboarding journey, setting the right expectation of "just a few more screens" rather than an intimidating open-ended flow.

  • Benefit-first messaging: Leads with an outcome ("easy to pay at home and away") rather than a feature list, aligning with best-practice onboarding copy that sells the transformation, not the mechanism.

screens.name: Revolut Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern during pre-login onboarding carousels for finance, brokerage, or super-app platforms that offer multiple distinct services (banking, crypto, stocks). It is highly effective when you need to:

  • Advertise a specific sub-feature (like Stocks) within a broader app ecosystem before requiring sign-up.

  • De-risk a historically intimidating category (investing) using familiar visual cues (famous brand logos).

  • Maintain legal compliance while keeping the primary marketing hook the dominant visual element.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, marketing-forward carousel approach for:

  • Utility or productivity apps where users expect to jump straight to the login/sign-up form without marketing friction.

  • B2B or enterprise software where flashy 3D visuals of competitor/partner logos might seem unprofessional or could imply unintended affiliations/endorsements.

  • Situations where the disclaimer needs higher visual prominence (e.g., high-risk derivatives trading) as this treatment intentionally minimizes the risk warning's visual weight.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new-to-investing consumers or existing Revolut banking users being cross-sold into the investment vertical. The messaging "From $1" specifically targets younger demographics (Gen Z/Millennials) or low-capital users who have been historically priced out of traditional brokerage account minimums.

Psychologically, the screen leverages Social Proof / Brand Authority (via recognizable logos like Apple and Google) to imply legitimacy and safety, alongside an Anchoring effect where the low dollar amount ("$1") anchors the perception of investing as low-risk/low-commitment rather than an activity reserved for the wealthy.
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.keyHighlights:
• Hybrid Input Strategy: Combines a high-level "Search address" typeahead with granular, editable fields below (Postal Code, Street, Unit), giving power users the speed of search while allowing manual correction for edge cases.

  • Localized Format Hints: Using real Singaporean context (National Gallery, Ayer Rajah Crescent) in placeholders builds immediate geographic trust and reduces formatting ambiguity.

  • Proactive Character Limits: Visible counters (22/50, 5/50) prevent frustrating truncation errors upon submission.

  • Compliance-Driven Copy: Explicitly linking the form to the "identity document" reduces the abandonment/rejection rate common in KYC flows by aligning user input with backend verification requirements upfront.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for account creation or login flows where you want to maximize completion rates by presenting one discrete, low-effort task per screen. It is ideal for consumer apps, subscription services, and any flow where user drop-off during registration is a key metric to optimize. Also effective when supporting platform-native privacy features (like Hide My Email or Sign in with Apple) to build trust.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this fully atomized single-field approach in enterprise/B2B contexts or forms where users expect to see the full scope of required information upfront (e.g., long compliance forms), as excessive step-by-step fragmentation can feel slow and patronizing. Also avoid if the app's user base skews toward power users who prefer filling multiple fields quickly on one screen, or in low-connectivity contexts where multiple screen transitions add perceptible latency.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets mainstream mobile-first consumer app users going through account creation, particularly those sensitive to friction and privacy. By breaking the sign-up process into atomic steps (email-only here), it caters to shorter attention spans and reduces the perceived effort of onboarding (a well-documented method for improving funnel conversion rates in consumer apps (fintech, social, subscription services)).

The reliance on native OS-level privacy affordances (Hide My Email) appeals to privacy-conscious users, particularly iOS users who are accustomed to and trust Apple's privacy ecosystem, thereby lowering the psychological barrier to giving out an email address.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-field focus: Isolating just the email field per screen (rather than bundling with password/name) drastically reduces cognitive load and abandonment risk.

  • Keyboard-first layout: Content is pre-composed to sit correctly above the system keyboard, eliminating jarring layout shifts when the keyboard appears.

  • Disabled CTA as validation gate: The greyed-out "Continue" button offers implicit, non-intrusive validation before any error messaging is needed.

  • Native "Hide My Email" integration: Leveraging Apple's built-in privacy feature builds trust and reduces the perceived risk of providing an email.

  • High-contrast gradient background: The vivid blue-to-black gradient creates visual hierarchy, drawing the eye to the top content while gracefully receding into the dark keyboard area.

screens.name: Revolut Post-Onboarding 10
screens.whereToUse:
• Sign-up or login flows where maximizing conversion/completion rate is the primary business goal.

  • Multi-step onboarding sequences where breaking data collection into digestible, single-purpose screens reduces perceived effort.

  • Products targeting mobile-first, on-the-go users who benefit from thumb-reachable CTAs and auto-focused inputs.

  • Brand experiences aiming for a premium, minimalist, distraction-free first impression.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this single-field-per-screen approach for internal/enterprise tools or data-heavy forms where users expect to see multiple related fields at once (e.g., billing address forms) - excessive fragmentation here creates fatigue rather than reducing it.

  • Not ideal when users need to reference multiple fields simultaneously (e.g., password confirmation fields benefit from being visible together).

  • Should be avoided if analytics show users abandon due to "step fatigue" from too many sequential screens rather than field complexity.

  • The stark, dark, minimal aesthetic may not suit brands requiring more warmth, imagery, or trust-building context (e.g., healthcare or financial services needing more reassurance copy).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users in the critical first-conversion moment of an app's lifecycle (the sign-up funnel). Because drop-off rates are highest during account creation, every element is engineered to minimize friction and cognitive burden.

Psychologically, breaking the form into single-field steps leverages the Zeigarnik effect (the tendency to feel compelled to complete a task once started) and reduces the intimidation of a long form by making progress feel incremental and effortless. The immediate keyboard presence exploits momentum (once a user is already typing, they are less likely to abandon the flow than if they had to first tap into a field).

This approach is best suited for consumer apps (social, entertainment, fintech onboarding) where maximizing sign-up completion is a primary KPI, and where the brand wants to project a slick, modern, low-friction identity.
screens.keyHighlights:
