• Single-field focus: Isolating email capture to its own screen (rather than bundling with password/name) dramatically reduces perceived effort and abandonment risk.

  • Auto-invoked keyboard: The keyboard is already active on screen load, saving the user a tap and creating a frictionless, momentum-driven entry experience.

  • Thumb-zone CTA placement: The "Continue" button sits directly above the keyboard, optimizing for one-handed reachability rather than being stranded at the top of the screen.

  • High contrast, distraction-free visual design: The deep gradient background with stark white typography creates a focused, premium "spotlight" effect on the single task at hand.

  • Inline clear (x) affordance: Allows instant field clearing, reducing friction for correcting typos in a field notorious for entry errors.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern when a regulated financial (or health) product feature requires mandatory disclosure before or immediately after activation (e.g., overdraft, credit, buy-now-pay-later, insurance).

  • Ideal for surfacing legal/compliance text without derailing the user into a separate full-page flow (keeps momentum while still being legally defensible).

  • Effective when pairing a positive benefit statement with a necessary risk disclosure, to maintain user trust and reduce drop-off/anxiety.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for complex multi-clause agreements requiring explicit affirmative consent per clause (e.g., multi-item T&Cs) - a single "Got it" button may not satisfy stricter legal consent requirements.

  • Don't use dimmed-background bottom sheets when the disclosure is critical enough to require undivided attention; a full-screen interstitial with explicit checkbox consent may be more appropriate for higher-stakes agreements.

  • Not suitable if the disclosure text is long enough to require scrolling within the sheet itself, as users may dismiss without reading (consider requiring scroll-to-bottom before enabling the CTA).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets users of Dave, a fintech app serving budget-conscious, often paycheck-to-paycheck consumers who rely on small-dollar cash advances (ExtraCash) to cover short-term gaps. The design leverages trust and transparency framing: by proactively explaining that the advance functions as an overdraft that creates a negative balance, Dave protects itself legally while also building credibility with a demographic that may be wary of hidden fees from traditional banks or predatory lenders.

Psychologically, the warm illustrated mascot bear and rounded, friendly UI in the background reduce anxiety around what is fundamentally a debt-like product, while the disclosure text satisfies CFPB/regulatory transparency expectations for overdraft-style advances.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual background dimming: Keeping the originating screen visible (though dimmed) behind the sheet preserves context and reduces the jarring "where am I" feeling common with full-screen legal modals.

  • Benefit-first, risk-second copy structure: Leading with the value prop headline before the overdraft/fee disclaimer softens the psychological impact of the negative-balance warning.

  • Single frictionless CTA: Only one exit path ("Got it") avoids decision fatigue and speeds users back into the product flow, which is ideal for a mandatory-read disclosure rather than a marketing decision point.

  • Inline legal link: Offloading the full account agreement to a hyperlink keeps the primary modal short while still legally covering the deeper terms.

screens.name: Cash App Login 1
screens.whereToUse: This Verification + Smart Defaults combination fits any account login or sensitive-action flow requiring two-factor or step-up authentication, where defaulting to the user's most likely-accessible method speeds up the common case while still supporting recovery scenarios.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a first-time account creation flow, where no default verification method or masked identifier yet exists and the user must actively supply contact information rather than confirm a pre-filled one.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• PayPal (2FA code request screen): uses the same masked-contact-plus-"Next" pattern for sending a one-time login code via email or SMS.

  • Venmo (login verification screen): offers a comparable default verification method with an alternate "try another way" fallback option.

  • Chase Mobile (identity verification for login): presents a similar pre-selected contact method with a masked identifier and a secondary path for alternate verification.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart defaults reduce friction: pre-selecting email as the verification method with the radio dot already filled lets most users complete this step with a single "Next" tap.

  • Privacy by design: masking the actual email address protects the user's personal information from shoulder-surfing while still confirming which account/method is in use.

  • Graceful degradation: "Verify another way" ensures users without access to this email (e.g., changed providers, lost access) aren't blocked, supporting account recovery scenarios.

  • Minimalism at a high-friction step: keeping the screen to a single option, two buttons, and no extraneous content reduces cognitive load at a step users want to move through quickly.

screens.name: Craft - Deleting a comment - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Collaborative document/content editors (specs, wikis, knowledge bases) where feedback needs precise textual anchoring.
  • Design or writing tools supporting asynchronous team review cycles.
  • Any product with a review/approval workflow where comment resolution status matters.
  • Apps wanting to preserve a clean, distraction-free reading surface while still supporting rich collaboration metadata.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Single-player, personal-only note apps where no collaboration ever occurs (the commenting chrome would be dead weight).
  • Dense, highly technical documents where many overlapping comment anchors could create visual clutter or ambiguity about which highlight maps to which thread.
  • Small screens with very short content where a bottom sheet would obscure too much of the source material, breaking the anchored-context benefit.
  • Real-time pair-editing scenarios where live cursors/presence are more appropriate than an asynchronous comment thread.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets collaborative knowledge workers, designers, and product teams who use Craft not just for personal note-taking but as a shared document/spec tool (likely small startup teams, design studios, or cross-functional product squads reviewing specs together). The psychological trigger at play is social accountability and clarity: by anchoring feedback directly to the contested text, the app reduces the cognitive friction of "what are they even talking about?" and encourages faster, more confident iteration. The realistic back-and-forth dialogue ("may attract the wrong audience" → "agree, will revise it") demonstrates a trust-building use case: showing prospective users that critique and consensus can happen asynchronously and painlessly inside the writing surface itself, rather than requiring context-switching to Slack or email.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Block-level, anchored commenting: Rather than attaching feedback to an entire page, Craft ties comments to a specific highlighted passage, which is a sophisticated editorial-document pattern rarely seen outside professional tools like Google Docs or Figma.
  • Non-intrusive visual anchor: The commented text is tinted with a soft, on-brand pale blue rather than a jarring highlighter-yellow, preserving the app's quiet, editorial aesthetic even while surfacing collaboration metadata.
  • Lightweight metadata strip: Avatars + comment count + relative timestamp condense collaboration status into a single scannable line, avoiding clutter.
  • Partial-height bottom sheet: Comments slide up without fully obscuring the source document, letting the user maintain context of what's being discussed while reading/replying.
  • Resolve affordance: The checkmark icon in the Comments header suggests a one-tap way to mark feedback as resolved, reinforcing a lightweight review workflow.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Any app requiring a brief initialization period for authentication checks, key decryption, or network handshakes before the home experience can render.

  • Fintech, banking, or security-sensitive apps where brand trust and calm confidence need to be established in the very first moment of interaction.

  • Apps that want to mask backend complexity (multichain RPC calls, wallet unlocking) behind a simple, reassuring visual rather than exposing granular loading states.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid if the loading process regularly exceeds 2-3 seconds (users will need feedback (a progress indicator) to avoid perceiving the app as frozen or broken).

  • Not ideal for first-time installs where value-prop education is needed; a static splash provides no marketing or onboarding value and should transition quickly into a Value-Prop Carousel or Setup Wizard.

  • Should not be used as a persistent branding tool beyond the technical load, prolonging it artificially (e.g., for marketing purposes) frustrates returning users who want instant access to their funds.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
For busy urban professionals managing crypto on the go, first impressions of speed and security are critical trust signals before they'll commit private keys or funds to an app. A clean, dark, branded splash screen triggers immediate associations with premium fintech products (banking apps, Apple Pay) rather than volatile or amateur crypto tools.

Psychologically, the instant, unadorned brand mark reduces the anxiety inherent in "waiting" states for financial apps (users subconsciously equate simplicity and restraint with technical competence and security rigor, which is essential for an app whose core value proposition is safely self-custodying irreversible on-chain assets).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Brand equity transfer: Leveraging the well-known "coinbase" name to instantly reassure users entering the more intimidating world of self-custody, while "WALLET" clearly demarcates it as a distinct, non-custodial product line.

  • Zero cognitive load: No interactive elements, text, or motion competing for attention (pure brand imprinting during the technical loading window).

  • Dark, high-contrast palette: Reinforces a premium, secure, "vault-like" feeling appropriate for an app safeguarding financial assets, and reduces OLED battery draw and eye strain for on-the-go urban users checking their wallet at all hours.

  • Seamless OS-level feel: The lack of a spinner mimics a native system transition, making the app feel fast, stable, and trustworthy from the very first frame.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for the first screen of any onboarding flow where the primary goal is to route the user into one of two mutually exclusive paths (e.g., sign up vs. log in, create vs. restore, start fresh vs. continue). It's ideal for consumer fintech, crypto, and identity-driven apps where trust and simplicity must be established immediately.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the app requires upfront explanation of complex risk (e.g., irreversible seed-phrase custody) - a purely decorative welcome screen without any educational framing could lead users to make an uninformed choice. Also avoid for B2B or utility apps where users expect to get straight to functional content rather than a branded moment; excessive animation/illustration in those contexts can feel like unnecessary friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both crypto newcomers and returning users of the broader Coinbase ecosystem, specifically "Busy Urbans" who want quick, low-friction access to a self-custody wallet without lengthy explanations. The minimal copy and single-decision layout cater to short attention spans and mobile-first usage patterns.

Psychologically, the screen leverages choice reduction (only two clear paths forward), aesthetic-usability effect (the vibrant token art makes the abstract concept of "digital assets" feel tangible and exciting rather than clinical), and trust signaling through polished dark-mode fintech visuals that echo premium banking and crypto-native apps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Playful token-art motion design: Floating crypto/NFT icons and sparkle accents around the central logo create a sense of liveliness, richness, and "digital treasure," reinforcing the value proposition of a wallet full of possibilities without saying a word.

  • Single dominant CTA: Using a stark white pill button against a black canvas ensures the primary action is impossible to miss, directly reducing onboarding drop-off.

  • Legally compliant but non-intrusive consent: Terms/privacy links are woven into a single sentence rather than requiring an explicit checkbox or blocking modal, striking a good balance between compliance and friction reduction.

  • Dark, premium aesthetic: The near-black background with vivid blue/green/purple gradients evokes a "digital vault" feeling appropriate for a self-custody financial product, building trust and a sense of security.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any short, non-cancelable background process critical to security or account setup (wallet/key generation, encryption setup, biometric enrollment, account provisioning, or backend account creation during sign-up). It's ideal whenever the operation takes a few seconds and cannot be meaningfully progressed by a progress bar (i.e., duration is unpredictable).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this indeterminate, full-screen blocking pattern for longer processes (over ~10-15 seconds) where users need a sense of progress (use a determinate progress bar with a percentage or step count instead). Also avoid it for interruptible or resumable tasks, where a cancel option should be provided to respect user control. Overusing full-screen blocking loaders across an app can also feel heavy-handed for trivial operations that could instead use inline skeleton loaders.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Coinbase Wallet's "Busy Urbans" target audience typically has low patience for friction and jargon. This screen is engineered to hold their attention for the few seconds required to securely generate a wallet without triggering doubt ("Did it freeze?") or drop-off. The dark, secure-vault aesthetic also plays to the psychological need for trust and safety when a user is about to be handed sole custody of their financial assets (a moment where perceived reliability of the underlying technology is critical to conversion).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radical minimalism: Removing all extraneous UI (no back button, no cancel, no branding clutter) signals to the user that this is a protected, atomic operation that shouldn't be interrupted.

  • Single-point focus: Pairing an indeterminate spinner with one short status line concentrates attention and reduces the perceived complexity of an inherently technical cryptographic task.

  • Reassurance through plain language: Translating a complex security operation into a simple, human sentence builds trust and reduces onboarding drop-off anxiety.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use native system permission dialogs with a custom rationale string whenever requesting sensitive OS-level permissions (biometrics, camera, location, notifications) in finance, health, or identity apps. Always trigger the prompt contextually (right after the user reaches a step where the permission's value is obvious) rather than immediately on app launch. Pair with a pre-permission "priming" screen beforehand when the ask is non-obvious, to increase acceptance rates since the system dialog itself cannot be visually persuaded.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid firing this system dialog blindly at first launch before the user understands why biometric access matters (this depresses opt-in rates and can trigger app-store-review-style rejection reflexes). Do not attempt to visually bias the "Allow" button (not possible on iOS, but relevant on Android custom equivalents) as it violates platform guidelines and erodes user trust. Also avoid re-prompting repeatedly after a "Don't Allow" response, since iOS suppresses re-prompting and repeated soft-asks feel naggy.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Targets "Busy Urbans" who need fast, frictionless access to their funds throughout the day (tapping to pay, checking balances on the go) without repeatedly entering PINs or passwords. Face ID satisfies both their need for speed (one-glance unlock) and their heightened need for security assurance, since this audience is managing real monetary value in a self-custody product with no bank-style fraud reversal safety net.

Psychologically, this leans on loss aversion (protecting money/data) and trust transfer from Apple's native biometric system, which users already trust for banking and payment apps, making them more willing to extend that trust to Coinbase Wallet.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom rationale string: Coinbase overrides the default system copy with a benefit-driven, security-framed sentence tailored to a financial wallet context.

  • Contextual timing: Presumably triggered after a relevant in-app moment (e.g., end of wallet setup) rather than an abrupt cold-start request, increasing acceptance likelihood.

  • Low-friction security upgrade: A single tap enables biometric lock, reducing future password/PIN entry friction while reinforcing the sense of a secure, self-custody product.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Pre-Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any dashboard, wallet, or account-balance screen that can legitimately be at zero (new accounts, financial apps, portfolio trackers). Ideal when there is one clear, dominant recovery action (e.g., "Add funds," "Connect account," "Import data") and you want to avoid a jarring blank screen. Especially effective when the product has an adjacent, trusted parent brand/account that can be leveraged as an easy funding source.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy illustration-driven empty state for screens where zero-state is rare or unexpected (e.g., a returning user who should have data (here an error state or reload prompt is more appropriate)). Also avoid duplicating the CTA at both top and bottom on very short-viewport screens, as it can feel repetitive or noisy if the whole screen already fits without scrolling. Not suitable when there are multiple equally important next steps, since the pattern is optimized for single-path conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Targets new or newly-onboarded crypto wallet users (including those migrating from a Coinbase exchange account) who have just created or imported a wallet and have zero on-chain assets. The design leverages the Zeigarnik effect and progress-oriented framing (presenting "$0.00" not as a dead end but as step one of an implied journey) plus reduction of decision paralysis by offering exactly one clear CTA. The Coinbase-brand link icon exploits trust transfer: users familiar with the centralized exchange are reassured that moving funds to the self-custody wallet is safe and easy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-illustration branding: The empty state graphic visually links the Coinbase (C) logo and Wallet logo via a chain icon, subtly reinforcing that funds can flow seamlessly from the Coinbase exchange account into the self-custody wallet (a key value proposition and cross-sell mechanic).

  • Persistent, redundant CTA: "Add crypto" appears both inline (attached to the empty state) and pinned near the tab bar, ensuring the primary action is always reachable regardless of scroll position.

  • Pre-populated navigation: Buy/Swap/Cash out and Crypto/NFTs/DeFi tabs remain visible and tappable even with $0 balance, letting curious users explore the app's structure before committing funds.

  • Contextual guidance over generic error: Instead of a blank void, the empty state proactively explains *why* it's empty and *how* to fix it in one sentence.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 8
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing an optional but high-value identity or convenience feature immediately after a core setup task (e.g., account creation, wallet generation) is completed. It's ideal for:

  • Turning technical/system-generated identifiers (IDs, hashes, URLs) into memorable, ownable handles.

  • Driving adoption of a free feature that increases platform lock-in or network effects (e.g., usernames, handles, custom URLs).

  • Any onboarding moment where you want to offer value without blocking progress, preserving a low-friction funnel.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen interstitial pattern for minor or low-value features, as it adds an extra step to onboarding and risks fatigue if used too many times in sequence. It's also inappropriate when the feature is mandatory for core functionality, framing something as an optional "claim" implies it's non-essential, so critical setup steps (like security backups or KYC) should use firmer, non-skippable UI instead. Additionally, this pattern should be skipped for expert/returning users who already understand and have configured their identity settings.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded Coinbase Wallet users, particularly crypto newcomers who are unfamiliar with or intimidated by long alphanumeric wallet addresses (e.g., 0x71C...). By offering a free, human-readable username, Coinbase reduces onboarding friction for peer-to-peer transfers and social sharing, while also increasing platform stickiness (a claimed username creates a sunk-cost/identity investment in the Coinbase ecosystem specifically).

The NFT-avatar imagery also signals to a crypto-native audience (holders of profile-picture NFTs) that this wallet supports and celebrates digital identity/collectibles culture, subtly appealing to that community's values around personalization and status signaling.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metaphorical Illustration: The wallet-as-ID-card visual instantly communicates an abstract Web3 concept (self-custody identity) through a familiar physical object metaphor.

  • Asymmetric Button Hierarchy: A stark contrast between the solid white primary CTA and the dark, muted secondary CTA visually funnels the user toward the desired action without removing choice.

  • Ownership-Framed Copy: Use of "Claim" and "my username" leverages loss-aversion and personal ownership psychology to boost adoption of an optional feature.

  • Non-Blocking Value-Add: Framed as an enhancement to an already-completed action (wallet creation) rather than a mandatory gate, keeping the onboarding funnel from feeling coercive.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for financial dashboards, wallets, brokerage, or portfolio-tracking apps where a single aggregate number is the most important piece of information a returning user needs. It's ideal when the product supports multiple asset types/categories that benefit from a lightweight tab/segment switcher, and when the primary actions are few and highly repeatable (buy, sell, transfer).

Also effective for multi-chain or multi-account products needing an "All networks/accounts" aggregation pattern to reduce fragmentation anxiety.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal, jargon-heavy approach for first-time user onboarding or consumer-facing apps targeting non-expert audiences (the lack of labels, explanations, or empty-state guidance would confuse users unfamiliar with terms like "Swap" or "DeFi)." Also unsuitable for information-dense enterprise dashboards where users need multiple data points (charts, historical trends) visible simultaneously rather than a single hero balance.

If the product anticipates predominantly zero-balance or churned users, a more directive empty-state with explanatory copy and a stronger single CTA would outperform this three-button pattern.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This design targets self-custody crypto users: ranging from active DeFi/NFT participants to casual holders (who value speed, control, and data density over hand-holding). The lack of explanatory text and reliance on symbols (arrows, percentages, chain icons) signals a design decision to serve an already-literate audience rather than first-time crypto users.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss/gain framing (green up-arrow percentage) to trigger dopamine responses tied to portfolio performance, a well-documented engagement driver in fintech apps. The prominent, high-contrast gradient Buy button exploits the path-of-least-resistance principle: with a near-empty balance, funding the wallet is the only rational next action, so the interface funnels attention there through color and positioning rather than copy.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Balance-first hierarchy: The total dollar value ($10.68) is rendered in the largest type on the screen, immediately answering the user's #1 question ("how much do I have?") before anything else.

  • Three-action pill row: Buy/Swap/Cash out condenses the entire transactional surface area of a wallet into one thumb-reachable row, with the gradient Buy button visually prioritized as the default entry action for low/zero balance states.

  • Segmented asset taxonomy: Crypto/NFTs/DeFi tabs let a single wallet address represent multiple asset classes without cluttering the main list, scaling gracefully as portfolios grow more complex.

  • Network filter chip: "All networks" dropdown quietly solves one of the biggest pain points of multi-chain wallets (chain fragmentation) by defaulting to an aggregated cross-chain view.

  • Icon-only bottom navigation: Maximizes content space in a chart/number-dense app while relying on universally recognized wallet iconography.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building any flow involving irreversible actions with high-stakes consequences (private key/seed phrase encryption, non-recoverable account deletion, or backup encryption for end-to-end encrypted data). It's ideal wherever standard "forgot password" recovery flows are impossible and users need explicit priming before proceeding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of friction and alarming language for low-stakes or recoverable actions (e.g., standard app login, everyday settings) as it will feel unnecessarily intimidating and increase drop-off. Also avoid disabling the CTA without clear visual/text feedback explaining why it's disabled (if there's no secondary hint (like field validation state or a tooltip), users may feel confused about what's blocking progress).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users (Coinbase Wallet) who are setting up encrypted cloud backups of their seed phrase (a mix of crypto-native and mainstream users who may not fully grasp the irreversibility of losing a non-custodial password). The psychological trigger here is loss aversion: by front-loading the catastrophic consequence of forgetting the password, the design leverages fear to increase attentiveness and encourage users to store the password securely (e.g., in a password manager) rather than treating it casually like a typical app password.

The forced checkbox also serves a commitment and consistency psychological principle, having users actively affirm understanding increases perceived personal responsibility and reduces blame-shifting behavior later.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit risk acknowledgment gate: Users must actively check a box confirming they understand irreversible loss consequences (this is a deliberate friction point that shifts responsibility and reduces support burden from "I lost my password" complaints).

  • Disabled CTA until requirements met: The visually muted "Continue" button acts as an implicit validation cue without needing explicit error messaging.

  • Password visibility toggle: Standard but essential affordance letting users confirm accuracy before committing to an unrecoverable secret.

  • Inline legal consent: Bundling terms/privacy acceptance with the security disclaimer streamlines compliance without adding a separate screen.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an application requires the user to create credentials or perform an action that is genuinely irreversible and has severe consequences (e).g., encryption keys, recovery phrases, wallet backups, or one-way account deletion. It's ideal when standard "forgot password" safety nets do not exist and the user must be made acutely aware of that fact before proceeding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed warning approach for low-stakes password creation (e.g., a standard app login) as it will feel alarmist and increase abandonment unnecessarily. Also avoid disabling primary CTAs without clear visual/textual feedback explaining why the button is inactive (some users may not immediately understand the checkbox is a hard gate, so pairing it with inline validation or a tooltip is recommended for lower-friction implementations).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets both crypto-curious newcomers and experienced self-custody users setting up a Coinbase Wallet (a non-custodial wallet, distinct from the custodial Coinbase exchange app). The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion combined with responsibility transfer: the app explicitly disclaims responsibility ("We can't reset it if you lose it") to set correct mental models about self-custody, preventing future support tickets and user frustration. The heavy warning language also serves a legal/liability purpose, protecting the company by ensuring informed consent is documented via the checkbox interaction.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit risk framing before action: Rather than burying the "no recovery" warning in fine print, it's placed front-and-center in both the header description and the checkbox copy, ensuring informed consent for an irreversible action.

  • Gated CTA via mandatory checkbox: The Continue button's disabled/low-emphasis state until the checkbox is ticked acts as a forcing function, guaranteeing the user cannot accidentally skip past critical risk disclosure.

  • Password reveal toggles: The masked eye icon on both fields lets users visually verify what they've typed before committing to a password that, if forgotten, causes permanent asset loss, reducing typo-induced lockouts.

  • Double entry confirmation pattern: Requiring the password twice (create + confirm) prevents fat-finger errors from locking a user out of an unrecoverable encrypted backup.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a user is about to set a credential or complete an action with severe, irreversible consequences (e).g., wallet seed phrase backups, account deletion, encryption keys, or financial transfers. It's ideal any time you need documented, active user acknowledgment of risk before enabling a destructive or high-stakes irreversible action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed, risk-laden approach for low-stakes or reversible actions (e.g., changing an app theme or a recoverable account password), as it will feel alarmist and increase drop-off/friction unnecessarily. Also avoid stacking multiple full paragraphs of risk copy on flows where the user is already fatigued (e.g., deep into a 10+ step onboarding), as comprehension will drop (consider chunking into a dedicated warning screen instead).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, ranging from crypto-native power users to newcomers migrating from custodial exchanges. Because losing this password results in permanent, irreversible loss of funds, the design leans heavily on loss aversion and explicit informed consent psychological triggers rather than persuasive/marketing techniques used elsewhere in the app. The stark black background and serious tone are intended to snap the user out of "casual app" mode and into a heightened state of attention, mirroring patterns used in legal/financial disclosure screens.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Risk-first copywriting: Explicitly states irreversible consequences before allowing progression, setting correct user expectations for self-custody wallets.

  • Double password entry: Confirms intent and reduces typos for a credential that has no recovery mechanism.

  • Checkbox-gated CTA: Forces active, conscious consent (not just a passive scroll) before enabling the high-stakes "Continue" action, functioning as a psychological commitment device.

  • High-contrast gradient CTA on black canvas: Creates a premium, security-vault aesthetic consistent with crypto/fintech branding while keeping visual focus on the single next action.

  • Reveal/hide password toggle: Reduces input errors for a critical, unrecoverable credential.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 13
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an application must surface highly sensitive, unrecoverable secrets (seed phrases, API keys, 2FA backup codes, encryption keys). It's ideal for:

  • Self-custody wallets and password managers exporting master credentials.

  • Any flow where a single leaked string can cause irreversible financial or security damage.

  • Situations requiring a mix of soft reassurance (backup status) and hard warnings (irreversible loss/theft language).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed security framing for low-stakes data (e.g., regular account settings, non-sensitive preferences) - it would create unnecessary anxiety and friction. Also avoid displaying sensitive secrets in plaintext by default; always default to an obscured state to prevent accidental exposure in screenshots, recordings, or over-the-shoulder viewing. Don't use alarming red destructive buttons for actions that are easily reversible, as this dilutes the signal for genuinely dangerous actions elsewhere in the app.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users (ranging from crypto-native power users to newcomers onboarded via Coinbase's ecosystem) who bear full personal responsibility for asset security. The design leans heavily on loss aversion and fear-based motivation (irreversible fund theft) balanced with reassurance (backup confirmation) to keep users engaged rather than panicked. It also exploits the authority/trust heuristic by explicitly stating "Coinbase will never ask you for them," building brand-level trust that outlasts the interaction itself and helps users recognize scams elsewhere.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Blurred/obscured seed phrase display prevents passive shoulder-surfing or accidental screen-recording leaks until the user deliberately interacts.

  • Status badge confirmation ("Backed up to iCloud") gives immediate peace of mind and reduces anxiety about data loss.

  • Color-coded action hierarchy: neutral gray for reversible actions vs. red for destructive/irreversible ones (Delete iCloud backup), leveraging color psychology to prevent costly mistakes.

  • Explicit anti-phishing messaging baked directly into the security copy, proactively inoculating users against social engineering.

  • Copy to clipboard shortcut reduces transcription errors when moving the phrase to a password manager or paper backup.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 14
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any irreversible, high-stakes action where user negligence could cause catastrophic loss (e.g., crypto key backup, account deletion with data loss, disabling 2FA). It's ideal when you need a documented, explicit user attestation before allowing progress, and when combining legal consent with safety confirmation streamlines the flow without diluting importance.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy-handed gating pattern for low-stakes or reversible actions (it adds unnecessary friction and can frustrate users completing routine tasks). Also avoid bundling unrelated consents (e.g., marketing opt-ins) into a security checkbox, as this can create legal ambiguity or erode trust. Do not use if the underlying action doesn't warrant the anxiety this UI intentionally provokes.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, many of whom are new to managing private keys and are highly vulnerable to loss-of-funds scenarios due to lost or unrecorded seed phrases. The design leverages fear of irreversible loss (loss aversion bias) to motivate careful action, while the explicit checkbox leverages the commitment and consistency principle: once a user affirms they've saved the phrase, they're more likely to have actually done so, and Coinbase gains a documented record of user acknowledgment for liability protection.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background layering: Creates focus and hierarchy, visually "locking" prior content until the current task is acknowledged.

  • Gated primary action via checkbox: Forces explicit user attestation before allowing progression, reducing support tickets from users who lost access due to skipped backups.

  • Combined legal + safety consent: Merges terms/privacy agreement with the security confirmation into a single checkbox, minimizing extra steps.

  • Reassuring iconography: The key + checkmark illustration transforms a stressful security task into a moment of visual accomplishment.

  • De-emphasized escape hatch: "Cancel" is available but styled to be subordinate, discouraging drop-off without fully blocking it.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Any flow involving generation or display of irreproducible secrets (seed phrases, private keys, one-time backup codes) where the consequence of loss is permanent and severe.

  • Legal/compliance moments where explicit, logged user consent is required before proceeding (e.g., terms acceptance bundled with a critical security action).

  • High-stakes destructive or irreversible actions where you want to add deliberate friction to prevent careless taps (e.g., wallet deletion, account closure, financial transfers).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy-handed, anxiety-inducing pattern for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (it will feel excessive and erode trust through unnecessary alarm).

  • Don't bundle unrelated consents (e.g., marketing opt-in) into a security checkbox; it dilutes the seriousness of the message and can create compliance ambiguity.

  • Avoid stacking multiple modal layers for routine confirmations, as excessive layering fatigues users and can lead to blind rapid-tap dismissal, undermining the very safeguard being designed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users, ranging from onboarding crypto newcomers to experienced holders, at the exact moment they take on full personal responsibility for their private keys. The design leans heavily on loss-aversion psychology: emphasizing catastrophic, irreversible consequences ("steal all of your crypto") to override the natural tendency to skip security steps during onboarding.

The mandatory checkbox exploits the commitment and consistency principle: by physically checking a box affirming "Yes, I saved my recovery phrase," users are nudged toward genuinely completing the backup rather than clicking through blindly, which reduces support tickets and irrecoverable fund loss down the line (a major business risk for a non-custodial wallet provider like Coinbase Wallet).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Two-layer confirmation architecture: Stacking a confirmation sheet on top of the informational backup screen visually and functionally separates "read the warning" from "confirm you understood it," reducing accidental dismissal.

  • Combined checkbox for security + legal consent: Efficiently merges an active-acknowledgment step with T&Cs/privacy agreement, minimizing extra steps without diluting the seriousness of the security warning.

  • Asymmetric button treatment: High-contrast gradient CTA vs. muted "Cancel" pill clearly communicates the intended path while preserving an easy way out.

  • Brand-consistent illustration used to soften a high-anxiety moment: The abstract shield/checkmark/key graphic injects a moment of calm and trust into an otherwise high-stakes security checkpoint.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 16
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an application must present highly sensitive, unrecoverable, one-time-view credentials (such as crypto seed phrases, API secret keys, 2FA backup codes, or encryption recovery keys). It's ideal for:

  • Self-custody wallet onboarding or wallet migration flows.

  • Developer platforms issuing one-time API secrets.

  • Password manager master-key or recovery-kit generation.

The blur-then-reveal plus dual backup-method approach is especially valuable when the cost of exposure (theft, screenshot leaks) is severe and irreversible.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy warning treatment for low-stakes or easily-recoverable data (excessive alarm fatigue will erode trust if applied to routine settings changes or non-destructive actions). Do not use blurred reveal-on-tap patterns for data users need to reference repeatedly during a flow, as it adds friction; and avoid pushing a single third-party backup method (like iCloud) as the sole "recommended" option in privacy-sensitive contexts where users may prefer fully offline custody, as this could conflict with self-sovereignty expectations of crypto-native audiences.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both crypto newcomers setting up their first self-custody wallet and experienced users who still need a guided, low-error backup flow. The design leans heavily on loss-aversion psychology: by foregrounding the catastrophic risk ("Anyone who learns them can steal all of your crypto") before showing the actual phrase, it primes users to treat the following screen with appropriate gravity.

The blur-by-default mechanic also reduces liability for Coinbase: it discourages careless screenshotting, which is a leading cause of seed-phrase theft via cloud photo-sync services or malware. The offering of iCloud backup as "recommended" nudges users toward a recoverable path (reducing support tickets and lost-wallet complaints) while still preserving the self-custody ethos by allowing manual copy as an alternative.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Blurred sensitive data by default: The seed phrase is obscured until explicitly revealed, protecting against shoulder-surfing, screen recording malware, and accidental screenshots.

  • Dual backup pathways: Offering both "Back up on iCloud" (primary, effortless) and "Copy to clipboard" (secondary, manual) respects different user risk tolerances and technical comfort levels.

  • Persistent status indicator: The "Not backed up to iCloud" badge acts as a lightweight progress/warning signal that can likely change state once the backup completes, giving the user closure.

  • High-contrast gradient CTA: The single vivid button on an otherwise dark, neutral screen unmistakably directs the eye toward the recommended safe action.

  • Explicit anti-phishing messaging: "Coinbase will never ask you for them" preemptively defends users against future scam attempts referencing the wallet's own brand authority.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Setting Up 17
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when onboarding users into systems with multiple valid security/backup mechanisms (e.g., crypto wallets, password managers, secure note apps) where the trade-offs (convenience vs. self-custody control) are significant enough to warrant explicit, informed user choice rather than a forced default.

Also effective when trying to widen the on-ramp for both technical and non-technical audiences within the same product, by presenting the lower-friction/modern option prominently while still preserving the legacy/expert option for continuity.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern if the choice is inconsequential or fully reversible later, as it introduces unnecessary friction into onboarding (in such cases, a single smart default should be used instead of forcing a decision upfront).

Also avoid presenting two security paradigms as equally weighted, unlabeled options if one is strictly better/safer for most users; consider adding a "Recommended" badge to reduce decision paralysis and prevent security-naive users from choosing a riskier path (e.g., self-storing a seed phrase insecurely) without proper warnings.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both crypto-native users who expect and trust the traditional 12-word recovery phrase standard, and mainstream/new users onboarding into Web3 who may be intimidated by seed phrases and prefer familiar biometric/passkey flows they already use for banking or social apps.

Psychologically, this leverages the familiarity heuristic: presenting Passkey using recognizable brand names (iCloud, Google, Yubikey) reduces perceived risk and taps into trust already established with those platforms. For the Recovery Phrase option, it appeals to autonomy and self-custody values prized by crypto purists who don't want reliance on third-party cloud providers.

Offering a choice rather than forcing one method also respects varying risk tolerances and technical literacy, which increases completion rates in onboarding funnels.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive disclosure via comparison cards: Both security paths are shown side-by-side (stacked) with just enough detail to make an informed choice without overwhelming the user with cryptographic detail.

  • Passkey-first ordering: Placing the more modern, lower-friction Passkey option above the traditional Recovery Phrase nudges new/mainstream users toward an easier, less error-prone security setup, reducing onboarding drop-off and support tickets from lost seed phrases.

  • Icon language reinforcement: The key/person icon and the asterisk/seed icon visually differentiate the two mental models (identity-based vs. secret-based) at a glance.

  • Neutral dark canvas: Removes visual distraction, appropriate for a decision that carries real financial/security stakes.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any financial, wallet, or account-based product's first-run or zero-balance state, banking apps, investment apps, loyalty/points apps, or storage apps. It's ideal whenever a user's core object (balance, inventory, playlist, project) is empty and you need to convert them into active use quickly. The combination of illustrated explanation + duplicate CTA (top and bottom) is especially effective on mobile where thumb-reach and scroll position vary.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy empty-state treatment for screens that are expected to be empty briefly or routinely (e.g., a search results tab before typing a query) - it would feel over-explained. Also avoid stacking two identical CTAs (top bar + bottom button) on data-dense screens, as redundancy that's useful in a zero-state becomes visual clutter once real content populates the list. For advanced/power users, the tutorial-style illustration should be dismissible or suppressed after first use to avoid feeling repetitive.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new or first-time crypto wallet users: likely people who just created a self-custody wallet (e.g., via MetaMask/Coinbase Wallet onboarding) and have not yet funded it. The psychological goal is to overcome the "blank slate anxiety" common in fintech apps: an empty balance can feel discouraging or confusing, so the design compensates with clear, low-friction guidance toward the very next action.

The design leans on the Zeigarnik effect (an unfinished task (an empty wallet) creates a mental itch to complete it) combined with reduced choice paralysis by highlighting a single primary gradient-colored button ("Buy") against neutral gray siblings (Swap, Cash out), visually signaling the recommended first step for someone with $0.00.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual redundant CTAs: Both the top action bar ("Buy") and a large bottom "Add crypto" button funnel the user to the same activation goal, maximizing conversion regardless of scroll position or scanning pattern.

  • Explanatory empty-state illustration: Rather than a generic "no data" icon, the illustration visually depicts the two funding sources (Coinbase, other wallets via Base) connected by a link icon, turning an empty state into a mini onboarding tutorial.

  • Progressive disclosure via segmented tabs: Crypto/NFTs/DeFi tabs let the wallet house multiple asset classes without overwhelming a first-time user, who lands on the simplest (Crypto) tab by default.

  • Zero-value transparency: Displaying "$0.00" honestly rather than hiding the balance builds trust and sets a clear baseline for the user's financial journey.

  • Notification dot on settings: A subtle red badge on the gear icon nudges users toward configuration (e.g., security backup) without interrupting the primary flow.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a core dashboard can be legitimately empty (new users, disconnected accounts, zero balances) but the app still has valuable secondary content (market data, education, promotions) to offer. It's ideal for fintech, crypto, and investment apps where market/discovery content can substitute for personal data and keep engagement high during dead moments in the user journey.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid stacking multiple promotional/discovery modules if the user already has an active portfolio (it would push high-value personal financial data (balances, holdings, transactions) below the fold, frustrating returning power users). Also avoid this density of merchandising in contexts requiring regulatory neutrality (e.g., if trending-token promotion could be construed as investment advice) or in markets with strict advertising compliance around crypto assets.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets the "Busy Urban" persona (professionals who want crypto exposure but lack time for deep research). For a first-time or currently-empty-balance user, the screen leverages several psychological triggers:

  • FOMO / Social Proof: Showing swap volume and trending tokens implies "others are active here," pressuring passive users to participate.

  • Anchoring on Yield: Leading with "4.1% rewards" anchors the user's mental model of the wallet as a productive asset, not just storage.

  • Reduced Cognitive Load: Rather than forcing users to seek out what to do next, the app pushes curated next-actions (earn, watchlist, swap) directly into their path.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empty-state monetization: Instead of showing a blank $0.00 dashboard, the screen immediately surfaces yield, watchlist, and trending-token modules to convert idle users into active participants.

  • Progressive disclosure via carousel: The page-control dots atop the rewards banner signal more tips/offers are swipeable, without cluttering the main view.

  • Social proof through live market data: The "495 swaps," buy/sell percentage bar, and price-change arrows lend third-party credibility that motivates action even absent personal holdings.

  • Persistent one-tap CTAs: A pill-shaped "Swap" button is embedded directly inside each trending token card, collapsing multiple navigation steps into a single tap.

  • Dismissible, non-blocking banner: The rewards card includes a close (X) affordance, respecting user autonomy while still defaulting to visible promotion.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern when a product's core value hinges on live market/content data and you need to keep unfunded, first-time, or otherwise "empty" users engaged. Ideal for fintech, trading, and marketplace apps where showing a blank dashboard would increase churn. Particularly effective when you have rich real-time data (trending items, sentiment, prices) that can substitute for personalized/owned content.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, multi-module approach for simple utility apps or onboarding flows where a single clear call-to-action (e.g., "Add funds," "Connect wallet") is more effective than competing content blocks. If the trending/discovery data isn't genuinely reliable or updated in real time, this pattern can feel like clutter or, worse, misleading marketing. Also avoid overloading first-time users with financial trading data before they understand basic app navigation, as it can increase perceived complexity and abandonment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets both crypto-curious newcomers who have just created a wallet (hence $0.00 balance) and active DeFi/Base-network traders looking for quick swap opportunities. The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Social proof & FOMO: "495 swaps," percentage bought/sold bars, and trending token rankings signal crowd activity, nudging users to act before missing out.

  • Curiosity gap: The BTC-onchain banner teases a new feature (cbBTC) without fully explaining it, prompting a tap-through.

  • Low-commitment engagement: The watchlist CTA offers a zero-cost way to start using the app (favoriting assets) before requiring any deposit, easing the funnel toward eventual funding.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empty-state disguised as content hub: Instead of showing a blank "$0.00, add funds" screen, the app fills the void with a promo carousel, watchlist CTA, and trending swaps, keeping the user engaged and reducing bounce risk.

  • In-line sentiment visualization: The green/red bought-vs-sold bar on each trending token card gives an at-a-glance social-proof signal that drives FOMO and swap intent without requiring the user to tap into details.

  • Dismissible, paginated promo banner: Page-control dots and an explicit close (X) button give users control over informational banners, respecting user agency while still surfacing new product features (cbBTC on Base).

  • Persistent quick actions: Search, QR scan, and notification icons are always accessible from the top bar, supporting power-user workflows like sending/receiving crypto via QR without deep navigation.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a product has meaningful zero/empty states (new users, no holdings, no data) that would otherwise feel like dead-ends. Populate them with relevant discovery content, light onboarding nudges, and low-commitment CTAs (like watchlists) to keep users engaged during the activation gap between signup and first meaningful action. Particularly effective in fintech, trading, and marketplace apps where "nothing here yet" is common for new accounts.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid overloading empty states with promotional content when the user's primary goal is unambiguous and time-sensitive (e.g., completing a specific setup task, verifying identity) - extra distractions can reduce task completion. Also avoid this pattern in enterprise/B2B contexts where market-style "trending" and sentiment bars would be seen as noise rather than useful signal, or where regulatory constraints limit promotion of financial instruments to unqualified users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets crypto-curious to intermediate DeFi users who have just created or connected a wallet but haven't yet funded it (a critical activation moment). The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Social proof (swap counts, buy/sell % bars) to reduce perceived risk of trading unfamiliar tokens.

  • FOMO/curiosity via "Trending" framing, implying momentum other users are already capturing.

  • Loss-aversion softened by utility framing in the watchlist CTA ("stay up to date") rather than urgency, appealing to more cautious/passive users.

  • Native advertising (MXNe/Brale banner) targets users interested in cross-border stablecoin remittance, a strong LATAM crypto use case.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empty state monetized as discovery surface: Rather than showing a blank $0.00 dashboard, the app immediately surfaces promotional and trending content to keep engagement high and guide the user toward an action (swap/fund).

  • Dismissible carousel with progress dots: The promo banner uses a segmented progress indicator (dash style) with an explicit close (X), giving users control while still surfacing sponsored/native content (MXNe/Brale).

  • Inline sentiment visualization: The bought/sold percentage bar on trending tokens gives an at-a-glance crowd-sentiment signal, leveraging social proof to drive swap action directly from the discovery card.

  • Contextual info icon next to "Trending swaps on Base" offers just-in-time clarification without cluttering the heading.

  • Persistent Swap CTA embedded in content cards collapses discovery and action into a single tap, reducing funnel steps for conversion.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a core screen might frequently be empty or low-value for new users (e.g., zero balance, zero saved items) but the app still has rich secondary content (market data, trends, recommendations) that can keep users engaged. It's ideal for fintech, crypto, and marketplace apps where discovery content can substitute for personal data on first-run or low-activity states.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in contexts where the empty state should prompt a specific, singular action (e.g., "Add your first payment method") - burying that CTA under multiple competing content modules (watchlist, trending, promos) can dilute focus and delay activation. Also avoid dense icon-only bottom navigation for non-expert audiences unfamiliar with crypto/wallet iconography, as it increases cognitive load and mis-taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets crypto-native or crypto-curious users, likely new wallet holders (indicated by the $0.00 balance) exploring the app before funding it, or seasoned traders using the app as a market-discovery hub even when their tracked wallet address is empty. The psychological levers at play include social proof (bought/sold percentages, swap counts) to validate token momentum, FOMO/urgency via live percentage movement (BRETT ↓3.54%), and autonomy appeal in the Morpho yield banner to attract self-directed DeFi users wary of centralized custodial products.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Productive empty state: Instead of a blank $0.00 dashboard, the void is filled with actionable discovery content (watchlist, trending swaps, yield promo), keeping a new/empty-balance user engaged rather than churning.

  • Dense but digestible trend cards: Each trending swap card packs price, % change, sentiment ratio bar, and a direct Swap CTA into one glanceable unit, reducing taps needed to act on a trending token.

  • Visual bought/sold sentiment bar: The green/red split bar communicates crowd sentiment instantly, leveraging social proof to nudge swap decisions.

  • Layered notification/scan/search utilities: Grouping search, QR (send/receive), and notifications together in the top bar keeps core wallet utilities one tap away without cluttering the primary content area.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a user lands on a dashboard with an empty or near-zero primary metric (balance, inventory, tasks) and you want to convert that dead-end moment into a guided next action. Particularly effective for fintech, crypto, or SaaS products where the "next best action" is well-defined (deposit, invite, upgrade). Pairing a first-party feature promo with a dismissible sponsored unit is effective for monetizing engagement without heavy-handedness, provided sponsorship is clearly labeled.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid stacking multiple promotional modules when the user's zero-state is due to a routine action (e.g., just logging out and back in) rather than genuine inactivity (repeated upsells can feel tone-deaf or spammy). Also avoid this pattern in contexts where trust is fragile (e.g., first-time onboarding before KYC/verification) since pushing deposits too early can raise suspicion or regulatory concerns. Never omit the "Sponsored" label, and never remove the dismiss option, as forcing exposure to ads in a financial context erodes trust quickly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets crypto-native or crypto-curious users who already hold a self-custody wallet but haven't yet deposited funds (likely a new or dormant user segment). The design leans on psychological principles including loss aversion (idle crypto = wasted opportunity), social proof and legitimacy (via the Morpho brand and reward eligibility badge), and reward incentives ($MORPHO token rewards) to trigger a deposit action. The "Trending onchain" section beneath further taps into FOMO/curiosity to keep even non-depositing users engaged and scrolling.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-state monetization: Instead of a passive empty state for the $0.00 balance, the screen immediately pivots to high-intent upsell content, turning a potential drop-off moment into a conversion opportunity.

  • Labeled sponsorship transparency: The "Sponsored" label above the native ad maintains user trust and regulatory/ethical clarity while still blending stylistically with organic content.

  • Dismiss affordance: Giving equal visual footing to "Deposit Now" and "Dismiss" respects user agency and prevents ad fatigue/annoyance, a subtle but important trust-building UX choice in a financial app.

  • Dot-grid decorative background: The card's subtle dot pattern adds visual sophistication and a "premium fintech" feel without competing with the text or CTA.

  • Redundant persuasion loop: Two consecutive modules (first-party promo + sponsored ad) both push the same "deposit/earn yield" action, maximizing the chance of conversion via repeated exposure.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 7
screens.whereToUse: Adapt this pattern for any app combining a personal dashboard with a content discovery feed (e).g., crypto wallets, creator economy platforms, or fintech apps introducing new "drops" or features. It's especially effective when you want to surface community-driven or time-sensitive content (mints, drops, limited offers) directly on the home screen with low-friction CTAs.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for first-time users unfamiliar with domain jargon, as the icon-only tab bar and dense terminology (onchain, mint) can create confusion without onboarding support. It's also risky when balance is zero and the primary content pushes spending/minting actions immediately (this can feel tone-deaf or overly sales-driven for users who haven't yet funded their account). Not ideal for apps prioritizing simplicity or first-run clarity over content density.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for crypto-native and Web3-curious users who already hold a self-custody wallet and are comfortable navigating onchain jargon (mint, onchain, address). The target user is likely an early adopter or NFT collector seeking new mini-apps and drops rather than a total beginner requiring hand-holding.

Psychologically, the design leverages social proof (showing dozens of other minters) and curiosity/FOMO (curated "Trending" carousel, truncated descriptions) to drive engagement and minting actions. The $0.00 balance juxtaposed against enticing mint opportunities and trending content also subtly nudges users to fund their wallet in order to participate.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero Carousel for App/Mini-App Discovery: Using a full-width, immersive carousel (Paperview) to surface trending onchain mini-apps treats discovery like a curated editorial feed rather than a boring app list, increasing engagement.

  • Social Proof-Driven Mint Cards: Each NFT mint opportunity shows "@user and X others minted," leveraging bandwagon psychology to reduce decision friction and imply FOMO-driven scarcity.

  • One-Tap Mint CTA: The persistent, high-contrast "Mint" pill button on each list item removes navigation friction (users can act immediately from the home feed without drilling into a detail page first).

  • Icon-Only Tab Bar: A minimalist bottom navigation using pure iconography (no text labels) keeps the UI clean and signals a power-user, crypto-native audience.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 8
screens.whereToUse:
Use this feed-based discovery pattern for crypto wallets, Web3 super-apps, or any platform bridging a technical/financial product with a content-discovery layer. It's especially effective for:

  • Onboarding new-to-category users by making unfamiliar actions (minting, connecting to dApps) feel like familiar social browsing.

  • Driving engagement in wallets/portfolios that would otherwise be static and only visited during transactions.

  • Merchandising time-sensitive or curated content (drops, trending apps) above static financial data.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for professional trading platforms, institutional finance dashboards, or any context where users expect immediate, dense access to portfolio performance, charts, and transaction history, burying that data below a media carousel would frustrate power users. Also avoid unlabeled icon-only tab bars for first-time users without a brief onboarding/coach mark, and avoid mixing high-risk financial actions (minting/spending) with casual social-feed framing for products serving risk-averse or compliance-heavy audiences.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets crypto-native and crypto-curious users on iOS who need a low-friction way to discover legitimate onchain apps and NFT drops without navigating opaque marketplaces or Etherscan-style interfaces. The design specifically caters to users who are more comfortable with consumer app UX (Instagram, TikTok, App Store) than with traditional finance dashboards, easing them into Web3 behaviors (minting, connecting to dApps) through familiar visual metaphors.

Psychologically, the screen leans on social proof (mutual mint counts), curiosity gaps (truncated descriptions), and low commitment framing (a single tappable "Mint" pill button) to convert passive scrolling into onchain action. The immediate visibility of $0.00 without gating or a heavy empty-state message keeps a new/empty wallet from feeling like a dead end.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Feed-ification of Web3: Reframes NFT minting and dApp discovery using familiar social/app-store UI (carousels, thumbnails, social handles) to lower the intimidation barrier of blockchain jargon.

  • Embedded Social Proof on CTA rows: Showing "@handle and 46 others" next to each mint opportunity leverages bandwagon effect to drive conversion without needing star ratings or download counts.

  • Zero-state balance without an empty-state screen: Rather than blocking the user with an empty wallet message, the $0.00 balance sits quietly at the top while the feed below gives the user something to do immediately (mint, explore) - turning a potentially discouraging moment into an engagement opportunity.

  • Info icon on "NFT mints for you": A small transparency affordance clarifying that this is an algorithmic/personalized recommendation, building trust around a feed the user didn't explicitly curate.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this dashboard-as-discovery-feed pattern for platforms where the core home screen risks feeling empty for new or low-activity users (e.g., wallets, investment apps, marketplaces). It's ideal for surfacing sponsored/partner content and personalized recommendations directly on the primary landing screen to drive activation and habitual return visits.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in contexts where users expect immediate, uncluttered access to their core financial data (e.g., banking apps) since mixing promotional carousels and merchandising with balance information can feel like it dilutes trust or introduces conflict-of-interest concerns. Also avoid icon-only, jargon-heavy tab bars and copy for less experienced or mainstream consumer audiences without added labels or onboarding cues.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets crypto-native power users: early adopters, NFT collectors, and DeFi/onchain app explorers (who are comfortable navigating wallets without heavy hand-holding text). The design assumes familiarity with concepts like "minting," "onchain," and wallet addresses (shown as truncated "Address 1").

Psychologically, the screen leverages social proof (mint counts, handles), curiosity/FOMO (trending carousel, scarcity implied by "for you" personalization), and low-friction discovery (one-tap Mint buttons) to keep users engaged even when their wallet holds no funds, effectively using content merchandising to drive re-engagement and transaction volume.
screens.keyHighlights:
Turning an empty balance into an opportunity: Rather than showing a stark "$0.00" with nothing else, the screen immediately pivots to curated discovery content, softening the potentially discouraging empty wallet state.

Native ad/content carousel: The trending onchain card behaves like a full-bleed sponsored placement with an embedded interactive prompt field, blurring the line between content and product, increasing engagement with third-party onchain apps.

Social-proof-driven mint list: Attaching "@handle and X others" to each NFT mint leverages bandwagon psychology, making minting decisions feel validated by community activity rather than solitary speculation.

Minimal icon-only tab bar: Reduces visual clutter and reinforces a power-user, symbol-literate audience who already understands wallet iconography conventions.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Post-Onboarding 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a product needs to blend transactional utility (balances, quick actions) with content-driven discovery to increase engagement time and transaction frequency (e).g., crypto wallets, investment apps surfacing tradable assets, or fintech apps cross-selling products via a feed. Effective when the core action (Mint, Buy, Invest) is singular and repeatable, allowing a consistent one-word CTA across heterogeneous content.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid combining a financial dashboard directly with an entertainment/discovery feed if the primary user job is quick balance-checking or sending money (the added scroll content can feel like clutter or dilute trust in a security-sensitive context). Also avoid single ambiguous CTAs like "Mint" for audiences unfamiliar with the term, as it hides underlying cost/gas fee implications and can create a false sense of "free" action, especially harmful for novice users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Targeted at "Busy Urbans": crypto-native or crypto-curious users who want quick, low-friction interactions rather than deep research sessions. The feed format exploits familiar social media scrolling habits (infinite scroll, image-first cards, single-tap action) to lower the learning curve for minting NFTs, a historically technical action. Showing "$0.00" balance alongside mint opportunities also subtly nudges deposit/funding behavior (users are shown desirable content requiring funds they don't yet have, creating a soft conversion funnel toward buying crypto).

The social-proof collaborator counts target FOMO and bandwagon psychology, common triggers for a mobile-first generation already primed by TikTok/Instagram engagement loops.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-purpose home screen: Combines financial dashboard (balance, address) with a content discovery feed, maximizing screen real estate for both utility and engagement.

  • Persistent, single-word CTA ("Mint"): Repeating the exact same pill button across every card creates a predictable interaction pattern users learn instantly, reducing decision fatigue.

  • Full-bleed media cards: Large edge-to-edge imagery (concert photo) mimics familiar social feed aesthetics, making Web3 minting feel as approachable as scrolling Instagram.

  • Collaborator social proof: "@user and X others" tags leverage crowd validation to nudge users toward minting drops that already have traction.

  • Compact top utility bar: Search, QR/scan, and notifications are condensed into icon-only buttons, preserving vertical space for the feed while keeping core wallet actions one tap away.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Purchasing & Ordering 8
screens.whereToUse:
Use this receipt-style detail pattern for any financial or high-stakes transaction confirmation: crypto transfers, bank wires, stock trades, or bill payments. It's ideal whenever:

  • The action is irreversible and users need a permanent, referenceable record.

  • Multiple technical metadata points (fees, network, addresses, timestamps) must be communicated without ambiguity.

  • Regulatory or support requirements mandate a clear audit trail visible to the end user.

  • You need to manage expectations about processing time via honest status states rather than premature success indicators.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, data-heavy layout for casual or low-stakes actions (e.g., in-app purchases of virtual goods, social interactions) where showing this much technical detail would feel overwhelming or paranoid. Also avoid full raw address/ID exposure in contexts where screen recording or shoulder-surfing is a security concern without an option to mask/copy discretely. For first-time crypto users, consider supplementing this screen with inline tooltips or a simplified summary view before revealing full technical metadata, as terms like "network fee" or "price per coin" may not yet be understood.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets retail cryptocurrency users (likely intermediate rather than first-time users, given the assumption of familiarity with concepts like "network fee," "price per coin," and raw wallet addresses). The Singapore Dollar (SGD) localization indicates a specific regional rollout (Singapore market).

Psychologically, the screen leverages transparency-as-trust: because cryptocurrency transactions are irreversible and often anxiety-inducing (fear of sending to the wrong address, losing funds, or being scammed), the design compensates by exposing every possible data point (full address, exact fee, timestamp, live status) rather than hiding complexity. This over-disclosure is intentional risk mitigation (it gives the user confidence that the platform has nothing to hide and gives them an audit trail if something goes wrong).

The "Secured by Coinbase" badge specifically targets users who may not trust the underlying network/wallet infra directly, borrowing brand equity from a well-known custodial exchange to reduce transactional anxiety for a self-custody or partner-embedded wallet experience.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-currency hero display: Showing both fiat (SGD) and crypto (BTC) amounts simultaneously bridges the mental model gap for users still thinking in local currency while transacting in crypto.

  • Full, unabbreviated wallet address: Resisting the temptation to truncate the destination address for aesthetics prioritizes user verification and security over visual tidiness (vital for irreversible transactions).

  • Neutral, honest status labeling: Using a gray dot + "Started" rather than a premature green success checkmark accurately reflects blockchain confirmation latency and prevents false confidence.

  • Persistent trust footer: The "Secured by Coinbase" lock badge is anchored at the screen's bottom on every financial detail screen, reinforcing brand trust at high-anxiety moments.

  • Contextual info tooltip on fee: Proactively addresses a known user confusion point (network fees) without needing to leave the screen.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Purchasing & Ordering 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any OAuth/API authorization flow where a third-party app requests scoped access to a user's account (especially in fintech, crypto wallets, or platforms with sensitive data/financial actions). It's ideal when you need to balance conversion (completing the connection) with regulatory/security transparency requirements.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when permissions are trivial or non-sensitive (e.g., read-only public profile data), where such a heavy, itemized consent screen would feel like unnecessary friction. Also avoid vague icon-only permission descriptions for highly technical or enterprise audiences who need precise scope definitions (e.g., exact API endpoints) rather than simplified consumer language.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets cryptocurrency users connecting a third-party dApp, exchange, or wallet integration to their Coinbase account (typically during a Web3 login or wallet-connect flow). This audience is security-conscious but also accustomed to friction in crypto UX, so the screen leverages authority and transparency (Coinbase branding, explicit scopes) to reduce hesitation before granting financial permissions.

Psychologically, the screen exploits the default/anchoring effect via CTA styling (primary blue vs. muted gray) and reduces perceived risk through granularity: listing permissions individually makes users feel they are consenting to specific, understood actions rather than a vague blanket authorization, even though the disclaimer clarifies it applies account-wide.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-led scannability: Each permission uses a unique, semantically relevant icon, letting users pattern-match risk level (a lock and a bank icon feel more consequential than a gear) without reading dense text.

  • Asymmetric CTA weighting: The solid blue "Authorize" button versus flat gray "Cancel" button visually nudges the user toward granting access while preserving an easy opt-out.

  • Trust chain disclosure: Displaying both the requesting wallet's icon/name and "by Coinbase" developer attribution builds layered trust and combats phishing concerns common in crypto.

  • Scope transparency with plain language: Translating technical OAuth scopes into human-readable permission statements reduces user anxiety and supports informed consent.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logout 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any irreversible or high-consequence action: deleting an account, wiping local data, disconnecting a wallet, revoking API keys, or removing a non-recoverable payment method.

  • Fintech, crypto, or security-sensitive products where standard "confirm/cancel" language is insufficient and users need concrete stakes spelled out.

  • Situations where you want to intentionally slow down power users who may otherwise tap through modals from muscle memory.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Low-risk or easily reversible actions (e.g., logging out of a standard SaaS app with password recovery) - this level of dramatic full-screen warning would feel excessive and erode user trust in the product's tone calibration.

  • High-frequency actions where friction would create fatigue (reserve heavy warnings for rare, catastrophic decisions only).

  • Contexts where users are already highly stressed or time-pressured (e.g., emergency flows), where an extra full-screen step could increase frustration without adding meaningful protection.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
