This screen targets self-custody crypto wallet users: a demographic ranging from crypto-curious newcomers to experienced holders - where the underlying psychological driver is loss aversion. Because non-custodial wallets have no "forgot password" recovery mechanism, signing out without saved seed phrases/private keys can mean permanent, unrecoverable loss of funds. The design leans hard into fear of loss (a stronger motivator than fear of inconvenience) to prevent support tickets, reputational damage, and user financial harm.

The friendly mascot also signals to a mainstream (non-technical) audience that the brand is approachable, helping offset the anxiety that comes from stark financial warnings, which is important for platforms trying to make crypto feel less intimidating to newcomers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inverted button hierarchy: The safe "Go back" option is visually dominant (neutral gray, top position) while the destructive "sign out" option is isolated in alarming red at the bottom, reducing accidental irreversible taps.

  • Explicit consequence messaging: Rather than vague warnings, the copy states the exact real-world loss (wallet + funds), leveraging concrete stakes to trigger System 2 (deliberate) thinking over System 1 (automatic) thinking.

  • Full-screen interruption instead of a small modal: Removing all other UI chrome and context ensures total user focus on the decision at hand.

  • Brand-consistent illustration softens severity: The mascot keeps the tone human and non-punitive despite delivering a financially catastrophic warning.

  • First-person confirmation copy: "I'm sure, sign out" forces active self-affirmation rather than passive button-pressing.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Logout 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for the entry point of any app that must split users into "new" vs. "returning/import" flows (wallets, password managers, backup/restore tools, or any product with irreversible, high-stakes account creation). It's ideal when the brand needs to simultaneously feel trustworthy, exciting, and simple before asking for sensitive setup steps (seed phrases, biometrics, KYC).

Also effective whenever a product wants to visually convey "breadth of ecosystem/compatibility" (e.g., supported chains, integrations, file types) without a text-heavy feature list (decorative iconography can do the persuasive work).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavily decorative, illustration-first approach for enterprise, B2B, or trust-sensitive financial contexts (e.g., banking, tax, insurance) where users expect a more sober, credibility-first first impression (playful mascots can undercut perceived seriousness. Also avoid burying the "returning user" path as a subtle text link if data shows a large proportion of your install base are returning users (e.g., a re-install after device change), since it may increase drop-off/support tickets for that segment. Finally, don't compress legal/compliance text this small in jurisdictions with strict consent requirements (e.g., GDPR)) an explicit opt-in checkbox may be legally necessary instead of implied consent via CTA tap.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets two overlapping audiences: brand-new crypto users who need reassurance and simplicity, and existing wallet holders migrating or re-installing the app who need a fast, low-friction path to recovery. The playful illustration style and mascot-driven iconography specifically target a mainstream, less-technical audience that Coinbase is trying to onboard beyond crypto-native early adopters, using visual familiarity and warmth to reduce anxiety about self-custody (a notoriously high-stakes, no-safety-net action).

Psychologically, the screen leverages primacy effect (first impression sets the emotional tone for a financial product), choice architecture (default path emphasized via button weight), and social/ecosystem proof (recognizable logos imply legitimacy and breadth of support) to build trust before asking the user to take on the serious responsibility of seed-phrase custody in later steps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Ecosystem visualization instead of feature list: Scattered token/NFT/protocol logos around the central mascot communicate "this wallet connects you to a whole universe of crypto assets" without a single word of copy.

  • Clear visual hierarchy between primary and secondary paths: A bold gradient pill button for the primary "create" action versus a plain-text link for "I already have a wallet" - guiding new users while not hiding the alternate path for returning users.

  • Compressed, non-blocking legal disclosure: Terms and privacy policy are embedded as inline links directly above the CTA, satisfying compliance without a separate screen or scroll.

  • Friendly mascot-based branding: The wallet's icon is anthropomorphized into a rounded, eye-like shape amid whimsical sparkles and creatures, softening the intimidating/technical connotation of "crypto wallet."

  • Page control dots signal more onboarding context exists, setting expectation this is step one of a short sequence rather than an isolated dead end.

results.query: How does Linear issue creation compare to Airtable record creation

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any "quick create" flow where speed of capture is more valuable than completeness of data (note-taking apps, task managers, bug trackers, or CRM lead capture). It's ideal when the core object has one mandatory field (title/name) and several optional metadata fields that can be added later. Auto-focusing the primary input and disabling submission until it's valid is a strong default for any lightweight creation modal.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the created object genuinely requires several mandatory fields upfront (e.g., a detailed support ticket needing severity and category for proper routing) - hiding required fields below the fold or behind extra taps could lead to incomplete, unusable records. Also avoid auto-focusing the keyboard if the form contains a prominent single-choice control (e.g., a type selector) that should be set before text entry, as immediate keyboard pop-up can obscure context or feel jarring on first load.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engineers, PMs, and designers who need to log a bug, idea, or task the instant it occurs to them (often while away from their desktop). The design leverages the psychological principle of minimizing "friction to capture": the fewer steps between having a thought and recording it, the more likely the thought gets captured before being lost. By front-loading the keyboard and title field, Linear caters to users who think in quick, low-effort bursts (e.g., "saw this bug on the train, log it now") rather than fully-specified tickets.

Deferring metadata (assignee, label, milestone, project) to secondary, optional taps respects the cognitive load limitations of mobile users, multitasking professionals who want speed over completeness, trusting that fields can be refined later on desktop.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-focused title input: The keyboard is already open and cursor active on launch, eliminating an extra tap and enabling true "capture-first" speed.
  • Metadata toolbar above keyboard: Assignee, Label, Milestone, and Project are accessible as quick-tap pills directly above the keyboard, so users never need to dismiss the keyboard to add context.
  • Disabled Submit state: Prevents premature/empty submissions and gives a clear visual cue of form completion status at a glance.
  • Contextual breadcrumb subtitle: Showing the repo/project name under the modal title keeps the user oriented about where this issue will be filed, critical when managing multiple projects.
  • Minimal chrome: No unnecessary labels, dividers, or decoration, maximizing screen real estate for actual content entry.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any quick-capture creation flow in productivity, project management, or developer tools (especially when the core content (title/description) is the critical path and secondary metadata (tags, assignees, dates) is optional). It's ideal for power-user audiences who prioritize speed, keyboard shortcuts, and minimal modal chrome, and where a flexible Markdown/rich-text body outperforms multiple rigid form fields.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for consumer-facing or novice audiences who need more guidance, validation, and visual separation between fields (the blended title/description text area and sparse labeling could cause confusion for less technical users). It's also unsuitable for workflows where metadata (e.g., priority, due date, compliance fields) is mandatory for downstream processes, since the deferred-chip approach allows incomplete records to be submitted. Highly regulated or data-integrity-critical forms should use explicit, validated fields instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers who need to capture a technical task the instant it comes to mind (often mid-conversation or mid-debugging) without breaking focus. The minimal chrome and keyboard-first design cater to technically fluent users who value speed and precision over hand-holding.

Psychologically, it leverages the reduction of friction principle: by making only the title mandatory and pushing all categorization (assignee, label, milestone, project) into optional, low-commitment chips, it lowers the activation energy needed to log a thought. The pre-filled Acceptance Criteria structure also exploits the anchoring effect, implicitly training users toward higher-quality issue writing by example rather than instruction.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-anchored header: Displaying the repo/project path directly below the modal title keeps the user oriented about where the issue will live, preventing misfiled tickets.
  • Unified title+description canvas: No visual boundary between the title line and the Markdown body creates a frictionless, document-like writing experience rather than a rigid form.
  • Deferred metadata via chips: Assignee, Label, Milestone, and Project are optional pill-shaped affordances rather than mandatory dropdowns, letting users fire off an issue in seconds and triage details later.
  • Inline Markdown toolbar: Formatting controls (bold, italic, link, image, mention, checklists) sit right above the keyboard, enabling rich documentation without breaking flow or requiring a separate "preview" mode.
  • Persistent primary action: The blue "Submit" button stays fixed at the top, always accessible even as the text area scrolls, reinforcing speed-of-capture.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for:

  • Quick-capture flows in productivity, task-management, or CRM apps where users need to log structured records (issues, tickets, leads) without interrupting their current context.
  • Any mobile form where metadata is secondary to a primary free-text field (e.g., note-taking apps with tags, bug trackers, support ticket submission).
  • Power-user tools where horizontal chip scrolling and a persistent rich-text toolbar can replace bulkier multi-screen forms, keeping everything within thumb's reach and above the keyboard.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The target audience is non-technical and needs guided, step-by-step input (the terse chip labels and lack of inline hints can confuse first-time or occasional users).
  • Metadata fields have complex validation or dependencies (e.g., conditional required fields) that a simple tap-to-cycle chip cannot represent without a secondary picker screen.
  • The form requires many more fields than can comfortably scroll horizontally (beyond 5-6 chips, discoverability drops sharply and a settings/detail screen becomes more appropriate).
  • Markdown/rich-text literacy cannot be assumed; showing raw markdown syntax (e.g., **bold**) without live preview may alienate casual users expecting WYSIWYG editing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and founders who think and write in structured, spec-like language (evidenced by the user's own acceptance-criteria formatting). The target user values speed of capture over form completeness; Linear's design assumes they will categorize (team/label/priority) in seconds via muscle-memory chip taps rather than labored dropdown menus.

Psychologically, the design exploits the low-friction commitment principle: by making Submit always-available and metadata optional, it lowers the activation energy to log an idea the instant it occurs (critical for capturing fleeting thoughts during a commute, meeting, or stand-up, which is why this is explicitly the mobile (on-the-go) version of issue creation).

The chip-and-caret metadata pattern also leverages recognition over recall: users scan familiar colored pills (SLMobbin, enhancement) instead of remembering exact field names, reducing cognitive load for frequent, repetitive task entry.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-screen capture, no wizard: Title, description, and all metadata are reachable without leaving the sheet or navigating steps, preserving flow and reducing abandonment.
  • Chip-based property selection: Team, Label, Status, and Estimate are condensed into tappable horizontal pill chips with dropdown carets, saving enormous vertical space versus traditional labeled form fields.
  • Floating formatting toolbar above keyboard: Bold, italic, link, image, mention, and list controls stay accessible exactly when text focus is active, without permanently occupying screen real estate.
  • Breadcrumb subtitle under the modal title: "SLMobbin/padel-score-counter" instantly orients the user to which workspace/project the issue is being filed into, critical for multi-project users.
  • Non-blocking required fields: The Submit button is live and unconditional on title text, letting power users fire off minimal issues instantly and enrich metadata later.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any creation flow aimed at expert/power users who perform the action frequently (ticket creation, note-taking, structured data entry) where speed and in-context metadata tagging matter more than guided hand-holding. It is especially effective when:

  • The form has a few essential metadata fields that benefit from being set at write-time rather than after submission.
  • Users are typing long-form or structured text and need the keyboard open continuously.
  • The audience is technical and comfortable with shorthand, markdown, and dense layouts.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, chrome-light, label-shorthand approach for first-time or non-technical users, where unlabeled chips ("enhancement", team acronyms) and lack of field hints will cause confusion. It's also inappropriate for forms requiring strict sequential validation or lengthy structured data entry (e.g., checkout, KYC) where a multi-step wizard with explicit progress feedback would reduce error rates better than a single freeform canvas. If the metadata fields exceed 4-5, a horizontal chip bar will overflow and require scrolling, breaking the frictionless promise this pattern depends on.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for engineers, QA, and product managers who need to capture detailed, structured issues on the go (often while in a stand-up, reviewing a bug on a device, or jotting a spec between meetings). The acceptance-criteria-style content in the example demonstrates the expected sophistication of the audience: they aren't casual note-takers, they are writing testable, binary pass/fail conditions.

Psychologically, the design reduces friction and cognitive switching costs: by keeping metadata selectors tethered to the keyboard, it avoids the "scroll up, tap, scroll back down" pattern that breaks flow state, respecting that engineers value momentum and resent context-switching. The breadcrumb subtitle also taps into a need for certainty and control; technical users are wary of misfiling work into the wrong repo, so immediate confirmation of destination builds trust in a tool that is otherwise invisible/fast by design.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Sticky metadata bar above keyboard: Team, Label, Priority/Workflow, and Project chips remain accessible directly above the keyboard toolbar, allowing triage without interrupting typing flow or dismissing the keyboard.
  • Contextual breadcrumb in header: Showing "SLMobbin/padel-score-counter" under the title gives instant confidence about destination context, critical for multi-repo/multi-team users.
  • Native markdown authoring: Power users can type raw markdown (`**bold**`, `-` lists) without relying on toolbar buttons, matching engineer muscle memory from GitHub/editors.
  • Minimal chrome, maximum content: No extraneous labels or borders around the title/description fields (they look like plain text, maximizing writing real estate on a small screen).
  • Single unmistakable CTA: The blue pill "Submit" button is the only saturated-color element on the screen, making the completion action impossible to miss amidst dense text.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any productivity, dev-tools, or B2B SaaS product where speed-of-capture outweighs completeness-of-metadata at creation time (e).g., issue trackers, note-taking apps, CRM quick-add, or task managers. It's especially effective when:

  • The user base is technical/power-users comfortable with Markdown or plain-text shorthand.
  • Secondary metadata (assignee, priority, due date) can reasonably be added later without blocking workflow.
  • You want to reduce abandonment on creation flows by minimizing required fields to just one (title).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal-field, Markdown-first pattern when:

  • Your audience is non-technical and would be confused or intimidated by raw Markdown syntax without a WYSIWYG toolbar.
  • Compliance, reporting, or downstream automation requires mandatory structured metadata (e.g., priority, category) at the moment of creation, deferring these fields could create backlog hygiene problems.
  • The product relies on heavy upfront categorization for routing (e.g., support ticketing systems that must classify issues immediately for SLA purposes).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and founders who need to capture a technical task the instant it comes to mind (often mid-conversation or mid-code-review) without breaking flow. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of friction to intention-to-record latency: by not forcing the user through dropdowns for priority, labels, or assignee before they can even write the issue body, Linear captures the thought before it's lost, a core tenet of fast-moving engineering teams praised for valuing speed over process ceremony.

The structured Acceptance Criteria formatting also reflects target-user behavior: teams that already think in Definition-of-Done checklists, so the tool is meeting them where their existing documentation habits already are rather than imposing new templates.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Markdown-native authoring: Users can type raw Markdown syntax (bold, bullet lists) directly in the description field, aligning with how engineers already write specs/tickets elsewhere, removing the need to learn a new formatting UI.
  • Minimal mandatory fields: Only a title is strictly required; everything else (labels, assignee, priority, cycle) is optional and deferred, dramatically lowering the activation energy to log an issue.
  • Contextual breadcrumb in header: Showing the repo/project path ("SLMobbin/padel-score-c...") directly under the modal title keeps the user oriented about where this issue will land without needing a separate dropdown field cluttering the body.
  • Full-screen modal over navigation: Using a card-style sheet that overlays rather than navigating away preserves the user's prior context/scroll position on the underlying screen.
  • Disabled Submit with loader: Prevents premature or duplicate submissions while background validation/sync resolves, an unobtrusive way to enforce data integrity.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any collaborative, stateful record that evolves over time (issue trackers, support tickets, order statuses, approval workflows, or CRM deal pages). It's ideal when users need both the current state (header/status) and historical context (activity feed) in a single scroll, and when a lightweight persistent action (comment, reply, approve) should remain accessible during review.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, static content (e.g., a profile view or a read-only article) where an activity log would be noise. It also breaks down on screens where many competing primary actions exist (the single floating action bar works because Linear limits itself to one dominant interaction (commenting); adding more buttons would clutter the thumb zone). For consumer apps prioritizing emotional engagement over auditability, this dense, log-style timeline would feel cold and overly technical.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engineers, PMs, and founders who need to triage or update issues on the go (e).g., reviewing acceptance criteria during a commute or quickly commenting from a phone during a standup. The density and GitHub-like structure cater to technically literate users who value information density over whitespace-heavy consumer UI.

Psychologically, the activity log leverages the Zeigarnik effect and transparency bias, seeing a running history of actions (assignment, labeling, milestone) builds trust that nothing is lost and creates accountability among collaborators. The always-visible comment action reduces friction for in-the-moment feedback, exploiting the "strike while the iron is hot" principle to increase engagement velocity.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent floating action bar: The "Comment" + info-icon cluster floats above the tab bar, keeping the primary interaction always within thumb reach regardless of scroll position.
  • Status pill as instant state signal: The green "Open" badge with a circular icon lets users parse issue state in a glance, no reading required.
  • Unified timeline of content + metadata events: Comments, labels, milestones, and assignments are rendered in one continuous feed, giving a single source of truth for issue history without separate tabs.
  • Breadcrumb-style repo context: "SLMobbin / padel-score-counter #2" instantly orients the user within the larger project hierarchy.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 10
screens.whereToUse:
• Any detail view for a record that has lifecycle state (tickets, orders, tasks, bugs) where status needs to be understood in under a second.
  • Collaborative tools where mentions, ownership, and accountability need lightweight visual emphasis inline with free-text content.
  • Apps with nested/hierarchical content (parent issue → sub-issues) that benefit from inline expansion rather than forced navigation.
  • Mobile companion experiences for desktop-first power tools, where users need fast read/triage/comment actions rather than full editing capability.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, text-heavy layout for casual consumer apps where users expect visual-first browsing (e.g., media, social feeds) - the information density here would feel overwhelming.
  • Not ideal when the primary user task is rapid bulk triage of many items; a list/table view with batch actions would serve that need better than a single-item detail drill-down.
  • If the target audience is non-technical or unfamiliar with issue-tracker conventions (acceptance criteria, sub-issues), this structure may require additional onboarding or simplification.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers who need to triage or action issues on the go (often between meetings or away from their desk). The dense but well-organized layout caters to power users who already understand issue-tracking conventions (acceptance criteria, sub-issues, status states) and simply need fast confirmation or lightweight commenting rather than full authoring.

Psychologically, the clear status badge and structured acceptance criteria reduce anxiety around ambiguous task ownership (everyone can see exactly what "done" looks like). The Owner tag and mention highlighting leverage social accountability, subtly encouraging responsiveness from tagged collaborators. The persistent bottom navigation exploits the Von Restorff/habit-loop principle: no matter how deep a user drills into a single issue, the path back to inbox or home never disappears, lowering the fear of "getting lost" in a dense tool.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Status pill as a first-class citizen: The green "Open" badge with icon is placed directly under the title, making state scannable before reading any detail (critical for triage-heavy workflows).
  • Breadcrumb-lite identity line: "SLMobbin / padel-score-counter #3" compresses team, project, and issue ID into one glanceable line, preserving context when deep-linked or shared.
  • Inline collaborator mention highlighting: Yellow-highlighted @mentions inside body text improve scanability of ownership/action items embedded in prose.
  • Progressive disclosure of sub-issues: A dedicated "Sub-issues" section with a quick-add (+) button supports hierarchical issue breakdown without leaving the detail view.
  • Persistent global tab bar: Even on a deep, content-dense detail screen, Home/Inbox/Explore/Copilot remain one tap away, reinforcing a hub-and-spoke IA.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 11
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when building detail/record views for technical or operational tools (issue trackers, CI/CD dashboards, support ticketing systems) where users need to see rich structured content, an audit trail, and a cross-tool shortcut all on one screen. It's especially effective when:

  • The record has a strong external linkage (e.g., GitHub, Jira, Figma) that deserves a persistent CTA.
  • An activity/audit trail adds trust and traceability for collaborative, asynchronous teams.
  • Content is naturally list/checklist-based (acceptance criteria, requirements, specs).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, log-heavy layout for consumer-facing apps or for users unfamiliar with technical/engineering jargon (the activity feed and checklist format can feel cold or overwhelming to non-technical audiences). It's also not ideal when the detail record has minimal metadata, as the extra chrome (breadcrumb, activity log, sub-issues) would feel like empty scaffolding on a simple object. Additionally, if the primary external action changes contextually (not always "Open in GitHub"), a static persistent button could create confusion or false affordances.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for engineers, founders, and technical product managers who need to triage or review issues while away from their desktop (e).g., approving acceptance criteria from a phone during a commute, or quickly checking an issue's status before a standup.

Psychologically, it leverages reduced cognitive load through familiar developer mental models (git-style activity logs, checklist-style acceptance criteria) so users don't have to re-learn a new paradigm on mobile. The immediate "Open" button also taps into minimizing perceived effort: engineers who live in GitHub expect a frictionless bridge between tools, and surfacing this action prominently builds trust that Linear won't trap them in a walled garden.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent "Open" CTA: Anchored directly under the header outside the scroll area, ensuring the primary cross-tool action (opening the linked GitHub resource) is never lost as content grows.
  • Inline Activity Timeline: Combines system events (label, milestone, assignee) into a single connected vertical thread, eliminating the need for a separate audit log screen.
  • Structured Acceptance Criteria as native checklist copy: Presents QA/test requirements as scannable bullet points directly within the issue body, supporting async engineering handoff.
  • Dual-layer bottom actions: Comment and Info buttons sit above the OS tab bar, cleanly separating "issue-level" actions from "app-level" navigation.
  • Compact metadata breadcrumb: Repo path (SLMobbin/padel-score-counter) under the title keeps full project context visible without consuming a dedicated header row.

screens.name: Linear - Creating an issue - Screen 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Any backlog, ticketing, or task-management app that needs to support multi-dimensional filtering (status, owner, label, project) without overwhelming the user with modals.
  • Professional/B2B tools where users are power users and value information density and speed over decorative or guided UX.
  • Mobile companion apps for desktop-first productivity tools, where screen real estate is limited but filter parity with desktop is still expected.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer-facing apps targeting non-technical or first-time users, where dense jargon-heavy rows (repo/issue syntax) and stacked filter chips would feel intimidating or cluttered.
  • Screens where the primary goal is conversion or emotional engagement (e.g., onboarding, marketing) - this utilitarian layout sacrifices visual delight for speed, which is inappropriate outside of professional tools.
  • Contexts with very few filter dimensions, where exposing 4+ chips would add unnecessary complexity instead of a single simple filter/sort control.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and founders who need to self-audit their personal workload ("Created by me") quickly, often between meetings or on mobile while away from their desk. The psychological driver here is control and accountability: by surfacing exactly what a user has created and its current open status, Linear taps into the desire for closure and ownership tracking (a Zeigarnik-effect-style pull to resolve open loops).

The dense, jargon-forward presentation (repo slugs, issue numbers, labels) signals to a technical audience that this tool speaks their language natively, reinforcing trust and reducing onboarding friction for anyone coming from GitHub/Jira-style workflows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Stacked filter chips as inline faceted search: Multiple independent filter dimensions (status, authorship, visibility, workspace) are exposed simultaneously as horizontally scrollable chips rather than buried in a single "Filter" button, reducing taps for power users who filter constantly.
  • Status ring as a micro-visualization: The small circular progress indicator before the issue title encodes workflow state (e.g., in-progress, backlog) in a glanceable, color-coded dot/ring rather than text, saving horizontal space.
  • Unified global actions in the nav bar: Placing Create (+) and Search as persistent icons beside the back button means users can jump to any action from any filtered context without extra navigation.
  • Graceful empty space handling: Rather than padding with placeholder content, the UI confidently shows whitespace below the single result, trusting the user's mental model that fewer issues is a good thing.

screens.name: Airtable - Creating a new record - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Any data-management mobile app that needs to expose spreadsheet-like records (CRMs, inventory trackers, project management tools) without a desktop-style grid.
  • Apps that support multiple structured collections (tables) within one workspace/project and need lightweight, tab-style switching between them.
  • Products targeting both technical and non-technical users, where surfacing filter/sort/group as primary actions builds confidence without requiring a settings deep-dive.
  • Any list where each item has rich attachments: using a stacked thumbnail with a "+N" badge is an efficient way to hint at extra media.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this card-based field-stacking pattern when a table has very few columns (2-3) - a simple list row would be less cluttered and faster to scan.
  • Not ideal for read-only or casual consumer apps where exposing Filter/Group/Sort toolbars would add unnecessary complexity and intimidate non-power-users.
  • If the underlying dataset has dozens of fields, this stacked-card approach can still create very tall cards requiring excessive scrolling (a dedicated detail/drill-down screen with a condensed summary card may serve better).
  • Avoid fixed bottom tab bars for table-switching when the number of tables can grow unbounded; this works for 3-4 tables but degrades with many more (would need an overflow/drawer pattern instead).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operationally-minded teams and prosumers: project managers, marketers, and "builders" who need structured data (not just freeform notes) but want the simplicity of a consumer app. The travel-planning example is a deliberate onboarding/demo choice: it's universally relatable, letting new users immediately grasp how fields, views, and tables map to a real scenario before they apply the same mental model to business workflows (CRM, inventory, content calendars).

Psychologically, the design leverages familiarity bias (spreadsheet terminology and right-aligned numbers feel instantly "correct" to anyone who has used Excel) combined with reduced intimidation (card-based layout, emoji-like destination icons, and friendly copy make the tool feel approachable rather than engineering-heavy). The visible toolbar also triggers a sense of control and mastery: users see immediately that they can reshape the view (filter/group/sort), which builds trust that the tool can scale with their complexity needs.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Spreadsheet-to-card transformation: Converts rigid tabular columns into vertically stacked, labeled fields per record, solving the classic "wide table on narrow screen" mobile UX problem without sacrificing data structure.
  • Persistent power-user toolbar: Filter, Group, Sort, and Hide Fields are surfaced directly in the toolbar rather than hidden in overflow menus, maintaining desktop-grade power on mobile.
  • Multi-table bottom navigation: The "Places / Packing List / Friends / +" bar turns a single database (base) into a multi-screen app experience, with an inline "+" for immediate table creation.
  • Attachment stacking with counter badge: The "+1" overlay on thumbnails elegantly communicates hidden content volume without requiring the user to open the record.
  • Prominent FAB for row creation: The floating blue "+" button anchors the primary action (add new place) in a thumb-reachable zone, consistent with mobile conventions despite the desktop-first origins of the product.

screens.name: Airtable - Creating a new record - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any mobile app that needs to present a "detail/edit" view for a single structured record composed of heterogeneous field types (CRM, inventory, field-service apps, forms builders).
  • Apps with user-customizable schemas where field type must be visually communicated without taking up excessive label space.
  • Situations requiring quick multi-source media attachment (camera vs. library vs. other) inline within a form row.
  • Any product that benefits from a friendly, non-blocking default name/title for incomplete entities.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, label-stacked form pattern for simple, single-purpose forms (e.g., login, checkout) where fewer, larger fields with more guidance text would convert better.
  • Not ideal for first-time or non-technical users who need more explanatory copy per field (the terse, icon-based labeling assumes schema familiarity and could confuse new users without onboarding).
  • Should be avoided when record data has strong visual/media priority (e.g., a photo-centric app) since this layout treats all fields with equal visual weight, burying rich content like images among plain text fields.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations staff, project managers, and field workers who need to capture or update structured data on the go (e).g., logging a site visit's location, scheduling days, attaching photos, and jotting notes directly from a phone rather than returning to a desktop. The design assumes users already understand the underlying table schema (since field names are self-authored), so it optimizes for speed of data entry over explanation.

Psychologically, the screen reduces cognitive load during interruption-prone contexts (standing at a job site, in a meeting) by using large touch targets, clear type-based icons, and an uncluttered one-field-at-a-time focus flow, letting the keyboard and current field dominate attention while other fields collapse quietly below.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Typed field iconography: Each field label is paired with a small glyph indicating its data type (text, number, attachment, long text), giving users an at-a-glance schema understanding without needing to tap in.
  • Inline multi-source attachment picker: The PICS field surfaces camera, gallery, and overflow options directly inline, reducing taps versus a separate modal just to decide the photo source.
  • Graceful default naming ("Unnamed record"): Prevents blank-title confusion and reassures users their row exists and is being tracked even before data entry is complete.
  • Vertical field stacking for row-to-form transformation: Converts a wide spreadsheet row into a single-column scrollable form, a necessary and well-executed adaptation for small screens.
  • Persistent minimal header actions: Back, record-switcher dropdown, and collaborators icon stay fixed, keeping navigation and collaboration accessible without stealing space from the data fields.

screens.name: Airtable - Creating a new record - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever an app must support file or media uploads from multiple competing storage ecosystems (documents, images, attachments) and when the audience is likely to have assets scattered across both local devices and professional cloud drives, such as B2B SaaS tools, productivity suites, CRM systems, and project management apps.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this exhaustive multi-source pattern for casual consumer apps where users almost always upload from a single source (e.g., a camera-only social app), as the extra choices add unnecessary decision fatigue. It is also not ideal when an app wants to funnel users toward its own proprietary storage/ecosystem (in that case, a single primary CTA with an "other options" fallback would be better).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Airtable's target users: operations teams, marketers, and project managers (frequently work across disparate tools and storage ecosystems (a marketer might store assets in Google Drive, an ops person in Dropbox or Box, enterprise users in OneDrive)). This screen respects that diversity instead of forcing a single workflow, which builds trust and reduces abandonment at the point of attaching critical files to records.

The psychological trigger here is reduced cognitive load through familiarity: by mirroring the native iOS share-sheet/file-picker pattern, users don't need to learn a new interaction model (it feels like an extension of the OS rather than a bespoke in-app control, lowering the perceived risk of connecting external accounts).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unified multi-source picker: Consolidates five cloud providers and three local sources into one coherent list, reducing fragmentation across integrations.
  • Iconographic recognition: Each row uses the source's actual brand icon/color, leveraging users' existing mental models (e.g., Dropbox's blue box, Google Drive's triangle) for near-instant scanning instead of reading.
  • Clear sectioning: Dividing "Local" from "Cloud" with bold section headers helps users quickly navigate to the storage type most relevant to their workflow (e.g., mobile camera roll vs. enterprise cloud drive).
  • Low-friction exit: A persistent, clearly labeled "Cancel" affordance in the header respects user control and prevents dead-end modals.

screens.name: Airtable - Creating a new record - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use contextual permission priming whenever a native OS capability (camera, microphone, location, notifications) is needed to fulfill a specific user-initiated action, attaching a photo, scanning a document, tagging a location, etc. Pair it with a record/detail view pattern for any app that lets users edit structured, multi-field data objects on mobile (CRMs, inventory apps, field-service tools, no-code database apps).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid requesting system permissions at app launch or before the user has expressed clear intent (this leads to higher denial rates and users being unable to understand the "why)." Also avoid the flattened field-row layout for extremely wide or highly relational data (e.g., linked records with many columns) where a tab-based or grouped-section layout would reduce scroll fatigue. Destructive actions like "Delete record" should never be placed this close to neutral actions without sufficient visual separation or confirmation step on less experienced user bases.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This flow targets operations staff, project managers, and mobile field workers who use Airtable to capture real-world data (e.g., travel logs, site visits, inventory checks) directly from their phone. The psychological trigger at play is reciprocity and trust-building through transparency: by explaining exactly why camera access is needed and tying it to a concrete, just-performed action, Airtable reduces the anxiety typically associated with permission requests, increasing opt-in rates and preserving user trust in the brand as a serious productivity tool rather than an intrusive consumer app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Just-in-time permission request: The camera prompt fires only after the user actively taps the Pics field, not preemptively on app load (dramatically increasing the likelihood of "OK" being tapped).
  • Field-as-row mobile reinterpretation: Complex relational table columns are elegantly flattened into a single scrollable record form, preserving Airtable's structured-data power while staying mobile-friendly.
  • Iconography per field type: Each field label has a distinct small icon (text "A", "#", paperclip, calendar) that mirrors the field-type icons used in Airtable's desktop grid, creating cross-platform consistency.
  • Clear destructive vs. constructive footer actions: Color and iconography (red trash vs. blue icon) make the irreversible "Delete record" action visually distinct from safe "Customize fields," reducing accidental data loss.

firstStageCandidates.flowName: Moving an issue to a project

screens.name: Linear - Moving an issue to a project - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any fast-capture / quick-create flow in productivity, task-management, or note-taking apps (anywhere the primary goal is to minimize the time between "I have a thought" and "it's recorded)." It's ideal for mobile contexts where typing is costly and every unnecessary field increases abandonment risk. Also effective when the app has rich downstream metadata (assignees, tags, projects) that can reasonably be deferred to a triage step rather than captured at creation time.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal-capture-then-defer approach when the created record is unusable or ambiguous without mandatory metadata (e.g., financial transactions, legal forms, or workflows where routing/ownership must be set immediately to avoid work being "lost" in an untriaged backlog). In such cases, deferring required fields can create a hidden pile of under-specified records that nobody takes ownership of. It's also unsuitable for first-time users who need more guidance (the terseness assumes familiarity with the team's existing taxonomy of labels/projects).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets engineers, PMs, and designers who need to capture a task or bug the instant they think of it (often mid-conversation, mid-standup, or mid-thought) before context is lost. The design leans on the psychological principle of reduced activation energy: by stripping the form down to just a title and optional description, Linear removes the "too much effort to log this now" excuse that kills team adoption of issue trackers.

The deferred metadata chips also reflect an understanding of cognitive load sequencing: asking "who should this be assigned to?" before the idea itself is written down would interrupt the user's train of thought. By allowing metadata entry after capture, Linear matches how technical teams actually think: capture first, triage later.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Title-first capture: The largest, boldest element on screen is the title input, correctly prioritizing fast idea capture over metadata configuration.
  • Deferred metadata: Assignee/Labels/Project/More are presented as optional chips below the fold of typing focus, so users aren't blocked by decisions they can make later.
  • Inline rich-text toolbar: Checklist, code block, mention, and quote formatting are available right above the keyboard, enabling structured, technical issue descriptions without a context switch.
  • Symmetrical escape/commit actions: Close (X) and Send (↑) are mirrored top-left/top-right for fast, confident one-handed exits in either direction.
  • Auto-generated issue ID (HBT-14): Immediately gives the draft a sense of being "real" and trackable, reducing the psychological weight of starting from a blank page.

screens.name: Linear - Moving an issue to a project - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when users need to reassign an item to one of many possible categories/containers (projects, folders, labels, teams, assignees) from within a detail view, especially on mobile where a full-page navigation would feel heavy. It's ideal for:

  • Issue/task management apps needing quick re-categorization
  • Any searchable single-select list exceeding ~5-7 items
  • Mobile contexts where preserving the underlying screen's context matters
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The selection requires multi-select or bulk assignment (a flat single-select list with a checkmark won't communicate multiple selections well).
  • The list is extremely short (2-3 items), where a search bar becomes unnecessary overhead.
  • Users need rich contextual info (e.g., project owner, status, progress) to decide (a bottom sheet with truncated text may be too cramped, requiring a fuller page instead).
  • Creating a new project is a frequent need from this entry point without a visible "+ New" affordance, which is notably absent here and could cause a dead end for users wanting an option not yet listed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets engineers, PMs, and designers who triage dozens of issues per day and need near-instant ways to reorganize work without breaking flow. The psychological driver here is reduction of cognitive and motor friction: by presenting a search-first, single-tap list instead of a nested folder browser or dropdown form, Linear caters to users who think in keyboard shortcuts and fast filtering rather than deliberate menu traversal.

The checkmark and "No project" default also leverage the recognition-over-recall principle, instantly orienting users amid frequent context-switching between many issues and projects.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-focused search with pre-raised keyboard: Eliminates an extra tap, letting power users start typing immediately to filter long project lists.
  • Inline selection state via checkmark: Removes the need for a separate confirmation step or secondary screen to see what's currently assigned.
  • Iconographic differentiation: Color-coded icons distinguish "No project" from actual projects and visually differentiate project types, aiding fast recognition over reading full labels.
  • Lightweight modal over full navigation: Using a partial-screen bottom sheet instead of a full page preserves context and signals a quick, reversible micro-interaction.
  • Single-tap commit: Presumably tapping any row instantly reassigns the project, avoiding a separate "Save" step (consistent with Linear's optimistic-UI, frictionless philosophy).

screens.name: Linear - Moving an issue to a project - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any high-frequency, low-friction content creation flow where speed and reduced cognitive load are more valuable than exhaustive upfront structure (e).g., task managers, note-taking apps, bug trackers, or quick-add modals in productivity tools. It's especially effective when:

  • Users need to capture an idea quickly before context-switching away.
  • Metadata (tags, assignees, categories) is useful but not mandatory at creation time.
  • The product's brand values speed and minimalism over guided hand-holding.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal, label-less composer pattern when:

  • Fields require strict validation or mandatory completion before submission (e.g., compliance forms, legal documents) - lack of visible labels and structure increases error rates for first-time or infrequent users.
  • The target audience is non-technical or unfamiliar with the domain's shorthand conventions (e.g., issue ID prefixes), as the absence of labels can reduce discoverability and increase onboarding time.
  • Accessibility is a primary concern: low-contrast, unlabeled text fields can be harder for screen reader users or those with cognitive disabilities to parse without explicit field labels.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers who think and work in short, high-frequency bursts: people who need to log a bug, feature request, or task mid-conversation or mid-thought without breaking flow. The design leans on the psychological principle of minimizing activation energy: by stripping away form labels, required fields, and multi-step wizards, it reduces the perceived effort of creating a ticket, which in turn increases the frequency with which team members actually document work (a common failure point in less frictionless tools like Jira).

The keyboard-first, mobile-native composer also targets users who capture ideas on the go (e.g., a PM noticing a bug while using a mobile prototype), leveraging the "strike while the iron is hot" principle, capturing intent immediately before it's lost or forgotten.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Borderless, chrome-free composer: Removing field borders and labels makes issue creation feel as lightweight as typing a note, dramatically reducing friction for a task (filing tickets) that is often perceived as tedious overhead.
  • Deferred metadata assignment: Assignee, labels, and project are surfaced as compact chips below the text body rather than as mandatory upfront form fields, letting users dump their thought first and categorize second, matching natural "capture now, organize later" cognitive flow.
  • Persistent rich-text toolbar: Inline formatting options (checklist, code block, quote, mention, image) are always accessible above the keyboard, enabling structured, detailed tickets without leaving the composer or opening a separate menu.
  • Single affirmative action: The up-arrow submit button in the top-right is the only primary CTA, keeping the exit paths binary (cancel via X, or submit), which minimizes decision fatigue.
  • Contextual breadcrumb chip: The "ASMobbin" workspace/team pill at the top anchors the user's location within the broader workspace hierarchy without consuming a full navigation bar.

screens.name: Linear - Applying a template - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any "quick add" or "fast capture" entry point in productivity, task-management, or note-taking apps where speed-to-save matters more than complete metadata at creation time (e).g., issue trackers, to-do apps, CRM lead capture, or support ticket intake. Ideal when the user base is technical/power-users comfortable with deferred organization and keyboard shortcuts.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal-field, deferred-metadata approach in contexts where compliance, data completeness, or routing accuracy is critical at the moment of submission (e.g., medical intake forms, financial applications, legal filings) - forcing required classification upfront prevents incomplete or misrouted records. It's also less appropriate for non-technical, mainstream consumer audiences who may feel lost without guided, labeled form fields and may not intuitively discover the chip row's functionality.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers who think and work in short bursts and need to capture issues the instant they occur (often mid-conversation, mid-bug-report, or mid-standup) without breaking flow to fill out a long form. The audience values speed and keyboard-first interaction over visual polish, consistent with Linear's "shortcut friendly, fast capture" ethos.

Psychologically, the design exploits the "low commitment to start" principle: by hiding all classification decisions until after the thought is captured, it removes the activation energy that stops people from logging minor bugs or ideas. The auto-numbered ticket ID (HBT-14) also taps into a sense of structure and permanence, reassuring technical users that nothing is lost and everything is traceable (important for engineering culture where accountability and historical context matter).
screens.keyHighlights:
Chip-based metadata bar with icons: Backlog (status), Priority, Assignee, and Label are rendered as pill-shaped buttons with corresponding icons positioned directly above the keyboard, letting users classify an issue without ever leaving the typing flow or opening a separate screen.

Inline rich-text toolbar: Attachment, mention, checklist, code block, and quote icons are embedded in a second row just above the system keyboard, giving power users (engineers/PMs) Markdown-like authoring speed on mobile.

Full-screen modal with dimmed backdrop: The rounded-corner card floating over a dimmed background clearly signals "quick capture" ephemeral context, distinct from the main navigational app chrome.

Zero mandatory fields before submission: Title and description are the only visible required inputs; all triage metadata is optional and deferred, dramatically lowering the barrier to logging an issue in the moment an idea strikes.

screens.name: Linear - Applying a template - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when:

  • Users need to select one item from a list that could grow large over time (templates, labels, assignees, projects).
  • The action occurs mid-flow (e.g., during issue/task creation) and should not interrupt the broader task context.
  • Your user base is keyboard-proficient or benefits from rapid, type-ahead filtering rather than visual scanning.
  • You want to maintain visual and interaction consistency between mobile and desktop surfaces that already use command-palette-style search.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The list of options is very short (2-3 items) and visually scanning would be faster than typing (a simple list or segmented control would suffice).
  • Your target users are non-technical or unfamiliar with search-driven interfaces, where a browsable, categorized list with visual previews would reduce cognitive effort.
  • The items being selected benefit from rich visual differentiation (icons, thumbnails, previews) that a plain text search list cannot adequately convey.
  • Immediate keyboard pop-up could be jarring or unwanted, such as when the modal is opened accidentally or unexpectedly during a passive browsing session.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern directly serves engineers, PMs, and designers who create many similar issues repeatedly (bugs, feature requests, tasks) and need a fast way to standardize issue structure without re-typing boilerplate fields each time. Templates reduce setup friction for recurring issue types, a high-frequency action for teams running structured workflows (e.g., sprint planning, bug triage).

Psychologically, the design leverages the recognition-over-recall principle by letting users type a few letters instead of remembering the exact label, and it exploits the power-user muscle memory Linear deliberately cultivates (the search-everything behavior trains users that virtually any action in the app can be accessed through instant filtering, increasing speed and reducing menu-diving fatigue over time).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-focused search input with keyboard pre-raised: Eliminates an extra tap, reducing the steps needed to find and apply a template to just typing + selecting.
  • Minimalist modal over full-screen navigation: Keeps users anchored in their original context (issue creation), reducing perceived navigation depth and making the interaction feel lightweight and reversible.
  • Search-first over list-browse: Mirrors the desktop Command Palette paradigm, giving mobile users the same fast, keyboard-centric mental model as desktop power users, improving cross-platform consistency.
  • Single, clear dismiss target (X): Provides an unambiguous escape hatch, reducing anxiety about getting "stuck" in a sub-flow.

screens.name: Linear - Applying a template - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any fast-capture creation flow where the core object has one or two essential fields and many optional ones (note-taking apps, task managers, CRM activity logging, or bug trackers). It's ideal when the goal is to minimize time-to-save and when users are expected to enrich records later (via desktop or a backlog grooming session). Also effective when you want in-context onboarding: using instructive placeholder text instead of tooltips or tutorials keeps guidance visible exactly when and where it's needed.
screens.whereNotToUse: This minimal, keyboard-first composer is inappropriate for workflows where metadata is compliance-critical or must be captured upfront (e.g., legal intake forms, financial transactions, medical records) - deferring required fields in those contexts creates downstream data-quality or compliance risk. It also breaks down for very long-form content creation, where a full-screen focused editor without a half-covering keyboard and chip row would serve better. Teams with rigid ticket templates that mandate fields like Sprint, Story Points, or Epic at creation time should surface those as required steps rather than optional ghost chips.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen directly serves engineers, PMs, and founders who think and work at high velocity and need to log an issue or idea the instant it occurs to them (often mid-conversation or mid-debugging session on mobile). The psychological trigger at play is reduction of friction and cognitive load: by deferring all non-essential decisions (priority, assignee, labels) and leading with just a title, Linear respects the user's limited attention and prevents the "I'll do this later" abandonment common in heavier PM tools like Jira.

The guided placeholder copy also serves a socialization function for teams adopting Linear's issue-writing philosophy (it quietly trains new users on what constitutes a good issue summary, reinforcing company-wide quality standards without requiring onboarding documentation).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Keyboard-first capture: The modal opens with the keyboard already active and cursor placed, eliminating a tap and optimizing for the "capture the thought now" moment.
  • Progressive disclosure of metadata: Status, Labels, Priority, and Assignee are rendered as low-contrast, optional chips below the fold of primary content, so the form never feels mandatory or heavy despite Linear's data-rich backend.
  • Guided empty-state copy: Placeholder text in the description field doubles as an in-context writing guide ("Why is this needed? What problem does it solve"), nudging better quality tickets without a separate tutorial.
  • Minimal chrome: Only three icons in the top bar (close, context, submit) keep the focus entirely on content creation rather than navigation.
  • Inline rich-text toolbar: A compact formatting bar (image, mention, list, checklist, code) sits directly above the keyboard, giving power-user formatting capability without a separate screen.

screens.name: Linear - Mentioning a user - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this modal quick-capture pattern for any tool where rapid, lightweight creation of structured records (tickets, tasks, notes, bugs) is core to the product's value proposition. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to create records quickly without losing their current context (e.g., issue trackers, CRMs, note apps).
  • Metadata exists but shouldn't block the primary creation action (use optional chips/pills instead of required form fields).
  • Your users are technical/power users who benefit from markdown or rich-text formatting tools embedded near the keyboard.
  • You want to encourage a specific content structure (like acceptance criteria) through smart defaults or placeholder text rather than rigid multi-field forms.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal, chip-heavy pattern when:

  • The majority of users are non-technical and need guided, labeled form fields rather than icon-only pills, which can be ambiguous without hover/tap discovery.
  • Compliance or data quality requires certain metadata (e.g., assignee, priority) to be mandatory at creation time (this pattern's optionality could lead to incomplete, hard-to-triage records).
  • The content being created is highly structured/tabular (e.g., financial records) where a free-text area is inappropriate and a multi-step form with validation is safer.
  • Screen real estate is very limited (smaller devices) and a long horizontal chip row combined with a formatting toolbar and keyboard could overwhelm or crowd the viewport.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, product managers, and designers who need to capture technical work items the instant they think of them (often mid-conversation or mid-debugging session). The low-friction chip-based metadata and markdown-friendly description field cater to technically fluent users who value speed and structure over guided hand-holding.

Psychologically, the design exploits the "capture now, organize later" principle: by not forcing categorization fields before text entry, it lowers the activation energy required to log an issue, increasing the likelihood that stray ideas or bugs actually get recorded instead of lost. The pre-populated acceptance-criteria style content also reflects social/professional modeling (teams that use Linear tend to internalize and replicate its implicit "write testable specs" culture, which is reinforced structurally by the UI's generous, unconstrained text area).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking metadata chips: Assignee, Label, Milestone, and Project are optional, icon-labeled pills rather than mandatory dropdown fields, letting users submit an issue in seconds and fill in detail later.
  • Context persistence: The repository/project name is shown directly beneath the modal title, so users always know the scope of the issue they're creating without needing a separate screen.
  • Inline rich-text toolbar: A compact formatting bar sits directly above the keyboard, enabling markdown-like formatting (bold, links, images, mentions, lists) without context-switching to a separate editor view.
  • Typographic hierarchy: Large bold title vs. monospace-style description text visually separates "what" from "how," mimicking the mental model of writing a ticket.
  • Modal-based quick capture: Presenting issue creation as an overlay (with X to dismiss) rather than full navigation preserves the user's previous screen state and minimizes perceived cost of starting a new issue.

screens.name: Linear - Mentioning a user - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any fast-capture creation flow within productivity, collaboration, or dev-tool apps (issue trackers, note-taking apps, task managers, or CRM activity logs). It is especially effective when:

  • Users need to jot unstructured content quickly, then tag collaborators or metadata without leaving the compose view.
  • The audience is comfortable with markdown or lightweight syntax.
  • Mentioning/tagging teammates is a core collaborative behavior (via @-mention autocomplete).
  • You want to minimize modal/step transitions for quick inputs on mobile.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Your audience is non-technical and would be confused or intimidated by raw markdown syntax rather than rendered rich text.
  • The creation flow requires many mandatory structured fields (e.g., compliance forms, e-commerce checkouts) where ambiguity about required inputs could cause errors (an explicit multi-step wizard with validation would serve better).
  • Screen real estate is extremely limited (smaller devices) and a floating autocomplete popover combined with a toolbar and keyboard could feel cramped or obscure context, as partially seen here where the popover covers prior body text.
  • Accessibility is a primary concern: dense floating overlays atop a keyboard can be difficult for screen reader or low-vision users to navigate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for engineers, product managers, and designers who need to capture issues the instant an idea or bug surfaces (often mid-conversation or mid-debug) without breaking flow to navigate a complex form. The markdown-first body and developer-standard terminology (Acceptance Criteria, Milestone) signal this is optimized for technically literate teams rather than general consumers.

The psychological trigger at play is reduction of friction/cognitive load: by allowing free-text capture with inline structured metadata (via chips and @-mentions) rather than forcing a rigid multi-field form upfront, Linear taps into the "capture now, organize later" behavior that matches how engineers actually think about tasks (fast, unstructured brainstorming followed by lightweight tagging).

The autocomplete's prioritization of a relevant team member (Sam Lee from SLMobbin) also leverages recognition over recall, letting users avoid typing full names and instead confirm a suggested match, which builds trust in the system's contextual intelligence.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-blocking @-mention autocomplete: Surfaces a smart contextual suggestion (the related repo/person) before a generic search field, reducing taps for the most likely action.
  • Floating metadata chips above the keyboard: Assignee/Label/Milestone/Project remain accessible without scrolling or dismissing the keyboard, enabling structured tagging mid-flow.
  • Persistent formatting toolbar: Markdown shortcuts (bold, italic, link, image, mention, lists) are docked directly above the keyboard for zero-context-switch editing.
  • Repository/project breadcrumb in the header: Immediately orients the user to *where* this issue will live, critical in multi-repo/multi-team environments.
  • Single prominent Submit CTA: Reduces decision fatigue; there's no competing secondary action fighting for attention.

screens.name: Linear - Mentioning a user - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Any fast-capture workflow (issue trackers, note apps, task managers) where speed-to-save matters more than complete categorization.
  • Tools serving technical/power users who value keyboard/markdown input over heavy form UI.
  • Scenarios where optional metadata should never block a core creation action.
  • Products that benefit from standardizing submission quality via smart content templates/defaults.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Consumer-facing apps where users are unfamiliar with markdown syntax and need WYSIWYG formatting instead.
  • Workflows where metadata (e.g., priority, due date) is compliance-critical and must be captured before submission, deferring it here would create data-quality gaps.
  • Low-literacy or non-technical audiences who may find an empty title + free-text body intimidating without more guided prompts.
  • Contexts requiring extensive required fields, where a single scrollable chip row would be insufficient and should be replaced by a multi-step form.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, PMs, and designers who need to capture issues the instant they're identified (often mid-conversation, mid-bug-report, or mid-code-review) without losing momentum to a cumbersome form. The psychological trigger here is reduction of activation energy: by leading with a blank title and a pre-seeded structured template rather than empty required fields, Linear lowers the perceived effort of starting, which is proven to increase completion rates for quick-capture tools.

The acceptance-criteria template also leverages the default-effect bias: users are far more likely to follow a given structure than to invent their own from scratch, which standardizes issue quality across a team without enforcing rigid validation rules.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Content-first field ordering: Title and description appear before any metadata, prioritizing idea capture over categorization friction.
  • Inline markdown template: Auto-populated "Acceptance Criteria" checklist pattern guides users toward writing higher-quality, testable issues without needing a separate guidance panel.
  • Persistent, always-visible Submit action: Anchored in the header regardless of scroll position or keyboard state, reducing friction to publish.
  • Horizontally scrollable metadata chip row: Assignee/Label/Milestone/Project are optional, deferred, and non-blocking (they don't gate submission).
  • Compact in-context repo breadcrumb: Confirms destination (SLMobbin/padel-score-counter) without a full navigation bar.
  • Thumb-reachable formatting toolbar: Rich text controls sit directly above the keyboard for one-handed mobile editing.

screens.name: Figma - Replying to a comment - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Any collaborative canvas/document tool where feedback must be tied to a specific visual location (design tools, whiteboards, PDF annotators).
  • Mobile companion apps for desktop-first collaboration tools, where quick-glance review and lightweight replies are the primary use case.
  • Asynchronous review workflows where context (what is being discussed) is as important as the comment text itself.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid pinned/contextual comment overlays in dense data interfaces (e.g., spreadsheets, tables) where precise pin placement is impractical and overlapping annotations become cluttered.
  • Not ideal for high-volume comment threads: a small bottom sheet won't scale well for long conversations and should expand to a full-screen thread view instead.
  • Skip this pattern on first-time/empty files with no collaborators yet, as it would be premature and could confuse new solo users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers and cross-functional collaborators (e.g., PMs, developers) reviewing design systems on the go via Figma's mobile app. The psychological trigger at play is social presence and accountability: seeing a colleague's avatar and comment pinned directly to a design artifact creates a sense of being watched/engaged by teammates, which drives faster response and reinforces team cohesion around shared libraries.

It also leverages reciprocity and momentum: a lightweight, casual comment like "Check this out, this is cool!" lowers the barrier to engage, nudging the recipient to reply quickly rather than feeling obligated to write a lengthy critique.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pinned, contextual commenting: The avatar marker sits exactly on the artifact being discussed, so feedback is never ambiguous about what it refers to.
  • Non-destructive overlay pattern: The bottom sheet floats above the canvas rather than replacing it, letting users scroll/reference the design while reading comments.
  • Persistent reply field: Always-visible input encourages fast, low-friction responses and keeps the conversation loop tight.
  • Grab handle affordance: The drag handle atop the sheet signals it's expandable/collapsible, a familiar mobile gesture reducing cognitive load.
  • @mention highlighting: "JudySmith" is styled as a link/mention, visually distinguishing directed feedback and enabling notification routing.

screens.name: Figma - Replying to a comment - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any threaded, contextual commenting system tied to a specific object, pin, or location in a larger canvas/document (e.g., design tools, PDF annotation apps, project management pins on a map or timeline). It's ideal when you want to preserve the user's place in a larger context while allowing deep-dive conversation, and when mobile quick-replies are a core use case.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for long-form or formal discussions requiring threading/nesting of replies, as the flat single-level comment list lacks visual hierarchy for complex conversations. It's also unsuitable for high-volume comment streams (e.g., social media) where sorting, filtering, or reaction aggregation are needed (this minimal layout would feel underpowered and require significant scrolling).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves design teams and developers reviewing work remotely or on-the-go, particularly stakeholders who need to catch up on feedback threads from a phone rather than at their desk. The psychological trigger at play is social responsiveness: being @mentioned creates an implicit obligation to respond, and the immediacy of "Just now" plus the ready-to-type reply box lowers the activation energy to reply instantly, keeping collaborative momentum alive even outside the desktop environment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Bottom Sheet: Keeps the user anchored to the canvas behind it, reducing navigation overhead (a hallmark of Figma's "canvas-first" philosophy even on mobile).
  • @Mention Highlighting: Instantly clarifies who the comment is directed at, supporting multi-person async collaboration.
  • Sticky Reply Field: Always-visible input at the bottom lowers the friction to respond, encouraging higher engagement rates on design feedback.
  • Relative Timestamps: "Just now" fosters a sense of real-time presence and urgency around active discussions.
  • Minimalist Overflow Menu: Keeps the primary reading experience clean while still surfacing edit/delete/resolve actions on demand.

screens.name: Figma - Replying to a comment - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when building collaborative annotation or commenting systems on mobile, especially in tools where feedback is tied to a specific visual or spatial object (design files, documents, video timestamps, images). It's ideal for:

  • Cross-platform collaboration tools extending desktop review workflows to mobile.
  • Any app where contextual, threaded conversation needs to coexist with a primary canvas/content view.
  • Scenarios requiring quick, low-friction replies (e.g., approvals, quick reactions, directed feedback via @mentions).

Avoid this lightweight bottom-sheet chat pattern when:

  • Feedback needs to be long-form, structured, or formally documented (e.g., legal review, detailed QA reports) - a full-screen or desktop-optimized interface would serve better.
  • The app's audience is not already familiar with @mention or chat-style conventions, as it assumes prior exposure to similar patterns from Slack/social apps.
  • Comments need rich context (e.g., multiple attachments, code snippets) that a compact mobile toolbar cannot adequately support.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers, developers, and cross-functional stakeholders (PMs, clients) who need to give or receive feedback on design work asynchronously while away from their desktop. The mobile commenting flow caters specifically to reviewers who may only check in on designs via phone (a common real-world pattern where a manager or client reviews a shared Figma link during a commute or between meetings).

Psychologically, the design leverages social validation and responsiveness norms: the @mention notifies a specific person, creating implicit social pressure to respond, while the casual tone and quick-reply affordance encourage low-friction, high-frequency engagement, turning design review into an ongoing conversation rather than a formal gate.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual mobile commenting: Brings Figma's signature in-canvas commenting feature to mobile without requiring a full desktop-style interface, preserving collaborative workflows on the go.
  • @Mention as a first-class formatting tool: Placed directly in the compose toolbar alongside text styling and link insertion, signaling that directed feedback is a core use case, not an afterthought.
  • Thumb-reachable toolbar placement: Formatting icons sit just above the keyboard rather than at the top of the screen, optimizing for one-handed mobile use.
  • Bottom sheet with drag handle: Keeps the design canvas contextually present behind the modal, reinforcing that comments are tied to a specific design artifact rather than existing in an isolated inbox.
