screens.name: Figma - Replying to a comment - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet threaded comment pattern when you need to let users discuss a specific object, pin, or location within a larger canvas/document without navigating away from that context. It's ideal for:

  • Design review and annotation tools (Figma, Miro, InVision)
  • Mapping/location-pin discussion apps
  • Any canvas-based product where comments are tied to spatial coordinates
  • Mobile companion apps where full-screen navigation would break spatial orientation
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for long-form, highly structured discussions that need rich formatting, file attachments, or deep threading (replies-to-replies), as the minimal bottom sheet lacks room for that complexity. It's also unsuitable when comments need to be a primary, persistent part of the main navigation rather than a transient overlay (in those cases, a dedicated full-screen inbox or discussion tab would serve better). Additionally, this lightweight style may feel too informal for enterprise approval workflows that require audit trails, status tracking, or formal sign-off.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for designers and developers collaborating asynchronously or in real-time on a shared design file. The target users are professionals used to fast-paced feedback loops where comments function like lightweight chat rather than formal review documents.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages social proof and low-friction communication: seeing "Just now" timestamps and casual language ("this is cool!") signals an active, living collaboration rather than a static review process, encouraging more team members to jump in and contribute. The @mention highlight taps into the same notification-driven engagement loop as Slack or Teams, being called out by name triggers a sense of personal relevance and prompts quicker replies.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Bottom sheet overlay: Keeps the canvas/context visible underneath while focusing attention on the conversation, avoidable full-screen navigation for a lightweight task.
  • Tinted @mention chip: Instantly differentiates directed call-outs from regular text, improving scannability in multi-person threads.
  • Consistent avatar-initial system: Removes dependency on profile photos, ensuring visual consistency across all users from day one.
  • Persistent reply composer: Fixed at the bottom, always accessible regardless of thread length, reducing friction to respond.
  • Per-comment overflow menu: Keeps secondary actions (edit/delete/resolve) out of the primary reading flow.

screens.name: Figma Adding a comment 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this "live example + explanation" canvas pattern when onboarding users into complex creative or technical tools (design tools, no-code builders, workflow automation canvases) where an infinite or non-linear workspace could otherwise cause disorientation. It's ideal for template files, starter kits, or any first-run file meant to teach by demonstration.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for linear, single-purpose mobile apps where screen real estate is limited and panning canvases would feel unnatural or inefficient. It's also inappropriate for time-sensitive transactional flows (checkout, forms) where large illustrative headlines and exploratory navigation would distract from task completion rather than aid it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets design teams and professional UI/UX practitioners (likely within an organization) who have just created or been invited to a shared "Team Library" file. It serves as an onboarding/template artifact for design system adoption. The psychological trigger here is reducing the intimidation of a blank/complex file by providing explicit, low-friction guidance ("Start here") combined with social proof of best practices (a pre-built example of colors and text field states), nudging the team toward standardization and away from fragmented, ad-hoc design work.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Canvas-as-Documentation: Using the actual design tool's infinite canvas to house an interactive "README" is brilliant because users learn the tool by looking at real artifacts within the native environment, rather than leaving the app to read a help doc.

  • Explicit Entry Point: The oversized "Start here" text with a directional arrow solves the classic "blank canvas"/orientation problem inherent to infinite-canvas tools, where users often don't know where to look first or which direction to scroll.

  • Paired Example + Explanation: Placing a live style-guide swatch sheet directly beside the explanatory text creates an immediate feedback loop between concept (library) and implementation (actual tokens/components).

screens.name: Figma Adding a comment 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when:

  • Introducing a new, non-obvious gesture or interaction model (e.g., tap-and-hold, swipe, multi-finger gestures) that cannot be conveyed through visible UI chrome alone.

  • Announcing feature parity between platforms (e.g., "now available on mobile/desktop") to re-engage existing users.

  • You need a lightweight, dismissible, one-time educational moment that doesn't require a full onboarding flow or tutorial.

  • The feature is core enough to warrant interruption but simple enough to explain in one short message.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The gesture or feature is already discoverable via visible affordances (e.g., a visible button) - an interruptive modal would be overkill and annoying.

  • The user has already dismissed this exact message before; repeating a "Got it" modal on every session creates fatigue and feature-blindness.

  • Multiple new features need to be communicated at once, stacking several of these modals in sequence overwhelms users and should instead be consolidated into a changelog or a guided multi-step tour.

  • The context is a first-time/new user onboarding, where the user has no prior mental model to compare against (in that case, a progressive onboarding flow integrated into first-use would be more appropriate than a "new feature" framing).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets existing, returning users of a collaborative design tool (e.g., Figma) who are already familiar with the desktop experience and are now encountering the mobile app, where interaction patterns differ meaningfully from a mouse-driven environment (hover, right-click, cursor-based commenting don't translate to touch).

The psychological trigger at play is reducing the "unknown gesture" anxiety: touch-and-hold is a powerful but non-obvious gesture that many users never discover organically. By proactively surfacing it at the first relevant moment (opening a file where commenting is possible), the product converts a potentially hidden feature into an immediately usable one, driving feature adoption metrics without relying on documentation or support tickets.

It also leverages the Zeigarnik/curiosity principle combined with reassurance: by announcing "Comments are now on mobile," it taps into the satisfaction of a long-awaited feature parity update, increasing goodwill and perceived product momentum.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Gesture-visualizing illustration: Instead of a static icon, the concentric-ripple graphic mimics the actual touch feedback animation the user will see in the real UI, making an invisible gesture (tap-and-hold) tangible and learnable at a glance.

  • Single CTA, no escape hatch: There's no 'X' or 'skip' within the modal itself (only the background screen's X in the top-left nav, which belongs to the underlying screen), forcing deliberate acknowledgment of the new feature before proceeding.

  • Dimmed background with content bleed-through: Preserves context and continuity, reducing the jarring, disorienting feeling of a full takeover screen while still focusing attention via contrast and scrim opacity.

  • Benefit-first, instruction-first copy ordering: Leads with the required action (headline) before justifying it (body copy), optimizing for users who skim.

screens.name: Figma Adding a comment 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this contextual bottom-sheet composer pattern when:

Also avoid for first-time or novice users unfamiliar with draggable sheets, since the drag handle alone may not sufficiently communicate expand/collapse behavior without onboarding or a tooltip.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets design teams and collaborators reviewing a shared component/style library on mobile (likely a secondary device used for quick async feedback rather than primary design work). The psychological driver is reducing context-switching cost: by keeping the design reference visible while composing a comment, users don't need to hold information in short-term memory or toggle between screens, lowering cognitive load and encouraging more specific, actionable feedback.

The @mention and link tools cater to collaborative review workflows where tagging teammates or referencing related files is common, appealing to users who value efficient, in-context team communication.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving composer: The comment input docks as a bottom sheet rather than a full-screen takeover, letting users reference the design content above while typing their feedback.

  • Rich inline tools without clutter: @mention, text styling, and link insertion are tucked into minimal icon buttons directly beneath the input, offering power-user functionality in a thumb-reachable zone.

  • Draggable sheet affordance: The grabber handle communicates that the panel height is adjustable, giving users control over how much canvas vs. input they see.

  • Clear exit path: A persistent close (X) in the top-left avoids trapping the user in the comment flow.

screens.name: Figma Adding a comment 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this mention-autocomplete-with-popover pattern in any collaborative tool where comments, tasks, or messages can be directed at specific team members (project management apps, design tools, document editors, or internal chat systems). It's especially valuable when workspaces have many members or potential name collisions, and when quick, low-context-switch tagging is essential to keep users in their creative or productive flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in consumer-facing apps with small or single-user contexts where tagging isn't relevant, or in flows where showing a user's email publicly could raise privacy concerns (e.g., public forums or open communities). It's also unnecessary overhead for simple, non-collaborative text inputs, and could clutter the UI if the suggestion list needs to show many simultaneous matches on a small mobile screen.

  • Dual-identifier suggestion: Showing both name and email in the mention suggestion prevents mis-tagging when names are ambiguous or duplicated across a workspace.

  • Persistent formatting toolbar: @mention, text styling, and link insertion icons are always visible above the keyboard, reducing the need to hunt through menus mid-typing.

  • Disabled-state submit button: The greyed-out send arrow communicates system status at a glance, preventing accidental empty submissions.

  • Context-preserving dim background: Rather than a full-screen takeover, the underlying library content remains partially visible, helping the user retain spatial memory of what they are commenting on.

This pattern targets professional and semi-professional collaborators (designers, product managers, and stakeholders working inside a shared design system or asset library). The psychological driver is social accountability and reduced ambiguity: by surfacing a verified identity (avatar + email) before confirming a tag, the system prevents the discomfort of mis-attributing feedback to the wrong person, which is especially critical in larger organizations with repeated first names. The low-friction composer also taps into the desire for quick, in-the-moment communication without breaking creative flow.

screens.name: Figma - Deleting a comment - Screen 1

screens.name: Figma - Deleting a comment - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The target user already understands Figma's commenting conventions from desktop and expects the mobile experience to replicate that power without dumbing it down.

Psychologically, the menu exploits recognition over recall (icons + labels), and the red "Delete thread" leverages loss-aversion cues to slow down accidental destructive taps. The persistent visibility of the underlying thread reduces cognitive load and context-switching anxiety, a key concern for mobile power users who often fear losing their place in long comment chains.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-anchored menu placement: The action sheet appears directly adjacent to the triggering comment rather than centered on screen, maintaining spatial continuity between cause and effect.

screens.name: Figma - Deleting a comment - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this confirmation dialog pattern whenever:

  • An action is irreversible or has cascading effects on data other users contributed (comments, threads, shared assets).

  • The content being deleted could easily be confused with similar items (e.g., multiple comment threads on a canvas), warranting a specific object name in the CTA.

  • Collaborative or multi-user contexts where "undo" isn't readily available or visible to all parties.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy modal confirmation pattern for:

  • Low-stakes, easily reversible actions (e.g., archiving a comment, muting a thread) - use an inline undo/snackbar instead to reduce friction.

  • High-frequency repeated actions, where a modal interruption every time would create workflow fatigue; consider a "don't ask again" option or swipe-to-delete with undo.

  • Situations where the destructive action only affects the current user's own private data with no collaborative impact (a lighter-weight confirmation may suffice).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers and collaborators working in shared Figma files, where comment threads often contain valuable design feedback, decisions, and discussion history from multiple stakeholders (not just the deleter). Because threads can include replies and reactions from teammates, accidental deletion has a real collaborative cost, losing someone else's input, not just your own.

The psychological trigger at play is loss aversion combined with social accountability: users are reminded that deleting affects not only their own content but also other people's contributions (replies/reactions), which raises the perceived stakes of the action and encourages a second thought before confirming. The dialog also serves a trust-building function for teams (by making destructive actions require explicit confirmation with clear consequences, Figma signals that collaborative work is protected from careless deletion).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit consequence messaging: Clearly states that replies and reactions cascade-delete, preventing silent data loss and surprise.

  • Color-coded action hierarchy: Blue "Cancel" (safe/default) vs. red "Delete thread" (destructive) leverages established color psychology to guide safe defaults.

  • Named action instead of generic label: "Delete thread" instead of "Delete" or "OK" removes ambiguity about what exactly will be removed.

  • Dimmed/blurred background: Visually locks focus onto the decision, preventing accidental interaction with underlying canvas or thread.

  • Context preserved behind the modal: The original thread (author, message, timestamp) remains partially visible, letting users mentally confirm they're deleting the correct thread before committing.

screens.name: Loom - Commenting on the video - Screen 1

screens.name: Loom - Commenting on the video - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any time-based media review workflow: video feedback tools, podcast annotation, design-review recordings, async standups, or e-learning platforms where feedback needs to be tied to a specific moment rather than the whole asset. screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for static content (documents, images) where there's no "timestamp" to anchor to (a simpler inline or margin comment pattern would be more appropriate). It's also overkill for very short clips (under a few seconds) where timestamp precision adds little value, or for casual social video apps where frictionless, non-contextual reactions (likes, simple emoji taps) are more fitting than a full comment composer.

screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense commenting/reaction overlay for short-form or ephemeral content (e.g., Stories, Reels) where the interaction model favors swipe-and-move-on rather than deep engagement. It's also overkill for single-viewer private recordings where no collaborative feedback is expected, as the extra UI chrome would add unnecessary visual clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Built for distributed teams and professionals who prioritize async updates over live meetings. The timestamped, threaded comment design specifically serves reviewers and collaborators (e.g., design critiques, code walkthroughs, status updates) who need to give precise, contextual feedback without a live call.

Psychologically, the design leverages social proof and lightweight reciprocity — seeing avatars, view counts, and quick reactions motivates others to join in with minimal effort. The emoji markers on the timeline also exploit curiosity gap (what made someone react there?) to drive re-watching and deeper engagement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Timestamped Comments: Each reply is pinned to an exact second in the recording, merging chat and video scrubber into one unified, navigable artifact.
  • Floating Emoji-on-Timeline Markers: Reaction emojis (😍) appear directly on the scrubber track at the moment they were triggered, giving an at-a-glance emotional heatmap of the video.
  • Activity / Transcript Segmented Toggle: Lets users instantly switch between social engagement and accessibility/searchable text without losing their place.
  • One-Tap Reaction Bar: Removes friction from feedback, encouraging lightweight engagement over typed comments.
  • Picture-in-Picture & Fullscreen Controls: Positioned top-right for power users who want to multitask while watching.

screens.name: Loom - Downloading a video - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom-sheet action pattern when:

  • A list or detail item has 3-6 frequently used contextual actions that would clutter a toolbar if always visible.
  • You want to preserve background context (title, thumbnail) while presenting options, rather than navigating away.
  • You need a universal, platform-consistent interaction for both iOS and Android via a single component.
  • Destructive actions need visual differentiation without necessarily blocking the flow with a confirmation dialog.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The action list exceeds ~6 items: it becomes a scroll-heavy, unscannable sheet; a dedicated menu or page is better.
  • The destructive action (e.g., permanent delete of shared organizational content) carries high risk (pair with an explicit confirmation dialog rather than relying on color alone).
  • Actions require additional input or configuration (e.g., share settings with permissions) - a full screen or multi-step flow would serve better than a flat action sheet.
  • On larger tablet/desktop surfaces, where a context menu or inline toolbar is more appropriate than a mobile-style bottom sheet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Targeted at professionals and teams managing multiple recorded videos, this pattern serves users who need rapid, low-friction management of their content library (e).g., deleting a bad take, downloading a clip for offline use, resharing a link, or correcting a typo in the title without navigating to a separate settings page.

Psychologically, the sheet exploits recognition over recall (icon + label pairing) and proximity grouping (all contextual actions for one video bundled together) to minimize cognitive load. The red Delete icon leverages learned color-danger associations (Fitts's Law + color psychology) to reduce accidental data loss without requiring an extra confirmation step at this stage.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded icon affordances: Red circle for Delete instantly signals irreversibility/danger, while other actions share a neutral brand-lavender tone (a lightweight visual hierarchy without needing extra copy).
  • Context preserved behind scrim: The dimmed background keeps the video title and scrubber visible, so users never lose track of which asset they're about to act on.
  • Compact 4-action sheet: Limiting choices to the most common post-recording tasks (Delete, Download, Share, Edit title) prevents choice overload and keeps the sheet glanceable and thumb-reachable.
  • Drag handle at bottom: Reinforces native, dismissible gesture affordance consistent with iOS/Android sheet conventions.

screens.name: Loom - Downloading a video - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this contextual, trigger-based permission request pattern whenever an app needs system-level access (camera, photos, microphone, location) for a feature that isn't essential to core onboarding. Pair it with a clear, action-driven entry point (e.g., tapping "Download" or "Save") rather than requesting access blindly at launch. The timeline-anchored reactions and timestamped comments pattern is ideal for any video, podcast, or audio product where contextual feedback at specific playback moments adds value (e.g., video reviews, e-learning, design feedback tools).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid requesting system permissions immediately on app launch or before the user has taken an action that implies need (this leads to high denial rates and permanently blocks re-prompting on iOS). Also avoid stacking multiple permission dialogs in sequence, as this overwhelms and frustrates users. The timeline-pinned reaction pattern should be avoided in short-form content (e.g., under 10 seconds) where the granularity of timestamped feedback adds more clutter than value, or in privacy-sensitive contexts where showing others' reaction placement could create social pressure or embarrassment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves professionals and teams reviewing async video updates (likely a manager or colleague watching a feedback/demo video and reacting with emojis and comments). The permission prompt specifically targets the moment a user wants to own the content (save it locally), appealing to users who want offline access or to repurpose the clip outside Loom.

Psychologically, the design leverages the principle of commitment and relevance: because the user initiated a download action, they are primed to expect and accept the subsequent system permission request (reduced friction/surprise). The emoji-on-timeline and threaded comments tap into social proof and reciprocity: seeing others' reactions encourages the viewer to also engage, reinforcing Loom's goal of replacing meetings with rich asynchronous dialogue.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Just-in-time permission request: The photo library prompt appears only when the user actively tries to download/save a video, not at app launch, maximizing context and acceptance likelihood.
  • Emoji reactions pinned to timeline: Reaction emojis (😍, 😂) are anchored at their exact timestamp on the scrub bar, giving an at-a-glance emotional heatmap of the video without needing to open the comment thread.
  • Timestamped threaded comments: Each comment is tagged with a precise video timecode (0:00, 0:09, 0:16), letting viewers jump straight to the relevant moment (a core differentiator for async video communication).
  • Activity/Transcript segmented toggle: Lets users switch between social proof (comments/reactions) and accessible text content (transcript), serving different consumption preferences.
  • Non-blocking modal design: Despite the dense background content, the native dialog is small, centered, and doesn't require navigating away from the video context.

results.query: Cleo versus Dave overdraft protection and financial coaching chat

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 15
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any single-value monetary or numeric input flow where the user needs undivided focus: fund transfers, top-ups, bill splitting, tipping screens, or ATM-style cash withdrawal amount entry. It is ideal when the next step (e.g., choosing a funding source or reviewing a summary) is handled on a subsequent screen, keeping this screen laser-focused on one micro-task.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this stripped-down approach when users need contextual information to make the decision correctly (for example, if there are minimum/maximum limits, fees, or multiple currency options that affect the amount being entered). In those cases, omitting helper text or limit indicators can lead to failed submissions or user frustration. It's also unsuitable for flows involving multiple simultaneous inputs (e.g., amount + recipient + note), where a single-field full-screen keypad would be too limiting.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers performing routine financial actions, topping up a digital wallet, transferring money to a friend, or funding a debit card balance. The design leverages the psychological principle of reduced cognitive load: by showing only the amount and a keypad, users are not distracted by fees, exchange rates, or promotional banners while making a monetary decision.

The large, bold amount typography also taps into a subtle confirmation bias trigger: seeing the number rendered in a prominent, currency-styled font makes users feel they are looking at "real money," reinforcing the seriousness and finality of the transaction and prompting more careful entry.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Oversized live amount display: The dollar figure is the single largest element on screen, functioning as a large-font confirmation mechanism that reduces data-entry errors before committing to the next step.

  • Custom full-bleed numeric keypad: Replacing the native OS keyboard with a bespoke calculator-style keypad gives the brand full control over spacing, tap targets, and visual consistency across iOS/Android.

  • CTA positioned above the keypad: Placing "Next" directly above the number pad (instead of pinned to the absolute bottom) keeps the primary action persistently visible and reachable without requiring the keyboard to be dismissed.

  • Minimalist chrome: A single close (X) icon is the only navigational escape hatch, reducing decision fatigue and keeping the user's attention locked on one task.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 16
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when designing any money-movement flow (transfers, subscriptions, savings plans, bill pay) where:

  • Users need both one-time and recurring options in a single, unified form instead of two separate flows.

  • Account selection carries decision-relevant metadata (fees, timing, balance) that should be visible without extra taps.

  • Regulatory consent is required for automated/recurring debits and needs to be captured inline without breaking flow.

  • The target user is anxious about fees or overdrafts, warranting explicit reassurance copy near the commitment point.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense single-screen approach when:

  • The transfer configuration involves many more variables (e.g., multi-currency, complex tax withholding) that would overwhelm a single scrollable form (a multi-step wizard would serve better).

  • The audience is enterprise/B2B, where more explicit confirmation steps and audit trails are expected rather than a lightweight inline checkbox.

  • Legal/compliance requirements mandate a dedicated, undivided disclosure screen (e.g., some jurisdictions require full-screen ACH authorization) rather than embedding it below a checkbox.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Dave's "Busy Urban" target demographic (often gig workers, hourly employees, or paycheck-to-paycheck earners who need small, frequent top-ups to their account rather than large lump transfers). The default $1 amount and weekly recurrence reflect a "set it and forget it" micro-saving/micro-funding behavior rather than one-time large deposits.

Psychologically, the screen taps into:

  • Loss-aversion relief: The overdraft-protection disclaimer removes the fear that automating a transfer could backfire and cost more fees, which is a top objection for financially stressed users.

  • Autonomy & control: Editable amount, selectable source/destination, and configurable frequency/day give the user granular control, important for users who have been burned by rigid or opaque bank automations before.

  • Habit formation: Recurring weekly transfers nudge users toward a savings/funding habit without requiring ongoing manual effort, aligning with Dave's mission to close the paycheck gap proactively.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero amount input: The dollar figure is rendered in oversized display type with an edit-pencil affordance, making the core action (set an amount) immediately obvious and delightful to interact with.

  • Progressive disclosure via toggle: The Recurring switch conditionally reveals Frequency and Transfer On fields, keeping the default form lean for simple transfers.

  • Contextual metadata inline: Transfer time, fees, and current balance are shown directly inside the account selector rows, so users don't need to cross-reference other screens before deciding.

  • Anti-overdraft reassurance copy: A single reassuring sentence placed exactly where anxiety would peak (right before authorizing a recurring auto-debit) reduces drop-off from fear of insufficient funds.

  • Inline legal consent: Compliance checkbox and disclosure text are embedded in the flow rather than requiring a separate screen, balancing regulatory needs with low friction.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 17
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any fintech recurring payment/transfer setup screen where regulatory consent (e.g., ACH authorization) is required. Ideal for subscription billing, recurring savings deposits, auto-invest configurations, or bill-pay scheduling where users must explicitly agree to recurring debit terms.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, multi-field layout for single, one-time transactions where recurring logic and legal agreements add unnecessary friction. For simple instant transfers, a lighter-weight, single-tap flow without a mandatory checkbox and expanded legal text would reduce drop-off and cognitive burden.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Targets Dave's "Busy Urban" demographic who likely live paycheck-to-paycheck and want automated savings/funding habits without the risk of bank penalties. The recurring transfer feature caters to users trying to build consistent saving/deposit habits into their Dave account (e.g., to qualify for or repay cash advances), while the overdraft-protection messaging specifically targets the psychological pain point of banking fee anxiety common among underbanked or financially stressed users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anti-Overdraft Reassurance: Explicit micro-copy assuring the system will "skip a payment" rather than overdraft the user, directly addressing the core anxiety of the target demographic.

  • Disabled State CTA: The "Set up transfer" button is visually disabled (grayed) until the required consent checkbox is ticked, preventing invalid submissions and enforcing compliance capture.

  • Visual Guidance Cue: The yellow directional arrow pointing at the unchecked checkbox acts as an implicit tooltip, guiding user attention without needing an explicit text instruction.

  • Structured Field Grouping: Bordered container labels for "Add to," "Frequency," and "Transfer On" create a clean, digestible visual hierarchy for a moderately complex multi-parameter form.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 18
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any financial or subscription flow where a user must configure a recurring or scheduled transaction (transfers, subscriptions, bill pay, auto-invest). It's ideal when:

  • You need to collect both a one-time and recurring transfer option in a single, low-friction form.

  • Regulatory/legal consent must be captured before executing an automated financial action.

  • Your users may have anxiety about insufficient funds or unexpected fees, requiring explicit reassurance copy.

  • You want to progressively disclose advanced scheduling options only when relevant, keeping the default path simple.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, multi-field pattern for simple, single-use transactions where recurrence is irrelevant (e.g., a one-time peer-to-peer payment) - it adds unnecessary cognitive load. Also avoid dense legal consent checkboxes in non-regulated, low-stakes contexts where they'd feel like unnecessary friction. If the target audience is not financially anxious (e.g., high-net-worth or B2B expense tools), the overdraft reassurance microcopy may come across as patronizing or irrelevant and could be omitted.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Dave's core demographic: financially underserved or paycheck-to-paycheck users who rely on the app to build savings buffers or fund their "Dave Checking"/ExtraCash features. The design leans on loss-aversion mitigation (explicit no-overdraft promise) and trust-building through transparency (clear consent language, visible fees/timing "4-5 business days • No fee") because this audience is often wary of hidden bank fees and automated withdrawals that could push them into overdraft.

The recurring transfer + small default amount ($1.00) pattern also suggests a habit-formation nudge, encouraging users to start an automatic savings habit with a trivially low-risk amount, lowering the psychological barrier to opting into automation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive disclosure via toggle: The Recurring switch conditionally reveals Frequency/Transfer On fields, keeping the default form short and only adding complexity when the user opts in.

  • Fieldset-style bordered inputs with bleeding labels: Each selector (From, Add to, Frequency, Transfer On) is contained in a rounded rectangle with a small label straddling the top border, giving strong visual grouping and a modern, uncluttered form aesthetic.

  • Overdraft reassurance microcopy: Explicitly stating the recurring transfer will be skipped if funds are insufficient reduces anxiety, directly targeting the financial-stress persona.

  • Explicit legal consent gate: A dedicated, unmissable checkbox with the exact terms (amount, frequency, day, source, destination) reiterated in plain language builds transparency and satisfies ACH authorization requirements simultaneously.

  • Animated/progress CTA state: The button showing "Transferring $1.00" with a moving knob confirms the action is in-flight, giving the user real-time feedback and reducing double-tap errors.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 19
screens.whereToUse:
Use this end-of-flow confirmation pattern whenever a user completes a multi-step configuration task with real-world consequences (financial transfers, subscription setup, recurring billing, automation rules, scheduled jobs). It's ideal when:

  • The action has a delayed or non-instant effect (e.g., ACH transfers, scheduled jobs) and users need reassurance about timing.

  • You want to reduce support burden by preemptively answering "what happens next?"

  • The flow is a wizard/stepper and needs an unambiguous terminal state.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, full-screen success pattern for:

  • Trivial or frequent actions (e.g., saving a single form field) where a lightweight toast/snackbar is more appropriate and less intrusive.

  • Flows where the user needs to take an immediate follow-up action, burying a critical next step behind a single "Done" button could cause it to be missed.

  • Contexts where introducing playful illustration would undermine seriousness (e.g., large wire transfers, irreversible high-stakes financial actions) - in such cases a more formal, detail-rich confirmation/receipt screen is preferable.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday retail banking or neobank customers setting up automated micro-savings or recurring transfers (e.g., "round-up" savings features, weekly auto-save rules). The target user is likely risk-averse about money automation and wants explicit reassurance that the rule was saved correctly and to understand exactly when money will move.

Psychologically, the screen leverages:

  • Closure/Completion bias: the checkmark and "All done" headline give the brain a satisfying sense of task completion, which increases the likelihood of continued app engagement and trust in the automation feature.

  • Reducing cognitive load & anxiety around recurring money movement by being explicit about dates and posting delays, since financial uncertainty is a major source of user stress in banking apps.

  • Reinforcement of habit formation: by confirming a recurring, automated savings behavior, the app nudges users toward passive, "set it and forget it" financial wellness habits.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Value re-confirmation: Restating the exact amount, frequency, and day the user selected turns a generic success screen into a personalized receipt, closing the loop on the setup wizard.

  • Proactive timeline transparency: Explicitly stating the first transfer date and the 4-5 business day posting delay preempts confusion and reduces "where's my money" support tickets.

  • Single decisive CTA: Only one button ("Done") is presented (no upsell, no secondary link) respecting the user's completed task and avoiding decision fatigue at a moment of closure.

  • Emotional softening via illustration: The lighthearted cloud/hill graphic humanizes a financial automation action, reinforcing a friendly, non-intimidating brand voice.

  • Iconography-led affirmation: The oversized green checkmark badge communicates success instantly, before any text is read, satisfying users who scan rather than read.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 20
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any flow involving recurring financial commitments (subscriptions, auto-invest, round-up savings, bill autopay) where the user needs to configure cadence and destination while feeling protected from negative consequences (fees, overdrafts, failed payments). It's ideal when regulatory consent is required alongside a friendly, low-friction toggle-based UI.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, multi-field configuration pattern for simple one-time actions or when the target user expects instant, frictionless transactions (e.g., peer-to-peer payments). Overloading a single modal with toggle, frequency picker, day picker, and legal consent can overwhelm users in a quick-transfer context; in such cases, split into a multi-step wizard or default straight to one-time transfer with recurring as a secondary, less prominent option.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets financially stretched or underbanked users (Dave's core demographic) who rely on small recurring transfers (e.g., $1/week) to build savings habits or fund a checking buffer. These users are highly overdraft-averse, so the explicit "no overdraft, we'll skip if low" promise is a critical trust signal that reduces transactional friction and anxiety. The recurring toggle and low $1 weekly default also nudge users toward habit-forming micro-savings behavior, a common growth/retention lever in neobanking apps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Conditional Progressive Disclosure: Frequency and Transfer Day fields only appear when the Recurring toggle is switched on, keeping the default one-time transfer flow clean and uncluttered.

  • Overdraft Reassurance Microcopy: Explicitly tells the user their account won't be overdrafted and payments will be skipped if funds are low, reducing anxiety around automating a debit.

  • Gated CTA via Explicit Consent: The primary "Set up transfer" button remains visually disabled until the compliance checkbox is checked, enforcing legal authorization order-of-operations.

  • Labeled Bordered Selectors: Fieldset-style bordered containers with floating labels ("Add to," "Frequency," "Transfer On") maintain persistent context even after a value is selected.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 21
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any screen managing recurring financial transactions (subscriptions, auto-invest, autopay, recurring transfers) where:

  • Legal/regulatory consent is required before activation or modification.

  • Users may have anxiety about funds availability or unexpected fees.

  • You need to support both "edit" and "cancel/destructive" actions on the same screen without confusing which is primary.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for: high-frequency or low-stakes settings changes where a legal checkbox would add unnecessary friction; contexts where the destructive action needs equal visual weight (e.g., safety-critical cancellations); or flows with many more fields, where stacking dropdowns and a checkbox before the CTA could push the button below the fold on smaller devices, hurting completion rates.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Dave's core "Busy Urban" demographic (users who rely on automated small recurring transfers (e).g., $1 weekly) to build savings habits or fund a linked account without manual effort. These users are often on tight, variable-income budgets, so fear of overdraft fees is a primary psychological barrier to enabling any automated debit.

By explicitly stating the transfer will be skipped rather than triggering an overdraft, Dave removes the single biggest objection to opting into automation, leveraging loss-aversion mitigation as a conversion/retention lever. The checkbox+disabled-button pattern also protects Dave legally while still feeling like a natural "unlock" moment rather than a compliance roadblock.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anxiety-reducing disclaimer placement: the no-overdraft/auto-skip promise is positioned immediately after the schedule inputs, at peak moment of user hesitation.

  • Checkbox-gated CTA: the primary "Update transfer" button is visually disabled until legal consent is checked, using progressive disclosure to combine compliance and usability.

  • De-emphasized but present destructive action: "Cancel recurring transfer" is available without being visually competitive with the primary action, respecting user autonomy without dark-pattern hiding.

  • Consistent outlined-field pattern: Account selector and schedule dropdowns share a unified visual language (bordered container + floating label), making the form scannable and predictable.

  • Mascot avatar humanizes the checking account row, reinforcing brand warmth even in a purely functional settings screen.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 22
screens.whereToUse:
• Before executing any destructive or hard-to-reverse action involving recurring payments, subscriptions, or automated transfers.

  • When users may have anxiety about unintended side effects (e.g., "will this affect what's already scheduled?") - proactively answer that question in the dialog copy.

  • Financial, subscription, or automation-based products where trust and transparency are core brand pillars.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for low-stakes, easily reversible actions, adding a confirmation dialog for trivial toggles creates unnecessary friction and "dialog fatigue."

  • Do not use guilt-tripping or exaggerated loss language ("You'll lose all your progress!") purely to retain users; this erodes trust, especially in finance apps where transparency is paramount.

  • Avoid if the underlying action is already easily undoable via an "Undo" snackbar (in those cases, a lighter-weight Undo-Instead-of-Confirm pattern is more efficient and less intrusive).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday banking app users managing automated/recurring money movements (e.g., savings transfers, bill pay). These users are often mid-task and financially cautious, recurring transfers touch real money, so any cancellation carries emotional weight and fear of mistakes.

Psychologically, the dialog leverages loss-aversion mitigation (assuring nothing already in motion is affected) and reversibility framing (assuring the user they aren't burning a bridge). Both reduce the anxiety and hesitation that typically accompanies "Are you sure?" prompts in financial contexts, where users are especially risk-averse due to real monetary stakes.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-manipulative confirmation copy: Explicitly reassures the user that canceling is low-risk and reversible, avoiding "confirmshaming" dark patterns common in cancellation flows.

  • Scrim + centered modal: Fully dims the background form, isolating the decision point and preventing accidental taps on underlying elements.

  • Asymmetric button treatment favoring the requested action: The solid pill button matches what the user just asked to do (cancel), respecting user intent rather than nudging them back to "Keep."

  • Contextual reassurance about in-progress transfers: Proactively answers the user's likely first question ("will this stop a transfer that's already happening?") within the dialog itself, reducing support burden.

screens.name: Dave Adding & Creating 23
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern as the final step of any settings change, cancellation, or deletion flow (especially in finance, subscriptions, or automation contexts (recurring payments, scheduled reminders, auto-renewals)). It's ideal whenever users need explicit written confirmation of exactly what changed, plus reassurance about what did NOT change (e.g., pending items still in flight).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-screen confirmation for low-stakes or high-frequency actions (e.g., toggling a minor preference), where a lightweight toast/snackbar would be less intrusive. Also avoid vague reassurance language if there are genuinely nuanced consequences the user must actively decide on (in those cases, a confirmation dialog with more detail or an undo option should precede this state rather than only appearing after the fact).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday banking/fintech app users managing automated savings or bill-pay rules (e.g., Chime, Ally, Varo-style consumer banking apps). These users are often modifying recurring transfers to adjust budgets, so the design must avoid triggering financial anxiety.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the peak-end rule: ending the cancellation flow on a positive, reassuring note (green checkmark, friendly copy) so the user's lasting impression of the interaction is calm and trustworthy rather than uncertain. The explicit callout about in-progress transfers also reduces cognitive dissonance by preempting a likely worry.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anticipatory clarification copy: Explicitly stating that in-flight transfers will still process removes ambiguity and builds trust in a money-moving context.

  • Bolded dynamic values: Amount, frequency, and day are bolded within the sentence, letting users scan and verify the exact rule that was affected without re-reading the whole paragraph.

  • Calming illustrative treatment: The soft cloud/hill illustration and generous whitespace de-dramatize what is otherwise a "cancellation," reducing any sense of loss or error.

  • Single exit path: Only one button ("Done") is offered, eliminating decision fatigue and firmly signaling task completion.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for the pre-authentication landing/splash screen of any consumer fintech, lending, or subscription app where the core value proposition can be reduced to a single, high-impact number or benefit. Ideal when the product UI itself is polished enough to be used as marketing collateral, and when the target audience needs urgent objection-handling (fees, credit checks, commitment) before they'll convert.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for B2B, enterprise, or complex multi-persona apps where a single benefit statement cannot represent the full value proposition (it will feel oversimplified or misleading). Also avoid if the underlying product UI isn't visually polished, as showcasing a rough interface here will undermine trust rather than build it. Not appropriate for apps requiring lengthy regulatory disclosures upfront, as the minimal copy space cannot accommodate necessary compliance context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Targets financially-stretched, busy urban workers living paycheck-to-paycheck who have likely felt shame or been burned by predatory payday lenders. The screen leverages loss-aversion and relief-seeking psychology: the promise of "$500 when you need it" taps into acute financial stress, while "no interest, no credit check" removes the shame/fear trigger associated with traditional short-term credit. The friendly bear mascot and rounded, mint-on-navy visual language work to disarm the anxiety and stigma typically tied to money-related apps, making the brand feel approachable rather than clinical or judgmental.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Device-in-device mockup: Showing the actual home screen UI inside a phone frame builds immediate trust and product transparency before the user has even signed up.

  • Physical card as trust signal: The fanned-out Mastercard debit card signals 'real bank account,' not just a loan app, subtly upgrading brand perception.

  • Objection-crushing subhead: "No interest, no credit check" directly neutralizes the exact fears that keep people away from cash-advance products.

  • Dual-CTA hierarchy: Outline vs. filled button styling cleanly separates returning users from new sign-ups without adding extra screens or copy.

  • Approved-amount preview: Displaying "You're approved for $500!" inside the mock UI plants an anchoring number that reappears in the headline, creating message match and reinforcing believability.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern when a regulated financial (or health) product feature requires mandatory disclosure before or immediately after activation (e.g., overdraft, credit, buy-now-pay-later, insurance).

  • Ideal for surfacing legal/compliance text without derailing the user into a separate full-page flow (keeps momentum while still being legally defensible).

  • Effective when pairing a positive benefit statement with a necessary risk disclosure, to maintain user trust and reduce drop-off/anxiety.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for complex multi-clause agreements requiring explicit affirmative consent per clause (e.g., multi-item T&Cs) - a single "Got it" button may not satisfy stricter legal consent requirements.

  • Don't use dimmed-background bottom sheets when the disclosure is critical enough to require undivided attention; a full-screen interstitial with explicit checkbox consent may be more appropriate for higher-stakes agreements.

  • Not suitable if the disclosure text is long enough to require scrolling within the sheet itself, as users may dismiss without reading (consider requiring scroll-to-bottom before enabling the CTA).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets users of Dave, a fintech app serving budget-conscious, often paycheck-to-paycheck consumers who rely on small-dollar cash advances (ExtraCash) to cover short-term gaps. The design leverages trust and transparency framing: by proactively explaining that the advance functions as an overdraft that creates a negative balance, Dave protects itself legally while also building credibility with a demographic that may be wary of hidden fees from traditional banks or predatory lenders.

Psychologically, the warm illustrated mascot bear and rounded, friendly UI in the background reduce anxiety around what is fundamentally a debt-like product, while the disclosure text satisfies CFPB/regulatory transparency expectations for overdraft-style advances.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual background dimming: Keeping the originating screen visible (though dimmed) behind the sheet preserves context and reduces the jarring "where am I" feeling common with full-screen legal modals.

  • Benefit-first, risk-second copy structure: Leading with the value prop headline before the overdraft/fee disclaimer softens the psychological impact of the negative-balance warning.

  • Single frictionless CTA: Only one exit path ("Got it") avoids decision fatigue and speeds users back into the product flow, which is ideal for a mandatory-read disclosure rather than a marketing decision point.

  • Inline legal link: Offloading the full account agreement to a hyperlink keeps the primary modal short while still legally covering the deeper terms.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for the first data-entry step of any account creation or onboarding funnel, especially in regulated industries (fintech, healthcare, insurance) where legal consent must be captured early. It's ideal when you want to:

  • Reduce drop-off by starting with the fewest possible fields.

  • Bundle legal/compliance consent invisibly into the primary CTA rather than an extra checkbox tap.

  • Signal multi-step progress without revealing the full length of the flow (avoiding "step 1 of 12" discouragement).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Regulatory requirements mandate an explicit, separately-checked consent checkbox rather than implied agreement via a button tap (some jurisdictions/GDPR contexts require this).

  • The flow needs to communicate exact progress length upfront (e.g., enterprise B2B forms where users expect to see "Step X of Y" for planning purposes).

  • Users are already authenticated elsewhere and re-entering credentials would feel redundant or annoying (in that case, a magic-link or SSO option may reduce friction better than a password field).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective users of Dave, a neobanking/fintech app aimed at budget-conscious consumers, often those who may have been underserved by traditional banks. The design leverages the commitment and consistency principle: by starting with an easy, low-effort action (email + password), users become psychologically invested and more likely to complete subsequent, harder steps (identity verification, linking a bank account, etc.).

The sparse layout and lack of distracting marketing content also reduces decision fatigue at a moment when the user has already decided to sign up (the job here is purely operational (credential creation), not persuasive, so the UI gets out of the way).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Minimal field count: Only two inputs are requested at this stage, deferring more sensitive/lengthy data (SSN, income, etc.) to later steps, which increases completion likelihood.

  • Implicit consent bundling: Legal agreement is tied to the primary action button rather than a separate checkbox, removing a friction point common in many sign-up flows.

  • Disabled CTA as guidance: The greyed "Agree and continue" button visually communicates incomplete input state without needing explicit error messaging.

  • Escape hatch preserved: The "X" close icon respects user autonomy and reduces the perceived risk of starting the flow.

  • Micro progress indicator: A subtle progress bar sets expectations of a multi-step journey without a discouraging step counter (e.g., "1 of 8").

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for the initial account-creation step of any regulated or trust-sensitive product (fintech, healthcare, insurance) where you need to collect credentials plus legal consent before proceeding to more sensitive data (SSN, bank linking, KYC). It's ideal when you want to front-load lightweight friction and defer heavier verification steps until after initial commitment is secured.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if your legal/compliance team requires explicit, separately-tracked consent checkboxes (some jurisdictions mandate unbundled consent from action buttons). Also avoid a bare progress bar without step labels/count if your flow is very long, as ambiguity about total steps can increase anxiety instead of reducing it; in such cases, use a numbered step indicator (e.g., "Step 1 of 5") instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users signing up for Dave, a mobile banking/cash-advance app, likely acquired through performance marketing (ads promising early paycheck access or overdraft protection). These users are often financially stressed and motivated by urgency, so the onboarding flow is deliberately kept short and low-friction to prevent abandonment before value is delivered.

Psychologically, the progress bar leverages the goal-gradient effect: users push harder to finish a task as they perceive proximity to completion (while the single-column, two-field form reduces the intimidation factor common in financial signups that typically require SSNs, bank links, and identity verification later in the funnel).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented progress bar: Visually communicates the user is early in a multi-step flow, setting realistic expectations and encouraging completion (sunk-cost/Zeigarnik effect).

  • Consent folded into CTA: Combining legal agreement with the primary action button reduces friction by eliminating an extra checkbox tap while still surfacing compliance links inline.

  • Minimal field set: Only two inputs (email, password) are shown at once, keeping the task laser-focused and reducing perceived effort.

  • Escape hatch (X): A visible close icon preserves user autonomy and reduces anxiety about being "trapped" in the flow.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this single-field-per-screen pattern during high-stakes onboarding flows (banking, insurance, healthcare) where you need to collect legally sensitive information but want to minimize perceived friction. It's ideal early in a multi-step KYC funnel when you need to build user confidence and momentum before harder questions (income, SSN, linking bank accounts) appear. Pair with a visible progress bar to set expectations of a short, finite process.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for low-stakes, high-familiarity forms (e.g., a simple login) where users expect to complete multiple fields on one screen and would find single-field pagination unnecessarily slow. Also avoid on flows where users are returning/repeat users who already expect a fast, one-screen experience (repeated screen transitions can feel tedious and increase abandonment for form types with many fields (e).g., 10+ step KYC without a clear payoff).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Dave's target user is a busy, urban, often financially-stressed individual who may have had negative experiences with predatory payday lenders or complex bank forms. This screen's brevity and gentle tone directly counteract "form fatigue" and payday-loan shame by making sign-up feel more like a quick chat than a bank application. Requiring "legal name" upfront (rather than deferring it) is a regulatory necessity for a chartered banking product, but framing it as the very first, simplest step builds early trust and momentum before requesting more sensitive data (SSN, income, bank linking) in later steps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• One-question-per-screen pacing: Isolates a single, low-friction ask (name) to build momentum before harder questions (SSN, income) appear later.

  • Disabled CTA as implicit validation: The greyed-out "Next" button communicates incompleteness without needing an error toast, reducing anxiety-inducing red error text.

  • Segmented progress bar: Visually commits the user to a "short journey," leveraging the sunk-cost/completion instinct to reduce drop-off.

  • Generous whitespace: Reinforces the mint-on-navy brand's calm, low-drama identity (even on a dense financial-services flow, the UI feels light and airy).

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when collecting sensitive personal data (phone, SSN, address) during onboarding or KYC flows, especially in fintech, healthcare, or identity-verification-heavy products. Ideal when you need to justify a slightly invasive request with a clear, benefit-driven explanation. Also effective for any multi-step form where breaking fields into single-question screens will improve completion rates over a monolithic form.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this single-field-per-screen approach for low-stakes, low-friction data (e.g., simple preferences) where breaking it into multiple screens would feel needlessly slow and increase abandonment due to excessive step count. Also avoid omitting the "why" microcopy for any sensitive field request, skipping justification on phone/SSN/financial fields significantly raises drop-off and distrust. Not suitable for desktop-first products where horizontal space allows multiple fields to be grouped without harming usability.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users mid-way through account creation for a service that requires identity verification (likely fintech, given the green branding and security-forward tone reminiscent of apps like Cash App or Chime). The design assumes users are on mobile, in a moment of intent-driven signup, but still susceptible to drop-off if the process feels invasive or lengthy.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Foot-in-the-door technique: having already committed to earlier onboarding steps (visible via the partially filled progress bar), users are primed to continue rather than abandon. The explicit security rationale also taps into trust-transfer: users are more willing to share sensitive data when the reason is framed around protecting their own account rather than the company's benefit.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Justification microcopy: Explicitly stating the security purpose (2FA) of the phone number pre-empts privacy concerns and increases form completion rates.

  • Personalized greeting: Using the user's name transforms a transactional form into a personalized, human interaction.

  • Single-field focus: Isolating one input per screen (progressive disclosure) minimizes cognitive load and maximizes completion likelihood compared to a long multi-field form.

  • Persistent progress bar: Gives users a mental model of flow length and reinforces momentum without revealing exact number of remaining steps, avoiding overwhelm.

  • Thumb-friendly fixed CTA: Large, full-width, bottom-anchored button ensures effortless one-handed interaction on mobile.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any account verification step requiring OTP/SMS confirmation, especially during signup, login recovery, or sensitive transaction confirmation. It's ideal when you need to simultaneously capture marketing consent in a legally compliant way without adding an extra screen. The progress bar treatment is well-suited for multi-step onboarding or KYC (Know Your Customer) flows where users benefit from seeing overall completion status.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid combining marketing consent capture with security-critical verification steps if regulatory context (e.g., GDPR strict consent separation) requires consent to be decoupled from transactional flows. Also avoid this pattern for high-frequency/low-friction re-authentication (e.g., app biometric unlock) where a full-page form would feel like unnecessary friction. If code auto-detection (e.g., iOS SMS autofill) isn't implemented, ensure the manual code entry doesn't add undue friction for repeat users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users completing account creation or phone-based identity verification for a consumer app (likely retail, fintech, or subscription service given the SMS marketing consent language typical of US commerce apps). The design leverages the psychological principle of commitment and progress: the visible progress bar exploits the sunk-cost/completion bias, encouraging users to push through the friction of retrieving and typing a code rather than abandoning the flow.

The clean, uncluttered layout also targets users on mobile devices in potentially distracted contexts (checking a text message on another app/screen), so minimizing choices and text ensures the user can quickly refocus and complete the field.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progress indicator retention: Keeping the top progress bar visible reassures the user they are partway through a finite process, reducing onboarding drop-off anxiety.

  • Masked phone number: Balances confirmation (user trusts the right number was used) with privacy (full number not exposed on-screen).

  • Inline resend affordance: Placing "Resend code" immediately below the reference text preempts the most likely user friction point (delayed/lost SMS) without requiring navigation away from the screen.

  • Ethical opt-in default: The marketing consent checkbox defaults to unchecked, respecting user autonomy and reducing legal risk (a best-practice deviation from manipulative pre-checked patterns).

  • Single fixed CTA: One clear, large, thumb-friendly action button eliminates decision paralysis at a critical conversion point.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any flow requiring phone number verification (2FA, account creation, fraud prevention) where you need to confirm ownership of a contact channel before proceeding. The progress bar + resend link + single CTA combination is ideal for regulated onboarding flows (fintech, healthcare, telecom) where trust and clarity are paramount.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid pre-checking marketing consent checkboxes by default (many jurisdictions (e).g., GDPR in the EU, and increasingly US state laws) require affirmative opt-in, making pre-checked boxes legally risky and ethically dubious. Do not bundle unrelated marketing consent with security-critical verification steps, as it creates confusion between "required to proceed" and "optional" actions. Additionally, for pure OTP entry, consider individual boxed digit inputs with auto-advance/auto-paste-detection instead of a single free-text field, which better supports autofill from SMS and reduces user error.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets general consumer users completing account or identity verification (likely for a fintech, insurance, or regulated service given the heavy compliance language). The design assumes a mobile-first audience comfortable with SMS-based 2FA.

Psychologically, the flow exploits the momentum/foot-in-the-door effect: once a user has committed to the effortful task of retrieving and entering an SMS code, they are primed to quickly tap through subsequent screens, including consent checkboxes, without close scrutiny. The pre-checked box leverages default bias (status-quo bias) - most users will not bother unchecking a box that is already in a "positive/accepted" state, especially when it's styled identically to a confirmation checkmark rather than a marketing opt-in.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progress visualization: The segmented progress bar reduces perceived friction by showing tangible advancement through onboarding.

  • Built-in error recovery: The "Resend code" link is placed immediately near the explanation text, anticipating the most common OTP failure (non-receipt) without extra taps.

  • Data masking for trust: The phone number is blurred/masked on screen, reassuring the user their PII isn't exposed to shoulder-surfers, even though they already know their own number.

  • Single, unmissable CTA: The full-width, high-contrast green "Next" button anchors the bottom of the screen with zero ambiguity about the next action.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 10
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately after account creation or first login, right before requesting a sensitive OS-level permission (biometrics, push notifications, location, camera/microphone access). It's especially effective when:

  • The permission has a clear, tangible user benefit (e.g., faster login, security).

  • You want to protect the "one-shot" native permission dialog from being prematurely denied.

  • The onboarding flow already uses a progress indicator, so inserting one more lightweight step doesn't feel excessive.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The permission request has no clear immediate benefit to the user (extra screens add friction without payoff).

  • The onboarding flow is already long; adding another full-screen step may increase drop-off (better to combine with adjacent steps).

  • Users are on devices without the corresponding hardware (always detect biometric capability first to avoid showing an irrelevant screen).

  • The app doesn't need repeated authentication (e.g., single-session tools), making biometric login prompts unnecessary and confusing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users completing account setup on biometric-capable devices (iPhone with Face ID). The goal is to drive adoption of frictionless authentication, which reduces future login drop-off and password-reset support costs for the business.

Psychologically, it leverages the principle of reciprocity and low commitment framing: by asking a simple yes/no question with an easy escape hatch, users feel in control rather than pressured, which increases opt-in rates compared to an abrupt native system prompt with no context. It also exploits familiarity bias: using Apple's own visual language makes the request feel like a natural extension of the OS rather than a third-party app asking for sensitive data.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-permission priming: Explains the benefit before the native OS Face ID prompt fires, increasing the likelihood the user accepts the actual system dialog (avoids wasting the one-shot OS permission prompt).

  • Soft decline language: "Skip for now" instead of "No thanks" reduces friction and guilt, keeping the flow feeling reversible and low-stakes.

  • Familiar iconography: Reusing Apple's own Face ID glyph and color palette builds instant trust and recognition without extra copy.

  • Clear visual hierarchy: Single bold headline, one primary and one secondary action (no distractions or competing choices).

  • Progress bar retention: Keeps the user oriented within the larger onboarding journey, reducing abandonment anxiety.

screens.name: Dave Pre-Onboarding 11
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pre-permission priming pattern before any OS-level permission request that is not immediately obvious in value (camera, notifications, location, biometrics, contacts). It's especially valuable in:

  • Financial, health, or identity apps where biometric/sensitive permissions carry higher perceived risk.

  • Onboarding flows where dropout after a poorly-timed system prompt would be costly.

  • Any flow where you want to control timing: asking only after the user understands the value, not immediately on app launch.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this two-step pattern when:

  • The permission is trivial or expected (e.g., basic microphone access mid-recording) - adding an extra screen would be unnecessary friction.

  • The user has already denied the permission at the OS level; re-prompting via a custom screen repeatedly can feel manipulative or nagging.

  • Regulatory/compliance contexts require the permission ask to be truly the first and only touchpoint, without pre-conditioning language that could be seen as steering consent.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers of a fintech/banking app (Dave) who prioritize fast, frictionless re-entry into a sensitive financial account. Biometric login removes password-entry friction on subsequent sessions, which is a major retention lever for financial apps where users check balances frequently.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the principle of consistency/commitment: by getting a "soft yes" on the custom screen first, users are primed to follow through with "Allow" on the harder, system-level ask. It also mitigates permission fatigue and loss-aversion around biometric data by explicitly tying the permission to a concrete benefit (speed + security) rather than leaving the user to guess why the app wants Face ID access.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Permission Priming: A custom-branded explainer screen precedes the native OS dialog, dramatically increasing opt-in rates versus a cold system prompt.

  • Non-blocking Escape Hatch: "Skip for now" is always visible, preventing users from feeling trapped and reducing onboarding drop-off/rage-quit.

  • Brand-Consistent Iconography: The green Face ID icon peeking behind the system dialog maintains brand presence even during an OS-owned interaction.

  • Progress Bar Context: Placing this step within a visible multi-step progress indicator reduces perceived friction by signaling "almost done."

  • Language Mirroring: The custom CTA text ("Yes, sign in with Face ID") mirrors the system dialog's "Allow" action, creating cognitive continuity between the two prompts.

screens.name: Dave Connecting & Linking 4
screens.whereToUse: This anticipatory-guidance pattern fits well when a flow must hand off to an external, third-party-controlled login/consent screen whose exact layout the primary app doesn't own, and where partial or incorrect consent selection would break the flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit when the next login step is fully controlled by the same product (no external handoff) or when the external screen's consent options are simple/unambiguous enough that pre-coaching would be redundant friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Venmo: uses the same Plaid pre-login instructional screens with mocked bank-specific checkboxes before OAuth handoffs to major banks.

  • Robinhood: presents similar bank-specific "what to check" guidance screens ahead of external login redirects during funding flows.

  • Acorns: uses this same Plaid pre-login coaching pattern with institution-specific mockups, a direct match since it's the shared third-party SDK behavior for OAuth-based banks.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Help users recognize, diagnose, and recover from errors: Pre-showing the exact checkboxes to select prevents a common failure mode (partial consent) before it can happen on an external site Plaid can't directly control.

  • Visibility of system status: The external-link icon on the CTA honestly signals an upcoming context switch to a different site/app.

  • Recognition over recall: A realistic mockup of Capital One's actual checkbox panel lets users match what they'll see rather than remembering abstract instructions.

  • User control and freedom: Back arrow and close X remain available, letting users exit or step back before committing to the external handoff.

screens.name: Dave Connecting & Linking 5
screens.whereToUse: This Determinate Progress + Social Proof pattern fits well during unavoidable processing waits (e.g., bank linking, account verification) in onboarding flows where reinforcing the value proposition can reduce drop-off or impatience.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for very short waits (under a second or two) where a statistic wouldn't be readable in time, or for processes where the wait itself needs undivided attention (e.g., security-critical confirmations) rather than supplementary marketing content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Chime: uses similar progress-bar loading screens with motivational statistics during account-linking or setup waits.

  • Albert: presents comparable "linking in progress" screens paired with benefit-reinforcing statistics during onboarding.

  • Empower: uses loading-state screens with social-proof-style statistics during bank-linking to maintain user engagement through wait periods.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visibility of system status: The determinate progress bar reassures the user that linking is actively happening and roughly how far along it is.

  • Perceived wait-time reduction: Filling loading time with relevant, credible content (a statistic) makes the wait feel more purposeful than a blank spinner would.

  • Social proof as motivation: Citing a specific outcome ("nearly 70%") for existing members reinforces the user's decision to continue linking at a moment they might otherwise hesitate.

  • Visual continuity: The bell/notification badge ties this loading screen back to the low-balance-alert benefit mentioned earlier in the flow, reinforcing a consistent value narrative.

screens.name: Dave Connecting & Linking 6
screens.whereToUse: This Permission Priming + Indeterminate Loading pattern fits well in cash-advance or lending-adjacent flows where a debit card is needed for repayment purposes and must be explicitly tied to a previously connected bank account.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for flows where no repayment/settlement mechanism exists, or where requesting a debit card in addition to a bank account would be redundant and add unjustified friction to the connection process.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Empower: uses similar institution-branded "add your debit card" screens explaining the card's use for advance repayment before card entry.

  • Brigit: presents comparable card-linking instructional screens tied to a specific connected bank, justifying the request for repayment purposes.

  • Albert: uses institution-specific card-linking loading/instructional screens as part of its cash-advance onboarding flow, a close structural match.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Match between system and real world: Explaining the card must be tied to the Capital One account mirrors how users think about their own banking relationships, reducing confusion about which card to use.

  • Error prevention: Proactively instructing the user to ensure card-account association helps prevent a downstream failure from linking an unrelated or incompatible card.

  • Visibility of system status: The loading spinner communicates that something is happening rather than leaving the screen looking stalled or broken.

  • Transparency of purpose: Stating the card "may be used to settle any advances" clearly ties this request to a concrete, expected outcome rather than an unexplained data ask.

screens.name: Dave Connecting & Linking 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech or lending apps requiring users to link a debit/credit card for repayment, subscription billing, or advance settlement.

  • Any flow where sensitive financial data is collected and user trust/anxiety is a primary conversion blocker.

  • Modal-based secondary tasks that shouldn't disrupt the primary app navigation stack (dismissible via X).

  • Situations requiring explicit legal/regulatory consent (e.g., ACH/EPA authorization) alongside the data entry.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid pre-checking legal consent checkboxes by default in jurisdictions where explicit opt-in is legally required (e.g., GDPR) or where it could be viewed as a dark pattern eroding user trust.

  • Don't use vague security phrases like "bank-level security" without a tooltip or link explaining actual encryption/compliance standards if targeting a security-conscious or enterprise audience.

  • Not suitable for low-stakes forms where the weight of trust signals and legal copy would feel disproportionate and slow down a simple task.
