  • Real-time/live data updates are expected rather than manual refresh, which would better suit a Live/Real-Time Updates pattern with auto-sync.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is designed for current vehicle owners or serious in-market buyers using a car manufacturer/dealer companion app (e.g., Hyundai's ownership app) to view specs of a purchased or shortlisted model (in this case, the Hyundai Venue).

The psychological triggers include:

  • Authority & Precision Bias: Presenting exact decimal figures (89.40 bhp, 220.0 kmph, 998.00 cc) rather than rounded numbers implies rigor and trustworthiness of the data source.

  • Ownership Pride / Social Proof: The "Share with friends" CTA taps into the identity-signaling behavior of new car owners wanting to showcase their purchase.

  • Trust through Transparency: Showing "last refreshed" timestamps reduces anxiety around outdated information, especially important if data is pulled from a live vehicle telemetry or dealer inventory system.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Hero product render as primary visual anchor: Placing a large, photorealistic car render above the fold (rather than starting with data) builds emotional connection and brand pride before diving into specs.

  • Data freshness transparency: The "last refreshed on 23 mar '24" timestamp paired with a manual "Refresh vehicle details" action builds user trust by being explicit about data staleness, a pattern rarely seen but highly valuable for connected-car or telemetry-style data.

  • Inverted color footer as functional zoning: Using a black background strip to house secondary/utility actions cleanly separates "content" from "system controls" without needing dividers or borders.

  • Minimalist spec typography: Small-caps grey labels over large bold numerals create scannable, premium-feeling data presentation similar to luxury automotive marketing materials.

  • Low-friction escape hatches: "report an issue" and "Share with friends" are both single-tap, low-commitment actions placed at natural resting points in the scroll.

screens.name: CRED Logging & Tracking 19
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for screens that aggregate official, verified, or government-sourced data (insurance, tax documents, licenses, vehicle records) where users need quick scanability plus trust signals. It's ideal for fintech, insurtech, or auto-tech apps that pull third-party verified data and want to visually differentiate "official facts" from "app actions." The refresh-with-timestamp pattern is broadly applicable anywhere data can go stale (stock prices, account balances, sync status).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy black/white sectioning and casual lowercase tone for enterprise, legal, or B2B contexts where formality and neutrality are expected (the playful typography could undermine perceived credibility). Also avoid embedding social sharing CTAs on screens containing sensitive personal data (full RC numbers, addresses) unless data is properly masked, as this could create privacy risks or user distrust. The manual refresh button should not be used for real-time critical data (e.g., live location) where automatic polling is expected instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday vehicle owners (likely in India, given RTO/RC terminology) who need quick, trustworthy access to their vehicle's legal and registration status (for insurance renewal, resale, compliance checks, or general peace of mind). The psychological trigger at play is authority and reassurance: showing "active" RC status and official RTO sourcing reduces anxiety about legal compliance.

The refresh mechanism taps into trust-through-transparency: users are wary of stale government data, so showing the last-refreshed date and giving manual refresh control builds confidence. The "Share with friends" CTA leverages social identity signaling, appealing to users' pride in vehicle ownership (especially relevant for new car buyers wanting to showcase their purchase).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Authentic state-code badge: The "SP" tile mimics real Indian license plate region codes, instantly grounding the data in real-world familiarity and trust.

  • Data freshness transparency: The persistent "last refreshed on" timestamp paired with a manual "Refresh vehicle details" button gives users explicit control and confidence in data accuracy (vital for legal/compliance information).

  • High-contrast sectioning: Alternating black and white blocks create clear visual chunking between marketing/social CTAs and factual data cards without needing heavy dividers or borders.

  • Casual typographic voice on formal content: Lowercase, rounded typography humanizes dry RTO/legal data, reducing user anxiety around compliance topics.

  • Embedded growth loop: "Share with friends" is placed prominently, turning a utility screen into a viral acquisition touchpoint.

screens.name: PayPal Redeeming 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for confirming enrollment in time-bound rewards, subscriptions, tier upgrades, or loyalty program category selections. It's ideal whenever you need to (1) confirm a user's choice, (2) explain usage mechanics in under 3 bullet points, and (3) set expectations for renewal or expiration (all while funneling to a single acknowledgment action).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy full-screen modal for low-stakes or frequently recurring confirmations, as repeated interruptions of this scale will feel intrusive over time. It's also unsuitable when more than 3 mechanics need explaining, cramming additional rows would break the clean scannability. If the reward has no time constraint or category rules, a simpler toast or banner would suffice instead of a full takeover.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets PayPal Debit Card holders enrolled in a rotating category cash-back program, likely triggered right after month-end category selection or as a reminder when the new cycle begins. The psychological drivers include:

  • Reward anticipation: Leading with the benefit ("Enjoy 5% cash back") triggers a dopamine-linked positive framing before any friction or rules are introduced.

  • Loss aversion via spending cap and expiry: The "$1,000 spending cap" and firm end date subtly encourage the user to actually spend using the card to not "waste" the earned rate.

  • Habit formation: The "Choose again next month" messaging primes users to return monthly, reinforcing recurring engagement with the card and app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose modal: One headline, one supporting card, one CTA (no competing actions or distractions).

  • Icon-led comprehension: The fuel pump glyph lets users identify the reward category in under a second, before reading any copy.

  • Mechanics list with icons: Breaking down "how to earn," "how much," and "renewal cadence" into three icon-labeled rows makes complex reward program rules digestible at a glance.

  • Explicit expiry timestamp: Down-to-the-minute precision builds trust and sets clear expectations for when the offer ends.

  • Compliance-friendly disclaimer placement: Legal text is present but visually subordinate, balancing regulatory needs with UX cleanliness.

results.query: Craft whiteboard tools versus Figma FigJam canvas stickies

screens.name: Craft - Drawing on a whiteboard - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when building tools for freeform ideation, diagramming, mind-mapping, or visual planning (especially within apps whose core experience is otherwise linear or document-based). It's ideal for:

  • Hybrid productivity apps offering a canvas mode alongside documents/notes (e.g., Craft, Notion, Apple Notes).
  • Flowchart, wireframing, or brainstorming tools where spatial relationships matter more than sequence.
  • Creative planning features where users benefit from a "whiteboard" metaphor to externalize thinking before formalizing it.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for core, high-frequency editing tasks where linear structure and reading order matter (e.g., formal document editing, long-form writing) - an infinite canvas adds cognitive overhead and navigation complexity in those contexts. It's also unsuitable for:

  • Small screens or low-dexterity contexts where precise placement and pinch-zoom gestures are difficult.
  • Users who need accessibility-first, screen-reader-friendly content, since spatial canvases are inherently hard to linearize for assistive tech.
  • Simple note-taking apps where added tooling (shapes, zoom, selection) would overwhelm a user expecting lightweight, fast capture.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves knowledge workers, designers, and writers who use Craft not just for linear prose but for early-stage ideation, mapping out site structures, project flows, or brainstorming sessions. The target user is someone who thinks visually and non-linearly before committing to structured text, such as product managers sketching a landing page flow or writers outlining a narrative arc.

Psychologically, the infinite canvas lowers the barrier to starting (there's no "blank page" pressure because elements can be placed loosely and rearranged freely). The dashed "start" node and sticky note format tap into familiar physical metaphors (whiteboards, Post-its), making the digital tool feel approachable and low-stakes, encouraging exploratory thinking over perfectionism.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Condensed pill toolbars: Zoom, undo/redo, and selection tools are grouped into a single floating capsule, reducing chrome and keeping focus on the canvas.
  • Dual-state node styling: Dashed vs. solid-fill shapes communicate semantic meaning (anchor vs. content) at a glance without labels or legends.
  • Dot-grid canvas: Provides just enough structure for alignment and spatial orientation while preserving the feeling of an infinite, unconstrained space.
  • Floating bottom dock: Primary creation tools (pan, select, shape, note, overflow) are always within thumb reach without obstructing the canvas.
  • Handwritten typography on notes: Adds a personal, sketch-like quality that differentiates "thinking" content from polished document text elsewhere in the app.

screens.name: Craft - Drawing on a whiteboard - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any productivity or note-taking app adding a brainstorming/whiteboard mode alongside structured documents.
  • Tools supporting early-stage ideation, flowcharting, or visual planning (product roadmaps, mind maps, moodboards).
  • Apps wanting to offer a lightweight, chrome-free canvas with on-demand tool access rather than a permanently busy toolbar.
  • Cross-functional collaboration tools where sticky notes and arrows are core interaction metaphors (retro boards, workshops).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for highly structured, data-heavy workflows (forms, tables, spreadsheets) where freeform placement adds no value and only increases disorganization risk.
  • Not ideal for users on small screens doing precision work for extended periods (infinite canvases demand pinch-zoom/pan gestures that can fatigue mobile users compared to desktop/trackpad).
  • Risky for first-time users without any onboarding/coach marks (a blank infinite canvas with a dense tool menu can feel intimidating without guidance on where to start).
  • Not suitable when the product's core value is linear reading/writing flow (e.g., long-form document editors) - mixing canvas and document paradigms can fragment the mental model if not clearly separated.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets visual and spatial thinkers within Craft's knowledge-worker audience: planners, product managers, designers, students, and writers who need to externalize ideas before they're ready to become structured prose. By offering a FigJam/Miro-style canvas inside a note-taking app, Craft captures users at the earliest, messiest stage of ideation (sticky notes, arrows, rough flows) and keeps them from switching to a separate whiteboarding tool, increasing retention and daily engagement.

Psychologically, the sticky-note and hand-drawn aesthetic exploits the IKEA effect and familiarity bias: users feel ownership and creative permission when the surface resembles analog tools they already trust (real sticky notes, whiteboards), lowering the intimidation factor of a blank digital canvas.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dotted infinite canvas: Signals boundless, non-linear space and subtly guides alignment without the visual noise of a full grid.
  • Hand-drawn typography for content elements: The "start" label and sticky note text use a handwriting font, reinforcing Craft's editorial, human-crafted brand identity even in a utility canvas.
  • Dashed-border shape as a placeholder/connector node: Visually distinct from solid sticky notes, implying a different semantic role (e.g., flow step vs. content block).
  • Lean persistent toolbar + expandable contextual menu: A textbook progressive-disclosure pattern that balances minimalism with full tool depth.
  • Magic wand "cleanup" icon in the top bar: Likely an auto-arrange/tidy feature, reducing the friction of manual alignment in freeform canvases.
  • Zoom percentage as a tappable affordance: Doubles as a status indicator and shortcut control, consistent with professional design-tool conventions (Figma, FigJam).

screens.name: Craft - Drawing on a whiteboard - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when building:

  • Whiteboard, mind-mapping, or diagramming features bolted onto a primarily linear/text-based product.
  • Creative tools needing both freeform drawing and structured shape/note primitives (e.g., note-taking apps, project planning tools, design handoff tools).
  • Mobile-first creative canvases where one-handed tool access and large touch targets are essential.
  • Products wanting to differentiate from plain text/list competitors by offering a visual, spatial thinking mode.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The core product is data-entry or form-driven, where spatial freedom adds confusion rather than value.
  • Users are primarily consuming content rather than creating/organizing it (freeform canvases add overhead for read-only use cases).
  • Small screen real estate makes precise manipulation of shapes/notes frustrating without stylus support (touch-only precision issues).
  • The app needs strict version control or structured data output (freeform canvases are hard to search, export, or parse programmatically compared to structured blocks).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This canvas mode targets knowledge workers, product thinkers, designers, and planners who use Craft not just for linear prose but for ideation, sketching site maps, flowcharts, mood boards, or project plans (e.g., "landing page" sticky note hints at product/marketing planning use cases). It appeals to users who already use physical whiteboards or sticky notes and want that tactile, spatial freedom digitally.

Psychologically, the infinite dotted canvas triggers a sense of unconstrained possibility: unlike a rigid document template, it signals "nothing is wrong here, arrange however you like," reducing the intimidation of a blank page. The autosave-implying "Done" button (rather than "Save") leverages a sense of safety and trust, letting users focus on creative flow instead of file management anxiety.
screens.keyHighlights:
Noteworthy UX decisions:

  • Dual-row tool dock: Separating stroke properties (size, line style) from tool mode (pan/select/shape/pen/color) reduces cognitive load by grouping related controls without cluttering a single bar.
  • Persistent zoom + undo/redo cluster: Always-visible zoom percentage and undo/redo in the top bar give users confidence to experiment freely on an infinite canvas without fear of losing control.
  • Color wheel as a live swatch: The rainbow-gradient circle doubles as both an icon and a direct preview of the currently selected color, saving a navigation step.
  • Dot-grid infinite canvas: Immediately communicates spatial freedom and invites non-linear, visual thinking (mind maps, wireframes, sticky-note brainstorms) distinct from Craft's structured document blocks.
  • Sticky note + dashed shape primitives: Pre-built object types (notes, shapes) lower the barrier to visual organization for users who aren't naturally "designers."

screens.name: Craft - Drawing on a whiteboard - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Apps offering freeform ideation, mind-mapping, or diagramming alongside structured content (note apps, project tools, design tools).
  • Any canvas-based creation tool needing a compact but powerful mobile toolbar that adapts to tool context.
  • Products that want to differentiate a "sketch/explore" mode from a "write/structure" mode within the same ecosystem.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this freeform canvas pattern for tasks requiring strict data entry, forms, or linear reading (the lack of structure would frustrate users seeking fast, predictable input).
  • Not ideal for users on very small screens without stylus support, where precise freehand drawing and small toolbar targets become error-prone.
  • Risky for first-time users without onboarding: an empty infinite canvas with icon-only tools can be intimidating or confusing without a guided tour or tooltips.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets visual thinkers, product designers, and planners: users who need to externalize non-linear ideas (flows, wireframe sketches, mind maps) before committing them to structured prose in a Craft document. It serves knowledge workers who already use Craft for writing but need a complementary space for sketching user flows, architecture diagrams, or brainstorms, appealing to the "second brain" / personal knowledge management crowd.

Psychologically, the blank dotted canvas combined with a low-pressure "start" bubble invites exploration and reduces the intimidation of a blank page (it signals "this is a sandbox," not a finished deliverable, encouraging rapid, judgment-free ideation).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual two-tier toolbar: the top row of the toolbar changes based on the selected tool (stroke size/style for pen, presumably different options for shapes), avoiding a cluttered, always-visible mega-toolbar.
  • Zoom + History cluster: grouping zoom percentage, undo, and redo into a single floating pill keeps canvas-manipulation controls spatially separate from drawing tools, reducing cognitive load.
  • Dot-grid canvas: an understated alignment aid that supports precision drawing without visually competing with ink content.
  • Mixed-media primitives: sticky notes, shapes, and freehand pen marks are first-class citizens on the same canvas, letting users mix diagram styles fluidly.
  • Full-bleed canvas with minimal chrome: maximizes usable drawing area on a small mobile screen, critical for a touch-based whiteboarding experience.

screens.name: Craft - Drawing on a whiteboard - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when building:

  • Freeform canvas, whiteboard, or mind-mapping features embedded inside a broader productivity app.
  • Any drawing/annotation experience needing a compact tool switcher that expands via a secondary action sheet.
  • Flows where users need confidence to experiment (undo/redo, non-destructive 'Done' exit) rather than rigid save/cancel semantics.
  • Apps wanting to differentiate a structured document editor from a looser, exploratory ideation mode without launching a separate app.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for:

  • Simple note-taking apps where users rarely need spatial/diagrammatic thinking (the added toolbar complexity would be unnecessary overhead).
  • Mobile screens with very limited vertical space, where a large popover list (8+ options) can feel cramped or require excessive scrolling; consider a horizontal icon strip instead on small devices.
  • Contexts requiring precision vector drawing (e.g., professional CAD/illustration) - a lightweight sketch toolbar lacks the depth (layers, boolean paths, precise snapping) such users need.
  • First-time user onboarding without any tooltip/coach marks (the dense icon-based toolbar could overwhelm novices unfamiliar with whiteboard conventions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets visual thinkers, planners, and product/design professionals who use Craft not just for text notes but for early-stage brainstorming, wireframing a flow (e.g., "start" → "landing page") before writing prose documentation. The whiteboard canvas taps into the psychological need for spatial, non-linear thinking: some ideas are better expressed as diagrams and sticky notes than paragraphs, and giving users this canvas inside the same app that houses their documents reduces context-switching to tools like Miro or FigJam.

The sticky-note and hand-drawn elements evoke a tactile, physical whiteboard-and-post-it session, triggering nostalgia and comfort for workshop/brainstorming veterans, while the polished tool palette reassures professional users that this isn't a "toy" feature but a serious, well-crafted capability consistent with Craft's premium design positioning.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-mode toolbar: Separates macro navigation (hand/select) from micro-drawing tools (pencil submenu), reducing clutter while keeping power-user functionality one tap away.
  • Contextual tool popover: Clicking the active pencil icon reveals an expanded list of related instruments, following the 'progressive disclosure' principle so the primary canvas isn't permanently crowded with a huge toolbox.
  • Dotted-grid canvas with hand-drawn shapes: Reinforces Craft's editorial, designed-document aesthetic even in a free-drawing context, rather than feeling like a sterile diagramming tool.
  • Persistent zoom/undo/redo cluster: Gives users confidence to experiment liberally, since any mistake is instantly reversible.
  • AI wand icon: Hints at smart shape-recognition or sketch-to-vector conversion, a delightful power feature for users who sketch messy diagrams.

screens.name: Craft - Drawing on a whiteboard - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern when an app needs to support non-linear, spatial ideation alongside its primary linear content model (e).g., note-taking apps adding a whiteboard mode, project tools mapping user flows, or educational apps for diagramming. It's ideal when users need to combine freehand drawing, shapes, and text notes in one exploratory space, and when the brand wants to signal flexibility and craftsmanship beyond plain text input.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for strictly data-entry or transactional screens where precision and speed matter more than creative expression (e.g., forms, checkout flows, settings). It's also unsuitable for small-screen contexts where a floating toolbar and infinite canvas would feel cramped, or for users who need strict accessibility/screen-reader support, since freeform canvases are inherently difficult to make fully accessible. Overusing hand-drawn/playful visual motifs can also undermine a professional or enterprise-grade product's tone if not carefully balanced.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets visual thinkers, planners, and designers within Craft's broader audience of writers and knowledge workers (people who want to whiteboard a flow (e).g., a product journey: "start → landing page") before or alongside writing structured notes. The psychological trigger is creative freedom within a safe, reversible sandbox: the omnipresent undo/redo and non-destructive "Done" flow reassure the user they can experiment without fear of ruining their document, encouraging looser, more exploratory sketching akin to a physical whiteboard session.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-mode editing: seamlessly embedding a freeform sketch canvas within a structured notes app, bridging visual brainstorming and text-based writing.
  • Floating, grouped toolbars: undo/redo, zoom %, and a "magic cleanup" wand are clustered together and visually separated from the destructive/exit "Done" action, reducing accidental data loss.
  • Hand-drawn aesthetic elements (the sticky note, the wobbly arrow, the dashed bubble) lean into the editorial, human, tactile brand feel rather than sterile vector perfection.
  • Minimalist dotted-grid background instead of harsh ruled lines, giving a softer "designer's canvas" feel that encourages spatial, non-linear thinking.
  • Bottom tool dock mirrors industry-standard creative tools (pan, select, shape, pen, more), lowering the learning curve for anyone familiar with Procreate, Figma, or Apple's Freeform.

screens.name: Craft - Drawing on a whiteboard - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this freeform canvas pattern when:

  • Your product needs to support non-linear, spatial thinking (mind maps, flowcharts, mood boards, brainstorming) alongside structured content.
  • You want power users and creative professionals to feel the app can "do more" than basic text entry, increasing perceived value and stickiness.
  • Users benefit from mixing handwriting/sketching, shapes, and sticky-note-like objects in one malleable space.
  • You want to visually differentiate a creative/ideation mode from the primary document/list editing mode via distinct background treatment (dot grid vs. blank page).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Your target users are non-technical or unfamiliar with canvas-based tools (unlabeled icon toolbars (pan/select/shape/pen) can create a steep learning curve without onboarding or tooltips).
  • The core product is strictly linear/text-based (e.g., simple note apps, to-do lists) where a freeform canvas would be feature bloat and increase cognitive load.
  • Screen real estate is extremely limited (very small devices) - pan/zoom/draw interactions require generous touch targets and space to be usable.
  • Accessibility is a priority and you lack alternative, non-spatial ways to consume the same content (canvases are inherently harder to navigate via screen readers).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets visual thinkers, planners, and creative professionals: designers, product managers, writers outlining structure, or students mapping ideas (who need to externalize non-linear thoughts before or alongside linear writing). It appeals to users who already associate dot-grid canvases and sticky notes with brainstorming (a nod to physical whiteboard/Post-it workflows), making the digital tool feel instantly familiar.

The minimal, chrome-light design leverages the psychological principle of flow state preservation: by hiding non-essential UI and using soft, muted tool palettes, the app avoids interrupting creative ideation. The inclusion of a precise, professional-grade toolset (pan/select/shape/pen, undo/redo, zoom) signals to power users that Craft is not "just a notes app" but a serious tool capable of supporting visual planning, widening its competitive positioning against tools like Notion, Miro, or Apple Notes' built-in canvas.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dot-grid infinite canvas clearly differentiates freeform/visual thinking mode from the structured document editor, using a well-established visual convention.
  • Floating pill toolbars (top and bottom) keep controls accessible without boxing in the canvas (they float above content like translucent cards, preserving the sense of infinite space beneath them).
  • Mixed content primitives (sticky note, dashed shape, freehand ink, arrow) shown coexisting demonstrate flexible, non-linear composition (a brainstorming/whiteboarding feature embedded in a writing app).
  • Zoom percentage indicator doubles as both a utility (shows current zoom level) and implicit affordance that the canvas is zoomable/pannable.
  • Dedicated Undo/Redo directly next to zoom controls caters to the exploratory, mistake-tolerant nature of sketching, distinct from the more deliberate editing of structured text.
  • "Done" instead of a back arrow alone for exiting (signals this is a distinct, committable mode/session (like entering a drawing sub-editor) rather than simple navigation).

screens.name: Craft - Adding content in a whiteboard - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Creative or document tools where typography/visual style is a core value proposition (note apps, whiteboards, design tools).
  • Any canvas-based editor needing scoped, contextual toolbars that avoid overwhelming users with global controls.
  • Font or style pickers where showing a live preview glyph dramatically improves decision speed over plain text labels.

screens.whereNotToUse:

  • Onboarding or first-run flows: this level of granular customization should appear only after a user has built basic familiarity with the app.
  • Accessibility-critical contexts where decorative fonts (like Script) could harm readability if applied by default or without sufficient contrast/legibility warnings.
  • Contexts with limited screen real estate where stacking multiple toolbars (global + canvas + text) risks cluttering a small viewport.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets power users and creative professionals (designers, writers, planners) who value visual craftsmanship and expect granular typographic control, similar to expectations set by tools like Figma, Notion, or GoodNotes. The psychological driver is creative ownership and aesthetic control: by offering font families with distinct personalities (clean System, technical Mono, classic Serif, expressive Script), Craft lets users imbue their notes with identity and mood, satisfying a desire for self-expression beyond plain text input. The low-friction, icon-driven popover also appeals to users who want quick, uninterrupted flow, minimizing modal interruptions to keep them "in the canvas."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Glyph-based font previews: Each font option (System, Mono, Serif, Script) is prefixed with a live rendering of "Aa"/"Ss"/"Sc" in that actual typeface, letting users preview the aesthetic instantly instead of parsing a plain-text label.
  • Checkmark for active state: The currently applied font ("System") is marked with a checkmark rather than highlighting or bolding, keeping the list visually quiet and consistent with the app's minimal aesthetic.
  • Scoped toolbar architecture: Controls are layered by scope (global nav (top), canvas tools (bottom bar), and contextual text formatting (bar above keyboard)) so the UI only ever shows what's relevant to the current selection.
  • Dot-grid canvas: Signals a spatial/freeform editing surface, differentiating this view from the structured block-based document editor elsewhere in the app.
  • Color wheel icon: A playful, visually rich affordance for accent/theme color sits amid otherwise monochrome icons, drawing the eye to Craft's signature customization feature.

screens.name: Craft - Adding content in a whiteboard - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any canvas-based creative tool embedded within a broader productivity app (freeform drawing, diagramming, whiteboarding, or annotation features). It's ideal when you need to let users switch between structured content (documents) and unstructured, spatial content (sketches) without introducing a jarring context switch. The two-tier toolbar with progressive disclosure is well suited to any screen offering many formatting options that would otherwise clutter a single row.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple text-editing or data-entry screens where a full drawing toolbar would be excessive and intimidating. It's also unsuitable for casual or non-creative audiences who may be confused by icon-only, tool-dense interfaces lacking text labels. On small screens or for first-time users without onboarding, the lack of labels (relying purely on icon literacy) could hurt discoverability and increase the need for tooltips or a guided tour.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves power users and creative professionals: writers, planners, and visual thinkers who use Craft not just for linear text but for freeform ideation (mind-mapping, sketchnoting, diagramming within a note). The target user is comfortable with tool-rich interfaces akin to Procreate, Apple Notes, or Notability, and expects precision controls like zoom percentage and undo/redo readily available.

Psychologically, the sparse, almost-empty canvas invites a blank-canvas / low-pressure creative state, while the visible but unobtrusive toolbar reassures users that powerful capabilities are available without overwhelming them upfront (a key trigger for creative flow and reduced anxiety when starting a new sketch or diagram).
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Color-wheel swatch as a toolbar icon doubles as both a tool and a visual flourish, hinting at Craft's "custom accents" brand identity even within a utility screen.

screens.name: Craft - Adding content in a whiteboard - Screen 6

• Embedded drawing/diagramming modules inside note-taking, documentation, or whiteboard apps.
  • Any creative tool needing a shape/sticker/asset picker that shouldn't permanently occupy screen real estate.
  • Apps that mix structured content (text, tables) with free-form canvases and need a clear mode switch between "write" and "draw."

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets visual thinkers, planners, and note-takers within Craft's broader audience of writers and knowledge workers who occasionally need to sketch a diagram, flowchart, or mind-map alongside their prose (not dedicated illustrators).   • Dot-grid canvas: Subtle alignment guide without being a rigid, distracting grid (balances freedom with precision).

screens.name: Craft - Adding content in a whiteboard - Screen 7

  • Creative tools where users toggle between content styling (text/paragraph) and spatial/drawing tools (pan, select, shape, ink).

• Collapsed, expandable toolbar: The bottom dock shows only the most-used tools with a chevron to reveal more, balancing minimal screen footprint against full tool access.
  • Dual-avatar presence indicator: Overlapping colored avatars in the header instantly communicate real-time co-presence without needing a labeled "collaborators" list.
  • Dot-grid canvas: Provides spatial/scale reference on an otherwise infinite blank plane, helping users judge zoom level and alignment via touch gestures.
  • Sample content as onboarding: Rather than an empty canvas, a populated demo board teaches new mobile users FigJam's building blocks (stickies, shapes, reactions, flow arrows) experientially.
  • Dedicated pan/select mode toggle: Separating the hand tool from the pointer tool at the very start of the toolbar acknowledges the unique navigation challenge of touch-based infinite canvases.

screens.name: Airtable -  Editing a record (note field) - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when designing mobile experiences for data-dense desktop-first products (spreadsheets, CRMs, inventory systems) that need a lightweight way to preview structured records. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to browse multiple fields per record without opening full detail view.
  • The underlying data model supports multiple views (filtered, grouped, sorted) that should be independently switchable.
  • Aggregate values (sums, counts) add immediate value to the user's at-a-glance understanding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense card/toolbar combination for casual consumer apps with simple, single-purpose data (e.g., a to-do list or social feed) where exposing Filter/Group/Sort controls would feel like unnecessary complexity. It also breaks down on very small screens if too many fields are configured to show per card, causing excessive vertical scrolling and card-height inconsistency. For first-time users unfamiliar with database concepts, this level of control should be progressively disclosed rather than shown upfront.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations-minded and detail-oriented users: project managers, trip planners, small business owners (who need the flexibility of a spreadsheet but the usability of a consumer app). The psychological trigger here is mastery and control: by exposing filter/sort/group tools alongside a friendly visual card design, Airtable reassures users they aren't sacrificing powerful data manipulation for simplicity.

The playful illustrated icons and informal notes tone build emotional familiarity, lowering the intimidation factor that traditionally accompanies database tools, making it approachable for non-technical users while still satisfying power users' need for structured, queryable data.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Card-based grid translation: Converts a traditionally dense spreadsheet row into a readable, touch-friendly card without losing column context (via small field labels and icons).
  • Dual-layer navigation: Separates "Table" (bottom tab bar: Places, Packing List, Friends) from "View" (top dropdown: Main View), letting users maintain multiple saved perspectives on the same dataset.
  • Automatic column aggregation: The "26 sum" footer under Days shows live computed totals, reinforcing Airtable's spreadsheet power even in a simplified mobile layout.
  • Persistent manipulation toolbar: Hide fields, Filter, Group, and Sort are always one tap away, keeping power-user data control accessible without a separate settings screen.
  • Attachment overflow badge ("+1"): Elegant compression of multiple images into a single thumbnail with a counter badge, preserving card height consistency.

screens.name: Figma - Editing FigJam file - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any file-management, document, or asset-library search experience where visual content (thumbnails, covers, icons) can meaningfully help users distinguish between items (e).g., cloud storage apps, design tools, photo libraries, or project management dashboards. It's especially effective when the corpus of searchable items is large and textual titles alone are ambiguous or frequently duplicated.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy thumbnail-centric layout for searches over purely textual or transactional data (e.g., searching contacts, settings, or commands), where a lightweight text-only list is faster to scan. Also reconsider the large keyboard-to-content ratio on screens where users commonly need to scroll through many results simultaneously, as it may force excessive scrolling and hide results below the fold.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern serves designers and developers managing dozens or hundreds of files, boards, and prototypes across personal drafts and team projects. In a canvas-first tool like Figma, file names alone are often insufficient to distinguish between similar documents, so the psychological reliance on visual recognition over recall is leveraged heavily (the thumbnail acts as a cognitive shortcut, letting users confirm "yes, that's the one" in milliseconds rather than reading full titles).

The immediacy of showing results as the user types (rather than requiring a submit action) caters to power users who expect sub-second feedback loops, consistent with Figma's reputation for responsive, real-time tooling.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live thumbnail previews in search results let users visually recognize files instead of relying on memory for exact names.
  • Explicit result count ("1 result") removes ambiguity about search completeness.
  • High-contrast search bar with a dedicated Cancel action provides an unambiguous, reversible entry/exit point for the search flow.
  • Dual metadata labels (location + recency) give enough context to differentiate similarly named files at a glance.

screens.name: Figma - Editing FigJam file - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any canvas-based, spatial, or whiteboard-style application being adapted to mobile (tools like diagramming apps, whiteboards, mind-mapping tools, or creative/drawing apps). It's ideal when:

  • The core value proposition is direct manipulation of freeform content (not list/form-based data).
  • Users are already trained on the tool via desktop and need a lightweight, consistent mobile companion.
  • Screen space is scarce and every pixel of chrome competing with content must be justified.
  • Real-time collaboration/presence is a core differentiator worth surfacing persistently.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal, icon-only, canvas-first approach when:

  • Your primary audience is first-time or non-technical users who need labeled controls and onboarding cues (unlabeled icons can create confusion without prior training).
  • The task is linear/form-based rather than spatial (e.g., checkout, settings, data entry), where a toolbar-heavy canvas paradigm would feel out of place and reduce task completion speed.
  • Accessibility is a primary concern and icon-only controls without text labels or robust VoiceOver/TalkBack descriptions could hinder screen-reader users.
  • The app needs to frequently promote features, upsells, or notifications (the extremely sparse chrome here leaves little room for such messaging without disrupting the canvas-first feel).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, developers, and cross-functional team members who need to review, annotate, or lightly edit a Figma/FigJam board while away from their desktop (e).g., in a stand-up meeting, on a commute, or during a whiteboard brainstorm. The target user already has mental models from the desktop app, so the mobile UI leans on icon recognition rather than teaching from scratch.

Psychologically, the minimal chrome and spacious empty canvas reduce anxiety and signal "this is a big, flexible space," inviting exploration and freeform annotation rather than rigid data entry. The persistent avatar leverages social presence cues (a known driver of engagement in collaborative tools) to remind the user that their actions are visible to teammates, encouraging more thoughtful and deliberate contributions even on a quick mobile check-in.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Edge-to-edge canvas: Nearly 100% of the viewport is dedicated to the dot-grid workspace, maximizing visual focus on content over chrome.
  • Split bottom toolbar: Tools are grouped into logical clusters (navigation mode, drawing/color, sticky notes, overflow) rather than one long row, reducing cognitive load and mis-taps on a small screen.
  • Hand/pointer mode toggle: A dedicated pan vs. select toggle solves the classic mobile canvas problem of distinguishing "move the camera" from "select/draw an object" gestures.
  • Persistent collaborator avatar: Reinforces Figma's multiplayer DNA at all times, even solo, by always surfacing presence UI in the top bar.
  • Frame thumbnails as overview: Showing shrunk frames in a horizontal strip lets users quickly reorient themselves on the whole board without needing a separate "minimap" screen.

screens.name: Figma - Editing FigJam file - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any canvas-based, freeform creation tool (whiteboards, mind-maps, mood boards, diagramming apps) being adapted to mobile. It's ideal when:

  • The core experience is spatial/visual manipulation rather than linear forms.
  • Real-time multiplayer presence is a core value proposition.
  • You need to compress a desktop-class toolbar into a mobile-friendly footprint via grouping and progressive disclosure.
  • The session is a "mode" users intentionally enter and exit (justifying the modal X vs. tab/back navigation).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for content-heavy, text-driven, or form-based mobile apps where an infinite freeform canvas would create disorientation rather than creativity. It's also unsuitable when:

  • Users need persistent, always-visible navigation (the modal "X" pattern breaks deep-linking and back-stack expectations).
  • The target audience is non-technical and unfamiliar with canvas/pan-zoom interaction paradigms (icon-only toolbars with no labels could create a steep learning curve).
  • Precision input (not freeform sketching) is the primary task (small touch targets on a collapsed toolbar are not ideal for pixel-level precision work).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers, PMs, and cross-functional teams who need to brainstorm or facilitate workshops on the go, often during standups, client calls, or hallway conversations where a laptop isn't convenient. The psychological trigger here is low-friction creative play: the playful colors, stickers, and emoji lower the intimidation barrier of an "empty canvas," encouraging spontaneous contribution rather than precise, high-stakes design work (which is reserved for Figma Design proper).

The presence indicators (avatars) also tap into social accountability and FOMO: seeing teammates "in the file" nudges users to engage in real time rather than defer participation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Modal "X" exit pattern: Using a close icon instead of a back arrow correctly signals this is a focused overlay session, not a nested navigation level, letting users understand they're "stepping into" a dedicated creation space.
  • Collapsed, expandable toolbar: Grouping tools into compact chips with chevron expanders is a masterclass in adapting a dense desktop toolbar for thumb ergonomics without losing functional depth.
  • Persistent active-color swatch: Surfacing the current pen color directly in the toolbar (rather than hiding it in a sub-menu) reduces taps for the most common action, drawing/annotating.
  • Collaborator avatars front and center: Placing presence avatars in the top bar (not buried in a menu) reinforces the real-time, multiplayer nature of the product at a glance.
  • Infinite dot-grid canvas: The subtle dotted background provides spatial orientation and alignment cues without visually competing with user-generated content.

screens.name: Figma - Editing FigJam file - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any canvas-based or spatial editing tool (whiteboards, diagramming, design tools) that must support both desktop and mobile without alienating power users.
  • Apps where objects can be selected individually or in groups and require quick, high-frequency actions (delete, duplicate, more) without navigating to a separate menu screen.
  • Collaborative tools that want to visually signal "who else is here" via persistent header avatars.
  • Any mobile adaptation of a complex desktop tool where progressive disclosure (collapsed toolbar + expand chevron) is needed to fit a constrained screen.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid icon-only contextual toolbars for novice or non-technical consumer audiences who may not recognize duplicate/delete iconography without labels.
  • Not suitable for simple content-consumption apps where users rarely select/manipulate objects (the overhead of bounding boxes and floating toolbars would be unnecessary complexity).
  • Risky on very small screens (e.g., smartwatches) where a floating toolbar could obscure the selected content itself.
  • Should not be used when actions are rare or destructive-by-default without a confirmation step, since quick-access Delete sitting one tap away can increase accidental data loss risk.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers, product managers, and cross-functional teams using FigJam on mobile (typically during live workshops, retrospectives, or when quickly reviewing/annotating a board away from their desktop). The psychological driver is control and confidence: by preserving familiar desktop interaction patterns (bounding box, corner handles, contextual toolbar) on a touch device, Figma reduces cognitive load and prevents the anxiety of "losing" precision when switching to a smaller screen.

The condensed, icon-only bottom toolbar appeals to the target audience's existing visual literacy (this is not a tool for first-time computer users, so icons alone (without labels) are an acceptable and even preferred efficiency trade-off).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Floating contextual action bar: Appears only on selection, positioned adjacent to the object rather than buried in a menu, minimizing travel distance and taps.
  • Faithful desktop-to-mobile translation: Selection handles, bounding box, and multi-tool toolbar mirror the desktop Figma/FigJam interaction model, reducing relearning cost for cross-platform users.
  • Chrome minimization: Top bar reduced to 4 essential icons, giving near-full-bleed canvas visibility (critical for a spatial, pan/zoom-heavy tool).
  • Collapsed, expandable toolbar: Chevron (^) lets power tools stay hidden until needed, solving the "too many tools, too little screen" constraint of mobile design tools.
  • Presence avatars: Two stacked collaborator avatars in the header reinforce FigJam's real-time multiplayer identity at a glance.

screens.name: Figma - FigJam file options - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when designing mobile companion experiences for complex desktop-first canvas or document tools (whiteboards, diagramming, design tools, map editors). It's ideal when:

  • The core interaction is spatial/freeform and benefits from an infinite canvas metaphor.
  • You need to preserve a large visual viewport while still exposing creation tools without modal interruptions.
  • Real-time collaboration/presence is a core value proposition that should be visible at all times.
  • Users will perform short, frequent "check-in" sessions rather than long focused work, justifying a reduced/simplified toolset versus the desktop version.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal floating-toolbar-on-canvas pattern when:

  • The tool requires dense, frequent access to many simultaneous options (e.g., full desktop-grade vector editing) - icon-only compressed toolbars will cause excessive nested menus and friction.
  • Users are predominantly first-time/non-technical and need labeled, explicit actions rather than icon-only affordances.
  • The app's primary content is linear/text-based rather than spatial, where an infinite dot-grid canvas would add confusion instead of clarity.
  • Precise, fine-grained manipulation is required that finger-based touch targets cannot adequately support without a stylus or zoom affordances.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers, product managers, and cross-functional team members who need to check in on, contribute to, or react to a brainstorming session while away from their desktop (e).g., during a stand-up, commute, or hallway conversation. The simplified mobile toolset assumes users are performing lightweight actions (adding a sticky note, reacting with an emoji, moving an object) rather than deep design work.

Psychologically, the design leans on social presence (avatars) and low-commitment engagement (big tap targets, undo-friendly canvas tools) to encourage spontaneous participation. The playful "FigJam basics" sticky and sticker pack also serves as implicit onboarding/demo content, lowering the intimidation factor for first-time FigJam mobile users by showing rather than telling them what's possible.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-mode floating toolbar: Separates navigation (select/pan) from creation (pen/shape) tools into distinct pill-shaped clusters, reducing accidental tool switches on a small touchscreen.
  • Infinite canvas affordance via dot grid: Instantly communicates spatial freedom and orientation without any onboarding copy.
  • Persistent collaborator avatars: Builds real-time social presence awareness at a glance, reinforcing FigJam's multiplayer value proposition even in a condensed mobile header.
  • Expandable tool trays (chevrons): Keeps the primary toolbar compact while still surfacing deeper customization (colors, shapes, sticky variants) on demand.
  • Minimal top bar with clear exit path: The "X" close button gives users unambiguous, low-friction control to leave the board, critical for a mobile companion/viewer experience.

screens.name: Figma - FigJam file options - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when a desktop-grade application needs to expose a long tail of secondary, power-user commands on a space-constrained mobile surface. It's ideal for:

  • Productivity, creative, or technical tools porting a rich menu-bar feature set to mobile/touch.
  • Contexts where command frequency varies widely (some used constantly, others rarely) and a flat always-visible toolbar would be impractical.
  • Apps that already have an established keyboard-shortcut/menu-bar culture on desktop, where consistency across platforms builds user confidence.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense list-menu approach for:

  • Consumer-facing, first-time-use apps where cognitive load must stay minimal (a 14-item menu would overwhelm casual users).
  • Primary, high-frequency actions that deserve dedicated, always-visible buttons rather than being buried in an overflow list (forcing two taps instead of one hurts efficiency for core workflows).
  • Situations lacking logical grouping: if items can't be clearly clustered, the undifferentiated list becomes a scroll-heavy, hard-to-scan wall of text.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This menu targets intermediate-to-power users: designers and developers already fluent in Figma's desktop conventions who need parity when working on a tablet/phone during a review, a quick edit, or while away from their workstation. The inclusion of niche commands like "Show timer" (a FigJam collaboration/workshop tool) and "Find in file" signals this is built for active collaborators, not first-time visitors.

Psychologically, the design leverages recognition over recall: by mirroring the structure of Figma's desktop right-click menu, returning users don't need to relearn where functions live, reducing friction and reinforcing platform consistency across devices, which builds trust and perceived reliability in a professional tool.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Grouping via Dividers: Related actions (clipboard, history, view) are clustered with subtle separators instead of labelled headers, saving vertical space while preserving scannability.
  • Disabled-but-Visible Pattern: Unavailable actions (Cut, Copy, Undo) are grayed out rather than hidden, maintaining a predictable, muscle-memory-friendly menu structure across sessions.
  • Icon + Label Redundancy: Every action pairs a trailing icon with its text label, speeding recognition and supporting accessibility/localization.
  • Porting Desktop Power to Mobile: The menu condenses Figma's desktop right-click/menu-bar functionality into a single scrollable sheet, proving that a touch-first surface can still support an expert, keyboard-shortcut-level workflow.
  • Persistent Trigger Visibility: The top bar (avatars, share, "...") stays visible above the menu, letting users understand the menu's origin and dismiss ambiguity about where it came from.

screens.name: Figma - Adding stamps - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this contextual, anchored tool-picker pattern when:

  • An app has many creation tools/object types that can't all fit in a persistent toolbar, especially on small touch screens.

  • You want to preserve spatial context (canvas, document, board) while letting users pick an action, rather than navigating away.

  • Your users range from casual/first-time to power users, and you want a single surface that serves both via inline shortcut hints.

  • Progressive disclosure of advanced features ("much, much more") is needed to keep the primary list lightweight and non-intimidating.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach when:

  • The tool/action list is very short (2-3 items): a popover with descriptions would be overkill; a simple icon row suffices.

  • Users are predominantly mobile-only with no keyboard access, surfacing keyboard shortcuts could add visual clutter with no payoff.

  • The underlying canvas content is not relevant to the decision being made (e.g., account settings, checkout flows) where a full-screen modal or dedicated page better isolates focus.

  • Screen real estate is extremely constrained (very small phones), where a dense popover list combined with a visible canvas could feel cramped or require excessive scrolling.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, product teams, and cross-functional collaborators (PMs, engineers, workshop facilitators) using FigJam on mobile/tablet to brainstorm or contribute asynchronously. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Recognition over recall: Icons paired with labels and descriptions reduce the memory burden of learning a new tool's iconography.

  • Progressive disclosure: Only a curated set of common tools (Table, Section, Connector, Text, Sticky note, Stamp) are shown by default, with "Much, much more" deferring advanced/rare tools to avoid overwhelming casual or first-time users.

  • Competence & mastery cues: Displaying keyboard shortcuts signals to prosumers that the app rewards efficiency and scales from casual touch use to expert workflows, supporting user retention as skill grows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual popover anchored to its trigger: The pointer/tail on the menu visually ties it back to the overflow button, maintaining spatial continuity and reducing cognitive load.

  • Icon + title + microcopy + shortcut pattern: A highly scannable, repeatable row template that balances discoverability (for new users reading descriptions) with efficiency (for power users scanning shortcuts).

  • Non-blocking overlay over live canvas: Keeps the user oriented in their document; the board content (sticky notes already on canvas) stays visible and dimmed rather than being hidden behind a full modal.

  • Persistent presence & sync indicators: Collaborator avatars and cloud-sync icon in the top bar reinforce FigJam's real-time multiplayer value proposition at all times, even mid-task.

screens.name: Figma - Adding stamps - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use a radial/pie selection menu when:

  • You need to present 5: 8 mutually exclusive quick-action options (reactions, tools, shortcuts) on a touch interface where speed and large hit targets matter.

  • The interaction is ephemeral and low-commitment (a reaction, a quick tag, a tool switch) rather than a complex configuration task.

  • You want to preserve context by overlaying the picker on live content instead of navigating to a new screen or full-screen modal.

  • Collaborative or real-time tools where social, expressive feedback (reactions, emotes) drives engagement and lightweight communication.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid radial menus when:

  • The option set exceeds ~8 items, as wedge targets become too thin and error-prone.

  • Users need to compare or read detailed labels: radial layouts favor icons/emoji over text, so they fail for content requiring explanation.

  • The action is destructive, high-stakes, or requires confirmation (radial pickers' speed and ambiguity (exact gesture endpoint) make them unsuitable for anything irreversible).

  • Targeting desktop-first users without touch input, where hover-based linear toolbars are more precise and discoverable.

  • Accessibility is a priority without additional work (circular layouts and gesture-based release are harder to make screen-reader and switch-control friendly than standard lists).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers, PMs, and cross-functional teams collaborating synchronously or asynchronously on a FigJam board from mobile devices (often during a workshop, brainstorm, or stand-up where quick, low-effort feedback (a 👍, 🔥, or 😂) communicates sentiment faster than typed comments).

Psychologically, the radial picker leverages Fitts's Law (larger, closer targets are faster and easier to hit) and reduces cognitive load by replacing a linear list (which would require scanning and precise vertical taps) with a spatial, gesture-friendly arrangement that can be operated with a single thumb swipe-and-release gesture, similar to familiar patterns from Slack and iMessage tapback menus. The emoji-only vocabulary also taps into the social proof and lightweight engagement principle: reacting takes less effort than commenting, which increases participation rates in collaborative sessions.
screens.keyHighlights:
Radial (pie) menu for reactions: Converts a desktop hover-driven stamp picker into a touch-optimized circular layout with large, evenly spaced hit targets (ideal for thumb reach and reducing mis-taps on small screens).

Non-modal overlay on live canvas: The picker floats above real board content rather than taking over the screen, preserving spatial context and signaling that reacting is a lightweight, non-committal action.

Central preview affordance: The purple semi-circle with a smiley/cursor glyph in the center acts as a live preview of the active stamp state, giving immediate visual feedback before commitment.

Persistent toolbar during picker use: Core tools (cursor, eraser, shape, stamp) remain accessible at the bottom, maintaining flow and avoiding a jarring context switch.

Collaborative presence cues: Overlapping avatar bubbles in the top bar reinforce the multiplayer, real-time nature of the session even while a secondary interaction (reacting) is in progress.

screens.name: Figma - Adding stamps - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Live collaboration tools (whiteboards, docs, video calls) needing fast, low-friction feedback without breaking flow.

  • Touch-first interfaces where several mutually exclusive or quick-fire options must be reachable from a single thumb position.

  • Any feature benefiting from gamified, icon-driven interaction (reactions, mood/rating pickers, tool selection in creative apps).

  • Scenarios where preserving underlying context (canvas, document, video) during selection is important.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid radial menus when there are more than ~8 options (recognition and tap accuracy degrade quickly as segments get smaller).

  • Not suitable for options requiring explanation or nuanced text labels, since the format depends on instantly recognizable icons.

  • Poor fit for accessibility-critical flows (screen reader users, motor-impaired users) unless a linear/list fallback is also provided.

  • Avoid on desktop-first, mouse-precision workflows where a simple dropdown or toolbar is faster and more familiar.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers, PMs, and cross-functional teammates collaborating live in FigJam, often during workshops, retros, or brainstorms where quick, non-verbal feedback (reactions/stamps) keeps momentum without interrupting a facilitator or typing comments. The radial layout specifically serves mobile/tablet attendees joining a session from a phone, where thumb reach and one-handed operation are primary constraints.

Psychologically, it leverages recognition over recall (icons instead of menus of words) and Fitts's Law (equal, short distances to all targets) to make reacting feel instantaneous and almost game-like, encouraging more frequent, spontaneous engagement, mirroring the dopamine-driven interaction patterns of social apps (quick reactions like Slack/Instagram) but repurposed for productivity collaboration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radial marking menu for reactions (all options sit on a circle equidistant from the thumb's resting point, reducing reach and mis-taps on mobile).

  • Center "stamp" icon doubles as a toggle/default, visually split blue/white to show an active/hover state before the user commits to an outer option.

  • Canvas remains visible and dimmed behind the menu, preserving spatial context of where the reaction will be placed.

  • Consistent chrome (top avatars/share, bottom tool switcher) stays present, so the reaction picker feels like a layered overlay rather than a separate screen/modal.

  • Icon-only vocabulary (no labels) speeds up recognition for a global, repeat-use audience already fluent in emoji semantics.

screens.name: Figma - Adding stamps - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for canvas-based, spatial, or whiteboard-style products (diagramming, mind-mapping, design tools) especially when adapting a dense desktop toolset for mobile. It's ideal when:

  • Real-time multiplayer editing requires visible presence indicators.

  • Autosave removes the need for explicit save actions and users need lightweight, non-blocking confirmation.

  • The primary content is non-linear/spatial and benefits from direct manipulation rather than scrolling lists.

  • Tool options are numerous but can be prioritized, with secondary tools tucked behind a "more" affordance.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for linear, form-based, or content-consumption apps where users expect standard navigation (tab bars, lists) rather than a freeform canvas. Icon-only toolbars without labels can hurt discoverability for first-time or infrequent users, so this works best for tools where users already understand the underlying metaphor (e.g., whiteboarding) or where onboarding/tooltips exist elsewhere. Overlapping avatar presence indicators should be skipped in single-user or non-collaborative contexts, as they add visual noise without functional benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets designers, product teams, and cross-functional collaborators using FigJam on mobile to review, annotate, or lightly contribute to a brainstorm/whiteboard session while away from their desktop. The psychological drivers at play include reduced cognitive load (icon-only toolbar, minimal chrome) so users can focus on content rather than UI, and social presence cues (avatars) that trigger accountability and engagement in shared work. The autosave toast taps into the need for control and certainty: users mid-collaboration want instant confidence that their edits (or others') are persisted without manual intervention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Autosave toast as implicit trust-builder: The "Changes saved" toast removes any anxiety about losing work on a collaborative canvas, replacing manual save actions with passive confirmation.

  • Presence avatars in the header: Overlapping colored initials avatars immediately communicate who else is active on the board, reinforcing FigJam's real-time collaborative identity even before any content loads.

  • Condensed, adaptive toolbar: A desktop-grade toolset is distilled into a single scrollable/expandable row with a chevron for "more," balancing power and simplicity for touch input.

  • Active tool state highlighting: The purple-filled stamp/sticker icon clearly shows which tool is currently selected, preventing ambiguity during direct manipulation.

  • Infinite dotted canvas: Reinforces the mental model of a boundless creative whiteboard, encouraging free-form placement of ideas.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Apply this canvas-first pattern when designing freeform creative or collaborative tools (whiteboards, mind-mapping apps, mood boards, diagramming tools) on mobile, where:

  • The primary value is the content/canvas itself, not navigation chrome.
  • Real-time multi-user collaboration is core, warranting persistent presence indicators.
  • Users need frequent access to a small set of creation tools without context-switching away from their work.
  • Onboarding can be accomplished via example content rather than modal tutorials, preserving flow.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal-chrome, icon-only approach when:

  • The target audience is non-technical or first-time users who need explicit textual guidance (icon-only toolbars can be ambiguous without prior exposure to similar tools).
  • The app's primary tasks require frequent navigation between many distinct sections (a persistent bottom tab bar would serve better than a floating tool tray).
  • Precision input is critical and screen space is at such a premium that condensed toolbars would force excessive nested menus, increasing tap depth and errors.
  • Accessibility is a top priority and icon-only controls aren't paired with adequate labels/tooltips for screen reader users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, developers, and cross-functional team members collaborating remotely who need a lightweight, visual brainstorming space accessible from a phone (e).g., checking in on a team's FigJam board during a meeting, adding a quick sticky note, or reacting with a stamp while away from desk.

Psychologically, the design leverages several triggers: social presence (seeing collaborator avatars creates accountability and reduces the solitude of staring at a blank canvas), low cognitive load via familiarity (icon-only toolbar mirrors tools professionals already know from physical whiteboarding - pens, sticky notes, pointers), and playfulness as an anxiety reducer (the pun-filled sample content and emoji stickers make an otherwise intimidating infinite canvas feel approachable and non-precious, encouraging experimentation rather than perfectionism).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Minimal, canvas-first chrome: UI controls are reduced to two thin strips at the very top and bottom, maximizing screen real estate for the actual work surface (critical on small mobile viewports where every pixel of canvas matters).
  • Live presence indicators: Overlapping avatar bubbles in the header immediately communicate "you are not alone here," reinforcing FigJam's core real-time, multiplayer value proposition even before any content is touched.
  • Active-state tool highlighting: The purple-filled cursor icon in the toolbar gives unambiguous, glanceable feedback on which tool mode is currently engaged (important since mobile touch targets are small and mode errors are costly).
  • Inline color swatch next to the pen tool: Surfacing the current drawing color directly in the primary toolbar (rather than burying it in a submenu) reduces taps for the most common action, changing ink color mid-brainstorm.
  • Sample content as onboarding: Rather than a tutorial overlay, the board ships with real-looking sticky notes, stickers, and a flowchart, letting users learn affordances by exploring and manipulating existing objects (a "learn by doing" approach that respects user agency).
  • Dotted grid background: Subtly communicates "infinite canvas" and spatial freedom without needing explanatory text.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this edge-anchored minimal-chrome pattern for any canvas-based, direct-manipulation tool (whiteboards, design tools, mind-mapping, diagramming apps) where the content area must dominate the viewport, especially on mobile. Use live cursors with name labels whenever real-time multiplayer editing is a core value proposition, as it builds trust and transparency in collaborative work. The avatar-stack presence indicator is ideal for toolbars with limited horizontal space when more than one collaborator may be active.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid pure icon-only toolbars for first-time or non-technical audiences where tool literacy can't be assumed — add labels or onboarding coach marks instead. Live cursors and presence become visual noise in single-player contexts or in apps where collaboration is incidental rather than central, and should be gated behind a toggle. Overlapping avatar stacks break down with large numbers of simultaneous collaborators (10+) and need a "+N more" fallback to remain legible.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, developers, and cross-functional teammates collaborating synchronously on brainstorms, workshops, or planning sessions, often while mobile or away from their desktop. The mobile FigJam experience specifically targets users who need to quickly glance at, annotate, or react to a board started on desktop — e.g., joining a workshop from a phone during a meeting.

Psychologically, the live cursor and presence avatars tap into social presence and accountability: knowing a named collaborator is actively present and visibly moving around the board increases engagement and reduces the feeling of working in isolation. The minimal, icon-driven chrome also appeals to the target audience's assumed tool literacy — designers and technical users are comfortable inferring icon meaning without text labels, and the reduced UI signals a "professional, precision-focused" tool rather than a hand-holding consumer app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live multiplayer cursor with name tag directly on the canvas, making remote collaboration tangible and spatially contextual rather than abstracted into a sidebar list.
  • Edge-anchored, icon-only chrome (top and bottom bars) that maximizes canvas real estate on a small mobile screen while keeping essential actions reachable by thumb.
  • Overlapping avatar stack as a space-efficient presence indicator that scales gracefully as more collaborators join.
  • Expandable bottom toolbar with chevron affordances, hinting at deeper tool options (color/stroke, shape variants, note styles) without cluttering the default view.
  • Sample content as onboarding — the pre-built "FigJam basics" board acts as an implicit tutorial/demo rather than a modal walkthrough.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any real-time collaborative canvas, document, or whiteboard product where multiple users can be simultaneously active. It's ideal when:

  • You need a lightweight, non-blocking way to show who's present without permanent UI real estate cost.
  • Facilitation or teaching use-cases require pulling group attention to a single viewport (e.g., Spotlight/Follow).
  • You want to reinforce a sense of liveness and reduce the "am I alone here?" anxiety in multiplayer tools.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in single-player or asynchronous-only apps where presence/collaboration isn't a core value prop (the added UI would be noise). It's also unnecessary for tools with very large concurrent user counts (50+) where showing every avatar becomes unwieldy and a simplified count or grouped indicator would be more appropriate. Additionally, "Spotlight"-type forced-navigation actions should be used cautiously, as hijacking another user's viewport without clear consent/visual warning can feel intrusive or disorienting.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets designers, product managers, and distributed teams running collaborative brainstorming or workshop sessions on a tablet/mobile device (likely in a room together or hybrid remote setting). The psychological driver here is social presence and co-creation: seeing avatars and live cursors satisfies the human need to feel "together" even in a digital space, which increases engagement and trust in the collaborative output.

The Spotlight feature specifically serves facilitators/teachers who need control over group attention (a direct response to the common pain point of "losing" participants who wander off exploring a large FigJam board during a workshop).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Stacked Avatar Entry Point: Overlapping circular avatars in the nav bar double as both a presence indicator and a tappable trigger for the full collaborator list (an elegant, space-efficient affordance).
  • Spotlight Action: A single-tap mechanism to broadcast your viewport to all collaborators, purpose-built for workshop facilitators and teachers running remote sessions.
  • Live Cursor Labels: Named cursors on canvas ("Julian") create an ambient, game-like sense of co-presence without needing a persistent sidebar.
  • Non-Modal Popover: The roster list floats above the canvas without dimming or blocking it, letting users keep visual context of the board while checking who's online.
  • Thumb-Optimized Floating Toolbar: Tools are condensed into a pill at the screen's bottom edge, optimized for one-handed mobile/tablet use during a creative session.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this "follow mode" pattern for any real-time collaborative canvas, document, or whiteboard product where multiple users navigate a shared infinite space (e.g., diagramming tools, collaborative slide decks, virtual whiteboards, or live code review tools). It's especially valuable for remote presentations, guided walkthroughs, mentorship/pairing sessions, and onboarding where one expert leads others through complex content.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in single-player or non-real-time apps, or in contexts where simultaneous multi-user viewports aren't relevant (e.g., static document viewers, form-based apps). It can also backfire if overused without a clear exit path (always pair persistent "following" states with an obvious, instantly accessible way to break away (as the X button here does), since locked navigation can feel disorienting or claustrophobic if users feel trapped following someone else's pace).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern serves teams and designers conducting remote walkthroughs, brainstorms, or workshops in FigJam, especially useful on mobile when someone wants to passively observe a facilitator's presentation of a board (e.g., during a remote standup or design critique) without needing to manually navigate. The psychological trigger is reduced cognitive load through delegated navigation: users don't need to figure out where to look; the system does it for them, mirroring the comfort of being guided on a tour. It also leverages social presence theory: visible cursors and names make remote collaboration feel co-located and trustworthy.
screens.keyHighlights:
Why this screen is excellent:

  • Color-coded identity consistency: Julian's avatar, cursor label, and the "Following" pill all share the same yellow hue, letting users track identity across multiple UI surfaces without re-reading names.
  • Persistent, unobtrusive mode indicator: The floating pill clearly communicates a non-default navigation state (being driven by someone else) without blocking the canvas content.
  • Minimal chrome maximizes canvas space: Only essential controls are exposed, reinforcing the "canvas-first" philosophy where content always takes visual priority over UI.
  • Live cursor as social proof of activity: Seeing a real named cursor moving through content makes the collaboration feel alive and synchronous rather than static.

screens.name: Figma - Following another user's action - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for canvas-based, creative, or collaborative tools (whiteboards, diagramming apps, design tools) being adapted to mobile or tablet form factors. It's ideal when:

  • The core value is a large, zoomable/pannable workspace that must not be obstructed by chrome.
  • Multiple simultaneous collaborators need lightweight, glanceable presence indicators.
  • Tool selection benefits from progressive disclosure (primary tool visible, sub-options behind a chevron) to conserve limited mobile screen space.
screens.whereNotToUse: This pattern is not suitable for form-heavy, linear, or transactional flows (e.g., checkout, settings, onboarding) where users need clear hierarchical navigation and persistent labels rather than icon-only, gesture-driven controls. It can also fail for new or first-time users without prior exposure to the desktop tool, since icon-only toolbars with minimal labeling rely heavily on learned mental models and may feel cryptic without onboarding/tooltips. Additionally, on very small screens, a floating toolbar can obscure canvas content near the bottom edge, so it should be paired with safe-area padding or auto-hide behavior.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
