It's ideal for fintech, healthtech, or any regulated app where trust and low cognitive load must be balanced with mandatory data/legal collection. Also effective when you want to visually communicate flow length via a segmented progress bar to reduce abandonment.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this single-field-per-screen approach for low-stakes, high-frequency forms (e.g., search filters, quick settings) where the extra screens/taps would feel needlessly slow. It's also inefficient for returning or power users who need speed over hand-holding; in those cases, consolidate fields into a single scrollable form. Additionally, if the total flow requires many steps (10+), a segmented bar with only 3 visible ticks can misrepresent true length and should be replaced with a percentage or numeric step counter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: For PayPal's target of busy urban users and students, phone number verification is often the very first gate to money movement (a moment where drop-off risk is high due to privacy hesitation). Students opening their first financial account and urban users switching between banking apps are typically impatient and skeptical of unnecessary data requests. The minimal, single-question screen respects that impatience (no multi-field wall) while the transparent SMS disclaimer specifically pre-empts the "will I get charged/spammed?" objection common among cost-conscious students. The stark navy-on-white, no-frills aesthetic reinforces the app's "cautious, ledger-minded" brand identity, signaling seriousness and security rather than gamified excitement, which builds subconscious trust during a sensitive identity step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented progress indicator: Immediately communicates scope (3 steps) and current position, reducing sign-up abandonment anxiety.

  • Single-field focus: Isolating the phone number field with no distractions maximizes completion rate per classic form UX principles (Hick's Law).

  • Conversational headline: "What's your number?" trades corporate tone for approachable, chat-like phrasing that eases friction around sharing personal data.

  • Inline compliance microcopy: Legal/SMS consent text is proactively surfaced rather than hidden, building trust without needing a separate consent screen.

  • Thumb-zone CTA placement: Full-width black "Next" button anchored at the bottom maximizes one-handed reachability and clarity of the single next action.

screens.name: PayPal Pre-Onboarding 8
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any early-stage identity verification or account-creation step in fintech, banking, or regulated apps where phone number collection is mandatory for 2FA or KYC purposes. It's ideal when:

  • You need to collect one sensitive piece of information without overwhelming the user.

  • The overall onboarding flow has a small, known number of steps that benefit from a visible progress indicator.

  • Regulatory disclosure text must accompany the input but shouldn't dominate the screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this single-field-per-screen approach for lower-stakes or high-volume data forms where step count would become excessive and annoying (e.g., collecting 10+ pieces of profile data would fatigue users if each is isolated to its own screen). Also avoid vague progress bars when the number of steps is highly variable or unknown, as this can breed false expectations and frustration if the flow turns out longer than implied.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is engineered for PayPal's core demographic of busy urban professionals and students who expect fast, frictionless digital experiences akin to consumer social apps, not legacy bank forms. The casual headline and generous whitespace speak to a mobile-native audience that associates dense forms with distrust or wasted time.

Psychologically, the progress bar leverages the Zeigarnik effect (a preference to complete unfinished tasks) and reduces uncertainty, a key driver of onboarding drop-off in fintech apps where users are naturally cautious about handing over personal data. The muted legal disclaimer builds trust through transparency without triggering suspicion, which is essential for a "cautious, ledger-minded" money app that must balance speed with credibility.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented progress indicator: Immediately sets expectations for a short, finite multi-step flow rather than an open-ended form, reducing abandonment anxiety.

  • Single-field focus: Only one input is presented at a time, applying the "one thing per screen" principle to maximize completion rates for a high-stakes financial onboarding flow.

  • Smart default country code: Pre-filling "+1" reduces typing effort and cognitive load for the primary market.

  • Bottom-anchored CTA: The "Next" button sits within natural thumb reach, optimized for on-the-go, one-handed mobile banking usage.

  • Transparent compliance copy: Legal SMS consent language is present but visually de-emphasized, balancing regulatory needs with a clean, non-intimidating UI.

screens.name: PayPal Pre-Onboarding 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use this segmented OTP + bottom sheet pattern whenever verifying a highly sensitive, time-boxed credential (phone, email, 2FA) within a broader linear flow such as onboarding, checkout, or account recovery. It's ideal when:

  • You need to keep users oriented within a multi-step wizard without a full page navigation.

  • The verification code has a fixed, known length (e.g., 6 digits).

  • You want to reduce input errors via auto-formatted, auto-advancing fields paired with the correct native keyboard.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The verification method doesn't have a fixed-length code (e.g., variable-length recovery keys) - a single text field with formatting may be better.

  • The flow requires displaying substantial supporting content (e.g., legal text, images) that a bottom sheet's limited real estate can't accommodate well.

  • Users may need to reference the background screen's full content simultaneously (the dimmed/cut-off background here (note the truncated "Who's opening this account)?" headline) can feel visually jarring or incomplete if not handled carefully.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets PayPal's core sign-up demographic (busy urban professionals and students opening a financial account, likely on mobile in transit or in short attention windows). Phone verification is a critical trust and security checkpoint for a money-movement app, and this audience expects the friction to be minimal but the process to feel secure (ledger-minded reassurance). The psychological trigger here is safety-through-verification: by explicitly showing "we sent a code to [your number]," PayPal reduces anxiety around account takeover or wrong-number errors, while the segmented input format subconsciously communicates precision and rigor befitting a financial institution.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Bottom Sheet Overlay Pattern: Retains onboarding context in the background (progress bar, previous screen) while focusing the user purely on OTP entry, minimizing the feeling of being "lost" in the flow.

  • Segmented OTP Boxes: Individual boxes per digit with active-state highlighting (blue border) give clear input affordance and progress feedback without needing a label.

  • Native Numeric Keypad: Automatically surfaces the correct keyboard type, removing unnecessary UI (letters) and speeding up entry (critical for security codes with short expiry windows).

  • Masked Phone Number Display: Confirms the right number was targeted without fully exposing PII on-screen, balancing usability with privacy.

  • Escape Hatch (X): Top-right close button lets users abandon or back out of verification without being trapped, respecting user control even inside a security-critical flow.

screens.name: PayPal Pre-Onboarding 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any OTP/2FA verification step in signup, login, password reset, or high-risk transaction flows, especially in fintech, banking, or identity-sensitive apps. It's ideal whenever you need to confirm ownership of a phone number or email while minimizing drop-off (pair it with native autofill APIs (SMS Retriever on Android, QuickType on iOS) wherever possible).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, modal-interrupting treatment for low-stakes or optional verifications, where a lighter inline prompt would suffice. Also avoid segmented OTP boxes if your platform doesn't reliably support autofill, since manual entry across six separate fields can become more error-prone and tedious than a single masked text field with formatting. Do not use masked phone display if the user has multiple phone numbers on file and needs full context to distinguish them.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: For PayPal's target demographic of busy urban professionals and students, speed and low cognitive friction during account setup are paramount (this audience is impatient with security steps that feel redundant or slow, yet they also expect financial-grade rigor from a money app). This screen resolves that tension by making the mandatory security check (phone verification, a form of 2FA) feel almost invisible through autofill, while still visually communicating "we are protecting your account" via the deliberate, boxed code-entry UI. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of perceived effort: even though the security requirement is non-negotiable, the design makes it feel like a near-zero-effort tap-to-confirm action rather than a manual chore.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented OTP boxes with real-time fill state and active-field highlighting for immediate visual feedback.

  • Native OS autofill integration (QuickType suggestion bar) eliminates manual code entry entirely for most users, dramatically reducing drop-off at this friction-prone step.

  • Bottom sheet over dimmed parent screen keeps onboarding progress and context visible, reducing the feeling of being lost in a separate flow.

  • Masked phone number confirmation balances trust-building transparency with privacy.

  • Low-friction resend link proactively solves for SMS delivery delays, a top cause of verification abandonment.

screens.name: PayPal Pre-Onboarding 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any account-creation or credential-setup flow, especially in fintech, banking, or other trust-sensitive apps where users need explicit confirmation that their input meets security standards. It's ideal for onboarding flows with multiple short steps, where breaking down complex requirements (password strength, format rules) into a live checklist reduces form abandonment and support requests caused by rejected passwords.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, standalone-screen approach for low-stakes apps or contexts where a lightweight modal or inline field within a longer form would suffice, dedicating a full screen and progress step to password creation can feel like overkill for less sensitive use cases. Additionally, avoid combining a visibility toggle with auto-fill/password-manager suggestions poorly, as conflicting UI elements can create confusion; and never omit real-time feedback if strict format rules are imposed, since delayed validation frustrates users far more than no validation at all.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets busy urban professionals and students signing up for PayPal, both of whom value speed but also need reassurance that their financial credentials are secure. The psychological trigger at play is reduction of uncertainty: by showing exactly what's required and confirming compliance instantly with green checkmarks, the design removes the guesswork and anxiety often associated with creating passwords for a money-handling app. The finite progress bar also leverages the goal-gradient effect: showing users they are near the start of a short journey motivates completion rather than abandonment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live checklist validation: Requirements turn green with a checkmark in real time as the user types, replacing a punitive "error on submit" model with encouraging, incremental positive reinforcement.

  • Password visibility toggle: Reduces re-entry errors and abandonment by letting cautious users verify exactly what they've typed before proceeding.

  • Segmented progress indicator: Sets clear expectations that this is step 1 of a short, finite (3-step) process, reducing perceived effort and drop-off.

  • Single-field focus: Isolating just the password field (no confirm-password field) minimizes friction while still enforcing strength via inline rules, striking a balance between security and speed.

screens.name: PayPal Pre-Onboarding 12
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for regulated onboarding flows (fintech, banking, insurance, healthcare) where legal/identity data must be collected but user patience is limited. It's ideal when:

  • The overall signup process has multiple steps and users need reassurance of a defined endpoint.

  • You need to collect legally binding consent but want to avoid an extra confirmation screen or checkbox tap.

  • Address entry can be enhanced with autocomplete to prevent invalid or fraudulent submissions.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid bundling consent into the primary CTA when:

  • Regulatory environments (e.g., GDPR-strict regions) require explicit, separate opt-in checkboxes for each legal agreement rather than implied consent via a button tap.

  • The form collects highly sensitive data (SSN, financial account numbers) where an extra explicit confirmation step reduces liability and reassures the user.

  • Users are unfamiliar with the brand: new/low-trust users may want to review terms before an all-in-one action, and combining steps could feel rushed or opaque.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets busy urban professionals and students signing up for PayPal to send money, get paid, or shop online (a group that is often on mobile, time-constrained, and impatient with lengthy forms). Students in particular may be creating their first-ever financial account and could be intimidated by formal KYC language; the plain-English framing and progress bar are designed to keep them from bailing mid-flow.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Zeigarnik effect (visible progress bar creates a pull to complete an already-started task) and minimizes decision fatigue by showing only essential fields at once, deferring more sensitive info (SSN, bank details) to later steps not shown here. The bundled consent-CTA also exploits default/path-of-least-resistance behavior: most users skim rather than read T&Cs, and PayPal's design accommodates this reality while still technically satisfying legal disclosure requirements.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consolidated Legal Consent: Rather than forcing a separate checkbox interaction, PayPal embeds Terms/Privacy/E-Sign acceptance directly into the primary CTA label, cutting one full interaction step out of the funnel while remaining legally defensible via linked text.

  • Segmented Progress Indicator: A minimal 3-bar tracker at the top manages expectations without a numeric "Step 1 of 3" label, keeping the UI clean while still reducing perceived effort anxiety.

  • Address Autocomplete Affordance: The search icon inside the Address field signals smart-search behavior, preventing manual entry errors that could later cause identity verification failures.

  • "Legal" Qualifier on Name Fields: A tiny but powerful copy choice that preemptively primes users to enter ID-matching information, reducing failed verifications downstream.

screens.name: PayPal Post-Onboarding 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this hub-and-spoke merchandising pattern on the home/dashboard screen of super-apps or fintech products that need to cross-sell multiple services (lending, crypto, cards) without cluttering the primary transactional flow.

  • Effective when you have several partner or brand-name integrations that can borrow trust to promote a newer or higher-risk feature (BNPL, investing).

  • Ideal for apps with a single dominant "hero action" (like Send/Request) that benefits from an elevated, differentiated FAB in the tab bar.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid stacking multiple promotional carousels above the fold if users primarily open the app for account balance/status checks (this can feel like an ad wall and delay time-to-task).

  • Not suitable for banking apps whose brand promise is minimalism/security-first, where cross-sell merchandising could undermine trust or feel intrusive.

  • Elevated central FAB should be avoided if the app doesn't have one single overwhelmingly dominant action, as it creates confusion about hierarchy among tab items.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially engaged but time-pressed users (busy urban professionals and students) who open the app primarily to send money but are also susceptible to passive discovery of adjacent financial products. Presenting Crypto and a Debit Card as swipeable, ad-like cards exploits the mere-exposure effect: repeated casual exposure during routine app visits builds familiarity and eventual conversion intent without requiring an active search.

The Pay Later merchant grid speaks to budget-conscious students and urban shoppers who want deferred payment options at trusted big-box retailers, using brand-authority transfer (borrowing Target/Home Depot's credibility) to reduce perceived risk of a lesser-known credit product. The "Link now, pay faster next time" section targets convenience-seekers who already use Uber/Grubhub, playing on friction-reduction psychology (the promise of a faster future checkout is a strong enough incentive to complete a small setup task now).

• Dark, high-contrast merchandising cards: The Crypto and Debit Card cards use black/navy gradients that visually break from the flat white cards elsewhere, immediately drawing the eye and signaling "premium/featured" content without needing a badge.

  • Repeated "+" affordance: Each carousel card has a circular add button, giving users a single, obvious, low-commitment next step (enroll/add) rather than forcing them to tap the whole card.

  • Elevated central FAB for Send/Request: Breaking tab-bar convention by floating the core action above the row instantly communicates the app's primary purpose and gives it disproportionate visual weight.

  • Recognizable third-party logos: Using Target, Home Depot, Grubhub, and Uber brand marks borrows their trust equity to make PayPal's Pay Later and linked-payment features feel safe and mainstream.

screens.name: PayPal Post-Onboarding 3

The horizontal-carousel-of-cards approach also works well for surfacing optional/advanced features (crypto, investing) to interested users while keeping the default view lightweight for mainstream users.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in apps where a single primary metric or account exists, introducing horizontal carousels for one item is unnecessary complexity. Also avoid stacking commercial offers (Walmart+, cashback banners) directly beneath sensitive financial data in apps serving highly vulnerable populations (e.g., low-income assistance apps) where this could feel exploitative or add decision fatigue at a moment users are anxious about their finances. screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Designed for busy urban professionals and students who check PayPal reflexively to confirm balances before a purchase or to split costs with peers. The low balance shown ($1.00) suggests the app is optimized to still feel useful and non-alarming even at near-zero balances (critical for a student demographic that may frequently run low on funds and needs reassurance rather than shame).

The tax-filing and Walmart+ offers are calibrated for cost-conscious users motivated by tangible savings (cashback, free services) rather than luxury or status signaling, aligning with the "cautious, ledger-minded" brand positioning. The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion-adjacent reciprocity: users feel they are "leaving value on the table" by not tapping into free tax filing or 40% cashback, nudging exploration of monetized surfaces.

• Horizontally scrollable account cards: Elegantly handles multiple financial products (fiat balance, crypto) without cluttering vertical space, letting power users swipe for more while casual users only see the essential balance.

screens.name: PayPal Post-Onboarding 5

screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen is engineered for the "Busy Urban" and "Student" personas who need quick, incentive-driven touchpoints rather than deep financial planning tools. The APY savings card and cash-back offers appeal to budget-conscious students and young professionals looking to make idle money work harder or offset everyday subscription/retail spend. Pay Later store tiles (Target, Home Depot) target cash-flow-sensitive users who want to spread out big-box purchases. The Pools feature with friend avatars specifically targets group-oriented use cases common among students (splitting trip costs, group gifts). screens.keyHighlights:

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

screens.name: Venmo Pre-Onboarding 1

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Targeted at a busy, urban, socially-connected demographic (roommates splitting rent, friends splitting a dinner bill, gig workers getting paid) who are quick to download an app off a recommendation and expect to be transacting within seconds. The illustration's inclusion of pizza, cash, and a QR code directly mirrors real-life triggers ("my friend just sent me a Venmo request for pizza") making the product instantly relatable rather than abstract.

• Illustration-as-value-proposition: Instead of a text-based value prop carousel, a single rich illustration conveys "pay anyone, split a pizza, use a QR code, even touch crypto" in one glance.
