  • On-brand iconography diversity: Cash, cards, crypto, and food icons hint at the breadth of use-cases (P2P, splitting bills, crypto) without needing explanatory copy.

  • Home indicator/gesture bar visible: Confirms this is a native, full-screen, chrome-less experience that maximizes immersion before commitment.

screens.name: Brilliant - Logging in - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for the first screen of an acquisition funnel when the product's core differentiator is a specific interaction model or methodology (e.g., "learn by doing," "swipe to decide," "build as you learn"). It's ideal when:

  • The brand wants to establish intellectual/premium positioning quickly via typography rather than imagery.
  • The product has a distinctive, teachable interaction mechanic that can be visually hinted at in miniature decorative elements.
  • You need a high-converting single-CTA screen with minimal choices to reduce onboarding drop-off.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimalist, type-dominant approach when:

  • Your value proposition depends on showing actual product screenshots or diverse feature breadth (a single slogan may feel vague or fail to differentiate from competitors).
  • Your target audience is less literate in the launch language or skews toward visual/emotional rather than text-driven decision-making, where imagery-led carousels convert better.
  • The brand's differentiation is emotional/social (e.g., community, connection) rather than mechanical/method-based (in which case human photography or social proof would be more persuasive than typographic art).
  • Localization is a concern: giant display typography is harder to adapt gracefully across languages with varying character lengths/scripts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
The target user here is a curious, often time-starved adult (students, professionals, lifelong learners) who has likely tried and bounced off passive video-based learning apps (YouTube explainers, MOOCs) and is skeptical that another app will hold their attention. By leading with "Learn by doing" and visually encoding tactile interaction elements, Brilliant pre-qualifies the user's expectation: this is not a watch-and-forget video course, it is a hands-on gym.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the mere-exposure/priming effect: showing fragments of the actual interaction UI (drag chips, dotted paths) before the user ever touches them reduces the "what do I do?" friction when the first real lesson appears. The oversized, confident typography also triggers a sense of editorial authority and seriousness (echoing print textbooks or TED-style branding), appealing to an audience that self-identifies as intellectually curious and wants to feel smart, not patronized by cartoonish mascots.
screens.keyHighlights:
Typography as the hero illustration. Instead of a stock photo or isolated icon, the headline itself becomes the primary visual asset, scaled to dominate the viewport (a bold choice that signals a content/text-first, no-fluff brand voice from the very first frame).

  • Diegetic foreshadowing of interaction model: the small draggable chip, dotted trajectory curve, and axis/scatter decorations subtly preview the "drag, slide, tag" mechanics used throughout lessons, priming muscle memory before onboarding even begins.
  • Single dominant CTA: one green pill button with no secondary buttons competing for attention, reducing decision fatigue at the most critical conversion point of the funnel.
  • De-emphasized sign-in: plain text link rather than a button, correctly prioritizing new-user acquisition over returning-user login on a first-touch screen.
  • Time-boxed value prop: "15 minutes a day" sets a concrete, low-friction expectation that reduces perceived commitment cost.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for account/profile hubs that double as lightweight onboarding checklists (especially in fintech, e-commerce, or subscription apps where completing setup (payment methods, verification, preferences) directly benefits both user and business). It's ideal when you have 2-4 setup steps that shouldn't feel forced but need gentle, persistent visibility. It also works well when combining identity display with quick-access settings and support links on a single scrollable screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern once a user has fully completed setup (the checklist card should be dismissed or replaced with more relevant content (e).g., transaction history) to prevent clutter and stale progress indicators. It's also unsuitable for high-security or enterprise contexts where profile screens need to prioritize account/security status over playful illustration, or where too many simultaneous CTAs (payment setup + referral + settings) could overwhelm a first-time user already navigating a complex financial task.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday users mid-onboarding or early in their Google Pay lifecycle (people who have signed up but haven't yet linked a bank account or card). The design leans on completion bias (the 1/3 counter), social reciprocity (referral rewards), and trust cues (Google's familiar visual language, clean layout, transparent status labels) to nudge users toward fuller product adoption without feeling like a hard sell. It's also built for users who value quick access to account controls (Settings, Help) without hunting through nested menus, reflecting a broad, non-technical mainstream audience rather than power users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fractional progress counter (1/3): A tiny numeric cue that turns an optional setup task into a completion-driven mini-goal, leveraging the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to finish unfinished tasks).

  • State-differentiated iconography: Active vs. not-yet-added payment methods are distinguished purely through color saturation and a "+" badge, avoiding redundant text labels.

  • Illustrated but functional hero: The playful background art humanizes a money app without sacrificing the information density needed on an account screen.

  • Decorative avatar ring with settings shortcut: Turns a static profile photo into an interactive entry point for account customization, saving a navigational step.

  • In-line referral code with copy icon: Removes friction from the invite flow by displaying the shareable code directly rather than requiring a secondary screen.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you need a low-friction way for two parties to establish a trusted connection (payment, contact-sharing, social linking) in person or over video/screen-share. It's ideal for peer-to-peer fintech apps, contact/business card sharing, event check-ins, or Wi-Fi/device pairing flows where a visual, scannable identity token reduces manual data entry and typo-related errors.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-frequency, repetitive actions where scanning would add unnecessary friction compared to a saved contact list or autocomplete search. It's also unsuitable for use cases requiring strong identity verification (e.g., KYC, large fund transfers) since a QR/code exchange alone lacks the security assurance of authenticated bank-level identifiers. Additionally, avoid on screens where accessibility for visually impaired users is a primary concern, since QR/code scanning relies heavily on camera-based visual interaction without a robust non-visual fallback.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who want to send/receive money from friends, family, or nearby contacts without manually entering phone numbers, UPI IDs, or bank accounts (a common pattern in markets with high QR/contactless payment adoption). The psychological trigger at play is frictionless trust: by visually presenting a name and photo/avatar alongside the code, the system reassures both parties that they are connecting with the correct person, reducing anxiety around mistaken transfers.

The design also leverages social parity with messaging/social apps (e.g., WhatsApp, Venmo, WeChat Pay) where QR-based "add contact" flows are already familiar mental models, making adoption near-instant for users coming from those ecosystems.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose full-screen focus: Removing tab bars, secondary content, and navigation chrome eliminates decision fatigue and mirrors the simplicity of "unremarkable" money movement the app is built around.

  • Identity-as-QR pattern: Turning the user's own profile into a scannable code reframes a technical pairing mechanism into a personal, shareable "digital business card," making peer-to-peer setup feel social rather than transactional.

  • Dual entry point symmetry: The screen simultaneously serves as a code to be scanned (passive) and offers a scanner to scan others (active), collapsing two flows into one lightweight screen via a single bottom CTA.

  • Soft gradient avatar: The blurred blob adds warmth and brand personality to an otherwise stark white/functional screen, softening the trust barrier around sharing financial connection details.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial onboarding flows requiring selection among a small, known set of institutions or providers (banks, insurers, brokers).

  • Any flow where trust and brand recognition materially reduce user hesitation (e.g., connecting a payroll provider, health insurer, or utility company).

  • Steps where reframing a mundane setup task into a benefit-driven narrative can increase completion rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when the list of options is large (20+ items) - a flat scrolling list of logo cards without search or alphabetization becomes unwieldy and should be replaced with a searchable list.

  • Not suitable when institutions don't have strong, recognizable visual branding, as the logo-first approach loses its scanning advantage.

  • Avoid if the underlying linking process (e.g., OAuth/Plaid-style flow) needs more contextual explanation (this minimal screen assumes users already understand what 'linking a bank' entails).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users in a critical trust-conversion moment: linking real financial credentials to a third-party wallet. The design choices (large cards, official bank branding, minimal text) are calibrated to reduce anxiety and signal legitimacy (users are more likely to trust a screen that visually mirrors their own bank's identity than one using generic financial iconography).

The psychological trigger at play is recognition over recall: rather than making users recall their bank's exact name and type it in, the app shows familiar logos they can instantly identify, lowering friction and hesitation at a step where drop-off risk is highest.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Logo-first recognition: Using full bank brand logos instead of plain text rows dramatically speeds up visual scanning and reduces misidentification errors in a high-stakes context.

  • Task reframing copy: The subheading connects an administrative chore (bank linking) to an emotionally resonant benefit (paying friends), increasing motivation to complete the step.

  • Single-column, large-target list: Removes any need for search or filtering at this stage, appropriate given the low number of expected results (likely geo/carrier-filtered to Singapore banks).

  • Secondary path for the unbanked: The 'Open a new account' fallback option prevents drop-off for users who don't have an existing account with any listed provider.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Any flow requiring a redirect to a third-party domain (bank OAuth, payment processor, identity verification) where users need reassurance before leaving the app.

  • Account linking/integration flows (e.g., connecting a calendar, CRM, or financial institution) where trust and one-time setup framing reduce friction.

  • Sensitive consent moments where regulatory disclosures must be shown without overwhelming the primary decision.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for low-stakes or purely internal navigation transitions (the ceremony (dedicated screen, diagram, legal text) would feel like unnecessary friction).

  • Not suitable when the redirect is instantaneous and reversible with no data-sharing implications; a lightweight toast or inline loading state would suffice instead.

  • Should not be used if the destination site cannot be clearly branded/logo-identified, as the trust-transfer visual relies entirely on recognizable brand marks.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users linking an external bank account (OCBC) to Google Pay for the first time (a high-stakes moment where users are naturally wary of financial data sharing). The design leans heavily on the psychological principle of reducing perceived risk through transparency and predictability: showing exactly who is involved (user + bank), what will happen (redirect and return), and how often (once only) removes ambiguity that typically causes drop-off in financial onboarding funnels.

The use of Google's own brand trust (blue avatar, familiar typography, Google Payments ToS) alongside the recognizable OCBC brand mark creates a "co-signed" trust transfer, borrowing credibility from both an established bank and Google's platform reputation simultaneously.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Handshake visualization: The avatar-to-logo bidirectional arrow diagram makes an invisible backend process (OAuth data exchange) instantly legible without technical jargon.

  • One-time reassurance messaging: Explicitly stating "You only need to do this once" reduces perceived effort and preempts abandonment.

  • Inline legal transparency: Terms and Privacy links are surfaced contextually at the exact moment of consent, satisfying both trust and regulatory needs without a separate modal.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: No secondary buttons or distractions. Only "Continue" and the back arrow, minimizing decision paralysis before a sensitive redirect.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Any OAuth-based account linking flow (banking, social login, third-party integrations) where the user must leave the native app environment.

  • Financial services requiring explicit consent and legal acknowledgment before transmitting data to an external processor.

  • Scenarios where you want to reduce drop-off by pre-explaining *why* a redirect is happening and reassuring users it's a one-time event.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for frequent/recurring actions (repeatedly showing a "redirecting" explanation screen for actions users perform often creates friction and annoyance).

  • Not suitable for flows where the destination isn't a well-known, trusted brand; unfamiliar third-party logos can increase suspicion rather than reduce it.

  • Should not be used without a fallback/error state if the external redirect fails to load promptly (avoid indefinite spinners).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users attempting to link an external bank account (OCBC) to Google Pay for the first time, likely for direct debit, bill pay, or bank transfer functionality. This demographic is typically security-conscious, as banking credentials are highly sensitive.

The psychological trigger at play is anxiety mitigation during a third-party handoff. Users are hesitant to leave a trusted app (Google Pay) for an external site (OCBC), fearing phishing or scams. By explicitly labeling the destination, showing official branding, and referencing legal Terms of Service, Google reduces the "leap of faith" required to proceed.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual Linking Metaphor: The dual-avatar-with-dotted-arrow illustration instantly communicates "connection" between the user's identity and the bank's identity, reducing cognitive load compared to a text-only explanation.

  • Preemptive Friction Reduction: Explicitly stating "You only need to do this once" manages expectations and reduces bounce risk during the external redirect.

  • Contextual Branding Trust: Placing the OCBC logo alongside Google Pay's own avatar system reassures the user that Google recognizes and vets this specific institution, transferring brand trust.

  • Loading State as Transition Buffer: The spinner over a dimmed/ghosted version of the confirmation screen prevents a jarring blank-white flash while the external site loads, maintaining perceived continuity.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when embedding third-party credential capture within your own app's flow (e.g., bank linking, OAuth-like partner logins, Plaid-style aggregators). It's ideal when the credentials belong to an external, trusted entity and you need to visually "hand off" trust without leaving your app's shell. Also effective for any short, high-stakes form where minimizing field count and maximizing brand reassurance are priorities.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if you cannot securely tunnel credentials directly to the third party (e.g., without passing through your own servers) - visually implying a secure bank hand-off while insecurely proxying credentials creates legal and trust liabilities. Also avoid for lower-stakes forms where the informal "Hello!" tone could feel out of place, or in flows targeting highly security-conscious enterprise users who may prefer a more formal, sober authentication UI (e.g., a dedicated OAuth redirect page) over an embedded native-feeling form.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who already bank with OCBC and are attempting to link that account to Google Pay for payments or transfers. The primary psychological trigger being managed here is security anxiety: asking a user to type their real banking PIN into a third-party app (Google) is inherently uncomfortable, so the design leans heavily on brand transference of trust (showing the bank's own logo and terminology) to make the moment feel like "banking with OCBC," not "giving my PIN to Google."

The friendly "Hello!" greeting and clean, uncluttered layout also reduce perceived risk by making the screen feel calm and unhurried rather than alarming, which is essential for compliance-heavy fintech flows where users are prone to abandoning if anything feels off-brand or suspicious.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Bank-branded trust anchor: Placing the OCBC logo front-and-center immediately before credential fields reassures users they're authenticating with their actual bank, not a spoofed Google form.

  • Contextual field labels: Using the bank's own terminology (Access Code, PIN) rather than generic labels reduces cognitive friction for returning banking customers.

  • Show/hide PIN toggle: Balances security-by-default masking with user control to verify correctness, reducing failed submission rates.

  • Persistent floating CTA: The circular arrow button stays fixed and thumb-accessible, disabled until inputs are valid, providing a lightweight inline validation signal.

  • Minimalist single-screen form: Only two fields are requested, keeping the highest-friction step of the entire linking flow as short as possible to minimize drop-off.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when an app needs to broker authentication with a trusted third-party institution (banks, insurers, payroll providers) via credential-based linking (as opposed to OAuth redirects). It's effective when:

  • The partner brand carries strong independent trust that can be borrowed.

  • The form is short and the ask is singular (login only, no extraneous fields).

  • Users need reassurance they are in a sanctioned, secure sub-flow (via modal presentation, drag handles, and partner branding).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid direct in-app credential capture for third-party services when a more secure, industry-standard alternative like OAuth/OpenBanking redirect or SDK-based linking is available, collecting raw bank PINs inside a non-bank app increases liability and can violate financial regulations or bank partnership terms in many regions. Also avoid this pattern if the partner brand is unfamiliar or low-trust, as it won't provide the reassurance effect and may instead raise suspicion of phishing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday banking customers: likely in a market where OCBC operates (e.g., Singapore/Southeast Asia) - who are being asked to link an existing bank account to Google Pay for the first time. This is a moment of heightened scrutiny: users are trained to be wary of entering banking PINs outside official banking apps.

The psychological trigger here is authority and brand transference: by prominently displaying the OCBC logo and using the bank's own language, Google Pay borrows the trust users already have in their bank to smooth over the discomfort of typing sensitive credentials into a third-party app. The friendly "Hello!" further lowers guardedness, framing the interaction as a casual login rather than a high-risk security event.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-brand trust transfer: Using the bank's own logo and terminology inside a Google-controlled flow reduces perceived risk and phishing anxiety.

  • Minimal, single-task form: Only two fields are visible, keeping the interaction focused and fast, lowering abandonment risk during a sensitive step.

  • Reveal/Hide PIN toggle: Gives users the confidence to verify their entry before submission, reducing failed-login frustration.

  • Modal/sheet presentation with drag handle: Visually communicates this is a temporary, dismissible sub-flow layered over the main app, preserving user orientation.

  • Single, unmistakable CTA: The floating arrow button removes ambiguity about the next step and prevents premature progression.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for terminal confirmation screens following any high-stakes, sensitive, or multi-step action (bank linking, identity verification, payment setup, security key registration, subscription purchase). It's ideal whenever the user's primary need in that moment is emotional reassurance ("it worked") rather than more information or choices.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this ultra-minimal approach when the user needs to take an immediate next action that isn't obvious (e.g., setting a default payment method) - the lack of a visible CTA can leave users unsure how to proceed if the flow doesn't auto-advance. Also avoid it for low-stakes confirmations (e.g., "profile picture updated"), where a lightweight toast/snackbar would suffice and a full-screen takeover would feel disproportionate and slow down the user's flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves any user who has just completed a sensitive, multi-step financial task (linking a bank account) - a moment psychologically loaded with uncertainty ("did that actually work?", "is my data safe?"). The design targets that anxiety directly with the fastest possible visual confirmation loop: a universally understood green/blue check-in-a-circle glyph processed by the brain in milliseconds, well before the text is even read.

It also targets Google Pay's broader audience of everyday consumers (not power users) who need reassurance rendered in plain English rather than banking terminology, reinforcing trust in a fintech-adjacent context where Google is not a traditional bank.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Extreme visual minimalism: Removing all navigation and competing UI elements makes the success state unmissable and anxiety-reducing at a high-stakes moment (financial data submission).

  • Reused iconography: The blue circular checkmark matches Google's system-wide success pattern, instantly legible without new learning.

  • Benefit-forward microcopy: Pairs the confirmation with a value reminder ("earn rewards"), turning a utilitarian task into a small motivational payoff.

  • No unnecessary friction: No additional confirmation, review, or upsell modal is forced before the user can proceed, respecting the user's time after a multi-step form.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for account/profile hubs in fintech or utility apps where you need to simultaneously surface identity, onboarding completion, and settings navigation. Ideal when you want to nudge users toward completing optional setup steps (payment methods, KYC, preferences) without a full-screen interruptive flow. The completion-counter card is especially effective for multi-item setup tasks (2-4 items) where visual icon differentiation (done vs. pending) can replace lengthy text.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are many more than 3-4 setup steps, as the horizontal icon row will become cramped or require scrolling, undermining the at-a-glance value. Decorative illustrations should be avoided in enterprise, B2B, or high-security banking contexts where users expect a more austere, purely-functional tone. Also avoid combining referral/marketing CTAs (Invite friends) directly inside a security-sensitive profile screen if regulatory or trust concerns require stricter separation of account management from growth features.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday users managing their financial identity within a broader payments app (likely users in markets with PayNow (e).g., Singapore) alongside global card/bank rails, indicating a localized fintech audience. The psychological levers at play include the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete progress "2/3" creates a mental itch to finish), social reciprocity/incentive (referral rewards), and trust-building through personalization (name, avatar initials, masked contact info). The soft illustrative backdrop specifically targets users who may feel anxious about handling money digitally, using approachable visual design to lower perceived risk.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progress-visualized completion card: The (2/3) counter combined with a dashed/outlined "locked" icon for the missing payment method is a highly effective, low-copy way to nudge task completion.

  • Decorative brand illustration behind functional UI: The playful island/dotted-halo artwork softens what is otherwise a sensitive financial identity screen, reducing anxiety around money management.

  • One-tap referral code with copy icon: Removes all friction from the invite flow (no separate screen or form needed).

  • Bottom sheet layering with drag handle: Reinforces that account settings are a lightweight, dismissible overlay rather than a heavy destination, keeping navigation feel light.

  • Icon-first row for payment methods: Uses brand logos (PayNow) and universal iconography (bank, card) so users recognize methods instantly without reading labels first.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 10
screens.whereToUse: Apply this pattern for any financial or identity-document data entry flow (payment cards, ID scanning, loyalty cards) where the primary input is long, error-prone, and OCR-scannable. It's especially effective when the manual keyboard is already visible, since the scan CTA can be docked adjacent to it without an extra navigation step. Also reuse the icon-rail + underline field layout for any short, vertically stacked utility form where speed and clarity trump visual richness.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for forms with fields that aren't scannable (e.g., free-text notes, complex multi-part addresses) since the scan shortcut becomes irrelevant clutter. Also avoid a bare-bones utilitarian layout like this for high-emotion purchases (e.g., luxury checkout) where richer visual merchandising and reassurance (progress indicators, order summaries) are needed to justify a larger spend. Additionally, dense legal text blocks should be avoided on smaller screens without a scroll cue, as they can bury the primary CTA below the fold.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets mainstream consumers adding their first card to Google Pay for tap-to-pay, in-app, or peer-to-peer transactions. Because entering financial data is inherently anxiety-inducing, the design leans heavily on trust signals: clean Google-blue branding, explicit legal links, and recognizable card network logos to reduce hesitation.

The psychological driver here is reduction of cognitive and physical effort: the Scan Card CTA exploits the fact that most users would rather point a camera than manually type 16+ digits, tapping into the "path of least resistance" principle that increases form completion rates and decreases abandonment at this critical monetization gate.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Scan Card shortcut docked above keyboard: Placed exactly where the user's attention already is, dramatically lowering the effort of entering a long card number via OCR camera capture.

  • Inline card network icons: Passive validation cue showing supported card types directly inside the input field instead of a separate help text or error.

  • Smart-filled name field: Pulling the user's Google Account name into the form removes a redundant typing step while still allowing an easy edit via pencil icon.

  • Icon-led field rail: Left-aligned iconography (#, person, pin) gives instant visual parsing of field purpose, useful for quick re-scanning if the user backs out and returns.

  • Modal dismiss via X: Signals this is a self-contained, cancelable task, reducing anxiety about being "trapped" in a payment flow.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when collecting sensitive personal information (phone numbers, financial data) during onboarding, especially in fintech, banking, or premium subscription services where trust and brand perception are equally important as functional data collection. Ideal for scenarios requiring regulatory consent (GDPR, RBI, financial data sharing) where user hesitation is high.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, editorial-style typography and slow, single-field-per-screen approach for utilitarian apps, B2B tools, or when speed is the primary user need (e.g., a quick re-login or simple account creation for a low-stakes app). Overly minimal single-input screens can feel tedious in a long form if there isn't enough narrative/brand payoff to justify the reduced information density per screen.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially-aware, credit-card-holding millennials and young professionals in India (CRED's core demographic) who are highly conscious of their credit scores. The design leverages Status/Exclusivity signaling (via "Membership Application") to appeal to users' desire for premium, aspirational branding.

The explicit reassurance about credit score impact directly targets a known psychological barrier: fear of "hard pulls" damaging credit history. By preemptively neutralizing this fear via copy and RBI regulatory backing, CRED increases the likelihood of consent and conversion at this critical funnel step.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Editorial Typography: Using a serif, lowercase headline transforms a standard data-collection screen into a premium, human-centric moment.

  • Anxiety Mitigation Copy: Explicitly stating "this does not impact your credit score" right at the point of consent removes a major psychological blocker to proceeding.

  • Framing as "Application": Calling it a "Membership Application" rather than "Sign Up" elevates the exclusivity and status appeal of the product.

  • Minimalist Progress Indicator: The thin grey bar at the bottom subtly communicates progress without adding cognitive load via numbered steps.

screens.name: Craft - Editing a separator pattern (patterns)   - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Document, note, or project cover customization in productivity/writing apps.
  • Any flow where users need to pick from a visually-driven set of options that benefit from live previews (themes, wallpapers, avatar backgrounds, card designs).
  • Design tools wanting to unify multiple asset types (pattern vs. photo) into a single, low-friction picker rather than separate screens.
  • Situations where retaining background context (half-sheet) is more valuable than maximizing picker real estate.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this minimal, label-only approach for first-time or non-expert users who may need more guidance on what "Pattern" cover selection actually affects.
  • Not ideal when the number of options is very large (e.g., 50+ patterns or colors) - a half-sheet grid would become cramped or require excessive scrolling; a full-screen gallery would serve better.
  • Avoid combining too many unrelated customization axes (pattern, color, opacity, blend mode) in one small sheet, as it can overwhelm; split into tabs or steps if complexity grows.
  • Not suitable for contexts where color/pattern choice carries business logic consequences (e.g., status tagging) since playful, exploratory UI implies low-stakes, purely cosmetic choices.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets design-conscious knowledge workers, writers, and PKM (personal knowledge management) enthusiasts who care about the aesthetic identity of their documents (e).g., treating a product brief or concept doc as a mini-presentation cover rather than a plain text file. It appeals to users coming from tools like Notion, Figma, or Pitch, who expect visual customization as a baseline capability.

Psychologically, this leverages the IKEA effect and sense of ownership: letting users personalize their document's cover with pattern + color increases emotional investment and perceived value of the content itself. The instant, no-commitment preview (tap to try) also reduces decision anxiety (users can freely experiment without a "confirm" step, encouraging playful exploration rather than cautious, hesitant customization).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Scrim + blur on background content: Keeps the editing context visually present but de-emphasized, reinforcing that this is a lightweight, transient customization step, not a navigation event.
  • Live color-matched pattern previews: Each pattern swatch dynamically renders in the currently selected accent color, letting users evaluate shape and color together instead of in isolation.
  • Segmented Pattern/Image toggle: Elegantly unifies two very different content types (generative patterns vs. uploaded photos) under one single "cover" mental model with a simple icon switch.
  • Persistent color picker + custom color wheel: Provides curated presets for fast decisions alongside an escape hatch (the rainbow wheel icon) for power users who want precise brand-matched colors.
  • Half-sheet modal sizing: Preserves spatial context of the parent document, reducing disorientation common in full-screen settings flows.

screens.name: Spotify - Filtering & Sorting - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any content library or catalog screen with lists long enough to benefit from quick reordering (podcasts, playlists, downloads, order history).
  • When users have a small number (2-5) of mutually exclusive filter/sort options that don't require complex multi-select logic.
  • Contexts where speed of selection matters more than advanced faceted search (use a bottom sheet instead of a full-screen filter page).
  • Mobile-first flows where preserving background context aids orientation and reduces perceived navigation depth.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when users need to combine multiple filters simultaneously (e.g., multi-select tags) - a single-select checkmark list implies mutual exclusivity and will confuse users who expect to combine criteria.
  • Not suitable for complex faceted browsing with many categories (price range, brand, size, etc.) - that requires a dedicated filter screen with apply/clear actions.
  • Avoid if users need to preview results before committing, since there's no explicit "Apply" step (instant commits can feel jarring for heavier/slower-loading filter operations).
  • Don't use on desktop/large-screen layouts where inline dropdowns or sidebar filters are more appropriate than a mobile bottom sheet metaphor.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets power listeners and binge-podcast consumers who subscribe to shows with large back catalogs (hundreds of episodes) and need to quickly narrow down to unplayed, downloaded, or chronologically relevant content. The "Downloaded" filter specifically serves users managing offline listening for commutes or flights, while "Not finished" serves habitual multitaskers who frequently pause episodes mid-way.

Psychologically, the pattern reduces choice overload: a show like this with 500K+ play episodes can have a long list, and surfacing a quick filter/sort mechanism helps users feel in control rather than overwhelmed, directly supporting the app's core promise of making "pressing play easier than deciding what to play."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving overlay: The dimmed background keeps the episode list visible, so users retain orientation while adjusting filters.
  • No Apply/Confirm button: Selections appear to commit immediately via optimistic UI, reducing an unnecessary extra tap.
  • Grouped mental model: Separating "Filter" (what to show) from "Sort By" (what order) maps directly to how users think about organizing content, avoiding a single confusing flat list.
  • Single checkmark affordance: Using a checkmark instead of radio buttons/switches keeps the visual weight light and consistent with Spotify's minimalist dark UI.
  • Drag handle & swipe-to-dismiss: Removes need for explicit close/cancel buttons, maximizing content space.

screens.name: Craft - Editing a separator pattern (washi gallery) - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Rich-text or document editors offering stylistic customization (dividers, headers, themes, covers).

  • Any settings panel where live, in-context preview materially improves decision confidence (fonts, colors, layouts).

  • Tools targeting creative/prosumer audiences who value aesthetic differentiation over purely functional UI.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for high-frequency, low-stakes micro-decisions where a bottom sheet adds unnecessary friction (e.g., simple bold/italic toggles should stay inline).

  • Not appropriate for enterprise/B2B tools where playful decorative assets (washi tape) could undermine a serious, formal brand tone.

  • Risky on small screens if the sheet's height plus background blur obscures too much editing context, hurting the very preview benefit it aims to provide.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets writers, note-takers, and knowledge workers who care about the visual craftsmanship of their documents—bloggers, designers, PMs drafting polished specs, or anyone treating Craft docs as presentation-ready artifacts rather than disposable scratch notes. The washi-tape motif specifically appeals to users with a journaling/scrapbooking sensibility, tapping into nostalgia and tactile aesthetics (similar to physical bullet journals) to differentiate from sterile competitors like plain Markdown editors. The live-preview mechanic exploits the psychological principle of immediate feedback, reducing the cognitive load of imagining "what will this look like" and increasing confidence to customize further.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed/blurred background with live preview: The underlying document stays partially visible and updates in real time as styles are chosen, letting users judge the result in context instead of guessing from a thumbnail.

  • Decorative, playful asset (washi tape) in a productivity tool: Offering a physical-world, scrapbook-style divider option elevates the "designed document" feel over generic horizontal-rule separators found in most note apps.

  • Icon-first segmented control: Three divider "families" (rule, tape, hand-drawn) are switched via compact icon buttons, keeping the sheet dense yet scannable without text clutter.

  • Undo/reset affordance next to the panel title: Placing a quick-revert icon directly in the header reduces the risk of commitment, encouraging experimentation with styles.

results.query: Compare corporate reimbursement submission in Brex versus personal expense tracking in Cleo

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any single-record detail view that mixes static facts with required follow-up actions, such as expense reports, invoice line items, order details, or claims processing. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to audit or verify a transaction/record after the fact.
  • Some fields are immutable (amount, merchant) while others need completion (tax, receipts, categorization).
  • Status at-a-glance matters more than exhaustive detail on first glance.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, sectioned detail pattern for high-frequency, low-complexity records where users just need a quick glance (e.g., a simple notification or balance check) - the multiple stacked sections and inline inputs would be overkill and slow. It's also unsuitable for consumer-facing, casual finance apps where terms like "assigned limit" and "tax rate" would be confusing jargon rather than clear context; in those cases, simplify to plain-language summaries instead of compliance-grade fields.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves employees and cardholders who need to reconcile a specific purchase, and secondarily finance admins auditing spend compliance. The psychological driver is reducing anxiety around accountability: employees spending company money want fast confirmation ("Approved") that they didn't do anything wrong, while incomplete items (tax info, unverified receipt) are flagged clearly so nothing slips through and creates friction later with finance/audit teams.

The inline "Switch limit" CTA targets users who may have accidentally charged the wrong budget/limit, giving them agency to self-correct rather than waiting on an admin, which reduces back-and-forth and support tickets.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded status pills (green Approved / orange Not verified) give instant visual triage of transaction health without reading text.
  • Inline actionable control ("Switch limit") embedded directly in a read-only detail view lets users correct a misapplied budget without navigating away.
  • Contextual compliance prompts ("This expense requires additional information") appear only when relevant, keeping the form lean for transactions that don't need tax handling.
  • Sectioned grey divider headers break a data-dense screen into clear, labeled zones (Amount/Merchant, Assigned limit, Tax rate, Receipts), reducing cognitive load.
  • Persistent back navigation and bottom Tab Bar keep the user oriented within the larger Wallet/Tasks ecosystem even while deep in a detail view.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any compliance-driven detail screen where a record (expense, application, claim, order) must pass through verification states before being finalized. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to supply supporting documents (receipts, IDs, proof of purchase).
  • There's a multi-stage review/approval workflow that benefits from a visible timeline.
  • Policy-specific messaging can reduce confusion (e.g., insurance claims, expense management, loan applications, KYC flows).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, warning-heavy layout for low-stakes or purely informational detail screens where no action is required (excessive banners and status indicators can create false urgency and alarm fatigue). It's also unsuitable for consumer-facing apps with casual, high-volume transactions (e.g., a coffee loyalty app), where this level of compliance friction would feel disproportionate and degrade the experience. Additionally, if policies vary widely or are too complex to summarize in one line, a static banner may oversimplify and mislead users about next steps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves employees who have made a small purchase on a corporate card and must now provide documentation to satisfy finance/compliance policies, as well as finance admins auditing the same record. The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion/compliance anxiety: by clearly flagging "Not verified" and explaining the consequence (manual review), the design nudges the employee to resolve the issue quickly to avoid being personally flagged or having the expense rejected.

The transparent status timeline also leverages the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to complete unfinished tasks) by visually showing an incomplete process, motivating the user to finish uploading valid receipts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive policy explanation: Instead of just flagging an error, the banner tells the user exactly *why* the receipt is problematic and references their specific company policy, reducing confusion and support escalations.
  • Inline character counter on Memo: The 50/800 counter gives real-time feedback, preventing surprise truncation and encouraging sufficiently detailed justifications for auditors.
  • Visual status timeline: Using a vertical checklist/stepper for "Status" turns an opaque back-office process (compliance review) into a transparent, trustworthy narrative the end-user can follow.
  • Low-friction receipt attachment: The "+" tile next to existing thumbnails keeps adding more proof as easy as a single tap, encouraging compliance completion in the moment.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a product needs to present a single record with both a status history and granular metadata, especially in regulated or scrutinized domains (expense management, compliance review, order/shipment tracking, support ticket detail, or insurance claims). It's ideal when trust and auditability matter more than persuasion, and when multiple stakeholders (submitter + reviewer) need a shared source of truth.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, document-style layout for high-frequency, low-stakes interactions where speed matters more than completeness (e.g., quick balance checks or casual browsing). It would also be inappropriate for consumer-facing, emotionally-driven experiences where a utilitarian tone could feel cold or bureaucratic. If a transaction has no review history, this layout should degrade gracefully with an empty state rather than showing an empty or confusing timeline.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves employees whose expenses have been flagged and finance admins/auditors who need to verify compliance status. For the employee, seeing a transparent timeline of "flagged → reviewed" reduces the stress and ambiguity of having a purchase questioned, invoking the psychological principle of procedural justice: people are far more accepting of a process outcome when they can see the steps taken to reach it, even before knowing the final verdict.

For finance teams, the structured transaction details satisfy the need for completeness and defensibility: every field needed for bookkeeping, tax categorization, or dispute resolution is present in one place, reducing back-and-forth queries. The comment/@-mention system taps into workplace familiarity with tools like Slack, lowering the learning curve and encouraging asynchronous resolution instead of requiring a meeting or email thread.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual audit-trail timeline: Checkmark-based vertical stepper turns an abstract compliance process into a transparent, reassuring narrative the employee can follow.
  • Dense but scannable key-value table: Consistent label/value alignment lets users quickly verify transaction facts without cognitive overload.
  • Contextual collaboration hint: The @-mention instructions inside the Comments section teaches functionality inline, right when it's relevant.
  • Balanced action hierarchy: "Add comment" (collaborative, low-stakes) and "File a dispute" (escalation, higher-stakes) are styled identically to avoid alarming the user, yet are clearly separated as distinct next steps.
  • Persistent context header: Merchant name and amount remain pinned at the top regardless of scroll, anchoring the user as they review granular details below.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this layered bottom-sheet + chip-based error pattern when:

  • An automated verification/validation process (OCR, fraud check, data matching) fails and the user needs specific, itemized reasons rather than a blanket error.
  • The failure is recoverable or has a fallback path (manual review, memo, re-upload) and shouldn't fully block the user's workflow.
  • You want to preserve form context and avoid navigating the user away from their in-progress task.
  • Financial, compliance, or document-verification flows where transparency about *why* something failed builds user trust.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The error is critical and must hard-block the user (e.g., legal/compliance violation) - a bottom sheet may under-communicate severity; a full-screen interstitial or disabled submit button may be more appropriate.
  • There are more than 3-4 failure reasons, as the chip row could wrap awkwardly or overwhelm the limited bottom-sheet real estate (consider a scrollable list or accordion instead).
  • The underlying cause is highly technical; surfacing raw field names like "Merchant" without guidance on remediation could confuse less technical users if no next-step CTA is provided within the sheet itself.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets employees submitting expenses on the go, often from imperfect conditions (bad lighting, crumpled receipts, foreign currency receipts, or no receipt at all as implied by the memo). It also serves finance/admin teams indirectly by ensuring exceptions are flagged and routed to manual review rather than silently approved, protecting compliance integrity.

Psychologically, the design reduces anxiety around making a financial mistake by externalizing the error to a system limitation rather than user fault, while the granular breakdown (Date/Amount/Merchant) gives the user actionable next steps (e.g., re-upload or add memo justification) instead of leaving them stuck. The manual-review fallback also builds trust that legitimate business expenses won't be rejected outright due to OCR failure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Bottom Sheet over Dimmed Background: Preserves the user's place in the underlying form while delivering a focused, modal-style alert, avoiding a jarring full-screen takeover for a non-blocking issue.
  • Field-Level Error Chips: Breaking the verification failure into discrete, labeled chips (Date, Amount, Merchant) gives granular diagnostic feedback instead of a vague generic error message.
  • Non-Blocking Error Pattern: The flow explicitly allows the user to proceed via manual review and memo justification rather than hard-locking submission, respecting real-world edge cases (e.g., lost receipts).
  • Dual-Surface Status Communication: The "Not verified" status label on the Receipts section header and the warning banner work together with the modal to reinforce the same message across multiple visual layers.

screens.name: Brex Reimbursement approved 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, banking, or expense management apps where a primary account/card visual needs to coexist with a transactional list. It's ideal when users need both an at-a-glance summary (balance, limit) and deep historical detail (expense list) on a single screen without extra navigation. The bottom-sheet-over-hero-card technique works well for multi-account switching contexts (e.g., switching between personal/corporate limits).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this layout for simple consumer banking apps where users have a single account and don't need to compare limits/policies (the added "Switch limit" and "View limit policy" complexity would be unnecessary friction). Also avoid dense status-icon rows for first-time or non-technical users, as the meaning of small iconography (sync, receipt, reimbursement status) may not be immediately legible without onboarding or tooltips.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets corporate employees and contractors managing company spend via Brex (likely non-finance staff who need quick visibility into "how much budget do I have left" and "did my expense get approved)." The psychological driver here is reducing anxiety around spending limits; by surfacing the available balance prominently and using green checkmarks for processed items, the app reassures users that their expenses are being tracked and resolved properly, reducing the cognitive load of manual expense tracking.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Draggable Bottom Sheet over Hero Card: Combines the emotional satisfaction of viewing a physical/virtual card with the functional density of a scrollable list, maximizing screen real estate.

  • Status Iconography: Tiny compliance icons (receipt attached, reimbursement pending, synced) next to each transaction amount allow users to scan for "what needs my attention" without opening individual records.

  • Masked/Blurred PII: Sensitive card numbers and merchant details are blurred by default, demonstrating a security-first design pattern appropriate for financial apps viewed in public spaces.

  • Eye Icon for Reveal: A dedicated "reveal" icon lets users intentionally expose sensitive card data, adding a friction point that protects against shoulder-surfing.

screens.name: Brex Reimbursement approved 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any financial transaction detail or reimbursement tracking screen where users need status transparency: expense management apps, insurance claim trackers, refund/return flows in e-commerce, or payroll disbursement detail views. It's ideal whenever a process has a waiting period and users are anxious about timing and destination of funds.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, sectioned layout for simple, instantaneous transactions (e.g., a completed in-person purchase) where tax/limit/attendee metadata would be irrelevant clutter. Also avoid surfacing full or even partially masked bank details in low-security contexts or public-facing screens, and avoid info banners for routine, already-completed transactions where reassurance copy would feel redundant or add visual noise.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees or finance administrators using a corporate expense/travel card platform (e.g., Brex, Ramp, Ramp-style fintech, or a business travel tool). The psychological trigger at play is anxiety reduction through transparency: employees fronting money for business travel (train tickets) want certainty about repayment timing and destination. The explicit ETA date and bank reference reduce the "where's my money" support burden and build trust in the platform.

The auto-verification badge leverages automation-as-reassurance: it signals to the user that no manual paperwork chase is required, appealing to busy professionals who want expense admin to be invisible.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive status banner: Instead of making users guess or dig through a support chat, the app surfaces the exact reimbursement ETA and destination bank account directly inline, preempting the most common support query in expense apps.

  • Auto-verified receipts: Automating OCR/receipt matching and surfacing a confident green checkmark state removes friction and manual review anxiety for the employee.

  • Masked bank details for security: Partially obscuring the account number ("•••• [masked]") balances transparency with security best practices.

  • Dual currency display: Showing both the GBP transaction amount and the USD limit/available balance clearly acknowledges multi-currency card usage without confusing the primary amount.

  • Actionable "Switch limit" CTA: Embedding an editable action (reassigning the spend to a different budget/limit) directly within a detail view avoids forcing the user into a separate edit flow.

screens.name: Brex Reimbursement approved 3
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any multi-stage approval or fulfillment workflow where a user is waiting on a third party: expense reimbursements, insurance claims, loan/credit applications, order fulfillment/shipping, support ticket resolution, or compliance review processes. It's especially valuable when stages are sequential and time-based, and when transparency about "who" and "when" meaningfully reduces user anxiety or support burden.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy timeline treatment for simple, instantaneous transactions (e.g., a completed peer-to-peer payment) where showing multiple steps would feel like unnecessary friction or make a fast process seem artificially slow. It's also overkill for internal admin tools where the reviewer doesn't need the empathetic step-by-step narrative (a compact status badge would suffice). Finally, this pattern can backfire if estimated dates are unreliable, since broken promises on "payment estimated" dates erode trust faster than no estimate at all.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees submitting business expense reimbursements within a company that uses a corporate card/wallet platform (finance ops, traveling employees, remote workers). The psychological driver at play is uncertainty reduction: nothing frustrates an employee more than spending their own money and not knowing when/if they'll be repaid. By visualizing every step of the approval chain and forecasting a payment date, the design leverages the Zeigarnik effect (people remember unfinished tasks) in reverse: it closes the loop of anxiety by showing clear progress and an end date, which increases trust in the employer's finance system and reduces repeated status-check support requests.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Vertical approval timeline: Converts an abstract multi-stage backend workflow (submit → approve → pay) into a tangible, scannable visual metaphor familiar from logistics/delivery tracking apps.

  • Estimated payment date forecasting: Proactively answers the user's most pressing question ("when will I get my money back?") before they have to ask, reducing support tickets.

  • Named approver with role tag: Builds trust and accountability by surfacing exactly who approved the claim and when.

  • Inline @-mention commenting: Turns a simple comment box into a lightweight task-assignment tool, blurring the line between communication and workflow action without requiring a separate feature.

  • Clear section segmentation with shaded headers: Makes a data-dense screen feel organized and easy to scan at a glance.

screens.name: Brex Reimbursement approved 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an automated or AI-driven decision affects something the user cares about (money, compliance, data matching) and you want to build trust without requiring the user to audit the decision manually. It's ideal for:

  • Fintech/expense tools confirming receipt-to-transaction matching

  • Fraud detection or verification flows that auto-approve/auto-flag items

  • Any "automatic" label that could otherwise feel like a black box
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy explanatory modal for low-stakes or purely cosmetic automated actions, where it would add unnecessary friction. Also avoid if the matching criteria are too complex to summarize in 2-3 simple chips, forcing oversimplification could mislead users about how robust the verification actually is. For highly technical/power users (e.g., accountants doing bulk reconciliation), a persistent inline indicator may be preferable to a modal interruption.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets finance teams, employees submitting expenses, and corporate card users within a B2B spend-management platform like Brex. The audience is often time-pressed professionals who need to trust that automated systems are handling compliance correctly without requiring manual review of every receipt.

The psychological trigger at play is trust-through-transparency: financial automation can feel risky or opaque, so explicitly naming the matched criteria (date, amount, merchant) reduces the user's need to double-check the work themselves, decreasing cognitive load and increasing confidence in the product's accounting accuracy (critical for retention in expense management SaaS where errors carry real monetary and compliance consequences).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explainable automation: Instead of just showing a "Verified" badge, the app proactively surfaces the reasoning (date, amount, merchant match) when the user wants more detail, reducing anxiety around automated financial decisions.

  • Non-disruptive disclosure: The bottom sheet preserves context by dimming rather than fully replacing the underlying expense screen, so users don't lose their place.

  • Iconography reinforces concept: The receipt-with-lightning-bolt icon visually encodes "fast, automatic processing" before the user even reads the text.

  • Granular trust chips: Breaking verification into three discrete, labeled checkmarks (rather than one generic "Verified" label) gives users confidence the system checked specific, relevant criteria rather than performing a vague blanket approval.

  • Contextual micro-interaction: The modal is triggered directly from the "Auto-verified" link/tag, following the principle of just-in-time information delivery rather than front-loading explanation nobody asked for.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when designing camera-capture flows embedded within a larger workflow (not a standalone camera app), especially when the captured artifact needs to be associated with an existing record (e.g., receipts, documents, ID verification). It's especially valuable when there's a possible mismatch between user intent and system state (proactively surfacing that mismatch before the user invests effort (e).g., taking a photo) saves frustration. The dual-path bottom CTA ("scan" vs. "manual entry/alternative") pattern is ideal whenever the primary capture method may not always be the right fit for every user's situation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid overlaying warning banners on a camera viewfinder when the warning is purely informational and not actionable (this adds visual clutter and can obscure the subject being photographed). If the warning condition is rare or edge-case only, consider handling it via a toast or pre-emptive screen before entering the camera, rather than cluttering the capture UI itself. Additionally, this pattern should not be used when receipt/document capture is the primary, context-free action of the app (e.g., a dedicated scanner app), since the "no expenses to attach" framing assumes a specific linked-record workflow that may not apply universally.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets business travelers, employees, and finance/ops teams who need to digitize paper receipts for expense reporting and reimbursement, likely within a corporate expense management or spend platform (e.g., similar to Ramp, Brex, or Expensify). The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion and effort-justification prevention: by warning the user before they waste time scanning a receipt that has nowhere to go, the app respects the user's time and avoids a frustrating "scan completed, but now what?" dead-end experience. The inline "Add to existing" and "create reimbursement" options also reduce decision paralysis by making the next best action obvious and low-friction, appealing to time-pressed professional users who value speed and certainty over exploration.
screens.keyHighlights:
Contextual Just-in-Time Guidance: Rather than letting the user scan a receipt into a dead end, the app proactively surfaces a system-state warning banner the moment it detects there's nothing to attach the receipt to, with an inline fix via "Add to existing."

Branching Escape Hatch: The "Or create reimbursement" button acknowledges that not all expense-logging starts with a physical receipt, offering a graceful fallback path without forcing the user to exit the flow and start over elsewhere.

High-Contrast Overlay Controls: White solid-fill circular buttons (close, retake) against the dark camera viewfinder ensure maximum legibility and touch-target confidence regardless of the background scene being photographed.

Minimal Chrome, Maximum Viewfinder: By stripping away navigation bars and status elements, the design maximizes the available frame for accurately capturing the receipt image, which directly impacts OCR/data-extraction accuracy downstream.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Expense management, corporate card, and reimbursement workflows where receipt capture is the core input.

  • Any financial form where cross-currency clarity is needed for distributed or international teams.

  • Tasks that are frequently interrupted mid-completion, warranting a visible draft-save option.

  • Scenarios where showing a real-time balance/limit constraint upfront can prevent invalid submissions downstream.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, single-focus modal pattern for simple, single-field forms (it adds unnecessary ceremony).

  • Don't surface a 'Save draft' button if the backend doesn't reliably support autosave/draft retrieval, as it creates false expectations.

  • Avoid displaying currency conversions using potentially stale/cached rates without a timestamp or disclaimer, as this could erode trust if the actual rate differs at processing time.

  • Not ideal for high-volume bulk expense submission flows, where a tabular/multi-row entry pattern would be more efficient than one modal per expense.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees at a company using a corporate card/spend management platform who need to request reimbursement for out-of-pocket business expenses. The psychological drivers at play include loss aversion (draft-saving prevents the frustration of re-entering data) and reduction of financial ambiguity (currency conversion and visible spend limits prevent surprises or distrust). The design also reduces the friction/dread typically associated with expense reporting (a notoriously tedious task) by minimizing the number of visible fields and emphasizing a single primary action (photo capture) before submission.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-currency display: Automatically converting the available balance into the user's local currency removes a mental math step and builds trust in global teams.

  • Draft-saving affordance: Positioning 'Save draft' as equal-sized but visually secondary to 'Submit' respects that reimbursement requests are often filled out in multiple sittings (e.g., waiting on a receipt).

  • Large receipt/photo upload area: Dedicating the majority of above-the-fold space to the attachment reinforces that proof-of-purchase is the most critical and often most friction-inducing step.

  • Contextual spend limit surfaced inline: Showing the 'Assigned spend limit' directly in the form (rather than requiring the user to navigate elsewhere) prevents the user from submitting requests that are likely to be rejected.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial, expense, or transactional forms where some data can be reliably pre-filled from an external source (receipts, calendar, transaction history, OCR). It's ideal for reducing friction in repetitive administrative tasks like expense reports, invoices, or tax forms. The draft-save + submit pattern is well suited to any multi-field form that users might need to pause and resume, especially on mobile where interruptions are common.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid heavy automation indicators (lightning bolts) if the underlying prefill confidence is low, mislabeling guesses as 'smart' erodes trust if users frequently need to correct them. This pattern is also unsuitable for simple, single-field transactional screens where a lightweight single-field flow would be faster, or for consumer apps where financial jargon like 'Merchant category' might feel overly corporate and reduce approachability.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees of a company using a corporate expense management platform (e.g., finance teams, remote/traveling staff) who need to file reimbursement claims for out-of-pocket business expenses, such as travel bookings. The psychological drivers at play include reduction of perceived effortcontrol and trust (users verify rather than blindly accept automation, which is essential when real money and accounting accuracy are involved).
screens.keyHighlights:
• AI/Automation Indicators: Green lightning bolt icons clearly flag which fields were auto-populated by the system, building trust through transparency while still allowing manual override via clear ('x') icons.

  • Inline Currency Conversion: Automatically displays the converted balance in a secondary currency, removing cognitive load for cross-border expense reporting.

  • Progressive Disclosure Toggle: The 'different currency' switch keeps the form uncluttered by default and only expands complexity when relevant.

  • Dual CTA Footer: Separates low-commitment ('Save draft') from high-commitment ('Submit') actions, reducing abandonment risk for incomplete expense reports.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when presenting a long, flat list of mutually exclusive options (10+) that benefit from both search and visual browsing (such as category pickers, country/language selectors, or merchant/industry classification). It's ideal for financial, e-commerce, or form-heavy apps where users need to quickly locate one specific item among many standardized options.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for short lists (under ~7 items), where a simple inline radio group or segmented control would be faster and avoid the overhead of opening a modal and keyboard. It's also unsuitable when multi-select is required (radio buttons imply single choice), or when categories have hierarchical/nested relationships better served by drill-down navigation or breadcrumbs.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets users managing business or personal finances who need to categorize transactions (likely small business owners, bookkeepers, or users of a corporate card/expense management product, given the formal accounting-style category names (e).g., "Bank & financial fees", "Airline expenses"). The psychological driver here is reducing cognitive load during a repetitive administrative task: categorization is tedious, so the interface minimizes friction via search-first interaction, iconography for fast recognition, and a flat single-select list instead of nested menus.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-focused search with live keyboard: Eliminates the extra tap to initiate search, assuming users know what they're looking for.

  • Icon + label + radio button row pattern: Creates fast visual scanning while unambiguously communicating single-select behavior.

  • Dedicated close affordance: The circular X button gives users a clear, low-risk way to dismiss the sheet without needing to select anything.

  • Hybrid search-and-browse model: Supports both fast typists and users who prefer visually scanning a categorized list, maximizing usability across user styles.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 10
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a user must select one option from a large, flat or loosely-grouped taxonomy (50+ items) where browsing would be inefficient (e).g., selecting a country, currency, industry/profession, merchant category, job title, or icon from a large library. It's ideal for:

  • Financial/accounting categorization tasks (expenses, budgets, invoices)

  • Settings screens requiring selection from long enumerated lists

  • Any single-select field where typeahead search meaningfully reduces time-to-selection
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The option set is small (under ~7-10 items): a simple scrollable list or segmented control would be faster and avoid forcing the keyboard open unnecessarily.

  • Users are likely to browse/explore rather than search with a specific term in mind (e.g., discovering new product categories) - in this case, a categorized/grouped browsing UI with sections would serve better than a flat search.

  • Multi-select is required: the radio button affordance here explicitly signals single-choice and would need to be swapped for checkboxes, changing the interaction model.

  • On low-connectivity or low-end devices where live filtering on every keystroke could introduce lag; a "search on submit" model might be more appropriate there.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of fintech/banking apps (likely small business owners, freelancers, or employees submitting expense reports) who need to classify a transaction quickly and accurately. The audience is assumed to be moderately tech-savvy but time-constrained, often performing this task repeatedly across many transactions (e.g., end-of-month bookkeeping), so speed and low-friction search matter more than discovery or delight.

Psychologically, the design leverages the Paradox of Choice mitigation: rather than presenting an exhaustive list of 50+ merchant categories upfront (which would induce decision fatigue), it defers to search, letting the user's own intent narrow the options. The radio button and single result set also invoke recognition over recall: users don't need to remember exact category names, just type a few relevant letters and recognize the right match visually.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Auto-focused search with instant keyboard: Eliminates the extra tap typically needed to engage the search field, respecting the user's time when they land on a search-heavy screen.

  • Live typeahead filtering: Narrows hundreds of possible merchant categories down to 3 relevant results instantly as "trav" is typed, turning an otherwise overwhelming list into a fast, guided lookup.

  • Consistent iconography per result: Each category gets a unique, relevant icon (WiFi symbol, briefcase, airplane), aiding rapid visual scanning and recognition over pure text reading.

  • Explicit single-select affordance: Radio buttons make the selection model unambiguous before any interaction occurs, reducing the cognitive load of guessing "can I pick more than one?"

  • Clear, always-visible dismiss control: The circular "X" button gives users confidence they can back out of the flow at any point without fear of losing progress or getting stuck.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 11
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any expense-reporting, reimbursement, or financial data-entry form where some fields can be reliably pre-filled (via OCR, receipt scanning, defaults, or prior context) and others are conditionally relevant (like foreign currency or tax). It's ideal for:

  • Expense management and corporate card apps

  • Invoice or receipt submission flows

  • Any multi-field financial form where reducing perceived effort drives completion rates

  • Modal-based "quick task" flows that need a clear escape hatch (close icon) and a save-for-later option
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Auto-filled values carry high risk if incorrect (e.g., legal or compliance-critical dates/amounts) without strong, unmissable warnings (users may trust the lightning-bolt icon blindly and skip verification).

  • The form is used by first-time users unfamiliar with the icon's meaning (the green bolt icon has no explicit label/tooltip, which could confuse new users about why it's there).

  • Draft-saving has no real backend persistence; offering "Save draft" without reliable storage undermines user trust.

  • The modal is used for very long, complex forms: scrolling within a modal (as hinted by the custom scrollbar) can be an awkward UX compared to a full-page flow for lengthy inputs.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees of a company using an internal expense management or corporate card platform (e.g., Ramp, Brex, Expensify users) who need to request reimbursement for a personal out-of-pocket business purchase. The persona is typically a busy knowledge worker who wants the reimbursement process to be as fast and frictionless as possible (they are not finance experts and don't want to engage with tax/currency complexity unless necessary).

Psychologically, the form leverages the effort reduction heuristic: by auto-filling data and visually flagging it (lightning bolt), the user feels the system is doing the heavy lifting, which increases task completion likelihood.   • Modular section architecture: Clear grey-divided blocks (Assigned limit, Receipts, Attendees, Memo) let users jump straight to the field they need without parsing a dense form.
  • Inline receipt management: Thumbnail + "+" add-tile pattern makes attaching additional proof frictionless and visually confirms what's already been captured.
  • Flexible attendee splitting: Dropdown for the primary user plus removable chips for external attendees supports common business-meal expense scenarios (clients, guests) without a separate screen.
  • Persistent limit visibility with quick switch: Showing "$27.97 USD available" alongside a one-tap "Switch limit" button lets users self-correct budget misallocation without leaving the record.

results.query: Brilliant interactive quizzes versus Spotify onboarding preference selection

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Transitional screens between onboarding segments (e.g., before a personalization quiz or setup wizard).

  • Apps with a mascot or brand character that benefit from humanizing the interface.

  • Flows where you want to justify upcoming data collection by previewing the benefit (a tailored experience).

  • Consumer apps targeting casual or younger audiences where playful, conversational tone increases engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise/B2B or professional tools where a playful mascot may undermine credibility or trust.

  • Flows requiring urgency or efficiency (e.g., checkout, account recovery) where a conversational pause adds unnecessary friction.

  • Contexts where users are already familiar with the app and don't need re-motivation to continue an in-progress flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets new users in the critical first-session window, likely for an educational, language-learning, or skill-building app (the visual style strongly resembles Duolingo's onboarding). The target demographic includes casual learners who may be skeptical about committing time to an app; this screen uses the mascot and friendly tone to lower psychological resistance and build rapport before asking for personal input.

Psychologically, it leverages the commitment and consistency principle: by framing the next steps as a collaborative path-building exercise, users feel more invested before they've even started answering questions, increasing completion rates of the subsequent quiz.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Mascot-led speech bubble: Converts a transactional onboarding step into a friendly conversation, boosting emotional engagement and reducing drop-off.

  • Minimal progress bar: Signals the start of a short journey without overwhelming the user with step counts.
