  • Single CTA, zero distractions: Removes all competing elements so the only possible action is to move forward.

  • Collaborative copy framing: "Let's build... just for you" sets an expectation of personalization before any questions are even asked, increasing perceived value of answering them.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during the initial app setup phase for consumer apps (health, fitness, education, finance) where the product offers multiple value propositions catering to different audiences. It is ideal when you need to algorithmically personalize the subsequent content feed or push notification strategy based on user intent.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for utility apps or B2B enterprise tools where the user's goal is already singular and obvious (e.g., a calculator app). Additionally, avoid overly whimsical mascot copy in enterprise or finance apps where a more serious, professional tone is expected by the brand.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets a broad demographic acquisition funnel, segmenting users immediately into distinct personas: working professionals, aging adults concerned with cognitive health, students, parents, and educators.

Psychologically, this leverages the Ikea Effect and Commitment & Consistency

biases; by having the user explicitly state their goal early, they become more invested in the app's outcome and are more likely to act in a way that is consistent with that stated goal later on (e.g., engaging with push notifications tied to that goal).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Mascot-led Conversation: Using a character and speech bubble turns a mundane onboarding question into an engaging, friendly interaction.

  • Segment-Specific Branching: By asking for the "top goal" upfront, the app can immediately tailor content (e.g., differentiating between "child" vs "student" vs "professional" goals) for the rest of the onboarding and content curation.

  • Visual Iconography: Pairing every text option with a relevant emoji significantly speeds up decision-making time by leveraging visual recognition over reading.

  • Linear Progress Visualization: The top progress bar manages user expectations regarding the length of the onboarding funnel.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during early onboarding for apps that serve multiple distinct user segments (education, fitness, finance, productivity) where personalizing content, tone, or feature recommendations based on motivation significantly improves relevance. Ideal when the app has enough branching logic downstream to actually act on the answer (otherwise the question feels performative). The mascot/feedback pattern works well for consumer apps with a friendly, approachable brand voice.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, illustrated single-question-per-screen approach for B2B/enterprise tools or utility apps where users expect speed over personality (it can feel slow and infantilizing). Also avoid if the collected answer isn't actually used to personalize the experience, as users will feel the step was a waste of time. Overusing playful mascot commentary on every selection can become repetitive or saccharine over a long multi-step quiz.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets a broad acquisition funnel spanning students, professionals, parents, and teachers (likely an edtech or brain-training app (e).g., flashcard/study tool). By asking "why" upfront, the app can tailor content recommendations, marketing messaging, and onboarding paths to each segment, increasing relevance and activation rates. Psychologically, it leverages the IKEA effect and commitment/consistency bias: by actively choosing a goal, users become more invested in completing onboarding and more likely to engage with content aligned to their stated motivation later on. The validating mascot copy exploits the human desire for approval/social validation, reinforcing that the user made a "smart" decision and reducing early drop-off.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reactive mascot feedback: The character comments on the user's selection in real time, turning a static form into a dialogue and increasing perceived app intelligence/personality.

  • Icon-led option cards: Pairing each goal with a unique, colorful emoji dramatically improves scannability and adds personality without extra copy.

  • Clear single-select visual state: The indigo highlight and border on the chosen card provide unambiguous confirmation, reducing user uncertainty.

  • Catch-all escape hatch: "Something else" ensures no user feels miscategorized, preserving data quality and user goodwill.

  • Persistent progress bar: Sets expectations for quiz length, reducing abandonment anxiety.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern during onboarding flows that require multiple steps of data collection (surveys, personalization quizzes, account setup) to break up friction with moments of positive reinforcement. It's especially effective:

  • After the user has invested some effort (e.g., mid-quiz) to combat drop-off via the sunk-cost/consistency principle.

  • When the product serves a broad, mainstream audience that benefits from "you belong here" messaging.

  • When illustrative or abstract previews of content can be shown without complex UI to build excitement.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The audience is highly technical or skeptical of vague social proof claims (e.g., enterprise B2B buyers who want hard data, logos, or case studies rather than generic "millions of users" statements).

  • Onboarding is already short; inserting a filler/reassurance screen in a 2-3 step flow may feel like unnecessary padding and increase time-to-value.

  • The product has low user volume: overstating or vaguely implying scale without evidence can damage trust if discovered to be exaggerated.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users: likely students, lifelong learners, or professionals brushing up on STEM skills (who are in the process of signing up for Brilliant, an interactive learning platform). At this stage in onboarding, users may have just answered profiling questions (goals, skill level, interests) and could be experiencing decision fatigue or self-doubt about committing to a learning app.

The psychological trigger here is social proof combined with belonging: by asserting that "millions" of similar users already engage with the product, the screen normalizes the decision to continue and alleviates imposter syndrome or skepticism. The illustrated content preview also builds anticipatory curiosity, a dopamine-driven nudge to keep progressing through the funnel.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotional checkpoint mid-onboarding: Instead of only collecting data, the flow inserts a reassurance screen to maintain motivation and reduce abandonment.

  • Social proof via scale, not specificity: "Millions of students" is vague but psychologically powerful, triggering bandwagon effect and reducing perceived risk of trying the product.

  • Illustrative card fan for content preview: The overlapping cards visually tease the diversity of the product's content (video, interactive diagrams, notebooks) without any cognitive load or reading required.

  • Uninterrupted single CTA: No alternate paths or skip options keep the user funneled forward, reducing decision fatigue.

  • Persistent progress bar: Reinforces that this is a short, finite journey, setting expectations and reducing perceived commitment.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during onboarding when a product needs to branch content difficulty, curriculum, or recommendations based on user self-reported skill/experience. It's ideal for edtech, fitness, language-learning, or any app with tiered content complexity. Especially effective when paired with a mascot/brand character to keep early funnel interactions friendly and reduce perceived effort.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, illustrative card-based quiz format for simple binary choices or when speed is paramount (e.g., checkout flows) since it adds scroll/visual overhead. Also avoid self-reported skill questions if the app can infer skill level via a short diagnostic test instead, as self-assessment is often inaccurate (users may overestimate or underestimate). Not suitable for enterprise/B2B tools where tone should remain more neutral/professional rather than playful.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new users signing up for a coding-learning app, spanning complete beginners to people with some programming background. The psychological driver is personalization and relevance: by asking about skill level upfront, the app signals it will tailor content difficulty, which increases perceived value and commitment (sunk-cost/investment loop). The friendly mascot and plain-language descriptions specifically target non-technical or anxious beginners who may feel intimidated by coding, lowering the barrier to continue the signup flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Code-snippet visual cues: Using actual syntax-highlighted code increases perceived credibility and helps users calibrate their skill level visually, not just via text.

  • Conversational mascot + speech bubble: Humanizes a data-collection step, making the quiz feel like a dialogue instead of a form.

  • First-person self-assessment copy: Reduces judgment/anxiety by letting users describe their own experience rather than being externally labeled.

  • Disabled CTA until selection: Clear, simple validation pattern that prevents incomplete submissions without needing error messages.

  • Prominent progress bar: Reduces onboarding abandonment by visualizing nearness to completion.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during onboarding for any skill-based or knowledge-based product (language learning, fitness, finance, coding) where personalizing content difficulty or pathway is critical to retention. It's ideal when you have 3-5 clearly differentiable tiers and want to use visual artifacts (like code, UI mockups, or icons) to aid in self-assessment rather than relying purely on text. Also effective when paired with a guide character to maintain engagement across multi-step onboarding flows.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the product doesn't meaningfully adapt content based on the selected tier, asking for self-assessment without delivering a personalized payoff feels like wasted effort and erodes trust. Also avoid overly granular tiers (6+) in a grid format, as this increases decision paralysis; a vertical list with more explanation may serve better in that case. For expert/professional tools where users expect to configure settings directly rather than being guided, this conversational quiz tone may feel patronizing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective learners of programming, ranging from complete novices to people with some prior exposure, who are onboarding into an educational coding app (similar to Mimo, SoloLearn, or Grasshopper). The design leverages the psychological principle of self-determination and autonomy: letting users choose their own starting point builds a sense of ownership over their learning path and reduces early drop-off caused by content being pitched at the wrong difficulty level.

The friendly mascot and casual tone specifically target younger or anxious beginners who may feel intimidated by coding, using social and emotional warmth to lower the psychological barrier to entry. The code snippets subtly prime advanced users with early credibility, signaling the app contains "real" programming content and isn't overly dumbed-down.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Code snippet as visual difficulty indicator: Each card shows actual code of increasing complexity, letting users intuitively gauge their fit before even reading the label.

  • First-person, self-assessed descriptions: Removes judgment and external labeling, encouraging honest self-placement for better downstream personalization.

  • Conversational mascot feedback: The reactive speech bubble turns a static quiz into a dialogue, reducing the clinical feel of a form.

  • 2x2 grid layout: Enables full-option visibility without scrolling, supporting fast comparative decision-making.

  • Persistent progress bar: Manages expectations and reduces abandonment by showing tangible onboarding progress.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during pre-signup or pre-paywall onboarding sequences when you need to build perceived value and justify why a user should invest time or money before they've experienced the core product. It's particularly effective for subscription or edtech apps where the user must be convinced of efficacy before commitment. Ideal for sequences of 3-6 slides, each isolating a single differentiated benefit with supporting visual and minimal text.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if the value proposition cannot be credibly supported by data (unsubstantiated statistics can damage trust if users later discover no citation or study backing the claim). Also avoid overusing multiple consecutive claim-only screens without interactivity, as users can disengage or skip through marketing-heavy onboarding; mixing in interactive/sample content screens keeps engagement higher. Not suitable for returning users or contexts where onboarding should be skippable/fast (e.g., utility apps).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets prospective learners (likely students, professionals, or lifelong-learning enthusiasts) who are evaluating whether Brilliant is worth their time compared to free alternatives like YouTube lecture videos. The psychological trigger at play is authority/evidence-based persuasion: citing a statistic ("6x more effective") taps into the user's desire for efficient, high-ROI learning, especially relevant to time-starved adults.

It also leverages the anchoring effect, setting up a comparison point (video lectures) that frames Brilliant's interactive format as superior before the user has even tried the product, priming them to view subsequent onboarding steps (quizzes, topic selection, paywall) favorably.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-claim focus: Only one value proposition is presented per screen, maximizing message retention and avoiding overload.

  • Quantified credibility: The "6x" statistic anchors an abstract benefit (effective learning) to a concrete, memorable number.

  • Friendly mascot reinforcement: The illustrated character physically "exercising" visually reinforces the metaphor of mental strength-building, adding warmth and personality to an otherwise data-driven claim.

  • Persistent progress bar: Signals the user is partway through a finite sequence, reducing drop-off anxiety by showing an end is in sight.

  • Unmissable CTA: The oversized, high-contrast "Continue" button at the thumb-friendly bottom zone drives frictionless progression.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 10
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during onboarding flows for habit-forming apps (fitness, language learning, meditation, productivity) when you want to collect scheduling or behavioral preferences that will later drive personalized push notifications or content recommendations. It's ideal when the goal is to make data collection feel conversational and low-friction rather than bureaucratic.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, illustrative, multi-step quiz format for returning users, power users, or B2B/enterprise tools where speed and efficiency are prioritized over emotional engagement. It's also inappropriate when exact time precision is functionally required (e.g., calendar scheduling apps) since vague lifestyle buckets like "morning routine" lack the specificity needed for precise reminder timing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new users in the critical first-run onboarding funnel of a habit-based learning app (e.g., language learning). The psychological trigger at play is the IKEA effect / sunk-cost investment: by having users explicitly state when they'll practice, the app creates an implicit personal commitment device, increasing the likelihood of adherence once reminders are later scheduled around this stated preference. It also leverages the foot-in-the-door technique, where small, easy commitments (selecting a time of day) prime users for bigger future commitments (daily streaks, subscriptions).
screens.keyHighlights:
Mascot speech-bubble framing: Turning the onboarding question into dialogue from a brand character builds emotional rapport and brand recall from the very first session.

Lifestyle-anchored options instead of time pickers: Asking "when does this fit your routine" via contextual rituals (commute, lunch break, bedtime) is far more frictionless and accurate than asking users to input exact times.

Disabled CTA until selection: Clearly communicates required input and prevents null-state submissions, feeding the personalization engine clean data for later reminder scheduling.

Generous card-based touch targets with icon + bold label + subtext hierarchy: Improves scannability and thumb reachability in a single-handed mobile context.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern during onboarding or personalization quizzes where you need to collect a preference that will drive future content curation, scheduling, or notification timing. It's ideal for apps that want to feel adaptive and conversational (wellness, education, meditation, audio/podcast, habit-tracking apps). Best used when there are a limited number (3-5) of mutually exclusive options that can be framed around real-life scenarios.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for utilitarian or enterprise/B2B tools where a playful mascot and whimsical copy would undermine credibility or professionalism. Also avoid if there are more than 5-6 options, as large card-based lists become inefficient compared to a compact list or dropdown. If the preference doesn't meaningfully affect downstream personalization, this heavy-weight UI would be overkill compared to a simpler toggle or settings field.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users in a lifestyle/habit-based app (likely an audio content, meditation, learning, or story app given the mention of "source code by starlight," hinting at sleep-story or audiobook content). The target demographic is likely consumers who value personalization and a "designed-for-me" experience (common in wellness, audio-learning, or bedtime-story apps targeting busy professionals or parents).

Psychologically, this leverages the IKEA effect and sunk-cost momentum: by investing time answering personalized questions, users feel increased ownership over the eventual recommendation output. The reactive mascot commentary also triggers parasocial bonding, making the brand feel attentive and witty rather than transactional, which increases emotional engagement and reduces onboarding drop-off.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual mascot callback: The speech bubble references the user's prior answer, creating a sense of continuity and personalization that most onboarding flows lack.

  • Scenario-based options instead of literal time ranges: Labeling choices by lifestyle moment (commute, lunch break, bedtime) rather than clock time lowers cognitive load and increases relatability.

  • Dual-weight typography within each card: Bold lead-in words paired with lighter descriptive text create fast visual scanning and hierarchy without needing separate labels.

  • Clear, high-contrast selected state: The chosen card uses both color and border-weight change, ensuring accessibility for color-blind users.

  • Icon-first visual language: Emoji-style icons (sun, pizza, moon, TV) give instant visual recognition and inject personality before the user even reads the text.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 12
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when notification permission is core to the product's value loop (reminders, streaks, habit-building, social messaging). Always pre-frame the native OS prompt with a custom contextual screen explaining the specific benefit, and position it after the user has had some context/investment in the product (not on the very first screen), so the "why" feels earned and relevant.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern if notifications aren't integral to the core value proposition (forced priming in that case feels manipulative and may increase early churn or App Store review friction). Avoid overly aggressive directional cues on the native dialog (like arrows) in regulated contexts or where App Store guidelines discourage manipulating system UI; keep it purely informational and let the choice remain genuinely neutral. Also avoid asking before any value has been demonstrated, as this increases decline rates and burns the permission request permanently on iOS.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets new users mid-onboarding for a habit-building/educational app (Brilliant), where long-term retention depends heavily on daily re-engagement. The psychological trigger is reciprocity and framing: by first explaining the benefit in human terms ("I'll remind you... so it becomes a habit"), the app reframes an intrusive system permission as a favor done on the user's behalf. The arrow leverages affordance signaling and visual momentum to subconsciously increase the "Allow" tap-through rate, which is critical since notification opt-in rates directly correlate with long-term retention and habit formation in streak-based learning apps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual priming before the native prompt: explains the benefit ("build a long-term habit") before the OS even asks, increasing accept rates versus a cold ask.

  • Directional arrow overlay: a bold green arrow visually points to the "Allow" button, guiding the eye and thumb to the desired outcome without technically manipulating the native control.

  • Progress bar continuity: keeps the permission ask feactored into the onboarding journey rather than feeling like an interruption.

  • Mascot-driven conversational tone: uses a friendly character and speech bubble to make a system-level request feel personal and low-stakes.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Educational or data-literacy apps teaching chart/graph interpretation skills.

  • Microlearning platforms where each screen should isolate a single testable concept.

  • Any onboarding or skills-assessment flow where tactile interaction (tap-to-select) increases engagement over passive reading.

  • Gamified learning products wanting to pair progress indicators with low-friction, single-question screens.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Data-dense analytics or BI dashboards where users need to compare many metrics simultaneously (this one-chart-per-screen pattern would be too slow and inefficient).

  • Professional/enterprise contexts where users expect exact numeric values and tooltips rather than estimation-based interaction.

  • Time-pressured workflows where forcing a single interaction per screen would feel like unnecessary friction rather than pedagogical pacing.

  • Accessibility-critical contexts without ensuring the chart has robust alternative text/data-table fallback for screen-reader users, since the core interaction relies heavily on visual bar comparison.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed adult learners and STEM-curious users who prefer active, bite-sized practice over passive video lectures (a demographic drawn to apps like Brilliant, Duolingo, or Khan Academy for skill-building in short daily sessions). The psychological trigger at play is active recall combined with low-stakes estimation: by asking users to physically interact with a chart rather than multiple-choice text, the app engages procedural memory and spatial reasoning, which research shows improves retention over passive reading.

The progress bar and streak icon tap into completion bias and habit-loop reinforcement, nudging users to finish the lesson and return daily, while the disabled "Check" button leverages the Zeigarnik effect: an unfinished task (an unselected answer) creates a subtle tension that motivates interaction completion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chart-as-interaction: The bar chart isn't a static illustration (it's the actual answer mechanism, embodying Brilliant's "do before explain" learning philosophy).

  • Disabled CTA state: The greyed-out "Check" button clearly communicates that an action (selecting a bar) is required before progression is possible, preventing premature or empty submissions.

  • Segmented progress + streak icon: Combines lesson-level progress tracking with gamified engagement (lightning bolt) in a single compact header, without cluttering the primary task area.

  • Generous whitespace: Isolates the chart as the sole object of attention, reducing extraneous cognitive load typical in dense dashboard-style data visualizations.

  • Estimation-friendly phrasing ("about 125"): Reduces precision pressure, making the exercise feel approachable rather than a math test.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when teaching data literacy, chart reading, statistics, or any skill where visual pattern recognition is the core competency being tested. It's ideal for microlearning platforms, interactive courses, and any "learn-by-doing" product where you want to assess comprehension immediately after (or instead of) an explanation.

Also effective wherever you want to reduce passive scrolling and increase active engagement per screen, pairing a single visual artifact with a single pointed question keeps attention squarely on the task.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for complex multi-variable data requiring extensive legends or context, as the minimal screen real estate and lack of explanatory text could leave users confused without prior setup. It's also unsuitable for first-time concept introduction (this works best as a reinforcement/check step after a concept has already been taught, not as the initial teaching moment).

Additionally, this approach may frustrate users who need review/backward navigation, since the pattern typically pairs with a weak-backward-review lesson spine; users who want to revisit the explanation before answering may feel stuck.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-directed, intrinsically motivated learners (students, professionals upskilling, lifelong learners) who prefer active problem-solving over lecture-style content consumption. The design leverages the generation effect psychological principle (people retain information better when they must generate or interact with an answer rather than passively receive it).

The approximate, visually-estimated question format also reduces math anxiety, making data literacy approachable for non-technical audiences while still being rigorous enough for STEM-focused learners. The minimalist, clutter-free screen caters to a global, diverse audience by relying on universal visual language (bar charts, color, numbers) rather than dense text, aiding localization and comprehension across markets.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chart-as-interaction: The bar chart isn't a passive illustration; it's the actual interactive quiz surface, collapsing explanation and assessment into a single tactile moment.

  • Minimal chrome, maximum focus: No app title, no distracting header text. Just an exit control, progress bar, and streak icon, keeping full visual weight on the data.

  • Low-stakes "Start over": Offering an easy reset below the chart removes fear of "messing up" while exploring data, encouraging experimentation.

  • Segmented progress bar: Communicates lesson position at a glance without numeric distraction, reducing cognitive load.

  • Single deferred CTA: The "Check" button is the only commitment point, letting users freely interact with the chart before submitting an answer.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Educational or training apps teaching data literacy, chart reading, or quantitative reasoning.

  • Any microlearning product where "learning by doing" beats passive video/reading content.

  • Gamified habit-building apps that benefit from frequent small wins (XP, streaks, checkmarks) to drive daily return visits.

  • Onboarding or skill-assessment flows where you want to diagnose user ability through interaction rather than a static quiz form.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for content requiring nuanced, multi-part answers where a single-tap interaction oversimplifies the assessment.

  • Not suitable for professional/enterprise tools where users expect dense, efficient data review rather than playful gamified pacing.

  • Risky for accessibility-sensitive contexts if color (yellow/green) is the sole signal (must pair with icons/text as done here, but motor-impaired users may still struggle with precise bar-tapping targets).

  • Avoid in contexts where speed matters more than reflection (the celebratory interstitial (confetti, banner) could feel like unnecessary friction for power users wanting to move quickly).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed, intrinsically curious learners (students, professionals, lifelong learners) who respond well to short, game-like bursts of learning rather than long-form lecture content. The design leans heavily on behavioral psychology: variable positive reinforcement (XP, confetti), low-friction interaction (single tap), and the sunk-cost/momentum effect created by the visible progress bar.

The "move before you learn" philosophy caters to kinesthetic and active-recall learning styles, which research shows improves retention over passive consumption, making this especially effective for a STEM-literacy audience that may otherwise find data visualization concepts dry or intimidating.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Interact-first assessment: The learner must tap directly on the chart itself to answer, turning a data-reading concept into a kinesthetic, memorable action rather than a multiple-choice abstraction.

  • Dual-channel feedback: Correctness is communicated through color (bar turns gold), iconography (green checkmark), and a bottom banner (redundant signals that cater to different attention styles and ensure the feedback is unmissable).

  • Optional "Why?" affordance: Decouples confirmation from explanation, letting fast learners move on instantly while curious learners can dig deeper (a elegant solution to pacing heterogeneity).

  • Minimal progress chrome: The segmented progress bar communicates momentum without overwhelming detail, sustaining motivation via the Zeigarnik effect (desire to complete an unfinished sequence).

  • Lightning bolt streak/energy icon: Ties the micro-lesson into a larger gamified ecosystem (likely streaks or energy/lives), reinforcing habitual daily engagement.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for micro-learning, skill-assessment, or data-literacy products where a single visual artifact (chart, diagram, equation) is both the teaching aid and the quiz input. It's ideal for:

  • Educational apps teaching chart/graph reading, statistics, or quantitative reasoning.

  • Any linear lesson flow where you want to force "doing" (selecting/estimating) over passive reading.

  • Products needing lightweight, low-anxiety progress indication within a longer course or module.

  • Scenarios where real-world, relatable framing (sales, scores, measurements) can de-jargonize abstract concepts.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The task requires precise numerical input rather than estimation (a chart-tap interaction is unsuitable for exact-value problems; a text/numeric field would be clearer).

  • Users need to review or edit past answers frequently (the implied weak backward navigation (only an X to exit, no back button) frustrates users who want to revisit previous questions).

  • The content is inherently list-based or textual (e.g., vocabulary quizzes) where a chart-based interactive artifact adds unnecessary complexity.

  • Accessibility is a major concern: relying on visual bar-height comparison and color-coded bars can disadvantage low-vision or colorblind users without additional data labels or alt-text support.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-directed adult learners and lifelong-learning enthusiasts (Brilliant's core demographic) who want bite-sized, active STEM practice rather than lecture-style video content. The coffee-shop sales scenario is deliberately mainstream and non-technical, designed to appeal worldwide without requiring domain expertise, lowering the barrier for users intimidated by "math" framing.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Generation Effect (people retain information better when they produce an answer rather than recognize one) and a Zeigarnik-like completion drive via the progress dots, nudging users to finish the step they've started. The disabled Check button also exploits a mild commitment and consistency trigger (users must mentally commit to an answer before the system validates it, deepening engagement with the material).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chart-as-interactive-content: The bar chart doubles as both the content and the input mechanism, embodying the brand's "doing over watching" philosophy rather than presenting a passive image with a separate answer list.

  • Segmented progress with color-coded completion: Green filled dots versus gray upcoming dots give lightweight, ambient progress feedback that doesn't distract from the task.

  • Disabled-state CTA: The grayed-out "Check" button enforces a deliberate action-then-validate loop, preventing accidental skips and reinforcing the "commit to an answer" moment.

  • Minimalist chrome: No tab bar, no header title, no extraneous iconography beyond essential navigation (X) and a streak/lightning indicator, maximizing focus on the single learning task.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when teaching any skill where visual/quantitative literacy is the goal (chart reading, statistics, finance, data science, or scientific reasoning apps). It's ideal for microlearning moments where a single concept (e.g., "reading combined values from a bar chart") needs to be reinforced through direct manipulation rather than passive video or text. Also effective in any product trying to replace lecture-style explainer screens with interactive, self-checking exercises to boost completion and retention rates.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex, multi-variable datasets where estimation from a static chart would be genuinely difficult or produce high error rates, causing frustration rather than productive struggle. It's also unsuitable for high-stakes assessments (certification exams, compliance tests) where "about" answers and forgiving approximation are inappropriate. Additionally, this minimal-chrome, no-hint approach can alienate complete beginners who need more scaffolding (axis labeling tutorials, worked examples) before being asked to perform an unassisted estimation task.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed adult learners and lifelong-learning enthusiasts (the core Brilliant demographic) who are motivated by mastery and curiosity rather than grades or external accountability. The design leans on the generation effect (people remember material better when they actively produce an answer rather than passively read it) and low-stakes testing effect (quizzing with immediate, judgment-free feedback strengthens retention far more than exposition).

The exit (X) and non-threatening "Check" button cater to intrinsically motivated users who may be studying in short bursts (commute, break) and need the psychological safety to stop at any point without feeling they've "failed" a course.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Question-as-interaction: The bar chart is simultaneously the explanatory content and the answer-input mechanism, collapsing two learning steps into one tactile motion.

  • Deliberate ambiguity ("about 225"): Using an approximate target number nudges users toward estimation and pattern recognition over brittle exact math, a subtle pedagogical trick.

  • Generous whitespace as pacing device: The large gap between question and chart forces sequential processing (read → scroll/look → analyze) rather than everything being parsed simultaneously.

  • Non-numeric progress indicator: Dots/pill segments communicate journey position without the pressure of a percentage countdown.

  • Single, unmissable CTA: The dark pill "Check" button is the only button on screen, eliminating decision paralysis about what to do next.

screens.name: Brilliant - Logging out - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
• Any app settings/preferences screen where users need a scannable index of account, notification, and support options.
  • Apps with a strong tactile or sensory interaction model that need explicit user control over sound/haptic feedback.
  • Products wanting to softly surface a premium upsell without disrupting the neutral, utilitarian tone of a settings area.
  • Educational or habit-building apps where Settings is a secondary modal space separate from the primary content flow (hence the "X" dismiss rather than back navigation).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this flat, icon-led list pattern when settings require deep configuration or complex interdependent options (a grouped list with no search becomes unwieldy past ~20-25 items).
  • Not suitable when monetization needs stronger visual emphasis; burying "Premium" in a plain row underperforms if the product relies heavily on settings-driven upgrade conversion.
  • Avoid demoting "Log out" purely via grey text in contexts where accidental logout has high cost (e.g., multi-account business tools) - consider explicit confirmation or more visual separation.
  • Not ideal for power users or admin tools needing bulk actions, search, or filtering within settings.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves all registered users of Brilliant, regardless of subscription tier, who need to manage account details, sensory preferences (sound/haptics for the tactile lesson interactions core to the app), notifications, and support channels. The inclusion of "Haptics" as a first-class toggle is particularly telling (it signals that Brilliant's "move something before it explains" interaction model relies heavily on tactile/haptic feedback, so users need granular control over that sensory channel).

Psychologically, the screen operates on predictability and control: users visiting Settings want quick, frictionless access to toggles and account info without being upsold or distracted. Placing "Premium" unobtrusively within the list (rather than as a banner or CTA) respects this intent while still providing a discoverable path to monetization for users who are self-motivated to explore it.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consistent row grammar: icon + label + chevron/switch pattern repeated throughout removes ambiguity about what's tappable vs. toggleable at a glance.
  • Visual demotion via color, not separation: Log out and Legal are pushed down in importance purely through lighter grey text and icon omission, a subtle hierarchy technique that avoids alarming red "danger" styling for a routine action.
  • Modal dismiss via "X": clearly frames Settings as a temporary detour from the core app experience, respecting the linear lesson spine metaphor.
  • Grouped sectioning via whitespace/dividers only: no section headers are used, keeping the screen uncluttered and trusting users to infer categories from proximity (consistent with the brand's minimalist, low-density aesthetic).
  • Version number transparency: displaying the build version at the bottom builds trust and aids support/debugging without cluttering the main content.

screens.name: Brilliant - Logging out - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• First screen of an app's onboarding flow where you need to communicate a core product mechanic (not just a vague value statement) in under 2 seconds.
  • Products whose primary differentiator is interactivity, tactility, or a novel UI paradigm, showing fragments of that UI inside the hero visual builds instant comprehension.
  • Any onboarding funnel needing to serve both brand-new and returning users on one screen (primary CTA + secondary sign-in link).
  • Apps targeting habit formation, where quantifying effort (e.g., "15 minutes a day") can meaningfully reduce activation friction.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Feature-dense or enterprise B2B products where users need concrete feature lists or trust signals (logos, security badges) before committing (this minimalist, abstract style would feel evasive or unserious).
  • Apps where the core value is emotional/social rather than mechanical/functional (the "interface fragments as decoration" trick only works when the product truly is about manipulation/interaction; otherwise it's a wasted, misleading metaphor).
  • Contexts needing immediate legal/compliance disclosures, pricing transparency, or regulatory consent (those must be present as the very first interaction, not deferred past a purely aspirational splash).
  • Low-literacy or icon-dependent markets where large stylized wordplay-driven typography may not translate well without localization rework.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets curious, often lapsed or skeptical self-improvement seekers (a worldwide, broad demographic) who have likely tried passive learning content (YouTube explainers, MOOCs) and felt it didn't stick. The "Learn by doing" framing and embedded interactive-looking tag chips speak directly to this pain point by visually promising an alternative: active, hands-on mastery.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the mere-exposure/preview effect: showing a glimpse of the actual interaction mechanics (drag tags, curve manipulation) builds instant product literacy and curiosity ("what do these floating labels do?") without requiring explanation. The "15 minutes a day" framing taps into the small-commitment bias, lowering the psychological barrier to starting a new habit-forming product, which is critical for an edtech app competing against short-form entertainment for attention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Typography-as-interface metaphor: Embedding draggable tag chips, axis ticks, and a curve-with-handle directly into the giant headline visually demonstrates the app's "manipulate-to-learn" mechanic before the user has done anything, turning branding copy into a functional preview.
  • Extreme content restraint: Only one headline, one sentence, and two actions appear on screen, reinforcing the "one idea per screen" design law used throughout the whole app's lesson spine.
  • Dual-path CTA hierarchy: A bold, full-width green "Continue" pill clearly signals the default path (try the product), while the quieter "Sign in" text link is deliberately deprioritized for returning users, avoiding decision paralysis for first-time visitors.
  • Low-commitment framing: "Continue" avoids the heavier cognitive/emotional weight of "Sign Up," keeping the funnel feeling exploratory and reversible.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 3
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (explicit scope + named personalization + honesty incentive + single-CTA continuation) fits any product moment where a short, bounded data-collection sequence will directly improve the personalization or accuracy of subsequent recommendations, and where user trust in the "why" of the ask affects response quality.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for lengthy or open-ended data collection, bounding expectations to "5 questions" works because it's true and manageable; using this same reassuring framing before a much longer or vaguer survey would erode trust once the user discovers the scope was understated.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: uses a similarly framed personalization quiz early in a chosen learning path, explaining why answers matter before asking.

  • Noom: frames its onboarding habit questions with comparable "the more you tell us, the better we can help" incentive language before a multi-question personalization sequence.

  • Headspace: personalizes onboarding copy with the user's name and bounds question sets to a known, small number to reduce perceived friction.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Bounded scope reduces perceived commitment: explicitly stating "5 qs" up front lets the user mentally commit to a small, known task rather than an open-ended one, reducing quiz abandonment risk.

  • Personalized addressing builds rapport: using the user's actual name mid-conversation reinforces the sense of individualized coaching rather than generic scripted output.

  • Explicit incentive for honest input: telling the user why honesty matters ("the better I can help you") is a deliberate design choice to improve data quality at the source, rather than assuming users will self-report accurately by default.

  • Progressive commitment through single-chip continuation: narrowing from multiple choice chips to one clear "let's go" chip mirrors the user's own narrowing intent (they picked a specific goal), keeping the interaction focused.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 4
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (ordinal graded scale + metaphorical/non-clinical labeling + bounded recall window + inclusive definitions) fits any self-assessment question touching a potentially sensitive or shame-prone topic (finances, health habits, mental wellbeing) where honest self-report is more valuable than precise numeric data.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit where precise, actionable numeric data is actually required for a downstream calculation (e.g., an actual budget needs real dollar figures eventually) - a qualitative weather-scale answer alone wouldn't suffice if Cleo's budgeting engine needs concrete numbers rather than a general spending disposition.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Noom: uses similarly non-clinical, metaphor-based response scales (rather than raw numeric input) when asking users to self-assess sensitive habits.

  • Cleo's own broader pattern: consistent with the "Swear Jar" and challenge-based tone observed in earlier product research, reinforcing that Cleo systematically avoids blunt, judgmental framing around money behavior.

  • Headspace: uses graded, illustrated response scales (rather than plain text options) for self-reported emotional/behavioral check-ins, a similar design logic applied here to financial behavior.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Ordinal scale reduces precision-reporting burden: offering five graded categories instead of requiring an exact percentage or number lowers the cognitive and emotional cost of answering (recognition over recall, reduced input friction).

  • Metaphorical framing de-stigmatizes a sensitive answer: using weather severity rather than blunt financial language ("I overspend") makes admitting financial strain feel less like a confession and more like a light self-assessment.

  • Inclusive definition of income: explicitly naming non-traditional income sources (government support, student loans) avoids alienating users whose financial situation doesn't fit a default "salaried employee" assumption.

  • Bounded recall window: anchoring to "the last 6 months" rather than an open-ended "generally" question improves the reliability of the self-reported answer.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 5
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (binary or scaled choice matched to the question's natural structure, displayed within a persistent conversational thread) fits any multi-question personalization sequence where maintaining engagement and honest self-report matters more than rigid format consistency across questions.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit if the underlying data actually needs to be precisely comparable across users in a structured database (e.g., a clinical intake form) - varying answer formats per question (binary here, five-point scale previously) can complicate downstream data analysis compared to a single standardized response type.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Noom: similarly varies its self-assessment question formats (scales vs. binary choices) based on what best fits each specific question's natural structure, rather than uniform templating.

  • Headspace: uses casual, friend-like phrasing in its own personalization quiz questions, matching Cleo's conversational register here.

  • Duolingo: displays user answers as persistent chat-style bubbles during its own placement/personalization flow, reinforcing the same "this is a real conversation" illusion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Answer format matches question structure: using a binary choice for an inherently two-state question (rather than forcing a five-point scale everywhere) shows appropriate interaction-design judgment rather than template reuse.

  • Conversational continuity reinforces engagement: displaying the user's own prior answer as a real sent message (rather than silently advancing) maintains the feeling of an actual back-and-forth conversation, not a disguised form.

  • Consistent de-stigmatizing tone: extending the playful emoji-metaphor pattern from the previous spending question maintains a uniform emotional register across the whole quiz, rather than shifting tone question to question.

  • Casual phrasing reduces perceived formality: "What are you like with bills?" invites a more honest, less guarded answer than a clinical survey-style question would.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 6
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (entertainment-only closing question + retroactive reframing + explicit opt-in to a confrontational payoff) fits products with a strong, established comedic or personality-driven brand voice, where a moment of genuine fun can be inserted into an otherwise functional flow without undermining trust in the surrounding data collection.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for products without an already-established permissive, jokey brand relationship with users, introducing "roast me" style confrontational content without the extensive tonal groundwork Cleo lays throughout its onboarding would risk feeling mean-spirited or presumptuous rather than charming.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: closes early quiz/placement sequences with a lighter, personality-driven closing beat before transitioning into its main app experience, similar to Cleo's fill-in-blank closer.

  • BuzzFeed-style personality quizzes: commonly use fill-in-the-blank or free-response questions as an engagement device distinct from the data-gathering questions around them.

  • Noom: offers a comparable "we'll use this to help you" framing after a habits questionnaire, though without Cleo's distinctive roast/confrontational payoff style.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Entertainment beats reinforce brand personality mid-task: inserting a non-data-driven, purely fun question at the close of a functional quiz builds emotional engagement without compromising the quiz's actual purpose.

  • Retroactive reframing builds anticipation: revealing that the quiz was "ammo" for a roast only after the fact creates a small narrative payoff, making the preceding functional questions feel more purposeful in hindsight.

  • Explicit consent before confrontational content: offering "roast me Cleo" as a distinct, tappable choice (rather than auto-launching into critique) respects the principle that even playful negative feedback should be opted into, not sprung on the user.

  • Format variety sustains engagement across a multi-question sequence: shifting from graded scale, to binary, to fill-in-blank across three consecutive questions prevents the repetitive fatigue a uniform format would risk over even a short 5-question quiz.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 7
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (result-ready confirmation + on-demand mechanic explanation + deferred link to the actual feature) fits any flow where a personalization process produces an ongoing, interactive feature (not just a static report), and where understanding the mechanic in advance meaningfully improves first-use comprehension.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for features that are simple, static, or self-explanatory on sight (e.g., a one-time summary page) - inserting an explanatory bulleted breakdown before something the user could understand instantly just by looking at it would add unnecessary friction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: similarly explains a new mechanic (e.g., the XP/streak system) in plain bullet form immediately after onboarding, before the user first encounters it live.

  • Noom: generates a personalized program summary after its own habits questionnaire, explaining how ongoing tracking will work before the user opens their plan.

  • Robinhood: introduces new account features (e.g., recurring investments) with a similar short mechanic explanation before linking to the live feature.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explain the mechanic before the user encounters it: describing how the daily spending limit and check-in behavior work before opening the overview reduces confusion at first contact with a new, ongoing product feature.

  • Escalating tone matched to explicit consent: the shift into unfiltered, casual-profanity language directly follows the user's own "roast me Cleo" opt-in, respecting that the tone shift was invited rather than imposed.

  • Concise, scannable feature explanation: three short bullet points (rather than a paragraph) make a genuinely new mechanic digestible in a chat-bubble format that wasn't designed for long-form text.

  • Deferred entry point: placing "My overview 👀" as a distinct link only after the explanation, rather than immediately upon quiz completion, ensures the user has context before landing in the actual feature.

screens.name: Cleo Setting Up 8
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (proverb-style wordplay + custom illustration + clear "all set" closure) fits any product moment introducing a new ongoing mechanic with real financial or behavioral stakes, where making the concept memorable and non-threatening improves the odds the user actually internalizes and uses the feature.
screens.whereNotToUse: Poor fit for regulatory or compliance-critical disclosures where precise, unambiguous language matters more than memorability (wordplay and metaphor risk obscuring exact terms in contexts requiring legal clarity (e).g., actual fee structures or terms of a cash advance).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Duolingo: uses similarly punny, proverb-style microcopy to reinforce app mechanics (e.g., streak reminders) in a memorable, non-threatening way.

  • Headspace: closes feature-explanation sequences with short, confidence-building confirmation screens ("You're all set") before returning the user to the main app.

  • Mint (Intuit), historically: used comparable illustrated metaphors to explain budgeting mechanics in a visually engaging, non-clinical way.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Metaphor aids retention: the coin-salt-shaker visual and proverb wordplay make an abstract mechanic (daily spend limit) more memorable than a plain text explanation would.

  • Consequence framed without alarm: referencing "overdraft" (a real financial penalty) inside a lighthearted proverb format keeps the stakes present without inducing anxiety, consistent with Cleo's established tone strategy.

  • Clear closure signal: "YOU'RE ALL SET" gives an unambiguous sense of completion after a multi-step explanation sequence, useful for orienting the user before the next screen/action.

  • Distinct avatar for tips/wisdom content: using a different icon (brain emoji) than Cleo's standard chat avatar may help visually distinguish "insight/tip" moments from regular conversational turns, aiding scannability in a chat-based interface.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 13
screens.whereToUse: Utilize this conversational pattern for financial wellness apps, health tracking, or any utility where the underlying data (spending, calories, screen time) is emotionally sensitive. It works exceptionally well for micro-decisions (quick queries that benefit from an immediate, natural-language answer rather than requiring the user to navigate multiple menus to find raw data and interpret it themselves).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex data visualization needs, such as detailed multi-month trend analysis or portfolio management, where a chat bubble format cannot adequately display graphs, charts, or granular transaction lists. Additionally, this high-frequency, casual tone may alienate high-net-worth users or enterprise clients who require a more formal, data-dense interface for serious financial planning.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets financially anxious or budget-novice users (likely Gen Z/Millennials, as evidenced by the casual tone and meme-adjacent language) who find traditional banking apps intimidating or boring. The primary psychological trigger is the reduction of decision fatigue: by outsourcing the "can I afford this?" calculation to an AI, the user avoids the mental math and shame spiral often associated with checking their bank balance.

The use of a "friend" persona (Cleo) rather than a "bank" persona leverages the parasocial relationship trigger, making users more likely to engage honestly and frequently with their finances because it feels like texting a buddy, not confessing to a bank teller.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anthropomorphized Financial Guardrails: Instead of a static "Available Balance" widget, the app frames budgeting as a dialogue, making the restrictive nature of budgeting feel like helpful advice from a friend rather than a punitive system.

  • Zero UI Input Friction: The user doesn't need to navigate to a "calculator" tool; they simply type a number ("20") directly into the chat, and the system contextually understands it refers to the previous question about cost.

  • Actionable Insight Injection: The chat bubble intelligently appends a "Set income" link when it detects incomplete data, turning a simple answer into an opportunity for data enrichment/onboarding completion.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 14
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern when building financial, wellness, or habit-forming apps aimed at a younger demographic that needs its subject matter de-stigmatized or made more approachable. It's ideal for products layering an AI assistant/chatbot as the core interaction model, where a feed of proactive insights can prime users before they even type a query. Also effective for apps needing to blend transactional utility with content marketing/education in a single screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this tone and layout for enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth financial products where users expect precision, gravity, and density of real data over personality-driven content cards. This pattern is also risky for regulatory-heavy contexts where irreverent humor about money ("Bezos" comparisons) could be seen as undermining trust or seriousness. Additionally, a chat-input-first home screen can frustrate power users who want instant access to structured dashboards/data rather than needing to phrase a query.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This design clearly targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z/Millennials) who are often intimidated, bored, or alienated by traditional banking/budgeting apps. The meme aesthetics, playful quizzes, and chatbot-first framing lower the psychological barrier to engaging with personal finances, a topic often associated with shame or anxiety for this demographic.

Psychologically, the design leverages anthropomorphism (the "Cleo" persona acting as a sassy financial friend) to build parasocial trust and habitual engagement, similar to how users interact with Duolingo's owl or a horoscope app. The gamified quiz card exploits curiosity gaps ("What's Your Spend Style?") to drive click-through, while the "Balance vs. Bezos" card uses social comparison humor to make abstract net-worth numbers feel relatable and less clinical.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-first architecture: Placing a persistent natural-language input bar at the bottom transforms complex financial queries into a single, low-friction text box, bypassing traditional menu-diving.

  • Personality-driven content cards: Using bold meme-style typography and irreverent copy ("Your Balance vs. Bezos") to reframe potentially stressful financial data as entertaining, shareable content.

  • Dual-intent content grid: The "Explore" (quiz/gamified) vs "Get Smarter" (educational) split elegantly serves both users seeking entertainment and users seeking utility within the same visual real estate.

  • Feedback loop invitation: The subtle "Got feedback about your feed?" link demonstrates a lightweight, low-commitment mechanism for improving algorithmic content relevance without a disruptive survey modal.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 15
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this conversational-dashboard pattern when a product deals with inherently intimidating or emotionally charged data (personal finance, health, mental wellness) and wants to reduce anxiety through personality and plain language. It's especially effective for apps targeting audiences fatigued by traditional enterprise-style dashboards, or for AI-assistant-driven products where natural language querying is a core value proposition. Quick-reply chips work well anywhere you want to reduce typing effort and guide exploration paths.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for power users, analysts, or B2B contexts where dense, comparative, at-a-glance data visualization (charts, tables, trends over time) is essential (chat-based delivery is slower to parse than a well-designed graph when users need to compare many data points). Also avoid an overly casual/meme tone in contexts requiring institutional trust and gravitas (e.g., large wealth management, enterprise banking, regulatory disclosures), where humor can undermine perceived competence or trustworthiness.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z/millennial) who are often financially anxious, under-served by legacy banking UX, and more receptive to informal, meme-based communication than corporate financial jargon. The design leans on parasocial trust: talking to "Cleo" like a witty friend rather than a bank (which lowers the psychological barrier to engaging with sensitive money topics).

The quick-reply suggestions leverage the path-of-least-resistance principle: users are far more likely to tap a button than compose a follow-up question, increasing engagement depth and data the app can use to personalize further insights or upsell premium features (a common freemium chatbot monetization funnel).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-as-Dashboard: Replacing static charts with a conversational Q&A format makes financial data feel personal and less intimidating, especially for anxious or first-time budgeters.

  • Suggested Quick Replies: Pre-written follow-up prompts remove typing friction and actively guide users toward deeper engagement (categories, merchants, insights feed) - a classic chatbot UX best practice.

  • Editorial Content Carousel: The top "Explore" cards inject discovery and light-hearted engagement (personality quiz, tax season tips) into what would otherwise be a purely utilitarian finance app, increasing session time and emotional connection to the brand.

  • Emoji-Enhanced Data: Using emoji as visual affordances (💰💸📈) within plain text speeds up scanning and softens the seriousness of money talk.

  • Persistent Multi-Product Tab Bar: Chat sits equally alongside Spend/Budget/Save/Borrow/Habits, signaling it's a first-class navigation destination, not a hidden support feature.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 16
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial wellness apps targeting younger or first-time banking users who benefit from simplified, guided data exploration.

  • Any AI-assistant interface where you want to constrain user queries to a supported subset via suggested replies.

  • Products aiming to humanize dry, numeric data (finance, health metrics, analytics) through personality-driven microcopy.

  • Apps building trust with anxious users around sensitive topics (money, health) where a friendly tone can reduce avoidance behavior.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise or B2B financial/accounting tools where users need precise, exportable, tabular data rather than conversational summaries.

  • Contexts requiring rapid multi-metric comparison (e.g., comparing 12 months of spend) - chat bubbles do not scale well for dense tabular analysis.

  • Older or less tech-savvy demographics who may find playful/casual tone at odds with the seriousness of their financial situation (e.g., debt collection, hardship notices).

  • Regulated disclosures or compliance-sensitive information where emoji and informal tone could undermine clarity or legal precision.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, mobile-native users (Gen Z/Millennial) who are more comfortable texting than navigating spreadsheets or complex dashboards. Cleo's brand is explicitly built around demystifying and destigmatizing personal finance through humor, making it approachable for users who may feel anxiety or avoidance around traditional banking apps.

Psychologically, the conversational format leverages the same engagement loops as social messaging apps (familiarity, low friction, and instant gratification) to keep users returning to check their finances rather than avoiding a stressful task. The playful emoji use also reduces the shame/anxiety often associated with reviewing spending (e.g., overdraft fees), reframing financial literacy as entertainment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Quick-reply chips instead of free text: Constrains user input to a finite, answerable set of queries, dramatically improving AI reliability and reducing dead-end conversations.

  • Emoji-coded financial categories: Using emoji (💀 for bills, 💩 for bank charges, 💰 for income) creates instant visual/emotional association and injects brand personality into raw numeric data.

  • Chat bubble math transparency: Explicitly showing "+/-/=" arithmetic builds trust and comprehension without needing a chart.

  • "See more" progressive disclosure: Truncates the category list to the top 3 spend categories, avoiding overwhelming the chat window while still allowing drill-down.

  • Persistent conversational memory: The chat retains context of the date range (Feb 1 (23) across follow-up queries, so the user doesn't need to re-specify the timeframe).

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 17
screens.whereToUse:
• Finance, health, or habit-tracking apps where raw data is emotionally sensitive and benefits from a softened, personality-driven delivery.

  • Products aiming to differentiate from data-dense competitors by offering a low-friction, query-based alternative to dashboards.

  • Scenarios where users have varied, unpredictable questions (ad hoc reporting) better served by NL queries than by pre-built dashboard views.

  • Apps targeting younger or first-time users unfamiliar with financial jargon/charts, where a guiding conversational voice reduces intimidation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Power users or professionals (e.g., accountants, active traders) who need to scan large datasets quickly (chat bubbles are slower and harder to compare at a glance than tables/charts).

  • Contexts requiring precise multi-dimensional analysis (e.g., comparing 12 months side-by-side) where a conversational thread becomes unwieldy to scroll through.

  • Situations where trust and seriousness are paramount (e.g., displaying a loan default warning) - excessive humor/emoji could undermine credibility or feel tonally inappropriate.

  • Accessibility-critical contexts where emoji-heavy, informally-formatted text may not read well with screen readers or for users who prefer structured, literal data.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets financially anxious or dashboard-averse users (often younger, less financially literate audiences (Gen Z/millennials) who find bank apps' bar charts and category tables intimidating or boring). By reframing financial review as a casual text conversation with a witty "friend," Cleo lowers the emotional barrier to checking one's spending.

Psychologically, this leverages the conversational interface heuristic: humans are wired to trust and engage with dialogue more readily than static reports (parasocial rapport with the Cleo mascot). The humor (skull/poop emojis) also uses tension release: talking about being broke or overspending is stressful, and comedy defuses shame, encouraging users to keep checking in rather than avoid their finances (a common behavior called financial avoidance).

The chip-driven follow-ups exploit the path of least resistance: users are more likely to continue engaging when the next action is pre-written for them, increasing session depth and data engagement metrics for the app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-UI data exploration: Complex financial querying (date-ranged aggregation, category breakdown) is accessed via plain-language chat rather than filters/dropdowns, removing the learning curve typically associated with finance dashboards.

  • Progressive disclosure via quick-reply chips: Each bot response ends with a suggested next action, guiding the user deeper into their data one bite-sized step at a time instead of overwhelming them with a full report.

  • Personality-infused data: Emoji annotations (💀 for Bills, 💩 for Bank Charges) turn dry financial categories into emotionally resonant, meme-able content, making the mundane act of expense tracking feel entertaining.

  • Typing indicator for perceived liveness: The animated dots reinforce a real-time, human-like conversational rhythm that increases trust and engagement compared to instant static loads.

  • Persistent bottom input + tab bar: The chat input stays anchored at the bottom, always ready for a new query, while Chat remains a top-level tab alongside Spend/Budget/Save, cementing it as the app's primary interaction surface, not an add-on.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 18
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for consumer fintech, wellness, or habit-building apps targeting younger demographics where reducing anxiety and building daily habitual engagement is the primary goal. It works well when the brand has permission to be irreverent and when the core function (chat/AI assistant) benefits from a distinct, memorable personality to differentiate from competitors' clinical UIs.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this tone and visual density for enterprise, B2B, wealth management, or older/high-net-worth demographics where credibility and seriousness are paramount trust signals. Overly meme-heavy language on sensitive topics (like debt or addiction) can also backfire if not carefully balanced, potentially seeming dismissive of genuine user distress; the graphic tone must be tested carefully against user financial stress levels.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen is clearly engineered for a younger, digitally-native audience (Gen Z / younger Millennials) who are typically disengaged or intimidated by traditional banking apps. The design leverages the psychological principle of "approachability through humor" - by using meme formats and casual slang, it lowers the guard of users who associate finance with shame or stress. The juxtaposition of a serious topic (gambling addiction awareness) within the same visual carousel as lighthearted content ("Hype Mode") signals emotional versatility, positioning Cleo as a "friend who gets it" rather than an institution, which is critical to building trust and daily engagement (retention) with users who might otherwise avoid opening a banking app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Personality-driven content merchandising: Using vibrant, poster-like cards instead of generic list items to market financial education content makes literacy topics feel like entertainment.

  • Emoji-augmented navigation: Placing expressive emojis directly in tab/section titles reduces the emotional distance typically felt with money apps.

  • Humor as an anxiety-reduction tool: Visualizing "Bills" with an exaggerated, comedic graphic acknowledges the dread of bill season while diffusing it with humor before the user engages with the underlying feature.

  • Persistent floating identity badge: The circular "CLEO" wordmark bridges scroll states and view transitions, keeping brand presence anchored even mid-animation.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 19
screens.whereToUse: Use this conversational, personality-driven pattern when the goal is to increase daily engagement/retention for a utility app (finance, health, habit tracking) that users would otherwise avoid due to anxiety or boredom. It works well for younger demographics or brands aiming to disrupt a stodgy incumbent industry.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth financial products where users expect clinical precision, trust signals, and formal data visualization (e.g., wealth management dashboards). Humor and memes can undermine perceived credibility for serious transactions like large loans, tax filing, or legal documents, and may not translate well across different cultural/international meme literacy levels.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets Gen Z and Millennial users who are digital natives fluent in meme culture and internet shorthand, and who are often disengaged or anxious about traditional, jargon-heavy banking apps. By adopting the visual and tonal language of texting a witty friend rather than a bank, Cleo lowers the psychological barrier to entry for financial engagement.

The psychological trigger here is parasocial relationship building: users are more likely to open a finance app daily if it feels like checking a message from a friend rather than confronting a spreadsheet of debts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Personality-Driven Interface: Using a chat bubble UI transforms a mundane task (bill review) into a relatable conversation, lowering the emotional barrier to engaging with finances.

  • Meme Integration: Embedding a recognizable pop-culture GIF/image directly in the chat feed creates an immediate emotional connection and shareability factor.

  • Quick Reply Chips: The pill-shaped suggested replies ("live", "laugh", "bills") allow for frictionless continuation of the conversation without requiring typing.

  • Hub & Spoke Navigation: The bottom tab bar cleanly separates the "fun" AI chat from the functional modules (Spend, Budget, Save, Borrow, Habits).

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 20
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building financial wellness, budgeting, or fintech products targeting younger or financially-anxious demographics who benefit from friendly framing rather than clinical data display. Effective for delivering potentially stressful information (low balance, bills due, overspending alerts) in a way that maintains user retention and reduces app abandonment/avoidance. Also useful in coaching, habit-tracking, or health apps where an AI persona can soften hard truths and drive daily re-engagement through conversational check-ins.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for enterprise, B2B, or professional financial tools (e.g., accounting software, investment platforms) where users expect precise, dense data and a serious, authoritative tone (playful chat bubbles would undermine credibility). Also inappropriate for older or less tech-savvy demographics who may find the chatbot metaphor confusing or prefer direct numerical dashboards. Overuse of full-screen typographic interruptions can also feel gimmicky or slow down power users who want quick, scannable data across multiple accounts at once.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern is targeted at younger users (Gen Z / young millennials), particularly those living paycheck-to-paycheck who experience financial anxiety around bill due dates. The conversational, meme-inspired tone and Cleo's "sassy but supportive friend" persona is specifically engineered to reduce the shame and avoidance behavior that often accompanies checking bank balances or bills.

Psychological triggers at play include: loss aversion/urgency (bills due before payday creates a ticking clock), social/emotional validation (removing blame lowers defensive avoidance), and anthropomorphism (chatting with "Cleo" as a friend increases trust and daily habitual engagement compared to a sterile balance screen).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Conversational UI as financial dashboard: Replacing charts/tables with a chatbot persona humanizes cold financial data and increases engagement/return visits.

  • Emotional pre-framing before data delivery: The bot validates the user's feelings ("no one's fault") before hitting them with a bill amount, reducing defensive/anxious reactions.

  • Oversized typographic "shock card": Using massive, bold, high-contrast type as a mid-conversation visual break dramatically increases recall and scannability of the single most important fact (amount + deadline).

  • Color-coded hierarchy: Light blue for narrative words vs. vivid orange for the critical number creates instant visual parsing without needing to read every word.

  • Chat input bar mimics native messaging apps (iMessage/WhatsApp), exploiting existing user muscle memory to make a finance app feel effortless and familiar.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 21
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for finance, health, or habit-tracking apps targeting emotionally sensitive topics where a purely clinical UI would cause avoidance. Effective when the product's differentiation is a distinct brand voice/personality and when frequent re-engagement (daily active use) is a core growth metric. Works well for conversational/AI-first products that want to reduce the intimidation factor of raw data.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this tone for enterprise, B2B, healthcare-compliance, or high-net-worth financial products where users expect neutral, authoritative, professional communication (humor here can undermine trust or feel dismissive of serious financial distress). Also inappropriate for users in acute financial crisis where shock headlines could increase anxiety rather than engagement; needs careful A/B testing and sensitivity thresholds.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets younger, often financially-stressed users (Gen Z/Millennial, frequently paycheck-to-paycheck) who are disengaged or intimidated by traditional banking UI. The psychological trigger is a blend of loss-aversion urgency (bold bill-due warning) and humor-based rapport building, which lowers defensiveness around a typically shame-laden topic (low balance, overdue bills). By personifying the AI as a sassy friend rather than a bank, Cleo builds parasocial trust and habitual daily check-ins, similar to checking messages from a friend.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-as-homescreen: Placing the AI conversation as the primary tab (not buried in a menu) reframes financial monitoring as an ongoing dialogue rather than a static report.
