  • Shock-then-humor pacing: The oversized alarming headline followed by a comedic illustration and casual question creates an emotional rollercoaster that increases engagement and memorability.

  • Inline feedback loop: Thumbs up/down on individual AI messages lets Cleo's tone/model be tuned per user, embedding a lightweight RLHF-style personalization mechanic directly into the chat.

  • Persistent quick-access home icon next to the chat input allows instant escape back to a dashboard without losing conversational context.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 22
screens.whereToUse:
• Financial wellness or budgeting apps targeting younger, digitally-native users who respond better to personality-driven brands than corporate tone.

  • Any app aiming to deliver potentially negative or corrective feedback (spending alerts, health warnings, habit tracking) in a way that reduces defensiveness through humor.

  • Products wanting to increase engagement/retention by making routine check-ins feel like a habitual, entertaining chat rather than a chore.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth financial platforms where users expect precision, formality, and data density rather than jokes.

  • Regulatory or compliance-heavy contexts (loan approvals, tax filing, legal disclosures) where humor could undermine trust or obscure critical information.

  • Users in genuine financial distress who may find joking about their balance tone-deaf or dismissive rather than supportive.

  • Accessibility-critical contexts where GIFs/emoji-heavy content may not be well-supported by screen readers.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets Gen Z and younger Millennial users, particularly those living paycheck-to-paycheck or new to financial independence, who are typically disengaged or anxious about traditional banking apps. The humor-forward, meme-literate tone taps into this demographic's comfort with social-media-style communication and their aversion to being lectured by authority figures (including their bank).

Psychologically, the screen leverages social proof through relatability (the GIF makes the user feel "seen"), loss aversion softened by humor (calling out overspending without triggering shame-driven avoidance), and the foot-in-the-door technique via low-commitment quick-reply buttons that ease users into deeper financial reflection.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Conversational UI for finance: Replacing dashboards/graphs with a chat thread makes complex budget data feel like advice from a friend, drastically lowering cognitive load.

  • Meme/GIF integration: Using pop-culture reaction GIFs and emoji spam as bot "replies" builds emotional rapport and virality/shareability, a rare pattern in fintech.

  • Ambiguous quick replies: Offering only "maybe..." and "mayBE" instead of a clear yes/no forces engagement and adds personality, avoiding the sterile feel of typical chatbot buttons.

  • Data-embedded dialogue: Injecting the actual account balance into natural language rather than a stat card personalizes the insight and increases perceived relevance.

  • Persistent multi-tool navigation: Bottom tab bar keeps the chat experience integrated within the broader spend/budget/save ecosystem rather than siloed.

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this bottom-sheet invite pattern when a feature requires rapidly pulling other people into a collaborative, real-time or near-real-time session (co-listening, watch parties, multiplayer games, collaborative documents). It's ideal when you have multiple invite channels of differing effort/reach tradeoffs and want to let users self-select the fastest path for their situation. The dimmed-background-plus-sheet approach is best for lightweight, task-focused interruptions that shouldn't break the user's sense of place in the app.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-stakes or infrequent invite flows (e.g., inviting a business collaborator to a formal workspace) where a full-screen flow with more configuration (roles, permissions) is warranted. Also avoid stacking too many invite mechanisms if your audience skews non-technical (the QR code and Bluetooth auto-invite options add complexity that could overwhelm users who just want a simple share link). If proximity-based auto-invite requires significant permissions (Bluetooth, location), be cautious about implying it's low-effort, as permission prompts can introduce unexpected friction or privacy concerns.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets social, group-listening users: people at parties, road trips, or hangouts who want to collaboratively control a shared queue. The psychological drivers at play are:

  • Social facilitation:
  • Reduced friction for viral/network growth: Every Jam invite is an implicit growth loop (non-Spotify users who click a share link or scan a QR code are exposed to the product, functioning as a soft acquisition channel).
  • Context-matching convenience: By offering Bluetooth/Wi-Fi auto-invite for in-person scenarios, the app removes the awkwardness of manually sending links to people standing in the same room, reducing the social cost of using the feature in a live setting.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background context preservation: The Home screen is visible-but-darkened behind the sheet, keeping spatial continuity so the invite flow doesn't feel like a full context switch.
  • Reach-ordered option hierarchy: Share link (universal) → Auto-invite nearby (proximity-based) → QR code (in-person), guiding users to the fastest path for their specific social context.
  • Self-explanatory microcopy: Every advanced feature (auto-invite, QR) includes a one-line plain-language explanation, eliminating the need for a separate help screen or tooltip.
  • Multi-modal invite redundancy: Offering three distinct sharing mechanisms (link, proximity, visual code) maximizes the odds that at least one method matches the recipient's context (remote friend vs. person standing next to you).

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any native OS permission request (camera, microphone, location, Bluetooth, notifications, contacts) especially when the permission isn't immediately self-evident in value. It's ideal for:

  • Features gated behind sensitive hardware/data permissions where context is not obvious.
  • Flows where permission denial would be costly to recover from (since the system prompt usually can't be re-triggered easily).
  • Onboarding or feature-discovery moments where building long-term trust outweighs the cost of one extra screen/tap.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The permission's purpose is already self-evident from context (e.g., asking for camera access directly after tapping a camera icon) — adding an extra screen here is redundant friction.
  • The app needs the permission immediately and urgently; an extra educational step may slow down a time-critical task.
  • Used too frequently across many permissions in a row, which can create "priming fatigue" and make users suspicious of over-justification.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are about to engage in a social/offline listening feature (e.g., Spotify's "Group Session" or device-sharing flows) that technically requires Bluetooth. The target demographic is broad — essentially any Spotify user on a flow that needs Bluetooth — but the design specifically counters the general public's heightened wariness of granting background hardware permissions (Bluetooth, in particular, is often associated with tracking concerns).

Psychologically, it leverages the foot-in-the-door technique: agreeing to a low-stakes, well-explained "Continue" makes users far more likely to also tap "Allow" on the subsequent native iOS prompt. It also uses reciprocity/transparency framing — by proactively disclosing data usage and reversibility, Spotify builds trust, which increases the probability of permission grant and reduces later distrust or app uninstalls tied to perceived overreach.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-permission priming: Explains value before invoking the native OS prompt, which research shows significantly increases opt-in rates versus a cold system dialog.
  • Benefit-first headline: Leads with the social use case ("listen with friends nearby") instead of the technical permission name.
  • Dual reassurance blocks: "How we'll use this" and "You're in control" preemptively answer privacy objections using calm iconography instead of warning symbols.
  • Warm, human illustration: Diverse hands and floating music notes humanize an otherwise cold technical request and reinforce the social/sharing use case.
  • Single low-friction CTA: "Continue" (not "Allow") lowers perceived commitment and funnels the user smoothly toward the actual OS permission dialog.

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a feature involves real-time collaborative sessions (shared playlists, watch parties, multiplayer games, collaborative docs) and you need to lower the barrier to inviting others. Ideal for scenarios with mixed invite contexts (remote, proximity-based, and in-person) where offering multiple invite channels in a single, dismissible surface increases conversion to multi-user engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-stakes or privacy-sensitive invites (e.g., financial account sharing) where "auto-invite nearby" could unintentionally expose data to unintended parties (proximity-based auto-invite requires very clear consent framing or it risks feeling invasive). Also unsuitable for single-user or non-collaborative features where surfacing invite options would be irrelevant clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Targets Spotify's highly social, group-listening user segment (friends at parties, in cars, or in shared physical spaces who want synchronized music control (Spotify Jam/Group Session feature)). The psychological driver is social facilitation and shared experience: music is inherently communal, and making group participation nearly effortless (auto-invite nearby) taps into spontaneity and reduces the setup tax that typically kills group activities. The QR code option additionally serves offline/low-connectivity social gatherings where typing or app-switching is impractical.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multi-modal invite strategy: Combines link sharing, proximity auto-invite, and QR code in one sheet, covering remote, ambient, and in-person social contexts.
  • Context-preserving dim overlay: Background Home screen remains visible (blurred/dimmed), anchoring the user in their existing session rather than navigating away.
  • Iconography reinforces concept: The pulsing-wave Bluetooth/nearby icon visually communicates the "auto-invite nearby" radius concept at a glance.
  • Low-commitment UI: Swipeable grabber handle and non-blocking design make it easy to dismiss without friction.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any content-heavy, subscription or engagement-driven app (streaming audio/video, news aggregators, e-commerce) where the primary goal is to get users consuming content immediately with minimal navigation. Ideal when you have rich behavioral/listening data to power genuine personalization, and when sustained daily engagement (not one-off task completion) is the core metric.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, algorithmic shelf-of-shelves approach for task-oriented or transactional apps (banking, productivity, utilities) where users need to find one specific item quickly (the scannability trade-off and lack of explicit search-first hierarchy would frustrate goal-driven users). It also fails for new users with no listening history, where empty or generic shelves can feel cold; a stronger onboarding/quiz flow should precede this view for cold-start users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Spotify's broad, habitual-listening user base (people who open the app expecting to press play within seconds rather than actively search). The design leans heavily on the psychological principle of reduced decision fatigue: by pre-curating "Start listening" and "To get you started" shelves based on listening history, Spotify removes the paralysis of an infinite music catalogue.

The personalized Mixes (named after specific artists the user already streams) exploit the mere-exposure and familiarity effect: users are far more likely to tap a tile branded with an artist they already love than a generic "Discover" playlist. The "Wrapped" chip taps into social proof and FOMO, since Wrapped is a widely shared, culturally-anticipated yearly event.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reasoned shelves: Every content row carries an explanatory subhead ("Jump into a session based on your tastes") that justifies the recommendation, increasing perceived relevance and reducing algorithm distrust.
  • Persistent now-playing bar: The mini-player survives across every scroll position and tab switch, making "pressing play" a near-zero-friction, always-available action.
  • Contextual overflow menus: The triple-dot icon on each track row offers quick actions (add to playlist, share, etc.) without leaving the feed, preserving flow state.
  • Horizontal, swipeable rows: Mixing vertical page scroll with horizontal carousel scroll maximizes content density on a small screen while keeping each category scannable.
  • Top filter chips double as a seasonal feature entry point: The "Wrapped" chip surfaces a time-bound campaign feature directly in primary navigation, driving engagement to a high-retention seasonal product.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse:
• Introducing a secondary, non-obvious feature (e.g., scanning, voice search, widgets) to users already engaged in a related primary flow (search, browse).
  • When a visual demonstration communicates the feature faster than text alone (especially for scannable codes, gestures, or camera-based features).
  • For feature adoption campaigns where you want to nudge usage of an underutilized but valuable capability without forcing a hard onboarding step.
  • Any app with physical/offline touchpoints (merch, posters, packaging) that benefit from a bridge to digital content.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid during first-run onboarding or immediately after login, when users are already absorbing multiple new concepts (this adds unnecessary cognitive load).
  • Don't use for core, frequently-needed features; reserve modal interruptions for genuinely optional, supplementary capabilities.
  • Avoid if no clear escape/dismiss path is visible (users need a frictionless way to decline without feeling trapped).
  • Not ideal for users who have already used the feature; repeated spotlighting of a known feature feels patronizing and breaks trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets existing, moderately engaged Spotify users browsing the Search tab who may never have noticed the small camera icon for scanning codes. It serves dual psychological purposes: (1) feature discovery for users who already trust the app and are open to learning shortcuts, and (2) social/physical-world bridging: Spotify Codes are often printed on posters, merchandise, or shared between friends, so this primes users to recognize and act on codes they'll encounter offline.

The trigger relies on curiosity and FOMO ("Everything on Spotify has a code") combined with low-friction action (one tap to "Scan"), capitalizing on a moment when the user is already in a content-seeking mindset within Search.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Show-don't-tell visual teaching: Instead of only describing what a Spotify Code is, the modal displays an actual stylized example (Shawn Mendes "Today's Top Hits" card) with a real code graphic, letting users pattern-match instantly.
  • Fanned card stack motif: The layered, slightly rotated cards behind the hero card imply "this works for many types of content" (songs, artists, playlists, podcasts) in a single glance, reducing the need for explanatory text.
  • Single CTA, no decision fatigue: Only one button is offered, funneling the user toward trying the feature rather than offering a menu of choices.
  • Contextual placement on Search: Surfacing this on the Search screen (next to the camera icon already present in the top bar) logically ties the "Scan" capability to an already-visible camera icon, reinforcing discoverability of an otherwise-hidden feature.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 10
screens.whereToUse:
• Introducing a net-new or under-adopted premium feature to engaged free users without a full-screen paywall interruption.
  • Social or collaborative features where group benefit framing increases perceived value.
  • Promotional moments that benefit from a distinct visual identity separate from core app chrome.
  • Soft upsell moments where you want to maintain goodwill by making dismissal easy and low-friction.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for first-time users during initial onboarding, introducing paywalled social features before any core value has been experienced can feel premature and pushy.
  • Not ideal for critical/transactional flows (e.g., checkout, settings changes) where unrelated promotional interruptions harm task completion and trust.
  • Overusing this modal pattern across many sessions risks "upsell fatigue," causing users to reflexively dismiss without reading (should be frequency-capped).
  • Should not be used when the feature being promoted has no meaningful utility for the specific user segment (e.g., users with no contacts/friends on the platform).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets existing free-tier or non-Premium users actively browsing Home, intercepting them during natural usage rather than at a hard wall. The psychological trigger is FOMO combined with social connection: framing the feature around shared experiences with friends taps into belonging and social validation needs, which are often more persuasive upsell levers than individual feature benefits.

It also leverages the curiosity gap and reciprocity pattern: showing full benefit-rich messaging before revealing it's a paywalled feature primes an emotional "yes" before the rational gate is disclosed, increasing the odds that the restriction is seen as a mere formality rather than a dealbreaker.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background retention: Keeps users spatially oriented in Home while fully focusing attention on the promotional card.
  • Emotion-first illustration: A custom 3D asset (boombox, equalizer bars, sparkles) communicates "fun social party" instantly, before any text is read.
  • Asymmetric CTA weighting: Bold pill-shaped, brand-green "Try it now" button vs. plain-text "Dismiss" creates strong visual bias toward conversion.
  • Delayed disclosure of restriction: The Premium-only requirement is shown in small muted text after the emotionally persuasive copy and CTA, reducing perceived friction.
  • On-brand gradient deviation: Breaking from the usual dark/green palette with a vibrant pink-purple gradient signals a special, limited, "event-like" feature.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 11
screens.whereToUse:
• Introducing a secondary, high-value feature to existing users without burying it in settings or menus.
  • Cross-promoting commerce or partner-driven features (tickets, merch, podcasts) that benefit from a higher visual energy than the core app chrome.
  • Any scenario needing a multi-message announcement carousel where users may only care about one of several updates.
  • Re-engagement moments (app relaunch, post-update) where a few seconds of user attention can be used for feature discovery.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, full-bleed takeover pattern for core, frequently-needed functionality (it adds friction to the primary task flow and should never gate access to essential features like playback). It's also inappropriate for first-time users with no behavioral data, since "tailored to your taste" claims will ring false before any personalization has occurred. Overusing vivid, off-brand colors across many promotional slides can dilute the dark/green brand identity and train users to habitually swipe past or dismiss without reading, reducing long-term effectiveness.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets existing, engaged listeners who already have an established taste profile (the copy assumes the app knows their "favorite artists"), not brand-new signups. It is designed to re-engage lapsed or passive streamers by connecting the passive act of listening to a higher-intent, often monetized real-world action (buying concert tickets), which also deepens emotional attachment to artists and, by extension, the platform.

Psychologically, it leverages personalization-as-relevance (the "tailored to your music taste" framing lowers perceived effort/risk of exploring a new feature) and curiosity/FOMO around live events tied to artists the user already loves. The vivid, non-standard color palette interrupts habitual dark-UI scanning patterns, forcing conscious attention (an intentional break from the "easy autopilot" of the rest of the app for this one high-value upsell moment).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Peeking next card: Deliberately cropping the following pink slide at the screen edge visually teaches the swipe gesture without any instructional text.
  • Mini product screenshot inside the card: Embedding a stylized, bite-sized preview of the actual search/browse UI builds trust and sets accurate expectations before the user commits to tapping through.
  • Color-coded card per topic: Each carousel slide uses a distinct saturated gradient (purple here), helping users mentally bookmark "which slide was that" and adding visual energy against the otherwise minimal dark app shell.
  • Dual navigation affordances: Page-control dots plus a card peek redundantly communicate "more content exists," catering to different user attention levels.
  • Low-commitment exit: "Dismiss" is one tap away and non-punitive, preserving user trust and reducing perceived manipulation.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 12
screens.whereToUse:
Use this shelf-based, color-differentiated carousel pattern for any content-heavy, personalization-driven home feed (streaming (audio/video), news aggregators, or e-commerce "recommended for you" surfaces) where the goal is to reduce user decision-making and surface a near-infinite catalog through algorithmically curated, bite-sized groupings. It's especially effective when:

  • You have rich visual assets (photos/artwork) per content item.
  • The brand needs to feel alive/personalized without a heavy onboarding quiz on every visit.
  • You want a scalable home screen that can mix editorial and algorithmic shelves interchangeably.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Content catalogs are small: endless horizontal shelves feel hollow or repetitive with few items.
  • Users need to compare items side-by-side or complete transactional tasks (e.g., checkout, forms) - shelf browsing adds friction instead of focus.
  • Accessibility is a primary concern; dense horizontal carousels with peeking cards and color-as-differentiator can be harder for screen-reader and low-vision users to navigate compared to a simple vertical list.
  • The brand/product requires deep, intentional discovery (e.g., search-first utility apps) rather than passive, scroll-and-tap consumption.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets returning, logged-in users (note the "Wrapped" chip, a seasonal/personalized feature only shown to existing listeners with history) rather than new sign-ups. The psychological drivers at play are:

  • Choice reduction / decision fatigue relief: Pre-curated "stations" and "mixes" remove the paradox-of-choice problem inherent to a catalog of 100M+ tracks.
  • Parasocial/artist affinity: Large, cinematic artist photography (Olivia Rodrigo, Taylor Swift, Gracie Abrams) leverages fan identification and celebrity recognition to drive clicks, more effectively than generic playlist art.
  • Mere-exposure & habit loop reinforcement: Familiar artists repeated across multiple shelves (Recommended Stations, Mixes) increase perceived relevance and comfort, encouraging a "press play" reflex over deliberation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded card system: Each playlist/station uses a unique saturated duotone (coral, mint, lime) purely as a wayfinding device against the otherwise monochrome dark UI, making the grid scannable at a glance and reinforcing brand's "sparingly used color" philosophy.
  • Edge-peeking carousels: Partial visibility of the next card is a low-cost affordance that communicates horizontal scrollability without needing explicit UI chrome (arrows, dots, "see more" labels).
  • Top filter chip bar with avatar entry point: Placing the user's profile avatar as the leftmost "chip" merges identity/settings access with content filtering in one compact row, saving vertical space.
  • One-tap resume bar: The "Start listening" row at the bottom functions as a zero-friction re-engagement point, always visible right above the tab bar.
  • Dense but legible typographic hierarchy: Bold 24px+ headers against 14px gray metadata create clear scan levels without needing visual dividers.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 13
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any content-heavy, personalization-driven app (streaming video, news aggregators, podcast apps, shopping apps with heavy catalogs) where the core value proposition is "help me decide" rather than "let me search." It excels when you have rich recommendation data and want to surface many categories of content on one home surface without forcing users into deep navigation trees. The chip-based content-type switcher at the top is ideal whenever an app serves multiple distinct content verticals (e.g., music + podcasts + audiobooks) under one roof.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, multi-shelf carousel approach for tasks that require precision or completion, such as transactional flows, forms, or settings (the lack of clear end-state and infinite horizontal/vertical scrolling can cause decision fatigue if applied outside of leisure/discovery contexts). It's also a poor fit for apps with sparse content libraries, new users with no listening history (cold-start problem), or accessibility-sensitive contexts where dense, small-text captions under tiny thumbnails reduce legibility and tap-target confidence.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Spotify's broad, global mainstream audience (casual listeners who want frictionless, mood-based music discovery rather than power users building meticulous libraries). The heavy skew toward pop artists (Olivia Rodrigo, Taylor Swift, Gracie Abrams, Ariana Grande) suggests this particular feed instance is tuned for a younger, pop-leaning demographic, demonstrating the algorithm's taste-clustering at work.

Psychologically, the screen exploits choice-reduction (pre-packaged "Mixes" and "Radio" remove the burden of playlist-building), social proof (familiar artist names build instant credibility), and the mere-exposure/familiarity effect (repeated artist imagery across multiple shelves reinforces recognition and trust in the recommendation quality). The "To get you started" framing also targets newer or returning users, easing them back into habitual use via a gentle onboarding-style nudge rather than an empty, intimidating blank canvas.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Content-type chip bar at the very top instantly re-scopes the entire home feed (Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks) without navigating away (a fast, low-friction filter layered over a recommendation engine).
  • Color-blocked, photo-forward tiles on a black canvas create strong shelf-to-shelf visual distinction and make the dense grid feel curated and editorial rather than cluttered.
  • Mixed card typologies (Radio stations vs. Artist Mixes) within the same scroll pattern teach the user multiple content formats using one consistent interaction model (tap to play), reducing learning cost.
  • "Start listening" continue-row at the bottom acts as a lightweight resume point, echoing the persistent mini-player and reinforcing one-tap re-engagement.
  • Artist-name captions under every tile provide just enough contextual metadata for an informed, confident tap without requiring a secondary screen view.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 14
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any content-heavy, habit-forming app (music, video, news, shopping) where:

  • You have rich behavioral/listening/viewing data to power personalization.
  • Users return frequently and benefit from near-zero-decision re-entry points.
  • Content can be visually represented (cover art, thumbnails) to support fast recognition-based browsing over text-based decision making.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The app has sparse or no historical user data (new users will see empty or generic, low-relevance shelves, eroding trust in personalization).
  • Content needs to be consumed in strict chronological or sequential order (e.g., task managers, financial transaction logs) - algorithmic shelves obscure recency and completeness.
  • Accessibility or low-vision contexts are a priority, since dense horizontal carousels with small truncated text are harder to navigate via screen readers or keyboard-only input.
  • The brand needs a curated, editorial-first storefront feel rather than an infinite, algorithmically-reordered browse experience.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets returning, habitual users rather than new sign-ups (it assumes a rich listening history and uses it immediately (the entire feed is personalized off known favorites)). The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Choice reduction / decision fatigue relief: by pre-curating stations and mixes, Spotify removes the paradox-of-choice friction from a catalog of 100M+ tracks.
  • Mere-exposure & familiarity bias: repeatedly surfacing the same favorite artists (Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo) across different shelf types builds trust in the algorithm and increases click-through likelihood.
  • Momentum/resumption bias: the "Start listening" row exploits the Zeigarnik effect (an incomplete/previously started listening session is more compelling to resume than to start fresh).
screens.keyHighlights:
Key UX decisions worth stealing:

  • Top segmented pills as a lightweight feed filter: switching between Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks without a full page navigation or loss of scroll context.
  • Color-coded cards per shelf row: distinct saturated backgrounds (coral/mint/cyan) make each horizontal carousel instantly distinguishable from its neighbors even on a quick scroll.
  • Artist-list microcopy as implicit social/taste proof: reusing recognizable names (Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo) across multiple shelves reinforces personalization credibility.
  • "Start listening" resume row: placed last but functionally first-priority, it's a near-zero-effort way to re-engage with recently played content, using an overflow menu (•••) for secondary actions instead of cluttering the row.
  • Dense, scroll-first density: no onboarding chrome or empty states; the screen is 100% content, which is ideal for a daily-habit app where returning users want immediate value.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 15
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any content-rich, habitual-use app (media, streaming, news aggregators) where the primary goal is fast re-engagement rather than deep navigation. It's ideal when you have multiple content types that benefit from cross-promotion, and when personalization/recency can meaningfully reduce the user's search burden. The segmented filter-plus-carousel-shelves approach also works well for apps transitioning from single-content-type to multi-content-type offerings.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, shelf-based home pattern for simple, single-purpose apps where a flat list or singular focused screen would reduce cognitive load. It's also unsuitable for first-time or low-content users (brand-new accounts without listening history will see sparse or awkward empty shelves, requiring a separate cold-start/onboarding strategy). Additionally, this pattern can overwhelm users seeking a specific item rather than passive browsing, who would be better served by a search-first entry point.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Spotify's full worldwide user base, especially habitual daily listeners who want frictionless re-entry into music/podcasts rather than active discovery. The psychological driver is the reduction of decision fatigue: by surfacing recently played and recommended content immediately, Spotify exploits the "path of least resistance" - pressing play is easier than choosing what to play, directly matching the app's core design philosophy.

The avatar notification dot and "Good Hang with Amy Po.." badge leverage curiosity-gap and social/novelty cues to pull users deeper into unexplored shelves, while the segmented filter caters to users with singular intent (e.g., podcast-only listeners) without forcing them into a separate app section.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-decision resumption grid: The top row of recent/continue items requires no scrolling or searching (users can resume exactly where they left off within one tap of opening the app).
  • Inline filter chips: The All/Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks segmented control reshapes the entire home feed instantly without navigation, giving a sense of control without complexity.
  • Graceful offline empty state: Rather than blocking the UI with an error, the offline notice is presented as just another shelf in the feed, maintaining flow and app usability perception.
  • Mixed content shelving: Podcasts, radio stations, and personalized DJ features are shelved together using identical card patterns, letting Spotify cross-merchandise disparate content types seamlessly.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 16
screens.whereToUse: Use this shelf-based, dual-axis home pattern for any content-rich app where the primary job is "reduce time-to-first-engagement" rather than "support deep deliberate search" - e.g., streaming (video/audio/podcasts), news aggregators, e-commerce homepages, or any app with a strong recommendation engine. It's ideal when you have multiple distinct personalization signals (recent activity, trending, genre-based) that don't fit into a single ranked list and benefit from being segmented into legible, labelled groups.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for task-oriented or utility apps (banking, productivity, settings) where users arrive with a specific goal (shelf browsing adds unnecessary scanning cost when users need direct, predictable paths. It also underperforms for small catalogs: if there isn't enough distinct content to fill multiple meaningfully different rails, the shelves will feel repetitive or sparse, exposing the recommendation engine's weaknesses rather than hiding them. Finally, be cautious embedding temporary campaigns (like Wrapped) as persistent navigation chips if the campaign isn't genuinely timely) stale promotional chips erode trust in the personalization system.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is engineered for Spotify's broadest possible segment: casual-to-habitual listeners who want frictionless audio, not crate-diggers who want to browse a catalog. The design leans heavily on the psychological principle of choice reduction: presenting 3 confident picks instead of a blank search bar reduces decision fatigue and shortens the time-to-first-play, which correlates directly with session length and retention.

The "Recents" and "Based on your recent listening" shelves exploit the mere-exposure and consistency principles, showing content the user has already engaged with increases the likelihood of re-engagement because it requires zero cognitive evaluation of whether the content is "good." The Wrapped chip taps into social/temporal relevance (a culturally-charged seasonal event) to re-activate dormant interest and drive sharing behavior later in the funnel.
screens.keyHighlights:
Several micro-decisions on this screen are worth stealing:

  • Decision-removal design: By pre-populating "Start listening" with three concrete, named tracks instead of a generic "Resume" button, Spotify removes the single biggest point of friction in media apps (choosing what to play) using algorithmic confidence instead of user effort.
  • Dual-axis scroll economy: Stacking independently-scrolling horizontal rails inside one vertical feed allows an almost unlimited number of personalization contexts to be surfaced on one screen without overwhelming the user, since each rail is optional to explore.
  • Overflow menu on recommendation rows: The persistent ••• next to each "Start listening" track gives users an escape hatch (e.g., "not interested," add to playlist) right at the point of recommendation, which both improves control and quietly feeds the recommender system more signal.
  • Campaign-as-filter-chip: Embedding "Wrapped" as a selectable chip in the primary navigational filter row (rather than as a separate banner) lets a seasonal marketing push feel like a native, integrated part of the experience rather than an interruption.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 17
screens.whereToUse:
Use this shelf-based home pattern when:

  • Your product aggregates large, heterogeneous content libraries (media, shopping, learning) that benefit from multiple parallel recommendation algorithms.
  • You need a single landing screen that serves both returning/habitual users (resume content) and discovery-seeking users (recommended content) simultaneously.
  • Visual thumbnails are strong, recognizable brand/content assets that can carry meaning without heavy text labels.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Your content catalog is small or narrow: shelves will feel redundant or sparse, exposing an empty-feeling product.
  • Users need a single, linear primary action (e.g., task-based utility apps, checkout flows) - horizontal carousels add unnecessary navigational complexity.
  • Accessibility/screen-reader users are a primary audience (nested horizontal scrolling grids are notoriously harder to navigate via assistive tech than linear lists).
  • You lack sufficient behavioral data to personalize shelves meaningfully, which would default users to the same generic/static ordering, losing the pattern's core value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Spotify's broadest possible audience (from casual music listeners to dedicated podcast binge-listeners) by using behavioral personalization rather than demographic targeting. The psychological trigger at play is the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to finish unfinished tasks): surfacing "Recents" first exploits the itch to continue an interrupted playlist or episode.

The "Your shows" and "Episodes you might like" shelves leverage habit formation and variable reward: mixing guaranteed, subscribed content (predictable reward) with fresh recommendations (variable reward) in the same scroll session, a core mechanic for maximizing daily active usage and session length.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Content-type segmented control pinned at the top lets users instantly re-scope the entire home feed (Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks) without navigating away (a lightweight filter that prevents content-type fatigue).
  • Recency-first shelf ordering: "Recents" appears before any algorithmic discovery content, optimizing for the single most common use case: resuming what you were just listening to.
  • Dense, image-forward grid with minimal text maximizes scanability; users recognize album/show art faster than they can read titles, leveraging visual memory over literal reading.
  • Avatar-as-nav-item in the top-left doubles as profile entry and establishes personalization/identity framing right where the eye lands first.
  • Four-item tab bar keeps the global navigation surface minimal, reducing decision fatigue and keeping "Home" as the obvious default re-entry point.

screens.name: Lemon8 - Watching a story - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this staggered grid + dual-navigation pattern for content-discovery apps where the primary job is inspiration and browsing rather than linear reading (e).g., shopping discovery, recipe apps, interior design, travel planning, or portfolio/mood-board tools. It's ideal when content pieces are highly visual and heterogeneous in shape/aspect ratio, and when you want to surface both a personalized algorithmic feed and manual topic browsing from a single home screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for task-oriented or utility apps (banking, productivity, messaging) where predictability and scanning order matter more than visual novelty (masonry grids disrupt left-to-right/top-to-bottom reading order and can hurt accessibility and screen-reader navigation). It's also a poor fit for content that is primarily text-based or requires consistent card sizing for comparison (e.g., pricing, job listings), since irregular heights make it harder to compare items at a glance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This feed is engineered for Gen Z and young millennial lifestyle enthusiasts who browse for aesthetic inspiration (home décor, beauty, food) in short, visually driven sessions. The masonry layout and cover-style thumbnails exploit the same browsing psychology as Pinterest (the "treasure hunt" effect, where irregular card heights and varied content types create unpredictable rewards, encouraging continued scrolling (a variable-ratio reinforcement loop)).

The emphasis on everyday creators (avatars, first names, relatable captions) rather than polished influencers builds parasocial trust and aspirational-but-attainable appeal (viewers believe "I could do this too," which is a strong psychological trigger for both continued consumption and eventual content creation, fueling Lemon8's creator flywheel).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Staggered Masonry Grid: Variable-height cards create visual rhythm and make the feed feel editorial/curated rather than templated, directly differentiating Lemon8 from square-grid competitors.
  • Dual-Layer Navigation (Feed Type + Topic): Stacking an algorithmic/social toggle above a horizontally scrollable topic chip rail lets users refine content on two axes instantly, without filters or menus.
  • Magazine-Style Cover Art as Thumbnail: Many cards use custom typographic covers (e.g., "Welcome," "WHY I THREW OUT ALL OF MY CANDLES") instead of raw photos, borrowing print-magazine cover conventions to boost click-through and stand out in a dense grid.
  • Highlighted FAB-style Create Button: The yellow-filled "+" icon breaks pattern from the rest of the monochrome tab bar, serving as a persistent, impossible-to-miss creation prompt that sustains the content supply loop.
  • Lightweight Social Proof: Each card discloses author avatar/name and a heart count, giving just enough credibility and popularity signal without cluttering the card with full engagement bars (comments, shares, etc.).

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Deleting & Removing 1
screens.whereToUse: Utilize this pattern for any list-based content that requires chronological logging and individual item management, such as browser history, search history, or transaction logs. It is ideal when users need to revisit previous states quickly without bookmarking every item, and when list decluttering (deletion) is a common secondary action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for critical, irreversible actions where a single swipe might be triggered accidentally (e.g., deleting a wallet seed phrase or confirming a crypto transaction). Additionally, if the target audience is less tech-savvy or unfamiliar with swipe gestures, relying solely on hidden actions without a visible "Edit" mode alternative could hide functionality and hurt discoverability.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves the "Busy Urban" persona who uses the wallet's dApp browser for frequent DeFi activities (like swapping tokens on PancakeSwap). Since crypto users often visit dozens of specific dApp URLs that are hard to remember or type manually, this history feature acts as a safety net for quick re-access.

Psychologically, the swipe-to-delete pattern taps into privacy concerns specific to crypto users; since financial dApp interactions can be sensitive, users are given an easy, discoverable way to clear specific traces of their activity without needing to dig through settings menus.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Familiar Mental Model: Adopting the standard mobile browser "History" list UI removes the learning curve for users navigating decentralized applications.

  • Non-Destructive Default View: Hiding delete controls behind a swipe gesture keeps the primary list clean and scannable, only exposing high-risk actions (deletion) upon deliberate user intent.

  • Metadata Hierarchy: Clear visual separation between the human-readable Site Title and the machine-readable URL/Timestamp aids quick scanning.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Deleting & Removing 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for any list-based screen (history, favorites, cart, notifications) that can legitimately be empty for new users.

  • Ideal when you want to convert a potentially discouraging "nothing here" moment into a motivational nudge toward a core action.

  • Effective in consumer-facing apps with a friendly or adventurous brand voice (travel, lifestyle, social, discovery apps).

  • Pair with a custom illustration that visually explains the screen's purpose to reduce reliance on text alone.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid overly casual copy ("Get out there and start exploring") in enterprise, financial, or medical contexts where users expect precise, neutral language.

  • Do not use a generic empty state illustration if the underlying feature is complex (consider adding a direct CTA button (e).g., "Start Browsing") rather than relying solely on passive suggestion.

  • Not suitable if the history list can be pre-populated with system-generated or synced data, where an empty state would rarely be seen and investment in custom illustration isn't justified.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets first-time users or users who have recently cleared their browsing history, most commonly within browser, maps, or travel-discovery apps. The design leverages the psychological principle of reframing absence as opportunity: rather than making the user feel like something is "missing" or "broken," the copy and illustration together trigger a sense of anticipation and invitation to engage with the core product (browsing/exploring).

The use of a friendly, informal tone ("Get out there") suggests the target demographic is casual consumers rather than enterprise/professional users, who typically respond well to encouraging, low-friction language that reduces the intimidation of an empty interface.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Purposeful, on-brand illustration: The browser-window-with-clock icon visually reinforces the concept of "history" instantly, reducing cognitive load.

  • Encouraging micro-copy: "No history yet" + "Get out there and start exploring" reframes an empty/negative state into a motivational, action-inviting moment.

  • Consistent chrome: Top bar and bottom tab bar remain fully functional and visible, preventing the empty state from feeling like a broken or dead-end screen.

  • Dark theme with high-contrast accent illustration: The light-blue illustration pops against the black background, drawing the eye directly to the focal point without visual clutter.

results.query: Compare account deletion friction between Brilliant and Dave

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any account/profile settings hub where users need to view and edit a small number of personal data fields alongside higher-stakes account lifecycle actions (export, deactivate, delete). It's ideal for:

  • Apps with GDPR/CCPA data export or deletion requirements.
  • Products prioritizing trust and transparency over retention tactics.
  • Any screen where visual calm and low cognitive load are priorities (education, wellness, productivity apps).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat, undifferentiated styling when:

  • Destructive actions carry severe, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., financial account closure) - these typically warrant stronger visual warning cues (red text, icons) and additional confirmation friction.
  • The settings list grows large (15+ items): at that scale, labeled section headers and search/filter become necessary instead of relying on dividers alone.
  • Regulatory or legal contexts require more prominent disclosure before data export/deletion, where a neutral chevron row may be seen as insufficiently informative.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Brilliant's audience is self-directed, intrinsically motivated learners (students, professionals, hobbyist problem-solvers) who value efficiency and clarity over flashy gamification. This settings screen caters to that same mindset: it respects the user's time and intelligence by not over-explaining or decorating basic account management.

Psychologically, grouping sensitive actions (export, delete) separately from everyday identity fields reduces the "fear of accidental taps" - users scanning for "Password" won't fear brushing against "Delete account" because of the clear visual separation. The neutral tone around deletion also reduces reactance; by not guilt-tripping or hiding the exit, Brilliant signals confidence in its product's value, which paradoxically builds trust and retention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Three-tier grouping via dividers: Separates identity, credentials, and account-lifecycle actions into clear risk tiers without needing labeled section headers, keeping the screen visually calm.
  • Non-alarming destructive action: "Deactivate or delete account" uses the same typography and black text as benign rows instead of red warning styling, avoiding unnecessary anxiety while still being fully accessible/transparent.
  • Consistent drill-down affordance: Every row uses the same chevron-and-value pattern, making the entire screen instantly scannable and predictable on first glance.
  • Privacy-aware masking: Password is hidden entirely (no value shown) while email is partially visible, reflecting sensible information-sensitivity tiering.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any subscription or account-based product's offboarding/deactivation flow, particularly when:

  • You want structured churn analytics without resorting to intrusive exit surveys or forced phone calls.
  • The brand value proposition relies on trust and non-manipulative design (e.g., education, wellness, productivity apps).
  • You want to close the loop gracefully, preserving goodwill for potential win-back campaigns later.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this exact pattern when:

  • The business genuinely needs a retention intervention (e.g., presenting a discount, pause option, or feature education) - in those cases, a reason selector should precede a tailored save-attempt screen rather than go straight to confirmation.
  • The checkbox list is so long or granular that it creates decision fatigue right as the user wants to leave quickly (simplicity and speed should be prioritized in exit flows).
  • Legal/compliance requirements mandate additional verification steps (e.g., re-authentication) before deactivation, which this screen does not surface.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already decided to leave (at this point, persuasion is futile and potentially damaging to brand perception). Instead, the design targets the company's internal product and growth teams as the secondary "audience," optimizing for structured churn-reason data collection. Psychologically, offering a reason selector gives departing users a sense of closure and voice, which can reduce negative word-of-mouth even among churned users ("they asked why, and listened").

The inclusion of options like "I am spending too much time on Brilliant" also signals self-awareness toward digital wellbeing-conscious users, appealing to the global, reflective STEM-learner demographic who may value a company that doesn't shame them for setting boundaries.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reframing churn as contribution: The headline positions the act of leaving as helpful to "future generations," softening the emotional friction of deactivation.
  • Multi-select checkboxes over radio buttons: Allows richer, more honest qualitative signal since churn is rarely caused by a single factor.
  • No dark patterns or last-minute discount offers: The screen respects user intent rather than inserting manipulative retention interstitials, which builds long-term brand trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Consistent minimalist chrome: Reusing the same top bar, typography, and spacing system as the rest of the app keeps even a "negative" flow feeling coherent and non-jarring.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any account-deletion or subscription-cancellation flow where:

  • You want structured, qualitative churn data without adding friction that feels manipulative.
  • Users need to choose between reversible (deactivate) and irreversible (delete) actions, and the distinction must be crystal clear.
  • Brand trust and long-term reputation (word-of-mouth, win-back potential) matter more than squeezing out one more retention save.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this low-friction approach if the business model depends heavily on short-term retention saves (e.g., subscription services with aggressive LTV targets) - some products legitimately need a single, well-crafted retention offer before this screen. Also avoid mixing checkbox and radio semantics on the same screen without a visual divider, as it can confuse users about whether multiple selections are allowed. Finally, never allow a "permanent delete" radio option without the explicit irreversibility disclaimer used here, as that invites support disputes and reduces trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves users who have already decided to leave (the target "demographic" here is a departing user, often someone who found Brilliant too difficult, redundant (duplicate accounts), privacy-conscious, or time-constrained). Pre-checked example states (shown with checkmarks) in the mock suggest common real-world churn reasons: difficulty, accidental duplicate accounts, and privacy concerns, implying Brilliant's actual churn data skews toward perceived difficulty and account-hygiene issues rather than lack of perceived value.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the sunk-cost-free exit principle (by not fighting the departure, Brilliant preserves brand goodwill and increases the odds of a future "boomerang" return (reinforced by the "temporarily deactivate" option)). The privacy-concern checkbox also signals awareness that STEM/edtech audiences (often data-conscious, intellectually engaged users) care about data ownership, hence offering a hard-delete path with explicit irreversibility language builds long-term trust even in the exit moment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Exit research, not exit prevention: No retention offer, discount, or guilt-trip modal precedes the actual deactivation choice (the product respects the user's decision and instead optimizes for learning).
  • Checkbox vs. radio button semantic clarity: Switching input type from checkboxes (top, multi-select reasons) to radio buttons (bottom, single-select severity) communicates selection rules without needing any instructional copy.
  • Transparent irreversibility disclosure: Explicitly stating deletion "can't be recovered, even by staff" removes ambiguity and builds trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Two-tier choice architecture: Separating "why" from "how severe" into two distinct question blocks, divided by a hairline rule, prevents cognitive overload and keeps the one-idea-per-section rhythm consistent with the app's lesson design philosophy.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any account deletion or cancellation flow where you want to (1) capture structured churn-reason data for product improvement, (2) differentiate between reversible and irreversible actions, and (3) add a final security/intent-confirmation gate. It's especially valuable for subscription, education, or SaaS products where re-engagement after a "cool-off" period is possible and worth protecting via a temporary deactivation default.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, multi-step flow for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., unsubscribing from a newsletter), where the added friction would feel punitive and out of proportion to risk. Also avoid for apps with no account recovery infrastructure, where offering a "temporary" option would be misleading. If legal/compliance requires immediate, frictionless deletion (e.g., GDPR right-to-erasure requests), this length of flow may need to be shortened or supplemented with a direct deletion path.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who have already decided to leave (learners who found the STEM content too difficult, privacy-conscious users, or those who created accidental duplicate accounts). Rather than fighting churn with dark patterns, Brilliant leans into transparency and data collection, which suits its brand as a trustworthy, pedagogically serious edtech platform aimed at a global, education-first audience.

Psychologically, the screen leverages loss aversion (bold warning about permanent, unrecoverable deletion) and commitment/consistency (requiring users to articulate their reason and re-enter a password) to slow impulsive cancellations while still respecting user autonomy (an ethical approach appropriate for an app whose value proposition is built on sustained, deliberate practice).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multi-select churn survey captures granular, actionable reasons for leaving before the deletion flow proceeds, turning an offboarding moment into a product-research opportunity.
  • Asymmetric default framing between "temporarily deactivate" and "permanently delete" nudges users toward reversible action without removing agency.
  • Password re-authentication gate as a final friction point, preventing impulsive, accidental, or malicious deletions.
  • Explicit irreversibility warning ("can't be recovered, even by staff") sets honest expectations and builds institutional trust even at the moment of loss.
  • Consistent one-idea-per-screen minimalism is preserved even in a utilitarian settings flow, keeping cognitive load low despite the emotionally charged context.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this multi-stage confirmation pattern (reason → reversibility choice → re-authentication → consequence disclosure → final action) for any high-stakes, irreversible user action: account deletion, financial withdrawal, data purge, or subscription cancellation with sunk-cost implications (e.g., losing saved progress or paid content).

It is especially valuable in subscription-based products where deletion has a secondary financial consequence (active billing) that users may not immediately realize.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, multi-step friction pattern for low-risk or reversible actions (e.g., removing a single saved item, logging out, or unsubscribing from a single notification type) - excessive friction on low-stakes tasks frustrates users and feels punitive rather than protective.

Also avoid requiring password re-entry if the user already recently re-authenticated in the same session, as redundant verification steps increase abandonment without adding security value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves users who have already decided to leave (likely frustrated, overwhelmed, or re-prioritizing their time) and targets two underlying psychological needs: agency (the explicit choice between temporary vs. permanent action respects that not everyone wants to fully sever ties) and trust (radical transparency about irreversibility and billing consequences signals the company isn't trying to trap or trick them).

For Brilliant specifically, whose brand promise is calm, focused, friction-light learning, maintaining that same respectful, low-pressure tone even during offboarding reinforces brand integrity (a company that is honest when you're leaving is more likely to be trusted if you return).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Password re-authentication gate: Converts a single destructive tap into a two-factor-like confirmation, preventing accidental or unauthorized deletion.
  • Inline password-reset recovery link: Solves the "I forgot my password and now I'm stuck" dead-end proactively within the flow itself.
  • Transparent subscription-cancellation disclosure: Surfaces a consequential business fact at the precise decision moment instead of hiding it in fine print, respecting informed consent.
  • Color-coded severity: The lone coral-red button amid an otherwise monochrome screen visually isolates risk without needing extra copy.
  • Reason capture before action: Collecting churn reasons (visible above the fold scroll) turns an exit into usable product feedback data.

screens.name: Brilliant - Deleting account - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
• First-touch splash/welcome screens for subscription or edtech apps where the product's core mechanic (interactivity, motion, hands-on learning) can be visually encoded into the hero graphic itself.
  • Apps that want to differentiate from generic stock-photo onboarding by using brand-specific illustration or kinetic typography.
  • Funnels where you want to softly bias users toward sign-up while still offering a low-friction path back to sign-in.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Apps where the core value proposition is emotional or social (e.g., dating, social networking) - an abstract typographic illustration would fail to build the human connection those categories require.
  • B2B or enterprise tools where users expect immediate utility/functional clarity rather than brand storytelling on the first screen (this pattern spends a full screen on persuasion before any functional UI is shown, which could frustrate task-driven users).
  • Contexts where regulatory or compliance screens (e.g., consent, age-gating) must appear before any marketing content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets a broad, worldwide audience of self-directed learners (likely skewing toward curious professionals, students, and lifelong learners who are often comparing Brilliant against competitors like Duolingo, Khan Academy, or Coursera in an app store search). Because this is the very first impression, the design leans heavily on the von Restorff effect (the oversized, unusual typographic illustration stands out from typical SaaS/EdTech splash screens that use photos of smiling people) to create immediate brand memorability.

The "15 minutes a day" claim taps into the psychological principle of minimal viable commitment: by framing the ask as small and time-boxed, it lowers the perceived barrier to trying the product, which is critical for conversion at the top of a mobile acquisition funnel where attention spans are short and competing apps are one tap away.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Typography-as-illustration: Instead of screenshots or stock imagery, the brand's core differentiator (interactivity) is literally woven into the headline using fake drag-tags, axes, and dotted plot lines (a highly original and on-brand way to visualize "doing" rather than "watching)."
  • Single, unmissable CTA: One full-bleed green button with no competing buttons of equal visual weight (removes decision paralysis at the most critical conversion point of the funnel).
  • Specific, benefit-driven subcopy: "Get smarter in 15 minutes a day" quantifies the value proposition, making an abstract benefit (intelligence growth) feel concrete and attainable.
  • Deferred sign-in: "Sign in" is present but visually subordinate, correctly prioritizing new-user acquisition while not alienating returning users.

screens.name: Brilliant Account 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this stacked, sectioned settings pattern whenever an app has a moderate-to-large number of configuration options that need to be organized without overwhelming the user. It's ideal for:

  • Account/profile management hubs

  • Apps needing a dedicated monetization entry point (Premium/Upgrade) within a trusted, low-pressure context

  • Any screen mixing instant toggles (sound, haptics) with deeper navigational settings (notifications, account)

  • Products wanting to visually separate frequent settings from rare/destructive actions (logout, legal)
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat list pattern when:

  • The number of settings is very small (2-3 items) - a simpler single section suffices and extra grouping adds unnecessary visual noise.

  • Settings require rich contextual explanation per item (this layout has no room for descriptive subtext, which could confuse users on ambiguous toggles).

  • The product is complex/enterprise-grade and needs search or categorized tabs for dozens of settings (a flat scroll becomes unwieldy past ~15-20 items).

  • Destructive actions like "Delete Account" need more friction/visibility (this minimal de-emphasized styling is appropriate for "Log out" but should not be reused for truly irreversible, high-stakes actions without additional confirmation safeguards).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets mainstream consumer app users (likely a language-learning, wellness, or gamified habit app given the playful icon style) who need quick, low-friction access to account, monetization, and preference controls. The psychological driver is predictability and reduced cognitive load: by mimicking the native iOS Settings paradigm, the designer leverages users' pre-existing mental models so zero learning curve is required. Placing "Premium" high in the list exploits the mere exposure effect and proximity to account management to nudge free users toward conversion during a moment when they're already engaging with app configuration (a natural reflection point about their relationship with the product).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual affordance system: Chevrons for navigational drill-down vs. toggles for instant state changes lets users instantly distinguish "this opens another screen" from "this changes a setting right now" without reading extra copy.

  • Three-tier visual hierarchy via grouping and whitespace: Primary settings, support/info links, and destructive/meta actions are separated purely with spacing and dividers (no heavy borders or color needed).

  • De-emphasized destructive actions: "Log out" is given no icon, no container, and muted styling, reducing accidental logouts while still being easily reachable at the bottom.

  • Modal dismissal via "X": Correctly signals this Settings screen is a temporary overlay, reinforcing a mental model of "I can always close this and return to where I was."

  • Premium entry placed near the top, directly under Account, maximizing visibility for monetization without being obnoxious or forced.

screens.name: Brilliant Account 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this grouped stacked-list pattern for any account/profile management screen where users need to view and edit personal identity fields, credentials, and perform rare, high-stakes actions. Ideal for settings hubs, admin profile pages, or any CRUD-style preference screen where scannability and predictability matter more than visual flourish. Also appropriate whenever regulatory compliance (GDPR/CCPA) requires exposing data export and account deletion options clearly.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimalist list style when fields require rich context, previews, or validation feedback inline (e.g., password strength, profile photo cropping) - those need dedicated editing screens or inline components. Do not bury destructive actions at the bottom if your product has legal/UX requirements for more prominent warnings (e.g., financial or healthcare apps may need explicit red flagging even at the list level). Also avoid this flat layout for screens with more than 8-10 settings, where sectioned headers and search become necessary to prevent scroll fatigue.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets all authenticated users managing their personal account, especially those who are privacy-conscious or need to update credentials periodically. The design leverages the psychological principle of reduced cognitive load through familiarity: by mimicking native iOS Settings conventions, users immediately understand how to interact without onboarding. Placing destructive actions last exploits spatial memory and friction-by-distance: users must deliberately scroll/reach further down, reducing impulsive account deletion. The inclusion of "Export your data" signals trust and regulatory compliance, which can reduce user anxiety about lock-in (a known churn-reduction/trust-building tactic).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Logical grouping via whitespace/dividers: Separates identity, credentials, and account-lifecycle actions without needing heavy visual containers, keeping the page light.

  • Deferred alarm color: The destructive "Deactivate or delete account" action is not colored red on this list screen, avoiding premature anxiety; the warning is reserved for the confirmation step (progressive disclosure of risk).

  • Consistent chevron affordance: Every row uses the same right-chevron, teaching the user a single predictable interaction model across all items regardless of destination type (edit field vs. navigate to sub-flow).

  • Transparency-first data controls: "Export your data" is given equal visual weight to profile fields, normalizing data portability as a standard, non-scary account feature.

screens.name: Brilliant - Changing password - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this grouped stacked-list pattern for any account/settings index screen where multiple categories of user data (profile, security, legal/data rights) need to coexist without overwhelming the user. It's ideal for apps that value a minimal, native-feeling settings experience, especially subscription or learning apps where trust and transparency around data are critical to conversion and retention. It also works well as a template for any screen that aggregates several single-field edit flows behind one entry point.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when settings require more context per item (e.g., showing descriptions, toggles with explanatory subtext, or multi-value previews) - the single-line row format would feel cramped. It's also unsuitable for highly destructive actions that require extra friction or warning; burying "Deactivate or delete account" in a neutral row with no visual distinction could be risky in contexts where accidental taps carry higher stakes (e.g., financial accounts), and a more explicit warning treatment (red text, separate section) would be safer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves any authenticated user who needs to manage core account hygiene tasks: updating personal info, securing their password, or exercising data rights. Given Brilliant's worldwide, STEM-learning audience (likely privacy-conscious, education-minded adults), the explicit inclusion of "Export your data" signals compliance maturity and builds trust with a global, regulation-aware user base (GDPR in EU, CCPA in US, etc.).

The psychological trigger at play is control and transparency: by clearly surfacing account deletion and data export as first-class, easily discoverable options rather than hiding them deep in nested menus, the app reduces user anxiety about being "locked in," which paradoxically increases trust and retention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grouped sectioning with whitespace dividers: Splits identity, security, and account-lifecycle actions into distinct visual clusters without needing headers, keeping the screen uncluttered.
  • Index-only pattern: Current values are shown read-only inline (e.g., "Sam Lee," "25") with navigation to dedicated edit screens, preventing accidental in-place edits and keeping the screen lightweight.
  • Calm treatment of destructive actions: "Deactivate or delete account" uses the same visual weight as benign rows, avoiding alarm fatigue while still being clearly labeled and accessible.
  • Truncated email display: Long email addresses are truncated with an ellipsis rather than wrapping or breaking layout, preserving the single-line rhythm of the list.

screens.name: Brilliant - Changing password - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any account security or credential-management flow (password, PIN, or passphrase changes).
  • Settings areas where the cost of error is high and users benefit from explicit, calm guidance.
  • Flows where disabling a CTA until all validation passes can meaningfully reduce failed submissions.
  • Any screen where changing a value will have a non-obvious side effect (e.g., session termination) that deserves proactive disclosure.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this static, no-feedback approach for high-friction forms where users need real-time password strength or match validation (this screen notably lacks inline validation cues, which could frustrate users who only discover a mismatch after tapping submit).
  • Not suitable for lower-stakes preference changes where such heavy warning banners would feel like overkill.
  • Don't reuse this stripped-down, charmless tone on consumer-facing marketing or learning screens where the brand's playful identity should be present.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves any authenticated user managing account security, a low-frequency but high-stakes task. Because trust and clarity are paramount here, the design leans on established security UX conventions (current + new + confirm password fields, session logout warning) rather than inventing novel interaction patterns (users expect this screen to look exactly like every other password-change screen they've used, so familiarity itself is the psychological trigger reducing anxiety).

The warning banner specifically targets the fear of being "locked out" or confused by losing access on other devices, addressing a real support-ticket-generating pain point before it occurs.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled-until-valid CTA: The greyed-out "Change password" button enforces correctness before submission is even possible, preventing wasted round trips to the server.
  • Proactive consequence messaging: Informing users upfront that other sessions will be logged out removes surprise and builds trust, rather than discovering this after the fact.
  • Required-field asterisks in brand accent color: Subtle use of the app's coral accent for required markers keeps the screen visually calm while still flagging mandatory fields.
  • Single-purpose screen: No unrelated settings, toggles, or distractions, reinforcing the "one idea per screen" design law seen throughout Brilliant.

screens.name: Brilliant - Changing password - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any sensitive account-security form (password changes, email changes, 2FA setup) where:

  • The user needs undivided focus on a short, linear task.
  • A side-effect of the action (like forced logout, data loss, or irreversible change) needs to be communicated before submission to avoid user confusion.
  • You want to minimize decision fatigue by presenting exactly one primary action and no distracting navigation.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this minimal single-column approach when:

  • The form requires real-time password strength feedback or complex validation rules (this screen lacks inline validation, which could lead to failed submissions and user frustration on first attempt).
  • Multiple related settings need to be changed together (e.g., security + notification preferences), where a more dashboard-like, multi-section layout would be more efficient.
  • The audience is less tech-savvy and may need additional guidance (e.g., password requirement hints like minimum length or character rules) directly adjacent to the input field rather than relying on post-submission error states.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves any authenticated user performing an account security maintenance task (typically triggered by a forgotten-password flow follow-up, a periodic security prompt, or voluntary account hygiene). Because Brilliant's audience skews toward self-directed learners who value efficiency and low friction (a STEM-focused, "do rather than watch" userbase), the screen is engineered to be completed in seconds without hand-holding.

The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion mitigation: by warning users upfront about being logged out everywhere, the design prevents the negative emotional reaction of surprise logout, which could otherwise be misread as a bug or security breach. This builds continued trust in the platform's handling of sensitive account data.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive Security Disclosure: The amber banner explaining the device logout consequence is placed before the user commits, turning a potentially confusing side-effect into an expected, trust-building outcome.
  • High-Contrast, Single Primary Action: The full-width black pill button removes any ambiguity about what to do next, and its singular presence (no secondary "cancel" button) keeps the screen decision-light.
  • Visual Hierarchy via Color-Coded Required Markers: Small red asterisks efficiently communicate validation requirements without needing explanatory microcopy under every field.
  • Generous Whitespace: The empty space before the CTA prevents visual crowding and keeps the eye moving naturally from problem (password fields) to warning (consequence) to resolution (button).

screens.name: Loom - Logging out - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Reuse this pattern for any settings or account management screen that combines routine account actions with one or more irreversible/destructive actions, such as:

  • Account/profile settings in SaaS, productivity, or collaboration apps
  • Subscription cancellation or data deletion flows
  • Any screen mixing "safe" exits (logout, sign out, archive) with "dangerous" ones (delete, deactivate, permanently remove)

It's particularly effective when you need users to quickly distinguish risk levels at a glance and want to funnel destructive actions through an additional confirmation step.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The destructive action needs much stronger friction (e.g., typing "DELETE" to confirm) - this screen alone is too lightweight if the stakes are extremely high (e.g., deleting an entire organization's data).
  • There are many account-related settings to manage (a flat single-section list won't scale and would need categorized sections, search, or an accordion).
  • The brand doesn't use a color system where red/orange reliably signals danger (e.g., color-blind accessibility concerns should always be paired with iconography or explicit copy, not color alone).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
