This screen serves Loom's broad professional user base (individuals and team members who may need to manage credentials, switch accounts between work/personal emails, or exit the platform entirely (e).g., offboarding from a company, or consolidating tools). Since Loom targets professionals and teams, account email visibility is important for confirming "which identity am I logged in as," a common point of confusion in B2B SaaS tools used across multiple organizations.

The deletion flow specifically caters to users exercising data ownership/control (often driven by privacy regulation awareness like GDPR), or those leaving the platform. Isolating and color-flagging this option leverages loss-aversion psychology and caution-conditioning: red signals danger, prompting users to pause and consider before proceeding, which protects both the user and Loom's support team from accidental, hard-to-reverse requests.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded action hierarchy: blue for benign actions (sign out), red/orange for destructive ones (delete account) - enabling instant risk recognition without reading text.
  • Deliberate spatial isolation: the delete action lives in its own grouped section, separated from account details, reducing accidental selection via Fitts's Law and visual grouping principles.
  • Progressive disclosure for destruction: the chevron on "Delete my account" indicates this leads to a confirmation step rather than instant deletion, respecting the principle that destructive actions should never be a single tap.
  • Minimalist grouped-list layout: uses native platform conventions (iOS settings style) so the screen feels instantly familiar and trustworthy, lowering cognitive load for a sensitive task.

screens.name: Loom - Logging out - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for moderate-consequence, easily reversible actions such as signing out, discarding unsaved changes, leaving a shared document, or removing a non-critical integration. It's ideal when you want to catch accidental taps without fully blocking or heavily penalizing the user with multi-step confirmation flows.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this lightweight dialog pattern for truly irreversible or high-stakes actions (e.g., permanent account deletion, billing cancellation, data purges) - these warrant stronger friction such as typed confirmation text, re-authentication, or a secondary review screen. Overusing simple confirm dialogs for low-risk, frequent actions (e.g., closing a panel) also causes "dialog fatigue," training users to blindly tap through without reading.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Loom's audience is busy professionals and teams who move quickly between devices and accounts. A sign-out confirmation prevents accidental taps (especially on mobile, where fat-finger errors are common) from disrupting an in-progress recording or losing access unexpectedly mid-workflow. The pattern leverages loss-aversion psychology: users pause for a split-second to confirm intent, reducing support tickets and frustration from accidental logouts, while still respecting the user's time with a single-tap resolution either way.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Color-coded button hierarchy: Blue "Cancel" (safe/default) vs. red "Sign Out" (destructive) gives instant visual affordance without needing to read text.
  • Dimmed background scrim: Forces single-task focus and visually subordinates the settings list beneath the decision point.
  • Proportional friction: A lightweight, one-tap-to-cancel dialog is used for a reversible action (sign out), reserving heavier friction for truly destructive actions like account deletion.
  • Grouped settings architecture: Separating benign account info from destructive actions ("Delete my account" in its own isolated row) pre-signals risk before the modal even appears.

screens.name: Loom - Logging out - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern as the opening screen of a value-proposition carousel for any app with a core feature that is visually demonstrable (collaboration tools, creative/media apps, productivity SaaS). It is ideal when you need to communicate a product's primary differentiator before requiring any sign-up commitment, and when you want to support both new-user acquisition and returning-user sign-in from a single, low-friction entry screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy illustrative, multi-screen onboarding approach for utility apps, tools used under time pressure, or returning-user-dominant apps where users expect to land directly on login or their last-used screen (the extra carousel steps would feel like unnecessary friction). Also avoid if the core value proposition cannot be meaningfully illustrated visually, as the mock-UI technique would lose its impact and risk looking generic or decorative.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets busy professionals, remote/distributed teams, and knowledge workers worldwide who are evaluating Loom for the first time, often during a quick app-store driven trial decision. The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Show-don't-tell / concrete imagery bias: people trust and understand a realistic mock screenshot faster than abstract marketing copy, lowering the barrier to understanding what the product actually does within seconds.
  • Social/collaborative cues: the avatar and reaction emojis (👍, 💬) imply other humans are already engaging, subtly invoking social proof and reducing the feeling of a solitary tool.
  • Autonomy and flexibility framing ("wherever, whenever," "on the go") appeals to professionals who value asynchronous work and want to avoid being tied to scheduled meetings (directly aligned with Loom's core pitch of replacing live meetings).
screens.keyHighlights:
Illustrative product preview instead of abstract graphics: showing a mocked real UI (document + video thumbnail + reactions) builds instant product comprehension over generic illustrations.

Two-tone headline typography cleverly splits emphasis between the core value ("Watch & engage," dark/bold) and the flexibility modifier ("wherever, whenever," light gray), guiding the eye and reading rhythm.

Dual-path CTA footer (Sign in / Sign up) removes friction for returning users while still prioritizing acquisition via visual weight on Sign up.

Page-control dots set correct expectations that this is step 1 of a short, skippable multi-screen story, reducing bounce from perceived long commitment.

results.query: Arc Search browse for me AI synthesis versus Shazam quick search

screens.name: Searching 01
screens.whereToUse: Same as the previous screen: fits reinforcing a feature already introduced during onboarding via a hint shown on the live interface at the moment of active engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse: Same as the previous screen: a poor fit if shown repeatedly after first engagement with the feature.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Gmail (Smart Compose hints): shows contextual tooltips as the user is actively typing, not just when a field is idle.

  2. Notion (slash-command hints): surfaces guidance the moment the text cursor becomes active in a relevant field.

  3. YouTube (live coach marks): ties hints to the exact interaction state (e.g., focused search field) rather than a generic screen view.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Just-in-Time Guidance: the active text cursor confirms the hint appears exactly as the user is engaging with the search field, maximizing relevance.

  2. Visibility of System Status: the blinking cursor is a small but clear signal that the field is focused and ready for input, distinct from the unfocused state in the prior screen.

  3. Von Restorff Effect: the single colored "Browse for Me" button remains isolated against three gray duplicates, continuing to direct attention.

  4. Consistency: reusing the identical tooltip, arrow, and layout from the previous screen keeps the hint experience coherent regardless of the exact focus state captured.

screens.name: Searching 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any AI-generated or synthesized-answer feature where processing takes a few seconds, and reassurance that the query was received is more important than a detailed progress indicator.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for longer processing times, where an empty canvas without a spinner, skeleton loader, or progress cue risks feeling broken or unresponsive rather than "in progress."
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (query-submitted loading state): similarly displays the user's query as a heading while the AI-generated answer is still being assembled.

  2. Google Search (Search Generative Experience loading): shows the query at the top with a placeholder/loading area before the AI overview renders.

  3. ChatGPT (prompt-submitted state): echoes the user's input prominently before the response streams in, similar to this heading-first loading treatment.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status: displaying the submitted query prominently while the rest loads reassures the user their input was received, even without a traditional spinner.

  2. Minimal Interruption: keeping the loading state visually quiet (empty gradient, no heavy loading animation) matches the app's broader "stay out of the way" design philosophy noted in earlier onboarding screens.

  3. User Control & Freedom: the Arc/Google toggle gives users an explicit way to bypass the AI-generated answer in favor of a standard search if desired.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law): the bottom three-button toolbar remains unchanged from the app's default browsing chrome, keeping the loading state visually anchored to the rest of the app.

screens.name: Searching 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any AI-synthesis loading state where naming real, credible sources during processing meaningfully builds trust in the eventual output, especially for research-style or fact-based queries.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when the underlying sources are numerous but low-value or undifferentiated (e.g., scraped forum posts with no recognizable authority), where listing them would add noise without building the intended credibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (source-reading loading state): shows a near-identical "reading N sources" list with fading source names while an AI answer is being compiled.

  2. Bing Chat / Copilot (searching-the-web state): displays which sites are being consulted during an AI-generated answer's loading phase for the same transparency purpose.

  3. You.com (AI search loading): surfaces a scrolling or fading list of sources being read as part of its multi-step search-and-synthesize loading sequence.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status: naming the exact number and identity of sources being processed goes beyond generic loading feedback, giving real insight into what's happening.

  2. Trust Through Transparency: surfacing recognizable, reputable domains during the loading state pre-builds credibility for the eventual AI-synthesized answer.

  3. Progressive Disclosure: the list reveals sources incrementally (implied by the fading opacity) rather than dumping all 20 at once, keeping the loading state readable.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law): the query heading, toolbar, and Arc/Google toggle remain in the same position as the prior loading screen, so this reads as a continuation of the same moment rather than a new screen.

screens.name: Searching 04
screens.whereToUse: This layout fits any AI-synthesized answer for a subjective, ranked-list-style query (best movies, top restaurants, recommended products) where visual media, credible sourcing, and concise editorial framing together make the answer more useful than a plain link list.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for factual, single-answer queries (e.g., "what year did X happen") where a rich, multi-section magazine layout would be overkill for content that could be answered in one line.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (finished answer page): uses the same image-carousel-plus-cited-write-up structure once a query finishes processing.

  2. Rotten Tomatoes' own "Certified Fresh" roundup articles: the emoji-and-rating format for individual movie entries closely mirrors this kind of curated critic listicle.

  3. Google's AI Overview (finished state): similarly surfaces source logos and linked cards above a synthesized summary once an AI-generated answer completes.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Progressive Disclosure: the page layers visual (posters) → credibility (source icons/cards) → substance (synthesized write-up), letting users stop scrolling as soon as they have what they need.

  2. Social Proof: recognizable outlet logos (Rotten Tomatoes, Forbes, IMDb) and specific rating percentages lend third-party credibility to AI-generated recommendations.

  3. Scannability: emoji markers and bolded titles let users skim multiple entries quickly rather than reading dense prose top to bottom.

  4. Persistent User Control: keeping the Arc/Google toggle visible even after the answer loads ensures the fallback option isn't buried once its "urgency" (during loading) has passed.

screens.name: Searching 05
screens.whereToUse: This repeated-entry format fits any AI-synthesized ranked or curated list (movies, restaurants, products) where consistency across entries helps users compare items quickly without re-learning the layout each time.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for answers with only one or two items, where imposing a repeated multi-entry structure would feel like unnecessary overhead for content that could be presented more simply.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Rotten Tomatoes' own "Certified Fresh" roundups: use the same rating-plus-blurb-per-entry format this write-up echoes.

  2. Letterboxd list pages: similarly present ranked film entries with a title, a quick descriptor, and consistent visual formatting per item.

  3. Perplexity AI (multi-item answer pages): structures list-style AI answers with the same repeated title/stat/description pattern across several entries.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Consistency (Jakob's Law): identical formatting across all entries lets the user's reading pattern become automatic after the first one or two items.

  2. Scannability: varied, meaningful emoji per entry let users visually differentiate genre/tone at a glance before committing to reading the text.

  3. Persistent Controls: the Arc/Google toggle remaining fixed in place while content scrolls ensures the fallback search option is always accessible without needing to scroll back up.

  4. Chunking: breaking a "top movies" answer into individually bounded entries (rather than one continuous paragraph) makes a long-form AI response digestible in a mobile context.

screens.name: Searching 06
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits long AI-synthesized answers covering multiple related but distinct angles on one topic (e.g., films and their performances), where topical sub-headings help users jump to the specific facet they care about.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for short, single-fact answers where introducing multiple sub-sections would add unnecessary structural overhead to content that doesn't naturally divide into separate topics.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. IMDb "Notable Performances" or awards-season roundup articles: use the same structure of underlined actor names with brief evaluative blurbs.

  2. Rotten Tomatoes editorial roundups: commonly segment a longer piece into named sub-sections (e.g., "Best Films" then "Best Performances") exactly as this page does.

  3. Wikipedia-style long-form AI answers (e.g., Perplexity's "Pro Search"): use inline linked names and topical sub-headings to organize an otherwise long synthesized response.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking with Sub-Headings: introducing a new "Notable Performances" heading partway down a long answer breaks the page into digestible topical sections rather than one continuous scroll.

  2. Affordance Signaling: underlining actor names as links signals they're interactive, inviting deeper exploration without cluttering the page with buttons.

  3. Consistency Across Sub-Sections: reusing the emoji-marker-plus-bolded-name-plus-description format from the movie list keeps the new section visually familiar despite the topic shift.

  4. Content Layering: transitioning toward a directly quoted excerpt (visible at the bottom) after several paraphrased sections suggests the page varies its content type to keep a long answer from feeling monotonous.

screens.name: Searching By Voice 01
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits enabling rapid, repeated searching within a session, where preserving visual continuity with prior results (rather than a hard navigation) helps users feel they can search again without losing their place.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when a new search represents a genuinely distinct task or context switch, where dimming rather than fully clearing the previous content could create confusion about whether the old results are still relevant or active.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Search app (new search overlay): uses a similar sliding sheet that layers a fresh search bar over previous results rather than fully navigating away.

  2. Spotlight Search on iOS: presents an overlay search sheet on top of dimmed background content, closely matching this layered transition pattern.

  3. Notion's quick-find overlay: similarly slides a search input over existing content while keeping the underlying page faintly visible for context.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Continuity of Context: keeping the previous page dimly visible behind the new search sheet reassures the user their prior results haven't been lost.

  2. Minimal Interruption: layering a new search sheet over existing content (rather than a full-screen replace) keeps the interaction feeling fast and non-disruptive.

  3. Visibility of System Status: the raised keyboard and focused cursor make it immediately clear the app is ready for new input.

  4. Progressive Disclosure: presenting an empty search field first, before any suggestions or results, keeps the entry point simple and unopinionated.

screens.name: Searching By Voice 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any voice-assistant entry point layered over existing app content, where a friendly greeting plus live waveform feedback reassures the user their voice is being captured, especially when invoked mid-task from another screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for silent or background voice capture (e.g., always-listening wake-word detection before invocation), where a full-screen animated overlay would be an unnecessary interruption before the user has confirmed intent to speak.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Siri (iOS voice assistant overlay): uses a nearly identical full-screen overlay with an animated orb/avatar and waveform to indicate active listening.

  2. Google Assistant: similarly greets users conversationally and shows a real-time waveform while listening, dimming background content behind the overlay.

  3. Alexa app (voice interaction screen): uses a friendly greeting plus live audio visualization to confirm the assistant is actively receiving speech input.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Anthropomorphism / Personification: the smiley-face avatar and greeting give the voice feature a friendly, approachable "character" rather than presenting it as a bare technical function.

  2. Visibility of System Status: the live waveform and status-bar call indicator together confirm the assistant is actively listening, critical feedback for a voice interface with no visible typed input.

  3. Continuity of Context: dimming rather than fully replacing the previous results page keeps the user oriented to what they were doing before invoking voice search.

  4. Conversational Design: greeting the user with a spoken-style prompt ("Hi! How can I help?") sets expectations for natural language input rather than keyword-style queries.

screens.name: Searching By Voice 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any voice-input flow where confirming correct speech recognition before acting on the query meaningfully reduces the cost of a misunderstood command, especially for open-ended or free-form spoken queries.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for extremely short, low-stakes voice commands (e.g., "next," "stop") where the action is reversible and the overhead of an explicit transcription-confirmation step would slow down an otherwise instant interaction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Siri (query confirmation): displays the transcribed spoken request on screen before or while executing the search, matching this pattern closely.

  2. Google Assistant (voice search transcription): shows recognized text beneath the listening animation as a confirmation step.

  3. Alexa app (voice query display): echoes transcribed speech on screen as part of its voice-interaction flow, serving the same error-prevention purpose.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status: displaying the transcribed query lets the user confirm the assistant correctly understood their speech before any search executes.

  2. Error Prevention: showing transcribed text as an intermediate step (rather than jumping straight to results) gives the user a chance to notice and correct a misheard query.

  3. Continuity of Interaction: reusing the identical avatar and layout from the listening screen keeps this feeling like one fluid voice interaction rather than a separate step.

  4. Recognition over Recall: the user doesn't need to remember what they said; it's echoed back to them directly on screen.

screens.name: Searching By Voice 04
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits multi-modal search products where maintaining one consistent loading and results experience across input methods (voice, text, etc.) is important for reducing user confusion and reinforcing a single mental model of the feature.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if voice and text queries genuinely warrant different follow-up experiences (e.g., voice results optimized for audio playback vs. text results for reading), where forcing identical visual treatment across modalities could obscure meaningful functional differences.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (voice and text search parity): surfaces the identical "reading sources" loading treatment regardless of whether a query was typed or spoken.

  2. Google Assistant → Search results: voice queries transition into the same visual search results loading pattern used for typed queries.

  3. Bing Chat / Copilot: unifies voice and text input into one consistent "searching the web" loading experience.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Consistency Across Input Modalities: using the identical loading pattern for both voice and text queries reduces cognitive load when switching between input methods.

  2. Visibility of System Status: naming specific, topically relevant sources continues to build trust and transparency during the loading period.

  3. Trust Through Transparency: recognizable domains relevant to the coffee recipe query (Starbucks, Pioneer Woman, AllRecipes) reinforce that the AI's source selection is meaningfully tailored to the query.

  4. Unified System Model: the persistent Arc/Google toggle and bottom toolbar remain fixed regardless of entry method, reinforcing one coherent mental model of the app.

screens.name: Global Site Settings 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any settings system where most users want consistent baseline behavior across all contexts, but some sites or contexts warrant individual exceptions, providing both a global default screen and per-instance override screens (with a clear explanation of their relationship) supports both needs without forcing users to configure every site individually.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings that should never vary by context (e.g., core account security settings), where offering a per-site override option would introduce unnecessary complexity or potential inconsistency for something that should behave identically everywhere.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's global vs. per-website settings: uses an identical default-plus-override model, where global settings (Content Blockers, Reader) apply everywhere unless a specific site's settings override them.

  2. Chrome's site settings hierarchy (global defaults vs. per-site permissions): follows the same cascading structure for privacy and behavior settings.

  3. Brave Browser's global Shields defaults vs. per-site Shields settings: closely mirrors this exact two-tier structure for ad/tracker blocking specifically.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Immediate Commit on Selection: choosing an option in the popover applies the change instantly upon dismissal, without a separate confirm step, reducing friction for a low-risk preference change.

  2. Consistent Value Display: the updated "From Anywhere" label matches the exact wording used in the selection popover, ensuring no disconnect between the choice made and its displayed result.

  3. Full Interaction Loop Demonstrated: across this and the two preceding screens, the complete cycle (view value → open selector → choose option → see updated value) is fully shown, confirming the setting behaves as expected end-to-end.

screens.name: Change Default Browser 01
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits browsers wanting to offer genuine search-provider choice while still promoting their own differentiated AI or search feature as a legitimate first-class option among established competitors, rather than hiding it as a secondary toggle.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if a browser's AI feature isn't yet reliable enough to serve as every query's default, presenting it as a full peer alongside Google or Bing sets an expectation of comprehensive search capability that an early-stage AI feature might not consistently meet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Default Search Engine settings: offers a comparable list of major providers (Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Ecosia) for users to choose from, though without an AI-native option like "Browse for Me."

  2. Brave Browser's search engine picker: includes both traditional and privacy-focused engines, plus a custom "add search engine" capability, closely matching this screen's structure.

  3. Opera's search engine settings: similarly lists multiple third-party engines with a checkmark-based single selection, though typically without a browser's own AI feature listed as a selectable "engine."
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Self-Referential Option Placement: listing "Browse for Me" first, ahead of the actual current default (Google), subtly promotes the app's own differentiated feature without forcing it as mandatory.

  2. Genuine Provider Choice: offering a range of philosophically distinct engines (privacy-focused DuckDuckGo, environmental Ecosia, AI-native Perplexity/Kagi) respects that different users have different search priorities beyond just "which engine is biggest."

  3. Clear Current-State Indication: a single checkmark unambiguously shows which engine is presently active, avoiding confusion in a list where any option could plausibly be selected.

  4. Extensibility: the "Add Search Engine" option signals this list isn't a closed, fixed set, allowing power users to add custom or niche search providers beyond the pre-populated options.

screens.name: Change Default Browser 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any AI-synthesis or answer-generation feature that depends on a genuine underlying search index, where exposing that dependency as a configurable secondary setting gives advanced users meaningful control without cluttering the interface for users who don't need to think about it.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit without at least a brief explanatory subtitle or tooltip, introducing a new, unexplained setting immediately after a primary choice risks confusing users about the relationship between the two, as this screen demonstrates by omission.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI's underlying search source settings: similarly exposes (in some configurations) which search backend powers its AI-synthesized answers.

  2. Microsoft Copilot/Bing Chat's search grounding: relies on an underlying traditional search engine to source content for its AI-generated responses, a comparable technical dependency.

  3. Brave Search's "Answer with AI" plus fallback engine settings: pairs an AI-answer feature with a configurable traditional search fallback, matching this exact dependent-setting pattern.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Conditional/Progressive Settings Disclosure: a dependent setting appearing only when relevant (i.e., only when an AI-synthesis option is primary) avoids showing an irrelevant control when a traditional engine is selected.

  2. Sensible Default Inheritance: the Secondary Search Engine defaulting to Google (the app's own prior default) provides a reasonable fallback without requiring the user to configure anything before "Browse for Me" works.

  3. Underlying Technical Transparency: surfacing that an AI-synthesis feature relies on a genuine underlying search engine gives technically curious users insight into how the feature actually sources its information.

  4. Missed Explanatory Opportunity: the setting's purpose isn't explicitly explained, which could leave some users confused about why this new option appeared or what selecting it accomplishes.

screens.name: Onboarding 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits onboarding sequences where a product has several distinct, easily-summarized differentiators that benefit from being seen together, especially when trying to justify a switch away from an incumbent (here, Safari).
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when a feature needs demonstration rather than description (e.g. a gesture-based interaction like "swipe anywhere to go back" is asserted here but not shown), or when there are more than four or five features, since additional rows would require scrolling and dilute the skimmability this pattern depends on.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Robinhood (onboarding feature list): uses the same icon-plus-benefit-row format to summarize app capabilities before account setup.

  2. 1Password / password managers: similarly lead onboarding with a "your logins carry over" reassurance row to lower switching friction.

  3. Opera / Brave browser onboarding: use comparable privacy-and-speed benefit lists early in first-run flows to differentiate from Safari/Chrome.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking: four short, uniformly formatted rows break a features list into digestible units instead of one dense paragraph.

  2. Recognition over Recall: icon + short title lets users scan for what a feature does at a glance rather than reading full sentences.

  3. Progressive Disclosure: only headline + one-line description per feature; deeper detail (e.g. how tracker-blocking works) is deferred past onboarding.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law): identical row structure across all four items sets a predictable reading pattern after the first row.

screens.name: Onboarding 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits onboarding moments where a single, specific interactive element (a button, gesture, or menu item) is the feature being taught, especially when it's easy to miss among visually similar sibling elements.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for teaching abstract concepts or multi-step workflows, since a single arrow-and-label can only clearly direct attention to one static target (sequences requiring several actions need a multi-step guided tour instead of one annotated screen).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo (feature coach marks): uses similar arrow-and-label overlays during onboarding to point at a specific first action.

  2. Slack (new-feature tooltips): highlights one interactive element among several identical-looking ones with color and a directional pointer.

  3. Google Search app ("I'm Feeling Lucky"-style call-outs): shows the real search suggestion UI with a highlighted alternate action button, similar to the "Browse for Me" row here.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Show, Don't Just Tell: using an actual UI mockup instead of icon+text rows lets the user preview the real interaction before it happens.

  2. Von Restorff Effect: the one colored "Browse for Me" button stands out against four gray twins, drawing the eye without extra explanation.

  3. Signifiers: the curved arrow is an explicit directional cue that removes any ambiguity about what to look at or tap next.

  4. Recognition over Recall: showing real example queries ("who are the beatles," "risotto vs paella") lets users recognize the feature's use case rather than imagining one abstractly.

screens.name: Onboarding 04
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits onboarding for any AI-generated or synthesized-output feature where the quality and richness of the result is the main selling point and is best proven by example rather than description.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when the actual output is highly variable, sparse, or low-quality in typical use, since showing a best-case curated example risks setting expectations the live product won't consistently meet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (onboarding/example answers): similarly shows a fully worked example query-to-answer page with cited sources to demonstrate AI search output during first use.

  2. Notion AI (feature preview screens): uses sample generated content in onboarding to prove value before the user tries it themselves.

  3. Google Discover/Search "AI Overview" intros: pair a sample query with a rich, sourced answer card to build trust in AI-generated summaries.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Show, Don't Just Tell: a fully rendered example answer page substitutes for further explanation of what "Browse for Me" does.

  2. Peak-End Rule: closing the feature demo on a checkmark and a rich, satisfying result page leaves a positive final impression of this onboarding step.

  3. Social Proof: recognizable publisher logos (BBC Good Food, Delish, RecipeTin Eats) lend third-party credibility to the AI-assembled answer.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law): reusing the same device-frame mockup, page control, and Next button from the prior screen keeps the sequence visually coherent.

screens.name: Onboarding 05
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits teaching gesture-based or otherwise "invisible" interactions where no static screenshot can fully demonstrate the action, especially when the feature is optional or supplementary to the app's core flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for teaching core, mandatory interactions users must understand to use the app at all (an optional-feeling "Skip" affordance undersells the importance of something the user actually needs to know).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Files by Google / Photos apps (pinch-to-zoom tips): use similar headline-plus-mockup coach marks to teach gestures that can't be shown with static arrows.

  2. Apple's own iOS feature tips (e.g., "Swipe down to search"): pair a short imperative phrase with a realistic content preview to teach system gestures during first use.

  3. Medium / Pocket (reading-mode features): use real article content in onboarding previews to demonstrate a reading-related feature in a relatable context.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Discoverability of Gestures: since pinch gestures are inherently invisible in a static UI, naming the gesture explicitly in the headline compensates for the lack of a visual affordance.

  2. User Control & Freedom: the "Skip" button lets users opt out of a tip they may already know, avoiding forced friction for returning or advanced users.

  3. Recognition over Recall: using a real, evocative example (a famous historic speech) makes the feature's value easier to picture than an abstract placeholder would.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law): the device-frame mockup and page-control layout convention (established across earlier screens) is reused here, keeping the tour visually coherent even without a page control visible in this crop.

screens.name: Onboarding 06
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any onboarding demo of an action with a brief processing delay, where showing an explicit "working" moment (rather than jumping straight from instruction to result) reassures the user that their action was registered.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's unnecessary for instantaneous actions with no real processing time, where inserting an artificial "in progress" beat would only slow down onboarding without adding useful reassurance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Photos ("Enhancing.."): uses a similarly brief, present-tense status label during onboarding demos of an AI-processing feature.

  2. Notion AI (generating content preview): shows a shrunk or transitional content card with a "Generating.." style label before revealing the AI output.

  3. Apple's "Cleanup" tool onboarding (Photos): depicts a mid-gesture visual state before showing the completed result, similar to this shrunk/rotated card.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status: the "Summarizing for you.." label ensures the user isn't left wondering whether the demonstrated gesture did anything.

  2. Continuity of Context: reusing the identical article card from the previous screen (same image, same headline) keeps this feeling like one fluid interaction rather than a new, disconnected example.

  3. Metaphorical Representation: shrinking and rotating the card visually mimics the physical pinch gesture without needing an animation to be described in a static screenshot.

  4. Progressive Disclosure: showing only a brief in-progress state (rather than jumping straight to a finished summary) sets an honest expectation that summarizing takes a moment.

screens.name: Summarizing Search 01
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any content-transformation feature (summarizing, translating, reading-mode) that should work consistently regardless of whether the underlying page is the app's own content or a third-party site, with a clear, dismissible in-progress state.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for pages where the "summary" would strip essential interactive functionality (e.g., a form, a checkout flow) rather than condense readable content, applying a text-summarization gesture to a non-text-heavy page would produce a poor or meaningless result.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari Reader Mode (activated on any site): similarly applies a content-transformation feature universally across both native and third-party pages.

  2. Instapaper / Pocket (save-and-summarize): condenses any web page's content regardless of source, matching this feature's cross-site applicability.

  3. Perplexity's browser extension (summarize any page): offers the same "works on any page, including competitor search results" capability shown here.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Consistency Across Contexts: reusing identical visual and textual treatment from onboarding for this live, real-content version reinforces recognition and reduces relearning.

  2. User Control & Freedom: the visible X button lets users abort an in-progress summarization, a safety net not present in the earlier onboarding demo of this same state.

  3. Reference Point Clarity: the small tab-style label above the shrunk card orients the user to exactly which page is being condensed, useful in a multi-tab browsing context.

  4. Universal Feature Availability: successfully applying summarization to a third-party Google page (not just Arc's own content) demonstrates the feature isn't limited to Arc-generated pages.

screens.name: Summarizing Search 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any feature that transforms or condenses third-party content, where clear attribution of the processing tool (versus the original source) is important for maintaining user trust and avoiding confusion about content origin.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for summarizing the app's own first-party content, where an explicit "summarized by [app name]" attribution would be redundant since there's no ambiguity about who generated the condensation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari Reader Mode with attribution: some reader/summary tools similarly label condensed content with its processing source to maintain transparency.

  2. Perplexity's page-summary attribution: labels AI-condensed content clearly as processed output rather than blending it seamlessly with the original source.

  3. Grammarly / browser extensions with "powered by" footers: use similar bottom-bar attribution to clarify which tool performed a transformation on third-party content.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Source Attribution / Content Provenance: explicitly labeling the summary as "by Arc Search" prevents ambiguity about whether this text came from Google's original page or Arc's own processing.

  2. Consistency Across Features: reusing the icon-labeled key-point row style from the "Browse for Me" answer pages unifies the visual language across Arc's different AI-powered tools.

  3. Trust Through Transparency: clear labeling of AI-generated content as such (rather than presenting it as though it were native to the summarized page) supports informed, trustworthy use.

  4. Closure / Explicit Completion Signal: the footer bar functions as an unambiguous "done" state, distinct from the "Summarizing for you.." in-progress label seen on the previous screen.

screens.name: Summarizing Search 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits summarizing content-rich pages where multiple distinct facets (recommendations, predictions, categories, platforms) can be meaningfully separated, giving users a scannable structured overview rather than one dense paragraph.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for pages with a single, narrow topic where forcing content into five artificially separated facets would feel padded or repetitive rather than genuinely distinct.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Notion AI (multi-facet page summaries): breaks a single source document into several icon-labeled thematic points, similar to this five-row structure.

  2. Perplexity's structured answer breakdowns: synthesizes information into multiple distinct topical facets with varied iconography, matching this pattern.

  3. Wikipedia's "Quick facts" infobox style (adapted for AI): organizes disparate facts about one subject into clearly labeled categorical rows, echoing this summary's structure.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visual Differentiation Within Structure: using five distinct icons rather than one repeated marker helps users visually parse different topics even while the overall row format stays consistent.

  2. Synthesis Beyond Visible Content: points like "Streaming Services" and "Box Office Predictions" suggest the AI drew from page content not immediately visible in the collapsed card, demonstrating real synthesis rather than surface extraction.

  3. Consistency (Jakob's Law): the row format (icon, bold title, description) matches the structure established in both this feature's onboarding demo and the earlier "Browse for Me" answer pages, unifying the product's AI-output visual language.

  4. Persistent Attribution: keeping the "Summarized for you by Arc Search" footer fixed regardless of scroll depth ensures the source is never ambiguous no matter how far the user scrolls.

screens.name: Home Screen
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits single-purpose, sensor-driven capture apps where one action dominates all others and the moment of use is fleeting (audio recognition, scanning, quick capture) and where secondary features exist mainly to store or extend the results.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for multi-purpose apps where two or more actions have comparable frequency, since elevating one to hero status makes the others feel buried; it also wastes a screen's worth of real estate in content-led products where the user arrives to browse rather than to act.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Snapchat: Opens directly on the capture surface with one dominant circular action and peer destinations relegated to a bottom rail. Same premise: the moment is perishable, so the app opens in the tool rather than in a menu.

  2. Yuka (and barcode-scanner apps generally): Hero scan button on the home screen, with scan history as a secondary tab. Structurally identical: a single sensor-driven capture that produces a saved record you can revisit.

  3. Google (Search a song / hum to search): The same audio-recognition task exposed as one prominent tap, and a fair comparison because it shows the pattern holds even when embedded inside a much larger app rather than given its own.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Fitts's law: Target acquisition time falls with size and rises with distance. A very large, centrally placed target is close to the theoretical best case for a task performed under time pressure and often without full visual attention.

  2. Signal-to-noise ratio: With one action in the content area, there is no visual search step. The user's eye does not have to scan, parse, or decide before acting.

  3. Recognition over recall: The hint text removes any need to remember what the circle does, which matters because Shazam is a low-frequency app for many users; sessions can be weeks apart.

  4. Progressive disclosure: Library, Concerts, search, and settings are all one tap away but contribute nothing to the primary task, so none of them occupy the primary zone.

  5. Thumb-zone ergonomics: Secondary navigation sits in the natural thumb arc at the bottom; the hero action sits higher, where a deliberate two-handed or reaching tap is fine because it is the action you are already committed to.

screens.name: Home Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits short, sensor-dependent operations of genuinely unpredictable length where success depends partly on the user's physical positioning (audio matching, live scanning, voice capture) and where abandoning mid-operation is free.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit for operations whose duration is knowable, where a determinate bar sets better expectations, and for long-running or irreversible processes such as uploads or payments, where a bare indeterminate animation with a one-tap exit gives the user neither a sense of progress nor protection against cancelling something costly.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Assistant / "Search a song": The same audio-capture wait rendered as an animated, level-responsive visual with a live status line. A fair comparison because it faces the identical constraint: unknown match time on a perishable input.

  2. Apple's Voice Memos and Siri: Waveform-as-loading-state, where the animation doubles as proof the microphone is receiving. Shazam is drawing on the same platform vocabulary, including the system-level recording indicator.

  3. Face ID enrollment / camera-based scanners: Concentric progress framing around a live sensor with a corner dismiss, comparable because the user must physically position a device correctly for the capture to succeed and needs real-time confirmation that they have.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status: Nielsen's first heuristic, executed twice over: one signal for process activity, one for input signal quality. The user is never left guessing whether the delay means working or stuck.

  2. Perceived duration and active waiting: Continuous motion plus a task to perform ("check it can hear") compresses felt wait time relative to a static spinner of identical real duration.

  3. User control and freedom: An always-available, unconfirmed exit from a running operation. Since abandoning costs nothing, adding a "Are you sure?" step would be pure friction.

  4. Feedforward, not just feedback: The audibility hint arrives at the only moment the user can still act on it, rather than after a failed match when it becomes a post-mortem.

  5. Continuity of the interaction model: The hero mark stays in place and grows into the pulse rather than being replaced by a new screen, so the button visibly becomes the process it started.

screens.name: Home Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: This fits short sensor-driven operations of unpredictable length where the user's physical positioning affects success and abandoning costs nothing (audio matching, device discovery, live scanning).
screens.whereNotToUse: Poorly suited to operations with knowable duration, where a determinate indicator sets better expectations, and to long or irreversible processes such as uploads or payments, where escalating full-screen motion with a bare one-tap exit gives neither progress information nor protection against accidental cancellation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Assistant / "Search a song": Same audio-capture wait rendered as expanding, audio-reactive motion around a fixed center; identical constraint of unknown match time on perishable input.

  2. Siri and Apple's Voice Memos: Waveform-as-status where the animation doubles as proof of microphone input, drawing on the same platform vocabulary including the OS recording indicator.

  3. Airdrop and Bluetooth pairing screens: Expanding concentric rings as the standard visual grammar for "sensing outward for something not yet found," a fair comparison because the wait is genuinely indeterminate and cancelling is free.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status, sustained: Activity remains legible not just at onset but throughout the wait, which is where most loading states quietly stop reassuring.

  2. Perceived duration: Rising amplitude resists the sense of stall that a constant-intensity loop invites after two or three seconds.

  3. Stable anchor amid motion: The opaque center gives the eye a fixed point, preventing a full-screen animation from becoming visually fatiguing or hard to focus on.

  4. Consistency of controls across states: Close and copy hold position between frames, so nothing the user might reach for moves while they are reaching for it.

  5. Motion restraint where it counts: The animation is slow, wide, and low-contrast; it fills the screen without flashing, strobing, or high-frequency movement.

screens.name: Home Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: This fits short two-phase operations where a local capture is followed by a remote lookup, and where naming the phases helps the user attribute any eventual failure correctly (audio or image recognition, scanning against a remote catalogue, lookup after sensor input).
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the phases are invisible to the user or complete in well under a second, since narrating them just adds flicker, and where latency is long or highly variable, in which case a bare indeterminate state with filler copy leaves the user with no basis to decide whether to keep waiting.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Assistant / "Search a song": Runs the same two-beat structure, shifting from an audio-reactive capture visual to a neutral processing indicator once the sample is sent. Same architecture, same constraint.

  2. Google Lens and barcode scanners generally: Capture phase with live camera feedback, then a distinct lookup phase against a remote index; a fair comparison because the user's physical contribution ends partway through and the interface must show that.

  3. Apple Pay / contactless payment sheets: Discrete named phases with tight, non-apologetic status strings and a persistent cancel affordance, comparable in how a short multi-stage wait is narrated without inflating it.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Match between system and the real world: Splitting "Listening" from "Searching" surfaces the app's actual two-stage architecture in plain language, which is what lets a failure be correctly attributed later.

  2. Honest signalling: The live meter is retired the moment it stops measuring anything real. Keeping an audio-reactive element running during a network call would be theatre.

  3. Consistency and standards: Close control, mark, and text block hold identical positions across states, so nothing the user might reach for shifts underneath them.

  4. Visibility of system status, weakened: This phase carries the thinnest feedback of the three states while being the one most exposed to network latency; a determinate or elapsed-time cue would be more useful here than in the capture phase.

  5. Aesthetic-usability tradeoff: The rings now animate without encoding anything, which keeps continuity and visual calm but converts a former information channel into decoration.

screens.name: Home Screen 5
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits recognition and lookup products where the answer is delivered free but the natural next action is monetizable, and where the moment of resolution is also the moment of highest user affinity (music, product, and media identification).
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit where the query is functional rather than affective (a translation, a unit conversion, a support answer) since layering a trial offer over a utilitarian result reads as opportunism, and it fails where the user is in a hurry or a public setting and auto-playing video is unwelcome.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Spotify (free tier track pages): Delivers the content, then gates full playback behind an upgrade at the exact point of intent. A fair comparison because both convert a moment of demonstrated interest into a subscription ask rather than interrupting earlier.

  2. SoundHound: The direct competitor's result screen pairs identification with lyrics, sharing, and streaming handoffs, showing the pattern is category-standard rather than Apple-specific.

  3. Google Lens results: Answer delivered as a full-bleed visual with actions layered over it and related results below the fold; comparable in treating a resolved query as the entry point to a browsing session.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Peak-end rule and moment-of-affinity conversion: The subscription ask lands at the emotional high point of the session, when the user has just gotten what they wanted, rather than at launch or on exit.

  2. Visibility of system status via content, not chrome: Success needs no announcement because the answer is the announcement; adding a confirmation banner would delay the payoff it describes.

  3. Colour as a hierarchy instrument: A single accent hue used only for playback and conversion means the revenue paths are the only saturated pixels; everything else recedes into video and dark neutral.

  4. Social proof as accuracy signal: The recognition count simultaneously validates the match ("a million people found this too") and reduces the user's doubt about whether to trust the result.

  5. Session extension over task completion: Related content positioned immediately below the fold converts a thirty-second utility interaction into a browsable session, which is how a single-purpose app earns retention.

screens.name: Home Screen 6
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits media detail views where several related items of the same type exist and the user is browsing rather than searching (video shelves, trailer collections, artist media) particularly where a contained player with an opt-in fullscreen respects the user's surroundings.
screens.whereNotToUse: It is a poor fit when only one item exists, where a carousel promises variety that is not there, and for long-form video, where a small contained player with a persistent CTA below is worse than a proper immersive player. It also fails where the horizontal swipe would compete with a vertical scroll of equal importance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Apple Music (music video sections): Same card-based horizontal video shelf, same expand affordance, same visual language. Shazam is reusing the parent product's pattern, which is why the handoff to Apple Music feels continuous rather than like leaving the app.

  2. Spotify (canvas and video previews on free tier): Video content shown in a contained frame with full playback gated behind an upgrade; comparable in using media as the hook for a subscription ask.

  3. YouTube Shorts shelves inside search results: Horizontally swipeable video cards nested inside a larger result page, a fair comparison for how a carousel signals "more of this type" without leaving the current context.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Affordance through partial visibility: The clipped neighbouring card is a textbook use of the boundary as a signifier; showing that content continues is more reliable than any indicator explaining that it does.

  2. Consistency across states: Close remains top-left and the teal accent remains reserved for the single monetized action, holding the conventions established through listening, searching, and result.

  3. User control over immersion: Offering fullscreen as an explicit choice rather than defaulting to it respects the user's context, which matters for a video that may be playing audio in public.

  4. Recognition over recall: The persistent header keeps track and artist visible while the user browses videos, so context is never lost to scrolling or swiping.

  5. Focused leaf view: Stripping secondary actions reduces this screen to one content type and one forward path, which is appropriate for a destination the user chose deliberately.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Deleting & Removing 1
screens.whereToUse: Utilize this pattern for any list-based content that requires chronological logging and individual item management, such as browser history, search history, or transaction logs. It is ideal when users need to revisit previous states quickly without bookmarking every item, and when list decluttering (deletion) is a common secondary action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for critical, irreversible actions where a single swipe might be triggered accidentally (e.g., deleting a wallet seed phrase or confirming a crypto transaction). Additionally, if the target audience is less tech-savvy or unfamiliar with swipe gestures, relying solely on hidden actions without a visible "Edit" mode alternative could hide functionality and hurt discoverability.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves the "Busy Urban" persona who uses the wallet's dApp browser for frequent DeFi activities (like swapping tokens on PancakeSwap). Since crypto users often visit dozens of specific dApp URLs that are hard to remember or type manually, this history feature acts as a safety net for quick re-access.

Psychologically, the swipe-to-delete pattern taps into privacy concerns specific to crypto users; since financial dApp interactions can be sensitive, users are given an easy, discoverable way to clear specific traces of their activity without needing to dig through settings menus.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Familiar Mental Model: Adopting the standard mobile browser "History" list UI removes the learning curve for users navigating decentralized applications.

  • Non-Destructive Default View: Hiding delete controls behind a swipe gesture keeps the primary list clean and scannable, only exposing high-risk actions (deletion) upon deliberate user intent.

  • Metadata Hierarchy: Clear visual separation between the human-readable Site Title and the machine-readable URL/Timestamp aids quick scanning.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Deleting & Removing 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for any list-based screen (history, favorites, cart, notifications) that can legitimately be empty for new users.

  • Ideal when you want to convert a potentially discouraging "nothing here" moment into a motivational nudge toward a core action.

  • Effective in consumer-facing apps with a friendly or adventurous brand voice (travel, lifestyle, social, discovery apps).

  • Pair with a custom illustration that visually explains the screen's purpose to reduce reliance on text alone.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid overly casual copy ("Get out there and start exploring") in enterprise, financial, or medical contexts where users expect precise, neutral language.

  • Do not use a generic empty state illustration if the underlying feature is complex (consider adding a direct CTA button (e).g., "Start Browsing") rather than relying solely on passive suggestion.

  • Not suitable if the history list can be pre-populated with system-generated or synced data, where an empty state would rarely be seen and investment in custom illustration isn't justified.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets first-time users or users who have recently cleared their browsing history, most commonly within browser, maps, or travel-discovery apps. The design leverages the psychological principle of reframing absence as opportunity: rather than making the user feel like something is "missing" or "broken," the copy and illustration together trigger a sense of anticipation and invitation to engage with the core product (browsing/exploring).

The use of a friendly, informal tone ("Get out there") suggests the target demographic is casual consumers rather than enterprise/professional users, who typically respond well to encouraging, low-friction language that reduces the intimidation of an empty interface.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Purposeful, on-brand illustration: The browser-window-with-clock icon visually reinforces the concept of "history" instantly, reducing cognitive load.

  • Encouraging micro-copy: "No history yet" + "Get out there and start exploring" reframes an empty/negative state into a motivational, action-inviting moment.

  • Consistent chrome: Top bar and bottom tab bar remain fully functional and visible, preventing the empty state from feeling like a broken or dead-end screen.

  • Dark theme with high-contrast accent illustration: The light-blue illustration pops against the black background, drawing the eye directly to the focal point without visual clutter.
