screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 16
screens.whereToUse:
• End states of any payment, transfer, donation, or purchase flow where the user needs unambiguous confirmation.

  • Any multi-step process (checkout, onboarding, form submission) that benefits from a calm, singular "success" resting point before returning users to the main app.

  • Situations where backend processing (e.g., bank clearing, verification) is delayed, and expectation-setting copy can prevent user confusion or repeat support requests.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when the action isn't fully guaranteed yet (e.g., pending fraud review) - declaring "complete" prematurely can create false confidence and support issues if it later fails.

  • Not ideal for flows where the user needs to take an immediate follow-up action (e.g., verify email); in that case, the CTA should drive them forward rather than just "Done."

  • Avoid overly festive celebration (confetti, animations) for small routine transactions, as it can feel disproportionate or gimmicky to the value of the action.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday users of a peer-to-peer payment, banking, or crowdfunding/donation app who need clear, low-anxiety confirmation that their financial action succeeded. Financial transactions are high-stakes emotionally even at small amounts (here, just $1), so users rely heavily on unambiguous visual and textual signals to feel confident the app "did the right thing."

Psychologically, this leverages the Peak-End Rule: users remember the end of an experience disproportionately, so ending on a clear, positive, reassuring note (green checkmark, calm copy) leaves a favorable impression of the entire transaction flow, even if prior steps involved friction (entering payment details, confirming amounts, etc.).

The expectation-setting about bank deduction timing also serves anxious or first-time users who might otherwise refresh their bank app repeatedly looking for the charge, reducing perceived risk of a "silent failure" or double charge.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Immediate visual confirmation: The green circular checkmark is universally recognized and processed faster than text, reducing the time to relief/certainty.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Explicitly stating the deduction may take a few days preempts confusion and reduces support burden.

  • Single, unmissable CTA: Only one primary action ("Done") is presented, removing decision fatigue at the end of a flow.

  • Generous whitespace: Signals finality and calm, letting the success message breathe without competing UI elements.

  • Dismissible via X: Provides a secondary, lower-commitment exit path consistent with modal/sheet conventions.

screens.name: Cash App Transferring Money 17
screens.whereToUse:
Use a radial progress + dual-CTA footer pattern for:

  • Crowdfunding, group gifting, or fundraising campaign screens where a single quantifiable goal needs to be communicated instantly.

  • Any collaborative/social finance product where growing participation (inviting people) is as important as the core transactional action (contributing money).

  • Screens where you want to combine identity (who created it), progress (how much has been achieved), and action (what to do next) in one concise, scannable view.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The goal metric is not naturally expressible as a percentage/progress toward a target (radial progress loses meaning without a clear numerator/denominator relationship).

  • Multiple competing goals or metrics need to be shown simultaneously; a single radial ring cannot scale well to comparative or multi-metric dashboards.

  • The user base skews toward power users needing dense data (e.g., transaction history, donor breakdown) immediately visible (here that data is hidden below a scroll, which could frustrate users wanting quick analytics).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users participating in group monetary pooling scenarios (friends splitting a group gift, coworkers pooling for a party fund, or informal fundraising among a social circle (the "Mobbin Party" name suggests a lighthearted, event-based collection, possibly a demo/test fund created by the Mobbin team)).

Psychologically, the design leans on:

  • Goal-gradient effect: Visualizing progress toward a concrete goal (even at 1%) motivates further contribution by making the target tangible.

  • Social accountability: Showing "By [Creator]" and an "Add people" action leverages social pressure and network effects (the more people added, the more social proof and obligation to contribute).

  • Low-commitment framing: "$1 of $100" reframes a large ask into small increments, reducing the psychological barrier to the first contribution.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radial progress ring instead of linear bar: Turns a mundane funding metric into a visually engaging, gauge-like centerpiece that feels more like a game meter than a spreadsheet stat.

  • Dual-action footer with clear hierarchy: "Add people" (neutral gray pill) vs. "Contribute" (bold black pill) visually encodes primary vs. secondary actions without needing labels like "primary/secondary."

  • Persistent bottom CTA pattern: Ensures conversion actions are always reachable regardless of scroll position, reducing friction to contribute.

  • Colorful avatar placeholder: The vibrant pink circle avatar personalizes an otherwise minimal, monochrome UI, and signals brand/identity customization is available for the fund.

  • Scroll affordance cue: Explicit "Scroll for activity" text with arrow icon compensates for the ambiguous empty space below the fold, directly telling users an activity feed exists.

screens.name: Venmo Dashboard 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when building any search experience where results span multiple entity types (users, businesses, organizations) and where accurate identification of the correct entity is high-stakes (e.g., financial transactions, contact/messaging apps, marketplace seller search). It's especially effective when usernames/handles are unique identifiers that can disambiguate common display names.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, single-entity-type search experiences where categorized tabs would add unnecessary complexity. It's also less suitable when the dataset is small enough that filtering/categorization offers no real value, or when speed is paramount and an unsegmented flat list would resolve queries faster. Additionally, relying heavily on user-generated avatars/initials can look inconsistent if a large percentage of accounts lack photos (consider more robust default avatar theming in that case).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using a P2P payments or social commerce app who need to quickly and confidently locate a specific individual or business among many similarly named entries (a common real-world problem given how frequent names like "John" are). The design leverages several psychological principles:

  • Recognition over recall: Showing avatar photos alongside names helps users visually confirm identity rather than relying purely on memory of a username.

  • Trust & safety cues: Unique @handles reduce the anxiety of sending money to an impersonator or wrong account, a critical trust factor in fintech UX.

  • Reduced choice overload: Capping visible results and using categorical tabs (Top/People/Businesses/Charities) prevents decision paralysis when many matches exist.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented "Top" filter as default: Surfacing a blended, ranked view of the most relevant people/businesses/charities before forcing users to manually filter reduces friction for the common case.

  • Consistent two-line list pattern: Avatar + Name + @handle repeated across both People and Business sections creates predictable scanning rhythm.

  • Progressive disclosure via "See more people": Caps initial results at 4 to avoid overwhelming the screen, while still allowing deep access to the full list on demand.

  • Persistent Invite CTA: Always-visible in the header, turning an unsuccessful or ambiguous search into an opportunity to grow the network via referral.

  • Graceful avatar fallback: Initials-in-circle avatars for users/businesses without profile photos maintain visual consistency and prevent broken-image states.

screens.name: Venmo Dashboard 2
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern when designing consumer P2P payment, expense-splitting, or fintech-social hybrid apps where user retention benefits from social engagement loops (likes, comments, feeds) layered on top of utility actions. It's ideal for products targeting younger demographics who respond to social validation and casual, informal tone, and for any app where you want to reduce the perceived seriousness/friction of a financial action by embedding it in a lightweight social context.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for B2B fintech, enterprise expense management, banking, or any context requiring privacy, compliance, or professional tone (publicly displaying transaction activity (even obscured) can create real security/privacy risks (e).g., revealing spending patterns, relationships, or routines) and would feel inappropriate or even alarming to older or privacy-conscious users. Also avoid if your user base skews toward high-value/sensitive transactions where playful captions and public visibility would undermine trust and gravity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, socially-networked users (Gen Z/Millennials) who are comfortable blending finances with public social identity (the same demographic driving Venmo's "public by default" feed culture). The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Social proof: the friend count and public feed make a user's financial activity feel validated by community size and visible engagement (likes/comments).

  • Norm establishment / peer pressure: seeing other users' casual payment captions normalizes sharing your own transactions, reducing friction and privacy anxiety.

  • Playfulness reduces money anxiety: using humor ("BOILING", "DRANK") in place of literal transaction descriptions reframes P2P payments as a fun social ritual rather than a serious financial event.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-mode feed toggle (Feed vs. Between You) elegantly reuses one UI to serve both public social content and private relationship history.

  • Single, unmissable primary CTA ("Pay or Request") that visually outranks all secondary profile actions via color, width, and placement.

  • Social-first information architecture: friend count and Add Friend button are prioritized above and visually equal to payment actions, reinforcing that money is secondary to relationship in this product's mental model.

  • Gamified, meme-able transaction captions that turn a mundane payment log into scroll-worthy, likeable/commentable social content, driving engagement loops typically reserved for photo/social apps.

  • Public visibility indicator (globe icon) on each transaction subtly communicates privacy scope without needing a settings menu.

screens.name: Venmo Dashboard 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when designing profile screens for social-financial or marketplace apps where trust-building and relationship context must precede a monetary transaction (P2P payments, marketplace seller profiles, gig-economy client profiles). It's ideal when you need to merge social identity with transactional history in a single, scannable view.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for B2B or enterprise financial tools where social metrics (friend counts, requested status) are irrelevant or could seem unprofessional. It's also unsuitable for high-security banking contexts where surfacing relationship/social data could create privacy concerns or regulatory complications. For one-off/anonymous transactions (e.g., checkout with a stranger merchant), the heavy social framing would add clutter rather than trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers using social-payment apps (e.g., Venmo, Cash App) to split bills, repay friends, or send money within a trusted social graph. The design leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Social proof: Friend count and mutual connections reduce perceived risk of transacting with this individual.

  • Relationship status transparency ("Requested"): Leverages the Zeigarnik effect (an unresolved pending request creates a subtle psychological itch to complete/accept the connection).

  • Reciprocity & convenience: The one-tap "Pay or Request" button lowers the activation energy needed to settle debts among friends, exploiting the ease-of-use bias to encourage more frequent transactions.
screens.keyHighlights:
Key UX decisions worth stealing:

  • Social-proof-before-payment framing: Displaying friend count and mutual network status before the payment action builds trust and reduces fraud anxiety in a P2P money context.

  • Segmented ledger view (Feed vs. Between You): Cleanly separates public social activity from private financial history, respecting both transparency and privacy needs within one profile.

  • Actionable empty state: Rather than a generic "nothing here" message, the empty state explicitly instructs the user on the next step, turning a dead-end into a conversion opportunity.

  • Single dominant CTA: "Pay or Request" is the only strongly colored button, ensuring zero ambiguity about the primary intended action on this screen.

screens.name: Venmo Dashboard 4
screens.whereToUse: Use a social/public feed pattern when a product's core value proposition benefits from network effects and habitual engagement (e).g., peer-to-peer payment apps, fitness apps (activity feeds), or collaborative tools where visibility of others' actions drives adoption and repeat usage. It's ideal when the underlying transaction type is low-stakes and shareable (e.g., splitting bills, casual purchases) and when a brand wants to differentiate from purely transactional competitors by adding a lifestyle/social layer.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-stakes, sensitive, or purely private financial contexts (e.g., mortgage payments, medical bills, salary transfers, B2B invoicing) where users expect confidentiality and a feed format would feel inappropriate or even alarming. It's also unsuitable for apps targeting older or privacy-sensitive demographics who may find social feeds cluttered or confusing when they simply want quick access to balance and transaction history.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This design targets a younger, social-native demographic (Gen Z/Millennials) who split bills, pay friends for shared expenses, and view money exchange as a routine social activity worth sharing (e.g., "Beignet", "Happy pup!"). The feed leverages social proof and fear of missing out psychology, seeing friends' activity nudges users to also transact and post, reinforcing habitual app usage. The visibility toggle (friends icon vs. globe icon) also plays into identity signaling: users can choose how much of their social financial behavior to broadcast, satisfying both privacy-conscious and exhibitionist user segments.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Social Feed as Homepage: Turning financial transactions into a public/semi-public feed with likes and comments transforms mundane payments into social content, driving daily engagement and return visits.

  • Privacy Icons on Each Transaction:

  • Overlapping FAB Tab Bar Icon: The central Venmo "V" button breaks tab-bar grid conventions to visually elevate the core action (pay/request money) above passive navigation items.

  • Native Merchandising Banner: The debit card promo is seamlessly woven into the feed using the same card-based visual language, reducing perceived intrusiveness of the ad.

  • Lightweight Engagement Controls: Heart/comment/overflow icons mirror familiar social app affordances (Instagram/Facebook), lowering the learning curve for interaction.

screens.name: Venmo Dashboard 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for financial or wallet-style dashboards where you need to surface a balance, provide quick access to a primary money-movement action, and simultaneously drive completion of a required but potentially friction-heavy step (like identity verification or linking a payment method). It's especially effective in fintech apps where user activation (adding a bank account) is a critical funnel step, and where showing an empty/zero state can be turned into a motivational nudge rather than a dead end.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this soft-nudge approach for verification steps that are hard legal/regulatory requirements (e.g., AML checks before any transaction can occur) - in those cases, a clearer, more directive hard-gate pattern is safer to avoid confusing users about why they can't transact. Also avoid pairing a prominent CTA (like "Transfer") next to a balance of $0, as it can create a dead-end tap that leads to an error state; consider disabling or contextually hiding primary actions when the underlying data (balance) cannot support them.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday consumers managing peer-to-peer payments (likely a mix of new users who haven't yet linked a funding source and existing users checking their balance before making a transfer or purchase). The design leverages the endowed progress effect and friction reduction psychological principles: by showing $0 prominently, it creates a mild sense of "incompleteness" that nudges the user toward the Transfer or Add-a-card actions to change that number. The soft verification prompt uses loss-framing softened by benefit language: reminding users they have inaccessible funds/features, which triggers curiosity and mild urgency to complete verification without feeling coerced.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Benefit-framed verification prompt: Instead of a scary "Verify Identity" compliance banner, the copy leads with a friendly illustration and a question that frames verification as unlocking value, reducing drop-off at a critical compliance checkpoint.

  • Segmented Wallet/Transactions toggle: Keeps balance and history in the same mental "space" while letting users flip context with a single tap, avoiding a full page navigation.

  • Dashed/empty-state card tile for adding a payment method: Visually communicates "this slot is empty" using a card-shaped placeholder with a "+" icon, leveraging the user's existing mental model of a physical wallet.

  • Primary balance + immediate Transfer CTA pairing: Placing the action button directly beside the number it acts upon reduces cognitive distance between insight and action.

screens.name: Venmo Inviting Teammates & Friends 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for growth-loop features in consumer apps with viral potential (especially fintech, marketplaces, delivery, and social apps) where both the referrer and referee benefit financially. It's ideal when the app already has contact/address book access and a well-defined, trackable reward structure.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy monetary-incentive approach for B2B or enterprise software where financial referral bonuses may be inappropriate or against compliance policies. Also avoid if the app cannot reliably track and pay out referrals quickly, as broken promises of "$10 per friend" can severely damage trust. Overusing contact-list access for invites can also trigger privacy concerns if not clearly opt-in and transparently explained.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets existing, engaged users of a peer-to-peer payments app (evidenced by the Cash App-style branding and iconography) who are likely to have friends within the same target demographic (young, mobile-first, social spenders). The design exploits several psychological triggers:

  • Loss Aversion / Endowed Progress: Pre-filling a sliver of the progress bar makes users feel they've already started and don't want to "lose" that momentum.

  • Reciprocity & Social Currency: Users are incentivized to share a "gift" of money with friends, which also flatters the referrer as generous.

  • Scarcity of Effort: By capping earnings at $100 (10 friends x $10), the product creates a bounded, achievable goal rather than infinite/vague earning potential, which increases perceived attainability.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual Progress Metrics: Tracking both "Referred" count and "$ Earned" in parallel gives users two satisfying ways to watch their progress grow.

  • Reward-First CTA Copy: Labeling each contact row button "Earn $10" instead of "Invite" keeps the financial incentive front-and-center at the moment of decision.

  • Frictionless Contact Integration: Surfacing the user's own address book with searchable, one-tap invite actions removes the multi-step hassle of manually finding and sharing a link.

  • Celebratory Illustration: The confetti-and-hand-holding-phone illustration visually reinforces the joyful, rewarding nature of referring friends.

  • Modal Presentation: Using a swipe-up sheet with a close "X" keeps the referral flow contextual and easily dismissible without derailing the user's main task.

screens.name: Venmo Inviting Teammates & Friends 3
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for peer-to-peer fintech apps, social commerce platforms, or any product where transactional or utilitarian actions benefit from social visibility and virality (e.g., splitting bills, gifting, tipping). It works well when the target audience is socially engaged and values transparency/status among a friend graph. Also useful for community apps wanting to gamify otherwise mundane actions by layering social feed mechanics (likes, comments, captions) atop functional events.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach for banking, enterprise, or B2B financial products where privacy, compliance, and confidentiality are paramount (publicly displaying transactions (even without amounts) could create trust, security, or regulatory concerns). Also inappropriate for older or privacy-conscious demographics who may find public transaction feeds invasive or confusing rather than fun. Not suitable for high-value, sensitive, or irregular transactions where levity in captions could be considered unprofessional or alarming.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets a young, social, mobile-native demographic (largely Gen Z/Millennial Venmo users) for whom peer visibility and social currency matter as much as the financial transaction itself. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Social proof: Seeing friends' payment activity normalizes app usage and encourages more transactions ("everyone's doing it").

  • FOMO/curiosity: Cryptic captions like "DRANK" or "BOILING" invite viewers to comment or ask what happened, driving engagement and retention.

  • Identity & belonging: Public friend counts and feeds mimic social networks, tapping into users' desire for visible social connection.

  • Low friction commerce: The persistent, prominent Pay/Request button caters to habitual, frequent peer-to-peer micro-transactions (splitting bills, drinks, rent).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Transaction-as-social-post: Turning a payment event into a feed post with likes/comments transforms a functional financial action into a shareable social artifact, driving engagement loops rare in traditional fintech.

  • Dual-scope segmented control: The "Feed" vs "Between You" toggle elegantly separates public social content from private financial history within the same screen real estate, avoiding extra navigation.

  • Clear CTA hierarchy: Outlined secondary buttons (Add Friend, Friends) vs. solid filled primary CTA (Pay or Request) instantly communicates which action matters most on a profile.

  • Deliberate ambiguity in captions: Vague one-word memos create intrigue and lower the psychological barrier of publicly displaying money transfers (no explicit dollar amounts are shown on the main feed, reducing financial exposure anxiety while retaining social visibility).

  • Visibility indicator (globe icon): Reinforces to users that this activity is public, subtly nudging privacy awareness without an interruptive dialog.

screens.name: Venmo Inviting Teammates & Friends 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when designing social-first fintech products (P2P payment apps, splitting bills, group expense apps) where you want to encourage repeat engagement through social visibility and light gamification. It's ideal for younger audiences who are comfortable with public sharing and enjoy playful, meme-able interactions layered onto utilitarian tasks. Also useful when you need to combine a person's social identity (friends, profile) with transactional capability (pay/request) on a single unified screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in B2B, enterprise, or high-security financial contexts (e.g., banking apps, investment platforms, corporate expense management) where users expect privacy, formality, and minimal social exposure of transaction data. It's also inappropriate for older or privacy-conscious demographics who may find public payment feeds unsettling or a compliance/security risk. Regulatory environments requiring strict transaction confidentiality (e.g., HIPAA-adjacent, GDPR-sensitive contexts) should not adopt public feed visibility by default.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets a younger, socially-driven demographic (Gen Z/Millennial) who view money transfers as a social activity rather than a purely private, transactional one. By gamifying and socializing payments (likes, comments, public captions) the product taps into psychological drivers like social proof (friend count, public feed visibility), reciprocity (Pay or Request), and social belonging (seeing friends' payment activity fosters a feeling of shared community/inside jokes).

The friend-request-like relationship status ("Requested") borrows directly from social network friending mechanics, lowering the psychological barrier to connecting with someone purely for financial reasons by making it feel like a normal social interaction.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-purpose CTA button: "Pay or Request" collapses two primary actions into one tappable element, saving space and simplifying the decision tree.

  • Segmented Feed / Between You toggle: Lets users instantly filter between the public social feed and their private transactional history with this specific person (a powerful mental model shift achieved with one control).

  • Social feed treatment of payments: Transforming payment descriptions into caption-style posts with likes/comments blurs the line between social media and fintech, driving engagement and virality.

  • Relationship status chips: "Requested" and "442 Friends" surface social graph context inline, reducing the need to navigate elsewhere to understand the relationship.

  • Public visibility icon (globe): Signals privacy/visibility settings directly in the feed item, reinforcing transparency and normalizing public sharing of otherwise sensitive data.

screens.name: Venmo Inviting Teammates & Friends 5
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern when designing peer-to-peer fintech or social-commerce products where you want to increase engagement/retention by layering a social feed on top of a core utility (payments, fitness activity, reading, etc.). It's especially effective when:

  • The core action (e.g., paying) is inherently mundane and needs a "fun" layer to drive habitual, repeat usage.

  • Your users already have an established social graph (friends/contacts) that can be leveraged for network effects.

  • You want to reduce the intimidation factor of a financial or transactional product for younger users.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for enterprise, B2B, or high-security financial products (e.g., business banking, wire transfers, wealth management) where users expect discretion, formality, and strict privacy (a public feed of transactions would be a serious trust and compliance liability).

It's also inappropriate for products serving older or more privacy-conscious demographics who may find publicly visible payment activity uncomfortable or even alarming (as has been publicly critiqued with Venmo's default public feed). Additionally, in regions with strict financial privacy regulations, exposing transaction metadata publicly by default could create legal/compliance risk.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets a young, socially-networked, mobile-native demographic (primarily Gen Z and younger Millennials) who are accustomed to sharing personal moments publicly and view money exchange between friends (splitting rent, dinner, drinks) as a normal, even fun, social activity rather than a private banking matter.

The psychological trigger at play is social proof combined with in-group belonging: seeing friends' payment activity in a feed format (complete with likes/comments) turns a transactional utility into a lightweight social network, increasing daily engagement and retention well beyond the actual utility of "sending money." The playful, coded memos ("DRANK," "BOILING") also tap into humor and inside-joke culture, driving virality and repeat visits to see what friends post next.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-intent CTA: "Pay or Request" merges two opposite financial actions into a single, prominent button, reducing screen real estate and decision fatigue.

  • Social-first framing of money: Using "Friends" and a friend counter instead of banking language reframes payments as social currency, decreasing the psychological friction typically associated with sharing financial activity.

  • Segmented Control for context switching: "Feed" vs "Between You" elegantly separates public social proof from private 1:1 transaction history within one screen, avoiding navigation overhead.

  • Public feed as social proof engine: Displaying real (if cryptic) transaction captions publicly leverages social proof and curiosity, encouraging engagement (likes/comments) on what is otherwise a mundane financial event.

  • Consistent iconography with global visibility indicator: The small globe icon on each feed item transparently communicates privacy scope, reinforcing trust and control.

screens.name: Venmo Purchasing & Ordering 18
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately following any high-friction, high-anxiety verification or approval process (KYC, background checks, account approvals, application reviews). It is highly effective for onboarding funnels in regulated industries (fintech, banking, healthcare) where the user needs explicit closure before feeling safe to proceed to core app functionality. It also works well as a bridge screen designed purely to redirect momentum into a specific monetizable action.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this ultra-minimal, single-CTA pattern for confirmations where users might need to review multiple next steps or details (e.g., complex order confirmations with shipping/tracking info), as it would feel like an oversimplification. Do not use this pattern if there's a chance the verification is only partially complete or requires additional user action, doing so risks creating false confidence and support tickets down the line. Additionally, avoid forcing a hard redirect to a purchase action if the user hasn't expressed purchase intent, as it can feel pushy rather than helpful.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users of a financial/crypto application who have just submitted sensitive personal documents (ID, selfie, address proof) for regulatory compliance. This demographic is often anxious about approval status, security, and the possibility of rejection or lengthy waiting periods.

Psychologically, this screen leverages the "Goal Gradient Effect" - users are more motivated to act as they perceive proximity to a goal, and this success state signals that the hardest, most tedious part (verification) is now behind them, making the "Buy crypto" CTA feel like a small, easy final step. It also uses relief-based reinforcement: by immediately confirming success, it prevents drop-off that could occur if users were left in uncertainty.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single Focal Point: Removing all navigational chrome (no header, no back arrow) eliminates escape routes and directs 100% of attention toward the confirmation and the next step.

  • Color Psychology: The use of a universally recognized green checkmark instantly communicates safety, success, and "all clear" status without requiring the user to read any text.

  • Momentum-Driven CTA: Placing "Buy crypto" as the only actionable element capitalizes on the peak emotional high of task completion (the "fresh start effect"), driving immediate conversion into the app's core revenue-generating action.

  • Reduced Cognitive Load: Extreme whitespace and short copy ensure the message is parsed in milliseconds, ideal for a moment where the user is eager to move past administrative friction.

screens.name: Venmo Purchasing & Ordering 19
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for short, curated selection lists in transactional flows: such as choosing a currency, payment method, investment asset, or subscription tier (where each option has 2-3 comparable data points (name, price, trend)). It's ideal when:

  • The list is short (under ~10 items) and doesn't require search/filtering.

  • Users need to compare live/dynamic values (price, change %) across options before committing.

  • Trust and clarity are more important than visual flair (fintech, healthcare, insurance).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the list of options is long (50+ items) - a flat scrolling list without search, filters, or categorization will become tedious and should instead use a searchable/filterable browse pattern. It's also unsuitable when options have highly heterogeneous attributes that don't map cleanly to the same two-column layout, or when the decision requires deeper comparison (e.g., detailed fee structures) that can't be conveyed in a single row and would benefit from a comparison table instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets mainstream, non-expert retail users of a widely trusted platform (PayPal) who are dipping into crypto for the first time or making casual, small-scale purchases (not power-user day traders). The design assumes low crypto literacy: only five, well-known assets are offered (no long scrollable list of hundreds of altcoins), reducing choice overload and the risk of users buying into scams or illiquid tokens.

Psychologically, the screen leverages familiarity and trust transfer: using PayPal's established brand credibility to make an inherently risky asset class (crypto) feel safe and simple. The stablecoin's placement at the top also exploits the anchoring effect, priming users to view $1 PYUSD as the "default" or "safe" comparison point before they see volatile double-digit percentage swings below.
screens.keyHighlights:
• PayPal USD pinned to the top: Placing the platform's own stablecoin above volatile assets like Bitcoin nudges users toward the "safer," fee-generating, in-house asset (a subtle business-driven default ordering rather than pure market-cap ranking).

  • Dual-column comparative layout: Separating identity (left) from performance data (right) lets users compare multiple assets' volatility at a glance without tapping into each one.

  • Color-coded gain/loss: Immediate red/green cues reduce the need to parse text, speeding up decision-making.

  • Card-based rows with generous whitespace: Reduces the "wall of numbers" anxiety common in trading apps and keeps touch targets large and error-tolerant.

  • Fixed $1 value for PYUSD: Reinforces the stablecoin's peg visually, distinguishing it from the fluctuating market prices below.

screens.name: Venmo Purchasing & Ordering 20
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any single-value monetary or numeric entry flow where speed and accuracy are paramount: buying/selling crypto or stocks, peer-to-peer money transfers, topping up a wallet, or entering a bid/donation amount. It's ideal when the entire screen's purpose is capturing one critical number.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when multiple related inputs are needed simultaneously (e.g., amount + payment method + date), as the full-screen numeric takeover doesn't accommodate multi-field forms well. It's also unsuitable for contexts where users need to reference other on-screen data (like current balance or price charts) while typing, since the layout intentionally minimizes competing information.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday retail investors and crypto-curious consumers using a mainstream fintech or exchange app (the PayPal USD stablecoin branding suggests a mass-market, non-technical audience rather than power traders). The design leverages several psychological principles:

  • Cognitive ease:

  • Anchoring via presets: Showing $20/$50/$100 chips subtly anchors the "normal" purchase amount higher than the $1 minimum, potentially nudging average order value upward.

  • Reduced friction=higher conversion: A custom, always-visible keypad removes the extra tap needed to summon a keyboard, shortening the path to purchase completion.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dominant, auto-scaling numeric display: The dollar amount is the largest element on screen, immediately communicating the primary action.

  • Quick-amount preset chips: $1/$20/$50/$100 shortcuts eliminate manual typing for common purchase amounts, drastically reducing time-to-purchase.

  • Custom numeric keypad: Replaces the system keyboard for full design control, larger touch targets, and a purpose-built layout including decimal and backspace keys.

  • Proactive minimum-order messaging: Prevents user frustration by surfacing the $1 minimum constraint before submission rather than via an error after the fact.

  • Minimal chrome: Simple back chevron and title keep focus entirely on the value-entry task with no distracting navigation elements.

screens.name: Venmo Purchasing & Ordering 21
screens.whereToUse:
• High-stakes financial confirmation flows (payments, transfers, crypto/stock purchases) where users need a clear final review before an irreversible action.

  • Any flow transitioning from an input screen to a summary/review step, where preserving context (via a dimmed background) reduces disorientation.

  • Situations requiring legal/compliance disclosures, placing them directly adjacent to the commit button rather than burying them in fine print elsewhere.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for low-stakes or frequently repeated actions, where a bottom sheet review step would add unnecessary friction (e.g., toggling a setting).

  • Not ideal if the itemized breakdown is very long (a bottom sheet has limited vertical space and could require scrolling, weakening the "everything visible at a glance" benefit).

  • Avoid burying critical irreversibility warnings in small gray text if the audience is non-expert; consider a stronger visual treatment (icon, color) for higher-risk transactions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets mainstream retail users experimenting with crypto/stablecoins via a trusted brand (PayPal) rather than a native crypto exchange. The design deliberately avoids crypto-native complexity (gas fees, wallet addresses, network selection) and instead frames the purchase like a simple currency exchange or online purchase receipt.

Psychologically, the screen leverages trust-building through transparency (itemized fee breakdown, $0 fee callout) and friction-at-the-right-moment (the cancellation warning) to reduce buyer's remorse and support tickets, while the low minimum ("as little as $1") lowers the psychological barrier to first-time crypto purchases - a classic foot-in-the-door tactic to convert curious users into active crypto holders.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background continuity: The amount-entry screen remains visible (dimmed) behind the sheet, reassuring users their input wasn't lost and providing spatial context.

  • Irreversibility warning placed at the point of maximum commitment: Rather than in a T&Cs page, the "cannot cancel" warning sits directly above the primary CTA (exactly when it's most relevant and most likely to be read).

  • Zero transaction fee highlighted: Explicitly showing "$0" fee (rather than omitting the line) builds trust and removes hidden-fee anxiety common in crypto purchases.

  • Bolded final total ("You pay $1"): Strong visual weighting on the final cost line ensures no ambiguity about what will be charged.

  • Payment method as an expandable row: Keeps the primary flow uncluttered while still surfacing an essential, changeable input at the top of the hierarchy.

screens.name: Google Pay Setting Up 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any settings/account hub in transactional, fintech, or trust-sensitive apps where users need to quickly locate a small, finite number of configuration categories. It's ideal when:

  • The total number of settings items is low (under ~10) and doesn't warrant search or filtering.

  • You want to visually separate 'account/identity' settings from 'app/session' actions using minimal chrome.

  • Brand consistency and calm, low-stimulation UI are priorities (finance, health, legal apps).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat single-list pattern when:

  • The settings surface area is large (20+ items), which would require section headers, search, or a nested/drill-down taxonomy to stay scannable.

  • Some settings require immediate visual differentiation for state (e.g., toggles, badges for unread counts) - this layout has no room for secondary metadata like a switch or status indicator.

  • The destructive action (Sign out / Delete account) needs stronger emphasis or confirmation gating; here it lacks any distinct color treatment or safeguard, which could be risky in higher-stakes contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves the entire Google Pay user base, but is especially critical for privacy- and security-conscious users who need quick, unambiguous access to controls over their financial data. Because Google Pay handles money, users arrive at this screen with heightened anxiety about data exposure, unauthorized transactions, and account control - the psychological driver here is reassurance through clarity.

By placing "Privacy and security" prominently near the top and using a trust-associated shield icon, Google leverages the psychological principle of primacy: important, anxiety-reducing options are seen first. The minimal, uncluttered layout also reduces the perceived complexity of managing sensitive settings, lowering the mental barrier to engaging with security features that many users otherwise avoid.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consistent Iconography System: Every row uses a matching-weight, single-color (Google Blue) line icon, creating strong visual rhythm and making the list scannable at a glance without reading every label.

  • Logical Grouping via Divider: Separating personal/account settings from app-level/meta actions (About, Help, Sign out) using a single hairline divider is a low-cost way to impose hierarchy without adding section headers or extra vertical space.

  • Destructive Action De-emphasized: "Sign out" is placed at the very bottom, styled identically to non-destructive items (no red color), preventing accidental taps while avoiding unnecessary alarm for a low-risk action.

  • Full-width Tap Targets: Despite minimal visual chrome (no card backgrounds or borders), each row likely has a generous tap area, aligning with Google's accessibility-first touch target guidelines.

screens.name: Google Pay Setting Up 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any settings/preferences screen managing multiple notification or communication channels (push, email, SMS).

  • Apps with both transactional (must-have) and promotional (optional) messaging that need to reassure users about the former while giving granular control over the latter.

  • Financial, e-commerce, or social apps where trust and perceived control directly impact retention and app-store review sentiment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this flat, long-scroll list pattern when there are dozens of notification types (it becomes overwhelming; use grouped accordions or a search/filter mechanism instead).

  • Don't use vague benefit copy without an actual technical toggle name if users are technical/power users who want precise control (e.g., enterprise or developer tools).

  • Not suitable when notification categories are highly interdependent (turning one off should logically disable another) - a flat toggle list won't communicate those dependencies.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves the broad, mainstream Google Pay user base who wants control over how "chatty" the app is across push and email channels. By defaulting most toggles to ON, Google leverages the default effect / status-quo bias: most users won't bother changing pre-set defaults, maximizing engagement and marketing reach while still legally and ethically offering an opt-out.

The clear separation of "guaranteed" transactional alerts from "optional" promotional ones builds trust: users feel Google isn't going to spam them about money movement, only about tips/offers/social activity, which are lower-stakes and easier to permit.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Benefit-framed subtext: Every toggle explains "why" in human terms rather than just naming the notification type, increasing the likelihood users leave things enabled.

  • Separation of critical vs. optional alerts: Explicitly stating that payment transaction notifications are always-on removes them from the toggle list entirely, simplifying the remaining decisions to purely optional/marketing content.

  • Consistent row pattern: Title + description + switch repeated identically across both Notification and Email sections, making the whole screen instantly learnable after the first row.

  • Section grouping via uppercase labels: A lightweight, low-visual-weight way to segment a long list without needing tabs or nested navigation.

screens.name: Google Pay Setting Up 3
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern whenever an app offers granular, multi-channel notification controls (push, email, SMS) and needs to communicate the "why" behind each toggle without overwhelming the user. It's ideal for financial, e-commerce, or subscription apps where trust and transparency around communication frequency directly impacts retention and complaint/opt-out rates. The title+description+switch triplet is especially effective when notification categories are not self-explanatory from their name alone.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, fully-expanded list approach when there are more than 8-10 notification types, as scrolling fatigue and decision paralysis increase; consider grouping into collapsible accordions instead. Also avoid defaulting all switches to "on" in jurisdictions with strict opt-in consent requirements (e.g., GDPR ePrivacy for marketing emails), where explicit affirmative consent must be captured rather than assumed via pre-enabled toggles.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves the entire Google Pay user base at the point where they seek to reduce notification fatigue or, conversely, opt further into marketing content (typically privacy-conscious or notification-averse users who have drilled into Settings specifically to curate their experience). The psychological trigger at play is the default effect / status quo bias: because every switch defaults to "on," most users will leave the majority enabled simply due to inertia, maximizing Google's owned marketing channels (tips, offers, transaction insights) without appearing coercive, since the control is technically present and easy to disable.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Co-located rationale: Every toggle is paired with a short, benefit-oriented explanation directly beneath it, eliminating the need for separate help documentation or tooltips.

  • Grouped mental model: Clear separation between in-product notifications and email channel via a divider and section header, so users understand exactly where each alert will surface.

  • Consistent, scannable rhythm: Identical title/description/switch layout for every row creates predictable scanning patterns, letting power users skim and toggle quickly.

  • Overflow menu: The "..." icon in the header likely surfaces advanced/rarely-used actions (e.g., reset to default), keeping the primary header uncluttered.

screens.name: Google Pay Setting Up 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this granular toggle-list pattern for any settings area where users need fine-grained control over communication channels (especially in fintech, e-commerce, or social apps where notification fatigue directly correlates with uninstall/opt-out rates). It's ideal when you have 4+ distinct notification types that warrant individual explanation and control, and when regulatory or trust considerations (e.g., GDPR, financial services) demand explicit, transparent consent per category.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this exhaustive per-item pattern for apps with only 1-2 notification types, where a single master switch suffices and granular lists would feel like over-engineering. It's also not ideal for onboarding flows where cognitive load must stay minimal (long descriptive toggle lists are better suited to deliberate settings visits than first-run experiences). Additionally, avoid pre-enabling any toggle whose value isn't immediately obvious to the user, as this can erode trust if perceived as opt-out dark patterns.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets privacy- and attention-conscious users, particularly relevant in a financial/payments app like Google Pay where trust is paramount. Users arriving at this screen are typically motivated by a desire to reduce notification fatigue or, conversely, ensure they don't miss critical transactional alerts.

Psychologically, granular control satisfies the need for autonomy (Self-Determination Theory) - users feel respected rather than "marketed at." The pre-enabled transactional toggles leverage a status-quo bias to keep users engaged with core utility features, while the opt-in-only marketing emails reduce perceived spam risk, which is critical for maintaining brand trust in a payments context.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual sub-copy under every toggle: Instead of a bare label, each setting explains the "why," reducing ambiguity and toggle-anxiety.

  • Segmented grouping by channel: Clear separation between in-app/push notifications and email preferences avoids a monolithic, overwhelming list.

  • Asymmetric smart defaults: High-utility, expected notifications (orders, chats) are on by default, while promotional-feeling content (Google Pay tips) is off by default, balancing engagement with trust.

  • Immediate visual state feedback: Color-coded switches (blue=on, gray/white=off) let users audit their full opt-in status in a single glance without opening each item.

screens.name: Google Pay Setting Up 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Settings/preferences screens where a mix of simple toggles and complex sub-flows need to coexist without overwhelming the user.

  • Fintech, healthcare, or any high-trust vertical where transparent, benefit-oriented copy can reduce opt-out rates for necessary permissions.

  • Any screen governing social discoverability (e.g., "find me by phone number") where inline toggles let users self-serve instantly.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid inline toggles for settings that require additional confirmation or have destructive/irreversible consequences (e.g., account deletion) - these need a Confirmation Dialog instead.

  • Don't use this flat list pattern when there are more than ~7-8 settings; grouping into collapsible sections (Accordion) would be more scalable.

  • Avoid soft, benefit-only framing for settings with genuine privacy trade-offs (regulators and privacy-focused users may see this as manipulative if the risk isn't also disclosed).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets privacy-conscious users and mainstream consumers alike who are handling financial transactions and therefore have heightened sensitivity to data-sharing settings. Because Google Pay moves money, users' trust threshold is higher than in a typical social app, so the design leans on Google's established brand equity (recognizable shield/people iconography, familiar Material typography) to reduce anxiety.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the illusion of control: presenting every switch as ON by default communicates a socially-engineered default (defaults bias) while still visibly giving the user agency to turn things off. The "avoid fraud" framing also taps into loss-aversion messaging, nudging users to keep contact sync enabled by associating it with protection rather than data harvesting.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Inline toggles over drill-down screens: Permission-based settings are resolved directly on the list with a Switch, dramatically reducing taps for one of the most frequently adjusted settings categories.

  • Benefit-framed microcopy: Descriptions like "avoid fraud" reframe data collection (contact syncing) as a safety feature, lowering the psychological resistance to enabling data sharing.

  • Consistent iconography language: Shield icons for security-hardening items (blocked people, data controls) vs. people icons for social/discoverability items create an instant visual taxonomy the user can pattern-match against.

  • Progressive disclosure: Complex topics (Data and personalisation) are pushed to a dedicated sub-page, while simple binary decisions stay inline (an effective triage of complexity vs). simplicity.

screens.name: Google Pay Setting Up 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any settings hub in a finance, health, or identity-sensitive app where users need to configure multiple independent privacy toggles and drill-down policy links in one place. It's ideal when:

  • You have a mix of instant-effect binary settings and deeper multi-screen settings that need to coexist on one page.

  • Trust and transparency are core to retention (fintech, health, social).

  • You want to reduce support tickets by clearly explaining the consequence of each toggle inline rather than requiring a help article.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when there are more than 10-12 settings, as a flat list without grouping/sectioning becomes a long, undifferentiated scroll that buries important items. In such cases, use accordion sections or categorized headers instead. Also avoid mixing navigational rows and toggle rows without any structural cue (like a divider or section label) in longer or more complex settings screens, as users may struggle to distinguish "tap to open" from "tap to toggle" once the list grows beyond 5-6 items.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets the general Google Pay user base at the exact moment they are seeking control or reassurance over their financial and personal data (often triggered by anxiety after reading a news story, receiving a spam contact request, or simply doing a periodic privacy audit). The psychological driver is locus of control: by exposing granular, individually toggleable settings (rather than a single opaque "privacy mode"), Google reduces the user's sense of helplessness around a fintech product handling sensitive data.

The mix of default-off (discoverability) and default-on (contact sync, group adds) toggles also reveals a dual audience being served simultaneously: privacy-conscious users who want the ability to lock down discoverability, and Google's own growth/network-effects goals which benefit from contacts being synced and groups being easy to join.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consistent row grammar: icon, bold title, grey explanatory subtext creates instant scannability and predictability across a long list of unrelated settings.

  • Segmented interaction model: drill-down rows (no toggle) vs. instant-toggle rows are visually and functionally distinct, letting users infer navigation behavior without extra affordances like chevrons.

  • Default states as trust signals: "Allow people to find you" defaults OFF (privacy-protective), while "Sync your contacts" and "Allow people to add you to groups" default ON (convenience-first) - a calculated default strategy balancing user trust with product growth needs.

  • Overflow menu in header: the three-dot icon keeps rarely used or advanced actions out of the primary flow, preserving the clean single-column layout.

screens.name: Google Pay Setting Up 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any legal/compliance/meta information hub. Settings > About sections in finance, health, or regulated apps where trust and transparency outweigh engagement metrics. Ideal when you need a low-maintenance, infinitely scalable list (new legal docs can be appended without redesign) and when the audience expects platform-standard conventions rather than novel navigation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this ultra-minimal treatment if the legal content itself needs contextual framing (e.g., a GDPR consent flow requiring active acknowledgement) - in those cases use dialogs or checkboxes with explicit consent capture instead of a passive link list. Also avoid for screens meant to drive engagement or feature discovery, as the deliberate blandness here would undersell any promotional content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves two distinct audiences: (1) the average user who occasionally needs to reference privacy/terms for reassurance or compliance reasons (e.g., before linking a bank account), and (2) power users, developers, or support agents who need the exact app version number for troubleshooting. Psychologically, the sparse, no-nonsense design reduces anxiety around "legal" content (users are not asked to read anything here, only given an easy off-ramp to detailed documents if they choose). The lack of persuasive design cues is itself a trust signal: Google isn't trying to sell or nudge anything on this screen, which subconsciously reinforces the app's credibility as a financial custodian.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-as-affordance coding: Blue icons signal tappable navigation rows, while the gray outlined "i" icon for Version visually demotes it to non-interactive status without needing a disabled state or extra label.

  • Radical minimalism: No banners, no illustrations, no CTAs. Just the four rows a user could conceivably need, respecting the low-engagement nature of a legal/compliance screen.

  • Overflow menu retained in header: The persistent "•••" icon in the top-right maintains consistency with other screens in the app even where its utility here is minimal, preserving muscle-memory navigation.

  • Version number transparency: Surfacing the exact build number aids support/debugging conversations and signals engineering transparency, a small trust cue for a finance app.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for account/profile hubs that double as lightweight onboarding checklists (especially in fintech, e-commerce, or subscription apps where completing setup (payment methods, verification, preferences) directly benefits both user and business). It's ideal when you have 2-4 setup steps that shouldn't feel forced but need gentle, persistent visibility. It also works well when combining identity display with quick-access settings and support links on a single scrollable screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern once a user has fully completed setup (the checklist card should be dismissed or replaced with more relevant content (e).g., transaction history) to prevent clutter and stale progress indicators. It's also unsuitable for high-security or enterprise contexts where profile screens need to prioritize account/security status over playful illustration, or where too many simultaneous CTAs (payment setup + referral + settings) could overwhelm a first-time user already navigating a complex financial task.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets everyday users mid-onboarding or early in their Google Pay lifecycle (people who have signed up but haven't yet linked a bank account or card). The design leans on completion bias (the 1/3 counter), social reciprocity (referral rewards), and trust cues (Google's familiar visual language, clean layout, transparent status labels) to nudge users toward fuller product adoption without feeling like a hard sell. It's also built for users who value quick access to account controls (Settings, Help) without hunting through nested menus, reflecting a broad, non-technical mainstream audience rather than power users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fractional progress counter (1/3): A tiny numeric cue that turns an optional setup task into a completion-driven mini-goal, leveraging the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to finish unfinished tasks).

  • State-differentiated iconography: Active vs. not-yet-added payment methods are distinguished purely through color saturation and a "+" badge, avoiding redundant text labels.

  • Illustrated but functional hero: The playful background art humanizes a money app without sacrificing the information density needed on an account screen.

  • Decorative avatar ring with settings shortcut: Turns a static profile photo into an interactive entry point for account customization, saving a navigational step.

  • In-line referral code with copy icon: Removes friction from the invite flow by displaying the shareable code directly rather than requiring a secondary screen.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you need a low-friction way for two parties to establish a trusted connection (payment, contact-sharing, social linking) in person or over video/screen-share. It's ideal for peer-to-peer fintech apps, contact/business card sharing, event check-ins, or Wi-Fi/device pairing flows where a visual, scannable identity token reduces manual data entry and typo-related errors.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-frequency, repetitive actions where scanning would add unnecessary friction compared to a saved contact list or autocomplete search. It's also unsuitable for use cases requiring strong identity verification (e.g., KYC, large fund transfers) since a QR/code exchange alone lacks the security assurance of authenticated bank-level identifiers. Additionally, avoid on screens where accessibility for visually impaired users is a primary concern, since QR/code scanning relies heavily on camera-based visual interaction without a robust non-visual fallback.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who want to send/receive money from friends, family, or nearby contacts without manually entering phone numbers, UPI IDs, or bank accounts (a common pattern in markets with high QR/contactless payment adoption). The psychological trigger at play is frictionless trust: by visually presenting a name and photo/avatar alongside the code, the system reassures both parties that they are connecting with the correct person, reducing anxiety around mistaken transfers.

The design also leverages social parity with messaging/social apps (e.g., WhatsApp, Venmo, WeChat Pay) where QR-based "add contact" flows are already familiar mental models, making adoption near-instant for users coming from those ecosystems.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-purpose full-screen focus: Removing tab bars, secondary content, and navigation chrome eliminates decision fatigue and mirrors the simplicity of "unremarkable" money movement the app is built around.

  • Identity-as-QR pattern: Turning the user's own profile into a scannable code reframes a technical pairing mechanism into a personal, shareable "digital business card," making peer-to-peer setup feel social rather than transactional.

  • Dual entry point symmetry: The screen simultaneously serves as a code to be scanned (passive) and offers a scanner to scan others (active), collapsing two flows into one lightweight screen via a single bottom CTA.

  • Soft gradient avatar: The blurred blob adds warmth and brand personality to an otherwise stark white/functional screen, softening the trust barrier around sharing financial connection details.

screens.name: Google Pay Connecting & Linking 3

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves the "on-the-go" user: someone standing at a hawker stall, retail counter, or across from a friend needing to split a bill. The design assumes high-stress, low-attention environmental conditions (crowds, noise, time pressure), which is why the UI relies on large, high-contrast iconography and minimal text.

Psychologically, the reticle exploits the "Von Restorff effect" (isolation effect) by using bright, distinct colors against a dark camera background, making the target area impossible to miss even in bad lighting. The persistent presence of network logos (PayNow) also serves a "trust transfer" purpose, borrowing the established credibility of national payment infrastructure to reassure users that Google Pay is a safe conduit for the transaction.

Brand-as-Function (Chromatic Reticle): Using Google's four signature colors for the scanning frame corners transforms a purely functional element (the viewfinder) into an unmistakable piece of brand identity, differentiating it instantly from generic QR scanners.

Bidirectional Mode Switch: The "Show your Spot code" pill efficiently merges two opposite payment flows (scanning vs. being scanned) into one screen, reducing the need for separate navigation paths for sending vs. receiving money.

Zero-Chrome Camera View: By defaulting to a full-bleed camera view with minimal floating icons, the app reduces cognitive load and gets the user to the "money moment" as fast as physically possible.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The reward messaging ("pay and earn") taps into variable reward psychology, priming users to associate scanning with potential upside, which increases the likelihood of choosing Google Pay over a bank's own QR scanner for the same transaction.

  • Real-time scan feedback (pulsing reticle): Builds confidence that the system is "listening" and actively working, reducing anxiety during the brief scan latency.

  • Scheme logo trust bar: Placing PayNow/FavePay logos at the bottom acts as a low-friction verification step, letting users self-serve compatibility checks instead of failing silently.

screens.name: Google Pay Transferring Money 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any final-step monetary or quantity input screen where accuracy and focus are paramount. P2P transfers, merchant checkout, bill payments, or in-app purchases. It's especially effective when:

  • The recipient/payee identity needs prominent, trust-building confirmation before committing funds.

  • A large numeric keypad is more efficient than a standard system keyboard (e.g., currency, PIN, OTP entry).

  • You want to minimize distractions and navigational escape routes to keep users on task during a critical conversion step.

  • You can offer a smart default (category, note, tip amount) to speed up completion without extra typing.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, single-purpose full-screen pattern when:

  • The amount entry is a minor sub-step in a longer, more exploratory flow (e.g., budgeting apps where users compare/edit multiple line items) - a modal or inline field may be more appropriate.

  • Users need to reference other information (e.g., account balance, previous transactions) simultaneously; the distraction-free design here sacrifices context.

  • The transaction requires more nuanced payee verification beyond a name/ID (e.g., in high-risk international wire transfers where additional fields like bank details are mandatory).

  • Desktop or larger-screen contexts, where a numeric keypad is unnecessary and a standard form input with real keyboard usage is more efficient.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

  • Authority/Verification bias: Displaying the UEN taps into trust heuristics (an official registration number feels more credible than a generic name, reducing anxiety about paying an unverified or fraudulent party).

  • Reduced friction anxiety: The prefilled note and oversized numeric display reduce the perceived effort and risk of the transaction, encouraging quick task completion.

  • Focus/scarcity of attention: By removing navigation and distractions, Google leverages a "narrow the funnel" design tactic common in checkout/payment flows to prevent drop-off or user error mid-transaction.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Smart Default Note: Pre-filled "Business transaction" placeholder removes the need for manual memo entry while still allowing customization, balancing speed with flexibility (Smart Defaults / Prefill).

  • Floating Confirm Button: The circular checkmark FAB positioned above the keypad keeps the primary action within thumb reach without cluttering the numeric input area.

  • Distraction-Free Chrome: Stripped-down top bar (only X and overflow menu) ensures full user focus on the singular task of entering an accurate amount.

screens.name: Google Pay Transferring Money 4

The docked funding-source + CTA footer pattern is especially valuable in flows where users may have multiple payment sources, as it keeps method-switching accessible without leaving the confirmation context.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for low-stakes or reversible actions (e.g., saving a draft, adding to a wishlist) where such heavy visual emphasis and friction would feel disproportionate and slow down the user unnecessarily.

Also avoid when a transaction requires multiple contextual details (e.g., itemized invoices, tax breakdowns, split payments) - the extreme minimalism here would need to be abandoned in favor of a more detailed line-item layout, or users may commit to payments without seeing critical breakdown information.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers making point-of-sale or QR-code payments to small/local businesses (evidenced by the UEN and PayNow business name (a Singapore-specific business registration and bank-linked payment identifier)). The design assumes a user who is often paying quickly, possibly in-person while a merchant waits, so decisiveness and speed are prioritized over exploration.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the peak-end verification effect: by foregrounding the amount and payee identity right before the commitment action, it reduces post-payment regret and buyer's remorse by ensuring the last thing seen matches the user's intent. The muted trust signals (UEN) subtly reduce anxiety around "Am I paying the right entity?" without requiring the user to actively seek out that reassurance.

  • Oversized amount typography: The dollar figure dominates the visual hierarchy, ensuring the last thing a user confirms before tapping "Pay" is the number that matters most.

  • Persistent payment method footer: Docking the bank account selector directly above the CTA lets users glance-verify the funding source without scrolling, reducing "wrong account" errors.

  • Verification metadata surfaced, not hidden: Showing UEN and registered PayNow name builds institutional trust for a business payment, which is where fraud risk (fake QR codes) is highest.

screens.name: Google Pay Transferring Money 5

Also avoid using an auto-generated initial avatar for entities where visual verification (like a logo or verified badge) is critical to prevent fraud (an unverified-looking orange circle could be mistaken as informal or non-secure by cautious users making large payments).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The target user values speed and certainty over decoration (they need instant confirmation that they're sending the right amount to the right recognized entity).

Psychologically, the design leans on loss-aversion mitigation: by making the recipient's identity and amount maximally legible and by using calm neutral colors (aside from the avatar), the interface reduces the anxiety naturally associated with parting with money. The bottom-sheet loading transition also exploits the Zeigarnik effect: keeping the prior screen visible signals an uninterrupted, trustworthy process rather than an app that has "moved on" and abandoned context.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Identity humanization for B2B/UEN payments: A colored initial avatar is generated even for a business/UEN identifier, applying the same trust-building visual pattern used for personal contacts to less personal, code-based entities.

  • Non-blocking progress transition: The processing/loading state appears as a bottom sheet overlay rather than a full-screen takeover, preserving context and giving the user a sense of continuity and control during the payment execution.

  • Redundant confirmation microcopy: Restating "Paying MACHI CREATION $12" in the loading sheet reinforces accuracy right at the point of no return, reducing post-transaction anxiety.

screens.name: Google Pay Transferring Money 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this minimalist processing pattern for:

  • High-stakes transactional flows (payments, transfers, purchases) where trust and correctness must be affirmed before confirming completion.

  • Screens designed to double as both the "pending" and "success" state shell, minimizing redesign effort and providing continuity.

  • Situations where backend confirmation may take a few seconds and you want to avoid a jarring full-screen loading takeover.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Processing times are unpredictable or long (>10-15 seconds) - a bare spinner without progress text or an estimated time can heighten anxiety rather than reduce it.

  • The transaction is reversible or complex (e.g., multi-item checkout) - users may need itemized confirmation rather than a single amount and generic category.

  • Errors are common in this flow: a silent spinner provides no scaffolding for graceful error recovery messaging if the transaction fails.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves everyday consumers and small-business customers making point-of-sale or P2P-style payments (e.g., paying a vendor like "MACHI CREATION"). The design leverages the psychology of transactional anxiety: money leaving one's account triggers heightened attention, so the interface strips away all distraction to keep the user's focus on the single fact that matters: the payment is in motion and being handled correctly.

The use of a large, unambiguous dollar amount and recognizable recipient identity taps into loss-aversion reassurance: users immediately double-check "is this the right amount, right person?" before worrying about status. Only after these are visually confirmed does the eye drop down to the loading indicator, at which point trust has already been partially established.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Persistent transaction-level actions: Keeping share/overflow icons active during the pending state signals architectural consistency (this is the same screen shell that will host the final receipt).

  • Generous whitespace as reassurance: The emptiness below the spinner avoids making the waiting period feel effortful or heavy, subtly reducing perceived wait time.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
