screens.name: Lemon8 - Reporting a story - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this bottom sheet pattern whenever:

  • Content needs to be exported or referenced outside the app (sharing to social platforms, copying links, sending via messaging apps).
  • You need to bundle a sensitive/destructive action (Report, Block, Delete) alongside benign utility actions, but want to visually de-risk accidental activation.
  • You want to preserve context (e.g., keep video playing/visible) while presenting secondary options, rather than forcing a full navigation change.
  • Your audience already has strong mental models of native OS share sheets, so adopting the same visual grammar increases usability instantly.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • There are more than 6-8 sharing destinations: the horizontal row would require scrolling or overwhelm users; consider a grid or "More" expansion instead.
  • The destructive action (e.g., Report, Delete Account) carries severe, irreversible consequences (in those cases, a dedicated confirmation dialog with explicit friction (e).g., typing to confirm) is safer than a sheet item.
  • The underlying content is sensitive and shouldn't remain partially visible behind a dimmed overlay (e.g., private user data, payment screens).
  • Users are on a low-dexterity or accessibility-constrained device, where small adjacent icons without sufficient hit-target spacing could cause accidental taps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Lemon8's target demographic: Gen Z and young lifestyle creators (are native "sharers)." Content only gains social currency once it leaves the app and circulates on Instagram Stories, Twitter, or group chats. This screen directly serves the psychological driver of social validation and curation identity: users want to be seen as the curator who found this interesting unboxing content first.

By placing Instagram and Stories as the top-left, most prominent options, the design acknowledges that cross-posting to Instagram (a near-ubiquitous app among this demographic) is the highest-value action for distribution and, indirectly, for Lemon8's own growth loop (content attribution/links driving new users back to the app).

The inclusion of "Report" caters to the platform's need for community moderation and trust & safety compliance, giving every piece of content an easily accessible, low-friction route for users to flag inappropriate content (crucial for maintaining a safe, brand-friendly, advertiser-viable environment for a lifestyle content platform).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background video keeps context alive: Users can still see a faded view of the content they're sharing, reinforcing what's being acted upon without a jarring full-screen transition.
  • Brand-colored icons for zero-friction recognition: Leveraging real-world familiarity with Instagram, Facebook, and Twitter iconography eliminates the need for text scanning.
  • Visual isolation of the destructive action: Separating "Report" into its own card below a gap drastically reduces mis-taps and signals a change in action severity.
  • Dual dismissal affordances: Both the "X" icon and the native swipe-down gesture (drag handle) are available, respecting varied user interaction habits.
  • Native, OS-consistent modal behavior: The bottom sheet pattern matches system-level share sheets users already know from iOS, lowering the learning curve to near zero.

screens.name: Lemon8 - Reporting a story - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a platform needs to let users flag content, users, or accounts for policy violations (particularly in social, marketplace, dating, or UGC-driven apps). It's ideal for:

  • Content moderation flows (posts, comments, profiles, messages)
  • Trust & safety reporting in any community-driven product
  • Any flow requiring a single, mutually exclusive classification before an action can proceed
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this exact pattern when:

  • Multiple reasons could apply simultaneously: a single-select list forces an artificial choice; consider multi-select in such cases.
  • The report requires additional context (e.g., screenshots, free-text description) - a plain list without a follow-up detail step may yield insufficient information for moderators.
  • The list of categories is very long (>12-15 items), which would require scrolling and could overwhelm a user already in a stressful emotional state, grouping into collapsible sections or a search/filter would be more appropriate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Lemon8's entire user base but is especially critical for Gen Z and young adult users, who are highly attuned to platform safety, community standards, and accountability. Given the app's social, UGC-heavy nature (photos, videos, comments on fashion/beauty/lifestyle content), robust and easy-to-use reporting tools are essential for trust & safety and regulatory compliance (e.g., minor protection laws, hate speech regulation).

Psychologically, the design reduces the emotional and cognitive burden of reporting (an action users may hesitate to take due to social anxiety ("will the person know)?") or uncertainty about categorization. By offering clear, pre-defined categories, Lemon8 removes decision paralysis and empowers users to act quickly, reinforcing a sense of agency and safety within the community.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled-until-valid CTA: The pale "OK" button enforces selection before submission without needing inline error states.
  • Severity-ordered taxonomy: Listing high-risk categories (minor safety, violence, self-harm) first helps prioritize urgent reports and nudges user attention appropriately.
  • Low-friction exit: The circular X button offers an unambiguous, easily tappable escape hatch.
  • Sensitive-topic-appropriate visual calm: Minimalist black-on-white list design with no color-coding or icons avoids trivializing or sensationalizing difficult topics.

screens.name: Craft - Commenting on a text block - Screen 1

  • Soft highlight instead of heavy chrome: The selected block is distinguished with a gentle light-blue wash rather than a harsh border or checkbox-heavy UI, preserving the editorial, document-like aesthetic even in an interactive state.
  • Peeking/partial element at tray edge: The action tray intentionally bleeds off the left edge, signaling more content/actions exist via horizontal scroll (a subtle wayfinding cue instead of an explicit arrow or label).

screens.name: Brex All expenses 1

Adopt this layered hero-card-plus-draggable-sheet pattern for any app where a single physical/visual asset (a card, a device, a ticket) is the primary mental anchor but needs to coexist with a long scrollable list of related records (transactions, logs, bookings). Psychological triggers at play include: trust-building through visual realism (the card mockup feels authentic and "owned"), reduction of anxiety via transparency (clearly showing "$36.14 USD available" prevents overspending surprises), and compliance nudging through status iconography (visually incomplete rows with red/missing icons would implicitly pressure the user to complete documentation, leveraging the Zeigarnik effect of unfinished tasks).
screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for micro-learning, skill-assessment, or data-literacy products where a single visual artifact (chart, diagram, equation) is both the teaching aid and the quiz input. It's ideal for:

  • Educational apps teaching chart/graph reading, statistics, or quantitative reasoning.

  • Any linear lesson flow where you want to force "doing" (selecting/estimating) over passive reading.

  • Products needing lightweight, low-anxiety progress indication within a longer course or module.

  • Scenarios where real-world, relatable framing (sales, scores, measurements) can de-jargonize abstract concepts.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The task requires precise numerical input rather than estimation (a chart-tap interaction is unsuitable for exact-value problems; a text/numeric field would be clearer).

  • Users need to review or edit past answers frequently (the implied weak backward navigation (only an X to exit, no back button) frustrates users who want to revisit previous questions).

  • The content is inherently list-based or textual (e.g., vocabulary quizzes) where a chart-based interactive artifact adds unnecessary complexity.

  • Accessibility is a major concern: relying on visual bar-height comparison and color-coded bars can disadvantage low-vision or colorblind users without additional data labels or alt-text support.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-directed adult learners and lifelong-learning enthusiasts (Brilliant's core demographic) who want bite-sized, active STEM practice rather than lecture-style video content. The coffee-shop sales scenario is deliberately mainstream and non-technical, designed to appeal worldwide without requiring domain expertise, lowering the barrier for users intimidated by "math" framing.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Generation Effect (people retain information better when they produce an answer rather than recognize one) and a Zeigarnik-like completion drive via the progress dots, nudging users to finish the step they've started. The disabled Check button also exploits a mild commitment and consistency trigger (users must mentally commit to an answer before the system validates it, deepening engagement with the material).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chart-as-interactive-content: The bar chart doubles as both the content and the input mechanism, embodying the brand's "doing over watching" philosophy rather than presenting a passive image with a separate answer list.

  • Segmented progress with color-coded completion: Green filled dots versus gray upcoming dots give lightweight, ambient progress feedback that doesn't distract from the task.

  • Disabled-state CTA: The grayed-out "Check" button enforces a deliberate action-then-validate loop, preventing accidental skips and reinforcing the "commit to an answer" moment.

  • Minimalist chrome: No tab bar, no header title, no extraneous iconography beyond essential navigation (X) and a streak/lightning indicator, maximizing focus on the single learning task.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when teaching any skill where visual/quantitative literacy is the goal (chart reading, statistics, finance, data science, or scientific reasoning apps). It's ideal for microlearning moments where a single concept (e.g., "reading combined values from a bar chart") needs to be reinforced through direct manipulation rather than passive video or text. Also effective in any product trying to replace lecture-style explainer screens with interactive, self-checking exercises to boost completion and retention rates.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex, multi-variable datasets where estimation from a static chart would be genuinely difficult or produce high error rates, causing frustration rather than productive struggle. It's also unsuitable for high-stakes assessments (certification exams, compliance tests) where "about" answers and forgiving approximation are inappropriate. Additionally, this minimal-chrome, no-hint approach can alienate complete beginners who need more scaffolding (axis labeling tutorials, worked examples) before being asked to perform an unassisted estimation task.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed adult learners and lifelong-learning enthusiasts (the core Brilliant demographic) who are motivated by mastery and curiosity rather than grades or external accountability. The design leans on the generation effect (people remember material better when they actively produce an answer rather than passively read it) and low-stakes testing effect (quizzing with immediate, judgment-free feedback strengthens retention far more than exposition).

The exit (X) and non-threatening "Check" button cater to intrinsically motivated users who may be studying in short bursts (commute, break) and need the psychological safety to stop at any point without feeling they've "failed" a course.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Question-as-interaction: The bar chart is simultaneously the explanatory content and the answer-input mechanism, collapsing two learning steps into one tactile motion.

  • Deliberate ambiguity ("about 225"): Using an approximate target number nudges users toward estimation and pattern recognition over brittle exact math, a subtle pedagogical trick.

  • Generous whitespace as pacing device: The large gap between question and chart forces sequential processing (read → scroll/look → analyze) rather than everything being parsed simultaneously.

  • Non-numeric progress indicator: Dots/pill segments communicate journey position without the pressure of a percentage countdown.

  • Single, unmissable CTA: The dark pill "Check" button is the only button on screen, eliminating decision paralysis about what to do next.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any educational, assessment, or skill-training product where interactive problem-solving (drag, tap, select) is central, and where you want to soften the emotional impact of wrong answers while still driving toward comprehension. Ideal for microlearning platforms, data-literacy or math tools, certification prep apps, and any flow where you want to incentivize reflection (via an optional "why" moment) over rote retry-until-correct loops.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this soft, non-urgent incorrect-state treatment in contexts where errors carry real-world consequences (e.g., financial transactions, medical data entry, compliance forms) - users need clear, high-salience error signaling there, not a gentle grey banner. Also avoid overlaying feedback badges directly onto charts/illustrations when the underlying visualization is dense or data-heavy, as it can obscure information; this works best with simple, sparse charts as shown here.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed adult learners (worldwide, STEM-curious audience) who want short, low-stakes, skill-building sessions rather than lecture-style content. By decoupling "being wrong" from negative emotion (muted color palette, no scolding copy), the design leverages a growth-mindset psychological trigger: mistakes are treated as data points in the learning loop, not as a verdict on the user's intelligence.

The optional-but-encouraged "Why?" button exploits curiosity gap psychology (rather than force-feeding the explanation, it invites the user to actively request it, increasing engagement and retention of the underlying concept (reading combined values off a bar chart)).
screens.keyHighlights:
• In-context error marking: Red "X" badges are placed directly on the incorrect bars in the chart itself, keeping feedback spatially tied to the user's actual selections rather than abstracted into text.

  • Non-shaming incorrect state: A calm grey banner with a simple icon and the word "Incorrect" avoids alarming red error treatments, preserving psychological safety for a learning context.

  • Behavioral button hierarchy: "Why?" is bold/dark and tappable; "Finish" is muted and secondary, nudging the learner toward reflection and understanding before progression.

  • Illustration-as-interaction: The bar chart isn't a passive graphic; it's the literal quiz mechanism, embodying the "move something before it explains" principle.

  • Persistent progress affordances: Progress dots and streak/lightning icon remain visible even during error states, keeping the learner oriented within the lesson module.

screens.name: Brilliant - Completing a lesson (data) - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately after any discrete, bite-sized unit of user effort (a completed lesson, workout, chapter, or task) especially in habit-building or edtech products. It's ideal when you want to create a clear psychological "checkpoint" that separates one unit of learning from the next, reinforcing a sense of closure and incremental mastery.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this full-screen interruption pattern for very short or frequent micro-actions (e.g., every single question answered), as it will feel repetitive and slow down power users. It's also unsuitable for productivity or utility apps where celebratory ceremony would feel patronizing or where users expect to move at their own, uninterrupted pace (e.g., enterprise dashboards, financial tools).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

The subdued color palette (green/orange on white) and lack of social elements (no friends, no leaderboard) suggest a solo, intrinsically-motivated audience (professionals or students using STEM practice as a personal habit, similar to a gym check-in).

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Goal-Gradient Effect and variable positive reinforcement: by confirming completion and quantifying progress (XP) immediately after effort, it closes the "operant loop," making the small amount of mental work invested feel rewarded and worth repeating tomorrow.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Single CTA, zero distractions: No back button, no skip, no secondary link (the user cannot do anything except move forward, reinforcing the linear lesson spine).

  • Restrained gamification: XP is shown but not overloaded with streak counters, leaderboards, or confetti animations, keeping the tone calm and "quiet gym"-like rather than chaotic.

  • Vertical light-beam motif: The glow effect behind the badge visually implies energy/value transfer from effort (podium) to reward (badge), a subtle use of visual metaphor instead of literal text explanation.

• Enterprise, B2B, or high-trust financial products (e.g., wealth management, tax software) where a playful/humorous tone could undermine perceived credibility and professionalism.

  • Contexts requiring precise, glanceable data comparison, peeking carousels hide information and require sequential swiping, which is inefficient for power users needing quick multi-category comparisons.

  • Accessibility-critical contexts, since edge-cropped cards and emoji-as-label patterns can be confusing for screen reader users or those needing high clarity/low ambiguity interfaces.

  • Older or less tech-savvy demographics who may find informal tone (skull emoji for bills) off-putting or unprofessional in a money context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z/Millennials) who are budget-conscious, often financially anxious, and respond better to informal, meme-literate communication than traditional banking UX. The gamified, chat-first approach appeals to users who find spreadsheets and bank apps intimidating or boring.

Psychologically, the design leverages anthropomorphism (Cleo as a "friend" character), affective reframing (turning bill anxiety into dark humor), and the Zeigarnik effect (peeking cards create an itch to swipe and see what's next). The "You're good" framing exploits positive reinforcement psychology to encourage continued engagement with budgeting rather than avoidance, a common behavior among people who feel guilt around finances.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Peeking Carousel Cards: Adjacent cards are intentionally cropped at both edges, creating a strong visual affordance for horizontal swiping without extra UI chrome like arrows or dot indicators.

  • Chat-as-Backdrop: The actual chat conversation persists faintly behind the cards (watermark + bubble), reinforcing that this dashboard-like carousel is embedded within the conversational AI experience rather than replacing it.

  • Emoji-as-Iconography: Using emojis (🎯🎮🚫💀🍎☀️) as functional icons for menu items reduces cognitive load, adds personality, and increases scannability versus generic line icons.

  • Data Visualization Snapshot: The donut chart gives an instant "at-a-glance" health check of budget categories before the user even reads the text.

  • Persistent Access Points: Home button and message input bar remain fixed at the bottom regardless of card in focus, ensuring users never lose their way back to the core chat function.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 40
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any financial summary-to-detail screen: category spending breakdowns, income statements, investment portfolio holdings, or expense reports. It's ideal whenever users need both a top-line aggregate figure and an itemized audit trail beneath it, especially in budgeting, expense-tracking, or accounting apps where trust and transparency in the numbers are critical.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when transaction volume is extremely high (hundreds+ per period) without robust search, filter, or grouping-by-date controls, as an undifferentiated flat list becomes hard to navigate. Also avoid decorative emoji iconography in enterprise, B2B, or high-net-worth wealth management contexts, where a more austere, data-table-driven UI conveys greater credibility and precision. If merchant names are frequently long, invest in adaptive truncation with tap-to-reveal rather than silent ellipsis clipping.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers using a personal budgeting or money-management app (similar to Mint, YNAB, or Koho-style apps) who want quick clarity on how much money has come in during a budget period. The design assumes a non-expert, possibly finance-anxious user, hence the playful emoji treatment and plain-language labels rather than banking jargon.

Psychologically, it leverages the peak-first disclosure principle, showing the reassuring total ("you received $22,440.71") before the granular details, which builds a sense of financial confidence and control before confronting the potentially overwhelming list of dozens of small transactions. The chronological ordering (most recent first) also taps into recency bias, letting users validate that their latest paycheck or transfer was properly captured.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Large hero metric first: Immediately answers the user's core question ("how much did I earn?") before any list scanning is required.

  • Decimal de-emphasis: Cents are rendered in a smaller font size than the whole-dollar amount, reducing cognitive load and emphasizing the meaningful digits.

  • Consistent iconography per source: Bank transfers get a building icon, generic deposits get a money-bag icon, helping users pattern-match transaction types at a glance without reading labels.

  • Two-tone background separation: The header's tinted background visually "docks" the summary card, creating a clear information hierarchy against the white transaction list beneath it.

  • Persistent back navigation: A simple top-left arrow keeps the drill-down mental model intact, letting users retreat to a broader budget overview.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 41
screens.whereToUse: Use this conversational card-carousel pattern when the product's core value proposition is built around an AI assistant or chatbot persona, especially in domains (finance, health, wellness) where users may feel intimidated, bored, or anxious about the subject matter. It's effective for surfacing multiple quick-access shortcuts without cluttering a chat interface with a traditional menu, and for reinforcing brand personality through tone and visual pacing.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for professional, B2B, or high-stakes financial tools (e.g., wealth management, enterprise accounting) where users expect precision, data density, and a serious tone rather than playful personification. It's also unsuitable for accessibility-critical contexts where emoji-as-functional-icons could confuse screen reader users, and for users who prefer fast, direct access to data over conversational indirection (the extra tap-through and swiping can add friction for power users who just want to see their balance immediately).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets younger users (Gen Z / millennials) who are less engaged by traditional dry banking dashboards and more responsive to app experiences that feel social, entertaining, and personified. By anthropomorphizing financial check-ins as "Cleo" texting suggestions, the app leverages the social proof and companionship heuristic: users are more likely to return daily ("Good to check every day") when the interaction feels like checking messages from a friend rather than doing a chore. The gamified, emoji-rich framing also lowers the psychological barrier to engaging with anxiety-inducing topics like spending and debt, using humor and casualness to reduce shame or avoidance behavior common in financial apps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Chat-as-navigation: Replacing static menus with conversational prompt cards blurs the line between UI navigation and dialogue, making finance feel like messaging a friend.

  • Peeking carousel cards: Partial visibility of neighboring cards is a subtle affordance that communicates "swipe for more" without needing explicit instruction text.

  • Emoji-as-icons: Using emoji instead of custom iconography for list items reduces design overhead while amplifying the friendly, informal tone consistent across the whole card.

  • Layered context: Showing the previous chat bubble above the card stack preserves conversational continuity, reminding the user this is one continuous thread with the AI, not a disconnected screen.

  • Persistent tab bar with home shortcut: Despite the chat-first paradigm, users are never more than one tap from core financial modules or the home icon, preventing feature discoverability loss.

screens.name: Cleo Chatting & sending Messages 42
screens.whereToUse: Use a conversational card-based UI when the product wants to humanize a traditionally intimidating or data-heavy domain (finance, health, legal). It's effective for quick, single-intent queries (checking balance, status lookups) where users benefit from natural-language framing plus structured, scannable data. Also ideal for apps aiming to build daily habitual engagement via a friendly assistant persona and for reducing onboarding friction to complex features by letting the AI surface deep links contextually.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex, high-frequency data tasks (e.g., detailed transaction reconciliation, multi-account portfolio management) where users need dense, persistent visual dashboards rather than a linear, scroll-based chat log that quickly becomes hard to reference. It's also less suitable for enterprise/B2B tools where efficiency and information density matter more than personality, or for users who find chatbot-style interactions patronizing when they just want fast, direct access to data without conversational overhead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z/Millennials) who are comfortable with messaging apps but may find traditional banking dashboards cold, complex, or anxiety-inducing. By reframing balance-checking as a "chat with a friend," Cleo lowers the psychological barrier to engaging with personal finances, particularly for users with low balances or financial stress who might otherwise avoid opening a banking app.

The streak/flame icon and emoji-laden microcopy tap into gamification and social-media-style engagement loops, exploiting habit-formation psychology (variable reward, daily engagement cues) to increase app stickiness and daily active usage (critical for a subscription-based fintech product).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Rich cards inside chat bubbles: Instead of plain text responses, the AI renders a structured, tappable card (balance, timestamp, Graph/Dashboard links) - merging conversational UI with functional data visualization affordances.

  • Dynamic contextual quick replies: "Home" and "Refresh Accounts" pills appear only after a relevant query, acting as smart, situational shortcuts that reduce typing effort and guide the conversation flow (Quick Actions / Shortcuts pattern).

  • Chat as primary nav paradigm: Placing "Chat" as the center tab-bar item elevates conversational interaction to be equal to core utilities like Spend/Save/Borrow, a differentiated architectural choice versus typical finance apps.

screens.name: Brex Itemize expense 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any workflow where a record (expense, invoice, order, application) has multiple compliance or completion requirements that must be satisfied before the user can proceed (e.g., submission, approval, payout). It's ideal when:

  • Actions can be conditionally disabled and you need to proactively explain the "why" rather than let users guess.

  • You must surface real-time balance/limit data alongside a transaction to prevent overspend errors.

  • Multiple status indicators (submitted, approved, missing, flagged) need to coexist in a single glanceable view.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, form-like detail pattern for consumer-facing or emotionally driven purchases (e.g., retail receipts, social payments) where rigid compliance language and red warning pills would feel punitive or overly bureaucratic. Also avoid stacking this many conditional states and red flags on a single screen in low-literacy or first-time-use contexts, as the volume of status pills, disabled states, and policy text can overwhelm users unfamiliar with internal expense policy (progressive disclosure or a guided wizard may serve those audiences better).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets employees submitting business expenses under a corporate card or reimbursement policy, as well as indirectly serving finance/compliance teams who set the underlying rules (receipt requirements, tax rates, spending limits). The psychological driver is loss-aversion and compliance anxiety: users are motivated to resolve red "Missing" flags quickly to avoid delayed reimbursement, rejected reports, or accounting friction. The disabled-state explanations and available-balance callouts also reduce cognitive load and uncertainty, key concerns for non-finance employees who find expense policy arcane.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Self-explaining disabled state: The greyed-out "Itemize expense" button is paired with inline grey text explaining the precondition, turning a potentially confusing dead-end into an educational micro-moment.

  • Color-coded compliance signaling: Blue "Submitted" vs. red "Missing" pills create an instant visual hierarchy of what's done vs. what requires action, letting users triage without reading full labels.

  • Dashed-border upload affordance: The "+" receipt tile uses a dashed red border, a universally recognized convention for "drop/add content here," combined with urgency-red to signal a blocking compliance issue.

  • Contextual available balance: Surfacing "$387.23 USD available" directly beneath the assigned limit lets the user self-verify they're not overspending without navigating to a separate budget screen.

  • Modal sheet for focused task: Presenting the expense as an overlay (with X to dismiss) rather than full navigation preserves the user's place in the parent list/report, reducing context loss.

screens.name: Brex Itemize expense 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a single transaction, receipt, or line item needs to be broken down into multiple categories, cost centers, or tags (such as expense management, invoicing, split billing, or budgeting apps). It's ideal when precise reconciliation (sum of parts = whole) is a functional requirement, and when users may want to toggle between absolute and relative (percentage) allocation methods.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, single-category transactions where itemization would add unnecessary friction (most consumer finance apps should keep single-category tagging as the default fast path and only surface this itemization flow as a secondary, opt-in action). Also avoid this level of granular form complexity on very small screens or for non-power users who may be overwhelmed by the repeated field sets; consider a simpler slider-based split for casual use cases instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets finance and expense-management app users: freelancers, small business owners, accountants, or employees submitting corporate expense reports (who need granular categorization for tax deductions or reimbursement accuracy). The psychological driver here is control and trust: by showing a live itemized total that must match the original charge, the app reduces anxiety about data entry errors and builds confidence that the categorization will be audit-ready. The repeatable, numbered "Expense #" cards also reduce cognitive load by chunking a potentially complex task (splitting a receipt) into small, identical, repeatable units.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live reconciliation total: The "Itemized total: £2.50" subtitle updates in real time, functioning as inline validation against the original transaction amount without needing a separate error message.

  • Dual allocation mode toggle (£/%): A segmented control lets users choose whether to split by fixed currency amount or percentage, accommodating both precise and proportional use cases.

  • Dynamic, countable CTA: The primary button text updates to reflect the number of itemized expenses ("Itemize 2 expenses"), giving explicit confirmation of scope before commit.

  • Redundant removal affordances: Both an inline (X) clear icon on fields and an explicit "Remove expense" link provide multiple, discoverable ways to undo an itemization block.

screens.name: Brex Itemize expense 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a single monetary value or quantity needs to be decomposed into multiple categorized parts that must sum to a fixed total (such as splitting a bill among categories, allocating a budget across line items, or itemizing a receipt for accounting/tax software). It's ideal for finance, expense management, invoicing, and budgeting apps where accuracy and auditability matter.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for casual or low-stakes splitting tasks (e.g., splitting a dinner bill between friends in a social app) where the dual £/% toggle and detailed category fields would feel like overkill and add unnecessary friction. Also avoid if users are likely to itemize only occasionally (in that case, a simpler single-step slider or stepper-based split may suffice rather than a full repeatable form with multiple fields per entry).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets small business owners, freelancers, and finance-savvy professionals who need to categorize blended purchases (e.g., a single receipt containing both a fee and a tax) for bookkeeping, expensing, or tax-deduction purposes. The psychological driver is a need for control and precision: these users are often anxious about compliance and accurate record-keeping, so the real-time total feedback and flexible allocation method serve as trust and accuracy mechanisms that reduce the fear of making an uncorrectable mistake.

The "Fees, licenses & taxes" example suggests this could be a card/expense management product like a UK business banking app (e.g., Monzo Business, Pleo, or similar), where itemization helps with VAT/expense reporting.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Allocate by £/% toggle: Gives users flexibility to split costs the way they naturally think about them, accommodating different mental models.

  • Live itemized total in header: Functions as an always-visible validation/progress indicator, preventing the common error of splits not summing to 100% or the original amount.

  • Dynamic, state-aware CTA copy: "Itemize 2 expenses" previews the exact outcome of the action, increasing user confidence before submission.

  • Granular removal controls: Inline "X" icons on both category and percentage fields, plus a dedicated "Remove expense" link per block, give users precise control without an all-or-nothing delete.

  • Repeatable block pattern with Add expense: Clearly scalable UI that supports splitting into as many categories as needed, resembling patterns used in invoice line-item builders.

screens.name: Brex Itemize expense 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a single record (transaction, invoice, order) needs to be decomposed into multiple sub-records that must sum to a fixed total (common in expense management, invoice line-item editing, budget allocation, or splitting a bill among people/categories). It's ideal when real-time validation against a fixed total is critical to prevent user error.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for simple, single-value edits where itemization adds unnecessary complexity, or for casual consumer apps where users are unlikely to need granular accounting breakdowns. It can also fail on small screens if too many expense blocks are added, since the vertical list requires significant scrolling with no overview/summary table (a compact table or inline list view may scale better for 5+ items).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets business expense trackers, freelancers, and corporate card users (likely within a fintech/expense management app like Expensify or Brex) who need to split a single purchase receipt across multiple accounting categories (a common requirement when one transaction includes mixed tax categories, cost centers, or personal/business splits).

Psychologically, the design reduces the anxiety of financial accuracy by giving constant total-matching feedback, which taps into the user's need for control and correctness when dealing with money and compliance (e.g., tax deductions). The granular, numbered breakdown also satisfies power users and accountants who want auditable, itemized records rather than lump-sum categorization.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live reconciliation header: The sticky "Itemized total: £2.50" instantly shows whether the sum of all line items matches the original charge, preventing submission errors before they happen.

  • Dynamic CTA labeling: The button text updates to "Itemize 3 expenses," giving explicit, numeric confirmation of the action's scope (a subtle trust-building microcopy pattern).

  • Repeatable, numbered expense blocks: Each line item is clearly labeled "Expense #2," "Expense #3," etc., helping users track their place in a growing list without visual clutter.

  • Inline clear/reset affordances: The × icon inside each field allows one-tap clearing of category or amount without needing to select-all and delete manually.

  • Low-friction add/remove flow: "Add expense" and "Remove expense" are symmetrically placed and styled, making the itemization list feel like a flexible, editable form rather than a rigid structure.

screens.name: Brex Itemize expense 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Any workflow where a single record is split or merged into multiple structural entities (expense itemization, invoice line splitting, group bill splitting).

  • Financial or data-integrity-sensitive actions where the user needs explicit confirmation of the mechanical outcome, not just a vague "Are you sure?"

  • Multi-step forms where destructive or structural actions (like "Remove expense") benefit from being paired with a final safety-net confirmation before committing.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid for low-stakes, easily reversible actions, adding a confirmation dialog for trivial actions creates unnecessary friction and feels patronizing.

  • Don't use vague confirmation language ("Are you sure?") when you have the opportunity to state the precise outcome (generic dialogs fail to build the same trust and clarity).

  • Avoid stacking multiple modal layers for simple, single-field edits; this pattern is best reserved for multi-entity or structural changes where the complexity justifies the extra confirmation step.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets business professionals, freelancers, or employees submitting expense reports who need to split a single purchase (e.g., a receipt with multiple tax categories or cost centers) into multiple line items for accounting/reimbursement purposes. These users are often under time pressure and need confidence that their financial data will be categorized correctly for compliance or reimbursement audits.

Psychologically, the confirmation dialog leverages loss-aversion and commitment anxiety: once itemized, the original single transaction is irreversibly broken into parts, which could complicate future edits or reconciliation. By pausing and explicitly stating the consequence, the design reduces regret and builds user trust in the system's transparency, which is crucial in fintech/expense products where accuracy directly impacts reimbursement and tax reporting.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-unit allocation toggle (£/%): Lets users itemize either by fixed currency amounts or percentage splits, accommodating varied real-world itemization scenarios (e.g., tax vs. tip vs. category split).

  • Live itemized total vs. original total: Displaying "Itemized total: £2.50" against the original "£2.50" header gives instant reconciliation feedback, helping users confirm their splits sum correctly before proceeding.

  • Consequence-explicit confirmation dialog: Instead of generic confirmation language, the modal explicitly states the structural outcome ("create 2 separate expenses"), setting accurate expectations for an action that alters the record structure in accounting systems.

  • Layered modal depth: Stacking a bottom sheet on top of a dimmed full-screen form visually communicates stakes and hierarchy (this is a "point of no return" step requiring undivided attention).

  • Per-item remove affordance: Each itemized card includes a clearly separated "Remove expense" action, letting users correct a bad split before committing, reducing reliance on the confirmation dialog as the only safety net.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 6
screens.whereToUse: This Compare View + Quick Actions combination fits any single-asset detail page in an investing or trading app where users need to evaluate recent performance and then act (buy, follow, sell) without leaving the screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a portfolio overview or multi-asset comparison screen, where users need to see several securities side-by-side rather than one asset's full transactional detail.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood (stock detail page): nearly identical layout: logo, price, colored change indicator, time-range tabs, Buy button, and an About section below.

  • Apple Stocks app: uses the same colored line chart plus time-range segmented control (1D/1W/1M..) pattern for individual securities.

  • Yahoo Finance (stock page): pairs a price chart, range selector, and company description in the same vertical order.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visibility of system status: the green upward chart line and matching green "↑2.60%" text reinforce the positive price movement through consistent color coding.

  • Recognition over recall: the NVIDIA logo anchors brand identity at the top, letting users confirm they're on the right stock before reading further.

  • Minimize user memory load: the segmented time-range control (1D/1W/1M/1Y/ALL) lets users compare performance windows without needing to recall or re-navigate to see historical data.

  • Progressive disclosure: the "About" text truncates with "read more," keeping the screen focused on price and action first, background information second.

  • Match between system and real world: separating "Buy" (transactional) from "Follow" (informational/tracking) respects that not every visitor to a stock page is ready to purchase.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 7
screens.whereToUse: This Drill-Down + Inline Help combination fits any investing app's company research screen, where users need both qualitative context (what the company does, who runs it) and quantitative metrics (valuation, growth) before committing capital.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a quick-glance watchlist or trending screen, where dense fact tables would slow down rapid comparison across many securities.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood (stock detail "About" page): uses the same CEO/Industry/Employees/Headquarters fact table followed by a Key Stats block with price, market cap, and revenue figures.

  • Yahoo Finance (Statistics tab): organizes company profile facts and financial key stats into comparable labeled two-column tables.

  • Google Finance: presents an "About" summary plus a structured key-stats grid (market cap, P/E, etc.) in the same drill-down-from-summary pattern.
screens.keyHighlights:

  • Progressive disclosure: both the truncated "About" text ("read more") and the "Details" link on Key Stats defer deeper content until requested, keeping the base screen digestible.

  • Consistency and standards: the same row layout (label left, value right, bold value) is reused across both the company-facts table and the Key Stats table, reducing learning cost between sections.

  • Information scent: section headers ("About," "Key Stats") clearly preview what's below, helping users jump to the data type they care about.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 8
screens.whereToUse: This Compare View + Horizontal Carousel combination fits investing app stock-detail pages where users need both historical financial trend data and current news context to evaluate a company before trading.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a quick-decision buy flow (e.g., a checkout or order-confirmation screen), where dense financial charts and news would add friction rather than help a user complete a simple transaction.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood (stock News + Financials tabs): combines a scrollable news carousel with a switchable Annually/Quarterly financials bar chart in the same stock-detail context.

  • Progressive disclosure: "Show more" on News defers the full article list, and the chart shows headline figures ($26.91B, $130.5B, etc.) with a partially cropped comparison row below for those who want more detail.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 9
screens.whereToUse: This Compare View + Social Proof combination fits investing app stock-detail pages where users benefit from a fast, visual read on both historical earnings performance and aggregated professional sentiment before deciding to trade.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for novice-focused, decision-light contexts (e.g., a simple round-up-savings or gift-card purchase flow), where analyst ratings and EPS beat/miss data would add complexity irrelevant to the task.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood (Earnings and Analyst Ratings tabs): uses a nearly identical Actual-vs-Estimated EPS bar comparison per quarter alongside an aggregated analyst-consensus gauge.

  • Yahoo Finance (Analysis tab): shows a comparable Sell/Hold/Buy recommendation gauge summarizing analyst ratings for a stock.

screens.name: Google Pay Transferring Money 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any payments, ticketing, or contactless-checkin app where speed-to-action is the primary KPI (e.g., transit apps, event check-ins, loyalty scanning).

  • Apps competing against entrenched habits, where reducing steps-to-task is a key differentiator.

  • Contexts where real-time feedback (focus reticle, haptic buzz) can reduce the perceived wait during a scan/recognition process.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid a camera-first default landing screen if the primary use case is NOT scanning (e.g., a banking app used mostly for balance checks) - forcing camera permission and viewfinder on every launch would frustrate users and drain battery/attention unnecessarily.

  • Not suitable when users frequently need to reference multiple pieces of information (balances, history) before acting (a full-screen camera hides all other context).

  • Avoid if regulatory/privacy concerns make an always-on camera view uncomfortable for users (e.g., healthcare or government apps).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday consumers in QR-heavy payment markets (e.g., Singapore's PayNow/SGQR ecosystem) who need to pay merchants, split bills, or transfer money on the go (often while physically holding a printed QR code sign in a shop or hawker stall, exactly as depicted). The design leans on the psychological principle of reduced friction = increased adoption: by making scanning the default landing screen rather than a secondary tab, Google Pay reinforces the "scan first" habit loop that competes directly with entrenched local apps.

The reward messaging ("pay and earn") taps into variable reward psychology, priming users to associate scanning with potential upside, which increases the likelihood of choosing Google Pay over a bank's own QR scanner for the same transaction.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Full-bleed camera-first interface: Removes any intermediate screen between intent ("I want to pay") and action (scanning), collapsing the task to a single gesture.

  • Borrowed mental model: Reuses native camera UI conventions (flash, gallery, close) so zero onboarding is needed.

  • Real-time scan feedback (pulsing reticle): Builds confidence that the system is "listening" and actively working, reducing anxiety during the brief scan latency.

  • Scheme logo trust bar: Placing PayNow/FavePay logos at the bottom acts as a low-friction verification step, letting users self-serve compatibility checks instead of failing silently.

  • Reward framing in microcopy: Embedding "and earn" into the instruction turns a transactional action into a slightly gamified one.

screens.name: Google Pay Transferring Money 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any final-step monetary or quantity input screen where accuracy and focus are paramount. P2P transfers, merchant checkout, bill payments, or in-app purchases. It's especially effective when:

  • The recipient/payee identity needs prominent, trust-building confirmation before committing funds.

  • A large numeric keypad is more efficient than a standard system keyboard (e.g., currency, PIN, OTP entry).

  • You want to minimize distractions and navigational escape routes to keep users on task during a critical conversion step.

  • You can offer a smart default (category, note, tip amount) to speed up completion without extra typing.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, single-purpose full-screen pattern when:

  • The amount entry is a minor sub-step in a longer, more exploratory flow (e.g., budgeting apps where users compare/edit multiple line items) - a modal or inline field may be more appropriate.

  • Users need to reference other information (e.g., account balance, previous transactions) simultaneously; the distraction-free design here sacrifices context.

  • The transaction requires more nuanced payee verification beyond a name/ID (e.g., in high-risk international wire transfers where additional fields like bank details are mandatory).

  • Desktop or larger-screen contexts, where a numeric keypad is unnecessary and a standard form input with real keyboard usage is more efficient.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves everyday consumers and small-business customers making point-of-sale or QR-code-based payments, particularly in markets like Singapore where UEN-based PayNow/GrabPay-style merchant payments are common. The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Authority/Verification bias: Displaying the UEN taps into trust heuristics (an official registration number feels more credible than a generic name, reducing anxiety about paying an unverified or fraudulent party).

  • Reduced friction anxiety: The prefilled note and oversized numeric display reduce the perceived effort and risk of the transaction, encouraging quick task completion.

  • Focus/scarcity of attention: By removing navigation and distractions, Google leverages a "narrow the funnel" design tactic common in checkout/payment flows to prevent drop-off or user error mid-transaction.
screens.keyHighlights:
• UEN Display for Trust: Surfacing the merchant's official business registration number builds institutional trust and confirms the user is paying the correct legal entity, critical for high-stakes irreversible transactions.

screens.name: Onboarding 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits onboarding sequences where a product has several distinct, easily-summarized differentiators that benefit from being seen together, especially when trying to justify a switch away from an incumbent (here, Safari).
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when a feature needs demonstration rather than description (e.g. a gesture-based interaction like "swipe anywhere to go back" is asserted here but not shown), or when there are more than four or five features, since additional rows would require scrolling and dilute the skimmability this pattern depends on.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Robinhood (onboarding feature list): uses the same icon-plus-benefit-row format to summarize app capabilities before account setup.

  2. 1Password / password managers: similarly lead onboarding with a "your logins carry over" reassurance row to lower switching friction.

  3. Opera / Brave browser onboarding: use comparable privacy-and-speed benefit lists early in first-run flows to differentiate from Safari/Chrome.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking: four short, uniformly formatted rows break a features list into digestible units instead of one dense paragraph.

  2. Recognition over Recall: icon + short title lets users scan for what a feature does at a glance rather than reading full sentences.

  3. Progressive Disclosure: only headline + one-line description per feature; deeper detail (e.g. how tracker-blocking works) is deferred past onboarding.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law): identical row structure across all four items sets a predictable reading pattern after the first row.

screens.name: Onboarding 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits onboarding moments where a single, specific interactive element (a button, gesture, or menu item) is the feature being taught, especially when it's easy to miss among visually similar sibling elements.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for teaching abstract concepts or multi-step workflows, since a single arrow-and-label can only clearly direct attention to one static target (sequences requiring several actions need a multi-step guided tour instead of one annotated screen).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Duolingo (feature coach marks): uses similar arrow-and-label overlays during onboarding to point at a specific first action.

  2. Slack (new-feature tooltips): highlights one interactive element among several identical-looking ones with color and a directional pointer.

  3. Google Search app ("I'm Feeling Lucky"-style call-outs): shows the real search suggestion UI with a highlighted alternate action button, similar to the "Browse for Me" row here.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Show, Don't Just Tell: using an actual UI mockup instead of icon+text rows lets the user preview the real interaction before it happens.

  2. Von Restorff Effect: the one colored "Browse for Me" button stands out against four gray twins, drawing the eye without extra explanation.

  3. Signifiers: the curved arrow is an explicit directional cue that removes any ambiguity about what to look at or tap next.

  4. Recognition over Recall: showing real example queries ("who are the beatles," "risotto vs paella") lets users recognize the feature's use case rather than imagining one abstractly.

screens.name: Onboarding 04
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits onboarding for any AI-generated or synthesized-output feature where the quality and richness of the result is the main selling point and is best proven by example rather than description.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when the actual output is highly variable, sparse, or low-quality in typical use, since showing a best-case curated example risks setting expectations the live product won't consistently meet.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Perplexity AI (onboarding/example answers): similarly shows a fully worked example query-to-answer page with cited sources to demonstrate AI search output during first use.

  2. Notion AI (feature preview screens): uses sample generated content in onboarding to prove value before the user tries it themselves.

  3. Google Discover/Search "AI Overview" intros: pair a sample query with a rich, sourced answer card to build trust in AI-generated summaries.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Show, Don't Just Tell: a fully rendered example answer page substitutes for further explanation of what "Browse for Me" does.

  2. Peak-End Rule: closing the feature demo on a checkmark and a rich, satisfying result page leaves a positive final impression of this onboarding step.

  3. Social Proof: recognizable publisher logos (BBC Good Food, Delish, RecipeTin Eats) lend third-party credibility to the AI-assembled answer.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law): reusing the same device-frame mockup, page control, and Next button from the prior screen keeps the sequence visually coherent.

screens.name: Onboarding 05
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits teaching gesture-based or otherwise "invisible" interactions where no static screenshot can fully demonstrate the action, especially when the feature is optional or supplementary to the app's core flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for teaching core, mandatory interactions users must understand to use the app at all (an optional-feeling "Skip" affordance undersells the importance of something the user actually needs to know).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Files by Google / Photos apps (pinch-to-zoom tips): use similar headline-plus-mockup coach marks to teach gestures that can't be shown with static arrows.

  2. Apple's own iOS feature tips (e.g., "Swipe down to search"): pair a short imperative phrase with a realistic content preview to teach system gestures during first use.

  3. Medium / Pocket (reading-mode features): use real article content in onboarding previews to demonstrate a reading-related feature in a relatable context.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Discoverability of Gestures: since pinch gestures are inherently invisible in a static UI, naming the gesture explicitly in the headline compensates for the lack of a visual affordance.

  2. User Control & Freedom: the "Skip" button lets users opt out of a tip they may already know, avoiding forced friction for returning or advanced users.

  3. Recognition over Recall: using a real, evocative example (a famous historic speech) makes the feature's value easier to picture than an abstract placeholder would.

  4. Consistency (Jakob's Law): the device-frame mockup and page-control layout convention (established across earlier screens) is reused here, keeping the tour visually coherent even without a page control visible in this crop.

screens.name: Onboarding 06
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any onboarding demo of an action with a brief processing delay, where showing an explicit "working" moment (rather than jumping straight from instruction to result) reassures the user that their action was registered.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's unnecessary for instantaneous actions with no real processing time, where inserting an artificial "in progress" beat would only slow down onboarding without adding useful reassurance.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google Photos ("Enhancing.."): uses a similarly brief, present-tense status label during onboarding demos of an AI-processing feature.

  2. Notion AI (generating content preview): shows a shrunk or transitional content card with a "Generating.." style label before revealing the AI output.

  3. Apple's "Cleanup" tool onboarding (Photos): depicts a mid-gesture visual state before showing the completed result, similar to this shrunk/rotated card.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of System Status: the "Summarizing for you.." label ensures the user isn't left wondering whether the demonstrated gesture did anything.

  2. Continuity of Context: reusing the identical article card from the previous screen (same image, same headline) keeps this feeling like one fluid interaction rather than a new, disconnected example.

  3. Metaphorical Representation: shrinking and rotating the card visually mimics the physical pinch gesture without needing an animation to be described in a static screenshot.

  4. Progressive Disclosure: showing only a brief in-progress state (rather than jumping straight to a finished summary) sets an honest expectation that summarizing takes a moment.

screens.name: Lemon8 - Creating a post - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any content-creation flow requiring multi-select media with order sensitivity (social posting apps, carousel ad builders, document/photo uploaders, or collage-making tools). It's ideal when users routinely select multiple assets and need visual confirmation of sequence and selection state before proceeding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, numbered multi-select grid for single-image use cases (e.g., profile photo upload) where it adds unnecessary complexity. It's also unsuitable for low-vision or accessibility-first contexts without supplementary labels, since the UI relies heavily on small numeric badges and color-coded highlights. For apps with small content libraries or infrequent uploads, the heavy grid/tray/segmented-control combination may be overengineered.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves Gen Z and young creative users who are visually driven and often build curated, multi-image lifestyle posts (outfits, food spreads, travel diaries). The numbered ordering system taps into their expectation of storytelling control honed by Instagram carousels and TikTok slideshows. The dense grid and quick filter tabs cater to users with large camera rolls who need to move fast between dozens of near-duplicate lifestyle shots, reducing friction and decision fatigue during content creation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Numbered selection badges: Instead of generic checkmarks, Lemon8 shows sequence numbers (1, 2) directly on thumbnails, letting users control the exact order images will appear in a multi-photo post/carousel.
  • Persistent selection tray: A horizontally scrollable strip of selected media sits above the CTA bar, letting users review and deselect items without scrolling back through the grid.
  • Dual-path CTA bar: Offering both "Collage" and "Next" as parallel primary actions respects different creative intents (quick multi-image layouts vs). standard sequential posting.
  • Branded dark theme on a system picker: Even this low-level OS-adjacent screen keeps the black/yellow Lemon8 identity, maintaining brand consistency across the entire creation funnel.

screens.name: Lemon8 - Creating a post - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Any content-creation or photo/video editing flow where users upload media that may need format correction (cropping, resizing, aspect ratio).
  • Multi-step creative pipelines (filters → text → stickers → publish) that benefit from a single persistent toolbar instead of nested menus.
  • Apps targeting visually-sensitive audiences where a neutral/dark background is needed to preserve true-to-life color judgment of user-generated images.
  • Scenarios where you want to proactively flag a technical issue (file size, resolution, format) with a direct, actionable shortcut rather than a blocking error dialog.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid dark, minimal chrome in editing contexts where brand personality/color needs to stay prominent throughout the flow (e.g., branded templates requiring visible UI styling).
  • Don't use passive contextual bubbles for critical blocking errors (e.g., invalid file type, corrupted upload) - those require an explicit modal/dialog to ensure the user cannot proceed without resolving them.
  • Not suitable for first-time users unfamiliar with iconography-heavy toolbars; novice audiences may need labeled onboarding or tooltips before relying purely on icon recognition.
  • Avoid overcrowding the bottom toolbar beyond 5-6 icons, as it can overwhelm users or require horizontal scrolling, undermining the simplicity this pattern aims for.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for Gen Z and young adult content creators who are used to fast, mobile-native editing tools (TikTok, CapCut, Instagram Stories) and expect professional-grade creative controls without leaving the app. The pattern leverages the Zeigarnik effect and momentum bias: once a user has imported a photo, the flow nudges them to keep refining and progressing ("Next") rather than abandoning midway.

The proactive quality-check bubble taps into loss-aversion and perfectionism common among visually-driven creators (nobody wants to publish a cropped-wrong or "too large" photo, especially on a platform where aesthetics drive social currency (likes, saves, follows)). By surfacing the fix immediately and specifically, Lemon8 reduces the cognitive load of noticing, diagnosing, and fixing issues on their own, which keeps less technically savvy creators from abandoning the post.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual inline warning with embedded fix: The "Photo is too large" bubble is spatially anchored to the exact tool (crop) needed to resolve it, collapsing diagnosis and remedy into a single glance-and-tap interaction.
  • Near-black editing chrome: Removes visual noise and color bias so the user judges photo quality/aesthetics accurately, a crucial detail for a visually-driven, image-first lifestyle app.

It also taps into the effort heuristic: users tend to trust results more when they perceive the system "worked hard" to produce them, even if the actual computation is instantaneous. A brief, visible loading state manufactures this perception of effort and algorithmic rigor, boosting confidence in the forthcoming learning path.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Determinate progress ring instead of a generic spinner (gives users a tangible sense of advancement and finite wait time).
  • Single-sentence status copy that personalizes the wait by referencing "your responses," transforming a technical loading state into a perceived act of personalization.
  • Extreme whitespace and vertical centering that enforces single-task focus and provides a cognitive pause after an interactive quiz sequence.
  • Brand-consistent accent color (yellow) used sparingly on the progress arc, keeping the palette restrained while still injecting warmth and energy.

screens.name: Brilliant - Selecting a learning path - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Post-onboarding or post-quiz recommendation screens where you need to convert personalization data into a single committed action.
  • Any flow where reducing choice overload among 3-5 comparable options is critical (subscription tiers, content tracks, skill levels).
  • Educational, wellness, or fintech apps that want to pair a "smart" algorithmic feel with warm, human-sounding copy to build early trust.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when the underlying recommendation isn't actually well-personalized, overusing "TOP PICK" language without real signal erodes trust once users notice it's generic.
  • Not suitable for catalogs with many (10+) comparable items, since the single-hero-card treatment only scales to a handful of choices before requiring scroll-heavy comparison.
  • Risky in contexts where switching later is actually costly or disruptive (e.g., paid plans with lock-in) - promising "switch any time" when it's not fully true damages credibility.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets the immediate post-quiz moment for a self-directed learner, worldwide, who has just revealed their interests/goals and is now expecting a tailored result (the classic "aha" payoff of a personalization funnel). The target user is motivated but also easily overwhelmed by too many course options (STEM content is famously intimidating), so the design leans heavily on authority bias (TOP PICK), default effect, and loss-aversion-softening (switch anytime) to usher them toward a single confident tap.

The muted secondary options are not dead weight (they serve skeptical or niche users who already know they want Data Analysis or Probability rather than the generic recommendation, preserving a sense of control for power users while still nudging the majority toward the suggested default).

• Single Recommended Default: Elevating one option visually (larger card, color border, shadow, badge) exploits the choice-architecture principle of a strong default, dramatically increasing conversion on the "Continue" action by removing decision paralysis.
  • Reversibility Messaging: "switch any time" directly neutralizes the fear of committing to the wrong path, a key psychological barrier in any personalization flow.
  • Illustration-as-Iconography: Each path uses a distinct, tactile 3D-style illustration instead of generic icons, making the list scannable and reinforcing the brand's playful, tactile identity even on a decision screen.
  • Conversational Framing: The speech-bubble mascot reframes a machine-generated recommendation as personal advice, increasing perceived trust and warmth.

screens.name: Brilliant Onboarding 6

Use this pattern during onboarding flows that require multiple steps of data collection (surveys, personalization quizzes, account setup) to break up friction with moments of positive reinforcement. It's especially effective:

screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

At this stage in onboarding, users may have just answered profiling questions (goals, skill level, interests) and could be experiencing decision fatigue or self-doubt about committing to a learning app.

The psychological trigger here is social proof combined with belonging: by asserting that "millions" of similar users already engage with the product, the screen normalizes the decision to continue and alleviates imposter syndrome or skepticism. The illustrated content preview also builds anticipatory curiosity, a dopamine-driven nudge to keep progressing through the funnel.

  • Illustrative card fan for content preview: The overlapping cards visually tease the diversity of the product's content (video, interactive diagrams, notebooks) without any cognitive load or reading required.

  • Uninterrupted single CTA: No alternate paths or skip options keep the user funneled forward, reducing decision fatigue.

  • Persistent progress bar: Reinforces that this is a short, finite journey, setting expectations and reducing perceived commitment.

screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new users at a critical conversion moment (the transition from passive browsing/onboarding to committed account creation, likely for an edtech or skill-learning app (e).g., language learning, course platform). The design leverages reduced friction bias (SSO options), loss aversion avoidance (emphasizing "free"), and goal-gradient effect (implying the learning path/discovery is just one tap away). The target demographic is likely mobile-first, time-constrained learners who abandon flows requiring manual form-filling, hence the heavy bias toward one-tap authentication.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-redirect for existing users: "Sign in" is offered both as a top-corner link and a bottom anchored link, eliminating dead ends for returning users regardless of where their eye lands.

  • Visual hierarchy inversion: Making the higher-friction "Continue with email" button the boldest, highest-contrast element nudges users toward first-party data capture (valuable for CRM/email marketing) while still offering frictionless SSO as equally accessible options.

  • Outcome-oriented headline: Framing sign-up around "discovering your learning path" rather than "create an account" lowers psychological resistance and ties the action to a personal benefit.

  • Minimalist single-focus layout: No distracting fields, forms, or legal text clutter the primary decision point (the user only has to choose a sign-up method).

screens.name: Brilliant Creating Account 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this disabled-button + full-field-visibility pattern when the signup form is short (under 6 fields) and all fields are mandatory (it works best for consumer apps that need basic demographic data (like age) for personalization or compliance). Ideal for apps where sign-up follows a value-prop/onboarding sequence, allowing this screen to stay purely functional and frictionless.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for longer or more complex registration flows (e.g., B2B signups requiring company details, billing info, or multi-role selection) - cramming many fields onto one static screen increases cognitive load and abandonment; a Multi-Step Form would perform better there. Also avoid an indefinitely disabled button without inline validation hints, as users may not understand *why* the button remains disabled if error states aren't surfaced live.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users who have already been convinced by onboarding/value-prop screens to create an account (likely students, lifelong learners, or professionals signing up for a STEM-learning platform like Brilliant). The inclusion of an "Age" field suggests the product serves a wide demographic range (including minors), and the app likely uses age for content curation, parental consent flows, or regulatory compliance (e.g., COPPA/GDPR-K).

Psychologically, the sparse, judgment-free layout reduces perceived effort and cognitive load during a typically high-abandonment step (account creation). The visibly disabled CTA leverages the Zeigarnik effect (users feel compelled to complete the "visible but blocked" task to unlock the button, turning form completion into a small sense of progress and achievement).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Disabled Submit State: The "Sign up" button is visibly grayed out until all required fields are validly filled, proactively communicating form requirements and preventing premature submission errors.

  • Smart Field Grouping: Pairing First/Last name side-by-side reduces perceived form length and scroll distance while keeping Email, Password, and Age as isolated full-width priority fields.

  • Implicit Legal Consent: Terms/Privacy agreement is handled via passive microcopy tied to the CTA action rather than a separate checkbox, reducing friction while still achieving legal compliance.

  • Dual Escape Routes: Both a top-left back arrow and a bottom "Sign in" link give users multiple ways to correct course without feeling trapped in the funnel.

screens.name: Brilliant Creating Account 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for consumer apps where quick conversion is prioritized over granular data validation (especially subscription or freemium products (education, fitness, productivity) where the goal is to get the user into the product experience as fast as possible). Ideal when the number of required fields is kept under 5-6 and when an alternate SSO/social sign-in isn't the primary path.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal-label approach for complex B2B forms, financial/compliance-heavy registration, or any flow where field ambiguity could cause costly errors (e.g., banking, legal documents) - here, explicit labels and inline validation are essential. Also avoid omitting an explicit consent checkbox in jurisdictions with strict opt-in legal requirements (e.g., GDPR strict interpretation) where implied consent via button tap may not be compliant.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets new users of an educational app (Brilliant) who have already seen the value proposition (via onboarding/carousel) and are now ready to commit. The age field is a strong signal this product personalizes content or enforces age-based compliance (e.g., COPPA), targeting a broad audience from teens to adults.

Psychologically, the form leverages the sunk-cost/momentum effect: by the time a user reaches this screen they've already invested attention in onboarding, so a short, frictionless form capitalizes on that momentum before motivation decays. The minimal number of fields and lack of email verification step before CTA reduces abandonment risk at the critical conversion moment.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Prefilled/sample data visible: The screenshot shows realistic sample values (email, name, age) already populated, suggesting either a smart-default/test-data pattern or a demo state used for app-store screenshots, reducing perceived effort by showing the form as nearly 'done'.

  • No explicit field labels: Reliance on entered content and context (e.g., email format, two name boxes) instead of labels keeps the UI extremely clean, trusting users' familiarity with form conventions.

  • Split first/last name fields: A simple grid-based micro-decision that improves data quality without added copy.

  • Implied-consent legal pattern: Avoids an extra checkbox tap by embedding consent into the CTA's action, which is a well-tested conversion-rate optimization technique.

  • Escape hatch via back chevron: Floating circular back button keeps navigation unobtrusive but always accessible.
