screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this layered bottom-sheet + action-sheet pattern when:

  • You need to let users drill into contextual details (like a specific card or account) without a full page transition, preserving spatial context.

  • The underlying task has multiple related but distinct sub-actions (e.g., reimbursement vs. mileage vs. drafts) that don't warrant separate screens.

  • You want to display compliance/status metadata compactly via iconography for power users scanning many rows quickly (expense reports, approvals, order history).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid stacking multiple modal sheets when:

  • The user needs to compare data across the obscured background screen and the sheet simultaneously, stacking reduces visible context the deeper it goes.

  • Actions require significant input (e.g., long forms); deeply nested sheets make it harder to back out gracefully and can disorient users on smaller screens.

  • Status icons are undocumented or inconsistent: icon-only communication risks confusing new users who haven't learned the meaning of each glyph; a tooltip or legend would be needed for first-time use.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets employees of a company using Brex for corporate card and expense management: likely non-finance staff who need a fast, low-friction way to check their remaining budget and submit reimbursement claims for out-of-pocket purchases (e.g., transit, coffee, travel). The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Loss aversion / budget anxiety:

  • Trust through transparency: Visible approval/reimbursement status icons reduce anxiety about whether a submitted expense is "stuck" or complete.

  • Reduced friction for compliance tasks: Separating "Request reimbursement" from "Request mileage" acknowledges that expense submission isn't one-size-fits-all, letting users self-select the correct flow quickly.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive disclosure via stacked sheets: Dashboard → Card detail sheet → Action sheet, each layer revealing only what's relevant to the current task without full-page navigation.

  • Status iconography row: Small compliance icons (upload, approval, reimbursement checkmarks) on each expense line let finance/ops users audit a list at a glance.

  • Persistent context card: Keeping the Brex card partially visible behind the sheet reinforces "which account am I looking at" without extra chrome.

  • Draft count transparency: Showing "(0)" next to View drafts manages expectations and subtly nudges completion behavior.

  • Grabber handles on both sheets: Reinforces the gesture-driven, dismissible nature of the modals, keeping the primary dashboard just one swipe away.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this full-screen camera capture pattern when the primary task requires scanning a physical object (payment cards, ID documents, QR/barcodes, receipts). Always pair it with:

  • A manual/alternate entry fallback for accessibility and failure recovery.

  • A clear, singular dismiss action.

  • Native-feeling capture controls (shutter, flash, gallery) to minimize cognitive load.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the data being captured can be reliably and faster entered via text input (e.g., short alphanumeric codes), as forcing a camera flow adds unnecessary friction. It's also unsuitable in low-connectivity or low-light contexts without robust fallback messaging, and should not be used without clearly communicating why camera access is needed (privacy/permission concerns) - a missing permission-priming step here could increase drop-off if this is the user's first camera-related ask.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets mainstream mobile users performing a transactional task (e.g., adding a payment card, scanning a QR/barcode coupon, or registering a loyalty card) who expect speed and minimal friction. It leverages the psychological principle of familiarity bias: by mimicking the stock iOS Camera app's control layout, the designer taps into years of existing muscle memory, meaning zero learning curve and higher completion rates. The manual fallback also addresses loss-aversion/frustration avoidance: users who fear wasting time on a failed scan are reassured there's always a guaranteed alternative path forward.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Manual entry fallback: Placing "Enter manually" prominently prevents a hard dead-end for users whose camera fails to recognize the object, respecting accessibility and real-world lighting/condition variance.

  • Familiar native camera affordances: Reusing the iOS system camera's shutter/flash/gallery layout dramatically lowers the learning curve (users don't need onboarding for how to operate the scanner).

  • Single, unambiguous exit: The circular X button is isolated top-right, matching platform conventions for modal dismissal, so users always know how to back out.

  • Distraction-free full-bleed canvas: No navigation chrome competes with the live camera feed, keeping 100% of visual attention on correctly framing the scan target.

  • Photo library shortcut: The "Select" option lets users scan from an already-captured photo instead of requiring a live camera pass, useful when the object isn't physically present.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for document/ID/card capture flows, KYC onboarding, receipt or check scanning, and any flow requiring an image of a physical object where camera access may fail or be inconvenient. Always pair the primary camera capture action with secondary import options (library, file) and a manual fallback to keep conversion high.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this multi-option action sheet for simple, low-stakes avatar or profile photo uploads where a single "choose photo" option is sufficient (too many choices can add friction). Also avoid if manual entry would violate compliance requirements (e.g., when optical capture is mandatory for fraud prevention), or if offering file upload introduces unnecessary security/format-validation complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets users completing identity verification, document upload, or payment-card linking flows (e.g., KYC, check deposit, expense receipt capture) where camera access is the primary path but not all users have the physical document on hand or a working camera at that moment. Offering photo library, file choice, and manual entry reduces drop-off by accommodating edge cases (scanned PDFs already on device, accessibility limits, poor lighting) and leverages the psychological principle of perceived control: giving users choice reduces anxiety and abandonment in sensitive flows like identity verification.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multiple capture fallbacks: Camera, photo library, file picker, and manual entry are all offered from a single surface, respecting different user contexts (e.g., document already saved vs. needing to snap a new photo).

  • Non-blocking modal overlay: The action sheet appears without fully replacing the camera screen, preserving spatial context and reducing perceived navigation depth.

  • High-contrast, distraction-free capture UI: Pure black background and minimal chrome keep focus on the real-world subject being captured.

  • Escape hatch always visible: The persistent close (X) button ensures users never feel trapped in the camera flow.

screens.name: Brex Request reimbursement 5
screens.whereToUse: Use the native OS photo/file picker (with its built-in limited-access messaging) whenever an app needs occasional, user-initiated access to personal media (such as attaching receipts, profile photos, documents, or support-ticket screenshots). It's ideal for expense management, customer support, document scanning, and social apps where trust and minimal permission footprint matter more than deep custom gallery curation.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid relying solely on the native picker if your product requires rich, branded media-browsing experiences (e.g., a photo-editing app, a social network's camera roll integration with custom filters/previews) where a custom UI with deeper curation, tagging, or AI-based suggestions adds real value. Also, if the app needs frequent, repeated media access (e.g., continuous background photo sync), prompting for full library access with a clear value explanation may be more appropriate than repeatedly surfacing the limited-access picker, which can create friction if users must reselect photos each time.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
The target user here is a Brex business cardholder or employee submitting an expense report who needs to attach a photo of a physical receipt. This persona is typically on the go, often in a hurry (e.g., right after a client dinner or purchase), and may be privacy-conscious about granting full photo library access to a finance/corporate app.

Psychologically, this screen addresses the "privacy paradox" tension in B2B fintech apps: users want convenience (quickly finding a photo) but are wary of corporate software having blanket access to personal photos (family pictures, personal moments). The limited-access disclosure directly defuses this anxiety, increasing the likelihood a user completes the attach-receipt flow instead of abandoning it or granting access reluctantly.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Leverages OS trust instead of rebuilding it: By using the native picker, Brex inherits Apple's privacy guarantees and polished interaction patterns for free, rather than building a bespoke (and less trusted) media picker.

  • Transparent limited-access disclosure: The "Private Access to Photos" card is a best-in-class example of proactive, in-context privacy communication rather than a one-time blocking permission dialog.

  • Dismissible, non-blocking education: The explanation is informative but optional (closable via the X), respecting the user's time if they already understand the concept.

  • Low-friction task completion: Search, sort, and collections toggle allow power users to quickly locate the exact receipt photo needed, reducing time-to-task-completion for an inherently tedious expense-reporting workflow.

screens.name: Verification Code Screen (Empty State)
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits best immediately after any step where a user submits contact information that needs to be confirmed as genuinely theirs (account creation, password reset, or high-trust financial actions like adding a new device).
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for low-stakes actions or flows where the contact method was already verified earlier in the same session, since re-verifying would add friction without a meaningful security or trust benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. WhatsApp (phone verification): uses the identical numeric-code-with-resend pattern immediately after phone number entry, a direct structural parallel.

  2. Revolut: verifies email/phone via a segmented OTP field with a disabled-until-valid Continue button, comparable because it's also a regulated finance app protecting account creation.

  3. Coinbase: applies the same Verification (2FA) pattern within its own multi-step signup, relevant given both are self-custody/crypto-adjacent products with similar trust requirements.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status: the progress bar and the dimmed/disabled Continue button both communicate exactly where the user stands and what's still required.

  2. Error prevention: disabling Continue until a code is entered stops users from submitting incomplete input and hitting an avoidable error.

  3. Recognition over recall: the placeholder "000 000" shows the expected code format before the user types anything, removing guesswork about digit count or grouping.

  4. User control & freedom: the "Resend" link and back arrow both give the user an explicit way out of a stuck state, rather than trapping them if the code never arrives.

  5. Consistency: the layout (progress bar, headline, subtext, input, primary button) mirrors the previous phone/email screen exactly, reinforcing a predictable step-by-step rhythm.

screens.name: Verification Code Screen (Filled State)
screens.whereToUse: This state-based button pattern fits best in any short, single-field verification step where the system can definitively judge input completeness (fixed-length codes, required checkboxes, etc.), giving users a clear, low-effort signal that they're ready to proceed.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for fields where "completeness" isn't a reliable proxy for "correctness" (e.g., free-text fields prone to typos) - enabling a button on completeness alone could let users submit clearly wrong input with false confidence.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. WhatsApp (phone verification): uses the same enabled/disabled button toggle tied to code completeness, a direct structural parallel.

  2. Revolut: activates its Continue/Confirm button only once a full OTP is entered, comparable given the shared regulated-finance verification context.

  3. Coinbase: applies an identical enabled-state pattern during its own account verification flow, relevant given both are self-custody/crypto-adjacent products.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status: the button's color change from disabled to active gives immediate, unambiguous feedback that the entered code is complete and accepted for submission.

  2. Error prevention: requiring the full code before activating Continue stops users from submitting a partial or invalid entry.

  3. Recognition over recall: the grouped digit format ("893 765") mirrors how OTP codes are typically communicated via SMS/email, making it easy to cross-check without re-reading digit by digit.

  4. Minimal user effort: the numeric keypad fills the bottom of the screen automatically, so the user never has to switch input modes or hunt for the right field.

  5. Consistency: layout, iconography, and progress indicator remain identical to the empty state, isolating the button's state change as the only meaningful visual difference between the two screens.

screens.name: Verification Code Screen (Error State)
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits best on any short, single-field verification step where failures are common and recoverable (mistyped OTPs, expired codes) - pairing a clear inline message with a still-editable field lets users fix the issue in place without restarting the flow.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for errors that require more explanation than a one-line message can carry (e.g., account already exists, code expired after multiple attempts) - in those cases, a more detailed error state or a redirect to account recovery would serve the user better than a generic "incorrect" message.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. WhatsApp (phone verification): shows an equivalent inline red-text-plus-message error when an OTP is entered incorrectly, a direct structural parallel.

  2. Revolut: reverts its Confirm button to disabled and highlights the field in red on a failed code check, comparable given the shared regulated-finance verification context.

  3. Coinbase: applies a similar Error State & Recovery pattern during account verification, relevant given both are self-custody/crypto-adjacent products with comparable trust requirements.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status: red text plus a dedicated error badge give redundant, unambiguous signals that the code was rejected.

  2. Error prevention & recovery: reverting Continue to disabled stops the user from re-submitting the same wrong code, while the "Resend" link offers a clear path if the code itself is the problem.

  3. Match between system and real world: the friendly "Oops!" phrasing softens what could otherwise feel like a harsh rejection, consistent with the app's warm tone from onboarding.

  4. Minimal user memory load: the incorrect code stays visible (rather than being cleared) so the user can see exactly what they entered and correct it rather than re-typing from scratch.

  5. Consistency: layout, icons, and progress bar remain unchanged from the success-state screen, isolating the red text, error badge, and disabled button as the only meaningful differences.

screens.name: Verification Code Screen (Loading / Submitting State)
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits best for short, fast backend operations (code validation, form submission, quick API calls) where a full-screen loading state would feel disproportionate to the wait time, and where keeping the user anchored to their point of action reduces perceived friction.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for longer operations (file uploads, multi-second processing, wallet creation itself) where an in-button spinner alone could leave users uncertain whether the app has stalled (those cases benefit more from a determinate progress indicator or a dedicated loading screen with status messaging).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Stripe (checkout confirmation): uses the same in-button spinner pattern immediately after a payment submission, a direct structural parallel for showing processing state without leaving the current screen.

  2. Revolut: shows a comparable inline loading indicator within its Confirm button during OTP validation, relevant given the shared regulated-finance verification context.

  3. Coinbase: applies a similar in-button Indeterminate Loading state during its own account verification flow, a fair comparison given both are self-custody/crypto-adjacent products with near-identical verification steps.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Visibility of system status: the in-button spinner immediately confirms the tap registered and processing is underway, preventing the user from wondering if their submission went through.

  2. Minimal disruption: keeping the loading state contained within the button (rather than a full-screen spinner or skeleton) preserves context and avoids an abrupt visual jump.

  3. Perceived performance: an indeterminate spinner is appropriate here since the operation is short; a determinate progress bar would be overkill and could make a fast process feel artificially longer.

  4. Consistency: layout, black (not red) text color for the code, and all surrounding elements remain unchanged from the prior screens, isolating the spinner as the only new element and keeping the pattern easy to recognize.

  5. Prevents duplicate submission: showing a loading state (implicitly disabling further taps) protects against the user tapping Continue multiple times while validation is in progress.

screens.name: Save Passkey Screen (Feature Pitch)
screens.whereToUse: This combination fits best immediately before any OS-level or otherwise unfamiliar permission/credential prompt (passkeys, biometrics, push notifications, camera access) where users are likely to reflexively decline without context.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for permissions or actions users already understand well and expect (e.g., a simple "Allow Photos access" when uploading a profile picture), where an extra educational screen would only add friction to an already-obvious request.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Google (passkey opt-in prompts): uses a nearly identical benefit-list format before requesting passkey creation, a direct structural parallel for priming users on a newer authentication method.

  2. PayPal: shows comparable "why passkeys" educational screens ahead of biometric setup, relevant given both are finance-adjacent apps needing to build trust before a security-relevant action.

  3. Robinhood: primes users with benefit-framed copy before requesting biometric/2FA setup, a fair comparison for the Permission Priming + Feature Spotlight combination in a fintech context.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Recognition over recall: defining "passkey" inline rather than assuming prior knowledge removes a common source of hesitation for less technical users.

  2. Objection handling before the ask: each benefit row preemptively answers a likely concern (forgetting passwords, security risk, losing password fallback) before the user has to voice it.

  3. Trust through reversibility: explicitly stating passkeys can be managed later in settings reduces the perceived stakes of the decision.

  4. Progressive disclosure: the screen focuses solely on the "why" of passkeys, deferring the "how" (the actual biometric setup) to the next system-level interaction.

  5. Consistency: the layout and progress bar carry over from prior onboarding screens, reinforcing that this is one more step in a familiar, ongoing sequence rather than a new context.

screens.name: Brex Add to Apple Wallet 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any fintech, banking, or corporate card management screen where sensitive payment credentials must be displayed, concealed, or copied. It's ideal for admin/self-service financial dashboards, virtual card issuance platforms, and any scenario where users need granular control (lock, replace, limits) over a tokenized payment instrument. The bottom sheet nudge pattern is reusable whenever a non-blocking but important account configuration gap needs surfacing in context.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid fully masking sensitive data by default in low-security contexts where users need constant visibility (e.g., a personal card display for a trusted single-user app) as the extra reveal/long-press step adds friction. Also avoid stacking a bottom sheet warning on top of an already dense screen if the issue isn't actionable immediately (this can feel like an interruption rather than a helpful nudge if the user lacks permission to resolve it themselves (e).g., non-admin employees seeing spend limit warnings they cannot act on).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets business professionals, finance administrators, and employees of a company using Brex for corporate spend management. These users are typically multitasking, cost-conscious, and security-aware, often accessing this screen in moments of urgency (e.g., lost card, need to make a purchase, verifying details for an expense report).

Psychologically, the design leverages the sense of control (lock/replace card instantly), trust through security transparencyloss-aversion framing in the bottom sheet (a pending/missing spend limit implies the card may not work, prompting quick resolution to avoid a blocked transaction later).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Security-first default masking of PAN/CVV/Expiry with a deliberate reveal toggle, balancing security compliance with user convenience.

  • Gesture-based copy interaction ("long press to copy details") that eliminates extra buttons while remaining discoverable via inline hint text.

  • Three-tile quick action row (Lock, Replace, More) gives users instant control over card security states (critical for fraud/loss scenarios) without navigating deeper menus.

  • Contextual bottom sheet nudge for spend limits that surfaces at the moment of card management, rather than as a generic notification, increasing the likelihood of action.

  • Apple Wallet integration CTA bridges the native OS payment ecosystem directly from the card management screen, reducing friction to real-world card usage.

screens.name: Brex Add to Apple Wallet 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an action depends on a third-party or OS-level service (payment provisioning, calendar sync, native share, push permission) that can fail unpredictably. It's ideal for:

  • Apple Wallet / Google Pay card provisioning flows

  • Payment processing failures

  • Any integration with external APIs where retry is a valid recovery path

  • Mobile contexts where a full-screen error would feel overly disruptive for a recoverable, non-destructive failure
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for silent, low-stakes background failures where interrupting the user adds more friction than value (use a toast instead). Also avoid it for critical/destructive errors (e.g., account security breaches, data loss) where a bottom sheet may under-communicate severity (a full-screen or modal dialog with stronger visual weight would be more appropriate. Don't use vague "try again later" messaging if the error is actionable by the user (e.g., permission not granted)) give specific remediation steps instead of a generic retry.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets business/corporate cardholders (Brex is a corporate card/spend management platform) who expect bank-grade security affordances (masked card numbers, lock card) alongside modern conveniences (Apple Wallet provisioning). The error-handling pattern specifically serves users attempting a device-level integration that depends on external APIs (Apple's PassKit/Wallet service), which can fail for reasons outside the app's control (network, device state, Apple servers).

Psychologically, the design reduces frustration by (1) not hiding the failure behind silent retries, (2) giving a human-readable apology-free but polite explanation, and (3) offering immediate recourse via "Try again" to restore a sense of control after a disrupted task flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Masked sensitive data by default: PAN, CVV, and expiry are hidden behind dots with an explicit reveal toggle, reducing shoulder-surfing risk for a corporate card.

  • Non-blocking, recoverable error pattern: The failure is surfaced in a bottom sheet rather than a full-screen takeover, preserving context of the underlying card screen.

  • Dual-path resolution: Offering both "Close" (dismiss) and "Try again" (retry) respects user agency (some users may want to retry immediately, others may want to abandon the Wallet flow and continue elsewhere).

  • Plain-language error messaging: Avoids technical jargon or error codes, reducing user anxiety around a failed native OS integration (Apple Wallet provisioning).

  • Visual hierarchy via color: The red alert icon and orange primary CTA create unambiguous visual cues about severity and recommended next action.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any compliance-driven detail screen where a record (expense, application, claim, order) must pass through verification states before being finalized. It's ideal when:

  • Users need to supply supporting documents (receipts, IDs, proof of purchase).
  • There's a multi-stage review/approval workflow that benefits from a visible timeline.
  • Policy-specific messaging can reduce confusion (e.g., insurance claims, expense management, loan applications, KYC flows).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, warning-heavy layout for low-stakes or purely informational detail screens where no action is required (excessive banners and status indicators can create false urgency and alarm fatigue). It's also unsuitable for consumer-facing apps with casual, high-volume transactions (e.g., a coffee loyalty app), where this level of compliance friction would feel disproportionate and degrade the experience. Additionally, if policies vary widely or are too complex to summarize in one line, a static banner may oversimplify and mislead users about next steps.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves employees who have made a small purchase on a corporate card and must now provide documentation to satisfy finance/compliance policies, as well as finance admins auditing the same record. The psychological trigger at play is loss-aversion/compliance anxiety: by clearly flagging "Not verified" and explaining the consequence (manual review), the design nudges the employee to resolve the issue quickly to avoid being personally flagged or having the expense rejected.

The transparent status timeline also leverages the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to complete unfinished tasks) by visually showing an incomplete process, motivating the user to finish uploading valid receipts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive policy explanation: Instead of just flagging an error, the banner tells the user exactly *why* the receipt is problematic and references their specific company policy, reducing confusion and support escalations.
  • Inline character counter on Memo: The 50/800 counter gives real-time feedback, preventing surprise truncation and encouraging sufficiently detailed justifications for auditors.
  • Visual status timeline: Using a vertical checklist/stepper for "Status" turns an opaque back-office process (compliance review) into a transparent, trustworthy narrative the end-user can follow.
  • Low-friction receipt attachment: The "+" tile next to existing thumbnails keeps adding more proof as easy as a single tap, encouraging compliance completion in the moment.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern whenever a product needs to present a single record with both a status history and granular metadata, especially in regulated or scrutinized domains (expense management, compliance review, order/shipment tracking, support ticket detail, or insurance claims). It's ideal when trust and auditability matter more than persuasion, and when multiple stakeholders (submitter + reviewer) need a shared source of truth.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, document-style layout for high-frequency, low-stakes interactions where speed matters more than completeness (e.g., quick balance checks or casual browsing). It would also be inappropriate for consumer-facing, emotionally-driven experiences where a utilitarian tone could feel cold or bureaucratic. If a transaction has no review history, this layout should degrade gracefully with an empty state rather than showing an empty or confusing timeline.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen primarily serves employees whose expenses have been flagged and finance admins/auditors who need to verify compliance status. For the employee, seeing a transparent timeline of "flagged → reviewed" reduces the stress and ambiguity of having a purchase questioned, invoking the psychological principle of procedural justice: people are far more accepting of a process outcome when they can see the steps taken to reach it, even before knowing the final verdict.

For finance teams, the structured transaction details satisfy the need for completeness and defensibility: every field needed for bookkeeping, tax categorization, or dispute resolution is present in one place, reducing back-and-forth queries. The comment/@-mention system taps into workplace familiarity with tools like Slack, lowering the learning curve and encouraging asynchronous resolution instead of requiring a meeting or email thread.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual audit-trail timeline: Checkmark-based vertical stepper turns an abstract compliance process into a transparent, reassuring narrative the employee can follow.
  • Dense but scannable key-value table: Consistent label/value alignment lets users quickly verify transaction facts without cognitive overload.
  • Contextual collaboration hint: The @-mention instructions inside the Comments section teaches functionality inline, right when it's relevant.
  • Balanced action hierarchy: "Add comment" (collaborative, low-stakes) and "File a dispute" (escalation, higher-stakes) are styled identically to avoid alarming the user, yet are clearly separated as distinct next steps.
  • Persistent context header: Merchant name and amount remain pinned at the top regardless of scroll, anchoring the user as they review granular details below.

screens.name: Brex - Reimbursement reviewed - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this layered bottom-sheet + chip-based error pattern when:

  • An automated verification/validation process (OCR, fraud check, data matching) fails and the user needs specific, itemized reasons rather than a blanket error.
  • The failure is recoverable or has a fallback path (manual review, memo, re-upload) and shouldn't fully block the user's workflow.
  • You want to preserve form context and avoid navigating the user away from their in-progress task.
  • Financial, compliance, or document-verification flows where transparency about *why* something failed builds user trust.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The error is critical and must hard-block the user (e.g., legal/compliance violation) - a bottom sheet may under-communicate severity; a full-screen interstitial or disabled submit button may be more appropriate.
  • There are more than 3-4 failure reasons, as the chip row could wrap awkwardly or overwhelm the limited bottom-sheet real estate (consider a scrollable list or accordion instead).
  • The underlying cause is highly technical; surfacing raw field names like "Merchant" without guidance on remediation could confuse less technical users if no next-step CTA is provided within the sheet itself.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets employees submitting expenses on the go, often from imperfect conditions (bad lighting, crumpled receipts, foreign currency receipts, or no receipt at all as implied by the memo). It also serves finance/admin teams indirectly by ensuring exceptions are flagged and routed to manual review rather than silently approved, protecting compliance integrity.

Psychologically, the design reduces anxiety around making a financial mistake by externalizing the error to a system limitation rather than user fault, while the granular breakdown (Date/Amount/Merchant) gives the user actionable next steps (e.g., re-upload or add memo justification) instead of leaving them stuck. The manual-review fallback also builds trust that legitimate business expenses won't be rejected outright due to OCR failure.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual Bottom Sheet over Dimmed Background: Preserves the user's place in the underlying form while delivering a focused, modal-style alert, avoiding a jarring full-screen takeover for a non-blocking issue.
  • Field-Level Error Chips: Breaking the verification failure into discrete, labeled chips (Date, Amount, Merchant) gives granular diagnostic feedback instead of a vague generic error message.
  • Non-Blocking Error Pattern: The flow explicitly allows the user to proceed via manual review and memo justification rather than hard-locking submission, respecting real-world edge cases (e.g., lost receipts).
  • Dual-Surface Status Communication: The "Not verified" status label on the Receipts section header and the warning banner work together with the modal to reinforce the same message across multiple visual layers.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 14
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any content-heavy, habit-forming app (music, video, news, shopping) where:

  • You have rich behavioral/listening/viewing data to power personalization.
  • Users return frequently and benefit from near-zero-decision re-entry points.
  • Content can be visually represented (cover art, thumbnails) to support fast recognition-based browsing over text-based decision making.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The app has sparse or no historical user data (new users will see empty or generic, low-relevance shelves, eroding trust in personalization).
  • Content needs to be consumed in strict chronological or sequential order (e.g., task managers, financial transaction logs) - algorithmic shelves obscure recency and completeness.
  • Accessibility or low-vision contexts are a priority, since dense horizontal carousels with small truncated text are harder to navigate via screen readers or keyboard-only input.
  • The brand needs a curated, editorial-first storefront feel rather than an infinite, algorithmically-reordered browse experience.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets returning, habitual users rather than new sign-ups (it assumes a rich listening history and uses it immediately (the entire feed is personalized off known favorites)). The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Choice reduction / decision fatigue relief: by pre-curating stations and mixes, Spotify removes the paradox-of-choice friction from a catalog of 100M+ tracks.
  • Mere-exposure & familiarity bias: repeatedly surfacing the same favorite artists (Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo) across different shelf types builds trust in the algorithm and increases click-through likelihood.
  • Momentum/resumption bias: the "Start listening" row exploits the Zeigarnik effect (an incomplete/previously started listening session is more compelling to resume than to start fresh).
screens.keyHighlights:
Key UX decisions worth stealing:

  • Top segmented pills as a lightweight feed filter: switching between Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks without a full page navigation or loss of scroll context.
  • Color-coded cards per shelf row: distinct saturated backgrounds (coral/mint/cyan) make each horizontal carousel instantly distinguishable from its neighbors even on a quick scroll.
  • Artist-list microcopy as implicit social/taste proof: reusing recognizable names (Taylor Swift, Olivia Rodrigo) across multiple shelves reinforces personalization credibility.
  • "Start listening" resume row: placed last but functionally first-priority, it's a near-zero-effort way to re-engage with recently played content, using an overflow menu (•••) for secondary actions instead of cluttering the row.
  • Dense, scroll-first density: no onboarding chrome or empty states; the screen is 100% content, which is ideal for a daily-habit app where returning users want immediate value.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 15
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any content-rich, habitual-use app (media, streaming, news aggregators) where the primary goal is fast re-engagement rather than deep navigation. It's ideal when you have multiple content types that benefit from cross-promotion, and when personalization/recency can meaningfully reduce the user's search burden. The segmented filter-plus-carousel-shelves approach also works well for apps transitioning from single-content-type to multi-content-type offerings.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, shelf-based home pattern for simple, single-purpose apps where a flat list or singular focused screen would reduce cognitive load. It's also unsuitable for first-time or low-content users (brand-new accounts without listening history will see sparse or awkward empty shelves, requiring a separate cold-start/onboarding strategy). Additionally, this pattern can overwhelm users seeking a specific item rather than passive browsing, who would be better served by a search-first entry point.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Spotify's full worldwide user base, especially habitual daily listeners who want frictionless re-entry into music/podcasts rather than active discovery. The psychological driver is the reduction of decision fatigue: by surfacing recently played and recommended content immediately, Spotify exploits the "path of least resistance" - pressing play is easier than choosing what to play, directly matching the app's core design philosophy.

The avatar notification dot and "Good Hang with Amy Po.." badge leverage curiosity-gap and social/novelty cues to pull users deeper into unexplored shelves, while the segmented filter caters to users with singular intent (e.g., podcast-only listeners) without forcing them into a separate app section.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Zero-decision resumption grid: The top row of recent/continue items requires no scrolling or searching (users can resume exactly where they left off within one tap of opening the app).
  • Inline filter chips: The All/Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks segmented control reshapes the entire home feed instantly without navigation, giving a sense of control without complexity.
  • Graceful offline empty state: Rather than blocking the UI with an error, the offline notice is presented as just another shelf in the feed, maintaining flow and app usability perception.
  • Mixed content shelving: Podcasts, radio stations, and personalized DJ features are shelved together using identical card patterns, letting Spotify cross-merchandise disparate content types seamlessly.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 16
screens.whereToUse: Use this shelf-based, dual-axis home pattern for any content-rich app where the primary job is "reduce time-to-first-engagement" rather than "support deep deliberate search" - e.g., streaming (video/audio/podcasts), news aggregators, e-commerce homepages, or any app with a strong recommendation engine. It's ideal when you have multiple distinct personalization signals (recent activity, trending, genre-based) that don't fit into a single ranked list and benefit from being segmented into legible, labelled groups.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for task-oriented or utility apps (banking, productivity, settings) where users arrive with a specific goal (shelf browsing adds unnecessary scanning cost when users need direct, predictable paths. It also underperforms for small catalogs: if there isn't enough distinct content to fill multiple meaningfully different rails, the shelves will feel repetitive or sparse, exposing the recommendation engine's weaknesses rather than hiding them. Finally, be cautious embedding temporary campaigns (like Wrapped) as persistent navigation chips if the campaign isn't genuinely timely) stale promotional chips erode trust in the personalization system.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is engineered for Spotify's broadest possible segment: casual-to-habitual listeners who want frictionless audio, not crate-diggers who want to browse a catalog. The design leans heavily on the psychological principle of choice reduction: presenting 3 confident picks instead of a blank search bar reduces decision fatigue and shortens the time-to-first-play, which correlates directly with session length and retention.

The "Recents" and "Based on your recent listening" shelves exploit the mere-exposure and consistency principles, showing content the user has already engaged with increases the likelihood of re-engagement because it requires zero cognitive evaluation of whether the content is "good." The Wrapped chip taps into social/temporal relevance (a culturally-charged seasonal event) to re-activate dormant interest and drive sharing behavior later in the funnel.
screens.keyHighlights:
Several micro-decisions on this screen are worth stealing:

  • Decision-removal design: By pre-populating "Start listening" with three concrete, named tracks instead of a generic "Resume" button, Spotify removes the single biggest point of friction in media apps (choosing what to play) using algorithmic confidence instead of user effort.
  • Dual-axis scroll economy: Stacking independently-scrolling horizontal rails inside one vertical feed allows an almost unlimited number of personalization contexts to be surfaced on one screen without overwhelming the user, since each rail is optional to explore.
  • Overflow menu on recommendation rows: The persistent ••• next to each "Start listening" track gives users an escape hatch (e.g., "not interested," add to playlist) right at the point of recommendation, which both improves control and quietly feeds the recommender system more signal.
  • Campaign-as-filter-chip: Embedding "Wrapped" as a selectable chip in the primary navigational filter row (rather than as a separate banner) lets a seasonal marketing push feel like a native, integrated part of the experience rather than an interruption.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 17
screens.whereToUse:
Use this shelf-based home pattern when:

  • Your product aggregates large, heterogeneous content libraries (media, shopping, learning) that benefit from multiple parallel recommendation algorithms.
  • You need a single landing screen that serves both returning/habitual users (resume content) and discovery-seeking users (recommended content) simultaneously.
  • Visual thumbnails are strong, recognizable brand/content assets that can carry meaning without heavy text labels.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Your content catalog is small or narrow: shelves will feel redundant or sparse, exposing an empty-feeling product.
  • Users need a single, linear primary action (e.g., task-based utility apps, checkout flows) - horizontal carousels add unnecessary navigational complexity.
  • Accessibility/screen-reader users are a primary audience (nested horizontal scrolling grids are notoriously harder to navigate via assistive tech than linear lists).
  • You lack sufficient behavioral data to personalize shelves meaningfully, which would default users to the same generic/static ordering, losing the pattern's core value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Spotify's broadest possible audience (from casual music listeners to dedicated podcast binge-listeners) by using behavioral personalization rather than demographic targeting. The psychological trigger at play is the Zeigarnik effect (people feel compelled to finish unfinished tasks): surfacing "Recents" first exploits the itch to continue an interrupted playlist or episode.

The "Your shows" and "Episodes you might like" shelves leverage habit formation and variable reward: mixing guaranteed, subscribed content (predictable reward) with fresh recommendations (variable reward) in the same scroll session, a core mechanic for maximizing daily active usage and session length.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Content-type segmented control pinned at the top lets users instantly re-scope the entire home feed (Music/Podcasts/Audiobooks) without navigating away (a lightweight filter that prevents content-type fatigue).
  • Recency-first shelf ordering: "Recents" appears before any algorithmic discovery content, optimizing for the single most common use case: resuming what you were just listening to.
  • Dense, image-forward grid with minimal text maximizes scanability; users recognize album/show art faster than they can read titles, leveraging visual memory over literal reading.
  • Avatar-as-nav-item in the top-left doubles as profile entry and establishes personalization/identity framing right where the eye lands first.
  • Four-item tab bar keeps the global navigation surface minimal, reducing decision fatigue and keeping "Home" as the obvious default re-entry point.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 18
screens.whereToUse:
Use this personalization-shelf + scoped-chip pattern in any content-rich app (streaming audio/video, e-commerce, news) where:

  • You have strong behavioral/taste signal on the user (listening history, purchase history, follows).
  • The catalog is large enough that curation materially reduces decision fatigue.
  • You want to reinforce retention by making the home screen feel like a living, personally-tailored space rather than a static menu.
  • You need a low-friction way to let users pivot their whole feed around one interest without navigating to a dedicated settings or search flow.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The app has thin or sparse content catalogs where personalization shelves would feel repetitive or redundant with only 1-2 real options.
  • There isn't enough reliable behavioral data yet (e.g., brand-new users), as fabricated "for fans of" shelves based on weak signal can feel creepy or inaccurate and erode trust.
  • The product's brand relies on a bright, light-first visual identity (the dark canvas/content-pop technique works specifically because of Spotify's dark aesthetic and wouldn't translate to bright, white-dominant interfaces without redesign).
  • Accessibility is a primary concern for low-vision users, since image-heavy tiles with only small caption text can be harder to parse than list-based, high-contrast text UI.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets highly engaged, habitual listeners (particularly fans with a strong single-artist affinity (stan culture), a demographic Spotify monetizes heavily through engagement and retention). By surfacing a named artist as a filter and two dedicated personalized shelves, Spotify leverages the psychological principle of identity affirmation: users feel "seen" and understood, which increases session length and perceived product intelligence.

The pattern also exploits choice-reduction psychology: rather than showing a blank search bar or an overwhelming genre grid, it pre-filters toward content statistically likely to be wanted, lowering the activation energy required to start listening. This is critical for an audio app where "frictionless background listening" is the core value proposition described in the app's positioning (pressing play should be easier than deciding what to play).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Artist-scoped personalization chip: Turning the user's own taste into a filter token (the green avatar) is a subtle but powerful way to let users re-center their entire home feed around one interest without a settings menu.
  • Dual Taylor Swift shelves ("For fans of" and "More like"): Reinforces relevance twice in one scroll using different framing (direct artist content vs. adjacent/similar artists), maximizing the chance of a satisfying match.
  • Dark canvas as a content amplifier: The near-black background isn't just aesthetic branding (it functions as a deliberate contrast tool that makes colorful album art and artist photography the visual hero of every shelf).
  • Horizontal carousels for zero-decision browsing: Users can passively swipe through dozens of options with minimal commitment, a frictionless entry point before pressing play.
  • Collaborator text as proof-of-relevance: listing featured artists under each radio tile lets users self-filter before tapping, saving time and preventing frustration.

screens.name: Spotify - Home - Screen 19
screens.whereToUse: Use this shelf-based, filter-chip browsing pattern for any content-rich, multi-category product (streaming video, e-commerce, news aggregators) where users arrive without a specific goal and need low-friction, exploratory discovery. It's ideal when you have strong editorial/algorithmic curation and want to minimize empty states or decision fatigue. The square-vs-circle card convention is a reusable, universally understood shorthand for "media" vs. "person" that should be adopted in any catalog browsing UI.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for task-oriented or utility apps (banking, productivity, settings) where users arrive with a specific goal (endless horizontal shelves add exploration overhead that actively slows down task completion). It also underperforms for new users with zero listening history, where shelves risk looking generic/cold without strong default/global popularity data to fall back on. Additionally, horizontal carousels have poor discoverability on their own (users often don't scroll past the first 3-4 items), so critical content should never live exclusively in a mid-carousel position.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves the broadest possible Spotify audience (from casual listeners to music superfans) by front-loading globally popular content (chart-topping artists like Kendrick Lamar, Bad Punny, The Weeknd) as social proof. Seeing mainstream, culturally dominant names validates the platform's relevance immediately, even for a brand-new or logged-out-feeling user, reducing the "what do I even listen to" paralysis.

The psychological trigger at play is largely recognition over recall: rather than asking users to think of what they want to hear, the screen passively surfaces familiar faces and album art, triggering impulse taps driven by curiosity or nostalgia. The personalized "Discover more from Gracie Abrams" shelf additionally leverages the mere-exposure/affinity effect: users are far more likely to engage with new content tied to an artist they already have an established relationship with.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Scrollable filter chips above the fold: Letting users pivot between Music, Podcasts, and Audiobooks instantly without a full page reload keeps cognitive and motor cost near zero.
  • Mixed card geometry (square vs. circle): Using shape semantically (albums = square, people = circle) lets users parse content type in milliseconds via peripheral vision alone, before even reading text.
  • Personalized "Discover more from [Artist]" shelf: Anchoring a recommendation shelf to a specific followed artist (with their avatar) rather than a generic "Recommended for you" label increases perceived relevance and trust in the algorithm.
  • Dense horizontal carousels with edge-peeking cards: Each shelf intentionally crops the next card at the screen edge, visually signaling "there's more" and inviting a swipe without needing a "see all" affordance on every row.
  • Dark canvas as a content amplifier: The near-black background makes vibrant album art and artist photography pop, turning the interface itself into a gallery rather than competing with the content.

screens.name: Spotify - Filtering & Sorting - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any content library composed of sequential, episodic media (podcasts, video series, audiobooks chapters, course lessons) where users need to quickly compare multiple items on recency, duration, and popularity before committing. It is especially effective when:

  • Content catalogs are long and need strong scannability.
  • Secondary actions (save, download, share) are valuable but shouldn't compete with the primary consumption action.
  • Social proof signals (play counts) are available and can build trust at a glance.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense list+metadata pattern when content items are not easily differentiated by date/duration/popularity (e.g., static article catalogs or evergreen reference content), as the metadata row adds clutter without decision value. It also underperforms for new or low-volume shows where play counts are embarrassingly low or absent, since surfacing weak social proof can undermine credibility rather than build it. For purely visual content (e.g., video thumbnails meant to be browsed cinematically), a larger card-based grid would outperform this compact row-list treatment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets returning, engaged listeners of a specific podcast franchise who are already past the discovery phase and are now deciding which specific episode to consume next. The psychological drivers at play include the mere-exposure and celebrity-proximity effect (guest names like Maya Rudolph, Julia Louis-Dreyfus drive curiosity among pop-culture audiences), social proof (play counts validate quality), and choice architecture simplification (the one-tap play button reduces decision fatigue for habitual, background-listening use cases common to podcast consumption during commutes or chores).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Isolated Play Affordance: The bold white circular play button is the only high-contrast interactive element per row, creating an unmistakable visual hierarchy that nudges toward immediate playback over exploration.
  • Scannable Social Proof: Play counts are baked directly into the metadata line of every episode, functioning as lightweight, ambient trust signals without requiring a separate ratings system.
  • Segmented Tabs for Content Types: Episodes / About / More Like This cleanly separates transactional content (listening) from informational content (show details) and discovery (recommendations), keeping the primary list uncluttered.
  • Truncated, Personality-Rich Descriptions: Two-line clamped summaries give enough narrative hook to drive curiosity while preserving scroll efficiency through a long episode list.

screens.name: Spotify - Filtering & Sorting - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Any content library or catalog screen with lists long enough to benefit from quick reordering (podcasts, playlists, downloads, order history).
  • When users have a small number (2-5) of mutually exclusive filter/sort options that don't require complex multi-select logic.
  • Contexts where speed of selection matters more than advanced faceted search (use a bottom sheet instead of a full-screen filter page).
  • Mobile-first flows where preserving background context aids orientation and reduces perceived navigation depth.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern when users need to combine multiple filters simultaneously (e.g., multi-select tags) - a single-select checkmark list implies mutual exclusivity and will confuse users who expect to combine criteria.
  • Not suitable for complex faceted browsing with many categories (price range, brand, size, etc.) - that requires a dedicated filter screen with apply/clear actions.
  • Avoid if users need to preview results before committing, since there's no explicit "Apply" step (instant commits can feel jarring for heavier/slower-loading filter operations).
  • Don't use on desktop/large-screen layouts where inline dropdowns or sidebar filters are more appropriate than a mobile bottom sheet metaphor.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets power listeners and binge-podcast consumers who subscribe to shows with large back catalogs (hundreds of episodes) and need to quickly narrow down to unplayed, downloaded, or chronologically relevant content. The "Downloaded" filter specifically serves users managing offline listening for commutes or flights, while "Not finished" serves habitual multitaskers who frequently pause episodes mid-way.

Psychologically, the pattern reduces choice overload: a show like this with 500K+ play episodes can have a long list, and surfacing a quick filter/sort mechanism helps users feel in control rather than overwhelmed, directly supporting the app's core promise of making "pressing play easier than deciding what to play."
screens.keyHighlights:
• Context-preserving overlay: The dimmed background keeps the episode list visible, so users retain orientation while adjusting filters.
  • No Apply/Confirm button: Selections appear to commit immediately via optimistic UI, reducing an unnecessary extra tap.
  • Grouped mental model: Separating "Filter" (what to show) from "Sort By" (what order) maps directly to how users think about organizing content, avoiding a single confusing flat list.
  • Single checkmark affordance: Using a checkmark instead of radio buttons/switches keeps the visual weight light and consistent with Spotify's minimalist dark UI.
  • Drag handle & swipe-to-dismiss: Removes need for explicit close/cancel buttons, maximizing content space.

screens.name: Spotify - Filtering & Sorting - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any catalog detail page representing a recurring content series: podcasts, YouTube channels, music artists, TV shows, newsletters, or blogs. It's ideal when:

  • Content is released episodically/serially and users need to track "what's new."
  • You need to build trust quickly via third-party social proof (ratings, charts).
  • You want to offer a low-friction trial (trailer/preview) before a longer commitment.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, review-heavy layout for single-use or ephemeral content (e.g., a one-off single track, a live event, or a short-form video) where series metadata like "episodes," "follow," and "charts" add irrelevant clutter. Also avoid heavy color-extraction gradients in contexts requiring strict brand consistency or high-accessibility contrast compliance, as dynamic backgrounds can sometimes reduce text legibility for low-vision users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
Targets casual podcast browsers and fans of a specific celebrity/host who arrive via search, recommendation, or social share link. The screen is engineered to convert a curious visitor into a "Follower" (subscriber) within seconds.

Psychological triggers include social proof (rating, rank, play counts), curiosity gap (truncated episode description, 1-minute trailer), and low-commitment sampling (play trailer before committing to a 1h23m episode). The Follow button (outlined, not filled) signals a low-pressure, reversible action, lowering the barrier to subscribing compared to a hard paywall or forced signup.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dynamic color extraction: The background gradient is algorithmically derived from the podcast cover art, giving every show page a bespoke, premium feel without manual design effort.
  • Compact social proof bar: Chart rank, star rating, and genre are condensed into one scannable line, borrowing credibility cues from the App Store and IMDb.
  • Trailer-as-CTA card: Placing a 1-minute trailer directly below the follow actions gives hesitant users a zero-commitment way to sample the show's tone before investing in a full episode.
  • "Newest • Unplayed" smart sort: Automatically filters/sorts the episode list to reduce decision fatigue (the user doesn't need to hunt for what's new).
  • Icon-only action row on episode cards: Save (+), Download, Share, More, and Play are compressed into a single row, enabling quick actions without leaving the list (bulk/library management pattern).

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this bottom-sheet invite pattern when a feature requires rapidly pulling other people into a collaborative, real-time or near-real-time session (co-listening, watch parties, multiplayer games, collaborative documents). It's ideal when you have multiple invite channels of differing effort/reach tradeoffs and want to let users self-select the fastest path for their situation. The dimmed-background-plus-sheet approach is best for lightweight, task-focused interruptions that shouldn't break the user's sense of place in the app.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-stakes or infrequent invite flows (e.g., inviting a business collaborator to a formal workspace) where a full-screen flow with more configuration (roles, permissions) is warranted. Also avoid stacking too many invite mechanisms if your audience skews non-technical (the QR code and Bluetooth auto-invite options add complexity that could overwhelm users who just want a simple share link). If proximity-based auto-invite requires significant permissions (Bluetooth, location), be cautious about implying it's low-effort, as permission prompts can introduce unexpected friction or privacy concerns.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets social, group-listening users: people at parties, road trips, or hangouts who want to collaboratively control a shared queue. The psychological drivers at play are:

  • Social facilitation:
  • Reduced friction for viral/network growth: Every Jam invite is an implicit growth loop (non-Spotify users who click a share link or scan a QR code are exposed to the product, functioning as a soft acquisition channel).
  • Context-matching convenience: By offering Bluetooth/Wi-Fi auto-invite for in-person scenarios, the app removes the awkwardness of manually sending links to people standing in the same room, reducing the social cost of using the feature in a live setting.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background context preservation: The Home screen is visible-but-darkened behind the sheet, keeping spatial continuity so the invite flow doesn't feel like a full context switch.
  • Reach-ordered option hierarchy: Share link (universal) → Auto-invite nearby (proximity-based) → QR code (in-person), guiding users to the fastest path for their specific social context.
  • Self-explanatory microcopy: Every advanced feature (auto-invite, QR) includes a one-line plain-language explanation, eliminating the need for a separate help screen or tooltip.
  • Multi-modal invite redundancy: Offering three distinct sharing mechanisms (link, proximity, visual code) maximizes the odds that at least one method matches the recipient's context (remote friend vs. person standing next to you).

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any native OS permission request (camera, microphone, location, Bluetooth, notifications, contacts) especially when the permission isn't immediately self-evident in value. It's ideal for:

  • Features gated behind sensitive hardware/data permissions where context is not obvious.
  • Flows where permission denial would be costly to recover from (since the system prompt usually can't be re-triggered easily).
  • Onboarding or feature-discovery moments where building long-term trust outweighs the cost of one extra screen/tap.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The permission's purpose is already self-evident from context (e.g., asking for camera access directly after tapping a camera icon) — adding an extra screen here is redundant friction.
  • The app needs the permission immediately and urgently; an extra educational step may slow down a time-critical task.
  • Used too frequently across many permissions in a row, which can create "priming fatigue" and make users suspicious of over-justification.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are about to engage in a social/offline listening feature (e.g., Spotify's "Group Session" or device-sharing flows) that technically requires Bluetooth. The target demographic is broad — essentially any Spotify user on a flow that needs Bluetooth — but the design specifically counters the general public's heightened wariness of granting background hardware permissions (Bluetooth, in particular, is often associated with tracking concerns).

Psychologically, it leverages the foot-in-the-door technique: agreeing to a low-stakes, well-explained "Continue" makes users far more likely to also tap "Allow" on the subsequent native iOS prompt. It also uses reciprocity/transparency framing — by proactively disclosing data usage and reversibility, Spotify builds trust, which increases the probability of permission grant and reduces later distrust or app uninstalls tied to perceived overreach.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Pre-permission priming: Explains value before invoking the native OS prompt, which research shows significantly increases opt-in rates versus a cold system dialog.
  • Benefit-first headline: Leads with the social use case ("listen with friends nearby") instead of the technical permission name.
  • Dual reassurance blocks: "How we'll use this" and "You're in control" preemptively answer privacy objections using calm iconography instead of warning symbols.
  • Warm, human illustration: Diverse hands and floating music notes humanize an otherwise cold technical request and reinforce the social/sharing use case.
  • Single low-friction CTA: "Continue" (not "Allow") lowers perceived commitment and funnels the user smoothly toward the actual OS permission dialog.

screens.name: Spotify - Turning on auto-invite - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a feature involves real-time collaborative sessions (shared playlists, watch parties, multiplayer games, collaborative docs) and you need to lower the barrier to inviting others. Ideal for scenarios with mixed invite contexts (remote, proximity-based, and in-person) where offering multiple invite channels in a single, dismissible surface increases conversion to multi-user engagement.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for high-stakes or privacy-sensitive invites (e.g., financial account sharing) where "auto-invite nearby" could unintentionally expose data to unintended parties (proximity-based auto-invite requires very clear consent framing or it risks feeling invasive). Also unsuitable for single-user or non-collaborative features where surfacing invite options would be irrelevant clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: Targets Spotify's highly social, group-listening user segment (friends at parties, in cars, or in shared physical spaces who want synchronized music control (Spotify Jam/Group Session feature)). The psychological driver is social facilitation and shared experience: music is inherently communal, and making group participation nearly effortless (auto-invite nearby) taps into spontaneity and reduces the setup tax that typically kills group activities. The QR code option additionally serves offline/low-connectivity social gatherings where typing or app-switching is impractical.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Multi-modal invite strategy: Combines link sharing, proximity auto-invite, and QR code in one sheet, covering remote, ambient, and in-person social contexts.
  • Context-preserving dim overlay: Background Home screen remains visible (blurred/dimmed), anchoring the user in their existing session rather than navigating away.
  • Iconography reinforces concept: The pulsing-wave Bluetooth/nearby icon visually communicates the "auto-invite nearby" radius concept at a glance.
  • Low-commitment UI: Swipeable grabber handle and non-blocking design make it easy to dismiss without friction.

screens.name: Venmo Requesting 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Help centers, FAQ hubs, and self-service support portals for apps handling sensitive/high-stakes actions (finance, healthcare, insurance).

  • Products with diverse user segments needing different types of support (billing vs. technical vs. account security).

  • Any screen where reducing support ticket volume via self-service deflection is a business goal.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for simple apps with very few help topics (an oversized categorized layout would feel like overkill and add unnecessary navigation steps).

  • Not ideal if most support inquiries are highly unique/long-tail; in that case a search-first minimal layout without heavy categorization would be more efficient.

  • Should not be used without a live chat/contact escalation path for time-critical issues (e.g., fraud, urgent account locks) since some users need human intervention immediately, not more reading.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets the full spectrum of Venmo users (from new users confused about basic profile settings to existing users facing acute issues like frozen accounts or failed transfers). The design leverages the psychological principle of reducing perceived effort: by pre-categorizing likely pain points, it lowers the anxiety and friction associated with seeking help, especially for financial issues where users may already feel stressed or vulnerable (e.g., "Troubleshooting: Frozen accounts & other concerns").

The prominent search bar caters to power users or those in urgent situations who want a direct answer fast, invoking the Search-First Navigation pattern to minimize time-to-resolution and prevent frustration/support ticket escalation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-path discovery: Combines a search-first affordance for users with specific questions and a browsable category list for users who need guidance, maximizing find-ability for different user intents.

  • Predictive subtitles: Each category pairs a bold heading with a plain-language description, letting users self-select the right path without needing to tap into each section speculatively.

  • Emotional design softening: The colorful doodle illustration and pill-shaped buttons reduce the inherent stress of visiting a "help" page for a money app, an emotionally charged context.

  • Visual consistency with brand: Rounded, bubbly shapes and Venmo-blue outlines maintain brand recognition even outside of the core app experience.

screens.name: Venmo Requesting 5
screens.whereToUse:
Utilize this pattern for any transactional history, support ticket, or status-tracking screen where the "zero state" is common (e.g., new users or specific filtered views). It is particularly effective for:

  • Support/Help center ticket histories.

  • Financial transaction dispute trackers.

  • Order tracking screens where no active orders exist.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid using dense, multi-paragraph text blocks like this for empty states in casual social or entertainment apps, where a simple illustration and single CTA (e.g., "Follow someone to see posts") is more appropriate and less overwhelming.

Additionally, if the exceptions being described (like the Synchrony redirect) apply to the majority of users rather than an edge case, this information should be moved to a primary, non-empty-state location, as users might filter/search and never actually land on this specific empty view.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves users of a banking or fintech application who are likely in a moment of financial friction, checking on the status of a transaction they believe was fraudulent or erroneous. The psychological state of the user here is typically anxiety or a need for control.

By providing immediate, clear links to "contact us" or "contact Synchrony," the design targets the need for a resolution path, ensuring that even in the absence of data, the user feels the "next step" is obvious and immediately actionable, thereby reducing frustration and cognitive load during a high-stakes financial workflow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive Bifurcation: The system anticipates that "credit card" disputes might be handled by a different backend entity (Synchrony) than other disputes, and clarifies this directly in the empty state rather than making the user guess or file an invalid dispute.

  • Actionable Emptiness: The empty state doesn't just describe an absence of data; it educates the user on the system's behavior ("Your dispute will be here once it's Submitted"), effectively serving as an on-demand tutorial.

  • Segmented Control for Status Filtering: Using a pill-shaped toggle for "Submitted" vs "Received" is an efficient way to manage two related but distinct data sets under one umbrella screen without adding tabs to the global navigation.

screens.name: Venmo Requesting 6
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-list settings pattern when:

  • Building an account/settings hub for any transactional, financial, or identity-sensitive app where trust and predictability matter more than visual flourish.

  • You have many discrete, unrelated settings that benefit from categorical grouping over a flat dashboard.

  • Users are expected to arrive with a specific task in mind (find password reset, sign out) rather than exploring casually.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The settings list is short (under ~6 items): grouping and section headers would add unnecessary visual overhead.

  • You want to surface personalization or visual richness (e.g., profile photo, plan status) - this flat list format buries such content.

  • The app targets a younger/more visual demographic where icons, colors, and imagery drive engagement (this style feels dated/corporate in consumer social contexts).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves existing, already-onboarded Venmo users who need to manage account security, redeem promotions, or exit their session (not new users being persuaded to convert). The psychological driver here is trust and control: because Venmo handles money, users expect settings related to password, device management, and identity verification to be easy to locate and unambiguous. The grouped hierarchy (Security section isolated from Information) leverages the peak-end and primacy effects: security-related actions are placed prominently near the top-middle so anxious users (e.g., someone who suspects fraud) can find "Change Password" or "Remembered Devices" quickly without scanning irrelevant legal content.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consistent row anatomy (icon + label + chevron) reduces cognitive load and speeds up scanning across a long, dense list.

  • Semantic grouping with muted section headers separates monetization/business features, security-critical actions, and informational/legal content without needing visual weight or extra chrome.

  • Differentiated Sign Out styling (blue text, no chevron, no icon slot) intuitively communicates a different interaction type (immediate action vs. navigation) without needing a confirmation-style warning color.

  • Version number footer provides a low-friction diagnostic touchpoint for support/debugging without cluttering the main UI.

  • Friendly micro-copy ("Have a code?") injected into an otherwise sterile, systematic list humanizes a promotional feature.

screens.name: Venmo Requesting 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any settings area consolidating static, rarely-updated reference documents (terms, privacy, licenses, fees, compliance disclosures). It's ideal for:

  • Fintech, healthcare, or regulated industry apps requiring easy access to compliance documents.

  • Settings/Profile menus where legal content needs to be present but not prominent.

  • Apps needing App Store/Play Store compliance (privacy policy & terms links are often mandatory).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat list approach when:

  • Legal documents require version history, acceptance tracking, or e-signatures (a more structured detail view with timestamps/audit trail would be needed).

  • Fee structures are complex or tiered: a dedicated pricing table or calculator would serve users better than a static document link.

  • Users need to search or filter across many legal jurisdictions/documents (e.g., a global app with region-specific terms) - a search or categorized/grouped list would scale better than a flat four-item list.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
