  • Clear single-tap back navigation preserves the user's place in the broader Settings hierarchy.

screens.name: Lemon8 - Privacy policy - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this long-form, typographically structured pattern for any legal, compliance, or policy document (Terms of Service, Privacy Policy, Community Guidelines, Cookie Policy) where accuracy and scannability outweigh visual flourish. It's ideal whenever:

  • Content must satisfy legal/regulatory disclosure requirements.
  • Users need to quickly locate specific clauses (via bolded sub-headers or an in-page search action).
  • The brand wants to maintain trust by being transparent and easy to navigate, even in "boring" but necessary screens.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, text-heavy pattern for primary marketing, onboarding, or engagement screens, where it would undermine the app's otherwise vibrant, visual-first brand identity. It should also be avoided if legal content could instead be summarized visually (icons, short cards) for simple consent flows (reserve full-text legal documents for users who specifically seek them out, not as a forced read during onboarding, since the length and density risk high drop-off or skimming without comprehension).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is targeted broadly at all Lemon8 users but is particularly relevant to privacy-conscious Gen Z users and users in regulated markets (EU/California) who are increasingly aware of and concerned about how their personal data (including photos and profile video, a data type unique to a content-sharing platform like Lemon8) is used. Presenting this information transparently and accessibly builds trust, which is critical for user retention in a platform that requires significant personal content (photos, videos, profile data) to function.

The psychological driver here is trust and transparency: rather than hiding legal obligations, Lemon8 surfaces a direct contact email and clearly labeled data categories to reduce user anxiety about surveillance or data misuse, which is especially important given that it is a TikTok-affiliated app facing public scrutiny over data privacy practices in several markets.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Bold lead-in labels: Each bullet point starts with a bolded phrase (e.g., "Your Profile Information.") functioning as a mini-heading, allowing users to scan the data categories quickly instead of reading dense paragraphs in full.
  • Clickable support email: The contact email is hyperlinked and color-coded in the brand's signature green, offering a frictionless escalation path for privacy concerns without burying it in a separate "Contact Us" flow.
  • Minimalist chrome: Stripping away tab bars, FABs, and decorative imagery keeps focus entirely on the text, which is the appropriate and expected pattern for a legal/compliance screen.
  • Overflow menu (•••): Preserves utility (likely search-in-page or share) without cluttering the header, keeping the focus on content consumption.

screens.name: Archive
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any browser or tab-management feature where content is automatically moved out of active view after a period of inactivity, requiring a dedicated, searchable, chronologically-organized location for users to retrieve or manage that archived content later.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit if archived content should be permanently and irretrievably removed rather than stored for later retrieval (in cases requiring true deletion rather than archiving, a distinct "delete" flow (rather than an archive-and-search model) would be more appropriate).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's Tab History / Recently Closed Tabs: organizes closed or archived tabs chronologically with title, URL, and favicon, closely matching this screen's structure.

  2. Chrome's History page: groups browsing history by date with search functionality, mirroring this Archive's date-grouped, searchable list.

  3. Arc Browser desktop's own Archive feature: the mobile app's Archive directly parallels the desktop Arc browser's auto-archiving tab-management system, maintaining feature consistency across platforms.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Feature Follow-Through: this screen delivers on the "auto-archive" promise made during onboarding and confirmed in Settings, showing archived tabs land somewhere retrievable rather than being silently lost.

  2. Chronological Grouping: organizing entries under date headers like "TODAY" follows familiar browser-history conventions, aiding quick temporal orientation.

  3. Scalable Management Tools: providing both Edit (bulk actions) and Search upfront anticipates the Archive growing significantly over time as tabs continue to auto-archive daily.

  4. Consistent Favicon Usage: using site favicons (the Google "G") alongside titles and URLs gives quick visual source recognition, consistent with standard browser history/bookmark list conventions.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 01
screens.whereToUse: This grouped Stacked List + Preference Center pattern fits any settings surface with a moderate-to-large number of independent preferences that benefit from being scanned at a glance, especially where some options are binary (toggle) and others need a dedicated picker screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit when there are only a handful of settings (a flat list would suffice) or when settings are highly interdependent and better presented as a guided wizard rather than an unordered menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari (iOS Settings): same grouped Stacked List + chevron drill-down pattern for browser preferences, a near-identical information architecture.

  2. Chrome (iOS Settings): uses the same colored-icon-plus-label row convention and trailing value text for settings like default search engine.

  3. Notion (iOS Settings): groups toggles and drill-down rows into dividered sections in a comparable Preference Center layout.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Chunking (Miller's Law): Dividers break ~14 settings into 5 digestible clusters instead of one long list.

  2. Recognition over recall: Trailing value text (e.g., "Google", "After 1 day", "Native App") shows current state inline, so users don't need to open each row to check it.

  3. Progressive disclosure: Chevron rows (Global Site Settings, Languages, Search Engine) push secondary complexity to nested screens, keeping this page scannable.

  4. Fitts's Law: Full-row tap targets (not just the switch/chevron) make toggles and navigation rows easier to hit on mobile.

  5. Consistency: Icon-label-value-chevron row pattern repeats identically throughout, lowering the learning curve as users scan down.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 02
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits any automated content-management feature (archiving, auto-deletion, auto-logout) where users benefit from choosing a personally appropriate threshold, especially when a single fixed default wouldn't suit meaningfully different usage patterns across the user base.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for settings where offering multiple duration options would create confusing inconsistency (e.g., security-critical timeouts where a single, carefully chosen default is safer than user-configurable flexibility).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. Safari's "Close Tabs Automatically" duration picker: offers a nearly identical range of duration options (1 day, 1 week, 1 month) for automatically closing inactive tabs.

  2. Chrome's "Auto Tab Groups" or memory-saver duration settings: provides comparable configurable timeframes for tab-management automation.

  3. Firefox's tab-unloading/archiving thresholds: similarly lets users choose how long inactive tabs remain before being archived or unloaded.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Resolving Prior Ambiguity: this screen retroactively confirms the "After 1 day" value seen in earlier Settings screenshots was genuinely configurable, not a fixed label.

  2. Range Accommodates Diverse Habits: offering both very short (12 hours) and long (30 days) options serves meaningfully different tab-management styles without forcing a one-size-fits-all default.

  3. Consistent Selector Pattern: reusing the same compact popover-with-checkmark format as the earlier "Swipe to Navigate" setting maintains a predictable interaction model for similar types of choices throughout Settings.

  4. Feature Follow-Through: this control makes the onboarding-promised "auto-archive" feature concretely adjustable, giving users direct control over how aggressively that promise is enforced.

screens.name: Change Archive Inactive Tabs 03
screens.whereToUse: This pattern (immediate persistence without explicit save) fits virtually all mobile settings interfaces, where requiring a separate save action for individual preference changes would add unnecessary friction and risk of lost changes if a user navigates away.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit only for settings with significant, hard-to-reverse consequences (e.g., account deletion, irreversible data actions), where an explicit confirm/save step is appropriate specifically to prevent accidental changes (a distinction correctly reflected in this app's separate use of confirmation dialogs (like the earlier "Clear All" archive action) for higher-stakes actions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
1. iOS Settings app (immediate value persistence): uses an identical pattern where sub-screen selections instantly update and display in the parent settings list without requiring a save step.

  2. Any well-designed settings architecture (Safari, Chrome, etc.): follows this same immediate-persistence convention as a baseline usability expectation for modern mobile settings.
screens.keyHighlights:
1. Reliable State Propagation: both changed settings correctly display their new values upon returning to the parent Settings screen, without requiring a manual refresh or save confirmation.

  2. Consistent Interaction Model Across Settings: the same select-then-confirm pattern (whether via popover or dedicated sub-screen) applies uniformly across different setting types (search engine, archive timing, language), giving the whole Settings experience a cohesive, predictable feel.

  3. Immediate Effect Without Explicit Save: no "Save" or "Apply" button was needed at any point in this sequence; each selection takes effect and displays immediately upon choice.

screens.name: Brilliant Course detail 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any structured, sequential learning or onboarding content (language apps, test-prep, coding tutorials, fitness programs, or compliance training) where you want to chunk a topic into a small number of bite-sized sub-tasks with a single clear entry point. It's ideal when you want to build anticipation and reduce overwhelm before a focused exercise session, and when you have a resource/energy economy you want to surface contextually.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex, non-linear content where forcing a fixed Warm-up → Main sequence feels artificial or condescending to advanced users. It's also unsuitable for professional/enterprise tools where playful 3D illustrations and gamified currency pills may undermine perceived credibility. If the module contains many sub-lessons (10+), a simple two-item checklist will feel insufficient and a fuller map/list view should be used instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed learners, students, and casual skill-builders (e.g., math learners, language learners) who need extrinsic motivation to continue habitual, bite-sized study sessions. The childlike, colorful 3D illustration style suggests the audience may skew toward younger students or adult learners who respond well to gamified, Duolingo-style encouragement rather than dense academic text.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the Zeigarnik effect (incomplete checklist items create a pull to finish), goal-gradient effect (clear small sub-steps feel more attainable), and scarcity (limited lightning/energy count) to drive daily engagement and reduce drop-off at the start of a learning session.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Playful 3D hero illustration doubles as subject-matter reinforcement (literally depicting a parabola function) while adding emotional warmth to an abstract math topic.

  • Two-tier task breakdown (Warm up → Graphing Solutions) sets clear, achievable expectations and uses sequencing to build momentum before the harder content.

  • Persistent resource counter (lightning/hearts pill) keeps scarcity top-of-mind even on a low-stakes overview screen, nudging retention and potential upsell.

  • Single sticky CTA at the bottom removes decision paralysis (there is exactly one thing to do next).

  • Page control dots subtly communicate a multi-level curriculum, reassuring the user of structured progress without needing a full map view.

screens.name: Brilliant Course detail 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when introducing a structured content module, course chapter, or skill unit inside a longer curriculum or roadmap (especially in edtech, habit-building, or skill-tree style apps). It's ideal when you want to set expectations (scope, effort, outcome) before a user commits to starting a sequence of lessons or tasks, and when the app already uses gamification elsewhere (streaks, levels, XP) so this screen feels consistent with the rest of the experience.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, illustration-led intro pattern for frequent, low-stakes micro-content (e.g., a single short lesson or a quick daily task) where the overhead of a full header would slow down users who already know what they want. It's also unsuitable for professional/enterprise tools where playful gamified language ("Supercharge," "Level 1") could undermine perceived credibility, or for contexts where screen real estate is at a premium and users need to see multiple lessons at once without scrolling past a large decorative block.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed learners (likely in math/STEM test-prep or skill-building apps such as Brilliant, Khan Academy, or Duolingo Math) who need frequent motivational reinforcement to persist through dry academic content. The design assumes a mobile-first, bite-sized learning context (users are expected to engage in short bursts, so the screen front-loads motivation (value prop + friendly illustration) before presenting commitment (lesson count) and then the actionable next step).

Psychologically, the screen leverages: (1) the mastery/competence motivator via gamified "Level" labeling, (2) curiosity gap via the peeking next node, and (3) reduced intimidation via playful illustration and encouraging copy for a subject (algebra/functions) that many users associate with anxiety or difficulty.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Collapsible unit header: Dual chevrons let users collapse the introductory copy once familiar with the unit, reducing scroll fatigue on repeat visits while still fully onboarding first-time users.

  • Peeking next-section preview: The faint "Seeing Solutions" node bleeding in from below the fold uses a Zeigarnik-effect style visual cue to pull users further down the path.

  • Custom isometric iconography: The satellite-dish/graph illustration visually encodes the abstract math concept (functions as graphs), making an abstract topic feel tangible and friendly.

  • Persistent gamification chrome: The streak/energy counter stays visible even on a content-description screen, keeping engagement metrics top-of-mind at all times.

  • Level framing as CTA: Wrapping "Level 1: Relationships and Points" in a bordered pill-button visually implies tappability/entry point, clearly marking where the user should tap to begin.

screens.name: Brilliant Course detail 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for sequential educational or skill-building content (courses, language learning, certifications, fitness programs) where you want to visualize ordered progress and gate content to encourage completion. It's especially effective for apps targeting habit formation, daily engagement, and lighter, game-ified learning experiences for consumer/B2C audiences.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for professional, reference, or non-linear content where users need to jump freely between topics (e.g., documentation, enterprise tools, or advanced courses where learners already know what they need). It can feel patronizing to expert audiences, and the gamification/energy-limiting mechanic may frustrate users who want unrestricted access or fast, searchable navigation rather than a guided path.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets learners (likely students or adult self-learners) who respond well to game-based motivation mechanics rather than traditional syllabus/list UIs. The psychological triggers at play include:

  • Progress & completion bias (Zeigarnik effect): seeing a trail of nodes with some checked off compels users to keep going to "finish the path."

  • Scarcity/loss aversion: the limited energy counter implies a cost to each lesson attempt, encouraging mindful, frequent engagement to avoid "wasting" turns.

  • Curiosity gap: faded/locked nodes below the fold hint at future content, pulling users forward.

  • Low cognitive friction: minimal copy and one clear CTA per interaction reduce the intimidation often tied to math education apps, appealing to anxious or casual learners.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Node-based path visualization turns a linear curriculum into a game-like journey, increasing motivation through visible progress and spatial metaphor.

  • Bottom sheet confirmation isolates the single next action (Start), preventing decision paralysis and keeping the main map free of persistent buttons.

  • Persistent energy/currency counter (2 ⚡) in the top bar sustains a resource-management loop that nudges daily engagement.

  • Completed vs. locked state differentiation (checkmark vs. faded/grayed nodes) gives immediate, glanceable feedback on progress and what's next.

  • Collapsible level header with chevron keeps orientation info visible without permanently consuming vertical space.

screens.name: Brilliant Course detail 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for structured, sequential educational or skill-building content (language learning, coding bootcamps, certification prep, fitness programs) where you want to visualize a long curriculum as an engaging, game-like journey. It's especially effective when you want to combine extrinsic motivation (streaks, levels, badges) with intrinsic curiosity-driven lesson naming.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavily gamified, linear-path pattern for professional/enterprise tools, reference documentation, or content that users need to access non-sequentially or urgently (e.g., troubleshooting guides, medical information) - the playful visual metaphor and locked-node gating would feel patronizing or create unnecessary friction. Also avoid for expert users who already know what they need and want direct search/access rather than a guided path.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed learners (students, career-switchers, lifelong learners) who need sustained motivation to complete long, potentially dry subject matter like algebra. The psychological levers at play include:

  • Progress visualization (Zeigarnik effect): Seeing a path with completed and locked nodes creates a compulsion to close the loop and keep moving forward.

  • Chunking: Breaking 45 lessons into "Levels" and discrete named nodes prevents overwhelm and leverages the sense of achievable, bite-sized goals.

  • Playful framing: Game-like iconography (coins, radar/satellite icon, colorful path) lowers the intimidation factor of a traditionally anxiety-inducing subject (algebra).

  • Scarcity of energy/lives (the "2 ⚡" counter): Classic engagement-loop mechanic that encourages daily return visits and controlled pacing.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual skill tree / path metaphor: Converts an abstract curriculum into a tangible, game-like journey with a clear sense of forward motion and spatial progress.

  • Layered information disclosure: The screen reveals unit-level context (title, description, stats) first, then lesson-level detail only on demand via the bottom sheet, reducing cognitive load.

  • Status-coded nodes: Checkmarks, color saturation, and iconography instantly communicate completed vs. locked vs. current lessons without needing text labels.

  • Low-friction re-engagement: The reset icon next to Practice subtly supports mastery-oriented learners who want to redo content, without competing visually with the primary CTA.

  • Dual engagement counters: The lightning/energy badge in the header keeps gamification currency visible at all times, reinforcing the app's reward loop even on a content-browsing screen.

screens.name: Brilliant - Giving Feedbacks - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for in-context feedback or bug-reporting forms embedded directly in a product experience, especially in educational, SaaS, or content-heavy apps where surfacing content errors quickly is valuable. It's ideal when:

  • You want users to report issues without navigating away from their current context (e.g., triggered by a shake gesture or a persistent feedback icon).
  • The form only needs 2-4 fields and benefits from a simple, single-screen structure instead of a multi-step wizard.
  • You need lightweight required-field cues (red dot) rather than heavy-handed error messaging before the user has even attempted submission.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the report needs significant context (e.g., screenshots, logs, device diagnostics) without a clear, labeled way to attach them (here the unlabeled "+" button is ambiguous and could confuse users about its function). Also avoid for flows requiring multiple categorized attachments or longer narrative input, where a single small text field is insufficient. If the feedback type requires branching logic (e.g., different follow-up fields depending on ticket type), this flat single-screen form would need to evolve into a multi-step form to avoid overwhelming or under-collecting information.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engaged, detail-oriented learners: the type of self-motivated STEM learner who notices when an explanation is "a bit vague" and cares enough to report it rather than simply bouncing. Brilliant's audience skews toward analytically-minded users who appreciate having a direct, low-ceremony channel to influence content quality.

Psychologically, the design leverages investment and ownership: by making it fast and easy to report a flaw, Brilliant turns a moment of frustration into a moment of contribution, which can increase loyalty and perceived product quality. The pre-populated email (already known from the user's account) reduces friction and signals that the system "already knows you," reinforcing trust and reducing abandonment at the final required field.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Low-friction exit points: both a back arrow and a circular close "X" are available at the top, respecting the user's time and preventing the feedback flow from feeling like a forced detour.
  • Required-field red dots: a lightweight, unobtrusive validation pattern that flags missing information without resorting to intrusive error banners until submission is attempted.
  • Dedicated vertical breathing room: the large empty space before the Email field visually separates "what happened" from "who you are," subtly structuring the mental model of the form into two logical groups.
  • Third-party trust badge: the "We run on Shake" mark builds credibility and signals that feedback is taken seriously and routed through dedicated tooling.

screens.name: Brilliant - Giving Feedbacks - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• In-app bug reporting or feedback forms where visual evidence dramatically improves the quality of support tickets.
  • Any attachment-picker use case needing to differentiate between multiple capture/source types (camera, gallery, files, screen).
  • Contexts where you want to preserve underlying screen context rather than fully navigating away, such as lightweight utility actions nested inside a longer form.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the attachment options exceed 5-6 items (a bottom sheet list becomes unwieldy and should shift to a grid or dedicated screen).
  • Not ideal for destructive or security-sensitive actions (e.g., sharing device location) without additional permission priming, since this list mixes casual item like "Pick from gallery" with more sensitive "Browse other locations" without differentiated weight.
  • Should be avoided on flows requiring strict user focus, where a dimmed-but-visible background could distract or create unintended context bleed between the ticket and the attachment flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets engaged, detail-oriented learners and power users of Brilliant who notice friction points (vague explanations, unclear visuals) and want to report them. Offering screenshot/screen-recording capture directly in-flow caters to users who think visually and want to show, not just tell, what's wrong, reducing the effort barrier that normally causes most users to abandon feedback forms before submission.

Psychologically, this leverages the effort-justification/investment principle: by making it trivially easy to attach rich evidence, Brilliant signals that it genuinely values granular feedback, which increases the likelihood of higher-quality, more actionable submissions from its most invested users.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed-but-visible background: The ticket form remains legible behind the sheet, maintaining context and reducing the cognitive cost of modal interruptions.
  • Color-coded icon system: Each attachment option gets a unique accent color, turning a plain text list into a fast, scannable menu without adding visual clutter.
  • Low-friction bug reporting: Native screen-grab and screen-record options are surfaced directly inside the feedback flow, removing the need for users to leave the app to attach evidence.
  • Dual exit paths: Both a back arrow and an explicit "X" close button give users flexible, low-risk ways to abandon or retreat from the flow.

screens.name: Brilliant - Giving Feedbacks - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Educational or training apps teaching quantitative, logical, or procedural concepts where a visual model can replace a wall of text.
  • Any linear micro-learning flow (language learning, coding, finance literacy) that benefits from one-question-per-screen pacing and instant feedback.
  • Gamified habit-building products wanting to reward correct actions with lightweight, non-intrusive XP/streak mechanics.
  • Products targeting global/multilingual audiences, since diagram-driven content minimizes localization burden.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Complex, multi-variable or open-ended problems that can't be reduced to a simple visual metaphor, forcing a diagram here could oversimplify or mislead.
  • Expert or advanced-level content where users want efficiency over hand-holding; the single-question-per-screen pacing would feel slow and condescending.
  • Contexts requiring robust review/backtracking (e.g., certification exams), since this app's "weak backward review" navigation would frustrate users needing to revisit prior questions.
  • Time-pressured assessment scenarios where XP/confetti celebrations would feel misplaced or distracting from serious evaluation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets self-directed adult learners and STEM-curious users (worldwide, language-agnostic since much of the content is mathematical notation and visuals) who want bite-sized, low-pressure practice rather than lecture-style video courses. The tactile, game-like mechanics (XP, streak icon, instant green checkmark) borrow proven psychological triggers from gamified habit apps: immediate positive reinforcement, small variable rewards (+15 XP), and visible incremental progress, all of which drive session completion and return visits.

The bar-diagram approach specifically appeals to visual/kinesthetic learners and those with math anxiety, since it reframes an intimidating equation as a concrete, colorful comparison task, lowering the barrier to engagement for non-expert audiences.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual proof before verbal explanation: The bar-model diagram lets users perceptually verify the algebra, embodying "move something before it explains anything."
  • Color-coded segment matching: Reusing purple/blue/orange across both bars creates an implicit visual legend that reduces the need for explanatory text.
  • Non-blocking feedback drawer: Correctness, XP reward, reporting, and deeper explanation ("Why?") are all bundled into one bottom sheet instead of separate modals, keeping flow momentum.
  • Granular progress bar: The segmented dash indicator at the top shows exact position within a short lesson, lowering perceived effort and anxiety about length.
  • Deferred depth via "Why?": Optional, low-commitment secondary action caters to varying learner needs without forcing extra steps on everyone.

screens.name: Brilliant - Giving Feedbacks - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse:
Adapt this pattern whenever you need frictionless, contextual bug/feedback reporting embedded directly inside a core product flow (especially in education, productivity, or gaming apps where interrupting the user's task to file a support ticket risks total drop-off). It's ideal for:

  • In-app bug reporting SDKs (support/QA tooling)
  • Any flow where automatic screen capture can replace manual description
  • Products with authenticated users where email/identity can be auto-filled
  • Low-density, card-based forms for lightweight data entry
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex, multi-faceted support requests that require conversational back-and-forth, nuanced triage, or attachments of multiple document types (a single static form with one screenshot slot will feel limiting). It's also unsuitable for anonymous/logged-out flows where there's no identity to auto-populate, as the email field would need to become a manual, friction-adding step. Finally, in apps with a more playful or highly branded voice, this utilitarian system-field tone may feel jarringly generic compared to the rest of the product's personality.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves engaged learners who hit a confusing or broken moment mid-lesson and want to flag it immediately rather than lose their place or motivation. Because Brilliant's core audience is self-directed, detail-oriented STEM learners, the design assumes they value efficiency and precision (hence the form favors structured fields (dropdown, description, auto-screenshot) over an open-ended chat-style support experience).

Psychologically, the auto-attached screenshot leverages the reduction of perceived effort: users are far more likely to complete a feedback loop when the system does the "showing" and they only need to do the "telling." The pre-filled email also exploits sunk-cost continuity: the user doesn't have to break flow to recall or type credentials, keeping the reporting action impulsive and immediate rather than deferred (and likely abandoned).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Automatic context capture: The exact in-lesson screen is auto-attached as a screenshot, eliminating the need for users to manually describe or recreate the bug.
  • Pre-filled email field: Removes friction by leveraging the logged-in user's identity, so the report can be routed and followed up on without extra typing.
  • Card-based field segmentation: Each form field is isolated in its own card, making the form feel scannable and low-density, consistent with the app's "one idea per screen" design philosophy.
  • Dual exit affordances: Both a back arrow (return to previous context) and a close "X" (abandon the flow entirely) are offered, respecting different user intents at the moment of quitting.
  • Required-field indicators: Red dots on Description and Email clearly communicate validation requirements before submission is attempted, pre-empting error states.

screens.name: H&M - Size guide - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for any e-commerce product configuration screen where a product has multiple visually distinguishable variants (color/pattern) plus a discrete, bounded set of secondary options (size, quantity). It is especially effective for:

  • Fashion, footwear, and accessories apps where variant appearance materially differs.
  • Retailers with omnichannel fulfillment (BOPIS - buy online, pick up in-store).
  • Products with a limited, well-known option set (standard sizing) that can be fully displayed without pagination or scrolling.
screens.whereNotToUse:
This pattern becomes less effective when:

  • Products have a very large number of variants (e.g., 20+ colors or custom sizes), where a full grid of photographic swatches would overwhelm the screen and require scrolling, negating the "scan at a glance" benefit.
  • Products require more complex configuration (e.g., bundles, engraving, multiple simultaneous attributes), where a single-screen form becomes cluttered and a multi-step or wizard flow is more appropriate.
  • Brands without physical retail presence, where the "Free pickup" option would be irrelevant and should be removed to avoid clutter.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets fashion-conscious shoppers, including existing H&M app users who already browsed a product and are now in high-intent, decision-making mode. The psychological design levers at play include:

  • Reduction of decision fatigue:
  • Loss-aversion/fit-anxiety mitigation: The adjacent Size Guide link addresses the #1 driver of apparel returns (incorrect sizing) directly at the point of hesitation.
  • Convenience-driven omnichannel behavior: The free in-store pickup option appeals to shoppers who want to avoid shipping costs/delays or wish to try before fully committing, which is common among budget-conscious young adults and families.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Photographic color swatches: Using cropped product photos instead of flat color chips lets shoppers preview texture, pattern, and fit nuances specific to fashion (e.g., pleat visibility) before switching variants.
  • Full-size-grid visibility: All 7 sizes (XXS. XXL) are shown simultaneously in a tappable grid, eliminating scrolling or dropdown friction at the highest-anxiety decision point in apparel shopping.
  • Contextual Size Guide placement: Positioning "SIZE GUIDE" directly above the CTA, right after size selection, intercepts doubt exactly when it occurs, reducing returns and cart abandonment.
  • Omnichannel pickup toggle: The "Free pickup at store" checkbox merges e-commerce and physical retail inventory, a strength unique to H&M's large store footprint.
  • High-contrast monochrome CTA: The pure black "ADD" button against white space follows strong visual hierarchy principles, impossible to miss amid otherwise neutral UI.

screens.name: H&M - Size guide - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever a product has variable, user-dependent fit (apparel, footwear, accessories, even furniture dimensions) and the catalog spans a wide size range that would otherwise require excessive scrolling. It's ideal for:

  • E-commerce PDP (Product Detail Page) size charts
  • Any global app needing to reconcile multiple measurement systems
  • Catalogs with sub-categories of fit (maternity, petite, plus, youth) that benefit from segmented tabs
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense tabular approach for products with simple, single-dimension sizing (e.g., one-size-fits-all accessories) where a full chart would add unnecessary complexity. It's also not appropriate for mobile contexts with very limited horizontal space if the table requires excessive horizontal scrolling (consider a simplified "find your size" quiz or recommendation algorithm instead for very small screens or less engaged users who may abandon a dense data table).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets online shoppers uncertain about fit: a universal pain point in fashion e-commerce where the inability to try on clothing physically drives purchase hesitation and high return rates. By front-loading detailed, categorized measurement data, H&M reduces the psychological risk associated with "will this fit me?" and builds purchase confidence before checkout.

The inclusion of Maternity and Petite tabs alongside Regular, plus "curvy" hip measurements, demonstrates an awareness of body diversity, appealing to a broader segment of the target audience (young adults, families) and reinforcing trust that H&M has sized thoughtfully for different body types, not just a generic standard.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Two-tier filtering (fit type + size range chips): Breaks an overwhelming size matrix into small, scannable chunks instead of one giant table.
  • Bottom sheet modal presentation: Keeps the user anchored to the product page context; dismissing the sheet returns them exactly where they left off.
  • Expandable "How to Measure" accordion: Keeps instructional content collapsed by default to prioritize the data table, but available on-demand for first-time or unsure users.
  • Dual-unit measurements (inch & cm): Serves a global audience without requiring a separate unit toggle.
  • Inclusive sizing (Maternity, Petite, Curvy hip measurements): Signals brand inclusivity and reduces return rates by helping diverse body types self-select correctly.

screens.name: H&M - Size guide - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern in any e-commerce or marketplace app selling physical apparel, footwear, or accessories where fit is subjective and return rates due to sizing errors are a business concern. It's ideal for:

  • Product detail pages with a "Size Guide" link near the size selector.
  • Categories with non-obvious measurement points (pants, bras, rings, hats).
  • Global apps needing to standardize understanding across different regional sizing norms.
  • Any flow where you need to educate users on a physical/manual process using diagrams rather than pure text.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, illustrated approach for:

  • Digital-only or simple products where sizing is binary or self-evident (e.g., one-size accessories, digital goods).
  • Contexts where screen real estate or user patience is extremely limited (this detailed modal adds a step before purchase and could feel excessive in a quick-buy/impulse checkout flow).
  • Products with universal/standardized sizing where users already have strong size intuition (e.g., basic unisex t-shirts across a single market), as the added friction of opening a modal may not be worth the marginal comprehension gain.
  • If illustrations aren't anatomically precise or lack sufficient contrast (e.g., poor color choices for colorblind users), this pattern can create false confidence and actually increase sizing errors.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern directly serves fashion-conscious online shoppers who cannot physically try on garments before purchase (a core friction point in apparel e-commerce). It is especially critical for first-time H&M shoppers unfamiliar with the brand's specific fit/sizing conventions, as well as international customers (H&M being a worldwide market) who may be used to different regional sizing standards.

Psychologically, this screen combats the fear of returns/wrong fit, which is one of the single largest drop-off points in fashion checkout flows. By proactively educating the user with clear, authoritative visuals, H&M builds purchase confidence and reduces anxiety, which in turn lowers cart abandonment and return rates.

The inclusion of "Maternity" and "Petite" size ranges signals an inclusive design consideration for specific body types/life-stages within the target demographic, widening the pattern's appeal to a broader segment of women shoppers.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-Mode Instruction: Combining a labeled anatomical illustration with numbered text creates redundancy that dramatically reduces measurement errors.
  • Numbered Visual Legend: Using matching circled numerals on both the diagram and the instructions creates an intuitive, language-agnostic mapping system (valuable for H&M's global/worldwide audience where visual cues transcend translation issues).
  • Front & Back Silhouettes: Showing both views clarifies measurements (like low hip) that wrap around the body and aren't fully visible from one angle alone.
  • Segmented Size Range Control: Surfacing Regular/Maternity/Petite options directly within the sizing modal ensures the educational content and the subsequent data table stay contextually relevant to the user's body type.
  • Collapsible Section: The minus/accordion icon lets returning or confident users skip the tutorial and go straight to the numeric chart, respecting varying levels of user expertise.

screens.name: H&M - Size guide - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Use this dense tabular approach for reference/utility information that requires precise cross-referencing, such as size charts, nutritional information, or technical specification sheets. It is ideal when users need to compare multiple variables (size tiers) against multiple metrics (waist, hip, leg) simultaneously.

The Bottom Sheet container is best used when this information is secondary/supplementary to a primary task (like viewing a product), allowing for quick consultation without full context loss.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this raw tabular format for first-time users who may need help determining what size to actually select; a purely numeric table requires the user to already know their own body measurements. For users who do not know their measurements, an interactive "Size Recommender" (input height/weight for an algorithmic suggestion) would be a more effective pattern than a static lookup table.

Additionally, avoid truncating important labels (such as "only for Curvy fit pr...") as seen in this design; if specific fit types have unique sizing criteria, ensure the full context fits within the viewport or utilize a tooltip/info icon to prevent ambiguity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves the anxious online shopper: a user who cannot physically try on the garment and needs to self-verify fit accuracy before purchasing to avoid the friction of a return. Given H&M's "worldwide" market, the inclusion of both inches and centimeters addresses the practical needs of American/UK customers alongside European and Asian customers simultaneously without requiring a settings toggle.

Psychologically, this screen aims to reduce purchase anxiety and pre-emptively solve for sizing friction, which is one of the primary deterrents to converting a browse into a sale in fashion e-commerce. By providing granular, trustworthy data (down to the half-inch), H&M builds confidence that the "Add to Bag" action will result in a correctly fitting item.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual Unit System: Provides both Imperial (inches) and Metric (cm) measurements for every category (Waist, Hip, Leg), removing geographic/regional barriers to understanding sizing for a global customer base.
  • Fit-Specific Rows: The specific inclusion of "Low hip curvy" rows demonstrates an attempt to cater to different body fit profiles (standard vs. curvy) within a single comprehensive chart rather than requiring separate screens.
  • Non-Modal Blocking (Bottom Sheet): Utilizing a draggable bottom sheet rather than a full-screen takeover maintains context, allowing users to quickly reference and dismiss the sizing info without a jarring navigation transition away from the product they are browsing.

screens.name: Figma - Adding stamps - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this contextual, anchored tool-picker pattern when:

  • An app has many creation tools/object types that can't all fit in a persistent toolbar, especially on small touch screens.

  • You want to preserve spatial context (canvas, document, board) while letting users pick an action, rather than navigating away.

  • Your users range from casual/first-time to power users, and you want a single surface that serves both via inline shortcut hints.

  • Progressive disclosure of advanced features ("much, much more") is needed to keep the primary list lightweight and non-intimidating.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach when:

  • The tool/action list is very short (2-3 items): a popover with descriptions would be overkill; a simple icon row suffices.

  • Users are predominantly mobile-only with no keyboard access, surfacing keyboard shortcuts could add visual clutter with no payoff.

  • The underlying canvas content is not relevant to the decision being made (e.g., account settings, checkout flows) where a full-screen modal or dedicated page better isolates focus.

  • Screen real estate is extremely constrained (very small phones), where a dense popover list combined with a visible canvas could feel cramped or require excessive scrolling.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, product teams, and cross-functional collaborators (PMs, engineers, workshop facilitators) using FigJam on mobile/tablet to brainstorm or contribute asynchronously. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Recognition over recall: Icons paired with labels and descriptions reduce the memory burden of learning a new tool's iconography.

  • Progressive disclosure: Only a curated set of common tools (Table, Section, Connector, Text, Sticky note, Stamp) are shown by default, with "Much, much more" deferring advanced/rare tools to avoid overwhelming casual or first-time users.

  • Competence & mastery cues: Displaying keyboard shortcuts signals to prosumers that the app rewards efficiency and scales from casual touch use to expert workflows, supporting user retention as skill grows.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual popover anchored to its trigger: The pointer/tail on the menu visually ties it back to the overflow button, maintaining spatial continuity and reducing cognitive load.

  • Icon + title + microcopy + shortcut pattern: A highly scannable, repeatable row template that balances discoverability (for new users reading descriptions) with efficiency (for power users scanning shortcuts).

  • Non-blocking overlay over live canvas: Keeps the user oriented in their document; the board content (sticky notes already on canvas) stays visible and dimmed rather than being hidden behind a full modal.

  • Persistent presence & sync indicators: Collaborator avatars and cloud-sync icon in the top bar reinforce FigJam's real-time multiplayer value proposition at all times, even mid-task.

screens.name: Figma - Adding stamps - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use a radial/pie selection menu when:

  • You need to present 5: 8 mutually exclusive quick-action options (reactions, tools, shortcuts) on a touch interface where speed and large hit targets matter.

  • The interaction is ephemeral and low-commitment (a reaction, a quick tag, a tool switch) rather than a complex configuration task.

  • You want to preserve context by overlaying the picker on live content instead of navigating to a new screen or full-screen modal.

  • Collaborative or real-time tools where social, expressive feedback (reactions, emotes) drives engagement and lightweight communication.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid radial menus when:

  • The option set exceeds ~8 items, as wedge targets become too thin and error-prone.

  • Users need to compare or read detailed labels: radial layouts favor icons/emoji over text, so they fail for content requiring explanation.

  • The action is destructive, high-stakes, or requires confirmation (radial pickers' speed and ambiguity (exact gesture endpoint) make them unsuitable for anything irreversible).

  • Targeting desktop-first users without touch input, where hover-based linear toolbars are more precise and discoverable.

  • Accessibility is a priority without additional work (circular layouts and gesture-based release are harder to make screen-reader and switch-control friendly than standard lists).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers, PMs, and cross-functional teams collaborating synchronously or asynchronously on a FigJam board from mobile devices (often during a workshop, brainstorm, or stand-up where quick, low-effort feedback (a 👍, 🔥, or 😂) communicates sentiment faster than typed comments).

Psychologically, the radial picker leverages Fitts's Law (larger, closer targets are faster and easier to hit) and reduces cognitive load by replacing a linear list (which would require scanning and precise vertical taps) with a spatial, gesture-friendly arrangement that can be operated with a single thumb swipe-and-release gesture, similar to familiar patterns from Slack and iMessage tapback menus. The emoji-only vocabulary also taps into the social proof and lightweight engagement principle: reacting takes less effort than commenting, which increases participation rates in collaborative sessions.
screens.keyHighlights:
Radial (pie) menu for reactions: Converts a desktop hover-driven stamp picker into a touch-optimized circular layout with large, evenly spaced hit targets (ideal for thumb reach and reducing mis-taps on small screens).

Non-modal overlay on live canvas: The picker floats above real board content rather than taking over the screen, preserving spatial context and signaling that reacting is a lightweight, non-committal action.

Central preview affordance: The purple semi-circle with a smiley/cursor glyph in the center acts as a live preview of the active stamp state, giving immediate visual feedback before commitment.

Persistent toolbar during picker use: Core tools (cursor, eraser, shape, stamp) remain accessible at the bottom, maintaining flow and avoiding a jarring context switch.

Collaborative presence cues: Overlapping avatar bubbles in the top bar reinforce the multiplayer, real-time nature of the session even while a secondary interaction (reacting) is in progress.

screens.name: Figma - Adding stamps - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Live collaboration tools (whiteboards, docs, video calls) needing fast, low-friction feedback without breaking flow.

  • Touch-first interfaces where several mutually exclusive or quick-fire options must be reachable from a single thumb position.

  • Any feature benefiting from gamified, icon-driven interaction (reactions, mood/rating pickers, tool selection in creative apps).

  • Scenarios where preserving underlying context (canvas, document, video) during selection is important.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid radial menus when there are more than ~8 options (recognition and tap accuracy degrade quickly as segments get smaller).

  • Not suitable for options requiring explanation or nuanced text labels, since the format depends on instantly recognizable icons.

  • Poor fit for accessibility-critical flows (screen reader users, motor-impaired users) unless a linear/list fallback is also provided.

  • Avoid on desktop-first, mouse-precision workflows where a simple dropdown or toolbar is faster and more familiar.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets designers, PMs, and cross-functional teammates collaborating live in FigJam, often during workshops, retros, or brainstorms where quick, non-verbal feedback (reactions/stamps) keeps momentum without interrupting a facilitator or typing comments. The radial layout specifically serves mobile/tablet attendees joining a session from a phone, where thumb reach and one-handed operation are primary constraints.

Psychologically, it leverages recognition over recall (icons instead of menus of words) and Fitts's Law (equal, short distances to all targets) to make reacting feel instantaneous and almost game-like, encouraging more frequent, spontaneous engagement, mirroring the dopamine-driven interaction patterns of social apps (quick reactions like Slack/Instagram) but repurposed for productivity collaboration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Radial marking menu for reactions (all options sit on a circle equidistant from the thumb's resting point, reducing reach and mis-taps on mobile).

  • Center "stamp" icon doubles as a toggle/default, visually split blue/white to show an active/hover state before the user commits to an outer option.

  • Canvas remains visible and dimmed behind the menu, preserving spatial context of where the reaction will be placed.

  • Consistent chrome (top avatars/share, bottom tool switcher) stays present, so the reaction picker feels like a layered overlay rather than a separate screen/modal.

  • Icon-only vocabulary (no labels) speeds up recognition for a global, repeat-use audience already fluent in emoji semantics.

screens.name: Figma - Adding stamps - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for canvas-based, spatial, or whiteboard-style products (diagramming, mind-mapping, design tools) especially when adapting a dense desktop toolset for mobile. It's ideal when:

  • Real-time multiplayer editing requires visible presence indicators.

  • Autosave removes the need for explicit save actions and users need lightweight, non-blocking confirmation.

  • The primary content is non-linear/spatial and benefits from direct manipulation rather than scrolling lists.

  • Tool options are numerous but can be prioritized, with secondary tools tucked behind a "more" affordance.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for linear, form-based, or content-consumption apps where users expect standard navigation (tab bars, lists) rather than a freeform canvas. Icon-only toolbars without labels can hurt discoverability for first-time or infrequent users, so this works best for tools where users already understand the underlying metaphor (e.g., whiteboarding) or where onboarding/tooltips exist elsewhere. Overlapping avatar presence indicators should be skipped in single-user or non-collaborative contexts, as they add visual noise without functional benefit.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets designers, product teams, and cross-functional collaborators using FigJam on mobile to review, annotate, or lightly contribute to a brainstorm/whiteboard session while away from their desktop. The psychological drivers at play include reduced cognitive load (icon-only toolbar, minimal chrome) so users can focus on content rather than UI, and social presence cues (avatars) that trigger accountability and engagement in shared work. The autosave toast taps into the need for control and certainty: users mid-collaboration want instant confidence that their edits (or others') are persisted without manual intervention.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Autosave toast as implicit trust-builder: The "Changes saved" toast removes any anxiety about losing work on a collaborative canvas, replacing manual save actions with passive confirmation.

  • Presence avatars in the header: Overlapping colored initials avatars immediately communicate who else is active on the board, reinforcing FigJam's real-time collaborative identity even before any content loads.

  • Condensed, adaptive toolbar: A desktop-grade toolset is distilled into a single scrollable/expandable row with a chevron for "more," balancing power and simplicity for touch input.

  • Active tool state highlighting: The purple-filled stamp/sticker icon clearly shows which tool is currently selected, preventing ambiguity during direct manipulation.

  • Infinite dotted canvas: Reinforces the mental model of a boundless creative whiteboard, encouraging free-form placement of ideas.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 4
screens.whereToUse: Use this grouped, search-first pattern when an app serves multiple distinct destination types (people, businesses, actions) through a single entry point, especially in fintech, food delivery, or super-app contexts where users may not remember the exact navigation path to a transaction. It's ideal when speed and unambiguous categorization matter more than rich visual merchandising.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal, text-first layout when results benefit from richer visual differentiation (e.g., product search with images, ratings, or price comparison), where flat list rows would force users to read every line to differentiate options. It's also not ideal if the app has many more than two or three category types, as stacked section headers would push relevant results below the fold and increase scrolling before the keyboard is dismissed.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday Google Pay users who already have an intent in mind (paying a friend, splitting a bill, or ordering food) and want the fastest path from typing to completing that transaction. By surfacing both people and merchants in one search box, Google Pay reduces the "where do I even start" friction common in finance apps, leaning on the psychological principle of recognition over recall: users don't need to remember which tab holds "send money" vs "order food," they just search.

The trust-first, low-decoration UI also caters to a broad, non-technical demographic who need confidence that they are searching correctly before money changes hands (ambiguity here has real financial stakes, so the design deliberately avoids visual noise that could cause misclicks).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented result grouping: Splitting results into "Businesses" vs "Contacts" removes ambiguity about what kind of payment action will follow.

  • Query pre-selection: The typed term "lao" appears highlighted in the search field, inviting quick refinement without extra taps to select-all.

  • Single dominant CTA per row: Only one blue actionable link per result ("Order food") avoids decision paralysis and mirrors Android/iOS system search conventions.

  • Consistent avatar language: Circular avatars (icon for businesses, colored initials for contacts) create fast visual scannability and reduce reliance on reading full text.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when embedding third-party merchant catalogs or marketplace listings inside a broader utility app (payments, maps, super-apps). It's ideal when you need to communicate business logistics (hours, fulfillment type, distance) upfront before a purchase decision, and when enabling fast, low-friction cart building for simple, low-consideration purchases like food items.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, quick-add list pattern for complex products requiring configuration (size, customization, add-ons) - a single tap "+" hides necessary decision points and can cause cart errors. Also avoid raw, unedited multilingual/truncated product names in consumer-facing marketplaces where brand polish and clarity are critical; truncated bilingual titles ("Che Pie..") can confuse users unfamiliar with the source language. Not suitable for high-consideration purchases needing rich product detail pages.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers already inside the Google Pay ecosystem who want to order food or goods from local merchants without downloading a separate delivery app. It's particularly suited to markets like Singapore/Southeast Asia (implied by the SGD pricing and bilingual Chinese/English menu) where Google Pay integrates local hawker/cafe ordering as a super-app style feature.

Psychologically, it leverages reduced context-switching: users trust Google Pay for payments already, so transacting with an unfamiliar small merchant feels safer when wrapped in a familiar, trusted UI shell. The star rating and distance serve as quick social-proof and convenience cues to reduce decision anxiety about an unfamiliar local business.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fulfillment chips overlaid on hero image: "Pick-Up Only" and "Order on G Pay" badges are placed directly on the photo so users instantly understand constraints before scrolling, reducing wasted browsing effort.

  • One-tap quick-add (+) buttons: Every menu row has an inline circular add button, allowing rapid cart-building without navigating to a product detail page (a low-friction pattern borrowed from top food-delivery apps).

  • Compact trust/logistics line: Address, hours, price tier, star rating, and distance are condensed into one line with bullet separators, giving maximum information density with minimal vertical space.

  • Modal-style navigation (X to close): Using a close icon instead of a back arrow signals this merchant page is a contextual overlay within Google Pay, not a permanent destination, keeping the core app's navigation model intact.

  • Embedded search icon: A magnifying glass beside the address allows users to jump directly to a specific menu item in a potentially long catalog rather than scrolling.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for any third-party integration/connected-account management screen: OAuth app permissions, connected loyalty programs, linked devices, or API integrations. It's ideal when you need to give users a single, clear place to review and revoke a specific entity's access without forcing them through multi-step settings menus.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal single-action layout when there are many distinct permission scopes that need individual toggles (e.g., location, contacts, payment history) - cramming multiple switches into this sparse layout would require a denser list UI instead. Also avoid decorative illustrations like this in enterprise/B2B security contexts where users expect a more clinical, information-dense audit log rather than playful branding.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves privacy-conscious users auditing which third parties (restaurants, loyalty programs, merchants) have access to their Google Pay data or payment credentials. The psychological driver is control and reassurance: by isolating this merchant's access into its own dedicated screen with a clear "kill switch," Google Pay reduces anxiety around data sharing and builds long-term trust in the platform's transparency, which is critical for a financial utility app where users must feel safe granting access to numerous vendors.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Decorative but restrained hero art: The dotted circular halo around the merchant icon draws the eye without adding functional clutter, giving an otherwise dry permissions screen personality.

  • Progressive disclosure via minimal rows: Only exposing "Notifications" and "Remove all access" avoids overwhelming users with granular permission toggles, deferring complexity to a nested screen.

  • Color-coded destructive action: Red text with no icon or button chrome keeps "Remove all access" discoverable but not accidentally tappable, following platform conventions for irreversible actions.

  • Contextual overflow menu: The "..." icon in the top right likely houses secondary/rare actions (e.g., report, help), keeping the primary view uncluttered.

screens.name: Google Pay Searching & Finding 7
screens.whereToUse:
Use this "numbered steps + illustration + proof + single CTA" pattern when introducing a discrete, self-contained feature inside a larger utility app (especially features involving a new interaction paradigm (like QR scanning) that users haven't encountered elsewhere in the product). It's ideal for:

  • In-app feature announcements or contextual "Learn More" deep links

  • Fintech/payments apps rolling out new merchant integrations

  • Any flow where trust and correct sequencing matter more than speed
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy explainer pattern for features that are already intuitive or that returning users will see repeatedly (it adds friction and feels condescending on repeat visits). It's also inappropriate for time-sensitive flows where the user just needs to complete a task quickly (e.g., an already-scanned QR code should jump straight to the menu/payment, not repeat the 3-step explainer). Additionally, this static, non-personalized version should be replaced with a dismissible or "don't show again" variant once the user has completed the flow once, to respect experienced users' time.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users who are already comfortable with Google Pay for basic P2P or online payments but have not yet used its in-restaurant/dine-in capabilities (likely surfaced via an "Explore" tab, a promotional banner, or contextual discovery near a participating merchant). The psychological trigger at play is uncertainty reduction: dining out involves social visibility (paying in front of a server or companions), so users need confidence the process won't fail or embarrass them.

The numbered walkthrough leverages the Zeigarnik effect and chunking principles from cognitive psychology, breaking an unfamiliar task into three sequential, visually distinct steps makes it feel achievable and memorable. The restaurant carousel taps into social proof, reassuring users that real, known brands (pizzerias, cafes) already support this, which reduces the risk perception of trying something new.

results.query: Stock market price analysis for Tesla TSLA earnings call

screens.name: CRED Logging & Tracking 26
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a critical, potentially urgent action (like an emergency call, delivery pickup, or service dispatch) depends on confirming context-specific data (vehicle, address, appointment) beforehand. It's ideal for multi-asset accounts (e.g., fleet or family vehicle management) where the wrong selection could cause real-world consequences. Also apply the just-in-time permission explanation pattern whenever requesting sensitive data (location, camera, contacts) immediately before a native OS permission dialog.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this extra confirmation step for low-stakes or single-asset contexts where there's no ambiguity (e.g., an account with only one registered vehicle) - it would introduce unnecessary friction. In true emergencies (e.g., a panic/SOS button), inserting a confirmation sheet before connecting help could be dangerous; the safer approach there is a smart default with an easy post-connection edit option instead of a pre-call gate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets vehicle owners (likely from an automotive brand's owner app, e.g., Hyundai) who are in a roadside emergency or need premium concierge support. The design leverages the psychological principle of reducing cognitive load under stress: emergencies impair decision-making, so the UI minimizes choices to one core confirmation plus one CTA. The reassurance copy exploits the trust-building "explain-before-ask" pattern, which is proven to increase permission-grant rates by addressing the "why" before the system-level "allow/deny" prompt appears.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual confirmation gate: Forces explicit vehicle confirmation before connecting to concierge, preventing misrouted assistance for multi-vehicle account holders.

  • Realistic vehicle representation: Using a license-plate UI element plus actual car photo builds trust and reduces selection ambiguity versus a plain text dropdown.

  • Just-in-time permission framing: Explains location usage contextually right before the action that requires it, rather than via a generic system prompt, increasing consent comprehension and reducing anxiety.

  • Layered modal architecture: A bottom sheet over a dimmed full-screen concierge page maintains context continuity while narrowing focus to one decision.

  • Single dominant CTA: The full-width black "Call now" button eliminates any ambiguity about the next step during a potentially stressful roadside situation.

screens.name: CRED Logging & Tracking 27
screens.whereToUse:
• Emergency, SOS, or roadside-assistance entry points within automotive, insurance, or fleet-management apps.

  • Any workflow where the user is likely to be stressed, distracted, or in a hurry (medical apps, safety apps, travel disruption flows).

  • Screens that need to build instant trust before asking the user to make a high-stakes call or commitment (e.g., calling a hotline, submitting a claim).
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this soft, illustrative tone for truly life-threatening emergencies (e.g., a 911/112 dialer) where speed and stark clarity outrank brand warmth (extra scrolling or narrative copy could cost critical seconds).

  • Not suitable for data-heavy or B2B admin contexts where users need dense information and multiple parallel actions rather than a single funneled CTA.

  • Should not be used if the service actually has slow response times or limited coverage, overpromising trust signals ("24x7", "20k+ garages") without operational backing will damage brand credibility during an already vulnerable moment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets vehicle owners in a stressful, time-sensitive situation: likely stranded on the roadside, dealing with a breakdown, flat tire, accident, or medical emergency involving their vehicle. The psychology at play is stress-reduction design: users in this state have narrowed attention spans and reduced patience, so the screen minimizes text density, uses reassuring tone, and surfaces one dominant action.

The "dedicated ambulance service" bullet suggests this is built for a premium or EV automotive brand (the car silhouette resembles a modern crossover/EV) targeting customers who expect white-glove, concierge-level support as part of their ownership experience (likely a differentiator versus mass-market roadside assistance apps).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Calming visual metaphor: A stylized, monochrome car-with-warning-sign illustration reduces panic compared to realistic crash/breakdown photography.

  • Single point of color: The red warning triangle is the only saturated color on the screen, creating a focal point without inducing alarm-fatigue.

  • Concierge framing: Reframing roadside assistance as a "concierge" service elevates trust and brand perception during a vulnerable user moment.

  • Credibility bullets with icons: Quantified trust signals (24x7, 20k+ garages) paired with whimsical hand-drawn icons balance seriousness with approachability.

  • High-contrast sticky CTA: The stark white "Call for assistance" button against a black background ensures the primary action is found in under a second, critical for stressed users.

  • Progressive disclosure: The screen teases "here are some of the services you can access" before presumably scrolling to a detailed list, preventing cognitive overload upfront.

screens.name: CRED Logging & Tracking 28
screens.whereToUse:
• Emergency or on-demand service apps (roadside assistance, home repair, medical dispatch) where users need to quickly understand service scope before requesting help.

  • Screens preceding a high-commitment action (call, paid request) that benefit from trust-building content like pricing transparency.

  • Onboarding or informational carousels explaining app capabilities to new users.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for truly time-critical emergencies (e.g., a 911/SOS screen) where any scrolling or reading delays could be harmful (those need an immediate single action, not a service list).

  • Not suitable for services with highly variable or unpredictable pricing, where an upfront "no guessing" promise could set false expectations and erode trust if broken.

  • Dark theme may reduce readability in bright outdoor sunlight, a common context for actual roadside breakdowns (should be tested against high-glare conditions).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets drivers experiencing or anticipating a vehicle emergency (breakdown, flat tyre, lockout, accident) who need immediate reassurance that help is comprehensive, fast, and financially predictable. The psychological trigger at play is anxiety reduction: stranded users fear both the mechanical problem and the unknown cost/reliability of help, so the screen front-loads scope-of-service clarity and pricing transparency to lower perceived risk before asking for a commitment (the call). The "concierge" framing and premium visual design also target users who expect app-based services (like ride-hailing or delivery) to extend the same on-demand convenience to automotive emergencies.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-led scannability: Each service uses a distinct, whimsical monochrome icon, allowing users to recognize the service type even faster than reading text (vital during stressful roadside situations).

  • Proactive price transparency card: Preemptively answers the "how much will this cost me" objection with a visually distinct card and illustration, reducing hesitation before the user taps the CTA.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: "Call for assistance" with an arrow icon is the only actionable element, eliminating decision paralysis in an emergency context.

  • Dark theme for calm urgency: The near-black palette avoids alarming red/orange emergency tones, instead projecting a controlled, premium "concierge" feel rather than panic.

screens.name: CRED Logging & Tracking 29
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for support-oriented conversational entry points in regulated or emotionally sensitive industries (insurance, banking, healthcare, travel disruption) where users need triage before reaching a human agent or deeper self-service flow. It's ideal when the range of user intents is well-known and finite, allowing quick-reply buttons to cover the majority of cases.

Also effective for first-touch bot interactions where setting scope expectations early prevents user frustration and abandonment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when user needs are highly varied, nuanced, or require detailed free-text description (e.g., complex complaint narratives) - forcing users into rigid quick-reply categories can feel dismissive or inadequate. Also avoid if the backend cannot handle open dialogue gracefully after the initial quick-replies, as users will hit a wall quickly.

Not suitable for flows where speed-to-human-agent is critical (e.g., emergency roadside assistance) - an extra chatbot layer before human contact adds friction and can increase user anxiety rather than reduce it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets insurance policyholders, likely following a stressful event (accident, theft, or damage) who need fast, low-friction access to claims support. Users in this state are often anxious, time-pressed, or unfamiliar with claims jargon and processes.

The design leverages the psychological principle of reduced choice paralysis by offering a small, curated set of next-step options rather than an open-ended chat box, which is especially valuable for stressed users who may not know how to articulate their exact need. The concierge framing and friendly avatar also invoke anthropomorphism and trust-building, making users more comfortable disclosing claim details to what is essentially an automated flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Personalization via name insertion in the greeting message immediately establishes a 1:1 relationship rather than generic bot messaging.

  • Guided quick-replies instead of open text input dramatically increases conversation completion rates and reduces the risk of chatbot misunderstanding during an emotionally sensitive claims process.

  • Scope-setting message upfront manages expectations about what the assistant is capable of, preventing dead-end queries.

  • High-contrast white response bubble for the bot's actual question visually separates "context" from "the actual ask," subtly directing attention flow.

  • Easy escape hatch (X button) respects user autonomy, critical in support flows where users may want to switch to human support or exit anxiety-inducing claim topics.

screens.name: CRED Logging & Tracking 30
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when prompting users to update or confirm time-sensitive, compliance-related, or renewal-based data (insurance, licenses, subscriptions, certifications) where forgetting has real-world consequences. It's ideal for:

  • Document/renewal management apps (vehicle, legal, healthcare, memberships)

  • Any flow requiring a single date input with clear consequence framing

  • Contextual triggers surfaced after detecting an expired or soon-to-expire status
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy benefit-explanation approach for high-frequency, low-stakes updates where users already understand the value (the extra copy would add unnecessary friction). Also avoid the casual, playful tone if the app serves a context requiring strict formality (e.g., government/legal filing tools) where regulatory precision and neutral tone are expected. Additionally, a scroll-wheel date picker becomes less ideal if the date range is extremely large (e.g., birthdates decades back) without smart defaults, as scrolling becomes tedious.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday vehicle owners (likely in India, given "PUC" - Pollution Under Control certificate terminology) who need to track multiple recurring vehicle documents (insurance, PUC, registration) and are prone to forgetting renewal dates due to the low frequency and low salience of these tasks.

Psychologically, the design leverages:

  • Loss aversion: "avoid being fined" taps into fear of financial penalty more effectively than a neutral instruction would.

  • Reduced friction/reciprocity: By making the update process trivially easy (pre-filled picker, one button), the app increases the likelihood users will actually complete the compliance task rather than procrastinate.

  • Reassurance/control: Framing the reminder system as something that will "never miss" builds trust that the app is a reliable delegate for administrative burden, encouraging habitual return to the app for all vehicle-document tracking (a retention/engagement driver for a vehicle management app).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual re-engagement trigger: The prompt is likely surfaced proactively (e.g., after the app detects the PUC date is near/past expiry) rather than buried in settings, increasing the odds of compliance.

  • Benefit-first micro-copy: Instead of a dry "Update PUC Expiry Date" form label, the screen sells the user on *why* this 10-second action matters using loss-aversion (penalty) and convenience (reminders) framing.

  • Native-feel date wheel picker: Provides fast, familiar, error-resistant date entry versus typing or navigating a full calendar.

  • Dimmed background continuity: Preserves spatial context of which vehicle/document is being edited without a jarring full-screen takeover.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: "Update →" is the only actionable button, eliminating decision paralysis.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 27
screens.whereToUse:
• Account status screens where a user has been placed in a restricted, pending, or waitlisted state (KYC holds, fraud review, capacity-limited betas).

  • Global settings/account action menus that need to remain accessible regardless of the user's account state.

  • Any scenario requiring you to pair a serious/negative status message with clear, low-friction recovery actions.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid vague waitlist messaging when regulatory or legal requirements mandate specific, detailed reasons for account restriction (e.g., certain financial regulations require explicit adverse action notices).
