  • Don't bury critical status information behind a secondary sheet if the user urgently needs to understand consequences (e.g., frozen funds) - this could increase anxiety or support ticket volume from confusion.

  • Avoid stacking multiple modal sheets in contexts where users may lose track of navigational depth or exit paths.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of a fintech/neobank-style app who have been flagged by an automated risk or KYC/AML engine. The design assumes users may be anxious, confused, or frustrated by being denied full access, so the psychology at play is trust preservation and controlled transparency: enough information is given to explain the hold without exposing internal fraud logic that bad actors could exploit.

By surfacing "change details" and "support" prominently at the top of the actions list, the design nudges users toward self-remediation first (cheaper for the business) before escalating to human support, reflecting a deflection-first support strategy common in scaled fintech products.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Empathetic reframing of a negative outcome: "good things are worth the wait" turns a compliance hold into a narrative of patience rather than rejection, reducing user frustration and churn risk.

  • Actionable recovery paths surfaced immediately: Rather than leaving the user stuck on a waitlist screen, the app immediately offers a menu of self-service actions (especially "change details"), empowering users to potentially resolve the flagged issue themselves.

  • Stacked/nested bottom sheets: The presence of a drag handle at both the top of the visible sheet and bottom of the screen suggests a layered sheet system, allowing users to peel back context without losing their place.

  • Consistent iconography and typographic hierarchy: Uniform icon style, spacing, and chevron affordances make the settings-like list highly scannable and reduce cognitive load during a stressful moment.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 28
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing a new, potentially unexpected or auxiliary feature within an existing trusted app, especially one that requires upcoming data-access permissions. It's ideal for:

  • Feature onboarding within a super-app (e.g., adding a new module like insurance, vehicle, or health tracking).

  • Priming users before requesting sensitive permissions (location, contacts, financial data) by first explaining the "why" visually before the "how."

  • Any onboarding flow where you want to set expectations for flow length via a page control while keeping cognitive load extremely low.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy illustration-led, multi-step onboarding approach for:

  • Time-sensitive or transactional flows where users want to complete a task immediately (e.g., checkout, urgent alerts) - the extra steps add unnecessary friction.

  • Return users who have already seen the value prop; repeating this flow on every session risks annoyance and should be gated to first-time feature discovery only.

  • Contexts where the permission being requested is highly sensitive (e.g., biometric or precise location) and requires an explicit, legally robust consent screen rather than soft inline disclosure text.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets CRED's core demographic: affluent, credit-conscious vehicle owners in India who already trust CRED with financial data and are being upsold into an adjacent utility (vehicle/traffic-challan tracking). The design leverages the trust transfer psychological principle (since users already trust CRED for bill payments and credit scores, extending that trust to fetch vehicle/insurance data feels like a natural, low-risk extension).

The illustration and minimal copy reduce cognitive load for a feature that could otherwise seem like a scope-creep ("why does my credit card app need my car's traffic challans?"), by focusing the value proposition on convenience and consolidation.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Custom isometric illustration: A bespoke 3D-style rendering of a car in a garage bay (complete with a traffic cone and floor markings) immediately communicates the feature's domain without requiring any copy (a strong visual-first onboarding technique).

  • Minimal, single-CTA bottom bar: Only one clear action ("Continue") is presented, eliminating decision fatigue and funneling the user toward the next onboarding step.

  • Inline permission disclosure below the CTA: Rather than a separate interruptive permission dialog, consent language is embedded directly beneath the button, reducing friction while maintaining transparency.

  • Page control dots: Sets clear expectations of onboarding length (3 steps), reducing perceived time investment.

  • Brand-consistent serif/mono type pairing: Elevates a mundane utility feature (traffic challans, vehicle spends) into a premium-feeling experience through typography alone.

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 29
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern when onboarding into a new feature vertical within an existing trusted app, where you need to justify an upcoming data or permission request with an emotional value preview first.

  • Ideal for reward/gamification-driven products where framing a utilitarian action (data sync, KYC, permissions) as an achievement or unlock increases completion rates.

  • Effective for premium/lifestyle brands wanting to maintain tonal consistency across a multi-screen onboarding carousel using minimal chrome and strong typographic hierarchy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavily stylized, abstract-icon approach for utility, healthcare, or B2B/enterprise apps where users need concrete, literal information immediately rather than an emotionally-framed teaser.

  • Not suitable when regulatory context requires explicit, itemized consent (e.g., GDPR-sensitive data) rather than a single bundled "permit CRED to fetch" statement (this could expose legal risk if used for highly sensitive data categories).

  • Risky for first-time/unfamiliar users unfamiliar with the brand's voice, as overly cute or identity-flattering copy ("obsessed") can feel presumptuous or gimmicky rather than trustworthy in cold-start scenarios.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets CRED's existing user base: financially disciplined, credit-card-paying professionals (who are now being cross-sold into a "Garage" or vehicle-management vertical). The messaging assumes a specific psychographic: car enthusiasts or owners who take pride in vehicle maintenance and see it as an extension of personal identity/status, not just a chore.

Psychological triggers at play include identity affirmation (labeling the user as someone who loves their machine flatters and validates them), curiosity/anticipation (abstract reward icons without full labels invite exploration), and foot-in-the-door commitment (a soft, exciting framing makes the subsequent data-permission request feel like a natural continuation rather than an intrusive ask).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotional reframing of a data-permission step: Instead of a dry "Allow access to vehicle data" screen, CRED reframes the ask as a reward-unlocking moment tied to identity ("obsessed with your vehicle"), reducing permission fatigue and resistance.

  • Isometric reward-preview illustration: The four-tile 3D icon cluster visually previews the categories of value (protection, fuel, documents, achievements) the user will get, building anticipation before the ask.

  • Front-loaded transparency: Placing the data-permission disclaimer directly below the CTA (in plain, non-legalese language) builds trust and preempts anxiety about "what happens when I tap Continue."

  • Minimal chrome, single decision point: No competing navigation, no skip button, no secondary CTA (the screen architecture forces a single binary decision (back or continue), reducing cognitive load).

screens.name: CRED Onboarding 30
screens.whereToUse:
• Pre-permission priming screens where you need to justify a data-access request (contacts, location, financial data) with an emotional or aspirational hook before the native OS permission dialog appears.

  • Multi-step onboarding flows for niche/passion-driven verticals (auto, fitness, finance) where framing the user as part of an "insider" group increases willingness to share data.

  • Premium/luxury branded apps that want onboarding to feel like an editorial narrative rather than a transactional form.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Utility or enterprise apps where users expect fast, no-nonsense onboarding; excessive brand narrative before a permission ask can feel like unnecessary friction.

  • Contexts where regulatory requirements demand prominent, high-contrast consent language (e.g., GDPR-sensitive flows) - burying disclosure in low-contrast grey text may not meet compliance/legibility standards.

  • Low-trust or first-time-user flows where flattery-based framing ("designed for the obsessive") could feel presumptuous before the user has formed any relationship with the brand.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets CRED's core demographic: affluent, status-conscious, detail-oriented individuals (often car/bike enthusiasts) who take pride in asset ownership and organization. The psychological trigger is identity affirmation ("the obsessive") combined with a sense of control and curation, positioning vehicle tracking as a premium lifestyle feature akin to a garage concierge rather than an insurance utility. This appeals to users who already associate CRED with exclusivity and rewards, priming them to trust the app with sensitive vehicle/insurance data because the brand consistently frames mundane financial tasks as premium experiences.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotional reframing of a technical permission: Instead of a dry "Allow access to vehicle data" prompt, the screen sells an aspirational identity ("designed for the obsessive") before the ask.

  • Progressive disclosure via carousel: The page-control dots indicate this is one step in a multi-screen narrative sequence, letting the value prop build gradually rather than front-loading everything at once.

  • Visual metaphor illustration: The phone-and-motorcycle isometric graphic concretely visualizes the abstract concept of "digitizing your vehicle," making the benefit tangible.

  • Premium dark theme with serif typography: Reinforces CRED's exclusive, high-end brand identity even during a functional onboarding flow.

  • Soft-touch consent copy: Placing legal/permission text below the CTA in low-contrast grey reduces friction and anxiety without hiding it entirely.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when introducing a financial or otherwise intimidating product category to a mass-market, non-expert audience for the first time. It is ideal for feature discovery screens, cross-sell modules within a broader financial app, or investment onboarding flows where the primary goal is to lower psychological barriers before requesting a transaction. It works particularly well when the underlying product has genuinely low friction (low minimums, no fees) that can be foregrounded as the headline hook.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this simplified, emotionally-driven approach for sophisticated or professional trading audiences (e.g., active day traders) who need ticker symbols, real-time quotes, and detailed metrics immediately rather than brand-logo carousels. It's also inappropriate in heavily regulated contexts where oversimplified "chance to grow" messaging without risk disclosures could raise compliance concerns (a full risk disclaimer should typically accompany or immediately follow this screen). Do not use for users already deep in a transaction flow, as the marketing-style framing will feel redundant and slow down conversion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets first-time or hesitant retail investors (likely younger users (Gen Z/Millennial) within a super-app or neobank ecosystem (the layout strongly resembles Cash App's investing tab) who have disposable cash sitting idle but have historically been intimidated by traditional brokerage complexity, high account minimums, or unfamiliar tickers).

The psychological drivers at play include: the endowment/familiarity effect (users are more willing to invest in brands they already emotionally trust and use daily), loss-aversion mitigation (the $1 minimum makes any potential downside feel negligible), and social proof via ubiquity (seeing globally dominant brands like Coca-Cola and Nike implies safety and legitimacy of the investment vehicle itself).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Logo-based stock carousel: Replacing ticker symbols with recognizable consumer brand logos (Nike, Coca-Cola, Walmart) dramatically reduces the intimidation factor of stock investing for beginners.

  • Micro-investment framing: Anchoring the headline on "$1" rather than "fractional shares" reframes an intimidating financial commitment as a trivially low-risk action.

  • Single decisive CTA: Only one primary action ("Buy stocks") is presented, eliminating choice overload at the critical conversion moment.

  • Sparkline visualization on cards: Abstract upward-trending line charts on each brand card visually imply growth and market activity without requiring numerical literacy.

  • Content-commerce blend: Pairing the promotional module with a real-time news feed (Reuters) builds credibility and gives non-ready users a reason to stay engaged rather than bounce.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 3
screens.whereToUse: This Flow/pattern combination fits any consumer trading or investing app home screen where the goal is to move a user quickly from passive browsing (news, trending assets) to an active purchase decision.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for professional/pro-trader tools where users need dense data tables, multi-asset comparison, or advanced order types up front rather than a merchandised, news-led browse experience.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood (Stocks tab): same combination of a prominent buy CTA, curated financial news feed, and "most popular" stock lists on one scrollable home.

  • Coinbase (Assets/Discover tab): uses horizontal carousels of colored category tiles and news cards to help users decide what to trade next.

  • Webull: similar hub-style stock discovery screen blending news, trending lists, and a persistent buy entry point.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Fitts's Law: the "Buy stocks" button is a large, high-contrast pill at the top of the scroll, making it an easy, low-effort target despite competing for space with news content.

  • Recognition over recall: company logos (Reuters, Tesla) let users scan and recognize sources/holdings instantly rather than reading full names first.

  • Progressive disclosure: category tiles (IPOs, Banking & Finance, Business Services) surface breadth without expanding the main scroll; users drill in only if interested.

  • Social proof: sourcing news from Reuters with timestamps builds credibility for a financial decision screen where trust matters.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 4
screens.whereToUse: This pattern fits investing or trading apps where users benefit from quick, pre-filtered stock rankings (popularity, volatility, sector) to jumpstart discovery before committing to a purchase.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a portfolio or holdings view, where users need their own positions and personal performance front and center rather than app-wide trending lists.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood (Discover tab): uses similarly labeled ranked lists ("Most Popular," "Top Movers") with logo-led rows and percentage badges.

  • Yahoo Finance app: pairs "Trending Tickers" and "Day Gainers/Losers" modules in the same stacked-card format.

screens.keyHighlights:
• Recognition over recall: company logos next to each row let users identify Tesla, NVIDIA, Apple, etc. at a glance rather than parsing ticker symbols.

  • Visibility of system status: up/down arrows paired with colored percentages make gain/loss direction legible in a split second, before reading the number.

  • Chunking: splitting stocks into two labeled cards (traded volume vs. daily movers) rather than one long list reduces cognitive load and clarifies what each ranking means.

  • Progress indication: the page-control dots under "Most Traded Monthly" tell users there's more content to page through without needing a "see all" tap.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 5
screens.whereToUse: This Feature Spotlight + Onboarding combination fits fintech or investing apps that want to build first-time-investor confidence and reduce intimidation before nudging toward a purchase, especially for users new to the asset class shown.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for experienced or professional traders' workflows, where an educational promo card interrupts efficient scanning of market data and adds visual noise rather than value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

  • Acorns app: pairs playful onboarding illustrations with "bite-sized" investing education modules in a comparable tone.

screens.keyHighlights:

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 6

screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a portfolio overview or multi-asset comparison screen, where users need to see several securities side-by-side rather than one asset's full transactional detail.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

screens.keyHighlights:
• Visibility of system status: the green upward chart line and matching green "↑2.60%" text reinforce the positive price movement through consistent color coding.

  • Minimize user memory load: the segmented time-range control (1D/1W/1M/1Y/ALL) lets users compare performance windows without needing to recall or re-navigate to see historical data.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 7
screens.whereToUse: This Drill-Down + Inline Help combination fits any investing app's company research screen, where users need both qualitative context (what the company does, who runs it) and quantitative metrics (valuation, growth) before committing capital.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a quick-glance watchlist or trending screen, where dense fact tables would slow down rapid comparison across many securities.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 8

screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a quick-decision buy flow (e.g., a checkout or order-confirmation screen), where dense financial charts and news would add friction rather than help a user complete a simple transaction.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 9

screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for novice-focused, decision-light contexts (e.g., a simple round-up-savings or gift-card purchase flow), where analyst ratings and EPS beat/miss data would add complexity irrelevant to the task.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 10

screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for purchases requiring precise, non-round quantities (e.g., buying an exact number of fractional shares to match a target allocation), where preset dollar buttons add little value over a direct numeric input field.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 11
screens.whereToUse: This Verification + Consent pattern fits any regulated fintech flow (investing, lending, crypto) where KYC/AML compliance requires identity verification before a feature unlocks, and reducing perceived friction at that gate directly affects completion rates.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for non-regulated, low-stakes features where bundling legal consent into a single "Get started" tap would be disproportionate or could obscure important terms the user should review more deliberately (e.g., agreements with real financial consequences that warrant explicit, separate acknowledgment rather than a bundled tap).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Robinhood (identity verification interstitial): uses a nearly identical reassurance-icon-plus-explanation pattern before collecting SSN and identity details for brokerage account opening.

  • Coinbase (identity verification step): pairs a trust-building icon and short explanatory copy with bundled legal consent before KYC data collection.

  • Chime / Venmo (bank account verification screens): use the same "we need a few more details" framing with a single CTA that bundles progression and consent for regulated financial features.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Framing effect: presenting identity verification behind a shield/checkmark icon and reassuring copy reframes a regulatory necessity as a protective, trust-building step rather than an obstacle.

  • Minimizing perceived effort: "a few more details" and "a few additional details" downplay the scope of what's actually a KYC (know-your-customer) verification process, keeping motivation high before the user sees the actual form.

  • Legal transparency at the point of consent: placing the agreement text immediately above the action button ensures users see what they're agreeing to at the moment of commitment, rather than in a separate, easily-skipped screen.

  • Progress indication: the thin bar at the bottom (partially visible) signals this is one step in a longer flow, setting expectations for what's ahead.

screens.name: Cash App Dashboard 5
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech or banking apps wanting to cross-sell multiple products (credit, investing, cards) without overwhelming users with data-heavy comparisons.

  • Home/dashboard screens where you want to blend transactional status (balances, paycheck state) with promotional merchandising in a single scrollable feed.

  • Products targeting younger, mobile-native audiences who respond better to lifestyle/aspirational framing than technical/feature-list framing.

  • Situations where you want to nudge users toward under-adopted features (crypto, borrowing, premium cards) via low-friction, single-tap "Start" entry points.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for power users, business/enterprise finance tools, or accounting dashboards where users expect immediate access to detailed numeric data (balances, transaction tables) rather than editorial merchandising.

  • Not ideal for compliance-heavy contexts where prominent promotion of credit or crypto products adjacent to account status could raise regulatory or dark-pattern concerns around suggestive selling.

  • Avoid when the app's core value is speed/utility (e.g., quick bill pay) - large hero-style promotional cards can slow down or distract from primary task completion.

  • Not suitable when users need to scan/compare many products quickly, as the tall card format increases scroll depth for accessing later list items.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets mass-market, often younger or first-time financial users (Cash App's core Gen Z/millennial demographic) who may be intimidated by traditional banking UI and more responsive to consumer-app conventions borrowed from social and e-commerce apps. By using bold, magazine-style typography and lifestyle imagery instead of numbers-heavy dashboards, the design lowers the psychological barrier to engaging with financial products like credit lines, crypto, and premium cards.

Psychological triggers at play include aspiration and identity signaling ("status"), curiosity/completion (the paycheck status nudge), and low-commitment framing via the single-word "Start" CTA, which reduces the perceived risk of exploring a new financial product. The "More for you" personalized feed label also invokes algorithmic-recommendation trust patterns familiar from social/shopping apps, making financial cross-sell feel like a tailored suggestion rather than an ad.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Editorial merchandising card: The "Turn spending into status" module uses full-bleed lifestyle typography and a horizontal product carousel, blurring the line between a banking app and a fashion/media brand to make a debit card upgrade feel desirable rather than transactional.

  • Contextual status framing: "Ready for first paycheck" personalizes the Paychecks feature based on the user's actual account state (no paycheck received yet), turning an empty/pre-activation state into a positive, forward-looking prompt instead of a blank slate.

  • Low-friction cross-sell rows: Borrow, Bitcoin, and Stocks are presented as a uniform stacked list with identical "Start" pill buttons, reducing cognitive load and making diverse financial products (credit, crypto, equities) feel equally simple to try.

  • Minimalist 3-icon tab bar: Reinforces a calm, uncluttered primary navigation, pushing product discovery into the scrollable feed rather than a crowded nav bar.

screens.name: Cash App Dashboard 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this repeating icon + title + subtitle + CTA row pattern when you need to merchandise multiple distinct product offerings within one app (super-app cross-sell, marketplace category entry points, or a settings-like feature launcher). It's ideal when each item leads to an isolated flow/module and you want a single consistent, low-cognitive-load action across all of them, especially in fintech, telco, or platform apps with many bundled services.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the listed actions have meaningfully different levels of risk, cost, or reversibility, using an identical neutral 'Start' CTA for both a low-stakes action (browsing stocks) and a high-stakes one (taking a loan) can obscure important distinctions and lead to regretted taps. It also doesn't work well when the number of cross-sell items grows too large, since an undifferentiated feed of 'Start' buttons can create decision fatigue or make the home screen feel cluttered with upsells rather than the core utility (in this case, money transfer) users came for.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This pattern targets everyday consumers, particularly younger and gig-economy users of Cash App who are already using the app for peer-to-peer payments and are being nudged toward higher-margin financial products (lending, investing, BNPL). The psychological triggers include: anchoring (showing a specific dollar figure like '$500' or '$1' minimum makes products feel accessible), curiosity/discovery (feed-like scroll surfaces products users may not have known the app offered), and low commitment framing ('Start' feels reversible and exploratory, not a hard sell). This design is optimized for cross-sell conversion and increasing product attach rate per user within a single financial super-app.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Uniform CTA pattern: Every single product row ends in the exact same 'Start' button, reducing decision fatigue and making the list scannable purely by icon and headline.

  • Value quantification in subtext: Instead of generic descriptions, each subtitle states a concrete number or outcome ($500, $1, $200, refund estimate), which is a strong motivator rooted in loss-aversion and specificity bias.

  • Cross-product merchandising as a feed: Treating unrelated financial products (lending, crypto, investing, tax, family, BNPL) as a single scrollable feed mimics a social/content feed's addictive scroll mechanic, encouraging discovery of features the user didn't know existed.

  • Iconography with photographic/textured assets: Using stylized photo-based icons (cash bills, coin, stock tickers, tax documents, keychain, Afterpay calendar) instead of flat icons adds visual richness and brand personality distinct from generic financial UI.

screens.name: Cash App Dashboard 7
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a single action (like "add money" or "top up") can be fulfilled through several distinct methods that each deserve their own flow. It's ideal for financial, wallet, or account-funding screens where users need clarity on discrete options before committing to a sub-flow. Also valuable for any regulated product needing to surface legal/compliance disclosures without letting them dominate the primary task.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this flat list approach when there are more than 6-7 options, as it will require excessive scrolling and lose scannability (in that case, categorize or group options). It's also unsuitable when one method is overwhelmingly the default/preferred choice; in that scenario, a single prominent CTA with an "other options" link is more efficient than presenting all methods with equal visual weight.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves everyday Cash App users: including unbanked or underbanked individuals, gig workers, and casual peer-to-peer payment users (who need multiple, flexible ways to load cash into their account (paycheck direct deposit, physical cash at a retail location, mailed checks, or bank transfers)).

The psychological driver here is reduction of choice friction combined with trust-building: by clearly enumerating discrete, well-labeled options rather than a single ambiguous "Add Money" button, the app reduces cognitive load while signaling flexibility and legitimacy. The FDIC/compliance footer specifically targets the trust and security concerns of users who may be wary of a mobile-first, non-traditional bank.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Persistent balance context: The "$200 available" strip at the top keeps the user oriented to their current funds even while navigating a funding sub-menu.

  • Icon-led scannability: Each funding method uses a distinct, simple line icon (inbox arrow, transfer arrows, bill, scan frame, reload loop) enabling fast visual differentiation without reading every label.

  • Progressive disclosure of legal content: Compliance text is present but visually de-emphasized (smaller, gray, dense) and positioned last, respecting the user's task-first mental model.

  • Consistent chevron affordance: Every row uses the same right-chevron, reinforcing a predictable drill-down mental model across the whole list.

screens.name: Cash App Dashboard 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when introducing a loyalty tier, membership status, or gamified achievement level tied to an existing product's usage metrics (spend, engagement, streaks). It's ideal for fintech, subscription, or rewards apps where you want to motivate a specific behavior (increased spend/usage) without a hard paywall, and where the benefits are compelling enough to warrant a visually rich, full-screen explainer.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy full-screen interstitial approach for minor or low-value features, as the visual weight and interruption cost don't justify small benefits. It's also inappropriate for new users who haven't yet built enough usage history to realistically qualify, showing an unattainable goal too early can create frustration rather than motivation. Additionally, if the underlying requirements are overly restrictive or unclear, this pattern risks feeling like bait, damaging trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets existing, moderately active Cash App users who already hold a Cash App Card and have some spending history (it is not a first-time onboarding screen but rather a retention/monetization upsell aimed at power users who could plausibly hit the $500/month spend threshold).

Psychologically, it leverages status signaling (exclusive card design, tier naming), gamification (earning a level), and loss-aversion-adjacent framing (implying you're missing out on cash back, overdraft protection, and interest by not qualifying). The premium card art and cash imagery specifically appeal to users motivated by financial upward mobility and visible wealth signaling.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Status-as-Reward Framing: Instead of pitching this as a paid subscription or fee-based tier, the entire narrative is built around 'earning' status through natural behavior (spending), which lowers psychological resistance compared to a hard sell.

  • Mood-Board Visual Carousel: Using a peeking/cropped image strip of card design, brand color, and cash imagery builds visual desire and brand identity association before any benefit is read.

  • Icon-Led Benefit List: Each requirement/benefit pairs a minimalist line icon with concise copy, enabling sub-3-second scanning and comprehension.

  • Single, Unmissable CTA: The pill-shaped black button strongly contrasts with the white/green palette, following the principle of one primary action per screen to eliminate decision paralysis.

  • Low-friction Exit: The top-left 'X' respects user autonomy, which increases trust and reduces feelings of being trapped in a forced sales funnel.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Introducing a signature, high-leverage feature (like a command palette, keyboard shortcut, or gesture) that differentiates the product from competitors.

  • Onboarding flows for productivity, developer, or power-user tools where speed and efficiency are core selling points.

  • Any scenario where the interaction method varies by device/input type and both paths need clear instruction.

  • Multi-step onboarding sequences where you want to balance education with user autonomy (skip option) and progress visibility.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this heavy, full-screen interruption pattern for minor or rarely-used features (reserve it for truly high-value, differentiating functionality).

  • Not ideal for first-time, non-technical consumer audiences who may find keyboard shortcut callouts (⌘K) confusing or irrelevant.

  • Should not be used if the feature can't actually be demonstrated/tried in context, forcing a "try it" prompt without real interactivity creates false expectations and frustration.

  • Avoid stacking too many of these full-screen coach mark steps in a row (fatigue risk) without allowing users to skip or revisit later via a help menu.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets productivity-focused, often technical users (engineers, designers, PMs) evaluating Linear as a project management tool. These users are typically efficiency-driven and skeptical of long onboarding flows, so the screen must quickly prove tangible value (speed) rather than rely on generic feature tours.

Psychologically, this leverages the testing/generation effect: users retain information far better when they perform an action themselves rather than just reading about it. It also uses reciprocity and competence framing: by immediately demonstrating a "power user" shortcut, Linear signals the product respects the user's time and skill level, which builds early trust and perceived product sophistication.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Device-adaptive instructions: The screen smartly provides both a touchscreen gesture ("tapping with two fingers") and a keyboard shortcut (⌘K), ensuring relevance regardless of input method.

  • Learn-by-doing microinteraction: Instead of just describing the feature, the card frames it as a task to "try," encouraging active engagement and muscle-memory formation over passive reading.

  • Keycap UI chips: Rendering the shortcut as skeuomorphic key chips (⌘ and K) rather than plain text instantly communicates "this is a keyboard shortcut" using a familiar visual convention.

  • Progress transparency: The page control dots at the bottom set expectations about onboarding length, reducing abandonment anxiety.

  • Low-friction exit: A persistent close (X) button respects user autonomy, letting advanced users skip onboarding entirely.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 13
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern immediately before any OAuth/third-party authentication handoff, especially when:

  • The integration requires sensitive or broad-sounding permissions (e.g., code, financial data, contacts, calendar).

  • You want to pre-explain *why* the permission is needed in your own branded voice before the native OS/platform permission dialog appears (which you cannot customize).

  • You need to differentiate your request from what users might assume (e.g., "we only need X, not Y") to reduce abandonment.

  • The feature is optional/supplementary rather than core, so offering a clear "skip for now" path is appropriate.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavier priming pattern when:

  • The permission requested is trivial or expected (e.g., basic notification permission) - adding an extra screen here only adds friction without added trust value.

  • The integration is mandatory for the app to function; in that case, framing it as skippable ("I'll do this later") would be misleading.

  • Users are already deep in a time-sensitive task, inserting a full-screen interstitial here could feel like an interruption rather than a helpful primer.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets software engineering teams and technical project managers who use Linear to track issues and want to connect their existing GitHub repositories. This audience is highly security-conscious and often skeptical of third-party tools requesting broad repo access, making trust and transparency the primary psychological lever at play.

The design leverages loss-aversion and risk-mitigation triggers: by explicitly ruling out code-read access, it removes the single biggest psychological barrier (fear of IP/code exposure) that would otherwise cause a drop-off at this step of the funnel. It also leverages the authority/competence heuristic: a clean, well-organized explanation signals that Linear is a professionally built, trustworthy product worthy of elevated permissions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Proactive Objection Handling: Explicitly stating what the integration will not do (read code) directly inside the value-prop list, rather than letting users discover/fear this on the native GitHub OAuth screen.

  • Permission Priming Pattern: A branded, friendly pre-screen before handing off to GitHub's native, less-customizable OAuth consent page, allowing Linear to control the narrative and context.

  • Low-Friction Opt-Out: The "I'll do this later" link ensures the integration prompt never feels like a hard gate blocking core app usage.

  • Checkmark Visual Language: Using checkmarks (vs. plain bullets) subconsciously signals "these boxes are already ticked/safe for you," increasing perceived trustworthiness.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 14
screens.whereToUse:
• B2B SaaS products where value scales with number of collaborators (project management, communication, whiteboarding tools).

  • Early onboarding flows where you want to seed network effects before the user's enthusiasm decays.

  • Any flow where you want to encourage an action but must not block progress for users unwilling to comply immediately.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Single-player or personal-use apps where there is no collaborative value proposition (invites would feel irrelevant or pushy).

  • Highly privacy-sensitive contexts where asking for colleague emails this early could raise trust/compliance concerns.

  • Flows where the user hasn't yet experienced core value, asking for a team invite before the product has proven itself can increase drop-off instead of reducing it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets new signups: typically a team lead, founder, or early adopter evaluating Linear for their organization. Since Linear's value is inherently networked (a project/issue tracker is far more useful with teammates present), this step exploits the "viral loop" growth pattern: converting a single-user trial into a multi-seat team account as early as possible. Psychologically, it capitalizes on the user's current high-motivation state (freshly signed up, curious, exploratory) to ask for an investment (inviting colleagues) before intent fades. It also uses social facilitation (once co-workers are invited, the user has public accountability to actually adopt and use the tool).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-exit strategy: Both "Continue" and "I'll do this later" give users multiple non-blocking ways to skip, drastically reducing onboarding abandonment risk.

  • Batch email input: A single text area accepting comma-separated emails lets power users invite an entire team in one action instead of repeating a form multiple times.

  • Visual progress transparency: The dot-based page control at the bottom sets expectations for how many steps remain, reducing onboarding fatigue/anxiety.

  • Strategic CTA hierarchy: The filled purple "Send invites" button draws the eye first, while skip options are intentionally muted in gray, nudging the desired behavior without forcing it.

screens.name: Linear Onboarding 15
screens.whereToUse:
• Post-onboarding or settings flows where you want to capture marketing/notification consent without blocking the primary task.

  • SaaS products with a technical or privacy-conscious audience where transparency drives higher-quality opt-ins.

  • Any flow requiring compliance with opt-in consent regulations (GDPR, CAN-SPAM, CCPA).

  • Situations where you want to separate distinct communication types (product updates vs. marketing) to improve long-term engagement and reduce unsubscribe rates.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this soft, skippable pattern if email capture is a core business-critical conversion metric that must be maximized (a more assertive single-choice prompt may perform better for growth-stage products).

  • Don't use pre-toggled OFF switches if your business model depends on default opt-ins and your jurisdiction does not legally require explicit consent (though this is generally not recommended).

  • Not ideal mid-task, where interrupting with a preference screen would break flow and frustrate users (e.g., during checkout or active editing).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets newly onboarded or existing Linear users at a natural checkpoint (likely post-signup or post-settings-visit) where communication preferences are most relevant. The audience is primarily technical/product teams who are highly sensitive to unsolicited marketing noise, so Linear's restrained, honest approach to opt-in (rather than pre-checked boxes) is tailored to a sophisticated, trust-sensitive user base that would otherwise bounce or immediately unsubscribe if manipulated into a list.

Psychologically, the pattern leverages the principle of autonomy (user controls every choice), reciprocity (transparent value exchange: "subscribe to learn about changes" implies tangible benefit), and reduced cognitive load (binary toggles, no required fields) to maximize genuine, lower-churn opt-ins rather than inflated but low-quality subscriber counts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Opt-in by default (toggles OFF): Respects user consent norms and regulatory best practice, building long-term trust over short-term list-growth metrics.

  • Frictionless exit via "X": Clearly communicates this is a non-mandatory step, reducing perceived pressure and modal fatigue.

  • Granular, specific choices: Separating "changelog" from "marketing/onboarding" emails lets users tailor exactly what they want, avoiding the all-or-nothing subscription trap.

  • Expectation-setting microcopy: Stating frequency ("bi-weekly," "occasional") directly addresses the top objection to subscribing (fear of spam).

  • Correct component semantics: Using a toggle for binary preferences but a button/pill for the external "Follow on X" action avoids UI pattern misuse.

screens.name: Wealthfront Setting Up 23
screens.whereToUse:
• Multi-condition automation setups (e.g., bill pay rules, subscription routing, round-up savings) where sequence and dependency matter.

  • Financial or productivity apps needing to explain "if X then Y" logic to non-technical users.

  • Onboarding flows for rule-based systems (budgeting apps, smart routing, workflow builders) where showing order of operations builds user trust and comprehension.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for simple, single-decision settings (the timeline/stepper visual overhead adds unnecessary friction if there's only one rule to configure).

  • Not ideal when steps have no real causal or sequential relationship; forcing an unrelated feature list into a "first/then" narrative can mislead users about dependency.

  • Risky for scenarios with many steps (5+) since the vertical scroll and expand/collapse pattern could become tedious; a table or matrix view may communicate priority faster.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets passive savers and first-time wealth builders who want their money managed intelligently without manually moving funds between checking, cash, and investment accounts every payday. The design leans on the psychological principle of automating willpower: by setting a rule once, users offload the ongoing decision fatigue of "how much should I save this month?" to the system, a proven behavioral finance tactic (similar to 401k auto-escalation) that increases actual savings rates.

The calm, editorial tone and muted violet palette are specifically chosen to counter the anxiety typically associated with automating money movement (fear of overdrafts, fear of losing control), making the feature feel safe for financial novices rather than only appealing to power users comfortable with spreadsheets.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Visual waterfall metaphor: Using a connected vertical timeline with directional icons (down arrow, coin stack, piggy bank) to represent the literal flow of money makes an abstract "if-then" automation rule instantly scannable and intuitive.

  • Progressive disclosure via expand/collapse cards: Only the active/relevant step is expanded with detail and a CTA, while subsequent steps stay collapsed, preventing decision fatigue while still previewing what's coming next.

  • Reassurance microcopy: "You can change this at any time" is strategically placed right after the headline to lower the psychological barrier to starting the setup.

  • Implicit reorder affordance: The hamburger/drag-handle icon on the collapsed step subtly signals to power users that priority order is customizable, without adding explicit UI chrome to the primary path.

screens.name: Wealthfront Setting Up 24
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech apps configuring automated money-movement rules, bill splitting, or "if-this-then-that" style rules engines.

  • Any workflow that benefits from expressing a sequence/priority order (e.g., waterfall budgeting, subscription tiers, notification escalation rules).

  • Multi-step setup wizards where you want to keep the primary CTA visible but disabled until prerequisite configuration is completed.

  • Situations requiring reassurance copy to reduce anxiety around automation or loss of manual control.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for simple, single-condition settings (the vertical waterfall metaphor adds unnecessary visual complexity for binary toggles).

  • Not ideal when users need to configure many (5+) sequential steps at once, as the expanding card approach could create excessive scrolling and cognitive load.

  • Disabled CTAs without clear inline messaging on *why* they're disabled can frustrate users who don't immediately notice the incomplete step above; always pair with a visible unmet requirement.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets self-directed, moderately financially literate users who want to automate saving/investing behavior without manually moving money between accounts each pay cycle (likely millennial/Gen-Z professionals using Wealthfront's cash management and investing products). These users are drawn to "set it and forget it" systems that reduce decision fatigue around personal finance.

Psychologically, the design leverages the endowed progress effect (the progress bar suggests the user is already partway to a rewarding automated system), loss aversion mitigation (reversibility messaging), and the default/mental accounting bias by framing savings as an automatic "leftover" after a protected cash buffer, appealing to users who struggle with the willpower required for manual saving.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Waterfall visualization metaphor: Using a connected vertical line with iconography (down arrow, purple bank icon, savings icon) to make an abstract "money routing" rule instantly scannable and comprehensible.

  • Contextual inline expansion card: Rather than routing users to a separate settings screen, the "How much cash should we keep?" explanation and CTA are embedded directly within the flow at the relevant step, reducing context-switching.

  • Disabled CTA as soft gating: The grayed-out "Turn on automated savings" button visually communicates incompleteness without needing an error message, nudging users toward finishing configuration first.

  • Implied reordering affordance: The hamburger/drag-handle icon next to "Then, save as much as possible" subtly signals that priority order is user-editable, giving a sense of control over automation logic.

  • Reassurance messaging embedded in the intro copy: Preemptively answers the "what if I want to undo this?" concern before the user even engages with the flow.

screens.name: Wealthfront Setting Up 25
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when configuring numeric thresholds, budgets, or limits in financial, health, or utility apps (e.g., savings goals, spending caps, low-balance alerts, calorie targets). It's ideal for:

  • Multi-step setup wizards where each screen should isolate a single, high-stakes decision.

  • Situations where a reasonable smart default can be computed from user data to reduce blank-slate anxiety.

  • Numeric inputs that benefit from both coarse (slider) and precise (direct entry) adjustment.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The value range is extremely wide or non-linear (e.g., $0 ($1,000,000), where a slider becomes imprecise and frustrating without logarithmic scaling).

  • Multiple interdependent settings need to be configured together, splitting them into too many single-focus screens can cause wizard fatigue.

  • There is no reliable way to compute a smart default, in which case presenting a pre-filled number may mislead or confuse users into thinking it's a recommendation.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen targets existing Wealthfront users setting up automated cash management ("Self-Driving Money") across linked accounts (typically financially engaged, moderately affluent individuals who want to optimize idle cash without manual transfers). The psychological trigger at play is automation trust + control: users are handing over a recurring financial decision to an algorithm, so the interface must feel transparent, adjustable, and safe. Showing an editable, pre-populated smart default triggers the anchoring effect, nudging users toward acceptance of a "good enough" number while still preserving a sense of agency via the slider/edit control.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual input modality: Combining a draggable slider with a tap-to-edit pencil icon caters to both quick approximate adjustments and precise numeric entry, satisfying different user preferences without cluttering the UI with two separate fields.

  • Smart default pre-fill: The $3,503 value is very likely algorithmically generated based on the user's real cash flow data, dramatically lowering the effort and anxiety of deciding "what number do I even pick?"

  • Single-focus screen: Isolating one configuration decision per screen in a multi-step wizard prevents overwhelm and keeps error rates low for a financially consequential setting.

  • Plain-language rule explanation: Translating a conditional logic statement ("if X then Y") into a friendly one-line paragraph builds trust and comprehension around an automated financial action.

  • Persistent account context: Keeping the account icon/name pinned at the top prevents users from losing track of which account the rule affects, critical in multi-account net-worth aggregation apps.

screens.name: Wealthfront Setting Up 26
screens.whereToUse:
• Multi-step configuration or setup wizards where sensible defaults exist and most users won't need to change them (e.g., automation rules, notification schedules, recurring transfers).

  • Financial or high-stakes flows where transparency about automated actions and safety nets (grace periods, cancellation windows) needs to be clearly communicated before the user commits.

  • Settings summary screens where you want to show current configuration state compactly with a lightweight path to edit.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this "display value + Edit link" pattern when the setting is critical enough that users should be forced to actively confirm each value rather than glossing over a pre-filled default (e.g., legal or compliance-sensitive selections).

  • Not ideal when there are many configurable parameters, condensing everything into review-style rows works well for 1-3 fields but becomes tedious and buries options if scaled to a long list.

  • Avoid if the underlying options require more nuanced comparison (e.g., choosing between several complex plans) where an inline selector would serve users better than a hidden edit flow.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets users setting up automated cash sweep / idle cash management features, typically in banking, brokerage, or neobank apps (e.g., moving excess checking balance into a high-yield or investment account). The audience is likely moderately financially engaged users who want "set it and forget it" automation but are still wary of losing control over their money movement.

Psychologically, the screen leverages the default effect (pre-selected "Daily" frequency reduces decision fatigue) and loss-aversion mitigation (the one-business-day cancellation window reduces perceived risk of automation). The clean, uncluttered design also invokes a sense of institutional competence and calm, which is critical for financial trust.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Smart Defaults presented as settled facts: Instead of empty form fields, the screen pre-fills "Daily" and a start date, drastically lowering the decision-making burden for the majority of users who will accept the default.

  • Decoupled Edit affordance: Placing "Edit" links beside display values (rather than embedding editable inputs directly) keeps the primary reading experience clean while still making customization one tap away (a pattern that reduces visual clutter on info-dense financial screens).

  • Proactive risk disclosure: Explaining the cancellation window and notification policy upfront builds trust and reduces support inquiries/anxiety around automated money movement.

  • Minimalist single-focus layout: Only one decision is asked per screen, aligning with the "one question per screen" wizard best practice that improves completion rates in multi-step forms.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 12
screens.whereToUse: This Value-Prop Carousel pattern fits any app introducing a new, potentially unfamiliar financial product (crypto, investing, credit) to an existing user base, where building motivation and basic understanding before the functional flow improves adoption.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for returning users who have already completed this onboarding or explicitly navigated to Bitcoin trading with clear intent, repeating a motivational carousel for them would add unnecessary friction rather than useful context.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Coinbase (onboarding carousel): uses nearly identical illustrated value-prop slides introducing Bitcoin/crypto with simple, aspirational language before account setup.

  • Robinhood (Crypto intro screens): pairs playful illustration with plain-language crypto explanations in a comparable multi-slide onboarding carousel.

  • PayPal (Crypto feature intro): uses a similar "invest in the future" framing with illustrated onboarding slides before enabling crypto trading within an existing payments app.
