  • Progressive disclosure: spreading Bitcoin's value proposition across multiple carousel slides (indicated by four dots) avoids overwhelming a new user with all information at once.

  • User control and freedom: the persistent close "X" lets users exit the onboarding at any point, respecting that Bitcoin investing is an opt-in feature rather than a mandatory step.

  • Familiar language over jargon: describing Bitcoin via familiar verbs ("sends, spends, and saves") rather than technical terminology reduces cognitive load for first-time crypto users.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 13
screens.whereToUse: This Hero Merchandising + Feature Spotlight combination fits any fintech app's crypto or investing home screen, where lowering the perceived barrier to entry (price, complexity) alongside optional education helps convert both ready buyers and hesitant newcomers.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a returning, active bitcoin holder's dashboard, where portfolio value, holdings, and price charts are more relevant than a beginner-oriented value-prop headline and educational content.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Coinbase (Home/Buy tab): uses the same low-minimum-price headline and prominent buy CTA paired with "Learn" content tiles for crypto education.

  • Robinhood (Crypto tab): pairs a hero buy CTA with educational "Learn" cards addressing common crypto questions, in a comparable layout.

  • PayPal (Crypto hub): combines a headline emphasizing low minimum purchase amounts with an adjacent educational content section before the buy flow.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anchoring: leading with "$1" reframes bitcoin investing as low-risk and accessible before the user considers cost as a barrier.

  • Recognition over recall: the Bitcoin symbol rendered prominently in the hero illustration reinforces what asset this screen concerns without requiring users to read first.

  • Progressive disclosure: separating the immediate "Buy bitcoin" action from the "Learn the basics" educational tiles lets ready buyers act fast while curious users can explore first.

  • Multiple entry points for different intents: pairing a transactional CTA with an educational carousel accommodates both experienced and first-time crypto users on the same screen, as directly stated in the subtext.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 14
screens.whereToUse: This Card Grid education pattern paired with a Preference Center for automation fits crypto or investing apps serving a mixed audience of beginners (who need conceptual grounding) and ready adopters (who want hands-off, recurring investment options) within the same feature area.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for an experienced trader's dashboard where beginner educational content would be redundant clutter above the automation settings they actually came to configure.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Coinbase (Coinbase Learn): uses a similar grid of beginner-question-style educational tiles ("What is Bitcoin?", "How does crypto work?") with illustrated thumbnails.

  • Acorns (Round-Ups feature): pioneered the "invest your spare change" automated round-up framing that Cash App's Bitcoin Round Ups directly mirrors.

  • Robinhood (Recurring Investments): offers a comparable "Auto Invest" toggle-based settings list for scheduling automatic crypto purchases.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Progressive onboarding / scaffolded learning: ordering the four educational tiles from foundational ("What is money?") to specific ("Why is bitcoin valuable?") builds understanding incrementally rather than assuming prior knowledge.

  • Recognition over recall: distinct, colorful illustration styles per tile help users visually distinguish topics at a glance in the grid.

  • Visibility of system status: showing "Off" next to Bitcoin Round Ups and Auto Invest clearly communicates the current (inactive) state before the user decides whether to enable them.

  • Reduced friction for automation: describing Round Ups as "Invest your spare change" translates a technical automation feature into a familiar, low-risk mental model (spare change saving).

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 15
screens.whereToUse: This Preference Center + Drill-Down combination fits any crypto or investing app's settings area where multiple related automation features (recurring buys, round-ups, direct-deposit allocation) need to be presented together with clear current-state visibility before the user commits to configuring any one of them.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a screen meant to drive urgency or a single decisive action (like a limited-time promotional buy), where a long list of settings options would dilute focus rather than support it.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Acorns (Round-Ups + Recurring Investments settings): uses the same paired "spare change" and "recurring buys" automation settings in a comparable list format.

  • Coinbase (Recurring Buy settings): offers an equivalent Auto Invest (style toggle list for scheduling automatic crypto purchases with clear Off/On status).

  • Robinhood (Recurring Investments + Deposit settings): presents a similar grouped settings list separating investment automation from deposit/transfer actions.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Consistency and standards: identical row structure (icon, bold title, gray description, status label, chevron) across both settings and usage sections reduces the learning curve as users scan down the page.

  • Visibility of system status: "Off" labels on all three growth features give an at-a-glance summary of what automation is and isn't active, without requiring the user to open each one.

  • Trust through transparency: explicitly stating "without a fee" on the Paid in bitcoin row proactively removes a likely objection at the point of decision.

  • Recognition over recall: distinct icons per row (refresh arrow, loop, deposit arrow, card) help users visually differentiate similar-sounding automation features.

  • Contextual relevance: placing the live "Price per bitcoin" figure between the settings and usage sections keeps market context visible without a separate lookup.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 16
screens.whereToUse: This Upsell / Cross-Sell pattern fits any multi-product fintech app where a secondary product (a card, a subscription tier) can be framed as directly enhancing the feature the user is already engaged with, placed at a natural stopping point rather than interrupting the primary task.
screens.whereNotToUse: It's a poor fit for a transactional confirmation or checkout screen, where introducing an unrelated product promotion at the moment of committing to a purchase would add distracting friction rather than complementary value.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
• Coinbase (Coinbase Card promotion within the crypto app): cross-promotes a debit card that earns crypto rewards directly within the main crypto browsing experience, similar to this Cash App Card tie-in.

  • PayPal (PayPal Debit Card + crypto rewards): uses a comparable "spend and earn crypto" framing to cross-sell its card product from within the crypto section.

  • Venmo (Venmo Credit Card cash-back promotion): places a card upsell with a rewards hook at the bottom of an unrelated feature tab, following the same end-of-scroll cross-sell placement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual relevance: placing the Cash App Card upsell inside the Bitcoin tab, framed around earning bitcoin, ties a cross-sell to the user's current context rather than treating it as an unrelated interruption.

  • Recognition over recall: the small blue Bitcoin badge overlaid on the card image visually reinforces the connection between the card product and the bitcoin-earning benefit before the user reads any text.

  • Transparency and compliance: the "Bitcoin services by Block, Inc. See disclosures" line at the natural end of the scroll satisfies regulatory disclosure requirements without interrupting the promotional flow above it.

  • Progressive disclosure: "Deposit bitcoin" is presented as a single drill-down row rather than expanding its address details inline, keeping the closing section of the tab lightweight.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 17
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when a product must route users between two or more distinct configuration paths that have meaningfully different downstream flows (e.g., recurring vs. one-time actions, simple vs. advanced modes). It works well for:

  • Fintech/investing apps offering multiple order or transaction types.

  • Any settings or setup flow where the "strategy" choice should be separated from "detail" configuration.

  • Onboarding moments where reducing jargon and giving plain-language explanations builds user trust.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • There are more than 3-4 options, as a simple vertical list becomes unwieldy and comparison becomes difficult (a table or comparison view would serve better).

  • The options are trivial or nearly identical, in which case adding this intermediate selection screen would only introduce unnecessary friction.

  • Users are highly expert and repeat this action frequently (in that case, the extra tap-through step (choice screen before configuration) could feel like an obstacle rather than a helpful decision aid, favoring a single combined form instead).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets retail crypto investors, ranging from beginners setting up their first recurring investment to more engaged users wanting tactical control over entry prices. The design leans heavily on psychological principles of reducing perceived risk and complexity in financial decision-making.

By framing "Auto Invest" first (the safer, "set-and-forget" default aligned with dollar-cost-averaging best practice for beginners) and "Custom purchase order" second (a more advanced, active-trading behavior), the hierarchy subtly guides less experienced users toward the lower-risk automated option while still empowering power users to self-select into manual control.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Jargon Translation: Complex trading concepts (recurring buys, limit orders) are re-labeled in plain consumer language, lowering the barrier to entry for novice crypto investors.

  • Icon-Led Differentiation: Distinct, simple line icons (a repeat/cycle icon for Auto Invest, a wave/curve icon for Custom order) provide instant visual differentiation between the two mental models being presented.

  • Deferred Complexity: The screen intentionally avoids configuration inputs (amounts, frequencies, price targets) at this stage, isolating the "choice of strategy" from the "configuration of strategy" to reduce decision fatigue.

  • Contextual Help Affordance: A persistent "?" icon in the header acknowledges that financial order types are a common point of confusion and offers an escape hatch to educational content without cluttering the main UI.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 18
screens.whereToUse: Use anchored coach marks like this when introducing a novel, high-stakes, or non-standard gesture (e.g., custom sliders, draggable chart elements, pinch-to-adjust) that isn't self-evident from visual design alone. Especially valuable in fintech, trading, and health-tracking apps where a misunderstood interaction could lead to a costly or irreversible mistake. Pair with a semi-transparent dimming of surrounding content to direct attention without fully blocking context.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for interactions that are already standard/expected (e.g., basic taps, standard sliders users have seen elsewhere) - over-explaining common gestures feels condescending and adds friction. Also avoid stacking multiple coach marks in sequence without a skip/dismiss option, as this can feel like forced tutorializing. If the feature is used frequently, ensure the hint only shows once (first-use) rather than repeating on every visit, or it becomes an annoyance rather than an aid.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets retail crypto investors and DCA (dollar-cost averaging) style traders who want automated, hands-off buying at target price dips rather than manually watching charts. It appeals to users who are price-sensitive and want to "buy the dip" without needing to monitor markets constantly (a common pain point for part-time crypto participants).

Psychologically, this leverages the human desire for control and optimization in volatile markets: setting a trigger price gives a sense of strategic mastery over an inherently unpredictable asset. The coach mark reduces the fear of "doing it wrong" for a feature that involves real money, which is critical for trust in fintech apps (a confused user might abandon a limit-order feature entirely if the interaction isn't crystal clear on first exposure).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Anchored contextual tooltip: The speech-bubble pointer connects directly to the interactive handle, creating an unambiguous visual link between instruction and action target.

  • Gesture-first teaching: Rather than relying on a generic "tap to learn more" pattern, the hint teaches a specific gesture (drag) that is unique to this feature and wouldn't be discovered through trial-and-error easily.

  • Non-blocking overlay: Unlike a full-screen modal, the coach mark sits within the live chart context, letting users see the real data they'll be interacting with immediately after dismissing the hint.

  • Visual affordance on the handle: The bright cyan circle with up/down chevrons signals draggability far better than a plain dot would, reinforcing the instructional text with an iconographic cue.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 19
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech or crypto apps introducing conditional/automated purchase rules (limit orders, recurring buys, price alerts with auto-execution).

  • Any monetary input screen where a small set of common amounts covers the majority of use cases (tipping, donations, top-ups, gift cards).

  • Multi-step flows where showing a dimmed preview of the prior step helps users retain context without formal breadcrumbs.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid preset-only tiles when transaction amounts are highly variable or unpredictable (e.g., enterprise invoicing, bill payments) - forcing users into the ".." escape hatch too often defeats the purpose of presets.

  • Do not use the dimmed background/bottom sheet stacking pattern for flows with more than 2-3 steps, as it can become visually cluttered and disorienting.

  • Avoid oversimplified if/then phrasing for advanced/professional trading tools where precise terminology (limit price, stop-loss, execution conditions) is expected and required for compliance or clarity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This flow targets retail/casual crypto investors, particularly those coming from a Cash-App or Venmo-like mental model rather than a traditional trading terminal background. The design leans heavily on familiar peer-to-peer payment UI conventions (rounded amount tiles, simple sentence-based instructions) rather than dense trading UI (order books, percentage sliders, decimal precision inputs), suggesting the audience is price-conscious but not necessarily financially sophisticated.

Psychologically, the preset dollar tiles exploit the anchoring effect and reduce choice overload by pre-selecting socially "reasonable" amounts, nudging users toward action rather than analysis paralysis. The conditional if/then phrasing also leverages a simple mental heuristic (a "rule" rather than a complex order type), making automated/conditional investing feel accessible to non-experts.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual layering: Keeping the previous step (price target) faintly visible behind the modal reinforces the causal relationship between "set a price" and "choose an amount," acting as an implicit breadcrumb without a formal breadcrumb component.

  • Preset denomination tiles: Removes numeric keypad friction for 90% of users while the ".." tile preserves flexibility for custom entries (a strong pattern for reducing decision fatigue).

  • Human-readable conditional statement: Restating the trigger price in plain if/then language just above the input choices ensures the user always understands what they are committing to before confirming an amount.

  • Disabled CTA until selection: Prevents accidental submission and visually communicates the required next action.

screens.name: Cash App Purchasing & Ordering 20
screens.whereToUse:
• Multi-step financial or e-commerce flows where a single decision (amount, quantity, plan tier) needs isolated focus without full-page navigation.

  • Conditional/automated order-setting flows (limit orders, price alerts, recurring purchases) where framing a hypothetical scenario reduces user anxiety.

  • Mobile-first flows where preserving context (dimmed background) while capturing quick input via a bottom sheet improves perceived continuity.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for complex forms requiring many fields (a bottom sheet with limited vertical space becomes cramped and forces scrolling, defeating its lightweight purpose).

  • Not suitable when users need to compare multiple data points simultaneously (e.g., full price history charts), since the sheet obscures a large portion of relevant background content.

  • Risky for irreversible high-stakes financial actions if not paired with a clear confirmation step afterward, as the frictionless preset-tap flow could lead to accidental over-commitment.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets retail/casual crypto investors, particularly beginners intimidated by traditional trading interfaces. By starting at $1 and using plain-language questions, the app lowers the entry barrier for users who may have never invested before, tapping into the psychological principle of micro-commitment: small, easy first steps increase the likelihood of completing a full transaction.

The conditional "if price drops to $X" framing appeals to loss-averse users who want to buy the dip without actively monitoring markets, leveraging automation and reducing FOMO/anxiety associated with market timing.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Layered Bottom Sheet over Contextual Backdrop: Preserves spatial context (the underlying price-setting screen remains visible but dimmed), reinforcing that this is one step within a larger flow rather than a disconnected screen.

  • Preset Amount Chips with Escape Hatch: Six large, evenly-spaced tap targets cover common amounts plus an ellipsis for custom input, balancing speed (one-tap selection) with flexibility.

  • Conditional Framing of Price: Tying the amount question to a hypothetical price drop reduces the emotional weight of committing capital, encouraging larger or more frequent investment decisions.

  • Single Primary CTA: The stark black "Next" button contrasts against the white sheet, leaving no ambiguity about the next action, and is fixed at the bottom for reachability.

screens.name: Linear - Adding a code block - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for any rich content editor (docs, notes, tickets, wikis) where users need to insert varied content types without leaving the writing flow. It's ideal for tools targeting technical or power users who value speed, such as project management, documentation, or note-taking apps. Use progressive disclosure (toolbar → expandable tray) whenever the full set of actions would otherwise overwhelm a compact mobile toolbar.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern in simple, single-purpose forms or apps where only one or two content types are ever needed (the categorized tray would add unnecessary complexity). It's also unsuitable for casual consumer apps where users may be intimidated by database/table-view terminology, or in contexts where screen real estate is too limited to comfortably render a two-column icon grid above the keyboard.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets knowledge workers: PMs, engineers, and designers (who need to rapidly capture structured information (tasks, specs, embedded data) without breaking their flow). The psychological driver is reduced friction for capture: by keeping the keyboard open and surfacing block options in a thumb-reachable sheet, the design respects the user's momentum and avoids forcing a context switch to a separate "insert" screen.

The categorized grid also leverages the recognition-over-recall principle (users scan icons and labels rather than needing to remember command syntax, which is critical for occasional or power users alike who may not use every block type daily).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Expandable block-insertion tray: A single "+" icon in the toolbar progressively discloses a categorized library of embeddable content types, keeping the primary editing surface uncluttered until the user explicitly requests more options.
  • Persistent formatting toolbar: Docked above the keyboard, it keeps core actions (checklist, indent, upload, format) within thumb's reach at all times, eliminating the need to scroll or navigate away from the text cursor.
  • Categorized content grid: Grouping options under "Media" and "Database" headers reduces cognitive load by chunking related actions, a well-established UX technique for large option sets.
  • Explicit dismiss affordance: The circled X icon gives users a clear, low-risk way to back out of the insertion tray without losing their editing context or cursor position.

screens.name: Linear - Adding a code block - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Adopt this pattern for document, note, or long-form content editors where the priority is uninterrupted reading/writing (knowledge bases, wikis, spec writers, or personal note apps). The floating AI/search bar pattern is ideal for products introducing conversational AI features that need to feel integrated and low-friction rather than bolted-on. Use the minimal top toolbar for any screen where content supremacy matters more than frequent navigational chrome (e.g., detail/editor views reached via drill-down).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this ultra-minimal toolbar approach on screens requiring frequent multi-action access (e.g., bulk editing, complex filtering) where hidden-behind-overflow actions would slow down power users. The floating bottom AI bar can also conflict with platform-native keyboards or other floating elements (FABs, tab bars) if not carefully coordinated, and may clutter the screen on smaller devices or when a software keyboard is active. For data-dense, tabular work (e.g., issue lists), this generous whitespace/large-title treatment would waste valuable screen real estate.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves product managers, engineers, and founders who use Linear not just for issue tracking but as a lightweight knowledge/document workspace for capturing notes, specs, or personal task lists. The inclusion of a code block signals this document editor is tailored to technical users who may paste snippets alongside prose.

Psychologically, the sparse chrome and oversized title tap into a sense of calm focus: reducing visual noise so users can think and write without distraction, a key value proposition for fast-moving teams drowning in tool clutter. The prominent "Ask AI" affordance exploits the path-of-least-resistance principle: by placing AI query input in the same reachable zone as search, it normalizes AI usage as a default habit rather than an opt-in novelty, nudging adoption through proximity and visual parity with core navigation elements.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Content-first typography: Large, bold serif-free title with ample line-height on bullets maximizes scannability and reduces cognitive load.
  • Mixed block editor: Seamless juxtaposition of a bulleted list and an embedded code block with its own mini-toolbar (language selector + overflow) shows a flexible, Notion-like block architecture within Linear's document surface.
  • Floating "Ask AI" bar: Elevated, pill-shaped, persistently docked at the thumb zone, turning AI assistance into an omnipresent, low-friction entry point rather than a hidden feature.
  • Minimal top toolbar: Icon-only share/comment/overflow cluster keeps the canvas clean while still surfacing collaboration (commenting) and export (share) as first-class actions.
  • Dual input modalities: Microphone icon alongside the AI text field offers voice-driven querying, accommodating different capture contexts (e.g., hands-busy scenarios).

screens.name: Linear - Adding a code block - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
• Productivity and knowledge-management apps that need to support mixed content types (text, lists, code, media) in a single flexible canvas.
  • Developer-facing tools where technical content (code, logs, configs) must be displayed with proper formatting inline with prose.
  • Apps introducing an AI assistant where you want adoption to be frictionless, embedding it in an existing trusted affordance like the search bar.
  • Any long-form content screen where maximizing reading/writing space by minimizing top-level chrome improves user focus.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, block-editor approach for casual consumer apps where users expect simpler, single-purpose note-taking without code or technical formatting overhead.
  • Not suitable for screens requiring frequent structured data entry (e.g., forms) - the freeform nature works against rigid validation or guided input needs.
  • If the primary user base is non-technical, embedding code-block tooling (language selectors, syntax highlighting) adds unnecessary complexity and visual noise.
  • A persistent multi-icon bottom bar can feel cluttered on smaller screens or when the app already has a tab bar, risking redundant or competing navigation zones.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for engineers, product managers, and technical writers who need to jot down quick personal to-dos alongside technical reference material (like code snippets) without leaving their primary workspace. The juxtaposition of a mundane to-do list and a JavaScript function speaks directly to the dual nature of a product/engineering professional's day: personal task management intermixed with technical problem-solving.

Psychologically, the sparse top bar and distraction-free body exploit the focus/flow principle: fewer visual interruptions mean lower cognitive load, which is critical for technical audiences doing deep work. The persistent AI/search bar taps into the availability heuristic: knowing help is always one tap away reduces anxiety about losing a thought or having to search elsewhere, encouraging continuous capture rather than deferred organization.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unified block editor: Seamlessly blends plain text, bulleted lists, and executable-looking code blocks in one scrollable document, avoiding context-switching between a notes app and a code viewer.
  • Inline language-aware code block: The dedicated "JavaScript" dropdown and syntax highlighting inside the note signal that Linear treats technical documentation as a first-class citizen, not an afterthought.
  • Persistent multi-modal input bar: Combining search, AI chat, voice dictation, and quick-compose into one fixed footer reduces the number of taps/screens needed to add or find information.
  • Minimal chrome, maximum canvas: The top bar is reduced to four icons, maximizing vertical real estate for content (a hallmark of tools designed for sustained focus work).
  • "Ask AI" as an ambient utility: Rather than a separate AI screen, assistance is embedded directly into the same input affordance as search, lowering the activation energy to use AI contextually while writing.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Enabling & Disabling 5
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any application requiring users to switch between distinct "environments" or "contexts," such as:

  • Crypto wallets or DeFi dashboards managing multi-chain assets.

  • Developer tools requiring switching between Production, Staging, and Development API environments.

  • Enterprise software allowing users to switch between different organizational tenants or workspaces.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this level of technical granularity and terminology for mainstream, non-technical consumer apps where the underlying infrastructure (like which specific blockchain is being used) should be abstracted away entirely. For a beginner-friendly fintech app, exposing "RPC networks" and "Chain IDs" directly would cause significant confusion and anxiety; the network switching should ideally happen silently in the background.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets Web3 developers, crypto power-users, and DeFi enthusiasts who interact with multiple blockchain ecosystems (L1s and L2s) regularly. The psychological driver here is control and trust: users need certainty regarding which network their assets and transactions are currently routed through, as switching networks incorrectly can result in lost funds or failed transactions.

By offering granular network management (including custom RPC addition via the "+" button), the design caters to the crypto-native ethos of decentralization and user sovereignty over infrastructure choices, rather than locking users into a single, curated blockchain experience.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Mainnet/Testnet Segregation: Isolating test networks behind a specific tab acts as a crucial safety rail, reducing the cognitive load and risk of a user accidentally trying to send real funds on a test network or vice versa.

  • Iconography for Rapid Scanning: Each network utilizes a distinct, colorful brand icon (Avalanche's red triangle, BNB's yellow diamond) allowing users to visually scan and identify chains faster than reading text alone.

  • Developer-Centric Utility: The presence of "Localhost 8545" alongside major public testnets demonstrates a feature set that caters not just to end-users but to the developer community building on the platform.

  • Persistent Bottom Tab Bar: Even within this deep settings/utility screen, the main app navigation (Home, Browser, Swap, Activity, Wallet) remains accessible, maintaining orientation within the larger app ecosystem.

screens.name: Coinbase Wallet Enabling & Disabling 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for advanced/technical configuration screens where users must input several interdependent, structured technical parameters (API keys, server endpoints, network configs, webhook URLs). It's ideal for settings buried under an "Advanced" or "Developer" section, aimed at a self-selected audience who already understands the domain vocabulary.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this bare-bones, label-only approach for mainstream consumer-facing forms or for any field where mistakes carry irreversible/financial consequences without added support (such raw forms lack inline validation, tooltips, or format hints, which is risky when a wrong RPC URL or Chain ID could break a wallet connection or route funds to the wrong chain). Add real-time chain validation, matching-network warnings, and contextual help before shipping this pattern to less technical audiences.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets technically sophisticated crypto users (developers, DeFi power-users, and multi-chain traders) who need to connect their wallet to networks not natively supported (testnets, new L2s, private chains). These users are motivated by control and flexibility, and they possess enough technical literacy to source an RPC URL and Chain ID independently.

The psychological driver here is trust and precision: a single incorrect Chain ID or RPC URL could result in failed transactions or exposure to a malicious/incorrect network, so the form's stripped-down, no-nonsense presentation signals "this is a serious technical operation" and implicitly encourages the user to double-check each value before saving.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Task-ordered field sequence: Fields are arranged in the exact logical order needed to define a chain (identity → connection → validation ID → currency → explorer), reducing cognitive load for a technically dense task.

  • Smart defaults/prefill: Populating the form with real, working values for an existing network (Base) rather than empty placeholders lowers the barrier for users editing or duplicating a known configuration.

  • Single responsibility per field: Each text field maps to exactly one on-chain parameter, avoiding combined/ambiguous inputs that could cause malformed network configs.

  • Clear optionality flag: Explicitly labeling the block explorer field as optional manages expectations and prevents unnecessary friction/blocking.

screens.name: Cleo Reviewing & Rating 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when introducing a new gamified feature, challenge, or habit-tracking module inside an existing app (especially for financial wellness, fitness, or productivity products where users need convincing before opting into a commitment (e).g., a savings challenge, workout streak, or reading goal). It works well as a feature-spotlight interstitial reached via a tab or nudge, not necessarily as first-run onboarding.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, bold-typography sales-page style for features that are frequently revisited or purely utilitarian (e.g., settings, account info) since the emotional build-up would feel exhausting on repeat views. Also avoid mock "success state" previews if the feature is unlikely to produce quick wins in reality, overpromising a completed streak/savings result can create disappointment and erode trust if actual usage rarely matches the idealized preview.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets financially stressed, habit-driven spenders (Cleo's core Gen Z/young millennial demographic) who respond better to playful, meme-literate coaching than to spreadsheet-style budgeting tools. The screen leverages several psychological triggers:

  • Loss/shame framing ("vices," "finally"): subtly signals the user's current spending is a problem, creating motivation to act.

  • Vicarious success priming: showing a completed 21-day streak taps into modeling/observational learning ("if the example did it, I can too)."

  • Micro-reward anticipation: the "$85" savings figure and celebratory emoji give a concrete, near-term payoff that feels achievable rather than abstract.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Functional preview instead of static illustration: Showing an actual mock habit-tracker card with a progress bar and streak status lets users instantly understand the mechanic before opting in, lowering cognitive friction and hesitation.

  • Pre-completed social proof state: The example shown is "Day 21 of 21: on track" (a fully successful, completed cycle) priming the user with a vivid picture of success rather than an ambiguous empty state.

  • Simulated encouragement bubbles: Overlaying chat-style affirmations onto the preview card lets the product "demo" its own positive-reinforcement/gamification loop within a static onboarding screen.

  • Single, unambiguous CTA: One large "Start 🚀" button removes decision paralysis and funnels 100% of intent toward challenge activation.

screens.name: Cleo Reviewing & Rating 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when introducing a new, potentially unfamiliar feature inside an already-installed app, especially one that requires behavior change (habit formation, financial discipline, fitness, learning). It's ideal for:

  • Feature-specific onboarding accessed via a tab or menu item, not the app's initial first-run experience.

  • Features that benefit from framing as a "challenge" or game to increase motivation and follow-through.

  • Situations where you want to set expectations across 2 (4 distinct sub-capabilities before the user dives in).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern for:

  • Frequently revisited screens: once a user has seen this explainer, it should not reappear on every visit to the Habits tab (it should convert into the actual challenge-creation flow going forward).

  • Features that are self-explanatory or icon-driven, where an explainer screen would feel like unnecessary friction before task completion.

  • Serious/regulated financial contexts (e.g., loan applications, tax tools) where playful, game-like language ("vice," "challenge") could undermine trust or feel tonally inappropriate.

  • Users who are already power users of the app: repeated exposure to marketing-style value props can feel patronizing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets everyday consumers: likely younger millennials/Gen Z users of a neobank or budgeting app (who struggle with impulse spending and are more motivated by gamified, competitive framing than by traditional budgeting spreadsheets or dry financial advice).

Psychologically, it leverages several triggers: loss aversion and self-competition (challenging your "vice" implies a battle with a personal flaw you want to overcome), goal-gradient effect (tracking savings growth visually motivates continued engagement), and curiosity/self-insight (the "Spot trends" card promises revealing, possibly uncomfortable truths about spending habits, which is intrinsically compelling). Framing money management as a game or "challenge" lowers the psychological barrier to engaging with a topic (personal finance) that often produces shame or avoidance.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Emotionally-charged reframing of a mundane task: Saving money is rebranded as a "challenge" against one's own "vice," tapping into gamification and self-improvement psychology rather than dry budgeting language.

  • Three-card benefit breakdown maps to a full behavioral loop (choose challenge → track progress → gain insight), giving users a mental model of the entire feature before they commit to using it.

  • Non-blocking onboarding: Persistent tab bar and back arrow ensure this educational screen never feels like a forced gate, preserving user autonomy and reducing bounce/frustration.

  • Consistent thematic iconography: The checkered flag emoji on the CTA button echoes the "challenge/race" metaphor set up in the headline, creating narrative and visual cohesion end-to-end.

  • High-contrast, bold typography immediately communicates energy and confidence, differentiating the feature from typically dry financial UI.

screens.name: Cleo Reviewing & Rating 3
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when trying to convert an infrequent, low-motivation task (financial reviews, health check-ins, journaling) into a recurring habit. It's ideal for apps with a defined cadence (e.g., twice weekly) where you want to visually preview upcoming touchpoints and reward consistency. Works well anywhere a "streak" or "path" metaphor can be layered onto a functional task to boost return visits.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for one-time or purely transactional tasks where a recurring cadence doesn't apply (the locked future nodes and streak framing would feel forced or confusing). Also avoid overly playful/gamified framing ("expose your vices") in contexts serving highly sensitive financial situations (e.g., debt collection, financial hardship tools) where a lighthearted tone could feel tone-deaf or trivializing.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:

Psychologically, the pattern exploits the IKEA effect (increased attachment to a product you helped create) and endowment effect: once a user has spent time dragging, pinching, and placing a sticker on "their" card, they feel more ownership and are more likely to complete the card order and share the result socially (driving organic referral/virality, especially if a "share your card" moment follows).

The low-friction, reversible nature (Start Over/Skip) also appeals to commitment-phobic users or those in a time-constrained banking flow, ensuring customization doesn't become a drop-off point in conversion funnels.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live, photorealistic card canvas: Users see their exact physical card updating in real time, closing the gap between digital customization and the tangible end product, building emotional investment before the card is even ordered.
  • Gesture-based direct manipulation: Pinch-to-resize/rotate on the sticker mirrors native OS photo-editing gestures, eliminating the need for sliders or numeric inputs.
  • Dashed guide boxes: Subtle overlay boundaries communicate safe zones (e.g., avoiding the chip or logo) without needing explicit copy, preventing user error before it happens.
  • Minimal floating toolbar: Three icon-only tools (sticker, emoji, text) keep the creative surface uncluttered while still offering multiple customization modes.
  • Dual escape hatches ("Skip" and "Start over"): Lowers perceived risk and commitment, encouraging experimentation.
  • Theatrical dark background: Pure black canvas functions as a spotlight, elevating the perceived premium-ness of the card product.

screens.name: Revolut Editing & Updating 5
screens.whereToUse: Use this live-preview-plus-inline-controls pattern whenever a product allows deep personalization of a physical or shareable digital artifact (e).g., custom debit/credit cards, phone case designers, merchandise print-on-demand tools, avatar/profile customization, or theme editors. It's ideal when the end result is something users will show off or carry physically, as the emotional payoff of "creation" drives loyalty and word-of-mouth.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy, real-time customization pattern for utilitarian or transactional flows where speed matters more than expression (e.g., core onboarding KYC, payment confirmation). It also fails in contexts where users have low intrinsic motivation to personalize (e.g., B2B admin tools) - the extra taps and decision fatigue from font/color selection would only add friction without emotional payoff. If bandwidth or device performance is limited, complex live-rendering previews can introduce lag that breaks the tactile magic this pattern relies on.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, design-conscious fintech users (Gen Z / Millennials) who view their debit card as a personal style statement and social artifact, not just a payment tool. Revolut's target audience skews toward digitally native, brand-aware consumers who appreciate Canva-like creative control and are likely to photograph/share a uniquely designed card on social media (indirect viral marketing).

Psychologically, the screen leverages the IKEA effect: users who invest personal creative effort into designing their own card feel greater ownership and attachment to the resulting product, increasing satisfaction and reducing the likelihood of switching to a competitor bank. The immediate visual feedback loop also taps into flow state principles, keeping users engaged in playful iteration.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live WYSIWYG Card Preview: Users see their exact customization rendered on a photorealistic card mockup in real time, eliminating any ambiguity about the final physical product.

  • Dashed Placement Guides: Subtle dashed-line bounding boxes indicate safe zones for text/graphics placement, teaching users the constraints without needing explicit instructional copy.

  • Inline Font Switching Carousel: Circular "Aa" swatches let users preview different typefaces at a glance before committing, turning a typically tedious settings list into a tactile, visual choice.

  • Low-Friction Exit via "Skip": Placing a Skip button in the top-right respects users who don't want to invest time in personalization, preventing this optional flourish from becoming a blocking step.

  • Persistent Keyboard Context: Keeping the keyboard open and cursor active removes extra taps, streamlining the text-input micro-interaction.

screens.name: Revolut Editing & Updating 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern immediately before a user finalizes and submits user-generated content for moderation or publication (such as custom emoji/sticker packs, marketplace listings, community posts, or profile customization assets). It's ideal whenever a platform has strict content policies (IP, legal, brand safety) and wants to reduce rejection rates and moderation overhead by educating users proactively at the point of highest attention.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when guidelines are overly long or legally dense (a bottom sheet with a short scrollable list works for 5-8 concise rules, but a full compliance policy should link out to a dedicated help/FAQ page instead). Also avoid presenting this as a blocking modal that cannot be dismissed if the user needs to reference it repeatedly during creation; in that case, a persistent inline helper or collapsible section embedded directly in the creation flow would serve users better than an interruptive overlay shown only post-completion.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of user-generated content (UGC) platforms: such as custom sticker, avatar, or theme marketplaces (where submissions are reviewed by a moderation team or automated system before being published or monetized). The audience is typically non-technical, creative users who may not be familiar with IP law, platform policy, or content moderation standards.

Psychologically, the screen leverages expectation-setting and loss-aversion: by clearly stating what will cause rejection before submission, it reduces the frustration and perceived unfairness a user would feel if their work were rejected without warning. This preemptive transparency also protects the platform, shifting some responsibility onto the user ("you were warned") while building trust through clarity.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual timing: Surfacing guidelines right after content creation (as evidenced by the "Looking good?" title behind the sheet) rather than before, ensures the rules are read at the exact moment of highest relevance (right before submission).

  • Bottom sheet over full page: Using a dismissible bottom sheet instead of a full-screen interstitial preserves the user's context and progress, reducing perceived friction while still delivering critical compliance information.

  • Icon-led scanning pattern: Repeating a simple info icon next to each bullet creates a predictable visual anchor, letting users skim seven rules in seconds rather than reading dense paragraphs.

  • Framing as help, not punishment: The "To avoid rejections" framing reduces the adversarial feel of a restrictions list by tying it to user benefit (successful approval).

screens.name: Craft - Filtering entries - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when a lightweight, in-context configuration (filters, sort options, quick settings) needs to be exposed without fully navigating away from the parent content (especially in document/database hybrid tools, table views, or any list/collection screen on mobile where screen real estate is limited). It's ideal when the action is transient, low-stakes, and benefits from spatial continuity with the source screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for complex, multi-field configurations that require more vertical space or involve several interdependent decisions (a bottom sheet can feel cramped and force excessive scrolling). It's also unsuitable for first-time or non-technical users unfamiliar with database query semantics ("Any Of," property/condition/value), who may need friendlier, more guided filter builders with natural-language framing instead of raw field names.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets power users, product designers, and knowledge workers who use Craft not just for journaling but for structured project management, tracking design assets, research, and specs inside the same tool they write briefs in. The filter modal's terse, technical labeling ("Any Of," "Category") assumes familiarity with database-style querying, appealing to users coming from tools like Notion, Airtable, or Coda who expect this level of control.

Psychologically, the sheet leverages recognition over recall (standard dropdown + value pattern) and reduces perceived risk via easy delete/close actions, encouraging users to experiment with filtering their collections without fear of making unrecoverable mistakes.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual dimming instead of full navigation: The background document remains visible but de-emphasized, maintaining spatial continuity and reducing the cognitive cost of switching contexts to configure a filter.
  • Compound filter builder pattern: Property dropdown ("Category") + Condition dropdown ("Any Of") + value field, mirroring familiar spreadsheet/database logic (Notion/Airtable-style) that power users instantly recognize.
  • Low-commitment UI: A visible trash icon next to an unconfigured filter row and a prominent close (X) make it clear this action is easily reversible, lowering the anxiety of experimentation.
  • Seamless doc-to-database fusion: Embedding a full relational table with filtering directly inside a freeform text document is a standout structural decision that differentiates Craft from simple note apps.

screens.name: Craft - Filtering entries - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Any app that embeds structured/tabular data inside a flexible document or note (hybrid doc+database tools).
  • Filter/query builders where users need to chain field → operator → value without a full-page context switch.
  • Power-user configuration flows where operator semantics (Is, Is Not, Is Empty, etc.) must be unambiguous and quickly scannable.
  • Mobile contexts where preserving background context behind a scrim improves orientation during multi-step tasks.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense operator-list approach for casual, non-technical end users who have no prior exposure to database filtering (the terminology (Is Not Empty, Any Of) can be confusing without onboarding or tooltips).
  • Not suitable when only one or two filter operators are ever needed; a simpler toggle or segmented control would reduce overhead.
  • Avoid stacking multiple overlapping sheets/popovers (as partially seen here) on small screens, since it can create ambiguous tap targets and visual clutter.
  • Don't use on flows requiring frequent repeated filtering by non-expert audiences (a saved-views/preset pattern would serve better than rebuilding filters each time).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets power users, designers, and knowledge workers who use Craft's database/collection blocks to organize research, design systems, or project data (e.g., the "Web3 Platform Landing" design doc shown). These users are comfortable with Notion/Airtable-style filtering mental models and expect granular control (Is, Is Not, Is Empty, Any Of, None Of) without leaving their writing environment.

Psychologically, the design reduces intimidation around "database" functionality by wrapping it in the same soft, editorial visual language as the rest of the app, lowering the barrier for writers who aren't naturally data-oriented but need lightweight structured views (e.g., tracking design components by category).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contextual dimming, not full navigation: the sheet overlays the document rather than replacing it, preserving spatial context and letting users see the table and column they're filtering.
  • Single-select radio-style list disguised as a simple menu: using a checkmark instead of explicit radio buttons keeps the UI visually quiet and editorial rather than clinical.
  • Layered filter construction (field → operator → value): breaking a complex query into sequential, digestible taps reduces cognitive load on a small screen.
  • Consistent corner-radius language: the large rounded corners of the sheet echo the rounded chips in the Category column, unifying the visual system across modal and content layers.
  • Document-embedded database: blending structured collections directly into a prose document view is a distinctive differentiator from typical note apps, reinforcing Craft's "doc, not database row" philosophy even inside a data-table context.

screens.name: Craft - Filtering entries - Screen 8
screens.whereToUse:
• Any app blending document/content authoring with structured data (tables, databases, CRMs embedded in notes).
  • Settings or query-builder overlays where you want to preserve background context via dimming rather than full navigation.
  • Filter/sort configuration for lists, tables, or kanban boards needing composable, stackable conditions.
  • Productivity tools targeting both casual and power users who need an approachable entry point into advanced functionality.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Simple apps with small, static lists where filtering adds unnecessary complexity and cognitive overhead.
  • Contexts where users need to compare the modal content against multiple background rows simultaneously (a bottom sheet may obscure too much of the table on small screens).
  • Mobile-only experiences with very limited vertical space, where a full-screen filter builder might work better than a partial sheet.
  • Novice-first products where even simplified query language ("None Of") could still confuse non-technical audiences without additional tooltips.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets power users, designers, and PMs

Psychologically, the modal leverages progressive disclosure to avoid overwhelming casual users with query-building complexity, while still satisfying power users' need for control. The soft, rounded, card-like filter UI reduces the cognitive "fear" often associated with database query interfaces.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background with visible context: The underlying document and table remain faintly visible behind the modal, preserving spatial orientation so users don't lose their place.
  • Composable filter builder: Property → Condition → Value is a clean three-part mental model that scales from simple to complex queries, with "Add Filter" enabling AND/OR stacking.
  • Inline delete affordance: A trash icon sits directly next to the filter row, letting users remove a condition without navigating away.
  • Database inside a document: Embedding a structured, filterable table within a free-flowing editorial page blurs the line between notes and databases, a signature Craft capability.
  • Low-friction entry point: The chip-style "Category" and "None Of" controls look tappable and inviting rather than form-like, reducing intimidation around a technically complex feature.

screens.name: Craft - Filtering entries - Screen 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when an app needs to let users attach structured, filterable metadata (tags, status, category) to rows/items without forcing a full navigation change. It's ideal for:

  • Hybrid document/database apps (Notion, Airtable, Coda, Craft) where tables are embedded inline in long-form content.
  • Mobile contexts where screen real estate is limited, so a bottom sheet is preferable to a full dropdown or new screen.
  • Multi-select tagging systems where visual color-coding aids fast recognition (project boards, CRM status, content categorization).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • The underlying data model doesn't benefit from tagging/categorization, adding database features to simple linear notes can clutter the writing experience and contradict a minimalist brand promise.
  • Users need to select from very long lists of categories (50+) - a bottom sheet with simple checkboxes becomes unwieldy; a searchable dropdown or full-screen picker would scale better.
  • On small screens where table columns already require horizontal scrolling, adding a half-screen sheet on top may over-complicate an already dense view; consider a dedicated edit screen instead.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets power users, designers, and PMs who use Craft not just for linear notes but as a lightweight project/database tool (professionals who've graduated from plain note apps and want Notion/Airtable-like structure without leaving the simplicity of a writing app). The psychological trigger here is mastery and control: giving users database-grade organization (filters, tags, structured columns) inside a tool whose brand promise is elegant writing taps into a sense of having "the best of both worlds" without context switching.

The quick-tag bottom sheet exploits the low-friction categorization principle (by reducing tagging to a single tap and checkbox selection, Craft encourages users to actually maintain metadata consistently, which compounds in value as collections grow (fast search, filtering later)).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Unified Doc + Database model: Freeform editorial text and a structured table coexist in the same scrollable canvas, reinforcing Craft's "every note is a document" philosophy rather than siloing data into a separate app section.
  • Contextual Bottom Sheet for Tagging: Tapping a Category cell surfaces a non-blocking bottom sheet with checkboxes, allowing multi-select tagging without a full-screen navigation detour (ideal for quick, in-flow metadata editing on mobile).
  • Color-coded Taxonomy Chips: Each category has a dedicated pastel color consistently applied both in the table and in the selection sheet, giving instant visual pattern-matching and reducing cognitive load when scanning rows.
  • Partial-height Scrim Overlay: The background table remains dimly visible beneath the sheet, preserving spatial context and letting users confirm which row/column they are editing before committing.
  • Inline "Add" and View Switcher: The "Table ▾" dropdown and "Add" button sit directly above the data, giving quick access to view-type switching (e.g., Table/Board/Gallery) and row creation without extra chrome.

screens.name: Brex - Limit policy - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for personal finance or allowance-style dashboards where a user needs an at-a-glance balance, a prominent primary action, and a scannable transaction history (e).g., corporate card apps, prepaid/allowance cards, benefits or stipend platforms, or any B2B tool where an individual operates within an admin-set budget. The card-peeking-from-wallet header treatment works well whenever the product's core object is a payment card and reinforces brand recall every time the user returns to the home screen.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this layout for admin/finance-manager personas who need org-wide, multi-employee visibility (this single-card, single-limit framing would feel reductive and force excessive drill-down. It's also unsuitable for apps with high-frequency, high-volume transaction logs (e.g., consumer banking with hundreds of daily transactions), where a denser table/list with filtering would outperform this card-style feed. Finally, the heavy use of masked/blurred placeholder values in real production should be replaced by genuinely dynamic data) if balances are frequently stale or slow to load, this calm, confident UI could backfire and erode trust.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees and card-holding staff at companies using Brex for corporate spend (not finance admins managing org-wide policy (that would show aggregate company spend, not "my" assigned limit)). The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Loss-aversion / budget anxiety reduction:
  • Autonomy and trust: giving employees direct visibility into their own limit and its governing policy fosters a sense of fairness and control rather than opaque corporate restriction.
  • Low cognitive load for frequent, quick checks: employees likely open this screen reflexively after a purchase to confirm it was captured correctly, so the design optimizes for glanceability over depth.
  • Social/professional accountability: the reimbursement status icons subtly nudge users to keep receipts and documentation current, as these are visible representations of compliance behavior.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Card-in-wallet visual metaphor: the overlapping dark header and white sheet mimic a physical card peeking out of a wallet, reinforcing brand familiarity through skeuomorphic cues without sacrificing a modern flat-design aesthetic.
  • Balance visibility toggle (eye icon): directly addresses the real-world privacy concern of viewing sensitive financial data on a phone in public.
  • Action embedded in the list: "Request reimbursement" is placed as the top row of the expenses feed rather than as a separate button or FAB, reducing visual clutter while keeping the action top-of-mind exactly where the user is scanning transactions.
  • Tri-icon status system: each expense row uses three small glyphs (payment method, receipt attached, approval) to compress complex state information into a compact, scannable visual language.
  • Policy transparency link: "View limit policy" proactively addresses the "why can't I spend more" friction point, reducing support tickets and building trust in the system's fairness.

screens.name: Brex - Limit policy - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app must surface conditional business rules or compliance policies that affect a user's next action (e).g., expense thresholds, approval workflows, SLA terms, or eligibility criteria. It's ideal for:

  • Finance/expense apps explaining receipt, approval, or spend-limit rules
  • HR apps explaining leave/benefits policy tiers
  • Any B2B SaaS surfacing admin-configured rules to end users in a scannable, read-only reference sheet
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, text-first format when the content needs to drive a decision or action in the moment (e).g., it's a poor fit for onboarding or urgent approval screens where a long scroll of static rules will cause abandonment. If the policy contains many categories or deeply nested exceptions, this flat list could become overwhelming; in that case, use an accordion or searchable FAQ structure instead. Also avoid this pattern if values are highly dynamic per-user; a static-feeling document can create false confidence if it isn't clearly tied to the user's specific role or entity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets employees submitting expenses or reimbursements who need to self-serve an answer to "what documentation do I need?" before or during a submission, reducing back-and-forth with finance teams. It also serves finance admins and founders who need to confirm what policy is currently enforced across the organization.

Psychologically, this leverages the need for certainty and procedural fairness: employees are more likely to comply with expense rules (receipts, memos) when the rationale and thresholds are transparent and easy to find, rather than hidden in a lengthy PDF handbook. Surfacing policy inline within the app (rather than requiring an email to HR/finance) also reduces perceived friction and builds trust that the system is self-consistent and automatable.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Threshold-based rule clarity: Dollar amounts are called out explicitly and repeatedly ($10, $50) so users never have to infer or calculate when a rule applies.
  • Consistent field pattern reuse: Every expense category (Card, Reimbursement, Travel) follows the identical Receipts/Itemized/Memos/Review template, reducing cognitive load as users scroll between sections.
  • Icon-led section anchors: Small glyphs next to each category name (card, reimbursement arrow, travel plane) aid quick visual scanning in a long, text-heavy scroll.
  • Dismiss-anywhere modal: The 'X' affordance communicates that this is a reference lookup, not a required step, minimizing friction and letting users return to their task instantly.

screens.name: Brex - Limit policy - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app needs to surface complex, rules-based, compliance-heavy information in a digestible format mid-flow (such as expense policies, insurance coverage details, terms of a loyalty program, or eligibility rules). It's ideal for:

  • Fintech/expense apps showing spend limits or approval thresholds
  • Insurance apps detailing coverage limits by category
  • Any scenario where a user needs quick reference info without leaving their current task (hence the modal treatment)
  • B2B SaaS admin-configured settings that end-users need to view (but not edit)
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this dense, text-heavy label/value layout when:

  • The target user is non-technical or policy is simple (in that case a short banner or tooltip would suffice instead of a full scrollable modal).
  • The information needs to be actionable/editable (this is a read-only view; if users need to request exceptions or edit values, a form-based pattern with inputs would be more appropriate).
  • Policy data changes frequently and must always be real-time accurate (static-feeling text blocks could become outdated and erode trust if not dynamically bound to the live policy engine).
  • On very small screens or low-literacy audiences, dense paragraphs of conditional rules may overwhelm rather than clarify; a progressive disclosure (accordion) per category might work better than one long scroll.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves employees and travelers at a company using Brex, specifically at the moment they are about to book travel or submit a meal/airline expense and want to self-check compliance before committing to a purchase. It also serves finance/admin teams indirectly by reducing manual review overhead (if employees can see thresholds up front, fewer out-of-policy expenses will be submitted unknowingly).

Psychologically, this screen leverages transparency to build trust and reduce anxiety. Corporate spend policies are often a source of friction and fear (will I get in trouble for this purchase?). By surfacing exact dollar thresholds and approval triggers in plain view, Brex reduces the cognitive load and uncertainty around spending, empowering employees to self-serve decisions rather than guessing or asking a manager.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-led category grouping: Each restriction category (Meals, Airline) has a distinct icon, making it a fast visual index for users to jump to the policy section relevant to their current expense.
  • Sticky contextual sectioning: The full-width gray divider bar for "Category and merchant restrictions" clearly separates general travel policy from itemized spending rules, aiding comprehension in a long scroll.
  • Label/value pattern: Bold field names paired with lighter gray descriptions create a spec-sheet readability pattern that scales well for dense regulatory content.
  • Modal "X" dismissal: Presenting policy as an overlay rather than a full page reinforces that this is supplementary reference information, letting users return instantly to their primary task (e.g., booking or expensing).
  • Footnote clarification: The "Notes" section proactively answers likely follow-up questions, reducing policy ambiguity and support tickets.

screens.name: Brex - Limit policy - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for any policy, terms, or rules reference that needs to be consulted mid-flow without abandoning the primary task (e.g., booking, checkout, form submission).
  • Ideal for B2B/enterprise tools where compliance, governance, or approval thresholds vary by category and need to be transparently communicated to reduce support tickets.
  • Appropriate when the content is read-only reference data that benefits from a repeatable, scannable structure (threshold tables, tiered pricing, eligibility rules).
  • Good fit for modal/sheet presentation when the content is supplementary to (but not part of) the main task flow (i.e., user needs to "peek and return").
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this dense, text-heavy layout for first-time users or onboarding contexts (it assumes familiarity with corporate expense terminology (e).g., "average daily rate," "review threshold") which could overwhelm novices without added tooltips.
  • Not suitable when policy data needs to be cross-referenced or compared across many variables simultaneously (a table/grid component would serve better than a long vertical scroll for power users doing side-by-side comparisons).
  • Don't use for content requiring frequent updates by the end user: this pattern is explicitly read-only; if editability is needed, a settings/form pattern is more appropriate.
  • Avoid on small screens without a search/jump mechanism if the policy list grows significantly longer than a few categories (currently it relies on manual scrolling, which won't scale well).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves employees actively booking travel or submitting expenses who need a fast answer to "will this purchase get flagged?" before they commit to a transaction. The psychological driver is anxiety reduction around compliance: employees fear submitting an expense that gets rejected or escalated, so having instant access to the exact dollar thresholds removes guesswork and builds confidence to book without hesitation.

For finance/admin teams, this screen is indirectly serving them too: by making policy self-service and transparent, it reduces the volume of "can I book this?" questions directed at finance, and decreases policy violations caused by ignorance rather than intent.

The underlying trigger is certainty and control: in expense management, uncertainty leads to either overly conservative spending (bad for productivity) or policy violations (bad for compliance). Surfacing exact numbers converts a vague corporate rule into a concrete, actionable data point.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Icon-anchored category headers: Small glyphs (car, bed, receipt) next to each section title give an instant visual anchor, letting users orient via iconography before reading text (useful for fast re-scanning).
  • Consistent threshold pattern across categories: Every spend category follows the identical "Review threshold → Through Brex Travel → Outside Brex Travel" structure, so once a user learns the pattern for flights, they can navigate car/lodging sections without relearning the mental model.
  • Explicit "N/A" states: Rather than omitting a field when it doesn't apply, Brex explicitly states "N/A." This removes ambiguity about whether data failed to load versus genuinely not applying.
  • Granular geographic thresholds: Lodging limits are broken out per high-cost city (e.g., New York) vs. "all other locations," reflecting real-world cost-of-living variance rather than a flat blanket number (a sign of policy sophistication translated faithfully into UI).
  • Non-interactive, dismiss-only modal: No edit controls reinforce that this is a trust/compliance reference layer, not a configuration screen, keeping the employee's mental model clear (I check, I don't change).
