screens.name: Figma - About - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this grouped-list settings pattern when:

  • Designing account/profile management screens for productivity or B2B SaaS tools where clarity and speed outrank visual flourish.

  • You need to support multi-tenant or multi-organization switching (the Teams and organizations block with checkmark is ideal for this).

  • The settings screen is a secondary, modal-style destination accessed frequently but briefly.

  • You want to expose both routine settings (Notifications) and power-user utilities (Shake to report) in the same screen without overwhelming the primary nav.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this flat, text-only grouped list when:

  • The target audience is less technical and would benefit from icons, illustrations, or more visual scaffolding to aid recognition.

  • The settings surface needs to highlight monetization or upsell opportunities (this minimal style under-communicates urgency or value and would bury a paywall/upgrade CTA).

  • Account switching involves many organizations (10+), where a flat list without search/filter would become unwieldy and require a dedicated picker screen instead.

  • Destructive actions like "Log out" need extra friction (e.g., shared/kiosk devices) - this pattern provides no confirmation step, which could cause accidental logouts in those contexts.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves designers, developers, and team administrators who need to quickly verify their identity, switch between organizational contexts, or manage account-level preferences without leaving their current design flow. The target audience values efficiency and predictability over delight (hence the stripped-down, native-feeling UI).

Psychologically, the modal "Done" pattern (vs. a stacked push navigation) reinforces that this is a transient, task-focused detour from the main canvas-first experience, not a core destination, respecting the user's primary goal of returning to their design work as fast as possible.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grouped list architecture: Logical sectioning (Identity → Teams → General → Help) mirrors native iOS settings conventions, minimizing the learning curve.

  • Checkmark for active context: The checkmark next to "JudySmith" under Teams communicates current workspace context at a glance, critical for multi-org users who switch between client/team accounts frequently.

  • Chevron affordance discipline: Only navigable rows get a chevron, creating a reliable visual grammar for tap behavior across the entire list.

  • Isolated destructive action: "Log out" is styled identically to neutral items (no red text, no icon) and positioned mid-list rather than buried or over-emphasized, balancing discoverability with accident prevention.

  • Power-user utility surfaced early: "Shake to report" toggle exposes an advanced debugging/feedback mechanism directly in top-level settings, reflecting Figma's developer-friendly culture.

screens.name: Figma - About - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for terminal settings screens that combine static diagnostic metadata with legal/compliance links and a single destructive action. It's ideal for app "About" pages, developer tools, or any B2B/productivity software where support teams will ask users for version/build numbers. The physical separation technique for destructive actions is reusable anywhere a low-frequency, high-consequence action (delete, logout, deactivate) needs to be present but de-prioritized.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this minimal approach if the destructive action (account deletion) carries significant consequences that warrant more friction (here it's only one tap away from a confirmation dialog, which may be too lightweight for highly sensitive consumer apps (e).g., banking). Also avoid this bare-bones layout for consumer-facing apps where users may not understand technical jargon like "Build" numbers; those audiences benefit more from help links or a support chat shortcut rather than raw version strings.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This screen serves Figma's core audience of designers and developers who may need build/version numbers for bug reporting or support tickets, as well as compliance-conscious users seeking legal documentation or account deletion rights (a requirement under GDPR/CCPA). The psychological design intent is to build trust through transparency (clear version/build data) while discouraging impulsive account deletion through visual de-emphasis and separation, without blocking the user's right to do so.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Spatial isolation of destructive action: "Delete account" is separated from the Legal/Version group by a large gap, acting as a non-verbal confirmation pattern that reduces accidental mis-taps.

  • Dark header, light body contrast: The near-black header anchors global navigation context visually, distinguishing chrome from content in a way consistent with Figma's branded dark-UI identity.

  • Non-interactive rows clearly marked: Version and Build rows have no chevron, correctly signaling they are copy-only/display-only data, avoiding user frustration from tapping dead rows.

  • Minimalist information architecture: Only four rows exist on the entire screen (an intentional reduction of an "About" screen to its legal and diagnostic essentials).

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
• Use this pattern for schema editing or settings configuration where a single object (like a column, field, or variable) has multiple distinct properties (Name, Type, Constraints) that need to be edited in one view.
  • Ideal for No-code/Low-code platforms where you need to translate complex technical configurations (data types) into simple, mobile-friendly toggles and list selectors.
  • Effective when you need to provide contextual safety nets, such as combining an editing action with a destructive delete action in a logically separated way.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern if the "Field Type" selection requires extensive sub-configuration (e.g., complex Formula fields or Linked Records with multiple options) that cannot be summarized in a single helper line; this would require a dedicated sub-screen rather than an inline toggle.
  • Do not use this dense, stacked form layout for simple, single-input tasks (like just renaming a file), as the heavy sectioning would feel bureaucratic and slow down a simple interaction.
  • Not suitable for public-facing consumer apps where users are unfamiliar with technical "Field Type" terminology; this density works for professional tools but could alienate casual users.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves Operations Managers, Project Managers, and Database Builders who need the flexibility to modify their business logic (the "schema") while on the go, perhaps during a meeting where a new business requirement arises.

The psychological trigger here is Mastery and Control. By exposing granular field-type controls directly in a mobile modal, Airtable reinforces the user's identity as a "builder" or "admin" of their own system, rather than just a passive data-entry clerk. The simplicity of the toggle and dropdown reduces the intimidation factor often associated with "editing a database," making the user feel capable of making structural changes without engineering help.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Type-Specific Contextual Help: The dynamic helper text ("Useful for checklists.") that changes based on the selected Field Type acts as an inline tooltip, educating users on database schema design without leaving the current screen.
  • Grouped Table Hierarchy: Using distinct card groupings for Name, Description, and Type creates clear visual rhythm and reduces the perceived complexity of editing a database schema on a small screen.
  • Isolated Destructive Action: Placing "Delete Field" in its own distinct section at the bottom, separated by whitespace/dividers from the editing fields, prevents accidental data deletion via fat-fingering.
  • Icon-based Type Identification: Using a colored icon (green circle) next to the field type name allows users to quickly visually scan and identify field types across the app, creating a consistent visual language for data types.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Apply this pattern whenever a user-initiated action is irreversible and affects data beyond the immediate view (e.g., deleting a column/field, removing a user from a shared workspace, deleting a database table, or archiving a project with dependent records). It's especially valuable in collaborative, multi-user tools where one person's action can silently affect others' data.

Use the inline expansion technique (Checkbox toggle appearing within the Field Type row) for simple configuration options to avoid unnecessary drill-down navigation, reserving full-screen or secondary modals only for field types requiring multiple settings.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy-handed confirmation flow for low-stakes or easily reversible actions (e.g., toggling a UI preference, hiding a column temporarily) - doing so would create unnecessary friction and training users to blindly dismiss dialogs ("confirmation fatigue"), which weakens the pattern's effectiveness when it truly matters.

Also avoid echoing overly long or technical field names verbatim in a confirmation button if space is constrained; truncate gracefully or use a secondary text input requiring the user to type the field name for extremely high-risk deletions (e.g., deleting an entire base).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations managers, database administrators, and power users who are actively structuring or maintaining a shared Airtable base (often under time pressure or while collaborating with a team that depends on data integrity). Because Airtable fields can hold months of accumulated team data, the psychological stakes of an accidental deletion are high (irreversible data loss affecting colleagues).

The design leans on loss aversion and friction-as-safety principles: by making the deletion path require multiple deliberate taps and explicit acknowledgment of data loss, Airtable reduces anxiety for cautious users while still allowing expert users to move through quickly once they've internalized the pattern.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Explicit consequence messaging: The dialog doesn't just ask "are you sure?" - it educates the user on exactly what will be lost (data across every record), reducing the chance of regret-driven support tickets.
  • Named re-confirmation: The button reads 'Delete "Visited?"' rather than a generic "Delete," reinforcing which specific field is about to be destroyed and guarding against misclicks when editing multiple fields in a session.
  • Inline type configuration: The Checkbox toggle and description appear directly within the Field Type row, minimizing navigation depth for simple field types.
  • Spatial separation of destructive action: Placing "Delete field" far below the primary editable fields, with a divider and trash icon, uses visual hierarchy to signal danger and reduce accidental taps.

screens.name: Airtable - Hiding fields - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
• Schema/configuration screens in no-code or low-code platforms where users define data structure (e.g., database builders, form builders, CRM customization panels).
  • Any settings list where each item represents a configurable "type" that benefits from a live visual preview rather than a text-only description.
  • Admin panels that need to onboard non-technical users to technical concepts through embedded contextual video and analogy-driven microcopy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Simple, flat forms with a small, fixed number of fields, adding live previews and type pickers would be over-engineering for a one-time contact form, for instance.
  • Screens targeting highly technical users (e.g., developers using a SQL schema editor) who may find the playful icon/analogy treatment patronizing and prefer dense, code-like table editors instead.
  • Contexts where field reordering has no real functional impact (e.g., static reports), since drag handles would add unnecessary complexity.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations leads, project managers, and "citizen developers" who build business systems without formal engineering backgrounds. These users need to configure data structures but are often unfamiliar with database terminology like "schema" or "field types." The design leans on recognition over recall (visual previews, icons, color coding) and analogy-based education (the blueprint metaphor) to build confidence and reduce the intimidation factor typically associated with database configuration tools.

The locked primary field and drag-to-reorder handles also speak to power users who need structural control and customization once they're comfortable, supporting Airtable's dual audience of beginners and advanced builders.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Live mini-previews per field type: Each row visually simulates its data type (progress bar, numeric input, file icons) instead of relying on text labels alone, dramatically improving scannability and comprehension.
  • Color-coded type icons: Each field type has a distinct icon/color combo (blue "A" for text, orange "#" for number, pink paperclip for attachment) creating a quick visual taxonomy that scales well as tables grow to dozens of fields.
  • Locked primary field affordance: The padlock icon on "Location" clearly communicates an immutable schema rule without needing a modal or error message.
  • Embedded contextual video/coach mark: Using a tappable video thumbnail inside the explanatory banner caters to varied learning styles (read vs. watch) and is dismissible via the "X" for repeat users.
  • Persistent "Add a new field" CTA: Anchored at the bottom of the list, it keeps the primary creation action always accessible regardless of scroll depth.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 8
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you want to increase engagement with an inherently infrequent or utilitarian check-in task (bill payments, compliance checks, health screenings, security audits). It's effective when the "good" outcome (zero violations, zero debt, clean record) can be framed as a countable streak worth protecting.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this approach when the underlying subject matter is severe or anxiety-driving for a meaningful subset of users (e.g., users who already have violations may feel shamed by streak-breaking framing). It can also feel tonally mismatched in serious legal, medical, or financial contexts where playful gamification undermines trust or trivializes real consequences.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This targets everyday vehicle owners in markets with digital traffic-fine (challan) lookup services, likely India given the terminology. The design leans heavily on loss aversion (don't break the streak) and status/social comparison (being among the "select few") to drive repeat check-ins on what would otherwise be a low-frequency, utilitarian task.

By gamifying a compliance record, the product increases session frequency and retention, turning a purely functional government-data lookup into an emotionally engaging ritual similar to fitness or habit-tracking apps.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Streak Gamification: Reframes a negative-avoidance behavior (not getting fined) into a positive, trackable streak with a flip-counter visualization.

  • Emotional Reward Before Data: Leads with affirming language and a green "0 challans" figure, front-loading positive emotion before any detail.

  • Exclusivity Social Proof: "only a select few outstanding drivers have no challans" nudges continued engagement via status signaling.

  • Single Clear CTA: One dominant, high-contrast button keeps the next step unambiguous and reduces decision fatigue.

  • Achievement Iconography: The certificate/medal illustration visually reinforces the "you've earned this" narrative typical of loyalty and gamification systems.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 9
screens.whereToUse:
Use this celebratory empty-state pattern when:

  • A "zero" or "no results" outcome is objectively good news for the user (e.g., no fines, no errors, no security issues, inbox zero, no bugs found).

  • You want to increase engagement or retention for infrequently-used utility features by making the outcome feel rewarding.

  • The brand voice supports a more playful, human tone even within a serious or bureaucratic domain (finance, legal, compliance, health checks, security scans).

  • You want to differentiate a checking/scanning feature from a purely transactional tool, encouraging repeat usage or social sharing of good results.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • A "zero" result could actually be ambiguous or concerning (e.g., zero results due to a system/search error rather than genuinely no violations) - celebrating incorrectly could erode trust if data is wrong or incomplete.

  • The user base or context demands a strictly formal, neutral tone (e.g., official government portals, legal documentation, enterprise compliance dashboards) where celebratory language may seem unprofessional or trivializing.

  • There is no clear next action and the celebratory screen becomes a dead-end; if used, ensure there's still a path back to core app value (e.g., check another vehicle, view details, share).

  • Users check this frequently: over-celebrating a routine, expected outcome can feel patronizing or gimmicky over repeated exposures.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets everyday vehicle owners in markets (likely India, given "challan" terminology) who use an app to check pending traffic fines associated with their vehicle registration number. The primary psychological trigger is positive reinforcement: users checking for fines often approach the screen with mild anxiety (fear of an unexpected penalty), and the app immediately converts that anxiety into relief and pride.

By labeling a "zero" result as an achievement ("mark of a great driver") rather than a neutral non-event, the app taps into identity-based motivation: users are subtly encouraged to see themselves as responsible, rule-abiding drivers, which can increase their emotional attachment to the app and likelihood of returning to check again (creating a habit loop around a otherwise infrequent utility action).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Reframing a null state as a celebration: Rather than a sterile "No records found," the absence of data (0 challans) is turned into a badge of honor, creating a small dopamine hit for the user.

  • Bold typographic hierarchy: Oversized, high-contrast, colorful headline against a near-black background maximizes emotional impact and readability in a single glance.

  • Radial burst background motif: Subtle sunburst rays behind the text mimic celebratory/spotlight effects (similar to confetti or achievement unlocks) without needing heavy animation or illustration assets.

  • Color-coded data point: The "0 challans" figure is rendered in green, instantly communicating a positive status via color psychology before the user even parses the words.

  • Minimal, single-action dismissal: Only one interactive element (the X), keeping the moment focused purely on the emotional payoff rather than pushing the user toward another task immediately.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 10
screens.whereToUse:
Adapt this pattern for rewards, loyalty, cashback, or coupon wallets where the goal is to maximize redemption rates and repeat visits. It works well for:

  • Fintech/neobank cashback and offer centers

  • Loyalty programs with rotating, time-limited perks

  • Gamified engagement surfaces (referral rewards, streak bonuses, spin-to-win outcomes)

  • Any context where you want to make a routine list feel like an exciting "prize reveal" moment
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this casino-esque, "you won" framing in contexts requiring trust, sobriety, or regulatory caution (such as investment products, insurance, loan offers, or any financial decision with real risk, where gamified urgency language could be seen as manipulative or even run afoul of financial advertising regulations).

It is also inappropriate for older, more conservative user bases or B2B/enterprise financial tools where a playful, gambling-adjacent tone could undermine perceived credibility. Additionally, artificial urgency (identical "expires in 05 days" on every card) should be used carefully and truthfully, reusing a static countdown across unrelated offers can erode trust once users notice the pattern is fake or non-dynamic.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of fintech, super-app, or cashback/rewards platforms (likely an Indian neobank or bill-payment/rewards aggregator given the Axis Bank/IOCL/RuPay branding) who respond well to gamified, dopamine-driven engagement loops rather than plain transactional lists.

The psychological triggers at play include the variable reward mechanism (borrowed from gambling/slot machines) to keep users checking back for new "wins," loss aversion and urgency via the persistent countdown badges, and status/progress signaling via the lifetime voucher count that encourages users to keep accumulating for bragging rights or a sense of achievement. This approach is best suited to younger, mobile-first, engagement-sensitive demographics (e.g., Gen Z/millennial users in emerging markets) who are more receptive to playful, high-energy financial UX than to sober, traditional banking interfaces.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Casino/Jackpot Framing: Using "you won" language and playing-card/poker chip artwork to describe a fintech cashback offer taps into variable-reward psychology, making mundane credit card perks feel like slot machine payouts.

  • Lifetime Counter as Trophy Case: Displaying "lifetime: 127" alongside "active: 3" instantly signals social/self status and progress, encouraging users to view voucher collection as an ongoing game with a running score.

  • Consistent Urgency Badge: The "EXPIRES IN 05 DAYS" clock chip is applied uniformly across disparate card types, systematizing urgency as a core structural element rather than an occasional promotional flourish.

  • Dual-Weight CTA Pairing: Pairing a low-commitment outlined 'Details' button with a high-contrast filled 'Redeem now' button visually biases users toward the desired conversion action while still offering an escape hatch.

  • Full-Bleed Hero Art per Card: Each voucher tile leads with an immersive, large-format image (bank card design, poker hand) rather than a small icon, making the reward feel tangible, valuable, and worth pausing on.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 11
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for reward, loyalty, or cashback-style features where users accumulate redeemable assets (coupons, points, badges) over time. It's ideal for apps that want a bold, non-traditional visual identity to differentiate from generic corporate finance/e-commerce UI, and for screens that need to simultaneously surface a primary redemption action alongside secondary engagement loops (like referrals).
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this high-contrast, oversized-typography aesthetic for enterprise, healthcare, or accessibility-sensitive contexts where a more neutral, conservative visual language and higher color-contrast compliance for all text (the faint gray watermark text may fail WCAG contrast checks) are required. It's also not suitable for information-dense dashboards where users need to scan many vouchers/items at once, since the generous whitespace and giant decorative text reduce information density per scroll.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This design targets a younger, digitally-native audience (likely users of a cashback, fintech, or rewards/coupon app) who respond well to bold, unconventional visual styling over traditional polished corporate UI. The gamified stats (active/lifetime counts) and referral "win more" language tap into completionist and social-sharing psychological triggers (users are nudged to check their voucher stash frequently (habit loop) and to invite friends for additional rewards (viral growth loop)).

The scarcity/urgency undertone of "127 lifetime" vouchers versus only "3 active" subtly signals to the user that many vouchers expire unused, creating FOMO that drives them toward the "Redeem now" CTA immediately rather than procrastinating.
screens.keyHighlights:
• High-contrast card-on-black layout: The off-white voucher card floating on a pure black background creates an immediate visual hierarchy and focal point without needing borders or shadows.

  • Dual-button hierarchy: Outlined "Details" vs. solid "Redeem now" clearly differentiates a passive/information action from the primary conversion action.

  • Oversized decorative typography: The giant faint "VOUCHER EXPIRED" text used as a background/section-divider adds editorial, poster-like visual interest to break monotony in a long scrolling page.

  • Color-coded cross-promotion: The green referral banner strategically breaks the black/white palette to funnel attention toward a secondary growth objective (referrals) without competing with the primary voucher CTA above.

  • Lightweight drill-down row: The "expired vouchers" list entry with a count and arrow is a minimal, low-cognitive-load way to expose historical/archived data without cluttering the main view.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 12
screens.whereToUse:
• Reward, cashback, or coupon aggregation apps needing a transaction/offer history log.

  • Gamified fintech apps (UPI apps, super-apps) wanting to reinforce a sense of ongoing "winning" and engagement.

  • Any screen documenting expired/used promotional content where maintaining brand recall and positive sentiment matters more than transactional accuracy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this playful, ticket-styled treatment for serious financial statements (e.g., transaction history, tax documents) where users need clarity and formality over gamified framing.

  • Not suitable for B2B or enterprise dashboards where users expect neutral, data-dense tables rather than illustrative card metaphors.

  • Should be avoided if the expired items list is very long, since a two-column card grid with truncated text is less scannable than a compact list/table for high-volume data.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets users of cashback/rewards/coupon aggregation apps (similar to CRED, Cheq, or coupon-stacking apps) who are motivated by gamification and deal-hunting psychology. Showing a history of "wins" (even expired ones) leverages the psychological principle of loss aversion and nostalgia: users see what they've earned/missed and are nudged to check the "active vouchers" section next time so they don't miss out again (a soft FOMO mechanic).

It also builds trust and credibility by proving the app has consistently delivered value over time, which is crucial for retention in reward-based fintech/shopping apps where skepticism about "fake" cashback offers is common.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Ticket/coupon skeuomorphism: The scalloped-edge, perforated-line card design mimics physical lottery/raffle tickets, subconsciously tying the digital reward to real-world excitement of scratch cards or coupons.

  • Desaturated archival state: Using grey cards on black to visually communicate "past/inactive" without needing heavy iconography, letting color remain a signal reserved for live, actionable offers elsewhere in the app.

  • Gamified framing of history: Even expired offers are labeled "you won X," turning a graveyard of missed deals into a subtle self-esteem/history log that reinforces the app as a rewarding experience worth returning to.

  • Brand-first scannability: Leading each card with a recognizable brand logo (Myntra, McDonald's, Agaro) allows rapid visual scanning/recall before reading text.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 13
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern when you want to convert a transactional confirmation (reward earned, level up, cashback credited) into a cross-sell or engagement moment. It's ideal for loyalty programs, fintech rewards, coupon/deal aggregators, or gamified apps that partner with third-party merchants and need to drive foot traffic or transactions toward those partners immediately after a positive user moment.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this heavy celebratory/gamified treatment in enterprise, B2B, healthcare, or highly regulated financial contexts where users expect sober, trustworthy, low-distraction UI. Also avoid if the partner list is very long or requires filtering/search (a swipeable carousel doesn't scale well past a handful of items and should hand off quickly to a searchable/filterable directory (as the "View all" CTA correctly does here)).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen likely targets younger, deal-savvy consumers (college students, young professionals) using a UPI-based rewards/cashback app in a market like India, given the UPI-specific payment instruction and rupee-style currency icon. This demographic responds strongly to gamification, visual brand storytelling, and instant gratification cues.

Psychological triggers at play include: variable reward/gamification (unlocked rewards framing), curiosity gap (peeking carousel edges inviting swipe), social proof via brand logos (recognizable local brands like Cantan, Guppy, Monkey Bar building trust), and loss aversion/FOMO implied by "meet our partner brands" suggesting exclusive access.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Achievement framing: Using "unlocked" language turns a standard partner-brand listing into a gamified reward moment, increasing emotional engagement.

  • Story-style carousel with peeking edges: Signals more content is swipeable without needing an explicit label, driving exploration.

  • Persistent balance chip in header: Keeps the earned currency visible during browsing, reinforcing the value of continued engagement/spend.

  • Dual-layer brand browsing: Large hero cards for immersive browsing + small avatar row for fast recognition/scanning cater to both slow and fast browsing behaviors.

  • High-contrast sticky CTA: The yellow "View all" button pops dramatically against the dark theme, making the next step unmissable.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 14
screens.whereToUse: Use this grid-card merchant pattern when showcasing a curated set of partner brands/offers where visual brand recognition (logos) is a strong trust and engagement driver (e).g., loyalty programs, cashback apps, coupon marketplaces, or travel/dining partner directories. It's especially effective when you want to elevate a transactional "offers" page into a premium, editorial browsing experience.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern when the offer list is very long or requires filtering/sorting by category, price, or proximity (a flat two-column grid without search or filter controls becomes tedious to scroll through at scale). It's also not ideal when offers are time-sensitive or highly numeric (e.g., "20% off," expiring today), since this format prioritizes brand storytelling over quick comparison of deal value. Lastly, the heavy stylistic branding (dark theme, custom copy tone) requires strong brand identity investment and may not suit more neutral, utilitarian financial products.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets CRED's core demographic: financially engaged, credit-card-owning urban millennials/Gen Z professionals who value status, curated experiences, and gamified rewards. These users are motivated less by pure monetary savings and more by exclusivity, discovery of premium brands, and the dopamine hit of "assured wins."

Psychologically, the screen leverages variable reward psychology tempered with certainty: using "assured rewards" to build trust while still framing the interaction as a rewarding "win," tapping into gamification instincts. The curated brand selection (specialty coffee, department stores, wellness, dining) also acts as aspirational social proof, aligning the CRED brand with premium lifestyle choices its target users want to associate with.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Contrast-driven card design: Placing vivid, colorful brand logos on stark white tiles against a near-black textured backdrop makes each merchant instantly recognizable and visually "pop," turning a plain list into a gallery-like browsing experience.

  • Contextual "IN-STORE" chip: A small, high-contrast green badge immediately tells users the redemption channel (physical store vs. app), reducing confusion before they even read the brand name.

  • Benefit-first microcopy: Rather than generic "10% off" labels, each card uses a punchy, personality-driven one-liner that sells an experience, increasing perceived value and emotional appeal.

  • Assured rewards framing: The word "assured" preemptively defuses skepticism common with reward programs (fear of not winning), lowering the psychological barrier to trying the QR-scan behavior.

  • Directional arrow micro-affordance: The simple arrow icon under each description subtly cues tappability without needing a heavy button, keeping the visual design light and uncluttered.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 15
screens.whereToUse: Use this bottom-sheet-over-dimmed-background pattern when presenting deal/offer details that require a secondary offline or external action (redeeming in-store, visiting a website, scanning a code). It's ideal for loyalty programs, coupon/voucher features, and any flow where you need to explain a multi-step process without navigating away from the current browsing context. The instructional list format is especially valuable for reducing support tickets on "how do I redeem this" type offers.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this pattern for purely in-app redeemable rewards where the CTA can directly complete the transaction, adding an extra explanatory step there would introduce unnecessary friction. Also avoid heavy dimming/modal stacking on already complex screens, as double-layered UI can feel disorienting on smaller screens or for less tech-savvy users. If the offer has no real conditions, skip the "How It Works" section to avoid over-explaining trivial actions.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy: This targets CRED's affluent, credit-card-holding user base who are motivated by status, exclusivity, and tangible ROI on spending they'd do anyway (coffee, retail). The psychological trigger is loss-aversion-adjacent: framing everyday purchases as "rewarding" makes users feel they're leaving value on the table if they pay any other way. The "assured" qualifier taps into trust-building for a demographic that is skeptical of gimmicky cashback schemes, while the coin/multiplier mechanic leverages CRED's existing gamified points economy to drive repeat engagement.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dimmed background context: Retains the sense of place (the offers carousel) while pushing full attention to the modal's decision-making content.

  • Assured Rewards framing: Using "2x assured" instead of vague "up to" language builds trust and removes lottery-style ambiguity common in reward programs.

  • Step-by-step redemption guide: Proactively answers "how do I actually get this?" for an offline/in-store action, which is a major source of drop-off in app-to-physical-world reward flows.

  • Single, directional CTA: "Visit the nearest outlet →" nudges a real-world action rather than trapping the user in a dead-end in-app confirmation.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 16
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern for card-linked offers, coupon detail pages, or partner promotion screens where a single reward needs to be explained in depth before redemption. It's ideal when:

  • Legal/compliance text is mandatory but shouldn't compete with the primary value proposition.

  • Eligibility varies by user attribute (e.g., specific card, membership tier) and needs quick visual confirmation.

  • The redemption action happens outside the current app (requiring a copyable code) rather than an in-app "Apply" button.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this heavy, text-dense pattern when:

  • The offer is simple and universally applicable: excessive T&Cs would create unnecessary friction and reading burden.

  • Redemption can happen natively in-app (in which case a direct "Apply/Redeem" button is better than "Copy code").

  • Users are on a fast-checkout flow where surfacing lengthy terms mid-purchase could cause drop-off or decision fatigue.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets price-sensitive, deal-seeking shoppers who use bank apps or card-linked-offer aggregators to find discounts before making a purchase on partner platforms like Myntra. The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Loss aversion/urgency: The "valid till mar 31, 2024" date nudges users to act before the offer expires.

  • Trust through transparency: Full disclosure of T&Cs builds credibility with financially cautious users who have likely been burned by hidden coupon restrictions before.

  • Effort reduction: The copy-code shortcut caters to users who want quick wins with minimal cognitive/manual effort, especially since they'll be switching apps to redeem it.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Segmented Legal Disclosure: Splitting a short marketing headline from a full, itemized bulleted T&C list balances persuasion (top) with compliance/trust (bottom) without cluttering the primary message.

  • Card Eligibility Preview: Showing masked bank card numbers with bank logos lets users instantly verify personal eligibility instead of guessing from generic text.

  • Sticky, High-Contrast Redemption Bar: The black "Copy code" button combined with the code and expiry date creates a clear, unmissable final action zone, visually distinct from the scrollable informational content above.

  • One-Tap Copy Interaction: Removing manual code entry (typing/memorizing) reduces friction and redemption errors, which is critical since the coupon must be pasted into a separate app (Myntra) to be used.

screens.name: CRED Redeeming 17
screens.whereToUse:
• Fintech, banking, or wallet apps looking to incentivize recurring bill payments (rent, utilities, subscriptions) through a dedicated rewards/offers hub.

  • Any product needing to merchandise multiple time-bound or category-specific promotions in a compact, swipeable format.

  • Consumer apps targeting younger demographics where playful, game-like framing increases engagement over dry transactional copy.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this pattern for enterprise, B2B, or high-trust financial contexts (e.g., wealth management, insurance) where playful "win/claim" language may undermine perceived seriousness and trustworthiness.

  • Not suitable when offers are extremely limited or rarely refresh (overuse of urgency/gamified CTAs without real new content will erode trust and feel manipulative).

  • Avoid if the target audience skews older or more risk-averse, as gamified reward framing around money can feel gimmicky or even predatory.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets younger, digitally-native users (Gen Z / young millennials) of fintech and credit card apps in markets like India, where cashback and rewards are major drivers of app engagement and card usage. The audience is likely price-sensitive but reward-motivated, and comfortable with gamified, app-based financial management.

Psychologically, the screen leverages variable reward framing (the "win" language), loss aversion / FOMO (locked offers, "claim now" urgency), and progress/achievement feedback (total cashback won ticker) to drive habitual bill payment through this specific app rather than competitors, increasing transaction volume and stickiness.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Gamified language ("win" vs "earn") reframes routine bill payments as a rewarding, lottery-like experience, increasing emotional engagement.

  • Padlock iconography on offer cards creates a subtle curiosity/reveal mechanic, implying the reward must be "unlocked" by claiming, which nudges toward action.

  • Dual-carousel structure (primary hero offers + secondary "earn more" strip) maximizes offer density on a single screen without requiring long vertical scrolling.

  • Social-proof-adjacent stat ("total cashback won ₹229") personalizes the value already captured, reinforcing that the reward system is real and already benefiting the user.

  • High-contrast neon-on-black color system gives the screen a premium, youthful, gamified brand identity distinct from traditional dull banking UI.

results.query: Weather forecast for Tokyo Japan next weekend

screens.name: Airtable - Filtering records - Screen 1
screens.whereToUse:
Use this card-based row pattern when designing mobile experiences for data-heavy, relational tools (CRMs, inventory trackers, project trackers) where a true grid is unusable on small screens. It's ideal when:

  • Each record has 3: 6 key fields that need to remain scannable at a glance.
  • Users need to preserve desktop power-features (filter/sort/group) in a condensed mobile toolbar.
  • The underlying data model is relational/multi-table, requiring an easy way to switch between linked tables (tab bar or similar).
  • Visual customization (cover images/icons) can increase user engagement and personal ownership of data.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this pattern when:

  • Users need to compare many fields across many rows simultaneously (true grid/spreadsheet editing) - cards force vertical scrolling and hide off-screen fields, which hurts bulk comparison tasks.
  • The app targets casual consumers unfamiliar with spreadsheet terminology like "Group" or "Sum" - the terminology and density could overwhelm non-technical audiences.
  • Screen real estate is extremely limited (smaller wearables) where even card content would need to be further truncated, risking loss of context.
  • High-frequency bulk editing is the primary use case (inline cell editing in a real grid is faster than opening/editing individual cards).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operationally-minded users: project managers, marketers, and small teams (who already think in spreadsheets but need to access and lightly edit that data on the go (e).g., checking a travel note while away from a desk). The design assumes familiarity with spreadsheet concepts (columns, sums, filters) and translates that mental model into a touch-friendly format rather than inventing a new paradigm, reducing the learning curve for Excel/Sheets veterans.

Psychologically, the card format reduces cognitive load compared to a cramped horizontal-scroll grid on a small screen, while retaining enough spreadsheet DNA (sort, filter, group) to reassure "builder" personas that they haven't lost functionality by going mobile. The colorful cover images also tap into personalization and ownership (users feel their workspace is "theirs," not a generic enterprise tool).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Grid-to-Card Responsive Transformation: Converts spreadsheet rows into scannable cards on mobile without losing column context (field labels remain visible per card).
  • Persistent Aggregate Row: The "26 sum" under Days keeps spreadsheet-level computation visible even in a non-tabular layout, satisfying power users who rely on totals.
  • Multi-Table Tab Bar: Bottom tabs (Places, Packing List, Friends) expose the relational nature of the base, letting users jump between linked tables without leaving the record context (a subtle nod to databases over flat sheets).
  • Full Toolbar Parity: Filter, Group, Sort, and Hide Fields are all present on mobile, avoiding feature loss compared to desktop (rare in mobile data apps).
  • Floating Action Button for Record Creation: Standardizes the "add new" action in the most reachable zone of the screen, regardless of scroll position.

screens.name: Airtable - Filtering records - Screen 2
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern when:

  • Building search over large, grouped, or hierarchical datasets on mobile (lists, grids, databases, CRMs, inventory apps).
  • You want to preserve spatial/contextual awareness of where the user was before invoking search.
  • Records have rich secondary content (images, notes, attachments) that benefit from a flexible preview toggle (e.g., Pics/Notes) to keep cards scannable yet information-dense.
  • Users need quick volumetric feedback (counts per group) before drilling into specific sections.
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach when:

  • The dataset is small or flat: an overlay search with grouping/count headers adds unnecessary complexity for simple lists.
  • The app is consumer-facing and benefits from more visual, marketing-driven search experiences (e.g., discovery feeds, image-heavy browsing) rather than this utilitarian, text-first layout.
  • Screen real estate is extremely limited: showing both dimmed background content and a full keyboard can feel cramped on smaller devices if not carefully tested.
  • Users primarily need fuzzy/semantic search; this pattern implies straightforward keyword matching and may disappoint users expecting smarter filtering without pairing it with robust Filter & Sort patterns.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves operations and project teams on the go: e.g., someone planning logistics (here, literally a travel/balloon adventure itinerary) who needs to quickly locate a specific record (a city, a note, a mention) from a mobile device rather than the desktop grid. The target user is comfortable with structured data but needs mobile-optimized retrieval, not data entry.

The psychological drivers at play include:

  • Reduction of search anxiety: Keeping the list visible behind the keyboard reassures users their data hasn't disappeared.
  • Trust through transparency: Explicit counts and grouped totals satisfy the "systems thinker" mindset of Airtable's core audience (ops/PM personas) who want quantifiable certainty over their datasets.
  • Familiarity bias: Leaning on native iOS search/keyboard patterns lowers the learning curve for a complex, power-user tool.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Non-destructive search overlay: The underlying grouped list stays rendered and scrollable in the background, so the user never fully loses their place in the data hierarchy while searching.
  • Field/view toggle (Pics vs Notes): A compact segmented affordance lets users swap which attachment/field is surfaced as the secondary line in each card (a clever way to pack dense tabular richness into a card-based mobile layout).
  • Grouped counts in section headers: Showing "Days X / Count Y" gives users an at-a-glance sense of data volume per group without opening each section, aiding quick scanning in large bases.
  • Cover image thumbnails with stacked attachment badges ("+1"): Signals multiple attachments exist per record without cluttering the card.
  • Standard iOS search ergonomics: Full-width text field, auto-focused keyboard, and a familiar "Cancel" button reduce friction and cognitive load by matching native OS patterns.

screens.name: Airtable - Filtering records - Screen 3
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern in any data-dense application where users manage categorized or grouped records (CRMs, project trackers, inventory apps, note systems). It is ideal when:

  • Content is naturally organized into collapsible groups or sections that should remain visible during search.
  • Instant visual feedback (highlighting) is more valuable than a separate "results list" because users benefit from seeing matches in their original context.
  • The underlying records contain multiple searchable fields (titles, notes, attachments) that benefit from a unified search affordance across fields/tabs (Pics/Notes).
screens.whereNotToUse:
Avoid this approach when:

  • The dataset is small enough that scrolling is faster than searching (in that case, a prominent search bar is unnecessary overhead).
  • Search needs to span multiple unrelated data types simultaneously (global search), where a unified results list with clear source labeling is more appropriate than preserving a single base's grouping structure.
  • The app targets casual consumer audiences unfamiliar with structured data (grouped headers like "Count" and "Days" may feel overly technical or spreadsheet-like for non-operations users).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This pattern targets operations users, project managers, and trip/task coordinators who manage growing datasets inside a single Airtable base and need to locate a specific record quickly without scrolling through dozens of grouped rows. The psychological driver is reduction of cognitive load: rather than forcing users to scan visually, the system does the matching work and highlights exactly where their query appears, building confidence and trust in the tool's intelligence.

The persistence of grouping and metadata (Count, Days) during search also caters to power users who rely on Airtable's relational structure daily (it reassures them that search is a lens on their existing system, not a separate disconnected feature, which is critical for retention among structured-data-heavy teams).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Real-time highlight matching: As the user types "S," matching characters are immediately highlighted in yellow across both titles and note previews, giving instant visual confirmation that the search is active and scoped correctly.
  • Context-preserving search: Group headers (Days 5 / Days 7) remain visible during search, so users never lose their place in the underlying data hierarchy (a crucial affordance for a tool built around structured records rather than flat feeds).
  • Full-screen takeover with clear exit: The orange header bar converts the base's icon/title area into a dedicated search bar with a visible "Cancel" action, following standard iOS search conventions so users always have a frictionless way back to the base view.
  • Attachment thumbnails as visual anchors: Emoji/photo icons attached to each record (balloon, tree) allow rapid visual scanning even in a text-search context, leveraging Airtable's flexible field types (attachments) for recognition over recall.

screens.name: Airtable - Filtering records - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for record- or document-scoped search inside data-heavy, multi-field apps (databases, CMS tools, project management platforms, note-taking apps). It's especially effective when:

  • Content spans multiple field types (attachments, text, mentions) that benefit from scoped filtering tabs.
  • Users need quick visual confirmation of match relevance via term highlighting.
  • Maintaining orientation within a larger hierarchy (base/table/record) is critical during a modal search task.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, metadata-heavy search pattern in consumer-facing or casual apps where users expect a lightweight, visually engaging search experience (e.g., social or media apps) - the "Days/Count" metadata strip and small scoped tabs would feel overly technical. It's also unsuitable for global cross-workspace search, where scoping to a single record would hide relevant results from other bases/tables, frustrating users looking for an all-encompassing search.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets operations-minded professionals, project managers, and team collaborators who use Airtable to manage structured but flexible projects (e.g., trip planning, content calendars, inventories). These users value speed and precision over visual flourish, which explains the dense, low-ornamentation layout.

Psychologically, the design leverages recognition over recall (highlighted matches, predictive keyboard suggestions) to reduce cognitive load during search. The visible @mention also taps into social accountability and relevance: seeing a teammate's name attached to content increases the perceived value and trustworthiness of the search result, nudging users to click through and engage with team content rather than treating the base as a solitary spreadsheet.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Instant highlight-matching: The matched search term "Singapore" is visually highlighted in the result card, giving immediate visual confirmation that the search succeeded and where the match occurred.
  • Scoped search tabs: The "Pics" and "Notes" segmented row lets users narrow search to specific content types within the record, avoiding noisy, undifferentiated results.
  • Persistent context header: Keeping the base name ("Balloon Adventure") and back/search/collaborator icons visible even during search prevents users from losing their place in the larger app hierarchy.
  • Rich preview snippet with @mention: Surfacing a collaborator tag inside the search result reinforces Airtable's collaborative, team-based value proposition even in a utilitarian search flow.
  • Metadata strip (Days/Count): Provides lightweight record context above the fold so users understand the scope of what they're searching before scrolling.

screens.name: MUBI GO - Home - Screen 4
screens.whereToUse:
Adopt this pattern for any limited-inventory booking or redemption flow where the content/product has already been chosen and the user only needs to resolve time and location (e).g., single-event ticketing, restaurant reservation time-slots, class/session booking, or appointment scheduling. It's especially effective when:

  • The catalog of choices is intentionally narrow (one film, one event, one class).
  • Multiple physical locations each have their own independent schedules.
  • Users need quick visual scanning across many venues/days with minimal cognitive load.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this flat list approach when the catalog is large or multi-dimensional (e).g., a general ticketing app with hundreds of films and venues would need robust filtering, search, and a map view to avoid overwhelming users with the same long-scroll pattern. It also becomes less effective without geolocation-based sorting; if venues aren't ordered by proximity or relevance, users in large metro areas may have to scroll through many irrelevant cinemas. Additionally, the lack of a map/visual distance indicator could frustrate users unfamiliar with the city's geography.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen is built for urban, time-pressed film enthusiasts in the US/Canada and UK markets who have already opted into MUBI GO's weekly pick and now need to convert that choice into a real-world plan. The design assumes a sophisticated, mobile-first user who wants fast, frictionless logistics rather than a browsing experience - the psychological driver here is reducing decision fatigue and eliminating anxiety around logistics (wrong time, wrong timezone, unfamiliar venue).

The condensed, editorial typography and bold color-blocking also subtly reinforce brand loyalty and premium positioning (even a routine scheduling screen feels designed, not default, appealing to users who self-identify as curators/connoisseurs of cinema rather than casual moviegoers).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Sticky date strip: The horizontal day selector remains pinned above the scrolling cinema list, letting users switch days without losing their scroll position among venues.
  • Outlined time-slot buttons: Showtimes are rendered as discrete tappable pills rather than plain text, making the primary action (pick a time) immediately obvious and thumb-friendly.
  • Grouped venue cards with dividers: Clear separation between cinemas via thin rule lines keeps a dense information set (name, address, times) scannable at a glance.
  • Proactive timezone disclosure: Explicitly labeling "SCREENING TIMES ARE IN GMT+1" per venue removes ambiguity for travelers or cross-timezone users, preventing missed screenings.
  • Single-film simplicity: By scoping the entire screen to one curated film's availability, MUBI GO avoids the choice paralysis typical of general ticketing apps like Fandango or AMC.

screens.name: MUBI GO - Home - Screen 5
screens.whereToUse:
Use this pattern whenever an app needs to convert a single curated or pre-selected item (an event, a class, a reservation) into a concrete real-world action requiring time/location coordination. It's ideal for:

  • Event ticketing or cinema/show listings where showtimes vary by venue and day.
  • Appointment or class booking apps where a service is offered across multiple locations/times.
  • Any "pick a slot" flow where date and venue filtering should feel instantaneous and non-modal.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense, all-caps, high-contrast treatment for primary discovery or browsing screens where the goal is delight and exploration rather than task completion (it would feel abrasive next to cinematic poster art). It's also unsuitable when there are very few venues/showtimes, where a simpler single-list view without a date carousel would be less overbuilt. Finally, on very small screens or for users with many simultaneous options, this flat list could get long and tedious; a map view or stronger filtering (by distance, by time) should supplement it at scale.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
MUBI GO's audience is urban, time-poor film enthusiasts who have already opted into a single curated weekly pick rather than browsing an endless catalogue. By the time they reach this screen, the psychological job is no longer about discovery or delight (it's about logistical confidence: confirming they can get to the right cinema at the right time).

The screen leans on reducing cognitive load and anxiety around a real-world commitment (leaving the house for a fixed-time event). Showing multiple cinema options per day also subtly reinforces choice and flexibility, which matters because MUBI GO's "one film a week" model could otherwise feel restrictive (multiple venues and showtimes per day soften that constraint and make the curation feel generous rather than limiting).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Single-screen date + venue filtering: Combining the day selector and the cinema list in one continuous scroll avoids a jarring drill-down navigation for a time-critical task.
  • Explicit timezone disclosure per venue: A small but high-value detail that reduces the risk of users missing their screening, directly protecting the core promise of the ticket.
  • Full street addresses inline: Removes the need to tap into a separate "view details" screen just to get wayfinding information.
  • Bold tonal shift to high-contrast yellow: Visually distinguishes "actionable logistics" screens from the moodier, poster-driven discovery screens, helping users subconsciously recognize this is a different mode.
  • Heavy, oversized typographic treatment for venue names: Maintains the editorial brand identity even in a purely functional, data-dense context.

screens.name: MUBI GO - Home - Screen 6
screens.whereToUse: Use this pattern for event or appointment-based redemption flows where a user must choose a specific venue and time slot tied to a limited, curated offering (e).g., ticketing apps, pop-up retail/restaurant reservations, or location-specific perks programs. It's ideal when the list of options is short enough (under ~10 items) to scan without needing filters or a map, and when timezone or local nuance needs explicit clarification.
screens.whereNotToUse: Avoid this dense list-only approach when the number of locations is large (dozens+) or geographically spread, where a map view or search/filter would serve users better. Also avoid an all-caps, heavy typographic treatment for long-form or frequently-referenced utility content, as it can fatigue readability over repeated use. If users frequently need directions or distance-based sorting, a plain text address list lacking geolocation context will frustrate rather than help.
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen targets urban, schedule-conscious film lovers in the US/Canada and UK markets who need quick, reliable logistics once they've committed to seeing the weekly pick. These users value precision (exact showtimes, correct addresses) because a wasted cinema trip undermines the premium feel of the subscription.

Psychologically, the dense but structured list reduces decision fatigue by narrowing choice to a short, curated set of partner cinemas (versus an open-ended map search), reinforcing MUBI GO's core promise of "curated over endless." The scarcity disclaimer also leverages exclusivity bias (a small pool of available screenings makes the experience feel special and worth planning around, rather than a flaw).
screens.keyHighlights:
• Repeating card rhythm: Name, address, timezone note, and times follow an identical structure for each venue, enabling fast F-pattern scanning.
  • Explicit timezone clarification per cinema prevents a common source of user error (missed screenings) without extra taps.
  • Bold, on-brand color block turns a purely functional "store locator" style screen into a cohesive piece of the cinematic editorial identity.
  • Scarcity framing at the bottom turns limited availability into a feature of exclusivity rather than a complaint-worthy bug.
  • Forward-looking teaser ("Next Week's Film") keeps users anticipating the next curated drop, reinforcing the weekly cadence habit loop.

screens.name: MUBI GO - Home - Screen 7
screens.whereToUse:
• Any subscription or membership product delivering a single curated item per cycle (weekly box, ticket, drop) where showing "what's next" increases retention.
  • Ticketing or event confirmation screens that benefit from a clear, scannable "ticket stub" visual metaphor.
  • Apps wanting to pair transactional utility (time/location) with brand storytelling/merchandising in one screen without resorting to tabs.
screens.whereNotToUse:
• Avoid this layout for multi-item or multi-session bookings, where a single large info card per item would create excessive scrolling.
  • Not suitable for transactional flows requiring immediate error recovery or multi-field data entry, since the page is read-only and lacks input affordances.
  • High-contrast yellow blocks should be avoided in contexts needing a calm, low-stimulation tone (e.g., financial statements, medical appointment confirmations).
screens.evidenceWhoWhy:
This screen serves urban cinephiles who have already committed to a weekly curated ticket and now need quick, unambiguous access to logistics (time, address) before heading out (likely checked on-the-go, hence large type and high contrast). The yellow/black palette ensures legibility even in bright daylight or low-attention glance scenarios typical of commute or pre-cinema checks.

The "Next Week's Film" teaser leverages anticipation and curiosity (a core psychological driver for MUBI's curation-over-choice value proposition) making users feel part of an ongoing cinematic journey rather than a one-off purchase. The scarcity language ("limited number of theaters") appeals to the premium, discerning audience who values exclusivity and considers curated restriction a feature, not a bug.
screens.keyHighlights:
• Dual-tone card system: The vivid yellow ticket-info card instantly separates "actionable logistics" from the "inspirational" dark film-teaser card below, letting users scan for what they need without visual competition.
  • Ticket-stub typography: Large time stamps and underline rules mimic a real cinema ticket, tapping into the emotional nostalgia and tangibility of physical moviegoing even within a digital interface.
  • Built-in anticipation loop: By revealing "Next Week's Film" immediately after ticket details, the screen converts a single transactional check into a forward-looking engagement hook, encouraging habitual weekly return visits.
  • Low-friction secondary actions: Outlined "Trailer" and "Previous Weekly Selections" buttons are visually de-emphasized (stroke-only) so they don't distract from the primary informational content but remain discoverable for deeper engagement.
